[p. 1]

## Einleitung — Introduction

When a researcher — whether due to an archaic temperament or because the particular shape of his destiny caused him to notice a feature of the world's appearance that has escaped his contemporaries — believes he has arrived at fundamental insights that deviate from all that is currently accepted, he will seek more often and more passionately than is usual, in the thought of the past, for traces of a kindred disposition and a kindred knowing; and he may have an advantage even over specialists in historical research in this: that he feels no inclination to presuppose that we today must somehow be "further along" than past ages were. Indeed, he will reckon from the outset rather with the probability of the opposite, and for this reason will see certain achievements of antiquity in a different light than someone accustomed to interpreting the entire course of human development in terms of the growing accumulation of its most valuable spiritual treasures, thereby regarding every earlier period of its capacity and achievement as a preparatory stage for later achievements.

There is hardly a question in philosophy, and hardly a fundamental answer to it, that we would not find anticipated in the intellectual history of the Greeks. But if, accordingly, the great systems of Western thought down to the most recent times — even in strictly scientific form — work only as more or less ingenious variations on a theme that three hundred years of Greek speculation had sufficed to produce, then it seems that one has seldom examined with full seriousness whether and to what degree those incomparable thinkers of pre-Christian centuries arrived, on their path of languageguided meditation, at a genuine and therefore universally binding knowledge. No one denies their pioneering work for certain methods and modes of inquiry; one [p. 2] shows us in their "worldviews" the seeds and beginnings of later formations; one concedes them certain lasting successes in the domain of logic and especially of mathematics; but one customarily agrees, at least tacitly, that their actual knowledge was meager and has been far surpassed by the discoveries of modern times.

We leave for the moment undecided how far the idea of "Empiricism" is involved in such a view — an idea that since the Renaissance has governed all research endeavors with the force of a spell and provides the modern belief in steady "progress," both of humanity as a whole and especially of its knowledge, with perhaps its most powerful nourishment; yet we would nonetheless urge consideration of whether one seriously wishes to maintain that we today are richer in it than, say, a Heraclitus! We have counted, weighed, measured whatever can be counted, weighed, measured; we have quantified the world in all its breadths, heights, and depths; we have accustomed ourselves to speak of "mechanisms" even of living and mental processes, just as we had earlier accustomed ourselves to see the great and small cosmos in the light of an extremely well-arranged laboratory, and with all this we have attained the famous "mastery over nature." But does this really mean that we have absorbed the knowledge of the Heraclituses, that it lies within ours, that we have developed its seeds and continued its beginnings? Were this the case, then we would first have to be shown that it means knowing the meaning and essence of the world when one eavesdrops on it for everything that could serve to subjugate it at will.

The skeptic, to be sure — and science and doubt are "twin siblings" — could counter us with much apparent justification that our charge of amateurishness against a direction of research whose legitimacy is already evident from the continuity of its development ultimately arises from belief in the apparent knowledge of metaphysics, regarding which a glance at the constant change of its systems permits the inference that it does not fundamentally aim at truth at all, but rather — though hidden from itself — fulfills the historically certainly interesting task of giving the prevailing disposition a more or less persuasive expression. Our progress consists precisely in this: that we have renounced fantastic anticipations and have learned to distinguish thoroughly between "belief" and "knowledge" — yet [p. 3] the very circumstance that such a view would arise with an air almost of self-evidence would have to arouse suspicion regarding its origins, and might tempt one to try whether an exactly contrary skepticism might not be equally defensible, one that would express itself roughly as follows. The very thing the anti-metaphysician insists upon bears the name of science by virtue of a belief — and indeed one that leads him to substitute mere acquaintance [Kenntnis] for knowledge [Wissen]. The connoisseur of horses is generally far from possessing the science of the horse; the connoisseur of wood is not the explorer of the vital process of plants; the connoisseur of human beings usually has least time of all to pursue the science of the soul. Behind every act of taking cognizance stands a guiding interest, and the taking of cognizance itself is, so to speak, the resultant of this interest and the image of actuality, and for this reason can never disclose the latter's essence. If we compare what goes summarily by the name of science — whether of "nature" or of "spirit" — with the circle of problems and the mode of inquiry of metaphysics, we see first that it merely continued only those threads of thought of its elder sister that at the same time promised a practical application, i.e., a sphere of influence for the will; and second, that its foremost hallmark of "truth-content" is the utility of its results "in the service of humanity." The "objectivity" of its propositions does not in the least exclude the possibility that the direction and course of its inquiry was determined far more by an interest than by the wish and inclination to mirror the character of the real. If we look behind the objectivity of its preparations and the apparent impartiality of its methods, we see at work among the driving forces a powerful tendency that surpasses every "private interest" in abstraction by as much as the concept of humanity surpasses the concept of the individual person. In scientific expertise there confronts us a constructive element whereby truth seems to owe its dignity to the contribution it makes to the human appropriation of its object; and the continuity of its development — which for a disinterested reflection, given the multiplicity of world-views, would not readily be expected — seems only the more to indicate that the entire enterprise rests on a process of selection allowing only such propositions to "survive" as also satisfy the demands of a comprehensive [p. 4] will to power. American "Pragmatism" gives us the epistemological caricature of the genuinely existing state of affairs: that the modern Spirit has fallen prey to the idol of the concept of purpose, whether it otherwise displays "realist" or "idealist" dress. — And perhaps our "doubter from metaphysics" would add this: that inquiry into essence, commonly and inaccurately called "Ontology," has sunk again far below the level of insight that antiquity had scaled and that the Middle Ages were in the process of scaling anew. For the same reason, that grandest attempt at the restoration of a contemplative spirituality — miscalled "Romanticism" — found a premature end in the bloom of its years; nor need one wonder further when the most powerful destroyer of ideological wish-ful constructions known to world history — Nietzsche — is already today considered "disposed of" by a generation that has been soul-blind enough to classify him, on account of his decisive error, the lamentable doctrine of the will to power, under "positivists" or "Darwinians" or "Schopenhauerians" as required for the easing of its conscience.

We do not yet say that we align ourselves with this spokesman; but we intend, with the following investigation, to furnish proof that those are mistaken who grant to inquiry into essence at best a merely preparatory role for genuine acquisition of knowledge. Without yet wishing to oppose the anti-metaphysician, we would ask him to direct his attention to the science of the soul. It is taught at all universities as though it too were a "science" like medicine, physics, jurisprudence, etc. Whereas these, however — at least as it initially appears — are compatible with quite different fundamental convictions, this is decidedly not the case with psychology. One does not practice psychology (and in fact no one has yet done so) without simultaneously practicing metaphysics, however many may suppose themselves capable of it. Whoever therefore denies the possibility of metaphysical insights should at least keep before his mind that thereby he has also denied the possibility of the science of the soul. Completely taken with the word "empiricism," most psychologists are reluctant to admit this, and misunderstand their own activity by regarding it after the manner of "natural-scientific induction" primarily as [p. 5] observing, experimenting, and registering that differs from other such activity only in being directed to inner rather than outer objects. — We are probably not wrong in supposing that it must be especially connected with this, what could hardly be painted more strangely: that there are, without exaggeration, approximately as many different psychologies as there are psychologists, and that in particular among independent researchers scarcely even two are in complete agreement on the delineation of their subject matter.

Some wish to dispense as far as possible with the concept of the soul and tell us that one is immediately concerned only with "phenomena of consciousness"; others call psychology a science of "inner (or immediate) experience," from which it is not far to the "inner perception" widely reviving today; yet others remain with the old concept of the doctrine of the soul, without however giving satisfactory information about what the soul really amounts to; for still others, research into the soul seems to be only a branch of the biology of the neuron; and yet others again, scenting false "naturalism" in all of this, wish to furnish us with an altogether new mode of thinking — sometimes called "intuitive," sometimes "subjectivizing" — that by its very nature avoids all the pitfalls of erroneous prior concepts. With all due respect for the acuteness of these researchers; yet we believe that here a great expenditure is wasted in vain out of aversion to a metaphysics that is ultimately unavoidable after all. Whichever of the named and unnamed conceptual definitions one chooses, one finds oneself at once within metaphysics, and will entangle oneself all the more badly in self-contradictory fundamental assumptions the more one feels obliged to avoid it. The talk of "phenomena of consciousness" leads to the question of the nature of consciousness, of its relation to the unconscious and, before one knows it, to some form of monism, dualism, or even "psychophysical parallelism"; the artificial and obscuring turn of phrase about inner or immediate experience demands as its counterpart an outer or mediate experience, and does not escape the same fate of having to instruct in monistic, dualistic, or parallelistic terms; the assumption of the soul already bears an "ontological" stamp in itself and forms the declared antithesis in content to the so-called materialism of the brainpsychologists; what finally concerns the "intuitives" and "subjectivists," [p. 6] they are usually only closet Platonists. But in truth it is the metaphysical conviction of the researcher that leads him to prefer one or another conceptual definition and — whether he knows it or not — thoroughly governs his entire treatment of the domain. One should cease speaking of psychology if one forbids oneself to be a metaphysician.

Before we decide the question whether this is not in truth the case for every science, and whether mechanistic natural inquiry in particular does not likewise rest upon a belief whose truth content — regardless of its supposed factual proofs — determines that of its results, we wish first to try to substantiate that at least in matters of the science of the soul the present-day bewilderment could take hold only because one forfeited what is perhaps the greatest discovery of the Greeks, or more precisely could not peel off the eternal core from the husk of false formulations with which the Greeks themselves had already distorted their best finding through a misdirected tendency. We mean the metaphysical assumption of a threefold substance of the human being: of soma (Body), psyche (Soul), and nous (Spirit, also to be called pneuma or logos) — which, prepared by the investigations of the Pre-Socratics, guides the broadly ramifying thought of the so-called Age of Flourishing under names that vary considerably, and forms a common center of crystallization for the otherwise so variously colored mythologems of Hellenism. This assumption remains, with occasional interchange of its terms, an unbreakable anchor of the tradition of soul-science even in the systems of will in the Middle Ages; is swept away by Cartesian rationalism; celebrates a brilliant but brief resurrection in the profound reveries of Romanticism; only to succumb entirely to the calculating intellect in the academic psychologies of the second half of the nineteenth century, whose spirit and nature no ideological restrictions can alter in any way.

In thus reaching back to an earliest achievement of thought, we at once guard against two possible misunderstandings. For reasons that will yet come to speech, neither the Greeks nor the Romantics — even supposing they had been able and willing — could give the concepts of the bodily, the soulful, and the spiritual that degree of definiteness that we today are — and rightly — accustomed to demand of scientific root-concepts. They knew [p. 7] of it, roughly as one has knowing of what one sees with one's eyes, but they had not grasped it in the stricter sense. With however much lived concurrence, we would nonetheless consider it presumptuous to call their knowing a discovery, were we not to feel ourselves capable of raising it from the realm of the merely meant into the realm of the most rigorous conceptuality. To speak of Body, Soul, Spirit in more than merely popular fashion requires today a knowing of distinguishing marks that permit one to indicate, with unwavering certainty, for every fact of consciousness — whether it be called a perceptual process or a mood or a surge of feeling or a decision or a reverie, etc. — what in it attests to the efficacy of the Body, what of the Soul, what of the Spirit. But if already with the claim of accomplishing exactly this we tread a ground that remained foreign to our predecessors, we take a standpoint that is also entirely different in substance regarding the doctrine of the nature of the relations among the three essential elements of historical humanity: for we are of the opinion that this doctrine was misconstrued from the very outset, indeed entirely misinterpreted, as a consequence of a deeply partisan valuation. While from the beginning one was accustomed to conceive of the Body as the foundation-wall, the Soul as the middle story, the Spirit as the upper floor or gable of the organic "articulated structure" of humanity, we intend to show what has guided all our investigations for some three decades: that Body and Soul are inseparably conjoined poles of the life-cell, into which the Spirit thrusts itself from without like a wedge, with the aim of driving them apart — so to desoul the Body, to disembody the Soul, and thus ultimately to put to death all life within its reach.

The theory whose main outlines we have elsewhere repeatedly sketched, but which we now wish to ground in its details and particularly to investigate with respect to its consequential phenomena, belongs therefore neither to the Greeks nor to Romanticism; yet it owes to earlier times its fundamental concepts as well as much of the apparatus of its method of proof. And it believes that it first clears the path for the original discoverer's gaze — to whom the threefoldness of the historical character of humanity was visible — by preserving it from the aberration that a false valuation had imposed upon it. Yet so little special acuity [p. 8] seems to us required for this, as conversely it does not follow from any lack of acuteness that the most eminent minds of today labor in vain at laying the foundations of soul-science; though it does require lived experience [Erlebnis] and a decision. The former one cannot communicate to anyone; but one can prompt all who have merely forgotten or misunderstood it, by means of indication, to reflect upon it; the latter, however, we can spare the reader, by inviting him to follow us for now, without prejudgment, in the examination of certain ancient questions to which, despite the participation of the most eminent thinkers over two and a half millennia, the universally binding answer is still outstanding.

[p. 9]

## Erstes Buch — Sein und Wirklichkeit — First Book — Being and Actuality

[p. 11]

### Erster Abschnitt — Zeit und Dauer — First Part — Time and Duration

#### 1. Kapitel — Die Außerzeitlichkeit des Gegenstandes — Chapter 1 — The Atemporality of the Object

If someone were to answer the trick question of how long the present lasts with the specification of some interval of time, one would have to counter that no temporal extension, however small, can be conceived that could not, for example, be bisected, so that in its second half the first would always already have elapsed. If, however, one wished to grant the only remaining assumption — that of absolute durationlessness for the measure of the present — merely the significance of a mathematical auxiliary concept, we would have to reply that without it no temporal consciousness can come about at all. For we apprehend time only with reference to the durationless point, as the following reflection may show.

If we place ourselves in the middle of any given time-interval — for example, a year — we call the half that is no longer present in the Now "past," and the half not yet present in the Now "future," thereby forming the concept of temporal succession from the standpoint of the existence of the present. If now, tentatively, we were to ascribe a temporal extension to the present as well, we could place ourselves once more in the middle of this, and from there, as from a Now of the second power so to speak, dissolve the former Now once more into past and future — and this procedure would evidently never reach a conclusion. Either, then, we must posit the dividing Now-point as durationless, or else deny succession and with it the concept of time; from which it follows that time cannot be thought without the mathematical present-point.

[p. 12] In fact we make use of it to articulate the ceaselessly flowing time. To anyone who cannot see that the present is without temporal extension, let it be recalled that he too exercises this knowing at least whenever he establishes what time it is! The division-points by means of which we divide the hour into sixty minutes are evidently durationless, for otherwise the hour would no longer consist of sixty minutes but of sixty minutes augmented by the duration of the division-points. Without the boundary that separates the earlier from the later, we would lack the capacity to distinguish an earlier from a later at all, and our temporal consciousness would be undone. But the boundary between two time-intervals means, in relation to both, the temporally unextended instant in which the earlier has already elapsed while the coming has not yet begun — it means the generalized Now!

If we pose the question how it comes about that we constantly, without giving any account of it, handle the concept of the durationless instant, then the answer cannot come to us from the outer world, in which there are no real and not even merely conceivable objects to which we would not have to attribute some temporal duration of existence. We can no more derive it from the recollection of experiences; for these too always seem to us to fill a shorter or longer span of time, whether we think of sensations or feelings, moods or surges of affect, judgments and thoughts or decisions, volitional tensions or reveries, and whatever other division one might prefer. The intended Now is certainly inexperienceable, and yet it underlies the experience of time, and hence all experience, since only temporal states of affairs are ever experienceable. But then nothing remains but to lend it to the act of apprehension itself! Only on the presupposition that the act of apprehension takes place at a temporally unextended point is it capable, with its help, of dividing the never-resting time.

We would, to be sure, have recognized this more quickly from the consideration that an event by which we are put in a position to find time, among other things, cannot itself be subject to the measuring of time. In order, however, to meet the objection at once that temporal difference is not the same as temporal opposition and still less the same as lack of duration, we have placed first the proof that time is ascertainable only with [p. 13] the assistance of the mathematical Now. With it, if one will, the act of apprehension "projects" itself into the stream of events, cutting the continuous medium of time through temporally unextended points into bounded intervals. — To the question of why one does not then acquire knowledge of this through recollection, we offer the consideration that the spiritual act which first makes all taking of cognizance possible cannot itself form an object of experience. Since everything that follows depends on one's having wholly understood the inviolability of this thesis, we offer one more ground for it that would alone already suffice to make it irrefutable.

The durationless point in time lays, so to speak, a cross-section through the entire universe, such that for every conceived instant all places in space appear to be connected in the concept of simultaneity. The Now-point is by its nature present in every point of space, or omnipresent. Even if we wished to set aside the absurdity involved in lending to a temporal process the discoverer's gaze for time, it could nonetheless never find something omnipresent, because its temporal constitution would prevent it from reaching, in the mathematical instant, an arbitrary multitude of different places. The act of temporal apprehension, and hence every act, is accordingly atemporal.

We cannot speak of the act of apprehension without positing a Something in which the capacity to perform it inheres. But we wish for now to call it only "the apprehending faculty," and at once reflect that it too must lack the character of temporality. If we represent a temporal state of affairs — for instance an electric generator — we must represent along with it that everything occurring in it or through it, such as the leaping of the spark, requires some temporal interval, however small. Conversely, what is to have the capacity to make incisions into time must reside outside of time! With the contrary conviction one would be maintaining that time itself divides itself into days, hours, minutes — which hardly anyone would concede. But if the apprehending faculty is atemporal, it must also be aspatial. For even if there were a temporal actuality without spatiality — as many suppose of mental processes — there is in any case no spatial actuality without some temporal duration of existence. Neither the process in the outer world nor even the volume of [p. 14] space in which it takes place can we mean without co-meaning a temporal span of its existence. If therefore we have removed the apprehending faculty from time, it can fitly have no existence in space any longer, and must accordingly be extra-spatio-temporal.

Whoever has sufficiently convinced himself of the atemporality of the apprehending faculty and of apprehension itself no longer requires proof of the atemporality of what is apprehensible, or of the "object"; for how could a temporally unextended act ever catch the temporal flowing! We just now considered that time itself cannot possibly ascertain itself; now we find ourselves pressed to the remarkable assumption that an atemporal something can do so no more! But here we encounter not only contrary prejudices, rooted for centuries and prepared for millennia, but also seem to entangle ourselves in a contradiction with our own presuppositions, insofar as these concern precisely the apprehension of time — the contradictory opposite of atemporality. In order to moderate at least in advance the extraordinary confusion of an investigation that constantly calls into question the discoverability of its own object, let it here be recalled that the commonly accepted concept of time conceals the strangest ambivalence. One distinguishes in time, among other things, past, present, and future, as though these were equally so many sections or parts of it. But if we replace the subject of the judgment in which the result of the apprehension of time is expressed — the judgment "time is" — with the first or last of the supposed divisions of time, we have unawares advanced to the assertion: the past is, and the future is — assertions that one would more credibly counter with: "past and future are not." It therefore seems to us that besides the time we articulate into sections, there is another kind hovering before us, for which a special name is lacking. Given this, if we call the measurable time the objective time or the time-object, and the other — about which for now we know nothing further — the real time, we have gained the advantage of having to confine the inapprehensibility solely to the latter. — With the indication of the non-being of past and future, the train of thought has already been introduced that is to lead us to insight into the atemporality of the objective.

Whatever else the judgment "something is" may imply, this much [p. 15] is certain: it does not mean that something was or will be, but that it simply is now. But if the object is a Being and the Being a "being-in-the-Now," then it can no more have temporal extension than the Now has, and we must resign ourselves to regarding it as atemporal — even though we cannot yet understand how time could nonetheless give itself as an object of apprehension. — Language is full of words and expressions that testify to the native knowing of this state of affairs. The word "Gegenwart" (present), formed from "gegenwärts" — analogous to "einwärts" (inward), "auswärts" (outward), "heimwärts" (homeward) — originally designates something directed toward one, hence an object present [gegenständlich Anwesendes], and acquires its relation to the Now-point of time only in the course of the eighteenth century; we still speak today of someone's "presence" [Gegenwart] or keep a matter "present" to ourselves, "make it present" [vergegenwärtigen]<sup>1</sup>. Language thus unmistakably sets up an equation between Being and being-present! The counterpart to this is the peculiar double meaning of the words "past" [vergangen], "pastness" [Vergangenheit], and "to pass" [vergehen], which mean sometimes a certain time-interval, sometimes the fact of nonexistence. "Past" events or events of the "past" are literally those within a time-interval that preceded other time-intervals and especially the present one; but they are also events of which we wish to deny existence. The word "vergehen" designates both the temporal flowing and the cessation of existence, the perishing, which is why one can also "vergehen" (be overcome) before rapture, fear, or shame; and the name "Vergänglichkeit" (transience) has developed into the bearer of the contrary of Being and being, gradually accumulating all the pathos that accompanies the flight of a thinking being from the certainty of its having-to-cease. In religious usage "transience," "temporality," and "mortality" form the nearly synonymous counter-words to the timelessly-being, which the wish for immortality calls an "eternal," and enter thereby into the closest proximity to actuality in general, which in the light of the thought of Being acquires the character of semblance. The proximity is perfected to coincidence, for example, in Goethe's verse: "All that is transient is but a symbol."

<sup>1</sup> On page 15. — Insofar as it is a matter of *present-day* German usage, and especially of bringing out a plurality of meanings of one and the same word, we rely here and elsewhere on the second edition (1908) of the "Deutsches Wörterbuch" by *Hermann Paul*, which, like scarcely any other, combines clarity and brevity with quite extraordinary richness!

The phrase just cited seems to us the fitting occasion, from [p. 16] what has been ascertained, to draw a conclusion that even those thinkers have regularly shied away from — for very understandable reasons — whose treatment of the problem of space and time ever moved in similar paths. The "transient," of which Goethe tells us it is only a symbol, is evidently actuality itself; and what is to reduce it to the level of a merely shadowy existence is its character of temporality. To be sure, Goethe did not say that all actuality is only a symbol; but he evidently did not do so only because he wished to present the Being in relation to which the "transient" fades to a symbol for him as a "higher" actuality — no longer burdened with the taint and deficiency of the one ordinarily so named: namely, instead of being, having to pass away in time. It is ultimately a question of linguistic convention whether one prefers to speak of two actualities or of the duality of Being and the actual; if we nonetheless consistently avoid the first formulation, it is because the entire history of thought furnishes proof that it has never served any other purpose than to suppose the duality to have been cancelled in that actuality that seemed "higher" not only to Goethe but to nearly all the philosophers of humanity: in the timelessly-being actuality. There can of course be no doubt that one must mean by "actuality" the temporally actual, if one is inclined to call one of the two Being. — The ambivalence of the actual, which Goethe's verse with the spell of prophetic poetry more conceals than reveals, has appeared to us in nakedness as a dilemma that no understanding of the understanding will ever resolve. Objecthood, we said, has the character of atemporality; but then the temporal never has the character of objecthood. As atemporal, the apprehending faculty finds, by means of timeless acts, the atemporal; but the temporally transient remains permanently closed to it. But if this is actuality, then there is no experience of the actual. What we call "knowing," presupposed to be empirical knowledge, must have an entirely different meaning from what the deceptive inclination to connect it with this word has suggested to humanity's spiritual will of appropriation. No faith in reason has ever led to any "knowledge," though it may supply an already existing knowledge with new material; and the collective name "science" for [p. 17] the products of the activity of conceptual thinking proves to be the result of the violent encroachment on the part of a "faculty" whose nature will be fully disclosed to us only from its "tendency." — We have made this anticipatory glance in order to make probable what goal our rudder is directed toward, and we now steer back into the more cautious course of developing exposition.

[p. 18]

#### 2. Kapitel — Vom Wesen der Existenz — Chapter 2 — On the Nature of Existence

We draw a great step closer to the peculiar difficulty that threatens, in view of the atemporality of the object, to make the concept of time impossible, when we first consider the temporal being of things. For since, as has already been expounded, neither thing nor process nor being can be thought without some temporal duration of existence, the concept of the actually existing appears no less called into question by the demonstrable atemporality of the object than does the concept of time itself — for which reason we may expect to illuminate each through the other. To simplify the inquiry, we take from the three forms of existence mentioned the unmoved thing, and consider first in what sense the perception by means of which we originally assure ourselves of its existence bears the character of an act.

When someone perceives a tree — whether through the most fleeting glimpse or through more prolonged examination — he receives not merely the impression of the tree's appearance, but simultaneously has the consciousness of the presential-being of an existing thing. If he puts this in the form of a judgment, it is at once evident that it does not refer precisely to the appearance of the tree. For this changes, even for the same observer, with every change of position, and can indeed never be the same for a new observer; whereas the existing tree is one and only one. Everyone accordingly distinguishes from the being tree the "aspect" [Ansicht] of the tree, and attributes to the former and not the tree, for instance, the color of the illumination. But even the "properties" of the tree do not assert themselves in the "aspect" of the tree. The existing tree has, say, a height of fifteen meters, while the appearance of the tree shrinks to a point at a sufficiently great distance. The adhering green [p. 19] of the leaves is entirely lost in darkness, although we count it among the permanent properties of that "persistent something" which had formed the object of the apprehension of existence. We must therefore distinguish with the utmost precision: the impression-experience and the apprehension of the existing thing — regardless of whether the latter customarily or legally and inseparably follows upon it. Just as certainly as the impression-experience can be conceived only as a temporal state of affairs of boundless transience, so certainly it would be impossible to see how we could preserve the apprehended existence from such evaporation, were we not to declare atemporal-unextended that act by which it became objective to us. The almost inescapably pressing assumption that it is accordingly itself an unextended point is compellingly confirmed the moment we attempt to set the content of the impression and the content of what we mean by the existing thing side by side for comparison. For since the numerically indefinitely great variability of the impression-contents in the face of a single thing forbids us to put any one of them in its place, nothing remains but to grasp it as an absolutely merely thinkable point — one, to be sure, that means a kind of relating-center for a manifold of images to be determined more closely in whatever way. (For this reason the point does not, of course, occupy a place within the thing, but is capable of representing it in a unique way — more about this follows later.) From this there follows for the relation of the apprehending faculty to the temporal actuality of appearances at least two things: it wrests its object from the world of appearances, and connects with this the peculiar gift of finding it again, in however various its aspects, as identical. The objectification accomplished by the act would thus not concern the actuality of the appearance at all, but an abstractum related to it for reasons as yet opaque. When medieval Scholasticism defended the doctrine of transubstantiation against the evidence of the senses with the argument that the persistence of the "accidents" of wine and bread does not contradict a transformation of their "substances," it exercised, in an admittedly contestable way, the incontestably correct assumption that even the perceived thing is an abstractum. — But how does it stand with the duration of the thing? Before we answer, however, certain objections press forward.

[p. 20] The apparent contradiction between the logical usage, according to which the perceived thing is rightly called a concrete, and the epistemological ascertainability of the opposite resolves itself through a fundamentally generalizing formulation. We have above distinguished the time-object from real time; we now distinguish the existence of the thing from the actuality underlying it. Concrete in relation to its properties, the actually present tree is nonetheless abstract in view of its appearance. "Concrete" says literally "grown together" and thereby indicates with surprising exactness that it does not concern the thought of being-actual at all, but of the (possibly demanded by actuality) cohering of properties. — Nevertheless, one might now object to the asserted abstractness of the thing: when someone perceives a tree, the "existential judgment" does not refer to a simply-being it, but to an individual it; for it has as its object a particular tree at a particular place at a particular time! That would be true, but offers a very peculiar reverse side that we must not let escape us. The appearance of the tree flows in time, and our looking also flows in time; but when I now perceive this tree and could accordingly judge: "Here stands a tree," I have not only detached the tree from the embrace of its appearance, but at the same time also the here and now of the appearing from the totality of space and the flowing of time! For there is no conceivable transformation of the universe that could alter by the least the established fact. One can fell the tree, devastate the ground, yes the globe might fall to pieces — this does not in the slightest affect the objective actuality of the conceived thing at the conceived place at the conceived time. Or: what has been cannot be unhappened, what has occurred cannot be unoccurred. As the tree-thing remains a selfsame, so too remains a selfsame the place of its existence and the span of its subsistence in the flowing of time. Not the tree alone is an abstractum — the place and instant of its existence are so equally. Its Now, at the moment of having-been-apprehended, has at once taken on the property of remaining as if forever "at its place and time," even though time and with it the whole world, including the bearer of perception, storms ceaselessly onward and has already left every Now behind in an instant. This appears [p. 21] in a truly paradoxical way when we consider that we speak of the Now-point in the plural, thereby looking toward a selfsame in the different Now-points — even though our actual Now is singular, unique, and without equal. Hardly need we add that no concept of the individual could be conceived that would escape the fate of meaning something abstract, if even the individual thing — together with the instant of its presence for the bearer of perception — is an abstractum! But then, one might ask, what would be the constitution of the metaphysical concrete from which we must abstract in order to apprehend the perceptual object?

Meanwhile we notice a gap in our earlier train of thought. We called the temporal point the generalized Now, but left open the question how a generalization of the Now can be thought. We have established of the Now only that, thanks to its point-like character, it can divide time — but we have not yet considered why, in dividing it, it designates a fixed position in time. If we consider only the state of affairs of its temporal unextendedness at the point, we can neither separate the temporal point from the spatial point, nor can we see how it comes about that no temporal point coincides with another temporal point, no spatial point with another spatial point. It is only in the positionality of the point that the fact is contained that it, although itself neither temporal nor spatial, nonetheless appears to be bound to time (as to space) in a peculiar way. We do not yet know what actually binds the point to a specific position; but this much we already see: the ground for it cannot possibly lie in the point itself, but solely in the nature of the medium in relation to which, with its help, the position is set. If accordingly it must always occupy some position — since wherever it may be it at once marks a position — it nonetheless assumes any position whatsoever without change of properties. In particular, the Now shares with every possible temporal point this: that it acquires the peculiarity of its character only from a factual sequence of points — that is to say, from a mere relation to other positions. The temporal point is the generalized Now insofar as already contained in the Now is the higher abstractum "temporal position." — Before proceeding, let the result at once be tested for its adequacy to the resolution of the contradiction that seemed to lie in the fact that a point-like act [p. 22] could find the stream of time. No mortal can indicate what time itself, space itself, is — because it would in truth be unthinkable to find, by means of timeless acts, real time, real space. Rather, what we apprehend and find is never anything other than the position in time to which time merely belongs, and the position in space to which space merely belongs. Or: the temporal position cannot be thought without reference to the totality of time, nor the spatial position without reference to the totality of space. — The resolution of the difficult question of what such belonging involves — from which we evidently receive the impulse to distinguish real time from the time-object — can we only undertake after we have shown more precisely wherein it does not consist.

Let us return to the question of abstraction. The conceived Now too, as has been shown, is already object and abstractum and therefore only a link in a chain of entirely uniform temporal positions. In fact we can transpose ourselves in thought to any position in time we wish, in order from there, as from an imagined present, to judge the events — a use historians and narrators sometimes make of this, reporting what is past in the present tense. This does not make it any less true, however, that only the Now enables the formation of the concept of temporal position. When we say that something has taken place, we mean that a temporal point is to be found in the past where the taking-place was present; and when we assert that something will take place, we assert the presential-being of the taking-place for a temporal point in the future. It is always the Now that — stripped of its uniqueness — recurs in every temporal position! But wherein lies this uniqueness? — No reflection on the act of apprehension would be capable of disclosing to us what is added to the ever-same temporal apprehension in order to lend to the consciousness of the Now its exemplary significance; which is why we must here, where we are discussing only apprehension, rest content with the negative verdict that there is something determining the act whose origin does not lie in the capacity of apprehension. The proto-concrete X we are seeking is doubtless there; but it belongs to its nature not to be able to become object for us in the same way as things (with their properties); so that the act of apprehension, in coming into existence, simultaneously tears itself away from its immediate ground of possibility. — The deepening of insight into the nature of the temporal point leads us [p. 23] a step further in the resolution of the question of the nature of the thing-point.

We have recognized in the thing the unextended relational-point for a temporally flowing manifold of images, and we find no further difficulty in knowing it to be somehow anchored in time. Whereas the mere temporal position remains where it is, the thing, on the contrary, demands to be thought as partaking of a temporal span that may be extremely great — such as the duration of the universe — or extremely small — such as the duration of a lightning flash — but can never shrink to the temporal point. There is no "existence" in the mathematical instant. But now we reflect that to the temporal point, because it forms a position in the time-object, belongs also the sequence of all other positions, and that already two of them suffice to fix, in the same way as the point fixes the position, any arbitrary stretch of time. It follows from this that the determinability of the thing-point derives from its self-sameness at at least two — moreover arbitrarily close — temporal positions. Or: the temporal sequence of appearances has an identical relational-point only in view of position-different points of time. If we imagined the apprehending gaze gliding along the time-line, it would find, in the objectified sequence of appearances, position by position the selfsame thing-point — which is why we can also say that the thing, though it does not exist in the mathematical instant, nonetheless passes continually through it. — We have earlier recalled that no extension, however short, can be conceived that cannot be divided into arbitrarily many parts. However small the distance at which we might choose the temporal positions where the apprehending act finds the thing-point, nothing prevents the insertion between them of an unrestricted number of further temporal positions where it would find it equally. But if it is thereby established that there would be absolutely no point in the temporal stretch where the thing would not be identically present for the finding gaze, then it suggests itself to replace the point-sequence by the stretch itself, and to understand the existence inseparable from the perceived thing as the persistence of the appearance-related point along a delimitable span of time. And only with this have we arrived at one of the most instructive and at the same time most consequential concepts that the human Spirit has created: the concept of "always" or of "Duration."

[p. 24]

#### 3. Kapitel — Der Begriff der Dauer — Chapter 3 — The Concept of Duration

[As long as a thing exists, it exists "always," or it "endures" that long — which means, as we now know, that for equally long it is, at every arbitrary temporal position, for whatever causes, a selfsame. Time in and for itself is never the same; it simply is not — it flows; but the thing in time does not merely subsist: it even persists in relation to the never-persisting time, and this we call its "Duration." {Were any doubt still able to prevail as to whether time has been apprehended not immediately but only as referred to the point in it, it would have to vanish in the face of the circumstance that the human Spirit has grown accustomed to transferring the concept of Duration to that which is in itself durationless — time! When above we remarked of our judgment "time is" that it strangely asserts the being of the past and even of the future, we might have referred at once for reinforcement to the still far worse paralogism of which we make ourselves guilty whenever, with the coupling-word "duration of time" [Zeitdauer], we quite untroubled express persistence of time. Since persistence presupposes at least two position-different temporal points, duration of time would evidently demand a second time, this a third, and so on ad infinitum — from which it is evidently manifest that the concept of time is burdened with an admittedly inevitable self-contradiction and can for this reason never form the foundation of adequate knowledge of the temporally actual. In the word "Zeitdauer" (time-duration) the situation is presented with particular sharpness: that thought is condemned to grasp without exception every Being — even that of the time-object — in conformity with the Being of things. The thing is the original Something and quite literally the model and prototype of the noun in general, which is why the history of human thought offers countless examples of the misleading reification of such concepts as: process, fate, life, [p. 25] childhood, age, youth, morning, evening, spring, enmity, sin, duty, and so on indefinitely. In this very fact is grounded the usage, common to so many languages, of the verb meaning "to exist" — in German, the verb "sein" — merely to link the predicate-word with the subject of predication. Every judgment about time as likewise about space is constructed as though it concerned a time-thing and a space-thing. In that we now, judging by analogy with Being, also treat that actuality which, while having no duration itself, nonetheless enables all enduring, time unawares becomes for us an existence of, as it were, surpassing all duration — or that arbitrarily extendable line along which we lay off stretch by stretch the conceived duration of things. We do not fail to make visible at least the fundamental impossibilities with which our entire conceptual image of the world is thereby overlaid.

Not too many people are in the habit of being clear about the fact that we do not measure the duration of a thing by means of time, but rather time by means of the duration of a thing. We apprehend two temporal positions and connect with them the consciousness of their succession; but we do not apprehend their temporal interval — we merely infer it according to the measure of the persisting of things that remain unchanged (or else according to the measure of the duration of a process, which in turn presupposes a temporally stable thing). Outstanding logicians have not missed the point that the so-called uniform progress of time is only an assumption, whose justification derives solely from its utility in explaining factual coincidences and successions. Whether the flow of actual time were uniform, ever-accelerating, or wholly irregular — no measurement of the objective whatsoever could settle even the least thing about it. Such indications, however, are suited to bring to our consciousness not so much the limits of knowing as rather its utter incommensurability with the time of actuality. In that we regard time at all from the standpoint of something endurable, we find ourselves in the position of being able to hold the line that it would thereby be, closed with every Now, while on the other hand we are incapable of establishing a starting-point for it. Time "reaches," according to this conception, from a beginningless infinity up to the present moment — it is thus of one-sided infinity, or rather both finite and infinite at once. In such contradictions [p. 26] there is manifestly revealed the incompatibility of the elements of the time-concept: namely, the unapprehended reality of time with the apprehended limit of time, through which alone we can in thought relate to the former.

With the last reflection we have already left behind the unavoidable contradictions and entered the ground of those mythologies of the understanding that rest on an emancipation of the concept of duration. The concept of duration — be it the paradigmatic duration of things or the analogically posited duration of time — has its conditioned right for the world of temporal existences, but leads at once into abysses of bottomless absurdity as soon as one employs it detached from these. — Every Now of our life lies in a flash already behind us again, so that we must continually add to our duration the measure of its temporal distance from the once-more-present Now. If we now forget that duration holds only of existences, but that for time it concerns only its relation to these, and allow ourselves to be led astray into lending our increment of duration to time itself, then it will appear to us at once under the image of a river flowing out of the past and into the future, gaining stretch by stretch anew with the Now as, so to speak, the crest of foam of its mobile front. The prejudice is so deeply rooted that we must not spare ourselves the effort of demonstrating the unavoidability of the assumption of the precisely opposite direction of the time-stream — if one dares here to speak of "direction" at all. The language leaves no doubt about it: with the idiom that time flows by, that the past lies behind us, that the future comes, the past goes, it unmistakably gives us to understand that the said flowing tears every momentary Now continually backward and into the past. Were it true, what a popular verse says, reinforcing common opinion:

One, two, three at rushing pace / Runs the time, we run with it, then we should never be able to age, because we would be eternally in the selfsame Now — since, in the absence of position-different temporal moments, there would of course be no duration and existence any longer. But this very assumption could not be avoided at all if we conflated the direction of increment of our supposed duration with the direction of movement of time and held the Now-point to be the moving hem of the time-stream [p. 27]. It would then no longer be any "fixed temporal position" to which we could ever return, but rather the same thing as the flowing of time "in itself"! Our actually present consciousness of ceaselessly increasing duration therefore demands that we take what exists in us as something timelessly standing, which marks point by point on the time flowing toward it the positions that its current unceasingly tears into the past. The faculty in us that finds time does not run with time, but time runs past it — as it runs past every thing — namely from the future into the past; and what we call its Duration is merely the measure, expressed in it, of our persisting in it.<sup>2</sup>

<sup>2</sup> On page 27. — We are speaking here of the time of actuality, and *not* of the objective and measurable time of physics. Why the latter necessarily appears as a "vector," and indeed with a direction into the future, will emerge in the second volume.

Whoever has, in opposition to this, made the exactly contrary conception one's own, finds nothing in the way of thinking the nonsense of "infinite duration" — in accordance with the unlimited extent one must claim for the continuation of the time-line — and the ground is laid on which the most absurd wishes for immortality find fulfillment. If we ask not the philosopher but the "common man" what he means by personal immortality, the answer is that he hopes, after his death, naturally, to continue existing without limit. But not only ordinary people believe this; the half-philosophers at least pronounce oracles about it, holding the question to be an "empirical" one; and as for the genuine thinkers, we have had to witness in the most recent times that one of the most celebrated erected an entire system on the explicit confusion of time and duration, and undertook to interpret — as will be shown — the purely temporal phenomena of cosmic life from the standpoint of an unstoppable increment of existence, thereby involuntarily likening them to the well-known penny given at interest upon interest at the time of Christ's birth. A brief consideration of the concept of "eternity" may serve us as an example of how the rigorous analysis of time-consciousness permits the compelling answer to certain much-contested questions.

There exists not merely one "eternity," but indeed two of them, although one would do well to crown only one of them with this name; but both are entirely different from "everlasting duration" (sempiternality). "Eternal" is the actual time, and only it is truly eternal — because it is not even present in the mathematical Now, let alone durable! [p. 28] Into eternity one would enter who, wholly divested of all existence, completely "passed away" in time — as perhaps the mystic had in mind when he wrote the thoughtful verses:

For whom time is as eternity

And eternity as time,

He is set free

From all strife.

An incomparably other "eternity" — namely independence from time — belongs to the object of every universal concept: the triangle, virtue, multiplicity; and at least atemporal is the object of thought as such. "Eternal" in such a sense would be any arbitrary judgment-content (whether true or false); for there is none that could not be thought, at the most various times, by the most various minds, as always the same. Yet this Being of more than Platonic character could scarcely satisfy the claims of those who dream of eternal duration. As for that, however, it is a genuine impossibility. The name "duration" signifies a necessary mark of existing, and existence is the form under which we posit a real thing as being, or a being thing as real. Since everything real is temporally changeable, everything being is atemporally identical, existence means self-sameness with respect to the temporal course, or within temporal limits, and duration signifies the magnitude of the distance between the limiting points. If we remove the limits, what is meant has at once lost its immediate relation to time — either by becoming the time-independent thing that, like the triangle, no longer exists in time, or by becoming the temporally actual itself, of which we have seen that, because it is always changing, it cannot be apprehended at all. "Infinite duration" is therefore a genuine contradictio in adjecto. Whatever exists, endures — and whatever endures, endures also finitely. Whatever we assume to possess existence must at some time in time have begun to subsist, as it will at some time in time cease to subsist. The objective universe of mechanics, for example, has no less a determinate duration than every objective body, every being, every process within it! Because finite durability belongs to the concept of real Being, one is already on the ground of fiction if one even permits the question of whether anything whatsoever — [p. 29] be it the universe or be it the soul — might perhaps after all endure infinitely.

It is very remarkable that, while everyone would dispute that zero added to zero often enough could yield more than zero — namely a something — most are nonetheless prepared to believe that something added to something often enough produces not merely a greater something but an infinite one; whereas this would be no less absurd than the former. Let one picture the case from the reverse side. When the inquisitive king in Grimm's fairy tale asks the wise shepherd boy: "Of how many seconds does eternity consist?" — no one fails to recognize the senselessness of the question, because "eternity," however often divided, would thereby no less remain eternal! But then one should grant that it would be equally unthinkable to build it up out of units. Unity implies countability, and countability excludes infinity. If we regard the universe already as a system of things, we have thereby already established its countability — both as regards the multiplicity of simultaneous things in space and the duration of each one in time — and we gain back by no conceivable expansion of the limits neither an infinite abundance for the former nor eternity for the latter. — The nonsense of "infinite duration" forms the conclusion, or perhaps better the persistent undercurrent, of the thousandfold errors that have arisen in the history of human thought from the confusion of actual time with objective time. Because we can fix the self-sameness of the thing-point in a temporal succession of appearances only with the help of two temporal positions, we imperceptibly make out of the temporally flowing actuality a permanent Always, composed of the stretches of existence that the duration of things lays off upon it.

As we survey once more the stopping-places of the completed course of thought, but in a different order, we reflect on what the investigation has gained and before what questions it has come to a halt. — With the indication that the sense of a judgment is independent of the moment of its occurrence, only in another way was expressed the atemporality of every possible judgment-content. We must, however, distinguish among the objects of thought those that are immediately related to the temporal phenomenon and those we have called time-independent. Of logical universal concepts, so far only one has been encountered whose object cannot be thought without reference to time: namely, the temporal position. [p. 30] Temporally unextended and wholly without part in the puzzling flight that we have, from as yet unconsidered necessity, attributed to the temporally actual — it has nevertheless its sense solely from its capacity to divide the continuous medium of that actual and thereby to insert itself into that sequence of homogeneous positions which, objectifying it, we underlay the ungraspable temporal stream. The concept of the temporal position served us as proof of the indivisible instantaneity of the act that posits it and of the necessity of locating the faculty for this in an absolutely atemporal Being. The temporal position, finally — as we ascertained — is abstracted from the strictly momentary Now; wherewith arose the question, so far only touched upon, concerning that property of actual presence which is capable of grounding the Now-concept.

But the most surprising prospect was opened by the consideration of the perceived thing, to which even immediate apprehension ascribes existence. Since to existing there belongs indispensably a span of existing — in other words, the persistence of a self-same in actuality — we had to think that point, in relation to which alone a spatiotemporal manifold of images closes into a thing, as identically present at at least two different temporal positions, or else as traversing a temporal "stretch." The dependence upon time thereby admittedly attributed to the thing was, however, as more precise consideration showed, wholly different from participation in it; and if above we had to detach from actual time as not belonging to it the unextended limit of time, so now still more completely the duration first to be founded on such limits. For, granted that the inescapable compulsion is right, out of which we take the actual time for something non-persisting, then it can of all things least possess duration — and hence also no existence, not even the Being of the present-point found in regard to it. Actual time is neither constant nor of the instantaneity of a mathematical position, but simply fleeting; and the phrase "temporal duration of a persisting state of affairs" expresses, in a most confusing way, rather its complete temporal otherness. With the concept of the temporal span, the atemporal object is smuggled into actual time — or rather, that object itself is described, albeit as seen through the layer of passing that is alien to it. Actual time and duration are incompatible; and the necessity of lending the existing thing duration, and [p. 31] of underlying that duration in turn — without which it would be ungraspable — the objective time of linear extension, certifies decisively that the object of thought is found only beyond temporal actuality.

Everything offered thus far is, if one will, a new formulation of the so-called principle of identity. That this is truly the supreme guiding principle of thought — or in some sense the most general instruction for correct thinking — can scarcely be disputed today. It is known, however, that the principle was fought over for centuries, and above all a Locke dismissed it with respect to the famous "A is A" as empty tautology. Now, admittedly, propositions such as "A is A" are incapable of designating the principle, because they merely repeat the finished product of an act of identification, instead of showing us in that act the ground of the object of thought. Yet, since the formula states the object of thought twice in the manner of an equation, it presupposes two acts of thinking in relation to it, and therefore demands the identity of the concept at two different points of time. The object of thought consequently possesses the property of atemporality; and this alone, and nothing else, to attest, is the sense of the identity principle.

With the exception of one thinker<sup>3</sup>, we find it not discussed in any textbook of logic that, according to the identity principle, comprehensibility is grounded in the atemporality of what is to be comprehended. The all the more frequently favored warning against confusing the self-sameness of the object of thought with duration already allows one to surmise why a meaningful formulation of the self-sameness principle has not hitherto succeeded. For just as certain as this principle — because it abstracts from the temporal flowing of actuality — contains no relation to duration, just as certain is it that without a knowledge of the state of affairs "time," it could be neither ascertained nor capable of any sense. As was elaborated in the second chapter, even the finding of what is by its nature identical with itself rests on the fact that the spiritual act tears what is to be found away from actuality and thereby, admittedly, as from something divested of all changeability, takes from it the possibility of ever ceasing to be what it is at the moment of its being found. But if identity means withdrawal from time, then nevertheless the name leaves no doubt that it is a never-identical that, through whose detachment, the object is "established"; and the laudable insight into the difference between self-sameness and duration must not cause us to forget [p. 32] that not even self-sameness, let alone duration, could be thought without an incessantly self-changing, however puzzling it may still be to us from where and in what form of thought we have the knowledge of it.

<sup>3</sup> On page 31. — Namely in his "Logik auf dem Scheidewege," *Melchior*-*Palágyi*, of whom there will very often be occasion to speak in what follows.

But the identity principle yields its metaphysical content to us first through application to this very self-changing (we have called it actual time), in that it reveals to us the impossibility of also comprehending the actual that we mean. For if we understand by time something incessantly fleeting, we make use of the concept of fleeing only by holding fast its meaning. However incessantly the fleeing may flee, our concept of the incessant fleeing does not flee with it. But if it remains one and always the same, then what it signifies also remains one and always the same — the fleeing; from which it emerges, as it were overwhelmingly, that through the act of comprehension the intended fleetingness falls prey to absolute rigidification — and with it also the most general property of actuality itself!

It is unfortunately too often overlooked in logic that every "positing" requires distinction — indeed, as we will show, rests on distinction and first takes place through it. We should not have the concept of time-independence without that of timedependence, not that of fleetingness without that of permanence, not that of change without that of persistence — and equally in reverse. The self-sameness principle is not a principle of duration; but it transforms itself into a principle of duration when applied to time-dependent states of affairs, whose model and originary case is to be sought in the thing. If I assert self-sameness of something that I rightly or wrongly hold to be real, I have already asserted its duration. Being as such therefore shows a double face: without immediate temporal reference it means the atemporality of the object of thought as such; with immediate temporal reference — something that endures unchangingly through the happening. With this latter we shall first concern ourselves. — The self-sameness principle forms the supreme summit to which abstracting soars. We must abstract from change in order to arrive at persistence; but we must also abstract further from time in order to ascertain what every object of thought — however it may stand with respect to time, and whether it be called "this table here" or "stream of time" or "identity principle" — shares with every other. In this is attested and expressed the durationlessness of the spiritual act that produces the object of thought. So much for now on the self-sameness principle. —

[p. 33] We had begun with the present-point and arrived at the concept of duration by the detour through the existing thing. The trajectory of human reflection ran in the opposite direction. Originally apprehended were existence and duration, and therewith the relation of the atemporal object to temporal actuality; only later the Now — and specifically as the beginning-point or end of existence. Now it begins, now it ceases, now it is there, now it is gone, and — pointing back into deeper backgrounds — once life begins, once it ends: at such fracture-points of a persistence barely noticed because all too habitual, there first flashed up the reflection that illuminated together: existence, duration, and Now. In the "infinite" actuality there is none of the three (for where would time find its end!), and we recall once more: duration and beginninglessness exclude each other, beginning and end demand one another. But where, in the actual, would the occasioning ground for these two lie?

[p. 34]

### Zweiter Abschnitt — Das Eleatenproblem — Second Part — The Eleatic Problem

#### 4. Kapitel — Die Seinsunfähigkeit der Bewegung — Chapter 4 — The Incapacity of Motion for Being

Our previous delimitation of the nature of the thing suffers from a certain uncertainty insofar as its oneness with respect to time would apply equally to the point in space. For there is no real place of zero duration! Furthermore, since the marking of the place takes place in relation to another place and, indirectly, thus in relation to the world of appearance, it seems as if the point of the thing coincides with the point in space. This would, however, be immediately countered by the fact that even the tiniest thing, for example, a "speck of sundust," within its necessarily included spatial extent, offers room for any number of mathematical points. Nevertheless, a lawful relationship between the two might exist, the clarification of which would finally provide the desired conclusion for the designation of the point of the thing; for just as the existence of the thing requires duration of existence, so too does every moment of its existence demand a place of residence in space. Moreover, however, the indicated factual situation seems to call into question the alleged abstraction of the thing once again. If we take, for example, one of the upper corners of a tangible cube into view, then it remains truly "in place and position" in relation to the other corners (as these, in turn, in relation to it). For the larger cube of the house, there also exists a fixed relationship of all outer points to the floor surface, which itself is immovably inserted into the surrounding land, and the continent of Africa has the shape assigned to it by the map, not only [p. 35] today, but also yesterday and tomorrow. Granted, even the hardest bulwark is gnawed at, and even the continents are gnawed at by the "tooth of time," and would have been noticeably altered in both cases already after the lapse of a century. Yet the fact of being fixed in form still seems to us to offer reality itself in the form of constancy and existence!

As long as humanity has sought with the understanding, it has pursued thought goals similar to the schema indicated here and has, precisely in its efforts to construct systems of knowledge, practiced the act of knowing in the manner of building and making habitable houses. (Incidentally, "system" means "assemblage".) Not only the Greeks, even though they did so with unsurpassed mastery (in finding as well as in missing!), but all philosophers of all times and peoples proceeded in this way, and, in particular, as we shall see later, modern "dynamicism," far from breaking with belief in being, has merely warmed itself to equally worse houses of knowledge, by preferring, as it were, railway carriages, automobiles, and airplanes to the "fixed residence." — We cannot yet decide what in a system-building thought is truly natural and indefeasible, and we wish first of all merely to show the unbridgeable chasm that separates the — real universe from more or less all system traditions. In order to awaken a feeling for this beforehand, let us for a moment recall the theory of ideas of Plato. Indeed, according to it, "ideas," whatever else they may represent, certainly possess the character of being and form an absolutely being order according to a mutual relation of being (or, more correctly, a one-sided dependence on one another). Everything in this world of ideas is, as one and always the same, placed before the observer, remaining and unchanging, "from eternity to eternity." "For God," it says in the "Timaeus," "found all visible things not in rest, but in disordered lawless motion, and led them out of disorder into order, because he held order to be absolutely better than disorder." Should not this God rather be merely the human understanding and, above all, the understanding of philosophers?! What system, however, would not have presented us with world orders? But does a world, in which no order has ever persisted, actually appear ordered, one that the statesman, the technician, or the schoolmaster has imposed upon it? And how would it be understandable from an order that no one can foresee, [p. 36] whom the storm, the plague, or the war will carry off, whom will spare, and that, all in all calculated, no day ever repeats the events of the previous day? Truly, if we wish to speak in similes, the world would resemble far more the lightning-swirled cloud that dissolves again in rain showers than the snail shell or weather roof with which perishable beings secure themselves for a while against storms and floods.

It took a cult of the understanding over millennia to predispose us with a readiness of belief for knowledge buildings that presume to express, in the guise of an absolutely being order, that which, as we are inclined to think, is absolutely unordered, and we wish already here to remind that before the turned-back eye lie longer millennia of humanity to which this mode of consideration was entirely foreign. For the myth itself meant, among other things, to report on actual occurrences. But if science believes it has sufficiently devalued it because it can hold up to it that it has fabricated demons instead of establishing facts, then it forgets that, conversely, it could reproach it for speaking with all its concepts of being entirely past the event-character of reality, of which it alone gives us an account! — But now one says to us that such arrows might at best hit the Platonic theory of ideas as well as the Platonizing thought-theology of the Middle Ages, but no longer the world picture of a Democritus, as it were, put together from atomic whirls, not to mention the electrodynamic systems of the newest physics, which are just about to dissolve the schema of being and to completely evaporate its last remnant, the supposed materiality of the world, into "energetics." To such objections we answer with the proposition that a faculty of judgment is incapable of making the factual situation of change its own; and we precede the proof with an overview of the science of appearance of the main types of change.

Beside the immediately perceptible stands the only indirectly perceptible change. If after some time we gain the impression that the blade of grass has grown longer, the bud fuller, the autumn leaf yellower, the mist denser, or that the hour hand of the clock has advanced, then we grasp this, as the statements themselves testify, not merely as a mere alternation of facts, but as the change of one and the same factual situation. What we establish in such cases by comparison are [p. 37] different factual situations; we indicate them, however, following an inner compulsion, in the sense of a continuous change of the states of one and the same thing identical with itself. On this we would never have fallen if we could not perceive such changes directly, such as: the getting louder of the whistle of an approaching locomotive; the continuous color change of a colored solution that we dilute; the apparent cooling of a warmed liquid into which we have dipped our hand. The peculiarity of such a transition of a certain quality of the thing into a conceptually new quality lies always in the fact that we can divide the path actually or as it were traversed into arbitrarily many parts. The growth of the blade of grass, which has become one centimeter larger, has traversed an arbitrarily divisible distance; the heat of the water, whose temperature has risen by one degree, has experienced an arbitrarily divisible increase, and so in every case.

Besides the continuous there are sudden changes. If we notice that a very fully bloomed rose has disappeared from the stem after a few minutes, then we again do not assume two different things, but the sudden change of a single thing and express this with the judgment that the blossom has fallen. Had we been present to the falling of the blossom, it would indeed have appeared to us in the light of a process, albeit one that plays out quickly, with certainly a series of intermediate links. But in countless cases we perceive the completely transitionless suddenness of the alternation of two qualities. The red litmus paper, moistened with a strongly alkaline solution, has turned blue in the apparently indivisible instant; the solution that was just clear but supersaturated has transformed in a single stroke into a deposit of crystals; the white powder of a diazo body disappears as soon as it dries, with a sharp bang, so that we only become aware of its non-existence afterwards. From direct experience we know of the (for this reason empirically named) instantaneity of the lightning, the clap of thunder, the blow and the sting, as well as of every appearance that suddenly appears before us unprepared or equally suddenly disappears from the field of vision. — Incidentally, let it be pointed out that certain qualities, which we have accustomed ourselves to consider from the standpoint of opposition, utterly resist the conception of an intermediate or even merely mediating [p. 38] quality. We cannot imagine an intermediate property between solid and liquid (for the soft, doughy would be from both merely a mixture), not between liquid and gaseous, between rest and movement, between being dead and being alive, and so on.

To the modern man it seems almost inconceivable that something should come into being from pure nothingness, or conversely, dissolve entirely into nothingness; yet even Robert Mayer believed he could justify his theory of the equivalence of forces by appealing to the principle ex nihilo nil fit, nil fit ad nihilum; but the "savage," just as much as the still young child, manifests with a thousand behaviors the precisely opposite belief. A child must, for example, generally have surpassed the age of five before one can successfully perform "magic tricks" for him. If one does so earlier, one will observe that he regards the sudden and seemingly causeless disappearance of an object as no less incomprehensible than its removal by visible means. The same thing happens, however, to the adult in many a night dream, where it does not surprise him at all if, out of the puppy that is jumping around him, a kitten suddenly becomes.
