Such highly questionable facts are intended here merely to serve as the prelude to the following train of thought: in order to arrive at the concept of change, we must start from the immediately perceptible change and regard among the perceptible those proceeding in the form of a continuous transition between two limiting states as fundamental. For we quite well understand that even sudden transformations of the kind of mere qualitative changes of a persistent fact can be interpreted, once one has seen others unfold through an arbitrarily divisible sequence of intermediate states; whereas we do not yet understand how one could ever have arrived at such an interpretation if the fact of continuous transition lay entirely outside the realm of immediate experience. — But just as the perceptible transition from one quality to some other provides the obvious basis for the concept of change in general, so again is the perceptible motion the pattern and as it were the archetype of all changes.

Besides (apparently) resting things we perceive moving things continually: be it the running animal, the thrown stone, the tree [p. 39] swaying in the wind, the rolling wave, the falling rain, the sailing cloud, the flowing river, or whatever else may be the case, and this means, we perceive: not the resting thing at various places in the course of time (such as, for example, the hour hand of a clock), but together with the thing and inseparable from it, its being moved. Although the natural-scientific distinction between rotatory and translatory motion also rests on a phenomenologically graspable and also ontologically significant difference, we may nevertheless for our purposes regard the latter as based on this insofar as any arbitrary fixed point of a body revolving around an axis is undoubtedly involved in translatory motion. If we define the latter more precisely as continuous change of place of the being, then, as one would not wish to overlook, the emphasis lies on the continuity of the transition from place to place and by no means on the difference of places which is of course tacitly included.

Countless linguistic expressions place it before our eyes in a striking manner that it was the perception of translatory motions that gave rise to the thought of mutability and whose object reappears covertly in the conception of every continuous succession of states or qualities. Time, as we have already heard, comes and passes, and the epochs follow one another; temperature rises and falls; the electrical "current" "goes" from the anode to the cathode, has a gradient, and so on; tones traverse a scale upwards as well as downwards; and, to grant at least a side glance to the supersensible, prices also rise and fall, someone sinks in our esteem, a thought passes through our head, and so on. A special case of translatory motion in the end lies before us when a body, for example an air balloon, swells. And thus we speak of the swelling of a tone, of the growing, increasing, decreasing of heat or cold, of brightness as well as darkness; and what is not everything do we become larger and smaller: the heat, the noise, the bodily pain, and so on, not to speak of the so-called transfers to the mental! It would be superfluous to add that the physical view of the world has always been primarily aimed at replacing all qualities with processes and all processes with motions. No doubt, we carry the concept of motion into every perceived as well as discovered change; and thus would indeed the incomprehensibility of change in [p. 40] general be proven, if it were possible for us to demonstrate that of motion.

It remains an eternal title of glory for the Greeks that, disregardlessly directed toward being, they provided the irrefutable proof for the impossibility of being of motion. We draw from the four arguments of the Eleatics against the possibility of being of motion — famously invented by Zeno according to Aristotle — only the strongest or at least tangibly convincing one, that of the flying arrow, in doing so, however, making use of the concepts that our own train of thought has put before us. If we consider the flying arrow during the period of its flight at an arbitrary present point, it always has a locally determined position, but against that also not the slightest motion. The same gaze of apprehension that gives me the arrow's position deprives this position of the possibility of being moved: this is the first and already decisive part of the proof. Should one now think, however, that we have indeed ourselves denied that a thing can exist in the mathematical instant, after which the whole phenomenal world, including the arrow together with its motion, would be nullified in it, then one would overlook that into the unextended place of time the existence of the arrow is not posited, but rather the position of the arrow and in that manner a quality or state which is conceived precisely as independent of any duration of existence. The arrow requires, in order to exist, a temporal interval, and during it it either rests or moves. Its property of position, however, requires, in order to be what it is, so little of a temporal span that rather its presence at the instant of apprehension forms one of the possible conditions under which the identity of the arrow is recognized. Two iron rails or two rulers or two matches "are" in time; but the angle which two iron rails or rulers or matches form "is" not in time, but belongs to the totality of time-independent properties, without which the identity of the thing in relation to time could not be understood.

We could have set forth much more briefly that the Eleatic train of thought gives the unanswerable answer to the question, not what the moving arrow is, but what the motion of the arrow is in the temporally unextended instant of apprehension: a position. We have chosen the longer path in order to demonstrate anew that the assumption of [p. 41] the indivisible point for the act of apprehension cannot be avoided. It was far from the Eleatics to engage in considerations regarding the duration of mental acts; yet their dissection of being forced them to presuppose unnoticed the necessity of taking place in the indivisible instant for the mental act by means of which it is found; and we believe that the reference to the relational properties of things is indeed particularly suitable to convince even the most stubborn doubter. Everyone must recognize that an angle stands outside every temporal relation and therefore could also be apprehended only by an instantaneous act of thought. This then applies no less to the shape of a thing and again to its position in space, which as it were gives the shape of the co-existence of things. But once one has advanced this far, it becomes easy to see that it must apply to all characteristics that we use for describing the thing, thus also to its color, hardness, weight, brittleness, flexibility, and so on; whereby it would already become apparent that they are one step more abstract than the thing found by means of them. Far from grasping the experienced phenomenon with the properties of the thing, we rather handle with them abstractions of time-independent being-character for the purpose of recognizing their time-constant basis. Just as little as the duration of existence of two crystals is connected with the difference of their edge angles, so little does the difference between the metallic smoothness of the one and the earthen roughness of the other. But if the possibility of identifying the thing rests on the assumption of time-independent properties, then we are not only entitled but absolutely forced to regard every state of it and thus its motion as time-independent as well, since it turns out that they immediately terminate in a position.

If one wished to avoid this by conceiving motion as an independently existing something, and thus as one and the same at least at two different points in time, one would have stamped it as a thing and thereby deprived oneself of the possibility of regarding it as merely a state of the thing (which, as we shall see, actually happens from the standpoint of the mechanistic view of the world). Yet even at the price of reifying motion the difficulty would not be removed. For if we compare what is found of the motion of a moving object at two different points in time, it is by no means something identical [p. 42] in itself, but on the contrary a difference between two positions. I find in the existing object at time-point B the same redness, the same density, as I found at time-point A, likewise, provided it is at rest, the same position; whereas, if it is in motion, by no means one and the same something called motion, but instead merely a position different from the first.

We must not leave this point without having thought of a serious error which had already crept into the Eleatic formulas, but there was happily compensated for by the interconnection of the arguments with one another, whereas in far too many repetitions of them this coherence is rendered null and void, and has already had to submit several times to the refutation of Eleaticism. So certain is it that the flying arrow has a locally determined position at any arbitrary present point, so certain would it be entirely mistaken to assert that it rests in it. Time is required for a body to continuously change its position in relation to one conceived as at rest, and time is also required for it to continuously remain in its position in relation to one that is in motion. If we remove time, we do not merely render motion impossible, but also rest, since it requires just as much a certain duration during which it takes place. The flying arrow rests no more in the timeless instant than it would be able to exist at all in the timeless instant; but it has at the moment of its passage through it no less unquestionably a locally determined position than it has such a one at the moment when it has landed again on the ground.

There is, it is well known, a means to make the necessity of the concept of the passage of the flying arrow through a position in every indivisible time-point appear in a manner that excludes all doubt. Without a doubt motion finds its conclusion in a certain instant. Now imagine this very one shifted to a point in time of that duration during which the arrow is still flying, or in other words let the moving arrow be seized by a sudden freezing, just as it happens to all motions of men, animals and things in the Sleeping Beauty fairy tale, and immediately it becomes clear that it infallibly held a certain position at the moment of the onset of this, in which it would now, however, remain. One can even visualize the matter by imagining that the arrow flies in complete darkness and is suddenly illuminated by a flash of lightning, [p. 43] so that one would see it hanging in the air as it were (understood, because our faculty of apprehension would no longer be able to follow the slight displacement, which in reality would nevertheless take place even during this duration).

After we have in this way believed to have removed all those doubts which would be based on a misinterpretation of the argument, the same strange contradiction now presses upon us which gave us trouble in the first chapter, where we attempted to prove the timelessness of the object by means of the example of its direct opposite, namely time. We have just considered and stated that motion requires a temporal duration and is necessarily rendered null as soon as one looks away from this. Then, however, it would seem, the denial of motion from the side of one who insists on ignoring its temporal course is like the behavior of one who would deny the existence of a noise, which he does not hear only because he has previously stuffed his ears! We remove the contradiction by the above already tested trick of distinguishing between the reality and the being of motion. By means of the concept which the mere act of apprehension gives us alone, and by means of the concept of the existing object, with which we attempt to grasp the known reality of motion for whatever reasons, we are inevitably forced to acknowledge their inability to be. The mere act of apprehension, aiming at being, gives us instead of the motion, whose reality is presupposed, the timeless position.

Perhaps one might say that the whole dissection of motion was actually superfluous; for whoever believes he has already proved the timelessness of the object in general and thus any being whatsoever need not also specially show that of (conceptually grasped) motion. Nevertheless, one thing is the general idea, another is its application to characteristic special cases. Did it not seem to us that numerous properties of the thing were involved in the existence of the thing in an obvious way: weight, shape, impenetrability, as well above all the locally determined position! Therefore it was necessary to provide a special proof that precisely the same mode of apprehension by means of which we come to the assumption of existing things makes perceptible motion of things and consequently change in general incomprehensible [p. 44]. Change and being exclude one another. If the former therefore applied to appearances, then the whole world of appearances lacks being: in this conclusion the Eleatic train of thought culminates.

With motion the real transience of time becomes visible in the apparent rigidity of space, so that in a certain sense the perception of motion is just as well called a perception of time as a perception of space (a proposition which we will of course have to restrict later). By beginning with it and proceeding from the perceptible to the imperceptible change, the apparent constancy of substantial existence seems to dissolve under our hands, and we gain thereby a deeper insight into the meaning of our concepts of properties of things. Just as the dimensionless point (of time as of space) so too is every conceivable property entirely detached from all change of the world and then also from all reality. If the sheet which I call reddish today appears to me yellowish with equal right after some time, nevertheless the conceptual meaning of the yellowish and of the reddish has meanwhile remained the same independently of time. With the expression that the property of a thing has changed, we express merely improperly the fact of a change, of which we hold the thing itself capable for its own sake by assuming different properties in the course of time. The real, which somehow gave us occasion to attribute "properties" to the thing, can in turn not be described by these properties, if otherwise it, as we do not doubt, belongs to time. Just as little as the points of time, which we must presuppose in order to think the existence of the thing, lie in the reality of the event itself, so too little do the properties of the thing lie in the reality itself of the images; and just as we cut up an absolutely continuous by means of those by setting limits, so too with these an absolutely changing. In that and only in that lies the conceptual and intelligible meaning of redness, that it differs, e.g., from blue; in that and only in that lies the conceptual meaning of color, that it differs, e.g., from sound; in that and only in that lies the conceptual meaning of spatial shape, that it differs, be it from another spatial shape, be it from whatever characteristics of the spatially shaped. Merely and exclusively drawing limits is what the apprehending can do, and for it to be able to do so, it must each time look away from the actually appearing, in [p. 45] another way, of course, when it sets the dimensionless but nevertheless attached to time and space points, and again in another way when the time-independent properties of things of color, hardness, spatial shape, etc. We take the opportunity for an extension of our explanations regarding the relationship of the logical abstract to the logical concrete.

Thing and property of the thing belong inseparably together. Without the logical abstractions of colorfulness, transparency, squareness, as well as further of virtue, goodness, striving, we could think neither things nor (personal) beings; but without the logical concretas of things and beings we could just as little arrive at the formation of those abstractions. Just as the timelessly extended time-point is apprehended only as related to time, the spaceless space-point as related to space, so too are the time-independent characteristics of colorfulness, transparency, squareness apprehended only as properties of time-dependent things; what of course does not exclude making them the object of consideration in and for itself once one has taken cognizance of them. If we without time would be unable to find the point on it, although we come to that only by means of this, so it stands no less firm that we would have no concept of its time-independent properties without the time-related thing, although they are recognizable only by means of things. When we above maintained the claim that the "existential judgment" at the sight of a tree concerned precisely not the appearance of the tree, we deliberately overlooked the obvious objection: even the appearance or "view" of the tree does after all every mentally healthy observer hold for something actually present, which he distinguishes, e.g., precisely from the non-existence of imagined wonder-beings; for now the answer becomes easy for us, whether we think ourselves referring to such features of the tree-appearance to which we think of attaching permanent underpinnings like spatial shape or solidity, or to such as we believe to be based on transient circumstantial conditions, like illumination colors, reflections, or finally on those belonging in the strictest sense to its "view", like perspective shortenings: for actually existing we hold of all this only what can be represented either as property or state of the existing tree or else as relation of its properties to the properties of other existences. Were it otherwise, so one could not in any way comprehend [p. 46] how we would come to identify the tree which we see now from a distance of five hundred meters with the same tree viewed from a distance of twenty meters. Without reflection we strike out in this way from actual being the extraordinary difference of the impression-images, to subject them fundamentally just as to a merely subjective order as any arbitrary dream-image. Yes, this "striking out" has passed over into us so thoroughly "into flesh and blood", that we continually seem to perceive something quite different from what we actually see; of which everyone knows a song to sing who begins with drawing exercises. Is he not, e.g., initially in danger of setting the four angles of the front wall of a house as rectangular instead of as he sees them: the upper left one extremely acute, the upper right one extremely obtuse! This does not prevent him, however, from remaining convinced that "in reality" the boundaries of the wall cut one another at right angles!

Should geometry seem to be called for here, it is so only because the same applies to each of its figures in relation to their appearance. Even the tangible triangle on paper, by means of which some theorem is proved, is a perceptual object that fundamentally does not coincide with the optical impression-contents to which it gives rise. Although, however, the visual images of geometric figures and bodies (such as square, ellipse, octahedron) can deviate considerably from themselves, we extract the intended shape from their appearance just as securely with the act of perception—and even with unfavorable foreshortenings—as we extract the actual tree from its aspects; and we owe our reflection on the actual, often far-reaching difference between the two solely to a special intellectual effort. With a single glance at any arbitrary page of this book, we grasp the straightness of the lines, their parallelism with the side edges of the page, the parallelism of the shadow strokes of all short letters with the side edges of the page, the rectangular shape of the type area, etc.; but in the visual image, the sides converge upwards, the side edges run in gracefully curved curves, and the angles change in manifold ways depending on the position of the book, and so on; how all this comes to light becomes apparent as soon as we try to sketch the book. Our firm conviction of the "objective" reality of all the aforementioned facts thus presupposes the object "book," "page," "type area," etc., already, or: [p. 47] only on the basis of the time-independent thing can Being be distinguished from Non-Being, and only that do we hold to be existing, with which the existing thing either permanently attributes itself to us or appears to temporarily clothe us— Thus it has already been stated that, detached from the logical concreteness of the thing, the logical abstraction of the property cannot possibly exist, or as it is commonly said: only the object of the logically concrete thing-concept has "independent" existence, not the object of the logically abstract property-concept. Nothing is more familiar to scientific logic, and against nothing is more often violated thanks to the unconquerable tendency of our mind to reify logical abstractions. 1 There is no light, color, heat, sound, weight, motion, or rest, but there are purely shining, colored, warm, sounding, heavy, moving, resting things. 1

We return to the Eleatics. The time-independence, the common and necessary characteristic of all thing-properties, fails at the fact of the variability of the thing, as it comes before us in a dramatic form in the shape of perceptible motion, which, viewed from the same standpoint, is irretrievably lost! Possibly even more sharply does the fact show itself from the opposite side. Only things, not properties of things, differ in durability (for it is, as we have heard, rather the thing that is subject to change, whether it be the change of properties and it alone that indicates the change to us!); two motions, however, differ among other things in their speeds: with which the element incompatible with unity of the time is incorporated into the characterization of the property "movability." In that, as we said, lies the intelligible sense of color, that it differs, e.g., from sound. If we now proceed, in that the intelligible sense of motion, that it differs from speed zero (= rest), then it becomes undeniably clear that we have conceived this quality only with reference to a temporal span! To bring the whole extent of that almost sensibly close to oneself, imagine all properties of the thing, so its color, solidity, shape, and whatever might be determinable in time-independent traits, to be seized by continuous change in exactly the same way for the immediate impression as is its position in the state of being in motion, and one immediately notices that then nothing more would remain [p. 48] by which the thing could be recognized, on account of which it itself—would vanish! We grasp the position of the arrow for any arbitrary present point of its being in motion because we refer it to the persisting arrow-thing, and we are again able to do so because its other properties such as solidity, form, shape are not affected at all by the fact of being in motion. But if they were all and completely continuously affected, then for the grasping glance there would indeed have ceased to exist not only the motion of the arrow, but the arrow-thing itself!<sup>4</sup> Now, of course, no perceptible change of all properties is offered to us, comparable to the perceptible continuity of the change of place in motion, and it must lie therein, then, perhaps, in the still unconsidered reasons which have first made possible the assumption of a fixed point of reference. Yet the temporal nature of reality inevitably demands their transience and thereby renders impossible the application of the concept of Being to the world of appearances!

<sup>4</sup> On page 48. — *Kant* remarks in a similar sense: "If cinnabar were now red, now blue, now light, now heavy, if a man were changed now into this, now into that animal shape, if on the longest day the land were now covered with fruits, now with ice and snow, my empirical imagination would not even find occasion to bring heavy cinnabar to mind at the representation of the color red . ."

The arrow argument has received an addition, the sense of which can be described briefly as follows: Just as adding zero to zero always yields only zero and never a magnitude, so billions of positionally different positions of the arrow never yield its motion of flying. No matter how often we might think of repeating the act of grasping in the face of the flying arrow, that would bring us no closer to the discovery of the Being of motion than a single act can. Insofar as each of them divides the path-line of the arrow at the same time at a point-like place, one can also say that no such large number of division points could possibly replace it itself, and would thereby immediately contain the core idea of the three remaining arguments, in particular that which concludes from the never-closable divisibility of every segment the impossibility of measuring it.

To have first proved the impossibility of the Being of motion is an achievement of such magnitude that it suffices to make its performer "immortal," and it is therefore not a matter of diminishing the significance of Zeno if one brings to mind that there were others before him, especially his teacher Parmenides, who had already asserted the more penetrating truth of which the incapacity of motion to be is merely an example, namely the incapacity of happening to be. In the language of that compact straightness which advantageously characterizes the still archaic [p. 49] thinking before the chatty of the Platonizing late period, Parmenides secures Being, just as with a powerful rampart against every mixture with happening<sup>5</sup>:

<sup>5</sup> On page 49. — We give all quotations from the pre-Socratic thinkers according to the excellent translation by *Nestle*.

"Never has it become, so it can also never pass away.

It is whole, unique in kind and without motion and end.

Never was it, nor will it ever be, only present is it,

Uninterrupted unity. . ."

". . . For far into the distance are cast Birth and Passing away ..."

This development of the concept of the Ever-presentness of Being preceded, before Zeno's soberer sharpness of sight provided the proof for it from the Never-presentness of motion. "What moves moves neither at the place where it is, nor there where it is not."

[p. 50]

#### 5. Kapitel — Wahrheit und Irrtum des Eleatismus — Chapter 5 — Truth and Error of Eleatism

We feel ourselves undesirably set aside with the confession that we hold his arguments up to here for unrefuted, because irrefutable; but we advise everyone to re-examine the attempted counter-proof in all main varieties, since it might after all perhaps diminish his trust in the position of the opponents if he must notice that thinkers of rank seek the alleged error of each elsewhere! To name some as possible as striking examples, let one recall, for instance, the epistemological standpoint of Kant, the positivist Dühring, and, to also do justice to the nearest present, the so-called dynamic one of Bergson, whose time-wise mobility one should not overestimate in the remainder.

Kant's "transcendental dialectic" is undoubtedly derived from Eleatism, although he lets this only occasionally become visible. What is one to say, however, if he thinks to have settled the "contradiction of reason," which his "antinomies" also wish to reveal even with regard to the divisibility, although not of space, but rather of the spatially extended appearance, by soothing it through the dozens of times uniformly repeated reference to the allegedly merely subjective nature of their object! Whether we hold space and time for so-called things in themselves or for their subjectively necessary "appearances" or finally for phantoms of a dream, that changes not the least bit in their properties! Red remains red, whether I perceive it or represent it or hallucinate, and the three-dimensional space is what it is, and does not find itself ready to spare me its problems because I might be inclined to doubt its reality! If one holds it to be demonstrable that a volume consists both of ultimate elements and also not of ultimate elements, then there is no possible consideration left to throw out the contradiction! So much for now; the more detailed critique of Kantianism follows later.

[p. 51] Dühring, to whom the great merit is due of first appreciating the significance of the Eleatics among the moderns and having presented it with unsurpassable clarity and sharpness in his "Critical History of Philosophy," denies (incidentally in rather close adherence to Kant) the cogency of their arguments by means of his fundamental critique of the concept of the Infinite, which certainly deserves all praise. Yet the excellent polemic against the assumption of a completed infinity would even then not be suited to shake the Eleatic demonstration, if one were to try to join in that utmost atomism in which the world-conception of "Positivism" culminates. His unflinching consistency in this relation leads this strongest carrier of mechanistic thinking to uphold the following conviction: not only does matter consist of indivisible ultimate and accordingly countable basic units, but even real space and real time itself. The arrow would thereby in reality traverse merely a finite and fundamentally again countable series of positions. Yet, since it is admittedly conceded that the position is something substantively and essentially different from motion, so a closable series of positions yields no more the smallest possible motion than would the uncloseable series. It is superfluous to remark that also the continuity of space cannot be built up from space-different, nor that of time from time-different basic units.

According to Bergson's view finally, Zeno would have exchanged motion with the traversed distance. This latter, of course, can be divided, whereas motion is something absolutely indivisible. In opposition to this it is to be remarked: the emphasis of all Eleatic meditations lies on the incomprehensibility of a continuous transition. But since the incomprehensible now already belongs to the mere line in relation to the point, so the incomprehensible roots no less in the impossibility of composing the line out of points than in that of composing motion out of positions; and it would not have been necessary at all to anchor oneself precisely to motion in order to lead the solely decisive proof that no interpolation approaches the Continuous. Bergson, fettered by the riddle of time, overlooks thereby quite the entirely analogous riddle of space. If we expressed above that in motion the ever-flowing time is embodied in the apparent stiffness of space, so we now add: in the form of the line the element of motion seems now to have even solidified spatially [p. 52]! Far from being the expression of a more or less arbitrary mode of consideration, this sentence expresses the circumstance that to every lineconception a motion-experience lies underlying; for which here for the present only some linguistic turns may testify: the path "goes," "bends," "rises," "descends," "wavers," the spiral line "turns," the vine "twists," the rocky edge "plunges" into the depth, two lines "intersect" or "run" parallel, and so on. In the remainder, one may think about it as one will, so much is undeniably fixed, that even the shortest line participates in the secret of the Continuous with what lies between its limits and is therefore forever withdrawn from the possession by a faculty whose whole and only act is the setting of the limit. If we nevertheless attribute to every process for the sake of calculation an extension, to motion the path-line, to time the extension as such, so it happens first, once, because only it allows us to mark off the points upon it of which we stand in need for orientation; furthermore, however, from a deeper reason, of which we shall speak again at a later place. The appearance, as if the line were thoroughly penetrated by the spirit, arises from its exceedingly sharp measurability; the measurement, however, presupposes a measuring unit, and this is again a line, from which it becomes evident that our measuring thinking remains at an ever-equal distance from the Real which it measures. Far from having covered the Continuous, even if only that of the line, with concepts, it presupposes for it the "knowledge" a system of mutually related points. Just as little does this ever coincide with the real connection which effects that they are mutually referable, so little does the thinkable Being coincide with the temporal continuum of the Real: this is the deepest and unassailable meaning of the Zenonian proof of the impossibility of restoring the flight-motion of the arrow out of a series of graspable positions.

Since, despite all of the foregoing, the objection will in all probability be raised here that such difficulties have by now been definitively overcome by "higher mathematics," we shall not, in passing, leave undiscussed why the invention of the "calculus of the infinite" — a discovery of extraordinary illuminating power for the history of culture — furnishes a new and powerful confirmation of the logical unattainability of the continuous. — Let us represent the first Eleatic argument in the form of the following equation: [p. 53] it becomes evident that the addition rule, while enabling us to continue indefinitely with adding, does not enable us to reach the value 1 for the sum ever, because obviously a difference of half the size of the last summand always remains. Eleatically spoken: Achilles never catches up with the tortoise, nor even the stake planted at any arbitrary distance; logically spoken: the Continuous is no magnitude-series and can therefore be represented by no, even if still so large, number of insertions. — The mathematician now believes to have eliminated the difficulty by the fact that he does not look at the difference as such but rather at the difference-change in the course of the addition or with other words the law of the unlimited magnitudereduction of the increment: the difference, so he is accustomed to express himself, "strives" accordingly or "converges" towards zero. This means, however: he invents for the uncloseable series a closure or a limit (limes), which would be reached in the moment where the difference would vanish.

The differential is consequently a vanishing difference, more generally a vanishing magnitude. (One should not say "infinitely small magnitude," because this favors the thought of something fixed, whereas in truth only by the symbol for the vanishing of a magnitude can the transition to the limit be effected. Indeed a Leibniz himself spoke sharply and precisely of differences which are in the concept to vanish!)

One needs only to take the concept of "vanishing magnitude" at its word, by seriously regarding the epithet as determination of the magnitude, in order to recognize immediately that it harbors two incompatible elements: namely both the still-existence and the already-vanished-existence of a magnitude! As long as we leave the magnitude a value, however small it may be, we are always at the beginning of the path; as soon as we conversely take it for simply not existing at all, we are already at its end. In order to effect the transition and thus to find the formula of the process, we must therefore think of it as a vanishing one, thus forming the contradictory concept of a Something which is yet also a Nothing, or of a Nothing which is yet also a Something. A magnitude "vanishes" not, but it is only marked off. [p. 54] The transition from magnitude to magnitude is a jump, but the happening flows. The arithmetical mastery of the Incomprehensible takes place therefore only by means of the inconcept of the "vanishing magnitude," more precisely with the help of a procedure which — an Eleatism turned upside down — takes away from the unlimited repeatability of the insertion the right to regard the difference as erasable. The Eleatic logic reads: because a distance always remains, however often I divide, so I never reach the goal. The mathematical counter-logic reads: precisely because I can continue indefinitely with the reduction of the distance, it is finally overcome.

The invention of the differential, alongside those of the O and the 00, is one of the most brilliant intellectual achievements of all time. Only those thinkers fundamentally err who, in the transition of thought from "static" to "dynamic" methods, perceive an approximation of the state of consciousness to the event itself. Precisely the opposite is the case! The dynamism of thought, standing at the threshold of the modern age, whose ultimate causes we cannot yet unfold here, rather signifies the final step in the complete thingification of the event. It is only at the moment that the mathematical point becomes the sole ruler, when one possesses the formula that expresses the process for the extensionless point upon it, thus rendering it independent of time!<sup>6</sup>

<sup>6</sup> On page 54. — A more detailed discussion of the basic concepts of the infinitesimal method would lead away from *our* train of thought without enriching it. We are concerned only with the circumstance that the famous limiting value is *logically* inconceivable, notwithstanding that it *computationally* works out; and this is illustrated quite sufficiently by the very elementary example of an interminable series of summands that is nevertheless supposed to yield a sum; for fundamentally it is always the vanishing of a magnitude that shows itself, in a thousand variants, throughout the whole calculus of the infinite. The often-mentioned peculiarity, too, that the so-called infinitely small is always the obverse of an infinitely great, and conversely, emerges clearly in our example: for the increment becomes "infinitely small" only for an "infinitely great" series of summands, and vice versa! Logically regarded, a tangent can never arise out of a secant, however closely we bring its two points of intersection with the curve together; logically, a circle can never arise out of an inscribed or circumscribed polygon, however often we imagine the number of its corners multiplied; logically, a cylinder can never arise out of a prism, even were we to grant it trillions upon trillions of sides, and so on: yet the *computational* passage to the limit works exactly! One can indeed pass computationally from the hyperbola to the parabola, from the parabola to the ellipse, and so on; *not* logically. It was of course inevitable that attempts should be made to eliminate this contradiction; but all such attempts have failed and will fail. Thus *Vaihinger*, for instance, holds that the computational result is logically unobjectionable thanks to the method of "compensating errors." That may hold for the solution of quadratic equations, or , for example, for the problem of dividing a line so that the product of the one part and the square of the other part be a maximum (x². (a − x) = maximum; first solved by Fermat); it certainly does not hold for the infinitesimal calculus, and, so far as we know, is by no means understood in this way by authoritative mathematicians. The ground of the computational correctness lies elsewhere, and deeper. Although it means a digression in relation to our train of thought, it may perhaps not be unwelcome to some reader who has ever been occupied with the logical riddle of the differential quotient if we set forth, at least by way of a note, how it appears from our standpoint. Here one must first be clear that the differential quotient (= the limiting value which the quotient of the increments of two mutually dependent variables approaches as the increment of the independent variable vanishes, or, as the mathematician would put it: the limiting value which the quotient Δy over Δx — where y is a function of x — approaches as Δx converges toward zero) makes it possible to state, with absolute precision, the strictly momentary state of a continuous process whose total course is known by a formula; while integration makes it possible, from a given differential quotient, to determine, with an equally absolute precision, the formula for the total course. Or: by means of the differential quotient, for a computationally expressible continuity, any point of passage whatever is calculated; by means of the integral, for a computationally expressible point of passage, the continuity; whereby the act of spirit referred to the point has computationally mastered the happening. But how has this been achieved? We know of no achievement of acumen (we do not say of profundity) in the whole history of the spirit that surpasses in genius the computational trick by which this is accomplished, and if for no other reason one would have to count its two inventors, Leibniz and Newton, among the greatest powers of understanding of humanity. Let us call to mind what problem they actually solved. — We need not concern ourselves this time with the logical objections that have been raised against arithmetic's use of zero as though it were a numerical magnitude. It is enough that, according to welltried computational rules, the quotient 0/0 signifies an indeterminate value, and so *could* have any value whatever from 0 to ∞. Taking as known the very simple computational operation that leads to the formation of the differential quotient (very simple, once it had been invented!), we need only point out that, from case to case, it determines *definite* values for the quotient in question, values whose "correctness" is not open to the slightest doubt. One notices at once that this logically violates the law of identity. For if 0/0 is an indeterminate value, then to all eternity I cannot tell from it which of the countless values properly belongs to it, of which, in accordance with its indeterminacy, it could have any *whatever*. Or: if 0/0 is valid — indeterminate, does there not also lie in that same 0/0 at the same time a principle of selection that, from the innumerable *possible* values, would in the individual case exclude all but a single one? If the calculation nevertheless yields a definite value, one might at first be tempted to believe that the mathematician knows two kinds of zeros: the ordinary zero, which, divided by itself, yields an indeterminate value, and an unusual zero — one might write it as 0̄ — which, divided by itself, yields in every case quite definite values. But the "unusual zero" would once again violate the law of identity, because the values for the quotient 0̄ /0̄ would, from case to case, always be different! It would thus have signified, each time, a different magnitude and consequently a different object of thought. To make matters worse, our assumption would be false. For even when we compute, say, 5 or 7 or 10 for 0̄ /0̄ , the zeros in the numerator and denominator of the fraction are real and genuine, namely quite ordinary, zeros! One must have thought this through once in this way in order to bring out what an astonishing riddle lies concealed in the computational operation in question. (Quite literally *concealed*; for the mathematician who *computes* with differentials is as little in the habit of noticing the riddle as the non-mathematician, in reckoning with the multiplication table, notices the astonishing riddle concealed in — the One.) We now show how, from our vantage point, the riddle and its solution present themselves, and in doing so we deliberately take refuge in a blunt example drawn from intuition. Let there stand before us on the table two tall glasses of cylindrical shape and equal size, 1 and 2. Since both are empty, we can designate the content of each as zero, or think a zero assigned to each (the atmosphere may be left out of the game). Nothing in the correctness of this designation would be changed by our learning that cylinder 1 had always, until now, been empty, whereas from cylinder 2 half a liter of water had just been drawn off drop by drop. But if we now include in the zero assigned to the second cylinder the thought of the process by which it came about that the cylinder *became* empty from being full, then, for *this* zero, the name "zero" would have acquired a different sense, without the least thing having been changed in the *value* of the zero. Now, precisely such a zero is that zero which, divided by itself, yields definite values. It is a zero that has swallowed its own history of coming-to-be and carries it within itself, or that has *become* what it is by way of continued diminution of magnitude. By accomplishing the unheard-of feat of distinguishing *becoming-zero* from *being* zero — or, to speak in the parable of the glasses, distinguishing the emptiness of the glass that *arose* through the gradual exhausting of its content from emptiness as such — the mathematician achieves, from case to case, a definite and indisputably correct result. Human acumen has never experienced a greater triumph. But logically, the manifest double use of zero is untenable; for it is logically impossible that in one and the same symbol, 0, there should lie both being zero and becoming zero. If, then, it is true that only a contradiction with the demands of logic enables such a computational feat, precisely this computational feat furnishes a new proof of the unattainability of the continuum for thought. Put in a strikingly evident phrase: because the continuum *cannot* be attained logically, an *error of thought* is needed to attain it *computationally*. Historians of mathematics have pointed out — with reference, for instance, to Euclid's infinite series of prime numbers, or to the proof, probably already known to Eudoxos, of the theorem that a three-sided pyramid fills a third of the space of a prism of equal base and height, or to the quadrature of the parabola and the spiral by Archimedes, and the like — that the concept of infinity was known to the ancients, at least in substance. This is certainly true. But it was scarcely their lack of an algebraic symbolic language that prevented them from making far-reaching applications of it. In view of the well-nigh incredible mathematical gift of the Greeks, one would rather have to think that, had they been so *minded*, they would at once have invented an algebra too! Against this, the Eleatic train of thought speaks for the view that the computational exploitation of the concept of infinity foundered on the *logic* of this people. — Here we permit ourselves a remark in advance. Epistemologists who still today maintain the astonishing assertion that the object of thought called continuity is a self-sovereign product of spirit, hence without any sensory basis, seem never to have called to mind that, since the mightiest intellectual achievements of the Greeks, nearly two millennia were needed before one was able to compute the continuous. How would this be explicable at all, if the concept of number stood on the same line as that of the continuous! The Eleatics possessed and made use of the concept of infinity, and proved by its means precisely the unattainability of the continuum. But in thereby denying its actuality, they denied the actuality of the world of the senses: truly a monumental piece of evidence, in the history of the spirit, that continuity lies on the side of the senses (in the sense of the side of lived experience), the countable series of points on the side of spirit! On this occasion let our reference to the paradoxes of Zeno finally be rounded out by recalling that he demonstrates the unthinkability of motion not only from the impossibility of its ever reaching an end, but equally from the impossibility of its ever beginning. The scheme of the proof is as follows. Suppose a moving body has, up to the present moment, traversed the distance a; then it must previously have traversed the distance a/2; but this in turn was traversed only insofar as, again previously, the distance a/4 had been traversed; and since the division in question — like, of course, any other — can be continued *without end*, the assumption of even the smallest displacement would force upon us the assumption of an *infinite* series of distances already traversed. From the *unthinkability* of this it follows that motion cannot begin at all! — Zeno had thus penetratingly recognized: whatever comes to an end somewhere and at some time has also had a beginning somewhere and at some time; in relation to what lies between beginning and ending, beginning and end are two extensionless *points* of time. Laying this down as his foundation, he establishes: the between cannot be thought, because it thereby disintegrates into a series of points, for any two neighboring ones of which the demand for the insertion of new points would repeat itself *to infinity*. From this one perceives three things: the aporia would remain even if motion were left entirely out of the game — the *instrument* of thought fashioned by spirit is the extensionless point — *the* state of affairs which he thereby vainly attempts to overcome by logical means, namely the continuity of the between, therefore cannot possibly have its source in *spirit*, and is accordingly found by it as already given.

Even if the more recent age could produce so-called identity systems, which mix thought and being, where indeed the one is the counterpart of the other, $0, one would hardly have occasion to reproach those early thinkers with having fallen into the same error. Such a passionate tension of the displacing intellect, as that must have been which first unveiled the far-reaching genus-concept of unchanging being, inevitably entails a stance of the spirit, according to which the faculty of comprehension also appears immediately in the light of a power that brings forth the ground of being.

"To think oneself into being and to be: these two are one and the same."

Such words of Parmenides reveal no little of the dialectical intoxication that overtakes him, who, like a breach struck through hard stone by the violence of speculative thought, suddenly sees flash before him the bare ore of a primal fact. Moreover, it even mitigates this [p. 55] boldest throw itself, in that it does not yet make the discoverer into a creative god— whither Christian thought alone strayed—, but merely asserts its identity with the found, and in so doing even harbors the germ of insight in the real identity of their essence. Yet the matter has a sinister secondary meaning.

If we replace the movement that appears merely as an illustrative example in Zeno's line of thought with the more comprehensive state of affairs of occurrence as such, then it would have unrestricted validity, provided only that this were his intention: the object of apprehension is Being, Being as an essentially present thing lacks the element of temporality, and consequently it has its place beyond the actual, which is a continuous occurrence. The demonstrated incapacity of motion for Being would in this way be only the supporting pillar of a knowledge concerning the unreality of Being. Essentially different, however, would be the picture if the guiding aim of the argument were to be sought precisely in the reverse direction — in the demonstration of the incapacity of the actual for Being — as though it were a metaphysical defect in the actual that it fits into no concept of Being whatsoever! Well, that is precisely where it leads in truth! It is not Being that is to be divested of reality, but reality that is to be devalued; and indeed, in accordance with the primordial tendency of Greek spirituality to clothe differences of value in the gradation of the reality of the thing valued, the devaluation takes place in a form whose very audacity of absurdity was bound to secure for it the most significant import. At the end of the road of the Eleatic undertaking stands the absurd conclusion: if occurrence is already not a graspable object, then it also has no reality; for I, the faculty of conceptual thought — so one would have to add — am the sole judge over the claim to reality! Instead of recognizing itself as the determining ground of Being and as essentially akin to it, conceptual thought takes itself for the determining ground of the actual as well, and fancies itself entitled to deny the pull of reality, of which it had to learn that it lies beyond its capacity for comprehension! The veil of dialectic is torn away; we cast a glance into the generative ground of the movement of thought, and perceive with horror that the driving force of its first deeply penetrating and exploratory thrust was hostility to the senses! Motion, although we see it — so Zeno had proven — lacks determination of Being, for it is ungraspable; but Parmenides had already let [p. 56] it be known that everything was "empty sound" that mortals had fixed in their language; and so, a pupil of both, Melissus, continues, therefore "it is clear that we did not see rightly, and that that multiplicity is only a false semblance." The driving force of this earliest onset, however, has remained the predominant one throughout the entire intellectual history of mankind, and has swept that history — seized as it was by this force — far beyond the Eleatic starting-point to so thorough a falsification of the image of reality that no one should hope ever to cure it of its blindness; just as all the voices that over the centuries called for a reversal were regularly bound to fade away unheard. — —

[p. 57]

#### 6. Kapitel — Erscheinung und Gedankending (Phainomenon und Noumenon) — Chapter 6 — Appearance and Thought-Thing (Phainomenon and Noumenon)

Today it is easy for everyone to laugh at that form of denial of reality as immaturity, with which the Eleatics made the relatively still almost harmless beginning. The phenomenon of movement does form the basis of the whole proof, without which it would be mere nonsensical chatter! How can it come to the philosopher, so one might say, simply to deny what he himself presupposed, be it even to demonstrate its inconsistency with the demands of thought! What does it change in the sense-confirmed reality of movement that it occurs to us to call it a deception! And it was certainly such considerations that for a time led to the misapprehension of Eleatism as a world-historical pattern of deceptive sophisms. — But "the devil is never perceived by the little folk, and if they had him by the collar". It would stand very well with such cheap improvements if only those, who could take them very easily at hand, thereby bound the slightest consciousness that they in such a manner snatched the entire world of appearance from the range of apprehension of comprehension and accordingly now, conversely, although not to the level of a "deceptive semblance", well rather to a logocentric construction, lowered that which they undoubtedly call their physical knowledge. Would they perhaps have easily decided themselves to what the occasion lay all the more closely, for instance to turn against a Kant and ask: what does it change in the reality of the spatio-temporal, that it occurs to us to call it a mode of intuition of our understanding? But the nihilism of the Kantian formula leaves, as we shall see, the one of the Eleatics behind!

To deny movement, that today looks almost like a useless joke. But movement and change too had to be denied not once, but dozens of times, and the conviction of the [p. 58] "higher" reality of the non-eventful being had to be fixed in consciousness with a hundred hammer-blows before humanity was ready and willing for the reception of the belief in a "mechanical world"! For this is now the peculiar thing about a mechanistic worldview, that it indeed knows calculable movement and sees the whole world under the figure of an ever raging machine; but only because it simply lost every relation to the real event therein. For it makes out of movement a thing, whose main distinguishing mark, the velocity, is determined by the ratio of a (objective) space-stretch to a (objective) time-stretch. It consequently had to invent strange beings, mechanical forces or then simply called forces, with whose help the movement-thing sets the body-things into movement or sets the moved ones back into rest. But no human being has been able to indicate up to this day how the moving force of a moved movement-carrier begins to communicate itself to other movement-carriers (and just as naturally not, how in view of the body in movement the moving force of the just elapsed time-unit communicates itself to the to-bemoved of the just beginning time-unit). The necessarily passing (transeunt) action of mechanical forces is such an impenetrable riddle that one tried the solution again and again with the help of the postulate, that the bodies themselves are simply nothing but forces or they consisted, more plainly put, entirely and throughly out of pure movability; whereas the indeed extremely sparse logicians of physics still brought to mind each time that without movement-differentiated, but movable existences the intended movement could not be thought at all. We return to this later and content ourselves here with the remark that mechanical movement approaches the again being thing in the form of a being something and accordingly does not enter into the mechanical equation at all as a form of the event, but as a numerically fixable partial quantity of the mechanical force, which is metaphysically indistinguishable from the mass-quantum of the body in movement! To the Eleatic, movement is still a case of application and, if one will, a symbol of the event, and his attack on their possibility of being presupposes the strongest feeling for the event-character of the Real, which appears to him incompatible with the thought-necessary assumption of persistent underpinnings. [p. 59] For if not guided by false intention, his result could also have sounded as follows: insofar as reality is entirely temporal, it is entirely change, whereas the apprehending gaze necessarily leaves nothing else behind but mere exchange at an identically persisting one. Then indeed everyone would have had to see that he could not be refuted with the reference to the fact of mechanical movement.

Yet the great discovery of the deepest of all oppositions — that of Phainomena and Noumena — which, following the path-breaking initiative of the Eleatics, finds its first completion in Plato, enters the stage of thought from the very outset with the hidden intention of annihilating the former and absorbing it, as it were, into the latter. For this very reason, even among the Greeks, that most extreme skepticism took hold of it quite soon, finding its classically apt expression in the brilliant formulation of Gorgias: "Being is something invisible that does not succeed in appearing; appearance is something weak that does not succeed in being." And what else does the Platonic formula mean but what was already familiar to the Eleatics: that in relation to the realm of Ideas, the world of appearances is at bottom merely a world of semblance! For while Plato effortlessly relocates all other predicaments to the "supracelestial place," he must forgo an archetype for the motion of things — consequently for change as such — consequently for the reality of events themselves, which in this way sinks to the level of the counter-image of deficient cognition ("opinion," doxa)!<sup>7</sup> With this, however, the theme was established that the development of "civilized" humanity would henceforth vary and carry forward into the indefinite: the theme of the disempowerment of the phenomenal by the noumenal, of the actual by the conceptual, of temporally flowing events by atemporal being. When, for example, the English empiricist can dispense with the Platonic dual world, it is because he has fully reified the phenomenal and, in place of images themselves, recognizes only the objective properties of things; and when Kant in turn explicitly denies them, it is for the oppositely equivalent reason that, by virtue of his erroneous doctrine of the "apriority" of space and time, he draws the whole world into the comprehending mind. "All that is transient is but a simile" — however beautifully this sounds and however much that is genuinely mysterious may resonate in the soul [p. 60] of the listener, it must nevertheless be said: if the transient is to be called a "simile" at all, then the simile-free imperishable is most certainly the multiplication table! Without further unrolling the clairvoyant symbolism of Faust II, we may nonetheless recall that Faust, after a life of pleasure aimlessly stormed through without lasting gain, experiences immediately before his end the "highest moment" in the consciousness of the worthiness of labor — as a capitalist entrepreneur; though — and here the poet's visionary gaze plunges into abysses — only in imagination, to the sound of the spades with which his grave is being dug! —

<sup>7</sup> On page 59. — However little an Aristotle, say, was able to overcome the dilemma, he had nonetheless recognized quite clearly the sorest point in Plato's philosophy, and never tires of reproaching him for being unable to derive motion, and for thus having to capitulate before the manifoldness of the world of the senses. Here are a few passages from his "Metaphysics" (after the translation by Bender): "But the question that most of all forces itself upon us is what the Idea really contributes to the eternal among sensible things, or to that which comes to be and that which passes away. For neither motion nor any change whatever can be derived from the Idea." "In the Phaedo it is said that the Ideas are the cause both of being and of becoming. But now, even granting that the Ideas exist, the individual things that participate in them still do not come to be, unless there is something present that gives motion. ." "For no account at all is given there of the cause that constitutes the principle of motion." "As for motion, again, the question is whether its principle lies in the great and the small. If this is so, the Ideas must be in motion; if it is not so, whence then does motion come? Then all consideration of nature is abolished."

[p. 61]

### Dritter Abschnitt — Die Zwiespältigkeit der Person — Third Part — The Duality of the Person

#### 7. Kapitel — Die Person als Geistesträger — Chapter 7 — The Person as Bearer of Spirit

We have deliberately employed, up to this point, the participial form of the verbal predicate to designate that which underlies the activity of apprehension, calling it simply "the apprehending"; for we were concerned not to create, by means of a premature presupposition, the appearance that the choice of name was left to personal preference. It is now clear that the avoidance of a substrate concept<sup>8</sup> in linguistic expression does not preserve us from the substrate concept itself. Just as we cannot think a motion without thinking something that is moved, so too are we unable to think any action without simultaneously assuming an agent. But should anyone harbor reservations against designating the ever-one point of origin of the apprehending acts with the sole word appropriate to it, "spirit," his doubt would in any case strike not the matter itself but only the verbal semblance of the matter, if we expressly add that by this is meant nothing other than the capacity for the production of those acts. Meanwhile, even linguistic reservations would seem to us to lack justification. For if we leave undecided for the moment whether there are acts other than merely apprehending ones, we find ourselves in clear agreement with a universally prevailing usage when we reckon judging, apprehending, and conceiving among the activities of spirit. From this standpoint it is of course entirely indifferent whether one prefers to say "faculty of judgment" [p. 62] or "understanding" or "reason." Even were spirit not the same as the faculty of judgment, the understanding, or reason, it would still always be through its presence in us that we possess a faculty of judgment — and that alone is what matters for our reflections.

<sup>8</sup> On page 61. — The excellent Germanization of "substrate" as "Unterlagsbegriff" [underlying concept] derives from Palágyi!

Even though the discovery of the essential properties of what is judged preceded that of spirit as the bearer of the act of judging by approximately three hundred years — as could hardly have been otherwise in a mode of thinking initially directed outward — it was nonetheless prepared by that latter inquiry, and fell at last as ripe fruit from the tree of a research that, occupied with the character of the product, found that of the producer in the end without seeking it. Already the one-god of Xenophanes displayed all the features of the faculty of judgment, albeit still mythically embodied:

"One god is greatest among gods and among men,

Not comparable to mortals in form, nor in thought.

All eye, all ear, and all thought is his being.

He remains forever in the same place and without motion, And it does not befit him to move now here, now there."

Heraclitus, the only one among all the Presocratics to be directed in an entirely opposite sense, whose incomparably profound discoveries concerning the nature of the real will yet occupy us, did not escape the fate of adulterating his doctrine through the assumption of a logos dwelling within it; we have already spoken of the Parmenidean identification of being with thinking; Anaxagoras made the mover of the world already that Nous, still conceived in material terms; Plato found the topos noetos and asomatos for the realm of the "Ideas"; and Aristotle finally opened the doctrine of transcendental spirit.

We have therefore to establish: there exists an extra-spatiotemporal being, spirit (logos, pneuma, nous), by virtue of which every being capable of judgment arrives at one and the same concept of unity, number, and measure, and is compelled to contemplate the temporally real from the standpoint of a system of relations of countable points. The strict objectivity or universal validity of truth is in the first instance the expression of the uniformity of the faculty of judgment in all beings that have the impulse and the capacity to form judgments at all. But the effective working of extra-temporal spirit into a temporal sphere of life demands their mutual connectedness, and this [p. 63] can be comprehended in no other way than as the presence of one and the same spirit in all moments of apprehension capable of the life-bearer. Accordingly, while the thing — indeed the object of thought in general — with respect to the entire world of appearances is merely laid into it by the act of apprehension, yet in that region of the world, let us say, from which the act springs, the time-abiding capacity for it must genuinely reside. Just as the ceaseless streaming of images is in no way compatible with subsistence and duration, we are nonetheless unable in any way to avoid lending subsistence and duration to that something in ourselves that was able to devise the concept of subsistence and the concept of duration! We call it the I or Self, and its bearer no longer merely the life-bearer, but the personal life-bearer.

Without yet unrolling the exceedingly difficult question concerning the ground of possibility of what is in truth an impossible state of affairs, we supplement at once the long chain of thought that compelled us to assume it with the immediate proof thereof. If someone were to insist on conceding acts of apprehension together with the capacity therefor, while yet denying the real existence of spirit in the judging-capable human being, the first thing to be urged against him would be that in every moment of judgment he can ascertain the said capacity as belonging to the I. He must concede, after all, that it is precisely he who judges concerning acts of apprehension! Now the subject of the sentence "I judge that..." unquestionably means something thing-like in its existence no less than does the subject of the factual-judging sentence "the oak grows." Let our denier of the I's existence not dispute this at all, but let him reply: how can one derive from the reification of the feeling of I a proof for the truth of belief in an I that persistently subsists in reality, when not even the sense-impression is supposed to be capable of validating belief in really existing things? We pass over the fact that this most common inversion sets aside, as though entirely non-existent, all that was already established concerning the origin of the concept of the thing, and merely suggest for consideration that in the judgment "I judge that..." the bearer of the judgment makes the content of a prior judgment the object of the judgment declared in the main clause, which content the subordinate clause reports. If now the I of the judgment-relating act were not one and the same something as the I of the prior act of apprehension, the judgment bearing upon it could not have occurred at all! I could impossibly relate what is judged, [p. 64] apprehended, meant, to myself, the one meaning — if it were another who establishes this relation, and yet another who had judged, meant, apprehended. There is therefore one (and moreover only one single) state of affairs whose mere concept (after the manner of the ontological proofs of God) indeed includes its existence — namely, the (apprehensioncapable) I; and the Cartesian cogito ergo sum would be right insofar as it sought to proclaim: judging, in order that it may really obtain, demands the existence of that something capable thereof, which is called I or Self.

If we confine ourselves, in the contemplation of the personal I, to the fact of its I-hood, we understand at once, on the one hand, why with regard to this the I repeats itself in all persons, and on the other, in what sense it is not at all affected by the personal course of life. The thought "I am" already contains the thought "I was" and "I will be," because "I am" merely unfolds in the sentence my consciousness of existence, which for its part is unavoidably consciousness of the duration of existence. As something that simply and purely is, every person resembles every other person without restriction. Nor will it escape us that the living ground of occasion for the development of the concept of the thing must be sought in the feeling of existence of the spirit-bearing life-bearer. When lifeless things are also called "objects" in the foreign-language usage, and personally living ones "subjects," one has already unintentionally demonstrated through the very words the existential character of both, and thereby at least mediately the dependence of the concept of object upon the real enduringness of the bearer of factual apprehension. Indeed, only to a being in which there really exists a something that remains identical with itself alongside time does temporal reality present itself as though it too were a structure of basic units persisting alongside time — and since this necessarily occurs already as a consequence of the act of perception, not the slightest change is effected in this by even the most thorough knowledge of the metaphysical impossibility thereof. For the one who exists, the real character of passing-away is indeed exchanged for the alternation of properties or states in what is "properly" and most fundamentally existing!

To the by no means idle question of what it is that leads us to think a plurality of I's, only this much need be remarked for the present, without further grounding: that this occurs in any case under a constraint just as immediate as that which aids us in our belief in things. [p. 65] We apprehend as existing outside ourselves not merely things in general, but also living things in particular, and among these again those that appear to us as the "seat" or site of the I. Living objects are called "organisms," that by which they live a "nature," but those additionally endowed with spirit are called "persons." Yet regardless of the path by which we arrived at such certainty, it inevitably includes the assumption that the personal I, inasmuch as it already participates in extra-temporal spirit, is moreover also a temporal reality; for without this, as goes without saying, the plurality of I's would indeed remain an unsolvable riddle! In doing so, however, we encounter — as it were from within — the very same contradiction that accompanied our previous investigation into the essence of being at every step, like a mocking echo!

[p. 66]

#### 8. Kapitel — Die Person als Lebensträger — Chapter 8 — The Person as Bearer of Life

What actually prompted us to re-examine the Eleatic problem? The refutation of the common prejudice that it is the world of appearances itself — including its media of time and space — that we are capable of apprehending directly. If, on the contrary, it is true that only relational points are apprehensible, then all the more urgently does the question arise: how can a subsisting point be related at all to a flowing occurrence? Or, in other words, whence do we derive knowledge of a reality that we hold to be unapprehensible? Let us recall the state of affairs once more by way of the Eleatic problem. Perceptible motion, the Eleatics had proven, is incapable of being; consequently, they concluded, it possesses absolutely no reality, but is merely a "false semblance." Yet how do we come to have such altogether certain knowledge of any such "semblance"? How is it possible that we believe ourselves to perceive motion, if the apprehending act — which is operative in every perception — is in and of itself never able to seize upon it? We do after all see motion, and only because we see it have we been compelled to frame the conceptual determination of the continuity of change of place. We thus see the continuity of space, and likewise the continuity of spatial processes, and we possess in them, inseparably from them, the continuity of time as well. What kind of power is it in us, by virtue of which we know the continuous, if under no circumstances can it be the spirit?

When one considers that the external world ceaselessly presents us with transformations — the motion of bodies, the drift of clouds, the flowing of waters, the swelling and fading of sounds, the gradual brightening and gradual darkening of the atmosphere — and that each time our senses are, as it were, the messengers that bring us word of it, one understands why the discovery of the metaphysical opposition of the Phainomena [p. 67] and Noumena had to go hand in hand with the erroneous attempt at explanation according to which "sensibility" serves the understanding as an auxiliary faculty. But before one were to assent to it even tentatively, one should note that the significance of what the Greek counted as sensibility is still fundamentally different from the significance of what is today called sensibility — little as he was able, or in accordance with the intent of his inquiry could be, to protect the concept by unambiguous delimitation from the process of deterioration to which it subsequently succumbed. For us, the content of "sensibility" is exhausted in an "immediately given" from which the understanding draws the stimulus for the development of its representations of being; for the Greek, in accordance with his more profound sensory life, it was and remained above all a reality of substrateless occurrence. We believe we attain the most certain knowledge precisely through the most comprehensive exploration of the sensible — and in truth for the reason that we long since succeeded in replacing it with the factual without yet becoming aware of the loss of "phenomenality"; the Greek had to turn away from the sensory world in order to arrive at the knowable world, because he saw not things but images, not existences but instability, change, occurrence! The evaluative division of the world into a "higher" and a "lower" sphere was originally based not at all on the merely thought distinction of the logically abstract from the logically concrete, but on the actually subsisting distinction of being from becoming, of the identically persisting from the ceaselessly fluctuating, of the always-present "essence" from the temporal life-bearer; and the aisthesis of the Platonic psyche means far less a perceiving than the source of the instinctive entanglement in the spatiotemporal mutability of appearances. The "soul," inseparable from images — though falsely conceived as an offshoot of "the ever-being God" — is, according to the content of the role that both Plato and Aristotle assign to it, the life-principle. After this historical prefatory reminder, we discuss our question dogmatically.

If instead of the Phainomena in general we take as our focus their most universal property of time and space, the question takes on the extremely simple form of how it comes about that we continually perceive the continuous, although we are capable of conceiving only the punctual. — It would be for the moment without decisive importance what name one might prefer for the [p. 68] mediating power, and we attach as yet no weight to the demand that the name we have chosen appear compelling as soon as it is uttered — which naturally occurs only in the course of a consecutively developed line of reasoning. Presupposing, however, that one has understood that the act of judgment apprehends being, and feels compelled to agree that spirit is in any case a capacity of judging reflection, then it is of altogether decisive importance to protect that function whose counterpart is occurrence from any admixture of an act-like doing, and to withdraw from its "organ" even the least addition of "spirituality." The sought-for X must be just as irreducibly different in essence from spirit as occurrence is irreducibly different in essence from being. For anyone who entertained even the possibility of a mediating concept, we would have attempted entirely in vain to make ourselves understood.

The answer reads: we become aware of the continuous by experiencing it. Just as outside ourselves there is "in reality" nothing but occurrences, which only we are compelled, on account of the activity of the spirit dwelling within us, to regard as though they were semblances and shadow-plays concealing a pointedly singular being always identical with itself — so it is now our participation in occurrence which, as we ceaselessly experience by virtue of it, compels spirit to an unlimited multiplication of the points of being, and already leaves its primal act, the act of perception, related not so much to being as such as rather always to particularized being that — independently of it — occupies a place in the spatiotemporal exteriority of reality. The personal I is the bearer both of spirit and of life, two powers whose relation to one another we now determine provisionally, drawing on the relation of being to reality, in the following way:

Spirit and object are the halves of being; life and image the poles of reality —

The Spirit "is"; life passes away —
