The Spirit judges; life experiences —

Judgment is an act, experience a pathos —

The Spirit grasps Being; life experiences the happening — Being (pure) is extra-spatial and extra-temporal, and so is the Spirit;

the happening is spatial and temporal, and so is life —

Being is in principle thinkable, but never immediately experienceable; the [p. 69] occurrence is in principle experienceable, but never immediately conceivable — The act of judgment requires experiencing life as the support upon which it rests; life does not require spirit in order to experience — Spirit, as dwelling within life, signifies a force directed against it; life, insofar as it became the bearer of spirit, resists it with an instinct of self-defense — The essence of the "historical" process of humanity (also called "progress") is the victoriously advancing struggle of spirit against life, with the (admittedly only logically foreseeable) end of the destruction of the latter. — These formulas, which require far-reaching interpretation, are intended only to give the concepts relief and to provide a guiding thread for later expositions.

[p. 70]

#### 9. Kapitel — Die Gegensätzlichkeit von Seele und Geist — Chapter 9 — The Opposition of Soul and Spirit

*[Page 70, the opening of the chapter, is missing from the scan;* *the text resumes mid-sentence on p. 71.]*

[p. 71] … of being and of actuality, in order nonetheless to shine a light far ahead along the path that lies before us, by deriving a few principal characteristics which make plain the fateful tension existing between them.

If it has been said that genuine poetry is always to a certain degree “romantic,” what was meant, at any rate, was that in order to deserve its name it must somehow be an expression of the soul. But it becomes an expression of the soul, among other ways, by giving voice, like myth, to a happening, thereby bearing witness to the happening-character of the experiencing soul itself. Insofar as we are experiencers, and thus always also bearers of soul, what is it, after all, that we experience? Parting and reunion, going and coming, coming-to-be and dying, day and night, awakening and falling asleep again, the change of the seasons, youth and age — not to count the thousands of events which, like unexpected gusts of wind, alter, blissfully or crushingly, the rhythm of the never-resting beat of the waves. Solely by virtue of its capacity for lived experience is this soul, whatever else it may be, a self-transformation alien to all persistence, or, put as pointedly as possible: the soul is the transience of the body. “The man,” says Plutarch, “dies when he becomes an old man; the youth dies in the man, the boy in the youth, the child in the boy. Yesterday’s self has died in today’s, and today’s dies in tomorrow’s.” As souls inescapably interwoven into an utterly fleeting actuality, we nevertheless stand, as spirits, literally outside it, incapable of fusing with it for even the briefest moment! No moment of experience in our life can ever repeat itself in us or in any other being; but the sense of any judgement whatever that we have passed is thought over again by any number of persons as always the selfsame; from which it shines forth that in the moment of being thought, and through being thought, it was torn away from the actuality of self-transformation. And so all “philosophy,” all “science,” indeed everything supposedly or actually apprehended, stands before us in an unmixable rigidity, as something that in the course of centuries or millennia may vanish from the memory of mankind in order, as it were, to make room for new “systems,” but that never grows and withers and could therefore never renew itself, as genuine poetry really does in every succeeding generation! We had already established something similar above. But that [p. 72] the personal bearer of life is for this reason traversed by a rift that nothing can paste over is shown us at once by a somewhat sharper look at the essential difference between the two “faculties,” of which the one enables us to experience and the other to apprehend, insofar as they must unavoidably be thought of as joined to each other within us.

For if the capacity for lived experience is a side of actuality itself, then we can indeed experience without apprehending the least thing, but by no means apprehend anything without the aid of experience; and if, now, the disposition to experience — which, with regard to profoundly meaningful waves of experience, we called the soul — consists inescapably in this, that something can happen to it, the soul, befall it, encounter it, then in relation to what befalls the soul the act of apprehension bears the character of an assertion, and the power of being that makes apprehension possible bears that of a compulsion to self-assertion. As a being of soul the person is a driven or a carried-away or a self-surrendering being; as a being of spirit it is a willing being, and so always a being that wants to hold fast to something, which unconditionally resists the surge of the soul and is compelled to judge every surrender to it now as weakness and lack of the power of resistance, now as distractibility, instability, seducibility. We shall discuss this much more precisely later, and for the present insert only two remarks, of which one is meant to reinforce what has just been set out, while the other, placed first, offers for it a thought-provoking testimony of language.

Every judgement “asserts” something, even the self-refuting sceptical one that no assertion has a claim to truth; and conversely: every “assertion” gives voice to a judgement already passed. According to the evidence of linguistics, the original sense of the word *behaupten* [to assert] was “to defend something victoriously against an attack,” and it passed over into the later sense of “to maintain an opinion” through the mediation of the thought that every opinion, insofar as it is stated, must be fortified against something that endangers it. If we add the phrase *eine Behauptung aufstellen* [to put forward an assertion] and the word *Feststellung* [establishing, literally “making fast”], we have already built the bridge to the same division of sense in the Latin verb *ponere*, which means both “to set down” in the sensory sense and, in the so-called figurative sense, “to assert.” Likewise the Greek *thesis* means first a position in space, then the laying down of a law (*latio legum*), and in [p. 73] philosophical language, as everyone knows, once again an assertion. Language thus reveals to us unmistakably not only that with every judgement a positing of being takes place, but also that there is no positing of being that would not have to be “asserted” and “held fast” against something threatening its continuance. With this we come to our second remark.

That against which every content of judgement is “established” and “asserted” is, practically, mostly only a counterjudgement, but metaphysically it is the element, contrary to being, of an ever-flowing actuality. Goethe’s rhyme of wisdom:

You must not confuse me with contradiction! / As soon as one speaks, one has begun to err.

— says, unfolded, something like: Spare me from giving my words that determinacy of content which they would have to take on in a dispute with counter-assertions; for thereby they become false, measured against actuality, which, strictly speaking, does not tolerate the form of assertion at all! If, now, the spirit capable of judgement has become actual in us through its attachment to an experiencing soul, then it too is a self-asserting actuality, and the proposition that the person, insofar as it is a being of spirit, stands under the compulsion to self-assertion contains not the slightest admixture of “hypothesis.” It follows necessarily from the nature of spirit as being and from its becoming actual in the personal I through its coupling (however this may be conceived) with the soul.

As already indicated, the I, insofar as it is a tendency to assertion, can also simply be called “the will,” of which only one inseparable side would in turn be illuminated by the formula of the “will to power”; but it may not be equated without qualification with so-called egoism, and still less with the animal drives of vital provision, which, because they prove themselves on this planet in struggle, people have most mistakenly sought to understand in terms of “self-preservation.” That compulsion to self-assertion of which we speak forms the basis of judging conduct as such — which, let it be noted only in passing for now, is always also an acting attitude — and articulates itself, for the special domains of action, into as many mainsprings or “interests,” which thus come into opposition both to the drives of the body and to the exuberances of the soul. Dependent on spirit and directed toward assertion, yet at the same time supra-personal, is the intellectually legislative [p. 74] will to knowledge, whose proper domain is logic; the will to order that regulates the objects of intuition (aesthetics); the practically legislative will to morality (ethics); but dependent on spirit and directed toward assertion are, besides, the personal egoisms as well, with their exceedingly numerous subspecies such as self-interest, acquisitiveness, greed for gain, craving for recognition, ambition, lust for domination, the need to have an effect, to exert influence, wishes for popularity, together with their forms of reaction against disturbances of their spheres of activity, such as the desire for retaliation, malice, cruelty, ill will, envy, etc.; dependent on spirit and directed toward assertion is every kind of self-mastery and self-formation (restraint, moderation, reserve, firmness, self-denial, self-overcoming, the drive to self-perfection, etc.); and once again directed toward assertion are all the varieties of the craving for self-esteem. Every special condition of self-assertion can fall out with every other, and in this is shown the atomizing effect of spirit on the scope of life assigned to it (as it showed itself in the image of the world through its fragmentation into a heap of individual things!). To what extent they nonetheless all belong together essentially, as dependent on spirit, is taught us at once by the consideration that any one of the “interests” listed here would run the risk of being estranged from its goal by the operation either of genuine drives or else of genuine passions and enthusiasms, which, while they hold sway, disempower the will and deliver its bearer, as it were, to a breaking wave of experience. If, therefore, the character of the soul is a being-surrendered, now drive-like, now enthusiastic, then the character of spirit appears over against it in the light of a recalcitrance that becomes actual in every stirring of the soul as intentional inhibition! Accordingly a reconciliation between spirit and soul is impossible, and what may at times strike us as such in outstanding personalities (as, say, in Goethe) always proves, on closer investigation, to be a mere compromise, an artificial “style,” never acquired without loss of immediacy of soul. As long as there is still a remnant of soul in the personality (and with its complete disappearance it would no longer be a “personality”!), it is something essentially divided and therefore, in contrast to all other individual beings, already endangered by nature with that derangement which, usually called “mental disturbance” [*Geistesstörung*, literally “disturbance of spirit”], is rather a disturbance of the soul, and indeed of such a nature that it is [p. 75] accompanied by some disturbances of consciousness (of apprehension, of thinking, of activity, etc.).

In the last place, finally, we cast a glance at that side of the division in question which was bound to force itself most readily upon untrained observation, but which has commonly been misinterpreted. Just as the thinkable world, as a structure of things (together with their properties and states), lies outside the world of happening, so, as a structure of related points, it lies outside the world of appearance, and for the one reason as for the other, outside the actuality of images. Since we become aware of these, among other ways, through sense-experiences, the chasm opens here once again: not, indeed, as has been supposed, between the objects of intuition — which are, after all, likewise already apprehended — and the objects of logically abstract concepts, but really between what is sensuously apprehended and the sensuous impression. For the content of the sensuous impression, even if its objective occasioning ground were a group of resting things perceived only for a moment, is, like the experience of the impression itself, a process, and moreover the expression of a “mood” that is again temporal, whether this may cling to it or stem from me, the one experiencing. This mood need not be noticed by the bearer of the impression; yet it always belongs to the operative elements of every possible impression, even the briefest, in that it establishes between the content of the impression and the soul of the one receiving it a pull, often remaining hidden from him, now of sympathy, now of antipathy. It is not by chance that the word *Sinnlichkeit* [sensuousness] in everyday speech hardly or not at all means the properties of the perceptual apparatus, as for instance “keenness of the senses” in fact does, but chiefly an openness of soul to that content of mood which the process of sensuous experience conveys, continually and inexhaustibly. For as long as mankind has philosophized, it has therefore been unable to overlook the conflict prevailing between this sensuousness and spiritual self-assertion, according to which spirit must forbid itself sensuousness if it does not wish to risk losing the “standpoint” indispensable to it, and with it the “independence” through which alone it is able to act. “In sense-experience the image of the world captivates, entices, seduces, carries away, overpowers; in judgement the apprehending spirit takes possession of it, objectifies it and locks it up in the ‘safe’ of ‘experience’!”<sup>9</sup> Sense-experience, [p. 76] the more it grows at once in strength and in depth, resembles all the more an irresistible whirlwind which suddenly and with primal violence tears down all the walls and dams that decades of labor of “level-headed” thinking have erected out of systematically mortared concepts and resolutions! In the divided double being of the personal I, a self-preserving sense of self thus resists the loosening and unbounding pull of elemental Eros.

<sup>9</sup> On page 75. — *From*: *Klages*, Mensch und Erde, 4th ed., Jena 1933, p. 87.

## Zweites Buch — Geist und Leben — Second Book — Spirit and Life

[p. 79]

### Erster Abschnitt — Der logistische Irrtum — First Part — The Logistic Error

#### 10. Kapitel — Akt und Leistung des Aktes — Chapter 10 — Act and Achievement of the Act

Since we henceforth cannot proceed further without coming into conflict at every step with the received scholastic opinions even of the past, but quite especially of the present, we will take the conflict itself as our point of departure, in order, by way of dismantling what bars us from our place, to build up our own doctrine. — Now it is admittedly, in the last analysis, a single basic error — namely the interchange of life with spirit — to which all the varieties of false system-building go back; but this error comes to light now more veiled, now more openly, and bears, in keeping with the twofold nature of every conceptual world, now an "idealist," now a "sensualist" stamp. If therefore we refute these two kinds of disposition one after another, and interpose between them a separate critique of the Kantian theory of knowledge, our chief attack is nevertheless directed at idealism — first because it is the trunk from which all the other isms merely branch off, second because the stronger minds have always still stood by it, and finally in view of the extravagances of its very latest embellishers. — It is not real difference of essence but merely supposed difference amid real sameness of essence that grounds the most irreconcilable enmities; hence it has long been good form among idealists and sensualists to inflict on one another every conceivable indignity. Ever since the former reserved logic for themselves alone, the strangest contempt for logic has flourished among the latter under the name of "empiricism"; and ever since the latter claim for themselves a natural-scientific science of the soul, the former mock at "psychologistics."

[p. 80] Since from this distorted word there has already come nearly a byword, it seems time to recall that the unwelcome psychologistics after all means only a partial manifestation of that very logistic in which, once life has been utterly abandoned, the idealist self-deification of the understanding is consummated. By refuting the logistic conclusions in which it necessarily culminates, we shall have proven the untenability of idealism as a whole. To this end we show in advance how our own preliminary findings would present themselves in the light of logistic.

This is roughly what the logistician would object to us: whoever speaks of "actuality," "happening," "continuity," "experience," and "life" has, by that very act, objectified or thought each of them. Actuality, happening, etc. are no different as contents of thought or concepts than "being," "sameness," "spirit," "act of judgement," "mathematical point," and so on; and since it is indeed the case that it is the judicial act which first brings forth the concept, we would have to do, in thinking, thoroughly and solely with products of thinking, and it would be absurd to speak of the unthinkability of that which one has, in the very act of doing so, thought, posited, conceived. — Objections of this kind almost invite the play of a Socratic dialogue, yet they have a more serious background, as will come to light in what follows.

First we would have to submit for consideration: it is one thing to think of something, and again another thing to apprehend it in thinking; the former merely "means," the latter "conceives" its object. We can form the concepts of the unknowable, the inconceivable, the non-objective; but no one will wish to maintain that the inconceivable is thereby conceived. There has probably never yet been an investigator occupied with this who has not admitted that every impression can never be exhausted by concepts. But is it not then a dispute over words, when one declares this very impression to be a product of spirit simply because one cannot after all avoid making it the bearer-word of a sentence in order to assert its inexhaustibility of it! — Panlogism is the worst of all the delusions of thinking, for it is the most incurable. Whoever has once sworn allegiance to it never again works his way out of the entanglement of taking something to be already conceived simply because he can mean it. If he has the consistency of a Hegel, he must hold the history of thought to be concluded and all riddles to be solved.

[p. 81] But quite apart from the fact that no logistician can ever be convinced, he might easily believe he could parry our attack by replying to us somewhat as follows: such distinctions as "thinking of something" and "conceiving something" are for him not in question at all; what object one has in mind in thinking, and how one feels oneself related to it, is wholly without significance; our example of the unknowable and the inconceivable does not shake the decisive fact that one nonetheless possesses of them too the concept that is in each case identical with itself, which alone first makes any assertion possible; and that alone is what matters. Had we not the concept of the inconceivable, we would not have been able to found anything with it either, and were the non-objective not a possible object of thought, we could not expatiate on it in any respect. But if, by our own admission, the concept is a product of the activity of spirit, then it is not to be seen how we intend to free the concept of inconceivability from this; indeed such concepts are so in an eminent way, because with them spirit sets itself new tasks; our standpoint, moreover, remains burdened with the otherwise quite ordinary self-contradiction of holding something thought to be unthought. — Driven in this way into a corner, we must, willingly or not, resolve to seize the error at its root, and in doing so we fortunately take the shortest path for pursuing our own train of thought further.

What do we actually understand by a "concept," what by "conceiving," what by the fully "conceived"? Quite different answers must be given to this. However certain it is that a concept is always something meaning (signifying) an object, it is just as certain that we have not thereby already conceived the meant object merely because we are able to mean it conceptually. Through being-conceived, the fully conceived is taken possession of by spirit, appropriated, "penetrated," whereas that which cannot be spiritually penetrated likewise constitutes an object of thought, and indeed a quite privileged object at that. If we clothe our meaning in the form of a judgement, according to which a conceptual B is predicated of an inconceivable X, then with the said "meaning" we have nonetheless, beyond all question, "conceived" something of that X. If I say, for instance, that happening is inconceivable, then I thereby "conceived" of happening even a very important, if one likes, "property" of it — its inaccessibility to the faculty of conceiving!

[p. 82] The deliberately antinomic pointedness of our sentences is meant to lead over to the new question, whether perhaps every concept necessarily means not only something conceived but also something unconceived.

As regards the conceived, the answer readily offers itself from our earlier considerations: that every concept indeed "conceives" the meant object without restriction, insofar as it posits in it a single one — and only this one! For however unsurveyably manifold a state of affairs the object of an assertion may be — the universe, for instance — as object of assertion it is nonetheless just as singular a one as, say, the mathematically determined place within the universe. Only insofar as our concepts of unboundedness, state, government, migration of peoples, tone-poem, etc. each time mean one thing, and this alone, can we, by means of them, as often as we please, mean again the meant as the selfsame. The actual divisibility of many objects of thought never corresponds to a divisibility of our concepts of them. One can divide an army into three armies; but what is meant by the concept of army is indivisibly the same in the three small armies as in the larger army from which they arose through its division. — In stretching Eleaticism further dialectically, the Megarians, notwithstanding their world-famous trifling with "eristic" questions and catch-syllogisms, earned not inconsiderable merit for the investigation of concepts, to which also belongs the proof that of quite numerous concepts the range of magnitude of certain determining elements cannot be fixed. But if accordingly we are indeed unable to state with which grain the heap begins, with the loss of which hair the bald head begins, or at what reduction of its complement of men the remainder of an army would have ceased to be called an army, or how the swarm is bounded against the pack, the pack against the herd, this changes nothing whatever in the transitionless difference between the concepts heap and grain, hairiness and baldness, army and troop, swarm and pack, pack and herd (provided these are not synonyms among themselves), and consequently nothing either in the unchangeable unity and sameness of what they mean. Our concepts remain quite untouched by the difficulties of their application to actual states of affairs, which of course does not exclude our dropping some concept as unusable in order to adopt another in its place. The Megarians, then, knew exactly about the [p. 83] indivisibility, or as they called it, the simplicity of concepts, and inferred from it, leaning on the Eleatic metaphysics of being, the unreality of the world of appearance spread out in boundless multiplicity. Against this, the same knowledge may help us to the essentially more modest insight that in the object of thought there is, through the concept of it, conceived that constitution with respect to which indivisibility belongs to it. Since now strictly indivisible is only the mathematical point, we choose it for the time being as the sign for what is conceived in the object of thought.

If the verb "to conceive" probably precedes, in virtually all languages, the noun "concept," this expresses the circumstance that mankind had always already been aware that it conceives something or has conceived something, before it noticed that this happens by means of concepts. Without yet entering upon the difficult investigation of the origin of concepts, we point out at once, in connection with what has already been remarked, that concepts have no existence whatsoever except in the consciousness of a conceiving I. The turn of phrase that the concept means the object was used only as a substitute for the proper one: that a conceiving I means the object by means of the concept. If we take away the conceiving I, we have thereby taken away all concepts together, but by no means thereby even a single experience! For it is not out of the impression of redness that there occurs in the recipient of the impression the judgement "there is something red"; but rather insofar as the impression prompts the I capable of judgement within it to the accomplishment of a judgement. In that it establishes, by means of the concept of redness, a relation between itself and the occasion of judgement, it clothes this occasion with the unity-character of the object of thought and thereby separates it unmistakably from every other object of thought. Since, according to our earlier findings, the I must be thought of as similar to the thing-point, we symbolize conceiving by the following schema, into which, until further notice, "self" or "subject" may also be inserted instead of "I-point," "thing" or "object" instead of "It-point," and "concept of the thing" instead of the arrowed direction of relation.

[p. 84] We established in the first section, concerning the time-point as well as the thing-point, that it is apprehended as related to the spatio-temporal continuity; we have now established, concerning every object of thought, that its being-conceived consists in its relatedness to a conceiving I and thus rests on the separateness of both, of the conceived and the conceiving; for which a point-distinct medium is likewise evidently needed. If we let the medium that separates the mutually related points also be conceived, along with the related points themselves, then everything would collapse into one and the same point, and with the being-outside-one-another the very ground that makes apprehension possible would vanish along with it. — One readily recognizes here the actual formative impetus of the Fichte-Hegelian triad: thesis, antithesis, and synthesis; and one now notices at once why these three would no longer have the slightest sense the moment we merely posited what is conceived by them without at the same time presupposing the continuous stream of an inconceivable actuality, in relation to which the conceived and conceivable finds the possibility of its otherwise-constituted existence only in that it stands out from that actuality as different in essence. We now turn our attention to what is thereby meant extra-conceptually.

Every thing has, at every moment, its place in space and "exists" by virtue of a shorter or longer duration in time; every property of a thing, because it participates in the thing, likewise has, even if only mediately, a necessary relation to space and time. Be it then thing or property or process, every conceived It-point is differently related to the actuality of happening and has the character not so much of a point pure and simple as rather of a point of relation. But the same holds also of the I, of which we indeed know that it is even really connected with that particular side of all happening which we call living life. It-point and I-point are mutually relatable only insofar as each of them is the relating midpoint of a happening — the It-point of so-called outer happening, the I-point of an inner happening. We leave it still undecided whether one can mean something wholly without concepts; but we need waste no further word on the fact that only by virtue of the co-relatedness of a meant object is the to-be-apprehended a conceived thing!

From this we gather: the outcome of apprehension goes far beyond the act of apprehension. Whether the act, too, does nothing other than [p. 85] forge the "rational" relation between It-point and I-point, relatability as such nonetheless requires the co-relatedness of every point to the "irrational" actuality; or: the achievement of the act allows us to recognize two sides that are indeed by no means separable, but different in essence: the positing of the point thereby conceived, and the division of the actuality co-related by it. It-point and I-point are (in possibility) mutually complementary objects of thought, insofar as they are positions relatable to one another; but they also form, besides, two unconceived and inconceivable meaning-contents, insofar as they are necessarily at the same time the relating midpoints of two sections of actuality. Accordingly the following figure symbolizes the state of affairs of apprehension, in which the broken line again signifies the relation between It-point and I-point, the dotted line the being-co-related of a section of actuality, and the solid line finally the sector of actuality itself.

The error of the panlogist rests, to use his own favorite word, on the "equivocation" of relation in general with apprehending relation. He has quite correctly noticed that only the act of spirit forges relations; but he has overlooked that there are two kinds of relations that are established through apprehension: the conceived relation from point to point, and the unconceived relation from point to happening. In that he throws together the wider concept of relating with the narrower one of apprehending, or the achieved outcome of the act with the act itself, he arrives at holding not only the apprehended to be something related, but also everything related to be apprehended, and at dividing up actuality wholly into objects of thought. In other words, he leaves nothing over at all but the apprehended sameness, without noticing that this would make absolutely everything identical, both the objects among themselves and each of them with the apprehending subject; whereby apprehension itself would be annihilated. His view amounts in the end to regarding finding as a bringing-forth and actuality as a mere noumenon, in which then the utmost intensification of the Eleatic error comes to light, [p. 86] and, as will emerge, at the same time its deepest ground. If the Eleatic exchanged actuality for being, the logistician goes considerably further by confusing actuality with truth! In him is fulfilled the Parmenidean impetus toward that most arrogant of all false doctrines, according to which actuality is one and the same as its thinkability. But there are no "propositions in themselves," as Bolzano would have it, and just as little "truths in themselves," as his modern outbidders would have it; rather there is anything of the kind only in the thinking consciousness of living individual beings, which for their part are neither truths nor propositions, but transient manifestations of the inconceivable happening. Before, however, we use the findings so far, after these already anticipatory remarks, for a sharper refutation of the objections that became our signposts, we turn once more back to the essence of conceiving.

[p. 87]

#### 11. Kapitel — Begreifendes und hinweisendes Denken — Chapter 11 — Conceiving and Indicating Thinking

The co-related actuality of happening, in our side view (Fig. 2) the straight line extending from W to W, would in front view be a circle that one had struck about its bisecting point with half of it as radius. The older logic was indeed fond of using such circles, in order to bring the extensional relations of concepts, according to their manifold relations, graphically to expression by their position to one another. If we take, say, the case that the conceptual circles intersect one another (e.g., that of air and that of transparency), this would look as follows in side view:

Only from this do we gather in what sense the co-related actually shares in the being-outside-one-another of It-point and I-point, and that an important property of being-related has hitherto been overlooked by us. The relating line is, namely, unmistakably not so much a line pure and simple as rather a directed line, and it has its direction without doubt through its relation to at least one further direction! For just as the findability of a line encloses within itself the co-findability of its direction, and this in turn its difference of direction from another line, so too the always direction-determined relation of a fact is established only in relation to a relation of fact differing in direction.

[p. 88] Because it overlooked this, epistemological research hitherto exhausted itself for centuries, and quite especially since Kant, in fruitless variations on the theme: subject and object — consciousness and being — thinking and being — consciousness and something — idea and actuality — I and not-I; and however the formulas, multipliable nearly without limit, may run, by which one and the same bipartition, in ever new guise, was held and offered up as the final solution of the problem of a world to be found. In that our schema conceives the all-too-famous pair of brothers (or really pair of enemies!) by analogy with two points, it at once comes to light that the relation of the objective point to the apprehending point requires at least a second objective point besides, and the bipartition subject-object (or self and thing) is thereby moved, from the outset, into the light of a high-level abstraction from the basic experience — repeated as often as one likes — in which, as a matter of fact, each time the I-relatedness of a particular thing occurs.

Everyone sees it: what is experienceable is not the thing at all, but a thing among — other things! But even the single thing is already, through its being-apprehended, distinguished from its properties, states, as well as from the processes that play themselves out on it or by means of it, and finally from its location in space and the duration of its existence in time. And we likewise think each of the following concepts as being every time somehow opposed to a complementary concept, in such a way indeed that none of them could be thought at all without the direction-determinacy thereby fixed: singularity — connectedness, unity — plurality, property — process, state — process, space — time, and further: quantity — quality, magnitude — degree, sameness — otherness, equality — difference, whole — part, inner — outer, cause — effect, and so forth. — Language has, as always, preserved the unambiguous knowledge of this. One "directs" not only one's thoughts toward something, one's attention, endeavors, feelings, one speaks not only quite unselfconsciously of "direction of drive," "direction of impulse," "direction of will," but one is even accustomed to call every discriminating peculiarity of belief, holding-for-true, conviction, approval, rejection, action, a "direction": direction of taste, direction of disposition, political direction, direction of faith, progressive direction, and so on. — The old circle-schematism of concept-representation lets it be recognized not in the [p. 89] slightest degree in what sense the geometrical locus of absolutely all concepts is the conceiving consciousness. Concerned exclusively with the extensional relations of concepts, and involuntarily always in danger of reifying concepts, it overlooks entirely the basic fact that concepts are nothing else than fixed direction-determinacies of apprehension, and could therefore not even raise the question, let alone solve it, of what belongs to life and what to spirit in the spiritual direction, what is merely meant by means of it, what is conceived. Only with the answer to this shall we have uncovered all that is for the time being necessary concerning the sense of conceiving and of the conceived.

If the spiritual act is altogether unable to posit the point except as a position of order, then with the positing a spiritual direction is unfailingly fixed, and if with the point a position is necessarily conceived, then to the conceived belongs also the particular location which the spiritual gaze is compelled to take up in order to find the position. We must accordingly, in the conceived of the meant, keep apart its character of unity and the position of order of the unity in question within series that otherwise cross one another in quite manifold ways. But just as a position does not change its nature as a position because it stands at the crossing-point of several series, and in particular does not gain, through participation in however many series, the least increase in similarity to the connected medium in relation to which its possibility of existing consists always only in dividing it at an extensionless boundary — so too, with the being-conceived of the direction of relation, it is not the co-related section of actuality that is thereby conceived, but only the fact of its difference from sections of other configuration. If the point-like character of objects of thought led us to the primal opposition of boundary and continuity, then their position-like character leads us to the primal opposition of conditionedness and unconditionedness, or, as one is misleadingly accustomed to formulate it, of the "relative" and the "absolute." Were the concept of direction transferable to actuality as such, there would likewise be an unconditioned actuality of direction, just as there is an unconditioned actuality of images. However that may stand, it remains fixed that a possible object of thought is formed only by the relation of two directions, with respect to which the actuality conditioning it is indeed lived and meant, but not conceived.

We would not have the concept of redness were there not also, for instance, the [p. 90] concept of blueness, and with it we conceive the difference of red, among other things, from blue; but we thereby mean, and are able, in consequence of the direction-determinacy of our being-related, to mean only the content of the impression of red — in the face of which everyone must admit that it could not even be touched, let alone apprehended, by statements of its being different from, say, hundreds of thousands of other colors! One can readily make it conceivable to a person born blind that red is different from blue; one can instruct him in the laws of optics; one can, finally, give him an idea of the difference in character of the two colors by comparing it, say, to the difference between a high tone and a low tone, or to the relation, in an instrument, between the tones generally of a bright timbre and those of a dark one; but with all this one cannot bring a single color to intuition for him. If we now mean, as no one will doubt, along with the concept of redness also the intuitive content of redness, then we clearly mean along with it something unconceived and never-to-be-conceived, which is co-thought with the conceived only insofar as the direction of relation toward red forms an (imaginary) angle with the direction of relation toward, say, blue. The "gaze" of our spirit actually goes in a different direction when we think redness than when we think blueness; but what is conceived (apprehended, spiritually taken possession of) thanks to such "gazing" is merely the relation of two directions to one another, and by no means, say, the phantasm of redness and the phantasm of blueness, which — comparable neither to a point nor to a direction — is received by an experiencing soul and can therefore vanish entirely in the process of thinking, once the direction of spiritual gazing thereby occasioned has consolidated itself.

In the process of thinking we must sharply distinguish the act of fixating from the process — which sometimes comes to its aid, more often disturbs it — of making-present, usually called "representing." For the most part no making-present of the objects of thought takes place at all in thinking, and it is a question that must be raised again and again from case to case, and is sometimes extremely difficult to decide, what exactly, and how much of it, is made present. Thinking consists in the continual transition, or more accurately leap, from one direction of gaze to another, and is quite properly a constant change of bearing on the part of spirit, which can also be confirmed by the science of expression and appearance.

[p. 91] One can convince oneself of this, moreover, easily by means of particles and conjunctions, these parts of speech that are not merely meaningful but wholly indispensable. We mean something different by "although" than by "in spite of that," something quite different by "if," something different again by "until" than by "before." Whereas to "and" there corresponds a gliding advance of spirit, what accompanies, according to the testimony of self-reflection, the perceiving of adverbs like "but," "however," "nevertheless" is comparable to a swing-about and a powerful pendulum-swing, and nonetheless it causes us the greatest difficulty to determine whether anything at all is made present thereby, and what!

With this we have now fully clarified what moved us to designate the conceived in the object of thought by the extensionless point. What matters is not the point itself but the direction to be fixed by means of it, and the indivisibility that first recommended the point to us is the indivisibility not of the atom but of the direction. It is true we cannot avoid positing a point at a certain distance behind the meant experiential content, because otherwise the co-relatedness of the experienced could not even be made schematically sensible; but this is a makeshift for the sake of provisionally avoiding the question, only to be raised later, of how that co-relatedness comes about at all. The direction itself, being lengthless, points into the "infinite," thereby also figuratively confirming the extra-temporality of the object of thought. But in that we isolate, out of the metaphor of the "ray," as really present, that side which it has in common with the metaphor of "gazing," namely direction, we thereby make it evident that for every conceivable judgement the origin must be demonstrable in the intuitive content of an experiencing, or more precisely in the medium — inseparable from any experiential content — of spatiality.

Instead of the strangely sounding formula that every concept means something conceived as well as something inconceivable, we now have the following two propositions. All conceiving consists in the sharply exact becoming-aware of the (imaginary) angle of two directions of spirit's gazing, and does not consist in the apprehending of the experiential contents that cross them. Further: however certain it is that nothing else is ever conceived but a direction (namely in relation to a second one), just as certain is it that the direction can at the same time signify an indication of the occasion of its origin: the experiential content that can never be conceived. We use this insight for the time being to weaken the objections of the logicist.

[p. 92] If he objected to us that even the non-objective is content of a concept and hence a product of thinking, we may reply to him, in a far deeper sense, that no object of thought whatever is found without the co-related foreground of an experiential content that, though meant with its help, can never be conceived! Even sameness could not be spoken of at all, were there not co-related an undivided continuity, in view of which self-identifying first acquires a sense. We do not deny that "actuality," "happening," "lived experience," "continuity," "inconceivability" are concepts and consequently marks of recognition for objects of thought; but we now show wherein their difference from such concepts as that of unity, number, sameness, point, thing, etc. lies.

If the relation to the object includes a being-co-related to the non-objective, then we can make every concept the bearer of our judgements with a double intent: on the one hand for the sake of unfolding the conceived, in that we set concept in relation to concept, object of thought to object of thought; on the other for the sake of indicating the inconceivable, from which we had to abstract for the sake of conceiving. We distinguish, then, in every concept its function of conceiving from its function of indicating. Since, however, we chose — and had to choose — the word direction in order precisely to clarify the sense of conceiving, and since in "direction" an indication already seems to lie, at least when, as here, a direction of gazing or something analogous to it is envisaged, let it once more, but by a somewhat coarser example, be made clear in what respect the function of indicating is essentially different from that of conceiving. With the indicative phrase "this table here" I distinguish the meant from the meant of the indicative phrase "that table there," and have thereby, without restriction, conceived and adequately expressed in language that two different tables are in question. On the other hand, in the meaning-content of the said turns of phrase there occurs not the least bit of the sensory images that would present themselves to me if I pointed alternately with my finger at the physically present tables, and thus nothing of that state of affairs without which the conceptual indication would lack its experienced ground of occasion. If, then, one understands by the indicative function of concepts the thought difference of the object of thought meant in each case from other objects of thought, this would be [p. 93] only, in a different light, the function of conceiving itself; but if one understands by it the necessarily-to-be-presupposed ground of occasion of conceptual distinguishing, then it is essentially different from the function of conceiving and has the office of linking the object of thought with a never-to-be-conceived actuality. It is then clear that we can put all concepts to a double use: sometimes for the ordering of objects of thought among one another, sometimes for the elucidation of their dependencies on the experienced ground of occasion of objectification; whereby then two fundamentally widely diverging directions of all thinking and research would be opened, of which we shall treat more closely still in this section. But the most cursory reflection on the meaning-content of names picked out at random already reveals, further, that in concepts now the conceiving, now the indicating note predominates.

Let one call to mind the sense of the following words: equality, difference, sameness, unity, plurality, majority, minority, number, point, line, thing, weight, possibility, impossibility, probability, certainty; and one will admit that one gains, by feeling, the impression that what is meant by them is each time something thoroughly conceived, penetrated by spirit as if with X-rays, completely "definable." This, however, is by no means so; rather these concepts too, however direction-exact and needle-sharp they may be honed, have behind them a layer of darkly surging inapprehensibilities; only this would first disclose itself to thought-work directed toward it, whereas it forces itself unbidden upon reflection at the mere sight of the meaning of the following words (which, moreover, one should understand in their proper and not in their so-called figurative sense): night, spring, youth, cold, darkness, glow, roaring, wonder, chance, mystery, actuality, happening, lived experience, infinity. Even the least schooled person, provided only he has ever tried his hand at a conceptual definition, feels straightaway that here the difficulty of such definitions might well be essentially greater than in the previous cases, and that what is meant by names of this kind might harbor altogether more of the indeterminable than of the determinable. It is no accident that the names of the first series play the greatest role in the linguistic usage of mathematics, mechanics, and logic, those of the second, by contrast, in the linguistic usage of poetry. The former serve chiefly the conceiving and ordering, the latter the constrained and indicating, kind of thinking, [p. 94] the former relate to the thinking spirit chiefly the interchangeably "fixed" object of thought, the latter use the objective predominantly for the co-relating of non-objective actualities; the former, to put it in a phrase that will only later be fully clarified, are meaning-poor concept-words, the latter concept-weak meaning-words. In this connection one should not overlook that in both cases we have chosen logically abstract concepts.

Since today, despite all the Goethe-cult, it has unfortunately become the custom for the author to underline twice and thrice whatever he holds to be important and valuable, and since the reader as a result sometimes no longer appreciates what is important unless it has not been underlined, we do not shrink from the immodesty of remarking that we attach to the distinction of a conceiving from an indicating side of thinking the significance of a logical discovery — certainly not exactly a world-shaking discovery, but one that nevertheless has consequences of considerable reach. — First and foremost, it puts an end, for once, to the millennia-old dispute over the possibility and the value of truth. Whereas the logisticians, as is well known, believe they can save the value of truth only by the extravagance of holding that it is spirit that spins the whole world out of itself, the avowed as well as the unavowed sensualists indulge in the complementary extravagance that all judgements are merely relatively true, or indeed only expediently — preferably one also says "economically" — devised "fictions," and that the progress of knowledge consists in replacing such fictions with still more expedient ones. We need explain here all the less in what respect our distinction disposes of both errors, since we shall have to return to it repeatedly; and only this one remark may be allowed to anticipate: all objects of thought are indeed fictions, insofar as one believes to have conceived actuality in them, and no object of thought needs to be a fiction, if one distinguishes what is actually conceived in it from that to which it can only, as to something inconceivable, point. But such concepts as stand in contradiction with the experienceable grounds of occasion of conceiving are not so much fictions as rather useless non-concepts.

Further, however, it seems to us that our finding first makes possible the investigation of concepts that has been under way since Plato, [p. 95] whose extraordinarily intricate apparatus stands in no proportion to the meagerness, hither-to, of its results. For we now find ourselves each time confronted with two easily distinguishable main questions, without knowledge of which one could never be safeguarded against consequential confusions. It is one thing to investigate the sense of the concept "this" in view of the concept "that," and again another thing to investigate the co-related experiential occasion which both concepts presuppose and without which their distinction would be impossible. If I mean "this" and "not that," I have compared two directions of spiritual gazing and conceived each in relation to the other without any "as if," and let it be said once more: in this and this alone does conceiving as such consist! But if I turn to the two concepts with a view to the experienced thing that has occasioned them, then I find myself related to the here and now, including the presence of objects of perception, and recognize readily that in the here and now, just as in the determinate object of perception, there lies an actuality that no conceivable concept would be able to encompass and pass on. Faced with it, the achievement of judgement consists in pointing to it, by means of fixed directions, as to something essentially unattainable for the faculty of judgement. From this, however, there results the decisive task of exploring the vital conditions to which the here and the now, etc., owe their arising, or more precisely, of distinguishing these conditions, by means once more of indicating acts, ever further from other experiential conditions, e.g., of the there and formerly and hereafter. We note at once, too, that for this purpose we must reverse the direction of gaze, because what has occasioned the forming of the concept of it always lies on this side of the object of thought. In relation to the merely "directing" function of conceiving thinking, the indicating function of (in the narrower sense) reflective thinking bears the character of a peculiar retrospectiveness, which might more precisely be termed "centripetality."

Finally, a brief justification of the names we have preferred. "Begreifen" [to conceive], coming from "umgreifen" [to grasp round], means the same as "erfassen" [to apprehend] and has its living wellspring in the grasping of a body with the hand. Now it is true that the angle formed by two directions cannot be handled, and it can therefore not have been the inner "gazing" that recommended, in numerous languages, the name "to apprehend" or "to conceive" for the share of spirit in the achievement of thinking. We shall come to know the true [p. 96] reasons step by step, and here recall only that the extratemporality of the object of thought, with respect to time, led to the concept of duration and finally of being, but that only something abiding, and not the thoroughly fleeting, can be grasped, seized, and held. Direction, or better the angle, shares with the graspable body — firmness, in relation, of course, of both to the changeable! — The grasping gesture is common to men and animals, the indicating gesture to man alone. We do not ask here yet for what reasons; but we recall that indication originally referred to such appearances as were not attainable by the grasping hand. The indicating gesture would never have arisen without man's vital connection with countless states of affairs which he either could not grasp, such as the stars or the fleeing deer or the attention-catching event on the far bank of the river, or which he shrank from grasping, such as the cave bear or the flame; and the favorite attempt to "derive" indicating from grasping fundamentally misses the mark. Today, it is true, now that we have been masters of indication for millennia, the teacher at the blackboard can, if he likes, touch with the pointing rod or finger the arithmetic problem he wishes to explain; originally, by contrast, indication was directed only at what could not be touched; wherefore the sense of indication must not be sought in the indicated goal, but solely in the — for the animal fundamentally incomprehensible — statement of a direction. From indicating there is, in the science of essence, no transition to touching and grasping; it is, however, capable of a higher development with respect to the degrees of precision of direction-taking, in which is grounded the invention, for instance, of sighting apparatus, those indispensable aids of exact measurement. Quite similarly, in higher thinking the mere gazing of spirit intensifies into sharply exact sighting. But whereas what is sighted with the bodily eye can very often also be reached and grasped, what is sighted with the eye of spirit can never be apprehended and "conceived," because there is no analogue, in spiritual sighting, to bodily apprehension. We call "conceived," in the object of thought, the imaginary angle of the spiritual "gaze" with the gaze upon another object of thought, because concerning it nothing further is in the least questionable; and we call unconceived, in the indicating direction, that which has compelled this direction to be taken.

[p. 97] With this it is now, incidentally, finally clarified in what sense the apprehended position of a time thereby made into an object of thought is to be related to the unapprehendable actual time (and likewise with regard to space). It is the conceiving function of thinking that permits us to apprehend objective time and, for example, to distinguish it most sharply from objective space; and it is the indicating function of thinking that permits us, by means of the same concept, to mean that without which the act of apprehension could not have taken place: the content of the experiencing of unapprehendable actual time as well as of unapprehendable actual space.

[p. 98]

#### 12. Kapitel — Vergegenständlichung und Entfremdung — Chapter 12 — Objectification and Estrangement

We have hitherto understood by the It-point always a now independent, now dependent object of the outer world, or at least a feature predicable of things among others — in short, in the narrowest sense, a thing. Now, however, we know that into the focal point of conceiving there can also move the conceiving I, and finally the activity of conceiving and its product. I can reflect on the thing (the alien-I included), on the I that reflects, and finally on the process of reflecting. The objectification of the thinking I could most simply be made sensible by placing it once more, namely in the place of the It-point.

With this a twofold thing would be represented: the boundedness of the relating power to the conceiving I, and its difference from the conceived I. For whoever apprehends his I at this moment is in any case not thereby thinking that which is thinking within him at the same moment! If, with utterances such as "I think myself" or "I think my I," reflection distinguishes a thought I from a thinking I, it follows the constraint of actuality in fundamentally the very same way as in the separation of the I from the thing in statements such as "I think of the moon" or "I see the tree." Psychologists have accordingly repeatedly given expression to the view that the conceived I relates to the conceiving I as a past relates to a present now, and is thus the I that has elapsed, even if only by a quarter of a second. So much, then, as our schema

[p. 99] Objectification and Estrangement 99 may agree with this, there is nonetheless no clue for answering the question how the I itself could actually get into the (related) place of the object without thereby forfeiting its nature as the relating power.

The German word "Gegenstand" [object], formerly even "Gegenwurf," carried over from the Latin "objectum," has again and again prompted philosophers to determine the object as that which "stands over against" or "stands opposed to" the thinking spirit; against which there is nothing whatever to object. Because, however, it was overlooked that a "vis- à-vis" as well as an "opposite" would lose all sense without the being-outside-one-another of the points standing opposed to each other, more recent psychologists in particular have believed they could now also psychologically support the age-old ideologism of thinking with the assertion that the achievement of the spiritual act consists precisely in this, that it sets something otherwise merely present in the soul, or say in consciousness, out of the soul and opposite to it, and thereby, as no one will fail to recognize, quite properly creates actuality itself. But if spirit is not even capable of conceiving, of the being-outside-one-another, so much as its generic property of continuity, then we shall have to deny it entirely the capacity for such an achievement. If we put the state of affairs into the equation: spirit + continuous medium = confrontation of two points of relation, and strike out on the left the continuous medium, then absolutely nothing at all remains on the other side, because everything collapses into one and the same point, which, being positionless, would be undiscoverable. If, on the other hand, we strike out spirit, then indeed the points of relation fall away on the right, but the condition of confrontation remains, because the actuality of the beingoutside-one-another would be unaffected, the same whether or not one marks positions on it. If, then, it is a lived actuality with respect to which the marking of positions can occur only on the part of spirit, then it must belong to the lived experience of actuality, and consequently to every experience of which the experiencing of actuality forms one side, that in it the experiencing and an experienced stand apart polarly. The duality of self and thing ("subject" and "object") is grounded in the polarity of experiencing life to appearing happening. Were there not, in the actuality of happening, a polarity between appearance and the being-experienced of appearance, spirit would find no counterpart at which its act of fixing could aim.<sup>10</sup> Spirit does not have the capacity to create a counterpart, [p. 100] but rather the capacity to find, in its own way, something that meets it, in that it wrests it from the totality of the stream of actuality, and thereby, admittedly, also from its connection with the experiencing soul. Happening, conversely, lacks the (conceptual) capacity to find, because it can divide and fix nothing; but only in it do experiencing life and the confronting-it of appearing actuality stand apart polarly. — We wish to corroborate this with a few examples and to take into consideration the most important consequences of it.

<sup>10</sup> On page 99. — The German word "Gegenstand" [object] is somewhat more instructive still than is commonly supposed. For while the first component, "Gegen" (= facing, opposite to), by no means signifies an opposite of spirit but the counter-pole of experience, the second component, "stand," really signifies the achieved result of the act, whose whole capacity consists precisely in positing a place and thereby "fixing" what was previously changing.

If I find myself below the level of spirit, that is, in the state of mere experiencing, then I stand in polar connection with something experienced that bears, in relation to the life-process, the character of foreignness, and in many cases that of the outer world; but by no means in polar connection with my experiencing itself. We see colors, lines, shapes, hear noises, sounds, tones, smell scents, taste the salty, the sweet, the bitter, the sour, touch the hard, the soft, the rough, the smooth, the dry, the wet, the warm, the cold, and so forth; but we do not see our seeing, do not hear our hearing, do not smell our smelling, do not taste our tasting, do not touch our touching. We therefore never experience the experiencing, but rather a counterpart foreign to experiencing, and it is by virtue of its foreignness, and by virtue of that alone, that we experience the actuality of the experienced, the actuality of color, of sound, of warmth. — But one must at once give oneself an account of the fact that actuality cannot be the same thing as objectivity, and that the determination of the objectivity of something actual, or in short of its "existence," is not to be understood from the lived experience of actuality alone.

For if a bearer of life experiences something actual, then he is, thanks to his experiential process, connected with the experienced and consequently also with the actuality of the experienced; but if a personal bearer of life (= personal I) thinks of something actually existing, he thereby knows himself to be separated from the object of his thinking; as, for instance, he is able to think of existences that existed millions of years ago (say, the saurians) or of the solar eclipse that will not take place for another seven months. His act of objectifying is thus different from his lived experience of actuality. This emerges still more palpably from the circumstance that objectification, considered purely in itself, would be incapable of separating objects foreign to consciousness (transcendent to consciousness) from objects proper to consciousness (immanent to consciousness); for [p. 101] object of thought is indeed not only the house, the table, the tree, but objects of thought are also mathematics, virtue, manifoldness, etc. The conceived always has, in the same way, the constitution of an object of thought, whether we think things and their properties, states, processes, or spirits and souls together with their properties, or finally concepts and conceiving itself. How, then, could we possibly begin, on the basis of objectification alone, to distinguish objects foreign to consciousness from objects proper to consciousness?!

Meanwhile we already know that objectification could not be carried out at all without estrangement. If we think of the saurians, and indeed in the firm conviction that they really once existed, we must not, to be sure, have experienced or perceived a saurian; but we must indeed have experienced the space of appearance together with the manifold things within it, including the temporal sequence of events in it, because otherwise we would lack, for the object of thought named saurian, the setting of its possible existence; and the space of appearance, again with everything to which it serves as a dwelling place, stands over against us in consequence of the estranging function of experiencing. But then the finding of one's own I likewise presupposes the process of estrangement.

If we call the apprehension of the thing the first step of reflection, then the second step of reflection, namely the apprehension of the I, has the character of a reflection-back, which the following schema would express:

If I am able to think "here stands a tree," I can also reflect, "I (see, believe, mean, think) judge that here a tree stands." In doing so I have turned back from the thought thing to that which already lay within the thinking of the thing, only without yet having "come to consciousness"; and I am able to do this because, through the thinking of the thing, the fetter was torn asunder that had previously bound my experiencing to the appearance, so that henceforth any arbitrary something can occupy the place of the object — hence also the I separated, in the act of thinking, from the thing. Of the state of affairs in question there tells, with unsurpassable sharpness, [p. 102] the foreign word "reflection." A thinking is reflected (or reflecting) insofar as it relates back to the thinking subject, and the capacity for thinking as such reveals itself in the capacity for back-relating thinking, in such a way indeed that, given the total absence of the capacity for self-reflection, one may no longer speak of a thinking state of life at all. Nonetheless a predominantly thing-related (also perhaps called "naive") and a predominantly self-related, or in the narrower sense "reflecting," thinking must be kept apart. The former would at the same time be, in the first instance, turned outward; the latter forms one side of thinking turned inward.

Our more recent schema, it is true, no longer clearly shows that the conceived I too occupies the place of the object; but it purchased for itself thereby the greater advantage of making the course of the apprehension of the I sensible. We gather from it, first, that self-apprehension can take place only by the roundabout way of the apprehension of the thing, and is thus just as dependent on the actuality of appearance as the apprehension of the thing is. But we gather from it something else besides. If, in consequence of polar connection with an actuality to be experienced, every experience is conditioned in its direction, then, in consequence of the breaking of that connection, thinking spirit has the capacity to dispose freely over the direction it wishes to take. It is able, for its part, to determine whither it will turn, whether from one thing to another thing, or from the thing back to the thinking I; whereby it first comes to our consciousness that every being-related has a direction! One is accustomed to keep chiefly in view the controllability of the directions of reflection with regard to the selection of the goals of the will, as well as the direction of so-called attention, and we shall have to develop, in the fourth book, that indeed only in the act of will is the key to the essence of the I to be found. But again it must be said: thinking too is inner steering, and the steering power is called the thinking I. It is true that we may again, indeed must, distinguish a strongly steered from a relatively unsteered process of thinking, as well as, further, the innate preconditions of both. But were we to think the steering power wholly abolished, we would thereby have robbed the bearer of life of the very capacity to think.

Here an occasion offers itself to explain why we set colors and seeing, sounds and hearing, scents and smelling polarly [p. 103] opposite each other. Everyone sees the unfulfillability of the conceptual demand that the following combinations of words would impose on us: unseeable colors, unhearable sounds, unsmellable scents, and would have thereby in any case admitted that not only can there be no seeing without colors, no hearing without sounds, no smelling without scents, but that there are likewise no colors without seeability, no sounds without hearability, no scents without smellability. Appearance and experienceability thus belong inseparably together. Besides this, however, they are essentially dissimilar in kind, which is at bottom already proved by the fact that we see colors but do not see seeing. Since, however, the life-process is confused not merely with the spiritual act but just as readily with bodily processes — according to which, for instance, seeing would be a molecular movement in the nervous system and hence fundamentally of the same kind as the seeable color — we prove it, moreover, indirectly by falling back on the result of reflection.

If, in consequence of the unavoidable being-confronted of the It-point, the original objectivity has the character of thing-ness, then it seems strange why spirit, when by virtue of a back-relating act it turns the relating into the related and thereby moves it into the place of the thing, is nonetheless by no means compelled to hold it to be something foreign to consciousness. It is true that the history of spirit offers whole sample-cards of false reifications; but there is no doubt that they are not unavoidable. Whoever reflects on spirit or on thinking is aware, or can at least be aware, of meaning determinations of inwardness and not, say, such of a possible outer world. The complete neutrality of the place of the object with respect to what occupies it does not exclude the sharpest possible separation of objects of thought foreign to consciousness from those proper to consciousness; which, however, would indeed remain inconceivable given a symmetrical oppositeness in the two-sided nature of experiencing. However one may explain seeing or hearing, one has in doing so always already presupposed that seeing is different from color in a different way than red is different from blue, that hearing is different from noises in a different way than high noises are from low noises, and has thus, in one's reflecting upon it, put into effect the essential dissimilarity of the two sides, of experiencing and the to-be-experienced. But two states of affairs that are both mutually dependent and mutually irreplaceable are called, in generally valid usage, poles. In the relation of polarity stand, among others, positive and negative magnetism, the right and left side [p. 104] of man, or, with regard to the process of reproduction, sperm and egg. Self and thing would always be merely different in position, and this difference of position could never be found without the difference in essence of objects belonging to consciousness and objects foreign to consciousness; which, however, can only be vitally grounded in the polarity of lived experience and image.

From this both things now explain themselves without constraint: both why the objectification of the I and its properties, as well as of concepts, need not lead to reification, and also, on the other hand, the not inconsiderable danger of confusing the two. If appearance and lived experience are polarly opposed to one another, then the co-related of reflection-back is polarly different from the co-related of thing-reflection. But because the place of the object has its character from the thing as its original placeholder, everything objective acquires the semblance of thing-ness, which it requires a special effort of discrimination to recognize and dispel — comparable to the effort of the eye required to determine the true color of a body under misleading illumination.

We conclude this part of the investigation by indicating a third and indeed last step of reflection, which can follow upon self-reflection only as the latter follows upon thing-reflection: we mean the knowledge of the being-related of the It-point to the I-point, or, in other words, the reflection upon what has chiefly occupied us here: conceiving and concepts. Thing-reflection is followed by self-reflection, and both finally by concept-reflection. — We refrain from a detailed depiction of how, with the help perhaps of the three planes of the usual coordinate cross, all the directional angles of relating might be symbolized, and add only that a difference in the state of affairs finds expression in the necessity of the transition from the planar to the spatial schema. Considered externally, concept-reflection is indeed nothing but the other side of self-reflection, since a conceiving consciousness inseparably belongs to the concept. Grasped more deeply, however, it represents a fundamentally higher stage of abstracting than any other kind either of thing-reflection or of self-reflection. Both of these, it is true, can likewise climb stages of abstractness differing in height. I think in a more abstract way as regards thing-reflection when I occupy myself with the laws of oscillation in springy media than when I occupy myself with the structure of a tulip blossom; more abstractly as regards self-reflection when occupied with I-ness than when with the [p. 105] capacity for envy. But I mount to a fundamentally higher stage of abstracting when I turn to the essence of concepts, whether of the I or of things. Looking toward the thing, I look away from the self; looking toward the self, I look away from the thing; looking toward the concept, I look away from both. To the thing belongs a co-related happening, to the self a co-related experiencing; to the concept as such neither of these belongs immediately, though indeed each of the two belongs to it mediately, inasmuch as self as well as thing have now themselves become co-relatednesses! As something wholly detached from actuality, it is true that concept-reflection alone has the extraordinary capacity to "survey" everything and to take up the solution of the question of the relation of spirit to life; but for that very reason it finds itself, as no other kind of reflection does, in the danger of unnoticedly losing sight of the two-sided dependence of conceiving — namely on the one hand on spirit, on the other on life — and thus of denying actuality and holding the concept to be the creator of the world. Socrates began with this; modern logistic celebrates its triumphs in it.

"The three steps of reflection stand out with wonderful sharpness in the history of Greek thought. The Ionian hylicists, insofar as they were not still symbolists, philosophized on the basis of thing-consciousness; the so-called Sophists, and above all the highly significant Protagoras, on the basis of self-consciousness; Plato on the basis of relation-consciousness. Unfortunately, however, Greek thinking already went astray here in the fateful way of confusing the object each time preferred with actuality itself and of dissolving the picture of the world into concepts of being; from which arose those three basic kinds of philosophical system-building that were ceaselessly repeated thereafter: from predominant thing-consciousness, "materialism" (realism, atomism, empiricism, sensualism, etc.); from predominant I-consciousness, "spiritualism" (pneumatology, illusionism, subjectivism, solipsism, etc.); from predominant relation-consciousness, "idealism" (panlogism, criticism, etc.). The ens realissimum of the first kind is called matter or stuff, of the second spirit, of the third idea (category, concept). All three are branches on the trunk of the very same basic error, according to which, over the mere substratum, the essentia was forgotten, over the cogitare the vivere, over the existere the fluctuare!"<sup>11</sup>

<sup>11</sup> On page 105. — *Klages*, Vom Wesen des Bewußtseins, 3rd ed., Leipzig 1933, pp. 59–60.

Having arrived at the end of the path that the Eleatics began with the [p. 106] denial of actuality, the logicist no longer has the slightest consciousness of having, for the sake of his belief in a world of mere noumena, first denied another world. Whereas the former still had to refute their own vitality in order to exchange the actual for being, he finds conceiving already in its place and sees nothing at all except what would confirm his inherited belief in the omnipotence of the faculty of judgement. Melchior Palágyi — among all the thinkers of the present, so far as we can see, the only one who is in fundamental feud with every kind of ideologism — digs out, with the following words, the root from which, branch by branch and leaf by leaf, has sprouted the unsurveyable series of fundamental errors that marks the course of development of the human spirit: "The source of the possibility of all human aberration is to be sought in the fact that we can take for spiritual what is merely alive, and for alive what is merely spiritual." Everything that we have already combated, and shall go on combating, proves in the end to be conditioned by one and the same compulsion: that of, on the basis of confusing experiencing with knowing, lying actuality away into a deed of spirit. Now that this tendency has been at work for millennia, determining not merely the direction of research but also the tradition of knowledge, whoever today wishes to bring experiencing into view at all must simply begin by clearing away the phantoms behind which the presumptions of a hybrid understanding have long since withdrawn it from our consciousness.

[p. 107]

#### 13. Kapitel — Vom Sinn der „Universalien“ — Chapter 13 — On the Sense of the “Universals”
