Let us imagine that someone were to raise the following objection: granted that it may well be true that estrangement must be experienced in order for us to find things of the outer world, the same could hardly hold in like manner for the finding of the content of numerous general concepts, such as virtue, government, manifoldness, sameness, plurality, etc. If someone occupied with the analysis of the process of thinking could, under no circumstances, mean that his thinking spirit and the thought object are spatially outside one another, since the latter has no spatial existence whatever, then it would become highly doubtful whether this is ever really the case at all, and in particular whether the "confrontation" of a thing-finding act may be equated with the spatial confrontation that alone would be experienceable by us. — Perhaps the reader already notices the misunderstanding of the objector we have invented; but we believe we can develop what we still need for the further investigation, for the time being, no better than in the form of a reply.

The apprehending and the apprehended as such are never spatially outside one another; and yet there is an apprehending at all only insofar as spirit as well as object have their place in spatio-temporal happening. How is this to be understood? We have the full equipment together to resolve the seeming antinomy. If only experiencing is estranged, then we must determine the achievement of the faculty of judgement more precisely as consisting in this, that, unconcerned with the actuality of a separating layer and, as it were, blind to it, it fixes the directing point. It required abstracting from the flowing of time in order to find time, abstracting from the change of image-appearance in order to find the thing, and it requires, finally, abstracting from the experienced counterpart in order to find the object as such at all. Meanwhile we could have inferred the latter from the former. If spirit must abstract from the being-outside-one-another in order thereby to find the [p. 108] relatable point, then it has thereby already abstracted also from the being-outside-one-another in which it itself occupies a place, and thus likewise from the mutual confrontation of both places. But however certain it is that the "abstracting" itself is an experience, or at least is rooted in one, just as certain is it that the counterpart is nonetheless experienced. With the help of this finding we complete our insight into the essence of conceiving and of concepts through the sharpest illumination of that which — formerly noted only in the so-called universals, that is, first of all in the generic concepts, but at bottom in general concepts as such — in truth belongs to every concept: its abstractness in relation to the actual.

First of all, as everyone recognizes, it is fundamentally immaterial whether, with the proposition that the concept as such is something abstract, one means the being-separated of the object of thought from the actual, or of the actual from the object of thought; for we cannot indeed separate the state of affairs B from the state of affairs A without, by that very act, having also separated the state of affairs A from the state of affairs B. But then the being-separated evidently concerns both alike: that which has been seized by spirit and which became its own through the seizing, as well as that from which it had to abstract for the sake of the seizing; and the co-relatedness of the actual, formerly so called, comes close to us in the new form of a separated presentness. Insofar as what is experienced by the bearer of life prescribes to spirit not, it is true, the direction of its relating, but indeed what it must leave aside in order to forge the intended relation, an actual is present in the object of thought, even if only as separated! It is open to me to think the shape of a surface or its color. If, however, I think the shape of the surface, I must look away from the color of the surface; hence, in the concept of surface-shape, the color of the surface participates through detachment. Now just as, in the concept of shape, color is contained in separated form, so too there is contained, in every concept, as separated, the being-outside-one-another of object of thought and thinking spirit. The line connecting the I-point and the It-point in our schema is thus only a symbolic line; as, moreover, is clear from the mere consideration that, in the contrary case, the evidently senseless question of the magnitude of the distance between the two points would necessarily arise. Stripped of every figure of speech, the schema states: only through abstraction from the being-outside-one-another of the experiencing and of an experienced does spirit arrive at the apprehension of the object. But the separated being-outside-one-another is [p. 109] actually that of which the line offers an example, namely spatial mutual exteriority.

At any thought-act whatsoever, space is thus involved as something set apart, as is attested not only by the felt sense of direction accompanying thinking, but also, according to the evidence of sharper self-observation, by the circumstance that any object of thought whatsoever — call it, for instance, identity — is grasped as something vaguely situated in the space of intuition, little as we are accustomed, of course, to attend to the moment when we are turned toward the object itself rather than to the mental posture we must adopt in order to think it. This explains what has indeed been carefully tested and described by researchers into expression, but by no means adequately understood: that the mimicry of *thinking*, for all its otherwise greatest variety, and for all the possible participation of nearly all the facial muscles as well as numerous muscles of the trunk, arms, and legs, nonetheless has its center in the mimicry of the eye — regardless of whether it is optical or acoustic appearances that excite the attention, and regardless of whether external or internal objects are being thought about.<sup>12</sup> Without knowledge of the separate presentness of experiences of space, the psychology of thinking is hopeless.

<sup>12</sup> On page 109. — Cf. *Sante de Sanctis*, Die Mimik des Denkens, Marhold, 1906.

Since Plato's theory of Ideas, the dispute has notoriously never come to rest as to whether "universals" exist only within thinking consciousness, or are rather the driving and shaping powers of actuality itself, and the very latest age has taken it up again at exactly the point where Scholasticism let it drop. One deceives oneself if one believes that the question which then split all thinking heads into the two great camps of the "Realists" and the "Nominalists" has meanwhile been decided. Although we have in fact already stated our solution in everything that has gone before, we shall not fail to formulate it once more with a view to that division. But first let us cast a glance at the present state of the problem.

If the medieval dispute turned chiefly on the question whether the determining power of all actuality — indeed actuality itself — was to be sought in general concepts, and especially in generic concepts, or rather in individual things, the logician of the present day will, by contrast, no doubt also assert the conceptuality of that very content of thought which the name "individual thing" means. It is also customary [p. 110] for the mode of thought then called "realist" — according to which the content of generic concepts was at bottom the only thing that truly existed — to be acknowledged by its present-day successors so little any longer, that one even believes one can defend its inventor, still held worthy of divine honors despite his rapturous descriptions of the pre-existence of souls in the realm of Ideas, against the assumption of a being of the Ideas as against an Aristotelian misunderstanding. Yet what is at issue is far more a mere alteration of the verbal semblance of the matter than of the matter itself, when instead, in answer to the now advanced question of the unconditional validity of true propositions, one responds with the founding of a "timeless realm of Ideas" and champions the assumption of contents of thought that, while indeed not being, are nonetheless independently present. What has been publicly proclaimed in this regard in the last two decades under the guise of purported acuity presents itself, however, to the knowing eye so much as a caricature bent on outdoing itself, and bears so obtrusively all the marks of an age of decline in metaphysical reflection, that we do not wish to illustrate by it the revival of scholastic "Realism," but rather by a subtle and highly cultivated thinker of the quite recent past, in whom must be seen the thoroughly serious immediate instigator of present-day logistic; for we shall in any case have to speak of the newest formalism later as well (namely in Chapter 38)!

In his in part excellent *Logik* (1874), Lotze discusses, on the occasion of a consideration of the Platonic world of Ideas, the difficulty involved in having to specify what a tone might be apart from being heard, a color apart from being seen, and notes in connection with this that not every language possesses an abstract expression of the desirable purity for what is meant in this way. He then continues: "For German usage, the word *actuality* serves this purpose. For we call actual a thing which is, as opposed to another which is not; actual, too, an event which occurs or has occurred, as opposed to one which does not occur; actual a relation which obtains, as opposed to one which does not obtain; and finally we call actually true a proposition which holds, as opposed to one whose holding is still in question. This linguistic usage is intelligible; it [p. 111] shows that by actuality we always mean an affirmation, though its sense takes a very different shape according to which of these various forms it assumes .., no one of which is reducible to the other.." (p. 511–512). Further: "Just as little as anyone can say how it comes about that something is or that something happens, just as little can it be specified how it comes about that a truth holds; one must regard this concept, too, as an utterly self-sustained fundamental concept, .., one which we cannot generate by a construction out of component parts that did not already contain it themselves" (p. 513). This is now used to justify Plato. "Plato meant to teach nothing else than what we have gone through above: the validity of truths apart from whether they are confirmed as being of the nature of some object of the external world; the eternally self-identical meaning of the Ideas, which are always what they are, regardless of whether there are things which, by participating in them, bring them to appearance in this external world, or whether there are spirits which, by thinking them, give them the actuality of a soul-state that occurs. But the Greek language lacked then, and still later, an expression for this concept of holding, which includes no being. .. Every content graspable for thought .. was to the Greek a being, ὄν or οὐσία; other than in this constant intermixture with the actuality of being, the language of ancient Greece never knew how to designate that actuality of mere holding.." (p. 513–514). The Ideas, then, are according to Plato to be thought of as separable or separate from things. "But," it goes on, "it was not Plato's opinion that they were merely independent of things, while, on the other hand, .. dependent on the spirit that thinks them; they enjoy the actuality of being, to be sure, only in the moment in which they, as .. products of a representing that is just now occurring, become component parts of this .. world of .. happening; but we are all convinced, in this moment in which we think the content of a truth, that we have not first created it but only acknowledged it; even when we were not thinking it, it held and will hold, separate from everything that is, from things as much as from us, and regardless of whether it ever, in the actuality .. of being-thought, becomes the object of a cognition.." (p. 515). By relocating the Ideas to a supracelestial and hence spaceless place, Plato, in view of the spatial emphasis of the Greek sense of actuality, clearly gives to understand that he is far [p. 112] from attributing to the Ideas an actuality of being. The opposite assumption is said to be due in part to misunderstandings of Aristotle. It then continues: "If one wished now to marvel at the fact that two of the greatest philosophers of antiquity wrestled, without complete success, for clarity about so simple a distinction (namely, that of being from holding), one would be unjust to both; for the perception of the simplest relations of thought is not the simplest act of thinking, and the whole long history of philosophy teaches how we are all, at every moment, ready to make ourselves guilty, in application, of the very same obscurity which, reduced to its simplest expression, we should like to hold impossible... And finally I must add that even we, when we distinguish the actuality proper to Ideas and laws, as holding, from the actuality of things, as being, have at first merely found, through the favor of our language, a convenient designation which can warn us against confusing the two; but the matter itself, which we designate by the name of holding, has thereby lost nothing of the wonder which contained the impulse to its confusion with being. We are merely, making use of our thinking artlessly as of a natural faculty, long accustomed to this, and now find it self-evident that the content of manifold perceptions .. must submit .. to general points of view; but that this is so, that there are general truths which are not themselves like things and which nevertheless govern the behavior of things — this, for the mind that immerses itself in it, is indeed an abyss of wonder, whose existence, discovered with astonishment and enthusiasm, always remains a great deed of Plato's, however many questions it may have left unsolved" (p. 518–520).

In view of the extraordinary self-importance of today's logisticians, it seemed to us fitting to recall to mind the train of thought of a Lotze by relatively broad repetition of his own words, since every expert will readily note his outstanding share — if not yet in a fully carried-out formalist world-view, then certainly in the authorization for it and in the fashioning of the conceptual armament for its defense. If we consider that even Lotze was already an epigone — though in part in the desirable sense of guardian and keeper-in-flow of the spiritual inheritances of a Plato, an Aristotle, a Leibniz, a Kant, a Hegel — then the modern logistician [p. 113] is, with his Scholasticism dressed up in the fashion of the day, in some sense removed even in his errors by a third hand; and his peculiar arrogance proves in the end to have sprung from the suppression of a feeling of superfluousness that secretly, though sometimes rebelliously, still stirs — Lotze, to be sure, was far from holding what he called the actuality of the valid or the true to be thinkable without presupposing the actuality of being as well as, besides, that of happening. "However great the value of the observation that actuality is such that we succeed, by connecting those ideas of ours with its course, in coinciding with it: still, one could not take this world of ideas for anything else than a system of abstractions or thoughtimages, which have actuality only insofar as they are regarded as the very mode of procedure of things, but which might in no way be set in opposition, as a prius, to the course of things, to which this course .. adapts itself as a second" (*Metaphysik* p. 80–81). Yet we need only shine into the sentences reproduced above the ray of light that can be kindled from our own findings, in order at once to discover in them a self-contradiction which, moreover, as it seems to us, did not entirely escape our thinker. Does he not himself concede that the distinction of an actuality of being from an actuality of holding cannot, in point of fact, remove the wonder at all which contains the impulse to the confusion of the two? But in this betrays itself the delicate point of this converted Platonism and its essential identity with the "Realism" of medieval Scholasticism.

Whoever — with Hegel — speaks of an actuality of truth can no longer say at all how this actuality is supposed to depend on another actuality, in Lotze's case even on two other actualities. But if he strikes out that dependency, then not even the miracle postulated by Lotze would be able to save the word "holding" from utter meaninglessness! Ever since Leibniz's all-too-famous *vérités de raison* (which became fixed in Kant's apriorism), professors of philosophy have repeated some tens of thousands of times that mere truths of experience (today gladly called "real laws") are something fundamentally lesser than logical and mathematical truths (today, ideal laws), which, in keeping with the apparatus peculiar to it, are supposed to be produced by reason in and for itself, and hence without the intrusion of any extra-rational actuality. Such joyful proclamations of [p. 114] legitimate reason's own omnipotence, bestowed upon itself, leave unmoved anyone who has become convinced that absolutely no concept — no matter of what — can be thought except by detaching a thereby co-related actuality. But even if we set aside the fact that it therefore follows, in the last analysis, that it is always something actual of which the holding thing holds (even in the case of mathematics), the said validity would nonetheless be utterly robbed of its sense without the actual existence of beings for whom it might obtain. The holding as well as the not-holding of a judgement requires, in order to be thought as a state of affairs somehow present, judging and judgement-receptive I's; hence Plato proceeded quite consistently indeed when he at once relegated these, too — or at least their "better part" — to the "supracelestial place" of the Ideas!

One more thing deserves our attention in Lotze's logistic prelude: his *coordination* of an actuality of being with an actuality of happening, which, taken seriously, would make our knowledge of both impossible. For either we would then live in the actuality of happening, or in the actuality of being, or, finally, alternately now in the one, now in the other; from which, however, it would follow that we would each time have forgotten that actuality to which we did not at the moment belong! Perhaps one objects: we do indeed, unquestionably, sometimes live in the actuality of dream, then again in the actuality of waking, and know of both of them nonetheless. Nothing could be more welcome to us than such an objection, in order to lay bare completely what in truth hides behind that apparent coordination of different actualities. We do not yet show here how it is that in dream we do experience an actuality, yet are by no means also able to think it; but we point out in advance that in the actuality of waking we do indeed also know of the dream-visions experienced, whereas in the actuality of dreaming we do not at all remember the actuality of waking. (The exception case of dreaming — moreover easily explained — that one is dreaming, always lies at the very onset of the process of waking.) And now, in the waking state, compared with what we now call the actuality of the external world, we judge our dream-contents to be "mere dreams," and that is to say, as external unactuality. Even one who, out of caution, would not commit himself to this, would still have to admit that he is not in a position to fit the experienced dream-space into the perceptual space of his waking [p. 115] world (or, conversely, the other way about), and consequently cannot in any case attribute actuality to both in the same manner! When Lotze unhesitatingly believes he may do just this with respect to the actualities of being and of happening, he betrays to us, against his own knowledge and will, that he — exactly like Descartes<sup>13</sup> — at bottom holds only being to be something actual, while of happening he knows only its form of existence, namely the *mechanical* processes and motions that play themselves out on things, which then, to be sure, coincide with existing things in the very same space. And because to being there corresponds the state of the consciousness of existence, the only state that makes the production of judgements possible, it can no longer surprise us that Lotze's determination of actuality ultimately comes down to the mark of spiritual being-affirmed, thereby quite unnoticed substituting, as the criterion of actuality's presence, the *assent of the understanding* to it. Since, finally, the model and archetype of the concept of being must be sought in the concept of the existing thing, we must state: the whole Western logistic since Plato is, exactly like its counterpart, "Materialism," in matters of metaphysics an instance of false *reification*; only that the latter takes its delight rather in massy matter, logistic in the most nearly weightless astral body possible! If we take up the books of contemporary logisticians, in which we are assured that one will, as the ghost-conjuring term of art has it, bring to "self-givenness" not merely sameness, difference, similarity, possibility, doubtfulness, permissibility, and the like — no, even the And and the How and the But — then we see in such extravagances even the "Realism" of the Middle Ages outdone, and feel tempted to consider illuminating the kinship of stock between the words Spiritualism and — Spiritism. So that, after such thoroughgoing renunciations, not even the smallest remainder of uncertainty may remain as to the conviction held by the author, we now give this, resting on all that has gone before, in the form of a threefold declaration unfolded in such a way that the qualification which the first would need finds expression only in the third:

<sup>13</sup> On page 115. — If even today many psychologists call their science that of "immediate experience," they thereby profess themselves adherents of the conviction, held first by *Augustine*, later by *Descartes*, that the originally certain is the apprehending spirit. The attempt to lend the self a fundamental position of privilege is undertaken here in a manner that stands out remarkably from the one most favored today, according to which among all objects of thought there is supposed to be one non-objectual one, namely the "pure subject." That, notwithstanding this, both turns of phrase are only differently expressed manifestations of the same basic idea comes at once to light when we set the starting points side by side as follows: everything belonging to the outer world is not the "pure subject," and everything belonging to the outer world is no being raised above all doubt. To these two premises, manifestly very similar to each other, two divergently mistaken inferences attach themselves under the pressure of the same tendency: the logistician is wrong to hold spirit to be non-objectual because it cannot be estranged; Augustine is wrong to hold it, for the same reason, to be immediately apprehended. Without a previously won certainty of alien being we should never arrive at certainty of our own being, and whoever insists on confusing psychology with epistemology ought to call it a science precisely of mediate experience. Yet Augustine nonetheless holds the stronger position, though he occupies it for a reason that is the opposite of the one with which it could be defended. The state of doubting, which certainly underlies the problem of immediate certainty not merely in appearance, can be clothed in the following question: What actually entitles us to ascribe real existence to perceived persons, things, and processes? For we believe we also perceive in dreams, and notice afterward that the dream-formations were not there at all. "How often does it not happen," remarks *Descartes*, "that the dream of the night tells me I am here, dressed in my coat, sitting by the fireside, while in fact I am lying in bed with my clothes laid aside!" What if the whole world were a stream of phantasms? What gives us the unshakable belief in a being existing *outside* the believing consciousness? To this the answer now given is: however this may stand, without doubt I, the one who questions, exist; and though I may doubt everything, I cannot possibly doubt the existence of myself as one who doubts. But granting the correctness of this inference, it still does not contain the least foothold for solving the question of an actuality independent of the I. From the fact that I hold myself, a questioning and doubting something, to be real, there follows to all eternity not the slightest thing regarding the belonging-to-the-I or the difference-from-the-I of, for example, dream-visions! But the Cartesian train of thought appears far more curious still when we note that his doubting, however seriously it was meant, rests covertly on the prior assumption that dream-visions are *merely* phantasms in relation to the existence of the perceptual things of waking consciousness! While apparently raising the question of actuality, he in truth raises the question of the ground of the applicability of the concept of being to an actuality already prejudged by him. And indeed it takes but little reflection to see that whoever calls into doubt the existence of perceptual things has already believed and assumed it, since otherwise there would be no occasion whatever for doubting. The belief in an immediate certainty of being of the I overlooks that the I always finds itself *in relation to things* *standing over against it*; of which, among other things, its state of doubting gives eloquent testimony. One notices the point of contact between the Augustinian-Cartesian and the logistic movement of thought. Both are on the hunt for the "pure subject," both want to make it unassailable, both strive for a determination of essence that would permit them to deny outer-worldly being the same *dignity*, and both disregard the relatedness of the subject to objects: the logistician, in order to declare it unrelatable; Descartes, in order to declare it existent without relation. Both are commanded, by the prudence of their thought-drive bought from spirit, *not* to keep being and actuality apart, because only in this way can they attempt to make the actuality of the outer world dependent on the necessarily-thought being of the I. — Let us, however, put the leading question as follows: what compels me to assume *existence*, be it of the outer world, be it even only of myself? — the answer must in fact run: this, that I can question and judge. For if I am a judging being, then I am, to begin with, a real being, but moreover also a being related to objects, itself relatable through reflection back upon itself, and consequently an objectual being. The cogito ergo sum is undeniably right, insofar as it is meant to ground the thought of existence in the *necessary* existing of the bearer of judgement. Existence as such demands the actuality of an existing spirit. What can be won from this for the thinking spirit is not the immediacy of certainty of being, but rather the assurance that the necessity of assuming existences is grounded in the determinateness of being of the thinking spirit. If we now designate more precisely, with the name of being, or here more correctly of existence, the object of thought held to be real, then "subject" and "object" — in the sense, that is, of self and perceptual thing — both fall under the genus of really existing objects, as indeed, as noted earlier, the names themselves already show; but if we ask further after the occasioning ground of the connectedness of being and actuality, then the perceptual thing belongs to actuality only for the one apprehending it, whereas the I or self belongs to it *absolutely*. The thing-point has, after all, only been posited by spirit — even if compelled to do so by the experience of actuality, and thus in dependence on the real — whereas the I-point is really connected with the happening, and hence connected *through* the happening itself. We must grasp both as immediately related to the real, only that for the one of them there lies before us not merely a ground in spirit, but also a real ground of the being-related. — Once this has been thoroughly understood, numerous states of affairs present themselves as explicable only from it, of which we shall here bring a few to notice. The history of thought gives us evidence in abundance that we can rethink any thing whatever, but in no way the I. In place of the *actual* sound I can put the fact "vibration of the air"; in place of the air, the mixture of two gases; in place of the gases, a — in principle countable — quantity of separate molecules; in place of the molecule, an assemblage of atoms; in place of the atoms, ions; in place of the ions, electron-systems moving within themselves; in place of the electrons, "elementary quanta," and so forth; whereas in place of a really existing I — more precisely, the I-ness of a real being — absolutely nothing else can be put; as indeed the manifold attempts to do so nonetheless, after the model of the analytic arts of natural science, have without exception come to grief. All things exist merely "relatively," every thinking I exists "absolutely." — Or: if we consider spirit as such, that is, the capacity for accomplishing temporally unextended acts, detached from its existence in a thinking bearer of life, then its time-independent being lacks any distinguishing determinability. Already the Middle Ages, following the lead of late antiquity, created the so-called negative theology, according to which of "God," as an entity wholly devoid of properties, only what he *is not* can be predicated. With the wholly correct characterization of this positive nothing as an "actus purus," it is quite fittingly made clear how it is nonetheless present and manifests itself through effects. But in this way an actuality different from spirit is posited; for without a material *on which* it could exercise itself, the mere *capacity for acts* would be as good as not present at all. But if this is how matters stand with spiritual being as such, then the real accomplishment of spiritual acts also demands the *real* existence of spirit in a bearer of life particularized in space, time, and kind. All objects of thought are identical with themselves; all things, moreover, are existences *on the basis* of acts of spirit; spirit itself, however, must exist in actuality if it is to be capable of performing those acts. — Finally, we point once more to the highly peculiar double use of the word "subject." It is no accident that by "subjects" one understands, on the one hand, I's (just as by the "pure subject" one understands spirit as such), and on the other hand the grammatical subject of a sentence, regardless of whether it is really a self, or a thing, a property, a state, a process, or even merely a relation, an actual or merely thought relationship; and we venture without hesitation the explanation that, in the grammatical use of "subject," linguistic instinct reached back from the merely derived being of things to the original being of the I, thereby instructing us that the act of judging — because that act of the I by which it transfers itself into actuality — is by its essence a *personifying* act! Whatever it may be of which something is predicated, it takes on, by virtue of the nature of judgement, the character of that object of thought which, of all possible objects of thought whatever, alone has a claim to actuality independent of thought — the character of the actperforming "subject."

1. To actuality there corresponds a conceptual counterpart, but there is no actuality of the conceived. Between actuality and conceptual knowability there does not obtain the relation of the members of a mathematical equation; rather, the two are non-interchangeable. One could call the truth [p. 116] insofar a function of the actual happening, in that it is in fact a product of the thinking being, but would thereby have concealed its relation of dependency on a spirit which does not, in and for itself, belong to actuality. Here, in the first place, the following claim is to be maintained: were one to remove the thinking being from actuality, one would not merely have eliminated the thinking-processes, but at the same time also the objects to be thought by means of them. "Were there no thinking, there would also be no truth" (G. E. Schulze). The metaphysical "place" of actuality lies as much on this side of true and false as it lies on this side of subject and object. Objects of thought are there only for a thinking consciousness, not without it, in actuality itself. This holds, as goes without saying, also for the content of this very declaration, notwithstanding that we hold it to be proven. — A child grasps this; for the understanding schooled astray for millennia, it wants to be established in detail. We therefore add a further remark, to guard against a misinterpretation that might otherwise perhaps be favored.

Color remains something visible without the faculty of sight, even though it would then no longer actually be seen; tone, something audible without a faculty of hearing; but what is thereby meant merely by the words "color" and "tone" is not the conceivable of color and not the conceivable of tone. The concept-content color and the concept-content tone are objects of thought lying beyond actuality. The actuality of color, then, does not depend on the presence of a faculty of sight, but the existence of color does depend on the presence of a faculty of conception. May we finally still express ourselves in popular terms: in actuality there are neither things, nor their properties and states, nor relations between them, and consequently nothing of lawfulness; since, then, in the last analysis a lawful world constitutes the (conceived) content of all possible judgements whatever, no content of a judgement has any part in actuality.

2. One has asked: what is truth; and one has learned to understand the impossibility of an answer to this, because every answer would already have to presuppose belief in a mode of procedure of thinking suited to the finding of truth. Against this, one may not merely, one must even ask: how does truth relate to actuality? Let us state in advance how it does *not* relate to it! It is not actuality once again, nor — as with the Greeks — a mirroring of it. What, then, would it be? First of all: a valid content of judgement, and hence a state of affairs that [p. 117] can be realized only in the thinking of a thinking being. Wherein, then, would the validity consist? It is characterized by tracing back to the conditions of the ascertainment of truth. And of these there are now two, fundamentally and metaphysically distinct from one another. The judgement, in order to be correct, must obey the law of spirit (in logic, the "principle of identity," or also the "principle of contradiction"), and the *impulse* to the judgement must come from an experienced actuality. We judge truly insofar as our spirit is compelled by the experience of actuality to judgement, and, in judging, follows its law of self-identification; in every other case, falsely. Had we already illuminated the experience of actuality more sharply, a theory of erring could be grounded upon this; here we content ourselves with adding, without proof, that the ultimate ground of every possible error (including, for instance, mere miscalculation) may never be sought in spirit, but always in a dislocation of the lived experience of actuality.

One will, however, still miss the answer as to how truth relates to actuality. Well, one thing is certain: it means the *trans*-ference of actuality into an *un*-actuality wholly incomparable with it, whose sign-language (not yet considered by us) guarantees to every thinking-capable individual being the conceptual reproduction of what is thereby meant, and, insofar as the meant is, as presupposed, something valid, the recovery of the actuality that conditions it. True judgements are only the *means of mutual understanding*, realizable only in thinking, among thinking beings concerning actuality. They cease to be, not merely somewhere, but even to be anything whatsoever, insofar and as soon as the said beings should come to an understanding without thinking.

With the qualification — offered even beyond what is always required — which the actual incomparability of the content of judgement and actuality imposes upon us, we offer, for the relation of the two to one another, a simile that seems to us especially fruitful: truth relates to actuality as the score does to the piece of music. The points which we line up in order to illuminate the relations between the two are so chosen that they remain correct if, in each case, one puts actuality in place of the piece of music, and the (valid) judgement in place of the score: a) The piece of music would remain what it is, even if there were no notes at all. b) The notes (here corresponding to declarative judgements) would still be, as before, points and strokes, but wholly devoid of meaning, if there were no tones at all. [p. 118] c) The two, the piece of music and the score, have not the slightest similarity to one another; and in particular the score by no means forms an echo of the piece of music. Could one make the note-heads dance (corresponding to the movement of thought), they would still always be only dancing note-heads, not songs and harmonies. d) This does not prevent a score from being correct, but also from being false, as it can be.

Only for the last point do we wish to assist the application — to be carried out independently by the reader — to the problem of "truth and actuality." Nietzsche remarks, in his posthumous notes on "The Will to Power": "Parmenides said: one does not think that which is not; we are at the other end and say: what can be thought must surely be a fiction." The remark is as profound as it is true, if it is meant to express the complete incomparability of the content of judgement and actuality; it is dangerously misleading if, by the word "fiction," it means to assert the impossibility of the finding of truth. In fact, Nietzsche remained stuck for life, in this respect, in Socratism, in that he never fought his way through to a clear distinction between truth and actuality. He, too, still takes truth for a kind of actuality which stands, in relation to the "proper" actuality, in the relation of a "fictive" actuality. But with that one falls into that skepticism whose impossibility can be excellently illustrated precisely by the foregoing turn of phrase. We cannot meaningfully speak of "fictions" without thinking of a *not* fictitious actuality and holding this thought to be true. With the proposition: there is no truth, one has also already said: there is neither error nor deception! "What can be thought," it should then continue, "surely has no actuality." It is not the note-head that sounds, and it is not truth that is actuality. But just as the knowledge of the (admittedly merely conventional) laws of musical notation makes possible the *correct* transposition of the piece of music into the score, wholly different in tonal nature, and thereby enables the person versed in notation to reproduce what has been transposed, so too the observance of certain inner requirements (whereby vital compulsions cooperate with the law of spirit) guarantees the *correct* transposition of actuality into the medium, foreign to actuality, of the contents of judgement, and thereby the conceptual reproduction of what has been transposed, in every judgement-receptive spirit. Only on the basis of insight into the complete incomparability of truth [p. 119] and actuality does the metaphysical knowledge of the unactuality of the contents of thought harbor, at the same time, the most invincible weapon against every kind of skepticism.

3. In these same posthumous notes of Nietzsche's is found the sentence: "Logic is bound to the condition: supposing there are identical cases" — with the accompanying thought: in actuality there are *no* identical cases; whereby the unactuality of all objects of thought would then be attested in yet another way. But this thesis, otherwise held by us as well, suffers now one — though indeed only a single — exception. If I think of myself as an existing something, I think a state of affairs which is actually present exactly as it is thought; for in the opposite case the fact of my thinking could not have taken place. There is, then, after all, an actuality of the thought, namely the actuality of the I thought as capable of thought.

The "Realists" of Scholasticism taught — in this at one with Plato — the actuality of generic and, ultimately, of general concepts; to which even today's logistician would be ready to reply that concepts occur only in the consciousness of thinking beings. He, however, now teaches a non-being actuality of the contents of concepts (or, alternatively, of the contents of judgements), which in substance comes to exactly the same thing! We have therefore taken the liberty, for the purposes of our counter-discussion, of assessing concepts and judgements from the outset solely with regard to the objects of thinking. It is not by pointing to the long-recognized difference between being and the thinking of being, but only through a critique exercised upon the thinkable itself, that logistic is uprooted. With every positing of objects, whether concrete or abstract, the one and same extra-spatiotemporal spirit answers, with always the same mode of procedure, the compulsions of the experiencing of actuality in the personal bearer of life, thus "projecting" into actuality the being that is foreign to actuality. In the thinking I, however, the sole ground of possibility of spiritual acts, the thinking coincides with the thought, actuality with being. The I belongs to the actuality of happening as a being that nonetheless at the same time endures through it. To the question how, then, the concept of the I is to be distinguished from the *content* of the concept of the I, the answer runs that the two would in truth be indistinguishable, provided the I that accomplishes the act were able to exist independently. It exists, however, only as attached to a changing living-space [p. 120] or, more briefly, as a personal I. How this is to be understood will be set forth further later; here let it only be mentioned that the said attachedness may not be conceived in the sense of a property of the personal bearer of life (as, say, the green color is a property of the leaf). The actuality of the I, as one notices, thereby becomes the central problem of metaphysics. It alone is worth questioning, and not the "timeless realm of Ideas," which results from it entirely of its own accord.

[p. 121]

#### 14. Kapitel — Die flache und die tiefe Besinnung — Chapter 14 — The Shallow and the Deep Reflection

We can now already explain somewhat more clearly what we understand by the relative seeming-validity of "cognition," by the deliberateness of "science," and by the counter-intention of genuine metaphysics. It does not suffice to say that thinking posits the point remaining identical with itself, to which a flowing actuality can be related; rather, we determine the full state of affairs only when we add that the thinking I thereby carries its own counterpart into actuality. With every fact that it finds, the finding I has thereby relocated itself into the judged world. Objects are estranged subjects, and being as such is estranged spirit. Accordingly, "cognition" would be the result of a logocentric reinterpretation of the actual and, insofar as only humanity serves as the seat of the Logos, also of an anthropocentric one. Belief in facts on the one hand and belief in concepts on the other would be only differently placed forms of a single logistic world-inspiriting, in relation to which the so-called animistic world-ensouling on the part of the prehistoric state of life would appear far less "subjective." Myth could sooner refute science than science could ever refute it. We wish also to lend words to the opposing standpoint, because this makes it easier for us to point out both the weaknesses and also the tenable core in each of the two.

If myth wished to refute science, it could do so only in the form of judgement, and would thereby, for its own part too, have obligated itself to the law that compels us to acknowledge every "fact" insofar as it is demonstrably established. For we call science the system of judgements insofar as it finds its support in facts. If, on the other hand, one denies the evidentiary force of states of affairs, one has thereby renounced judging itself and can henceforth neither prove nor dispute anything. Supposing, then, that one were even able to refrain from objectification, [p. 122] one would still, in that very moment, have forfeited the capacity to determine the least thing about truth and untruth. Not even the assertion could be maintained that the judging state is something deliberate, since this assertion, too, would already presuppose it. We must therefore ourselves set foot on the ground of science, in order to ascertain the latter, namely whether some tendency may have formed the ground for a falsification of the truth.

The self-evaluation put into words in the foregoing sentences, which attaches even to the most modest scientificity, whether expressed or not, has, as far as we can see, hitherto by no means sufficed to weaken rapturous prophecies (which rather agree excellently with scientificity, indeed as its indispensable counterpart), but has sufficed to take the courage away from the historically quite rare mythical thinking to offer a well-founded counter-declaration. How might such a counter-declaration have to be voiced? It would, without in the least shaking those sentences, bring to light only the hidden thought which they conceal. It is one thing, it would have to note, to translate actuality into the language of facts, and quite another thing to take this translation itself for a fact. Whoever, faced with a tree, judges that here stands a tree, is unquestionably right logically, but wrong metaphysically, insofar as he takes the noumenon tree for a phenomenon and accordingly for an actuality.

The "advocate" of reason may retort: since the inconceivability of "appearance," even were it demonstrable, does not exempt one from transforming what appears, for the purpose of conceiving it, into a world of facts, knowledge of this remains not only wholly unfruitful for the gaining of cognition, but might, on the contrary, even form a serious hindrance, since it fundamentally diminishes the value of all findings and robs cognition itself of its dignity. Against this, however, we ourselves now wish to represent the metaphysician, and first of all to consider whether belief in the self-sufficiency of the understanding does not constitute an even worse hindrance to the formation of knowledge.

All truths are equally valuable, or else equally worthless, if we evaluate only their being-true. We have, in other words, no standard whatever by which to evaluate truths, so long as we consider only the finished truth instead of the process through which it comes into existence. But if we do this, a difference results which [p. 123] compels us to distinguish two very different classes of truths from one another. — Let us place ourselves in the state of a most original ignorance, such as that of the child or of an as yet early humanity: then it is, from case to case, the estranging experience which brings it about that the impulse to objectify finds its occasion. If we designate such an inclination by the name of a *questioning after* *actuality*, and call the finding, accordingly, simply the fulfillment of a question of actuality, then we already sense, perhaps, with a feeling, that there is present here something other than the dissecting, calculating, and experimenting of science. For seeking and questioning go together better, say, with "musing" than with observing or calculating, and musing, in turn, would already be closely akin to that "contemplating" and "speculating" of which science commonly speaks only as of degenerations of the effort at cognition. — Now the following is to be noted: whenever we have found something, that is, established a fact, the conditions are thereby also at once given for a further seeking, whose peculiarity it is to lead us step by step *away* from actuality, the more we yield to it. For because in actuality everything is connected with everything — embedded, as it were, in a medium of uninterrupted continuity — the findable fixed thing that we call a fact demands to be brought into relation with all facts whatever that are at all possible, in such a way that only a gapless system of facts satisfies the drive for cognition, even if it had at first been concerned with only a single one of them. It lies in the nature of the found fact to drive the capacity for questioning on to the finding of ever new facts, and thereby to exchange the original delight in questioning (not to say: the pain of questioning!) for the far different interest in the establishment of (calculable) relations between fact and fact. The more the spirit follows this compulsion, the more it will be, in place of the compelling force of an experienced actuality, rather the demanding force of an experienced fact that gives it occasion for the finding of further facts. It looks upon the actual only mediately now, namely only insofar as it might be suited to enter into connection with facts already established. And so it must in the end come about that the scientist's will to objectivity is held together with actuality only by a thin thread, which grows thinner in the same measure as the mass of judgements grows that he must make use of, in order, for his part, to arrive at a [p. 124] judgement. The finding lived experience sees itself displaced by finding experience [Erfahren], and the lived-through itself, to a great extent, by what is merely learned.

Let one picture to oneself the typical scholar of the old and best style, who has, over today's average, the double distinction of strictly conscientious thoroughness and of a lack of so-called practice, and one will not be able to avoid admitting that, as a rule, not only his own life but life itself was lost to him behind a dense mesh of mere items of knowledge and formulas, whose shadowiness he himself could do nothing to change, even if they all had the merit of being correct. We state the same matter in only somewhat different words when we say that every declarative sentence conveys, indeed, its sense, but not, at the same time, the experience which originally enabled its discovery. The movement of thought by which a Galileo found the laws of falling bodies encloses within it a fullness of lived experience of which the physics student still knows not the slightest, even when he has already grasped, in the best way, that a body sliding down an inclined plane attains the same final velocity as in free fall from the same height. By no means only truths of so-called philosophy, but equally also those of science, have, at the moment of being found, a weight of depth of meaning which we ourselves, however devotedly we immerse ourselves in them, can never again recover once they have belonged, for centuries — indeed even for mere decades — to the armory of the tradition of knowledge. Cognitions are ceaselessly turned into items of knowledge; but the process of the gaining of cognition (= discovery) remains abysmally different from the process of the learning of what has been discovered. We appreciate, for the present, only one side of this most peculiar state of affairs, which will meet us again and again in what follows.

Concerned only to build further, along the line of least resistance to possible objectification, upon inherited propositions, science turns away from every actuality as soon as it merely possesses for it a formula suited to connection, in order henceforth to regard it as though it were something actual. In doing so, however, it has taken a path not so much toward a deepening of knowledge as rather toward an increase in the abstractness of knowledge and toward an expansion of the range of application for each of a moderate number of basic concepts. The quantity of mechanical, optical, and acoustic knowledge available today stands in a downright glaring disproportion to the meagerness of our knowledge of the [p. 125] essence of motion, of color, of sound — indeed even of cause and of force; the mathematical fluency in higher calculation contrasts almost ridiculously with our nearly complete ignorance concerning the origin and the scope of the concept of number; and who would deny that science, too, may well be a life-crushing burden, if one dares to compare, with the mountain-piling rubble of daily-growing historical tradition, the hopeless ignorance in which we still find ourselves to this hour concerning the driving powers of the life of peoples and concerning the meaning and course of the process of culture! But let one not take this for something merely not yet attained: it is not attainable at all by the questions and methods of research of customary "science," and it would have been attainable even centuries ago, with a thousandfold smaller expenditure of means of knowledge, by way of a contemplation saturated with life! The more a research renounces lived experience, the further it removes itself from actuality, and the more it falls prey to the false wishful image of an all-leveling concept of magnitude. One does not go too far in asserting that man is never further removed from the experiencing of space than in his capacity as measuring geometer, nor from the experiencing of the heavenly body than in his capacity as calculating astronomer. What distinguishes the scientific mental attitude from the unscientific is far less the capacity to hold back "emotional needs" than the cultivated inclination to conduct research by means of the sole exercise of the understanding and under the far-reaching exclusion of *lived experience*. If the understanding-believing disposition were resolved to examine itself without ulterior regard, it would have to confess that it regards lived experience as a disturbing addition and, quite properly, as the most decisive hindrance to that very activity which is needed for the finding of those truths which alone have meaning for it. We strike the vital nerve of this disposition when we add that what has been accomplished by it is: intellectually, the logicization of actuality; materially, its subjugation under the human Logos by means of that instrument called the "logic of facts." The "real symbol" of this is the machine, which, with the help of nature, outwits nature!

The judging activity is always one and the same, regardless of what it is directed upon. If we look only at the individual judgement, it can only be either false or correct, and if it is indeed correct, then [p. 126] the compelling lived experience has somehow had a share in it, because without this no fact whatever would have been found. It is present as much in the occupation with the highest mathematics as in the extremely concrete occupation of the painter with the landscape, and it can degenerate no less in the one case than in the other. The picture changes, however, as soon as we fix our eye on the system of judgements and, in doing so, raise the question of the measure of immediacy of the lived experience that was required for its production. For then it becomes evident that comprehensive systems of judgement could only be created on the basis of an increasing dilution of lived experience, and carry within themselves the tendency to volatilize their truth-content, as it were, into an unboundedly intensifiable conceptuality. — We now wish to call a truth *known through lived experience* insofar as its possession is the result of a finding lived experience, but merely *known through learning* when it required only experience and learning to come to share in it. If we consider, finally, that accordingly one and the same truth can be both known-through-learning and knownthrough-lived-experience, then, quite apart from later elucidations, the justification of the proposition should already become somewhat clear: that every judgement whatever, whether true or false, is grounded now in a shallow, now in a deep reflection, and that, accordingly, the development of knowledge gravitates either toward the side of the increase of items of knowledge, or toward the side of the deepening of insight.

Logic and the theory of science as they have existed hitherto know nothing of deep and shallow reflection, because, being themselves logocentrically oriented, they also know nothing of the life-source of discovery, and therefore remain wholly incapable of finding any mark by which to evaluate truths. One is given guidelines for checking the completeness of a proof-procedure, rules of investigation for individual fields of research, and, at best, certain principles for weighing the significance of a proposition within the total system of the sciences; but the question has never even been raised, let alone answered, whether, behind the allegedly impartial "search for truth," there do not stand wholly different motives of research, from which alone it could first be decided what degree of essentiality inheres in the findings. We now assert that, hitherto, only shallow reflection has been able to establish itself as "science," whereas deep reflection — pushed out of the development of the spirit and, as it were, rendered unlawful — runs an increasing danger of losing entirely the claim of its propositions to universal [p. 127] validity, and of sinking, for the reason-believing consciousness, to the level of a decorative play with arbitrarily extravagant and, at best, personally satisfying conjectures. Before we also, for the sake of clarification, mark out the direction in which every genuinely metaphysical research has branched off from the exemplarily scientific, it is indispensable to cast a fleeting glance at the circumstances which brought it about that the achievements of shallow reflection won undisputed precedence.

Dühring, perhaps the most consistent representative of the belief in the self-sufficiency of the understanding, and at the same time a thorough connoisseur of the prehistory of science, feels moved, in his *Kritische Geschichte der Philosophie*, to the highly characteristic remark that the natural-philosophical endeavors of all ages and peoples have thus far "never yet led to any real increase of existing insights." For this reason, he thinks, "the task of the historian of mere philosophy, in this direction, is a relatively thankless one even for the more recent centuries"; for he must renounce letting come to the fore precisely that which, in thinking about nature, represented the truly creative element and the genuine speculative power. We believe, indeed, for reasons soon to be touched upon, that Dühring has overlooked an important side of the matter; but we agree with him in regard to what he himself has in mind here, only in a somewhat different sense than he means it. Let one harbor no illusion about this: the Brunos or the Caruses have very rarely increased the knowledge of the Newtons or the Darwins; but we hold that the opposite has been just as rarely the case. If, on Dühring's view, the so-called philosophers, at least as regards their knowledge of the universe, were one and all hopeless fools, it might be well to bear in mind that the scientificity which here serves as the standard has existed for barely four hundred years, namely since the Renaissance. It is true that antiquity had a few so-tospeak natural researchers (Hippocrates, Aristarchus, Ptolemy, Euclid, Philolaus, Archimedes, Alcmaeon, Galen, Pliny, and so forth); yet what does this amount to against the hundreds, nay thousands, who have come forward since the sixteenth century with more or less independent discoveries! But if one wished to bring some inhibiting "belief" into account for this "backwardness" of earlier ages, which nonetheless distinguished itself, for example, in imperishable [p. 128] structures, then one would have to ask — and this in contrast to Dühring — how this is to be reconciled with the fact that the philosophy of antiquity, at least, was capable of discovering nearly all the methods of research, of further developing the basic conceptions to which we still resort today whenever we wish to explain something, and finally of achieving many profound insights into the soul, to which we shall scarcely deny our recognition. But if we have thereby become sufficiently skeptical toward every supposed "progress," it will not escape us that this progress, too, forms the expression of a *belief*, with which bourgeois "Liberalism" forced its breakthrough, and finally its victory, against the feudal and priestly orders of value! The spirit of scientificity is only a part, or more correctly a phenomenal form, of the very same spirit that called into life the modern state and, in the last analysis, modern capitalism, and we do not yet know whether a longer existence will be granted to it than, say, to the spirit of medieval Scholasticism! Whoever has grown accustomed also to consider spiritual matters biologically would find, in the mere circumstance of the simultaneous onset and the parallel intensification of otherwise very different formations of culture, sufficient reason to suspect a common ground for the whole series, even where the kinship of soul lies less openly exposed than between scientificity and the sense for utility. It is no accident that, from the very outset, the following stepped onto the stage of world history together, in order thereafter to fight together and to conquer together: the "ideal of freedom" of bourgeois self-government — the incorporation of Roman law — "Protestantism" of every kind — the idea of expansion and progress — the self-interest that makes everything calculable — and finally a science storming onward from invention to invention; and it would probably not cast a favorable light, in every respect, on the "modern age" thus circumscribed, if one were to undertake, for once, to confront it with everything it had to destroy in order to gain room for its achievements. — In now turning our attention once more to the epistemological side, we make use of a consideration which, it seems to us, ought to be convincing even if its premises had not been discussed at length in the foregoing exposition.

Whatever we possess the concept of at all is, as something conceived, one [p. 129] and always the same thing. Not only is every number what it is, in the same way for the Babylonian of antiquity as for the inhabitant of America in the modern age, but so too the color red, the tone C-sharp, the thing, the body, the span of two minutes, the length of a hundred meters, similarity, manifoldness, plurality, equality, sameness, possibility, probability, certainty, anger, holding-true, doubt, love, hatred, belief, and so on. But if actuality flows temporally, ceaselessly changes, neither endures nor recurs, and is hence a pauseless coming and going of eternally original and altogether ungraspable worlds, then no second time either can there be *lived*: the same number, the same magnitude of time, the same tone, the same manifoldness, the same anger — however often it may again and again be *thought*; and an unbridgeable abyss opens between the inclination of our being, which compels us, day by day, generation by generation, century by century, to join together, ever more firmly, the time-withdrawn, growing edifice of the noumenal, and that sphinx-like, menacing necessity which, however violently forgotten and however wisely kept silent, nonetheless drags generation after generation no less into the maelstrom of passing away, weaving this handful of millennia of conceptclamped humanity into the storm-driven flight of images as into "the dream of a shadow."<sup>14</sup> Now — the *spiritual* gaze into this abyss engenders an astonishment and a musing which, when it takes form and is grasped, is called metaphysical knowledge. In it, man comprehends himself as a double being: as bearer of spirit and as bearer of life. He feels, at the very least, even should he no longer be able to know it, that the spirit dwelling within him is a stranger in the world of happening, that the form of existence of conceivable things throws back to him only the world-piercing ray of the I addicted to persistence, and that actuality has long since slipped away from the judging being, even as he fancies he has captured it in judgement and fixed it into something possessable. These, too, are judgements; but such judgements for which the spirit receives both matter and formative impulse solely from the depth of life. If one wants a rounded formula: historical man stands under the double compulsion either to bind life within spirit or to loose spirit within life. According as spirit rules over life within him, or life over spirit, his questioning striving aims either at finding being within happening, or, supported by the sign-language of being, at finding its way back from being [p. 130] into the world of happening, unconceivable though it be. On the one path are gathered up and collected the facts and their relations; the other issues, from case to case, in the discovery of their essence. Whoever proceeds in the first way builds on the straight-rising Eiffel Tower of science, which is destined never to be finished; whoever proceeds in the second has entered a labyrinth with innumerable passages of innumerable direction, which, however, all run together in one and the same center: the essence of actuality, only ever to be lived. The one is progressive and logocentric in disposition, the other contemplative and biocentric. — If we survey the cognitive endeavors of historical humanity in their totality, they indeed stand, from the very beginning and among the most various peoples, under the sign of the preponderance of the logocentric spirituality over the biocentric, yet it is only within Christendom that this preponderance has been able to lead all the way to the exclusion of the latter by the former. On the whole, we in any case do not go wrong if we equate the logocentric with the basic disposition of science, the biocentric with the basic disposition of metaphysics, notwithstanding that no metaphysician of purely biocentric stamp has yet been found. —

<sup>14</sup> On page 129. — We recall *Goethe's* saying: "Thoughts return, convictions propagate themselves, states pass away irretrievably."

The supposed impartiality of the "search for truth" is a pious fraud, hatched by shallow reflection in order to cut off deep reflection's claim to science. There is so little an unintentional questioning that the state of questioning is, rather, the purest expression of spiritual "tending," and this stands inescapably in the service either of life or of the Logos. With the either-or of "true" or "false," one has decided nothing whatever yet as to for which need the system of findings is an instrument: whether of the will to the objectification of the world and to taking possession of it through the apprehending spirit, or rather of the will to the re-dissolution of the merely objectified and to the generation of the consciousness of the unpossessable essence. We do not conceal from ourselves that new questions at once demand to be heard, above all: to what extent this still deserves at all to be called a knowledge, which is really nothing but the conviction of the inconceivability of the actual and accordingly seems to amount to a renunciation of knowledge. We content ourselves, for the time being, with recalling that we have just now characterized the properly "world-view"-forming success of this pointing function of thinking, but hold it fitting to cast a glance at the peculiar [p. 131] -ity of the modes of procedure that we must employ in order to arrive at such insights.

The individual judgement, as already noted, can be the object of both shallow and deep reflection, and in particular each of the two is capable of making use of the judgements of the other as well. If I use the number-concept created in prehistoric times in order to form the equation "two times two is four," I have found a shallow truth with the help of deep truths; if, conversely, I use the shallow truths of arithmetic to fathom the essence of unity, I have at least taken the direction toward the unveiling of a finding lived experience, and would, even with the Eleatic denial of happening, still find myself in possession of an error of the character of depth, which holds out more prospect of fertilizing the formation of knowledge meant here than a thousand shallow truths. Yet the possibility, fundamentally present, of mutual help must not let us overlook that the goals of the two kinds of reflection lie far apart from each other, and would certainly have entailed two wholly different branches of the development of knowledge, had it ever succeeded for deep reflection to explain itself about itself as clearly as its late sister, science. In the first place, namely: if for deep reflection alone the fact holds for what it really is, for the point of orientation with regard to the stream of happening, then it must draw the *choice* of the point solely from the *pulse-beat of lived experience*. Through this, facts can become important to it which have no significance for science, whereas, conversely, many findings of science lose all value for it. — In the second place, the nevercompletable striving of shallow reflection for the ascertainment of objective relations turns, for deep reflection, into a mere aid toward the solution of the question of the building-element of actuality, which compels acts of objective relating. It will wish to learn whence it comes that we carry the relation of cause and effect into the temporal one-after-another, the relation of substrate to its properties into the spatial side-by-side; but it will not hold this to be a deepening of knowledge, but rather the effect of a will to the expansion of the human sphere of power, when the effort at cognition exhausts itself in the condensation of causal chains. — Thirdly, finally (and this is by far the most sharply dividing point), there sink for it to the level [p. 132] of almost a mere makeshift of method, experience and "induction," while self-reflection by way of the *examination of names* is raised to the chief instrument of the formation of knowledge! Before we turn our particular attention to the latter point as well, let what has been said above be illustrated by an example.

The number-speculations of the Pythagoreans are, from the standpoint of science, actually sheer madness; from the standpoint of metaphysics, on the other hand, they are the thoroughly intelligible attempt to comprehend actuality out of the interweaving of an essentially boundless with an essentially bounding principle — an attempt of which we have to this day not in the least decided how far it succeeded. This emerges somewhat more clearly if we compare with those supposedly fantastic assumptions the by no means doubtful ignorance in which we currently find ourselves regarding a quite objective question. Modern scholarship, in its undertaking to explain the almost universally human "sanctity" of the number three, has, among other things, arrived at the famous solution that human beings were for many millennia able to count only as far as two, and took the next counting-step, when it was finally achieved, with such lasting emotional emphasis that threeness thenceforth remained something sacred. But no modern scholarship has so much as raised the question which Romanticism believed it had to answer in the affirmative: whether the tripartite division might not indeed actually constitute a feature of the apparent universe. There are, to pick out only a few instances, three dimensions of space, not more than three kinds of temporal relation (past, present, future), three livable basic states of life (waking, dreaming, sleeping), three individual stages of existence (at least in the case of woman, most sharply delimited by the onset of puberty and the climacteric), three intuitively distinct forms of cohesion of matter (solid, liquid, gaseous), three soul-different kinds of living being (plant, animal, human), three objectively groundable grammatical genders (der, die, das — not identical with, but similar to, man, woman, child), three "germ layers" of every embryo, three sensibly distinguishable parts of corporeality (head, trunk, limbs), three main sections of the legs and arms (thigh, shank, foot; upper arm, forearm, hand), three finger-joints, three sharply standing-out basic lines of every human palm, three main convolutions of the human frontal brain, three main parts of every insect's thorax, and so on. We do not fail to recognize that such considerations could lead as far as [p. 133] the domain of astrology; but we are wary of assuming, without examination, that Chaldean and medieval astrology were versed only in false equations (quite apart from their practice of "nativities" and "prophecies"). The triads adduced are "facts"; but one notices at once that "science" would never do anything with facts of this kind; for that the three main lines of the human hand should stand in some, however remote, causal connection with the three dimensions of space is something not even he will wish to assert who should hold the *tripartite* articulation of a building-element of *actuality* to be demonstrable. But had he now succeeded in showing this, he would, as a metaphysician, go on to ask whether there is, for that threeness, a model which would enable him to ascertain its meaning, and, granted that he succeeded in this too, he would have obtained, for instance, the reagent for the reliable distinguishing of all merely apparent from genuine triads; whereupon he would, as we wish to note in passing, not only find at least one deceptive one among those we have enumerated above, but would also, for example, be able to sort out the true from the false in the table of dichotomies bequeathed to us by the Pythagoreans.

From a single example of this kind it should become clearer, better than with many words, that the motive as well as the formative means of thinking are different in the camp of science and different again in the camp of metaphysics. If the former today resembles a fortress armed with the heaviest ordnance, the latter resembles, at best, the gathering-places of homelessly wandering, ever more dwindling gypsies with their meager covered wagons. But were someone to point us, against this, to the high tide of philosophical publications, we should have to reply that we have been unable to discover in it the least content of genuine metaphysics, and cannot, even if we disregard the charlatanism that clamors today in every street, grant to the productions belonging to it anything approaching the rank that is due to the achievements of solid scientificity within its own limits. To furnish the counter-proof, however, we challenge him to name to us even a single "history of philosophy" which could seriously attempt, and would be in a position, to decide with any evidentiary force between truth and error in the Pythagorean dichotomies!

We have above called the examination of names the chief means of metaphysical formation of knowledge, and wish, for the present, [p. 134] at least to indicate the reasons for this, and, factually, to augment with a few especially convincing ones the evidence which our work has already offered in various forms. — Man would not be a thinking being, if he were not a speaking one. In order to hold fast a concept even in a single judgement, we must be capable of the re-recognition of the linguistic expression for it. Just as little as we have, in the face of the very same thing, twice the wholly identical lived experience, just as little do we produce twice the wholly identical sound, or receive twice the wholly identical impression, when we perceive it by hearing or read it by seeing. As the thing recurs identically in a temporal succession of appearances never wholly like one another, so does the concept in a temporal succession of sounds never wholly like one another. It is thus anchored two-sidedly in the image: there, in the appearing occasioning-ground of the matter; here, in the appearance of its sign. It would help me nothing to find the object in flowing actuality, did the experience of finding not have an expression peculiar to it in a distinctive way, which could signify the concept of the meant in just the same way as this signifies the object. As the impression is, as it were, the experience of the question for the seeking inclination, so is the speech-sound, for the finding, the experience of the answer. This indication suffices to make us certain that the name necessarily says something, too, of the finding lived experience: in one way in the original roots, and again in another in their derivative forms. If, then, the verbal garb is already for this reason a natural point of attachment for that direction of research which has set itself the goal of tracing back to the content of lived experience, its orienting power comes fully to light only when we consider against what aberrations it promises, from the outset, to preserve us. — The sense of a word tends, in the course often of mere decades, quite certainly of centuries, to shed certain component parts of meaning, taking on others instead, while at the same time the embodying sound grows on according to its own law, as soon as the original bond has become in some measure loosened. Of the consequences, we are concerned here only with the tendency of the concept to remove itself ever further from the intuitive content of the language-forming lived experience. There is, in particular, no linguistic sign for the non-intuitively abstract whose meaning would not be intuitive, as soon as we take it literally! In many cases this can now be ascertained only by the history of language, as when we establish that "Zweck" [purpose], formerly "Zwecke," originally meant the peg [p. 135] in the middle of the target at which one meant to shoot. In numerous others, mere reflection on the content of the name suffices to get on the track of the course by which its meaning developed. "Object," "representation," "impression," "to remember," "to conceive," "to apprehend," "reason" are transparent examples of this. — If we now surrender ourselves uncritically to inherited concepts, we are in danger of seeking actuality, as it were, in the wrong place, and of filling the gaps in our lived experience with the products of the appropriating labor of the logos.
