For one must know that experiences of unreflective primordiality are granted to man scarcely beyond the first seven years of his life, and that from then on he almost exclusively has "experiences" — which is to say, he still lives through something only insofar as it occurs in relation to objects for which he possesses *named concepts*!

Scientifically one might replace "understanding" with the capacity for apprehension or the capacity for judgement; one would do full justice to everyday usage only if one let apprehensions or judgements refer primarily to states of affairs in the external world. Of the capacity for experience — as, with regard to this, we would have to call it — it is customary to say, with everyone's approval, that it draws upon "life" and thereby brings about successes of knowledge that are thoroughly and fundamentally superior to "book-learning." It is indeed indisputable that the character type of the "experienced man of the world," and likewise that of the "empiricist," differs considerably from the type of the "bookworm" — only, precisely, not through any greater nearness to life on the part of his store of knowledge. To see this, let us examine the much-vaunted "experience" somewhat more closely, though leaving aside the earliest years of childhood, in which the spirit of the personal self is indeed still able to make contact with actuality outside of concepts.

I would never arrive at the meaningful use of even a single word, if I had already forgotten its meaning as soon as I had grasped it; never at the understanding of a sentence heard or read, unless the apprehension of each word were borne up by the apprehension of the words already gone by; never at the understanding of a book, were the content of pages one through nine not still spiritually present in me while reading the tenth page; but likewise never at any experience whatever without the presence of knowledge, already previously acquired, concerning the meaning of objects. Of this much, at least, there is no doubt: whatever experiences I am having r i g h t n o w [p. 136] whatever experiences I am now having, they rest upon the deposit of experience left by the whole of my life thus far. But that, in turn, rests unfailingly upon that other deposit of experience which was instilled into me, before I myself had even begun to have experience independently, through the transmission of my mother tongue! It was not I who discovered the difference between day and night, between water and air, between plant and animal; rather, I merely rediscovered it, compelled by the names for these things, in which the researching and finding of a prehistory tens of thousands of years long lies consolidated, and whatever I may in future observe and learn that is new about plants or animals as a botanist or zoologist, it rests, without prejudice to its truth or its usefulness, no differently upon phylogenetic pre-judgements than, moreover, every experience I make rests upon the residue of all the experience of my own life gone by, or than my understanding of the last line of a letter rests upon the continued presence of the sense of the first. Nor would I certainly have the same experiences of plants and animals were I by chance a member of a "primitive people" that, for instance, did not linguistically distinguish plant from animal but instead distinguished the living from the unliving. According to a saying of Hobbes: homo animal rationale, quia orationale [man is a rational animal, because a speaking one]. Language is, according to W. v. Humboldt, "the formative organ of thought." "The words in which we think," remarks Max Müller, "are channels of thought which we ourselves did not dig, but which we find ready for our use." No one, however, has demonstrated the dependence in question more penetratingly than Geiger in his profound, unfinished work on "Origin and Development of Human Language and Reason." Philosophy, he says, "seeks to this very day the nature of beings . ., that have no other actuality and independent existence than in the intuitions of a distant past, as they live on in those wondrous sounds" (p. 100); indeed, "it is not something born from the womb of the surrounding present that determines our will by a stimulus, our belief by an intuition, our conceiving by an appearance, but rather it is the prehistoric world, from the very beginning down to the present moment, that acts, believes, thinks, and feels within us, and behind us, not beside us, lies the key to the riddle within us and around us and of all existence. Ground and source" (p. 108)

Of one who acquires his knowledge chiefly from books, it is customary to say that he has learned his trade. But however the reading of the small books may differ from the reading of the great book called the world— [p. 137] —called, learning and mere learning take place in both cases, and the shared schoolmistress is called the mother tongue! To be sure, learning it demands of everyone who learns it a renewal, in himself, of language-creating processes; but renewal does not coincide with original creation. At the moment of discovery, the discoverer is a "pathbreaker," the first to "strike out" in a direction (1); the learner, by contrast, receives along with the words the directions in which his entire understanding of the world will henceforth move. To have experience means to learn, and to learn means "to orient oneself by something." Experience rests on a spiritual gift for adaptation, and the *metaphysically* direction-giving power is, for the man of the world just as much as for the bookworm, the inherited language.

If, by contrast, the discovering genius comes into immediate contact with a feature of actuality not yet thought of before, then the precondition for this indeed lies in a gift of nature that no one passes on by teaching and no one gains by learning; but the precondition for removing the obstacles to finding is not, in the same way, a natural gift! Rather there exists, as far as we can see, at least one methodical means for bursting the fetters of conceptuality in which all our thinking and striving was forged, long before we awoke to a clear consciousness of ourselves — namely, reflection on the content of names! — It is not for nothing that the warlike fanfares of the second Bacon, in whose company empiricism first entered the arena of the spirit, are directed above all at the fight against the "idols" of names! The result has been that no direction of thought since Confucius has been led more willingly on a leash by conceptual schemata than the word-blind cult of experience, none has more fatally misjudged nature than fact-believing "naturalism"!

The "genius of language," were it a sentient being, would scarcely fail to note, and not without malicious pleasure, that precisely those who are most inwardly convinced of the mechanical constitution of the universe daily and unwittingly testify to the anthropocentric origin of their belief when they take extra-human nature to be governed by l a w! Were they to look at the name itself rather than merely at the communicative purpose attached to it, they would have to notice at once that "laws" require a person who lays them down, and, in turn, other persons who obey them, and perhaps they would then [p. 138] also discover the lawgiver in the shape of the human logos, who, with the aid of cleverly adapted formulas, takes possession of a nature that is wholly and entirely ignorant of law. Indeed, mere consideration of the word "lawfulness" ought to suffice to teach us that nothing of the sort can exist in an actuality which is the actuality of happening! Or does one take it for chance that precisely this word had to serve to drive out the fickle demons when one began to organize nature and fate scientifically? Then let one look at the "fruits" by which, fittingly enough, every belief is known: at the canalized rivers, at the thinned-out forests set in rows, the machine-captured waters, winds, and electricities, at the murder-weapons that fetch the eagle from the ether of heaven, the whale from the polar sea, and the last elephant from the last of the primeval forests, and with whatever else science digs its traces into the face of the earth! "Laws of nature" reach exactly as far as the field of play of the human will reaches (astronomy notwithstanding!), and it goes without saying, of course, that one could not master that from which one had not overheard some features of its real constitution! But by exactly as much as the essence of a thing is more and other than what I must ascertain about it in order to make it a tool for my purposes, by exactly so much is the *ousia* of world-happening more and other than what can be transposed from it into the legal language of the logos. Moreover, there is no chance in the coining of names. Not even the deliberately purposive nomenclatures of science, let alone words of common use, such as this one is, are ever found or borrowed without the secretly selecting inclination of the "unconscious." To make matters more than sufficiently clear, the historical proof can be furnished that the concept of the law of nature was originally created to give shape to the belief that an ordering reason rules over the entire universe, and only after this belief had been absorbed did it lose its meaning as a law of reason. We shall have to deal at length, later, with the Stoics, who, if not the first inventors, were at least the most eloquent agitators of the belief in question, and we therefore confine ourselves here to three utterances that lay bare the connection. Zeno: the primal matter "is governed throughout by the universal reason, which is also called the law of nature"; further: "the universal law, which consists in right reason . . , is identical with . . the ruler of the order of the world." Chrysippus: "the law of nature is [p. 139] the world-reason (!)." — We now set beside this merely critical point a positive example as well. — To call something "senseless" and to call something "purposeless" is, at present, almost the same thing, and the "sense" of a thing usually amounts to its serviceability in the cause of rational intentions. The "direction of sense," too, points in the first instance to the prevailing disposition of the will. In the teleological interpretation of the world, the content of this and related concepts is at work in the same way as, in the mechanistic interpretation, the concept of law; hence one may call the one the metaphysical projection outward of the conceiving I, the other that of the willing I. But whereas the word "law" betrays to us the person-dependence of all so-called laws, the name "sense" conversely gives us to understand that we have falsified the essence of its meaning through rationalizing, whenever we seek it in the neighborhood of the determining grounds of the will. Scarcely any of those who today speak of "sensible" or "senseless" tend to notice that this very same sound also means the bodily senses, the messengers of images at least in the waking state, thereby pointing to "sensibility" as the true substratum of "sense"! Far from locating "sense" in rationality, the finding experience instead places it in the impression-giving *appearance*! If the wisdom of the word "law" guards us against the error of taking laws to be actual outside the spirit, then the deeper wisdom of the word "sense" not only lets us avoid the teleological detour, but also helps us to find the sense-filled soul where it actually is, namely in the world of appearance.

From the extreme right of philosophy, against which we first turned in order to make room for determining the concept of life, the course of our examination has led us imperceptibly to the extreme left, and has in doing so already let pass by the most important facts, which suggest to us that we should count both sides among shallow reflection and take as mere apparent oppositions the parties of "idealism" and "materialism" (more correctly: mechanism) — which have been feuding for centuries — or, what amounts to the same thing, of "rationalism" and "sensualism." Both stand on the ground of the judged world, and both fail to recognize the lived world. The party of the right is enchanted by the knowing spirit, the party of the left by the knowable being, but neither of the two has any consciousness of the living life, without which the relating activity could not be thought at all. Clever minds have pointed out, jokingly, that one arrives at "idealism" if one reads the famous [p. 140] equa-tion esse = percipi from left to right; but at "materialism" if one reads it from right to left. Before we devote a longer pause to this latter as well, let us cast a glance at the peculiar intermediate standpoint which, since Kant, has perhaps enjoyed the most approval among thinking minds, because it creates the appearance of having corrected, if not abolished, the twofoldness of these ways of looking at things from a higher point of view; for which purpose, however, the Kantian concept of space will already fully suffice us.

[p. 141]

### Zweiter Abschnitt — Der Kantische Irrtum — Second Part — The Kantian Error

#### 15. Kapitel — Der subjektivierte Raum — Chapter 15 — Subjectivized Space

We do not venture to decide how often other readers, too, of the certainly acute, but in our view never profound, Critique of Pure Reason have been unable to suppress an immediate astonishment at the fact that a thinker who explicitly sets out to find the ground that makes knowing possible transposes what he believes he has thereby ascertained into knowing itself! When Nietzsche remarks in Beyond [Good and Evil] that Kant, asked how knowledge is possible, answered "by virtue of a faculty," he is at any rate voicing, in perhaps a somewhat drastic form, the very astonishment we mean. We may hope to make ourselves understood most quickly if we point at once to a difficulty in which Kant sees himself entangled from the very outset and which he never manages to master, although it repeatedly demands a hearing and evidently gives him no small trouble. In order for me to perceive colors, I must have a faculty of sight; in order to perceive sounds, a faculty of hearing; in order to perceive scents, a faculty of smell, and so on. Now if such and related faculties do not yet in themselves contain the conditions for the specific properties to be apprehended also displaying a spatial characteristic, then I am free to further associate with them a faculty of spatial intuition. But the very condition which I thus find it necessary to assume, in order to make the perception of something extended thinkable, however different it may be from the sensory dispositions, nonetheless agrees with them entirely [p. 142] in this: that they constitute an indispensable side of the capacity for experience in general. If it pleases me to call such dispositions an a priori, then I must call each and every one of them an a priori; if, conversely, it pleases me, with regard to the so-called a posteriority of the contents of experience, to dispute the a priori, then I have not the slightest reason to exempt spatial intuition from this. We shall hear presently what moved our epistemologist nonetheless to do so in so decided a fashion; here we are concerned, for the moment, with the fact that the reference to the necessity of a capacity for experience merely paraphrases the state of affairs already contained in the very concept of experience itself, according to which a "subject" as that which relates unfailingly belongs to the "object" as that which is related, and a capacity for relating belongs to whatever is capable of being related at all. If, with regard to all merely possible objects of the external world, I fix my eye on the fact that there must correspond to them, to speak in Kantian language, a "capacity of my senses to be modified," so that these senses can be modified by them, then a "modification of sensibility" is just as much the "intuition" of space as it is the "sensation" of a color, and it becomes altogether impossible to see what could lend the former the special character of apriority, if the latter, as we are emphatically assured, lacks it. Self-contradictions in a thinker are regularly the signal that his wishes have come into conflict with the facts and that, in order to settle this, he has fallen prey to a substitution, whether by identifying the different or by multiplying the identical. Our foregoing investigations have put us in a position to state at once, too, which substitution is here in question.

Kant's investigations are directed, only in appearance, at the ground that makes knowing possible, but in truth at knowing itself, for the purpose of distinguishing two cognitive faculties, of which one is supposed to guarantee only "empirical," the other, by contrast, universally valid and necessary truths. In doing so he spins further the misguided thought of Leibniz concerning the two classes of truth, the vérités de fait and vérités de raison. We leave aside, however, the logical untenability of a division of judgements according to degrees of truth, and note only that Kant, in supposing that he grasps, in the special power of conviction inherent in "apodictic" certainties, the condition of the formation of knowledge as such, has in view not the actuality of space at all, but solely the being of space, the object-of-thought [p. 143] space, the objective space, or what we call the space-object. For the assertion, so stubbornly maintained, of the apriority of spatial intuition in fact answers, or at least believes itself to answer, the question as to the cause of the inviolability of the basic judgements of mathematics, and the Kantian concept of space stands, from the outset, in the service of the aim of supplying the sufficient ground for the necessities of thought in geometry. The capacity of the spirit to be "modified" by something spatial is consequently transformed, for him, into a capacity rather to produce the spatial in exactly the same way as he does indeed produce the points, lines, and figures that divide up space. In doing so, however, he confuses — in a manner which, by virtue of its extraordinary paradoxicality, can both baffle and seduce, and certainly constitutes the "charm" of his reflections — the *alienating lived experience* with the *ascertaining* *apprehension*.

In view of the downright hypnotic effect that his doctrine of the consciousness-dependence of space has produced, it may not be superfluous to repeat briefly the reasons that lead us to reject it without qualification. First, then: if we carried space in our "mind" — and that is what it ultimately amounts to — then we would also be able to find it nowhere else but there, since the finding act indeed ascertains, but in no way alienates. But then, secondly, we would have made the mind, to which Kant attributes precisely non-spatiality, willy-nilly into a spatial fact, indeed strictly speaking into a volume, which could no longer be distinguished from a bodily volume. It is the peculiarity of the spatial that it cannot be inside anything that is not itself in turn spatial and hence, for its part, again "in" space: whatever encompasses space is always also encompassed by space! If one objects, on the other hand, that Kant did not really place space "in" the mind at all, but merely the condition whereby, by virtue of the mind, space "comes to appearance," then this assumption too — which is, incidentally, quite unthinkable — leads to the very consequence just shown, and hence to self-cancellation. For if spatial intuition is attached to inwardness as a condition of its being experienced, then it, too, must be found within space, exactly as it finds a stone or tree or brook within it; whereby it would, however, be robbed of the very mark required to establish its difference from objects of that kind, and hence also, completely, of the capacity to make these, in turn, "appear" spatially in the first place. — Here, [p. 144] thirdly, can we no longer escape the circle in which anyone moves who believes himself entitled to use the preposition "in" for the purpose of deriving space, without noticing that he has, with it, already presupposed the very thing to be derived. For it is only by letting "sensibility" be doubly directed — toward "outer" and toward "inner" — or by adjoining an "inner sense" to the "outer sense," that Kant is able to set a merely temporal "mind" over against the spatio-temporal thing. Had not a thousand-years-long history of logocentric thinking made minds trained in scholastic meditation compliant toward every kind of subjectivization of actuality, it would be inexplicable that the manifest sleight of hand should have gone unnoticed even for a single moment, which supposedly critical idealism perpetrates when it grounds the origin of the opposition between space and time on the difference between two faculties, whose characteristics it unmistakably borrowed from that very opposition! The sentence with which Kant opens his "metaphysical exposition" of the concept of space — "by virtue of outer sense . . we represent objects to ourselves as o u t s i d e us and all of them together in space" — is an unambiguous tautology, since there can be no talk at all of externality as the distinguishing mark of a "sense" that represents it, except with regard to a spatially extended world in which the said "sense" has its place. We hardly need add that, with the destruction of the actuality of the spatial, the distinction between "spontaneity" and "receptivity" likewise collapses. There is no spiritual doing except in relation to impressions of "sensibility" that have actually occurred, and there is still less any impression-capable "sensibility" without the being-outside-one-another that alone makes it possible, in the first place, to distinguish a receiving from a giving! Should a Kantian wish to object that this is exactly what the master expressed with his much-discussed antithesis, "thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind," we would have to remark emphatically that such word-combinations as "empty thoughts" and "blind intuitions" belong entirely to the class of those about wooden iron. Thoughts without content are not so much empty as, rather, simply incapable of existing at all; intuitions without concepts, however, are indeed capable of existing, but in that case by no means blind! (Compare the animal world!) — Although we have not yet brought the problem of "inner" and "outer" actuality to its conclusion, let it nonetheless be permitted to anticipate at least so far as is necessary, in order, fourthly, [p. 145] to demonstrate the untenability of the mark which, according to Kant, is supposed to guarantee the concept of inwardness. "Receptions" are things undergone, and everything undergone runs its course in time. But now let one try to represent something real which, although exposed to temporal influences that must of course arise outside it in order for the change to be experienced as an "influence," is nonetheless something absolutely spaceless, and one will confirm the impossibility of the undertaking — not merely a factual impossibility, but even a conceptual one. As should already be clear from our earlier discussions, and as will be brought to certainty in what follows, space and time stand to one another in a relation of polarity, in such a way that neither a timeless space nor, equally, a spaceless time comes to "appearance." In despatializing inwardness, Kant has in fact also detemporalized it, and consequently has in view, not the experiencing inwardness alone capable of being affected, but the thinking inwardness, or consciousness; but since he nonetheless immerses this very consciousness in the stream of time, he suppresses the life-principle and puts spirit in its place — a consequence, indeed, no longer avoidable, of his proton pseudos [primal falsehood], the confusion of alienating lived experience with ascertaining judicial act. — The name "sensibility" serves only to conceal the fact that, in truth, the understanding has been endowed with the faculty whose function is Kant's "intuiting"; the name "receptivity," that the condition of the possibility of receiving, namely space, is instead produced by the receiving "mind"; and however express the disclaimer against assuming the conceptuality of this space may be, it must not deceive us as to the fact that it is exclusively the conceived space, or the space-object, that forms the object and motive of the "transcendental aesthetic"; with which we come to the fifth objection, decisive in itself already, which can be briefly formulated thus: it is completely false that objective space is one and the same as the actuality itself of spatial appearance. The space-object arises through acts of spatial delimitation. Just as certainly as the boundary of space is not, in turn, space, but something related to space, just as certainly the origin of what is already presupposed in the concept of the boundary of space — the boundless uniformity of spatial appearance<sup>15</sup> — cannot lie in the boundary apprehending spirit. Kant's "faculty of intuition" is the willing helpmate of the mathematics-practicing understanding, and, apart from that, a nothing.

<sup>15</sup> On page 145. — Whoever should doubt the soundness of our interpretation of the Kantian conception of space, we recommend for exact verification the following sentence from the "Transcendental Aesthetic": "Were it not the boundlessness in the progress of intuition, no concept of relations would carry with it a principle of the infinity of the same." Space is, then, according to Kant's view, infinite insofar as one cannot represent to oneself any space that is not part of a greater space, this again of a still greater one, that again of a still greater one, and because such a "*progress* of intuition" finds simply no limit. But in this way, in place of phenomenal or positive boundlessness, there is put logical or negative infinity, which consists merely in the *inability to be completed* of a "progress," a Kantian "synthesis." Consequently there is talk neither of intuitive space nor of intuition, but of the "formal" operation of dividing and composing in relation to an object that can be divided by no division and completed by no composition out of parts. His considerations, then, aim exclusively at space as an object of thought, and wholly fail to recognize the *experience of continuity* which, even *within* the limits that the act of apprehension has in each case drawn for it, guarantees to *every* space an *extra*-*subjective* boundlessness.

[p. 146] "All intuitions," he states verbatim, "are n o t h i n g to us and do n o t c o n c e r n u s i n t h e l e a s t, if they are n o t t a k e n u p i n t o consciousness . ." His "sensibility" and "imagination" are two entirely powerless arrangements without "transcendental apperception," which alone gives birth to a world out of the formless "matter" of those two.

Resting on the decisive fifth objection, we can combine our rejection with a concession that will admittedly give the Kantians little pleasure: the space of which the Critique of Reason speaks is indeed subjective; the actuality of the beingoutside-one-another, meanable only through co-relation, on the other hand, does not occur at all in the "transcendental aesthetic"! The space-thing situated beyond time, which remains left over, for the ray of the apprehending spirit piercing through it, in place of real space, is indeed no different, as thought-thing and reflected-back I, from all the other "proper" things of which we have treated at such length, and would unquestionably vanish with the vanishing of the spirits related to it. But the said relating would not have taken place at all, and there would then not even have been any assumption of a space-object, without the compulsion that befell the spirit from the lived experience of the being-outside-one-another of actuality. And here we do not fail at least to raise a question to be resolved only later, from which one may gather anew what the metaphysical disposition of mind means for the choice of the direction of research to be pursued.

If both, the space-object and any thing whatever, seem to agree in demanding the predicate of existence, then we naturally wish to know wherein, then, their fundamental difference consists. However the answer to this may turn out, it leads inescapably to differing features in the lived experience of actuality. If space-object and existing thing are merely compelled products of the objectifying activity of the I, then we must seek to investigate those differences of character in the experienced compulsions by which it comes about that we arrive, at one time, at the finding of objective space, and, at another, at the finding of the thing. Even the most modest result reached along this path, however, would allow us to give at least some account of a matter about which neither Kant nor any other epistemologist was accustomed to ask: concerning the necessity of the interconnection of space and time, and, in turn, concerning the relations of dependence of the thing on both of them.

[p. 147] Anyone who thinks his way even a little into our conception will find it, step by step, more astonishing that anyone could ever seriously have argued for the consciousness-independent actuality of the space-object, given the complete unanimity concerning the merely noumenal presence of the figures and theorems of Euclidean geometry! And he will be baffled to a possibly still higher degree when he has to notice that not a few, precisely among the most acute successors of Kant, see through entirely the sameness of the space of the "transcendental aesthetic" with the space of geometry, admittedly merely detached from it, and yet nonetheless take the actuality of the being-outside-one-another to be refuted by means of the — thereby admittedly indisputable — subjectivity of the latter. Lotze, mentioned by us several times above, for instance, begins his excellent discussion of the nature of space with the demolition of all the grounds that Kant believed himself to have adduced for the apriority of spatial intuition. He never tires of illuminating, with hints as ingenious as they are, admittedly, also dispensable, the absurdity into which we irretrievably fall as soon as we take mathematical points and lines for something actual independent of consciousness. But instead of concluding from this that real space — without which it would remain quite incomprehensible how one arrives at the representation of points and lines at all — cannot be grasped by means of constructions of that kind, he falls, with regard to their occasioning ground, into exactly the same error into which the Eleatics fell with regard to the actuality of motion, and believes himself, incomprehensibly, to have supplied after the fact the proof, still omitted by Kant, that it is not we who are in space, but space that is in us!

Yet let us reflect: that such lunacy was, and is, not merely seriously believed but even held to be proved, and that too with the help of grounds each of which would seem to us admirably suited to establishing the opposite — this is something incomprehensible only to one who has ceased to confuse: spirit with soul, thinking with lived experience, being without happening with actuality that is forever happening. Whoever suppresses soul, lived experience, and actuality from the outset will notice nothing at all of those difficulties, but will instead have exchanged them for the conviction that a state of affairs is demonstrable which becomes a kind of madness when measured against the sense of actuality that is peculiar to him too!

[p. 148]

#### 16. Kapitel — Vorläufiges vom Wirklichkeitssinn — Chapter 16 — Preliminary Remarks on the Sense of Actuality

We have emphasized the downright hypnotic effect of the doctrine of the consciousness-dependence of space, and in view of this we have just concluded our counter-discussion with the word "sense of actuality." For to declare the actuality of space to be a fact of consciousness means to derealize it, or to substitute for it the actuality — consisting only in concepts of it — of geometrical figures. We shall presently also touch upon that supposedly "intelligible" actuality of the occasioning ground of spatial appearance, with which "transcendental idealism" intends to compensate us for the despatialization of the world. Here we discuss briefly, too, that it is this very same misapprehension of the question of actuality on which idealism, with its proofs, and "positivism," with its refutations of them, rest! For we could not hope to have disturbed the hypnotic spell even a little, unless we called to mind the ways of fallacious reasoning, beginning with Descartes and culminating in a Berkeley or also a Schopenhauer, by means of which one sought to campaign for the credibility of idealism precisely by invoking the sense of actuality.

In the camp of positivism, the disposition we are combating is gladly mocked as "dream-idealism"; but as yet no positivist has come our way who has demolished the sham proof which the "dream-idealist" draws, for his fundamental conviction of the subjectivity of space, from the undeniable fact that even in dreaming one experiences a spatially extended actuality, and that upon awakening one nonetheless considers oneself entitled to assume its unreality outside the dreamer. From the dream-phantasm, it is said, it clearly follows that no spatial actuality need be given at all in order for the mere appearance of it nonetheless to arise. Countless times the following is further added: just as the dream-phantasm of space exists o n l y within the dreaming self, so [p. 149] too, among other things, is the "representation" of space within the representing self, indeed, the perception of space within the perceiving self. The assumption of a space existing independently of this thus proves to be superfluous, since it does not prevent one from converting it into a representation, if it is to be capable of being known at all. We do not yet decide the question of actuality here; but we show what a dreadful sophism lies hidden in utterances of this kind.

Since the character of person-independent actuality is indeed denied to dream-images by the waking person, but by no means by the dreamer, it is evidently not some quality of the dream-images themselves from which the supposed unreality of dream-space derives. Whatever the stage of their appearing — indispensable for dream-images too — may differ from the stage of sensory space, it is, just like the latter, experienced as real in the dream-state, and can therefore not serve to establish the opposite. Nor does the secretly coinvolved thought of the difference between the dream-spaces of different persons do any damage to the tone of actuality of dream-space, any more than damage is done to the tone of actuality of sensory space by the less obvious consideration that the sensory spaces of different bearers of impressions are likewise, in principle, different from one another. The experience of actuality is consequently p r e s u p p o s e d whenever someone astonishingly philosophizes about whether sensory space might not, after all, take place somehow in his soul. In substituting for the appearances of space a product of spirit, namely the space-object, idealism hopes to win us over to the — so to speak — merely conceptual nature of these appearances too, by bringing the sham actuality of dream-space into the field. Instead of posing the natural question, by what right the waking person denies dream-space an extra-personal actuality, idealism, with its thought-thing, strikes down the extra-personal actuality of spaces altogether, and hence of the world — not considering that no judgement could ever have been passed, no discourse conducted, concerning space, without the person-independence of its appearing — co-experienced by the recipient of any intuited images whatever — and thus likewise of the appearing of its very settings. — But if today it causes difficulty to think through something so simple, this rests on the fallacies to which idealism has accustomed us through its centuries-long cultivated confusion of perceiving with [p. 150] "representing"! Only now are we at the core of the non-thought which a Schopenhauer cast into the dazzling and blinding formula: "The world is my representation."

A child can understand that no two persons could ever have come to an understanding with one another about their experience of space, and that there would thus be no concept of space at all, unless those otherwise so very different experiences resembled one another at least in this: that each time there was co-experienced a compulsion — not stemming from the soul of the one experiencing it — to assume both the existence and the how-being of the spatiality experienced in each case. Whereas I can normally "represent" to myself whatever I please, at any time, it is by no means open to me to perceive something momentarily to be perceived otherwise than as it g i v e s i t s e l f. The impression-experience underlying the act of perceiving is something that befalls the bearer of the perception, and is, as such, taken up, received, undergone by him; whereas the occasioning ground of his representational activity is never undergone by the one representing, and, even in the exceptional case of the so-called compulsive representation, does not in any case bear the character of being alien to the soul. I may, indeed, while perceiving, turn my attention at will now to this, now to that side of the object; but I am wholly incapable of seeing blackness in place of the redness of a perceived cloth, or an unspatial "thing in itself" in place of the spatially extended actuality. I can "represent" to myself, at my own pleasure and whim, white or red or black cloths, and, in thinking, I can even look away from the spatiality of the world altogether. In the state of perceiving, by contrast, I am bound, from moment to moment, in an incomparable manner, according to which the binding factor proves to be something different from the soul.

In view of the confusion of spirit that the English concept of "idea" has conjured up, let it be stated here that "to represent" is nothing other than "to think," namely in the narrower sense of thinking of something, and with the secondary meaning of thinking of something intuitable. "To represent something to oneself" means: to visualize or call something before oneself in thinking. Accordingly, the laws of representing belong to a subdivision of the laws of thinking. Only what is thinkable can be represented, and the "movement" of representations depends wholly and entirely on the willed activity of thinking. From representations we must sharply distinguish self-arising *phantasms*, which [p. 151] take consciousness captive like an actuality and disempower the free will of the spirit — ordinarily interrupted by interludes of representing in the state of daydreaming, but uncontested rulers in the state of sleep-dreaming. We can "represent" to ourselves, with the clearest consciousness thereof, both the real and the unreal, whereas what is dreamed and what is fantasized claims full validity of actuality for as long as we are dreaming. How dream-space relates to perceptual space will occupy us elsewhere; here we develop, from what has been set forth, the essential marks of the representable.

If I represent to myself, with closed eyes, the space of the room in which I sit at my desk, then the represented (i.e. thought) obviously coincides no more with my activity of representing than the perceived space of the room coincides with my activity of perceiving. Moreover, my representing (= thinking) differs from my perceiving not merely in degree, but down to the very ground — only not, however, with regard to the object meant, which is, after all, presupposed to be just one and the same. Rather, when people unanimously tend to bemoan the paleness and gappiness of the contents of representation, this can only mean: that thinking presentification concerns the intuitable properties of objects of perception, which naturally prove themselves to be what they are only in being perceived; whence, on the contrary, precisely the opposite would be fit to arouse astonishment, for, while I think of the space of my room with closed eyes, I do after all perceive a formless black, and similarly in every case! The talk of the indistinctness of the contents of representation leaves no doubt that even in the case of presentifying arbitrary fabulous beings, the represented is measured against the object of perception. Representing thought, in other words, draws the whole of its intuitable material from occasions of impression! In contrast to this, idealism of every shade pays homage to the deluded belief in the sameness of representing thought with the process of perceiving, and it does this, to be sure, with the very best conscience, because, out of blindness to it, it has struck the impression-experience out of the process of perceiving, thereby leaving over of it only that in which it resembles mere thinking-of: the spiritual act! With this, however, it has itself removed the very ground from under the distinction that forms the starting point of its own reflections as well — [p. 152] that is, the distinction of perceiving from the perceived, of thinking from the thought, of consciousness itself from the object of consciousness. For if the world were a representation of the one representing it, then no one would henceforth know anything more of the world; but then no one, either, would know anything of himself as a being capable of representing. Whoever falsifies actuality into a fact of consciousness has thereby at once annihilated consciousness itself!

It would be unnecessary today to refute a Kant, if only one in every hundred of those who study the Critique of Pure Reason, or take note of its basic ideas from histories of philosophy, were to study just as thoroughly the Critique of Theoretical Philosophy which the Göttingen philosopher Gottlob Ernst Schulze published in two volumes in 1801; and it is surely one of the most curious proofs of the interestdependence of judgement that the utter demolition of Kant — accomplished sine ira et studio [without anger and without partiality] and with the richest expenditure of the most thoroughly considered counter-arguments, and moreover in classical form of presentation, more than four generations ago — has not in the least managed to shake the erroneous doctrines of the Königsberg thinker in the consciousness of educated people today. For this reason it seems fitting to us to conclude our counter-critique with a longer series of verbatim quotations from the second volume of the work named, which uproot chiefly the fundamental error of confusing perceiving with representing, but alongside this also certain conclusions drawn from it.

"In the state of intuiting external things, by contrast, what is present to the consciousness of the subject is not some modification located in it, but a thing wholly and entirely different from it and subsisting for itself, and indeed present with the utmost evidence." But representations by themselves never tend to become external objects for us. Accordingly, if all intuitions were mere representations, then it would be expected "that we should be conscious of no objectively present thing, differing from the existence of our subject, as present at all, but would think of everything external only as absent, so that consequently no difference at all could hold between the cognition of God and his omnipresence through mere concepts, and the cognition, through intuitions, of the world surrounding and present to us" (p. 30). — "By virtue of the supposed identity of external sensations with mere representations, joy and pain, which occur combined with mere representations, would have to be just as strong as the feelings of the pleasant [p. 153] and the unpleasant, which occur in us simultaneously with the sensations, and the mere representation of the presence of the scent of a rose would have to affect us just as pleasantly as the sensation of the scent itself — whereas the opposite occurs" (p. 37). — "For representations, according to the consciousness of them, constitute mere modifications of our I. They are no more present outside it, for it, than an existence separate from the existence of the I belongs to them. Now if the intuiting and sensing of external objects were originally the consciousness of a mere representing of these objects, then the I could originally be conscious of what it feels, sees, hears, tastes, and smells only as a particular modification of itself, and the whole external world would at first have to appear to it merely as a variation of the determination of itself" (p. 43). — "Even if one were to bring the omnipotence of the deity into play here, and wished to derive the origin of the concept of a truly objective existence of things from an immediate influence of that omnipotence on the human spirit, one would still be far from having said anything conceivable about the possibility of such an origin. For suppose the case that an intelligence possessed in its consciousness always only a consciousness of its own representing; then, even if the deity acted upon it, this effect would in turn constitute only a representation and a consciousness of mere modifications in it, and nothing at all would yet have been given in such a consciousness by which the intelligence could arrive at the concept of the objective existence of the deity and of other things besides the deity and besides the intelligence" (p. 45). — Ordinary human understanding "holds fast, in its confidence in the reality of this insight (namely, into the existence of external things), solely to what is immediately given of itself in the consciousness of external objects . . and knows nothing at all of an inference that is supposed to be present in intuiting and that is supposed to lead us, in the first place, to the knowledge that there are things which exist outside the cognizing subject. This inference was devised only in the schools of the philosophers and was added to the intuitions of external objects after these intuitions had been converted into mere representations, in order to explain how it comes about that we regard objectively existing things as real, notwithstanding that our consciousness is supposed to have before it merely mere representations of things" (p. 57). — "But the notion, stemming from Descartes, [p. 154] pretense that all cognition of external objects would have to be mediated by a representation of these objects, has, because it was applauded without anyone conducting exact investigations of it, caused all the attempts made since this philosopher to render external empirical knowledge comprehensible to take a wholly false direction; and that these attempts, instead of determining the grounds of the intuiting of external objects, aimed only at demonstrating the grounds of those representations, related to external objects, out of which representations external experience is supposed to consist" (p. 76). — "The grounds of truth of mathematics are to be sought in the intuitions that are laid beneath its concepts . ., so that the intuitions of mathematics do not serve merely, say, to clarify the concepts . . but are absolutely indispensable for proving the truth of mathematical judgements" (p. 189). — "The fixed order in external objects can be explained just as well from the mode of operation of a passive faculty of representation as from an a priori. For one may very well assume that this faculty first receives its whole direction and determination in its mode of operation only through the impressions made upon it, so that, by virtue of such impressions, it is also compelled to present the manifold of the representations received to consciousness in a lasting manner" (p. 193). — Through mere subsumption of representations under concepts of the understanding, no relation whatever to a really existing thing can ever be produced. "Just as little can it be assumed that, through the combination of sensory representations with concepts of the understanding, the consciousness of those representations . . is transformed into the consciousness of an object different from the . . states of the subject." Rather, one would be inclined to think, quite to the contrary, that, in view of the spontaneity required for this, these representations would appear as products of arbitrary will, and that thereby all delusion "concerning the existence of present . . objects, which might perhaps have been occasioned by perception, would be wholly destroyed!" (pp. 276–277). — "The most peculiar idea underlying the idealism set up in the Critique of Reason is really this: that all being present for us . . arises out of thinking, and that whatever is, really is something only for the understanding, according to the particular concepts lying within it." But if one takes this thought seriously, "then no actuality at all remains, not even [p. 155] the actuality of thinking, . . but what we call the inner and outer world is then only a sum of representations connected with one another, whose entire actuality in turn consists only in a concept of it" (p. 512). — Kant's idealism is no better than Berkeley's. For: "whether the origin of external experience can be made comprehensible more easily from the influence of things in themselves, wholly unknown to us, upon our mind, than from the efficacy of God upon that very same mind, this surely requires no investigation" (p. 548). — Had the Critique of Reason wished to proceed consistently, it would have had to let the world arise out of purely rational grounds alone. "One must therefore at the very least confess that those who have attempted to give the transcendental explanation of the origin of an objective world in this manner have not at all become apostates from the ideas about the transcendental that lie in the Critique of Reason, but have merely made complete use of these ideas, and have thereby also been able to avoid the contradictions into which one unavoidably falls when one still admits, into the transcendental-idealist manner of explaining the world, something of the doctrines peculiar to metaphysical realism" (p. 701).

Whoever has seen through the utter untenability of the doctrine of the subjectivity of space need not go on to prove that of the subjectivity of time as well; for a spatial actuality that would at the same time be outside time is unthinkable. Sufficiently conclusive grounds against it have, moreover, already been advanced from other quarters.

[p. 156]

#### 17. Kapitel — Überleitung zum Begriff des Schauens — Chapter 17 — Transition to the Concept of Beholding

We leave the Kantian concept of space with a reference to the extremely confusing usage that arises from the fact that our thinker, in keeping with his interchange of being and actuality, calls precisely objects "appearances" . The world of so-<sup>16</sup> called appearances, that is, with which he deals exclusively, is indeed the world of objects, whose logocentric origin we have illuminated. But because, according to his doctrine, the spirit-alien medium of continuity, through which it comes to "appearance," itself belongs to the object (or, if one prefers, to "the appearance insofar as it is thought as an object according to the unity of the categories"), there must evidently be yet another object, in relation to which his object first becomes "appearance"; from which it then follows that precisely actuality receives the form of the object, or of the "thing in itself." With this the following has come about since the Eleatics: the incomprehensible happening has become a moment of comprehensible being, the phenomenal a property of the noumenal, actuality as such the product of a supra-personal spirit which, in us, as it were rendered finite, emerges only in a relating capacity and requires, for this, a sensibility burdened with space and time, as that in which the sole truly present object scatters apart into the sham world of a manifold of objects. The hidden intention of this ideologism perhaps nowhere comes to light more clearly than on the occasion of the remark that our capacity for grasping is confined to appearances for the reason that sensory intuition naturally depends on something already given, whereas at least the possibility remains open of a "primal being" whose "intellectual intuition" (!), by means of an intuitus originarius [originary intuition], likewise also produces the intuited object — understood, of course, as much materially as "formally." One was, accordingly, in [p. 157] full right to call the "thing in itself," or the "primal being," now also by its name (however wrong one was to actually take it for the creator of the world!), and one meant, in fact, one and the same thing, and disputed far more about words than about the matter itself, when one preferred, by turns, to say instead: "I," "consciousness as such," "the Absolute," "spirit," "will," "transcendental reason," or "God."

<sup>16</sup> On page 156. — One eases one's understanding of Kant's scholastically cumbersome, in many places confused, and by no means self-consistent terminology quite enormously as soon as one keeps constantly and sharply before one's eyes that, without exception, it is erected upon the following fundamentally erroneous equation: actuality = being = object (of sensible intuition) or thing = appearance. Of the many dozens of passages that could be adduced as proof of this, only a few of the most pregnant ones shall be cited here, and we may leave it to the reader to establish, in each case, their relation to the four terms of the equation. "*Appearances* are the only *objects* that can be given to us immediately, and that in them which relates immediately to the object is called *intuition*" (Kehrbach edition in Reclam's Universal-Bibliothek, p. 122; all letter-spacings ours). ". . Without the relation to an at least possible consciousness, appearance could never become for us an object of cognition, and would thus *be nothing* for us, and because it has in itself no objective reality and exists only in cognition, *be nothing whatever*" (p. 130). ". . If everywhere we have to do only with appearances, it is not merely possible but also necessary that certain concepts a priori should precede the empirical cognition of objects. For as appearances they constitute an *object*, Notes — . . which *is merely in us*, because a mere modification of our senses is nowhere to be met with outside us" (p. 137). — In view of such a passage, dropped in the second edition of the "Kritik der reinen Vernunft," to which many similar ones could again be added, surely only a quite blindly reverent Kantian could still doubt that Schopenhauer was right when he saw one motive for the later deletions in Kant's concern for the originality of his system, after he had been reproached — and, we think, not without reason — with the charge that "his doctrine was merely refurbished Berkeleyan idealism"! — "Reality *is* .. that .. whose concept in itself indicates a being (in time)" (p. 146). "The schema of *actuality* is *existence* at a determinate time" (p. 147). "The real, that which corresponds to sensations in general, .. represents only something whose concept in itself contains a being, and signifies nothing but the synthesis in *an empirical consciousness* in general" (p. 165). "All appearances *contain* the persistent .. as the object itself, and the changeable as a mere determination of it, i.e., a way in which the object exists" (p. 174). "The transcendental use of a concept in any principle is this: that it is referred to things in general and in themselves; the empirical use, however, when it is referred merely to appearances, that is, to objects of a possible experience" (p. 223).

All non-ideologists in any way capable of judgement (among them, once again exemplary, Schulze) discovered early on the astonishing contradiction that lies in making a "thing in itself," however more precisely it may be designated, into the cause of the world of appearance, while at the same time, with Kant, attaching the thought of causality to the very same arrangement by virtue of which alone there are appearances at all, for the human being burdened with it! Yet it is not enough to deny the "thing in itself" the capacity to cause appearances; one has, rather, to recall without reservation that the statement, a "thing in itself" can come to appearance, is exactly as meaningful as if one were to say that nothingness comes to appearance! If the "thing in itself" — merely a new name for Parmenidean being, or for the deity of negative theology, and in fact an actuality-analogous mirroring of "spirit in itself" — demands, as required, the exclusion of all determinations to which the impetus might come from the world of appearances, then it is, in relation to that world, a nothing, with regard to which its convertibility into an "appearance" cannot merely not be thought, but must even be thought as impossible to think. Every attempt to stamp it as the bearer of appearance would inevitably chain it to the manifoldness that already characterizes the individual appearance, and, still more, the spatio-temporal immensity of that appearance, and would thus falsely smuggle, into what is absolutely devoid of constitution, the of course determined (because determining) preconditions of innumerable differences of property. But if, in such straits, one managed to pluralize the "thing in itself" (as it were, for household use) and, with perfect equanimity, to replace the multiplicity of appearances so emphatically abolished by an equally great multiplicity of "intelligible" places and characters, then this expresses a degree of absurdity measured against which belief in ghosts becomes a very harmless aberration of the understanding. If ideologism wishes to avoid this cliff of imbecility, however, it leads, when thought consistently through to the end, [p. 158] in the end, unfailingly, to itself ad absurdum: for if space and time were indeed merely forms of intuition, it would nonetheless stand fixed that their cause, or condition, or occasioning ground, must precisely not be sought in the intelligible "thing in itself"; whereby not only would a metaphysical duality of actualities, the phenomenal and the noumenal, be conceded, but also the irreducibility of the former to the latter!

As certainly as the Kantian attempt at a solution of the space-time problem has failed, just as certainly is its author owed the credit, through the incomparable decisiveness with which he undertakes it, of having tied every further advance of epistemological inquiry to the answering of a question that leads by the most direct route into the world of images. His effort to ground the act of knowing on what he calls "intuition," and to locate, in turn, the distinguishing constitution of intuiting in its receptivity to space and time, ought indeed to have led beyond Eleaticism, had not the said intuition already been knowledge, and the intuited already objective space (alongside objective time). But the ground that makes knowing possible cannot in turn be knowledge, but must lie in lived experience, and the actuality of space and time cannot already have objectivity, but must belong to the content of what is lived through. Accordingly, our answer to the question he poses himself diverges from his in the following way. We deny, first of all, that it would be possible to separate from one another: whether real space from real time, or, from their spatio-temporal character, the data of sensibility. There are no experienced colors, sounds, scents, temperatures without spatio-temporal character, no experienced space that would not be actualized in data of sensibility and, with them, subject to the flow of time, no experienced time except insofar as it appears in the change of images. But if it is thereby established that we must look away — from space, in order to find time; from time, in order to find space; from both, in order to find the data of sensibility; in short, from the mutually interpenetrating actuality of all of them, in order to be able to objectify each for itself — then we shall no longer imagine that the primal appearance of the temporal stream of images is, rather, pieced together out of the "matter" of so-called contents of sensation and out of the "forms of intuition" of space and time; whereby then [p. 159] at the same time the opinion is rejected as utterly absurd that any kind of conceptual composition could bestow upon the object to be found the character of being-outside-us, unless the compelling actuality already possessed it by virtue of an alienating lived experience.

If we henceforth call the lived experience, insofar as it gives us the stream of images, a "beholding lived experience," then the unfortunately unavoidable similarity of name with "intuiting" must not lead us to lose sight of the fundamental differences between the two processes. What Kant calls intuition is simply perception, that is, the act, resting upon an alienating lived experience, by whose aid we find things; but how we ourselves intend to use the word "intuition" shall be explained only in the next section. By beholding lived experience, however, or, more briefly, beholding, we understand the inward counterpart of the actuality of images, ceaselessly caught up in change, and thus a process that is itself temporal and wholly without deed, which is not merely unable to find things, but does not possess the capacity for finding at all. We must still set aside the question whether we have, besides this, some far more immediate knowledge of the experience of beholding, which hitherto we have only been able to disclose by analyzing the process of cognition; but we attach at once, to the considerations to which the examination of the Kantian doctrine gave us occasion, a negative decision of the greatest importance, and thereby enter upon the path indicated above, directed toward the investigation of the lived experience of actuality. Through whatever means we have become beings that actively perceive rather than merely passively behold, this much stands fixed: that on the basis of a merely beholding lived experience, the act of apprehension could not be accomplished. Without a world of spatio-temporal images there would, to be sure, be no world of spatio-temporally related things; but we do not yet see what could have brought it about that the poles were able to separate from one another, so as to be assigned to the two points of relation "subject" and "object," and thereby at once also to the two systems of relation, time and space. We suspect, therefore, that the lived experience of actuality must consist of at least two partial processes, of which we have so far only touched upon the process of beholding.

[p. 160]

### Dritter Abschnitt — Der sensualistische Irrtum — Third Part — The Sensualist Error

#### 18. Kapitel — Selbstwidersprüche des Sensualismus — Chapter 18 — Self-Contradictions of Sensualism

Although in the exceedingly numerous directions into which the logistic misconception of life diverges, the fundamental error is always the same, it nowhere emerges so wholly unveiled as in the sensualist direction: hence there has scarcely been a doctrine that has entangled its adherents so thoroughly in contradictions, and split them, on purely psychological grounds alone, into so many factions, as the theory of so-called sensation — not to speak of the thousandfold mutually warring varieties that arise once the physiological question is also taken into account. — Although we naturally cannot altogether avoid touching on certain basic conceptions of the psychology of sensation, it is nevertheless not that psychology which is our object, but the sensualist world-view, which admittedly shares with it no small range of views. Apart from that, what is properly to be understood by "sensualism" can, given the extraordinary confusion of concepts prevailing in the sensualist camp, only be indicated approximately and, so to speak, by estimate. Thus much, at any rate, should find the approval of all sensualists: the whole world consists of sensations, or, that is, of contents of sensation. Sensations are sense experiences or "receptions" by means of the senses. "Esse est percipi." Since most sensualists do not distinguish at all between the sensed and the sensing, the little game of question and answer that we now let follow takes equal account of the one and the other article of faith.

[p. 161] The sensations are in us; but is what is sensed also in us? Some answer yes and declare the outer world to be a bundle of "ideas" ("perceptions," "representations," "sensations," "impressions," etc.) with the special mark of spatiality; some answer no and conversely make the impression a function of that which gives the impression; still others say half yes, half no: what is smelled, tasted, heard, seen is in fact within us, whereas what is touched is outside us; what is objectively present is a materiality determined by density, extension, position, motion. Or: everything sensible has its place in space and time; are space and time, then, also sensed? Some say yes, at least space is in some sense co-sensed; others say no, such a thing is rather owed to a reflection that seeks to explain the simultaneity of impressions. Or: what is sensible is always also a state or property of enduring things; are these, too, sensed? Here most, presumably, say no; yet to the further question of where such things then come from, some declare them to be real substrates of which nothing further can in any case be known; others, bundles of ideas arising from the habitual association of representations; still others, rules of the connection of ideas inspired by God. Or: in order for something to be sensed, there must be a sensing subject; is this, too, sensed? Some answer that it is once again a wrongly reified bundle of ideas; others, that it is rather a (Cartesian) res cogitans. Or: in sensing, the sensing subject is passive or undergoing; does it also undergo the connecting of sensations? Some say yes, whence follows the "habit" of "associating"; others say no, this springs rather from a self-activity of the sensing subject. — The world is a bundle of representations, that which represents is likewise a bundle of representations, the bundle is again represented — the bundle is "given" through things, through matter, through God, and it is not given but rather thought in addition out of (evidently faulty) habit — representing is an undergoing, and representing is an activity of that which represents, and so on and so forth: one could go on like this for pages, and might in the end find the most incomprehensible circumstance of all to be that the theorists of sensation were and are borne along by the unshakeable conviction that they had, for the first time, replaced the word-juggling thought of scholasticism — indeed of practically all earlier philosophy — with a solid and, as it were, actuality-saturated research! The English may understand much; of philosophy, at any rate, they understand [p. 162] nothing. But if their supposed sensualism, mediated through France, has laid waste the continental spirit down to this very day, it might be difficult to decide where the more regrettable deficiency lies: in English shallowness or in the continental incapacity for sober critique. — We wish to show the error at its root; but since we shall bring our own solution only later, and must for the present content ourselves with setting up a postulate, we expressly state in advance that, in our conviction, the undoubtedly real life-function of sensing *has not yet been discovered*<sup>17</sup>. We must therefore ask, in the sense of our view, that a "so-called" always be understood as added to the supposed sensing that we now have to deal with.

<sup>17</sup> On page 162. — We ourselves, however, have already treated the problem of sensation programmatically in our work "Vom Wesen des Bewußtseins."

Since at least the original concept of sensation (that of a Locke, for instance) does not distinguish sensing from perceiving, we shall for the present use both in the same meaning. If, accordingly, what is sensed or "perceived" or perceived were, say, the colour red, it is advisable to recall from the outset that what is actually perceived is, in each case, something like a red raspberry, a red drop of blood, the red of evening. These are, first, three reds different not merely in number but in kind; second, reds of three different objects; and third, reds at three different places — from which it follows that, in order to arrive at "redness," we must have looked away, first from the location of the red thing, then from the thing itself to which the red belongs as an adherent or illumination colour, and finally from the particular kind of red in each case. Granted, then, that there is something in our lived experience that enables us to form the general concept "redness," or the still more general concept "colour," we shall nonetheless not look, within it, for an element or atom of this experience that combines with other atoms of experience into the in each case unique impression we receive from a red raspberry, a red drop of blood, the red evening sky; and we shall therefore harbour, in advance, the suspicion against any doctrine that gives itself the appearance of undertaking such a thing, that it foists upon us, as lived experience, the knowledge of the objective partial cause of what is experienced.

In order to examine this more closely, let us imagine that someone fixes his eye on one and the same red of a red sphere lying before him, and let us ask about the character of his lived experience so far as it bears precisely on this red. [p. 163] Here it is above all recent sense research that has furnished the compelling proof of the necessity of change which every content of sensation whatever, and especially every content of visual sensation, undergoes, despite the sameness of the object perceived, from every change of accompanying contents of sensation. The red sphere looks different against a black background than against a white one, and against both essentially different than against a red one. If we give it a green background outright, then, through so-called contrast-experience, such an intensification of the degree of saturation of the red would occur that anyone who had not observed the process would be inclined to doubt the sameness of the objects. But even simultaneous auditory impressions, as has been confirmed by experiment, and simultaneous impressions of temperature, smell, taste, as can be inferred with no less certainty, act to modify the visual impression (and equally well the reverse). And what holds of the side-by-side holds in principle just as much of the succession of impressions: the particular kind of what I am sensing at this very moment proves to be co-dependent on what I sensed immediately before. If, then, the accompanying sensations can already be subject to the greatest change, an at least approximate equality with respect to the preceding sensations can, in general, only be produced artificially and under quite special circumstances — and apart from that, it never occurs at all; from which alone it follows that the impressions produced by the selfsame red are never, either in two persons or in two moments of life of a single person, ever completely alike. The process of sensing red, and hence visual sensation as such, is thus a thought-thing, whose establishment could be achieved only by at least two omissions: first, of the simultaneously occurring accompanying sensations, and then, and above all, of the course of the sensations.

Yet we should still have committed an error of presupposition in characterizing the momentary content of experience in each case, were we to confine ourselves to sense-data, however far more accurately these themselves might be conceived than with the aid of the customary concept of sensation. For it seems that the entire outer world, hence also the red sphere within it, is always steeped in the inner colour of the observer's mood, were it only the grey of indifference. Whoever finds this unpersuasive should picture the matter by reference to such extremely opposed states of life as are brought about either [p. 164] by very different dispositions of character, or by the distance between stages of age, or finally by contrary forms in which the course of life proceeds. Who would deny that the redness of the sphere "acts" differently on one highly receptive to colour than on one highly receptive to tone, "shines" more splendidly to the child than to the old man, "speaks" more vividly to the rested than to the one exhausted to death! For all three cases, as is understood, the examples could be multiplied without limit, so much so that in the end there is no trait of character, no stage of age, no degree of freshness or fatigue, indeed not even a thought just now passing through my head, without an unrepeatably peculiar "mood-colour"! Long ago, indeed, the elective affinity was noted, for instance, between dejection and a preference for blue, between elation and a preference for red; in accordance with which the redness that pleasantly affects the euphoric person is felt by the depressive to be, in some measure, a nuisance! There must, of course, be grounds that make it possible to find a red of a given shade again as belonging to an object, and we shall have to deal with this at length; but this much we can see now: what is thus found again cannot be, or at least cannot without qualification be, something-to-beexperienced.

If, accordingly, sensation were recognized as the side — distinguishable at best, but certainly not separable — of a life-process whose other side would have to be called, say, "mood," or, in the terminology of today, "feeling," then by virtue of this reverse side the total process would appear so embedded in the course of life of its bearer that every content of sensation would gain, so to speak, a particular aftertaste from the position, in the sequence, of the segment of life within which the sensation was to take place. The form, most familiar to science, though by no means thought through to its final consequences, of the dependence of the present impression on the prior history of the recipient of the impression is the loss of consciousness for the contents of such sensations as repeat themselves often enough. The object of perception which, clothed in the character of novelty, "makes an impression," forfeits this capacity in the measure of its familiarity, until at last it no longer comes to consciousness at all for one who has grown wholly "accustomed" to its presence. This holds of the individual thing as of the whole world surrounding us, and for the latter it has, besides, the particular sense that its capacity to stir life-processes diminishes, quite apart from the dispositions of character of the bearer of life, [p. 165] in proportion to the fullness and variety of impressions that have already previously taken place. What do we not experience, taken purely sensuously, in a city or landscape that we are wandering through for the first time — and how vainly we search for it after we have been settled there for years!

One is accustomed to call the properties of things, insofar as they call forth sensations, "stimuli," and with this unfortunate coinage one veils what one cannot help but notice at every step, namely that the stimulus-value of the said properties, of itself and for the same person, becomes different and ever again different, usually in the sense of diminishing, though occasionally also of increasing. "Darkness, gazed at longer, grows lighter; the radiantly bright fades; the vivid grows grey; the smell of the heated stove can scarcely be perceived any longer after but a short presence in the room; the pressure of our clothes we feel, even when we wish to, only imperfectly; and whatever further occurrences of this kind there are, which one is accustomed to describe as blunting (adaptation)." It is admitted that every impression, scarcely<sup>18</sup> begun, at once falls prey to a modification; and one nonetheless continues to regard the contents of impressions as building-blocks that one need only correctly clamp together, and the durable thing would then already be complete! Some researchers have rightly emphasized that every impression rests on a change of the state of life, and a Hobbes already taught: to sense always the same thing means to sense nothing at all! Yet such insights served only to deny sensations any determinacy of content, instead of yielding that knowledge with whose proclamation we now turn back to the starting point of all the investigations of this book: sensation, whatever else its essence may consist in, is in any case a *never* *motionless* process (more precisely, indeed, only one side of one), and once again merely a wave in the individually personal stream of life. Whether someone looks at the red of a red sphere for a quarter second or for five minutes, the impression is in both cases a flowing happening, for which there are no two mathematical points in time at which it would be identically the same.

<sup>18</sup> On page 165. — Vom Wesen des Bewußtseins, 3rd ed., p. 15.

What we earlier set forth in a different way has again resulted from the consideration of the so-called contents of sensation: namely that neither the process of sensing nor what is sensed by means of it is of the nature of time-stable units out of which anything [p. 166] could be bundled together. If we nonetheless undertake to assess colours, temperatures, shapes, sizes, and other qualities "objectively," this happens solely with respect to objects of thought already presupposed, more precisely, to existing things; and the measurement aimed at, however constantly mediated through life-processes, refers by no means to what is experienced, but to its objective ground. In overlooking this, sensualism of every shade confuses sense experiences with their transcendental occasioning grounds, or — insofar as it distinguishes the sensed at all — with the suprasensible property of the thing! Without giving itself an account of this, it lays down, as an article of faith, a world of things, properties, and functions, in order thereafter, with a rich expenditure of the most artificial apparatus, to spin these out of — lived experience! Just as platonizing logistic is only supposedly concerned with psychic life-processes, but in truth with judgements and concepts, so sensualist logistic is only supposedly concerned with sensuous life-processes, but in truth with mechanisms; in consequence of which there is today scarcely anything more unknown and more misjudged than human and animal sensibility! — In the meantime, with this we have only pointed out one error in the calculation on which sensualism is based.

[p. 167]
