The act of apprehension rests on sensing wakefulness, and apprehensible thingness is founded on a sensible corporeality. Experience is the unboundedly progressive dissection which spirit, guided by the separating life-process of sensing, performs upon the actuality of appearance.

In that sensualism confused sense experience with the process of perception and suppressed the spiritual act which, in the process of perception — at least in man's case — inescapably joins itself to sense experience, it found itself faced with the hopeless task of having to derive, from one and the same event, the achievement of the act of perception, that is, the thing and its properties — the boundary and the matter to be bounded. Nor was that all: it overlooked that the senses are organs both of body and of soul, or that in every experience the process of beholding images and the process of sensing their corporeality work together, and it fancied that it could bundle together the appearance of the world out of disparate "contents of sensation." We shall not repeat how, in this fashion, it very involuntarily strangled itself. Now that, once insight into the twofold function of the senses has been gained, whole chains of questions fall away as chimerical — questions on whose unanswerability sensualism was shattered — the task presses upon us all the more urgently, not only to point out the means for the *separation* of beholding from sensation, but also to shed light deep into the structure of their interconnection. Since the way from the thing to the image led us by way of the intuitive image (= appearance), we have found ourselves obliged to interpose a third process between beholding and sensation, namely the process of intuition. If its difference from the process of sensation has up to now stood in the foreground of our consideration, while its difference from the process of beholding could so far only be surmised, the chapters that follow shall be devoted precisely to clarifying this latter difference; and let the remark below form the prelude to it.

[p. 199] As surely as a body without a soul would no longer be a living body, just as surely must the soul's sensory process of beholding be involved in the body's sensory process of sensing, if the latter is to deserve the name of a life-process at all. The third process, then, that must therefore be interposed, in which the two fuse with one another, now presents itself differently thanks to its participation in sensing, and differently thanks to its participation in beholding. According to the former, we should have to investigate the conditions under which corporeality is experienced in images; according to the latter, the conditions under which the non-intuitive happening appears — or, in other words, the conditions of the transformation of beholding as such into an intuition always underpinned by corporeality. This investigation, to be taken up in earnest only later, we have introduced by marking the difference between improper image-properties and proper thing-properties, and we shall for now continue it by winning back for sensibility, step by step, its capacity for beholding, which the scholasticism of sensation has falsified away.

[p. 200]

#### 23. Kapitel — Vom Schauvermögen der Sinne — Chapter 23 — On the Beholding-Capacity of the Senses

Even though language lacks designations for tone as such, it nonetheless distinguishes tone-characters of high and low, or bright and dark, or light and heavy, or sharp and broad, from which indeed the arrangement of objective tones upon a "scale" derives. While, then, every higher tone is objectively different from every lower tone, there nonetheless obtains a kinship of character between all comparatively high tones and the content of spatial aboveness, and between all comparatively low tones and the content of spatial belowness; and likewise with respect to bright and dark, sharp and broad, light and heavy. What linguistic usage thus makes known to us concerning the world of tone holds generally: what is experienced are never thing-properties, for which we possess sharply delimiting generic concepts, but rather — to put it now more precisely — similarities and oppositions, the former arising from kinship of essence, the latter from conflict of essence; and the comparison of what is in and for itself incomparable is grounded in the experience of its expressive content. Before we go on, let us clear away a few difficulties, even if only apparent ones.

One might wish to deny all comparability between the world of things and the world of essences. It might well be objected: granted that certain tone-qualities and spatial aboveness, or a glaring red and the sound of a scream, may become experienceable as the expression of one and the same essence, yet the "high tone" or the "screaming red" has not the slightest similarity to the connection of specific marks in the property-complex of a thing however constituted! For quite apart from the fact that the high tone does not belong at all to the genus of things, but rather, say, to that of properties or of an effect of things (as likewise the screaming red), it is in any case of necessity high, the glaring red of necessity loud; whereas the red ball before my eyes could equally well be green, or rough instead of smooth, or [p. 201] light instead of heavy — With such an objection one would indeed raise a question soon to be touched on further, and would only have overlooked what quite different question of the apprehension of things it is to which we may expect to find an answer solely by virtue of insight into the beholding of the appearance of essence. Just as language, on the one hand, strictly speaking never names the contents of what has to this day been called sensation, so, on the other hand, it has no designation for the determinate individual thing. If I say that before my eyes there lies a smooth, red, solid sphere of ten centimeters' diameter, I have, for the purpose of germinally designating this individual thing, made use of the general concepts of smoothness, redness, density, material fullness, spherical shape, and length — which I can only do because I already have these at my disposal. The concept of substratum, in order to come about at all, requires the concept of property; but the concept of property is a relational concept, of which, for other reasons, we have already treated at length in Chapter 11. The problem of the finding of the thing must therefore be preceded by the question of the ground that makes possible the finding of the properties of the thing; and, in order now to obtain an answer to this, we must enter the life-domain of that *sensibility* which halves the scope of the world available to every essence whatsoever into two groups of intuitive images: at the level from the single-celled organism *up* to man, into the appearance of friendly, serviceable, alluring powers and into the appearance of hostile, disturbing, dangerous powers; but at the primordial-human level, as will moreover be peeled out step by step, into *polarly* opposed and, precisely for that reason, despite all tension, mutually complementary powers. — Two further remarks on this.

In order to separate the concept of essence as clearly as possible from the concept of the thing, we have among cohering expressive traits given particular preference to those which, like height and tone for instance, fall entirely apart in terms of thing-properties. This by no means excludes there being a character of the visible in relation to the character of the audible, to the character of the tangible, and so on — on the contrary: unless, in one way, everything that appears to sight cohered with everything else of its kind, and, in another way, everything that sounds, and in yet another, everything that offers resistance, the apprehension of visible, audible, tangible thing-properties would never have come about at all, and we would have no concept of dissimilar sense-zones. Nonetheless we must never wish to interchange the unity of existence of the thing with the unity of effect of the essence [p. 202] — for which we again call to mind: just as the appearance, strictly speaking, cannot be dissected into substratum and property (except perhaps by way of analogy), no more can the essence appearing within it. There are gods of water, and gods even of a particular body of water, gods of the plant kingdom as well as of a particular tree, gods of the hearth as well as of a particular house, but also gods of night, of day, of the dawn, of light, of darkness, of storm, of tempest, of thunder, further of love, joy, revenge, atonement, wrath, further of death, sickness, fertility, and finally of praying, sacrificing, exchanging, healing, waging war, swearing oaths, averting evil, and so on without end. If, then, it belongs to the generic hallmark of all thing-bound thinking that thing, property of the thing, state, and process are never to be confused with one another, then things are matched neither by thing-like essences, nor by property-like ones, nor by state-like ones — since, after all, "essences" always stand on one and the same line of acting powers, and there is no possible predicate that could not figure as a subject of statement in the world of essences! If, in the course of our exposition, we have repeatedly come upon the invincible propensity of the human spirit to reify general concepts, and to regard light, color, warmth, sound, motion in the same way as colored, warm, or moving things, we now also know a vital impulse behind this. Could we pass only such judgements as: the brown stove is warm, we would speak less readily of brownness or of warmth than happens by virtue of that manner of judging, likewise still peculiar to us, as: this brown is warm! There is no such thing as light, warmth, sound; but there really is, and even still for us, the *character* of light, of warmth, of sound. The world of congealed "Ideas" offers, so to speak, the silhouette of an actuality of once-living gods!

To a mode of thought guided by the theory of sensation, the following difficulty — most briefly made recognizable by example — may well seem more troubling. When we hear the noise meant by the word "rattling," there lights up before the eye of the soul, say, the image of chains striking against one another; whereas at the noise of "pattering" there arises perhaps the image of rain breaking down and dripping leaves. The theorist of sensation would want to explain this by "associations," a matter we shall come to only later, but would otherwise maintain that rattling as well as pattering is in any case something heard, and hence for the deaf as good [p. 203] as not present at all; that nothing we have adduced in the least shakes the dependence of impressions on determinate sensory processes — to which it should be replied that the question of dependencies has indeed scarcely been touched, but that we have again and again recalled the indispensability of sensory excitation. Only one capable of hearing, we do not doubt, perceives noises, be it waking or in a dream; only to one capable of sight do colors appear, only to one capable of smell, scents, and so on.<sup>26</sup> But we believe we have proved that by means of hearing there is perceived a working and acting of the very same space-time powers that appear to the soul in another way through sight, again in another way through touch, and that must therefore also become known to one born deaf — only, to be sure, not in the appearance-form of noises. Far from diminishing the significance of the senses, whoever turns them from mere stimulus-receptive organs of sensation into just as many, each singularly gifted, messengers of the soul, through which it gains touch and enters into contact of essence with the distance of images, raises that significance on the contrary quite immeasurably; and we do indeed maintain, and have shown, that the opposite attempt — namely to work an image out of stimuli — must fail hopelessly, and thereby even abolishes itself, because it renders our knowledge of stimulus-exerting thing-properties inexplicable, indeed unthinkable!

<sup>26</sup> On page 203. — One might raise the question, and it has been raised, whether such sensory qualities might not also appear for which no corresponding stimulus-occasion had ever preceded. Would it, for example, be wholly excluded that one born blind should *dream* of colors, although in waking he had never seen any? It is advisable not to be too hasty with an answer to questions of this kind. Purely physiologically one can only make conjectures about this. The bodily causes of congenital blindness can be very various, but lie mostly either in the receiving apparatus or in the optic nerve (or in both together) and only rarely in the central organ. It would therefore not be simply excludable that, with an intact quadrigeminal body, color-visions might arise through inner-bodily excitation. Apart from this, however, we cannot assert with full certainty that it is precisely an excitation of the optical sensorium that is required for one to *dream colors*. We come closer to the state of affairs only on psychological ground. First we recall that inner-bodily processes can call forth *intuitive* appearances of the most manifold kind (as indeed dreaming itself alone already proves), which admittedly often differ not inconsiderably from the character of external stimulus-occasions. The same holds also of inadequate stimulations. To remain with the visual sense: the flickering welter of luminous points that arises from a blow or pressure on the closed eye is not entirely equivalent to any other visual perception. Next we bear in mind that stimulus-occasions always initiate self-activities of the sensorium, which entail not only continual alterations of the appearance (one recalls the state of affairs of the blunting discussed earlier) but can also occasion wholly new appearances. To these belong the contrast-phenomena and after-images. Here we already meet the possibility of the *generation* of appearance-qualities — as, for example, when after gazing for some time at a green surface we, on turning the eye away, generate through its inner activity the complementary color and seem to see a colorless ground now as *red*. Might there not lie, one could think, in the extension of such observations in principle the possibility that appearance-qualities of an entire sensory zone might be produced by the self-activity of the sensorium — better, of the beholding-faculty of the soul? But even if the bodily preconditions of original blindness should in certain cases by no means permit the exclusion of such an assumption, the following would still speak against it. Innate "ideas," including "representations," phantasms and intuitive contents of every kind, may be regarded as definitively disposed of. On the other hand, the dispositions of sensing, of intuiting and of beholding really are inherited, and we shall learn later that this means considerably more than the inheritance merely of receptivities to impressions (according to the hitherto customary conception of impressions), inasmuch as to each of these belongs also the disposition and tendency to a specific *interpretation* of the impressions. But however certain it is that actuality is, in substance and metaphysically, the counter-pole of the living soul, so certain is it that we know of no evidence that the psychic pole should of itself create a substitute for actuality. The multiplicity of qualities belonging together through kinship of character within an entire sensory zone is, however, unquestionably a piece of actuality. Even if we, with the Romantics, were to posit a primal sense or central sense that had only later branched into the individual senses, we still ought not to let the sides of actuality already correspond to it for which, after the *completed* differentiation, the soul becomes receptive by means of the individual senses. There are undoubtedly persons of exceedingly heightened sensitivity to changes of air pressure as well as to electrical and magnetic fluctuations; but even to them the coming change of weather announces itself through impressions (and especially through inner-bodily sensations) that are equally familiar to everyone far less sensitive, and *not* through impressions that would differ from the sensory qualities known to us in the way that, say, color-appearances differ from tone-appearances. In short, we doubt the possibility of the inner generation of, for instance, col-or-appearances by the originally blind, in view of the absence of the *polarity* of lived experience required for it, even though we must admit that, given the beholding-faculty of the soul that spans all the senses, a *strict* proof of the impossibility cannot for the present be furnished.

From this vantage point there now opens up the prospect of a countless number of questions, most of which have to this day been neglected, and not one of which is conclusively decided. On the ground of the doctrine of beholding, the capacity of the senses as such first of all steps into an essentially new light. What we have learned about it from sensation-research hitherto concerns not so much sensibility itself as rather the physics of the outer and inner-bodily processes accompanying certain differences in the thing-relatedness of its experiencing. Not only have the conducting nerves been examined, but the organs of stimulus-transmission most precisely too, in their relation to the chemical and oscillatory influences to which they are exposed; the limits, for every single and sub-sense, both of its receptivity to stimuli in general and of its receptivity to changes of stimuli, have been numerically determined; the after-effect duration of stimuli has been investigated, their mixability and unmixability; and finally, by ingenious experiments, it has been established on a considerable scale at what tempo the activity of apprehension follows the sensory processes, and what regularities the disturbances [p. 204] to which it is subject display. Yet, however highly one may rate all this, what is thereby illuminated is the *mechanics* of the sensory processes, or in other words sensibility minus its *ensoulment* —

Millennia-long breeding of spirits in the service of purpose-guided belief in facts has accustomed us to take sense experience for a sign-language of things, and to extract from it on the instant whatever it may have to tell us about them. But now we also perceive, in the noise of rattling, the *character* of rattling and hence, for example, the character of iron; in the noise of pattering, the character of raining, hailing, or a rockfall — and are thereby enabled to soulful exchange with the powers revealing themselves in the happening. Apart, however, from the poets already extinct today and the artists lying in their death-throes, no one indeed still troubles to gain knowledge from what is thus overheard. How much it nonetheless fructifies even our knowledge will be gathered with astonishment from the recollection that, among other things, it is indeed on this that rests the gift, lacking wholly in no one, of reading off from a human countenance, in a flash, the moods, stirrings, surgings, and, to a not inconsiderable degree, even the character-traits of its bearer. And here, then, let the occasion be taken for a side glance at the Copernican reversal which the conception of the sources of knowledge undergoes through a doctrine that, with the rediscovered capacity of beholding, restores to sensibility the forgotten wonders of its power.

On the victory of belief in the actuality of things rests the astonishing development of the two sciences that, before all others, have founded the fame of modern scientificity — which, in view of the acumen expended on it and the tremendous growth of power in the *mastery* of things, is fully justified: we mean physics and chemistry. Yet while no one could dispute away the sensory ungraspability of all those objects underlying their arts of calculation — molecules, atoms, electrons, affinities, energies, ether-vibrations, and so on — one nonetheless goes on, confusing outward appearance with the substrata thought into it, to hold for intuitively given that which is expressly compounded out of the transcendencies in question, namely the things themselves, and has thereby been compelled to consign to a peculiar supersensibility [p. 205] precisely the most life-deep and most powerfully effective achievements of the senses. Even today there are found fairly numerous such persons (especially among women) who at first glance quite properly "see through" their fellow man, indeed divine important features of his past and even his impending fate, often with the use either of especially suited organs of transmission, such as the symbolically most eloquent hand, or of thought-fructifying points of attachment (horoscopy!); and finally, in extraordinary cases, are even able to feel out from an implement what it has been used for, and, to cite a historical example, to pick out from a large series of axes the one with whose aid a murder was committed. If we add the thousandfold attested "telepathies," presentiments, and true "clairvoyances," the by no means doubtable successes of dowsers sensitive to water and metal, we stand before a vast field of manifestations of primordial beholding, grown rarer today but once popularly widespread, which the intelligence imprisoned in thing-consciousness must either deny outright or is compelled to hand over to a downright incomprehensible supersensibility. For however such achievements may in detail be explained, this much is certain: they never become intelligible from the activity of the image-estranged and image-piercing spirit in us, which has indeed precisely torn apart the immediate connection of soul and world, in order to endow us instead, to be sure, with the calculability not of happening as such, but of one side of it.

Although the magnificent systems of Romanticism were unable to press through to a clear formation of the concept of the soul's beholding-power, they were nonetheless on the way to it with their assumption of an "Ur-sense" or "central sense" or "all-sense," as it were the stem from which the individual senses — which only later became dissimilar — branched off in the course of a development lasting hundreds of thousands of years, and which precisely for that reason works into each of them in its own particularized way, just as, conversely, it is stimulated by each of them to supplementations of what is sensed, far beyond disparate special contents. With this they groped their way, besides, to an access on the one hand to the life-content of the sleep-state and so-called somnambulism, whose occasional gift of the true dream became, in their view, intelligible from the heightened all-capacity of the soul, less disturbed by stimuli and therefore more concentrated; and on the other hand, and above all, to the "instincts," become today [p. 206] more enigmatic than ever, whether of man himself or especially of animals — in which, with a few sentences, we can once again uncover dispositions of sensibility that had to remain foreign to sensualism.

"How does the animal recognize in water the means to quench its thirst, how does the carnivorous animal recognize its food in flesh, the herbivorous in plants?" asks *Treviranus* in his Erscheinungen des organischen Lebens [Phenomena of Organic Life]. Why, we continue, is the hen stimulated by the sight of the egg to brood it, the still wholly inexperienced duckling by the sight of the pool of water to plunge into it, why the bee by the scent of linden blossom to draw out the nectar and store its prey for later use in the artfully wrought honeycomb structure? Why does the young cat snatch at the mouse before anyone has ever shown it how? Why does the silkworm greedily devour the mulberry leaf that serves its future cocoon, and not a beech leaf, although it could; and what induces it to spin the web of threads many thousand meters long more loosely at one spot, when it is surely not informed that otherwise the butterfly could not tear the cocoon open? Why does the hermit crab load itself with sea anemones, without having tested up to then that they protect it by defensive measures in case of danger? Why, as soon as its wings have grown, does the gnat shun the water in which it grew up, and why does the female — never the male — seek it out again when it is necessary for laying the eggs, which can develop only in water? How did the leopard learn that it must spring at the giraffe's neck and tear open the artery, if it is to have any prospect of bringing down that so much larger animal? Does it not become sun-clear, from such examples from the animal world multipliable a millionfold, that whoever has merely traced the mechanics of the genesis of their thing-relatable data has explored nothing whatsoever of the life of the senses; and should not the almost infallible certainty of such recognitions, precisely on the part of the animal itself, teach even the most inveterate rationalist that it is quite certainly not to be comprehended from capacities of the spirit! Often the thirsting rider's own thirsting horse, given free rein over miles of arid steppe, led him to a spring or oasis several hours' journey away. Wild animals, but also many domesticated ones, feel things in advance and, through shelter-seeking behavior, signal the impending onset of unusually severe storms, and especially of an earthquake. If we think further of the orientational capacity called the sense of place [p. 207] of the homing pigeon, which, carried off a hundred kilometers in a dark box and by roundabout ways, returns to its home, if possible in a straight line, one can hardly help agreeing with the Romantics when they were inclined to understand such things from the same point of view as the clairvoyance mentioned above, and one will no longer find it ridiculous that all primordial peoples venerated in the animal the working of planetary powers held to be divine.

Were we further to urge that it also belongs to sensibility that the sight of a figure can fill us instantly and immediately with the deepest affection, indeed irresistible desire, and at times even the sound of a voice, and conversely, both times just as immediately, with violent aversion, the theorist of sensation would again come at us with his "associations," and would moreover refer us to the supposed elucidations of his doctrine of the "accompanying feeling-tone." But if something fundamentally similar takes place also in the animal world, and indeed preferably by means of the sense of smell, then surely no one will want to explain from "associations" the fact that the dog follows the trail of the bitch, or that the horse flees on scenting the panther! And besides, animals are exceedingly rich in the strangest "idiosyncrasies," against which Darwinian evasions fail. The bull hates the red cloth, ants flee from blue light, the horse avoids the camel, badger and fox avoid each other, likewise shark and alligator. Were, moreover, the "association of ideas" even more and other than a mere emergency exit of the scholasticism of sensation, it would nonetheless have to content itself with tracing the soul's effect of one image back to that of another image, only in the end to come to a halt before the soul's effect of "elementary sensations" — which, as we know, are sides of images and expressive traits of appearing essences. "Were one to call to one's aid the whole poetry of the seasons in order to interpret the awe-striking power, for example, of the scents of flowers, one would nonetheless find no point of attachment for the fabric of feelings and phantasms without the presupposition that there already lies within sense experience itself what we are indeed able to depict to some extent only in the "mood-images" that it allows to arise upon unhindered unfolding: the scent of the rose, say, mild fullness; that of jasmine, hot intoxication; lime-blossom, foretaste of bliss; violet, happiness-promising memory; lilac, the youthful exuberance of rapture; forest- and resin-scent [p. 208] the fairy-tale mood; hay, brooding absorption; damp foliage, primordial self-gathering." Not by chance, then, does the name of the stimulus<sup>27</sup> [Reiz] (from the verb "to charm/stimulate" [reizen]) denote, in colloquial speech, instead of the occasioning ground of sensory-nerve processes, rather the source of the soul's delight in sensibly experienced images; to which one may further compare "charm" [Liebreiz] and "charming" [reizend]. Since we emphasized in the previous section that no delimitation of the feelings should yet be expected, but have just now at least touched on their close connection with beholding, we add at least so much as is necessary to forestall the distortions of the state of affairs that the fashionable false doctrine of the merely "subjective" character of feeling almost inevitably brings with it — restricted, however, to feelings that occur together with sensory processes.

<sup>27</sup> On page 208. — From *Klages*, Vom Traumbewußtsein, Zeitschrift für Pathopsychologie, vol. III, no. 4 (1919), p. 409.

If it occurs to no one to deny the sense-datum its referability to the outer world, however else he may interpret it, notwithstanding that the process conveying it runs its course no less completely within the organism of its bearer than does the process of feeling, then it is of course not to be seen why the data that a sense-mediated feeling furnishes us should lack that same referability. Led astray by the undeniable fact that one and the same sight arouses now pleasure, now displeasure, now joy, now fright, now tension, now boredom, one has wanted to lock feeling away outright within the bodiliness of the one feeling, whereas in truth at least three principal cases are to be distinguished: it speaks preferentially of the life-state of the one feeling; it speaks of the relation of his life-state to the life-content of the impression; and it speaks preferentially of the latter, though of course always mediated through his own life-state. If in this case we call the feelingdatum the "felt character of the image," or more briefly an essence-feeling, then, contrary to present-day views, it must be most decisively emphasized that essence-feelings are not causes but rather effects of the soul's beholdings within the personality of the one feeling. It is not through essence-feelings that characters are beheld; rather it is appearing characters to whose beholding essence-feelings can attach themselves, without, however, having to accompany them with equal strength from case to case and from person to person. The characters of redness or of burning, in two life-different moments — although never recurring as the selfsame, in the manner [p. 209] of the measurable properties of the time-persistent thing — nonetheless resemble one another to that degree which infallibly results in re-recognition, whereas the "feeling-tones" of the character of redness or of burning fluctuate far more considerably in kind and degree — for reasons, it is understood, of the fluctuation of personal receptivity to them. If we look about for a mark distinguishing essence-feelings from merely self-personal state-feelings, or, more precisely, with regard to relational feelings, the essence-revealing trait of feelings from their other traits, we come upon the depth already reported earlier, which gains ground to a higher degree only at the cost of the mark of affective violence or *intensity*, and whose utmost heightening lets the feeling-process flow, beyond its own bounds, into the state of being-beside-oneself, or what the ancients called Ekstasis. If beholding is thus completed only in a being-beside-oneself different in kind from feeling, then it becomes fully manifest that even to the essence-feeling there falls only the task of *announcing* the beholdable image-content within the consciousness-capable bearer of life. Ordinarily beholding will not come to completion, and will either merely assist animal sensibility in its unconscious recognitions, or else, by virtue of exclusively human essence-feelings, support the soul's intercourse with the intuitively present characters of the world; but in the exceptional moments of its completion, it is with the worldessence's *substance* — deeper in stratum and never belonging to the moment alone — that the soul of a now transformation-capable body enters into connection, partaking in the pulse-beat of universal happening. In an exposition, however, whose emphasis lies on the capacity of the senses, we do not press forward to the "primordial images"; it is enough if one learns to recognize that it is sensibility which, thanks to its participation in the soul's gift of beholding, opens for the soul the ways to all heights and depths!

For our purposes almost still more important than the indication of the capacity of sensibility in general, insofar namely as it is grounded in beholding, are the questions — scarcely yet unrolled — concerning the relative beholding-power of the individual senses, the difference in their content of characterizing data, their degree of fitness to stand in for one another, the particular aptitude of sense-differing specific marks for representing the spatiality or the temporality of happening, the essence of the relation of image to thing, and by what means and in [p. 210] what respect the soul's beholding is involved in the compulsion that lets the spirit's positing of the relating point appear at the same time as the *finding* of the properties necessarily to be related to it. It is not at this point that we intend even to attempt an answer to such questions, and we attach the indication, without which we would not wish to take leave of the subject, to a closing word on the how-constitution, to clarify whose concept was the most important subsidiary task of our defense against "sensualism."

Are the properties of things then really qualities, or are they not? — thus we hear it asked. If they are, how then can they be objectively compared with one another, which doubtless constantly happens; but if not, how are they to be distinguished from real qualities? Are we seriously to believe that the warmth (whether sensed or beheld) of the heat-giving stove is a different warmth from that meant by the expression "warm red"; and how then would we come to state, in both cases, the selfsame state of affairs, namely being-warm? Nor, indeed, does color cease to be color when we attribute warmth to it! Does not whoever takes mere transferences literally and wants to derive facts from similes fall into an abyss of nonsense? — The last question we can quickly dispose of. Everyone recognizes without further ado that, and why, a transference has taken place when we speak of the "leg" of a table. For if I point to the leg of a human being and then to the improper leg of the table, the intuitive similarity of the two is scarcely less visible than that of the human leg to the leg, say, of the horse; to which is added a similarity of functions that we need not further elucidate. No one, on the other hand, could intuitively point out the similarity of the stove's warmth to the warmth of the red of a peony, let alone to warmth of heart. Similes and transferences presuppose things already thought to completion, whereas the similarity of qualities belongs to the immediate content of an experiencing that first makes possible at all the finding of the thing-properties and hence of the thing itself. — But the preceding questions, too, prepare no difficulty whatsoever for us.

Actuality is experienced; being, on the ground of experienced actuality, is always only thought. Accordingly we have already earlier distinguished the actuality of space from the being of space, the actuality of time from the being of time, the actuality of happening from the being of happening, the actuality [p. 211] of motion from the being of motion, and we have now besides distinguished the actuality of the how from the being of the how. In the form of the thing-property, the being of the how, which is only to be thought, takes the place of the actuality of the experienced how. Color remains color, even when we call it warm; warmth remains warmth, even when we lend it to a color. But we thus use the names of thing-properties for experienced sides of appearance, and elucidate the character of a color by the character of warmth. In the thing-world of being, space, time, rest, motion, how splinter apart from one another. That we nonetheless find them related to one another, and must fit what has been atomized into a system of ordering-places, the impulse for this the spirit receives from experienced images, to which its work of dissolution remains bound, even though, in regrouping what has been dissolved, it may besides be guided by demands inherent in itself. Let us leave it open, given in whatever way it may be, for which — as will be shown — the vital occasioning ground must be sought in the genuine process of sensation: the place; then we can for now determine the relation of thing-property to impression-quality as follows: severed from its essence-context, the image-quality becomes the timeless specific property of a thing, insofar as it falls to the sphere of effect of the place posited by the spirit.

If, to the question why a thing-like substratum can be thought for all colors, and again for all temperatures, but none for the "warm color," the answer is given that colors are indeed mixable with colors and temperatures with temperatures, but not colors with temperatures, then this indisputably correct indication leaves unexplained precisely what would need explaining: namely, why the concept of the shining should exclude the warming, when the experience of the warm color seemed to demand precisely the opposite! Our grounding of the illusoriness of the recourse to the supposed or real dissimilarity of the sense-zones may here be supplemented by the reminder that the still unresolved dispute over the number of the senses already testifies to a degree of difficulty in keeping them apart that finds no counterpart in the nature of the specific properties of the thing. We can indicate much more precisely whether we mean smells or tastes than we are able to indicate whether a taste was indeed really tasted or rather smelled; whence stems the double sense of the verb [p. 212] "to taste," which some dialects use in the phrase "it tastes" for exactly the state of affairs that others convey with "it smells." Impressions of warmth and impressions of cold are indeed generically different, but only painstaking scientific labor has been able to uncover that they always also take place at different spots of the skin; and how, without artificial experiments, would we ever have gained any inkling of the peculiarity of the sense of pain! The immediate ground for the classification of specific properties, which is always already presupposed in every classification of the senses, lies grounded in their relation to the selfsameness of a place.

What, then, does the thing-point — not temporal, indeed, but time-persistent — actually achieve in respect of the timeless universals of colors and temperatures? It links them in the concept of the possible simultaneity of being-related to it! Redness and blueness on the one hand, warmth and cold on the other, contend, so to speak, for the time-place of that relatedness, whereas colors and temperatures can in principle occur simultaneously in any pairing whatever, and thus appear objectively independent of one another. The red ball before my eyes cannot simultaneously be blue, but it can indeed simultaneously be warm, or instead simultaneously cold. We close ourselves off for the present to the manifold new questions that might at once press forward; for the provisional result gives us for the time being enough to think about, and, in the reflected light of the place-bound thing, makes more sharply recognizable, in the essence-experience, the placelessness of the essence-appearance. As surely as the redness of which we judge that it is warm is a space-time revelation of its essence, just as little does it belong to warm red to be in this or that place. The redness of the spherical thing, by contrast, finds itself, together with all its other properties, precisely *now* right here, where at the same moment cold, too, *could* find itself, and, as it were nailed down, has forfeited the expressive power that belongs only to the essence acting out of itself: what is experienced transforms itself into the objective how as soon as it is bound to the delimiting place.

Whoever has followed thus far now finds himself confronted with those numerous questions, some of which we named above and to which many more could still be added. Why is there a complete absence of generic names for smells? Why, apart from pitch and depth, can sounds be depicted only with verbs? Why are not they, but only colors, fit to depict things, their spatial relations included? [p. 213] Or would the echo, too, be a likeness? Is there a depictability only of bodies, or also of the original images, and how does reflection stand in relation to the likeness? If it is true, as was maintained above, that in the actuality of essence-appearances the difference between substratum and property does not yet obtain at all, or does so only analogically, then it must in principle be possible, in characterizing sentences, to interchange subject of statement and statement with one another — as indeed really happens when we speak now of "tone-col-or" [Klangfarbe], now of "color-sound" or "color-tone." Why, then, do we speak of warm colors, but never, conversely, of colored warmth? As one notices, only with this would the soul-research of the senses begin, and no one will fail to recognize how extraordinarily it will diverge from so-called sensualism. Here let a mere indication prepare that subject which, from the doctrine of the essence of the senses, will especially occupy us later: the law of composition of the thing in its relation to the "given" intuitive image.

Polar to one another, like space and time, are also the two most pronounced distance-senses, sight and hearing, of which the former marks the preponderance of the spatial pole of sensibility, the latter that of the temporal pole. If we earlier had to emphasize the time-independence of all thing-properties in relation to the thing itself, and, in contrast to this, the temporality of motion, indeed of process as such, we see at once that sounds, tones, noises belong especially to the process-side, however much they are besides still of qualitative character. Geometry treats of the properties of certain figures, but not of the duration of figures; color-theory, of the intensities and qualities of colors, but not of the duration of colors; the theory of tone, by contrast, must also pay heed to the duration of tones, and shows us that processes such as, for example, beats can even partake in the how-constitution of sounds. To be sure, there are as few purely temporal as purely spatial intuitabilities, and sound, too, noise, seems to us to spring up somewhere in space and to come toward us from somewhere; not to speak of the very differing "massiveness" of noise-characters; but there can be not the slightest doubt that the appearance of sound bears the character of a process, and thus stands in the utmost opposition to the appearance of color.

Because it always covers the surface present in the moment, color is [p. 214] an appearance-mark immediately of space; because it forever articulates a happening, sound is an appearance-mark *immediately* of time. As time-persistent, however, the thing has the greater elective affinity to space than to happening, and accordingly also the greater elective affinity to color than to sound. It is colors and their shapes that the thing of perception seizes upon most violently and links to itself most indissolubly, whereas sound, so to speak, hovers midway between thing and happening and, although likewise caught up in the world of things, nonetheless does not cease to speak the language of essences. Herein one of the relational laws announces itself, one that grows for the dissecting activity of the understanding out of the exigencies of experiencing. With the more precise investigation of it, we would take a further step toward the most important goal of our inquiry: the recovery of experienced connections from the meshed network of lines of separation, crossing them a thousandfold, that the relating faculty of judgement has drawn. In order, however, not to go astray in doing so, we must now let the concept of experiencing measure itself against its most dangerous adversary, the modern concept of consciousness.

[p. 215]

## Drittes Buch — Bewußtsein und Erlebnis — Third Book — Consciousness and Experience

[p. 217]

### Erster Abschnitt — Das Bewußtsein als Lebensstörung — First Part — Consciousness as a Disturbance of Life

#### 24. Kapitel — Kritik der herrschenden Bewußtseinsauffassung — Chapter 24 — Critique of the Prevailing Conception of Consciousness

One may simply call the concept of consciousness the Achilles' heel of modern thought, and explain, at least in part, from unfamiliarity with it the superiority which the Greeks displayed in their treatment of the problem of life. For as long as the logocentric intention of inquiry keeps spirit and life apart, it remains relatively harmless and capable of findings serviceable to the science of life. If, however, it succeeds in creating a hybrid concept that imperceptibly draws life into spirit, then in place of a Logos that at least still contends there steps its good-faith, unwitting ecclesia triumphans, in which henceforth the most honest objectivity appears paired precisely with an ineradicable blindness. This is exactly what the modern concept of consciousness accomplishes.

We find its present-day sense — which, incidentally, was already the same from the outset — by interrogating the name. The word "consciousness [Bewußtsein]" is the subjectively used infinitive corresponding to the statement: I am conscious of myself (of a thing), that is, I know of something, think of it, reflect upon it, take note of it. That the scientific coinage of the concept proceeded by way of the word may be attested by two determinations, without which it is never encountered since its first occurrence in philosophy. Because every reflecting upon whatever it may be also makes possible a reflecting upon the one who reflects, the theory of consciousness already found in Augustine (as, before him, somewhat more vaguely in the Neoplatonist) sets up as essential [p. 218] that proposition of the self-certainty of consciousness which the Cartesian "Meditations" only spin further. Because, moreover, self-reflection is in any case the taking-note of some something, among whose ineliminable features (conceptual) simplicity is counted, everything knowable counts from the outset as "gathered together" by the relating I. — It makes no difference, incidentally, whether the considerations circle around the word "consciousness" or around the Latin cogitare or the Greek phronesis, so long as they are directed precisely at that taking-note whose fulfillment, in the state of affairs of being-related, has found in the German word its sharpest and at the same time most compelling expression; yet let it be recommended to the reflection of those who have spoiled their feeling for the sense of the word through the daily use of such phrases as the "appearances," "formations," or "contents" of consciousness, that precisely in the meaning of what is later intended by "consciousness," a Descartes uses "cogitare," a Malebranche "raison," a Spinoza "intellectus."

The dependence of the concept on general linguistic usage would of course be only welcome, given a concordant insight into its meaning. But once the word has been seized by the tendency toward spiritualization, it serves, as no other does, to veil the following falsification: in order to be related in consciousness to what has been sensed, perceived, imagined, dreamed, fantasized, I must have sensed, perceived, imagined, dreamed, fantasized; consequently — consciousness consists of such processes as sensing, perceiving, imagining, dreaming, fantasizing. If the Eleatic exchanged actuality for being, the theorist of consciousness falls prey to the still far worse confusion of lived experience with knowledge about lived experience, in such a way that he speaks unceasingly of experiences while he never has anything else in view than — consciousness of them! Taken on principle, everything so called "psychology" in the school sense is a self-denying theory of knowledge, just as, conversely, the so-called theory of knowledge might just as well have been called "psychology." It is not quite without a comic aftertaste that the dispute over where exactly the boundary between the two lies never comes to rest. For even the understanding of a god would strive in vain to determine the difference in competence between two disciplines that, given at most a slightly different inclination on the part of their representatives, cultivate exactly the same object! Before we [p. 219] pursue this up into the higher elaborations of the concept, we wish to show it more sharply in its unavoidable counterpart, the humorous "unconsciousness."

This "unconsciousness" or "unconscious" occurs, on the surface, in two meanings, a functional one and a dispositional one. Functional sense: someone, absorbed in gripping reading, fails to hear the striking of a clock in front of him, but can nonetheless afterward recollect it; so he has, then, heard it "unconsciously." Dispositional sense: what someone has "in consciousness" at a given moment falls far short of what he possesses knowledge of, in order to "call it to memory" case by case, whether prompted or of his own accord; his knowledge thus bears the character of "unconsciousness." Likewise every practiced skill rests on a disposition to skill that has become "unconscious." But when one calls it unconscious, this evidently does not happen in order to make the essence of the disposition recognizable, but rather to indicate the circumstance that it appears to have been formed from the deposits of consciousness-acts that once took place. The naming intention, in both cases, thus aims at processes that one assumes either are not yet, or are no *longer*, "in consciousness," but *could* well arrive there; and it is of course natural now to posit consciousness-like processes as well, which, even though they possibly never become conscious, otherwise resemble in every respect the "appearances" of consciousness. "Unconsciousness" — differing from consciousness only by degree, or better still by place, but again, as regards kind, itself consciousness — relates to consciousness roughly as darkness to brightness, rest to motion, silence to sound, or again as below to above. It is in precisely this shape that the ill-thought-out notion first steps onto the scene in the system of *Leibniz*, whose "unconscious" representations are emphatically "infinitely small," "dark" representations or differentials of consciousness, and whose "unconscious" altogether still presents itself, pleasantly unabashed, as an unconscious consciousness. If a physicist wanted to instruct us that visible luminosity arises from invisible luminosity or from darkness, audible sound from inaudible sound or from silence, perceptible motion from imperceptible motion or from rest, one would doubtless find that absurd. But does one not notice that, instead of an explanation, one is in fact only offering a doubling of what is to be explained, insofar as one lets "appearances of consciousness" issue from precisely the same appearances of a so-called [p. 220] unconscious?! However certain it is that a doctrine of this kind is indeed the only possible way out once one has surrendered oneself to the false alternative "consciousness or being," it is just as certain that it needs only the care and cultivation of lesser spirits to ripen its seed of absurdity into that chimera of thought which we today see behaving in parody in the most sought-after fables of the unconscious. Present-day humanity delights in an unconscious of the nature of more than an ordinary calculating machine, one that not merely carries out the arts of calculation but of its own accord also makes the initial approach. It represents, thinks and wills; it jests, tinkers, calculates; it forges plans and carries them out with the cunning of the shrewdest trader, knows how to steer clear of ill consequences or to disarm them with lawyerly tricks, and, all in all, perceives its advantage just as unassailably and shortsightedlycleverly as one ever imagined of the consciousness of the one who wills. Only, as every parody contains at least something of the essence of what is parodied, so too the "unconsciousness" of today's writers is after all only a caricature of Leibniz's "unconsciousness." Once one has doubled any single "content" of consciousness, one has doubled consciousness altogether; and once one has doubled it, it will unnoticed soon have tripled, decupled, centupled itself! Quite consistently, then, there exists at present, besides the "unconscious," a "preconscious," "subconscious," "superconscious," "co-consciousness," and whatever other relational words may further offer themselves, in order to place at the side of consciousness any number of varieties of an exceptional consciousness. We must not spare ourselves the task of bringing the most important derailments especially to light, in order to secure it against every possible dispute that the concept of consciousness constitutes the basic malady of contemporary thought.

If, besides consciousness, there is also an unconscious whose "contents" are the same, only without the exponent of consciousness-having, both necessarily appear under the image of two realms or spaces, between which a continual exchange of the said "contents" takes place. There a representation is now in the bright space of consciousness, now in the dark space of the unconscious; it "sinks" from the former into the latter, or it "rises" from the latter into the former; it naturally crosses a "threshold" of the bright space, or falls again "beneath" the threshold into the dark space; it is what it is, but at one time "supraliminal," at another "subliminal" (in [p. 221] German "subliminal"). Since, further, a space, however large it may be, at some point becomes full, it is understood that the "contents" pressing forward must sometimes wait in an antechamber because of the "narrowness of consciousness." A struggle for place also seems to prevail in the illuminated room, whence the weaker party occasionally gets thrown out and, under threat of painful penalties, is condemned to avoid the disputed place for the time being. A doorkeeper or guardian of the threshold has to watch over such outlawed or "repressed" contents of consciousness actually remaining outside, but is either shortsighted or corruptible, because he frequently lets them slip through nonetheless under rather clumsy disguises. — We recommend as a doctoral question: how many "contents" go into consciousness altogether; can this be stated in general, or only for the individual person? And what befalls consciousness should it happen to be entirely empty for once, or would that perhaps be excluded, and why? — The mythologies of the ancients were often extravagantly fantastical, yet always richly colored and generally substantial; the mythology of double consciousness, by contrast, is indeed forsaken by all the gods of fantasy, but — perhaps for that very reason — is unfortunately outstandingly simple-minded.

We hardly need to counter the suspicion that we wished to make war on figurative speech. Our earlier discussions should have sufficiently made clear that we attach no weight whatever to whether one prefers to make use of a highly abstract or a broadly concrete, a maximally unpictorial or an itself image-rich manner of communication, since we are convinced that even the most abstracted concept is rooted in intuitable particulars and must prove itself against "images." Nor, indeed, is there scarcely a psychologist who would not assure us in advance that by consciousness he means nothing remotely spatial, even though he must speak of its "contents," its "narrowness," its "threshold." What is in question is not the fact of figurative speech but, granted that it is a figure, the thoroughly misleading figure. Whether a doctrine is to be understood literally or figuratively, its right to exist is won either from the contribution it makes toward deepening our insights, or from its capacity to unlock facts unknown until then. The first thing we should wish to know about an unconscious from which "appearances of consciousness" are supposed to be explained would surely be its peculiar [p. 222] nature and mode of operation. Instead, one offers us consciousness once again, by attaching an "unconscious" with peculiar emphasis to all proceedings of practical as well as theoretical thinking, as though they were thereby better understood or could unlock something more. — But the helpless wonder at the seeming emptiness of the undertaking transforms into a knowing wonder at the cleverness of an unconscious grown poor in life, as soon as we inquire, following the thread of the thought, what purpose it helps to fulfill. If we put the ground of life in the place of the unconscious, the doctrine has indeed told us not the least thing about its nature, but has instead quite deliberately barred the way to it through a complete Logi*cization* of lived experience. Whoever surrenders himself to it never again finds the way to the — unconscious, because in its place he has been fobbed off with an unconscious — consciousness! It is in the unconscious that the nihilism of the concept of consciousness is first unveiled. If the latter lets experiences have understanding, its counter-concept lets a hairsplitting understanding possess — lived experience! The consummating complement to the disempowerment of lived experience through its incorporation into thinking spirit is formed by the displacement of spirit out into vitality! Whoever might still have hesitated, when offered knowledge about lived experience in place of lived experience itself, must concede himself overcome, once it has been shown him at length that the entire ground of life is permeated and leavened by a calculating understanding, "unconscious" though it be! — After this sharpening of our view by way of the doctrine of the unconscious, we turn back to the doctrine of consciousness.

Although the act of consciousness by which we take note of what is experienced as well as of the experiencing itself was empowered to enclose lived experience within itself, in the end it proves impossible to avoid somehow keeping the two apart, and thus dividing consciousness once again into the bright space of a knowing and the dark space of a merely-asyet-experiencing consciousness. Thus there arose, and had to arise, the embarrassment-doctrine of a "perceiving" and an "apperceiving" consciousness, which, addressed to more finely fashioned minds, discloses the truly Laocoön-like struggle with the serpent-coils of unresolvable contradictions into which everyone falls who, lacking the capacity for self-deception, has lost the concept of life. — Consciousness is here supposed at first merely to "have" certain "contents," and only at a higher stage [p. 223] does knowledge of them come to be added; the merely had or "perceived" content is indeed already "in" consciousness, but not yet "for" consciousness, or is indeed "experienced" by consciousness but not yet "attended to" by it. Against this we permit ourselves the prior question: if someone, gazing at the evening sky "lost in thought," fails to notice a star located there, how then is the star nonetheless "perceived" by him? How does one hit upon making the process of seeing a "process of consciousness" when consciousness is dwelling precisely on something else? Who has ever come into the peculiar situation of finding something "in" his consciousness which at the same time had no existence whatsoever "for" his consciousness? The play with the prepositions "in" and "for" seems to us to serve the finer deceit of the divisibility of consciousness no more happily than the play with the prepositions "under" and "over" served the cruder deceit of double consciousness.

We urgently recommend to anyone who has not yet resolved on the unreserved rejection of the fiction in question the reading of the most honest work that seeks to defend it, the work "Bewußtsein und Gegenstände" by Theodor Lipps, unquestionably the sharpest analyst of consciousness of the most recent past. One must have inwardly shared in the agonizing struggle with which the author torments himself and the reader in order to make clear the difference between "perception," or the conscious "having" of a "content," and "apperception," or the conscious "thinking" of an "object," and one will thereafter no longer doubt that it is a struggle with the impossible. For whoever turns experiences into "contents" of a consciousness no longer has any possibility of ever again stepping outside consciousness, and, in a consistent train of thought, unavoidably flows into that variously fashionable modern doctrine of the Logos which sees in actuality itself a product of the activity of the I. It is not without interest to see how a researcher of the rank of a Lipps, from an apparently wholly opposed starting point, arrives at the most consistent logicization of inner life thus far, and, so to speak, at a Fichteanism of psychology, after having, in keeping with the erroneous concept of perception, condemned himself on principle to taking experiences for data of consciousness. Striving to give the actuality-character of the external world its due, he never tires of emphasizing its objecthood, independent of consciousness. Since, however, notwithstanding his own definition of "apperceiving" as a merely [p. 224] extracting act, he must nonetheless endow this act with the miraculous gift of displacing experienced "contents of consciousness" out of consciousness, his external-worldly is from the outset that which it finally, openly reveals itself to be by way of a train of thought as convoluted as it is superfluous: a — product of consciousness! The chain of grounds that develops almost by necessity has the following principal shape: actuality is factuality; factuality is the experienced demand of an object to be thought; every individually actual thing belongs to the one Actual; unity is found only in the "gathering" act of consciousness; consequently actuality is the creative doing of a transcendent I, whose volitions are "perceived" by the individual I as a demand. The kernel of the matter has been laid bare: the external world so readily conceded has become the content of a detached reason, lived experience, forever being summoned up, has become a kind of echo of its commands, actuality as a whole has become the conceptual web of the pure subject! Yet there was no need at all of the difficult, winding path along which we have only made visible the turning points and waystations, in order to reach a goal that in truth lies at its — beginning. Whoever speaks at all seriously of experiences of consciousness has, once and for all, already transformed experiences into thoughts, appearances into objects, the whole of actuality into a contrivance of "apperception"! And he<sup>28</sup> thereby abolished, quite against his own supposition, consciousness itself, because he took from it the precondition of all finding and apprehending, the *being-outside-one-another*!

<sup>28</sup> On page 224. — Of the hopeless double-bind into which one is inevitably entangled by the non-concept "consciousness-experience," the following sentences may give a sample. "And in thinking, consciousness *actually* goes or reaches beyond itself, or *spirit* reaches *beyond consciousness*. It is precisely the peculiarity of consciousness that it does *not* remain enclosed within itself or its experiences, but goes beyond them and thinks objects. — But as surely as objects are not consciousness-experiences, so surely are the *demands* of objects also not consciousness-experiences. This is excluded by the very fact that they are precisely demands of *the objects*. This does not mean that the demands could not be *experienced*; rather they always are, whenever I have a consciousness of them. But my consciousness of a demand is not the demand *itself*, but is my consciousness of it, or (1) my lived experience of it" (pp. 83–84). — Meanwhile Lipps cannot help continually being astonished himself at how consciousness actually manages to find something sweeter present in itself that, by presupposition, is supposed to be only in it. "I have something," he says with reference to the act of thinking, "that at first was only *in* my consciousness, or was simply *experienced*, *apprehended*, and thereby merely set over against, or . . set *myself* over against it. That I am capable of this is by no means self-evident, but can appear as the strangest of all facts of consciousness. And one may well add: whoever this fact has never struck as strange . . has never fully brought it to consciousness" (pp. 20–21). "Now, after I have thus set it over against myself, it is no longer merely (!) in consciousness, but for consciousness . ." "As long as blue is merely content, whether of sensation or of representation, it is indeed not identical with me, but different from me. But it is still one with me (1), that is, not yet consciously *distinguished* from me" (p. 22). — We permit ourselves to interject: this separating-out of a "Different" "within" consciousness could of course lead only to a distinguishing of "contents of consciousness," but not to a distinguishing of consciousness itself from what is alien to consciousness. Let us hear how the author, for the impossible, is compelled to choose an impossible metaphor as well: "In the psychic eye there are *contents*; *for* the spiritual eye there are *objects*" (p. 25). One thinks involuntarily of entoptic opacities! And further: "In me is the content; opposite me stands *the* object" (p. 30). "If one finds the state of affairs described here wonderful, I again draw attention to the fact that I am speaking here of consciousness, the *most wonderful thing* in the *world* . ." (p. 31). "The actuality of objects, I said, is the demand of the objects to be thought . . Only thus do I *experience* them . ." "With this, one might think, actuality is transformed into a consciousness-experience . .; but this view denies a fact. It knows nothing of thinking and of objects. Objects are not consciousness-experiences . . rather objects are that which . . stands opposed to all consciousness-experiences as something toto coelo different." With the thinking of objects "consciousness reaches . . beyond its own limits. And now one perhaps thinks this is as *impossible* as that a man should *jump* over *his own* shadow (emphasis ours)." Yet "it may be impossible to jump over one's own shadow, but consciousness is after all neither a shadow nor a body with a shadow, but is consciousness, and thinking is not the jumping over a shadow, but is thinking" (!) (p. 83). No doubt remains: consciousness makes the impossible possible, namely the jumping over its own shadow! One would like to believe it a parody, and yet the thinker is bitterly in earnest about it! But immediately thereafter come the sentences in which the turning-point becomes visible! In thinking "objects are posited . . which are not in consciousness, but *for* consciousness, in themselves something transcendent to consciousness. It is a further question whether the objects are also transcendent to an all-consciousness or whether they are immanent to it. Perhaps they are *experiences* of such an all-consciousness and nothing but this" (2) (p. 83). At last, then, after a long sham search, the researcher *finds* in the casket of consciousness what he himself had laid into it: the — world!

But what, actually, is the point of the detour? Well, in selfreflective minds, even when they may not know it at all, it perhaps always has that same ground which, in Lipps, thanks to an abnormally developed drive toward conceptual clarity, comes candidly to expression — we mean the compulsion to acknowledge two classes of "experiences of consciousness," of which, as it appears, only the one gives occasion to acts that are at the same time alienating. If, in the usage of science, one "senses" the color blue, say, then on the basis of this content of consciousness the finding act apprehends the mark of a thing foreign to consciousness; if, by contrast, one "feels" joy or sorrow, say, then on the basis of this differently constituted content of consciousness the finding act apprehends the mark merely of a consciousness. (We are not here, of course, speaking of our own conception of the difference between these two data of experience, but [p. 225] of the manner in which it necessarily presents itself to today's psychologist.) One may well say that genuine investigators of the soul — of whom, to be sure, there are only extremely rarely and extremely few — are wont to be gripped more deeply by no question than that of wherein lies the essential difference between feeling and sensing; and now let one not hesitate to admit to oneself that the possibility of determining it is cut off by the imprisonment of both processes within an allegedly experiencing consciousness. The almost tragic self-dismemberment-in-thought, for which a work such as Lipps's "Bewußtsein und Gegenstände" furnishes us the historically most significant evidence, is rooted in the painful conflict between the unavoidably obtruding conviction of the autonomous lawfulness of feelings and the inability to delimit what is felt against the bodily-vivid character of what is sensed, once one has already locked both — sensing together with feeling — into consciousness. For if what is sensed and what is felt sit seriously inside consciousness, then neither of the two can be found outside consciousness either; if, notwithstanding this, one takes the liberty of letting them "affect" the I, then that which affects stands in a relation of otherness not only to the sensing but equally to the feeling I, and there no longer offers itself any way out for deriving the particular cognitive value of sensation. But precisely the circumstance that what can only be found in lived experience is nonetheless sought entirely in knowledge forms the ever-renewing incentive to the fear-inspiring torment of that deceptive "self-observation" and "self-dissection" which will later be cited among the psychic pathological phenomena of the most recent turn of the century. The modern investigator of the soul, when he pursues his research activity, lies constantly in wait in order to intercept and gather in, without pause, what has just been "in" his consciousness or is in it, imagining that he thereby beholds with his eyes, as it were, or grasps with his hands, the difference between feeling and sensing, between willing and thinking, between apprehension and lived experience! Nailed fast to the historically hallowed idea of a space of consciousness filled with experiences, he undertakes, as though he had things before him, to describe and dissect what has, at the very moment it becomes the object of his contemplation, already ceased to be a determination of his lived experience — comparable to a man who strives desperately to catch the movement of his own gaze in a mirror, or to take note [p. 226] of the instant of his falling asleep! Such a procedure, however, evidently taken over from the only possible observing of thing-like data, cannot and will never lead to anything other than a reinterpretation of lived experience into those peculiarly hybrid processes, partly cognition-like, partly will-like in character, which one is accustomed to call "processes of consciousness." This very same manner of thinking, which created the mixed concept of an experiencing consciousness, has also produced — to pick out only a few of the most famous from the long series of psychological errors — "inner perception" (Locke) — the interpretation of the emotions as confused thoughts (Descartes, Leibniz) or as inner-bodily sensations (James, Lange) — the division of feelings according to "pleasure" and "displeasure," which is to say, according to success and failure, or their division into "activities of the I" — the multiform unification of the boundless multiplicity of drives (we recall Schopenhauer's "will," the naturalists' "drive to self-preservation," the physicians' sole-beatifying "sexus") — the "feeling-tone" of sensations, as though only sensing were something actual and feeling merely its accompanying circumstance — the impregnation of the ground of life (down into the pathic quality of its dreaming wave-beat) with purposefulness or "finality" — and above all, methodologically, the kind-hostile compulsion to reduction which, secretly led by the nose by the noumenon of a mere unit of calculation, stoichiometrically divides the bearer of life into historical acquisitions, and with the help of backboneless and ultimately never-graspable elements of experience, contrives into a thing-become — actuality itself!

While the exchange of opinion over the concept of consciousness remained within the circle of specialists, the corresponding unconscious enjoys a popular esteem whose devastating effect on the intellectual bearing of the age we must here refrain from characterizing. But before, taking it as our starting point, we let the constructive activity follow upon our efforts hitherto preferentially devoted to demolition, let us ward off one more misunderstanding that lies close at hand. One might think that, since vitality is at any rate also something unconscious, as at least seems to emerge from our discussions, it would suffice to substitute the word "life" for the so-called unconscious in order to check the evil of the doubling of consciousness; indeed, one might perhaps point, in support of this, to the history of another concept whose initially [p. 227] likewise negative formulation did not prevent it from finally being truthfully filled with positive content. Relatively early in the history of Greek thought, an immaterial appears alongside the material, only to flow, after two centuries of inquiry, into the spiritual. According to closer investigation, however, the opposition was from the outset already one of essence, roughly as though one, beginning with the consideration of light, had at first described heat as lightless; whereas the unconscious, formed from the standpoint of a gradation of degree of consciousness, stands beside the latter as darkness stands beside brightness. Now, as surely as the same laws govern brightness and darkness — namely, those of light — just as surely is it the substance of the presumed consciousness from which the material for building up the "unconscious" was taken; hence it could not be protected by any change of name from the fate of being, instead of life itself, rather a repetition of the understanding, or at best its vitalized ground. This point requires, for the sake of the simile, an explanatory addition.

Darkness arises out of brightness through the sudden or gradual vanishing of the latter. Likewise, for many performances — speaking now within the simile — the light of consciousness dwindles away after they have, for instance, been practiced into habit. Now, as surely as we of course would not understand what now takes place in the dark without the brightness that was at first necessary for it to occur, just as surely will one not, presumably, wish to explain the unlit course of events from the absence of brightness! Rather, to remain within the simile, if it was previously the light of consciousness that at least took part in the arising of certain performances, then it must now presumably be a warmth different from consciousness that accomplishes the very same thing without the help of light! Consequently, whoever wishes, without the concept of life, to ascertain the unconscious merely by considering the activity of consciousness becomes inextricably entangled in the net of a fundamental error, comparable step by step to the error into which a physicist would fall who, confronted with the fact of the convertibility of heat into light (and conversely), saw in heat only its lightlessness, and accordingly concluded that darkness was hidden brightness and therefore capable of producing brightness! That it is in fact hopeless to breathe vitality into an unconscious thus corrupted was already proven by the attempt of Romanticism to call by the name of the unconscious the all-life which it had rediscovered out of "magical" experiences and celebrated in philosophical epics of incomparable [p. 228] splendor of language, with which it wished (erroneously) to declare that from the bearing maternal ground of life there springs at last even the act of finding reflection. For just as little as its living unconscious could link up with the doctrines of consciousness of preceding thought (Goethe's at most excepted), just so little has it been able to have any effect on the rationalized unconscious of the thought that followed, and nowhere has it in the least halted the confusion of a chthonic world of images with the — cellar-rooms of the barracks of the understanding. It is therefore better to refrain from designating life, in terms of a theory of consciousness, by the mark of its unconsciousness, and to content oneself with applying the name "unconscious" only adjectivally, insofar as it cannot be avoided as a way of pointing to the absence of consciousness-making acts of spirit. — But before we now shine our light down into the living dark stratum that underlies the arising of consciousness, we must, more sharply than through mere critique of what is wrong-headed about them, demonstrate in the processes themselves the difference from consciousness even of such life-processes whose occurrence appears inseparably bound up with the capacity for consciousness of their bearer.

[p. 229]

#### 25. Kapitel — Die Bewußtlosigkeit der Lebensvorgänge — Chapter 25 — The Unconsciousness of the Life-Processes

When the completely "absorbed" reader sometimes only becomes aware, after several seconds or even minutes, of the striking of the clock that has taken place, then, in view of the circumstance that a deaf person would not have been capable of this, we are unquestionably entitled to call the process that made the after-the-fact reference possible a hearing, and must therefore assume of this hearing that it occurred, at any rate, *without* consciousness. Since hearing now falls under the concept of lived experience, we would thus have at least one special case that furnishes us the first immediate evidence for the this-sidedness relative to consciousness of lived experience in general, which up to now has only been inferred.
