But then we may hope to find further witnesses as well for the proven dual nature of spirit and life, and to see confirmed by consciousness itself what, translated from the metaphysical into the psychological language, would have to read as follows: no *lived* *experience* is conscious, and no *consciousness can* experience anything. — We have just spoken of a special case; for ordinarily, it seems, one is indeed accustomed to take note of what is heard while one is hearing it! But even the most cursory survey can teach us that it does not constitute an exception at all, since, rather, no so-called appearance of consciousness whatever is to be found that is not, depending on circumstances, merely — a lived experience! We pick out — at first deliberately at random — a few particularly striking examples from the multitude of textbook cases, and leave it to the reader to call others to mind himself or to look such up in any textbook.

The passionate smoker who has resolved not to smoke today for once occasionally finds himself, during a walk, suddenly and to his own astonishment with a lit cigar in his mouth, and has thus, without being conscious of it, carried out a rather intricate sequence of movements that appear to be guided by the end-purpose of smoking. — [p. 230] Accustomed to winding the clock as soon as one takes off one's clothes to go to sleep, one sometimes does it without intending to even when one is merely about to change clothes. — "Who has never," remarks the witty conversationalist *James*, "drawn the house key from his pocket on standing before the door of a good acquaintance." The Huxley whom he cites<sup>29</sup> tells "of a clever prankster who, on seeing an old veteran carrying his dinner home, suddenly called out: 'Attention!'; whereupon the man instantly put his hands to the seam of his trousers and let his mutton, with the potatoes, fall into the gutter!" — The first glance at a person new to us sometimes reminds us of a person we know, even though, often after hours of reflection, we cannot work out which person it actually was. — What do we generally know of a friend's features, in such a way that we could state it or even sketch it "from memory," even though we are able, without reflecting, to recognize him among dozens! — Of the thousands who are extremely sensitive to the faintest hint of a disparaging judgment in the expressions of their fellow men, scarcely one in every hundred would know how to tell us with any accuracy how a disparaging judgment betrays itself in the play of features. — Someone has studied an extensive book with full understanding without afterward being able to state with certainty whether it was printed in roman or in blackletter type. And who has not often already read on through whole paragraphs merely with the eyes, while his spirit was "not on the matter"! — Let one call to mind the difference between the child laboriously learning notes and the accomplished musician who "plays at sight" the most difficult piece of music, in order to be clear at a single stroke that every "ability" is a matter of vitality, and of vitality alone! "The marksman sees a bird, and before he knows it, has aimed and fired. A flash in the eye of his opponent, a momentary pressure of his blade, and the fencer becomes aware that he *has* parried and riposted correctly without delay." Impressions, inferences,<sup>30</sup> conclusions, combinations without the activity of apprehending, inferring, concluding, combining; sequences of movement of apparently the most deliberate purposiveness, without any thinking at all, and only too often against the intention! Indeed, if we consider it rightly, all examples of this kind have, at bottom, something comic about them, because they wish, with great expenditure of effort, to instruct us in things that ought to belong among the most self-evident of all self-evident matters — provided [p. 231] we were not caught in the strangest superstition concerning the nature of consciousness. One writer holds that someone who had to accompany an action unceasingly with consciousness would probably remain restricted, for his whole life long, to two or three actions, or would at least need a whole day merely to dress or undress himself; hence it is a most expedient arrangement that every action gains in ease through repeated performance. Against this, however, it must be remarked that a consciousness which accompanies life-processes could not be conceived at all, and that, moreover, not the very smallest action would ever come about if there were any such thing! It is not consciousness that senses, feels, fantasizes, and it is not consciousness that produces movements! It is only because such a — one feels tempted to say — truism has been lost that one must fall back on examples which set it drastically before our eyes that even life-processes of this kind, which previously seemed most intimately bound up with the act of apprehension, are to be detached from it.

<sup>29</sup> On page 230. — Psychologie, translated by Dürr, p. 137.

<sup>30</sup> On page 230. — Same place, p. 137.

The adherent of belief in the omnipotence of the understanding will scarcely let the opportunity slip to call out to us: well, there we have precisely the logic of the "unconscious"! We ask, however, to be granted a little more patience on this point, and for the time being give only this to consider: that the processes predominantly adduced so far had repeatedly to traverse the cutting-line of the moment of reflection, and thereby acquired the property of a substitute for consciousness. If, then, they admittedly proceed in this way without consciousness, yet nonetheless only fully "logically," "purposively," and so to speak with error-free rationality, this speaks no more for the existence of a hidden activity of thinking than the fact that the interplay of cells, of a purposiveness that simply cannot be surpassed, brings about life-sustaining assimilation of nourishment, or even the healing of countless disturbances of the body's tissues (one need only think of a wound caused by a cut), speaks for a thinking on the part of the cells. Either the word "think" has no meaning whatsoever, or it designates an activity of consciousness. In that case, however, let one finally renounce the folly that declares any arbitrary state of affairs to be something thought merely because its outcome bears a far-reaching resemblance to the outcome of certain acts of reflection. With the falsification of all life-processes thereby delivered — of those simply and wholly separate from consciousness as well [p. 232] as of those capable of being linked with it — one blocks off for oneself, among other things, and indeed without hope of ever finding it again, the path to insight into the nature and the enabling grounds of the act of reflection itself. — Whatever, now, may be the truth about the "automatizing" effect of "habit" and "practice," neither of which has ever yet been thoroughly investigated, in any case both offer us inexhaustible storehouses full of evidence for the separability of reflection from any and every "content of consciousness"; so much so that "consciousness" and "contents" at last fall apart again, and the former becomes remotely similar to a spectator sitting by, whose pauses of sleep have not the slightest influence on the tumult of the latter. Comparable, by way of exception, to that power "which always wills evil and always works the good," the logocentric intention has, with the concept of consciousness, laid the axe to the tree of its own existence, because only now could there rise up as a fact what, without belonging to the external world, is nonetheless not a "fact of consciousness"! Just as if one had uttered a magic formula with the word "consciousness," one sees oneself at once threateningly surrounded and hemmed in by a veritable ghostly chorus of such experiences as perform their dance unconsciously! A confirmation as curious as it is instructive of this is given us by a glance at more recent literature.

Whoever wanders, even only cursorily, through the literature of representation from the oldest to the most recent times cannot fail to notice that, the nearer to the present, the more numerous also appear those figures who do not so much will, speak, and act as rather know themselves compelled to do all this out of dark necessities of their own being. In vain would we search for an ancient Hamlet, an ancient Tasso, an ancient Brother Medardus (from Hoffmann's "Elixiere"), each of whom is driven, as it were, by life-powers dwelling within himself that stand more or less at feud with his conscious personality. The fatalism of the ancients saw an external-worldly necessity of fate to which even the highest gods themselves were still subject; for the fatalism of the moderns, an inner doom holds sway no less irresistibly! This mode of conception found both the high point of its strength and its most richly colored form of appearance in the poetic literature of Romanticism, whose mightiest creations show us man, without exception, in the light of a plaything of secret powers of the soul, or of the will-less conduit of "magical" streams. It is the [p. 233] common element in the distinguishing nimbus of nearly all the poetic works of a Jean Paul, Hölderlin, Kleist, Novalis, Tieck, Achim v. Arnim, Hoffmann, Eichendorff, Lenau — to single out, from the strongest representatives of the Romantic feeling for life, only such as, taken personally, diverge from one another to the point of incomparability. One could hardly find more different types of humanity than, say, Hoffmann's demonic René Cardillac, who piles murder upon murder, and Eichendorff's ever-blissful ne'er-do-well, who, fiddling and rejoicing, travels his roads like the spring wind itself; and yet the polar feelings of the darkest horror and the brightest intoxication, into which we fall when we alternately make their fate our own, are joined by the deeperlying, stratum-deep basic feeling of a being-driven that is now accursed, now graced. Irresistibly spellbound by the glittering gleam of stones and gold, Cardillac must murder, and irresistibly drawn by the alluring blue of the distance, the ne'erdo-well must wander! Both are pathics, but the one of "black," the other of "white" magic. — And the poetry of the period that followed, notwithstanding its contrary tendencies and predominantly "realistic" means of representation, gravitates unawares once again toward the side of inner being-driven, insofar as it at all dares to touch on deeper questions, in such a way that since then one has essentially rightly judged the significance of a poet by the degree to which his work embodies pathic experience convincingly. Ibsen's by far greatest, if not indeed his only, poetic work, Peer Gynt, unrolls the changing panorama of a life-course pathic through and through, and the relevant figures of Dostoevsky, who shines his light down into the abysses of the soul, are without exception "compelled" pathics whose personality, as a result, almost regularly goes to pieces. Here we have everything that today, with particular predilection, occupies the doctrine of psychic illness: "flight" into the night of forgetting, "twilight states" up to the exemplary "splitting of the personality," reifications of every unconscious tactic of behavior, somnambulisms, sham actions of the most precisely calculated purposiveness without, indeed against, the will of the one acting. A few examples!

After the murder has already been committed, Raskolnikov wanders, or rather staggers, wholly aimlessly, as he believes, through the city, driven only by revulsion against every human surrounding. "Everyone he met was repulsive to him, their faces hideous, as were their gait and their movements . . . When he reached the quay of the Little Neva on Vasilevsky Island [p. 234], he stopped by the bridge. 'He lives here, in this house,' thought Raskolnikov, 'but what do I want, I have never gone to Razumikhin's myself; it is exactly the same story as before, and yet odd all the same — I have come myself, or rather have just run along for my own sake and ended up here! And yet, I said — the day before yesterday — *that* I would go to him the day after the deed; well, what is there still to consider, I shall simply do it, then!'" Or: "At another time it seemed to him that he had lain ill for a whole month already; then again, that everything had happened on a single day — but that monstrous thing, that deed, he had wholly forgotten. And yet at every moment he was conscious that he had forgotten something which he must *not* forget . . ." Or: "He walked with his gaze fixed on the ground. Suddenly it seemed as though *someone* hissed into his ear; he raised his head and became aware *that* he was standing before that dreadful house, right at its entrance. Since that evening he had not been in this part of town again, but he did not walk past it." There follows the visit, carried out under feelings of the strongest reluctance, yet compulsively, to the scene of his crime. Or: staggering aimlessly about once again, Raskolnikov comes into a district little known to him, where the following soon takes place: "A leaden feeling weighed on his heart; he stopped in the middle of the street and looked about him; where was he actually, and where did he want to go?" He catches sight of a dirty tavern. "Women's voices sounded. He wanted to turn back again, unclear as to why he had run here, when suddenly, in one of the last open windows . . he saw Svidrigailov sitting with a pipe between his teeth." Both at first act as though they had not noticed each other; the maneuver fails, however — Svidrigailov calls to Raskolnikov, who steps in and declares: "I was just going to you, to seek you out; but why I have now turned into the X-sky Prospect from S Street — I perhaps never come here, never frequent this place; the way to you never leads past here either — I had lost my way and meet you here. Strange, indeed!" "Why do you not say straight out: 'odd'?" "Because this is a matter of chance." "What slipperiness there is in this people," laughed Svidrigailov, "he will not admit it, although inwardly he is firmly convinced of it! You say yourselves that you have come here only by chance, 'perhaps'; what cowards people are regarding their own opinions! . . . But as for the 'oddness' [p. 235], I must tell you that you seem to have been asleep these last two or three days. I myself told you of this tavern. I myself even described the way to you, named the place where it is, the hour at which I can be met here. Do you recall it?" "I had forgotten it," answered Raskolnikov in astonishment. "I well believe it — I even told you twice! . . You have come here quite mechanically, yet strictly according to the address, without becoming aware of it . . ." — Who would not have to think here of posthypnotic suggestions! It may be recalled, for good measure, that it was only the nineteenth century that presented us, on a scale never before seen, with a casuistry of "mesmerism," "animal magnetism," "hypnotism," of "hallucinations," "pseudo-hallucinations," and so on, together with countless discussions concerning them.

One would, however, be altogether mistaken in the view that mankind has in the meantime become somehow more pathic, since, quite the reverse, the much-praised "progress" consists entirely in the gradual overpowering of the dreaming stance toward life by the willing, waking and conscious one. Nor is the ready assumption of a sharpening of the opposition between the two likely to suffice to explain so extraordinary a change of type in imaginative literature. Rather, the reason lies on the surface: the "unconscious" processes have remained what they were, while the conception of them has changed completely; the saga, myth and poetry of the ancients (as of the Middle Ages) are in fact overflowing with depictions of pathic states, some devastating, some beatifying, and already the age of Plato possessed a strictly elaborated theory of the matter. Can a "psychogenic delirium," to speak medically, be portrayed more convincingly than in the "Ajax" of Sophocles, more brilliantly than the Agave of Euripides' "Bacchae," or a theory of pathism be developed more clearly than in Plato's "Phaedrus"? But in those days there was no "unconscious," because there was as yet no consciousness in the present-day sense, and all the stirrings that in some way overcame the personality, or even rendered it absent — the erotic not least among them — were held to be the effects of demonic powers upon the soul of man. Even we today still find, surviving from that stage of thought, words in our language such as "inspiration," "Inspiration," "illumination," "revelation," "enthusiasm," "ecstasy," "possession." A god took possession of the man, sometimes only in soul, sometimes even bodily (the succubus [p. 236] and incubus of the Middle Ages), unveiled the future to him, brightened or clouded his senses, swept the will-less man away into "holy" or diabolical deeds, indeed entered directly into him in order to speak and act in his place. There was no deed so gloriously noble and no crime so wicked that a demon had not breathed it into man! "Merit" and "guilt" were only quite external marks, and "free will" had not yet been invented! For:

"All things indeed the play of change moves, / and ever transformed is men's / unsteady wandering course of life."<sup>31</sup>

<sup>31</sup> On page 236. — *Euripides*, Hippolytos.

Can there be a worse infamy than that of the spurned Phaedra, whose slander brings upon Hippolytus, the man she loved, an end as shameful as it is agonizing, a more culpable recklessness than that of Theseus, who without any examination delivers his innocent son to a cruel destruction! And yet the poet has the deity herself excuse them both:

"So has Cypris contrived it, the treacherous one" and / "...unwillingly you destroyed him; the mortal / must indeed sin, when the gods so *ordain*."<sup>32</sup>

<sup>32</sup> On page 236. — *Euripides*, Hippolytos.

Behind the terrible drama, indeed, stands the jealousy of Aphrodite, goddess of desire, toward the virginal Artemis, whose enthusiastic servant Hippolytus must atone for his austere chastity! Pathism still bears so little the character of an exception that, for its higher and originally unconditionally distinguishing degrees, it wrests the right to exist even from its grimmest enemy, the proletarian Socrates, who was the first of all the Greeks to create the opposite goal of an everunderstanding consciousness: 1 "madness" (= mania), far different from present-day "insanity," was then the name for the reflection-robbing surrender of the conscious personality to the life-impulses held to be *divine*, and counted for this reason as an essentially higher good than the wisest circumspection.

"And frenzy wonderfully resembles the seer's art. / *When* the *power* of the mighty one fills our bodies, / then, *raving*, we speak what is to come."<sup>33</sup>

<sup>33</sup> On page 236. — *Euripides*, Bacchen.

So, roused by Dionysus, the seer Teiresias — and the philosopher concurs! Plato says in the "Phaedrus" that "the greatest goods [p. 237] come to us by way of a madness which is, however, given through a divine gift; for both the prophetess at Delphi and the priestesses at Dodona have, in the state of madness, accomplished much that is splendid for Greece, but in the state of sober-mindedness little or nothing; and if we were also to speak of the Sibyl and others, who by the exercise of a god-inspired art of divination have already foretold much to many concerning the future and thereby preserved them from error, we should prolong the discourse by repeating what is generally known... Also out of sicknesses... the greatest afflictions... madness, appearing in those who had need of it and arising prophetically, found a release..., for those seized by it, a deliverance..., devising remedies with regard to present ills. But there is a third kind of possession and madness, proceeding from the Muses, which, having seized upon a tender and undefiled soul, rouses it to eruption in songs and the rest of poetry, and thereby, glorifying countless deeds of the forefathers, forms their descendants. But whoever comes to the gates of the poetic art without the madness of the Muses, persuading himself that by mere skill he will be a sufficient poet, is himself deficient, and his poetry, that of the sober-minded man, is brought to nothing by that of the mad."

Now even though modern times — leaving aside the truly inspired Romantic movement, which for that matter found its way back to full-blown demonologies — tend to halt at the logicized zone of the individual life, while antiquity, thrusting down to the very ground, brought up far more of those phenomena which today have fallen prey to a dubious "occultism," there is nonetheless no doubt that in both cases we see the same processes, described in two conceptual languages entirely different from one another. Only because the cultic Greek had already created the symbolic opposition of "gods and men," or more correctly "demons and men," was the philosophizing Greek able to discover the conceptual opposition of phenomenon and noumenon, or of life and spirit — however systematically mistaken he may have been in his evaluation of it! Taking this in turn as our foundation, we now set out, by way of anticipation, the following guiding propositions, which may indicate in advance the first steps into the structure of the matter.

I. There are no "appearances" or "contents" or "processes" of [p. 238] consciousness; there are only temporally unextended acts of spirit, which, themselves devoid of lived experience, give consciousness of what is lived.

II. Life is uninterrupted lived experience; consciousness is the momentarily present achievement of the point-like act of reflection, each of which can refer back to the result of every preceding one, in that they are all clamped together by the one and same stream of experience.

III. In the temporally unextended instant of reflection upon it, what has been lived through has always already flowed away, regardless of whether the reflection follows immediately or only much later.

IV. Spirit and life would remain eternally separate, and individual beings would remain in (vegetative) unconsciousness, were there not disturbances in the stream of experience. The reach of the acts of reflection corresponds, among other things, to the degree of susceptibility of life to disturbance.

V. The ultimate ground of possibility of any disturbance whatsoever lies in the particular life-process of sensation (not yet analyzable at this point). Once this is presupposed, the seemingly constant wakefulness of consciousness requires the temporal articulation of the stream of experience, comparable to a regular wave-motion.

VI. The act of reflection fixes the unextended instant, in each case, at which the wave of experience just flowed away ends and the one just coming *begins*. It puts division in the place of articulation. The change of phase in what is lived becomes the consciousness of the separateness of objects.

VII. The question of what, in the instant of reflection, is present of the experience already flowed away leads to the disclosure of a profound difference between the act-bearing boundary-quality of lived experience and the act-less intervening qualities, a difference that forms the foundation of the doctrine of voluntary recollection, and thus of consciousness in the sense of the *capacity* for apprehension and judgement.

[p. 239]

#### 26. Kapitel — Lebendiger und mechanischer Vorgang — Chapter 26 — Living and Mechanical Process

Although, as we know, actuality itself does not consist of things and therefore actuality itself does not know mechanical processes either, we must nevertheless now, where lived experience has become our object, determine first of all — without any side-glance at what is metaphysically warranted — wherein living and mechanical process differ from one another according to our conception. Since every conceptual determination requires the specification of a mark that makes it impossible to confuse the genus to be determined with any other genus, and since the mechanical process points back to the activity of apprehension, we may expect to have truly fenced in the life-process only if this occurs through a determination that at the same time also bounds it against the spiritual act.

Although we must, of course, distinguish between the compelled and the autonomous act, every intervention of spirit nonetheless bears no less the stamp of activity, and activity is always I-activity. If anywhere in the world thinking occurs, it occurs on the part of some thinking someone, and if anywhere in the world willing occurs, it occurs on the part of some willing someone; and likewise too: if someone thinks, he necessarily thinks something; if someone wills, he necessarily wills something. What takes place "in" consciousness are activities, and activities stand in need of completion through the aim of the activity — they are inwardly *transitive* (note well: *inwardly* transitive, and by no means always so according to grammatical form, of which more shortly). Now if mechanical events, like living ones, are without doubt processes, their bearer can never be the I. We turn first to the mechanical process.

Whether it be man or animal whose body is in motion, whether it be the stone rolling will-lessly down the mountain, the flying arrow, or [p. 240] the slowly reshaping cloud: we must in every case disregard the real or supposed liveliness of the moving thing, whenever its being-in-motion is called by us a mechanical one. However violent an undertaking such a beginning may be in the face of a language that partly spiritualizes and partly animates all processes, it is nonetheless actually carried out every time we fix our eye on an event's character as a mechanical process. Not only the customary manner of speech, according to which the cloud wanders, the dust turns, leaves dance in the wind, but even the physicist cannot help, through the transitive use of the verb, placing the objects of his statements in the light of active beings, since he too, after all, lets the falling tree "strike down" the animal, the steam "drive" the piston, the sunbeam "decompose" the light-sensitive layer. Notwithstanding this, what hovers before him is by no means the goal that completes every activity, but a finished state of affairs, only, to be sure, inseparably linked with a preceding state of affairs, to which it relates analogously as an activity's result relates to the activity. He means the striking-down, driving, decomposing to have been expressed only figuratively, just as when it is said of the house that it "casts" a shadow, or of the road that it "runs" across the meadow. Just as certainly as we should know nothing of forces or causes were we not ourselves beings capable of activity, just as certainly do things, causes, forces figure in the mechanical equation merely as computational quantities, stripped entirely even of the scantiest remnant of inherent self-activity. So astonishing a feat of abstraction would hardly have succeeded for the human spirit without the help that language nonetheless lent it, in turn, through its long-since-accomplished creation of the impersonal pronoun. One certainly need not assume that expressions such as "it lightens, it thunders, it rains" originally meant something mechanical; but one must proceed from the fact that in any case they mean nothing personal. With the impersonal pronoun, language furnishes the convincing proof that, as a possible bearer of an event, it recognizes, besides the I capable of activity, a power of yet another kind, and consequently needs the verb by no means only in the sense of the activity-word, but moreover for the purpose of announcing genuine processes, whose motive power — however constituted it may otherwise be — may not even be thought of by analogy with a spirit. If there is for the I no other mode of manifestation than that of activity, [p. 241] and if activity, for its part, always springs from the I, then it belongs to the essence of the process to be the *manifestation-form* of an It.

We interject that the linguistic-historical question of the impersonals is not thereby meant to be decided. The It is used today a thousandfold, as one is wont to say, as a "pure formword" (e.g., it is right, it is good, it is in no hurry, it will not do, it cannot be denied, etc.) and often stands there alongside quite definite grammatical subjects, as in: it is someone coming, it is a storm drawing up, it is the children shouting for joy. But this does not already shake its original opposition to the personal pronoun, which still betrays itself today in the unusualness of expressions like: "it you-talk," and in the impossibility of saying, say: "it he-rejoices." From the relative lateness of its appearance in more or less all the languages to which it has become known at all, we conclude that it originally had to replace a *vanishing* class of grammatical subjects, and this still lies openly evident in a number of cases. If the It of the Greek heuei (= it rains), contained though it is only in the ending, was long preceded by a Zeus heuei (= Zeus lets it rain), then this Zeus was indeed likewise a personal being, at least since the days of Homer, but originally a purely demonic being; and demonic beings are *not* persons. Only the extensive unfamiliarity of many scholars with the symbolic thought of early times makes it seem understandable that the opinion should seriously have been held that the application, customary among several peoples, of gender-designations to things and processes (whether achieved through differences of ending or through specially appointed words) was, at the time it arose, the expression of a tendency toward personification — according to which, in the mind of the primal creators of grammatical genders, the way should have counted for a man, the surf for a woman, water for neither of the two. No age at all, and least of all the primally creative prehistoric age, *had to* take something for a person because it took it for something living, and the river or stream was, for all the peoples who made it masculine, already an incalculably long time a masculine living being before it became for them the dwelling-place of humanly shaped gods of the same gender! Only as a consequence of the growing independence of consciousness from lived experience, and the accompanying narrowing of the concept of life to men and animals, did the efficacious being of extra-human [p. 242] events acquire the character of that indeterminacy — both general and, in particular, also of gender — for which the in every respect neutral It offers itself as linguistic expression. We hold that sentences with the bearer-word It are neither grammatically nor, indeed, originally, in their meaning, "subjectless," and we think that its present-day indeterminacy pure and simple could fall to it only because, at the time of its origin, it was called upon to take the place of the object-class — slipping away from consciousness — of *extra-human* living powers. We do not place the emphasis on the now, admittedly, undoubted indeterminacy or fadedness, since it would then be hard to understand why, in a mankind thinking in ever more conceptually determinate fashion, the need for the use of an indeterminate sentence-bearer-word could increase; rather we place it on the impersonality, which had to interpenetrate all the more intimately with the lack of determinacy, the more, for the consciousness of mankind, everything extra-personally actual was stripped of inner liveliness. Should one wish, on linguistic grounds, to dispute the fundamental correctness of this conception, it is enough for us already to maintain it for such impersonals as: it thunders, it lightens, it rains, it snows, it hails, it storms, it thaws, it burns, it smokes, it shines, it glows, it flames, etc., to which we shall, to be sure, at once have to assign a series akin to them in essence.

While one could fill whole libraries with the volumes that philosophers have written about the I, there is as yet no system that has the far more mysterious It as its center of growth. For thanks to the logocentric direction of human intellectual history, the It has become, in accordance with a logic of semantic development as compelling as it is easily deciphered, the substructure of mechanistic thinking, in that it conceptually preserved of its original sense only its relation of opposition to the I, while being able, precisely for that reason, to save itself all the more fully into the singing nimbus with which the fairy-tale opening "Once upon a time" [Es war einmal] is wont to enfold us. If, in the 13th chapter (note 13), we believed we had found, for the certainly explanationrequiring circumstance that the name of the subject denotes on the one occasion the personal I, and on another any bearer of a statement, the reason in the coloring of personality that falls to the grammatical subject from the unconscious reference, made by the one who pronounces judgement, to the place of origin of objective being, namely the I, then we already know, by this very fact, why [p. 243] as nothing else could, the impersonal pronoun had to ease and favor a direction of thought whose hidden drive was aimed at the de-animation of the object. If the grammatical "subject" had secretly been a personal and hence active subject, then, through the introduction of a markedly impersonal bearer-word, in the measure that its demonistic primal meaning dwindled away, the verb had to forfeit its character not only as active efficient cause but as efficient cause altogether, and to exchange it instead for that of a process-word "in itself," so to speak. In this way there was linguistically prefigured what mechanistic thinking undertook to elaborate into the complete system of a world-view which, for the sake of the calculability of events, eliminates the concept of causing. The mechanical process is an intransitive It-process. To give an example: the metaphorical turn of phrase that the falling stone had (transitively) shattered a vessel would have to be replaced by the statement that, as a consequence of its falling, the vessel broke — if one wished to describe the process in a strictly mechanistic way, within, of course, the limits that the living and organically grown word sets against every Lullian misuse!

If we had already had occasion earlier to remark that mechanical "force" lacks a goal, we now know that it lacks even more completely the capacity for causing; and by this alone every attempt at a system of world-mechanics would be uprooted. If, in the great machine-house of the mechanistically interpreted universe, some process takes place, then, as one is wont to say, another process follows upon it lawfully. But no physicist has been able to tell us, and none will ever be able to tell us, how the first process sets about bringing forth the second, given that the bearer of the process as such — call it matter, atom, or ether — has been expressly stripped of all liveliness and consequently, being devoid of impulse, would neither exert effects nor receive them. If it belongs to the determinateness of the mechanical process to be an intransitive process, then it does not exist in actuality, because in actuality it would not only be capable of effecting nothing, but could not even have been brought about by another process. If this already presignified why every real process must be conceived as a living process, we have at the same time also ascertained what separates the mechanical process from the living one, and can at once [p. 244] define: the life-process is transitive. No intransitive verb describes the verb "to live through" [erleben]; for to lived experience belongs something lived through, as to what is lived through belongs one who lives it.

Perhaps one will object that what does the living-through is precisely an I, and that lived experience is therefore in turn merely the being-directed-toward-something of spiritual doing. If it already reads, I think, will, apprehend, then, with no lesser right, I see, hear, smell, taste, touch, live through, feel, hate, love, dream; moreover, some of the most important life-verbs, such as wake, sleep, live, die, are intransitive. — We leave it still undecided that today surely no one would deny animals waking, sleeping, living and dying, touching, tasting, smelling, hearing and seeing, even though he might not for that reason be ready to endow them with I-consciousness as well; for one must first, by another route, recover from the logocentric blindness of the foregoing objection and have escaped the downright fatal error into which, in dependence on the active form of the verb common more or less to all Indo-European languages, the thinking of the Aryan peoples was led astray from the very beginning with regard to life-processes, before one would then also find oneself prompted to draw means of proof, from considerations of the psychic life of animals, for the fundamental difference between the roles of the bearer of life in immediate lived experience and in the spiritual apprehension of what is lived through! Here we show what interpretation that linguistic usage requires, and that it is able to offer weighty testimony for our conception, once it has been rightly understood.

Let us first remain with the verb "to live through" [erleben]; the most modest self-reflection suffices to convey the recognition that, in the statement "I live through," the I is a suffering subject and thus, in point of fact, rather the object of an event that has sprung up outside the subject. This also emerges linguistically as soon as we direct our attention, for example, to the emotions, to which the term "to live through" finds its preferred application. If the person not yet distorted in his thinking reckons his thinking and his willing, to be sure, among the activities of spirit, but quite certainly not his emotions, he instinctively follows the directions of language, which, equally with the Greek "pathos," the Latin "passio," and the German "Leidenschaft," assigns to the I violently living-through something the role of a being that lets something happen to it, and which holds even the learned "affect" and "emotion" [p. 245] under the spell of the same image. According to a usage of language valid without exception, we have the will, and are had by feeling. "No one will say that his will drives him to pluck the rose, but rather that he wills it; perhaps, though, because his desire drives him to it. Desire 'compels,' admiration 'seizes,' grief 'shakes,' hatred 'blinds,' rage 'grips' — in short, the affect moves *me*, who am, for my part, in turn the mover of my will. It can either be followed by feeling or resisted, but it cannot be called forth of one's own accord, which, on the contrary, in renunciation of activity, would be a letting-happen and a suffering." — <sup>34</sup> *What* we feel in joy, grief, love, wistfulness, hope, is hardly less alien to consciousness than are colors, sounds, scents, dream-visions. How else, indeed, could it be understood that man has, since ancient times, distinguished his feelings not only from one another but even from himself, has beheld them opposite himself like beings, and has outright created gods of love, of desire, of warlike courage! One need only think of the "temptations" of the saints, of the "evil enemy" of the Middle Ages, and of the fact that, even in the 17th century, many books dealing with disapprovingly judged drives or addictions were preferably titled: der Eheteufel [the marriage-devil], Saufteufel [drinkdevil], Spielteufel [gambling-devil], Hofteufel [court-devil], Jagdteufel [hunting-devil]; or one may read the Stoics, how they speak of the affects quite as of wild beasts that lie in feud around the rational I of man, and one will give up denying the character of the emotions as something one undergoes, and disputing the opposition that holds between the I's falling prey to a living event and its own autonomous act of apprehension. — Why, and under what conditions, it is nonetheless precisely the surge of feeling that is called upon to extort acts of reflection from consciousness, we shall consider further below.

<sup>34</sup> On page 245. — *Klages*, Die Grundlagen der Charakterkunde, 11th ed., p. 135.

Had one heeded such unmistakable indications, one would never have fallen into the momentous illusion that presumes to interpret "I live through" in the same sense as "I think" or "I will." For if the difference is exactly the same as that between an "I suffer" and an "I do," and if "I suffer" can thus be represented by a "it happens to me," then in the lived experience the I is, in point of sense, the point of attack of a process which, stemming from the body living its own life, has awakened in consciousness the — to be sure always I-guided — act of apprehension! While every "I do" says literally what it means, "I live through" always means this: I apprehend, or take cognizance, [p. 246] of, or reflect upon, the fact that something *befell me*. — But if this holds firm for the feelings and affects, whose I-nature the psychology hitherto has never tired of emphasizing, it applies all the more fully to sensing, beholding and dreaming — names by which we do not at all mean the processes in question themselves, but rather what is sensed, beheld, dreamed, in the face of which the I sinks down to an activity-unconscious recipient; according to which it would, strictly speaking, have to read: to me appears the dreamable, the sensible, the visible, the audible, the smellable, the tastable, the touchable! Whoever created a work, solved a task, completed a piece of work rightly asserts that he performed, did, accomplished the thing; but no one of sound mind would hit upon declaring, as his achievement or deed, the resistance his groping hand encountered, the colors that met his eye, the dream-vision that the night's sleep bestowed upon him. — As for, finally, the intransitive form "I wake, sleep, live, die," it is surely enough to point to the fact that we should know not the least thing of any of those states, were they not able to overwhelm the I just as any feeling can; for which one may recall the transitional moments of awakening, of being awakened, of falling asleep, and finally, too, of fainting, which gave us a foretaste even of the act of dying.

And here we must now append to the foregoing another series of It-expressions, from which it emerges compellingly that in each case a living power is envisaged which stands out unmistakably against the I capable of activity. Sentences such as "it grips, seizes, shakes, overwhelms me" or "it tenses, delights, horrifies me" may well leave it open whether the It perhaps does not mean some external event; but in any case what is meant exclusively is the inner, and thus living, power that confronts the I, subduing it, in expressions such as: it freezes, hungers, thirsts me; it pains, gnaws, rues me; it makes me laugh, makes me drowsy; it makes me anxious, it dreamed to me — and likewise in "it lures, entices, desires, drives, tempts me," insofar as this or that doing depends on it. Through such possibilities of expression, language directly discloses to us the I-opposed essence of an It that nonetheless bears living effects, and thereby, at the same time, the character of undergoing that belongs to feeling as much as to sensing and beholding; whereby, admittedly, the new question becomes pressing, how it could ever have come about [p. 247] that, at least in the case of sensing, the I's undergoing is marked quite predominantly by means of the active form! How did it come about that, with "I see, hear, smell, taste, touch," something happening to the I was forced into the very same active form of the word that, in "I throw, strike, run," designates an achievement of will, and that "I reflect" or "I have reflected" should be set alongside, as apparently equivalent, an "I have forgotten it," as though even forgetting could be an activity?! Why was the sole appropriate passive form exchanged for the active form, and this, moreover, particularly in the case of sensing, which, as nothing else does, stamps our essence as a mere receiving-apparatus for I-independent "impressions"? Even the recollection that there exist whole linguistic circles, such as, say, the Greenlandic, which have kept themselves entirely free of such a confusion, would not relieve us of the obligation to ascertain the reasons for its common occurrence in languages not even remotely related to one another, such as, for example, the Germanic and the Chinese. — Our answer takes into account for the present only what is necessary in order to protect the character of undergoing that belongs to the life-process against doubts that might perhaps appeal to such linguistic usages.

The possibility of announcing a passio through an intentio is at all times given for the very simple reason that man, as the bearer of consciousness, remembers — by no means always, as we have heard, but nonetheless by far predominantly — such experiences-undergone to which an act of apprehension immediately attached itself. It is, after all, the ordinary case that I suppose myself now to be sensing something, now to be feeling something, and am accordingly quite unable, through recollection, to distinguish my act of apprehension of what was sensed or felt from the processes of sensing or feeling. We may assume that it was either the peoples endowed with more than average strength of understanding (e.g., the Chinese) or those endowed with more than average strength of will (e.g., the Aryans) who therefore gave preference quite generally to the active form of the verb. — Against this, we have still other grounds to adduce for the special favoring of the active form for the purpose of announcing sense-processes, where their character of undergoing rather still exceeds that of the emotions.

There are, as will be shown, several kinds of estrangement, one of which presses in the first instance toward the judgement of the object's difference from the I, another of which presses, besides and especially, toward the judgement of its difference [p. 248] from the experiencing soul. In the state of being sad, everyone can indeed effortlessly give himself an account of the fact that it is grief that has seized his I, and he can give this expression by setting it, with "I feel grief," "I have a feeling of grief," over against the I, or even by raising it to a living power in expressions such as "grief befalls me"; but as a rational being, who no longer holds grief to be a demon, he is compelled to hold it to be a process of his own soul, which he naturally has to think of as somehow attached to his spirit. Through this, the process of feeling gains, in the mirror of self-observation, so considerable a preponderance that untrained reflection runs the danger of putting it in the place of what is felt — for which a single example may suffice instead of many. Every sensuously lived-through thing can, through intensification, take on the aftertaste of painfulness that is ordinarily accompanied by a peculiar state of displeasure of the soul. Because this state, in taking hold of us in a preeminent way, at once fuses with its content, we are accustomed to call many kindred states of the soul simply "pains," even though the occasion for them lies by no means in a disturbance of the body, but, say, in the thought of a beloved's infidelity. We speak of soul-pain as we speak of toothache, and this usage is common to numerous languages; from which one may see how readily the content of feeling is constantly, as it were, ready to vanish behind the process of feeling, which is thereby able to preserve its independence relatively well against spirit.

Exactly the reverse is true of the process of sensuous lived experience, be it beholding or genuine sensation: it is constantly ready to vanish behind what is sensuously lived through, whose alienness to consciousness carries the character — at the same time distinct from the soul — of the image or the body. If feeling conceals from us what is felt, then what is beheld conceals from us the beholding, what is sensed the sensing; and if the apprehension of feeling always related preponderantly to the feeling, then to a far higher degree still does the apprehension of sensuous lived experience relate to what is sensuously lived through. A person in a state of grieving usually returns involuntarily, from the occasion as from the content of the grief, to his grieving, whereas one who watches fireworks being set off, if his senses are sound, never finds himself prompted, on that account, to think of the process of seeing! All the defects of the doctrine of sense-experiences are most deeply grounded in their confusion [p. 249] with things, and this, in turn, was at the outset a consequence of the darkening that sense-experience suffered from its opposition to the outshining brilliance of the lived appearance. Accordingly we see Greek thought dominated by the tendency to explain beholding from the beholdable, and, for example, to take the eye for something luminous, because it is able to receive effects of light; modern thought, on the other hand, to explain sensing from the sensible, and to take, say, all sense-processes for nothing but bodily processes, because they bring us tidings of bodily processes outside us! But if the sense-experience thus manifestly recedes entirely behind the colors, shapes, sounds, smells, resistances that appear to us with its help, then we understand why so many languages pass over it almost entirely and take note only of the acts of perception that commonly follow close upon its heels; and we understand all the more fully how greatly, precisely thereby, aid was lent to the aberrations of a thinking that was intent on falsifying lived experiences generally, either into acts of spirit or into mechanical processes. Against this, we may, after so far-reaching a refutation of all counter-positions, now take it as settled and proven: the bearer of doing is the I, the bearer of happening the It; the mechanical process is intransitive, the life-process transitive. — Before we draw further conclusions from this, we return once more to the difference between alienness-to-spirit and alienness-to-soul.

The polarity that we had to set forth for the purpose of characterizing the life-process is that of the movements of the soul toward something that moves the soul. Accordingly, lived experiences would be, quite simply, things undergone — namely, by the soul — and, in the second instance, then also things undergone by the I or by spirit. We must, however, distinguish these two kinds of undergoing from one another in more than one respect. — The I, or, let us say, the I-shaped spirit, receives directly only psychic (or bodily) effects, and becomes aware only through and by means of these of the effects that the soul suffered from actuality itself; whereas the soul, besides those just named, also undergoes impulses on the part of spirit. As a consequence, we must thoroughly remodel our concepts of activity and undergoing (passivity) in their application to the soul, and for this purpose we take up the term, handed down from antiquity and already used without explanatory comment in the previous chapter, of pathic. In calling the soul pathic through and through, we [p. 250] mean to say: it moves, insofar as it is movable, out of undergoing, never out of exertion of force; it answers, as it were, now the question, now the demanding and commanding call, and only in consequence of this does it enter into the circle of efficacious powers; it is not, of itself, an active power, but rather so out of the necessity of a reverberation peculiar to it alone and characteristic of its kind. (Lest one take offense at the seeming contradiction with our claim above, that only something capable of effecting could receive effects, we add here already that we do not mean to deny the soul the capacity to effect altogether, but rather that we place its center of gravity in undergoing.)

Quite the opposite is true of spirit! In and for itself "actus purus," or sheer act, it becomes, through coupling with the living soul, a capacity for activity that reveals itself either in doing (activity) or in being-done-to (passivity). Were the efficacy of the soul not an efficacy out of undergoing, and were this not (for reasons that will emerge later) communicated by it to spirit, spirit would for its part experience no effect at all, and we should accordingly lack the I-experience of passivity, and then, in consequence, of activity too, because every doing requires something resisting, in the overcoming of which it proves itself. But just as even the efficacy of the soul takes place not out of arbitrary choice but out of necessity, and is thus rather a having-to, so the passivity of the I thereby made possible proves, on closer consideration, to be another mode of being active. For we experience being-done-to only on the strength of just such a capacity, in which every impulse that touches it awakens the urge to counter-activity. While, then, we must regard the soul as a being that simply undergoes, spirit, shaped in the form of I, by contrast becomes the being that simply acts — only that its manifestations come to consciousness for us now as autonomous, now as compelled. If we consider the compelled manifestations by themselves alone, they in turn fall apart into several kinds, according as in them the I braces itself against what is efficacious, or succumbs to the psychic influence, or, finally, renouncing all self-assertion, surrenders itself to it and thereby gives itself up. Leaving the latter case aside for the time being, we shall henceforth, so far as possible, use "thing undergone" [Widerfahrnis], in part, and "suffering" [Erleidnis], in part, exclusively to denote the psychic pathic, but, with an easily intelligible variation, "succumbing" or "falling prey" for the compelled forms of activity of spirit.

[p. 251] In the interconnection of the mutually conditioning poles of the efficacious world and the undergoing soul lies the sense of lived experience, and thus the no-further-resolvable meaning of all "sense" whatsoever. Essentially meaningful is the interconnection of the distinguishable members of a manifold, and the most original manifold is a twofold. The return to this twofold, far from following a mere caprice of dividing and counting, is demanded by the polarity between the appearing actuality and the soul that lives it through; a polarity without which there would be no concept of a living being, and then none of a thinking being either. In it, as may be stated in advance, is grounded the actual significance of the number three. The primordial view is correct which ascribed to the middle one of every sacred three the primacy over the two flanking units: for in it, as the whole, are joined the two poles distinguishable from one another in each case! But just as the unsupported happening articulates itself into an efficacious agent and a sufferer of the effect, so the *appearance* of the world everywhere presents us with that sidedness which we can think only in the form of poled unities. The magnet is the connecting third out of negative and positive force, the body of numerous animals — but also of leaves — out of left and right, the day out of darkness and brightness, and so on. We call to mind a result in which the life-scientific part of our investigations thus far is summed up, by means of the following equation: life-process = lived experience = poled happening = polarity between efficacious power and undergoing soul = reciprocity of estrangement and transition = primal schema of the meaningful process = point of origin of the appearing triad.

If, then, the life-process consists in the process of lived experience, every living thing, so long as it lives, finds itself in the state of lived experience, and we should accordingly have to determine life as the capacity for *uninterrupted* lived experience. No one denies that, between the birth and death of the living individual being, being-alive is not broken off for a single instant, and all are ready to acknowledge, once again, the continuity of the stream of life for every chain of individual beings sprung one from another, up to the cellular primal ancestor who lived millions of years ago; but very few consider that the continuity of the stream of life is by no means yet guaranteed by the connection of all the single waves distinguishable within it, but that this requires, in addition, for every instant of every single wave, the interconnection of the receiving soul with the efficacious happening. Being-alive, [p. 252] in other words, presents itself, in the individual life as also even in the sequence of generations, as a succession of lived experiences that suffers, at no point, an interruption by anything that would *not* be lived experience!

Scarcely anything else casts a deeper light into the devastating consequences of the confusion of spirit and life than the fact that people are inclined to claim, for spirit — indeed for consciousness — the uninterruptibility of the ever-changing happening, of which one hears, astonished and reluctant, once it is disclosed in the form of the continuity of lived experience! If, as has been shown, the act of reflection takes place in the boundary-setting instant, then each such act is separated from every other by an intervening interval of unconsciousness, and would remain, wholly isolated, condemned to ineffectiveness, without the stream of life that binds them all together. Just as certainly as, in the bearer of life, lived experience hangs together with lived experience, and, thanks to lived experience, the experiencing soul with the experienced image, just as certainly does "consciousness" of the bearer of life mean the series of strictly momentary acts of spirit, which are clamped together with one another and thereby become referable to one another solely through the continuity of that lived experience. With this proposition the doctrine of consciousness begins for us, and thus, for the first time, the science of the soul as well, because without a doctrine of consciousness no science of the soul could come about. In contrast to this, the textbooks of "psychology" are accustomed to begin with the assurance that consciousness precisely has the nature of a continuous stream, out of which reflective consideration first lifts sides and parts! Where, we might already<sup>35</sup> ask here, does the said stream of consciousness hide in dreamless deep sleep? We cannot judge what those persons actually think, and whether they think anything at all by it, who speak in the same breath of spiritual acts and of the stream of consciousness; but we think that so scruple-free a conceptual confusion suffices to justify *every* conflation of life and spirit, and to fill up lived experience at will with unconscious acts of reflection!

<sup>35</sup> On page 252. — *James*, for example, gives the eleventh chapter of his "Psychology" the heading "The Stream of Consciousness" and lists, in third place among his four criteria of consciousness: "Every personal consciousness is sensibly continuous." Loc. cit., p. 149.

There are poets' words whose mere conceptual content could hardly explain why they are at once, and often for centuries, on everyone's lips. We would not understand why the most varied occurrences in the life of modern man again and again call forth the couplet from Hamlet's soliloquy: "the native hue of resolution / is sicklied o'er with the pale cast of thought," [p. 253] if we thought we had thereby declared nothing more than the rather obvious, and certainly not startling, discovery that too much pensiveness and scrupulousness hinders their bearer from acting. But these verses belong to those weather-signs which, here and there suddenly illuminating the oppressive darkness of a mighty poetry, make threatening visions emerge out of mist and desolation, and in this way let us divine the incomparably deeper science of the conflict between lived experience and consciousness — a science for which the inquiry into essence has been wrestling since the "Renaissance," and which our book undertakes to conclude with a *final* answer. The deep gulf that seemed to open between life and spirit has unmistakably met us again in the relation of consciousness to lived experience. Lived experience has the character of continuity, consciousness that of a series of gaps; in lived experience the experiencing soul, even if as opposite poles, hangs together with the experienced image, while in consciousness the knowing I and its object are separated from one another; lived experience is extinguished in the act of reflection, the act of reflection is without lived experience; lived experience, never to be wearied, rolls on through aeons, while consciousness, suspended a thousand times over in the numbness of sleep, endures only the comparatively tiny span of a human existence; lived experience embraces and joins together all organisms, and perhaps beyond them even the stars and indeed space and time itself, while consciousness parts from its own vitality and tears out of the whole All, insofar as it is that All, the bearer of consciousness. Compared with such a gulf, the space between the stars must count as less unbridgeable; for it connects suns with earths, earths with moons, through gravitation and light; but consciousness can only sunder: it is the irresistible and never-to-be-appeased aqua fortis for all connections! Spirit and life — thus a Gorgon's head rounds itself more firmly before us — are two actualities hostile to one another from the ground up: the power outside space and time, whose timelessly twitching act shatters actuality into atoms of being within the cosmos; and the ocean of happening within space and time, out of whose ceaselessly quivering mirror breaks the dancing reflection of the farthest stars. There is no third thing of which they would be parts or sides, and hence there is no intelligible reason why it should have had to *happen* that they clashed together in man, and in him alone — whereby, in respect of the bearer of consciousness, every "monism," and in respect of actuality every "dualism" as well, is disposed of for good! — [p. 254] Conceptually still undeveloped, yet sufficiently recognizable, the profound thought has at least once been present, that accordingly the highest and last goal of humanity consists in this: with the aqua fortis of spirit, at the end to loose from life spirit itself, the great sunderer of all things, and thus to restore to each of the two, life and spirit, the undisturbed being-for-itself of their primordial existence — namely more than two and a half thousand years ago, in the Sāṃkhya philosophy of the Indians, which in clear-sightedness and truth-content leaves the Buddhist doctrine of Nirvana behind it. — Before one could approach such highly metaphysical problems, however, one would first have to have traversed a whole throng of other questions, of which we shall name a few.

How was it possible for spirit and life to clash, when they are yet of wholly different essence? When and where did it first happen? How could reflection upon the occasion of lived experience come to be joined to lived experience? Why is there consciousness only of the swiftly transient single life, and why not a consciousness of boundless lived experience itself? Why, above all, has life balled itself up into creatures, and wherein consists — in contrast to unbounded lived experience — that particular connectedness of life-processes which forms the substratum of a consciousness? Does thinking-consciousness really belong to man alone? What modification of his mode of life gave room for the incursion of spirit? How do the consciousness-capable life-processes within him differ from those never capable of consciousness? What does his lived experience effect in his consciousness, and what is altered in his lived experience by this consciousness? How are the relatabilities of spirit related to the connections of life? — We shall not be able to answer every one of these questions; but it will become clear that those which cannot for the present be decided all hang, one and all, on a single one, comparable to the little bells and jingles that chime in officiously whenever the great tambourine, to whose rim they are tied fast, is struck. And likewise the answer to all the rest will be found without difficulty, as soon as we have illumined just one down to its depths: namely the question of which property of lived experience it is to which the act of reflection is immediately bound, insofar as the existence of the intervention-ready spirit is provisionally presupposed.

[p. 255]

#### 27. Kapitel — Das Gefälle des Lebensstromes — Chapter 27 — The Gradient of the Stream of Life

Up to this point we have, standing on the side of spirit, looked across at life. Let us now for a moment take our stand on the side of life and look across at spirit; then the act of reflection at once moves into the light of a having-to-stop, a stepping-out of the stream of lived experience, a sudden finding-oneself-beside-oneself as the result of a lightning-like blow that has taken place. Measured against that flow of lived experience which we in fact only infer, yet believe, as if in recollection, to know immediately when we look back, say, on the enjoyment of a symphony, every coming-to-consciousness resembles being awakened from deep sleep and presents itself, like this, as an experience of disturbance. Should it not, then, be disturbance-like shock-points in the stream of life itself that in a sense open the gate to the incursion of spirit, and let us recognize the primal meaning of its working as consisting in this: that it hardens into lifeless matters-of-fact what was rock of fate surf-beaten by life? We shall try to substantiate this conjecture step by step, and begin with a series of irrefutable testimonies that far-reaching acts of self-reflection regularly appear bound to an unusually steep gradient of the *stream of life*.

All the textbook examples of unconscious lived experience to which we deliberately confined ourselves above suffer from the defect of picking out only such experiences as merely seem, in retrospect, to lack the consciousness that once accompanied them, and which therefore lend support to the erroneous view that their unconsciousness is merely a sideeffect of the repetition of acts of reflection identical in meaning. Against this, a comprehensive view of the unconscious stream of original lived experience is opened to us by taking note of those kinds of happening which, throughout the uniformity of their working upon the soul of the bearer of life, can never become conscious, even though the span of time involved may [p. 256] be measured in years. Whoever, capable even to some small degree of remembering feelings, looks back in youth upon the years of childhood, makes without exception the surprising finding of an unbroken fundamental tone of mood running through them, of which he had at the time not the slightest knowledge. It was, then, not his lived experience as such, but its transformation reaching down into the depths, that enabled him to take cognizance of those depths. The stream of his lived experience had to leave the level surface of its upper course near the source and, after a cascading or sudden fall, gain a new level, in order that the transformed roar might bring him a belated consciousness of what had passed. Had the stream in its course never undergone a fall, had it never been cast "from cliff to cliff," there would be no knowledge of natural sections of the single life that was more than knowledge of merely bodily changes. To appreciate the full meaning of this, however, we must consider the fundamental mood in question somewhat more closely.

In retrospect it can seem to us to swim about a whole section of life like a nimbus, yet it commonly stands before us in fixed colors — whether luminous or dimming the light — and almost tangibly before our eyes, only when we manage to catch it by immersing ourselves in quite definite events, actions, words, surges of feeling, thoughts of the past. Now that it has vanished, we believe we perceive, in countless impressions, with complete clarity, a timbre of the soul which we are infallibly certain we can no longer live through, while at the same time we are compelled to establish that in the former fullness of what was livingly possessed we lacked all consciousness of it. Be it the bite into a juicy apple, the sight of the light-giving Christmas tree, the smell of the honeycomb, the high garden wall, the game with the kidney-beans, the majestic cumulus cloud in the summer sky, the blowing of the wind and the rustling of leaves, the favorite playmate, the circus performance, a fearsome thunderstorm, the terror of darkness, the dread of the churchyard, the throbbing of "conscience," the scarlet fever, or whatever it may have been — we know now that at the time a shimmer lay over everything and anything, a shimmer that today is a riddle to us, and which, so it appears, remained just as undisclosable and hidden to us for exactly as long as we were lost in the living awareness of it! The experience of the youth with his childhood years is repeated for the man when he [p. 257] looks back on his youth, and for the old man with the years of middle manhood. No mortal is empowered to grasp the ever-present fundamental color of his lived experience. Neither the reflective sage, who of all characters possesses the clearest knowledge of life, nor the poet who lives from the root, who of all men calls the deepest knowledge of life his own, penetrates down to the groundwater from which they are fed — the life-powers that work in him again and again — even though he makes the past present again far more vividly than the restlessly purpose-bound man of action or the researcher who bleeds himself out upon concepts.

To this is added, for everyone who has the middle of life behind him, a further experience that confirms our interpretation of the previous one: namely, that a sequence of increasing degrees of his "awareness" corresponded to the succession of differently elevated river-sections of the life he has left behind him. Only in the last two centuries, with the fearful increase of the inclination to analysis, did insight ripen into that curious opposition of ways of holding oneself in life which the distinction between a predominantly "naive" and a predominantly "conscious" ("reflective," "sentimental") type of character seeks to found. If we seek the shaping core within this somewhat fluid formation, the two concepts stand out against one another as follows: a character is, other circumstances being comparable, the more "naive" the stronger the rapids of his lived experience must be before he wins a consciousness of it from it, and conversely the more conscious the smaller the changes of his pulse of lived experience that suffice to let the act of reflection spring from them. The transition from the one to the other appears as one from a difficult to an easy triggering of retrospective acts of reflection. — If we consider that, accordingly, the child, thanks to unquestionably greater "naiveté," is absorbed in experiences by comparison with the adult, from which the latter, scarcely had they taken place, would already be torn away again by consciousness of them, then we see, with the increasing automatism of life, the easing of reflectiveness agreeing surprisingly well with it, and are thereby fully guarded against confusing the, so to speak, consciousness-saturated "unconscious" with the unconsciousness of original lived experience. The more a bearer of consciousness has "experienced," the greater became his store of incorporated rules of experience, and the weaker is the effort of reflection required on the occasion of applying those rules to the individual case. But the waters that drift, as if alive, in [p. 258] the channels of habit are withdrawn from the riverbed of lived experience; from which it follows that the achievements of the act of reflection must flatten out at the same pace, and the ever-repeating disturbance would be called upon to carry life, through intervening stretches of spiritual wrestling, into a final *rigidity* perhaps even robbed of consciousness altogether. — But we wish to wander to the end of the way, and therefore rein in, lest appearance deceive us, the desire for beams of light that run ahead of it.

What holds for the single life in respect of its year-spanning sections is confirmed once again for the weaker and stronger bends within them. Only after entry into school has been accomplished does the child know of any happiness in its school-free idleness, of which until then it had no knowledge whatsoever; only after entry into the apprenticeship of a trade has been accomplished does the youth know of certain tones of mood belonging to his schooldays, which were unknown to him while he lived within them; and only after the passage into professional independence has been accomplished does the ripening man know the quite peculiar color of the sufferings and joys of being led on a leash, and perhaps longs back into a state of dependence which could not possibly have appeared valuable to him so long as it was merely — lived experience! An old folk saying runs:

When love is with love, / love does not know what love is; / but when love has come from love, / only then does love know what love has been.

We know the most blissful fullness, but equally the most tormenting lack, only when we have lost what we possessed, or gained that of which we suffered a lack. — Should one wish to regard it as an objection that this rests upon a comparison of states, which by its nature could only be undertaken once one had exchanged the first and one state for a subsequent state, we would only have to remark that every apprehension is also a comparative apprehension, and that consciousness as such is a capacity for measuring and comparing. Wherever there is consciousness, there is also comparative consciousness (although comparison itself, as will later become apparent, could not take place at all without an analogous feature of constitution belonging to lived experience). Beyond this, however, the seeming objection would prove to be a fresh confirmation; for comparison demands, taken purely logically, at least a numerical difference — though in the case in question actually, originally, a difference in kind — between the [p. 259] states of affairs to be compared, and thus again what was illustrated under the image of the gradient of the stream: the transformation in the course of life. If the act of reflection is, among other things, an act of comparison, it points necessarily back to a change of lived experience. If, accordingly, the said objection in truth serves to illuminate what it disputes, then, by contrast, the widespread view testifies to a misapprehension of the state of affairs — the view that those moods which we believe we find, in retrospect, in past sections of life were first carried into them afterward.

It is true that, for reasons not to be discussed here, every temporal as well as every spatial distance has its transfiguring atmosphere, and a sifting power in the memory of the body comes to its aid, a power that drives us to make present again and again what was blissful, thereby consolidating it, while it presses what was repugnant into the darkness of what is to be forgotten. The conception of consciousness as a disturbance of life also explains to us why its "ray" penetrates more deeply, more cleavingly, when passing from fullness into lack than in the reverse direction. Yet all this, doubtless well suited to steeping the past as a whole in a blissful nimbus and to painting its hardships and fissures in fair colors, does not in the least explain the quite enormous difference in coloring of the stretches of development we have traversed. Whoever possesses even a meager gift of retrospective reflection will by no means discover only lost blissfulnesses, but alongside them also abandoned wastelands, of which he can afterward scarcely comprehend how he was able to cross them unbroken! How often does it not happen that someone whom a liberating turn of life has, after long bondage of soul and spirit, opened for the first time to fuller enjoyment, only now notices with horror an innermost torment that he had borne for years without apprehending it! When, in Stifter's moving tale "The Old Seal," the hero, after many years of confused soldiering, suddenly rediscovers the mysteriously vanished beloved of his youth, only then, in the moment of the first stormy embrace, does he know that he had meanwhile "long, long not lived." And it is a wholly mantic flash of consciousness, piercing through the nullity of the whole of his manhood years, that puts into the mouth of the aged Peer Gynt, at the sensed nearness of the lost Solveig, in the foreboding of approaching death, the shattering words: "I was long dead before my death!" — Beyond this, however, what matters essentially for the arising of retrospective reflection is not at all the magnitude of the temporal [p. 260] distance separating the taking-cognizance from the lived experience, but the magnitude of the difference in elevation between the two states of life, of which the one brings knowledge of the other. The sudden fall of the stream of life in a week of most dangerous illness, on a day after the death of the person most dearly loved, in the hour of torment of a difficult birth, can unleash flashes of consciousness that make their bearer, without mediation, into one who "knows" the whole of his life thus far; and it is certainly no mere legend when, since the oldest days, we are told of the prophetic gifts of so many of the dying, especially in the case of violent death.

"Take care lest I stir up against you the wrath of the gods, / on the day when Paris and Phoebus Apollo, / valiant as you are, destroy you at the Scaean gate!"

With these words, which foretell to the cruelly merciless enemy his own fate, Hector, fallen in battle, breathes forth his soul. Only in passing let us recall the occurrence, at least to be set alongside this, that in moments of extreme mortal danger, especially in falls in the mountains, according to the most definite testimony of those affected, fear is occasionally overlaid by a flash of consciousness that seemed in an instant to illuminate the whole sequence of events of the life that had passed.

Without yet touching upon the puzzling-seeming question of how it comes about that far-reaching acts of reflection can strike not merely the past, but even what is only to come, let us recall once more the already-mentioned mantic gift of inspiration, which numerous "savages" of the present share with the peoples of antiquity.
