Already the Romantics rightly placed every kind of second sight, and in particular of course the mantic gift of inspiration, in the closest neighborhood of ecstasy; yet this must not hinder us from establishing that ecstasy is not, in and for itself, already prophetic. In its consummation most nearly resembling the self-forgetfulness of one wholly intoxicated with happiness, it leads temporarily to the extinguishing of consciousness altogether, in a surf of lifewaves stirred up from the ground, flooding the one seized by it with a sea of images that robs him of all reflection upon it. But because, in order to accomplish this in a person, it must first burst the shell of the I, it goes hand in hand with a shock to consciousness-capable lived experience that may distantly be compared to the outbreak of the most violent passions [p. 261] (more on this presently), and it is this shock that, under special conditions, dies away in the sudden ray of mantically prefiguring consciousness. It is not the wave of life bedded in purple darkness that makes one a seer, but rather: that it is whipped up and broken against the resistance of the I-shaped spirit. No condition seems to us more fittingly crowned than this by the luminous word of the seer-like *Hölderlin*: "The heart's wave would not foam up so beautifully and become spirit, did not the ancient, mute rock, fate, stand against it."

To the after-all understandable question whether, given his restless agitation and constant feud with a thousandfold resistances, the man of action does not thereby become the most knowing type — of which, however, experience rather bears witness to the opposite — we would reply that we, far from joining in the overestimation of the man of action that has today become almost a substitute for religion, are led by far-reaching investigations to trace back not only the busyness of the leisureless perpetual laborer and tradesman, but also the performance-conditions of "world-historical" figures, to a peculiar impoverishment and flattening of life. Supposing that consciousness really comes about through spirit making a leap or a bend of lived experience harden into a no-longereffaceable mark, then the receptive capacity of spiritual acts would depend, on the one hand, on the magnitude of the shock to life, but on the other hand also on the possible power and force of the lived experience itself — comparable to the difference in strength and fullness of tone of the sounds that a narrow brook and a broad river would produce given a fall of equal depth. Were now, as we believe, the acting consciousness attached to a meager vitality, then its ever-disturbed agitation would nevertheless not guarantee that reach of acts of reflection which marks the character deep in essence. With this, however, an altogether different question crosses our path, whose solution is indeed only broached by the following consideration, yet at a very essential point.

We have so far explained the arising of consciousness exclusively by reference to retrospective or self-reflection, and accordingly have done justice only to the inward-turned taking-cognizance. If in this respect the man of action should fall behind, even given considerable fullness of life, because he looks to the highest degree ⦅after⦆ outward, then his constitution of life would all the more readily go together with more than ordinary reflection upon matters, and we would have to ask [p. 262] whether there is evidence that the wakefulness of reflection upon matters, too, is heightened by shocks to life. We begin by disarming an objection which, were it to hold, would irretrievably overturn the whole line of thought pursued so far. — Tying in with our proposition above, that reflection is always also comparative reflection, one might wish to object as follows: if I become aware through comparison of the life-moods lying behind me, then the present lifemood must have served me as the measure, of which I would thus possess knowledge; but this would evidently overturn the claim that such knowledge occurs only of past moods! We shall use this objection, for the time being, to throw sharper light on the comparison meant here.

Its (conditioning) first moment is the experienced difference; and from it follows, as a (possible) second, the side-by-side of two feelings of life. Supposing that retrospective reflection did not get beyond the first stage at all, its judgment would run: formerly I felt differently; and supposing that it finally did arrive at a determination of the otherness, then the layering would thereby have unfolded itself even into a temporal sequence. But even if the color of the past mood became conscious at once, the comparison thereby presupposed would still, in the first place, have to be distinguished from the comparison, say, of the colors of two flowers. Both of these are objects before me, and I can compare them with the greatest care without exercising the least self-reflection (e.g., through the incidental thought of my visual acuity or state of mind); whereas in the case of retrospective reflection only the former mood stands before my eyes, in the first instance. If we nonetheless call the act of apprehension an act of comparison, this expresses, for one thing, that it takes place only because the past feeling of life stands out against the present one as differently constituted in kind; and it thereby recalls, moreover, the circumstance known to us, that every apprehension of a matter, to speak with a favorite word of physics, already "potentially" means self-apprehension as well — according to which, then, even the present feeling of life might come to become an object through retrospective reflection. Only at this point would the objection become dangerous.

But if it is true that we find, in past moods, a fundamental color that remained undiscoverably hidden from us while it prevailed, then we must, under all circumstances, deny to the ever-present fundamental color the capacity for consciousness [p. 263]. The seeming difficulty resolves itself quite simply. We can, at every moment, reflect that we exist, and we can accordingly likewise reflect on how we feel just now. But even setting aside the astonishingly manifold self-deceptions to which we are exposed in assessing our momentary state of mind, the gaze even of the most truthful and clear-sighted character never penetrates as far as that ⦅fundamental color⦆, which becomes visible to him only after a ⦅transformation⦆ has taken place. The duality of moods required for comparison stands ready at hand; but the depth-power of the comparing acts weakens in the measure of the nearness and familiarity of the object, and increases in the measure of its distance and strangeness.

With this it has already been disclosed, in principle, how far reflection upon matters too must anchor in a shock to life. We called lived experience a poled process, which can be grasped equally from the point of view of the connectedness as of the estrangement of its poles. … ; The primal act of consciousness attaches itself to the strangeness of the image and is thus always reflection upon a matter. Now if the strength and reach of retrospective reflection grows with growing self-estrangement, and if this in turn corresponds to the magnitude of the gradient of life, then we may assume that the degree of estrangement required for the onset of reflection upon a matter, too, rests upon a break in continuity; according to which the arousal of consciousness for objects of the outer world should go hand in hand, most decisively, with just those images that could be lived through by the receiving soul only under shocks. This leads us from the moods considered so far to the movements of the heart, surges of feeling, "affects".

Its pronounced character of something undergone stamps every stronger surge of feeling, as the very name indicates, as a shock to the course of lived experience, and must accordingly lend it, to a special degree, the capacity to awaken consciousness. It need not confuse us that someone, out of sudden anger, for example, "loses reflection," gets wholly "beside himself," is no longer "with himself," afterward "comes to himself" again, and becomes aware with horror of the consequences of an action which he committed only because, "blind" with rage, he had "forgotten himself"; for expressions of this kind speak, at any rate ⦅among other things⦆, of an occurred lapsing of the I into abandonment, and remain, for that very reason, nonetheless compatible with the required increase of a merely [p. 264] but thoroughly compelled activity of consciousness. Leaving aside for the present the question whether and why excessive intensifications of feeling might actually be capable of extinguishing consciousness, it admits of no doubt that, with regard to the corresponding constitution of consciousness, every movement of the heart is marked by the irresistibility with which it calls forth acts of reflection turned toward the outside. We need only recall by what means the aptly so-named attention is most effectively awakened, and we convince ourselves at once that it unfailingly happens through "affect-laden," drive-arousing impressions. The tree stump that I had overlooked by day I most certainly notice if, in the dark, I take fright before it; the person most indifferent to me I notice instantly if his presence in company ⦅surprises⦆ me; and the laziest and sleepiest pupil is awakened by the threat that he fears. It is always the real or supposed occasion of a surge of feeling for which the consciousness of the one filled with stormy joy, of the violently enraged, of the astonished, annoyed, indignant, affected, tense, dismayed, and so forth, was unfailingly awakened; and we shall not close ourselves off from the conviction that there can be no compelled acts of reflection at all except as a consequence of ready-lying impulses that occasion the bearer of life to answer certain impressions with a surge of feeling, however faint it may sometimes be. For it must be grounded in this, and in this alone, that the choice of direction of attention is afterward ⦅recognized⦆ as compelled, and that, owing in some sense to the insistence with which this recognition asserts itself, retrospective reflection finds feelings and surges of feeling more easily than sense-processes, and originally saw them in the light of alien-souled powers! Whatever we notice at all ⦅involuntarily⦆ — be it the fly buzzing about us, or the crowd gathering in the street, or a lowered barrier — bears, ⦅as⦆ involuntarily noticed, the character of a disturbance, or, if one prefers, the character of an excitation (since it may, after all, also be the figure of the beloved), and we notice it because our "interest" has answered the impression — following the order of the examples — with reluctance, curiosity, impatience, delight. This obliges us to add an important qualification to the previously cited dictum of Hobbes, that to sense always the same thing is to sense nothing at all: namely, that even something sensed out of a change in sense-processes could nevertheless not [p. 265] become an object of perception without the assistance of the surge of feeling bound up with it. Whoever could experience none of the entirety of feelings for which we have names — that is, none of love, hatred, veneration, abhorrence, contempt, dejection, grief, care, longing, hope, pity, remorse, shame, envy, malicious joy, cruelty, boredom, indifference, and so on — would doubtless no longer be capable of consciousness! Against the absurd opinion that feelings must cloud the faculty of judgement, it is to be objected that, wholly without feelings, the faculty of judgement would no longer become "actual" at all. The primal act of spirit is a "reacting" act, and its occasion the abrupt shock to life.

The more or less sudden changes of course in lived experience — more precisely, in the drive-side of it — which one calls movements of the heart, surges of feeling, "affects," teach us incontrovertibly that the awakening of attention for what is outwardly objective points back, all the more, to shocks in the stream of life! "Attention" comes from "aufmerken" [to mark, heed], in which the preposition "auf" [upon, to] is used in exactly the same sense as in: to watch out for, to heed, to listen for something, to hearken, to hear, and so on; hence one should, so far as possible, understand by "the awakening of attention" the onset of the outward-turned acts of reflection, and not the acts of retrospective reflection. We shall have to examine much later whether the susceptibility of drives and "interests" to disturbance may not possibly be intelligible from a feature of essence common to all of them, which would explain to us, even better than has just been done, even the almost indifferent acts of involuntary reflection upon matters; remaining here with the surge of feeling proper, we sharpen our gaze for the inhibiting side of every shock to life, and elucidate, by reference to the corresponding consciousness of matters, the most dangerous consequence of its, so to speak, sleepless wakefulness.

The appearance, linguistically attested above for violent surges of feeling, of a lapsing of reflection proves, on closer consideration, to be grounded in the fragmenting effect that accompanies irresistibly extorted acts of consciousness of a matter. If the soldier, to choose a favorite example, feels not the least of the wound in the tumult of battle that would cause him violent pain once he had "come back to himself," this by no means testifies to a simply weakened capacity for reflection; rather it occurs because, sprung from a surge of feeling far stronger even than that which could accompany bodily pain, the [p. 266] consciousness-capable life-space of the combatant is chained, as if with a steel hawser, wholly to the sight of the enemy! On the occasion of kindred occurrences, ⦅Herbart⦆ speaks of the "one-sidedness" of passion, and the moderns like to speak of a "narrowing" of consciousness, whereby, characteristically, they pursue now the direction toward heightened concentration, now that toward "clouding" and disintegration of consciousness. With regard to the spellbinding overemphasis of the object, we, by contrast, extract from the state of affairs first and foremost the certainty that reflection is capable of isolating the occasion of lived experience and, with it, what is related to it, and thus appears directed, by tendency, toward the splitting-off of the consciousness-capable outer layer of life from the non-consciousness-capable core of life.

For the present it will be found highly questionable that we use, to characterize the activity of spirit, what has hither-to, so far as it has been given attention, been used solely to characterize the affects, and we do not wish to claim full persuasive force for our finding before we have been able to demonstrate the same tendency for the acts of volition of spirit not yet touched upon. Meanwhile the discussion here is not of feelings and surges of feeling as such, but an attempt is being made to ascertain, from certain in any case possible consequences for the attendant constitution of consciousness, a feature belonging to the essence of reflection upon a matter. — If the splitting-off of the outer layer just referred to really occurs, even if only temporarily, then one act of reflection can no longer be related to another, and a standstill of consciousness sets in, usually in the shape of a lapse and a gap no longer capable of being remembered, but sometimes also followed by complete loss of consciousness. Since the relating of the acts of reflection to one another takes place through the personal I, we draw from the manifold expressions of "no-longer-beingwith-oneself" and "not-being-master-of-oneself" the fitting indication of the impossibility, in states of violently extorted consciousness of a matter, of reflecting upon oneself, and at the same time find the key to a curious fluctuation to which unreflective usage of language seems, on this occasion, exposed in another respect. For while expressions such as: one was fettered, seized, overpowered by something, emphasize an overwhelming bond, on the other hand an unboundedness hovers before us when it is said of one seized by a surge of feeling that he behaves without restraint, without check, without measure. With boundedness, usage of language aims [p. 267] at the particular force either of the overemphasized object, of which we have just been treating, or else, as we must not overlook, of a (psychic) image; with unboundedness, however, unambiguously at the, in either case unavoidable, disempowerment of the will. With this sentence we have touched upon a new problem that opens wide vistas before us.

If ecstasy, as we have allowed to be glimpsed, lets a world of images become master over things, then, contrary to a widespread prejudice, the surge of feeling bound to reflection upon a matter would not lie on the way to it at all, but rather in just the opposite direction. At once, however, the question would arise whether feelings ought not perhaps to be arranged in strata according to differences of degree in image-content, and might even fall apart by kind, according to whether, laden with images, they reinforce inwardness, or, violent in movement, prepare the way for their splitting through the act of reflection. We do not decide this now, and wish, with this pointing-ahead to two kinds of ecstasy, only to have indicated them for the present. — Sharply distinct from the image-intoxication that antiquity called ekstasis is the Asian-Christian "rapture." Whereas the former, elective-affine with feelings of bursting joy and intoxicating happiness, sometimes takes its start from there, the latter seems to break forth, in the "supersensible" glory of a glaringly dissolving light, soundlessly and yet comparable to a scream, out of the most horrible agonies and torments. "The history of the martyrs of all times and peoples is rich in evidence for the capacity of just the most violent torments to detach themselves from the consciousness of pain and to deliver the tortured one over, as if with a sudden jerk, to a dominion of dream-sense that veils from him the harshest present entirely with inspiring “visions.” On the glowing gridiron, out of the flames of the pyre, on the horns of the bull, the suddenly “raptured” begin to “exult,” or show, “transfigured,” the expression of blissful ecstasy. What here vouches to the believer for the nearness of God serves, conversely, as proof of the devil’s assistance in the witch trials, where the so frequent observation of effortless silence amid the worst tortures increased the canon of infallible proofs of guilt by the “maleficium taciturnitatis.”" But however it may stand with such "raptures,"<sup>36</sup> they in any case end the surge of feeling that preceded them with a state of life quite different from it, which can at best be remembered afterward, but can never, while it prevails [p. 268], be known. For this too we take the most general grounding from our findings. — If the disturbing intervention succeeds, by virtue of terrible strength, in splitting off the capacity for reflection, then, given an inwardness still sufficiently full of life, the unconscious current of beholding can, now temporarily free of inhibition, come to dominion in possibly rememberable "visions." We may already surmise here that these differ essentially from those glowing or flaming images that become visible not out of an impotence of consciousness, but out of a reflection-drowning fullness of the elemental soul.

<sup>36</sup> On page 267. — *Klages*, Vom Traumbewußtsein, loc. cit., pp. 416–417.

[p. 269]

#### 28. Kapitel — Bedingungen und Grenzen weltgeschichtlicher Erkenntnis — Chapter 28 — Conditions and Limits of World- Historical Knowledge

We should not like, in this connection, to pass over a state of affairs which, withdrawn indeed from the gaze of the more life-blunted, tends to captivate sensitive natures only the more passionately, the more it lures them into bottomless abysses of brooding contemplation. — There have been, at all times, protesting spirits who knew themselves to be in irreconcilable opposition to their contemporary world, who rejected the values of the multitude, refused their approval to the prevailing laws and customs, their recognition to the ruling convictions, and hoped for the rescue of all the soul's treasures either from the bursting of age-hallowed fetters, or else from a complete turning-back and the recovery of vanished forms of life. Their constitution of character decided whether they became solitary despisers or those Promethean breakers after whom the great curves in the course of historical humanity are named. Among them we find inventors, discoverers, secular reformers and re-shapers, overturners and rebels, founders of faiths and "saviors," martyrs of heavenly as well as of earthly high thoughts; among them, too, we find the lonely "knowing ones" who, like Heraclitus, scarcely consider it worth the trouble to make their knowledge "generally comprehensible," or who, like Cassandra, must proclaim the disaster which they lack the power to avert. Yet however threateningly the gulf may open between the individual and his "fartoo-many": there never was so powerful and free a spirit, never so archaic and belated a one, never so hating and corrosive a one, that was not nevertheless called upon to bear witness also to the feeling of life of its own day! Every age has outer layers and inner layers of its becoming and passing away, and sets at enmity, with the outer layer of its norms, the few, or the one, whose flame of essence was kindled at the hearth of its transformation. If, then, lived life is never at the same time known, it remains denied even to the most penetrating spirit to find the source of his [p. 270] willing in the undercurrent of his own time, however much further his gaze may reach than that of all his contemporaries, and regardless of whether his "mission" forbids or permits him to think the thought of the dependence, even of his most inspiration-rich shocks, upon the secret "law" of the cosmic as of the human course of the world. He too is a shade of color in the picture of an age of man that becomes fully objective only to a later one, and of him too holds the melancholy truth of the fatalistic verse:

What he weaves, no weaver knows. It repeats itself, at the turning of the ages, what we have just set forth concerning the turning of the sections of the single life: that only a new — we might now say — direction of the stream of life, differing from that of the course now past, brings forth consciousness: no today of humanity has ever been able to look into the ground of life of its own reflecting and contemplating; and all knowledge of the driving powers, of historical happening too, is necessarily posthumous!

When we who are present today step before the temple ruins of Paestum, we grasp, deeply shaken, with a single glance, determining traits out of the soul of antiquity of which, in no line of Empedocles, Plato, or Plotinus, even the faintest consciousness dawns. An inward radiance seems to stream forth from the ruins, translating them beneath one and the same sky, and into the transparent gold of the very same ether, together with the Olympian epic of Homer and the metallically clear, resounding rhythms of the Greek tragedians. Into strange, wondrous phantoms — a playful smoke about altars close to the gods — fade the scholastic quarrels of the thinkers; into a rippling of waves on the surface above wine-dark depths become, for us, even the most tremendous political struggles; it no longer touches the meaning of antiquity, whether Sparta or Athens won the mastery, and even between the hostile focal points of Hellas and Rome the arc of a shared feeling of life unexpectedly spans a circle of humanity, one that could still shelter itself, behind an aegis ringed with lightning, beneath the "shield of necessity."

Or, immersing ourselves in the sublime shudders of Gothic cathedrals and in the congealed conflict between the founding life of the earth-grown stone and the sucking draw of an otherworldly ⦅order⦆, we unexpectedly grasp the spirit, too, of the strict and rigid systems of Scholasticism, and see [p. 271] both, unbeknownst to themselves, mirroring in the work of the arts and the concepts the path of disembodiment of the thought of ⦅world-dominion⦆ which — an uncompleted ladder of deeds — "world history" designates with the centuries of the tragic struggle of annihilation between Emperor and Pope.

And how much more revealing than any thinker's word from the time of its flowering does our gaze dart into the soul of a lordship doomed to death, when we surrender ourselves, for only a few minutes, to the improbable enchantment of the clipped hedges, the planimetric flowerbeds, the writhing Tritons and nymphs, the grottoes, cascades, and stage-like backdrops that surround the, in the adornment of their all too spacious mirrors, their glittering glass chandeliers, their phantasmal ornamentation, doubly dead and yet ghostly-alive pleasure-palaces and summer residences of the Rococo! What the dying nobility of the eighteenth century lived, without being able to know it, with its shepherd-plays and masked balls, its marionette dances and wandering hunts, its confused adventures and hellishly ingenious intrigues, its despot's whims and orgies of extravagance, its idolization of woman, its gallant feuds and amorous festivities, the solemn theatricality of its sociability, the sudden juxtaposition of roving miracle-mongering and scornful free-thinking, of pietistic renunciation of the world and cynical viciousness — this its legacy tells us, and we recognize it as the apostate's attempt at a ⦅restoration⦆ of the pagan ⦅Eros⦆, which, fed on the blood of overripe and already uprooted lineages, stood, from the outset, under the sign of hopeless decline. It was, in an unsurpassed turn of phrase of Nietzsche's, "the century of ⦅fleeting⦆ happiness."

We place no weight on the formulas by which we have just now sought to characterize the vital elements of three worldages of history, and wish by means of them only to make intuitively evident the tremendous distance between a nearreflection capable, so to speak, of merely groping, and the images — as clear as they are incontrovertible — which the mirror of far-reflection is able to design of the "spirit of the ages." — Since Plato it has been the endeavor of philosophers to ascertain the ultimate presuppositions of cognition and to pursue that critique of reason after which a Kant named his principal work. But only our age has conceived a critical task of an essentially different kind, in relation to which the selfreflections of earlier thinkers seem childlike: we mean the ascertaining of the relations between the decisions of [p. 272] thinking and the course of destiny. Through Nietzsche — in whom a later generation (insofar as one of astonished spirit should still exist) will recognize the pathbreaker of that inquiry which alone might first deserve the name "science of the soul" — questions have become familiar to us whose answering promises to lead into darker depths than any speculative acumen could ever reach, an acumen which, for all its caution in the choice of major premises, nevertheless never scrupled to place itself, as the best-known or rather the measuring magnitude, within the equation of humanity itself. Both the dialectical doubt as to what cognition achieves, what conditions it has and where its limits lie, and the skeptical doubt as to whether there is any cognition at all and whether what is known is not deception or mere habituation, stand to the suspicion — compared even to the mere question why it should appear valuable to us to translate the images of life into *graspabilities* — as play stands to earnest; upon which, nevertheless, every step of the supposed urge toward cognition, whether in a skeptical or a positivistic intent, was directed without doubt as to its own entitlement. Only when we cast the plumb line beneath the understanding may we hope to bring up a grain from strata of essence which have not yet had to congeal in any conceptual matrix, in order to become aware, through it, of steeper barriers to the thirst for knowledge — even if only through a divining surmise of the world-historical connections of which every invention, every discovery, every system of thought, together with the arts and the deeds of peoples, is merely a manifestation, and indeed on the outer side of life, in the medium of wakefulness. With countless discoverer's flashes, in which just as many "ideals" burned up, Nietzsche for the first time proves, upon past cultures, the destiny-seeking guiding thought that the meaning of his doing is closed to the doer, and that above all even a thinking that tests itself never grasps its own imperative and that imperative's relation of allegiance to the life-powers that shape the age. A single example, in place of many, may show us, precisely from the undertakings of thinkers, that they played their role in the drama of humanity no less caught up in illusion than, with the blaze of their deeds, those driven by — other passions.

In respect of the opposition of theses between philosophical dispositions there is scarcely a sharper one than that of the Stoics to the Epicureans. No one suspects the sincerity of the bitterness with which they contended with one another, just as even today the partisanship which gave these [p. 273] schools their names has not wholly vanished. Yet even the somewhat critical reporters of the history of thought have long ceased to doubt that the real opposition between the two lay elsewhere than where the doctrine supposed it, while the supposed opposition was rather a — misunderstanding! For both accompany and express, with only slightly differing formulas, the dying process of the feeling of symbiotic community that bound together the still bodily orders of the perishing "autochthons." Both teach, in sharpest contradiction to the age-old belief in the sanctifying beauty of transporting enthusiasm, the blessedness of ataraxia, of freedom from emotional disturbance, of standing above in the artificial equilibrium of a rationality no longer possessed but possessing. And both devalue that from which they tore themselves loose, the soul of the people, and set against it, didactically or disdainfully, but equally bluntly, the model of the better-instructed "sage." The Stoic, however, is power-minded and prone to attack, eager to act, legislative, secretly in need of struggle — even with the affects! — an advocate of duties and intent on the fortification of the state's coercive apparatus; the Epicurean, on the other hand, inclined to a renunciatory withdrawal of the self, stands, with the contemplativeness of his garden pleasures, a little nearer, for whoever likes it, to the lost field of life. The Stoic "endure and renounce" resembles a military command to the point of confusion, whereas the same confession in the mouth of the Epicurean already sounds as suspect as the Buddhist "pass the world by — it is nothing." Here lie the oppositions between the two kinds of disposition otherwise sprung from a single root: but none of their contemporaries would have been able to decide this, and even today not too many eyes are opened to it. — The knowledge-embittered demand, "by their fruits ye shall know them," may for once preserve us from seeking the depth-content of a work in the intention of its accomplisher. What storms or calms of sea have been lived through, of that we learn only once the weather has changed: the "spirit of the ages" is venal only at the price of the death of the ages!

But we feel ourselves moved to yet other renunciations of judgement by a glance at the reverse side of this finding. If distance alone gives us the coherence that was closed to every near view, then it thereby denies us precisely the science of the reflective constitution of soul of the bearer of the near view. No matter how deeply penetrating a glance into the shaping [p. 274] powers of prehistory, it does not teach us how it was "in the mind" of earlier men! The content of what they left behind tells us what they lived, far beyond their consciousness of it; but neither their doing and refraining nor the content of their reports discloses to us how they cared and wished, nourished hope and suffered fear. Even if we escaped the temptation to place a meaning of their destiny into their deeds and words — a meaning which indeed became known to us from their consequences, but could not have been known to them — the actions were nevertheless carried out, the customs practiced and experienced, the words spoken and received, out of a state of consciousness for whose reproduction we lack the indispensable precondition, namely the corresponding formation of essence, which is irretrievably gone!

What we today call hating, loving, revering, despising, despairing, differs widely from the like-named feelings of a Carthaginian, and not a little already from those of a German of the Thirty Years' War. If, for example, the "savage," upon the violent death of a relative — instead of seeming to mourn — even today aims in the first place at revenge, then the customary reference to the fear of spirits supposedly peculiar to him gives us not the slightest insight into a state of mind that, on the occasion of death and dying, awakens such thoughts; and we recognize indeed the fact of the difference, but not the kind of difference between his mourning and ours, between his demand for retribution and our own. — — Let no one imagine that the age which delighted in autos-da-fé and witch-burnings was crueler than our own! It is, however, a different cruelty when tortures, performed with the best of consciences, serve as a shared feast for the eyes of a spectaclehungry crowd, and yet another, again, that books its atrocities, visible far and wide — one need only think of Russia, murdered by terror and hunger! — with a greasy grin, on the profit side of gigantic "businesses," and spices the mockery of its triumph with mobile hypocritical laments over the lot of the strangled, out of the lie-dripping mouths of newspaperwriters specially paid for the purpose!

We still draw lots, but in doing so we live through something far different from the long-vanished age — or the age that has survived only among "primitive peoples" — for which the casting of lots was a preferred means of divining the decisions of demonic powers! One may state it as a rule: from cultic symbols and magical observances there arise, in a later age, sense-altered customs of profane festivals, [p. 275] and in a still later age, customs practiced without understanding as children's games and entertainments, or else, wholly reinterpreted, arrangements in the service of utility. But these are merely crude, palpable signs of the completed accomplishment of unstoppable transformations of lived experience. Modern man, if he possesses any depth at all, gathers himself, or scatters himself, however one wishes to put it, on lonely mountain peaks or on the most remote sea coves; the man of antiquity and the Middle Ages found the heightening — to be named in the same way, but certainly different in coloring — in the now noisy, now solemn pomp of festivals, popular or aristocratic. — — What a change — by no means only of the branch, but with it infallibly also of the mode of life — confronts us when our glance surveys the history of spectacles, from the agons of the Greeks to the gladiatorial combats of the Romans and from these to the tournaments of the Middle Ages; or that of festivals, from the nightly revelling thiasoi of Dionysus to the darkly sensuous Saturnalia and from these to the jest-filled brightness of German-burgher marksmen's festivals; or even merely that of the forms of entertainment, from the ancient board game to today's ninepins and cardplaying!

How differently from us did those generations feel, who made every public appearance of their conduct more palatable by the pepper of folly! What we, at most, still tolerate as the buffoon in the puppet theater or as the "silly August" in the circus, was to them, as jester, mace-bearer, and court fool, an officially appointed accessory to every public self-display, of certainly no lesser vital importance than the policeman is to us. — — As long as humanity has existed, there has been what is today called "occultism." Nonetheless an unbridgeable gulf separates the mode of experience in the initiation rites of a novice of the Mithraic mysteries from that in the reception customs of a present-day Freemasons' lodge; not to speak at all of the fact that the occult *appearances* change step by step with the cultures within whose frame they take place. One need only set beside the medieval mortifications, incombustibilities, incorruptibilities, luminosities, auras, stigmatizations, ecstatic flights, transformations, possessions, vampirisms, witches' salves and magic potions the American-spiritualist table-rapping and "psychography," and one will abandon as hopeless the attempt to re-experience from it the feelings of those magically graced or bewitched in the age of eucharistic miracles and counter-miracles! — — How [p. 276] different the experience of marriage looked in the age of the world-wide purchase of brides, compared with our own age of the — in the form of the woman's dowry — actually existing, but veiled and therefore unavowed, purchase of men! Whoever will not believe this, let him be told that in the equatorial jungle the negro woman even today is filled with pride at having been bought by her husband for as high a sum as possible, and that she is apt to be regarded as an insufferable companion for as long as she is, so to speak, married only on loan, because the amount has not yet been paid in full! — — Today as before there is a delight in self-abasement and sexual servitude; but what lover of pain would undertake to relive the feelings of that knight who had himself sewn into a wolf's pelt in honor of his lady, in order to be nearly torn to pieces by sheepdogs!

But the reports too leave us in the lurch; for words, spoken in the style of their age, are heard exactly by no one in the meaning with which another once bore them on his lips. Change of sound and shift of concept form only the step-by-step deepened watermarks of the ceaseless oscillations between life and spirit, which are accompanied by a ceaseless change of color in reflective lived experience and hence also in the feelings attached to the meanings of words. — If we compare attentively, with the works of Homer, who stands culturally far nearer to us than, say, the Edda-skalds, the creation modeled on his technique, "Hermann und Dorothea," then, notwithstanding the exemplary "classicism" and the much-praised "naïveté" of Goethe, we are struck at first by the difference of the entire lived experience. "Hermann und Dorothea" brings to life for us the soulful inwardness of the love of a youth for a maiden. Homer, on the other hand, who, as guardian of the honor of the family, indeed sets up model examples of the most tested fidelity and mutual attachment of both spouses, with unmistakable emphasis of heart (Hector and Andromache, Odysseus and Penelope), knows nothing, for the rest, of "romantic" love. Only once, as is well known, namely in the Nausicaa episode, does something remotely comparable flash up, whereas his otherwise emotionally uninvolved, sensuous conception of the relation between the sexes stands before us with disconcerting clarity when we learn that Odysseus, at the very moment of hewing the sorceress Circe to pieces for crimes partly committed against his companions, partly threatening himself, followed, the instant she had given, under compulsion, the oath of fidelity he had forced from her, her wish for union:

[p. 277] Then I climbed with Circe onto the splendidly prepared couch. Carried along by the mightiest stream of epic that history knows, we are apt, in reading Homer, to forget how strange to us has become the state of mind of a humanity that, out of murderous wrath (of the hero) or mortal terror (of the sorceress), was able to glide over with such swiftness and grace into the mood of sensuous love. — A more penetrating examination shows us an entirely different distribution of mass in the structure of the reports. Whereas Homer indeed lets his men speak with the broadest circumstantiality, and interrupts, say, the preparation for battle with the description of a shield of such artisanal exactness, or the beginning of the single combat of two heroes with an account of their lineage of such prolixity, that it would be felt as disturbing in any more recent author, Goethe, on the other hand, for all his partly unconscious, partly deliberate closeness to the Greeks, cannot forbear to name various expressive traits of emotional agitation — for example, a flying blush — which for the Greek poet seem scarcely to exist at all.<sup>37</sup> And this brings us already to the third and here decisive point, namely to the difference in the content of word-meaning, according to which at that time unthinkably more lay enclosed in any given sentence than does today! Homer is rich in descriptions splendid even for us; but we should have to be able to exchange our own for a kind of childhood stage of spirit in order to hear out of them what they gave to the Greek of, say, the fifth century B.C. The mighty event of a shipwreck and the toilsome rescue of a single survivor from it is rendered in the following verses:

<sup>37</sup> On page 277. — Even one who did not know that Homeric scholarship, so far as is known to us, recognized the mighty verses in the twentieth book of the Odyssey — where the suitors are overcome as if by a dreadful foreboding of impending doom — as a later interpolation, might perhaps infer it from the wholly altered bearing of the poetry, which suddenly speaks a language of mien and gesture that, different from the otherwise preferred primal expressive phenomena (turning pale, weeping, sobbing, trembling of the knees, swooning, etc.), comparable to a dreadful flickering apparition, would naturally befit only an inwardly convulsed age: And behold, a great mirthless laughter Pallas Athene stirred up in the hall and confounded the minds of the suitors. And now they all laughed with faces horribly convulsed. Blood-befouled flesh they now devoured. There follows the uncanny vision of Theoklymenos, who already sees the spirits of the slain fluttering away to Erebos.

... after the god of high-rolling thunder, in the midst of the sea, had shattered my ship with the smoking bolt, all my brave companions sank there into the abyss. But I, who clung to the keel of the shattered ship, drifted about for nine days. Nothing of the approach and breaking of the storm, nothing of the scenes that must have played out among the crew of the ship as it went down, and not a word of the feelings of the man who, clinging to a plank, is tossed about by the waves for days and nights! And even where, in other passages, the descriptions turn out richer [p. 278] in yield, each still retains something of the lapidary sparseness of this report. Goethe, however, finds occasion to voice, through the mouth of the lion-keeper's wife, how some strollers are to be regarded who return wearied from watching the procession of the exiles: "See how dusty are everyone's shoes! How the faces glow! And each one brings out his handkerchief and wipes away his sweat. I myself, in this heat, after such a spectacle, would not wish to walk and suffer so far!" Not only a wholly altered kind of *sensitivity* speaks out of such verses; they also let us surmise how much more must be said today than formerly, in order that it be heard at all. Whereas, within the range of his sensitivity, all that was worth communicating would no doubt have been sufficiently revealed to a Homeric Greek by, say, the words: dusty they come home!

But what holds of the language of poetry holds — only to a far higher degree — of the language of the chronicler, the researcher, and the thinker. If we set forth in the 14th chapter why a truth does not mean the same thing for the learner as for the finder, we now know why it is denied to the discoverer to hand down, together with his report, also the pathos and the depth-content of his findings. What is handed down from him is the transferable content of judgement, not handed down is the content of meaning, whose precondition of existence is the reflective constitution of soul of the discoverer's personality, together with that of his people and his age. — Already today we are incapable of hearing, out of the words "Kraft und Stoff," the uproar with which they were able to shake the industrially rising bourgeoisie of the second half of the last century. We must read the whole of Schopenhauer in order to bring out even somewhat what the insatiable "Will" meant for him — not merely as a conceptual building-block of his system; the whole of Hegel, in order to sip a little at the intoxication into which word-combinations such as "spirit in itself," "spirit for itself," "spirit in and for itself," "absolute spirit," could carry his contemporaries. — It may succeed us, with some effort, to follow logically the conceptual hair-splittings of the Scholastics; but let no one imagine that in so doing he even remotely reawakens the soul-vibrations that were unquestionably bound up, in those men, with their realitas, qualitas, unitas, equalitas, alteritas, quiditas, [p. 279] haecceitas, and so on! No reader of today could so much as guess at the pathos with which the name "Idea" once made a disciple of Plato shudder.

Two source-spirits so exceedingly different from one another, but both gifted with the highest self-knowledge — Goethe and Nietzsche — met in their rejection of belief in "history," in which they were inclined to see an afterwardinvented fable. In that we add, from our own inquiries, the decisive ground of right to their conception, we may take this as a new confirmation of that view. Because reflection upon the sap-hearth of a state of life is only made possible by another state of life, neither of them had knowledge of the "spirit" of himself; and because the state of life capable of deep sounding is no longer the one sounded, precisely his own science takes from him the capacity to place himself within a state of mind to which this knowledge remained closed. — The only end-task possible for the science of history would lie, renouncing the fathoming of vanished states of consciousness, in the objectification of the shaping forces of past periods of time, whereas the criticism, hitherto cultivated with preference, of so-called political events from the supposed motives of their traditionally accessible bearers would prove wholly impracticable. For the solution, however, of what is in principle solvable, a comparison would be presupposed of all the remains left behind from the period in question: its buildings, images, writings, symbols, songs, poems, works of tone, garments, weapons, utensils, coins, sepulchral monuments, and so on, and thereafter a testing of the *from these* gained results against everything the reports offer concerning contemporary estates, callings, offices, legal concepts, concerning agriculture, craft, trade, money-economy, concerning technique, science, philosophy, concerning instruction, the educational system and means of formation, concerning forms of intercourse, modes of conveyance and inns, sociability, banquets and table-luxury, garden arts and feeling for nature, marriage and "fornication," belief and "superstition," burial customs and ancestor-worship, and so forth. Such a "history of culture and morals," on the basis of the divined content of expression of present-day precipitates of the past, does not, to be sure, yet exist — Whether and how far, by other means than<sup>38</sup> those which stand at the disposal of the drive to research, a making-present of the past might nevertheless, exceptionally, succeed, of that something more will be said in what follows.

<sup>38</sup> On page 279. — The one who, in our judgment, has advanced furthest in this direction is J. J. *Bachofen*, though only mediately in the service of opening up antiquity, and immediately, rather, that prehistoric early age out of which antiquity itself first grew. We call it, with him and with the Romantics, "Pelasgianism." It is an essential trait of Bachofen's individuality that he makes the reports accessible to us with the help of symbols and myths that he himself has interpreted, and not, say, the reverse.

[p. 280]

### Zweiter Abschnitt — Vom spiegelnden Schauen — Second Part — On Mirroring Beholding

#### 29. Kapitel — Schauung und Spiegelung — Chapter 29 — Beholding and Mirroring

Everything that we shall further adduce, indeed at bottom everything that is henceforth at all to be ascertained, will be guided by the fundamental thought just now set forth, that reflection springs from points of disturbance of lived experience and makes the occasion of disturbance congeal into that lawfully regulated world of facts into which the wakefulness of the thinking-reflective bearer of life finds itself inescapably clamped. If, accordingly, it is only the coming chapters that have compellingly to substantiate the equation between consciousness and disturbance of life, we shall henceforth, however, only step by step call to mind what weight of grounding they add to the guiding thought, and shall moreover take up the problem of the origin of consciousness from various points of departure, without expressly reading off, each time, their relation to the direction-showing weathervane. For the present, however, let the transition to a new direction of consideration be at least indicated.

We have seen that with the pauseless flowing of the stream of life the assumption of arbitrary points of disturbance is without contradiction compatible. Just as little as a fall into the depths brought the real stream to a breaking-off, just as little did the temporal stream of lived experience suffer breaking-off through the gradual or sudden change of constitution that we have described under the image of the gradient; and just as little as a water's surface shows breaks because its smoothness vanished in the breaking of waves, just as little would lived experience forfeit its undividedness, were its continuity, say, afflicted [p. 281] with a constantly recurring change of phase. The motion of waves now gives us, out of the world of outer happening, the most exact simile for that articulation of life which underlies the seemingly uninterrupted waking consciousness. Even without regard to the necessity of points of disturbance, as shall now be shown, the earlier-explored opposition between the temporality of lived experience and the timelessness of apprehension would compel us to the assumption of a vitally articulated time. For, on the presupposition of a merely even flowing, it would remain, given the never-presentness of lived experience, wholly incomprehensible at what the absolutely present act could then properly be aimed. If the apprehensible now of my life is impossible to be the same as the life-moment of apprehending, because in it, instead of being within lived experience, I have rather left it, in order to look at something already lived — then the nowconsciousness would be a logically impossible miracle, unless turning-points occurred within lived experience, at which the act of apprehension might find a lasting substitute for the vanished actual now. As surely as lived experience continues flowing without a gap, so surely must its passage through every timeless instant of dividing apprehension be of distinguishing particularity, if the spirit is to succeed in the delimiting act. Only insofar as there is, in lived experience, again and again an ending new-beginning and a new-beginning ending, do we understand the place-positing place-boundedness of beginning and end, each time divided by a temporally unextended cutting-line, dividing act.

Striving to smooth the ground, in the reader's readiness to grasp it, for a disclosure as new as it is difficult to formulate, by linking it to something already at hand, we send ahead of our own exposition a series of sentences from the closely related work, on the same subject, of the repeatedly mentioned Melchior Palágyi, whose research results we shall have to appraise later. On the occasion of the, so far as we know, hitherto uniquely standing undertaking, in his "Logik auf dem Scheidewege," to develop the vital foundations of judgement out of the state of sensing, this thinker ascertains, in the sensory process, a rhythmic articulation, and knows how to set it forth with clairvoyant insight in a language of admirable simplicity. In order effortlessly to hold fast, in sensing, the precondition of the "impression-judgement," he sets, namely, the sensation-experience actually meant by him, as "sensing or determined reflection," over against the "judging or determining [p. 282] reflection." While his exposition leaves no doubt as to the impropriety of this formula, he makes use, on the other hand, in its proper meaning, of the word "recollection," to designate what, in the punctual instant of apprehending, is available of the already elapsed sensing. By the aid of this nomenclature he now opens up the important new finding, that every "impression-judgement" passed in the face of a sense-fact is in truth a "recollection-judgement," and sensation itself a pendulation between *impression* and *recollecting*.

"An impression never takes place in a mathematical point of time.." (p. 175). We shall rather think it — "however small its duration may be — as consisting of temporal sections, and indeed of boundlessly many temporal sections. If one holds this vividly before one's eyes, one also sees that these.. cannot be simultaneous, that therefore, when an impression is spoken of, there must in any case also be talk of past sections of the impression" (pp. 175–176). "We must, however, bring impression and recollection into a far closer relation with one another than we are accustomed to do.. We must distinguish, in our sensing, two opposed currents, of which the one lends our sensing the character of the impression, the other, however, the character of recollection.. It is (now) the recollectiontendency in our sensing by which we free ourselves from the fetters of the impression, in order to be able to pass over into judging reflection. — We cannot, with mathematical simultaneity, be subject both to the impression and to recollection: we come from the impression to recollection and from recollection to the impression. Our sensing reflection is a rocking between two antagonistic *states*.." (spaced by us; p. 177). "One commonly holds only those states to be recollections in which, after some considerable time, we come back to a past fact. But if one considers that that faculty which one calls memory must always be present when one wishes to establish an impression — because otherwise the impression would be forgotten in an instant — then one sees at once that the passage from the impression to the judgement upon it necessarily takes place, even when we pass the judgement in the very face of the fact, likewise on the basis of recollection. It might be objected to this that we can, after all, look uninterruptedly at a body — for instance, at this red ball — and meanwhile also utter the judgement: 'I see something red'; that something like a recollection is thus not at all necessary, since [p. 283] the impression, after all, continues without interruption even during the judging. To this it may only be answered that it takes a wholly imperceptibly short time until we pass from the impression to recollection, from there to the judgement, and again back to the impression. Just as one does not notice one's own pulse and one's breathing unless one especially attends to it, so too one does not notice the pulsing of one's own sensing between impression and recollection" (pp. 178– 179). "Every sensory impression is comparable to a boundless ocean, on whose shore we stand in order to scoop from it a handful of recollection, which we preserve in the judgement. Even when the impression is designated as 'present,' we have, in our judgement upon it, nevertheless only so much as recollection offers us. We are then merely, as a rule, in the advantageous position that we can proceed at once to like, repeated impressions.. The difference between the impression-judgement and the recollection-judgement can thus be illustrated by the following simile. Whoever judges merely from recollection is comparable to a man who has drawn water from a spring with his jug and then withdraws from the spring, and so is unable to draw from it again. But whoever judges on the basis of the 'present impression' remains standing with his jug at the spring and can.. fill the jug again and again.. But he too is not spared the trouble of drawing" (pp. 186–187). "In order to escape the dangerous confusion of sensing and judging reflection, it is expedient to direct the gaze straight at the transition from sensing to judging. That there must, on each occasion, be a moment at which we come over from sensing reflection into judging reflection, anyone may tell himself: but what happens in that moment is a most captious question.." (p. 193). It can, in that moment, "add to what is sensed, once again, no new sensation or new feeling, because we would then still find ourselves within sensing reflection" (p. 193). "Since this moment is no sensing and no feeling, it must be conceived as a mathematical point of time" (p. 195). "In it we take away nothing from the impression and from the recollection that have just taken place. Nor do we add anything to it, beyond merely their validity.. For the impression has, after all, already elapsed, and the recollection of it has just now reached its closing limit; and our thinking thus refers to something already past" [p. 284] (pp. 195–196; the last sentence spaced by us). — Let us add that the author, in his principal work, replaces the easily misunderstood "recollection" by "phantasm," so that we are in the fortunate position of being able, exceptionally, to rest a most difficult part of our own train of thought on the results of a contemporary researcher.

To this end we once more extract from the foregoing sentences what confirms what was discussed earlier, and complete it as a prelude to what is now to be discussed:

1. Lived experience flows in time; the judgement is the consequent appearance of a temporally punctual act.

2. What has been lived is, at the instant of reflection upon it, always already elapsed. 3. The process of lived experience must be an articulated process, because otherwise the act would lack a place at which to attach itself.

4. At the instant of the act of reflection, a substitute for what has been lived must be available. 5. The turning-point of every wave of lived experience is, in respect of state, fundamentally different from its preceding sections, and indeed in such a way that the corresponding content of experience offers, in relation to the intervening sections of what has been lived, an object-like quid pro quo.

Our attempt to bring nearer to the understanding that peculiarity of state of the turning-points of lived experience which might explain the success of the spirit's intervention, is undertaken here indeed on sense-experience, yet not, as one might wish to hold fast, from its bodily or sensation side, but from its psychic or beholding side.

Certain errors of the history of spirit have been overcome only once one was not content with their refutation, but at the same time also ascertained the grounds to which they owe their origin. Among them belongs the still popular belief, first systematized by the epistemological inquiry of the Greeks, that all conceiving rests upon a kind of mirroring-capacity of consciousness. The theory of judgement of the ancients, as is well known, conceived the process of the attainment of cognition after the pattern of an eye-experience, whether it assigned to consciousness the role of the light-sensitive plate and to concepts the peculiar character of photograms, or whether it resolutely let the world-appearance duplicate itself and let the detached eidola storm the spirit through the senses and pores. Neither the Greek fullness of beholding, which was lost to the head-man [p. 285] of "civilization," nor the overemphasis on the sense of sight suffices to make clear to us why the people of the most extravagant dialectic, who climbed to Eleatic heights of generalization, remained wholly closed to the act-nature of cognition. We must seek, if not the cause of this, then at least the occasioning ground for it, wholly elsewhere.

Of the countless judgements that a man has to pass in the course of his life, by far the most stand, without his being conscious of it, in the service of willing, and it takes the rare hours of self-sufficient meditation before the thinker comes to reflect upon his — thinking. Thus, however, shifted for a time out of the role of co-agent into that of spectator of the action, and perhaps experiencing this as a peculiar kind of happiness, he inclines to confuse the activity of thinking with the state of contemplation which gave him the knowledge of that activity. The equation is false; for we need neither think in contemplativeness nor need we, in thinking, be precisely contemplative; but it explains itself and brings us near an important truth, if we examine the state by which it was occasioned. There are as few objects that can be beheld as there are objectlike images; but there are in fact two kinds of images, namely the original ones and the copies, or, as we have hitherto said, the intuitive images, and to them correspond two kinds of beholding, namely beholding pure and simple, and spectating beholding, which, in turn, is again different from thinking apprehension. We are now of the opinion that the apprehending act attaches to the passage of beholding through a turning-point of spectating, which mirrors the beheld images. Spoken without simile, the wave-beat of the movement of life proves to be a constant alternation of intervening stretches of beholding and closing points of spectating, whose opposite pole is no longer original images, but after-shines of what has already been lived through.

Before we explain this more closely, it is advisable first to disarm the absurdity that seems to lie in the fact that recollection of the particular life-feeling should serve precisely the spectator, in order to find the living precondition for the disturbance of life through the apprehending act. The spectator, one might think, is after all rather the undisturbed one, the one who calmly surrenders himself to life, freed from the compulsion to act! To what other end, indeed, would humanity have invented the theater, if not to taste something of the Olympian happiness of the divine [p. 286] beholding, which is heightened and enhanced precisely by the sight of the restlessness of those who act! So it might seem, and this seeming has deceived the greatest thinkers, until Nietzsche's youthful work, the "Geburt der Tragödie," for once destroyed it. To be sure, Nietzsche did not employ precisely the foregoing turns of phrase; but he showed that the beholder is one "enraptured," to whose soul the images stand in the relation of soulparticipating "visions"; whereas, running parallel with the increasing predominance of the man of action and "naturalist," the "theoretician" develops, who, removed from the state of beholding, henceforth merely contemplates the images; whereby we do not at once forget that the name, today customary for the highest achievements of the understanding, of "theory," derives from the Greek theoria = intuition, feast for the eyes, just as likewise our "speculate," for high-valued endeavors of thinking, derives from the Latin speculari — to take in sight, to look about. — Spectating is by no means beholding, and the inclination to a mere contemplation of life presupposes, as already attained, a stage of active wakefulness which — having already become a torment to itself — craves "redemption" from the whip of willing. The theater, for example, arose among all peoples out of cultic festivals of excitation or of consecration, which indeed knew the duality of demon and man, or of hierophant and neophyte, but by no means that of the performer and an otherwise uninvolved spectator. Man has long since exchanged the pathos-filled being-within for the ever-hungry standing-without, whenever he strives after rest and undisturbedness, and confuses the mere holiday-stillness of his "interests," which "fair semblance" grants him as does "contemplation," with a return into the fullness of beholding.

What, in truth, is the case with such a happiness of repose, and that it is the pre-form of the thinking subjugation of life, is attested, incidentally, by a system which, among more recent ones, like no other, praised in the contemplative disposition of spirit the well-spring of metaphysical insights. Without doubt it is the state of mirroring, deeply thought through by him, that recommended to Schopenhauer his artistic interpretation of the Platonic "Ideas"; and equally without doubt he fell victim to a self-deception when he thought that what he too cannot help declaring to be the sense of the "Idea" — the lawful schema of the world-course — had sprung from a surrender of the soul. Whoever really succeeded, in ecstatic beholding, in bursting the "principium individuationis," would never have hit upon [p. 287] the notion of taking the certainty he had suffered for a kind of rational cognition, and of equating the unrecoverable uniqueness of the genuine image with the time-independent objectivity of universally binding being! Neither Schopenhauer nor even the assuredly stricter *Plato* ever penetrates through to the *actuality* of images; rather, both, each in his own personal way, devalue the phainomena and teach the "higher" reality of a being, noumenal, conceptual world. But what gives even the "Ideas" of Plato, and altogether, in the wholly other-worldly conception of Schopenhauer, their ambiguously shimmering coloring, is the unappeasable wish of these proclaimers to represent the objectivity — in their own sense even "a priori" — of these Ideas as at the same time something intuitable, remembered, phasmic, in short mirroring actuality. Herein now is expressed and reveals its nature the basic experience of peculiar nearness of spirit in which the two meet and which both misjudge — the experience no longer of beholding, but of looking-back upon something already beheld. Not streaming images, but standing copies, underlie, in the process of life, the things of Idea meant, whether inwardly or outwardly. The movement of life must be neutralized at the turning-point, and the stream of images must be present in the aftershine, in order that the spirit may succeed in binding the eternally-passing within the object which is, to be sure, imperishable, because, namely, extratemporal.

Already the unrestricted character of happening in beholding should suffice to show the act-releasing kinks in the light of a kind of stoppage of the pulse, which forms, so to speak, the prelude to its real cessation in the dividing act of the spirit within life. Being essentially timeless, the spirit could not enter into connection with life if life's temporality were not articulated, and, although connected with it, the dividing act, being essentially instantaneous, would nevertheless find nothing to allot, if, in its passage through the consciousness-capable turning-point, the wave did not linger, for a briefly limited detention, in the mere after-shining of what has already been beheld. The state of mirroring presents itself differently, according as we think of the repose of contemplation, which relieves the restlessness of willing, or of the uninvolvedness of "reflecting," which exchanged the streaming rapture of beholding for an outside-and-beside. There one has, to be sure, drawn nearer to life, as one who has fled from the arbitrariness of apprehension into the necessity of apprehension; here, however, one would stand on the point of [p. 288] leaving it, because the consciousness-unthreatened seizedness of the eternal flooding would have given way to a lookingabout pause, which would seem at least in danger of flowing into the congealing act of objectification. The moment of mirroring — in the literal sense a glance of the eye, and more than merely similar to the sense-process of seeing — stands to the continuity of beholding as the moment of waking stands to the continuity of sleeping, and designates, on the psychic side, the very same point of reversal of the life-process that, on the bodily side, lies in the onset of sensation. Images we can, among other things, dream; but in order to experience impressions, we must be awake. And let it now be noted, already here, that in dreaming we are withdrawn not only from the bodily zone of sensing, but equally also from the psychic zone of mirroring. Wholly enclosed by it, we are also wholly within it, and shall never find ourselves in that role of a mere spectator of our visions, in which we can at least find ourselves in the face of every possible impression.

If it is true, as this anticipatory silhouette at least allows us to surmise, that the "mirroring" state is one and the same with the state of soul of wakefulness, whose indispensability for the accomplishment of the act was never doubted, then we may hope to make clear the essence of mirroring by ascertaining what distinguishes, from the image in general, those particular images that give us "impressions." We do not yet enter into the analysis of sensing; but we wish to show that, taken as a psychic process, the sense-impression bears the character of the copy, and waking receptivity bears the character no longer of the beholding, but of a mirroring form of life. — The inquiry into the nature of the mirror-image or copy that is thereby required will proceed from the following points of view.

The copy is never the repetition of the object copied. Of several rulers, knives, penholders, plates, books, intuitively indistinguishable, manufactured after the same pattern, none is called a copy of another, but each, rightly, a piece or "specimen." Our fundamentally intended equation between copy and mirror-image relocates copy-hood, from the outset, into the special domain of the sense of sight, or, as we shall henceforth say throughout, of visible appearance. Were one to point, against this, to wood-carved or stone sculptural works, the reply would be that corporeality alone can guarantee only existence, but not copy-hood. Merely by virtue of its [p. 289] bodily presence, the sculptural work of wood would stand, in relation to the object represented, exactly as much a second object as, beside the first plate, the second plate of the same pattern. What makes it a copy are features of visible appearance. Of these the most important is grounded in the highly peculiar capacity of visible appearance to replace bodily presence, as emerges with particular clarity in the mirror-image. This, however, is bound up with that, to be sure, self-evident, but ordinarily unheeded, *freedom of place* of visible appearance, which qualifies it for a kind of *omnipresence*. The bodily waterfall is "in its own place," and I perceive it when I betake myself there. Its copy, on the other hand, shows it simultaneously in the most various places of the earth: to the copy there belongs, in actuality, no place proper to it. If, by contrast, their place is indeed occupied by the film-strip or the colored cardboard, whose visible appearance "presents" the waterfall to us, then only the more sharply is the corporeality of its meaningless substratum distinguished from the copy itself, and thus, from the place-determinedness of the contents of touch, the place-indeterminedness of the contents of sight, which are able to depict, and in this manner to mean, those contents of touch. The program hereby laid down shall be carried out in a depth-sounding investigation of visible appearance.

[p. 290]

#### 30. Kapitel — Die Begriffsverwandtschaft des Augenscheins — Chapter 30 — The Conceptual Affinity of Visible Appearance

Although we call the fragrant constituent of the rose in rose oil merely its aroma, the child already believes it beholds the rose itself in the image of the rose, and thereby betrays that its apprehension of the thing clings to the optical impression. The mirror-image of the cloud in the pond is for us not so much an effect of the cloud as, in a peculiar way to be sure, the cloud itself once more, whereas the rain with which it drenches us is taken for something other than the cloud itself — indeed it does not even always pass for its product. The lion cast in bronze is for us far more a bronze lion than, say, a piece of metal, while we unhesitatingly count the actual hide of the slain lion, once it lies spread on the floor, among the genus of carpets — evidently guided, in doing so, by just such a similarity of the merely visible shape as gave us the lion in the bronze copy. Pointing to the fact of imitability would not suffice to explain why the capacity to reproduce conceptual meaning belongs exclusively to visible appearance. When a phonograph deceptively lets us hear a lion's roar, and we are no longer tempted, as the child is, to go looking for the real lion on that account, we call what we heard an imitated lion's roar, but by no means a depicted lion. Attempts have been made to divide human characters, by the pictorial content of their mode of apprehension, into visual types, auditory types and motor types; but even granting the questionableness of such concepts, we could hope for a useful application of this only on the strength of the insight that *only* visible appearance *constitutes* the substratum of all universals belonging to the properties of things. We now offer a series of littlenoticed proofs of this.

The sight of a well-painted winter landscape may perhaps stir the phantasm of cold, which can complete itself in an "imagined" [p. 291] shiver; the sight of a strikingly rendered torture scene can lead as far as the co-sensing of real pain. One does not hear the voice of an acquaintance without at once also having before the inner eye a silhouette of his appearance; but it happens to even the most musical of spirits at best as an exception that, with nearly equal distinctness, the sight of someone stirs in him an image of that person's voice. Sounds, noises, and above all smells sometimes overcome us with intoxicating force and surrender us to a stream of inner images that for a while wholly "transports" us out of the bonds of sensory presence; but when we afterward reflect on what we have experienced, it invariably turns out that the auditory impression conjured up not an auditory phantasm, nor the olfactory impression an olfactory phantasm, but each of the two conjured up images of visible appearance, to which imaginations from other sensory domains might then only afterward attach themselves. We are able to retain in memory for years some meaningful sentences we once heard, and to renew in imagination every attendant circumstance of the conversation down to the last detail, at a time when even the last trace of memory of the speaker's vocal timbre has long since died out . It weighs more heavily, and, as we hold, decisively, for<sup>39</sup> our guiding thesis, that the attempt to "picture" the sense of a word never succeeds without the aid of visible appearances. One will labor entirely in vain to make present the meaning-content of the sweet, the sour, the salty, the bitter, if one denies oneself every sidelong glance at the visual representation both of a tastable body and of the palate and the moving tongue. In noises and sounds, as we showed earlier, powers operating spatially become perceptible; now we add: not even the shadow of a substitute phantasm can be mustered for the objective sense of thundering, roaring, crashing, howling, din, once every image of spatial position is ruthlessly banished. Or let one choose any general concept one likes — virtue, multiplicity, mathematics, lying, sensual pleasure — and one will confirm that the attempt at sensualizing it demands, without a single exception, the representation of shapes; just as countless generic concepts became, for earlier peoples, gods in human form, and for later ones served at least still as the theme of allegorical paintings and sculptures. The same holds for the pronoun, the article, the numeral, the adjective, the conjunction, and so on. The conjunction "and," for example, calls up the representation of two bodies standing side by side [p. 292], perhaps even with a visible middle term, but certainly not of two tones, smells or tastes — and where it does so nonetheless, only on the basis of visible appearances already formed beforehand, which have crept in unnoticed.

<sup>39</sup> On page 291. — Something worth noting in this respect, though for another purpose, is offered by *Stricker*, Studien über Sprachvorstellungen (Vienna 1880). On p. 19 it says: "Immediately after some stranger has spoken to me, I can indeed easily recall his voice and also the words *heard*. But this recollection gradually fades. The words remain, it is true, in my memory, but not the voice along with them. I can, for instance, recall exactly the words with which I was accosted by a beggar in the street a few days ago; I also recall the beggar's figure, but of his voice I have no longer any notion."

As already indicated, our conception is borne out by language, which for designating both the most general objects of thought and the mental activities directed upon them borrows its names quite preferentially from the world of visible appearances. The word "Vorstellung" [representation], in use far earlier for a theatrical performance than for the inner representation, shows from the outset a most peculiar oscillation between "bringing something to intuition" and "meaning something." To "vorstellig machen" [make representation of] a matter means to set it before someone's eyes, to bring it into sensibly present proximity to him; but "that actor over there represents [stellt vor] a king" means that he signifies a king. Since it is now the appearance-of-meaning, now precisely the meaning-of-appearance, that is designated by one and the same name, we understand why "representation," scarcely taken up by science, at once became a source of endless disputes and gradually grew into the worst problem child of psychology. For if one lays the stress on the intuitability of what is representable, then "representing" means an inner havingpresent of variously "pale, bodiless, gap-ridden, indeterminate, fleeting" after-images; if, on the other hand, one lays the stress on the meaning-content, it simply has the sense of "thinking of something" and merges with meaning the *thing* itself.
