It would have to astonish us that so ambiguous a name could assert itself with such tenacity, were it not grounded in the secret kinship of the images of visible appearance with concepts! — We do not hesitate, and are unquestionably right, to call sounds, smells, and taste-impressions "intuitive" contents; yet there is no doubting that we would not speak of "intuition" [Anschauung] at all if we were not seeing beings; and, in exact analogy to the double meaning of "vorstellen," the name "Anschauung" likewise soon acquired the secondary sense of "conviction." — With words such as "Erscheinung" [appearance], "Sinnenschein" [sensory semblance], "Phantasma" (from phainesthai = to appear), language furnishes still stronger evidence of its all-governing tendency to derive the broader concept of that-which-gives-impressions as such from the narrower one of visible impressions, and even the comparatively most neutral word "Bild" [image] aims directly at something [p. 293] visible. — With the very common compound words "Zeitraum" [space of time], "Zeitstrecke" [stretch of time], "Zeitspanne" [span of time], we grasp time as a perceptible line, and with the utterance that we are "still far removed" from the goal, we again put spatially visible extension in the place of every conceivable obstacle separating resolve from accomplishment. — "Clarity of spirit," "bright head," "view" [Ansicht], "insight" [Einsicht], "intent" [Absicht], "point of view" [Gesichtspunkt] borrow, for the purpose of designating properties, achievements and activities of the intelligence, the state- and process-images of the world of visible appearance, or the performances of sight directed upon it. The Aryan case-endings, according to the leading philologists, originally had the meaning of place and direction; and, as ethnology attests, the same holds of the well-nigh innumerable case-designations of more or less all primitive peoples! — If, in this way, making-present occurs at all only by the roundabout way of making-present of visible appearance — which is why only this is fitted to represent units of meaning — we readily see why "concept" and "shape" (eidos) could be confused, and we note, to the strengthening of human modesty, that so mighty a system as the Platonic doctrine of Ideas is at bottom only an ornamental flourish (a metaphysical misreading) upon the far mightier edifice of language.

*Lazarus* Geiger, already mentioned in passing, was, unless we are mistaken, the only one among philologists who at least surmised the conceptual affinity of visible appearance and its fundamental importance for the development of communicative language. "An invisible gas," it says on p. 39 of his book on "Ursprung und Entwicklung der menschlichen Sprache und Vernunft" [Origin and Development of Human Language and Reason], "is at first thought under the image of a visible vapor, the negation of its density being added in fantasy only as though it were a matter of the opposition of a fine tissue to a coarser one; we no sooner begin to think of warmth, sound, light as independent things than they also step before the soul shaped, radiating, wave-forming; we speak of electric currents, ask ourselves whether electricity and magnetism are fluids, proceeding in this from the fluid we see, thinking away, to be sure, the property of visibility, but always tacitly substituting the thought of a possible visibility, say for senses more capable of it. Now, through the [p. 294] operation of thinkingaway, everything can apparently be negated; indeed we can even, through abstraction from all properties, represent to ourselves pure being or nothingness, which two, comprehensibly enough, may then no longer be different; but with these arts we do not banish the nature of our representing and thinking, which remains forever bound merely to the repetition of what has been sensed, and, where things are concerned, of what has been seen. Even a spiritual being is for us only a refined bodily shape, demanded by the understanding as invisible yet still hovering visibly before the fantasy; and even the effort to deny precisely corporeality and visible shape in order to arrive at the thought of pure spirit — what is it but a concession of the preponderant significance which shape possesses in everything that is not spirit, that is, in all things?" — We were wrong to reproach the author for not knowing, and being unable to know, of the process of beholding and of the process of mirroring; for an insight is never devalued by the fact that the development of thought founded upon it outgrew it. Nor does the almost unanimous rejection on the part of philologists amount to much, since Geiger's attempt to substantiate his finding with examples failed completely, owing to quite inadequate skill in word-derivation. It cannot be denied, however, that this significant thinker remained caught, by a "sensualism" ultimately peculiar to himself as well, in two fundamental errors. First, he confused visible appearance and concept (just as he also confused representation and sensation); second, he sought the principal cause of the concept-supporting capacity of visible appearance in a particularly highly developed power of discrimination, and, quite properly speaking, in the "delicacy" of the eye.

For one would remain stuck in a literally superficial conception were one to hold the undeniable dependence of the development of word-meaning, among all peoples without exception, upon visible appearance to be sufficiently explained by some or other superiority of sight over the other senses. We wish to make this palpable by means of yet another favorite concept of ideological thinking — one standing exceedingly close to the concept of the Idea, or rather being that very concept itself grown old — namely, that one wholly misses the cause of the vicarious power of visible appearance so long as one thinks to find it anywhere in specific traits of optical experience. Ever since the "formae substantiales, separatae, inhaerentes, nativae, corporationis etc." of the Scholastics, the half [p. 295] and whole Platonists have held it their foremost task to visit their distinction of "form and content," "form and matter," "form and material" upon every possible field of knowledge, claiming "form" or "forms" for themselves as the ideal, the proper, the "eternal," and leaving the transient, material, and so to speak ordinary "contents," not without a certain complacent forbearance, to the "crude empiricists." Now "form" is precisely the same hybrid of concept and sensory semblance as "Idea," but offers the advantage of at the same time revealing to what end the mating took place. "Forma" means "shape" and originally also designated the device for bringing something into a shape — for instance the vessel that one can now fill with this "content," now with that. The vessel is manifestly no less a thing of sense than the material within it, and both belong, among other things, to the zone of visible appearance. If we ask, however, what gave the vessel preference over its content to serve as vicar of the ideal, there can be no doubt that the property of its color — one that cannot be thought away optically and is "given" to the eye alone as such — drops out immediately as the answer, and that the conceptual affinity must rather be sought in its relative *rigidity*. Shape — here in the first instance that of the vessel, but thereby every shape — stands to the other traits of sensory semblance as the abiding to the changing, the solid to the fluid, the standing to the mobile, the enduring to the fleeting, the sempiternal to the temporal. It was not from a predominance of the visual impression that visible appearance offered itself as the substratum of logical meaning, but the reverse: visible appearances came to predominate within human sensibility in step with the development of a thinking that, as the basis for the timelessness of objects, could make use only of those traits of appearances that bear the character of being withdrawn from time. From the lived archetype of actuality, its spatial shape became the meaning-symbol, because and insofar as it was the counter-pole of its temporal flux. The chain of proof for this would be closed if the question had to be answered affirmatively, whether tangible resistance too, insofar as it outlasts the moment, is not entitled to a similar privileged position for the development of concepts. A quite obvious consideration brings us certainty on this point!

If ideological thinking, out of the confusion of the visibly rigid with the conceptual, indulges a cult of "eternal forms," then it is [p. 296] quite plainly the confusion of the conceptual with the tangibly rigid that has, since the most ancient times, helped empiricist thinking to its no less blind cult of "eternal matter"! The tertium comparationis of shape and the solidity of matter — as against, say, colors of illumination — is the relative withdrawnness from time of both: beheld, the one time, in colored appearance, the other time in tangible appearance; there joined to the materially indeterminate figural, the outline-like, the shadow-actual, the semblance-like, the mirror-image-like; here joined to the form-indeterminate resistant, solid, corporeal; there as though withdrawn from the stream of time into a separate presentness, here as frozen within it into an indestructibility that outlasts time. Whereas, then, the two world-historical opposed forms of belief in reason stem, in terms of the science of life, from the rivalry of visual experience and tactile experience, there has never yet been a philosophy whose formation of concepts was guided by audibilities, smellabilities, tastabilities — and doubtless for no other reason than that, in the middle senses, the spatial pole of experience remains more or less dependent upon the temporal pole of experience, so that the elements of appearance experienced in this fashion lack that measure of rigidity, whether sensible or pictorial, which the temporal oppositeness of thought-things requires for its support. — To the preponderance of the sensation of touch, and its particular role in the generation of concepts, the German language pays homage with words such as: "Eindruck" [impression], which borrows the general concept of the experienceability of appearance through the senses from tactile experience; "Reiz" [stimulus], which likewise raises the excitation of the sense of touch to the pattern for sensory excitation as such; "Einprägung" [imprinting], which makes the retention in memory dependent on a material performance of the impression; "Erinnerungsspur" [memory-trace], which makes it conditioned by the once again materially conceived plasticity of the receiving soul; and finally, above all, with "Begriff" [concept] itself, which comes from "begreifen" [to grasp/conceive] = to feel by touch.

Let us survey in quick succession the waystations of the path of thought we have traversed. Depictability belongs to the world of visible appearance. Every depiction or mirroring takes place through the repetition not of the beholdable image but of the visible shape of the image, which, compared with the former, has the property of being relatively withdrawn from the stream of time; and it is this that now enables it to signify the strictly extratemporal properties of things and, consequently, the things themselves that are, so to speak, [p. 297] clothed with them; or in a brief formula: the conceptual affinity of visible appearance is grounded in the empirical timelessness of shape. — Here the intervening question presses itself upon us, whether shape is not also to be felt by touch, and, if this should be the case, on what, all the same, the superiority of visible over tangible shape for the formation of concepts rests.

We spoke in the 23rd Chapter of the twofold capacity of sensibility, according to which this always consists of beholding and sensation. What is sensed, we indicated, is always a resistance, whereas what is beheld is every sensory quality, and indeed inescapably within the totality of spatiotemporal images. Accordingly, space too would be beheld, whether through sight or through hearing or through touch. What profound significance belongs to the sense of touch for the formation of the image of space we shall see later; here let it merely be pointed out, for the time being, that neither a resistance by itself, nor the character of the resisting surface — its roughness, smoothness, hardness, and so on — could by itself build up an image of space. If, nonetheless, space is unquestionably felt by touch even with sight wholly excluded, since every tangible resistance at once appears also as an aspect of spatial images, and with it inescapably the roughness, smoothness, hardness of the resisting surface, this is grounded in the capacity of the tactile organ for self-moved traversal of space. Now every movement has the distinguishable properties of speed of movement and shape of movement (which in turn can be resolved into path-lengths and directions). If, then — what has here only been asserted without proof — movement can be experienced and apprehended, then the shape of the movement is also co-experienced and is likewise apprehensible. Not, to be sure, a resistance felt by touch, but rather the sequence of movement — for instance of the groping hands along the resisting surfaces — leads in this way to the apprehension of the shape of the touched body. The movement that traces out a shape requires for this a longer or shorter span of time, whereas the outlined shape appears in the empirical now. From this it follows that, in the shape of the path traversed, even the movement itself appears in the empirical now. With this important preliminary finding we turn to the question of the particular conceptual affinity of visible appearance.

If lightning flashes over an evening landscape behind us, we perceive, with the aid of sight alone, in a fraction of a second, [p. 298] the depth of space together with the manifold figures that the things in space signify to us: the poplar bent by the wind, the rippled mirror of the pond, the bowed-down reeds, the clouds caught in drifting, the houses and hills, and so forth; but we suppose that, beyond this, we perceive the movements themselves of the trees, the reeds, the water, the clouds. Because the shape of moving things tends, more or less, to have the shape of the movement participating in it, figures that are in and of themselves unmoving (such as the shortest experienceable instant gives us of what is actually moving) can not merely denote but simply represent the swinging, circling or hurrying-past! Long before it is able to give itself an account of the objective unmovedness of what it sees, the child, in the colored or drawn image of the waterfall, already supposes it sees, in place of a resting figure of lines, the actual plunging-down of the masses of water — thereby indisputably attesting that it has taken up even the wildly moving into itself with the aid of standing schemata of visible appearance. — The answer, suitably to be inserted here, to some questions at least partly raised already earlier, will let us reach, imperceptibly, the actual point of forking of tactile experience and visual experience, and thereby, for the first time, that question whose settling coincides with the final disclosure of the meaning of mirroring beholding.

Not by virtue of their qualities, as we should like to decide a question raised in the 23rd Chapter, do colors cling to the spatial pole of world-appearance, but thanks to their capacity for sensualizing forms, figures, shapes. Only the shape of the color becomes for us the surface of the body needing shape, and precisely thereby runs the risk of being understood henceforth merely as a property of the thing. Darkness, night, murk, twilight, brightness, pallor, fog, day and light belong to the world of visible appearances as surely as they remain wholly closed to the blind; but, being unshaped, they stand no less remote from the thing than do noises and sounds, and therefore serve, as we offered numerous examples to show, in the first instance for the depiction of character. If, by contrast, the name-determined red or blue or yellow or green or white meets us a thousand times more often shaped — whether as the covering color of objects of use, or as the inner pigment especially of the plant world — we now understand without further ado why it had gradually to lose in content of character. One speaks of "warm red," because warmth, notwithstanding all its property-character, [p. 299] remains preferentially an event and therefore expression, but not of "red warm," because we are accustomed to represent red as shaped, and in shape behold something like a mode of appearance of being.<sup>40</sup>

<sup>40</sup> On page 299. — It may be mentioned in passing: the blind loses, through the absence of colors, in a twofold respect less than the deaf through the absence of sounds and noises. The deaf has lost, along with the sounds, also the movement of the sounds; the blind has *not* lost, along with the colors, the world of shapes as well, which is represented, among other things, by those colors. Because, further, sounds and noises, thanks to the overemphasized temporality of their appearing, are in the highest degree *qualitative* expression of operative powers, the deaf finds himself largely cut off from the *character* of the actual and sees himself, as it were, set outside into a world of shadows and semblances, unless he too, through touch and sight, experiences the mutability of appearance; whereas the blind, being reliant on touch and hearing, communes with the *character* of the world far more intimately still than the man of sight, referred quite predominantly to optical shapes! Hence stems the "cheerfulness" of the blind, attested even by folk song, and the moroseness of the deaf! "As soon as he but feels life, the blind man already begins to sing," runs the opening of a Portuguese folk song.

We do not forget that it was shown in the same chapter that even the meaningless figure of lines expresses the inwardness of a happening, more precisely of a movement, since nothing strictly expressionless is to be found at all in the image of the world. For this reason it is nonetheless true that, given comparable attendant circumstances, sounds carry more weight of expression than colors, unformed colors more weight than formed ones. To escape confusing content of expression with content of meaning, let us briefly elucidate both by the same case: the image of the waterfall. — Suppose an artistically highly gifted draughtsman and an artistically very poor but adroit one had each represented the waterfall foaming down through a rocky gate; nothing prevents the intended object from being equally recognizable in both pictures, or even seeming better "hit off" in the artistically far weaker one. But whereas the latter would offer only water and rock, the former would disclose to us, together with the motion of the water, its down-tearing force and trail-breaking unstoppability, and, with the rigidity of the rock, the violence of its resistance and the wave-splitting inflexibility of its defiance — thus revealing the combative encountering and the alternating self-renewal in victory of contrapuntal modes of the world's course. By virtue of what traits does the motionless figure of lines in the drawing signify plunging water, and by virtue of what other traits does it express a little of the soul of the water? That would be a question for so-called aesthetics, if this were ever minded to sacrifice its delight in self-satisfied phrases to the passion of inquiry. — The standing shape of visible appearance can thus even take up into itself all that which we set against it above for the sake of the special characterization of qualitative color: brightness and darkness, night and fog, the shining and flickering of the atmosphere, the spray of water, glittering reflections, moisture, wetness and drought, receding weather, the onset of twilight, even icy cold and boiling heat; and it can consequently saturate itself with expression to such a degree that we suppose ourselves to meet in it a rather intensified than diminished actuality. But if, in this way, a great artist manages to disclose to us, by means of a mere figure of lines, all the riddles [p. 300] and distances of the richer actuality of a beholding nearer to the primal source, this is in any case only because the figure in question is properly capable of "counterfeiting" the most delightful actualities, and exactly to the measure of its capacity to do so. Mere arabesques, too, are wonderfully capable of expression; but what soul-content would appear there, the figure of lines would owe, as certainly, to what is represented, just as the tangled lines of a hasty hand owe the legible forms to their character as written signs. Since, now, every possible drawing consists in the end of a relation of lines (or then of darker and lighter cut-out areas), it must therefore be given to us to perceive that innumerable manifold of processual appearances in standing relations of lines. From this there follows, in the first place, an immeasurable superiority of visible over tangible shape in respect of the breadth of the range of meaning; for no tangible shape can be conceived that could signify: the shining and flickering of the atmosphere, the spray of water, glittering reflections, moisture, wetness and drought, icy cold and boiling heat! — Even if man did not in fact surpass, comparatively speaking, all animal species in the development of sight, it would still stand unshakably firm that he far surpasses them all in receptiveness to shapes, which, as has been shown, amounts to the same as receptiveness for the relation of lines, or of light and dark cut-out areas. Every six-year-old child, but only rarely an animal, recognizes in the motionless photographic image the object drawn in light! The adult, who at the sight of a well-succeeded photograph is accustomed to think far less of it than of the person meant, must first bring to consciousness, with an effort, the monstrous difference between her and the image of her. The photograph, the length of an index finger, presents the pictured head, with the sharpest distinctness of all its features, in a smallness to which, in actuality, there would correspond an interval that would make it wholly unrecognizable; the photograph is flat, the head corporeal; the one shows merely gradations of brightness, the other manifold colors! The child who produces on a slate lying flat, above two parallel lines, two lines intersecting each other at an obtuse angle (and even white on black!) believes it recognizes, in the unspeakably meager figure, a standing house — indeed the particular house of its parents! So astonishing a degree of schematizing apprehension of relations can originally be borne only by the [p. 301] sense of sight. But should not, then, all and every apprehension of relations — of man, that is to say — occur according to the measure of, and mediated through, such an apprehension of visible appearance; and would not, conversely, the indubitable superiority of man in the apprehension of sensory proportions generally point once again to the preponderance of meaning of his world of visible appearance? We offer a single example that at least does not stand in the way of so bold a conclusion.

If, among the senses, sight and touch stand at the outermost opposite ends of the *range of visual field* of beholding, then sight and hearing stand at outermost opposite ends of another kind: in the image of sight the spatial pole rules, in the image of hearing no less the temporal pole. The visible figure is perceived in an almost timeless-seeming instant and is thought without the least inclusion of any lateral duration; a sequence of tones is never perceived in the empirical instant and never thought without the inclusion of temporal intervals; yet the customary turn of phrase "musical *figures*" betrays to us that we think even the sequence of tones as designated by the shape of the movements we experience in passing from tone to tone. We venture the conclusion that here lies the key to the problem of the origin of melody. The mode of song peculiar to man alone differs, as is well known, from the natural cries of animals — including the merely improper songs of birds — through fixed degrees of pitch and the transposability into any register of pitch grounded only on these. No grey parrot that has learned to whistle down a shorter or longer melody ever takes it up in a changed key, whereas the six-year-old child (like the "natural man" as well) either renders it of its own accord in varying registers or is at least able to continue in any key whatever, as soon as it is given the opening notes. If, in the animal, the apprehension of tones by duration, strength and mood predominates, then in man it is unquestionably the apprehension of their relations; and this, again, is apprehension of the shape of movement, for which words like "Tonleiter" [scale, lit. tone-ladder], "Tonstufen" [tone-steps], "Tonschritte" [tone-steps/strides] may further be adduced. The original apprehension of shape meant a relation in juxtaposition; it climbed, in step with the development of thought, to the most dizzying heights of its receptivity for differences in the domain of visible appearances, and it finds the standing presence realized only in the impression of sight, through which its object, shape, seems, as it were, to offer an example of intuition for [p. 302] the object of thought itself. For this reason we hold that the particular receptivity to relations, which places man, even as one who merely lives-through, into a supra-animal realm of, so to speak, concept-related units of meaning, is grounded quite generally, and thus also for decidedly temporally-poled traits of appearance, in shaped visible appearance.<sup>41</sup> This already presaged what, besides the difference in scope of their experiential contents, sets a boundary — itself to be construed in kind — between the touching and the seeing of forms.

<sup>41</sup> On page 302. — As we recognize, in the flat differences of brightness of the small postcard picture, the wave-beaten Helgoland, so we recognize the one and same melody in the high solo voice of the singing child, the low voice of the singing man, and in the roaring concord of the instruments of the largest orchestra.

Although the blind man is without question actually able to mean the same shape that the sighted man sees, he has nonetheless had to abstract from the tactile movement the temporality of its course in order to become aware of it; whereas in the instantaneous visual impression the result lies ready-made before him. Indeed, he has had to abstract even something more! In the one single glance of the eye, besides the "point of fixation," there always stands at the same time its positional relation to other points of space, and accordingly always the shape as well; in the simultaneous pressure of the forefinger against the tabletop there stands, of that same shape, only a single empirical position. Were positions now strung together, one after another, by a groping glide, and were the abstraction carried out that leaves over, of the process of movement, only the shape of the path, this would nonetheless differ from the visual shape through its boundness to position; and only once the substratum too had been thought away would the remainder that is left coincide with the thing-signifying side of the relational properties in the visual image. It is true that in the world of objects there subsists a mutual dependence between timeless universals and enduring substrata, as indeed we grounded above upon this the thing-property-character of shaped colors. That thinking, for that reason, no less chooses precisely opposite directions, according as it uses the property in order to arrive at the substratum, or rather the latter in order to arrive at the property, was already proven by our derivation of the mutually warring world-view forms of "materialism" and "idealism" from the rivalry of tactile experience and visual experience. We now touch upon the point of forking, in that, turning back to the guiding thought of depictability with the aid of visible appearance alone, we elucidate in visual shape that trait through which it enters, in terms of the science of appearance, into opposition to tactile shape.

Had a blind man, by feeling over a human shape, ascertained the identity of its bearer, and had the latter then, as silently as possible, [p. 303] changed places, the blind man would have to carry out the feeling-over once again at the new place: the process of touching and the tactile shape are position-determined. Whoever, by contrast, sees his own body mirrored fivefold in a double mirror grasps the mirror-images and, in them, the sameness of the object without any change of position — indeed, under certain circumstances, two or three of them at a single glance: the process of seeing and the visual shape are free of position. Should one object that the process of seeing takes place, after all, in the place-bound optic nerve, one would have confused it, in exactly the same way, with a merely optical process — as happens, though without harm, when one is in the habit of calling "real" images the place of effect of the rays that are thrown back by concave mirrors and lenses, or captured in a dark chamber. For physics, the "virtual" image, e.g. in a plane mirror, which does not act at the apparent place of its appearing, is usefully distinguished from these; but in terms of the science of appearance both are merely semblance-images, because both lack a real place. The bodily shape is really located where it is felt by touch; the image-shape *without* the body is located nowhere, or everywhere! The place-determined bromide-silver plate and the place-determined optic nerve are sensitive to, again, place-determined effects of the objective light; but no chemical substance in the world is sensitive to shape! Light-rays — and by no means images — decompose the plate and decompose the retina! We do, it is true, also assign mere visual images to particular places in space, but only because the space of things coincides for us with tactile space, which, for reasons not yet ripe for judgment here, is the immediate bearer of the space of things. Let one strictly forbid oneself every side-thought of the tangibility of visual shape, and one will at least not be able to avoid acknowledging its freedom from place — stressed at the outset — as evidencing itself in the fact that it can occur, at any given moment, at any place whatever, and thus at a thousand and ten thousand places at once. (One need only think of the illustrations in a widely circulated illustrated newspaper!) Only in the visual impression is the *omnipresence* of shape realized, and this now forms the living abutment of the arch of the bridge that spans from it over to the placelessness of objects, for which we have coined the *concepts* of warmth, cold, solidity, fluidity, color, fragrance, bitterness, sweetness, loudness, softness, movement, change, and so on — in short, of all the properties and states of things.<sup>42</sup>

<sup>42</sup> On page 303. — Since this note has a personal undertone, the "we"- form must be dropped. — A friend, to whom I had read the chapter on the conceptual kinship of visible appearance, believed he detected points of contact with so-called Gestalt psychology; whereupon I at once recalled having read something similar in some review of earlier writings of mine. I therefore resolved to inform myself what was involved in Gestalt psychology, hitherto unknown to me. I was told the essential work was: *Wolfgang Köhler*, Die physischen Gestalten in Ruhe und im stationären Zustand, Vieweg und Sohn, Braunschweig 1920. It is the same author to whom we owe the excellent investigations into the intelligence of anthropoids. And so, during the printing of this volume, and as it were at the eleventh hour, I borrowed the book just named and at least read it *through*, guided throughout solely by the question whether a kindred direction of thought was present here and, if so, whether of alien origin or dependent on my own researches. These latter, namely, have for more than thirty years moved along *the same* line, as anyone can convince himself who takes in hand the collected volume "Zur Ausdruckslehre und Charakterkunde," in which I have united 21 individual investigations from 1897–1927 that today would otherwise be hard or altogether impossible to obtain (Niels Kampmann Verlag, Heidelberg). I now communicate the result of my re-examination. I must say first: my almost unreservedly critical marginal remarks are not to be understood as a value-judgment on Köhler's work *as such*. Even if I possessed more physical training than I do, it would not be possible for me, on the strength of a mere reading-through, to judge the overall value of a work that unconditionally demands to be *studied*. If I am not mistaken, the author, with his conceptually theoretical survey of *physical* states of affairs, has struck out on a promising path, one that could with advantage have been considered sooner, and I am inclined to believe that his book may claim high merit in *that* regard. Quite otherwise, however, does the matter stand in *psychological* respect, and it is of this alone that we shall speak here. Let me say it outright: the Gestalt-psychological tendency, so far at least as it emerges from the work in question, is neither dependent on my views nor akin to them. It is true that it, like me, renounces sensualist atomism and provides several fine proofs of the impossibility of piecing intuitive images together out of fragments of perception. But with this agreement in the *negative* the matter is already exhausted, and at once the roads fork, fork so widely that I consider mutual understanding excluded. For the *positive* aims are not merely different from one another but are also wholly incompatible with one another. In agreement evidently with other Gestalt psychologists, Köhler seeks first to furnish proof of the like-naturedness of essential criteria of neurophysiological processes with those of general physical processes. What he brings out, to this end, concerning *nonadditive* states of affairs in physics deserves close examination, while the neurophysiological parallels make, on the uninitiated, the impression of rather bold hypotheses and fail to indicate the experiments by which they could be verified. The conclusions, however, that are drawn from this for *psychology* rest, in my judgment, on a fundamental misunderstanding. I show this by means of a single example that, incidentally, occupies broad space in Köhler's work. In order to prove that the apprehension of objective figures — for instance, an intuitively given circular figure — is derivable from the *nerve* processes that accompany seeing, he makes the wholly arbitrary assumption that to the circular object of perception there corresponds a circular reaction-district of the retina. "Suppose we had before us, on an otherwise homogeneous, say gray, ground, . . a *circle*. The retinal image yields, over an equally circular area, *one* kind of reaction, and, widely around it, a second kind of reaction" (p. 206). "To the, in the geometrical sense, perfect symmetry of the retinal circle-*form* corresponds, in perception, phenomenal uniformity of the 'shape' all around . ." (p. 232). To this it must be replied: this is in fact so only under rare exceptional conditions, whereas in the great preponderance of cases, in the perception of circular figures — of plates and ashtrays, for instance — the visual images are *ellipses*, and moreover often very narrow ellipses; compare in this connection our remarks on p. 46. Yet although we have had hundreds of times elliptical visual images of the rims of cups and beakers, we perceive the circularity of the objects, and this holds, with corresponding variations, *generally*. It has repeatedly happened to me that someone, whom I pointed out to, that in the upper corners of a room the edges appearance-wise meet at *obtuse* angles and not, say, at right angles, refused to believe it, until I asked him to draw what he saw! From this it follows that it cannot possibly be the visual data *alone* to which we owe the apprehension of intuitive spatial shapes. How we actually accomplish this is foreshadowed in the concluding chapter of this volume and will occupy us more closely in the third volume. This much, however, has already become familiar to us: that it would be hopeless to want to understand, from the physics of sensory processes, the units of meaning into which without exception all sensory experiences — even those of animals — flow. The initial error of the Gestalt psychologists is therefore of a fundamental nature. It requires no far-reaching considerations to recognize that the Gestalt-psychological mode of thought is a variety of ideologism. It does indeed turn away from atomism; but, like all sensualists and idealists, its representatives know nothing of lived experience and know only the Cartesian duality: here being — there consciousness! In that they — confounding being and actuality — seek to find products of thinking within the contents of lived experience, they carry — and this is their novelty — the supersensuous objects of physics (such as force-fields, lines of force, potentials, ions, electrons, etc.) into the world of the senses, and subordinate the abstracta of the most abstract thinking to the *actuality* of *appearance*. They believe they are investigating phenomena while they are investigating thought-things, and should therefore hardly be surprised when they hit upon the most perfect agreement of the former with physics, and, conversely, of physics with the facts of consciousness! I was at first astonished, on reading Köhler's book, to find nowhere an unmistakable forerunner from the previous generation mentioned. Although *Theodor Lipps* does not in general use the terms "Gestalt" and "Gestalt-property," the *matter* itself is indeed downright a principal theme of his entire psychology and "Aesthetics," which in *that* regard had already, by around the nineties, likewise abandoned atomism. Because he was continually in search of the "unity in multiplicity," he arrived at his doctrine of geometrical-optical illusions, which he, out of the explanatory principle he had posited, augmented by many hitherto unknown ones. I waited in vain for Köhler to demonstrate his neurophysiological interpretation on at least three or four fundamentally important optical illusions. But I soon recognized the reason for this silence in the circumstance that, in *another* respect, the Gestalt psychologists feel themselves, and indeed must feel themselves, precisely opposed to a Lipps. For whereas the latter lets shapes and forms first arise in us through an "apperceptive" activity of consciousness (more precisely, of spirit), it matters to the Gestalt psychologists to demonstrate that the shapes lie in the appearances themselves, from where they are supposed to be transported, by processes of like nature, partly chemical, partly electrical, into the center of the nervous system. What was misguided in Lipps's conception appears here on an enlarged scale. For in order to furnish the proof in question, the concept of Gestalt is given a new and incomparably more abstract sense, according to which it is henceforth to be called "Gestalt" when a process, indeed a state of affairs generally, cannot be composed of parts, but part after part appears determined by the totality of the process. What falls out of this for physics is — I repeat it — very interesting. But if we consider that in this way "proper structures" would be = shapes — for instance the distribution of electric charge over the surface of a conductor, or even the communicating system of two electrolytic solutions — and *Gestalt-properties*: the charge-density at any arbitrary point of the conductor, or the electric potential at any arbitrary point of the solution, then surely no one fails to see that it would scarcely be possible to remove oneself still further from the world of intuition with the concept of Gestalt! If a Lipps let the "apperceptive activity" weave the picture of the world out of atoms of perception, it is now the theories constructed for the explanation of physical processes that the Gestalt psychologist holds to be, as it were, imprints (ectypes) of the appearances themselves! Out of the esse est percipi there has become, for a change, and admittedly in a novel guise, once more a percipi est esse, and even the famous "unity in multiplicity" puts in an appearance, but at the opposite end: considerations on magnetic-field patterns and equilibrium figures of liquid films must serve to impute to *nature* a tendency toward the formation of the simplest, most regular, most symmetrical shapes possible! One can investigate neurophysiological processes physically and chemically, as one can other processes too, and one thereby achieves their ever more far-reaching incorporation into the general causal nexus. But if this is to serve a deepening of our insight into the processes of life, we must first have investigated the life-processes themselves; otherwise we achieve nothing physically. May my consideration for the very widespread unfamiliarity with the equation: life-process = lived experience be credited to me, if I once more illustrate the sentence just cited, self-evident though it is, by a robust example. If humanity had been completely deaf from time immemorial, but had brought physics so far that it could calculate all the processes in an animal's hearing-apparatus by means of differential and integral equations for the movements of electrons, it would for all that know no more of tones, sounds, noises than it does *without* physics — that is, nothing. Generalized: from the extra-sensory objects of thought of physics no bridge leads to the contents of sensory lived experience. Worse for the formation of knowledge than ignorance of them, however, is the misapprehension into which we fall when we *exchange* the images of the world of appearance for the objects of the world of being, as the sensualists do with their belief in atoms, and the spiritualists with their belief in a creative power of the Logos: for both, in this way, the world of appearance becomes a world of *semblance*, though of a different tinge. The Gestalt psychologist, finally, phenomenalizes highly abstract relational concepts and thereby bends fundamentally back to the early forms of ideologism. — I take, in conclusion, a further piece of evidence for this, if one may say so, extremely cerebral reinterpretation of the sensory world for the Gestalt psychologist's own conception of Gestalt. Because the visual image, as has been shown, is a vital analogue of the object of thought, shape (eidos, "idea") and concept gravitated, so to speak, toward one another (at least in the thinking of the Occident) from the very beginning. Far from being, then, a turning toward the world of images, the emphasis on the *gestalt-like* character of nature signifies rather the beginning of the turning-away of the mind from it, and of the "way upward." But then it is the *conceptual* kinship of visible appearance that is once again demonstrated to us, when one recently feels driven to borrow the word Gestalt once more from the visual domain for every kind of reciprocal dependency of any states of affairs upon one another; and we no longer doubt *whither* one will arrive if one keeps to the line thus traced out: to the volatilization of actuality into a — now, to be sure, scientifically equipped — realm of Platonic ideas!

Just as the visual image of the thing — and this alone — can be experienced in the empirical [p. 304] instant, and yet is able to signify even the never instantaneously occurring movement of the thing, so the object of thought is grasped in the mathematical point of time and is nonetheless able to hold fast countless traits from the world of happening; and just as the visual image, and this alone, can be detached from the thing and yet goes on representing it, so every object of thought is (though only unintuitively) "abstract" and yet capable of pointing to a world of intuitable things; and just as it never belongs to the mere visual image to be exactly here and to linger long or briefly, so there is no conceivable property of a thing in which being-referred to a determinate place in space and time would already be contained. Rather, it consists precisely in this that the genus-founding "universality" of all property- and state-predicables (predicaments) lies in their occurring everywhere and at all times. Redness, cubic shape, weight, temperature, speed, acceleration, smoothness, acidity, dryness, and so on and so forth, have no seat in space and time; and if, now, the dry, cubic, warm, red, heavy thing, etc., unfailingly has them, then dryness, cubic form, warmth, redness, speed themselves stand to it in exact analogy to how, within sensibility, the visual impression stands to the tactile impression — the visual impression, detached in the copy, leading a place-free, hovering existence. If the sense of sight is indeed, in breadth of horizon, the most beholding of the senses, this is, all the same, precisely not for the sake of a capacity for mirroring by which it lures us, as no other sense does, out of the inwardness of beholding into the outwardness of that mere looking-on which, when it turns enthusiastic, crowns itself with concepts of a not yet explained enmity to actuality, but indeed of a deceptive turning-away from actuality. In truth, only a being of the eye could become a detached, and therefore a thinking, being, and only the need for redemption of a thinking being could cheat itself up into the uprooted belief in the "better beyond" of mere semblances — as, for Europe, Plato dialectically prefigured it, and Schiller glorified it in fire-colored tints:

Only the body belongs to those powers / That weave dark fate; / But free from every power of time, / The playmate of blessed natures, / Wanders above in the meadows of light / Divine among gods, the Form.

[p. 305] If we draw the sum of what has been said, it seems to us to be expressed in the following statement: visible shape, archetype and pattern of shape as such, signifies, represents, "stands for," in the form of an ever-instantaneous presence, the actuality of happening — or rather: it gives, of the fleeting, its experienceable presentness, and thus, in the sensibly present, the sensibly *already* elapsed. In view of this, it hardly needs interpreting why it prepares the thinkability of the actual and, in a certain sense, renders the eternally-transient capable of being; only the more urgently, on the other hand, does the question thrust itself upon us as to the inner ground of possibility of so strange a state of affairs. If we consider that, in respect of its nature as the beholdable image, actuality possesses spatial mutual-externality, and, in respect of its nature as operative happening, temporal fleetingness, then we arrive, for the experience of shape, at the final and simplest formula: that it offers time in the medium of *space*. The key to the problem of actuality-signifying shape lies in the essence of sense-space!

[p. 306]

#### 31. Kapitel — Das Wesen des Sinnenraums — Chapter 31 — The Essence of Sense-Space

We have distinguished from actuality-space the space of things, or the spatial object; but we must now interpose between the two a third space: impression-space, or intuition-space, or sense-space. If we occasionally also use for it the word "perception-space," it should be noted that what then hovers before us is not the mental act within the process of perception, of which we treated in the first chapters, but the psychic peculiarity of the experience that bears it. As a space to be experienced, sense-space too belongs to actuality-space — the sense-space that animals (though not plants) have in common with us — except that we now wish to prove that it is not given to us by original beholding, but by the *mirroring* of what has already been beheld beforehand. According to this, the ultimate ground, in terms of the science of appearance, for the strange capacity of visible appearance to signify things and processes, would be a property of space not yet ascertained to this day and, to be sure, at first sight thoroughly strange, according to which sense-space would have the form of actuality of a mirror-semblance — and then, of course, so too, as derived from it, would the space of things. Let us recall here in advance that the mirror-image's character of being a mere semblance cannot, in principle, be *seen* in it at all. Who has not, at some time, been on the point of running into an insufficiently lit mirror, because for a moment he had mistaken the mirrored space for the space of things! *Within* the world of visible appearances, then, the mirror-image of the perceived thing would stand on *the same* level as the thing itself, since this, in turn, can again be mirrored, and its mirror-image again, and so on, possibly, into infinity. If we now conclude that the mirrorability of mirror-images points back to the substantial semblance-character of the impression-contents themselves, then the initial member of the series now to be posited — namely the original actuality, or, more briefly henceforth, the "archetype" — would indeed lie *on this side* of the [p. 307] world of visible appearances, and that process of mirroring, through whose occurrence the archetype is exchanged for the intuitable impression-content, would differ essentially from the process of mirroring in physical usage. We should have to keep the optical and the vital mirroring apart, and we mitigate at once, with a preliminary explanation, the very justified misgiving to which the extension of an optical concept here indicated may well be exposed. The right to borrow the name of mirroring for the life-process that gives us, in place of beholdable archetypes, intuitable impression-contents, we gain from the proposition — to be grounded step by step — that the intuitability of impression-contents capable of becoming objects stands to archetypal actuality, in essential respects, similarly as the mirror-semblance of the thing stands to the thing. It is, in other words, a similarity (not, say, an identity) of the relations between the respectively independent and the respectively dependent state of affairs that leads us to set a vital mirroring alongside optical mirroring.<sup>43</sup>

<sup>43</sup> On page 307. — Only to forestall a possible misunderstanding do we briefly recall the customary conception, according to which, at bottom, one may not speak of a depictability of sense-space and of appearances, but only of *things*. One expatiates on this somewhat as follows. It has no sense to say that the green of the painted landscape depicts the tree-green of the actual landscape, the painted blue an actual sky-blue; rather the matter stands thus, that the colors of the painting, repeating the colored impression, offer a picture of the objective landscape. Because formed color has, among other things, the capacity to represent something bodily actual, it accomplishes this without distinction both in the thing itself and in the picture of the thing; the picture, however, is a picture in that it evokes, *only* with the help of visible appearance, the illusion of the existence of a thing to whose nature it belongs to be, in principle, attestable by *all* the senses, but especially by the sense of touch. This consideration, unquestionably correct, leaves open precisely the question that stands at the center of ours: namely, how a sense-datum can "represent" something wholly different from itself, and on what it rests that the essential content of an actuality is feigned by a few relational properties of its colored appearance. Whoever proceeds from the thing as the "given" need not concern himself with such questions at all, and can nevertheless present us with valuable disclosures — for instance concerning the fundamental requirements of pictorial reproduction. *We*, however, are in search of the occasioning grounds precisely of the *origination* of the perceptual thing, and set about to understand its psychic side from its capacity for mirroring.

Since the following inquiry brings answers to a series of questions that were left undecided in earlier chapters, our linking up with some findings already secured there may help chart the direction of our path. We had established that the thing-point holds, at every instant, a determinate spatial place, while it remained as yet open in what respect it differs from this place. With regard to the spatial place itself, we must of course first of all keep apart the lived experience of place and the mental act that, resting upon it, marks mathematical points. But within the conditions of that lived experience we must again keep apart the receptivity for the space in which places reside and the receptivity for place within space. Without sense-space, no place, and without place, no thing: in this it is expressed that one basis in life for the finding of the thing is the lived experience of space, the other the lived experience of place. The latter marks, within the capacity for impression, the bodily side, the former the psychic side; and it is this latter that we shall for the present examine by itself alone.

Proceeding from the consideration that there is no state of affairs capable of appearing that does not partake of the happening-character of actuality, actuality-space has, using the customary image of the stream of time, been called a "flowing space," and thereby the ceaselessly self-transforming space has been transposed into the domain of intuitability. That [p. 308] a self-transforming space is something through and through different from the spatial object needs no saying. But we assure ourselves expressly that it can also never be beheld. So far as we follow the process of beholding in thought, there results for the archetype assigned to it, trait by trait, an incompatibility with intuitable determinations. By virtue of its boundless fleetingness it is an ever-already-past image, and in no instant the same image, and by virtue of the continuity of its coherence, the character of each respective image-phase would moreover be co-determined by that of all that had already elapsed. — By contrast, intuition-space is never experienced as past, and every intuitable change is referred to bodies and materials, and by no means to intuition-space itself. A space not presently present can indeed be "represented" but not perceived, because, were this to happen, it would at once show itself as present. Even the customary view, on beholding a star a thousand light-years distant, that one beholds the past of the star and of the space it occupies, would leave untouched the intuitable state of affairs itself, which would bear the character of presentness just as surely as it would be able to form the substratum of an act of perception taking place in the instant. Both — presentness and unchangeability — hang together inseparably, of which we shall give a somewhat more detailed account.

If we examine carefully the counterpart of our sensibility, we find, in accordance with the flowing character of all lived experience, a never really interrupted change of qualities in our impressions too, however imperceptible it may at first sometimes be — but not a change of the appearance-space co-experienced with them. The specific qualities of something touched, tasted, smelled, heard, seen are caught up in a change now swift, now extremely slow; but the space of their appearing does not flow *along*. Space-intuition has been subjected to very exact analyses, and in the process, contrary to a widespread view, the apt remark has among other things been made that the so-called empty visual space at all times presents certain optical features which one is not entitled to disregard, even though they do not fall precisely under the concept of actual color; from which it would appear as though even it itself could be woven into the flux of images. Yet one would be mistaken to assume on that account that it is only by virtue of the act of objectification that there comes to appear that space which, [p. 309] though as it were clothed in the specific contents of appearance, nonetheless remains unaffected by their coming and going. The finding of the sameness of space with regard to points of time that differ in their place presupposes rather its experienced presence, and the distinguishability of so-called contents of sensation from the spatiality assigned to them without exception demands, as intuited, the polar opposition of the successive to the simultaneous. To assure oneself of this for once, let one make the following simple reflection.

As participating in the outside-one-another, the thing-property of smoothness is among other things something spatial — in such a way that its outside-one-another can indeed be distinguished from its quality, but not separated from it without at the same time abolishing that quality. Now one and the same thing-smoothness is now touched, now seen. But the specific content of a touched smoothness is wholly incomparable with the specific content of a seen smoothness. Supposing, then, that there were an act directed solely upon it, it would find in the touched smoothness a tactile space, in the seen smoothness a visual space — but not, in both, one and the same space. Indeed, even this is still a borrowed manner of speaking. For if the outside-one-another that would be found on the basis of the touched smoothness is, in the occasioning experience, an element or aspect of an image that in no way resembles a seen smoothness, then it would fall under the same concept as the outside-one-another to be found in the seen smoothness no more than, say, a noise falls under the same concept as a smell. The touched and the seen outside-one-another of smoothness would differ from each other no less and no differently than the touched and seen smoothnesses themselves — which would inescapably have the consequence that no *concept of space at all* could any longer come about. If we generalize what the example teaches us, we obtain the following proposition: the "spatial characteristic" of any given impression means the "spatial characteristic" of every impression; sense-space must have been experienced if it is to be understood that it is *perceived*. No speculation about feelings of movement, about the reversibility of sequences of movement by means of self-movement, about the possibility of occlusion, and whatever else has in some partially apt way been adduced to explain how the impressions of the various sensory domains come to be connected with one another, could derive that which gives intuition-space its determining stamp: to be, for everything sensuously experienced, the common medium that alone makes it possible [p. 310] to reinterpret, objectifyingly, qualities incomparable in and for themselves into properties of things. Just as surely as the act of reification requires sense-impressions and nothing further, just as surely does the sense-impression, in order to enter into appearance as what it is, require intuition-space, which, though pervading the qualities and never to be caught in its nakedness, nonetheless again and again releases one after another from itself — comparable to the cone of light of a searchlight, which persists intuitively, notwithstanding that it is perceived only as thrown back by the dust particles and water-vapor droplets of the atmosphere ceaselessly sinking through it.

Sense-space may well appear to us now larger, now smaller, and this happens by no means only owing to differences of visibility, weather influences, and colors of lighting, but also owing to peculiarities of our soul's constitution (to which we shall return in later chapters); yet that which remains, after the separation of all specific qualities, from the momentary impression-image of the world in each case — its pervading spatiality — never takes part in any of those changes that can intuitively play themselves out in lines, colors, forms, temperatures, tactile qualities, tastes, smells, as well as in all the data of inner bodily impressions; wherefore we feel driven, by a compulsion intuitively grounded, to distinguish their occasioning grounds from sense-space. Every quality, as we heard, can be continuously increased or diminished: bright — brighter, dark — darker, loud — louder, soft — softer, smooth — smoother, rough — rougher, and so on, whereas the concept of degree finds no application to the outside-one-another, without whose participation the qualities would not come to appearance. Even though the brighter surface may already seem larger to us than the equally large but less bright one beside it, two things nonetheless remain unmistakably distinct on that account: increase of brightness and enlargement of surface, decrease of brightness and diminution of surface. Indeed, it proves to be the case that we relate the differences of size, extent, and height of sense-space to it itself always only mediately, but immediately to contents of impression differing in space.

If someone stands at a window and sees a carriage drive past on a country road leading away from the house, so that it moves ever farther away, he feels himself occasioned by an inner necessity to understand the growth of the intervening space from the movement of the carriage, and not, say, from an event of space. It would be conceivable that we should judge [p. 311], not "the distance grows because the carriage moves away," but "the carriage moves away because the depth-extension of space grows"! If this now never happened and never happens, then the experience of the appearance of space must possess a characteristic feature that permits only one, and just the one, of the two equally possible judgments to be made. And the very same holds with regard to (relatively) resting objects. We earlier called to mind the wonderful line with which Goethe's revelatory depth of vision summons twilight into appearance: "Already all nearness is far." Were we now to reflect on the discursive content of the line, we should have to establish that it expresses that what is near at hand seems to have become something far off, and not, say, that a dimension of space has extended itself. The poet, to whom the merely conceptual meaning of his lines can and must be a matter of indifference, was indeed permitted to say even this, insofar as it served still better to "summon into appearance" the event meant: but what would always be to be conceived in it is only the removal of the objects of intuition — owing, however, not to their locomotion, but on the occasion of the falling of twilight, which as it were carries them off into the distance. It is, moreover, evident that words like farness and nearness would lose their sense as soon as we burdened space itself with the change that we experience in the transition from spatial nearness to spatial farness.

If, accordingly, sense-space is something never past and passing away, but changelessly present, then it coincides with the actual now that we have repeatedly and vainly inquired after: the *actual* now and *intuition-space* are one and the same, even though judged from two essentially different points of view. The actual now is not beheld, but it is indeed intuited, namely in the only possible form of the sense-space that is present at all times; whereby, incidentally, the meaning of the linguistic equation between presence and presentness has revealed itself to us. Everything present is also something present, and that which is present absolutely is sense-space. This finding permits far-reaching conclusions, of which a few will already suffice to bring about important decisions that we had still had to forgo in the second chapter.

How, we asked there, would the metaphysical concretum be constituted, from which we must abstract in order to apprehend the object of perception? With our answer, now ripe for pronouncement, that it is [p. 312] intuition-space, we mean at first only to characterize the intuitive outside-one-another that attaches to any given content of impression, partly in and for itself, partly by virtue of the co-experienced distance of that content from the recipient of the impression. But if the intuitive outside-one-another originally coincides with the presentness of the image, then, with the help of sense-space, it must be possible to apprehend — and there was in fact originally apprehended — a being-there, and then, with regard to the changeability of the features of the impression, at once also an always. For if, thanks to the changes of the images of intuition, we are able to know that something is just now no longer present which was present just before, then, with regard to the absolutely present intuition-space — whether the contents of impression persist or rush past — we find ourselves occasioned to the conviction that it, as what it is, is always present. In relation to the fleetingness of a sound, for example, the place from which it seems to come to us, and the space it seems to traverse, are for us something intuitively persisting, from which the sound stands out as something non-persisting and thus emphatically temporal.

The thought of the always of space, once it has gained a footing, is, as one notices, bent on making us forget the nowtone of space, and has even more or less obscured for thinkers the fact that even the most fleeting image of intuition — a bang, say, or a flash of lightning — in order to take place, must be there at some time and thus must take part in the appearing now. If, on the other hand, one knows that sense-space, and it alone, is the ever-again-appearing now and consequently the counter-pole of happening, then one also knows that it can indeed be pointed to, but can be conceived just as little as happening can, and one is in a position to avoid the errors that the concept of the always — briefly considered before and now to be considered once more — has occasioned. — Just as the appearance of lapse separates itself from the always of space, so does that which has in each case been separate itself from that which is in each case present, and thus, from space itself, the succession of the points of time, for which the schema of a line therefore inevitably results, as the extension of the ever-present space through all the moments that have ever been. With this we have made the leap from intuition-space to thing-space, and we establish — probably to the reader's astonishment — that objective time is merely one aspect of objective space! As governed by the thought of the always of space, time becomes spatialized time, more precisely the imperishability of the object of space.

[p. 313] With more justified astonishment, however, we might well ask why, for millennia, a state of affairs was overlooked (and could only be uncovered by logicians of mathematics of the last few decades) which we clothe in words every day, as often as we speak of a span of time, a stretch of time, the *length* or shortness of time, of a period and a duration of time, and thereby characterize the element of ceaseless flowing-by with turns of phrase that would be admirably in place for spatial distances. Nor, indeed, does anyone seem to doubt that time is a line, and everyone is even accustomed to take it for a straight line, though usually without knowing why. Meanwhile, the straightness is explained as follows. With regard to any two moments of the past, we can always ascertain only this: which seems to lie farther from us, which nearer — we thus see both separated by nothing but a distance; and then the series of all of them is extension absolutely, and thus straight extension.<sup>44</sup> That this straight line cannot be inscribed into sense-space (or can be so only figuratively) is self-evident; for it means nothing other than its unintuitable always reaching backward. Finally we uncover one of the reasons why it is a backward glance with which we sight the geometrically directionless line of the past. Without the aid of a mirror we see only the space situated before us; if this now is the present, then the past lies *behind* us.

<sup>44</sup> On page 313. — With merely mathematical means of thought, the definition of the straight line seems to encounter the greatest difficulties, if it is not indeed altogether impossible; from the standpoint of the science of consciousness these difficulties do *not* exist. There are, in fact, even two determinations of the straight line, which, more closely considered, admittedly come to the same thing: an immediate one and a mediate one, namely, by the specification of a defining property. The former runs: the straight line is direction as such; the latter: the straight line is distance as such. The latter is indirect, because it, strictly taken, expresses only that the straight line alone is fit to measure the distance of two points. The *former*, however, can also be reversed: direction as such is the straight line. In it lies at the same time the ground in right of the other. Only by keeping to the direction from A to B, or from B to A, can we ascertain the distance of the two points, whereas the slightest deviation from the direction would entail a measurement error; but the points do not belong to the meaning-content of the straight line. Antiquity had grasped the decisive marks more practically than theoretically, and perhaps it is partly on this account that modern mathematics no longer wishes to content itself with this. *Euclid* comes at least close to the truth with the proposition: "A straight line is a line all of whose parts lie in one and the same direction." *Archimedes*, in his book on the sphere, makes it easy for himself: "I assume and posit as known that, among all lines having the same endpoints, the straight line is the shortest." Eminent logicians have, however, repeatedly expatiated on both the definitions we have offered, none, it seems to us, more luminously than *Lotze*, in the excellent chapter "Deduction of Space" in his "Metaphysik" (Meiner 1922). We cite from it the sentences decisive for the definition, and take the liberty of letter-spacing what is essential for us. "As for direction, however, one soon notices that one deceives oneself if one believes one has a concept of it under which straightness and curvature could be subordinated as coordinate species: its concept is intelligible only *if it coincides entirely with that of* *the straight line*, which one calls, from another point of view, with reference to its endpoints, the distance of these; every representation of a curvature includes that of a deviation from the straight direction of the tangents . . One can therefore give *for* an extended line a criterion that guarantees its straightness: the distance of its endpoints *must* be the sum of the intervening distances of any two of the points one wishes to distinguish in it; but of course one does not thereby avoid the concept of the straight line in principle: both the distance of the endpoints and each of these intervening distances can only be thought under its image. It is therefore in fact not proper to say that the straight line is the shortest distance between two points; *it is* *rather precisely the distance itself* . ." (pp. 244–245). One does not trust one's eyes when one sees a mathematician like *Poincaré* come forward, by contrast, with the following definition of the straight line. "It may happen that the motion of an unchanging figure is such that all points of a line belonging to this figure remain immobile, while all points lying outside this line move. Such a line one will call a straight line." (Science and Hypothesis, translated by F. and L. Lindemann, Teubner, Leipzig 1914, p. 47.) That may be mathematically extremely acute, and touches, incidentally, on the definition of *Leibniz*, according to which the straight line is the line that remains immobile when one lets it rotate about two of its points, which are held fixed; but logically it is untenable. Lotze expresses himself on similar definitions (and perhaps with Leibniz in mind) *with* fine irony as follows: "Whoever should go so far as to designate the straight as that line which, on rotation between its endpoints, does not change its position, would plunge us into quiet reflection as to how he conceives the axis of this rotation, and by what, without anywhere presupposing the straight line, he would measure the change of position that the curved line would undergo under the same rotation" (p. 246). Probably one shuns, out of a preference for the a priori, the concept of direction, because it at once brings to bear the dependence of the whole of geometry on intuitive space; and indeed one not only can but must ask further after the essence of direction, on whose noogenesis we shall still have occasion to speak in the second volume. But for all that, the concept of direction is no less presupposed by the concept of the straight line. Without it the straight line would no longer be definable at all. If one wishes to circumscribe the state of affairs *intuitively*, one can also give the straight line the following further definition: the straight line is that line which can be sighted in such a way that its (hypothetical) starting point conceals the whole line. (The objection that might occur to a physicist — that this presupposes rectilinear propagation of light — would not hold water. It is true that it would actually be curved lines that we should take for straight lines under curvilinear propagation of light; but this would in no way affect the *criterion* of straightness. For the curved lines in question would, in their *optical appearance*, fall under the genus of straight lines, even though we should have to convince ourselves, by tactile perception, of their factual nonstraightness; just as, conversely, we convince ourselves of the unbrokenness of the straight rod set obliquely into water, without thereby being able to change in the least its optical brokenness. The *criterion* of straightness is the same, whether we seem to see straightness or to feel it by touch; and were it otherwise, we should know nothing of straightness. From this, however, it does not follow that in the visual experience the "direction as such" *necessarily* coincides with the "direction as such" in the experience of movement.)1)

Thanks to their participation in sense-space, all images of impression present a side that forces itself upon the reflection that succeeds them as unchangeable. If we let places already be found, there follows at once their unshiftability with respect to one another, and with it the possibility of founding a geometry, as well as the unavoidability of borrowing from the rigidity of space the material for all units of measure (weights, temperatures, quantities of heat, etc.) — not least of spatialized time! If we can indeed think everything as changing, but not the distance between two points of space, then there is expressed in this the unchangeability and timeremovedness of the space-thing; and if we even attribute the same unchangeability to a "stretch of time," then we have purchased the measurability of time at the price of its — de-temporalization.

We are now equipped for the distinction between thing-point and space-point. If place in space is motionless (as, again, is the point of time modeled on it), then movement requires a movable point, or: *place* is the *immovable*, *thing* the movable [p. 314] position in space. With the help of the concept of thing, then, the manifold of intuition-images related to it — which mean for us, e.g., a solid body — is replaced by a strictly mathematical point, which, however, in contrast to the points of geometry, demands to be thought of as moving, in that it ceaselessly crosses other places, and thereby, just as ceaselessly, other positions of time.<sup>45</sup> There are mathematicians and physicists who believe the self-contradictions of the mechanistic view of the world to be removed by the "relativization" of all movements — already sketched out by Newton, but which has recently attained popular fame — according to which the movement of the thing-point A can be determined only with regard to the thing-point B. If A and B approach one another, then, in their opinion, two assumptions would be equally justified: A is at rest and B moves toward A; or B is at rest and A moves toward B. The logician would, to be sure, immediately point out that the law of identity of thinking would thereby be abolished, because it would now be asserted of point A, and equally of point B, with a claim to validity, that it is simultaneously both at rest and in motion. Whoever, on the other hand, has practiced thinking merely mathematically but unfortunately not logically will indeed inevitably succumb to the fiction in question, unless he has given himself an account of the fact that the concept of movement, besides the movable thing-point, requires the immovable space-point — notwithstanding that the definition planted at the entrance to the theory of movement, that movement is continuous change of place, could have convinced him of the impossibility of forming the concept of movement without the concomitant assumption of immovable places! Just as surely as there would be no movement without the movable thing, just as surely is there none without the immovable place.

<sup>45</sup> On page 314. — The thing-point thus represents *metaphysically* the thing in exactly the same way as its center of mass does *mechanically*. Herein lies the ground, from the standpoint of the science of consciousness, why every consideration of the world proceeding from the *thing* must terminate in mass-points.

Accordingly we find in the universe no possible thing of which it could be maintained that it rests not merely "relatively" but "absolutely" — wherefore the concept of movement could not be won from the concept of thing alone. Whoever forbids himself a glance at the immovable space-point will therefore catch only an illusory image of the movable, and will henceforth believe it left to the arbitrary choice of the calculator whether he finds it good to exchange the moving for the resting, or the resting for the moving. As much, then, as the complete dissolution of thinking stands at the door in this way, even this most brazen attempt at de-actualizing the world offers, once again, only an example of false reification — namely, the reification of the space-point (as likewise also of the time-point) through its [p. 315] being made movable; whereby, to be sure, the Kantian subjectivization of space would be disposed of, but only in favor of its futuristic dissolution.<sup>46</sup>
