Could we look on at a stream of experience from outside, and read off the successive moments of experience much as, in a material stream, stretch by stretch, we should perceive: the character of experience B is determined by the preceding experience A, that of experience C by the preceding A and B, that of experience D by the preceding A and B and C; in short, that of each by the whole series of those that preceded it. Life on the one side, the images on the other, would be caught not only in restless flight but also in ceaseless transformation, and there would never come about a presence. It is not the streaming but its wave-beat or pulsing that makes the impression possible, and it makes it possible by having, on occasion of the turning-points, a mirroring of the original images insert itself each time into the stream of beholding — images that have occurred between one boundary-experience and the next. Were we to remain with the ever-merely-happening experiencing of the soul, then every life-moment would hang together with an image, each following one, as developing out of the previous one, with an image different on that account, none with anything even merely seemingly abiding. If, by contrast, we add in the turning-points, then each of them, too, would indeed hang together with the fore-moments of an experiencing that glided on, through the zero-point of motion, without measurable standstill; but besides this also with the images of all the fore-moments since the previous turning-point, because it "mirrors" them all, as we called it. The "present impression" thus designated coincides with unconscious recollection. If we now replace the simileword "mirroring" by the ground of all mirrorability that we have set forth, namely making-present, then we stand before the formula — certainly no longer incomprehensible-seeming — that the relative pausing at the "sensing" turning-point enables the soul to make present, in the momentary impression, the fleeting images of its own motion. But we must go one step further, [p. 346] to find out where, within the life-process itself, lie the conditions for "unconscious recollection" to become consciousness of having-been-past. — If even at the turning-point the beholding motion does not measurably linger, then the moment of making-present, too, must hang together with original images, and its hanging-together with already-past images would accordingly appear in the light of a connectedness of these with the image assigned to *it*. But then it should be possible to ascertain, in the impression-content, a property from which it would follow compellingly that it rests twofold on a coupling of images: that, not capable of consciousness, between turning-point and turning-point in the intuitive image, and further that of the intuitive image with the original image during the moment of the mirroring turn. Leaving the twofoldness aside for the present, it would in any case have to be shown that any impression whatever is a connectedness of images. That is the gap which we promised above to make recognizable and to fill.

If someone unselfconsciously regards an object and its mirror image, he judges the appearances of both to be completely identical (notwithstanding that in the mirror image right and left are, as is well known, interchanged). How, by contrast, must we more closely determine the relation of the fleeting images of the primal space to the ever-present impression-image of sense-space, since equality by no means prevails here in any case? Our answer runs: both are connected by force of *elementary similarity* — The "apperception psychologist" will at once object that similarity is a "subjective relation," produced, like plurality, difference, number, and so on, through the "thinking-together" of objects in the "comparing consciousness." We reply: that indeed holds for the judged similarity of two things, but not for the elementary similarity, without the presupposition of which we should know nothing whatever of things. Things are self-identical compendia of properties. But how could we ever have managed to find a compendium of properties in the stream of happening, had the similarity of at least two images not been experienced by us! — As against the view, happily now on the wane, that similarity is diminished equality, one would have to point to the fact that we assert equality times without number where similarities are wholly absent, and search for equalities times without number on the occasion of a similarity already ascertained. Every arithmetical equation sensuously represents, in keeping with its name, the equality of its two sides, which yet commonly have [p. 347] not the slightest similarity to one another; and the kilogram weight on the left pan of the scale is no more similar to the apples of equal weight on the right. Who, conversely, has not often met with the experience that the first glance at a hitherto unknown person assured him of that person's similarity to someone he knew, without his at once making out whom she actually resembled and by which traits, accordingly, the two persons would have to be compared with one another! He thus already has the experience of similarity without yet having together the objects to which it might be referred.

The judgement of equality touched on here reminds us of the dependence of the concept of equality upon the concept of sameness. The assertion that two times two equals four represents sameness of numerical magnitude on both sides, given a different distribution of the elements composing it; and the assertion that on the right pan of the scale lies a kilogram of apples represents sameness of the mass-quantity of the apples with the mass-quantity of the solid metal cylinder on the other pan, given otherwise arbitrarily great differences of colour, shape, and material properties. But if equality is thus always sameness *of some* determining constituents, then the judgement of equality is rooted in the judgement of sameness and receives its measure from it. Now when Nietzsche, with the cunning sentence, "Logic is bound to the condition: supposing there are identical cases," wished to prompt reflection on the fact that identical cases simply cannot occur in the world of appearance, that skeptical ulterior motive should not keep us from once more raising the question anew — now, however, with regard to the necessary specific differences among the contents of an experiencing that flows uninterruptedly — as to what could bring it about that we nonetheless feel ourselves capable of continually applying judgements of sameness to the actual.

Let the prelude to the disclosure of a most important precondition be formed by the utterance of *Kant*'s, already cited earlier in a note: "Were cinnabar now red, now blue, now light, now heavy, were a man changed now into this, now into that animal shape, were the land, on the longest day, covered now with fruits, now with ice and snow, then my empirical imagination could not even find occasion, in the representation of the colour red, to bring heavy cinnabar to mind . ." Had Kant, instead of merely uttering it, thought this sentence further through, the insight [p. 348] would probably have fallen to him too that not only things but even their properties of blueness, redness, heaviness, and so forth could not become known at all to a being that experienced nothing but the fleetingness of appearance, and he would then at least have had to ask what other property of experiencing, besides the very lack of persistence which he himself indeed granted to "inner sense," makes possible the formation of concepts of properties. To bring the state of affairs palpably home to us, let us weigh for a moment the instructive psychology of the *spot*. — If the one and only glance with which we perceive a patterned or plain-coloured tablecloth permits us to notice the ink-spot upon it, then it must already have been decided, with that same glance, that the spot cannot be reconciled with any rule of distribution of the cloth's coloured appearance. The same naturally holds of every hole or tear. But how can the rule of distribution of its surface colours also come to be known together with the perception of the cloth? Were every empirical point of sense-space simply colour-different from every other, then a spot would nowhere be found any longer. If, conversely, even the empirical point can actually take on the meaning of a spot, then within the arbitrarily small patch of surface surrounding it, the *similarity* of its subparts must have been co-apprehended. A colour impression, however small it might be, would not come about at all without co-experienced similarities; for the coloured point is what it is only by standing out against the differently coloured surface, and that surface, in turn, is by no means to be composed of points. If a testing glance wanders, from close range, place to place over the uniform grey of a flatly spread cloth of one square metre in extent, the associated impressions are not point-impressions but shape-impressions, and consequently all different from one another. If they nevertheless all combine into the image of uniform colour, it happens out of similarity, and that similarity must accordingly already have been experienced with regard to the parts of every surface-shape that was referred to any one fixation point. But what holds in this way of the colour impression holds of every impression whatever, so that we must extend the above proposition into the "law," undisclosed to this day: every *sense impression whatever* presupposes the *beholding of the* simi- *larity* of *images*. We judge a line, a surface, a volume to be something continuous insofar as every smallest possible section of it seems to us to *continue* into its neighbour, and this requires a [p. 349] similarity of unconsciously beheld images. But should one find the name "image," in the sense of the original image, ill-suited to designate co-experienced similarities of experienced moments of happening, one should note that this in no way characterizes the happening as such, still less the content of the happening, but solely its capacity, under determinate conditions, to enter into appearance.<sup>51</sup>

<sup>51</sup> On page 349. — From this there follows, convincingly for anyone open to rational grounds, the utter untenability of the assumption that continuity in particular forms no content of *intuition*. Taken literally, this would include the impossible assertion that the object of perception is mathematical points. By restricting the claim to empirical points one would in principle already have abandoned the theory, since the empirical point is a surface and thus, within its bounds, something continuous. But even if we were unwilling to give weight to that, there would still have to be something from which the empirical point stood out and by which it was distinguished from a second point; and that would be the continuity of an intervening space. If one wished finally to save the theory by appealing to the experience of direction in the process of perception, and to explain the between-the-points from an experience of change of direction, one would at best have offered a contribution to the *genesis* of the perception of continuity, but would not have hit upon the perception of continuity itself, which remains an intuitive state of affairs, whatever apparatus we may deem necessary in order to render the receptivity for it intelligible. Moreover, one would have overlooked that *perceptual* processes are experiences of direction only insofar as, together with the object of perception, *some* distance of it from the bearer of perception is co-perceived; and this distance is in turn something continuous, regardless of whether we are thinking of perceptions mediated visually or tactilely, and again regardless of whether we trace visual depth-perception back to experiences of movement or not. Whoever strikes the moment of continuity from the content of intuition has struck out the content of intuition itself.

But to the space-pole of world-appearance there belongs the time-pole, and to the experienced side-by-side there belongs an at least co-experienced succession. This shows itself more clearly through a glance at the time-pole itself. Were every empirical now simply different from every other, we should experience no temporal continuity and would consequently have neither the concept of duration nor that of the instant, which, as we have learned, enters into appearance only by standing out against duration. The impression of the instant presupposes the experience of a course, since otherwise it could not enter as a link or section into the succession of instants, and the experience of a course is grounded in a co-experienced similarity of images situated apart from one another in time. — Through the demonstration of the flowing-together of spatiotemporal images in the intuitive image, the pulsing of experiencing is for the first time secured, and "vital mirroring," without recourse to simile, is recognized as consisting in this: that from every life-wave that has just now reached its end, at the turning-point, the images belonging to it are united thanks to their similarities, which only now first come into effect. — In that ill-starred sensualism, in complete unacquaintance with the process of beholding, pretended to derive the impression from sense-data specifically disparate and separated from one another in time, it first tore the impression out of space and time, second barred, by an insulating layer, the way from each datum to each, and has consequently exhausted itself for some centuries in the hopeless endeavour of gluing back together what it had itself fundamentally dismembered — not, indeed, into the intuitive images actually given in actuality, but at least into localized and property-bearing things, which, once reflection has been accomplished, are taken to represent them. It did not consider that things, like properties, require judgements of sameness as already accomplished, and that judgements of sameness could not be pronounced at all upon separately experienced, unspatial and untemporal sense-data!

[p. 350] The proposition, probably striking many readers as difficult, that experienced presentness forms the cross-section of experienced having-been, we can accordingly exchange for the one intelligible without comment: that in the experience of presentness there lies, by virtue of its similarity with the course of experiencing, a temporal sequence, as co-experienced. But let us at once add why, beyond that, even the emphasis on *fleetingness* can attach to it, in accordance with the participation of the images, *occurring* as demanded above in the second place, in the "representing" intuitive image as well. When we set forth in Chapter 3 that the now is originally apprehended as the instant of ending or beginning ("now it comes, now it is gone," and so on), and later found occasion to mention that it is the ever-presentness of space which makes the concept of the now possible while at the same time concealing its origin, we have now ascertained a most important partial cause of this. Insofar as the intuitive image is the utterly present mirroring of happening that itself has no present, it contains the condition for the separation of the persisting sense-space from the never-persisting time; but since, moreover, moments of happening attach to *every* content of experience, there dwells, in relation to the ever-presence of sense-space, in the impression of presentness too a tension and the *readiness* to glide off in the "direction" of happening and thus into the past, and it is this above all that lends its presentness the high accent of the now. — According as, within the impression of presentness, the experience of existence or that of fleetingness predominates, differences of character emerge in the intuitive image that entail far other differences of interpretations of actuality than those arising from the rivalry of the tendency to embodiment with the tendency to making-present. Measured against the thoroughly static bearing of Greek philosophizing (of which modern dynamism is merely a side-branch, which will occupy us later), the absence of the auxiliary verb "to be" among almost all primitive peoples, besides folk-song and myth, testifies above all to the event-character of the actuality of early human thinking. Here, however, we turn our attention to something else.

Although, according to our account, the impression of presentness includes the experience of time within itself, it might still be asked, in view of the "line" of time as an object of thought, why a not-present thing that has actually taken place necessarily appears to us in the light of having-been and not equally, on occasion, in that of the still-coming, seeing that thanks to our wishing and hoping we find ourselves referred to the future of [p. 351] time just as much. In other words, what compels us to place the "remembered" state of affairs into an instant now *no longer* present, and normally never into an instant *not yet* present? Answer: because, in accordance with the "potential direction of movement" of the present impression as well, we are unable to reverse the "direction of time." From this it follows, among other things, that makings-present are originally *always* makings-present of a (supposedly) having-been (the fabulous constructs of cults and myths are so too!), and that other means of thought are still needed to clarify the making-present, only subsequently added, of a (supposedly) future thing. — Now that it should be sufficiently established that in the impression of presentness, by virtue of elementary similarity, a manifold of images unintuitable in and for themselves comes to intuition, and indeed in a twofold manner, let us examine what such insight can contribute to the doctrine of the process of recollection.

So far we have spoken solely of the mirroring of images that have happened, and have recognized in it the ground that makes perceptual space possible as well as an indispensable source of the experience of time. But if the (mirroring) turning-point of experiencing is connected with happening, then, precisely by that very fact, it is connected also with the intuitive image of the previous turning-point, of which the same holds with regard to its being the forerunner of the next, and so on without end; and if it is elementary similarity that catches the images in the mirror of the intuitive image, then it will also be elementary similarity that stretches connecting threads between the intuitive images. That intuitive images cannot combine with one another in the same way as *original* images do within the intuitive image needs no saying; for each of them already possesses the character of presence which the images within the intuitive image only first attain! A further glance back at the simile of mirroring leads us first of all to the separation of two basic possibilities of the association of intuitive images.

Just as the mirror is able to mirror not only the object but also mirror images, so too the moment of impression may be able to mirror earlier intuitive images. If what is mirrored is a mirror image, then the mirror itself is mirrored as well. Let us now suppose that we noticed *only* the mirror image, and not that it was the mirroring of a mirror image; to this there would correspond a bygone content of impression, akin to the present impression through elementary similarity, which, to distinguish it [p. 352] from the latter, is called a *phantasm*. If, on the other hand, we were to notice the mirror as well, there would correspond to this the same intuitive image, but bound up with the *consciousness* of its having-been, and only such a one deserves the name *recollection-image*. We should thus have the following basic possibilities: the present impression, by force of elementary similarity, "awakens" a recollection-image, and the present impression, for the same reason, "calls forth" a phantasm. For the present we remain with the phantasm.

If every impression has the character of presentness, and if simultaneously with it a making-present of an earlier impression takes place, then, however great the kinship of essence between the two intuitive images, there exists a conflict which we may most briefly define as a struggle for space, or a struggle of spaces. If the phantasm is victorious, the dream-space takes the place of perceptual space, and the recipient of impressions finds himself no longer referred to the impression but to phantasms: a state that interrupts, off and on, the wakefulness of all human beings without exception during waking life — in one person rarely, and each time only for fractions of a second, in another frequently, and each time for longer. "Man of action" and "dreamer" thus come to stand opposed to one another. — If, conversely, the phantasm must yield, then the impression, from the conflict victoriously resolved, gains a new note in addition, which, given sufficient strength, is called the "knownness" or "familiarity" of the impression and, as remarked earlier, with growing intensification withdraws the content of the impression more and more from consciousness. But before the efficacy of the phantasm dwindles to a mere tinge of knownness in the impression, it asserts itself more clearly in the experience of original *recognition*. Let us dwell a moment on recognizing, because it belongs to those kinds of experience whose excessive familiarity makes it extraordinarily hard for us to notice their wonderful and enigmatic character at all.

Although most investigators have probably seen this rightly, it cannot be repeated often enough: recognitions not only need not go together with recollections, but originally, and above all in animals, never do so. When the dying dog of Odysseus, after twenty years, attests by a feeble wagging of the tail that he recognized his returned master, this by no means signifies that he remembered the experiences of his earliest youth, but signifies, [p. 353] to put it first of all in the closest possible accommodation to present-day ways of thinking, that through the scent received he fell into a state of excitement resembling those states which he experienced at that time, when he was still together with his master. This, however, does not suffice to explain the recognition that undoubtedly takes place. For, apart from the fact that we should know nothing whatever of similarities of inner states without their connection with images similar in essence, the mere linkage of experiences would also found only habits of behaviour and by no means yet recognitions. Even in the plant there exist experiential connections, both of its parts with one another and of the whole plant with its earlier states as well as with the states of its line of ancestors; in consequence of which it begins, according to the season, now to sprout and now to wither, even when it has been transplanted to the other hemisphere of the earth, where its germination and flowering now fall in the winter season. Recognitions, however, require the mirrorability of the contents of experience, and thus the impression-experience proper only to animal being.

In connection with the dog of Odysseus, let us point here already to the fundamentally different process by which the old nurse Eurykleia recognizes the hero. Although she has already remarked that of all the strangers who had called in the course of the years, none resembled Odysseus so much in voice, form and feet as this one, she is not remotely led thereby to take him for Odysseus himself, until, on the occasion of a foot-washing, she recognizes the scar on his leg which the youth once carried away, hunting, from a boar. Her feat of recognition differs from the dog's feat of recognition by two main features, of which the one separates human recognition from animal recognition only as a rule, while the other separates them without exception. The mark, to be discovered with the aid of the sense of touch or of the sense of sight, by which she recognizes the hero is, namely, characteristically a mark of shape, whereas animal recognition takes place through scent, at least here and in the majority of cases. But to this there is now added the fundamentally distinguishing feature, that on the occasion of the recognized peculiarity of shape the spiritual act of the *identification* of its bearer takes place, which thus precedes the recognition of him! To appreciate the full significance of this, let us bear in mind that identity is also ascertained without the process of recognition. Countless times the human being, and he alone, accomplishes the act of equating [p. 354] in the face of a duality of objects, without any possibility of recognizing what is one and the same in both. Whoever, armed with the equipment of scientific handwriting analysis, identifies an outstandingly disguised hand with the natural handwriting of the suspect, or by means of dactyloscopic and anthropometric measurements identifies the prisoner with a known criminal, or by chemical analysis identifies the blood of a stain with human blood, has gained knowledge of the sameness of the fact in question with a known fact, without, however, recognizing the one in the other. Animals recognize, but they do not identify.

Now that we have made sure that recognition may be confused neither with the recollection of a state of affairs nor with the equating of two states of affairs, the question would naturally suggest itself: what, then, is recognition actually? Or: by which properties does a recognized state of affairs differ from a new one? To this, however, we should at first find no answer, however thoroughly we might reflect back upon an experience of recognizing. Every attempt in particular to characterize mechanistically the modifications which the occasion of an impression undergoes through being recognized — for instance with the quite erroneous talk of an intensification of the impression — is doomed to failure, as in principle are all attempts to resolve properties of essence into properties of things. We shall be right if we say that, in relation to the first impression, the recognized impression has a new character; but we shall be able to make the particular character hovering before us here intelligible only to a being that knows how to experience recognitions and to reflect upon the experience of recognizing. Let us instead go back to the *condition* of recognition just discussed; but we must not dismiss it without a more precise determination of its content and without having at least to some extent weighed its scope and its consequences.

Because original images have not yet fallen prey to "independence," they "constitute," so to speak, the intuitive image, and because intuitive images, by virtue of their presentness, have won a kind of vital existence or sensuous being-there, being lost in the stream of experiencing is henceforth denied to them. But precisely thereby possibilities of effect upon other moments of being-there have fallen to their share. If the phantasm, to which a recognition is owed, does not remain [p. 355] self-present, it can, by induction, alter the meaning of the intuitive image, and it is such an alteration of meaning that transforms the intuitive image into a recognized intuitive image. Before we draw further conclusions from the peculiarity of character which the intuitive image thereby acquires, let us ask in passing wherein, for recognition, the guarantee of its correctness lies.

The whole science of the soul scarcely shows a second question of such confusing and difficult problematic character. The person untrained in such considerations, to be sure, believes he has heard something quite superfluous, and already has the answer ready: recognition is correct when the present occasion of impression is the same as the bygone occasion of impression. But in the world of experiencing and of appearances there are no identities, and neither are any two impressions ever identical with one another, nor does an (experienced) occasion of impression ever recur identically. The dog of Odysseus recognized Odysseus, although the Odysseus aged by twenty years was by no means the same, appearance-wise, as the Odysseus of former days! Only when, in later parts of our work, we uncover the decisive reason that occasions spirit to apply the act of equating to actuality (Volume III), shall we encounter in it, at the same time, an aid to recognition still veiled for the present. But in principle no standard whatever can be derived from the mere feat of recognition to determine whether it has hit upon what is "correct" or not! The experience of similarity by which it is borne occurs beneath the region of data capable of becoming conscious as individual items, and the similarity of life-processes undoubtedly corresponding to it cannot be graded by degrees in such a way that a determinate and verifiable degree would guarantee the correctness of the recognition. If recognition leads back to a similarity of origination (= sameness of kind of origination) between the impression and the phantasm that alters its meaning, then we cannot borrow from the process of recognition the means of cognition that would exclude the possibility of mistakes. Thereby these lose much of the oddity that seems to attach to them each time we make use of the thought-objective equality and sameness in order to assess the feat of recognition.

So-called false recognition, far more correctly called the phenomenon of déjà vu, is, strictly speaking, a delusion of memory, which [p. 356], however, is commonly preceded, at least for a moment, by an experience of recognition. Example: on a walk through regions never before entered, one catches sight of a house which one believes one ⦅knows⦆ down to the most exact details, only immediately thereafter, straining one's power of recollection, to ponder where one has actually already seen this garden gate, these two poplars, this greenpainted vaulted door, and so on. Here too the impression has conjured up a phantasm similar in origination, which lent it the character of knownness, and which then, admittedly, out of the incredibility of the alteration of meaning of the intuitive image, became independent and exchanged it for the character of a recollection-image, which, measured against the store of experience of its bearer, again appears astonishing. Conversely and similarly, in the case of so-called estrangement from the world of perception, everything is correctly recognized, while hidden phantasms clothe the well-known with the semblance of strangeness. If one goes somewhat deeply into examples of this kind, one will no longer fail to recognize that it is not so much "false" recognition as precisely "correct" recognition that stands in need of explanation, and that it cannot at all be comprehended from the state of affairs of the vital association of intuitive images alone.

If recognition, with regard to something recognized, repeats itself often enough, the recognized thing takes on the character of familiarity; and this now underlies the units of meaning of both originally human and animal sensibility. — The capacity for comparing, which, as will later appear, is quite unintelligible from consciousness, is rooted in the fact that the starting-material of all comparing, namely the content of the impression, is already the consequent appearance of life-processes, which we must apprehend ⦅by⦆ analogy with comparing. Because every impression whatever — for instance of a silence, of a cold, or also of what, by reifying it, we call a flame — has, as it were, drawn the sum out of images continuously passing into one another according to the measure of their elementary similarity, and because the finished intuitive images again enter into relations of effect out of elementary similarity, the new impression accordingly behaves toward the ever-bygone one as something either similar or dissimilar to it, either continuing it or interrupting it. Just as, thanks to elementary similarity, it can seem as though impressions persisted or repeated themselves, so too, thanks to their dissimilarity, as though they disturbed one another. Now that we were earlier able to establish, with numerous [p. 357] examples, that every intuitive image originally has the meaning of the expression of a living stirring, we may designate the operative power of elementary similarity by the word "kinship of essence," and accordingly have to posit, for the crystallizations that accomplish themselves preconsciously, the most general determining ground — as it were empedoclean — in inclination and conflict. Since it is decisively important that one recognize the efficacy of this distributive motive already within the domain of unreflected impulses, let us illustrate it by an animal trait of all sensuous life-processes.

These are impressions from the great class of the inner-bodily, in consequence of which we judge: I am hungry. Being hungry offers a convincing example of the fact that the persistence of an impression is by no means always accompanied by its dulling, but sometimes also by a temporary intensification, and it makes exceedingly vivid to us the co-experiencedness of phases of impression. Now, in a manner not to be traced more closely here, the impulse to search for food develops out of the impression of hunger. But once the food has been found and sufficiently incorporated, no one, presumably, would doubt that even the animal must experience the immediately following impression of satiety in the sense of its opposition to the impression of hunger. To the experience of hunger there thus belongs a peculiar tension, which strives, through the intermediate link of instinctive movements, to carry it over into the impression, opposite to it, of satiety. Thereupon, however, occasions of impression that promise the stilling of hunger will likewise come to stand in opposition to those that promise nothing of the kind, and we see the similarity that helped us to the concept of the edible, or of food, vitally grounded in the co-experience of an oppositeness, in consequence of which, among other things, certain occasions of impression stand out, by virtue as it were of the lustre of a particular allurement, against those lacking a lustre of this kind. In like manner, the thirst-quenching — or, as we may now perhaps say, the liquid, moist and soft — stands vitally opposed to the dry-hard, the habitable to the unhabitable, and, with the force of unmistakable conflict, the life-protecting fully opposed to the life-threatening. All these are pre-conceptual units of meaning which demonstrate irrefutably that in the experience of an impression the experience of similarities and oppositions lies ⦅within it⦆. And what holds of these impressions, which we called animal for easily evident reasons, necessarily holds [p. 358] of all impressions, however hard it may sometimes be to bring their stimulus-value to consciousness. But as surely as such experiencing manifests itself inwardly through inclination and aversion, outwardly through seeking and fleeing, so surely is it exciting or indifferent, friendly or hostile ⦅beings⦆ that originally lend the intuitive images their meaning and compel them to act upon one another according to kinship and conflict.

After these remarks, running not inconsiderably ahead of ourselves, on the extraordinary scope of the ⦅effects⦆ of elementary similarities, let us turn once more back to the duality of recollection-image and phantasm. If the intuitive image is victorious over the phantasm, then perceptual space is victorious over dream-space as well; but if the phantasm is victorious over the intuitive image, then dream-space is victorious over perceptual space, with which there normally goes a removal of the recipient of impressions into the latter. In somewhat other words: the content of the impression asserts itself insofar as, vis-à-vis the phantasm, it possesses the greater power of appropriating ⦅space⦆, and conversely likewise. But it is, as we know, sense-space = presence of bodies, dream-space = presence of mere appearances. Now if, as has been shown, the ratio of strength between readiness for embodiment and readiness for making-present fluctuates according to races, peoples, persons, and if we suppose the case that readiness for making-present comes more and more to predominate, then the corporeality of the intuitive images would dwindle to the same degree, from which a possible consequence would be that phantasms would penetrate into sense-space and mix with objects of perception. With this we should have uncovered the ⦅proximate⦆ cause of all formations of semblance, deceptive perceptions, hallucinations, and should at the same time find occasion to test our assumption of a, so to speak, racial predominance of readiness for making-present in East Asian man. For verification it suffices to reproduce a few typical painter-legends of former China.

"Thus it is told of Han Kan, China's most famous painter of horses: In the year 780 a man leading a horse by the bridle inquired after a veterinarian. This man looked the animal over and cried out laughing: Why, this looks like one of Han Kan's horses — real horses never look like that! Han Kan happened to come by and said with astonishment: Yes, this horse I have indeed painted. You know: whatever we create up here [p. 359] is at once copied in the world down there. Then he stroked the horse and found that it was limping from an injury to its forefoot, and discovered to his surprise, at home, that the horse in his own picture had a small blemish at precisely that spot. Thus he learned how pictures put us in connection with the spirit-world... Of the landscape painter Li Ssu-hsün we hear that he painted a fish, but the wind blew the silk into a pond, whereupon the fish swam away alive... Finally the legend of the magical end of Wu Tao-tzu leads us into the landscape itself: before the eyes of the emperor he vanishes into the opened cave of the great landscape which he had previously painted on a wall of the palace: behind him the rock closes, and before the ruler can take a single step, the whole painting has vanished and the wall is white as before. But the master was never seen again by any man."<sup>52</sup>

<sup>52</sup> On page 359. — From: *Otto Fischer*, Chinesische Landschaftsmalerei, Kurt Wolff Verlag, Munich 1921, pp. 145–146.

Whichever example we might pick out from the overabundant multiplicity of similar legends, they are all, without exception, mere variant forms of the one and only theme, that to what is represented in painting or drawing — in short, to the image — there belongs the same actuality as to the depicted ⦅body⦆! And the Chinese fairy tale makes use of the same motif many times over. If we now think of a Western master of so powerful an imagination as Böcklin, to whom certainly nothing of the kind, let alone a hallucination, ever happened, one could scarcely withhold assent from the following propositions:

1. Strength of imagination (= gift for waking dream) testifies — apart from the ⦅fullness⦆ of inwardness thereby posited — to a considerable power of appropriation on the part of phantasms (= readiness of dream-space to arise easily).

2. The ease of arising of illusory images (namely within perceptual space — thus = the faculty of illusory perception), which is to be strictly distinguished from the foregoing, rests upon a relative predominance of the faculty of making-present over the faculty of embodiment, speaks therefore neither for nor against the power of appropriation of phantasms, and can accordingly go together with a great imagination as well as with the most meagre one.

3. Illusory perceptions are, from the standpoint of the science of life, ambiguous, in that they arise now from the strength of the gift of intuition (as is doubtless the case among the Chinese), now from a shrinking and disturbance of the faculty of sensation. (The ⦅deeper⦆ cause, above all of the illusory perception to be interpreted negatively, [p. 360] will be treated only in Volume II of our work.)

Before we now turn briefly to the conditions under which the conjured-up phantasm takes on the fundamentally new form of the recollection-image, let us cast a sidelong glance at the exceedingly many-membered group of the most original of all ⦅recognitions⦆, which, in view of their inescapable connection with animal ⦅drives⦆, are still today, in accordance with older usage, sometimes called "instincts" (properly = incitements). The word "to recognize" is here taken by us in its earlier sense, which it still preserves today when we say: he recognized the beauty by her earrings. The recognitions belonging here occur thanks to the bodily efficacy of original beholding, which — being impressionless and unconscious as it is — is not interrupted by deep sleep, and therefore permits the germ-plasmic transmission of the disposition to beholding, and in this way links the succession of generations by a demonstrable form of experiencing. If, then, the young chick pecks at grains without having learned their edibility, if the bird builds the nest for a brood not yet in existence at all, if the males "instinctively" find the females at mating time, and if many animals from the outset avoid at least some of their enemies as well as numerous dangers which they have never encountered, then in every such case there are indeed recognitions present, but not recognitions arising from bygone impressions.

If one calls the substrate of all the experiential traces hereby indicated "memory," then one must set up within it essentially new dispositions, both to mark off the gift of dreaming and also the faculty of recollection from the gift of instinctive recognizing. Since everyday speech makes no distinction between memory and the faculty of recollection, there have been investigators who wished to explain even "instinctive" recognitions too from a memory-gift of living matter. At about the same time that ⦅Hering⦆ gave his engaging, yet more captivating than penetrating, lecture "On Memory as a General Function of Organized Matter" (1876), the poet ⦅Wilhelm Jordan⦆ announced something similar, more profoundly, in his "Andachten," which appeared in 1877 and which, despite their unrewarding Darwinism and not a few views now outlived, deserve in their entirety to be set beside the didactic poem of ⦅Lucretius⦆. Given the extraordinary obscurity that a Jordan enjoys today, we consider it fitting to bring an extract from the verse-chapter headed "Erinnerung" [Recollection]. After the poet has set forth that [p. 361] perhaps no particle of matter of the whole earth is to be found that has not already, on other planets, ages ago, lived along in organized combinations of matter, he continues: What was it, then, that once in tepid wave / Won for matter the form of the first cell? / Recollection of an earlier shaping / And power of wishing toward a like unfolding. / "Fantast!" so you cry, dear reader, and take fright — / And yet it is no fairy tale! Wherever you look / You will find the enchantress Recollection; / Recognize her — and a thousand riddles vanish. / She bears art, the cunning of the fight, unweakened, / As a bridge from generation to generation. / Recognize her and cast the foolish word / Instinct, as empty, out of our language. / It is recollection of its own cradle / When the red spike-fly, sensing grains of sand — / As soon as it feels its egg has ripened and quickened — / Glues into a pointed vault for its brood. / It is recollection of its own fodder / At larval time, when the anxious mother / Drags the caterpillar astride over long stretches / And lays her egg, locking it into that dungeon. / The stag-beetle's larva feels and knows, / Recollecting, the length of the antlers beforehand, / And chisels for itself in the old oak tree / Already twice as wide the space for its transformation. / What teaches the huntress of the air to weave / Her net by set-square and delicate law, / And with feeler-threads for angling / To hang it, from branch to branch, at her chosen seat? / No — more lightly still she takes up her mother's [p. 362] duty: / The brood creeps out, cast off, untended, / From the sac into which the eggs were laid; / Yet, three, four days later, the young spiderling / Already spans, just as deftly, / With its small net the fronds of a fern, / And yet has never seen its mother's fly-snare. / The caterpillar has no eye to behold / How others knit their silken coffins / For their rising again. Whence, in all these spinners, / Comes the fine art? Solely from ancestral memory. / Only because in man what he learned in his lifetime / Puts the ancestors' harvest of labour into shadow / Does he fail to recognize, foolish from a pupil's presumption, / How rich he too is in the store of ancestral memory. / Recollection of what, a thousand times before, / Was done in like manner by the whole choir of ancestors, / Teaches, skilfully, though still blind, / The newborn child already how to be milked. / It is recollection by which, in the mother's womb, / You yourself, O man, are first enabled / To fly through, in months, all the destinies of existence / That your forebears once slowly climbed. / To the oftattained goal, by the accustomed path, / Leads ancestral memory, not dull compulsion. / What is most secret it makes plain and manifest, / Admirable, what was thought a mere wonder. / Nature gives nothing free. To win strength in struggle / And the right of victory, to bequeath it onward, / Is her commandment, her means to the legacy / Of the hard-won art that is the memory of bodily matter. The remarkable [p. 363] and highly significant didactic poem goes still further in its speculative boldness, and undertakes to derive all the poetizing and striving of humanity, insofar as it seems to grow together into the goal-directed impulse of an overall development, from the unconscious recollection of a perfection formerly already attained on a more perfect star. We, however, end here with the remark that the two closing words of the verse last cited by us also designate the intended state of affairs in a scientifically unimpeachable manner; whereas the word "recollection" ought to be used only for conscious remembering, of which, naturally, there can be no question in any of the cases that Jordan adduces. While "the memory of bodily matter" forms the rightly conceived disposition which we must add in thought to the experience of beholdings whenever our statements refer to living substance, phantasms as well as recognitions rest upon the special dispositions of a living substance that is not merely receptive to images but also capable of impressions. Now that we bring their efficacy to bear upon the experience of recollection, we must for a moment leave the ground of pure vitality in order to set foot instead upon the ground of spirit-coupled vitality. For the experience of recollection occurs exclusively in such a recipient of impressions as accomplishes acts of reflection, but never in the unspirited recipient of impressions.

The animals have an astonishing memory, on the strength of which they recognize what has long passed and also dream of what has long passed; but they remember nothing! In<sup>53</sup> order for me to apprehend a phantasm as a recollection-image, I must take my momentary consciousness to be the same consciousness that earlier underwent the impression of which I now have available only a phantasm; or, to turn once more to the simile, I must notice in the mirror of the impression not merely the earlier content of impression but at the same time the mirror in which it was caught, and consequently, as mirrored together with it, the — now, to be sure, temporal — distance, which, incidentally, suffers all the more perspectival foreshortening, exactly like the distance of real mirror-images, the further the pastness of the experience grows. Recollection presupposes the consciousness of the self identical with itself, and every remembering is in fact, as German usage indicates, a remembering ⦅of oneself⦆. In view of this there are also partial conditions of involuntary remembering, which become fully comprehensible only from the foundations of voluntary remembering, not yet to be discussed here [p. 364] (Volume II). If we turn, with this restriction, to involuntary remembering, we naturally have to seek its precondition likewise in the conflict between the impression and the phantasm of the impression, or, more briefly, in the conflict of spaces. We have learned: the space of the impression retains the preponderance = recognized impression. The dream-space attains the preponderance = phantasm. In both cases the bearer of life is connected with an image, and the consciousness of the spirited bearer of life is referred to things or to imagined things; and only when, and then, however, unfailingly, the said conflict occasions an act of self-reflection, does the phantasm of the impression separate off from the present impression as a formerly received impression. Because "I" find myself in the present sense-space, where the phantasm has no place, the space of the phantasm becomes a bygone space. Were we to unfold, into judgements, what takes place in an instant, they would run: not I, who am, receive the impression from the intuitive image that obtrudes itself upon me; but I, who ⦅was⦆, received it. If we said earlier that, with the finding of an existence within the impression, the finding of the duration of that existence, of before and after, is already prepared as well, we now see more precisely that this actually takes place insofar as the finding of the thing guarantees the finding of the finder, and we arrive at the fundamentally important proposition: ⦅acts⦆ of ⦅remembering-oneself take place only through the mediation⦆ of acts ⦅of self-reflection⦆. To remember something means, without exception, also: to remember oneself. — One errs with the view that recollection-images carry within themselves the tendency to become objects of perception; but they are indeed always ready to return to their homeland, the actuality of phantasms, and do so, by virtue of an inherent falling-power, without effort, whenever, through a passing fatigue of spirit in the one who remembers, the obstacle yields that barred the way: his consciousness of his own presence here! We do not yet speak of the decisive occasioning ground of the act, but we can, from among the grounds in consequence of which it becomes, by way of self-reflection, an act of remembering, already make at least one intelligible here, from the finding of the thing familiar to us.

<sup>53</sup> On page 363. — If one states it baldly, "animals recall nothing," one is again and again in danger of being misunderstood. The bee "takes note of" its hive as soon as it sets out on distant flights, and likewise takes note of a particularly rewarding meadow of blossoms; the house-dog, after hours of roaming about, finds its way back to its dwelling, and it *seeks* its master when it has lost him; songbirds that one has fed for two or three days already appear of their own accord at the feeding-place today, and indeed with surprising exactness at the very time at which the food was scattered yesterday; the cow, the bull, the horse, the cat, the dog "retain" it astonishingly long "in the head" when someone has maliciously teased them, just as when someone has treated them to their favorite food. For such feats to be possible, there is need not merely of memory in general but of impression-memory in particular, for whose durability the dog of Odysseus, *provided* we are willing to believe the poet, would furnish an example scarcely to be surpassed. The only question is whether performances of impression-memory of this kind necessarily include a recollecting-oneself; and this we now dispute. Schopen*hauer*, whose works, despite a mistaken metaphysics, are rich in shrewd particular remarks on the inner grounds of both human and animal behavior, observes aptly in the third book of the first volume of his "Welt als Wille und Vorstellung": "The animal really has no representation whatsoever of the past as such, although this past acts upon the animal through the medium of habit — hence, for instance, the dog recognizes its former master again even after years, that is, receives from the sight of him the accustomed impression, but of the time that has since elapsed it has no recollection at all." To the conclusion of our demonstration in Volume II let there at least be sent ahead here one indication of the direction in which it must be sought. Whatever it is that we recall involuntarily, that very same thing we can *in principle* also recall *voluntarily*. Let us accordingly assume for once that the key to understanding involuntary recollecting lies in voluntary recollecting; then scarcely anyone would be ready to agree, were one to try to persuade him, that an animal could voluntarily call up recollections. For if it were capable of that, it could also engage in deliberation quite as we do, could raise questions and seek their solution, and would thus in principle be capable of the achievements of understanding of homo sapiens. Since it evidently is not capable of this, the cause of that lies in its incapacity for voluntary recollecting, and then — should the connection we have posited in fact hold — in its incapacity for recollecting at all. One can express this in principle as follows: the "higher" animal disposes of a comprehensive and lasting impression-memory, but is so completely ruled by it that its doings and abstentions appear in the light of a function of its memory; man, by contrast, however often he too depends on his memory (= his past), is *in principle* in a position to rule his memory (= to place the past *consciously* in the service of his present); and of this the next (dispositional) condition is called: the faculty of recollection.

In so far as the impression-image, though always filled with meaning, is, as in the animal, merely lived through, its conflict with the phantasm can never attain that sharpness which it unfailingly attains once the finding of the [p. 365] thing has been accomplished, because this finding involves the cofinding of the place — in space and time — and, with a view to this, what the thing is remains for all eternity unchanging. Only thereby does it become, from a merely unconsciously effective disturbance, a palpably felt one, before which spirit recoils, as it were; and thus we see the seemingly feeling-free act of wholly abstract I-am-reflection once more chained to a kink in lived experience or, as Palágyi, aptly for a different purpose, called it, to a "refraction of fantasy." In passing we recognize the neighborhood and reciprocity of acts of recollection and acts of self-reflection, and surmise something common in the personal foundations of both; though it must not be forgotten that spirit, in the act of recollection, makes use of the act of self-reflection only as a support, in order to exercise that other kind of reflection-on-things which extends to things that have been, whereas in genuine self-contemplation it has torn itself free from the occasion of the backward reflection and has thereby climbed to a higher stage of abstraction in its activity.

In this connection let mention once more be made of an irregularity that forms a kind of counterpart to those touched on above. In certain disorders of apprehension it happens that someone who is able to describe an object from memory with sufficient accuracy is nonetheless unable to recognize it when he sees it. Just as, in "false recognition," in so far as it can be counted among recognitions at all, a hidden phantasm lends the object of perception a character of familiarity although it is unknown, so in the case of agnosia the *phantasm* of a *memory-image* makes the recognition of an object of perception difficult or impossible. This shows us with the utmost clarity that phantasms, and even phantasms of memory, can distract from the present impression and thereby impede recognition itself, if the impression — for whatever reasons — has lost its power of appropriation. The dog of Odysseus, lying mortally sick on the dung-heap, was surely given over wholly to the moment — and recognized his master; Penelope, Eurycleia, Eumaeus dwelt unceasingly on memories of Odysseus and did not recognize him. With these preliminary considerations on remembering we must content ourselves, since a deeper penetration would require far more comprehensive knowledge of the nature of consciousness than we have so far attained.

[p. 366] The proposition, repeatedly and rightly put forward by several investigators, that no content of an impression can be exhausted in concepts, suggests to us, after the foregoing findings, the inexhaustibility also of the relations of similarity between the impression and the impression-phantasm. By what unconscious selection out of this most proper infinitude the recognizable congeals depends, both generically and individually, on the life-character of the recipient of the impression or, if one prefers, on its life-needs, and is therefore never calculated in advance but only confirmed afterward. Yet the original recognition always comes about through an essential kinship of images, and hence, already on the animal stage of life, what is recognized stands opposed to contents of conflicting essence. Besides the inherited recognitions already spoken of, it is above all impressions lived through earlier that bring it about that, on suspicion of danger, the hare flees to the nearest attainable cornfield, the browsing roe-deer to the nearest attainable thicket of the wood, or the duck to the nearest attainable pond. If the animals thereby *recognize*, without concepts, units of meaning such as brightness, shadow, clearing, thicket, grasses, rain, foliage, and so on, then the basic sameness of the processes leading there with the process of recognition just discussed will of course be familiar only to a way of considering things that rests on the insight that it is an essence which, in every lived unit of meaning, links the objectively distinguishable marks of appearance, and that there is accordingly, in like manner, an essence of darkness or of the forest, just as there is an essence of the animal and, finally, of this particular cat. However immeasurable the difference in essence may seem to us, on the one hand, between what we have become accustomed to regard as properties, states, processes of things — for instance brightness, stillness, morning, cold, stoniness, twilight, redness, bitterness, lying, moving, and so forth — and the things themselves on the other, and however wide the gulf may threaten to open between the non-living and the living things which we call organisms and see fall into several main kingdoms besides countless subkingdoms: this — being essences that can appear — is common to all intuitively understandable units of meaning. Thanks to co-experienced similarity and dissimilarity, agreement and disagreement, every impression stands at once within an intuitive image of the world, and there is thus prefigured, in the contents of lived experience, what for spirited beings grounds the conceptual pairs of sameness [p. 367] and non-sameness, equality and difference, being and non-being. Whereas, however, developed thinking begins with these most general positings and advances from them, by the addition of specifying marks (differentiae specificae), to objective differences among which opposition occurs as a subordinate case, insight into the origin of the impression of difference out of the *conflict* of essential appearances has taught us that the vital source-point of all dualities must be sought in intuitively lived oppositions; whence all, so to speak, natural thinking receives the compulsion to master whatever material is at hand by way of bipartitions. The symbol-formations of probably all the peoples of the earth are doubly poled (Vol. III); the myths and sagas of the Aryans, at least, are dominated by the thought of a struggle between a bright and a dark principle: one need only think of the battles of the Kurus with the Pandavas in the Indian epic, of the Iranians with the Turanians in the Persian, of the Völsungs with the Nibelungs in the Germanic; and ethics, for example, has to this day not ceased to pursue, with highly abstract investigations, the primeval division of all men into "good" and "evil"! Fully so on the plane of the animal units of meaning, which stand solely in the service of the care of life: all modes of behavior are organized according to lived oppositions. Surely no one able even a little to immerse himself in the originality of lived experience will doubt that already for the animal the impression-images of brightness and darkness, of day and night, of motion and rest, of noise and stillness, of cold and heat, and countless other essentially polar appearances, fall apart into oppositions. The squirrel, setting from branch to branch in hasty flight, gauges the distance in a flash before every leap and accordingly distinguishes, not nearness from farness, but certainly attainable from unattainable nearness, and avoids, just as swiftly, branches that would not bear it, thereby distinguishing thickness and thinness of the twigs, firmness and brittleness. But if, in view of such recognitions, we can scarcely fail to arrive at a fitting estimate of animal soul-life, we have on the other hand all the more to guard against overestimating its agreement with our own, which differs quite extraordinarily from that of animals for two reasons now to be considered more closely.

[p. 368]

#### 35. Kapitel — Vom tierischen und menschlichen Erkennen — Chapter 35 — On Animal and Human Cognition

If, from the dependence — now known to us — of all human impression-images on impression-form there followed, on the one side, the almost boundless sole rule of the sense of sight, then, on the other side, there inescapably went along with it the most extraordinary atrophy, above all, of the sense of smell, and, in consequence, the almost complete loss of a whole world of scents in which the most deeply moving experiences of by far the greater number of animals are played out. A thousand things which we are wrongly inclined to understand from the "intelligence" of animals would reveal themselves quite differently if even the tiniest fraction of those connections and oppositions which the animal is able to live through directly and intuitively, thanks to its scents, were accessible to us. Not even of the world of impressions of the domestic dog, which stands comparatively very close to us, do we, with the utmost exertion of imagination, gain so much as a "notion," and we are therefore always in danger of tracing countless of its achievements back to form-impressions and then wishing to derive them from a thinking consciousness, when in truth they take place without any such thing, on the occasion of contents of meaning apprehended by scent. If we add to this the receptivity of not a few animals to changes of air pressure, to electrical and magnetic natural influences, to differences of horizontal direction, to fluids perhaps still unknown to us, we may feel assured that there are sides to the essence of the world that remain forever withdrawn from the whole compass of our possible experience — not to speak of the impression-less contents of experience of purely vegetative life-processes! But whereas in such differences of cognition it is chiefly differences of power among the senses that come into play, there are others, far more deeply incisive, arising from that fundamental difference of the souls themselves which grounds, among other things, the capacity for reflection belonging to the human soul alone.

[p. 369] The view expressed in the phrase "homo sapiens," that man is distinguished from the animal by conscious thought or, by disposition, by his being spirited, is inadequate because it leaves us entirely in the dark as to by virtue of what transformation of the nature of life spirit entered into connection with life in man, and in him alone. On the basis of a doctrine that lets spirit come to life from without (= thyrathen, in Aristotle's coinage), the question would at once have to be asked whether the transformation of life by which an animal species became the human species already had spiritedness as its immediate consequence too; and we are now convinced that this was by no means the case at first. For we believe we have recognized that the transformation of an animal into original man — whose state of soul counted, for the next following stage of development, in memory of it, as divine or demonic — consisted in a change of poles, and indeed in this sense: that the soul-pole, previously dependent on the bodily pole, henceforth became determining for it. Out of sentient, or bodily awakened, animality original man detached himself by the liberation of beholding from the rule of sensing. The difference does not have the form of a transition that would allow one to think of intermediate forms, but the stepwise form of a change of state that transforms the whole of lived experience just as abruptly, profoundly upheavingly, and boundlessly as, in another way, the leap from the state of sleep into the waking state does. But it is now not so much a becoming-awake as rather the waking of a new side of essence, whose wakefulness disempowers the already existing wakefulness of the animal and, on another plane, once more makes the form of livingness more similar to the world-interwoven sleep of plant-being. With the wakefulness of the body and the gift of locomotion, by which it separated itself from the plant, the animal exchanged, for the all-capability of all slumbering life, the insurmountable barrier of presentness belonging to a drive directed merely at the impression; from this barrier original man tore himself free and plunged back into the all-capability of lived experience through the awakening of the beholding soul. While the animal lives in a world of bodies differing in appearance, original man lives in a world of bodily images; while the animal's expression of life is necessarily the expression of the changing states of the living body, the elementary expression of life of man is the expression of the states of his soul; and while, finally, [p. 370] in the expression of bodily livingness the disturbances and surgings of the drives of its living bearer appear, in the expression of the soul, merely selected out by the body, there appears, in the form of the images that only thereby reveal themselves, the essence of actuality itself!

The grazing cow has the sensuous impression of the meadow, with which she is connected through drives of inclination, and, on the basis of the impression, picks out the juiciest and fattest grasses without any deliberation whatever. She also has the sense-impression of the dog, with which she is connected through drives of defense, and knows, on the basis of the impression, how to drive it off in a highly "purposeful" manner. She has the intuition of these and many other units of meaning in common with us; but her intuition, wholly led on a leash by the attractions and repulsions of the body, never attains, within the context of her lived experience, that independence which would permit comparing the impression to the projecting of an inner image, and therefore, notwithstanding a great wealth of possibilities of reaction, under no circumstances releases the urge toward the *representation* of what has been lived through. Animals can build the most artful dwellings and nests, can in many ways imitate movements as well as voices; but no animal on earth has ever *so much asproduced* a likeness of what it, like us, is able to behold; whereas man, scarcely had he begun to think, brought countless contents of impression to representation by drawing or by modeling. Since in the likeness a phantasm of the impression-image is made into an object, a phantasm which, in relation to sense-space, belongs to a space of the past, we may give the memory-lessness of the animal which we have ascertained, with regard to the constitution of its intuition of space, the more general formulation that it lacks the life-content of distance, and that the animal's power of making-present is thus confined to spatial images belonging to a place.

If we emphasized above that in the animal beholding depends on sensing, and in original man sensing depends on beholding, we have now taken a turn that allows us to express the same state of affairs, with a view to the life-bearer capable of consciousness, as follows: in the animal's impression-experience, the making-present (which of course is never lacking!) of units of meaning is governed by their bodily determinability, whereas in the impression-experience of original man, conversely, the selection of what is capable of embodiment is governed by intuitive images that were made present out of *psychic* necessity. The [p. 371] soul of the cow, although it too "mirrors," is able to do so only in dependence on what is sensed, and her consciousness, supposing she had one, could never grasp: the drifting bank of cloud, the outline of the mountains, the snowy blue of the névés, the broadly rolling peal of thunder, the fragrant orchestra of the alpine herbs. With these images too she lives through connections and answers their changes with the most well-adapted behavior, in so far as changes proceed from them partly of her vegetative, and partly, above all, of her sentient bodiliness; in doing so, as we have learned, she far outstrips man in fineness of scent — for instance at the coming of a storm, the imminence of an earthquake, the approach of an untimely snowfall — but to gain an image of it, and now even to "picture" such a thing to herself, remains wholly denied her. The sheep on the alp enjoys, just as we do, the freshness of the brook and the shade of the tree, only not — the view! The eagle, which, hovering a mile high above labyrinths of mountains, finds its way back effortlessly to its eyrie; the buzzard, which from a considerable height espies the little mouse that serves it for food; the birds of passage, which cover many hundreds of miles on most fittingly chosen air-routes, often running along coasts and used again and again, preferably, as is known, by night, when sensuous orientation would be most difficult (!): none of these has intuitive images of the landscapes inhabited or traversed, and they would find themselves suddenly transported into an almost wholly alien world, one that would make vitally important recognitions exceedingly difficult, were they compelled to perceive these same regions by the means of human form- and image-apprehension!<sup>54</sup>

<sup>54</sup> On page 371. — Since a new teaching cannot guard against misunderstanding too often, let it be stressed once more that animals in general, and above all the so-called higher animals, naturally possess a faculty of intuition just as we do. It is indeed we ourselves who hold the conviction that sensations never occur at all without some basis of intuition. What is at issue is not the presence or absence of intuitions, but whether the soul-conditioned intuition is *determin* ative for bodily sensing, or bodily sensing for soul-conditioned intuition. Through the latter the animal is characterized, through the former, man. Borrowing a mathematical turn of phrase, one might also say that in the animal, beholding is the dependent variable, while in man, sensing is the dependent variable. Only *within the framework* of this dependency, and for the closer characterization of *intuitive images*, can one then indeed speak, within mankind, of a *relative* predominance now of the inclination toward making-present, now of the inclination toward embodiment. Similarly, however, within animality too, an extraordinarily long series of *degrees* of the participation of beholding in sensing must be distinguished. If late Romantic philosophy was somewhat too ready, for many feats of animals, to reach for "life-magnetic" explanations, the opposite fashion prevails today: to regard everything from the standpoint of mere differences of degree. Thanks to ingenious (though often also dreadfully cruel) experiments, an almost unsurveyable mass of factual material has been assembled concerning the constitution of the sense-organs, indeed of the entire bodily nature of animal creatures from the anthropoid down to the world of protists; but the art of interpretation has not kept pace with it. Let this be illustrated by an example. Whereas formerly one was accustomed to hold a mysterious sense of direction responsible for the bee's power of orientation and its capacity to find its way home, it is now supposed to be established that the bee orients itself optically with the help of landmarks. Proof of this is held to be the fact that bees on land easily find their way back to the hive from a distance of 3 to 5, sometimes even 8 to 10 kilometers, but *never* from a distance of as little as 2 kilometers if one carries them out onto a lake and releases them there. Now it is self-evident that every animal makes use, for orientation too, of every sense it possesses, so far as orientation requires it. If it is endowed, say, with genuine visual capacity and not merely with light-sensitivity, then its visual capacity likewise weaves into its image of the world; from which everything further follows of itself. But it does not follow in the remotest degree that *its* orientation by means of the eye may be equated with *our* orientation by means of the eye — as one evidently assumes at present. The bee, it is held, takes in on its outward flight a series of optical intuitive images of its surroundings and retains them in memory so admirably that on the return flight it can use the series of images in the reverse direction! There is no life-magnetic explanation of any Romantic that could measure up to this one in improbability. For, first, the bee for the most part does not return to the hive even approximately by the same route it used on the outward flight , but mostly on a straighter course. Second, the bee is supposed to be able to see *distinctly* only at two, or at the very most three, meters, in the sense especially of the capacity for distinguishing shapes. If it now covers even as little as two kilometers, then, despite the great speed of its flight (about 10 m per second), it would have had to take in a series of some 1000 intuitive images and carry them in its head so excellently ordered that it could readily run through the series in the direction 1000–1! Third and finally: if one shifts the beehive two meters to the left or to the right, the returning bees gather *in the air* at the very spot where it had previously stood, and sometimes need more than half an hour to find it. This one *knows*, and nonetheless speaks as though bees could orient themselves optically after the manner of human beings! And that is not all: if one carries so-called potter wasps two kilometers away from the nest in a box, they nonetheless return to it at once! Orientation, however it may come about in the individual case, and whether it is chiefly visual experiences or olfactory experiences or experiences of position and movement on which it rests, certainly takes place, in every instance, with the help of bodily overemphasized *experiences*, and *not*, as in man, through those thing-related and thing-discriminating "representations," notings, conscious recollections, to which vitally there corresponds a world of intuitive images. Compare also Note 59 and Note 69 on this.

With this, so far as the literature is known to us, that difference between original man and animal has for the first time been ascertained which allows of no further reinterpretation. For if one answers the question by what the intelligence of man differs from that of all animals with, say, a reference to the use of tools, the zoologists will be able to name for us more than one animal species that likewise employs tools. Certain insects, for example, knock shut with a little stone the small hole in which they have laid their eggs. And the provisions made, for instance, by fungus-cultivating ants are of so intricate a nature that they can scarcely fall behind tool-use in ingenuity. Here half-circular pieces of leaf are cut out and carried in by special workers, so-called leaf-cutters, chewed to a pulp by others and kneaded together into a [p. 372] sponge-like nest, which then, besides unusable "mycelia" that are bitten off by workers specially appointed for the task, and besides mold-fungi which are likewise systematically rooted out, produces the species of fungus that serves the ants for food (Deegener, Die Formen der Vergesellschaftung im Tierreich, pp. 199–200). — If one answers that only man possesses a language, one will first be told of ape-languages, which is a matter with its own peculiar bearing , and will then be drawn<sup>55</sup> into an endless dispute over whether and to what extent the mutual understanding of animals through manifoldly modulated sounds does not likewise fall under the genus of linguistic utterances. The misgivings are unfounded; but their refutation does not lie ready to hand and will probably long remain a matter of controversy. — Fully disputed, too, is the capacity of animals for thought. While mechanistic biologists, walking in the footsteps of Descartes, labor to resolve the behavior of animals into machine-movements, animal-lovers and trainers are inclined to place the deliberative achievements of animals on very nearly the same level as those of man, not to speak of allegedly calculating horses and dogs. — If, finally, one decides with Schiller, "Art, O man, thou alone hast," naturalists will tell us of artistic drives in numerous animals and cite, for instance, a species of bird of paradise in New Guinea which, for the purpose of attracting the females, lays out a "love-garden," arranging sand, shells, stones, and berries alternately and with unmistakable feeling for color. All attempts at distinction thus lack an unassailable foundation.

<sup>55</sup> On page 372. — Whether, and to what extent, one may speak of linguistic understanding among certain species of apes, shall remain undiscussed here. Regarding a *faculty of intelligent experience* essentially of the same kind as ours, however, in the so-called anthropoid apes, no doubt is any longer possible after the studies of W. *Köhler*, as thorough as they are cautious, "Intelligenzprüfungen an Anthropoiden" (1917 and 1918).
