There we hear how the chimpanzee, after first searching in vain for hidden fruit, digs it up and continues doing so until it has convinced itself of the completeness of its success quite as one of us would; how it teases hens in a maliciously sly manner quite like human children; how it makes use of a stick as a weapon or as a lever; how it hangs itself about with scraps of cloth and the like, evidently thereby fancying itself grander, much as many a Central African does; how it playfully "paints" with white clay; how, after prolonged attempts, it fits several pipes into one another in order, with the instrument thus lengthened, to draw a banana toward itself through the bars; how it likewise, though only gradually, piles two, three, even exceptionally as many as four crates on top of one another in order to reach the desired goal, and so forth. — Only as a curiosity let there be mentioned here the view that the author of this book had already formed as a young student concerning apes (and indeed all apes without exception), since it still corresponds to his conviction today. The apes are *remnants of* a round of mankind that existed who knows how *many hundreds of thousands of years* ago. That vanished mankind will indeed have differed from the mankind known to us in many particulars; but it was certainly in possession of a human understanding. It is the relics of that understanding which we admire in the intelligent feats of the anthropoids. — The grounds that impelled us very early to this assumption lie in the domain of expressive movements, and are indeed such as to convince instantly anyone who becomes aware of the indications in question at a "fruitful moment," but otherwise are without evidential value; for which reason we present our view, too, only as a curiosity. Should there, in some very distant time, again be a *new* mankind — which is of course extremely improbable — it may perhaps observe, in the trees still left standing, a likewise *new* species of anthropoid, representing the no longer further transformable final stage of the "progress" of present-day mankind. —

Whoever might still wish to doubt the aptness of metaphysical inquiry for fructifying our knowledge of the facts too would have to be given pause by the circumstance that just such inquiry has now led us to an intuitive example of the difference of achievement between man and animal, in which the biologists have hitherto failed to discern what is *decisive*. How often have we not marveled, in the circus or the vaudeville theater, at the well-nigh unbelievable feats of skill to which the trainer had been able to bring elephants, bears, dogs, horses, sea-lions, and so on; but how far would this be surpassed by the astonishment — no, by the utter bewilderment — that would seize us if the trained horse were able, with one of its forehooves, to sketch out in the sand of the arena the outlines of some object of the simplest shape, [p. 373] even though, taken purely mechanically, this achievement would fall considerably short of many another we have already seen horses perform! But should one wish to cast doubt on the mobility of the hooves required for this in the horse's case, then let one take the dog, or even the cat — animals of which no one will make it credible that the construction of their legs and paws does not permit them to draw triangles, squares, or simple curves in the sand and thereby, without a doubt, produce the schematic likeness of the front of a house, a bowl, a cone; all of which we see our children accomplish of their own impulse, with a finger in wet earth, with lead or slate on tablet and paper, before they have even come to school, and which stone-age man already achieved, even with a high degree of perfection, on his cave walls, on bone plates and antler staves, just as, down to the most recent times, the primitive achieved it by scratching on pieces of tree-bark, on the inner side of hides, or with clay, ochre, and charcoal on rock walls. Here we have hit upon the difference which no dispute of opinions can any longer reach; but not because we had been hunting for it, but because it emerged as a demand out of our investigation of the faculty of perception.

If we now recall the countless motor achievements of the most intricate kind of which the so-called higher animals are capable on their own, adding to this the fineness and sharpness of their attentiveness (one need only recall dogs as guides for the blind), we must confess that their complete incapacity to copy even the simplest object cannot be explained either by motor deficiencies or by a low state of "intelligence." Rather: they do not draw, not because they could not carry out the movement of drawing, but because their optical world of perception deviates from ours into the very depths! For their beholding is led on a leash by their sensing, instead of, as in original man, sensing being led by beholding. They distinguish shapes in so far as differences of shape serve to distinguish (vitally important) bodies; but they never distinguish shapes as such. They lack the independence of the gift of intuition, and thus, of course, also that strength of phantasms which alone first permits their realization in drawing. For original drawing, whether of children or of primitives, is and never was, anywhere, a copying, but rather a bringing-forth of what is to be represented on the basis of memory-phantasms, [p. 374] which, moreover, can deviate quite extraordinarily from the occasions of impression that were meant.

If the stress on beholding as against sensing *can* lead at least to a stress on making-present as against embodying, or, in short, to a stress on intuition, and if the intuitive image, for the sake of its presentness, stands opposed, in another way, also to the primal images, namely by virtue of that object-like independence which we described above from the point of view of freedom of place, we believe we understand why, already with the generation of original man out of the character of divinity, nature ran the risk of becoming, in him and through him, vulnerable to the cleaving blow of spirit, and we may consider the event of his coupling with life to have been prepared by a growth of independence of the intuitive image, however grounded, by which it made ready, as it were, to tip over into a separate form of existence. But once, in a moment of the most far-advanced loosening, the severing blow had somewhere first occurred and the split had been accomplished which left, out of the still temporal intuitive image, the thing that is in itself non-temporal and now merely time-related, spirit had — if we may put it so — in a twofold respect only just begun its task, and by no means already completed it: for one thing, in a sense quantitatively, in so far as consciousness could take possession only slowly and step by step of ever new contents of experience; and then, too, as a consequence of a specific peculiarity of original reflection, which makes it possible to divide the spiritual history even of prehistoric humanity into the two sections — actually interplaying with one another, yet in principle sharply distinguishable — of life-dependent and relatively life-detached, but in any case spirit-dependent, thinking. For reasons to be communicated later, we call the life-dependent stage that of *Promethean* thinking, the life-detached that of Heraclean thinking, and, with regard to the fundamental units of meaning, we expand and deepen what we earlier initiated, on the occasion of distinguishing a shallow from a deep reflection, with our discussions of "biocentric" and "logocentric" direction of spirit.

Here it is to be noted from the outset that the life-dependent activity of consciousness — which, even long after spirit had attained life-detachment, [p. 375] could again and again on occasion rally itself into preferentially biocentric systems of thought — did indeed precede, in time, the life-detached kind, but nonetheless did not cease to be there, and continued to act, in the form of a now, however, unconscious motive force, in every, however detached, thought-endeavor tending toward still further detachment, down to the present day. What unfolds, in retrospect, into a temporal sequence presents itself, in cross-section, as a layering of strata. For a thinking absolutely detached would not merely be thinking no longer, it would not exist at all! Let us suppose the line of spiritual history strives toward the complete detachment of consciousness from lived experience; then the attainment of that goal would be equivalent to the real ending of consciousness itself, or, put metaphorically, to the re-excretion of spirit out of life (of man, and thereby of the earth), presumably after the completion of the work of destruction which it was spirit's destiny to accomplish upon it. We hold this, in fact, to be the fate of mankind — already decided inwardly, not yet concluded outwardly, but unavoidably impending — yet wish here, by such remarks, only to have underscored that the comparatively life-detached mode of reflection of conceptual thinking could neither be understood nor even take place at all without the underlying stratum of life-dependent or symbolic thinking; and it is in accordance with this that the characterization now to be offered, in a few main strokes, of the units of meaning of original apprehension wishes to be appreciated partly as the epistemologically indispensable underpainting of thinking apprehension by the understanding, partly as the exhibiting of that intermediate link which, granted of course the soul's receptivity to spirit, connected the soul with spirit and thereby forms the immediate precondition of the thinking-consciousness familiar to us.

If we sum up, in a fresh abridgment, what has been established concerning the process of as-yet-unspirited recognitions, we would have, in the first place, the proposition: *impression-images* congeal out of co-experienced similarities of *beheld* primal images. Were we to add, in the second place: the *grouping according to meaning* of *impression-images* takes place according to the measure of *elementary* similarities, we would thereby only have asserted, in somewhat different words, the essential similarity in which we have shown the impulse to all original combinings [p. 376] as well as separatings, but would now, in view of the difference — meanwhile illuminated — of the experiential bases of animal and human recognition, have to clarify to what extent what holds good for both nonetheless allows two fundamentally different kinds of selection. We found the animal characterized by a predominantly bodily, man by a predominantly psychic, understanding of meaning, and we bring to notice, of the latter's higher independence of contents, only the reverse side, by stressing the far narrower connections between animal understanding and the proper states of animal life. Should an elementary formula seem called for here too, we would have to recall that the continuity of lived experience, which suffers no interruption even at its turning-points, serves not only the linking of images but also, alongside this, the linking of the moments of life, and thereby places the living moment of the impression occurring into two mutually crossing contexts, whereby it is dependent, on the one hand, on the chain of all previous moments, and, on the other, on that flight of images which has gained presence in the impression. Since the sequence of impressions again belongs, to a wide extent, to the fate of the proper essence, and likewise takes part in the interpretation of intuitive images, the world of meanings will always appear fed from two tributaries, in such a way that now the soul, now the extra-psychic actuality, has predominantly the say. Even apart from the regrettable ambiguity of the names "subjective" and "objective," it would not do to call the one the subjective and the other the objective tributary, because the state of the soul — which after all likewise belongs to actuality — is indicated by its reactive bearing just as factually as a facet of the actuality of images is indicated by the reflection of happening alien to soul. One could, however, drawing on the sequences of reflection, speak of the (relative) opposition of weakly objectivizing to strongly objectivizing states of soul. In the animal, to put it in somewhat different words, the meaning of the impression is determined far predominantly by its vital importance for the being receptive to the impression; in original man, far predominantly by the character of the impression itself.

In the character of a sudden bang there doubtless lies something of what, given the unexpectedness of its occurrence, justifies our animal fright [p. 377] and "startling"; but by no means that life-threatening quality of its occasion which only became experienceable after the invention of firearms and explosive devices. The soul of that creature, then, for which — like all grown game — the bang means, in the first place, a signal to flee, has subordinated the little that it too has of course necessarily taken up of the character of the bang wholly to a co-experienced motion of its own, which in the given case naturally stems from the past of its impressions. The lion's roar, however meaningful, conceals in the least degree nothing of the lion's dangerousness, and it is obvious that one hears out of it one sense, if it awakens the fear of the beast of prey's nearness, and another again, if one perceives it, say, in comparison with the character of the cow's bellowing. In principle the same difference of experience, only arising from a difference in the degree of the body's participation, doubles the character of the equatorial sun's heat, according as we are able to mirror it ourselves (in comparison, say, with the character of the warmth of a spring) or only the deadly exhaustion of our body through it. Even in the red glow of a glowing iron, both characters split apart according to sense-zones, when we perceive it once with the help of sight, another time sense it by touch; for the fearful pain on touching would of course also betray something of the character of the red glow, but as it were swallowed up by the excitationcharacter of the sentient body. Indeed, sense-processes divide, by kind, into those of the strongest power of objectivization and those of the weakest. Compared with the almost invariably objectivizing experience of seeing, the inner-bodily sensations belonging chiefly to the class of muscular experiences, whose interplay eventually produces the overwhelming feeling of fatigue, have virtually no power of objectivization at all.

These few examples have at the same time given us certainty that the duality of drives toward immediate exploration by the senses, which we have just developed in connection with the difference between animal and human cognition, likewise halves human impression-experiences, or, more correctly, concerns, in every impression-experience, two sides of differing origin, of which now the one, now the other predominates in giving it its coloring. But if, in consequence of inwardly bodily conditioned "moods," there does indeed take place a selection and shaping of meaning of impressions [p. 378] for which we could find no other clue in the impressions themselves than the degree of their fittingness to the already existing state, then, conversely, however great the difference among recipients of impressions, we shall find the key to the states of excitation that occur on the occasion of impressions only in the proper character of these impressions themselves; and it is precisely this which, in contrast to the animalism of lived experience, decisively governs the formation of cognition at the Promethean stage of spirit.

[p. 379]

#### 36. Kapitel — Symbolisches und begriffliches Denken — Chapter 36 — Symbolic and Conceptual Thinking

Whoever holds the original units of meaning, one and all, to have been won from elementary similarities has raised the hovering similarity to an effective power, by which, on this side of things, the grouping of images is determined in a manner analogous to the way the grouping of things within the world of things is determined, say, by gravitational force. We must first give account of the quite extraordinary opposition into which such a view enters with the principles of conceiving that have become habitual to us, principles which, because they always ultimately rest on things, seem to have abolished relations of similarity by replacing them with the relation of cause and effect. Just as, according to this view, there is not, and cannot be, in the realm of things any connection according to similarities, so, correspondingly, there would now be, in the *actuality* of life, no *connection* of cause and *effect*, but exclusively one of elementary similarities. If, according to Jean *Paul's* memorable saying, language is a "dictionary of faded metaphors," then this means, in this light: the contents of word-meaning bear witness to the working of elementary similarities, and pale into mere metaphors only for thinking by the understanding, which stands under the compulsion of substituting, for every living and therefore directly-only-livable unity, a merely objective and therefore directly conceivable unity. Since, however, the faculty of judgment cannot make itself heard otherwise than by employing the great dictionary of language, we shall not go wrong in assuming that the efficacy, mentioned above, of the life-dependent formative impulses of spirit must be demonstrable, even in strictly objective thinking, through its already earlier indicated relationship of dependency on the means of communication, and we therefore cast our glance, in the first place, on the persistence of elementary laws of grouping arising from the compulsions of language.

[p. 380] One will never make out what was "earlier," the noun or the verb, because every original content of meaning was an essence, and an essence a living power whose actuality could not be apprehended without the co-apprehension of its working, and whose working could not be apprehended without the co-apprehension of its actuality. The merely external question, whether the primal linguistic sound is to be reckoned equal to a sentence or to a member of a sentence, becomes pointless, in so far as the distinction of noun and verb finds no application at all to primal linguistic sounds. However much the use of the same root-sound — often stressed by linguistics — now to denote an effective something, now the activity of this something, now the instrument by which the effect is brought about, now the result, may seem, viewed from without, like a stringing together of meaning-related thoughts, it is in truth the product of a progressive *analysis* of what still lay undivided within the originally apprehended content of meaning; and only this much, to be sure, remains correct, in agreement with the most usual manner of presentation: that, once the division has occurred, and running parallel with the degree of determinacy that meanings come to assume, verbal formations — and indeed originally thanks to the stressed event-character of their sense — furnish the preferred means of countless linkages and represent, quite properly, the generative element of language, whereas the nominal ones prepare the way for individuation and reification.

The Latin serpens, the snake, does indeed come from serpere = to creep, to slink, exactly as the German "Schlange" was formed by ablaut from "schlingen," which in its Middle High German form "dingen" likewise meant "to creep" (analogously: Blindschleiche, the slow-worm, from "schleichen," to slink); but for the *understanding* of the genesis of meaning it would in principle come to the same thing whether we think of the already known sense of slinking and creeping as applied to the something called "snake," or, conversely, think the content of meaning of a word for a process, now to be derived from it, as having first emerged from the intuition of the already known snake. Among the kinds of words as parts of speech, for which a uniform ordering rule has still not been found — one need only think of the usual distinction of noun (Hauptwort/Substantiv), pronoun (Fürwort), article (Geschlechtswort), adjective (Beiwort), numeral (Zahlwort), verb (Zeitwort), adverb (Umstandswort), preposition (Verhältniswort), conjunction (Bindewort) [p. 381], interjection (Ausrufswort) — any one can in principle develop out of *any* *other*. In particular, to remain only with the principal opposition of nouns to verbs, linguistics teaches and attests the threefold possibility: common descent from the same stem (example: Fall [fall] and fallen [to fall], Schlag [blow] and schlagen [to strike], Sang [song] and singen [to sing]) — verb from noun (rauchen [to smoke] from Rauch [smoke], morden [to murder] from Mord [murder], schallen [to resound] from Schall [sound], fragen [to ask] from Frage [question]; or, for proper thing-words: krebsen [to crawl like a crab] from Krebs [crab], ankreiden [to chalk up] from Kreide [chalk], harken [to rake] from Harke [rake]) — noun from verb (Betrag [amount] from betragen [to amount to], Erfolg [success] from erfolgen [to ensue], Brauch [custom] from brauchen [to need/use], Begriff [concept] from begreifen [to conceive]); and thereby attests the same degree of aptitude for generalization in both. If the snake is indeed a creeping thing, there must nonetheless in any case have been some other creeping thing on whose occasion the word for creeping was found; hence, in the state of coming-into-being of their separating out, noun and verb, for all their difference, cannot present any difference of scope in their contents of meaning; just as, for instance, the very general "capricious" owes its name to the particular animal genus of the goat (=capra), or the no less general "miniature," and even the far more general "en miniature," derive from the quite particular minium = red lead, with which miniaturepainters used to color.

From proper names generic names occasionally arise, as Kaiser from Caesar, or Academy from the name of the hero Akademos, whose grove Plato had chosen for his place of teaching, or magnet and magnetize from the name of the city of Magnesia, near which iron ores were found, or pistol, originally a Spanish coin, once again from a city, namely Pistoia in Italy, where it is said to have first been minted, or "verballhornen" [to bowdlerize/botch] from the bookseller Ballhorn (end of the 16th and beginning of the 17th century), of whom it was said that, instead of improving the primer, he had made it immeasurably worse; but every linguist also knows that there are few proper names that would not be derived from generic names (appellatives, or, as sometimes in Hebrew, indeed from whole sentences) and thus have originally been meaningful. Just as little, however, is there any original thing-name that does not offer the *characterization* of that which it names, regardless of whether it arose, say, from a verb, or let the verb arise from itself; and if the Scholastics taught the abstractness of all properties, we infer, reaching beyond this in a twofold respect, [p. 382] from the abstractness of everything nameable whatsoever the life-foundation out of the sheer *essentiality* of the contents of word-meaning, among which, for this very reason, none is found that would not be a knot in the fabric of similarities and would not, so to speak, carry within itself the seed for a reflection upon countless comparabilities. The conceiving consciousness could not pass a single judgment, were not every name, still today, at least co-naming an essence which, coming to appearance in manifold ways, enters into intercourse with other essences, partly through attraction, partly through repulsion.

As a creeping thing, the snake is a form of representation of an essence that comes to representation on a thousand occasions, now thing-like, now property-like, now state-like, and is thereby linkable, through some trait of kinship or other, with, for instance, the human "sneak" (Schleicher) and the "tricks" (Schliche) that serve him! If, according to the report of Diogenes Laertius, a Thales, asked which came into being earlier, night or day, is supposed to have answered, "Night, a day earlier," then, however inclined one may be to see in this a reification of day and night — even supposing this held true of Thales — one must not lose sight of the still more important reverse side, according to which reification, arising from a non-distinguishing of essence and thing, originally succeeded only because, at the start, all thing-denoting names too were essence-denoting names! Instead of having meant that night is a thing-like matter, Thales *could* equally have meant that all things are essences, like night — which would in any case fit better with the grand animations of the whole world of appearance, in view of which the systems of the Ionian philosophers are wont to be called "hylozoistic." Linguistically, in any case, night has remained to this day what it was originally apprehended as; for no one fails to recognize that we are speaking of an effective essence when we say that it "breaks in" or "recedes" — indeed, we once more essentialize the effect by substantivizing the predicative word, in turns of phrase like "the breaking-in of night."

In etymological dictionaries one finds it remarked again and again that some name or other originally had such-and-such a "proper" and "physical" meaning and was subsequently "transferred" to states of soul, achievements of thought, and other modes of behavior of man. Should anyone draw from this the conclusion that thing-related thinking [p. 383] tends to precede essence-meaning thinking, he would, quite apart from our demonstration of the contrary, first have to be reminded that the origin of no word can be traced back into the primal stratum of language, and would then have to be pointed to the circumstance, repeatedly urged and, so far as we know, especially by Max Müller, that with many a bold "transference" the poet who ventures it "only draws forth again the latent metaphors of language." In fact, a complete cycle of the supposed transferences can be traced, on a wealth of examples, from a comparatively still recent time. In today's "Sonnenblick" [sun-glance/sunshine] the second component seems to be used figuratively. In reality, however, Blick comes from the Old High German blic, which meant "lightning," as still audibly echoes in the miners' terms "Goldblick" and "Silberblick" [the bright flash of gold or silver at the moment of smelting]; and the "transference" had accordingly already once taken place, only in the opposite direction, in that people thought they rediscovered the sudden flashing of lightning, of gleaming metal, of a fleeting illumination by the sun, in the — "beam" (Strahl) of the human eye! The sun can today "glance" (blicken) because long before, the eye had been able to "flash" (blitzen). Should one object that here too the "physical" beam forms the starting point after all, we would have to reply that the physical beam would scarcely have been ascertained even in the glance of the eye, and certainly not in "radiant" beauty, "radiant" smile, "radiant" joy, had not the essence already been grasped, from the beginning, equally from the radiance of the sun or of lightning — just as afterward, demonstrably, it happened, by a back-transference of human glancing onto the sun, meanwhile so very much reified, with the fusion-word "Sonnenblick"!

The assumption of a higher originality of thing-related thinking rests on a falsification, smuggling our matter-of-factness into the word-forming processes, whose grown contents never name things alone, but always also appearances — that is to say, of essences. We readily recognize what must have favored such a falsification. For if every finding of essence rests on co-experienced similarities of images, then in all the languages of the earth there is no name, however abstract, that was not at some point branched off from another name with an intuitively graspable content of meaning; and since we are accustomed, out of the consciousness's overemphasized need for objecthood, to bring every content of intuition at once into connection [p. 384] with things and their properties, it will of course be easy for us to atomize even the oldest word-meaning as well! But just as physical atomism founders on the *organically* living, so linguistic atomism founders on the demonstrably intuitive primal content of all words and turns of phrase for what is *of the soul* and *of thought*. Having thereby incidentally weighed the decisive ground for the intuitiveness of all essence-designations, which we have already amply documented earlier, we do in fact pay homage to the still far more far-reaching conviction that not only are all these not transferences at all, but that even the genuine transferences — such as "table-leg," "weathercock," "meadow foam-cress," "wood anemone," "nightshade," "blossom-snow," "sea of flowers," "spit of land," "bay," "grasshopper," "seal," "cabbage head," "mountain basin," "forest's hem," and so on — could occur only because the matter-of-fact or poetically comparing gaze had itself secretly suffered the pull of the mutual striving of soul-related images!

One would resist such at-bottom readily accessible insights less than one does, were they not opposed, ever since the victory of merely conceiving over image-forming thinking, by the false doctrine that the finding of essence rests upon a poeticizing-in of essence, upon "empathy," ensoulment, "animism," and so forth (since it simply remains unknowable whence the *finding* essence derives, and whether this essence perhaps invents itself!), and that "empathy," in turn, is inescapably personification! Once again it was Max Müller who with resolve rejected the understanding's haughty nonsense that souls must coincide with personified souls. "Because one called the moon the measurer, the dawn the awakener, the thunder the roarer, the rain the rainer, the fire the swift-runner," it says in his "Origin of Religion," "we may not on that account assume that one took these things to be human beings with arms and legs." Unfortunately he immediately abandons the path leading in quite another direction, to exchange it, without being aware of the turn, for the customary one, adding, in keeping with his belief in the creative power of the Logos, that all this was merely simile! For it is by no means "figurative" versus "literal" speech that stands to be chosen between; rather, what must be decided is whether a roaring person, or even merely a roaring ox, must be meant by the essence of roaring which the listening soul met again, among other places, in thunder. Persons are certainly *not* what, as has been shown, [p. 385] after the world's far-advanced de-souling, could so often save itself by retreating into the impersonal pronoun — from which we sense the afterglow of the essence of night even more strongly than from the above semi-poetic turns of phrase, when we say "it is nighting"!

But even if the most fully conscious matter-of-fact thinking cannot dispense with the binding and dividing pull of hidden units of meaning out of the workshop of essence-meaning thinking, one still wishes to learn wherein it sets itself apart from the latter; for which purpose it would first have to be clarified how thinking, today the underlying stratum, was shaped in the age before its supremacy. In particular one will want to hear whether we seriously meant to maintain that a thinking humanity ever got along without things together with their properties, states, and processes, and, since that can hardly be our meaning, in what else the so-called symbolic thinking then consisted, other than in the presence of certain compulsions for the thought-selection of what was to be compared. We develop the answer with the help of a few examples. The "heavy heart" grounds, for objective thinking, no connection between bodily weight and human temperament; talk of "warm" colors just as little a connection between optical and thermal properties; the distinction of "high" and "low" tones no connection of the tone-thing with the extensions of space; for the self-identical something "human temperament" or "tone" or "color" was won at the price of its severance from lived contexts, in such a way that we believe we must renounce thinking itself the moment we would surrender the matter-of-fact and property-of-matter units whose concepts are designated by those words. But it was precisely in this that the decisive trait of symbolic thinking consisted: that, far from perceiving similes in such linguistic signs, it took the designated contents for consciousness-independent *actualities*. Without thing-relatedness, thinking would of course be impossible. But whereas in conceptual thinking things are the actual, or, say, the skeletal frame of actuality, and essences a mere fantastic invention (with the now, admittedly, absurd exception of animal and man!), conversely in symbolic thinking essences are the actual, while things, by contrast, are either unheeded tools used only in the service of the appearance of life, or dwelling-places of essence ("idols").

[p. 386] In view of the circumstance that even the extremely enlightened late age of the Greeks lets us hear, from the mouth of its professor Aristotle, that the myths were "remnants of age-old, vanished wisdom," we are in any case in unsuspect company when we consider the two spiritual attitudes not from the viewpoint of two developmental stages but of a difference of kinds, and hold them against one another, phenomenologically, as follows. The understanding-based manner of thinking uses insights already present in symbolic form for the ascertaining and comparing of the things that are for it exclusively actual; the soul-based manner uses co-apprehended things for the finding of characters of appearance; the understanding-based manner divests the coherence of images of its power through the substitute system of matters relatable to one another, the soul-based manner subjects the system of things, insofar as it has one, to the coherence of images through the *transference* of the *thought of sameness* onto *characters of appearance* of *essential similarity*; the understanding-based manner believes, with regard to things, in the causability of the noumena and invented for that purpose the riddle-essences of the physical "forces," the soul-based manner believes in the *transformability* of the phainomena and derives them from the working of living essences. Both form series and kinds. But if the one follows the properties of things, the other the characters of images, then the series must not only diverge completely from one another but must also have logically opposite meanings. The lived and symbolically apprehended similarity between the above of space and the height of a tonal quality is not a matter-of-fact relatability; but the matter-of-fact relation between air vibrations and tone is, for its part, no similarity to be lived. A thinking thus proves itself life-dependent insofar as it arrives at the finding of its units out of the essential kinship of beheld images, which units thereafter at once diverge polarly. Both series, always formable according to oppositions, form the core, still capable of germination today, of linguistic contents of meaning, without whose continuing pull matter-of-fact comparisons and distinctions would not take place at all. In relation to linguistic symbols, however, matter-of-fact comparison is always the result of an act of dissection, entirely regardless of whether it thereafter proceeds by binding or by separating.

If we now ask: how does matter-of-fact thinking detach itself from the living meanings from which it takes its departure; or: what makes possible, [p. 387] in the psychic process, the impulse toward conceiving thinking, and what transformation does the symbolic unit of meaning suffer through the appropriating power of spirit — then the next answer to this falls to us as thoroughly prepared, out of the assumption of an overemphasis of making-present, according to which the happening of images runs the danger of being swallowed up by their omnipresent form. Because the above of space beheld in tone-pitch is not intuitively present in the tonal quality, the warmth beheld in purple not intuitively present in the colorquality, and so on, the accentuation of making-present, with regard to each of the two pairs, prepares its falling-apart, whose actual occurrence through the spiritual act could at the least be accompanied by the correlating of tones to tones, of spatial properties to spatial properties, of colors to colors, of warmths to warmths, and in this way by the finding of the general concepts of tone, of vertical extension, of color, of temperature.

But the timelessness of the general concepts of thing-properties requires being related to the thing, which is in turn space-time-related; hence, in relation to the original beholding, the overemphasis of making-present forms only the complementary reverse side to the overemphasis of embodying — no longer, however, as with animals, in the service of the finding of body, but of the positing of local *anchoring points* for universals that would otherwise no longer be capable of a home in the totality of appearance! However much, in consequence, outward-turned thinking thereafter strikes out in opposite directions, according to whether it "idealistically" follows the making-present readiness of the sense of sight or "materialistically" the embodying readiness of the sense of touch, these are nonetheless directional oppositions on the plane merely of matter-of-fact reflection, which — as it were, situated higher up — no longer intersects anywhere with the abandoned plane of essence-reflection. If we said that warmth and purple must threaten to fall apart all the more, the more the purple is made-present, we can just as well say: the more it becomes the property of a thing. For even though the conceived how-constitution of the space-timeless purple color is one and the same on any purple-colored thing whatsoever of all times, it exchanges, for this merely noumenal existence, a semblance of actuality only by surrendering itself, from case to case, to the individual thing, always determined in place both spatially and temporally — on which there cools into [p. 388] a mere simile what was formerly the space-temporally *occurring* appearance of a through-and-through living essence: the warmth of purple. Conversely: it is not that the itself space-temporal warmth of purple lacks, in and for itself, a home-place in the space-temporal totality of appearances; rather, what clasps it together into an image proves to be unrelatable to the thing's place of existence.

Whoever is able to apprehend what we call "warm redness" has without doubt both the warmth and the redness. If, then, the symbolic units of meaning actually preceded the matter-of-fact ones, the finding of matter-of-fact concepts would all along the line be the consequence of a dissection, and in no case of a so-called synthesis. This is exactly the view we hold. That redness of which, in the above word-combination, being-warm is predicated, is not the matter-of-fact redness but an appearance of essence, and this appearance of essence is struck apart for the purpose of the finding both of matter-of-fact redness and of matter-of-fact warmth. The concept of color (like the concept of temperature) that thus arises would accordingly be nothing new with regard to the mode of appearance of objects, but would indeed be something thoroughly new with regard to the boundaries now running, impassably, between the contents. As the image side, the determinate redness realizes itself out of the efficacy of an essence that furthermore realizes itself, on one occasion in another redness, but then also in warmth; as the thing side, it is isolated and could be compared neither with other colors of the same thing nor with the rednesses of other things, unless it already had, as the product of the disintegration of the symbolically already posited redness, the character of the general concept in its very state of arising. But its isolatedness nonetheless asserts itself in that henceforth its existence demands an efficient cause existing outside it, or (in the broadest sense of the word) a *causation*. The causes, again — this may only be indicated — soon divide themselves into the "dispositions" of the thing, to which they cling, and into other conditions of the development of the disposition. If we name among them, for example, light, then the findability of matter-of-fact light will of course again have to presuppose a symbolic "light" as already known; and this would in turn be one and the same something in those appearances that we derive from matter-of-fact light, and in that content of meaning which today only metaphorically the coupling-word "life's light" indicates. Had not, under the compulsion [p. 389] of elementary similarities, the soul lived-through and the still life-dependent spirit apprehended the characters of warmth, of color, of light, there would be no general concepts of warmth, color, light at all, and a matter-of-factly comparing thinking would never have arisen! We shall return to this in the 38th chapter. If, accordingly, essence-science investigation will in numerous cases effortlessly find its way back, by means of names, to the originally meant units of meaning, of which, in the depths of the word-meaning of all the languages of the earth, a remnant germ, however meager, has been preserved, there are yet far more concepts still whose object has lost every relation to the world of intuition, and entirely to the world of images. We called these, in the 11th chapter, poor in meaning, and refer to the evidence offered there. In particular it is the essence-concepts themselves that no longer have any place in the matter-of-facted totality, and are therefore never understood in the originally intuitive meanings that, in by far the most frequent cases, can be read off without further ado from their names — for which we have indeed again and again offered examples. It is precisely of these, accordingly, that a deeply penetrating essence-research can avail itself as the irresistible lever that uproots the whole of mechanistic thinking. For only from the primal actuality of the living totality can there be understood, it is true, also a mechanized totality, but not from the being of the mechanized totality — though we measure it by thousands of light-years — the tiniest living being!

Having thereby grounded more sharply than before why we can attribute the capacity to win metaphysical insights only to life-dependent symbolic thinking and by no means to life-detached matter-of-fact thinking, we do not wish, after our discussion, which in principle confines itself to units of meaning of a property-like kind, to pass entirely here already over the thing-like units of meaning, which in the narrower sense of the word are preferably called symbols, and which, far more even than those others, helped to entrench the conviction of the superstitious erroneousness of life-fettered thinking. For there is no doubt about this: that with the thing-like symbols too, there can be no talk whatever of similes! Because the serpent — *among* other things — coils into a ring, it was for the Pelasgian symbolist the cycle of life, whose sensible presence brought blessing to the house, recovery to the sick; because the bird, silently hastening away, presses into the farthest spaces, it was a "swarming" soul and a fateannouncing soul-messenger; [p. 390] because the meta sudans towers steeply upward and is moistly trickled over, it was phallic begetting-power, indeed a constantly life-renewing Gamos!

If we ask what, confronted with such facts, was the opinion of otherwise meritorious ethnologists of the second half of the last century, the answer runs: primitive man confused his representation of things (facts) with the things themselves. If we ask further what the currently best-approved opinion is, we come up against the same nonsense, altered, however, by an interpretive procedure that — drawn by average minds from *Nietzsche* and, as goes without saying, entirely distorted through adaptation to their own measure — merely somewhat worsens the matter: primitive man — as a kind of neurotic! — confused with the facts the images of his *wishes*.<sup>56</sup> If we recall the proverb according to which the wish is father to the thought, it becomes glaringly evident how the newest wisdom of diagnostic symbol-interpretation eks out its garrulous existence only from those stale remnants which the most life-thin and culture-less span of spirit's most recent past has left behind. When a few representatives of the currently, amid mockingly cheap clamor of renown, so much talked-of school fable, with fondness, following a coinage of Burckhardt's, about "primordial images," this is, in such mouths, entirely synonymous with — venerable tomfoolery. In the meantime, however, there was one man who, inheriting the profundity of Romanticism and in a certain way crowning it, at exactly the same time when the presumptuous doctrine of confusion was in full bloom, already possessed the key to the early world of the soul — without, however, making any other use of it than to thereby unlock that early world! We mean J. J. *Bachofen*, of whom detailed mention will be made in Volume III.

<sup>56</sup> On page 390. — A noteworthy exception is formed by the French sociological school of *Durkheim*, out of which arose the work of *Lévy*-*Bruhl* named in Note 21, Das Denken der Naturvölker. According to Lévy-Bruhl there exists, besides the logical, a "prelogical" state of mind, which — differing from the logical in kind and not merely in degree — persists alongside it and, in primeval times, governed the behavior of human beings to a great extent. The mere rejection of the belief in progress and of the doctrine of confusion has sufficed by itself to render the exceedingly manifold assemblage of rites, customs, institutions, symbols, linguistic peculiarities, and modes of apprehension of primitives considerably more interesting than the vast material, mastered almost only classificatorily, that a *Wundt* was able to set forth in his many-volumed "Völkerpsychologie"; but scarcely more interesting than the writings of, say, a *Tylor*. It is true that the latter is governed by the idea of animism and is thereby prevented from a deeper grasp of primitive phenomena, but he pursues with great consistency the power of intuitive images — which he places at the center — for the genesis of the units of meaning of original thinking. Lévy-Bruhl, by contrast, free of the constraint of the demand to hunt everywhere for logically transparent connections, and incomparably more supple in his interpretations, is nonetheless scarcely able to penetrate more deeply beneath the surfaces, because in place of solutions he presents us with a (partly new) posing of the problem, which he unfortunately confuses with an explanation. For the "prelogical" constitution of mind is supposed to come about through the individual taking over his thinking and striving as fundamentally pre-shaped by the group of human beings to which he belongs. Just as, accordingly, he becomes, with the whole of his lived experience, a mere instance and application-case of his group, so too he "participates" in the phenomena of nature around him, insofar as, in keeping with traditional tribal experience, they can have vital importance for him. In this way it comes down in the end to two concepts — the "collective representation" and the "mystical participation" — with the help of which the author undertakes to explain the direction of sense of primitives; an attempt that is carried out with wit and a wealth of supporting material. Now there is no doubt whatsoever that the manner of thinking and of behaving of any human being, today as formerly, is in some way co-dependent upon the manner of thinking and behaving of his time and his people; and this dependency is, in a certain respect whose closer characterization must be omitted here, greater for the primitive than for the bearer of civilization. Therein lies a problem, and to point it out has merit. But even granting that we had solved it completely, we would thereby still know not the slightest thing about the *genesis* of the manner of thinking and behaving in question. We would merely have shifted it from the individual to the tribe, without, however, being able to state whence it arose in the tribe! If, then, the "collective representations" cannot help us further, it must moreover not be passed over in silence that, with a doctrine that employs them for the purpose of explanation, the subjectivist mode of apprehension that had been rejected has, so to speak, crept back in by the back door. Whether one calls the so-called participations prelogical or mystical, they gain nothing in content of actuality from the circumstance that the experiences underlying them are common to all members of a clan. It is agreeable that Lévy-Bruhl holds a merely logical procedure to be insufficient to do them justice, but we are not told by what means of thought this is to take place, and least of all where the content of actuality of a mysticism is to be sought that, in his opinion, stands in contradiction with the most elementary requirements of logic. Here, before the discussions of our third volume, let the rejection be sent ahead of a view that has of late liked to appeal to Lévy-Bruhl, who himself, however, advocates it only in passing and with caution. To that stretch of mankind for which there existed spirits, demons, ancestors, and the like, there is supposed to have preceded, as the very most primitive stretch, one for which everything that fell within its field of vision would have been pervaded by a single mysterious substance connecting each thing with every other; of which the "wakanda," say, or "orenda" of the North American Indians, or the "mana" of the Melanesians, is offered as an example. We do not deny that the earliest groups attainable to us were capable of generalization to a far higher degree than is commonly assumed; but a *generalization* of this kind would be attainable only by a procedure of abstraction ; and *abstracta* are something the original human being does not know at all. The inner causes of the view in question are too transparent for it to be worth the trouble of examining the grounds by which one seeks to support it. The scholar of today is delighted by "mana" because in it, without noticing it, he rediscovers the — physical principle of energy! But behind that principle stands, viewed in terms of the history of the spirit, pantheism, and behind pantheism, — monotheism. — It would be wrong to wish to burden a Lévy-Bruhl in particular with the chief responsibility for the newest readiness of belief in *Codrington's* mana; but his "participation" in it already betrays the fact that one can advocate a "prelogical" without being rid of the presuppositions of intellectualism.

If it occurred, among the thinker-people of the Greeks, that one put a roof-tile on trial for having struck a man dead, or brought suit for murder against the axe with which the sacrificial animal had been killed, must we then truly imagine that those Greeks were unable to distinguish a stone or an axe from a living human being?! If the cruel but highly gifted Aztecs rendered burial honors to the wooden images of the drowned, are we seriously to believe that they had forgotten that they themselves had fashioned those images out of wood?! If the Chinese, whose philosophy and art we have no prospect of approaching even [p. 391] remotely, gave the dead paper replicas of his favorite possessions, indeed of his favorite dishes, into the grave, so that he should not lack his belongings in the realm of souls, are we foolish enough to imagine that one took paper oranges to be the very same thing as those grown on the tree?! And how now, if a pious Lutheran drinks of the wine of the communion chalice with the believing words in his heart: the wine is blood (namely, of the Redeemer), or the Catholic even swears to believe that the priest's gesture transforms the wine into blood — are the two, then, less simple-minded than those Greeks, Chinese, Aztecs?! One will forever break one's head over such questions in vain, and with all the talk about them merely waste lung-power or ink, so long as one does not have the key to the insight offered here: that there are two kinds of sameness — the conceptual, or *identity of matter*, and the symbolic, or identity of essence! But far more sharply even than with property-like ones can it be shown, with thing-like symbols, that their content of meaning rests on elementary similarity of images.

If we take as the simplest case the similarity between original and copy, it is evident: if, to a consciousness, the sameness of a soul appearing in both has become manifest out of the similarity of the two, then the knowledge of the duality of the objects stands no more in the way of the apprehension of this sameness than the difference between a steel-hard bar and glowing molten flow stands in the way of *our* apprehension of the iron identical in both! It is astonishing what objects and states of affairs we do not hesitate for a moment to hold to be identical, even where there is not the remotest possibility of comparing them intuitively. At bottom, this very astonishment gave rise to the so-called evolutionist theories of those biologists who believed they could explain the sprouting-up of the tree from the tiny seed-grain, and finally, more or less, of all animal living beings from the fertilized egg, only by supposing that the tree was already hidden in the tree-seed, the animal in the fertilized egg. A summer cumulus cloud, white powdery snow, and a clear solid piece of ice are, intuitively, as different as can be. Let one consider for a moment what sum of hypotheses was and is required in order that one may meaningfully believe that the three are, materially, nonetheless one and the same thing — water! But a further multiple of hypotheses is needed [p. 392] if it is to be conceivable that the transparent liquid named water is materially the same as the two invisible gases hydrogen and oxygen, or that the entire world of forms of the organically living "consists" essentially of the four "elements" carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen — of which each, with whatever animal or plant, shows not only no intuitive similarity but also no equality of any other property! Should it not, in view of this, seem far more natural to us that symbolic thinking posits the identical on the basis of similarities, and should we not then also have to consider whether there might not be a *direction* of thinking that permits such an identical to be *found* just as well, and probably more easily, than the other direction of thinking, to which we have become accustomed, permits, say, the finding of the hydrogen atom in countless states of affairs that are intuitively simply incomparable? We, to be sure, also bring to consciousness, from case to case, conceptually, what we wish to regard as identical, and have, with the supposedly identical, quite generally the thing in view, or the atom, in turn conceived thing-wise, whereas the bearer of symbolic thinking was not able, in like manner, to give an account that it was always the sameness of an essence that he rediscovered in similar intuitive images. But now that this has been ascertained by us, the possibility of symbolic truths is thereby demonstrated, and at the same time also the impossibility of warring against them with objections from the domain of matter-of-fact thinking. The plastic likeness, thingwise a piece of wood, can be the appearance of the soul of the original; the thingly wine, the appearance of the soul of blood — if, that is, they are indeed images in which, and in which alone, souls express themselves! He who comports himself in accordance with such thinking has not, it is true, judged the profound truth, but has lived through and practiced it, that the intuitive images of the world are the appearances of the souls of the world, and he thereby remains a hundred times in the right against our entire matter-of-fact science, as often as the latter, misunderstanding itself, pretends to want to explain even a single fact of life!

From the, so to speak, external case of the likeness, however, the similarity-reflection of image-thinking can rise just as well to higher generalities of essence and venture essencelinkages flashing through everything, as, out of cause-reflection, matter-of-fact thinking rises to ever poorer-in-meaning objects of thought, and in this way links together structures between [p. 393] which the gulf could no longer be spanned by any bridge of similarity. — Because the quartered moon has the shape of a little boat, it becomes the appearance of the soul of the ship; the ship, because it harbors all that is living within itself, becomes the appearance of the soul, on the one hand of the mother's womb, but then also, on the other, of the grave's darkness that again demands everything back: these few similarities, with which dozens of kindred ones cross — the sickle, for instance, with which one cuts grass, the winnowing-fan for grain, the cradle, and so on — would suffice to let us understand why, to the Egyptians, the crescent moon was the gondola of Isis, and to the Greeks the moon altogether the region of Persephone and the "element of souls" which, according to the statement of *Plutarch*, "are dissolved into it as the bodies of the dead into the earth." This did not exclude the same Greeks from philosophizing, alongside this, about the size and distance and materiality of that same moon, even though they were unable to keep apart, and to guard from mutual disturbance, image-service and fact-service. The two combat one another to this very day, and *had to* do so, ever since fact-service presumed to charge image-service either with devilry or with folly! Now, when for the first time its life-detachment and estrangement from actuality is unmasked by us, it is — too late. The earth drips with the heart's-blood of shattered and mutilated images, and the strangled souls wither away. — Over and above the possibility, in principle existing, that the elementary similarity of images might also emerge intuitively and could therefore be subsequently confirmed through matter-of-fact comparison, we must not, however, forget its derivation from a kinship of essence that is in and for itself non-intuitive. It is not the serially arranged succession of tonal qualities but, in the first place, the kinship-relation of the tone-characters that makes possible the comparison of their differences with the "rungs" of a "ladder." When many "nature-peoples" infer, from the similarity of a child to a deceased person, the return of the ancestral soul in question, or attest the greatest dread of having their likeness taken, because the possessor of the likeness gains power over the soul of the original, such examples reveal, together with the principle of intuitive similarity, at the same time the ground of its capacity for the creation of meaning, and we thus have no more occasion for astonishment that, for instance, in ancient China as also in India, identity of name counted as an impediment to marriage. For if it is indeed the soul that forms the features of a human being and [p. 394] reappears in the features of a similar human being, then it may well also be the soul that expresses itself in the name of the human being and reappears in all identical and many similar names. The essential kinship of two twins from intuitive similarity need not be any greater than the wholly non-intuitive kinship of a thing with its name!

Hard by symbolic truth lies symbolic error; but hard by logical truth, too, lies logical error. There *is* genuine "superstition" in abundant fullness, yet it vanishes like a light haze beside the knotty, tenacious phantasms out of the history of the understanding! The wisdom of image-service turns into the delusion of ghost-belief as soon as it degrades its actualities into things; but the acuity of fact-service perverts itself into soul-denying dullness whenever it screws its units of calculation up into — actualities! Let one ask oneself what, on both sides, is the rule and what the exception, and one will know from which side the greater horrors threaten.

[p. 395]

#### 37. Kapitel — Die Vergesellschaftungsmechanik — Chapter 37 — The Mechanics of Association

The only large-scale attempt of thinking hitherto to pursue what, if we may put it so, is a sub-spiritual science of the soul, has had the tragic, or rather tragicomic, fate of perishing already in its very state of arising, through its downright fatal self-surrender to the mechanics of association still dominant today. After the critique, at once cogent and annihilating, of what he aptly called "association-scholasticism," by a Palágyi in his "Naturphilosophische Vorlesungen," it would be storming open doors were we to begin the refutation all over again from the start. For Palágyi has demonstrated, with irrefutable grounds: first, that the assertion of the existence of the associations in question at best designates a problem, but by no means solves it, so long as it does not even lead to the question of what links the associated contents together; second, and above all, that the customary "factors of association" are simply invented on the basis of a logical comparison of the objects of experience. "If one knows that the representation a has associated itself with the representation b, one can begin to speculate about what logical relation the two representations stand in to one another; for some kind of logical relation must, after all, in any case be establishable between two representations. One will enumerate all the possible categories of relation that could obtain between two representations, and will then be able to be certain that, as soon as two representations x and y are spoken of, one will always find some category-box in which the pair of representations can be accommodated. Hume constructs three such category-boxes, other thinkers construct four of them, James Mill strove to replace them with a single box" (loc. cit. II, pp. 199–200). To this, in a merely critical intent, scarcely anything more would need to be added. Since, however, we do not so much wish to dissolve the customary mechanics of association [p. 396] as rather to win, from its dissolution, further facts for the confirmation of our own view, we bring forward, on the presupposition of what has just been heard, another inadequacy into the foreground, and to that end first assemble, from the bestnamed "psychologies" of the present, a motley series of examples of the application of the mechanistic doctrine of association.<sup>57</sup>

<sup>57</sup> On page 396. — The very *name* "Vergesellschaftung," or, as it has now become naturalized, "Assoziation," is by no means an accident either; but it *alone* would of course give *no* occasion for objection, provided only that one meant something tenable by it — as we ourselves have indeed spoken of a "consorting" of intuitive images! — The examples given below for so-called associations are, be it noted in passing, taken not from this or that psychological camp-follower, but from the works of the following authors: *Wundt*, *Lipps*, *James*, *Ebbinghaus*.

The following occurrences — among others — are customarily derived by their proponents from the association, whether of psychic or of brain processes: 1) the thinking, or even the uttering, of the words "through night and wind," as often as one heard spoken the words "Who rides so late" — 2) the expectation of a thunderstorm when the sky clouds over — 3) the expectation of warmth when the hand approaches the flame — 4) the tendency to link rhyming words such as "hound" and "bound" — 5) the tendency to link words of opposite meaning such as

"mountain" and "valley" — 6) the linking of the property with the thing to which it belongs — 7) the linking of a thing with the name of the thing — 8) the linking of a name with the representation of the named

thing — 9) the linking of a sound with the written character for it — 10) recognition — 11) remembering — 12) the ability to recognize, in a drawing, the object represented — 13) the ability to estimate distance with the help of the sense of sight — 14) the visibility of the roughness of a surface — 15) the joining of simultaneous tones into sounds, consonances, noises —.

⁠16) the compulsion to think a tone as afflicted with temporal duration — 17) the combining of supposedly simple feelings into affects, passions, and so on — 18) the disposition, on hearing a song, to carry out rhythmic movements. We could, instead of the above 18, just as well have gathered together 180, indeed, with sufficient patience in collecting and subdividing, perhaps even 1800 occurrences [p. 397], which according to the customary view would, one and all, be brought about by "association." But we think our more modest series already suffices to entrench the conviction that in the word "association" one possesses a magic formula that explains no more and no less than — everything! It is not to be seen why one should not transfer it at once to the external world as well, and thus, say, to the question why the moon revolves around the earth, answer curtly: out of association! Far worse, however, than the confusion of a mere naming with an explanation is the circumstance that, being thus baptized with the same name and hence taken to be in need of the same explanation, states of affairs are coupled together that in part have no more to do with one another than the revolution of the moon around the earth has to do with the association of two simultaneous impressions.

In the painted orange I believe I see a likeness of the actual orange (Case 12); but has there ever been a mentally sound human being who took lightning for a likeness of thunder, because on perceiving the lightning he expected to hear the thunder?! (Case 2 and 1). If, then, we wished to call the condition of such expectation an association of representations, we would *not* be permitted to call the condition of the recognizability of the thing in the likeness of the thing by the same name! The warmth that I expect to feel when my hand approaches a flame (Case 3) is a property of the flame; but thunder is no property of lightning; consequently, again, it can *not* be an association of representations that occasions us to relate properties of the thing to the thing (Case 6), *supposing* that the sequence "lightning and thunder" were indeed such a case. As for the recognition of a speech-sound intelligible to us (Case 8) or of a written character intelligible to us (Case 9), their meanings are *inherent* in the sensible states of affairs as their signs, in such a way indeed that it is only with the help of the sense that we understand the signs in question at all. But thunder is not inherent in lightning; the latter is at most a forewarning-sign, by no means, however, a sign of thunder, and is therefore recognized out of itself and not first *by virtue* of thunder! To this we add: *after* man has created for himself a fixed sign-language for all the units of meaning he was able to apprehend, he simply apprehends nothing further except with the help of some sign or other for it (Case 7). If I recognize an animal as a dog, this occurs by means of the word "dog" (or an equivalent [p. 398] sign); if I do not indeed recognize the dog, but yet an animal, then precisely by means of the word "animal," or also the word-combination "unknown animal"; if finally I perceive something wholly unknown to me, then by means of the word "something," or also "something unknown to me." We have thus far already the following fundamentally different groups of process: I. Habitual sequence of intuitive units of meaning — II. Linking of properties into the sum of properties of the

thing — III. Recognition of the thing in the likeness of the thing — IV. Recognition of the sign through apprehension of its meaning — V. Apprehension of a state of affairs with the help of the sign for it.

Whoever's power of judgment is not yet hopelessly and utterly wrecked by the doctrine of association must recognize that its application called into life a *system* of *confusions* that will probably stand unique, in the previous history of thinking, in the extent of its devastating consequences for the formation of knowledge. — But whereas, now, despite all fundamental differences, the above five groups agree at least in the presence, in each case, of two distinguishable states of affairs, there lies before us even only a single state of affairs when, with one glance into the landscape, we also perceive the distance between the nearer tree and the more distant house (Case 13), or perceive with the sense of sight the roughness of a surface (Case 14). If one calls in, say, the position of the eyeaxes, the movements of the eye, the so-called inner tactile sensations, and so on, to explain the perception of distance, or, to explain the perception with the eyes of the roughness of a surface, some experiences of touching by contact, these are in both cases processes of lived experience that were either merely inferred, or else, in exceptional cases, become accessible only to an observation expressly aimed at them — in no case, however, impression-contents to be co-ordinated alongside the impression of distance or the impression of roughness. The equating of the arising of an impression with the stringing-together of ready-made impressions through association may give us a concept of the degree to which the science of life hitherto is merely a mechanics that misconstrues itself, and how little illumination one may expect from it even of the most elementary traits of lived experience.

[p. 399] After these samples we may leave it to the reader to think through the remaining ones of the 18 enumerated occurrences and to furnish, batch by batch, further evidence for the masterly aptitude of the non-concept of association for erasing differences! — We turn once more to the five twomembered groups and establish that only the first of them has the air of a linking of two independent states of affairs, whereas in all the others there are present, of one single state of affairs, two distinct sides, which, regardless of ever so great differences of connection, stand to one another in a relation of mutual *interpenetration*. If we take as the model for the relation of interpenetration the connection of the thing with its properties, and provisionally name, with "association," the condition of the involuntary stringing-together of meaning-determined intuitive contents, then we have — apart from a single fundamental exception, to be discussed further below — above all to set against the boundless mechanics of association the bulwark of the proposition that through mere consorting of impression-contents matter-of-fact units of meaning never arise. Thing and property of the thing interpenetrate one another; but the intuitive contents named lightning and thunder, associated out of the experienced frequency of their succession, do not interpenetrate one another, and remain, notwithstanding their temporal neighborhood, in strictly separate independence. Exactly the same holds, of course, for all associations that one is pleased to trace back to matter-of-fact simultaneity or spatial juxtaposition. Whoever fell in love for the first time in his life, at a dancing lesson, to the strains of a waltz, will not, even as a man of fifty, hear this melody without at once being reminded of the figure, the bearing, the eyes, and so on, of a girl; but for all that the melody remains melody and the girl's figure remains the girl's figure, and there does not exist even the remotest possibility that the two might ever fuse into a new whole, comparable to the whole that each of them is in itself!

Following upon a critique of the mechanics of association, we are not dealing with the life-foundations of animal and human units of meaning that we have already largely uncovered, but we may not pass over the question of how, then, from the standpoint of our doctrine, those undeniably existing seriations of content present themselves which, in relation to the character of necessity of the essence-dependent [p. 400] connections, bear the character of contingency. Before we enter upon this, we once more make plain, with the utmost sharpness, the fundamental difference between the previous manner of research and our life-scientific one. — Modern psychology stands under the spell of English "naturalism," which raised the interchanging of consciousness and lived experience to a principle. It has instilled in us a conception of living processes which — entirely led on a leash by the model of the conception of things — issues in a quantifying atomism. It reports of "simultaneous" and "successive" impressions, quite as one indeed rightly speaks of the juxtaposition and succession of things in space. It counts and measures its "psychic structures" just as one may ever only count and measure to compare things in space. It observes and notes the coming and going of "contents of consciousness" as the astronomer, say, notes the transit of a star across the crosshairs; and it therefore *had to* exchange, for vital connections, the matter-of-fact relations of that which, by virtue of them, "came to consciousness." Thus it brought about such peculiar "laws" as that it is the matter-of-fact simultaneity of apprehended things and processes, or their matter-of-fact similarity, that effects all manner of linkages in the soul. It made, drastically and not without an ulterior motive, the child into the cause of the sexual drive, and along with it, say, even the joys of family life, and it did so in a language that seems taken from business life, where indeed a few people likewise sometimes "associate themselves" for the realization of an idea of gain.

As against this, we must first of all hold fast to the fact that even all thing-units that one thinks of as associated cannot be identical with lived impression-contents, and were accordingly extracted only subsequently, out of the connections of image-elements and image-sequences, through the dissecting labor of conceiving thinking. However little the thing-positing thinking could dispense with already-lived units of meaning before it, these nonetheless concern the kinship and conflict of living essences. To the intuitive image of a figure that delights me there also belongs the beautiful garment with which it is clothed. If, then, I objectifyingly separate figure and garment from one another, it is an original connection, comparable to "warm red," and by no means something linked through simultaneity that the dissecting art of spirit had cut apart into two facts. Every successful painting, [p. 401] every successful building, every successful inscription of a book, every chord, every melody gives me, thanks to its unitary distinctive character, in each case a whole, in relation to which only the subsequent procedure of dissection ascertains parts and sides upon it. A net I can regard thingwise in two ways: on the one hand as a net, on the other as a jumble of cords; but even the wide-meshed net, so long only as it really is what the name means, offers itself intuitively as a network, and opens to symbolic thinking essence-related series, on the one hand in the direction of an untold number of web-like image-forms, whence "street network," the retina of the eye, the mesentery; on the other hand toward countless activities of catching as well as occurrences of entangling oneself, whence turns of phrase such as: to draw someone into one's nets, to set snares for him, to become caught in one's own net.

With this, however, it has already become manifest that, in principle, what is thought as linked, in whatever sense, never stands in need of an explanation; rather, what does is the inner compulsion by virtue of which what belongs together of itself and thus inwardly, and what is merely outwardly co-present, seem to us to fall apart — within which, again, the occurrences provisionally to be called "chance-linkages" stand out in particular. Fixing our eye, for the present, on these alone, we aim at answering the question of what, within the impression-image itself, occasions the distinguishing of independent units of meaning from contingencies of their consorting. Before, however, we approach this target question more closely, we recall once more the corresponding opposite one. — We had found the weaving power of everything belonging together, whether by kinship or by opposition, in the efficacy of essences that appear in the intuitive images. But if, demonstrably, impression-contents link themselves with one another between which, as for instance between the waltz-melody and a girl's figure, no relations of meaning obtain, either out of similarity or out of opposition, must we not then assume a second power, entirely different from the previous one, in order to explain such things? And if perhaps not, how then would that one and single power bring into connection both what belongs together and what in no way belongs together? So we would then have two questions, of which the one, however, forms only the reverse side of the other — wherefore we shall have answered both if we should succeed in answering one of them.

As certainly as no essential connection [p. 402] of simultaneously occurring events could be derived from the concept of simultaneity, just as certainly does such a connection nonetheless exist once we go back to the vital point of origin of the thought of simultaneity. The mathematical concept of the time-point would never have arisen without the empirical concept of the now, and the empirical concept of the now would never have arisen without the lived experience of the now, whose intuitive substratum, as has been shown, must be sought in sense-space. If we now call empirically simultaneous all events that supposedly or actually take place in the empirical now, then everything simultaneously occurring that becomes intuitive to us inescapably partakes of the image of sense-space, in such a way that no mood of our wakingly conscious state of life can be conceived that is not underlaid by the intuitive image of the spatiality surrounding us. (This holds, as is self-evident, in principle also for the blind, however much their spatial intuition may diverge from that of the sighted.) I can recollect no joy or grief or despair without corecollecting a locality at which I actually lingered while the emotion in question was occurring, or which I am compelled to imagine in connection with it; and I would simply have "lost from memory" a feeling once suffered, given a total loss of the capacity to assign it to some locality.
