Likewise, of course, the mood-color of the bearer of life at the time of the thought-process, and consequently the locality underlying it, belongs to every thought-experience as well, and we would again lack the capacity to know when we thought this or that, were we not able at least vaguely to associate the time-point<sup>58</sup> with a locality — say, this or that city. Thanks to their inescapable participation in the image of intuitive space, empirically simultaneous psychic processes, insofar as they depend on occasions of impression, are — however strange it may sound — clamped together by a trait of similarity and belong to a context of actuality which, to be sure, as everyone sees, could never take part in the construction of the thing, and which, to the extent that a perceptual activity oriented toward the thing predominates, yields the field, as comparatively accidental, to the intuitive images that permit exploitation in the service of factual thinking. We soon convince ourselves, however, that the kinship of essence thereby indicated must gain, and indeed does gain, in significance for the predominantly appearance-oriented thinking of primeval times — But there is something more to add to this.

<sup>58</sup> On page 402. — Let it be noted that we are speaking here of the recollection of the former *emergence* of a thought, and not of the recollection of the thought itself. The latter, anchored as it is in linguistic form, can rest upon the spoken word, or upon the written word, or, for instance, upon a page-image that resounds again, and so forth.

[p. 403] Every moment of lived experience belongs to the stream of lived experience; every turning-point of lived experience belongs, moreover, to the sequence of vital mirrorings; hence, as was emphasized earlier, two different contexts cross in the experience of impression. If we transfer the sense of the river-bed metaphor to the substance of life, we arrive at the image of the wrinkle or trace or notch engraved into it by every impression, which brings it about, for instance, that new impressions become familiar ones. The most cursory reflection teaches us the necessity of constant alteration in every trace or fold — partly because the substance of life is never at a standstill in its growth and withering, partly because ever new little folds overlie, bend, and blur the earlier ones. Habits form, stiffen, and are lost; what has been practiced is unlearned again after a long interruption of practice; recognitions founded on experience grow uncertain if not tested for a long time, until they finally sink down into the night of an all-effacing forgetfulness. But if the moment of appearance is thus rooted in the entire prehistory of the bearer of life, then the shaping of the images of impression must at least co-depend upon that prehistory — of which we most readily convince ourselves in the case of images of recollection. — The consciousness of pastness, inseparable from the image of recollection, is, more precisely, the consciousness of a temporal distance between the phantasm of recollection and the impression of the present — in short, of a temporal extension backward, whose magnitude, however, is now measured by the fullness and manifoldness of the impressions experienced in the interim, and thereby bears the stamp of a magnitude-character. A week rich in "experiences" seems, in retrospect, to stretch to the length of months, while one laden with trivialities — regardless of the "tedium" *during* its occurrence — seems to have elapsed with the swiftness of hours. Just as visual impressions carry marks of spatial depth, so do images of recollection carry marks of temporal depth, and both are found incorporated into the opposites of extreme nearness and extreme distance.

Not only is night an essence, polar-opposite to the essence of day, but distance too is one, and nearness, its polar opposite. Already for animals, the greater nearness separates itself from the lesser according to a difference of character; but for man, capable of beholding-into-the-distance and gifted with recollection, all contents of lived experience are, among other things, deposited between two poles which come to appearance in the intuitive opposition of *spatial* nearness and spatial distance. [p. 404] If, accordingly, all images of the character of temporal nearness stand polarly opposed to those of the character of temporal distance, then it is thereby already expressed that everything participating in the near-character, as also everything participating in the far-character, closes together group-wise. Just as it is a shared appearance-space common to them all that can connect empirically simultaneous life-processes with one another, however great their differences of significance may otherwise be, so, conversely, it is their space-analogous relation of distance to immediate sense-space on which the elective affinity of phantasms with impressions in part depends. If, for example, spatial breadth and spatial distance set the tone in the image of impression, because the soul is, say, held fast by the horizon or the starry sky, then there exists a greater kinship of essence between the impressions and phantasms of distance-in-the-past than of nearness-in-the-past, and conversely with the latter in the bustle and street-noise of a small town. Whoever now once more surveys our earlier assembled series of symbolic names for spatial properties will not only be convinced of the predominant significance of intuitive space for the apprehension of essence as such, but will also readily recognize clearly distinguished circles of kinship, by which the preferential directions of connecting are determined.<sup>59</sup>

<sup>59</sup> On page 404. — It would indeed be grotesque, yet perhaps not impossible, that this or that reader might object to us: in ascribing to sense-space a linking power, we would — merely in a somewhat different guise — have let the rejected "contiguity-association" back in by the back door! Let such a possibility, then, be forestalled by the following (partly recapitulating) lines. The mechanics of association speaks of objects in general, of things and their properties in particular. It breaks things down into parts and aspects, and likewise the side-by-sideness and succession of things, and lets the products of this breaking-down correspond now to psychical processes, now expressly to facts of consciousness. If now, it further concludes, the object of perception A, which earlier formed a part or an aspect of the object of perception B, occurs again, or at least an object of perception A' similar to it, then the soul — *or* the brain! — "reproduces" the remainder that does not occur, thus completing the A' into B. The yellow color of the orange, say, was perceived together with the scent of the orange; if one now, on another occasion, smells the scent of orange, one thinks of the yellow color of the orange, or indeed straightaway of the orange itself. That, in essence, is the main point. Besides this, there is dispute about countless variants, which it would be idle to mention, because the fundamental error remains always the same. By contrast, we speak of contents of lived experience in general, of intuitive images in particular. We deny that a patchwork labor of the soul is needed to bring them forth. We know no "reproductions," but only original processes of fantasy. We see the grouping power, if one may say so, in the kinship and conflict of essences as they appear, and we had only one thing to explain: how it is that even such consortings as, from the standpoint of factual thinking, possess the character of contingency, become intelligible from kinship of essence. To this end we called to mind sense-space as an accessory of *all* intuitive images (as likewise of all feelings!), which participates in the appearance of essence, and indeed without exception. That one can, as goes without saying, also set factual simultaneity and factual succession into conceptual relation *to* sense-space, has as much — that is, as little — to do with its capacity to accomplish psychical linkings as if one were to regard it, say, as the concrete point of departure for Euclidean space! If someone, on thinking of fried fish, at once thinks of white wine, he does so because a total image lights up (or is on the point of lighting up) , to which both the wine and the fish belong, or else because a sense-spatial locality embraces both the wine and the fish and thereby makes both, so to speak, into data of the appearance of a mood-character that would not be what it is without the participation of both in *one and the same* intuitive image. The said "mood-character" is the band linking the two, and this very mood-character is at the same time the character of a sense-spatial locality. Once one knows this, one can at once state why our epicure thinks precisely of white wine. Factually simultaneous would also be, say, a white tablecloth, plates, knives and forks, and whatever else besides; and indeed it *can* happen that, from the thought of fried fish, another person feels moved to pass over to the thought of plate and knife and fork. That signifies that these belong, quite essentially, to *his* image. If, by contrast, for the epicure the second accent lies on the white wine, then it is quite evidently tastephantasms that have determined, for *him*, the character of the intuitive image! — To what extent all this can also be regarded from the standpoint of "feeling-emphases" will be discussed further in what follows. Here, however, let a remark anticipating that discussion be permitted. The "appearing essence," as is set forth further in the main text, is now predominantly the essence of the intuitive image *itself*, now predominantly carried *into* it out of the soul of the one who lives through the situation. But whether it behaves in the one way or the other, the linking power lies in the essence of the image, or — adapting to present-day usage — in the "mood-character" of the image, and only to that extent, admittedly, always also in the feelings of the one experiencing it, insofar as feelings *wholly* without image-content do not exist at all. To think anything of the kind was impossible for the generation of researchers around 1890 (and is even today still something essentially unknown). Apart from that, however, among those men from whose works we have drawn our examples of "associations," none stood nearer the truth in this regard than *Lipps*. For he teaches: 1. All associations are ones of similarity, or rather of sameness-in-kind (against which Ebbinghaus argues with choicely foolish specious grounds). 2. This samenessin-kind refers to "psychical processes" and only secondarily to "experiences of consciousness." 3. Their efficacy increases with the increase of agreement of "the total essence of the psychical processes," and this regardless of whether and how far that essence expresses itself in the "content" (namely of consciousness) (Leitfaden der Psychologie, III, pp. 92–93). To be sure, something other is meant by all this than what we mean. "Sameness-in-kind" is likewise read off by him from aspects and parts of the objects of thought; the "psychical processes" are constructed after the fashion of physical forces and stand to the "experiences of consciousness" (which do not exist at all!) roughly as weight stands to the acceleration of a falling body, and "essence" is the so-called affective character. Consequently his conception, too, is erroneous. Notwithstanding this, it is a conception with which, covertly, the *turning-away* from the whole mechanics of association is being prepared, little as Lipps, with his mistaken concept of "experiences of consciousness," was able to manifest that turning-away. The polemic of the others against him proves it! In that he posits the decisive factor in the "sameness-in-kind of psychical processes," he is on the point of leaving the ground of associationist psychology. Finally, let the animal faculty of cognition be illuminated once more here, of which we treated in Chapter 34 and above all in Chapter 35. — The animal's faculty of impression reaches exactly as far as the animal's faculty of self-movement, and the *consorting* of impression-contents reaches exactly as far as the faculty of impression. This is now commonly called "associative memory," and it manifests itself according to the following experiment, which has become famous and can count as a model for countless experiments of a similar kind. Certain crabs, which normally always seek out the light, were lured in an aquarium into the darkness of a shading screen by placing there fish-flesh, which serves them as food. Whereas on the first day of the experiment, of 30 crabs, only 3 went under the screen in the course of 15 minutes, on the eighth day of the experiment, of 29 crabs , no fewer than 28 were already to be found under the screen after 5 minutes. If one now set up the screen *without* the food, the crabs continued to seek out the shade, to such a degree that on the thirteenth day, of 27 crabs, after 5 minutes 25 still did as before, and had thus become "negatively phototropic" (= light-fleeing), as the designation, as learned as it is misleading, is wont to run. In reality, no "associations" whatsoever take place here, any more than in man, but rather it is impression-memory that governs. From the moment of the first discovery of the fish-flesh onward, the shadow of the screen belongs to the intuitive image lived through, more precisely to the situation-character of the taking of food, and it is only we who separate, in thought, shadow and fish-flesh. The alluring force therefore adheres, in what follows, no less to the shadow than to the fish-flesh. But just as certainly it will again be lost after some time; for when the crab repeatedly no longer finds the food in the shade, the situation-character changes from an alluring one into an indifferent one, in accordance with which the shadow, too, then loses its power of attraction. Pavlov's experiments on dogs are too well known for us to need to repeat them or to demonstrate specially their belonging to the same mode of behavior. But even if we descend as far down as the region of starfish, we encounter exactly the same state of affairs. Impression-memory is fundamentally the same from the protist up to man, and it is only in two respects that vast differences show themselves: first, between man and animal in general, in that in human impression-memory the contents of sensation are always dominated by the contents of intuition, in the animal the reverse; and second, among the animal species, according to the extraordinarily varying degrees of participation of intuitive images. In keeping with the former state of affairs, no animal lives in the world, familiar to us, of embodiments of properties that we call things — for which let there stand here yet another example, no less famous than the experiment with the crabs. The dragonfly feeds, among other things, on mosquitoes, which, being one of the most agile fliers among animals, it is able to catch in a flash. But this same dragonfly starves to death if shut up in a gauze cage on whose inner walls flies and mosquitoes are crawling about. It thus does not even know what we call a fly or a mosquito, notwithstanding that both serve it as food; rather, it is invariably related to the intuitive image of *hovering* flies and mosquitoes, in such a way that the intuitive data form only the nonautonomous occasioning ground of tonic *tensions* and "virtual movements" of its bodily nature, in consequence of which it instantly prepares itself for the hunt! — As for the second-named state of affairs, the difference of degree in the participation of beholding in the behavior of animals, the crabs already mentioned, for instance, already possess visual capacity, whereas countless protists possess only light-sensitivity. If we now, beginning with ourselves, let visual capacity decrease and light-sensitivity (relatively) increase as we proceed through the animal species, we pass more and more out of worlds relatively characterized by intuition and into worlds of mere differences of intensity, which, to be sure, likewise already bear the character of an outside, but of an outside step by step more weakly estranged. If we now think back to the bee returning home to its hive from a distance of kilometers, we shall no longer wonder that it, transported onto a lake, loses its power of orientation; for the new situation-character is *fundamentally* different from all the situation-characters it has experienced on land. Almost everything that belongs to *its* sense-space is now lacking: the scents of blossoms and the accustomed chemisms, the colors of blossoms, as well as all the impression-images familiar to it — whether it can see distinctly for two meters or even for as much as twenty! Even if it *had*, moreover, a sense of direction, it would still have to fall into confusion, because its image of the world, unlike that of birds, is an image of *very great* nearness, and consequently its relation, on the lake, to its image on land is roughly similar to the relation, for man, of the world that would present itself to him if he suddenly found himself transposed into the zone of gravitational equilibrium between moon and earth, as against the accustomed outer world of the planet earth!

We conclude our critique of the mechanics of association with a reference to a psychic state of affairs that has forced itself upon reflection since the earliest times, and that plays now a greater, now a lesser role in the particular formulations of the doctrine of association — we mean the abruptness of what are therefore called "sudden ideas." — In accordance with the flowing nature of lived experience, and with the pendulum-movement that immediately underlies reflection, consciousness is never able to linger on any given object for longer than a single moment, and is, so to speak, ceaselessly engaged in a wandering that moves ever new and again new objects, step by step, into its "focal point." Just as thus the mere apprehension of contents of impression might already be compared to the flaring-up of a ray whose connection with the preceding and the following ray at first remains hidden from us, so too does the association of meaning-filling phantasms take place suddenly and by leaps, even embroidering our purposive thinking again and again with all manner of sudden ideas, "intuitions," and notations, whose origin is now easier, now more difficult, and sometimes not at all to be ascertained. The difficulty of exhibiting the connection, and the impossibility [p. 405] of calculating it in advance, is grounded in the unsurveyable variation of the conditions that determine, from moment to moment, the drawing-power of the phantasms, since now a kinship of essence between appearances (in the narrower sense), now merely their sharing in the same near- or far-character owing to the prehistory of the recipient of the impression, tips the scale. The connection darkens completely and lets the sudden idea appear in the light of a mysterious "inspiration" when the phantasm entering consciousness forms the final link of a more or less long series of intermediate links, none of which became conscious. Someone catches sight of a fruit-bowl of hammered copper, and instantly the word "Syndetikon" occurs to him, without his even guessing its meaning: neither that it had once been rendered for him in German as "fish-glue," nor had he noticed the fish in the bowl's ornamentation! Because the relatively little-steered movement of thought follows the pulsing of the soul more willingly, it is by no means rare that it is precisely this movement that grants us flashes of discovering insight.

If the mechanics of association treats its other motives of connection by analogy with those of so-called contiguity, or, consistently, holds contiguity alone sufficient to underpin even the origin of, say, concepts of things, it does so out of the hidden compulsion to think psychic "structures," after the manner of things, as added together out of atoms; hence one must again and again remind it of the fundamental difference between the merely accidental separable juxtaposition of images that happen to meet, and the relation of interpenetration that obtains, for instance, between a thing and its properties. If, on the other hand, symbolic thinking rather let every juxtaposition and succession be woven, conversely, from the same necessity of happening as the original images themselves, then, in view of the kinship of essence we have demonstrated even among all merely coinciding impressions — arising, namely, from participation in the very same near-character — we shall not fail to recognize in this a trait of surprising profundity, provided only that we keep before our eyes that "accidents" occur solely in opposition to conceived lawful regularities, and hence only in the world of facts (causes), but not at all in the actuality of images.

We left it undecided above, in the case of Thales, whether he held night to be a thing or all things to be essences. On the ground of symbolic thinking the question would be decided, and we would no longer have [p. 406] any criterion at all for distinguishing what merely represents subjective compulsions to *us* from objective necessities! That in the Pythagorean rule "Do not pluck apart the garland" an essence was meant by the garland, we can still relive today as soon as we think of the bridal garland or the victor's garland; but that, for instance, in the other rule "Do not turn back from the journey" even the journey was an essence is already far harder for us to understand; and yet we too command a thousand turns of phrase that presuppose the essence-character of analogous states of affairs, as when we speak of "wings of song," or breathe the strongest pathos into the mere passage of time with the phrase "the years flee." But if the journey was an essence, then a side of it, or a sub-essence, was also the day and hour of departure, as well as much, and in the end everything, that met the traveler on the journey. We today would hold the opposition of the east point to the west point to be an objective one, that of the right side to the left a subjective one; in the intuitive image of the world, however, both polarities stand fundamentally on the same line, and if there is an essence of the east, say, as opposed to the essence of the west, then no less is there an essence of the right side as opposed to the essence of the left — of which, again, language has preserved the memory for us in the value-superiority of the right, insofar as from it came the correct (das Richtige), over the left and its — leftishness (Linkischkeit); hence it was only consistent when a Pythagorean wayfarer at a fork in the road preferred, say, the road to the right hand, and carefully noted whether a significant bird crossed his path from the right or from the left. Here we see intuitive space grasped from the standpoint of a weaving and working essence whose significance stands on equal footing beside the consequent appearances of things, and happening itself grasped from the standpoint of a necessity within which no room is left any longer for the inessential.

Let it only be recalled in passing that units of meaning can thereby arise that are incomprehensible to factual thinking, although they reach in massed numbers into the present. As we shall investigate more closely in Volume III, the ethnographer again and again encounters, among primitive peoples, the fact that the distinction of certain tribes is shared in by the difference between the eastern and the western direction of the sky, indeed by the diversity of the landscapes they inhabit. But we too still speak, with reference to peoples, of Orientals and Occidentals! [p. 407] Now if the appearance-space of landscape A undoubtedly diverges likewise from the appearance-space of landscape B, while nonetheless beingoutside-one-another is common to both, then the appearance-spaces acquire place-accents capable of communicating themselves to the objects entering into them, down to the least particulars. The same sign can mean something different on a pole than on a stone, and again something different on the pole in the house than on the pole in the temple, something different on profane ground than on consecrated ground (Spencer). Thereby, seen from the standpoint of factuality, what is identical is continually posited as non-identical, and conversely. But even today, in believing strata of Catholic peoples, the Mother of God at Maria Zell is a different one from that at Maria Schutz, and again a different one from that at Maria Wörth — notwithstanding that by no means is belief held in *several* Mothers of God!

Applied to what we call accidents, the necessity of happening becomes fate or doom (Moira, Ananke, Heimarmene). The investigation of causes has never calculated fate and never will calculate it; the investigation of essence has never ascertained causes and would misunderstand itself were it nonetheless to give the appearance of doing so. Instead, however, it early on already built up a science of chance, and believed it had discovered numerous omens. But even if the inspection of entrails, the interpretation of bird-flight, horoscopy, and so forth, were nothing but systems of errors, that would still not prove the fundamental erroneousness of an impulse which, raised into consciousness, signifies the belief in the necessity of every intuitive image of the world. The Christian distortion, to be sure, in particular of the astral image-cult into the "astra inclinant, neque tamen necessitant," marks only the prelude to the, admittedly impossible, attempt of modern-day glossers of the misunderstood symbolisms of antiquity to unravel connections of essence into causal relations! Astra necessitant: only not in the sense that by means of gravitation and light and other "forces" they determine the course of life of Paul or Peter!

But let us leave aside the, here still questionable, background of a possible connection of essence among all the images of the cosmos, and ask what would first have to be ascertained, with regard to connections arising from temporal neighborhood, as to what other, intersecting compulsion moves us to attribute to a determinate kind of occurrence the factual significance of the being-effected of the consequent member by the [p. 408] initial member. Since, ever since *Hume's* misleading interchange of causality with frequency of succession, however great the readiness to reject it, no fundamental insight into its presupposition has yet been achieved — namely, the confusion of units of intuition with things — the concept of cause lies, to this very day, in an almost impenetrable fog, which we can only undertake to clear away later. Let us then remain, for now, with connections of chance in the narrower sense: their actual occurrence would depend, in each case, on the receptivity of the recipient, this in turn partly on his character, partly on his prehistory; from which would result a modest usefulness of the connections in question for the investigation of characters and their fates.

Whoever, on hearing a bang, even a distant one, thinks at once of danger and of his own personal safety, is more than ordinarily fearful. Whoever, when a furious bull charges, cannot help admiring, despite the perhaps genuinely threatening danger, the irresistible force in the bearing and movement of the animal, probably has an artistic sense, and so on. If a seven-year-old child breaks into a crying fit as soon as a match is struck before its eyes, one may be sure that it was once badly frightened by a fire that broke out suddenly close at hand (trauma). The calling-out of so-called stimulus-words for the purpose of tracking down psychic "complexes," however, given the unsurveyable manifoldness of the motives of connection, will never get beyond the level of a perhaps entertaining parlor game, and the expectations once tied to it for criminology have grown ever more modest.

Since the doctrine of feelings will be treated only later, we confine ourselves for now to the preliminary remark that we, in contrast to all opinions currently in circulation, ascribe to feelings no *producing* power whatever over the course of life-processes, but see in them, rather, by far the most important indications of everything occurring inwardly. If, for example, someone were to suffer for years from a morbid fear of water because as a child he had once nearly drowned, we would see in the deadly fright that is usually held responsible for this merely the sign of a disturbance of equilibrium among the drives, arising from the overemphasized efficacy of a single one of them for the shaping of impressions — by which, then, the study of occasion would bend back *too* into the study of character. [p. 409] In particular we do *not* mean that it is intelligible as a self-sufficient sovereignty of some feeling or other, when the "high tone" acquires an "affective character" the same as the above of space; rather we mean that both, the high tone and the above of space, can acquire that affective character (not must, and in fact do so, in each case, to a different degree from person to person), insofar as they are, from elementary similarity, appearances of one and the same essence. In the meantime, however, before the final clarification of the matter, we too wish to express ourselves as though feelings possessed a productive significance for the shaping of impressions.

And here it must now be said that all those moods and emotions, too, with which the recipient of an impression answers not so much the character of the impressions as, rather, merely their relation to his own drives and (in man) to his interests, one and all color off, more or less, onto the character of the impression. The waltz-melody to which I first fell in love will not only awaken in me phantasms that it would not equally awaken in others, but will also possess for me an excitation-value behind which its real significance may lag as far as one pleases. Examples of a similar kind offer themselves to everyone in the greatest number. — This is what we had in mind above when, in announcing the rule that no mere juxtaposition of impressions weaves at all into their content of meaning, we had to register a fundamental exception. Even the feeling generated by the mere coincidence of impressions, and hence, in the end, the momentary relation of the recipient of the impression to the impression, takes part in the interpretation of sense — which, for such cases, would more correctly be called a lending of sense. If, in particular, the characters of the contents of impression mix with the character of the given appearance-space, it cannot fail that the psychic bearing of the recipient of the impression colors off even onto the latter, and clothes rooms of a house, and even regions, with a tone foreign to them. If we take our stand on the assumption of an absolutely necessary connection among all appearances, then the room where a murder took place would *really* have acquired something uncanny (if the murder had not indeed been drawn there by the room's own being under a spell!) — something that would then, to be sure, given sufficient receptivity in the observer, have to cling to it even for one who had not the slightest knowledge of the event. But if the room appeared uncanny to me merely because I thought a murder had taken place there which in truth took place [p. 410] somewhere quite different, then a lending of sense would be present, one that would speak *only* of the lender. Thus, for instance, with the interiors of barracks — indeed of entire quarters of towns in which they lay — there became bound up, in the years of the "World War," for many soldiers, a mood of horror that could not be understood from the character of the impressions in and of themselves. For that, and for that alone, the name "empathy" [Einfühlung], unfortunately much in vogue in support of false doctrines, could be used without danger. Empathy rightly understood in this way, however, would present us with a series of highly important problems unknown to the misunderstood kind, of which we wish to indicate at least a few.

If we must also admit that the momentary relational feelings of the recipient of an impression color off onto the character of the impression, this nonetheless does not thereby make impossible the apprehension of the impressions' own proper character, because the said colors are far more fluctuating quantities than the proper colors they overlie. This holds especially for all encounters of the impression with a *passing* mood. If a landscape, a scent, a form strikes me as melancholy because I myself happen at the moment to be in a melancholy mood, then, in view of the circumstance that I experience the same states of affairs, or, to speak in the language of the science of life, their renewed intuitive images, another time in a joyful mood, the mood-color would after all be comparable only to a detachable color of illumination and not to an adhering opaque color. But even those colors that fall to impressions from their encounters with one another remain, if not in constancy, then at any rate in firmness of connection, behind the proper colors, and *can*, at least on that account, be distinguished from them. If I hear that waltz-melody once so fateful for me, I would, with attention directed to the purpose, nonetheless be largely able to keep apart its proper worth and its memory-worth. Finally, all colors of occasion undergo, in the course of life, still stronger transformation than those peculiar to the image. It is, moreover, evident that individual personalities will differ extraordinarily according to the degree of their inclination to empathy. The extreme opposite to the great artist in the spirit of antiquity, whose intuition, saturated with actuality, mirrors the characters of images almost undimmed by colors of occasion, is marked by the psychically disturbed person, for whom the proper colors of essences vanish completely behind the reflections of his moods and [p. 411] ill-humors. "It is," according to *Eichendorff*, "the peculiarity of distinguished human beings, that every appearance mirrors itself in their pure breast in its original individuality, without their spoiling it by an admixture of their own self." We add: every "subjectivism" of world-contemplation is on the way to psychic disturbance, and in every psychic disturbance a diminished feeling for actuality has its share!

Beyond this, however, one can test the life-states of every bearer of perception for their receptivity to actuality, and, in that regard, order all feelings according to the degree of their fitness to open the soul to the characters of images, or to close it against them. In this way negative stirrings such as anxiety, terror, hatred, envy, malice, and so on, separate themselves, in terms of the science of life, from the positive ones of love, admiration, veneration, and so on — which, however, as will be shown later, is not an ultimate state of affairs, but comes down to the opposed degrees of strength with which the process of beholding takes part in the process of feeling, of which only one side may be spoken of here. Just as one rightly distinguishes deep and shallow personalities, so too can everyone distinguish, in himself, deep and shallow moods, and will then also confirm that from the comparatively deeper mood a comparatively deeper glimpse into the essence of actuality is inseparable. Notwithstanding the difference that obtains between depth-experience and distance-experience, every depth-experience nevertheless also has a far-character, every far-experience also a depth-character; hence we may measure the pathos of the depth of a mood, among other things, by its content of distance. From this result two determinations of heightened feeling for actuality.

The one lies in the co-experience of distance in time, of which we made so far-reaching a use in Chapter 28. We look more deeply into the distance of time than into nearness. If, then, someone returns after decades for the first time to the landscape of his homeland, externally perhaps scarcely changed, and sees it therefore with wholly different eyes than would be the case had he not spent his childhood years there, we may be sure that this "empathy" has rather felt *out* the innermost soul-content of the perceived images. But the same holds equally of all first moments. Compared with the accustomed impression, the new impression is richer in content of distance, and therefore opens itself [p. 412] to the soul down into far deeper depths than the everyday does. But if the seeingpower of the soul grows blind before what is habitual, we sense what dangers threaten the discovering power of the spirit from that microscopically exact groping-over of objects which science demands (and in part must demand), and we understand why so often pathbreaking first findings did not originate with the guild-professionals, but with a layman, to whom, in a favored moment, a state of affairs wooed a hundred times in vain unveiled its unsuspected core, because under his eyes it regained the shimmer of primal freshness.

[p. 413]

#### 38. Kapitel — Die Ein-Bildung des Auffassungsaktes (Zum Problem der Begriffsentstehung) — Chapter 38 — The In-Forming of the Act of Apprehension (On the Problem of the Origin of Concepts)

We state in advance: in what follows we shall speak of the act of apprehension always as the immediate occasioning ground of the act of judgement; why this remark is necessary will emerge in Volume II. — If for a moment we look back along the path we have traversed, we become aware that we have indeed shown how the transformation must be constituted through which the life-process becomes, in the end, receptive to the intervention of spirit, but have, by contrast, only just touched upon the manner in which the two are connected. For if an A is connected with a B, then not only will something happen to B when something happens to A, but also to A when something happens to B. In the personal I, as the form of the connection of life and spirit, nothing can therefore happen on the side of life without a consequent appearance on the side of spirit, but just as little can anything happen on the side of spirit without a consequent appearance on that of life. The realization of the deed of spirit coincides with the generation of a precipitate of the deed of spirit within the region of life available to it, or: no *lived experience passes unaltered* through the act of reflection. When, in Chapter 25, we sharply separated consciousness and the contents of lived experience, we assigned to the former, "removed" as it was, the role of a spectator whose pauses of sleep could exert no influence on the tumult of the latter; but it does not for that reason have the role of a genuine spectator, because the moments of its waking most decisively co-determine the course of the play! Herein consists its I-hood: that a vitality which admits the intervention of the spiritual act is itself immediately altered, down into its depths, in a unique way, by the act that actually occurs. What, seen from the side of life, is the deed of spirit, is, seen from the side of spirit, the in-forming of the effect of the deed into a receptive scope of life. The nous poietikos [the active intellect], to speak in Aristotelian terms, requires a nous pathetikos [the passive intellect], because without it it would remain in extra-temporal concealment. — Now [p. 414] we have indeed already shown earlier that the achievement of the deed consists in the splitting of something previously bound together, and in the de-limitation that thereby falls to its lot; but we now wish to gain, step by step, insight into the reshaping of lived experience itself that is undergone under the effect of spirit, and we therefore turn our attention, in the first place, to the experience of spiritsupported or *intelligent* understanding.

According to a nice experiment of *Wundt's*, of five colorgraded discs (white, light gray, gray, dark gray, black), each gradation is, after a single showing, recognized again without further ado, and indeed correctly identified; but of several — up to nine — only after the introduction of distinguishing names for the newly added color-shades. Wundt conjectures that the achievement of identification, even of the first five, already finds a hidden aid in the shading-names commonly available for the purpose. What is going on here? If we consider that concepts, among other things, correspond to names, we may conclude that the extended series, still unnamed, is indeed apprehended link by link, but only becomes, once provided with property-designations, at the same time conceptually articulated in the apprehending. If, then, we identify what is conceptually determinate, not what is conceptually indeterminate, it follows compellingly that the impression is trans*formed* by the act of conceiving.

Less simple examples offer themselves by the hundred, and occur in the textbooks of psychology as evidence for the most diverse conceivable views. One likes, with predilection, to adduce the admittedly downright startling, but more difficult to interpret, case of hearing a foreign language. If we imagine, present at the conversation of two persons, two others, of whom the one understands their language and the other does not, then the extent of the difference in the purely auditory impressions of the two listeners can scarcely still be pictured. The one who understands will perceive a succession of articulated sounds, where the one who does not understand hears a confused jumble of vocal noises. Or: consider the extent of the difference in the visual impressions when the object is a sheet full of Chinese characters and the one observer is a Chinese able to read it, the other a European ignorant of Chinese! Of many an illegible handwriting no letter of the entire alphabet can any longer be "deciphered" if one carefully isolates it from the structure of the words, yet it remains legible in the context of the text.

[p. 415] To forestall the misunderstanding that the achievement of the act resembles the effect of a mechanical force, let us say rather that it is the in-souling of its having-been-conceived that transforms the impression. We shall not, to be sure, therefore look for an alteration in that fragment of lived experience which sensualism called "sensation"; but we shall hope to find it in the experience of meaning with which, as has been shown, every sensory process comes to its conclusion. Since, however, we now wish to learn wherein the conceptual feeling of meaning differs both from the feelings of meaning that make animal recognition possible, and from the symbolic feelings of meaning of primal man, we must, for the time being, leave wholly aside, in the meaning of names, the essence-meaning under-stratum, even though conceptual thinking, to be sure, could not have taken place without it.

If someone, for lack of color-designations, confuses some of seven shades on their second presentation, he does not do so because he failed to recognize the color — for he is quite well able to recall having just seen it — but rather because, notwithstanding his recognition, he could not self-identify the individual color. From this it follows compellingly that the achievement of self-identification is *differentiation* and nothing else! What enables me to judge that the one disc is light gray, the other gray, is the holding-fast of a line that *separates* gray from light gray, and insofar as the name has helped me toward this, it must have done so by virtue of its capacity to designate the line of separation in question. If in thinking we place the emphasis on the line of separation between object and object, then we have extracted that side of the thought-process which stems exclusively from spirit, without any admixture, that is, of life-impulses, and whose predominance, still to be more closely circumscribed, separates conceptual from symbolic thinking. We arrived at the same result through the separation of the referring from the conceiving function of the concept in Chapter 11, and we found it confirmed by the preliminary considerations on the origin of concepts out of symbols. Here we encounter an obvious objection.

Even in animal recognition, one might say, there is differentiation, and even in animal recognition confusions occur — as, for instance, when the sparrow takes the scarecrow for a real human being. In this one would be right; but insight into the vital precipitate [p. 416] of conceiving depends entirely on the clear apprehension of the fundamental difference between the two kinds of differentiating, and this in turn on an appreciation of the difference between the object of thought and the experienced content of meaning of its sign. Whoever is capable of judging: that is the gray, that the light-gray disc, would, if expressly asked about it, undoubtedly also be able to judge that he means the sameness of the colors thus named, and not, say, of the colored things — since the discs of the first series might, in the second case, possibly have been exchanged for other discs of merely the same size and coloring. So exclusively would his color-statements refer to the colors alone, that in order to decide on the identity of the colored things he would have to carry out *several* comparisons and perform several acts of self-identification. The line that separates for him the conceptual meaning-content of the one color-designation from the conceptual meaning-content of the other, or, more briefly, the object Gray from the object Light-Gray, at the same time also separates each of the two colors from the thing to which they adhere. In order to distinguish what is meant by the speech-sound "gray" from what is meant by the speech-sound "light-gray," we must already command what is meant by the speech-sound "color" — or: the conceptual apprehension of any given individual color takes place with the aid of the object of thought "color in general," which stands to the colored material or thing in the relation of a property to its substratum.

Nothing even remotely similar occurs in the understanding of the animal, for which all units of meaning that it seeks or flees lie on the level of essences, now attracting, now repelling. Whether it answers, with a cognizing mode of behavior, an illumination, a color, a sound, a smell, a movement, or the massive body itself, it answers, each time, the experienced effect of an essence, and however manifold its modes of behavior may differ, we shall find no difference of behavior that would offer any sign that it had been concerned with the distinguishing of the thing from its properties, or with the distinguishing of two properties of the thing as properties. If the bull, out of aversion to the essence of redness, or at any rate of a glaring red, attacks the red cloth persistently and incorrigibly, he thereby manifests that he does not distinguish the red color from the body that bears it, and thus, notwithstanding his capacity to recognize red and certainly not to confuse it with blue, nonetheless does not command the meaning-content [p. 417] of the concept of red, and hence also not of the concept of color.<sup>60</sup> Just as the feeling of hunger renews itself always similarly, and calls in an always similarly constituted way for the oppositely constituted satiation, so too do the units of meaning of animal understanding already separate themselves according to kinship and opposition. But just as little as a boundary-representation is needed for the difference of behavior to correspond to the opposition of hunger and satiation, or of hunger and thirst, just as little does any apprehension of difference take place in animal understanding out of a knowledge of the boundaries of what is to be understood. It is, by contrast, boundaries of content, and these alone, whose efficacy enables us to conceive. Before, however, we characterize the transformation, now readily statable, which lived experience undergoes from the so often already touched-upon process of the drawing of boundaries, let this process itself be thought through to its end in every respect.

<sup>60</sup> On page 417. — In reality the bull is by no means so incapable of learning as is commonly believed, and the holding-out of the cloth is far more dangerous for the capeador than *if* it were otherwise. The "higher" animals are apt to find out very quickly where the being "of interest" to them, which they have to seek or to flee, is to be found. But this does not touch our train of thought. For if the bull in the end nonetheless attacks the capeador instead of the cloth, this does not happen because it has recognized the innocuous character of the red that irritates it, but because the *movements* of the capeadores have meanwhile become more interesting to it than red *and* cloth. — If more recent authors assert that *red* leaves the bull altogether indifferent, we should like to call that into question for the time being.

Far from working shapes, let alone images, the mere boundary signifies only the end of the one, the beginning of another state of affairs, and thus contains not the least trace of the states of affairs thereby divided apart. Whereas the states of affairs, without boundary-consciousness, would remain what they are, boundary-consciousness, if it could be detached from every context of life, would coincide with the consciousness of a nothing no longer even distinguishable from the something. Were it objected that the concept of boundary does, after all, include within itself that which is to be bounded, the answer would be that — even granting this — the bounding, by virtue of its nature as a nothing foreign to actuality, would nonetheless likewise threaten with annihilation that which it bounds, by tearing it out of the universe. For since any openness of a content, with regard to the drawing of boundaries, would only indicate that this has not yet taken place there, we may make only what is bounded on all sides the object of a consideration seeking to get at the sense of conceiving from the essence of the boundary. Could the trot, for instance, not be delimited with the same sharpness against the gallop as against the walk, we would to that extent lack the possibility of applying the concept of trotting. But something bounded on all sides, as wholly cut out of actuality, could be compared with nothing further, and would thus stand, henceforth, in no relation whatever to anything.

The Eleatics had, in their first storming of the concept of being, at once laid bare what was decisive: the unchangeability of its content. If we put in place of the change without which it could not be conceived [p. 418] a succession of different states of affairs, then out of the impossibility of conceiving change arises the impossibility of conceiving difference, and this comes out most glaringly in the concept of difference itself, whose content cannot be determined except by pointing to some states of affairs that, in and of themselves, have not the least thing in common with it. But if difference cannot be conceived, then neither can its most abstract case: plurality; and with that there opens before us a gaping rift between any general concept whatever and the "cases" to which it is supposed to be applied, and which yet seem, in the first place, to found its existence! *Stilpo* explains his conviction of the impossibility of inherence with the drastic utterance: "What is being shown to me here is not cabbage; for cabbage existed ten thousand years ago, therefore this is not cabbage." He means to say, or has rather said, thereby, even if he could not have put it that way: what is meant by the concept of cabbage concerns solely and exclusively certain differences of cabbage from all other produce of the earth's soil; but that is made present only with the aid of the "representation" of a determinate head of cabbage, and of that, now, absolutely nothing is contained in those differences; consequently the individual head of cabbage and "cabbage in general" mutually exclude one another. But had someone hoped to refute him by declaring, with a pointing gesture: "I mean this cabbage here" — he would, without doubt, have received the instruction that with the this-being and the here-being, further with the I-being and the meaning, he had equally named generalities, just as with the cabbage-being, and had thus by no means taken up the individual case meant into the conceptual content of his limiting statement. For could not any human being whatever, at any time whatever, in any place whatever, maintain with equal right the very same assertion, while the structure called "cabbage" would be one thing, and ever again another?

Whoever, hearing something of this kind for the first time, perhaps not without astonishment gains the conviction of the abstractness of all possible objects of thought, should not forget over this that their general*ity* would scarcely have sufficed to produce the Cynic-Megarian aporias, had it not been aided, from the nature of conceiving, by an inhibiting feeling that forbids the gaze aimed at the core of the concept to think it as participating in a multiplicity! To the consciously hovering opposition of generality and particularity there joins itself, unconsciously, the [p. 419] only more effective contradiction between the indivisibility of the general concept and the claims to participation of countless "cases," of which, precisely by virtue of its generality, it is asserted to hold. Grafted onto Socratic conceptual inquiry, the negation of actuality of Eleaticism intensified into the self-negation of conceiving, and prepared, indeed inaugurated, that with which the intellectual history of Greekdom came to its close: systematic doubt (skepticism) — inasmuch as one did not, indeed, bring to consciousness, but did put into effect, in a dissolving dialectic, the supposed incompatibility of the apartness of every conceptual content with the demand to enter into any connections whatever. Since, however, every judgement in fact places such connections before our eyes, one had thereby in truth unrolled an epistemological problem that awaits, to this very day, a generally approved solution.

If, in the extensionless time-point, movement stiffens into mere position, we need only extract what it too still offers in the form of an application — the boundary *as such* — in order to find actuality itself annihilated in it and through it. Just as unchangeability forms the reverse side of the sameness of the object of thought, so does that isolatedness which the mathematical point offers us in space-time relation, and the arithmetical 1 in pure abstraction, form the reverse side of its unity — a unity whose sense *exhausts* itself in the capacity to remain, in every combination, separated off and by itself. We believed we had just now found that the unadded content of conceiving is differentiation; and we now believe we have found that the model of all inconceivability lies in the meaning-content of — difference: in this self-contradiction, disguised, the question as to the ground of the *relatability* of what has been isolated by spirit ought to have become sufficiently pressing for us.

Whoever surveys the history of European logic, even only in broad outline, will, notwithstanding a bewildering wealth of admirably acute individual considerations — the professional mastery of which would, moreover, probably require a human lifetime — miss a convincing doctrine of the course of concept-formation. This is reflected, among other things, in the battles of opinion over the most elementary problems, which testify certainly not to a flagging of logical reflection, but indeed to its lack of clarification. If one were to ask, say, all contemporary logicians of note what "categories" are, the number of by no means mutually compatible answers would be exactly as great as the number of authors; [p. 420] and scarcely more favorably would matters stand with the answer to the question of the genesis of the concept. However much, to be sure, seen from our standpoint, it is in the end always an insufficient knowledge of the essential difference of spirit and life that entangles every attempt at solution in difficulties, *closer* grounds of the failure and of the general uncertainty can nonetheless be shown quite generally; and here it seems to us that one has hitherto not been able to keep fundamentally apart the process of abstracting and the process of generalizing — from which alone never-concluding tournaments of debate arise. If the sensualist, who believes in a "given" and therefore does homage to abstracting, hopes to demonstrate its success with concepts like redness, horse, or water, the idealist at once troubles him with the question by what processes of abstraction general concepts like sum, relation, difference, or illness, experiment, could have been produced, in order presently even to deny outright that, by the mere omission, say, of what distinguishes a fir from a willow and again from a linden (an example of Kant's), the concept of tree could come about. If, however, he hopes, conversely, to make his fortune with apriorities, the sensualist troubles him at every step with the quasi-opposite question of how he manages to apply concepts that are *not* detached from actuality nonetheless to it, and in particular to test his *general* on a *particular* which, by presupposition, has no part in it whatsoever; whereupon the one finds himself finally forced into the monstrous confession of the existence of "general representations," the other, as we know, into the still more monstrous one of the production of the world by mere concepts! We shall illuminate this conflict of opinion more closely below, and wish for now only to have pointed out that the one, like the other, locates the origin of both processes, of abstracting and of generalizing, in spirit. But that is precisely what is fundamentally wrong.

As surely as there would be no concepts, and hence no general concepts, without spirit, just as surely it cannot be the work of spirit that *has* conferred generality upon the general concept and finally upon every concept. In our consideration of symbolic thinking we have indeed already become acquainted with the true ground that makes generality of meaning possible, but we now wish to consolidate our result from the other side, taking as our starting point the peculiar difficulty [p. 421] that the question of the applicability of concepts to intuitive images brings with it. When the Roman called the elephant, hitherto unknown to him, the "Libyan ox," the Algonquin Indian called the horse the "big dog," the typesetter called quotation marks "goose feet," the butcher called the ruminant's leaf-shaped stomach the "calendar," and everyone called his newfangled writing implement a "steel pen" , one must not be content with the usual observation of<sup>61</sup> so-called transferences, but must direct one's attention to the circumstance that in each of these cases a name is being used in a far more general meaning than the one intended for it by other habits of speech. If we pursue the matter, we come upon, if not the law, then certainly the rule that in the life of peoples as of the individual human being, there inheres in meaning-units grounded in intuition a tendency toward generalization that, at first, reaches beyond the scope of their conceptual sense — whether they already had such a sense or only acquired it later. This, however, as will be shown, leads us to the ground of generalizing as such.

<sup>61</sup> On page 421. — Numerous examples are offered by G. *von der* *Gabelentz*, Die Sprachwissenschaft, Leipzig 1891, pp. 40–41.

Wundt (in his "Völkerpsychologie") tells of a seventeenmonth-old child who, without further ado, transferred the name "eijebapp" for railway to a line of dogs walking one behind another. Of the thousands of examples of the same kind that offer themselves, familiar to every linguist and occasionally cited by each, let one be mentioned here that the author himself had occasion to observe in earlier years and later to investigate more closely, because it seems extraordinarily well suited to disclose the significance of elementary similarities for the primary apprehension of generality. — A boy of four or five had seen, pictured in a picture-book, a group of animals designated to him as a "hamster family," whose roundly bulging forms aroused in him the greatest delight. A few days later, meeting in a larger company of adults a boy of about the same age with particularly fat cheeks, he went up to him and, with every sign of tenderness, exclaimed: "You little, little hamster family!" The laughter of the adults, which broke out at once, made so bewildering and wounding an impression on the boy that he retained the event in his memory for the rest of his life and in later years was able to give an exact account of what he had experienced in it. According to this, he had seen a hamster family before him in the boy, had not in the least [p. 422] grasped what he might have disgraced himself by, as he gave joyful expression to his perception, and only at a later stage of his development suddenly understood that the boy had simply not been a hamster family — whereupon his utterance of that time at once appeared to him too in the light of comedy. The exceedingly far-reaching differences between the picture of a hamster family and the sight of a chubby-cheeked child had thus been completely obliterated by the trait common to both — a roundness that could invite a tender touch.

The case shows us palpably that it is the soul's resonance to elementary similarities of images, more precisely of image-forms, that grounds, in original lived experience, meaning-units which, if we measure them by concepts, surpass in generality the objects of thought that later congealed out of them. And that is not all: the "hamster family" had been for the boy a plastic and, as it were, kneadable roundness, because this — to speak entirely in today's manner of expression — had spoken to his feeling, to his eros, and had thereby indicated to him the sense of the image, which could meet him again in the appearance of his chubby-cheeked contemporary. Images would not be what they are — namely, connections of data of appearance — without their character, and it is this, and this alone, that grounds *original* similarities and lets an identical something appear in objects of intuition that are, in their factual properties, extremely different. Here lies the source of the meaning-units of primitive apprehension, without exception underpinned by intuition.

The state of affairs is not accurately set forth by the turn of phrase — favored even by *Geiger* and often repeated since — that confusion precedes distinction. Our boy, who took another boy for a hamster family, had confused nothing whatsoever; what he had done was to lay, from the outset, beneath the designation "hamster family" a sense that would correspond roughly to the conceptual meaning-content of the much more general "plastic roundness." Geiger, however, at least *touches on* the truth with the following sentences: "That words and concepts, as abstract and general, should run counter to and disturb the sensuous freshness of this world of appearance, is a prejudice that experience wholly contradicts. The object of concepts is, to be sure, what is common to many particulars; hence it may seem as though their formation required some [p. 423] insight into precisely this commonality. But whether there is a single human being or many, one sun or several; whether the property of whiteness repeats itself innumerable times in things or not, is wholly indifferent to the arising, in the soul, of the images — thrown back by language — of those objects, of which the soul, in by far the most cases, actually perceives only an extremely small fraction of what it thus gathers into unities. It was some particular human being whose sight first gave it material for that image, and as soon as a second human being then appeared to it, he seemed to it like the first, indeed to be the same as him; some single and particular animal was, in a single moment, the occasion for the name common to all individuals, and however manifold the living creatures that subsequently crowded before man's eyes, man had no senses for such differences."

Only because it is essences renewing themselves in similar image-forms that the deed of spirit split off from the content of intuition, does there arise the wonder — no longer to be explained thereafter from the precipitate of thought alone — that the things thus detached are without exception generalities, which now recur identically in countless individual cases. The unity as well as the sameness of what is delimited attests the delimiting act, whereas generality originally accrues to it only in the measure of the unboundedness of the co-related (= omitted) meaning-content, which in turn cannot again be conceived, since only within the boundary, and solely within it, can what corresponds to the concept of the object be sought. It is true that only through such a drawing of boundaries does the co-related acquire the mode of existence, in principle alien to it, of the non-spatio-temporal and hence always and everywhere available universal (be it redness, sound, or body); nonetheless it is no less the unboundedness of the essence that can never be conceived which makes it possible for the universal to exchange its nowhere-home for the determinateness, identically repeated in the now and here, of images occurring. Never, then, out of the sharpness of spirit but solely out of the depth of the soul did and does there come about the "bold generalizations" and daring analogies (of the discoverer-metaphysician) that tend to provoke the contradiction of scholars, and it is only ever in the critical limitation of the claims of the drive toward generalization that the efficacy of the latter has proved and proves itself!

[p. 424] The extraordinary importance of an inquiry that — in contrast to nearly all traditional teachings, but also to the currently most fashionable ones — wishes to show the power of abstraction to be far more an obstacle to the formation of general meaning-units than their cause of origin, may justify our carrying, for the sake of a sharper delineation of the main thought, the insight so far gained into the everyday dissensions of philosophical thinking that were already spoken of above — namely by judging the most right-wing flank of the most modern logistic by the counter-arguments with which it proposes to shake the most delicate position of sensualism, we mean the notorious "general idea," usually illustrated since Locke by the concept of the triangle. Since the individual triangle always has a determinate size of sides and angles and cannot, say, be at once acute-angled and obtuse-angled, a general idea of the triangle would of course be an absurdity. Equally untenable are all the attempts (ultimately traceable to Berkeley) that seek to explain how the individual triangle sets about exercising a kind of representation for the triangle as such. Consequently, the logicist triumphs, you sensualists and nominalists have failed to give an account of what you are actually talking about! The triangle is a thoroughly determinate object of thought, which therefore does not cease to be different from the individual triangle because it can be exemplified in it. You have overlooked, he adds, that in speaking of the triangle you are moving on the ground of the "ideal unity of the species," of "intentional objects," or, in our language, of pure thought-things. With that the matter is settled for him. For he holds the "ideal units of validity" to be a "realm" — presumably situated in Cloud-Cuckoo-Land — that is not in the least concerned with whether a faculty of thought is at home anywhere in the universe. He knows how to give us a report, down to the smallest detail, of this realm of modern ideals and its constitutional order, namely thanks to "immediate evidence," and he supposes that he has thereby, for the first time, discovered true logic, which is accordingly to be carefully and "cleanly" separated from such trifles as the thinking of human beings, which always takes place somewhere and at some time.

Whoever was not endowed with the miraculous gift of a consciousness of evidence that first attained self-revelation in the twentieth century may, by contrast, hold something else to be evident. The splitting [p. 425] of being into two kinds of being, "ideal being" and "real being," makes it logically impossible that our thinking, which belongs to "real being," should ever know the least thing about "ideal being," since through such knowledge the said ideality would be taken up into the reality of the process of thinking and would thus have been robbed of its ideality; hence the corresponding two-world theory has presupposed, as belonging to it, something through which, if not ideality itself, then certainly its knowability is logically denied.<sup>62</sup> Formalism in truth offers, as is understood, merely determinations of concepts (and, indeed, correct ones alongside a preponderance of unserviceable ones), but otherwise, as was already noted earlier, a new edition of Platonism, though as it were on miserable paper. In that it defines not only with Socrates but also, with Plato, reinterprets everything definable as something existing, it substitutes, in keeping with its anemic spirituality, for the Platonic Ideas mere lawfulnesses which — if one may speak of an intensification within the absurd — could, without an actuality that obeys the laws, exist even less than Plato's at least idol-like essences.

<sup>62</sup> On page 425. — This was demonstrated in exemplary form by *Palágyi* in his work published in 1902 (!), "Der Streit der Psychologisten und der Formalisten in der modernen Logik" (Engelmann, Leipzig). One took pains to pass over it in silence. Otherwise, indeed, no success would any longer have been granted to *those* logical investigations which flattered the logically corrupted taste of the age by finding an expression for it. And so the valuable work has for the time being fallen into oblivion, in accordance with a long-proven recipe; for the time being.

But if we were, by way of trial, to assume that a god had granted the formalist to enter into connection with the realm — situated we know not where — of the "eternal units of validity," even that, unfortunately, would help us nothing. For now we wish to learn how the "ideal species," named, say, triangle, sets about being "exemplified" in the individual triangle. And here we call ourselves to reflection: not only the species triangle, but also the individual triangle is, from the standpoint of the science of consciousness, an abstractum, because it has been wrested from the stream of passing away and becoming, and thus detached from actuality, and then, moreover, only completely detached from every other abstractum. The same cut that separates the thought-thing from actuality separates any given thought-thing from any other — or, to speak with Stilpo, the cabbage in general from the cabbage here in this place. How, then, does the logically singular thought-thing called the individual triangle manage to take part in the logically general thought-thing called the triangle as such?! Here the formalist falls silent (or rather he does not fall silent, since he does not fall silent even when he has nothing further to say). He has rejected the sham solutions of the nominalists and sensualists, but has simply left the gap open, and if the "psychologists" could at least attempt [p. 426] to answer the decisive question, formalism itself must renounce doing so, since in the meantime it dances, with comical gesticulating ghostliness, around the word-idol "evidence."

We hardly need say that the practice of *taking* mathematical concepts *as a starting point* in inquiries into concepts is fundamentally mistaken — first, because mathematical concepts belong to an exceedingly late section not only of the history of mankind but even of the history of understanding, and further, because they concern immediately *pure* thought-things, whose relation to the concepts of what really exists is *at first* itself the problem. Mankind possessed, for tens of thousands of years, meaning-units such as sky, earth, night, brightness, darkness, tree, animal, stone, and so on, or running, standing, lying, waking, sleeping, and so on (or analogues of such meaning-units), before it was able to grasp the concept of the Euclidean triangle, and even in the numerical speculations of the Pythagoreans it emerges that number — found, to be sure, in prehistoric times, but belonging to the late period of prehistory — was not originally the number (= quantity) of arithmetic, but a numerical *character*. It would therefore be far from our purpose to illustrate the relation of species to individual case, or of the logically general to the logically singular, or finally of conceptual generality to conceptual particularity and singularity, precisely by the triangle. But if one wishes to hear how our findings bear out in this application, well then, the reference just offered to Pythagorean number-symbolism should already make the path to be taken surmisable, even apart from its already being foreshadowed by everything that has been set forth concerning symbolic and conceptual thinking.

Just as man originally did not in the least behold, mean, or name the individual tree, but rather, on the occasion of it, the tree-like or the tree-character, so too he originally neither beheld, meant, nor uttered the individual triangle, but rather, on the occasion of it, the triangle-like or the triangle-character. The meaning-units with which human thinking began, and with which it begins anew, again and again, in the face of everything not yet conceptually fixed, never relate to the singularly objective, but without exception to object-characters, and thus to something that, when translated into the language of concepts, has the nature now of the general mark, now of the genus. Mankind proceeds, at all times and everywhere, from *the logically more general* to the logically *more particular* (which is in no way in contradiction with a strongly individualizing mode of apprehension [p. 427]) , and the opposite direc-<sup>63</sup> tion has been taken solely and exclusively by science, which, wherever it came to the fore, could rely upon a world of general as well as particular meaning-units, and then, to be sure, with the aid of abstraction promptly scaled heights of generality that no *intuitive* thinking could ever reach. Only when the fact-character "this" or "this here" — whose vital ground of possibility lies in the demonstrative function of the process of perception — is added to the tree-like or the triangle-like or whatever other fact-characters, does the original character become particularized, which is to say that it gains, in addition to its hitherto features, which remain untouched by this, still others.

<sup>63</sup> On page 427. — We shall here be confronted with the "concretizing" manner of speech of primitives, for which we ourselves offered some striking examples in Chapter 20. It will also be recalled that among them there frequently exist "concepts" of species or subspecies, while such concepts for the genus are still lacking. In the work of *Abegg* that we cited (Note 20) we read, for instance: "Thus there exists (namely among many primitive peoples) indeed a rich terminology for individual species of animal or plant, but no expression for animal or plant in general, nor even for comprehensive groups among them; for instance, there are words in Indian languages for white oak, black oak, red oak, but none for tree. Occasionally the individualization goes so far that quite different designations exist for the same animal, according to the situation in which it finds itself; thus Eskimo has several expressions for the seal: one counts as the general designation; a second is used for the seal that lies in the sun; the third, when it lets itself drift on an ice-floe. The extreme consequence of such an individualizing rendering of reality is given when, as among the Maori, the objects of daily use and ordinary life, such as houses, canoes, weapons, articles of clothing, are designated not by generic names but by formal *proper names*." The list of similar occurrences could be multiplied without end from every part of the globe where primitives still dwell, but the customary interpretation seems to us mistaken. If what we take as our basis should prove correct — that the primitive, resembling in this the original human being as well as the child, does not know *concepts* at all — then his linguistic units of meaning are as little concrete as abstract, but are partly mediately, partly immediately, *intuitive*. In slogan-like characterization one would have to call the languages of culture languages of thought, but the primitive as well as the original languages, by contrast, image-languages or sense-languages. From this, and from this alone, all the peculiarities of prelogical speech are to be explained, at least so far as it stands in contrast to speech that thinks in concepts. — Because the intuitive image of the seal that lies in the sun on the beach is thoroughly different from the intuitive image of the seal that drifts on an ice-floe, the designations for them can also be different in an image-language; and it is always similarly the case. In very many instances this can be described as though primitive thinking were more concrete; in other instances not. Precisely the example cited gives a fine piece of evidence for the opposite. The Eskimos *have*, after all, a designation for "seal in general," and what they designate, by contrast, with "seal lying in the sun" and "seal drifting on an ice-floe" are not more concrete subspecies, but intuitive situations, both highly characteristic of the life of the seal. — Our conception of the state of affairs, far from being, say, merely another formulation, gives an application of the fundamental distinction between the process of generalizing and the process of abstracting. If one proceeds from the antithesis of the abstract to the concrete *without* knowledge of its difference from the antithesis of the general to the particular, one runs the risk of denying to the image-language of primitives the generality of meanings, and thereby places oneself in contradiction with other features of the state of affairs. If the Oneida can say: I seek a village, and thus not: this or that particular village, then he disposes of means of utterance for generalities. For this he actually has the sound sl, which he inserts into the word-structure that stands for the sentence. We quote verbatim from *Abegg*: "Gnaglaslizaks = g I; nagla to dwell; —sl— abstractum; i verbal particle; zak to seek; —s— continuative."
