"To dwell" and "to seek," too, and the expression of the continuative, are of course generalities. It is further grounded in the intuitive character of original thinking that quasi more-concrete units of meaning have no need of the more abstract ones in order to be grasped. On the plane of factual-logical thinking one could not meaningfully speak of white oaks, black oaks, red oaks without having the concept of the oak and that of the tree; on the plane of intuitive thinking this encounters no difficulties. One can have experienced the white-oak-like without having experienced, with equal distinctness, the tree-like, and so forth. But one can just as well have experienced the ostensibly living as against the ostensibly non-living, and will then at times dispose of intuitive units of meaning that exceed, in generality, the concept of tree, of plant, of animal; and this too is nothing unusual among primitives. On the occasion of his many years of study among the South Sea peoples of the Bismarck Archipelago and the Solomon Islands, R. *Thurnwald* (Beihefte zur Zeitschrift für angewandte Psychologie 6, 1913, pp. 92–99) compiled a small vocabulary of so-called pidgin English, which he introduces with the statement that ordinarily "the meaning of words is *extended* a great deal." Thus, for instance, the word nothing can, in the mouths of the natives, mean both "without" and "pointless," in which an original faculty of generalizing manifests itself. And this comes to light elsewhere too, among the Buin people, quite in the manner of the examples we have offered in the main text. For "railway" one invents on the spot "steamer of the land." Further: "When colored sailors on the Australian coast saw a railway train for the first time from the ship, they hurried in consternation to the captain and cried out (in English): 'Look there, captain, many *houses* are moving away'" (loc. cit., p. 95). In their own language "koku" designates both the bottom of a basket and swampy ground, and finally also the somewhat rotten tip of a banana (p. 91); what is common to these is the *character* of the dirty and the unclean, which is experienced *intuitively* in three, incidentally very different, objects, and thereby grounds a unit of meaning that we are unable to render in a single word, because, despite great generality, the detachment has not yet taken place that would permit the formation of the *concept* of the dirty. For the rest, we must never overlook the fact that every property that varies among individual persons also varies among peoples and races. With regard to the inclination and capacity for generalizing, we must therefore assume, among different tribes, *original* differences of disposition. The "world-historical" evidence for this is furnished by Hellas and Rome. There, in consequence of a roving fantasy and a wide-ranging power of generalization, the swift victory of myth over gods and cults, and, running parallel with the sundering of the poles of life, the invention of philosophy; here, in consequence of a clinging "earth-heaviness" and a nearness-bound attitude of solicitude persisting through all transformations right into the orientalizing period of the late Empire, *something* of the spirit of that poetry-hostile service of ceremony, as it was originally expressed in the pontifical indigitamenta. Thus it could, thus it had to, come about that, despite passionate efforts of appropriation, of the results of Greek speculation only the relatively more concrete part, namely ethics, was taken up and further developed, while "theory" grew ever coarser and flatter the longer this went on. Quite similarly, of the individual sciences, the most concrete, medicine, expanded, while the most abstract, mathematics, retreated more and more and finally fell into complete oblivion! But we turn once more to the early age of language. Apart from all that has been set forth here, there is no sound-sign that could be brought, so to speak, to coincidence with the intuitive image, since it would utterly lack generality. The intuitive image is by its nature a momentary intuitive image. If we now attach a special designation to the particular house, the particular ship, the particular person (== proper name), it holds for *all* the intuitive images that we receive of the house, the ship, the person at the most various times. Instead of meaning the ever-momentary intuitive image, the proper name thus means the contents of countless experiences of re-recognition, and stands, in terms of the science of consciousness, to the intuitive image itself as the generic concept of the horse stands logically to the individual concept of the particular horse. It suffices to recall once more our remarks on the dying dog of Odysseus to know that intuitive generality is lived and not thought generality. To invent designations for this only the original human being was able to do, because his re-recognition is guided by beholding, and not, on the other hand, the animal, whose re-recognition is guided by sensing. Here let one more remark be permitted, which would give occasion for the most manifold inferences, were one to think the problem of the origin of concepts through down to its individual features. If we leave aside *the* concepts that relate to concepts, such as identity, equality, difference, etc., we can think of the remainder as stretched between two endpoints, one utterly most concrete and one utterly most abstract. The utterly most concrete would be the particular individual thing, the utterly most abstract the arithmetical number. To the former corresponds the proper name, to the latter the name of a numeral. For both now, the proper name and the name of the number, the scope of meaning coincides with the concept. The degree of generality of the proper name is the lowest of all degrees of generality, and the concept belonging to the proper name is the most concrete of all concepts. The degree of generality of the number-word is the highest of all degrees of generality, and the concept belonging to the number-word is the most abstract of all concepts that are not merely relational concepts. It might therefore seem as though proper names and number-words had only conceptual content but no meaning-content whatever; and that is indeed the case as regards the scope of meaning. But it is not the case when we keep the process of finding in view. The unit of meaning for which the proper name is the sign is found through vital re-recognition, the concept through spiritual identification. The unit of meaning for which the number-word is the sign is originally likewise re-recognized, though naturally within narrow limits (on the basis of the estimation of intuitive quantities, or more precisely on the basis of the apprehension of *quantity-characters*), while the corresponding concept is the product of abstract counting. This can also be put the other way about, by saying: if, with the help of the proper name or the number-word, what is named is merely re-recognized, then the meaning-content of the name is conceptless; if it is — with or without re-recognition — identified, then the name means a concept. Both, meaning and concept, are thus as before entirely different from one another, only this time not in respect of scope. With such knowledge one holds in one's hands the key to many otherwise incomprehensible peculiarities of original thinking, as it has been preserved, at least in part, among dying-out primitive peoples.

The tree-character, the triangle-character, has nothing in itself that would compel it to enter into appearance here and now, and just as little anything that would forbid it to do so. But if it now appears here and now, then its meaning too — that is, its hereness and nowness — can be apprehended, from which arises the possibility of a comparison between the tree-like, the triangle-like on the one side, and the tree-like or triangle-like here and now on the other; a comparison which, if actually carried out, measures the occasion of perception against a phantasm — to which a number of the sensualists' considerations could then be attached. But the ground of right for such considerations, one not even surmised by any sensualist, is supplied by the circumstance that the pre-conceptual unit of apprehension signifies a character to which generality is proper, because and insofar as hereness and nowness do not adhere to it.

Not, indeed, for the windy understanding of the formalist, but very much for a still root-firm concern with the matter, one repeatedly and successfully calls upon the early-historical stage of thinking. Long before mankind possessed a single concept, it knew, meant, and gave voice to gods, demons, "spirits," nymphs, fairies, elves, dwarfs, sprites, wood-spirits, trudes, witches, werewolves, and so on. But the identical thing that was in each case posited with such and kindred meaning-units has, among all the peoples of the earth, the capacity to appear suddenly as well as to disappear suddenly, and — which represents merely a special case of this — the capacity for change of shape. Every demon can assume very different shapes without thereby ceasing to be this one and the same demon, to whom one must, say, sacrifice and pay homage in quite a particular manner [p. 428]. Even one who has long ceased to "believe" in miracle-stories reads with pleasure that Athena transforms herself into Mentor, Zeus into a bull, the young witch into an age-old little crone, and curiously does not tend to dwell on the question of what, say, Proteus "actually" is, when he looks now like a boar, now like a dragon, now like a lion. This has its good reasons. For it is at the very least no more wonderful than that we find the triangle in the individual triangle. In gods, demons, fairies, and so on, there have been preserved for us original unities of essence belonging to all human thinking. Now if it evidently belongs to the meaning-unit "essence" to be able to become manifest in changing images, then it must also belong to the *essence* of the tree to be able to become manifest in manifoldly different trees, to the essence of the triangle, in manifoldly different triangles. And just as the thoroughly determinate character of the demonic essence grounds a kinship of character among all the images of its appearing — according to which an earthdeity, for instance, would never appear as an eagle, a lightdeity never as a serpent — so it is a lived kinship of character among the images that makes it possible for the meaning-unit of, say, the tree-like or the triangle-like to "enter into appearance" at different times and in different places.<sup>64</sup>

<sup>64</sup> On page 428. — If we measure, against the original contents of meaning, what later takes their place, namely the objects of thought, three fundamental differences emerge peripherally , which are however three different features of a single one: experienceable beings are living units of effect, whose differences of character so little abolish their context of effect that they rather establish its particular kind; objects of thought are effectdead units of being — experienceable beings, as not chained to being-here and being-now, have the character of generality and yet belong to the world of intuition; objects of thought are, as contents of concepts, non-intuitive, because removed from the self-transforming of actuality — experienceable beings commune with one another; objects of thought are separated from one another. The interconnectedness of the three distinguishing marks can be derived in several ways: here we consider their non-intuitiveness and "deadness" from the point of view of consequent properties of their being isolated.

The character of the tree is different from that of grass, the character of volume from that of surface, the character of the triangle from that of the quadrilateral; but the beholdings that correspond polarly to such differences do not differ from one another essentially otherwise than, on the side of the *body*, say hunger differs from thirst, and are therefore unable to set boundaries to the content of intuition: *the world of pre-* *conceptual intuitive images is boundless*. Whoever wished to object that the shadow, after all, sets itself off in a sharp boundary against the brightness, the pond's mirror against the bank, the rock against the airspace, would have confused the boundary belonging to the object of thought with the pre-conceptual *form*. If by the intuitive image we understand a form of connectedness of qualities that are themselves in turn formed, then the forms partake of the qualities and the qualities of the forms, whereas the boundary, through participation in what is to be bounded, would forfeit its capacity to bound and thus cease to exist. If the shadow is to be not a dark-colored planar form — of a very determinate character, to be sure — upon a bright field, but rather something bounded against [p. 429] this field, then I have mentally cut it up into a dark surface lacking form and an added second thing, namely the boundary, which first *forces upon* it what it "had" intuitively, namely, the form. Forms transform themselves, boundaries merely shift; forms are intuitive, boundaries purely ideal states of affairs.<sup>65</sup> If, then, this is the sense of conceiving, that it sets boundaries and thereby isolates, it would be inconceivable how the products of conceiving, that is, the objects of thought, could be related to one another; indeed, the object itself, being unrelatable, would have become an impossibility for thought, were it not for lived characters — *left aside* but co-understood — in relation to which the world of intuition is quite properly the scene of their appearing.

<sup>65</sup> On page 429. — The new consequent appearance of the opposition of life and spirit, or of lived experience and thinking, thus laid bare, is of such importance that we do not consider it superfluous to demonstrate it intuitively. The following Figure 7 shows, on a dark ground, whose circular form is here immaterial, a bright surface of *circular* shape. We leave it open how the concept of the circle was found; it is enough that everyone who has it *perceives* the circular form. But what he thus perceives is neither the same as a boundary that sets off the light surface against the dark one, nor could it be found through the process by which the boundary is found. More than that: the boundary itself is not a possible object of perception at all! We may indeed regard the circular surface from the point of view of a bounded surface; but only because, when we first grasped what a boundary is, we did so with the help of a movement of thought which, "raised into consciousness," looks the way we now wish to characterize it in Figure 7. We transport ourselves in spirit to a point outside, or here more conveniently inside (A), the circle, and imagine that we were moving in the direction of the arrow toward the circle's periphery. Then a moment will come when we still find ourselves on the bright surface, and immediately thereafter a moment when we *no longer* find ourselves on the bright surface, or already find ourselves on the dark one. *Between* the two moments lies the temporally unextended moment of crossing the spatially unextended *boundary*. The same will result if, starting from point B, we move in the direction of the other arrow. From this it follows that the boundary as such possesses no shape and can possess none. From whatever point outside or inside the circle we may move toward the circle's periphery, the path-line of our movement always intersects it at a *point*. But from however many points, no shape can be composed. If one already *knows* the form, one can indeed abstract from the bearer of the form, i.e. from the *thing that has the form*, and then retain pure boundaries, which awaken the appearance of being forms (figures) for the reason that the form, though left out, is co-related. It is with figures of this kind that geometry has to do, whose "elements," i.e. points, lines, surfaces and so-called bodies, betray their origin — namely through abstraction from intuitive forms — only insofar as the constructions performable with them can be tested and elucidated on intuitive (moreover, for the most part open) figures (e.g. angles). In and for themselves, however, it is not a matter of figures at all, but of strictly groundable rules for the *construction* of *boundaries*. This reveals itself, among other things, in the practice — avoidable perhaps in words but not in fact — of defining curves as *loci* of *points*. Example: the circle is the geometric *locus* of all points that have the same distance from a fixed point; the parabola is the geometric *locus* of all points that have the same distance from a fixed point and a fixed straight line; the ellipse is the geometric *locus* of all points for which the sum of their distances from two fixed points has a constant value, etc. A glance at the foregoing definitions could suffice to confirm the following convictions: in terms of the science of consciousness there is only one element of geometry, namely points in space; all remaining elements are to be derived from the spatial point; the spatial point is the "primal image" of the boundary; all other boundaries are to be derived from the spatial point; the object of geometry is the laws of the constructibility of spatial *boundaries*. (If one says spatial "*magnitudes*," that is only a derived word for the same thing; for everything bounded — but also only something bounded — is, in relation to something else bounded, a "magnitude.") One will now understand what we meant in Note 40, where we called intuitive space formed but unbounded, and so-called Euclidean space formless and boundless. Since the boundary has meaning at all only in relation to something continuous, the boundless-continuous is co-related through the boundary; and since, further, it is the intuitive *form of space* through whose omission the geometric "figure" arose, geometric space lacks form. With this it is already stated that unboundedness coincides for it with infinity; for with the assumption of an end, the boundary would be attached to the *medium itself*, *in reference to* which geometry *posits* boundaries. With regard to a medium itself bounded, all constructions of geometry would be false. Not even the straight line would exist any longer; for, whether one determines it from the point of view of distance or of direction, it itself lacks the mark of finitude. (The conceptual construction of n-fold manifolds remains unaffected and can be mathematically as well as physically valuable, provided only one did not forget: first, that the use of the name "space" for it is merely borrowed usage; second, that speculations of this kind can never extend our knowledge of the *actuality* of space.) Further pursuit of these thoughts could contribute something, even if only on the most modest scale, to the philosophy of mathematics. This, admittedly, would have to be done by men who understood mathematics a hundred times better than the author! Here let only three more remarks be permitted. To begin with, the famous dispute between "empiricists" and "apriorists" is hereby decided. Insofar as geometry has to do merely with boundaries, that is, with a state of affairs that does not occur in actuality at all, its constructions (Euclidean as well as non-Euclidean) are pure thought-things or pure creations of the spirit, which are neither proved nor refuted by way of experience. But insofar as it is space into which it carries its boundaries, it remains, with all its speculations, dependent on one *side* of actuality. In precisely this dependence, and only in it, lies grounded the possibility of the *application* of its results to actual occurrences. — Secondly, one recognizes at once from what *inner* grounds geometry could and had to be "arithmetized." Number is discontinuous, form continuous. The transition from the discontinuous to the continuous is, as we have seen, *logically* impossible. The (geometric) curve, on the other hand, permits the transition by means of calculation, because its continuity accrues to it only apparently, namely through the co-relatedness of space, while it itself is a constructible *locus*. — Thirdly, finally, one notices that, in relation to the geometric figure, number belongs to a *still* higher degree of abstraction, in that it depends immediately neither on the spatial pole nor on the temporal pole. To what extent it too nevertheless presupposes actuality will occupy us only in Volume III.

One can sharpen the problem into the following antinomy: we would not have the *concept* of the individual triangle if we did not have that of the triangle; and yet the object of thought "individual triangle" is absolutely different from the object of thought "triangle as such," and even though it remains true that we arrive, where applicable, from the latter to the former, and certainly not the reverse, one still asks in vain how the triangle is to be found in the individual triangle. One will never conceive how a real atom could act upon a second atom; but one will just as little conceive how *the* triangle is lodged within the individual triangle, or how the individual triangle takes part in its species; and by far the greater part of what has been put forward on this is "evident" failures. No wonder! One wanted to explain what does not exist at all; for the real atom does not act upon a second atom, and the conceptual species "triangle" does not occur in any way in the conceptual individual triangle. Only in a much later chapter (namely of Volume III) shall the fundamental confusion responsible for these failures find its final possible clarification; here, however, we end our excursus on the triangle, turning back in a wide curve to our starting point.

When we let atoms act upon one another, we have substituted, for an actually occurring and wholly inconceivable happening, a conceptual relation of (calculable) units, with which we thereafter conduct ourselves as though it were itself a real connection; and when we suppose ourselves to find *the* triangle in the individual triangle, we have again — only in a different respect — established a relation between two objects of thought. There are indispensable and dispensable relations. The [p. 430] relation of the individual case to the species, or of the species to the still more general genus (in the case of the triangle, say, to the genus "figure"), is an indispensable relation, because without it the individual case could not be apprehended as an object of thought at all. We suppose ourselves to find the triangle-species in the individual triangle because the apprehension of the individual triangle as an object of thought takes place with the aid of the conceptual relatedness of it to the triangle as such. We can also bring the mental act of relating to consciousness, and do so (at least potentially), as often as we call the individual triangle a triangle. Instead of the misguided question of how the species partakes in its applied cases, we have the meaningful question of the ground of the being-related of the two to one another.

If there were in us one essence that produced the contents of lived experience, and again another that, as though from outside, performed acts upon them, then neither the first essence nor the second would have (thinking) consciousness: the former not, because something would merely befall it; the latter not, because it would merely do something; for pure undergoing is no (objective) finding, and pure doing is likewise no finding. The acting essence would cut, and the suffering essence would be cut; the latter would resemble the bread, the former the knife; but, however convincingly we speak of the "sharpness" of the understanding, who could fail to recognize that an understanding that were *nothing* but a knife would not have the very least prospect of "apprehending" (= grasping around), of "conceiving" (= encompassing), and of taking spiritual possession of anything! Only, then, insofar as it is its own lived experiences on which an essence performs the act of dividing, can what is thereby separated be relatable to one another and accordingly be a *differentiated thing*. Distinguishing and relating are correlative concepts. If a is distinguished from b, then both are related to one another, and if a and b are related to one another, then they are also distinguished. But as surely as the state of affairs of distinguishing stands in interaction with the state of affairs of relating, just as surely can we *not* derive the parting and the joining from the same side of the essence that apprehends as an object of thought. Rather, it is the spirit of this essence by which it is compelled to separate, and it is its vitality thanks to which it remains capable of joining together again what has been separated, and it is, finally, the *mutual counter-working* of the two from which thinking consciousness stems, by which we would have to understand something of this kind: the knowledge of *what is mutually related yet different*. The indispensable difference of the species from the individual case is also an indispensable [p. 431] relatedness of the two to one another; but the generative ground of the being-related is the lived connectedness of a general character with a particular character, or, that is, of an essence with the forms of its appearing, whereas the generative ground of the being-differentiated is the conceptual boundary as, so to speak, the remaining trace of a cleaving deed of spirit; with which we have, for a second time, circumscribed the receptivity of vitality for the working of spirit, and have ended our excursus.

The chief yield of the inquiry is the insight: general meaning-units do not arise through the essentially dividing activity of spirit, but by virtue of lived connections, and only *after* they have arisen does the process of abstraction intervene, in that it replaces meaning-units by concepts, connections by mere relations, which, as no longer bound to any intuitiveness, are capable of a generality both fundamentally different and incomparably higher in degree. — If, then, the sensualist believed he arrived at the general by way of abstracting, it must be objected to him that the process of abstracting would, of itself, rather isolate, and would render impossible even the most modest scope of a concept. If, conversely, the formalist believes he can dictate concepts to actuality, it must be objected to him that even concepts constructed by the understanding (as by far most of those of mathematics and mechanics are) would lack the character of generality, and thus applicability, were there not also present in them, by way of co-relatedness, traits of actuality, in relation to which they themselves are — abstracta! *Every* concept, in other words, is an abstractum, and no concept has *therefore* the character of generality, but rather by virtue of that from which it was "detached." Once we have concepts, we can combine them ourselves and thereby form relational concepts, of which, to be sure, it could never again be seen in respect of what they were "abstracta" were we not to trace the path of combination back; hence it bespeaks a complete misapprehension of the matter when some proponents of an "autonomous" origin of concepts believe they have refuted the process of abstraction by pointing to the unfulfillability of the demand to specify the state of affairs by whose omission objects of thought such as elasticity, electron, quotient, square root, logarithm, cube, conic section, business, credit, trade, guarantee, benefit, authority, correction, and so on, have as it were "remained over." For it plainly stands with such concepts very much [p. 432] as with the tools and machines that we have assembled from pieces for a purpose of use, each of which, *severed* from *natural* connections, received its machine-serviceable form through a more or less vigorous *simplification*! (That this is even more than a mere simile will be shown in Volume II.) Above all, however, the paths and goals of abstracting are different according as abstracting or generalizing *leads the way*.

Let us assume that the meaning of the one — however it may be — has been found; then, for the *concept* of it to arise, its *character* would first have to be split off. This would in any case yield the possibility of counting, even though it might take a considerable time before one got beyond the first steps of counting. If now the comparing gaze fell upon the finished numbers, it would sooner or later infallibly succeed in the making-autonomous of concepts of difference and equality of magnitude, which would leave the *intuitive* difference — say, of the heights of two trees or the thicknesses of their trunks — behind by just as much in generality as in abstractness, and henceforth spirit would find itself in possession of a "greater" and "smaller," a "more" and "less," for which it would be in vain to seek a starting point in the world of the senses. But to whatever utmost generalities it might thus raise itself, the sense even of the very utmost of them would still be borne by the one, whose point of contact with the world of intuition will be shown later, and the work of climbing would have been accomplished solely thanks to a sign-language that is, once again, sensuous! But if we set alongside the generalities *out of* abstractness the abstractnesses *out of* generality, such as morning and evening, summer and winter, youth and age, friendship and enmity, love and hate, it is impossible to fail to recognize the fundamental differences between the two groups. The former, won through continued splittings-off, are poor in meaning far beyond their generality; the latter, abstract only because they represent concepts, that is, closures, seem, precisely through their generality, to carry weight of meaning; the former, with growing generality, are pushed further and further out into an outside-the-world, resembling projections of something in itself incomprehensible onto the plane of actuality; in the latter, so it seems to us, powers of actuality have, notwithstanding their abstractness, had a coforming share; the former are on the "way upward," the latter on the "way downward," that is, toward the center. There, finally, in the service of demarcation, reigns the unintuitive difference (differentia specifica), which in the end [p. 433] invariably terminates in relativism; here, the (contrary) opposition, pointing to polarities of life.

Striving to ascertain the effect of the deed of spirit upon the process of lived experience within the substance of life, we have brought into the beam of the sharpest illumination the two elements, if one will, of the state of affairs "concept," which we had earlier illumined from other sides: the complete demarcatedness (isolatedness) by which it attests its origin from spirit, and the now greater, now lesser generality with which the boundless and boundary-dissolving process of life has a share in it. In the second chapter it was said of the sensuous act of apprehension that it *wrests* its object from the world of appearance and thereby joins to it, "for reasons still opaque for the time being," the peculiar gift of finding it again identically in its ever so different views. We recall that the ground of co-relatedness in general — the conceptual facade, so to speak — has meanwhile been unveiled. The individual object too, bearing the name "this tree here," or a determinate point of time, a determinate point of space, has indeed, as has been repeatedly emphasized, the character of generality, in that it remains, for any arbitrary sequence of spirit's finding glances, the selfsame something. But as surely as the conviction of identity can only take hold because its object, at the moment of being found through the act of apprehension, is wrested from the stream of time and thus "fixed" once and for all, just as surely does the *re*-finding of what has been fixed require the elementary similarity that manifests itself immediately in the animal's and the human being's capacity for impression. Of the two moments or sides that can again be distinguished in it — the specifically psychic gift of intuition and the specifically bodily capacity of sensing — we have hitherto given detailed appreciation only to the former, and have arrived at the following conclusion: the applicability of the thought of sameness to what is actual presupposes the concept of the time-position, this in turn presupposes the empirical now, and the empirical now is grounded in the lived experience of the space of intuition, insofar as it is regarded from the point of view of the "cross-section" of the time of actuality. The most general co-relatedness of any object of thought whatever is called spatiality, and, because lived temporality cannot be separated from lived spatiality, space-temporality; and it is only in *relation* to the space-temporality of the content of lived experience that the purely dividing deed of spirit leads to the success of positing a boundary. But to the question of what the process of life thereby suffers, and how an [p. 434] essence must change that serves a spirit engaged in deeds as its dwelling-place, the answer is given us by a look at the sensuous precipitates of thinking, we mean at its sign-language.

Since the logicist pays homage to the belief in the possibility of truths not only free of images but also free of signs, let it be recalled once more that signless thinking could no more take place than thinking without the foundation of intuitive lived experience. All thinking is, by its nature, a dialogical process, for which the conversational form of Platonic philosophy offers a monumental example, or, as *Palágyi* puts it, a "self-intercourse" of consciousness which, like every intercourse, requires a form of utterance, though distinctively a sign-language. Already the animal essence is determined from moment to moment by lived meaning-units and answers to them with phenomena of expression; but a consciousness of images, bodies, and essences, or of facts in general, or of one's own existing, or of thinking spirit, or finally of relations and concepts, exists solely by virtue of the signs through which we subsequently relate ourselves to what has been lived. We leave it undecided here why, within mankind, it was precisely the vocal sign that gained dominion all along the line; for it suffices to emphasize: just as the deed of spirit, springing up at fracture-points of lived experience, could not arise without the material of intuition which it is its function to break up into fragments, so it could, even once it had arisen, "apprehend" at the very least nothing, unless it were also able to hold fast the boundaries it had created — and it fixes them only by once again calling vitality to its aid for the purpose of coining signs that permit the "enclosed" to be communicated, in the first instance to other moments of life of the bearer of spirit, but thereby to the bearer of thinking consciousness as such. Accordingly, the name would have two kinds of "energies" proper to it: the symbolically indicating, of, as it were, kinetic nature, and the conceptually delimiting, of potential nature. If we let the former prevail, we come into the phenomenal world of essences revealing themselves; if, however, the latter, then into the noumenal world of objects setting themselves off against one another. The name by itself calls preeminently for beholding: think of words like Montenegro or sea-surf or sunset, or of cries like "fire!," or even of interjections like "ah"; but in the setting of names against one another, the consciousness of boundaries, as it were, flashes up and consolidates itself. To place the stress on the former is to conjure up the meaning [p. 435] of the word, by means of which the faculty of judgement points to something unattainable by it; to place the stress on the latter is to reflect on the *concept* and thereby to become aware of the meaning-related boundaries. But with this it has already been said what happens, by virtue of delimitation, within the play-space of life.

For if, as was shown earlier, lived experience in general, and above all the lived experience of impression, is a polarized and polarizing process, or an uninterrupted exchange between the receiving actuality of the soul and the acting actuality of happening, then there follows for the bearer of life, from the delimiting deed of spirit, a barrier to the unfolding of his lived experience of *actuality* that is comparable to nothing else. The first deed of spirit founds in him the first barrier to his feeling of actuality; each following one, a new barrier, vitally linked to the earlier one; the connectedness of all of them is the content of the personal I. The in-forming of spirit coincides, in sense and extent, with a *rule-* *governed* narrowing of life. — Whoever, by means of a color-designation, finds again a shading that he would not have been able to find again without it, for him it is, within the sign's meaning-content, not the meant color but that which distinguishes it from a differently designated color that has enabled him to find it again. Insofar as an essence is able, with the help of signs signifying processes or marks, to relate itself to what is signified, to that extent it is a thinking essence.<sup>66</sup> (With his witty utterance, "In the beginning is the sign," the mathematician Hilbert would thus be right, provided that by "the beginning" the beginning of thinking is meant.) And insofar as we human beings communicate with one another through meaning-laden signs, there correspond, to the opposition of content and boundary in the words of speaker as of hearer, two mutually contending impulses, each of a particular degree of strength: the one, indicating and connecting, which fulfills itself in phantasms; the other, continually commanding a halt and hindering the lived experience from gliding over into a lived experience of kindred content, which fulfills itself in concepts of unintuitive differences. It is the former that *expresses itself* in the sound of speech; the latter, that which, by means of such expression, turns to a consciousness for the sake of understanding. Contents of meaning can be expressed symbolically; boundaries of meaning, by contrast, wholly inexpressible, can, borne by the former, only be *communicated* — and that exclusively to a reflective I.

<sup>66</sup> On page 435. — Here one will object: but we do come to an understanding with the "higher" animals, and especially with domestic animals, precisely through sign-giving; but then the animal too would be a thinking being! And certainly, if I say to my dog "Stay!", he stays home when I leave, albeit with the most doleful expression; if I say "Come," he comes bounding; he sits at "Sit!", lies down at "Down!" and so forth. It looks as though he understands human speech to a modest extent and answers, through his behavior, to "meaning-laden" signs. — Since most animal-lovers are probably inclined to credit the animal with an understanding of speech, we must not pass over the objection in silence. Since in our "Grundlegung der Wissenschaft vom Ausdruck" we devoted a thorough investigation to the origin of language, we make use here in part, almost verbatim, of some sentences from it, at the risk that they are already known to some readers. All the theories of language that have ever existed agree, knowingly or unknowingly, in the assumption, and must do so, that the speech-sound is such a sound as means something wholly different from itself, and therefore finds use as a *sign* of what it means. That is indisputably correct. Only the name "sign," for all its apparent unambiguity, has several meanings, of which the following stand out even linguistically from one another: indication, omen — mark, badge, characteristic, token, signal-sign (or signal) — symbol-image. By the two dividing strokes three main groups are marked off. The omen is only a variety of the indication or *symptom*; mark, characteristic, and signal-sign all serve at least to distinguish, and are thus in any case *signs of distinction* (diacritics); "symbol-image," finally, gives Ramler's rendering of *symbol*. Whereas now marks and signal-signs merely indicate something different from themselves, the speech-sound *contains* what it means, whether or not it also thereby indicates it. We must therefore sharply separate from the indications — partly symptomatic, partly serving distinction — the *meaning-laden* signs, which among original humanity were one and all symbol-images. But however much, in the matter-of-fact thinking of today, symbolic thinking may now participate only as an underlying stratum, the difference nonetheless persists without restriction between the meaning-laden sound and the signal-sign or signal. We offer for this a few convincing examples. Meaning-laden, quite generally, is what we call such signs in which what they mean *inheres* — thus linguistic signs, further written signs, finally pantomimic gestures. If, on the other hand, a hooting sounds for five minutes beside my house, from which every fireman gathers that he must report at once for a drill, that is a *signal*, which admittedly *has* an agreed sign-value but by no means represents it. The same holds of the whistles of factory sirens, of locomotives, of the many optical and acoustic signals of railway operation, of the bell-signs in schools, of the trumpet signals in military service, and of numerous sign-givings of a similar kind. We, who already have meaning-laden signs at our disposal, can convey such things, at least in part, *also* by signals (drum-language, flag-language); for that reason signals and meaning-laden signs are no less different in essence, and the latter can never develop out of the former, as some researchers would still like to assume (on the basis, as it seems, chiefly of certain facts from the prehistory of the origin of writing, whose discussion here, however, would lead too far). One thing at least admits not the slightest doubt: linguistic intercourse rests on meaning-signs, and these are *not* mere signal-signs! Once we have become clear about the difference, we assure ourselves at once that domestic animals obey our linguistically uttered wishes and commands thanks to their understanding of signals, and in no case out of an understanding of speech. If I have trained my dog to search for the cat as soon as I call to him "Find the cat!", he will likewise search just as often as I instead make use of one of the following turns of phrase: Are you finding the cat? — Were you finding the cat? — Don't find the cat! etc. This admittedly has its limits. If I alter the little sentence more and more, he will look at me doubtfully, because he no longer recognizes the signal with sufficient certainty. And to this is added something else, which was bound to favor, to an extraordinary degree, the belief in at least a modest understanding of speech among animals. — Dogs and horses fundamentally surpass humans in the understanding of expressive movements. Now the intonation is different in the imperative sentence, different in the interrogative sentence, different in the declarative sentence, and so on. If, then, I put *very* distinct interrogative *stress* into the interrogative sentence, the signal changes for the dog far beyond the mere difference of sound and is consequently likewise not recognized. But if I omit this, he follows the signal, notwithstanding that the sense of the sentence has become an entirely different one. One convinces oneself of this in yet another way. From angry rebuke through mild reproof to tender approval runs a very long ladder of gradations of tone in the human voice, which an animal like the dog grasps with an almost unbelievable sensitivity to difference. Let us take the case that someone habitually uses similar turns of phrase throughout when he scolds his dog, and other, likewise similar ones among themselves, when he shows it tender affection; then the dog will react with the signs of grief or fear as soon as one hurls at him a "You dear, good animal" with an expression of anger, but will fawn and make up to him at the tenderness-stressed address: You colossal idiot! In short, our domestic animals have by nature, in part, quite outstanding understanding of expressive phenomena and *acquire* through us, to a considerable extent, an understanding of signals; but they neither have nor acquire the least understanding of speech. The world of meaning-laden signs is closed to animals, and thus they do *not think*.

[p. 436] Two people converse meaningfully about state, politics, government, empire, law, but would at first exhaust themselves in groping attempts if set the task of specifying the concept of one of those words. We believe we know, as well as anyone could, what a plant is, and nonetheless run into difficulties in the effort to state it, as soon as it occurs to us that there are, among plants, also such as move and consume flesh. We predicate being in countless declarative sentences and nonetheless fall into doubt whether, for instance, our contents of judgement belong to being, and whether truths are facts. Who does not know exactly, in practical life, what it means to make someone ridiculous, and who could state without fail what it is that "ridiculousness" actually consists in? We gather from this that it cannot be concepts with whose help we speak meaningfully. Rather, what allows us, in keeping with the sole consciously intended purpose of communication, to choose words unconsciously with assurance and to combine them consistently, are meaning-filled *attitudes*, with regard to which anyone can readily verify that they stand, as it were, constantly on the point of calling forth those sense-spatial intuitive images in which we have shown the connecting link between actuality and conceptuality. Whenever we begin to reflect on what state, what government, what empire is, there seems to press up, first of all, out of the immediate underlayer of consciousness, a formation now hazily wavering, now fairly determinate (for instance, a government building), which had secretly co-determined our choice of words and is therefore even ready to offer itself as material for the attempt at conceptual delimitation. But we at once also note the impulse contending with it, to leave the whole domain of intuitiveness and to draw nearer to the concept by stringing together names of kindred meaning, which set themselves off from one another more or less sharply. If we define government, say, as the legislative body and necessary part of the state, then there is no longer any talk even of remnants of intuitiveness, and we have instead arrived at a setting of names against one another, which comes to its conclusion in the drawing of boundaries. Because the sense, as object of thought, of all contents of meaning is exhausted in the mutual relation of the concepts of them, we can hope to track it down only beyond any intuitiveness whatever, in the relations that have consolidated themselves in meaning-laden signs. Whereas, in order to discover actuality in the vocal sign [p. 437], we would have to feel our way back from it to the lived experience that made use of the sign to represent its content (which, as is understood, would in most cases happen only through a long series of intermediate links), we ascertain, under an artificial exclusion of this connection, the object of thought solely in those properties of the signs that ground their *mutual ordering*. That every determination of a concept demands reflection on the matter needs no saying; but reflection on the matter, widely different from reflection on lived experience, breathes, so to speak, the atmosphere of meaning-signs, and would, without them, be condemned to suffocation. Let one recall any cases one likes. If someone without graphic talent wants to tell another, say, about the construction of a machine, and the name centrifuge or step-grate or ball valve suddenly fails him, there sets in, first, an often agonizing search for the names of kindred objects, and, if he does not succeed, with their help, in finding the unknown sign, or at least a substitute word, there follows at once the disappointing knowledge of having, of the matter, indeed a vague intuitive image, but by no means the concept! Conversely, it suffices to name to someone wholly unfamiliar with mechanical engineering the terms flue gases, heating gases, combustion air, in order, by that alone, to have already somewhat increased his conceptual knowledge. From this it follows that we would be unable to employ language for purposes of communication, were there not, *besides* the content-phantasm, also, in the feeling of word-meaning, the condition for the delimitation of meaning. Added to the speech-experience long since completed beforehand, through the in-forming of the activity of spirit, it must be conceived as a *reining force*, adhering to the content-phantasm, upon its urge to expand, with which, at the same time, the counter-claims of conceptually neighboring signs announce themselves as claimants to the word.

We can illustrate the state of affairs by any pair of concepts we choose, or indeed by any pair of words; for in a language that serves thinking and is guided by communicative purposes, there are no names whose meaning-phantasms have not grown together with limits upon their drive to spread, set against other names; but nowhere do these come home to us more convincingly than when we consider that the sound-sign forms themselves enclose grammatical and syntactic meaning-contents. Even with regard to these, to be sure, we are far from holding them to be mere products of spirit, and here and there we have already [p. 438] taken the opportunity to cast, however fleeting, a sidelight on the lived-experience foundations *also* of grammar; yet there is no doubt that a language would be without them only if it were nothing but a language of images! The undoubtable circumstance that there are, say, nominal experiences alongside verbal experiences shows us language as it were impregnated with the consequences of deeds already performed by the spirit that splits apart and thereby conceptually delimits. If now, with every language still living, its heir also inherited the dispositions that compel him to experience: feelings of declension and conjugation; feelings for case, tense, mood; feelings that enable one to distinguish the nomen agentis from the nomen actionis; feelings for root, stem, suffix; for the relation of subject and predicate; for numbers, conjunctions, prepositions; pronominal and adverbial feelings — then we shall not hesitate to acknowledge that with the acquisition of language the organism was implanted not only with an unsurveyable manifold of historically arisen content-phantasms, but also with the equally unsurveyable manifold of consciousness-sustaining inclinations toward classes of *objects* that *bound themselves off against* *one another*, beginning with things and reaching into the thousandfold ways of human doing and refraining. Hidden overseers of our manifold conduct wait upon the call that would empower them to make themselves known in prohibitions against the crossing of boundaries: attitudes of understanding — of believing, holding-true, meaning, representing, judging, thinking, inferring, concluding, conceiving, explaining, apprehending, understanding, cognizing, knowing; attitudes of will — of seeking, asking, finding, resolving, commanding, obeying, ruling, serving, being-able, having-to; attitudes of the body — of resting, moving, lying, sitting, standing, walking, riding, carrying, lifting, and so on. Take away these attitudes, and man is by no means deaf of soul, but he has indeed become blind of spirit and incapable of thought!

But we must not yet call a halt, and once more take up the expedient of self-contestation in order to drive the thought to its end. Boundary-checks upon lived experience, one might object, exist equally in the lived experience of any animal whatever — as when, say, fear prevents the bird from pecking crumbs from a human being's open hand. Wherein, then, would lie the peculiarity of that boundary-check which alone is supposed to be capable of bearing a boundary-consciousness, and why should the same success be denied to the animal occurrence of mutually conflicting impulses? [p. 439] How do we know that it does not happen through the drawing of boundaries when the bull quite certainly distinguishes something red from something blue, and why, conversely, *must* the drawing of the boundary also detach the color from the colored thing? Objections of this kind could also be cast in the form of a question. Whoever distinguishes gray from light gray has, one might say, indeed distinguished color as such from the colored thing, and with this further distinction has set a new boundary within what was already conceptually bounded. It is thus already a thought-thing with respect to which its apprehension of color takes place. But then nothing at all has yet been said of the transformation of the impression-content through the act of apprehension, but only of what happens to the thing through an act of restriction of what is apprehended. How, then, is the boundary-check constituted which guarantees not so much conceptual understanding as rather conceiving itself — or, in other words: what alteration does the impression-experience undergo through the first and most fundamental act of apprehension?

Contrary to a widespread opinion, there obtains between conceptual understanding and original reflection on the matter merely a difference of degree, not of kind. As soon as a being has entered into that vital attitude with reference to which we call it a thinking being, it henceforth perceives nothing without spiritually apprehending it, and it apprehends nothing whatever, however slight, without the assistance of some concept or other. Even "plain" perception, however certainly an act of apprehension declares itself in it within the consciousness-capable bearer of life, already includes a conceiving within itself; only that the object thereby posited can, among all objects of actuality, be the poorest in co-related content, namely a something that is simply and merely present. The most original transformation of an impression, that is, the one effected by plain attention, consists in the flipping-over of the mirrored counterpart of an image into the merely thinkable counterpart of the existing something, and thus in the flipping-over of mirroring lived experience itself into the meaning-feeling of the actuality of a being-there. Every act of apprehension, hence the very first no less than the very latest, includes within itself a positing of being, insofar as it takes place only with regard to a world that is. The turn whereby the experience of something actual is forced to pass over into an experience of the being of this actuality conveys the feature common to all boundaries of lived experience arising from deeds of the spirit.

[p. 440] In the judgement, one thing is gray, the other light gray, there lies, as a possibility, that there is something gray as there is something light gray; but in it, too, lies insight into the difference between the gray and the light gray and things colored gray or light gray. The thing, identical with itself, changes its color among other things; but the object which the concept of gray or of light gray delimits never changes. The same act that compels us to strike something experienced as actual into the fetters of being separates the content of experience from actuality and would let it vanish into the point outside space and time, were it not that the experienced pull of images compels us to take up, along with the connecting band of actuality, the form of being into the object as well — which object thereby becomes now the universal, immediately related to space and time, of the thing, now the universal, related to the thing, of the property. In the world of things, as it was put in the 23rd Chapter, space, time, rest, motion, how splinter apart from one another; in the world of things, as we now continue, they all remain related to one another, because they were sides of an image of actuality, from which the spirit found itself compelled to detach them for the sake of objectification. The positing of being tears apart all objects of thought, and the positing of being now links them together again in a new way, by letting them all be related to this one and the same thing which, although it is outside space and time and outside the world, on account of its origin takes over the representation precisely of actuality — that is to say, of that side of all happening to which the units of meaning stand related as appearances to the appearing essence. — An application of the content of the highly abstract concept of being is given us, with its "there is something," by every, as it were, downright naked perceptual judgement, and hence also the content-poorest of all judgements that we are ever occasioned to pronounce in the face of an intuitive image. If, accordingly, the soul is henceforth denied the experience of the transformation of actuality, it has nevertheless received in exchange the experience of the mutual relatedness of independencies that are otherwise strictly confined within boundaries.

All the investigations of this book that bear on this matter resemble concentric circles, with whose help we encompass, step by step, ever more narrowly the essential content of the concept of being. In spite of all this, even the most willing reader will presumably again come to a halt and inwardly resist when we now assert in the most definite terms that no animal, however adapted the behavior with which it responds to the actuality of the most various events, ever experiences so much as the precondition of the judgement: there is something; [p. 441] and that it accordingly lives, notwithstanding a thousandfold similarity of its awareness to our awareness, in a fundamentally different *actuality* than we do. But now consider: if I can judge, there is something, then also, it was there or was not there, and it will be there or probably will not, and then, further: it *could* be here, even though it is not here! But who would not come fully to a halt if one tried to persuade him that the deer perceives not merely the meadow but occasionally is also wont to ask, or to comport itself in accordance with the question, why are there not a few trees standing here on the meadow? (Remarked in passing: it would also somehow find the means to plant the trees, if only it thought of such a thing.) If one now says no to this, one should not overlook that in doing so one has at the same time denied the condition of judgements of being in the lived experience of animals! — We scarcely need add what the gradation men-<sup>67</sup> tioned above was meant to say. If, in the spirit-endowed being, the perceptual act that is as relationless as possible lets the intuitive image congeal into the thing that is as indeterminate as possible, this thing narrows into an ever more determinate object through every subsequent act of apprehension; and if the "naked" act of apprehension erects, in the stream of lived experience, the boundary-feeling of being-there, then, within the feeling of being-there, every subsequent act of conceptual interpretation erects boundary upon boundary of its field of extension. For this reason it is a matter of indifference which point in the series one chooses in order to demonstrate the incorporation of the precipitate of spiritual acts. But it is time that we close the third-innermost ring of our consideration.

<sup>67</sup> On page 441. — Animals *search*, but they do not ask. Searching and asking are no more and no less different from one another than animal and man, in such a way that of all earth's inhabitants man alone is a questioning being. The motif of the pain of questioning in the countless myths, legends, and fairy tales of countless peoples, whose most powerful symbol is the Sphinx, will occupy us elsewhere. When Nietzsche remarks in one passage that the cow sometimes has the look of an astonishment that has come to a halt halfway to the question, we convince ourselves at once, through attentive examination, that the facial expression of the cow scarcely ever betrays any particular astonishment, let alone even the *beginning* of a question, but we see no less clearly from that ingenious little sentence that Nietzsche too accords the state of questioning exclusively to man. Searching reaches down into the world of the protists, above all the searching for a way out of a distressing situation, and the characteristic thing about it is this: that it either finds — now the alluring goal, now the state of equilibrium that a disturbance had temporarily abolished — or does not find; in which case it continues, under certain circumstances to the point of exhaustion, whereas questioning, in relation to searching, signifies a state entirely different in essence, which we can further describe as follows. At the moment of the transition to the question, vital or psychic searching is replaced by the *searching of the spirit*. Being able to question therefore means: being able to think, and in thinking, in place of outer movement there steps that - *inner* movement whose outcome, becoming conscious to us, we for that reason like to call "movement of thought." But thinking is impossible without relatedness to being, and relatedness to being is impossible without the omission — co-related, to be sure, for that very reason — of actuality! If I ask someone to *think of* the blast of a trombone, he really hears the sounds spoken by me and not at all the trombone-blast of which he is now, as requested, thinking. If he, in thinking of the trombone-blast, had not actually detached its actuality from the object of his thinking, he could either not think of it at all, but merely perceive the trombone-blast like the animal, or else, as soon as he did so, the trombone-blast would have to sound audibly to him as well! Now, this thought-of thing, this uniquely de-actualized being, is that in view of which all spiritual searching, in short, questioning, takes place.

Whence comes the compulsion to the positing of being?<sup>68</sup> Not from lived experience, which hangs wholly and exclusively upon the appearance of actuality, and not from the (extra-spatio-temporal) spirit alone, were a place not prepared for it in the play-space of life. We would not find outside us the semblance of being, did there not lie in us *actually* being in the form of the time-constant pivot of life and spirit: one calls it the I or self. Only because spirit is in fact connected, through the actuality of our lived experience, with the self that is, do all images of actuality mirror back to us independently existing points! Even the perception-capable animal continually experiences something that meets it as alien, something different from its own state, but not something different from a self; and only what meets the self as its externality has the de-actualized form of actuality that is being!

<sup>68</sup> On page 441. — The reader will notice that we are hereby bending back to the remarks with which we anticipated, by way of pointer, in the 9th chapter. Meanwhile, of the "theses" with which the 8th chapter closed, not indeed all, but most, have now been unfolded and proven.

Attempts to distinguish essentially the sense of the I from the sense of the self are hopeless and have been rejected throughout [p. 442] by linguistic usage. Just as the mystics of the fourteenth century already used Ichheit [I-hood] in the sense of egoism, so too analogous formations attach themselves to "self": selfhood, self-seeker, selfishness, self-praise, self-love, selfish, self-deception, and so on. That from the I-am consciousness the consciousness of being, and hence the consciousness of sameness, wells up can, taken purely linguistically, be shown nowhere more clearly than in the derivatives of "self." "Derselbe" [the same], earlier written "derselbe," originally meant "der nämliche" [the very one]; hence we have translated word for word when we rendered "identify" repeatedly by "verselbigen" [to render-selfsame]. "Self-consciousness" was at first not yet consciousness of self-worth, but consciousness of oneself and consequently consciousness of one's own being-there. To this add "self-active" and "self-activity," which lets a happening break forth from the separated point of being; further the archaic "self-stand," left to us only in the adjectival "independent" [selbständig], with which one sought, unsurpassably, to render into German the sense of — substance! Finally let mention be made of the etymological conjecture according to which the original meaning of "self" was as much as "lord, owner."

The *first* boundary-check in the lived experience of actuality, instituted by the *first* act of spirit, is the I — though not yet consciousness of the I, but first of all consciousness of its mirror-semblance, that is, of actuality sensibly congealed into a matter. Yet with this there was in fact accomplished what philosophy is wont falsely to grasp as a mark of actuality: the splitting of the world into "subject" and "object"; and this now draws after it, unstoppably, countless other splittings, all of them, in a sense, of the same caliber, and lets them step by step enter "into consciousness," by occasioning the one who reflects upon it to separate: thing from thing, thing from time and space, time from space, thing from property, from state of the thing, subject from subject, subject from property and state of the subject, property of the subject from property of the matter, and so forth. Thus selfhood expands, in the play-space of life, through the *ever-new boundary-checks it forms into* the beholding of actuality.

We have approached spirit, from the side of life, through the zone of visible evidence as far as possible; we have approached life, from the side of spirit, through the mediation of the boundary-checks of the impression of actuality, as far as possible; but we have found no answer to the question how, phylogenetically, at some time or other, spirit was first able to work its way into life. [p. 443] We know, and believe we can prove, that this happened exclusively in man, and indeed not even in original man, but only in a late stratum of prehistoric man; but the how and why remain, for the present, an insoluble riddle. The vitality of present-day man, of this there can be no doubt, already brings with it germ-plasmically a disposition for the reception of spiritual acts, and this disposition becomes actual by way of the acquisition of a language which, along with the primal store of symbolic meaning-contents, also communicates the traces of the millennia-long arts of separation of the logos. Before we consider a little more closely our final result, according to which the fundamental content of the I is to be regarded as equivalent to a system of unique feeling-inhibitions, let us document with a few examples how one attains something like immediate knowledge of the flipping-over of mere lived experience into the experience of the separating and distinguishing boundary, by recollecting suitable cases.

Already a foretaste of this is gained by anyone who has misunderstood an impression and now makes the peculiar experience that some subsequent act of apprehension transforms the object of perception abruptly and completely. One need only think of those jesting pictures whose grinning skull turns out, on closer inspection, unexpectedly to be a bright semicircle in which two children sit playing, facing one another; or of the still more feeling-laden change of understanding whereby, in what was taken for the whimpering of a child, one suddenly hears the yowling of a cat. As, in a labile equilibrium, the slightest push suffices to rearrange the whole system, so here an almost imperceptible and in any case no longer analyzable change of impression has had as its consequence the complete exchange of the things perceived. Since, however, it would require detailed working-out to demonstrate the difference between occurrences of this kind and outwardly similar ones from the animal kingdom, we illustrate the state of affairs more compellingly by the transition of the actuality of the impression into the actuality of the thing. For we can also become aware that an impression-content, experienced indeed but as yet not objectlike, gives way to the meaning-determined object, however unthinkable this may appear and however much it can, to be sure, be known only afterward. For reasons to be developed later, it happens, namely, that the impression must repeat itself several times before attaining a degree of corporeality that first suffices to offer the act an assailable support; and then it sometimes happens that we, in a similar way, only immediately remember an unconsciously mirrored something, just as we are always able to recollect something unconsciously dreamed. — [p. 444] Whoever is woken from deep sleep by a knocking at the door not seldom knows, at the moment of perceiving it, that it had already knocked twice before, without his being-present having gained the character of selfhood or the waking sound the character of thinghood. One who is caught up in a passionate conversation, to whom an interrupting message is brought to notice only through repeated repetition, has nevertheless already had the impression of it, which is only now, renewed, perceived by him. After act-diminished pauses of "thoughtless," "absent," "distracted" staring at some sensible thing, one who suddenly "comes to himself" often at once realizes that he has already been facing it for a good while, but without the capacity to objectify and separate out his own state from the image bound up with it. Whoever eavesdrops on himself in such moments will most likely feel, like a blow, the transforming jolt that has befallen the impression through the separating lightning-flash of the act of apprehension.<sup>69</sup>

<sup>69</sup> On page 444. — Finally, to ward off an obvious misunderstanding: we do *not* mean that the animal's lived experience is to be compared in the remotest degree to what we have just called "thoughtless staring," "absence," and so on. Mere pausing of the spirit cannot transpose back into the life-state of animality a being that, as has been shown, was long ago compelled, even before the intervention of the spirit, to separate itself vitally from it. As a result of the enormous preponderance of the gift of beholding over the capacity for sensation in us, even the contents of impression (thus the material of the act of apprehension) are already different in character from those of animality; hence we would have to draw on essentially different occurrences of our lived experience in order to find, however narrow, an access to the animalism of impressions. Although this otherwise does not belong here, let an example still be offered for it, such as has probably happened to everyone already, in this or at least a similar way. — On the occasion of a walk of several hours, someone had lost his way in an extensive forest. He tries a path to the right and turns back again, one to the left and turns back again, he walks back along the main path and turns back once more; finally he resolves to go on for the time being, but soon forgets "path and track," because he becomes absorbed in sharp reflection on a question of worldview that has long occupied him, and behold, if one may say so, his *body*, unburdened by doubts of questioning, leads him so bravely and surely that he arrives back at his starting point without any considerable detour! This experience of finding-the-way with absent understanding and without *judgement* of the path stands at least close to the impression-experience of animals, and would coincide with it, provided it could be linked to an *other* kind of wakefulness than the one alone familiar to us, in which acts of thought of the spirit follow step by step.

[p. 445]

#### 39. Kapitel — Vom Verhängnis der Selbstheit — Chapter 39 — On the Fatality of Selfhood

Spirit is outside space and time; spirit-made-alive, because rooted in temporal life, is spatial and temporal; life is boundless; personal life, because broken upon the spiritual boundary, is finite and historical. In contrast to the organic growth of the unspirited bearer of life, the historical progress of the spirited bearer has the character of self-multiplication through a kind of petrifying preservation. Against the saying with which the deepest life-philosopher the West has yet produced, *Heraclitus*, nevertheless takes the side of spirit — that the soul has proper to it a self-multiplying logos — we set the objection that this holds in no way of the soul, but certainly does hold of the I-shaped soul, or of the psychic self. The living and growing (physis) stands under the sign of eternal otherness, of a similarity that links everything with everything, finally of unceasing pulsation, and has for its equally weighty symbols the wave and the circle, whose smallest elements of direction are all different from one another, all similar to one another, and at every point signify beginning and end at once; the historically progressing (ethos) is the tangent of the circle, extensible at will, and departs to the same degree from the sense-bestowing point of origin as it is in turn able to enlarge itself. More than merely outwardly comparable to capitalism, the empirical I is the process, in each case localized in space and time, of the self-*consumption* of the stuff of *life* — a process that would, golem-like, devour the world, did it not, as essentially finite, find a brazen boundary in the death both of the individual bearer and, in the end, of the species that serves it as the site of its working.

With the first boundary of actuality implanted in it, vitality already does homage as well to the scepter of a drive that negates it, a drive which, by making images into mere matters-of-fact, withdraws them from its beholding and transmutes, [p. 446] into checks upon their course, whatever it may seize. Every new "experience" increases the distance of the personality from the original source of life, since step by step it also loads new prohibitions both upon receiving and upon striving, until at last the "experienced" person no longer lives except through experience, instead of experiencing while living! Attached to the most voracious of all passions, the mania for regulation — which, as we shall see, is one and the same as the mania to possess and to rule — as though to a band that unceasingly shortens itself, the living cell, by virtue of its "spiritual progress," draws near to a point of rigidification where, excluded from its participation in the life of the All, it falls prey to a *destruction* that no renewal follows. The way of self-becoming, and to that extent the way of fate of every personality, is the way from the moistness of life to the withering of life, from the sovereign majesty of rhythm to the compulsory rule of the regulation, from the relation of complementation to the sundering of the poles, from concord with the necessity of what happens to conflict with the ought of the law, from the being-within of the whole in the unrepeatable being proper to it to the being-a-part of merely existing individual beings within the mechanism of division; and running exactly parallel to it, "in world-historical terms," is the way from the symbiotic custom of the village commons to the detached legislature of the machinery of state! At the stage of levelling already now reached, even the one richest in life preserves, beyond his thirtieth year, scarcely a remnant of the All of the soul, even though up to twice that age he may still feed and nourish the "ordering" spirit from the urn of his own proper life. This is the reason why the person stands in need of that overwhelming eruption which the ancients already christened "ecstasy," if he is to be capable of diving back, even if only for a while, into the still-unfinitized stream of life.

This picture, to be sure, seems to fit but ill with the hymns with which logicians, philologists, and philosophers have from time immemorial celebrated the superiority of man over "nature," of intellect over so-called instinct, of will over drive, and might, to that extent, seem even to contradict our own account, insofar as the examples we adduced to illustrate the meaning-feelings likewise placed the understanding experience of meaning at an advantage over the unintelligent. Writing, a confused and unretainable scrawl for the illiterate, is transformed for the reader into an articulated sequence of meaningful signs; the speech-sound that, ununderstood, flits past the ear as noise that is at best [p. 447] indifferent, but commonly indeed disturbing, has for the one who knows the language acquired a face that he recognizes with as much certainty through every difference of voices, and even of dialects, as a human countenance in all the changes of its expression; and how utterly convincingly, finally, does the gain of conceiving show itself to us when we consider that the free availability of the treasury of memory, which alone makes it possible for us to turn experiences to account and to steer the future, coincides essentially with the scope of name-giving and finds in it a boundary that cannot be overstepped. Considering this, we may perhaps be tempted to agree with the Sophoclean chorus (in Jordan's translation):

Of things mighty / most mighty of all / is man. / Over the seas themselves / he fares in the southern / winter storm; / beneath the roaring, / breaking surge of waves / he glides *onward* . . . / for / he devised for himself the word, the airy breath / of thought. It is easy to demonstrate, by comparison with the animal, the well-nigh incalculable superiority of man, as soon as one takes, whether consciously or unspoken, the magnitude of power as the measure of worth. By taking as the basis of one's consideration not life itself but, from the outset, the consciousness of being-there, the constant momentariness of the sensory faculty of impression appears in the light of an oppressive fetter, and the animality bound to it appears the poorer for the capacity for all those achievements whose accomplishment requires a stepping-out from the spell of the present image. Every animal, too, lives the continuation of its past, but not of its "experiences," let alone that of its<sup>70</sup> forebears. It can fashion no tool for itself, because, being wholly within the experience of impression, it is not able, as man is, to "represent to itself" what, at the moment of experience, is not yet present at all [p. 448].
