With its natural weapons it defends itself, to our astonishment, admirably; "but its life or death may depend on its rolling down upon its adversary a stone which lies before it and which, merely pushed forward, would suffice to crush him: it dies without rising to any such consideration, and the utmost necessity never makes it inventive. For it has no intuition of the stone and no representation of its mobility and of the effect, still to be expected, of that mobility," however much it would, for its own part, know<sup>71</sup> how to expect and avoid that effect if it had been sensibly experienced as the threat of a fall. Its present is the living link between what has been and what is coming; but it has not the slightest foreknowledge of the future and wholly lacks that planning which would forestall and disarm a merely conceivable evil.

<sup>70</sup> On page 447. — In the sense of the word "experience" customary hitherto, the animal has experiences just as we do; but it no longer has experiences if one understands by this, as is done in this book, experiences of the understanding, i.e. the intelligent processing of the contents of lived experience.

<sup>71</sup> On page 448. — L. *Geiger*, Ursprung und Entwicklung der menschlichen Sprache und Vernunft, p. 61.

The most perceptive researchers have, to be sure, not failed to recognize that this reckoning, too, calls for a counter-balance: consciousness of being-there is one and the same as consciousness of finitude, and foreknowledge as such is bought only with the knowledge of the impending of *death*! Unceasingly, in the measure of his awareness, the science of his having-to-end accompanies consciousness-capable man, and his capacity, which subjugates every other creature, breaks tragically against the eternal unconquerability of death. "Everything grows old and grows young again; why are we alone excepted from nature's beautiful circling course?" asks *Hölderlin*, and reveals it in the sentence as fateful as it is profound: "The child is immortal; for it knows nothing of death!" In that man, and man alone, gained the knowledge of death, he alone of all creatures has, along with the thinking spirit, also drawn the constant reprieve of the gallows, whose unbearable bitterness — to cheat it with the dogma of a bodiless continuance — forms the deepest ground of origin of all religions of the spirit. Whatever ever gave priests and prophets their influence, whatever drove men and women into the "bosom of the church," into secret cults and discipleships, it was never anything other than the implacable horror of having to cease and the provision for a post-mortal immortality. There is no canonical article of faith in the world that would not lose all sense for one who, unacquainted with the fact of dying, could not wish the wish that inspired its fictions, now fantastic, now dialectical: the wish for the *de-actualization* of *death*, even [p. 449] at the price of a de-actualization of life! — When the Persian king Gustaspes had accepted the doctrine of Zarathustra, he asked to see four wishes fulfilled: that he need fear none of his enemies; that he might distinguish all the good and evil that should ever occur in the world; that his soul should remain in his body until the day of resurrection; and finally, that he be let to know what place in the other world was allotted to him. "I will indeed," said Zarathustra, "beg these four things of God for you; but you must content yourself with one, and leave the others to the three most eminent men of your court, for God does not grant them to one man alone, lest he be able to say: I am almighty." Then Gustaspes *desired* to know his place in the other *world*.<sup>72</sup>

<sup>72</sup> On page 449. — *Karl Kiesewetter*, Der Okkultismus des Altertums, p. 92.

Yet even if one, moved by such and similar considerations, makes the antagonist of understanding, so-called instinct, the starting point of those deep-penetrating investigations that led a Nietzsche to see in consciousness far rather a sickness and imperfection of life than its perfection, or even resolutely sets aside the measure of the feeling of power and poses the truly decisive question, what changes the conditions of happiness of animality have undergone through the accession of foreknowing reflectiveness, one still seems to us to be standing on the ground of an erroneous presupposition and to be assessing the worth or unworth of reason from a false point of view. — We have shown that it cannot have been the faculty of thought that distinguished original man from the animal. Man dwelt upon the earth for at least a hundred thousand years, but in all likelihood for very much longer, before even a single people entered into that historical course which is the expression of a rationality that subjugates "nature" in successive thrusts. A sign of all humanity from the very beginning was certainly language; but a glance at the symbolic thinking of the early historical period, or even at poetic usage of words, so far as it seriously deserves that name, suffices to show us language in yet another light than merely that of a means for animating spiritual acts. If, in mythic-poetic speech, the act of judgement is guided by elementary similarities, the thought would for that very reason lie near at hand that the transition of life from the animal to the human stage is to be sought not so much in the transition to a capacity for thought as rather in a [p. 450] transformation of beholding, which must be determined without regard to its capacity for being coupled with spirit; and we think it needs only a recollection of the, so to speak, poetic moments — which, after all, are wholly absent from the history of not even the soberest of men — to grasp with our hands what is at stake in the binding of life through the "power of facts"! It is not the animal stage of life, which we never experience immediately, that we must set beside the human, if we wish to compare lived experience and consciousness, but rather our own wakefulness of thinking and willing beside our own *being-carried* along by the "stream of thoughts." We search in vain in the world out there for essential differences of lived experience, if we have not been able to discover them within ourselves! We know of animal drive so far as we know of drive within ourselves, of the animal momentariness of lived experience so far as we experience it in ourselves, of animal immemoriality from the recollection of the one-day consciousness of the stage of childhood. One succumbs to a self-deception if one deems the detour by way of animality necessary for the ascertainment of the epimethean form of life, and it comes in the end to this, that one poeticizes into the animal what, by way of contrast, is fit to serve as a foil that sets off an already presupposed glory of reason. Nor should one object that the person given over to enjoyment likewise remains related to objects and would certainly lose all hold, were he, suddenly de-spirited, no longer to comprehend the world around him. We must direct our attention not to the already-given form of actuality, but to the transition of lived experience from a less conceiving to a more conceiving apprehension, if we wish to inquire whether lived experience itself is thereby widened or narrowed.

Everyone knows the peculiar shudder of sublimity that a glance into the clear starry splendor of the winter sky affords. But if he has now thoroughly learned to gather the stars in groups according to traditional figures — to see here Aldebaran, there the Crown, there the Wain, the Lyre, the Serpent, Orion, Cassiopeia — then, in the measure of his acquaintance with it, his nocturnal universe has become poorer, nearer, and flatter! To be sure, he has exchanged something else for it. Now that we have once become questioning beings, beings full of curiosity and with the unconquerable inclination to interpret, to determine, and to solve riddles, every moment of finding satisfies and sates our will to knowledge and widens our [p. 451] feeling of possession, and every boundary of our having-conceived in turn lures and entices us to ever new voyages of discovery. But this is the contradictory fate of all taking-possession, or rather of the deed as such: that the accomplishing heightens us, while the accomplished strikes us into fetters! By that very thing by which we imagine ourselves enriched through finding, because in finding we taste the pleasure of triumphing over an obstacle of consciousness, by that very thing we despoiled actuality and narrowed the infinity of lived experience, to which every find prescribes a new law, draws a new boundary, engraves a new irrevocable ought! The pleasure of conquest is a pleasure in the I; the bliss of beholding is a bliss in the actual. The former is offered for sale only at the price of an equally weighted impoverishment of the latter: every satisfaction of the "will to power" is atoned for with a loss in the capacity for bliss! To the Sophoclean song of praise there answers, with menacing insistence, the cry of lament of Hyperion: "I have thoroughly learned to distinguish myself from what surrounds me, am now solitary in the beautiful world, am thus cast out of the garden of nature, where I grew and bloomed, and wither in the noonday sun. A god is man, when he dreams; a beggar, when he reflects."

The characteristic mark of the unconscious source of happiness is ageless originality, eternal well-spring nature, a remoteness with which we merge without ever drawing near it, a familiarity that nevertheless remains strangeness, an undivided and indivisible fullness. Understanding, however, measures and counts, brings the most distant into a palpable and yet separate nearness, unveils the strangeness and makes us "acquainted" with it, displaces fullness with "order," draws off from the sea of images the unmixable rigidity of objects, gives us, in place of the born, lifeless things on which time becomes a gnawing tooth and happening a maelstrom of destruction — in short, it de-actualizes the world and leaves behind a mechanism, the field of operation of the craving for deeds, which, even as it compels and demands, is in turn itself also capable of being mastered, whereas it is experienceable only as a boundary of life. — Convincing examples, needing no further argument, offer themselves by the hundred to anyone. The labyrinthine confusion of a luxuriant park, where at every step new wonders seemed to blossom for me, is already on the way to disenchantment as soon as I have had to discover that all the crossing paths run radially to the same center point. Scarcely have I begun to "orient" myself when the secret already threatens to slip away from me [p. 452] — the secret that was the very heart-nerve of the image's power to loosen and release! The well that frightfully allures, gazing at the child with the eye of unfathomability, suddenly has an everyday face that no longer awakens presentiment-laden shudders, once the child has for the first time measured its depth with a plumb-line. The clouds cease to be storming hosts of demons once I have become acquainted with the law of the precipitation of water vapor, which, dead as it is, follows in turn the regularly fluctuating air pressure. Or: "When, in that beautiful uncertain night of first acquaintance, day little by little begins to peer across and the sober cocks crow, then one wondrous spirit after another steals away to the side; what stood there like a dark giant becomes a crooked tree, the valley that looked like an overturned, age-old Roman city becomes a common ploughed field, and the whole fairy tale comes to a stale end" (Eichendorff).

Present-day man is inclined to regard experiences of this kind as a fantastical display, to be esteemed at most as the superstitious aberration of an immature stage of life. And indeed our examples may well let it be seen how far we are from seeking the key to the originality of lived experience in the animalism of lived experience. Even one who has not fallen for the fools' belief in an unceasing "struggle for existence" of animality, and who rejects the blindness that mangles the wondrous work of the organism into the fortress and armory of a mendacious "drive of self-preservation," will nonetheless not be in doubt for a moment that the dimension of lived experience just described remains wholly closed to the animal. But as regards "superstition" and "fantasy," one should not forget that to be free of these makes up only the questionable privilege of the "educated," whereas we fall deeper and deeper into both the further down we descend to the level of the folk-consciousness, where alone the threads are tied that lead to human prehistory. If it is methodically permitted, indeed required, to seek the animal in man, it is required all the more to excavate, within rational consciousness, the mythic consciousness as the older and founding stratum between it and the animal stage of life — without the most exact knowledge of which all allegedly critical pronouncements on the faculty of thought are nothing but learned gibberish.

Meanwhile, since even from the "educated" man at least the sharp mountain-ridge [p. 453] of his arts and poems leads across to mythic consciousness, let one last example from this domain be granted us. Let one dare to *study* the harmony of color of the richest painting, the line of beauty of the most living statue, the structural fabric of the most space-vanquishing cathedral, the musical "thought" of the most surging symphony, the rhythmic "law" of the most rapt poem, and one will presently see their secret escape and find oneself cheated of the innermost enchantment with which the work encompassed and held captive the *lover* bereft of understanding. In defiance of an age whose supreme intellectual conceit is a barren connoisseurship and a bloodless "aesthetics," and whose artists are for the most part nothing more than practicing connoisseurs, let it be said that the connoisseur stands to the man of enthusiasm as the master tailor stands to the bridegroom, in relation to the bride! Goethe, who out of a great poet became almost a great connoisseur, and moreover a truly wise man, and who therefore knows the matter from his own experience, has somewhere expressed it (in substance) that one must beware of wishing to penetrate, in the manner of a connoisseur, into a matter for which one is receptive with the heart; it is precisely "science" that robs us of familiarity with its object, because, as we may add, it unravels its image into fibers and in the end leaves us nothing but a handful of facts. How many a one has not grown weary halfway on the road to mastery because he got stuck in "problems of technique"; and what youthful enthusiast for flowers, animals, or stars has not long since lost the images of his love, after his errant zeal seduced him into botany, zoology, or astronomy! The cloud that shines of itself — called by the ancients "nimbus" — which veils the images of the world, softening and transfiguring them, for the *lover*, evaporates and dissolves in the corrosive ray of understanding before the curious gaze of the researcher. In order to find and hold fast what alone is to be found and made fast, the hard and separate kernel, the spirit has already wiped away what can never be grasped: the loosening and fusing veil that shines only for the midnight eye of the soul.<sup>73</sup>

<sup>73</sup> On page 453. — A concession should not be withheld even here. The foregoing assessment of the activity of cognition refers in the first instance to so-called causal explanation, which by no means prevailed originally in the Occident, but which, since antiquity, gained more and more, and since the Renaissance decisively, the upper hand; or else to what we have elsewhere called now the "shallow reflection," now the "logocentric" reflection, and finally, already by way of intimation, the "Heraclitean" spirituality, whose most precise analysis the Second Volume will have to undertake. And it does not refer in equal measure to the "biocentric" or "deep" or "Promethean," or, according to an earlier prevailing usage, the "contemplative" direction of reflection. What this latter is capable of achieving, not only in principle at all, but also to what extent still other felicities accompany it than merely those of the power-claims of the spirit, will emerge ever more clearly only in what follows. But *this* no reflection can alter: that, in relation to the experience of beholding itself, even soul-conditioned flashes of cognition signify the answer to that deepest *disturbance* which can befall only a being whose life-space has in some respect been *severed* from the general life through the separating power of the *spirit*.

But we may not take our leave of the thought of selfhood with this turn, because we must anticipate and touch upon a fact of life without whose exhibition even the most exact rendering of account of the relation of spiritual act to living process would leave in the dark the ground on which an Ishapedness of vitality is possible at all. The [p. 454] deferral of the problem of sensation has brought it about that our considerations of the conditions under which consciousness arises suffer from a peculiar gap, in that we have neglected to ask whether, and how far, life itself is characterized by them. Are those properties by virtue of which spiritual acts are made possible properties of life in general, or rather of certain forms of life, and are there, above all within ourselves, only such life-processes as would be capable of serving as the substructure of consciousness? One cannot pose this question without at the same time also answering it in the negative. Already the most superficial glance at our own vitality shows us two groups of life-processes: those that are at all times to be connected with spirit, and those that are never to be connected with it. Acts of apprehension are commonly wont to go along with our sensory functions, while the functions of the cells, whose interplay we call organic growth, never "call an act into life." One might, to be sure, wish to explain these as mere chemistry; for whoever has taken life up into spirit has by that very act taken it out of the body, and will find, in place of the living body, nothing more than a machine. But if the sensory organs surely do live, by whose help we are able to sense, then one will labor in vain to make it credible that their structural elements, the cells, should lack life. But if they live in exactly the same sense as the sensation-mediating sense organ, then each of them, too, has an experiencing inwardness, and it thus stands fast of this kind of lived experience that it never *bears* spiritual acts.

The reference to the life of the cell reminds us that so far we have spoken only of the actuality of life, but have just now leapt without mediation to the state of affairs, only just touched upon, of the objectlike character of the bearer of life. No consideration of the livingness of the cell would have been needed to give us full certainty on this point, that the consciousness-capable bearer of life is compelled to distinguish between its own life and life foreign to it. However he may have come to such knowledge, that he has it thanks to a compulsion evidently just as original as the one that compels him to hold the straight line to be the shortest line between two points stands fast for everyone who does not perhaps pay homage to the delusion that he alone lives amid what is, as it were, a desert swarming with larvae. With this, however, we have passed from life as such to such life as we think of as bound to relatively isolated [p. 455] centers of life, which one customarily regards from the point of view of existences somehow endowed with life, and we thus make up for the first time for the omission that the one vitality that is to be coupled with spirit is that of the living thing, or better, of the individual being. We do not encounter consciousness in the world except in dependence on the vitality of objectlike, distinguishable individual beings. — In view of the act-incapable life of the cell, we establish, in the second place, that the totality of living beings falls apart into at least two different classes: the unspirited and the spirited. Man is a spirited bearer of life, the plant an unspirited one. Cells, like plants, live, and if they live, then they also have lived experience; but neither cells nor plants have the slightest consciousness of it. "No age and no people has ever harbored doubt as to the livingness of the vegetative; indeed, unspoiled thinking shares with that of primitive peoples the inclination to behold, precisely in the luxuriantly welling plant growth of, say, the primeval forest, the fullness of life even more than in the restless movement of the animal, and the tree cult, almost universally diffused in prehistoric times, has its very root in just this." No one, however, who has not already succumbed<sup>74</sup> entirely to the ill-taught interchanging of spirit and life, attributes consciousness to the plant on that account — be it consciousness of the being-there of the sunray, be it of its own experience of light, which, for reasons to follow later, could not even be permitted to be called "sensation."

<sup>74</sup> On page 455. — *Klages*, Mensch und Erde, pp. 49—60.

The question of objective symptoms of life that thereupon arises leads us — as can here be no more than touched upon — to the dimension of sense-things describable, on the testimony of an ever-truthful usage of language, only negatively, the dimension in which their livingness announces itself to us as something unattainable to the dissecting gaze: the dimension of the individual. Every bearer of life is individual, which literally means "not to be divided," and because indivisible, necessarily singular. Striving to hold fast wherein the living thing is, to sensuous understanding, distinct from the lifeless thing, and by what it is immediately to be recognized, spirit finds not properties that would stand to one another as size to smallness, roundness to angularity, softness to hardness, warmth to cold, noise to stillness, brightness to darkness, motion to rest, and whatever else of bodily data might be seized upon — since none of these could fail to be met with in the unliving thing as well — but rather it finds, in the sum total of the properties of the living thing, or of any thing at all, [p. 456] insofar as it is taken for a living one, the *uniqueness* of this sum total, and consequently the uniqueness also of the individual property, provided a sign of life is beheld in it. Against the ancient and readily intelligible opinion that livingness speaks out of self-movedness, it would have to be objected, first, that even what is wholly unmoved can be recognized as filled with life, and further, that its aseity does not belong to the *factual* marks of a function and consequently becomes an object of perception only insofar as it has been experienced. But the factual mark of it is in every case its unrepeatable singularity. Of every process, insofar as it is a mechanical one, and of every thing, insofar as it is unliving, one can furnish hundreds and thousands of copies; of the individual, insofar as it is living, not a single one! In respect of their livingness, the sole factual point of comparison among the many millions upon millions of living beings is, paradoxically put, solely their — incomparability!<sup>75</sup>

<sup>75</sup> On page 456. — In our "Grundlegung der Wissenschaft vom Ausdruck" we furnished, in the third chapter, under the heading "Die Wahrnehmbarkeit der Eigenbewegung," the proof that, within their species-specific horizons, animals distinguish the living from the non-living and are thus capable of finding essence. The proof rests on the statement of a characteristic by virtue of which, even for the animal, organismic movements become recognizable in contrast to extra-organismic ones; but this character of movement, which can only ever be experienced, is called: incalculability, or more precisely, intuitive unforeseeability of the course of movement; by which, evidently, the moment of incomparability is illustrated as the most general mark of animal aliveness. We offer below a fragment of what was set forth there. "Let one call to mind translatory movements of earnest purpose or of play in dogs, cats, calves, foals, weasels, martens, hares, deer, mice, or in birds or fish or any insects whatever, or even in reptiles; let one hold up beside them, in spirit, movements such as those of a rolling ball, of falling rain, of a passing stream, of waves breaking on the shore, or even of rising smoke, and one certainly need not think of the incalculability of the former in order to gain the conviction that they are distinguished, in relation to the latter, by *intuitive unforeseeability*, and that in this is rooted the inner necessity of taking them for *spontaneous* movements. If we only stick to the main point and do not at once let ourselves be disturbed by deceptive exceptions, we must acknowledge that every spontaneous movement places the perceiver in an *uncertainty of expectation* that has no equal within the range of the perception of machine-movement. But since spontaneous movements are such movements as break forth from the interior of the bearer of the movement and accordingly manifest the working of a *being*, we would then have arrived at the conclusion that animal self-life appears, among other things, in movements that deviate from the movement-phenomena of the life of the landscape through the characteristic unforeseeability of their course, and, owing to the surprises they can prepare and not too rarely actually do prepare, have in common an essential feature with the effect-content of the unusual. — This is indeed not a physical, but certainly a phenomenological, truth. — It is *not* the experienced harmlessness that lets even shy animals remain in closest proximity to the roaring passing train; for it would never have been experienced, had not a quite different experience first made possible the *attempt* at remaining in the face of this crashingly moving monster at all — namely the quickly completing experience of a *fulfillment of* *expectation* with regard to the course of the forward movement, which contrasts powerfully with the unforeseeability of organic phenomena of locomotion" (pp. 45—46). "If one wishes to place it beyond doubt that animals, like us, distinguish through mere perception the animally living from the non-living, one should indeed not straightaway adduce their intercourse with fellow members of their species, and likewise not their hunting of living prey, because against this the objection could be raised that they are dependent on both these occurrences of appearance; but rather their play. If two dogs play together, the one chasing does not experience the chasing to the same degree charged with desire as in the chasing of prey, the one fleeing does not experience the fleeing to the same degree charged with fear as in fleeing before an enemy, or, more briefly put, neither of the two takes the playmate in full earnest for what it means to him in play. Just as little, however, do cats and dogs and other animals, which occasionally play with lifeless bodies as though they were alive, take the non-living thing in full earnest for what it appears as in play, in that they, as everyone knows and as is unanimously confirmed by animal researchers, first themselves set their sham prey in motion. — Finally, there are examples enough that reveal that the unforeseeability of the courses of movement, in which we see the decisive indication of living motor activity, has an essential component in common with the unusual and, through its novelty, now surprising, now frightening, but always disconcerting, character. In his outstandingly careful work on 'Die Seele des Kindes,' *Preyer* reports of a dog that used to fling dry bones about in play. His owner once fastens a long, thin thread to one of the bones and begins, by means of it, to pull the bone away; the dog rushes off and observes, most alarmed, how the bone seems to move of itself! No further explanation of this is surely needed" (pp. 46—47).

Accordingly the "empirical," "concrete," "existent," "vital" I, or, more briefly, the person, would be an individual I, and the consciousness that is by essence necessarily personal would also be necessarily individual consciousness. Hardly anything else has abetted this confounding of spirit and life as much as this state of affairs, because it puts us in the strange position of having to depict, in the "personal character" of the human being, vitality according to its spiritual effects, and thereby continually exposes us to the danger of speaking the word "I" when we mean the individual! Since for the human being every life-disposition is at the same time a precondition of intelligent achievements, life seems on the one hand to possess spirit — one need only think of expressions like "spiritual life" — and spirit seems on the other hand to disperse into an unsurveyable wealth of living individual traits! Against this we hold fast that personality owes its distinguishing stamp exclusively to its vitality, however much, in order to *read it off*, we may with the greatest right consult its thinking and willing, its spiritual capacities and its "interests." Every plant individual deviates from every other plant individual just as much, and for no other reasons, as those from which every personality differs from every other personality; but what distinguishes the personal bearer of life from the impersonal bearer of life is the participation, identical in essence for all persons, in one and the same spirit.

[p. 457] Before we, continuing the train of thought, bring to bear upon the foundations of consciousness still quite different features than those hitherto examined by us, we now give an overview, however, of the research findings of the one thinker, among all contemporary thinkers, with whom we touch at essential points and to whose kindred-minded propositions we have already repeatedly found occasion to appeal — the research findings of Melchior Palágyi.

[p. 458]

#### 40. Kapitel — Die Forschungen Melchior Palágyis — Chapter 40 — The Researches of Melchior Palágyi

Palágyi — uniting, with a discoverer's clear-sightedness, the most profound knowledge in mathematics, biology, logic, epistemology, and the history of philosophy — belongs to those rare minds who prefer to prove the light-giving power of their supposed or genuine principal finding, be it ever so foundation-shattering in nature, on circumscribed problems of special disciplines, before they feel moved to unveil the hidden lamp itself. In possession of a central metaphysical thought which not too many of his readers are likely to guess, he nonetheless adopts the bearing of the specialist scholar who, soberly, in the language of the school and by means of its approved methods of investigation, seems intent on critically re-examining precisely the best-credited "laws," so far as possible even of the exact field of research — with the surprising result, however, that one after another they prove inadequate, where not untenable. Put in a martial image, he sets the front of the sciences tottering at the most various points, in order — this, to be sure, must be anticipated — perhaps in the end to "roll it up" altogether. The specialist scholar senses just enough of this to be loath to make friends with this kind of scientificity; the layman, however, who wants to be won over by vague and pompous general ideas and is accustomed to rate the spice of resounding catchwords and brilliant antitheses higher than the classical charm of consummate clarity, has not so far set eyes on the *philosopher* Palágyi and feels obligated meanwhile to the ingenious calligraphy of, say, a Bergson, just as, in less lean times, he let himself be caught by the pathos of certainty of the not wholly unrelated, but truly stylish and, as a writer, highly significant sham-metaphysician *Schopenhauer*. — As already mentioned earlier, it was Palágyi who in 1901, in the "metageometrical" [p. 459] special investigation concerning "a new theory of space and time," came forward with the setting-up, at that time completely new, of that four-axis coordinate system which later became the showpiece of the theories of relativity. In fact this signified for its inventor the foundation-wall of his system of "world-mechanics." Here, however, we lay the stress on another side of the state of affairs, one which has made it easy for the obscurers of his merits to suppress his significance for the conception of the "four-dimensional manifold": namely, the circumstance that Palágyi, not indeed avowedly, but in fact, takes as his basis, in place of the advanced line of time, rather *actuality-time*, in order to set against the world-space of Copernicus — still anchored in intuitive space — a space that changes *fluidly*. But whoever, for the first time bringing Heracliteanism to completion, is in earnest with the "flowing," or more correctly the happening, space, *must* also be in earnest with the abolition of the concept of duration, and consequently also of the thing and of the motion of the thing, and has thereby uprooted the very possibility of the mechanistic interpretation of the world.

Palágyi is entirely right that the concept of space cannot be grasped without the help of the concept of time; but it is one thing to think space as related to flowing time, and again another to make out of it itself something flowing. In the former case two objects hover before us, the succession and the side-by-sideness, and the law of relation only expresses that the side-by-sideness remains the same, unconcerned with its change of place within the succession; in the latter case, by contrast, the flowing has now seized space too, together with time, whereby we would be forbidden to apply the law of identity to the world of appearance at all! A happening space admits not merely no things, but no longer even geometrical figures. Palágyi overlooks that he must first again abstract from this very flowing in order to enunciate the "law of conservation" of space. "Conservation" and "flowing" are contradictory concepts, unless one wishes to insist, in a play upon words, that it is precisely the — flowing that remains conserved. When he recommends to the reader, in order to ease the thought of a temporal series of spaces, that he imagine space as having just now a red coloring which in the stream of time gradually passes over into yellow, orange, green, and so on, it is evident that we posit the space in question as identical in order to think, in respect of it, a change of color. But if we exchange it itself for something [p. 460] continuously flowing, then, just as its color did before, its place, its extension, its spatial figure now also changes without interruption, whereby it inevitably ceases to be an object of our conceiving. If we simply cannot apprehend the individual triangle without co-apprehending its sameness in respect of any points of time whatever, then the sameness of space as such already lies within it; if we accordingly abolish this sameness by making of it something continuously changing, then volume, surface, line, place are already abolished along with it; and what would then still remain would by no means be those two orders, objective space and objective time, but would be solely the spatio-temporal polarity of the experienced, which is not merely inexhaustible by judgements, but is not objectified at all.

Should this be misunderstood as though we meant to say that the straight line thereupon passes over into the curved line, the circle into the ellipse, and so on, we would have to repeat emphatically that in respect of a happening space simply no concept whatever of a geometrical figure could any longer come about. The straight line would indeed not pass over into the curved, nor the circle into the ellipse, because there would no longer be either straight or curved, circle or ellipse. In order that a configuration of points in space become objective to us, space itself must become objective to us, and it can do so only if we abstract from the flowing of time, or if we think it as maintaining its identity through the stream of time. That, however, would be the "standing space," regardless of whether we let time flow through it or — with the usual reversal of the direction of time — let it flow along with time. The latter conception would indeed be erroneous (for nothing objective flows along with time); but it would no more take from space its selfsameness than a piece of wood would become another piece for drifting upon a river. Palágyi, on the other hand, has not in the least left us in doubt, in his "New Theory of Space and Time," that he takes the flowing of world-space literally and in the proper sense. "If the point of time becomes another, then I have the logical warrant to speak also of another world-space" (p. 11).

If a certain contradiction between the tendencies and the intentions of our author already seems to meet us here, it emerges now far more sharply still in his epistemological and psychological findings, as they are comprehensively developed in his "Naturphilosophische Vorlesungen über [p. 461] die Grundprobleme des Bewußtseins und des Lebens" (first published 1907). — Through an analysis of the process of perception that has as yet had no equal in penetrating power, he becomes the founder of the doctrine of the opposition between temporally flowing life and the intermittence of temporally *punctual* acts of spirit. To give the right idea of the complete novelty and fundamental significance of the matter, perhaps nothing can serve better than the remark that he opposes to the erroneous notion of "psychophysical measurement" the demand for a *counting* of the acts of spirit. The supposed "psychophysical measurement" aims in reality at a control, by mechanical methods of measurement, of vital estimating-achievements, for the purpose of the indirect measurement of the course of life-processes; the "indirect vitalistic measurement," however, opens up the prospect of an indirect counting of the acts of spirit. For if the measurement of the time of the vital process that links two acts with one another should succeed, then the way would also be leveled toward an experimental counting of our spiritual acts. Palágyi calls the time-interval between two immediately successive acts a "spiritual pulse-beat" and then continues: "The investigation of the spiritual pulses constitutes the proper task of scientific psychology. It is a pulse-theory of human consciousness." A single sentence of this kind, to which we at least would know of no counterpart to offer from any "psychology," may instruct us that it is really only herewith that the concept of the act is set up and the ground laid on which one could begin to erect the doctrine of the nature of consciousness! Whole series of problems light up that one could not previously even pose: whether and to what degree the "pulse of consciousness" is subject to fluctuations in the individual life — which experiences are bound up with its shortening and acceleration, which with its slowing and lengthening — how, according to it, the various periods of the individual life may stand to one another — how, further, say, dreaming stands to waking — which traits of character belong to its individual constitution — whether there are typical "pulse-disturbances" of consciousness, and so on, and so on.

Meanwhile, however, the expression "pulse-theory" already lets it be surmised that its creator, notwithstanding the most sharply emphasized instantaneousness of the act, interprets its connection with the life-process not at all, as we do, from the standpoint of a *disturbance* of vitality, [p. 462] but in keeping with an organic coherence; whereby we are at least prepared now to have to hear that he places the two in the relation of *correlation* to one another! The eternal stream of life is for him "only a stream because it presents itself to a pulsating consciousness as a stream; and this consciousness is only a pulse because it is borne by that stream, to which it relates itself, thinkingly, by means of its acts." We leave it undecided whether it can be logically reconciled with the concept of correlate that the temporal should stand complementarily to the extra-temporal; for it suffices to point out that the thought of correspondence demands the dependence not only of the existence of consciousness upon the actuality of life, but also of the actuality of life upon the existence of consciousness, in order to show us the deep gulf that separates Palágyi's conception of life from our own. He too, to be sure, distinguishes those life-processes that stand in connection with consciousness (he calls them the animal ones) from the "vegetative" life-processes, which are not capable of this, and we are unable to conceive how he means to rescue their livingness for the latter, provided life in general has need of the spiritual act as its correlate. But whatever solution he may have to offer for this, his determination of the animal life-processes shows with unmistakable clarity that his extremely vitalistic philosophy, astonishing as it may sound, at bottom lacks the concept of *original lived experience*! We single out a few sentences, with the advantage for us of being able to illuminate our own view, perhaps more sharply than by anything positively set forth, through its utter opposition to the views of precisely a kindred-minded thinker.

After Palágyi has, within animal vitality, separated out three classes of processes, namely sensation, feeling, and phantasm, he expresses himself on their relation to consciousness as follows: "If the epistemological position of biology within the circle of the other sciences is to be truly clarified, one must above all seek to put an end to the psychologistic confusion of the tree of life and the tree of knowledge. This, however, is certainly no easy task: the animal life-processes, namely, that we designate as feeling, sensation, and phantasm, agree completely with our spiritual activity in this, that they can all have one and only one immediate witness. This seduces us into confusing the animal-vital [p. 463] processes that come to our consciousness with the spiritual acts of perception through which they are apprehended. It lies in the nature of the case that the vital process must flow together with the spiritual act of perception into a concrete unity. For as soon as we become conscious of a sensation, the union of the vital process of sensing with the activity of consciousness must already have taken place, that is, must belong to the nearest past. We can never say: now the sensation is approaching our consciousness, now it is already quite close to it, now it is knocking at the gates of consciousness, now, in this mathematical instant, it has found entry. For a *process of sensation* that has not yet united with *our* activity of consciousness does *not* yet exist *for* us; and a sensation that already exists for us has already accomplished its union with the activity of consciousness in an unnoticed manner" (pp. 11-12). We have set the passage most decisive for us in spaced type.

The still unconscious sensation does not exist for us, it is consequently as good as not present at all, it is a *nothing*; feeling and phantasm will fare no better. But how in all the world are we then still supposed to pursue biology, the word understood in Palágyi's sense? How can one even assert the existence of living processes, let alone want to fathom their nature, if these processes sink irresistibly into hopeless darkness the moment they are severed from consciousness? What else, indeed, does the mechanist say, who derives sensations from objective processes in the brain, what else the spiritualist, who has them produced by consciousness? Indeed, are we not at once reminded of Kant (contested by Palágyi without reservation), where he expresses: "All intuitions are nothing to us and do not concern us in the least, if they are not taken up into consciousness"! If we draw the extract from Palágyi's sentences, they assert: there is no actless living-through! Since he nonetheless posits actless life-processes, his life-processes are not "lived experiences" at all; but what, then, would they be? Let us hear his determination of the concept: sensations are life-processes by means of which we take cognizance of mechanical processes, feelings such as procure us a knowledge of our own life-process. Two things interest us in this: first, that it does not betray to us a single syllable about the sensation (or the feeling) itself, but speaks exclusively of its consequences; second, that it believes it has ascertained its marks [p. 464] in each case in a characteristic achievement of the correlated act. Far from holding sensations and feelings to be actualities, our thinker evidently has in mind only the elements of the process of the acquisition of knowledge! We wish to show, at least by the supposed criterion of sensation, that his determination is a perfect circle, since only in this way do we hold ourselves assured of not having fallen into any illusion as to where, for him, the truly actual lies.

Sensation is supposed to be a living process for the reason that it gives us the possibility, with its help, of taking cognizance of a "mechanical world." If we call sensation the unknown X to be determined, then we must designate the world of things, which is supposed to make its determination possible for us, say, by A. Now, however, we hear that it is precisely the process X that enables us to find A. We therefore know not the slightest thing about a mechanical world except on the basis of precisely that X whose "magnitude" is in question. Accordingly the author appeals for his X not to an A at all, but to a Y, and for this Y again to his X! Without mathematical symbolic finery: a "mechanical world" becomes known to us only in the first place as a consequence of sensation; accordingly it is a circle if we hope to mediate acquaintance with the sensation posited as unknown by pointing to a "mechanical world"! — But if one of the most outstanding logicians overlooks so manifest a circular inference, we may be sure that elementary motive-forces stand behind it. The solution reads: it is his belief in the *actuality* of things that prompts him to make reference to them the starting point for the determination of life-processes. Well then: the world of things is the world of existences, the objective world, the world of the intellect, and to take it for actuality means to strike out the actuality of life. We were not deceiving ourselves when we beheld, in his sentences above, a declaration of the nullity of lived experience!

We hardly need to assure the reader that in this way he succeeds no better in keeping feeling and sensation apart than any mere "psychologist" ever has. For if one posits the world of things as unknown, one is no longer in a position to distinguish sensation from feeling by thinking only the former as related to the said unknown; but if one posits the world of things as known, then our body too becomes a thing among things, the life-process accordingly an intra-corporeal one [p. 465], and feeling, in relation to sensation, inescapably an intra-corporeal or "visceral" sensation! Palágyi takes the utmost pains to evade this wholly unavoidable consequence of his pre-existing belief in mechanics; but he is led, against his will, to admit it, if with a peculiar restriction. — On the occasion of his truly illuminating investigation of the sensation of touch, which forms the crystallization-nucleus of his book, he sets alongside the double sensations in self-touching simultaneous double feelings. The former, he teaches, are active in the touching limb, passive in the touched limb, whereas the feeling of pressure that occurs in each limb has the character both of activity (a) and of passivity (b), of pressure as well as of resistance, and accordingly contains a and b as components. "On the basis of this remark," he continues, "one can render intuitive the relation of sensation and feeling in the following metaphorical manner. Feeling springs from the organic union of the sensation-pair a and b, which now no longer confront one another as strangers, that is, are no longer distributed over two different limbs, but, fusing with one another in a single limb, become a feeling composed of two opposed components. Conversely one can think (in a metaphorical manner) sensation as arising out of feeling, in that the two opposed components of feeling separate from one another . . . so that they can confront one another as if strangers." When, however, he adds that he must nevertheless emphasize that sensation and feeling are in reality not reducible to one another, it must be answered him that he has, rather, actually accomplished precisely that reduction which was laid out from the outset in the mechanistic premises of his determination of the concept, and no one will fail to recognize that it quite unambiguously carries the sense of an annihilation of feeling, which is equated with the *fusion-product* of two *sensations*.

We may not spare ourselves the pursuit of yet another fundamental determination of a concept, which alone would already have sufficed to support our critique, but which appears in the full light of its significance only here. — Vital processes are, according to Palágyi, such processes as tolerate only a single witness, mechanical processes such as are able to have as many witnesses as one likes. We shall no longer be surprised, after what has preceded, if the distinguishing mark of the vital [p. 466] as against the mechanical is once again sought not in them *themselves*, but in the witness- *hood* of *consciousness*, and if in this way the decisive question is beforehand suppressed, namely whence the owner should actually know that his life-process is exclusively his own! Determinations of this kind always possess a popular power of conviction; for everyone does indeed believe he must confirm that at least immediately he alone is in a position to attest his own lived experience, whereas a mechanical process, in the end, anyone may attest. And yet they are not merely vacuous, but even only conditionally correct. If a graphic exaggeration is permitted us, in order to underline in advance the vacuousness, we ask the reader to imagine that someone should undertake to define a particular class of meteors by the remark that they had the curious peculiarity of being seen exclusively by Nansen! — Meanwhile, however, the *choice* of such a stopgap determination of a concept has a very significant prehistory, at which we must linger somewhat more fully, all the more as it seems capable of showing our own doctrine in a new light.

The definition gives itself the appearance of delimiting vital processes from mechanical ones, but in reality aims at the delimitation of individual processes from extra-individual ones. Let us assume for the moment that "life" is identical with "individual life"; it must nevertheless be said that the state of affairs of individuation could not be ascertained at all except on the basis of an already antecedent determination of lived experience. The mere exclusion of alien witnessing by no means suffices to guarantee the individual character of life-processes, and therefore does not guarantee livingness either. But in the following way our thinker refutes himself. According to him, life-processes are those by means of which we relate ourselves to a mechanical world; this world is what is common to all, or what is simply attestable, at which, accordingly, in principle everyone can "be present." Suppose now that we could, *without further ado*, recollect our way back from the sensed thing to the process of sensing: it would then be nothing to us but the vehicle in the hunt after mechanical processes, and it would be utterly impossible to see why we should therefore hold it to be a process of our own *livingness*, simply because we alone could still assist at it! Here we *preserve* the unconditional exclusion of alien witnessing *without* the success of the self-finding of the individual: from which it follows that the source-point of life-consciousness may not be sought [p. 467] in that exclusion either. To be sure, the example is imaginary, since sensing always forms only one side of the life-process, so that we can discover the sensing vitality only by means of abstracting recollection; but this does not touch the conclusiveness of the challenge to a formula that defines sensing by the mechanical process, and the life-process in general by the impossibility of becoming attestable for any consciousness other than the one correlated to it.

To our advantage, Palágyi is aware of this and carries it out with all desirable sharpness by the example of the spiritual taking-possession of voluntary movements. "The movement of one's own hand," he says, "must be given to us, besides through sensations, in some quite different way as well, in order that we recognize it as our own movement. We can also *sense* any alien movement whatever, and insofar as our own movement is merely a sensed one, it may not properly be designated as our own at all. For in its mere sensedness it is as foreign to us as any alien movement..." It announces itself as our own, by contrast, "in no case through sensations, but *always* through *feelings*" (p. 69). And this holds not merely of movements; it holds generally: "We discover our own life-process by means of our *feelings*" (p. 78). With this, however, he has overturned his own determination of the concept. For now we know that it is not at all the being-present of a consciousness that could instruct us about the individual and consequently also the vital nature of a process, but the *peculiarity* of the attested process. Only from its particular constitution can it be derived that it is a lived process, and only insofar as consciousness attests it as lived does consciousness take itself as correlated to it and only now become self-consciousness. It is not from the singular of the consciousness present at it that the individual nature of the attested process follows, but the reverse: a quite determinate peculiarity of what is attested first makes possible the concept of a consciousness that believes alien consciousness excluded from certain attestations. Palágyi's self-contradiction reaches its climax where even he cannot avoid admitting the individual character of processes that are withdrawn from the correlated consciousness. Every individual bearer of life wakes his own waking, sleeps his own sleep, dies his own death. Either, then, the said peculiarity is *not* grounded in the fact that precisely only the consciousness of the bearer enjoys the privilege of assisting [p. 468], or his sleeping and dying would at least not befall him, since he can indeed no longer — "be present." — To the question, hardly to be evaded, why our thinker does not define (for which he himself indeed created the tools): mechanical processes are only perceived (or inferred from what is perceived), vital ones are, moreover, also felt, one would have to answer: because his concept of feeling is only a disguised concept of sensation, and his concept of sensation merely a reflection of his concept of the mechanical, or, more briefly, because of lived experience he has only the word and not the thing. On this account, namely, the determination of the concept just proposed would at best be a — tautology! — We take the occasion to set our fundamentally divergent conception in all the brighter light by the contrast. "I live through [something]," we explained, means in every case: I take cognizance of the fact that something befell me. It is not the taking-cognizance as such that gives me a consciousness that that of which I take cognizance is a lived thing and accordingly, generally speaking, something individual ( = something distinctively *my own*), but the content of the apprehended as of something suffered. To live through is to suffer, to apprehend is to do, and "mechanical process" is neither of the two. It is never the apprehending that guarantees the vital character of the apprehended, but the element of a distinctively suffered compulsion, without which, to be sure, no deed either — whether of apprehending or of willing — could be accomplished. With words like "suffering" or "befalling" one expresses sharply that the life-process is in and for itself bipolar and transitive, which the witnessing presence of a correlated consciousness does not first have to remove from the domain of intransitive processes. And with this we come to the more substantial part of our critique, namely to the problem of the relation of life in general to individual life.

The concept of lived experience is sighted from a wholly different point of view than the concept of the peculiar character of lived experience. I can know about experiences without yet also knowing about the peculiarity of what is experienced; I shall then, and indeed only then, at once know about this, if I moreover reflect on the connectedness of the experienced with consciousness: life-awareness is not yet consciousness-awareness, but awareness of the peculiarity of lived experience is under all circumstances also awareness of the peculiarity of consciousness. It is not, then, because [p. 469] we were thinking of something that only each individual, and not also a second, could assist at, that we know of the peculiarity both of our lived experience and of our consciousness, but rather insofar as we, keeping being-present in view, must now attest our being-compelled to this as well. But because consciousness is precisely a being-present, life becomes objective to us in the same act — more precisely, becomes localized, bounded, bound life — and this now, and this alone, is the sense of its individuatedness. If life has its space, then spirited life has, moreover, its place; and if, accordingly, thing and the life of the thing are separated, then one's own life and alien life must also separate; and the two belong together inseparably. There is no own-I without an alien-I, but there is also no own-life without alien life! As surely as every factually fixable vitality is an individual one, just as surely do we apprehend, when we call its functions our own, not so much it itself as rather its sphere of operation. If one chooses the individuatedness of life for the purpose of a consciousness-theoretical delimitation of life-processes from mechanical ones, then the formula would have to read: only vital processes can enter into interaction with spirit, mechanical ones stand over against *it* (and enter into interaction with it only through the mediation of the living body). But of this we have spoken earlier.

It is, however, not the improvement of a determination of a concept that matters to us, but its consequence in thought. If "individuality" is life's sphere of play, we have not the slightest right to exchange its possible boundness to place for life itself. And, what is more decisive: we may not even want to assert that the attestability of lived experience must be bound up with the attestability of the peculiarity of what is experienced. There is no "law" that could bound the sphere of play of life. If an ecstatic capable of recollection feels driven to declare: "I was *beside* myself," this can mean, at the least: I was no longer even an own-being; it was not I that lived it through, but it, life "in itself," lived it, the hither side of the bounds of a consciousness-capable corporeality, that lived it. Now, to be sure, once returned and "come back to himself," he can hardly do otherwise than relate the experienced to himself and his person. But relatability alone no more makes the experienced into his lived experience than it makes a factual thing into a lived experience. Already the boundaries of the peculiarity of lived experience are comparatively fluctuating, and altogether still more so the boundaries of that which becomes experienceable as belonging to consciousness; hence the awareness of the [p. 470] peculiarity of what is experienced stands far behind, in certainty, the certainty of life-consciousness! We are moving here exclusively on the ground of the doctrine of appearance, and may lay no other "material" at the base of our conclusions than the testimonies of recollection. Should the science of the soul seek information from poets and mystics, it would in all likelihood find itself in the position of having to augment the familiar kinds of feelings and fellow-feelings by two further kinds, namely "all-feelings" and "directly lived alien feelings" — assuming that the name feeling should still seem at all suitable for them. Instead of many, only a single example! Hebbel concludes three strophes upon a mysterious unknown woman, of which at least the last breathes the revealing shudder of genuine poetry, with the two lines:

Perhaps, when I shudder, exult, or weep, / It is your sensation that thrills through me.

(Let it be noted that what is spoken of here is not fellow-feelings!) — If the like sounds "rhapsodic" and strange nowadays, we may nevertheless remark that this was not always so. If we hold, beside Palágyi's mechanistically tinged determination of life, the following lapidary saying of Heraclitus: "For the waking there is only one single and common world, but in sleep each one turns to his own particular one," it becomes manifest to us at a single stroke how incomparably stronger the standpoint of the Greek thinker is. Still wholly free of the devastating belief in an actuality of the mechanical, and untouched by the wearing doubts that the concept of consciousness has conjured up, he aims without circumlocution at life itself, brings its two poles at once into view, and sets the actuality of the sleeping soul as of equal worth beside the actuality of the waking soul! We would, however, only be completing the saying in the spirit of early antiquity were we to supplement it as follows: the world of the dreamer is indeed non-objective, but it, and it alone, is the actual world, provided and insofar as he — dreams true.

Over this, to be sure, we must not now lose from sight the reverse side of the matter. As surely as life in general reaches beyond the individual and thus beyond organic life, just as surely is organic life individual life, and the experiences of every organic being are, in the first instance, only its own experiences, between which and the experiences [p. 471] of another organic being no direct connection exists. A more deeply penetrating investigation would teach us that the bounds which every individuation unavoidably brings with it are now looser, now more rigid: looser in plant lived experience than in animal lived experience, loose in another way in the elementary lived experience of primordial man than in the already spiritual lived experience of promethean man of the late period of prehistory, but of an inflexible hardness, which only death still breaks, in the heraclean man of "world-history," that is, in the man of will and doer, of whom we shall have to treat in Volume II. The plant carefully tended in the earthen pot blossoms and gives off fragrance, while the other beside it, which one forgot to water, withers; the hunting cat experiences an intoxication of pleasure when it tears apart the little bird dying under its claws; in the same house dwell the aging hypochondriac and the boy blossoming toward life, whose singing still embitters the former; there dwell the feasting exploiter and the woman worker who hungers and starves for her children; the market rates rise and the stock-exchange jobbers triumph when the poison-gas war against a speararmed little people of exotic regions has been "happily" concluded and the gold-sand-bearing site of smoking villages has been opened up to "culture": in such examples, multipliable without number, it emerges shatteringly that in individuals life has severed itself from life, up to the agonizing perishing of the one at the power-craving of the other. Death, finally, presses its seal upon the solitude of all. — Yet, however abysmal the riddle of the clusterings of life may ever be, the being-born and dying of beings, their breathing and nourishing of themselves, must attest that the essence of life was merely lent to its particularized bearer, and could therefore never be understood out of that bearer. Without the feeling of life no feeling of the peculiarity of what is experienced, and without the feeling of one's own no consciousness: in this order it is grounded that we try in vain to illumine the sense of lived experience so long as we believe we can find its criteria in the impossibility of having one's own lived experience attested by any consciousness other than one's own.

Only in this way, finally, do we penetrate into a state of affairs that has been wholly obscured by the reason-faith of more recent thought, namely that the judgement upon the boundaries of "dead" and "living" is subject not merely from man to man, but above all with the course of time, to unavoidable fluctuations within an extraordinary breadth, and [p. 472] at bottom only seals whatever metaphysics happens to prevail. Palágyi's determination of the concept would, strictly taken, have the consequence — though it neither states this nor wants to have meant it — that we should arrive at the concept of the vital, as that which is attestable by only one witness at a time in each case, by restriction from the concept of the mechanical as that which is simply attestable; whereas ours expresses what alone can be supported by both the history of the race and of the individual, namely that we arrive, rather, at the concept of the mechanical as the isolated by abstraction from the concept of the living as the connected. We find what is merely attestable (the objective, the thing-like, the "mechanical") by learning, step by step, to abstract: "outwardly," from the coherence of images; "inwardly," from the sufferedness of the impulse to the passing of judgement. The world that is mechanical in the proper sense knows, indeed, neither a working nor a suffering, and if, notwithstanding this, we believe we can even extract a working from "causing," then we have enriched the objective process with a non-objective element out of the well of lived experience. Given a logocentric development of mankind, the concept of the thing must therefore constantly grow in span, that of the living own-being shrink in the same measure. For the sorcerer-priest of primeval times millions of things are alive that for the mechanist are no more than units of computation of mechanical processes. Accordingly the mechanist "acts" upon them (and experiences their acting) only mechanically, where the sorcerer-priest vitally influences them (and, in turn, may succumb to their influence) through the lived-through action-at-a-distance of "magical" spells and rites. Here it is not truth standing against error, but a disposition of mind that remains largely fettered by life, standing against one that has in wide measure detached itself from it. An "objective" decision as to what here might be "correct," what "incorrect," simply cannot be reached, for the reason that the picture of actuality depends on lived experience, and the scope of possibility of objective experiences depends, in turn, on the picture of actuality. The dreamer, so long as he dreams, cannot be brought to acknowledge the unreality of his dream-visions, and indeed no one at all can be logically compelled to sacrifice the lived meaning of the picture of the world to mere "matter-of-factness." — If one holds it necessary to contest so far-reachingly the system of a contemporary thinker, one must hold his merits to be so significant that they oblige one to the most serious appreciation even of [p. 473] his errors. Although, accordingly, our beginning was a beginning of approbation and reverence, one might nevertheless perhaps think that a critique which visibly strikes at the foundations must, if consistently carried through, lay the whole edifice in ruins; and we by no means wish to deny that we should see ourselves compelled to refute still dozens of Palágyi's principal propositions, were we to measure them point by point against our concept of the sovereign actuality of lived experience. But, as already signaled at the outset, this thinker's conscious intentions are at odds with his vital tendencies, so much so that biocentric findings come to light in abundance, which a stylizing understanding, of the most virtuoso gift for combination, puts to use in the service of a logocentric plan. Although it would not be particularly difficult for us to find the key to this, we content ourselves with the general remark that many a Columbus has sought an India and found an America instead, which not even the fact that his all too legislative reason should stubbornly persist in denying it could alter in the least. And so we add, in conclusion, that this researcher's mechanistic conception of actuality has not prevented him from furnishing a characterization, at least of animal lived experience, that leads far out into vitalistic new territory!

Strange as it may sound, he states outright that sleep is an experience, and argues on this basis in the happiest possible way. — He is the first to bring the fully convincing proof of the impossibility of apprehending processes of movement with the help of sensations alone, and he shatters the sensualism of the science of the soul more thoroughly than even the most irresistible critique could, with what one may call the explosive force of his new concept of the irreducibility of "vital" or "imagined" movement, which must take its place beside sensation and feeling as a third and final life-process. He shows that every perception of the outer world requires the cooperation of sensing with feeling, and in turn of both with processes of fantasy, whose core, or more correctly essence, must be sought in the very imagination of movement just mentioned. We enter all the less into a critique of these findings as we should have to anticipate later discussions to do so, but we remark even here that we hold his doctrine of the phantasms to be just as epoch-making, though not in the same sense complete, as his doctrine of the intermittence of the acts of reflection. What seems to us, however, perhaps the most sublime masterstroke is his dissection of the sensation of touch, [p. 474] which now removes even the last doubt that he *handles* the concept of self-sovereign lived experience which his definition denied him! For with a turn of phrase that unquestionably hits the mark, he describes, in the particular case of sensing experience, the estranging function of experience as such, when he conceives the experience of touch as grounded in a "*self-estrangement* of the *process* of life." "We stand here," he says, "before the wonderful fact that our life-process ... is able to confront itself as if it were something alien. How alien the one hand grasps and presses the other, as though it did not belong to one's own body. Only through this self-estrangement of the life-process does one find one's own life-process no longer as a mere life-process, but as — a body. And only because one is able to find one's own body can one also speak of wholly alien bodies, which touch and press our hand just as we ourselves have touched and pressed it. Were the life-process incapable of self-estrangement, we should be able to find nothing alien whatsoever in this world. On *the* *self-estrangement* of *one's own life-process rests the whole perception* of an *outer world*" (p. 118).

It should be noted that our thinker, in distinguishing as sharply as possible between the self-estrangement of the life-process and the perception and finding of the outer world that rests upon it, is far from truly thinking of the former as dependent on the latter. We should doubtless find no world of things without sensation; but there can be no question of our failing to sense without (conceptual) capacity to find(1). The dependence is one-sided, not reciprocal. Sensation remains what it is, whether or not an act of perception joins itself to it; and it is what it is, not because a correlated act of apprehension refers by its means to "mechanical processes," but because in it too there manifests itself the *polarized* happening that we call "experience." Polarized within *itself*, the life-process is sovereign, and not, say, the counter-pole of a correlated spirit. And with this we close the circle: with his biological formula of the "self-estrangement of the life-process," Palágyi bears witness, just as irrefutably, to the independence of *lived-experiential* actuality, as he does to the independence of *happening* with his cosmic formula of "flowing space."

[p. 475] *Afterword* — The foregoing essay was written in 1917 and published for the most part in 1919 in the (since discontinued) "Deutsche Psychologie" (vol. II, issue 5).<sup>76</sup> Personally acquainted with Palágyi since 1908, but during the years of the World War cut off even from correspondence with him, the author had the great good fortune, in early 1924, to have the friendly Hungarian thinker as his guest for fourteen days. Intensive spoken exchange of ideas (which in the time before had been possible only once, namely in the winter of 1912) led to a mutual clarification of essential components of as yet unpublished sections of both systems, and thereby to such a rapprochement of the two thinkers that joint plans of research could be envisaged. The author was inclined to attribute Palágyi's repeatedly expressed premonitions of death to a somewhat hypochondriac state of mind. A return visit was planned for the summer. But the dreams and premonitions were to prove right. On July 13, 1924, Palágyi, sixty-four years old, succumbed in Darmstadt to a stroke, leaving behind, unfinished and unfinishable, the mighty "Weltmechanik" on which he had been at work for three decades. This is not the place to speak of the irreplaceability of this loss for the author. But our characterization of the insights of this towering thinker should be completed by taking into account parts of his literary remains that have since appeared.

<sup>76</sup> On page 475. — We quote, in accordance with our original text, always from the first editions of the writings of *Palagyi*; but it will present no difficulty for any reader to find the passages in question again in the meanwhile-published new editions, namely in the second edition of the "Naturphilosophische Vorlesungen" and the two collected volumes that have appeared from the literary estate under the titles "Wahrnehmungslehre" and "Zur Weltmechanik," all published by Barth. The volume on world-mechanics contains all the works that Palagyi published on fundamental questions of physics in earlier years.

It turned out, in fact, that besides extensive but unfinished manuscripts there existed several completed individual works, which could be combined into two posthumous volumes: "Zur Weltmechanik," with a foreword by Gehrcke, and "Wahrnehmungslehre," with a comprehensive introduction to Palágyi's collected work by Klages (both published by Barth, Leipzig). The Wahrnehmungslehre, whose sequence of essays affords instructive insight into the development of Palágyi's convictions in the science of consciousness, does not in principle go beyond the content of the "Naturphilosophische Vorlesungen," but brings important applications and conclusions, above all in the classic essay "Theorie der Phantasie." It makes it easier for us to refer later to partial results of Palágyi's still passed over here, but changes nothing in the basic ideas we have appraised. The "Weltmechanik," on the other hand, offers, besides the previously published works such as the "Neue Theorie des Raumes und der Zeit" (1901) and the illuminating engagement with the "Relativitätstheorie [p. 476] in der neueren Physik" (1914, following Palágyi's lecture of the same title at the 85th Convention of German Natural Scientists in Vienna), a series of highly significant essays that lead considerably beyond what had previously been disclosed, and that now, indeed, bring openly to expression the guiding mainspring of Palágyi's thought which we earlier called still a hidden one: we mean the idea of the polar character of actuality.

To deal with this in a way that furthers understanding, however, we should have to measure the conception of actuality held by physics, on which Palágyi tests his idea of polarity, against the conception of actuality of the theory of appearance that we ourselves represent. But this can be done only at the close of the next volume, after we shall have examined, in connection with the doctrine of the will, two or three basic concepts of mechanics as to their noogenesis. In connection with this, the reader will find what remains to be said here in the chapter headed "Galilei und Palägyi."

[p. 513]

## Viertes Buch — Die Lehre vom Willen — Fourth Book — The Doctrine of the Will

What could not be miracle wills to become work; what could not be work becomes deed.

[p. 515]

### Erster Abschnitt — Gesetz und Willkür — First Part — Law and Arbitrary Will

#### 41. Kapitel — Tatbestand und vorläufige Ableitung des Wollens — Chapter 41 — The State of the Case and a Preliminary Derivation of Willing

The doctrine of the will is an essential part of the doctrine of the conditions under which consciousness arises. If we nonetheless treat it in a book of its own, this happens partly out of regard for the circumstance that we shall be obliged, far more than hitherto, to read off the nature of the enabling grounds of the state of affairs to be investigated — namely, of the act of will — from the nature of its *effects*, which therefore demand a very extensive investigation; partly, and above all, on account of the quite preponderant importance which the doctrine of the will possesses for the science not only of consciousness but of the essence of historical man as such; and finally in view of the extraordinary preparations which the mapping of a territory hitherto, on the whole, unknown demands.

The mere conceivability of the coming-into-being of acts, as we saw, still gives us no insight into the origin of consciousness so long as we leave life-process and spiritual deed each standing for itself and do not instead think of both as united into a new totality, within which they would be mutually conditioning sides. Following the general considerations on this matter, we now take up again — and shall later bring in the main to a conclusion — what was indicated in the 9th Chapter and, in particular, advanced a few steps further in the 38th and 39th Chapters: the investigation of the concrete or personal I, whose existence we have proven to be a necessity of thought.
