Though no answer [p. 516] was granted us to the question of how it could come about that spirit and life became entangled with one another in man, still only our knowledge of their metaphysical difference makes possible an accurate conception of the nature of the I, in that it preserves us from seeking in the I anything other than the strictly indivisible pivot of the two. Said with a robust simile: the I relates to its bearer as the earth's axis of rotation relates to the globe itself, and not, say, as to a sphere the detachable rod which we have stuck through it in order to give it a bodily axis. It is neither spirit nor life, and just as little a new essence alongside them, but the extensionless point of relation of their interworking. From this we may likewise conclude: if life in and for itself is unconscious and temporal, and spirit is strictly non-temporal and lifeless, then the connection of life and spirit, in which alone consciousness is rooted, must have arisen at some point in time and must again dissolve at some point in time — exactly analogous to the limited duration of that which arose through the I's externalization, by which we mean the thing.

In the 9th Chapter we had set forth that, in relation to the liveliness of its bearer, the I can be determined as an assertion of existence, or simply as will. If, on the other hand, in the 26th Chapter, with the remark that all thinking requires a thinking someone and all willing a willing someone, we asserted, with regard to both processes equally, their character as activities of the I, then reflection on linguistic usage would nonetheless teach us that, notwithstanding this, the activity of thinking is by no means as suited to the disclosure of the I as the activity of willing. For while the word "arbitrary will [Willkür]" expressly links the exercise of will with the pleasure of the one willing, there is no designation at all for a choicedependency of thinking. Only a life-blind intellectualism could overlook what language has thus so sharply prefigured for us — namely, that the doctrine of the will is to be developed only out of the doctrine of the I, since conversely this latter would have to find its completion in the former.

Yet the doctrine of the will was scarcely less forfeited by an "individualism" which the state of affairs we have named led astray into errors of just the opposite kind. — One speaks of objective thinking and sets against it partisan thinking; but one would speak only in a transferred sense of objective willing, and no longer at all of objective [p. 517] arbitrary will, and thereby seems to declare that the activity of the I which we call willing can partake of the superpersonal power of a norm only indirectly. If we exchange "norm" for "law" and recall the already-intimated derivation of all laws from demands of the spirit, it at first appears as though, in relation to willing, thinking stood nearer to spirit. Moreover, it is quite often personal wishes that bring forth personal resolutions, and again scarcely less often personal wishes that rob the movement of thought of its objectivity. If, accordingly, the personal can never be wholly separated from the will, then, on the contrary, its non-intervention is demanded on the part of a thinking to which the finding of truth is supposed to fall. Now, if we truly have the choice only between two powers, namely spirit and life, then, in respect of its norm-unconcerned arbitrariness, willing would seem not merely to stand further from spirit than thinking does, but, by that very fact, also nearer to life.

However little the primal opposition of spirit and life has hitherto been brought to clear expression, it nevertheless worked as a hidden driving force in every direction of sentiment that undertook to champion the "right of passion" , of "nature," of the "heart" against the statutes and commandments of the "head." Unfortunately, however, for the reasons adduced, every one of these has misunderstood itself as "individualism," or more aptly as personalism! For the Greek sophists, who began it, for the spokesmen of the so-called Renaissance, for the herald-spirits of the "Storm and Stress" of the 18th century, indeed in part even for a Nietzsche, "nature" coincided with "freedom of personality," and the demanded right of the heart with an approval of the power-claims of the stronger! One believed oneself to be taking the side of life by taking the side of the personal I, and one hoped to have broken through the barriers of lawfulness by acknowledging personal arbitrary will. Considerations such as these, and similar ones, are what caused the word "spirit" to resonate more strongly with the faculty of thought than with the will.

Against this, whoever sees in the I the actualization of spirit, and in the act of will the most immediate manifestation of the I, must believe, precisely conversely, that he can read off the essence of spirit from the act of will; let the way to the proof of this be broken here only by pointing to two fundamental errors of all personalism. — Only insofar as there is a willing is there a conscious oughtness. We do indeed sometimes say [p. 518] of our dog that he knows very well what he "may not" do. Yet he "knows" nothing whatsoever in the sense there intended, even though, from impression-memory, he really has learned to shun bad consequences should he yield to the impulse to steal meat from the kitchen. He behaves similarly, though not from the same ground, to the child who would refrain from the same actions in remembrance of a prohibition. If now we set side by side the hunger which makes the child — like the animal — crave nourishment, and the consciousness of an ought-to-do or ought-torefrain, everyone must recognize that here two fundamentally different kinds of inner compulsion are present, of which the one is experienced as demand or determination, the other as necessity. According to the testimony of self-reflection, the I has "freedom" of decision in every case. But what else could be meant by this than that it would be able to oppose to the demand, as also to the need, its *own* demand! To be able to determine oneself we call freedom; to have to renounce self-determination, unfreedom. Demand, however, remains demand whether I issue it or receive it; from which it clearly follows that law and arbitrary will are woven from the very same stuff! The Pauline "But where no law is, there is no transgression" only particularizes, for moral laws, the reciprocity of law and arbitrary will. "Individualism" of every shade fails to distinguish — and this is its first error — lawfulness and necessity, and therefore holds the arbitrary willing to be something different from *both*, and the person capable of arbitrary will to be a counter-instance to the law-giving spirit.

But just as the participation in life that is indeed peculiar to the person could by no means be inferred from its capacity for arbitrary will, so too it is precisely not the objectivity of the mode of apprehension but, as we shall see, its purposiveness through which the power of spirit asserts itself in the "laws of nature." One finds in the fact the law of spirit when one measures it against actuality; but one also finds in it necessity when one *measures* it against arbitrary will. Because the individualism of factual logic, out of the self-sovereignty of arbitrary will, resists this, it devalues — and this is its graver error — the act that is, after all, still a compelled one, in favor of the absolute command, and aims in fact at enslavement instead of, as it fancies, at the liberation of life! Thus it never attained to any insight into the image-forming undercurrent of thinking, but ended, after a brief [p. 519] blaze of splendid rockets of wit, invariably in a purely negating addiction to doubt. — We have made mention of it here, however, only in order, by refuting a view that experience shows to be seductive, to light the way at least a little for the thought that has been entirely lost to our rationalistic epistemology: namely, that the unconscious sense of spirit promises to be disclosed, even in the act of apprehension, only by a deep glance into the nature of the act of will, and that it is not in the thinking but in the willing I that the supreme power of spirit steers toward its most fateful triumphs. — We have, many dozens of times, used for fundamental facts a name which the critical reader, insofar as he were still unfamiliar with the customary usage of epistemology, should not have heard without suspicious astonishment: the name act of apprehension, deed of apprehension. Thus, then, he might perhaps voice his suspicion:

"I am willing to grant, after all that has gone before, that a drawing of boundaries on the part of spirit cooperates in the experiential process of human perceiving, and let it pass unchallenged if one sees in the being thereby found the product of a "positing" of spirit; but I withhold my assent from the — at the very least still unfounded — assertion that the positing thus conceived is invariably a deed, and that consciousness therefore, without exception, always bears the character of being-active . I do not deny that every act of thinking bears witness to an activity; but I seek in vain for anything even comparable to thinking in countless acts of perceiving. Nothing seems to me more evident than that experiences are things undergone. But how then can one deny an involuntary process of perceiving the character of a thing undergone? If I cannot help but *perceive* the thunderclap that sounds before my ears during a storm, then something has unquestionably *befallen* me. And if I were moreover absorbed in a train of thought, then I experience the event of the thunderclap as a painful disturbance of my mental activity, and the process of perceiving itself as forced and wrung from me. Where, then, would there nonetheless lie in it a "deed"?" Only a little later will the answer to such questions follow — one, moreover, largely already prepared — which for the present shall serve us merely as a transition to the state of the case of the act of will.

If I notice a blade of grass, I am compelled to notice it [p. 520] in accordance with its concept, and it is not open to me to behold a shrub in its place; and if the property of its color catches me, I am compelled to find it similar to, say, the color of the walnut leaf, and it is not open to me to equate it with that of a carnation blossom. But I am not compelled to notice the blade of grass at all; it stands unquestionably open to me to attend to its color or its form; it is my affair whether I wish to compare it, in this respect or that, with other things: I possess the gift of the deliberate direction of attention. And conversely: every "sudden idea" forces itself upon me, is there as though summoned, holds me captive, even if only for seconds; but I decide over its use: I possess the gift of the logical guidance of my acts of reflection. Alongside the bound spiritual deed, so it appears, there stands an unbound one; alongside the consciousness that is led, willingly or unwillingly, on a leash by the stream of lived experience, the self-determining stride of a free one. And what everyone in this way already knows from himself is fully confirmed by a glance at the diversity of persons. As long as there has been a historical mankind, there have stood apart — indeed, in ancient days, waged bitter war — and will stand apart until the downfall of thinking consciousness, the pathics, who abandon themselves will-lessly to the play of their sudden ideas and phantasms, and the makers, doers, and men of action, who, scarcely is it there, at once press every impression, like a flash of thought, into the service of their inner or outer willing. However it may stand with the compelled attending, and regardless of whether we are occupied with things of perception or with representations or with thoughts, of this at least there is no doubt: that we are in principle in a position to steer our consciousness and to give to attention (understood in its widest sense) the direction which we wish to impart to it. Insofar now as this happens through acts of spirit, the acts are called acts of will; and let it for the present merely be stated, without proof: only because we are capable of accomplishing acts of will did the concept of the act come about; but were we not capable of that, then there would likewise be no — act of reflection! We may sooner hope to understand the involuntary process of apprehension from the willed one than the other way about.

It is of decisive importance to grasp the act of will at its root, because otherwise one does not grasp it at all. Instead of going back to it itself, certain attempts at the disclosure of the will turn, like [p. 521] a veritable polyp, to inner occurrences, and would therefore be condemned to failure even were it not for the deeper reason of the non-distinction of spirit and life. We hear of the "conflict of motives," of the weighing of reasons and counter-reasons, of the efficacy of moral principles and their conflicts with personal inclination, of approval and rejection according to the measure of generally binding values; whereupon, in the end, the formally dramatic final decision is deemed worthy to be called a decision of will. That fables of this kind are, without exception, perfectly compatible with every sort of blindness to the act of will itself follows from what comes next. If I find myself in the state of weighing, be it of "motives," be it of whatever else, then my steps of thought are either willed or not willed. If they are not willed, then the goal or end to which the sequence of them all — comparable to the passing-by of a series of phantasms — is able to lead me cannot possibly be willed. If, conversely, this end is to be called a willed decision, then every step on the way to it *must* likewise be willed. Whoever overlooks this has, countless times unnoticed, already presupposed the very act of will which he pretends to want to illuminate, and will, with all his talk about it, infallibly in the end only confirm one of the usual erring doctrines that flatly deny it on principle. Either one finds the volition in every deliberate act of reflecting, or one finds it never and nowhere, however rich an apparatus of psychic processes and facts of consciousness one may bring into play.

It is worth casting a side-glance at the history of a problem which, like no other, is called upon to decide the value of the metaphysical presuppositions of every system of thought. — For reasons partly already discussed, antiquity penetrated to the psychology of the will just as little as it was able to penetrate to the discovery of the act. To be sure, one speculated on the imputability of actions and on freedom of choice (Aristotle), affirmed or disputed the law-governed necessity of decisions of will (the determinism of the Stoics against the relative indeterminism of the Epicureans), and, with the concept of a purely active world-reason, created the model for the actus purus of scholasticism; but by "will" one understood thereby a kind of natural or divine force, and believed its working was to be found in the formation in which matter, through its receptivity for it, came to partake. One pursued not so much a psychology of the [p. 522] will as a psychology of the achievement of will, but conceived this, analogously to perception, as an occurrence which the bearer of life underwent by looking toward the existing end! Against this, it was Christian philosophy that conquered the will, as it were, in a headlong charge, by first of all bringing the inwardness of its distinctive character to consciousness. But just as the Greek, deeply entangled in the experience of mirroring, could not find the spiritual act because he remained fettered by the compelled doing of cognition — though he was thereby able to preserve the dependency of reflection on the image of the world — so, conversely, it befalls the Christian philosophers to confuse the fervor of their willing with the very ground of the origin of consciousness, and, in exchange, to develop the concept of the act out of reflection on the experience of self-determination. It is always the same thinkers whose psychology accords to the spiritual deed (intentio) a well-nigh creative preponderance over lived experience (passio), and whose metaphysical convictions culminate in the belief in the omnipotence of *arbitrary will*. Prefigured by Augustine, this direction of thought reaches its high point in a Duns Scotus and a William of Occam; and from this there arose that passionately conducted controversy which marks the wrong path from which the treatment of the problem of the will has not, to this very day, departed: namely, whether to willing or to cognition, whether in man or in God, the "primacy" is due.

One could scarcely find a more fitting formula for the essence of spirit than the "actus purus," and there is no doubt that it was arrived at through reflection back upon that self-sovereignty which cannot be separated from any intentionality, however insignificant, of inner or outer comportment; but one would commit a dangerous "equivocation" were one to equate the act thus distinguished with willing and acting. It is different from the spiritual act not only in that every deed of will requires a subject persisting in time, but also because, at the moment of its accomplishment, the act of willing lies in the — past. The concept of omnipotence, by no means merely rapturously believed but thoroughly consistent, can instruct us that the temporally unextended momentariness of the spiritual act necessitates the assumption of a coincidence of its occurring with the success of its occurring. God is omnipotent because, and insofar as, the pure act is already the pure accomplishment [p. 523] as well! Were the omnipotence of God a temporal omnipotence, it would already no longer be "omnipotence," because he would first have to will in order to attain to the deed; and were he himself a willing God, he would already no longer be spirit, because he would then no longer be non-temporal. — Before we proceed, however, with our retrospect on historical crystallizations of the problem, let us bring to the state of the case of willing a fundamental preliminary decision.

If that deed which we designate by the foreign word "act" — so as to keep open its capacity to participate both in willing and in perceiving — is a temporally unextended intervention of spirit, then it cannot, in any case, coincide with the processes either of cognition or of action. Furthermore, because a temporally unextended act could, besides its deed-nature (still to be more closely grounded), impossibly exhibit any other determining features (which would, after all, one and all have to be borrowed only from spatio-temporal actuality), there seem to remain for us only two possibilities for distinguishing the act of apprehension from the act of will: derivation either from the sequence of the acts, or from a difference of the *life-processes* that would have occasioned the accomplishment of the act. The first assumption would lead us back into the erroneous doctrine already rejected, while the second encounters difficulties of another kind.

As will be recalled, we inferred in the 7th Chapter the inescapability of assuming a really existing I from our capacity to relate, by means of an act now taking place, to a preceding act. Accordingly we can assert innumerable relations of dependency among the acts, and, if one likes, ground on this a so-called doctrine of categories. The act of self-reflection, for instance, rests upon that of reflection-on-a-matter, the act of reflection-on-a-property upon that of reflection-on-a-substratum, every act of reflection-on-a-relation upon at least two already accomplished acts, and so on. But who could overlook that in this way we never get out of the domain of the process of reflection! Nor would it help to weave in feeling-related acts, for the consciousness of a mood is just as much mere consciousness as that of any other state of affairs. One likewise convinces oneself at once, from any example whatever, that no possible feature of a content of reflection would let one recognize whether the reflection upon it was intended or not. I think, on one occasion, deliberately of a theorem of geometry for the purpose of solving a mathematical problem, and I think, on another occasion, of the same [p. 524] theorem involuntarily, because it simply "occurs" to me. But if no combination of acts of reflection, however rich, leads to anything other than higher acts of reflection, then it cannot possibly be determined from the sequence of the acts what would confer upon the act the significance of an act of will, and the question of primacy proves for that very reason to be pointless. Even were one to grant that willing avails itself of some precipitates of thinking, these would still, under no circumstances, be that out of which it itself arose.

If, accordingly, only the assumption of a difference in the occasioning life-processes seems to remain for the purpose of distinguishing the act of apprehension from the act of will, we shall nevertheless do well to hold before our eyes at once the new difficulty which we thereby conjure up. We have recognized in the life-process an uninterrupted wave-motion which, passing continually through turning-points, intermediately exchanges the inwardness of unconscious beholding for the consciousness-capable inwardness of making-present. We shall later make probable, for another purpose, that the point of impact of the act can shift; but no one will expect that the act thereby becomes an act of will. At the turning-point its arresting call fixes an intuitive image (of the nature of a mirror-reflection of already-elapsed primal images); at every other point it would strike the primal images themselves, which are not fixable at all, and thus, neither there in place of the impression nor elsewhere in place of the primal images, would there be an actuality whose arrest would yield the end, if it were in this that we were minded to seek the distinguishing feature of the effect of the willing act.

Meanwhile we have already, on repeated occasions, let it shine through that at least the animal mode of life would be characterized only by half, were one to interpret it solely from the standpoint of receptivity to impressions. With cogent grounds it was shown, especially in the 31st Chapter, that something sensibly experienced becomes an object of perception only with the assistance of a surge bound up with it; and it was added that "the deed of spirit is a reacting deed, and its occasion the sudden life-convulsion." — As long as there has been an epistemological thinking, that is, at least since Plato, one has seen oneself compelled to separate, within lived experience, impression and impulse. When our physicians, speaking of a sensory-motor system, mean by the sensorium both the senses and sensing, and by [p. 525] motility both the movement-experience and the movement itself, they only repeat in other words what, for example, Aristotle already taught, in that he distinguished, within the animal domain of life: the kinetikón katá tópon [that which moves in respect of place], or self-motion, and the aisthetikón [that which senses], or sensation, tracing the former back to the órexis [desire, appetite], that is, the impulse arising from desire. Over the difference between these two states of affairs, as likewise over their equally vital character, no doubt has ever prevailed; but only the most recent times have allowed the insight to ripen, in the most advanced minds, that they are inseparably interbelonging halves of a vital circle that is always closed, whether it be the impression that awakens the stirring, or the stirring that calls forth the image. We experience no impression without answering it with a stirring (however little this need become conscious to us at every moment), and we experience no stirring that would not be directed toward an image essentially corresponding to it. The impression comes about only in a drive-endowed being and is itself already a form of "hexis," just as, conversely, the impulse occurs only in a being receptive to impressions and is always also a form of beholding. The two kinds of lived experience differ only in this: that in the one the impression seems to generate the stirring, in the other the stirring seems to generate the image. The hungry man *dreams* of images of satiation in the state of sleep, and feels himself drawn by them in the state of waking, even when no edible things at all are present; in the one receptive to impressions there stirs softly now a feeling of hunger, now a feeling of aversion, on the occasion of the intuitive image of edible things.

With this we have reached the point at which it is possible for us to give a preliminary answer to the question of the essence of the act of will. The act of apprehension occurs when, at the moment of passage through the act-bearing boundary-quality, lived experience stands under the guidance of the impression (more generally: of the intuitive image); the act of willing, when it stands under the guidance of the impulse. If the impression-side of lived experience is split, then the halves of the split are the cognizing subject and its object; if the impulse-side is split, then they are the willing subject and its end. There, the experience itself transforms into the feeling-of-meaning of the existence of something undergone; here, into the feeling-of-meaning of the self-activity of the bearer of life. There is no "potentia nobilior," neither of cognition over willing nor of willing [p. 526] over cognition; but there is, from case to case, a preponderance now of the intuitive image over the impulse, now of the impulse over the intuitive image. The difference of the predominantly cognizing type from the predominantly willing type stems not from a difference of spiritual acts, but springs from the opposition of a predominantly drive-governed to a predominantly impression-receptive stance of life.

With this, however, we have so far anticipated the sequence of thought that we must first turn back again, as is a custom familiar to our readers, by way of doubts which reinforce the above still further. Is it not the case, one might object, that with a declaration of dependency on the vital stirring, the deed-nature even of the act of will is called into question; indeed, would it not now coincide with those acts of perceiving that occur in response to strongly feeling-toned impressions? We preface the answer with the grounding of the deed-nature of the act of apprehension as well. — In the 9th Chapter it was set forth: set into the stream of happening, the I becomes, thanks to its nature opposed to transience, subject to the compulsion of self-assertion, or to a being that wills-to-be-there, or, more briefly, to will. We meanwhile discovered the immediate sign of this in the feeling of self-activity which, according to the testimony of retrospective reflection, accompanies every deliberateness of inner bearing, but saw this stand in opposition to the feeling of being-compelled in occasions of perception — for instance, of surprising suddenness — and recognized in it the enabling ground of the finding of undergoing in every lived experience. Yet the phrase "being-compelled," chosen earlier already, and again just now, in indisputable accord with experience, would be devoid of any sense unless the I remained, even at the moment of being overcome, an active being — one that does not so much take something in as, in taking it in, "reacts." Were the counter-acting deed not present even in the utterly compelled process of apprehending that before which we violently take fright, we would indeed nonetheless take fright, but could never become conscious of the compulsion thereby befalling us. Only in that the undergoing touches a deed-capable core, whose answer to it has the ever-same form of the act — however involuntary it may be — does the occasion for it become not merely suffered but thereby, at the same time, also *known* as a thing undergone. It is in the having-to-apprehend, in its reacting, and in this alone, that the I's existence manifests itself to itself as opposed to the living It of [p. 527] actuality. Without the capacity for acts of arbitrary will we could, to be sure, not have formed the concept of the act; but without the deed-capacity, which in the act of will merely comes to light directly, the act of apprehension too could not be wrung from us. The voluntarist scholastics were right when, supported by the experienceability of arbitrary will, they circumscribed the spiritual foundation of consciousness as such from the standpoint of a capacity for the accomplishment of (timeless) acts; they scented a still deeper truth in their intimation of a dependency of the object of apprehension on the end of will; but they erred insofar as they held that the process of willing generates the process of finding.

"Be it so," our doubter might reply, "still my questions have found no answer. If the act is always the same event, why then would it be less compelled when it splits the stirring than when it splits the impression? If the life-process is two-sided, the assumption would lie even closer that each time both sides are split; in which case it would be a matter of my own pleasure to name the act 'act of will' or 'act of apprehension.' The difference of feelings can explain so little that it would rather itself require an explanation from a difference of acts, the key to which, despite all that has been advanced, I still lack!" Objections of this kind make us aware how far, up to now, we have still reported too superficially on the state of the case of the difference between volition and finding; hence we shall now, step by step, bring this difference to its sharpest expression. We have just now established an acting within compelled apprehending; we now reflect that, conversely, a being-compelled also lies within deliberate apprehension. Whether I notice the blade of grass involuntarily or turn my attention to it voluntarily: it, the noticeable blade of grass, remains wholly untouched by the difference of the processes through which it came to my consciousness; and whether I reflect on the mathematical theorem because I need it, or whether it occurs to me unsought: it, the theorem to be thought just as it is, does not care in the least. If I purpose a journey, it is a long chain of facts, simply to be found as given, on which I lean in deliberation just as I would if I were merely considering what steps another would take who had the journey in question in mind. If, accordingly, the fact itself must be distinguished quite generally from its determination in the service of an intention, then it is evident, first of all, that the cognizing act and the willing act cannot possibly take place in the same timeless instant. [p. 528] It is also, beyond question, one thing to know ends (and duties) with complete clarity, and another thing again to will these very same ends (and duties). The mere thinking of the end has just as little to do with the willing of the end as, for example, the expectation of an occurrence has to do with the actions or events that bring it about. A second step will now lead us considerably further.

It has hitherto been overlooked that, to the bare act of perceiving, "there is something," there corresponds a voluntary counterpart in the bare act of will: "I will something." Just as the former seemingly lacks an object, because the being that actually stands over against it lacks determinacy, so the latter seemingly lacks an end, out of the indecision of the choice to be made. Whoever finds it difficult to recall that he found himself, here and there, in a state of willing without yet willing anything determinate, let him be reminded that this, among other things, characterizes typical obstinacy. To be sure, the one who wills out of obstinacy *resists* a demand to do or to refrain from something, even though he would do or refrain from the very same thing were he permitted to decide unbidden; but the impulse to such "unreasonableness" stems from the need for *willing as such*, or, if one likes, for self-determination, arising either from a still undeveloped determinacy of ends (childhood) or from a lack thereof owing to an inherent indeterminacy of the stamp of character. The same propensity to become conscious of freedom of choice and of "one's own" will favors an arbitrariness of decisions in the narrower sense so called, as well as certain kinds of "moody" caprice. The indeterminate "I will something" means not so much "I will this or that" as rather "I will to will." So long as we direct our attention only to determinate ends, it can appear as though it were the thought of the end that calls forth the willing; but the more we leave the end in the indeterminate, the clearer it becomes that the state of willing is required in order that a thought may take on the form of an end. In brief formula: *it is the volition that generates* the end, and not the reverse! As soon as I no longer merely think the goal but actually will it, it *transforms* itself, only then, into the end! The thing of perception, even though cut out of the stream of images by a counter-acting deed of spirit, is nonetheless found by the bearer of perception, whereas the end, by contrast, is generated by the bearer of will. Before we plumb the lowest ground of such a gulf, let us complete [p. 529] our insight into the relational connection of the two acts by allaying a nearby misgiving.

Contrary to those profound scholastics, the almost universally held view is that the act of will rests upon a preceding act of cognition. In order to will a journey, must I not know what a journey is? — and similarly with each single step I undertake toward its realization. Even if acts of will never arose through mere concatenation of acts of apprehension, still, in any case, acts of reflection would have had to take place in order that positings of ends could take place. This is undeniably correct, but it has an obverse side which most will not hear without astonishment, if we express it as follows: in order that the fact be available of which the volition could avail itself, the act of apprehension that gave it to us had to be, in a certain sense, sealed by an act of will directly following upon it. Such acts of will, whose end is nothing other than the realization of the achievement of apprehension, are called acts of judgement — which incidentally furnishes the grounds why we remarked, at the beginning of the 38th Chapter, that we spoke of the act of apprehension as the immediate condition of the act of judgement. Whoever should be inclined to identify the two acts, the act of apprehension and the act of judgement, must be reminded that there certainly are characters of outstanding power of apprehension who come to judging only with an expenditure of effort, and again others whose constant readiness to judge damagingly anticipates their apprehension. We meet the deepest difference between the typically feminine and the typically masculine intelligence in the observation of a preponderance of the gift of apprehension in the former, of the capacity for judgement in the latter. Equipped with the sharpest attentiveness and a logically unmediated clairvoyance, not a few women are nonetheless incapable of making known, in judgement, what they know best, whereas the man, conversely, frequently has to guard against falsifying his apprehension through a will to judgement that speaks too soon. If of him all too often the saying holds, stat pro ratione voluntas [the will stands in place of reason], then of her no less would hold: ratio eget voluntate! [reason has need of will]. If, in the words of Palágyi, judgement adds nothing to the impression but its validity, we must say more sharply: it adds nothing but the validity to the apprehension! The act of apprehension gives us the object; the act of judgement raises its own to a law. Did a commanding (= legislative) act not seal the find of the giving (= simply positing) act with even the most ordinary [p. 530] seal, "there is something," the finder would not have the least prospect of ever finding again what he had found, and this would be as good as not present at all for his treasury of experience! Without knowledge of facts, no purposing; but the volition is already implicated in the fact, insofar as only through the passing of judgement did the finding become spiritual property.

As will be noted, we have with this expanded our previous analysis of spiritual apprehension by a very essential addition, though even now not yet brought to a close, and we touch, in a few words, on some of its consequences. When we just now denied the possibility of refinding for every find that was not also immediately judged, we naturally had in mind conceptually graspable finds, and, in place of sensory refinding, which is likewise proper to the animal, refinding by means of thinking-back-upon. If we said earlier that animals do indeed have an astonishing memory but recollect nothing, we now know — what we had likewise already intimated at that time — that the involuntary gift of recollection rests upon the voluntarycapability of recollecting, which is proper only to the bearer of spirit. Whatever may occur to us involuntarily out of the past, nothing ever occurs to us that we could not, in principle, also voluntarily call to memory. Quite often we do not succeed in this; but however much may in this way have "escaped" us, it nonetheless always belongs to the stock of that of which we could also, at another time, have deliberately thought. The process of involuntary recollecting is different from the process of intentional recollecting, but the contents of what is recollected are fundamentally the same, because only those acts of apprehension to which an (inner) act of judgement immediately attached themselves convey what is recollectable (as opposed to mere phantasms). In this way there has confronted us, for the first time, a kind of dependency — not, to be sure, of the act of apprehension, but indeed truly of the object of thought — upon the act of will, which certainly does not resemble a generation of the object by the act of will. To forestall misunderstandings we add: if an occurrence occurs to us only afterward, one which at the moment of its effect upon us we had not attended to at all, then only now do both the act of apprehension and the act of judgement first take place. — In turning back, accordingly, to the questions raised above, we bring the distinction, as regards the state of the case, between reflection and volition to a conclusion in a manner that at least answers some of them definitively.

[p. 531] If I receive a violent blow on the arm and am consequently compelled to notice the pain felt in the arm, retrospective reflection tells me that the compelled act of noticing was the *consequence* of life-processes. If I resolve to raise this same arm to shoulder height, and carry it out, retrospective reflection tells me that the self-sovereign act of willing *occasioned* life-processes. What holds of the compelled act of apprehension holds no less of the willed act of apprehension (since I am in turn compelled to notice some of the occasioned life-processes); and what holds of the self-sovereign act of will holds no less of the enforced act of will (because even a command, for instance, which I must obey, is realized only through the intermediary link of my willing): without exception the act of apprehension follows upon preceding life-processes, and without exception the act of will precedes the life-processes which we call the action; whereby the difference between the basic feelings of being-compelled and self-activity has presented itself to us in a new light. The latter arises insofar as a deed of the I seems to occasion life-processes; the former, insofar as, on the occasion of life-processes, a deed of the I comes to pass. From this there follows irrefutably at least this: that the difference between the two deeds may not be sought in their relation to one another, but must be sought in the difference of their connections with lived experience.

Now, however, we already know: the lived stirring, when it is attended to, is alien to consciousness in a different way than the lived impression is. By the stirring too the soul is moved, or rather is moved by it above all; but wherever the origin of such a movement may lie (we have scarcely inquired into it, let alone decided it), it lies, under all circumstances, not, like the occasion of the impression, in sense-space. It was shown in detail: we find in the impression the sense-thing, and we find the stirring only indirectly, by means, namely, of the "subject" which we have found in opposition to the "object." The source-point of all findings whatever is the sense-impression, and an object of perception is that primal finding in relation to which all other finds — be they even the most abstract relations between the most content-poor general concepts — appear as derivatives. Were there, then, a splitting of the stirring-side of the life-process, as there certainly is a splitting of its image-side, the result of the splitting could be no "fact"! We assert: it is the end generated by willing [p. 532]. Of it too, naturally, we can reflect, as indeed we constantly do here; but in doing so we have reflected upon the willing itself! The attempt to treat the end after the manner of a thing, or even merely of a fact, as antiquity undertook and countless "teleologies" repeated, has, of all attempts at false reification, in a sense the worst prospect, in that it does not even bring about the semblance of a solution — to which we shall return. We can make things the object of contemplation without regard to the spirit that thinks them, because in them the person-independent actuality directly partakes *as well*; we cannot, by contrast, make the end the object of contemplation without regard to the willing that generates it, because it does not, in and for itself, partake of actuality at all, though indeed indirectly through its relatedness to objects of thought.

If we now look back at our preliminarily sketched explanation of the origin of the act of will, we have indeed sharpened the distinctions, clarified dependencies, and forestalled the possibilities of confusion indicated above; but we have left undecided how it could be conceivable that the act of will should seem to occasion life-processes, when after all it ultimately depended in some way on the fact that, in traversing the turning-point in the life-process, the stirring determined the beholding. This question, however, requires a preliminary investigation concerning the splitting of the drive and the generation of the purpose, and we might in turn ease this for ourselves if we first extend our historical retrospect to a hitherto unconsidered point of dispute.

[p. 533]

#### 42. Kapitel — Gesetzlichkeit und Notwendigkeit — Chapter 42 — Lawfulness and Necessity

The failure to distinguish spirit and life has brought it about that all attempts at an explanation of the feeling of freedom were shipwrecked, so to speak, on a false exchange. For they interchanged, as was already indicated with another intention, necessity with lawfulness, and in turn arbitrary will with lawlessness. Now, however, a process could run its course entirely lawlessly and yet necessarily, and as regards lawfulness, it would first have to be asked how great a share in it belongs to the will and how great a share to necessity; for the two, necessity and law, are as different in essence as — life and spirit.

When the Stoics first, borrowing the Heraclitean concept of logos and the Democritean conception of causality, raised the question over whose answer the still unresolved dispute broke out between "determinists" and "indeterminists" — the question whether the event of willing takes place conditioned or unconditioned — they believed they had at once also to understand the presumed conditionedness from a lawful *order* of the course of the world. We offer some evidence for this from the older and middle Stoa. Zeno: "Everything proceeds according to the law of nature"; the primal matter "is governed throughout by universal reason, which is also called the law of nature." Chrysippus: "The law of nature is world-reason ..., according to which what has become has become, what is becoming becomes, and what is to become will become"; "The law of nature is the natural order of the world-whole, according to which from eternity one thing follows from another and changes, this interweaving being inviolable"; "For it is impossible that anything, however slight, should happen otherwise in particular than in accordance with the common nature and the law of reason ruling within it." Poseidonios: "The law of nature is the sequence of causes, according to which cause linked with cause generates an effect from itself... Therefore nothing has happened that ought not [p. 534] to have happened, and likewise nothing will happen for which nature did not contain the very causes that bring it about."

After having already pointed out earlier what testimony of origin the derivation of the lawful order from a world-*reason* implies, we hope now to explore something still deeper from the quite peculiar consequences to which these first "determinists" saw themselves driven. If a world-reason has, according to inviolable laws, predetermined the entire course of the world once and for all, then every act of volition too takes place with just such inevitability as the falling of leaves in autumn when the wind blows, and the experience — not to be argued away — according to which I must judge that my act of will sprang up in myself, would amount to a delusion. Now, however, it is precisely the Stoics who maintain that the origin (arche) of willing lies in the personality that is for that very reason responsible for its actions, and indeed because, in relation to the merely subsidiary-causal influences from outside, it is itself the chief cause of its resolutions. Far more than such logical mediations between apparently conflicting findings, however, must occupy us the circumstance that, through the belief in an irresistibly compelling law of effect, the Stoics were not prevented from issuing *precepts* to the bearer of will, with that concept of duty which, under their leadership, made its entry into antiquity with gestures almost already those of the old Jewish God Yahweh as penal judge! If we call dutiful willing right willing, and willing contrary to duty wrong willing, then in the spirit of the Stoics the mark of right willing was — submission to the law of the world. "Every right fulfilment of duty *is* . . . *obedience* to the law" (Chrysippus). At once, of course, the question would arise how the opposite of this, namely non-submission out of disobedience, could even be thought at all, if it was legislating reason that had planned everything down to the last particular; and, after the answer given to this — because passions could entangle the rational part of the soul in errors, or — in the spirit of antiquity — because errors could entangle the rational part of the soul in irrational passions — the new question arises of the conceivability of errors arising from contra-rational stirrings, or then of the conceivability of contra-rational stirrings resulting from errors, within a world of reason. We pass over here, however, this genuine self-contradiction and insuperable stumbling-block of all the later so-called "theodicies" [p. 535] and hold instead to the exceedingly remarkable fact that the Stoic considers compatible with an all-regulating world-law various degrees of the capacity to obey it, and thence, astonishing as it may sound, regains for the wholly determined will the possibility of complete "freedom" with the help of the concept of unrestricted fullness of acknowledgment of the law by it. "Freedom, then, may be called the knowledge of what is permitted and forbidden, and slavery the ignorance of what is permitted and not permitted." Further: "Everything belongs to the wise; for the law gives them perfect *freedom*"; it being understood, of course, that they follow it without resistance! And: "It is precisely in this that the virtue of the happy man consists ..., that everything is done in accordance with the agreement of the individual personality of the particular person with the will of the ruler of the world" (Chrysippus). Even if we were not already better informed than we would be from the ill-conceived groundings that the Stoics offer us for it: must not, in the face of such trains of thought, a suspicion dawn on us that omnipotence of the law and omnipotence of the arbitrary will flow essentially from the very same source?

The Stoics denied the possibility of chance. Now, certainly in no sense was it chance that they reconciled freedom of the will with the pressure of law through the assumption of a capacity for voluntary obedience to the law! For it is only from an inner compulsion that it can be understood why all the moral advocates of subsequent centuries who at all concerned themselves with the problem of freedom end, at bottom, at exactly the same point, however much the formulas in which they clothe this may diverge from one another. To be sure, the web of lies of Stoic pantheism was at first torn apart — and in fact and in truth incurably — by the otherworldliness that the Christian faith demanded for its God of spirit, and then undertook to prove with the help of the Aristotelian nous; but in return the peculiar nature of law and its connection with the peculiar nature of the will only emerged the more sharply. Three samples may suffice. — According to Abelard, morally good is a willing that takes place in agreement with the conscience of the one willing — that is, unconstrained; in conscience the natural law makes itself known; but the natural law is the will of God. — According to Spinoza, natural law and moral law are identical, and all decisions of will occur with natural-lawful necessity. If, however, he derives the freedom of self-determination, likewise known to him [p. 536], from an activity of the soul, and this activity from the mastery of clear and distinct thinking, whose most perfect achievement is to be sought in the knowledge of *God*, then it becomes glaringly evident that he conceived the determining power by analogy with the self-activity of the human will, and in this way located the ground of origin of that lawfulness in a willing world-reason. — According to *Kant* the world of appearance, and hence also human willing, is in every train of its course strictly determined. The freedom of the personality, required for the sake of the moral law, nevertheless results from its capacity to obey that law unconditionally. "The... moral worth of an action consists solely... in its subjection to the principle of universal validity"; and the "dignity" of the human being is rooted in his "*freedom* as a rational being under moral laws." (In Schiller's language: "Take up the<sup>1</sup> Godhead into your will — And it descends from its throne of worlds.")

<sup>1</sup> On page 536. — Even among those who find much to object to in Kant's theory of knowledge, it is customary to praise the extraordinary novelty of his grounding of morality. We search in vain for even a single new turn of thought. For not even his separation of the fulfillment of duty from happiness can count as such. Did not the Stoics already say: "Pleasure is something unnatural and has no value for life" (Zeno); or: "The highest good is the end for the sake of which everything is done dutifully, but which itself has no end lying outside itself" (Chrysippus); and did not Kant himself, in the end, likewise reintroduce a "highest good," and with it that, so to speak, supernatural blessedness which is allotted, in a better beyond, to the — though for men unattainable — perfection of the accord between personal disposition and the moral law! We need only translate the seemingly monistic principles of the Stoa, each time, into the language of conscious dualism, and we have the principles of Kant. Did the Stoics teach: "The *world* is a great state with *a* constitution and *a* law; natural reason commands in it what is to be done, and forbids what is to be omitted" (Chrysippus) — then Kant, to be sure, knows of the complete incomparability of nature with the realm of legislative reason, but has located that institution of man through which obedience is rendered to the ordinances of reason in — the state.

The Kantian dualism now makes it recognizable even to short-sighted eyes wherein the common element of law and arbitrary will is to be sought. For if we appeal, against the moral law, to the inexorability of our actions from causality, it hurls back at us an inexorable: "You can, *for* you *ought*!" In a formula already familiar to us: "primacy" of the practical, i.e. the willing, reason over the theoretical, i.e. the cognizing, reason! If we translate this back from the epistemologically convoluted into the simpler mode of expression of medieval metaphysics, we stand at the Augustinian: "Omnes nihil aliud quam voluntates sunt," or we conclude with a Duns Scotus that the world owes its existence and its being-thus to a pleasure of the spirit-god, and that the moral worthiness of action is ungroundable, because the commandment obeyed comes from the pure arbitrary will of the "Almighty," whose resolutions are determined by nothing, and hence not by grounds of cognition either. Yahweh spoke: "Let there be light"; and there was light. He could equally have spoken: "Let there be darkness"; and it would then have become darker still. Everything that exists, and then also the cognition of it, exists and lets itself be known in consequence of an absolute command. The endeavor to find a lawful order in necessity springs from the sometimes concealed, sometimes openly avowed prejudice that necessity, too, *also* is what it is from a — now, however, creative — *command* of spirit.

[p. 537] We have already touched on the Semitism of the Stoa. We now see more precisely which "spirit" it was that furnished a Kant with the at first bewildering formula of the "categorical imperative." Over the Greek belief in willing from grounds, the Judaic belief has triumphed in a cognizing from purposes, which an omnipotent arbitrary will, occasioned by nothing but itself, posited. Instead of speaking of the sham monism of the Stoa, one might just as correctly speak of the sham dualism of Kant; for the ultimately real element of both is reason, no longer, however, in the sense of the ever-constrained power of cognition, but of an unrestricted power of command, which also produces the very thing by which the command is carried out. The Old Testament tyrant of the will, without whose doing no sparrow falls from the roof, nor even one of the hairs, numbered by him, from a man's head, is merely the same principle in Judaically exaggerated form that has driven up the belief in a lawful dependency of the world's course and thereby, indeed, the more modern belief in causes itself. "Determinism," whether that of servants of God, or of the Stoa, or of Kant, means: *determination* of the cognizing spirit for the purpose of the complete absolution of the willing spirit!

It has, if we do not err, hitherto been left unremarked in which word and which thought the allegedly sacred scriptures of Christendom astonishingly agree with the "natural sciences" of this same Christendom: we mean the word "law." None occurs more often in the "sacred scriptures," none more often in the sciences, and to none is an equally high rank granted in both cases, and a ban-power so irresistible. Was there perhaps involved, as co-instigator, in the European discovery of the so-called laws of nature — which helped to de-soul the elements and to traffic away the de-souled — that all too famous "God, the Lord," who partly dictated laws and partly cursed gods? Guided by such a question of a mistrust no longer merely harmlessly scholarly, the theory of knowledge might perhaps have restored what "natural science" dissolved, instead of merely, walking in its tracks, confirming the destructions!<sup>2</sup>

<sup>2</sup> On page 537. — Similar direction of the senses breeds similar wishes, similar wishes lead to similar meaning-contents and similar apparent proofs. *Schopenhauer* supports the determinism he adopted, among other things, with the following consideration: „If we do not assume the strict necessity of everything that happens by virtue of a causal chain linking all processes without distinction, but instead let this latter be interrupted at countless points by an absolute freedom, then all *foreseeing* of the *future*, in dreams, in clairvoyant somnambulism, and in second sight . . becomes absolutely impossible, and hence unthinkable . . ." It had thus scarcely escaped him — who was forever looking about for forerunners and oath-helpers, and who, thanks to his outstanding knowledge of the history of the spirit, could point out, for example, the difference between early Greek fate (Heimarmene, Moira, Ananke) and Jewish-Christian as well as Stoic providence (Pronoia) — and hardly by chance, that Chrysippus had already judged exactly thus before him: „No one could hold the perceptions of seers to be true, if everything were not governed by the law of nature," or, at greater length, Posidonius and other Stoics! Schopenhauer was aware of no essential kinship of conviction with the Stoics whatever, and yet far surpassed them in infecting the course of the world with elaborately contrived concepts of purpose 1 Whoever doubts this need only read, in the second part of his principal work, the single chapter on the „Metaphysics of Sexual Love," which teems with turns of phrase and sentences such as the following: „Nature implants it (the instinct) there, where the acting individual would be incapable of understanding the purpose.." — The individual, in satisfying the sexual drive, serves „a purpose . . that is not at all its own". — „This investigating and testing (namely in mutual selection) is the *meditation* of the *genius* of the *species* about, etc." — The pains of love are „sighs of the spirit of the species, which here sees an irreplaceable means to its end being either gained or lost, and therefore groans deeply". — „The spirit of the species is able to see at a glance what value it (love) has *for it*, for its purposes" — under certain circumstances nature has „no other choice but to choose the lesser of two evils ( ! )" — accordingly, driven "into a corner . ., it resorts to a makeshift, a stratagem (!)". — While in this way he sees in the faculty of cognition nothing but the tool of a will cut to human measure, he never hits upon the thought that the very linkage of cause and effect that makes everything *foreseeable* forms only an indispensable precondition for the enslavement of the course of the world by the spirit of — intentionality; as he himself betrays, with regard to the „freedom" and power of the sage, in Seneca's words: „Si vis tibi omnia subjicere, te subjice rationi!"

With the thereafter unmistakably compulsory-seeming inclination — after the essential distinction of law and arbitrary will had been carried out — to limit the understanding by the demands of an absolutely omnipotent will, one involuntarily supplied the intellectual-historical evidence for the derivation of the concept of law not so much from spirit alone [p. 538] as rather from those presuppositions of its existence in life, of which we become directly aware in the self-authority (aseity) of every act of volition. All the less, however, may we any longer postpone the question of what it actually was that prevented the "determinists" from stating their secret "indeterminism" plainly and clearly and setting up a system of, if we may put it so, monism of will! We shall for the present give a one-sided account of this by putting ourselves in the procedure of the arbitrary will.

If I raise my act of will to a law, this means a compulsion, coming from outside, for the volitions of all who are obliged to obey the law; or, generalized: simply because will stands against will, the force of law — as, namely, the expression of the stronger will — separates itself from obedience to the law by the weaker will. At once, however, we recall that even for the capacity of the conceivably strongest will there is a barrier of the most general character, which without exception burdens every one of its exercises with the encumbering weight of a matter wholly alien to it. Suppose a despot has vanquished another despot and taken many of his people captive. He demands of them unconditional submission, on pain of death. They do not submit, and he has them executed. He may give the order with a few words, or he may, like Caesar in the amphitheater, content himself with merely pointing his thumb downward: in any case he must make the command known bodily, and it will always be the bodies of his servants, together with the bodily instruments of killing, by which the command is carried out. The decision of will is not the same thing as its manifestation, and the manifestation of the command would remain an empty sound or gesture without the assistance of that bodily actuality, in respect of whose constitution the self-authoritative act of willing finds itself quite sensibly crossed by the constrained act of cognition. One may perhaps object that this is precisely what the law of causality aims at. We, however, wish to emphasize that in this way law and arbitrary will have separated themselves together from the resistance of *actuality*.

Not actuality, as we determined, can *consist* of things and their properties, or of that matter to which alone "laws of nature" find application. One would not speak of constrained acts, and not of finding, and then not even any more of willing, were there not something that resists the act of spirit and that changes its omnipotence into a mere will [p. 539] to omnipotence. But this is now, on the part of the world, not its thinghood, which is in principle conceivable and which, in the measure of its being conceived, becomes the property of the will, but rather its life, in principle inconceivable, by virtue of which even the thing — distributable among laws and amenable to calculation — pays tribute to the element of corporeality that runs counter to the will! In relation to actuality itself, the things regulated in accordance with natural law are already a mixed result of it and of spirit, and express quite properly the compromise into which the will had to enter in order to have any prospect of overpowering actuality. In that one, driven by spirit, took for simply actual the most original achievement-result of the act, the object of perception, there confronted the arbitrary will, as essentially different, precisely what betrays, in the object, the share of the (willing) spirit: lawfulness. If in this way the deed of spirit has already been taken up into the state of affairs supposedly limiting it, it can no longer be too surprising if one ends, notwithstanding the alleged spiritlessness of the mechanical course of the world, at last with the "freedom" of the will.

Meanwhile the service to cognition that this train of thought renders us for the correct estimation of the concept of law does not preserve it either from the self-contradiction of teaching a kind of freedom of the will and, in the same breath, tying it to the condition of voluntary obedience to law. Let the sham opposition of law and arbitrary will pretend, as it may, the compatibility of the incompatible, because it seems plausible to us that an obeying will should subordinate itself voluntarily to a commanding will: all the arts of even the most finely spun dialectic founder on the unavoidable splitting of the law into two laws, the natural law and the moral law, of which the one carries out, though not with forces of its own, what it commands and demands, while the other has already accomplished before it would even have demanded. Freedom, thinks Kant, is a "causality according to immutable laws, but of a special kind," and the will that natural fact which "acts according to concepts"; but he too, unfortunately, has not been able to tell us how a lawfulness acting according to concepts could be compatible with a lawfulness acting mechanically, without the one entirely abolishing and annihilating the other. We decide a little differently: there are *no* natural laws, and the moral law is *rebaptized* [p. 540]- *arbitrary will*. But in the fact that "laws" nevertheless emerge in both cases — the moral law that merely demands, and the natural law that merely enforces the demand read into it — there expresses itself the hostile opposition of deed-doing spirit and necessity. For, just as little as nature of itself obeys laws, just as little would spirit be content merely to give laws, were it granted to it also to produce that in respect of which the concept of law first receives a meaning: the life-process. To dissolve this — whose being-actual coincides with beingnecessary — in such a way that it becomes conquerable, the contemplation of the universe sub specie of a state administrable according to laws serves! — After this searching weighing of the so-called "determinism," we cast only a fleeting glance at the so-called "indeterminism."

Whether one calls the law, according to which the process now taking place follows, by compulsion, upon another equally constrained one, natural law or rational law, I am, for the process of will that I oddly enough call my own, no longer responsible; for however completely I may understand the demanding statute, and however gladly I may wish to satisfy it, it will not change my must and will not increase my can. We would be nothing but wound-up automata! Therefore, thinks *Epicurus*, it would be better "to follow the fables about the gods than to be the slave of natural law; for the former at least afford hope of the hearing of prayers . . ., whereas natural necessity is inexorable." In accordance with the intellectual-<sup>3</sup> ism of antiquity repeatedly emphasized in the conception of the will, he too, however, remained far from making, like the will-metaphysicians of the Middle Ages, absolute arbitrary will the determining ground of cognition and from advocating that genuine indeterminism with which the precedence of the willing act over the finding act works itself out for the problem of freedom — a disposition to which, as we saw, the Stoa stood far closer. In that Epicurus likewise advocated a course of events, though thought of only mechanically, he nevertheless left room besides for two other powers, for the personal will and for chance. "Everything happens by necessity, by design, by chance." His effort to restrict, at least, the efficacy of the law testifies to the older cast of mind; but in that he did so with the concepts "design" and "chance," it follows that he too lacked insight into the fundamental difference [p. 541] of legislating reason from the creative powers of life. The "law of nature," namely, was from the beginning, and could be nothing other than, what it fully revealed itself to be only in the "natural sciences": the designation of the general rule according to which a process B occurs whenever a process A takes place — it being understood, unhindered by third processes. Should, then, even once a process X follow upon process A, without a process C having been at work that would in turn, in accordance with the law, be able to change process B into X, then either that presumed law would have to yield to another, actually valid law, or else there would be no lawfulness at all. — Our retrospect has taught us: "determinism" and "indeterminism" are sham oppositions that at any point can always turn into one another, because what they set over against willing and its freedom, general lawfulness, already contains within it the generating ground of willing. For the question of the conditionedness or unconditionedness of willing we gather from this, among other things, that one cannot even seriously discuss it, let alone answer it, if one has from the outset laid beneath actuality a world of things regulated along the guiding thread of "sufficient grounds."

<sup>3</sup> On page 540. — Striving to secure a multiplicity of conditions to match the multiplicity of what happens, he shrewdly insists on the recognition of the principle that the assumption of a universal law of nature excludes not merely malice and negligence, but especially also compels error, and hence its defender, to grant judgements that negate one another. The judgement, for example, that nothing happens of necessity would be just as necessary as the judgement that everything happens of necessity. The objection weighed more heavily then than it would weigh today, in an age which, thanks to its ethical Socratism, saw in error far more the origin of unlawful commotions than their consequence. It will, of course, be objected that this proves only that erring, too, lies within the plan of necessity. Yet it is a thing impossible to hold the incorrect judgement, without mental reservation, to be just as valuable as the correct one; and even one who, with Nietzsche, might wish to declare deception and error vital, indeed life-furthering, could not help but regard precisely this declaration as correct, and to that extent as more valuable than its counterpart. But how, Epicurus might then say, can one devalue error, when it testifies, together with truth, to one and the same necessity! „Whoever maintains that everything happens by natural necessity can make no *reproach* against one who says that not everything happens by natural necessity"; a remark that receives its particular light from the very readiness of the Stoics to heap spirited abuse on the deniers of the constraint of natural law!

In the first main section of Nietzsche's "Beyond Good and Evil" occurs the passage, communicated below in extract: "That 'conformity to law in nature,' of which you physicists talk so proudly, as though —

— it existed only owing to your interpretation and bad 'philology' — it is not a matter of fact, not a 'text,' but rather only a naively humanitarian arrangement and distortion of meaning, with which you amply accommodate the democratic instincts of the modern soul! ... Someone could come along who, with the opposite intention and art of interpretation, could read out of the same nature, and with regard to the same phenomena, precisely the tyrannically inconsiderate and inexorable enforcement of claims to power ... and who nevertheless ended by asserting the same thing about this world that you assert, namely that it has a 'necessary' and 'calculable' course, but *not* because laws rule in it, but because laws are absolutely *lacking*, and every power draws its ultimate consequence at every moment." One does not, indeed, quite know how Nietzsche believes he can understand from this not only the compulsoriness of events but also their calculability; but, apart from this, he — and unmistakably for the sake of rescuing [p. 542] the unconditionedness of which his "will to power" could least of all be deprived — has proposed a bold innovation, in that he suggests to us that we multiply the centers of will, or more correctly monads of power, without limit, while availing ourselves of the wholly surprising auxiliary assumption that each of them would vanish from the course of the world after its exercise of power had taken place. (Might calculability perhaps lie in a foreseeability of the sequence of such manifestations of power?) Since we wish to represent a wholly different conception with regard to necessity, we may the less spare ourselves the examination of an interpretive proposal that likewise wants to do without laws, as the seemingly strange notion of a plurality of power-monads merely circumscribes, in Nietzschean fashion, the actual state of affairs of the multiplicity of personal I's! We ask, then: could power-monads that are simply unconditioned bring about a world-happening of the character of necessity? And we anticipate the answer: they would bring about not only no necessity, but nothing at all!

If we first choose the standpoint of the observer, which we must after all adopt in order that what Nietzsche's power-monads are supposed to explain may become ascertainable, then it would seem to befall the world observed, and hence indirectly ourselves, the observers, what the power-monads would accomplish wholly out of themselves and hence unoccasioned. But with this we would have set over against the active something that suffers the activity, and thereby inevitably limited the active by, as it were, the matter upon which it would be dependent with its activity. If nothing existed but the power-monads in question, no one would gain any knowledge of them, not even the one who himself belonged to them, because he too would first have to cease being merely an effector in order to find anything at all! If, on the other hand, we choose the standpoint of the power-monad, it becomes clear that it would have nothing to do, nothing to effect, were there not for it a moment at which what will be effected through it is not yet there, notwithstanding that as something-to-be-effected it would already have to hover before it, if it is what it is supposed to be, namely a "consequence-drawing" power and not, say, merely a mechanical cause; and with this it is already stated that in every moment of its acting it would suffer the urge measured against the pertaining condition of the world, and thus the condition of the world itself; whereby it would simply and unquestionably be stripped of its nature as a power! The nothing-but-powermonad, in other words, would become an all-power-monad, and the all-power-monad [p. 543] (= God) would lie beyond every conceivable actuality; for it could neither become perceptible within an actuality, nor would it, for its part, find an — actuality before it. The monad, however, as bearer of a measure of force and of capacity, would by that very fact also have limits to its capacity, and would see its willing and accomplishing bound, step by step, to conditions.

In the language of a science of the soul that is not, precisely, concerned with power-monads, the verdict would run: the willing I would have no possibility of experiencing its power without the possibility of experiencing its powerlessness, and consequently no experience of willing takes place at all without experience of the resistance of necessity! Only with a view and in relation to it does a willing exist. If I will to do the one thing, I must leave the other undone: the recollection of this alone could suffice to uproot once and for all the delusive thought of an unconditionedness of willing. Let us, however, call to mind a few fundamental instances of our not-being-able in relation to the volitions that build precisely upon it! I cannot be in two places at once; therefore I will to traverse, as quickly as possible, the distance separating the two. I cannot turn back time in order to make what has happened not have happened; so I will at least to mitigate the after-effects of what has happened. I cannot make the unhappened happen; so I will to make up, so far as at all possible, for what was missed. I cannot transform a point in time of the future into the present; so I will to hasten the course of events. I cannot change it that an event will occur, provided its occurrence is necessarily connected with an event of the present or the past; so I can still meaningfully will to slow down the course of things. Willing breaks against the barrier of being-able, and being-able, however, is made of the matter of necessity. Measured by willing, the "Almighty" becomes an all-powerless one, because he, though he could will everything already — only, however, by no means — to will. Would the experience of the self-authority of willing then be a deception, or more correctly a figment of the brain, which might just as well be absent without the least thing in the course of the world being thereby altered — or would it speak of the manifestation of a power that really contended with necessity, and of which, then, the consequences would also somehow have to become apparent in necessity itself? Before we indicate why we answer the second question just as decidedly in the affirmative as we deny the first, we shall touch upon that necessity which has so utterly nothing to do with lawfulness.

[p. 544] We today can scarcely speak any longer of causes without at the same time meaning their lawfulness, and natural science in particular deliberately means it so. To forestall confusions, we shall therefore always use the name "cause," without further qualification, in the natural-scientific sense, but may not on that account forget that humanity for many millennia thought connections of effect without in the least co-thinking their lawfulness, let alone a dependency, pointing into the boundless, on other connections of effect. Must not we too — perhaps to our own astonishment — notice that it sometimes falls harder to us to keep that unsurveyable series in view than to content ourselves with the very nearest link as with something ultimately determining, as when we believe we discover, for our resolve and even for the arbitrary movement, the origin in our I, and reject the derivation from more remotely lying causes as something artificial; since, indeed, the continuing dispute over dependencies of willing lying further back leaves no doubt at all that here, at bottom, it is two different causalities that are being disputed over. If we call the natural-scientific concept of effecting, more precisely, the mechanical one, then there would step alongside it, in the first place, that of personal effecting, and this, now, would at least touch upon a concept of magical effecting, insofar as the mediating links between resolve and executing movement remain hidden from us a thousandfold. Under personal effecting there fall, therefore, to no small extent, divine effectings as well, and it in fact forms the transition from the primal state of humanity to humanity thinking in terms of factual logic — a humanity, to be read off roughly at the epic or heroic age, to whom the processes of nature appeared in the light of manifestations of agitation or manifestations of will of person-like gods. Thus it is a magical expression of affect when, at the frowning of the brows of Zeus, the whole of Olympus trembles, and it is a magical manifestation of will by virtue of which Leto transforms the hostile peasants into frogs, Dionysus the pirates into dolphins; in accordance with which, there the agitation of Zeus, here the wish of Leto, of Dionysus, counts quite certainly indeed as cause, but just as certainly also as the ultimate cause of the process following upon it in each case.
