If we trace the development of spirit back through this comparatively short intermediate age, we come upon, already within it, traces of an incomparably older mode of intuition, whose somewhat more precise consideration might make it easier for us [p. 545] to illuminate what is for the present required concerning the concept of unfalsified necessity. Alongside the gods and demigods — now associated and allied with them, now wholly independent of them, now even superior to them — stand peculiar powers of *fate*, which, to be sure, were with time often personified and correspondingly represented by peoples of plastic disposition such as the Greeks, but which for the most part, in relation to the Olympian figures of light, retained that quite properly darker character that points back into the far more original world of extra-personal, daemonic formations. If some students of religion, especially on linguistic grounds, wish to find in them merely humanized or weakly humanized general concepts, then they commit, with regard to them, the same error that was committed with the merely mechanical conception of the impersonal pronoun or the merely person-like conception of the gender-words, and in any case set the actual course of the matter squarely on its head; for it was not out of factual general concepts that concepts of powers of fate arose, but rather out of these that certain general concepts arose! For it is, namely, by preference, among others, the names of powers of fate that fall prey to the absorption by the conceptual drive to generalization — with the drive to personification naturally always co-operating to some extent — because their emphatically extra-personal daemonism clothes them, for the understanding, with an indefiniteness that meets the demand for generalization halfway, so to speak, and, after the objectification has taken place, delivers the intuitable content of word-meaning over to a more or less rapid fading-away. Were it the other way round, we should probably try in vain to explain why the fate-daemons appear not only in great multiplicity but throughout also in the plural, and are, moreover, quite predominantly, and by no means merely for linguistic reasons, of the female sex — for which one may compare, for instance, Greek formations such as: the Moirai, Parcae (Clotho, Lachesis, Atropos), Horae, Keres, Erinyes, Tychai, further Ananke, Ate, Nemesis, Hybris, Themis, Adrasteia, Eileithyia, etc., alongside these, say, the Fortunae and Fatae of the Romans, the fairies of the Celts, the Norns, Valkyries, and swan-maidens of the Germans. Long since, too, has the close kinship and partial complete sameness of such powers with the spinning and weaving earth-mothers been recognized, for which the mere concept of chance or of doom would offer no basis, as has the thousandfold attestable fact [p. 546] that it was predominantly women who, as priestesses, seeresses, sorceresses, represented the thought of fate in cult or magic; one need only think of the witch of Endor, the Pythias, Sibyls, Vestals, Druidesses, Idisi! Nor is this all: a graduated series of transitions can be traced to the Agathodaemons, Genii, Junos, family and attendant spirits, or, more briefly, to that daemonic double who, attached to every thing and person, signifies, among other things, the particular fate of the given state or people or person. A side-glance at certain events in the 22nd book of the Iliad will bring us fully to our goal!

Athene has vehemently demanded that Hector, "long since marked out for doom," should not escape destruction yet again. Zeus grants her request: "I will be kindly disposed toward you." But, although he does allow Athene to hasten forthwith to the aid of her Achilles, he by no means draws the decision as to whether Hector shall fall or not from his own breast; but instead:

Now the Father stretched aloft the golden scales, / and laid into the pans two dark lots of death, / this one for the son of Peleus, and that for horse-taming Hector, / grasped the middle and weighed: then Hector's fate sank / heavy toward Hades; and Phoebus Apollo forsook him.

He decides, then, only after having, by means of the scale and lot — to speak in today's language — ascertained the will of fate; with which finding we have descended to the stratum of symbolic thinking, and find ourselves transported back, unnoticed, into the train of thought that dealt with the "conditionedness of the accidental." If, now, numerous kinds of mantic ascertainment of the future from antiquity or the Middle Ages are, according to the testimony of ethnology, still practiced today by primitives and semi-primitives — for example the casting of lots, inspection of entrails, interpretation of the flight of birds, interpretation of dreams, palmistry, sieve-oracle, "sidereal pendulum," etc. — then we shall seek the motive for the action of Zeus just now heard in darker times than the almost already understanding-bright ones that created the Olympian gods and the Homeric epics, and shall regard as an extreme falsification of receptivity to fate the calculatingly intelligent considerations with which the Stoa, and later Schopenhauer (cf. note 2), thought to come to the aid of the possibility of divination. [p. 547] For it is, after all, in relation to the so-called laws of nature, precisely through-andthrough accidental happenings, and they alone, to which the capacity for foretokening an inescapable event is attributed; whereas the slightest secondary thought of a regularity of happening, and even the mere impulse aiming toward it on this side, would have had to reject any such arts of oracle unconditionally, or rather would never have hit upon them at all!

If we translate into the form of a fundamental principle of conscious conviction what at that time was not thought, not judged, but worked irresistibly in the minds of men from case to case, then the following propositions might serve, in the first place, to characterize the conviction that we obtain in place of the mood of fate: everything that happens to a human being, and likewise everything that happens through him, is a befalling — including, therefore, his feelings, resolves, and deeds — the must that reigns over him, as well as the one that pervades him, means now torment and ruin, now good fortune and blessedness — every event hangs together with every other, and the (in our sense) most incidental action can shake the whole just as much as, or more than, the (in our sense) mightiest, and can call forth an avenging doom, comparable to the touching of but a single thread of a spiderweb, when it makes the artful net tremble to its center. Let us sink ourselves especially into the above Homeric verses, and above all into the line rendered by Voß with admirable delicacy — rete d hektoros aisimon hämar ocheto d eis Aidao — = then Hector's fate sank heavy toward Hades — and Zeus will not appear to us as effecting, only the scale as co-effecting, but quite properly "decisive" that "lot of death" which "fell" to the hero, to use a phrase still current today; while at the same time even this effecting, conceptually ungraspable and yet palpable, in turn fits itself into the world-web of the great "effectress" Moira. Finally, however, notwithstanding that in this way all human work is no longer achieved but must be, and doing entirely dissolves into happening, we shall not close ourselves to the impression that there exists a mysterious belonging-together of the lot of doom with the hero who suffers it, or, more broadly, of fate with the one whom it strikes! The human being and his fate seem to us like two sides of a higher unity, and the necessity of what happens seems to us the expression of an essence in which we ourselves, and out of ourselves, are participant.

[p. 548] Let us recall to memory what was made known at several points concerning the pathic character of lived experience in antiquity; let us remember above all that with words like "inspiration," "afflatus," "enthusiasm" language attests that there *can* be a must which appears as an exuberant happiness leaving far behind it the line of ordinary feelings; and let us consider, finally, that Plato, the deifier of concepts, was still Greek enough to praise, in "divine madness," the source of the highest goods of humanity, and that, on the other hand, from a *Nietzsche*, whose nature of will was coupled in irreconcilable strife with the quite opposite drive to intoxication, sentences like these were wrung: "My love kindles itself eternally only at necessity!" — then we shall henceforth see in the light of extreme questionableness what, thanks to the mode of thought presupposing it in all apostles of morality, became the best-unproven habitual opinion: the belief, bearing itself as something self-evident, that the suffering of must is nothing but the suffering of being-compelled, and accordingly is to be compared either to the painfully futile rattling of the slave at his chain, or, at best, to a self-denial thereby deeming itself grand! How dreadfully estranged from life were all these thinkers, if, wholly blind to the case of precisely the most highly intensified moments of existence, they confused necessity with the ever-adverse hindrance of a prohibition, and thus imputed to it the lawful compulsion that one at least ideally overcomes only by submitting to it slavishly! Yet we now see clearly the scarcely concealed underlying thought. Just as necessity becomes a blessed must solely for the reason, and exactly to the extent, that the soul suffering it momentarily merges itself with the essence that expresses itself in it, so the demanded obedience to law is likewise affirmed only for this reason and to this extent: that the obeying personality knows itself, in the most personal way, participant in the power-will of a spirit that commands and forbids through laws! The daemonization of *life* in the belief in fate is met, with glorification of law, by the canonization of an arbitrary will not so much estranged from life as rather hostile to life. But we also know that on the side of life there corresponds to this what *Nietzsche* proclaims, as strikingly brief as it is profoundly true, in the words: "Where life *grows rigid*, the law piles itself up!"

Without having so far discussed them all exhaustively, we here range together, in the form of judgments of their bearers, six basic kinds of the feeling of life, to which correspond [p. 549] six basic kinds of personal ethos. The "egoist" does: I will — the "altruist": I ought — the "man of feeling": you will — the "ascetic": he wills, I must — the "animal man": it drives, I must — the "elemental man": it happens, I must. Of these, however, the two middle ones signify mere intermediate varieties, while the first two and the last two each signify sub-varieties of a single kind; for the ought of the second is only the willing of the first generalized and turned into law, and the must of the I out of the necessity of essence is common to the last two. Starting from the feeling of life of affirmed must, we could without difficulty show that neither the concept of willing nor the concept of lawfulness could have arisen if necessity alone determined the lived experience of thinking man; but here the bifurcation shall for the time being serve us to elucidate the difference between self-determination and fate from the difference of two states, of which the one affirms willing, the other must. Both agree in deriving the inner process from an essence directly effecting it: but this is, for the doer, the I, for the pathic, the It — or for the former a command of spirit, for the latter a power weaving actuality itself and, insofar as it also wove him, the sufferer of fate, at the same time the impulse that comes to his consciousness from the depths of his own essence. If we call the one attitude to life that of I-originatedness, the other that of life-originatedness, then it follows in the first place: because the life-original attitude understands itself from the efficacy of an essence that is literally akin in blood to the working essence of the growth of the tree, and in turn to that of the thunderbolt that shatters the tree, an outer and inner fate may indeed become distinguishable for it, but it cannot fall apart, for it, into two fundamentally different kinds of must; whereas, since the I-original attitude understands itself from the efficacy of a power from which being-for-itself is inseparable, there *must* fall apart for it, first of all, willing and event, and then also willing and lived experience. We indicated why the "natural law," or, according to the less anxious naming of the Stoics, the law of reason (namely in its application to natural processes) represents an important concession on the part of the purpose-positing power to necessity, and shall [p. 550] later have to examine precisely why such a concession calls forth the inexhaustible chain of causes that indeed, at least apparently, stands in the starkest opposition to I-originatedness. For the present, however, we return to the problem of freedom with the question now thus altered: not how I-originatedness accommodates itself with any lawful compulsion, but how it finds a place within necessity. First, however, it seems requisite to establish beyond all doubt whether what we set out to seek, in the actuality of happening, as a scope for exercise, is indeed what is actually meant by the experienceable self-authority of willing.

[p. 551]

#### 43. Kapitel — Bedingtheit und Unbedingtheit des Wollens — Chapter 43 — Conditionedness and Unconditionedness of Willing

It is certainly a characterization of the state of affairs that is inaccurate from the standpoint of the science of appearances, when most thinkers of rank (thus in antiquity more or less Aristotle, Epicurus, Carneades, Cicero, Chrysippus, thus in modern times more decisively Hobbes, Locke, Leibniz, Hume, Herbart, Schopenhauer) interpret unschooled self-reflection to mean that by freedom of the will it means that the bearer of the will could *do* what he wills (so-called freedom of action); and one has already imputed to natural reflection the false either/or which we have rejected, when one adds by way of grounding, say, that the unspoiled (also gladly called "naive"!) observer does not understand at all the question whether he could also *will* what he wills. For, however certain it is that he would indeed have to fall silent before this question, just as certain would he be right with the rejoinder that the little sentence "I will" means, in an emphatic sense, that it is the I of the one willing which makes or brings forth what he calls his willing, and, insofar as there is any question here at all, it is in any case only whether it merely seems to be so, while in actuality another power had brought forth the willing. Whereas one can frequently enough *not do* what one wills, and not too rarely one also does something that one had not willed at all. (Example: actions out of sudden anger or out of negligence.) Without self-contradiction one may say: "I do indeed will it, but I cannot do it" and: "I did it, but I did not will it"; whereas the turn of phrase would contain a self-contradiction: "It was not I who willed my willing."

If we consider what it is that reflection, in giving such an account of the experience of willing, actually relies upon, we come upon the command which goes forth, as it were from the midpoint of the personality, to that personality itself, and thereby at once upon the ability, proper to the one who issues the command, to test his independence at any time. If, on setting out [p. 552] on a walk, I waver even for a moment as to whether I would prefer the path to the right or to the left, I can, in view of this, bring to consciousness that it stands open to me to will either the one or the other. Such wavering, be it noted, need not necessarily precede our resolutions. In countless cases we will something, e.g. to read a book, without retrospective reflection being able to show us that a wavering had preceded the resolution. Only, if for the cases of wavering we are compelled to conclude that it was our I that gave the decisive turn, then we must judge of all cases without exception that it stood with us to will or also not to will, and may *to that extent* call every act of willing a choosing (= electing, arbitrary will). If accordingly the uniquely distinguishing mark of the impulse of will lies in the fact that it takes place on the occasion of a command, then we may draw from this an important confirmation of the fact that the linguistic communication of one's own willing to others took the form of the imperative, which, in contrast to the statement and partly also to the question (insofar, namely, as we take it merely as the posing of a problem), cannot be detached from the person of the speaker without losing its essential content. The sentence that reports to me the death of Charlemagne has, in its content, no connection with the speaker, whereas the sentence "Come here" gains its accent of meaning precisely from this connection.<sup>4</sup>

<sup>4</sup> On page 552. — Should one object that general precepts too, beginning with „thou shalt" and „thou shalt not," that is, commandments and prohibitions, are linguistically disguised imperatives, which moreover could just as well be uttered in imperative form, then we for our part maintain, going further still, that the same holds even of all laws, including the so-called laws of nature, and that precisely this attests their co-dependence on commands of the spirit — yet we can scarcely expect contradiction, and in any case none of any force, if we must add that this does not touch the fact, equally secured by linguistics, that declarative sentences with the *meaning* of imperatives could only come into being on the basis of imperatives long since linguistically formed beforehand. To be sure, it was not only generalized imperatives that the personal imperative preceded, but the personal statement preceded all general statements whatsoever; but this does not affect the circumstance that only in the genuine declarative sentence *can* the person of the speaker vanish entirely, never however in general imperatives, however deeply they may be concealed in declarative forms; of which one at once assures oneself by the consideration that every commandment, every statute, every moral law invariably betrays something of the disposition of the group of persons that devised and established the precept in question. For the so-called laws of nature, however, only an extremely penetrating analysis could demonstrate the same, and that analysis we have by no means yet carried through to its end.

Both properties of the impulse of will — its developing out of a command and the very electedness thereby accorded to the goal of the will — make it possible to display the I-originatedness of the process of willing in the sharpest possible light by comparison with any mechanical process whatever. For whoever can at all climb up to this level of reflection will, on beholding a leaf swaying on its branch and then sinking to the ground, certainly not entertain the opinion that the leaf, while it swayed, had also wavered inwardly and thereupon come to the resolution to detach itself from the twig; and conversely he will indeed credit the storm with the force to break trees, but not endow it with the gift of issuing the command to fell trees. He will further find no difficulty in deriving the falling of the leaf and the blowing of the wind from causes which in turn require more remote causes, and again more remote ones, and so on; but he will have to admit to himself that he would have annulled the very cause which he felt compelled to adduce, rightly or wrongly, for the [p. 553] impulse of will — namely, the command of the I — were he to let it be brought about by a more remote cause. Only because the science of appearances has hitherto remained stuck in mere beginnings can it be somewhat understandable that one believed one could so lightly subordinate two sequences of process so fundamentally different to one and the same lawfulness of effect!

If we examine what path "determinism" is accustomed to take for this purpose (as likewise "indeterminism," from which we shall for simplicity's sake here abstract), we meet with the following ever-similarly recurring train of thought. In the willing momentary-self only the thing-like persisting personality announces itself, whose constitution derives from an endless chain of causes no less unambiguously than does the constitution of the leaf on the tree; and upon this personality there now act motives or "reasons," in consequence of which the result, i.e. the volition, occurs with exactly the same compulsory inevitability as, at the appointed time, the falling of the leaf when the wind blows. With this the relation of the personality to the willing momentary-self was correctly described, probably the personality itself already incorrectly, though this would for the present remain mere conjecture, and, out of a false reification, the meaning of the motive or "reason" was entirely missed. For supposing it were as we set forth above, that the purpose, instead of resembling a fact that is simply found, is rather generated by the willing I, then every motive too that in any way asserted itself in the "conflict of motives" would be generated by it, and the view here presented would have committed the ineradicable error of ranking certain consequences of the activity of the I among its causes! Yet let one consider: it would merely be describing once more, in other words, the carefully set-forth state of affairs, if one described it thus: precisely in this does the falling of the leaf differ from an action, that the blowing wind, to be sure, causes it directly, but simply does *not* form a motive for it. Even if we were to disregard that the motive would, among other things, be a thought and to that extent not at all comparable with the fact called "the blowing of the wind," still the reference to the fact that might correspond to such a thought would precisely *fail* to designate in it that by which it received the character and the peculiar power of a [p. 554]- *motive*! Everyone has the ability, to repeat, to reckon up all the motives that might determine an *other* to act this way or that, without meanwhile harboring on his own part any other intention than that of — solving a calculation of probability; from which it is clear that the mere thinking-through of purposes and motives never coincides with the motivating force of these purposes.

Whoever has followed the path traveled thus far attentively enough with us to be able to call to mind all its bends and turns will perhaps hold at least one point to be insufficiently grounded, or, put otherwise, will think he perceives a gap between two propositions. As regards "determinism," he might suggest for consideration, the author seems to share the assumption of a "given" constitution of will of the one acting: but he then also adds, in place of the rejected "motives," a second "given" quantity, namely the ability of the agent, or more correctly its limits. Now, however, a decision of will certainly often occurs without regard to difficulties of execution; but if not, then the regard in question would likewise be a motive. How does the consciousness of ability relate to the "motives," and how do both relate to the command of spirit?

There are wishes whose realization is unthinkable, e.g. that what has happened should be unhappened; others that merely exceed human powers, e.g. a journey to the moon; still others to which merely my own powers would not be equal, e.g. to lift three hundredweight or to buy a castle; finally wishes fulfillable both in principle and personally. Insofar as, in the case of a wish, I normally forgo making the first three into objects of my willing, the motive for these acts of not-willing lies in the consciousness of my incapacity. Remaining within the fulfillable wishes, and leaving unaddressed the occurrence that difficulties of execution, depending on the type of personality, can both heighten and paralyze resoluteness and tension of will, the thought of my ability at least no longer weighs directly on the choice of the goal. But even in such cases some *motive or other* has undoubtedly given the decisive turn, even though I am by no means always in a position to name it offhand, and still less may I always hold myself assured, in attempting to do so, that I have not confused it with another. In order [p. 555] to pick out, by way of example, possibilities from the unlimited number of motives that might induce the walker to choose the path to the left instead of the path to the right, let us suppose it happened because he wished to avoid the probable encounter, on the path to the right, with a certain person, or because he indeed expected, precisely on the path to the left, the encounter unwelcome to him, yet was minded to allow no such consideration any codetermination of his action; further, because he somewhat superstitiously held the road to the right to be unlucky, or because, on the contrary, he feared just that of the road to the left, yet again wished to ignore such fears. One notices at once that with decisions in each case from the second ground there would be bound up in quite special measure the consciousness of being able to choose at one's own pleasure, because, despite objective expediency, the tentatively envisaged goal was rejected in high-handed fashion by the person with an "I don't care about that." — But what, then, was actually the decisive factor? Why did one thought "win" over the other in the "conflict of motives"? Did that perhaps lie in its logical power of conviction? But then we ought largely to be able to calculate how someone will decide under surveyable conditions, which we can at best only surmise, never know for certain in advance. While, for example, we are in no doubt that whoever we publicly hurl a grave insult in the face of will fall prey to the feeling of indignation, we can be completely mistaken about the action that results from it for him: for there now comes into play his — arbitrary will!

In order to get out of this unpleasant circle, let us not hesitate to make an end, once and for all, of an old legend: motives or "reasons" in the sense hitherto believed do not exist at all! Here Nietzsche, more than any other, has broken the path for us. "One did not doubt," he says in "Götzendämmerung," "that all the antecedents of an action, its causes, were to be sought in consciousness and would be found there again if one sought them — as 'motives': one would otherwise not have been free for it, not responsible for it." But the so-called motive is an error. "Merely a surface phenomenon of consciousness, an accompaniment of the deed, which rather conceals the antecedents of a deed than represents them." In the 32nd section of "Jenseits" he sets forth that in a pre-moral period of humanity one derived the worth or unworth [p. 556] of an action from its consequences, whereas in the moral period, thanks to a first attempt at self-knowledge, from its *origin*. Meanwhile, he goes on, "a fateful new superstition... came to power with just this: one interpreted the origin of an action, in the most definite sense, as origin from an *intention*... The intention as the whole... prehistory of an action: under this prejudice one has praised, blamed... and even philosophized almost down to the most recent *time*." As against this, everything that can be known of an action "still belongs to its surface and skin," which indeed betrays something, but conceals more. If, finally, we hold beside this the Zarathustra saying: "One thing is the thought, another the deed, another the image of the deed; the wheel of the reason does not roll between them," we see, first of all, that Nietzsche attacks, at its most sensitive point, the belief, now open, now concealed, in an efficacious power of consciousness, in that he strikes from the causes of the resolution — and hence of that whereby alone consciousness could attest itself as capable of effect, namely of action — the thought of the purpose, to which only a symptomatic value is left. And we see him, further, using the words "motive" and "intention" in the same or nearly the same meaning.

That "motive" may indeed be used for "purpose" and conversely is shown by the fact that, as often as we prefer, in place of the turn of phrase "I am pursuing with this such-and-such a purpose," the turn of phrase "the ground (= motive) why I do this is such-and-such." If we call motives tentatively envisaged purposes, we reflect once more: if it is the willing I that posits purposes, then it can also only be the willing I that posits motives. However much, then, Nietzsche is right to lend to the motive meant in each case (= thought of purpose) merely the significance of an indication of the real causes of the resolution, it nonetheless remains just as true that there can be talk of a decision of will only with reference to the fact of consciousness of the intention. We call it purpose with regard to the goal of our willing that hovers before us, and, on the other hand, motive insofar as we wish to state why, in our opinion, precisely this goal was chosen by us. In view of the extraordinary tenacity of life that the false doctrine of "motives" has manifested, let us illuminate its illusoriness once more from another side.

As has been indicated several times, the process of deliberation is a [p. 557] deliberate and hence a will-steered process, or, in short, an inner action. Since the weighing of so-called motives, which precedes not all but yet many resolutions, is naturally no exception to this, such preliminaries of the outer action are again activities of will and by no means, say, preparations of a pure reason, which lets given "motives," upon a will still unawakened for the time being, "repeatedly try out their force against one another," as Schopenhauer describes it in a manner that turns the will into the will-less prey of two beings quite willfully battling over it! To explain the volition from so-called motives would accordingly be roughly equivalent to explaining burning by the remark that the burning stems from the fire! — Let us consider, on the other hand, the purpose in the meaning of the motive, and three features strike us about it more sharply.

The motive is, first, always a thought. If it is objected that the motive of someone who, say, ran away at the sight of an explosion without reflecting, was an object of perception, indeed a mere impression, we would counter that either the mere impression actually occasioned the running away, in which case, however, there is no decision of will at all and no action at all present, but a sequence of impulse-movements; or the running away happened with intention, in which case the apprehension of the fire must infallibly have preceded it, and indeed as containing in itself the thought of its danger. Secondly, far from being nothing but thought, the motive appears to its bearer rather in the light of the ground of a positing of purpose. If it is now true, as we repeatedly convinced ourselves, that no mere thinking-through of motives coincides with the intending of the action that would correspond to them, then we recognize, thirdly, that its actually motivating force must have flowed to the thought of purpose from elsewhere. Whatever hidden mediations may be at play here (and we shall later learn to distinguish the true purpose from the merely supposed purpose), so much stands fast in principle: it must be a vital impulse whereby the thought gained the high accent of the goal toward which it presses the one willing, and it must be a command of spirit whereby the impulse was fettered to a thought! With this we can now, as it were from within, separate out what in the process of willing falls to necessity and what to arbitrary will.

Given to the I, because suffered by it and accordingly necessarily [p. 558] given, are impulses; not given in the same sense, but rather become its own, and therefore to be subsumed under no concept of necessity, is the command of spirit, which makes out of impulses positings of purpose and thereby, out of the driven I, an I that wills for the first time. One searches in vain for the autonomy of the bearer of will so long as one hopes to find it in the generation of impulses, and one falsifies, conversely, necessity, when one imagines oneself able to derive from mere commands of spirit that whereby an impulse announces itself in the process of willing. If we conceive the personal I as the point of attack of two powers, life and spirit, then the personal volition arises out of the struggle between the manifestation of life named impulse, which the I, by virtue of its livingness, suffers, and the manifestation of spirit named command, which the I itself, by virtue of its spirituality, seems to issue. With regard to the impulses, the volition belongs to the web of necessity; with regard to the command, there is realized with it, on that same web, the act of this spirit intelligible from nothing but spirit itself. If the having-to of the pathic being proceeds simply from its essence, then the volition proceeds from the personal I, and that is to say from an essence riven within itself, whose having-to and necessary side is disturbed again and again by an active side, and whose active side is hindered again and again by a having-to side. Or: in that a command, apparently of the I, in truth of spirit, enters into connection with a living impulse, it is superseded by the impulse of will, which, exactly as indivisible as the I that comes immediately to activity in it, nonetheless attests its double nature in that it must first carry the goal, even though it brings it forth, into actuality. The volition is thus, to be sure, wholly preconditioned by the personality of the one willing; but in the personality of the one willing there are found coupled together two fundamentally different kinds of conditions: the vital constitution, in consequence of which the I receives impulses by essential necessity, and the spiritual constitution, in consequence of which it accomplishes acts on its own authority, even though solely on the basis of impulses received. The connection, finally, again "given," of vital constitution with spiritual constitution can no longer be grasped from the standpoint of necessity. — The clarification, now ripe for utterance, of the relation of the motive to the consciousness of our ability shall [p. 559] serve us to find a distinguishing mark, extremely important for the whole problem of will, of those impulses which are qualified to form the substratum of commands of spirit.

For the I-original stance, as was said above, there fall apart, on the one hand, willing and event, and, on the other, willing and experience. Let us replace "event" by "outer necessity," "experience" by "inner necessity"; then to the former belong all the, however variously distinguishable, limits of my ability, to the latter all the impulses that become in any way motives for me. As surely, then, as everyone long ago noted various limits of his ability before he became aware of his motives, so surely does the mere reference to the fact of factual reflection suffice to demonstrate, among the enabling grounds of willing, the existence of an element which — independent of the command of spirit — stems from necessity. But as surely, on the other hand, as we could recognize and acknowledge the bindingness of no really subsisting fact and the bindingness of no logical connection for our thinking without having experienced and suffered an impulse that occurred independently of our pleasure, so surely is that outer necessity for us necessity only to just the extent that it was able to announce itself in the medium of inner necessity. If we further consider that, at least at the moment of coming to a resolution, the belief in the executability of the resolution can never be lacking, whether or not it be expressly thought, then we must think of what in the language of the understanding is called the "world of facts" as involved in without exception every impulse-experience capable of will, and accordingly formulate the requiring proposition: commands of spirit go forth *exclusive*ly on occasion of impulses referable to fact. If we recall, finally, that it is a previously exactly circumscribed limit of process whereby the act of apprehension engraves itself into impression-experiences, then only inner processes afflicted with such limits of process, and in this way already riven within themselves, would be capable of will.

We believe we now see very clearly why, after the blindness that has occurred for life-processes, in the so-called question of primacy, opposite decisions could present themselves with an equally convincing semblance of correctness. If one lays the emphasis on the logical relation between purpose and means, it is usually not much further to the attempt to compose willing out of nothing but [p. 560] thoughts; if, conversely, one lays the emphasis on the delimiting selection in apprehension, or even merely on the "reactivity" of the act of apprehension, it is usually not much further to the attempt to compose thinking out of nothing but deeds. Both views are false; but the second, if it is permitted to speak of degrees of wrongness, stands a little closer to the truth; for in the inspirited being the will-ready stance is more original than the merely apprehending stance. Before we bring this fully to light later, let us first give information about the relation, inquired into, between motive and consciousness of ability, with the following overall characterization of willing: it is the autonomy of the commanding spirit whereby the feeling of free pleasure rightly attaches itself in the willing I, and it is the I's experience of being driven, on whose account the determining grounds of the positing of purpose appear in the light of motives, and it is, finally, the limit of process, clamped to the will-capable pull toward the goal, on whose account every motive always also means a thought-ground, and in this way a constituent of the knowledge of the ability to accomplish.

With the insight into the dependence of the volition on the two-fold, divided nature of a will-capable being, the question of more remote causes of the resolution is finally set aside, and in its place there steps the task of a characterization of the enabling grounds of willing according to the measure of the character-constitution of the bearer of will. Although such a task, as will be shown, ultimately comes down to a single double problem, we must nonetheless, with a statement not yet touching on this, make all the more a concession to the customary way of conceiving fundamental differences of character of will, as it is only thereby that we may hope to forestall the misunderstandings which the habitual relapse into consideration "along the guiding thread of causality" always brings with it anew. In doing so we have, besides some dispositions of will that determinism too asserts, others to mention that have escaped research hitherto. With these we begin.

Grounded in the constitution of character is the personally uncrossable how-much of the capacity to will, which, however, unfolds under an analyzing investigation into at least three thoroughly different dispositions of intensity or strength. We first name the personal tensibility of will, corresponding to what is popularly called "energy," in consequence of which the one can, with his effort of will, more or less exceed the possible highest degree [p. 561] of will-tension of another. In second place we single out the personal degree of nimbleness of the realization of will, also to be called will-talent or ease of will, in consequence of which, under like external circumstances, the one needs each time a lesser measure of exertion for the execution of a resolution than another. In third place there would already be to mention here the personal degree of ease of the transition from feeling-impulse to will-impulse, or, in short, personal resoluteness, in consequence of which, given like-situated "interests" and external circumstances, the one resolves far more swiftly than another, and especially in the case of wavering comes out of the wavering far more easily. One sees at once in what respect the willing of man depends on such dispositions, and that he is also not able to exchange them for other dispositions.

Now someone might wish to renew a long-since-settled question as follows: granted all that, this still does not decide anything about an essential dependence of the act of choice. If one remains this side of the limits of personal energy, of personal ease of will, of personal resoluteness, then it stands in the free pleasure of everyone whether to wish to exert himself or not, to take upon himself difficulties of execution or to shrink back before them, to come to the resolution or to renounce it, finally and above all, to end states of wavering between different possibilities with a "sic volo." Is the capacity for freedom of choice to be denied him, then? The answer runs: as surely as it would have no assignable sense at all to deny him a capacity in whose exercise willing precisely and variably consists, so surely does it lie grounded in the constitution of his character which choice he will make from case to case. The personal I, and nothing besides, has the decision! But if the personal I is, so to speak, the geometrical locus for the cooperation of spirit and life, and nothing besides, then the decision can impossibly turn out otherwise than according to the measure of the partly vital, partly spiritual constitution of this personal I! The opposite assumption would compel belief in a second I behind the first, this again belief in a third, and so on into infinity. Let us, however, call to mind the state of affairs by means of everything that we were able to determine about the structure of volition!

[p. 562] If my I is to be able to generate a purpose, it must have suffered impulses; for without any impulse to it, it could purpose nothing. That is not yet enough: they must be impulses referable to fact that I have suffered, because otherwise I would remain unable to bring what drives me into connection with the world of facts. Here let it be permitted to anticipate coming chapters: only "elementary" and only "animalic" impulses are impulses *not* referable to fact, and a being that is only "animalic" as well as one that is only "elementary" can harbor no intentions whatsoever, generate no purposes whatsoever. If we call the substratum of such impulses drives, the substratum of impulses referable to fact motive-springs (= "interests"), then the problem of will coincides with the problem of the genesis of motive-springs out of mere drives. — Well then, our questioner might reply, let us take motive-springs or "interests" as "given," and accordingly impulses referable to fact as given; does it not then stand within the discretion of the purpose-positing I to make the choice between different impulses, and would it not thereby have decided on its own authority whether it wished to follow the one or the other motive-spring?! Many a one, he might perhaps add, has indeed begun, of his own free will, from one day to the next, "a new life," in that he by no means merely condemned perverse habits, but simply laid them aside and suppressed them with "iron energy"! Does it not come to light irrefutably, in view of so many "conversions," changes of mind, complete reorientations, which occurred thanks to a single resolution, that the personality, instead of letting itself be led about by its motive-springs, is rather in a position to master its motive-springs?! The answer runs: quite without question the personality can choose between two impulses and has thereby also already chosen between two motive-springs; only this too, however, happens in consequence of a suffered impulse, underlying which again lies a motive-spring! We repeat briefly the proof of this.

The thought of purpose includes by its nature the relation to a motive, or rather both are only a single state of affairs, but considered from two different sides. Whether and how far I, in willing, think of my motives, whether and how far I think of them rightly, does not touch the indubitable fact of the belonging-together of the purpose with a motive. No intention can be conceived without a belonging Because. If I will, for instance, nothing but to will, or to manifest my will, be it before others, be it even only before [p. 563] myself, then the motive for this was perhaps the intention to prove to myself or to others that I am able to do this, because it so pleased me. All the same, Nietzsche is doubly right to call the motive a mere accompaniment of the deed; for, first, as will come to light only later, the true motive is wont usually to remain hidden from us; and, second, as we have shown, it can by no means be something adhering to a (thought-) ground whereby it appears in the light of a moving force. If this, to be sure, necessarily couples itself in willing with a thought, it nonetheless stems no less from a suffered impulse. It is, in other words, indifferent what I hold to be the motive of my willing, and in particular no decision can occur for which some motives or other could not be given; but neither must the motive I mean be the true motive, nor, again, would I hold a mere thought to be a moving force, did it not have at its disposal the vehicle of an (by spirit cleft) impulse. The cause of willing is thus in general no thought at all, but a life-process driving from within, to which, however — and indeed already in statu nascendi, namely by virtue of that cleavage — a (groundable) thought of goal has attached itself. Then it also holds, however: whatever ground I may suppose myself to have for preferring impulse A to impulse B, it has become a motive for me only insofar as the occasion of its taking place was in turn a suffered impulse; from which it is to be seen that into every decision that ends a wavering and generates the resolution we must take along the suffered impulse, and then, too, the motive-spring dwelling within us that brought it to bear at the I-point.

Since the habit, hopelessly misleading for our problem, of researching "along the guiding thread of causality," might intrude with the accessory thought that then there would surely be no change of the "innate" character and every upbringing would accordingly be superfluous, we note that the question of the innateness of the dispositions has not even been touched by our discussions hitherto. In every somewhat matured character there are found, besides innate motive-springs, other motive-springs that were acquired through habit or practice, and no one could seriously wish to dispute that every acquired motive-spring resembles a mean proportional of innate motive-springs and outer life-circumstances, which, in relation to those, possess the character [p. 564] of contingency. *How* a character will further develop, if we transplant it early enough out of determinate life-circumstances into life-circumstances as opposite as possible, can at best be gauged with some probability, and often not at all; but that it will change somehow, we may set down as certain. Character is not a fixed but a variable quantity, or, if one prefers, a system of dispositions *together with* the, for the present, unknown-to-us breadth of variation which we must add to each of them, and thereby also to the "force" of each in connection with the rest. This alone, however, is not touched or restricted by the "givenness" of character! Two twins, placed from the first day of their life under conceivably like-kind surroundings and educational influences, will by the fourteenth year already have *acquired* as surely different dispositions as they *brought with them* from the outset different dispositions; and the "conversion" that succeeds in the one person, and fails in another under the same circumstances, succeeds or fails according to the character-constitutions as they were "given" at the time of the operative circumstances.

By what, then, one hears asked further, does this whole conception still differ from that of "determinism"? With the answer to this, prepared down to the last detail, we bring the first part of the book to a close. — The autonomous command of spirit, as we had signified in advance, *really* contends with necessity and accordingly calls forth in the world of appearance changes that could not take place without it. If we consider what is meant by this, first of all as it were from within, we find ourselves faced with the question of what befalls, through the act of spirit, that life-process which we called the suffered impulse. For if the act of spirit, without indeed being able to generate impulses, is nonetheless to bring forth effects, these must in any case consist in certain modifications which already available impulses undergo through it. Our decision, already put forward earlier, that the impulse is cleft by the spiritual act, would, to be sure, remain a problem clothed merely in the form of an assertion so long as we could not state which side is thereby separated off from which other side of the life-process, and what the consequence of this is in the life-process. However the answer to this question may more precisely turn out, the supposed effect would unquestionably signify an intervention of spirit into the necessity of happening. [p. 565] But no transformation can take place in happening that would not also bring with it transformations in the world of appearances, and no transformation can take place in the world of appearances that would not somehow become perceptible and would have to be accessible to demonstration in the world of facts. With this we come to the "outer side" of the state of affairs.

If the volition is not, being what it is, without the command of spirit, then all the movements called movements of arbitrary will are not, being what they are, without the command of spirit. Whether we hold things, together with their properties, states, processes, to be constituent parts of actuality itself, or, with the author of this work, only for thought-things which spirit, on occasion of the experiencing of actuality, has cut to its own "law" in order to become master of that actuality, there is no doubt that without actuality and without *its* principle of the necessity of happening there could be no talk either of things, their properties, states, processes, or of any "laws" concerning things and processes. Has it not been indicated more than once already that with the concept of a natural lawfulness the all-powerful will of spirit has had to resign itself to a concession to — necessity! But the foundation-wall and cornerstone of all lawfulness is the concatenation of (mechanical) causes with (mechanical) effects, in consequence of which the recurrence of the former inviolably brings about the recurrence of the latter. From the indubitable impossibility of ranking the purely spiritual act among the causes follows the impossibility of ascribing to the purely spiritual act any effects whatsoever within the framework of natural laws! That is precisely the standpoint of a consistent determinism, which we leave untouched. For we intend to show that demonstrably immeasurable effects, with which acts of spirit unceasingly break into actuality, take place this side of all possible "causal connections" whatsoever, and that it is entirely a matter of indifference for the discoverability of "causal connections" whether we take as our basis the extra-human world of facts or the achieved results of our willing; whereby, indeed, it would be shown by the most powerful example possible that, in relation to the necessity of happening, the sham-necessity of the mechanics of law resembles an extremely artificial net with which one imagined one could scoop out the — ocean.

[p. 566]

### Zweiter Abschnitt — Trieb und Wille — Second Part — Drive and Will

#### 44. Kapitel — Kritik bisheriger Triebauffassungen — Chapter 44 — Critique of Previous Conceptions of Drive

We begin with the inner side of the state of affairs just so named, and would have, then, to disclose plainly and clearly what is separated off from what, in the life-process bearing the name "impulse," through the act of spirit. — If we call the impulse-conditions drives, we have entered a territory concerning which, to speak bluntly and without mincing words, nothing but a heap of nonsense has hitherto been put forward. We would indeed have said too little with the remark that a psychology of drives does not exist, because what has been repeatedly offered for it represents so thorough a falsification of all drive-life that the state of mere absence of knowledge would be by far preferable to the prevailing state. So at least it appears, if we provisionally disregard the, however consequenceless, attempts of a great part of Romantic philosophy, and of a considerably smaller part, however, of the trains of thought of Nietzsche, whose in itself very deep-penetrating conception of drive was deflected from its guiding line by the importing of a "will to power" into the life-processes. We survey, summarizing, the occasioning grounds of the distortion of drive already familiar to us throughout, and test them on a classical example.

Whoever, blinded to the concept of life, investigates drives, will always interpret them by analogy with the will, indifferent to whether he does so deliberately, as among analyzers of consciousness, say, a Lipps, or rather, conversely, wishes [p. 567] to interpret the impulses of will by analogy with the impulses of drive, as among thinkers, say, a Schopenhauer. Lacking insight into the essential difference between drive-impulse and will-impulse, he — because man rarely experiences drive-impulses without accompanying will-impulses — infallibly carries spirit into the sub-spiritual drives, and will, precisely with the endeavor to interpret willing from mere drive-impulses, deliver the very worst misconstruals of drive. — Because the will pursues purposes, the life-impulse is likewise understood as though it purposed something, and the whole of nature as though it were a system of purposes. Because the purpose of will is realized in achievements, from which we are accustomed to read it off, certain consequences of their operation are investigated in place of the drives, and thought into the drives themselves as intentions directed at the effect. Because only an I is capable of willing, which in every act of willing asserts itself, the self-preservation-interest of the bearer of will transforms itself into a self-preservationdrive of all living beings. Examples may make this clearer. Our domestic animals eat as we do and drink as we do. They indeed do not know it, but we know it, that one cannot go on living if one wholly abstains from eating and drinking. We accordingly know purposes of nourishment and can come to resolutions such as to nourish ourselves better or to abstain from superfluous gluttony; consequently, so runs the conclusion, eating and drinking occurs originally and generally out of a "nourishment-drive," and in the drive for food there compellingly announces itself the drive of self-preservation.

If someone now said: but the animals have not the least knowledge that, in order not to die, they must take in calories; for even the assumption that they are capable of acquiring such knowledge would not help us past the fact that they already perform what is so called purposive even beforehand (one need think of the pecking of grain by a chick just crept out of the egg), and indeed by no means only in respect of the taking of nourishment, but of a thousandfold other activities besides (one need think of the migrating away of the birds of passage in autumn) — then the believing confessor of the religion of self-preservation, of the sacro egoismo, holds ready, in most honest conviction, those phrases which, stripped of all evasions and befoggings, proclaim that all this happens out of unpurposed purposes, unthought thoughts, unconscious consciousness! Who thinks here, and who does not think? The "self-preserving" being does not think, yet the "nature" dwelling within it is indeed intent on its preservation. In the non-thinking being there sits a planning, calculating, indeed, without doubt, financially [p. 568] trained "nature," which lays out its undertakings for the long view, whereof we shall presently hear still more astonishing things.

For the purpose of self-preservation alone will not suffice. Like human beings, animals too pair off, and one does not fail — in view of the reproduction that quite frequently, indeed among animals normally always, follows upon it — to call the mating drive a "reproductive drive." But man knows from himself, and finds it readily confirmed by the behavior of numerous animals, that the young brood causes the parents all manner of inconveniences which a drive of mere self-assertion would certainly not endure. Food must be procured for the young, often at the cost of effort and danger, not to speak of the instances of a maternal love — *also* among animals — that sacrifices its own life in cases of danger. Nor is that all: the mating process is, for not a few animals, fraught with mortal danger. The male spider, by copulating with the female spider, exposes himself to the danger of being devoured by her! There is perhaps no more beautiful proof of the self-assertive nature of the I than that a thinking estranged from life by spirit should feel itself irresistibly moved to explain even the so-called reproductive drive — which it sets over against the "nutritive drive" — from a purpose of preservation! And once "nature" as a whole has already been made autonomous and self-identical, why should it not, like a bank director, pay out an entire host of department heads, business managers, financial advisers, arbitrageurs, and chiefs of advertising — namely the genera, species, and varieties? Without foreseeing the consequences, and at times thereby endangering themselves in the extreme, the animals nonetheless pair according to the preservative purposes of the provident *species*, to belonging to some one of which they can in no way help. (One notices, incidentally, the conceptual pattern of the human state!)

We stand in the midst of a conception of drives which, without ever having so much as asked about the drives, without ever having examined them itself, circles with everything it puts forward about them around the answering of a single question: what *use* are the drives, and consequently whom do they benefit? They are useful because they preserve, and they preserve either the self-being or the species of the self-being; they are a will directed toward the one or the other! Should some uninvited doubter again recall that to every purposing there belongs an I that purposes it, since no one has ever experienced the contrary, indeed could not even conceive it, [p. 569] which would then compel the conclusion that a *person* is the bearer of the properties of the species, notwithstanding that the self-beings belonging to the species, with whose disappearance the species itself would disappear, are found scattered over the most various places of the earth and through the millennia — it would not in the least trouble the representative of "natural-scientific" experience not merely to deny the personhood of the species but at once to dissolve the personal I itself into nothing but natural drives — because into *the* two thought-things he takes for natural drives, the nutritive drive and the reproductive drive, he has already, unnoticed, smuggled in the calculating I!

It scarcely needs to be affirmed that the sense of utility, in the end, is never at a loss for an answer, however much that is useless or superfluous one may hold up to it. Point to the feelings, the surges, the raptures that accompany so many manifestations of drive, and it shows us that the species attains its purposes the better for taking the self-beings into its service by paying them all manner of "pleasure-premiums," as we heard above in a note from Schopenhauer, and as the very latest physicians have spun out with a wit that would unquestionably earn the authors of student beer-papers a round of applause. Should one venture to remark that, even granting those two drives to be truly established, there would still evidently be a whole pack of other drives — drives of self-expression, of movement, of play, of wandering, of formation, of adornment, of imitation, and so on — it cannot fail that he discover some profit in each and every one of them, always having the advantage of calling in the species where the self-being shows no benefit, and the self-being where the species shows none. As for symbiosis, we had best not bring that up with him at all, for advantages of one kind or another for the cohabiting beings will certainly not be lacking. Were we to count up the rowan-berries that a rowan tree produces in a year, or the numerous hips of a luxuriant briar bush, and set beside that the number of rowan trees and briar bushes that on average come newly into being from them, it would certainly emerge that thousands, indeed tens of thousands, of fruits continually rot away without any "useful effect." Our apostle of purpose would nevertheless prove to us that, in this world of self-beings locked in struggle with one another, the spirit of the species must reckon with enormous obstacles and resistances and must therefore scatter about a great superfluity of seeds, so that the continuance of its house be assured. Were we to persist, we should indeed still be able to trouble him with tiresome counter-questions. [p. 570] We might point him, for instance, to all manner of superfluous organs, to atrophies, indeed to countless malformations. We should wish enlightenment from him as to why so many blossoms display themselves in the most splendid colors. As recently as a generation ago he would have answered without hesitation: so that they be found by the insects, which — even though for their part they pursue partly selfish purposes of their own and partly selfish purposes of the species — unwittingly attend, as a mere by-product of their visits, to the reproductive process of the plants; evidently in consequence of an extremely far-sighted arrangement made by the superintelligence of nature that once again governs behind the species. Meanwhile, however, it appeared to emerge that not a few insects are at least partially color-blind; as are some fish, which nonetheless adorn themselves at mating time with the most gorgeously colored garb. The most recent researches, to be sure, again incline toward the contrary assumption. Yet according to the researches of Erhard, diurnal birds, for instance, are nearly blue-blind, notwithstanding that many of them have precisely a blue plumage! But who knows — perhaps our indestructible confessor of purposive reason would counter that those colors, though invisible to the "parties concerned," are just as important and effective as the moneys and monetary values in the vaults of banks, which perform their services even though they generally remain hidden from the eyes of the customers! But it is not worth pursuing such questions further, because they give the appearance of assenting on principle to a way of thinking that, not unlike late myths, not only personifies every extra-human appearance in the crudest fashion, but moreover attributes to the acting powers a disposition that makes the universe indistinguishable from a colossal factory. For anyone still unprejudiced can see readily enough that here — astonishingly naive as it is — the "competitive struggles" of the "business life" of a society enslaved to Mammon have been transferred onto a so-called nature.

So lauten jener Afterweisheit Sprüche, / for which all things grow for the oven or the kitchen, / for which whatever creeps and flies and swims / appears foreordained for us as food, / which grants even the giant ball that flames above / only the office of heating the earth; / for which the moon hangs in the sky, to aid the feeble stars, / as our night-lantern. / (Jordan.)

[p. 571] It was in the money-economic age of the Greeks that the "plebeian Socrates" (as Nietzsche calls him) began a slander of life that was subsequently spiritualized to the utmost by countless "teleologies." And again it suffices to dig down only a little beneath the surface to find "idealism" and "materialism," however fiercely they quarrel over words, secretly arm in arm, both laboring — with, though different, instruments of thought — to fortify and support belief in this plainly petty-bourgeois rationality of the world's arrangement; whereupon, to be sure, "idealism" once again shows the greater consistency in error, and hence the comparatively greater strength. It is to idealism alone that we wish here to grant a sidelong glance, all the more since the essential kinship of "materialism" with it will become evident not merely from the example about to be adduced, but will also come up for discussion on the occasion of the dissolution, to be offered later, of the concept of mechanical causation.

If the talk of so-called natural purposes is to be more, and other, than an entertaining metaphor, there must be a person who thinks the purposes of the species on behalf of the self-beings, and finally a commander or monarch who in turn thinks the species. Kant, whose peculiar consistency we have had occasion enough to appreciate, calls the concept of the purposive merely regulative, yet nonetheless holds that there will never come a Newton able to explain even a single blade of grass "according to natural laws that no intention has ordered"! The self-beings would thus become thoughts (or intentions) of the varieties, the varieties thoughts of the species, the species thoughts of the genus, the genera thoughts of God — whereby one may, if one pleases, insert as further naturae naturantes et naturatae [natures naturing and natured] the classes of living beings, the planet earth, the solar system, and so forth. And so we should arrive at the creative Logos. This is precisely what "idealism," roughly since *Plato*, means when it reflects on stirrings, impulses, and formative powers; and because our thoughts lack the capacity to bring anything forth without bodily mediation, it makes use, by way of distinguishing the thoughts of the creative Logos from ours, preferably of the Platonic word "Idea." The "Idea" of the whole determines, according to *Kant*, the connection of all the parts. Even a *Carus*, insofar as he Platonizes, lets it be "Ideas" that come to appearance in all the formations of the world of perception; likewise Schiller, likewise Schopenhauer, and so on. According to [p. 572] Carus in particular, there exists in the Godhead the Idea of the total organism of the world, of the organism of each individual star, of the organism of the crystals, of the organism of the species, of the organism of each individual being; it is extra-temporal and imperishable, while the appearances belonging to it are temporal and perishable; it shapes, forms, and fructifies "nature," which, over against it, signifies merely a malleable matter, or else a mere possibility for realization.

The heavy, well-nigh impenetrable cloud of meaning that envelops the old magic name "Idea" like a nimbus enables its stewards and priests to make themselves believe that they have comprehended the most various states of affairs under a single concept. At one moment the Idea is the organism itself, insofar namely as it "appears"; at another it is the invisible Archeus of its formative processes; at another it is the purpose *prior* to its realization, at another the product achieved through purposive activity; at another it takes on the form of a physical force that is added to the other physical forces (vis vitalis, vis essentialia, occasionally nisus formativus); at another it is a higher principle that avails itself of the physical forces exactly as human intelligence does, and indeed already in their inorganic manifestations. The dubiousness that naturally forces itself upon us in the face of so peculiar an interchangeability of the concept drives one to ever new attempts at naming, as for instance Carus introduces, in place of "Idea," the following substitute words by turns: image — prototype — type — schema of organization — form — forming force — ideal form — cause of existence — entelechy — life. One readily recognizes that already the first great teleologist, namely Ari*stotle*, placed the entire conceptual apparatus of an ideological doctrine of world-purpose completely at disposal, and that no accumulation of turns of phrase, however fanciful, could free the purpose-positing or forming or driving Idea or entelechy or vis from being the effluence of that intelligence, essentially different from the processes of nature, which we find in ourselves and exclusively in ourselves, and whose intentionality would simply abolish the presupposed laws of nature, were it actually able to intervene in them. Aristotle knew this in the end; the vitalisms of modern times were able to conceal it, because hidden behind them, as it turns out, stands the Judaic belief that a purposing will *begets* the world. In the Romantic Carus, however, to whose profound researches we shall return, the point of view of preservation withdraws altogether [p. 573] behind, as it were, artistic intentions of design on the part of the Idea-generating Godhead. All the less shall we fail to recognize it — to pick out only a few instances — in the all-dominating drive of self-preservation of Spinoza, in the monads of Leibniz, in the I of Fichte, in the "Reals" of Herbart, in the "Will" of Schopenhauer. — Upon this we shall offer, in conclusion, a model example of what has been set forth.

An extreme idealist, at least in his intellectual achievements, is *Schiller*. Whoever has not yet given himself an account of the deeper essential sameness of idealism with "materialism" may therefore justly be astonished that it was precisely Schiller who composed the following often-cited stanza:

Meanwhile, until philosophy / holds the fabric of the world together, / *it* keeps the machinery going / through hunger and through love.

It scarcely needs to be stressed that "hunger" here means "nutritive drive" and "love" "reproductive drive," since otherwise it would be quite impossible to see why these two in question should be just what keeps the fabric of the world together. — Between Schiller and *Darwin* there certainly exist some differences; and yet it is precisely these same two supposed drives, prompted by the thought of self-preservation and preservation of the species, which the otherwise mechanistically explaining Darwinism must presuppose step by step, and indeed actually does, in order to be able to present its system of purposiveness — now, to be sure, already cut down to poorhouse dimensions — with some plausibility. For the means which the will to preservation, in the Darwinian sense, makes use of could be paraphrased, in the form of a precept, by the sentence: "You must stretch yourself to fit the blanket," and the being that survives in the competitive struggle of the bearers of existence-assertion, and is allegedly the stronger, always purchases so successful an advantage by having been able, at the astonishing price of surrendering its own peculiar character, to *adapt* itself to God knows what straits! But what, thanks to this cast of mind, comes unvarnished to light in Darwinism — the devaluation of all drives and other properties of the organism according to the measure of their competitive fitness and their officious readiness to fall into line — underlies, though less obviously, all doctrines of life, spiritual and unspiritual, teleological and mechanistic alike, and has laid waste the conception of the drives, down to the present day, to an extent that could not be surpassed.

[p. 574] Let it further be mentioned that by far the majority of doctrines of life proceed "optimistically." But one sees readily enough how easily the optimism in question can turn into a Schopenhauerian pessimism. If the "war of all against all," as Hobbes set it up for human society and Darwin extended it to the entire world of organisms, is in and of itself not exactly apt to nourish our confidence in the powers that shape the world, then, with regard to the "nutritive drive" (= hunger), one need only stress that according to it every living being devours other living beings to the best of its power, and one can, if one likes, just as well call it a drive to murder, and thus armed, set about proving with it that this planet at least, with the life that swarms upon it in the millions, is the spawn of a Satan who wished to procure for himself the sadistic pleasure of watching endlessly self-devouring egoisms; whereby one would have grounded quite prettily, in "natural-scientific" fashion, the equation — not exactly new to many a reader versed in cultural history — God = Satan. What a positively infernal prospect opens up, moreover, when one considers that everything and anything is always only means, never end — the individual being, for instance, a means of reproduction, the new being thereby produced once again a means, and so on ad infinitum, without an ultimate end even being conceivable that would lend some kind of sense to the ghastly expenditure — unless it be the annihilation of the entire machinery, the return into the spirit of depravity that invented and hatched it! — It is superfluous to depict in detail what hideous caricatures result when modern hollow heads, without even themselves knowing their dependence on such a conception of life, nonetheless make use of it in order to peddle what lies close to their hearts — their repugnant twaddle about sexuality and eroticism!

Even one who did not see new "dawns" rising, but who shared the opinion of the author of this book that humanity will shortly have played itself out, might, without any gift of prophecy, foretell that this kind of life-philosophical slander of the drives will come to an end even before the end. However quickly, indeed, the spiritual atmosphere of humanity as a whole may fall into decomposition even after the final victory of all destructive powers, it was charged, by the unprecedented volcanic eruption that bears the name "Nietzsche's works," far too violently with the glowing germinal matter of a new doctrine of life for the offspring not to have had to set in already — even if for the present only in the form of a reawakening of [p. 575] reflection upon the world of appearance; and this manner of reflection, notwithstanding the gesticulating press of greedy pettifoggers busy entangling it in formalistic verbal noise, may still, before the iron curtain falls, present us with the beginning of a piece of an entirely new natural science, one far more unlike what has hitherto gone by that name than are the "humane sciences." But what has hitherto been advanced about the drives in relation to a doctrine of appearance stands to the drives themselves rather as, say, the disclosure that water is good for softening legumes by boiling stands to the properties of water! — With regard to our attempt now to open up an approach to the doctrine of appearance from the side of the drives, let it be kept in mind that the unfolding of a doctrine of drives cannot be planned here, at least not at this point, where all that matters is to grasp, with regard to the drive in general, how it comes to take effect in the impulse-experience, and, with regard to the impulse-experience, what purchase it offers to the intervention of spirit and what befalls it through the spiritual deed—

[p. 576]

#### 45. Kapitel — Trieb und Triebantrieb — Chapter 45 — Drive and Drive-Impulse

The concept of drive was formed because impulses could be experienced, and no impulse can be experienced that is not, among other things, an impulse of the body. Whether we say that a horse is being driven on, or that we ourselves feel ourselves inwardly impelled to do something or to leave it undone, we always mean by the word "impulse," and can only mean by it, the occasioning ground of movements. Every impulse is a movement-impulse, and the psychic impulse-experience coincides with the experience of a (now driving, now reining-in) urge to movement. Just as little as something, merely because it is a body, would already have to be capable of experiencing impulses, just as surely could the soul feel no impulses without belonging to a body capable of movement; and just as little, admittedly, as an experienced impulse would always have to work itself out in the movement toward whose realization it presses, just as surely does it actually do so, to the extent that counter-impulses do not cross the process of movement. Instead, therefore, of defining the drive as the abiding foundation of impulse-experiences, we may more briefly call it the vital cause of movement. If, by contrast, mainsprings or "interests" are the abiding basis of the positing of purposes, or, more briefly, causes of will, then we should have sharply separated the vital causes of movement from these, and thereby taken on the task — still paradoxical-seeming today — of explaining without evasion how spirit alters the life-impulse without the addition of a new impulse!

If we seek to gain a deeper insight into the vital cause of movement by placing ourselves within the drive-like impulse-experience, which stands open to us through reflection on our own experience and is readily completed by observation of the behavior of animals, then, according to the most usual account, there are distinguished from one another the two polar and opposed features of its strength or intensity and of its quality or kind, which is in turn further [p. 577] decomposable. The impulse-feeling of thirsting, for example, differs in kind from the impulse-feeling of hungering, but violent thirsting differs, analogously, from faint thirsting just as violent hungering differs from faint hungering, which is why we occasionally equate the impulse-feelings of hungering and thirsting, so wholly different in kind, with respect to their strength. In actuality, strength is only one side of the vital cause of movement, whose other side would be the cause of direction. For the present, however, we shall remain with the opposition of strength and kind.

If we first fix our gaze upon the specific characteristic by itself, it forces itself upon us above all that it can in no way be determined more closely as regards its object, except by indicating those images with which, in the case of fulfillment, the bearer of the impulse would unite in accordance with my impulse, or from which, in accordance with its impulse, it would flee; and from this we see, more sharply than before, why to the pre-conceptual experience of actuality there become visible essential features of images which, measured against concepts, possess a high degree of generality.
