If, for example, *Aristo*teles rightly calls hunger an urge toward union with the dry or the solid, and thirst an urge toward union with the liquid or the moist, then the two quite abstract properties of the dry and the moist appear as mediately underpinned by the difference of goal between two drives. But just as surely as the difference of goal between impulses is marked only by differences in kind of the fulfilling images, just as surely are there no experienceable differences of the images, within the being capable of impulse, that would not go together with a specific modification of the impulses. Thus, for example, within the general specific character of thirsting, which would correspond to the character of the liquid, there separate out precisely as many particular kinds of thirsting as there are liquids differing in image that could quench the thirst of the thirsting being. Thus it is not merely hungering that differs in kind from thirsting, but also the pleasure of drinking water from that of drinking milk or of drinking wine — indeed the pleasure of Bordeaux from that of Rhine wine or Tokay. If we further take into the images their character of distance, to which, to a higher degree, only man responds, then all manner of seemingly merely incidental circumstances can attain any degree of significance whatever for the shaping of the drive, such that someone, for instance, although thirsty, will disdain the water offered him in a cup, which he would eagerly drink from a glass. To

Klages, [p. 578] at this stage, then, the drives of the individual being alone already multiply into the sheerly indeterminate, so that one could easily enumerate hundreds, indeed thousands, of them. The number arrived at would, moreover, have to be raised to a higher power every time one included the modifications of drive that accompany the larger periods of life, and this power would again have to be raised further once different individual beings were taken into account, each of which would have its own particular character and hence also its own peculiarly constituted drives. For humanity in its full unfolding, figures in the millions do not suffice to enumerate all the subspecies of the drives according to the well-distinguishable classes of situations differing in image that might be capable of awakening any of them. Pointing to only a few principal features of the moods of love capable of impulse, within the essential limits merely of the individual human being, is meant to make this a little clearer to us.

To begin with, everyone loves everything he is at all capable of loving, in an ever again different manner in each of the first four seven-year periods of his life, after which, following a longer-lasting evenness, there occurs, with the gradual waning of the sexual component of the drive, once more a considerable change, which is finally followed, in the more or less asexual phase, by a further retuning of the stirrings of love. Further, he loves differently in each single period of his life, when, with the love natural to the object, he loves the father, the mother, the brother, the sister, comrades, the friend, the superior, the subordinate, the fellow-worker, the bearer of rank, the ruler, the people, the son, the daughter, the grandson, the granddaughter, the wife, the beloved, and so on: still far more differently, however, love-tinged things (such as keepsakes), and, entirely differently again, animals, plants, regions (such as the high mountains, the heath, the sea, and so on), one's homeland, one's youth, and so forth — not to speak of wholly non-intuitable objects of love such as vocation, science, art, religion, fatherland, and so on. But even within the sphere merely of the decidedly sexually accented impulses of love, there opens up, for one and the same person within one and the same period of life, a wealth of varieties hard to exhaust. For, quite apart from the fact that, given a rich shaping of drive, she might experience by turns widely divergent processes as bestowing voluptuous pleasure — ordinary mating, touchings and fondlings, visual perceptions of the most manifold kind, active doings as well as sufferings, torments that she might inflict or let be inflicted upon her — her inclination of love toward *one* person will just as certainly differ in kind [p. 579] from her inclination of love toward *another*, as the love-inspiring images of the two differ from one another.

Were we now to pass from the individual bearer of love taken as our basis to another individual bearer of love, we should find, first of all, numerous differences of impulse that accompany every otherness of character in general; we should moreover, without difficulty, even be able to distinguish principal varieties of all loving in the event of a change of sex among the preferred objects of love. If, for instance, we do not doubt that the character-type of woman is partly opposed to the character-type of man, and rightly drew from this the conclusion that the love of the typical man must also be partly opposed to the love of the typical woman, then we should have been just as entitled to infer not merely a fundamental difference of character between the sexes, but, still more, a fundamental difference in their loving from the sexual difference of the objects that stand at the focal point of the inclinations of both. For how could the loving of the woman be one in kind with the loving of the man, when for her it is the image of the man that awakens her strongest inclinations, but for him the image of womanhood! Infallibly, therefore, it means *not* the same thing when the woman says to the man: I love you inexpressibly, as when the man says to the woman: I love you inexpressibly! And the same sentence means something essentially different again in the mouth of the man with respect to a man, and in the mouth of the woman with respect to a woman; and if the loving of the typical man is certainly not like the loving of the typical woman, then the loving of the (strongly predominantly) homosexually excitable man and the loving of the (strongly predominantly) homosexually excitable woman differ widely again from the loving of both. It would be, as goes without saying, fundamentally erroneous — however much it might hold good outwardly for one group of cases — to interpret the state of love of the man-loving-man lover from a corresponding preponderance of feminine properties in his character, because he, as the man that he is, under all circumstances also partakes of the type of masculinity, while she, as the woman that she is, partakes even more unrestrictedly of the type of womanhood — not to speak of the hopeless attempts to think of homosexual love-inclination as having arisen from some (additional) deflections of heterosexual inclination. A Caesar, a Michelangelo, a Shakespeare were more or less capable of homosexual [p. 580] love; and yet in none of the three should we hit upon the notion of positing that measure of feminine admixture from which we would infer and demand the existence of the love-inclination in question, unless we already knew of it! It is a great blunder, in matters concerning the conception of the drives, to take exclusively homosexual eroticism for exactly the same kind of drive as exclusively heterosexual eroticism, which had then — just think of it! — *merely* hopped over, as it were, onto the sexually opposite class of objects; and one has thereby, from the outset, blocked the path of inquiry, by forbidding it to trace the differences of essence, reaching down into the very root-layer, from which alone it could be understood how the arousal-value of the image of the sexual characters came to be, quite simply, reversed. Whoever is able to follow the interconnections of life even a little can have no doubt that for the man dominated by homosexual passions, the *entire* world-*image* must, in one fundamental respect, diverge from the world-image of the heterosexually excitable man.

If, after all this, we cannot help but set up the proposition: as many differences of image among exciting impressions, so many differences of goal in seeking and fleeing — or else: the greater the range of qualities of its needing, the richer, for a being endowed with sense, the world of appearance unfolds — then the task of finding, by means of a few principal and higher concepts, the conscious thread of Ariadne that would lead us not merely into the labyrinth of the drives but also, unharmed and, as we should have to hope, enriched, out of it again, might well appear downright insoluble to us; and we hold it, indeed, in view of the simplifications set forth above with which the sense of utility has afflicted the life of the drives, to be an indispensable requirement that one should have thoroughly grasped the, so to speak, immoderate difficulty of the task in question before so much as thinking of devoting oneself to it. Little as this is to be attempted here, we shall nevertheless not entirely bypass the question whether, through such a multiplication of the subspecies, the concept of species itself does not run the risk of being dissolved.

Here, however, it should first be recalled that *exactly the* *same* abundance, in the domain of intuitive images, has in no way hindered us from dividing and subdividing, however much difficulties of arrangement may often prevail in particular cases. We have formed the specific concept of redness, notwithstanding that the manifold variety [p. 581] of reds is considerable; the specific concept of liquidity, despite the well-nigh unsurveyable differences among the substances that find themselves, at the same temperature, in the liquid state; the specific concept of the dove, notwithstanding extremely numerous subspecies; and it is always *also* certain common features of their appearing by which all the occurrences of one species are distinguished from the occurrences of another species. If, however, we step onto the ground of *pure* species (= qualities) — that is, for instance, of colors — then, as was shown in Volume I, the distinction can be communicated only by our *pointing*, with the help of names for them, to contents of experience that are in and of themselves inconceivable. Where the intuitable content of experience is lacking, or even an entire range of contents of experience — as the seeing of colors is lacking to the born blind, the hearing of noises and sounds to the deaf-mute — we are not in a position, with however many declarative sentences, to call forth a "representation" of the intuitive images meant. The same holds of the qualities of feeling by which we have, for the present, elucidated the drives. However mighty, for example, the effects may be by which a violent passion of love attests itself in the world of appearance, whoever is himself incapable of loving will be instructed neither by this nor otherwise as to what love *is*; and just as the extremely red-blind must forgo the intuition of no small number of color-tones, so too will even the bearer of extremely heterosexual stirrings of love know how to interpret, to some degree, only one side of the feelings of a bearer of extremely homosexual stirrings of love.

If we are thereby reminded to remain conscious of the limits which, in the apprehending and interpreting of the *meaning* of the appearances, the peculiar character of his own nature has set for each of us, then, nevertheless, *within* such limits conceptual delimitations are by no means hopeless — only that they lead us, before we notice it, over to the other side of the stirring of drive, we mean into the movement, to be characterized more closely as to shape and strength, of which the drive, already according to the testimony of its very name, *has* primarily to count as the cause. For it can escape no one that — with reference to our example — in *every* kind of love there lies a being-drawn toward the object of love. Were we now to try, with the help of this, to stake out that species of drive which manifests itself in feelings of love, regardless of their particular kind, it would at once emerge that, in order to indicate, say, how the being-drawn toward the object of love differs from the being-drawn toward food or drink or the exercise of an [p. 582] activity, we should again have to have recourse to *qualities*, by calling to mind how differently we find ourselves "disposed" on the occasion of such various cases of desiring; and the same would hold of the finer differences of our "inclinations" toward different persons. We shall not pursue this further here, but shall state one result of our reflections which — won, so to speak, in passing — may light the way for the investigation to come: there is no specific peculiarity of a feeling in which the peculiarity of a stirring does not share, and no peculiarity of a stirring without a peculiarity of the quality of feeling belonging to it. If, then, we have described more closely the impulse-side peculiar to a mood of life, we have thereby at the same time also contributed to the characterization of the mood in question itself.

We have hitherto considered, so far as possible, the specific constitution of the impulses by themselves. But even had it not already been indicated in advance that this alone does not in any case suffice for characterizing impulse, an obvious consideration might instruct us as to how, in one most important point, it has itself even been given only incompletely. According to the considerations which we offered in earlier chapters on the essence of beholding, beholding proved to rest upon a polarity of experiencing soul and effective image, this polarity in turn consisting in a reciprocal belonging-together of being-estranged and being-connected. Having in the meantime claimed *this same* polarity for the drive-impulse and its goal, we do not fail to recall that, accordingly, the drive-impulse *is connected* with the complementary image and is by no means merely related to the image (in the manner of the relatedness of the personal bearer of life to the purpose posited by the will). But before we consider what follows from this for the development of the impulse, we must ask why being-estranged possesses the form of an impulse and the image the form of a goal! Everything set forth up to this point about the complements of drive by no means lets us recognize wherein there attaches to them the character of goals that allure or are to be fled, and would, were we to content ourselves with it, positively compel us to equate the beholding of images — or, more precisely, the impression-experience, insofar as beholding too has a part in it — completely with the drive-like impulse-experience.

Indeed, a critical reader might urge: for the concept of impulse, or of the vital cause of movement, [p. 583] introduced rather abruptly, the foundation laid in Volume I is quite lacking in compelling premises. Such a reminder would stand justified, and if at some point we must regret that the structure of our book, as well as the subject-matter itself, requires a very long postponement of the discussion of the problem of sensation, it is here, where we are obliged to treat of the impulses, that we must take up a number of unproven propositions, if the inquiry is not to hang in the air. However much the discussion of the impulses may itself contribute something of the utmost importance toward their grounding, gaps are nonetheless unavoidable for as long as it has not been clarified down to the last detail what, within the world of images, the world of bodies is, and how the world of things stands in relation to it — and that can only take place through a characterization of sensing. — Let us, however, provisionally assume that we had already shown how and whereby images are embodied; then it would also have been demonstrated, which is what now matters to us, that in this way the actuality of movements stands out from the actuality of mere happening — movements which the understanding had to try to render tractable to itself with the help of the concepts of spatial as well as temporal distances.

If, in the actuality of *merely* the appearances, there were no corporeality of the appearances and therefore also no appearance of movement, but solely the phenomenon of transformation, then it suffices to place oneself within an actuality of bodies in order at once to hold the appearance of movement to be unavoidable as well. If, in other words, the soul is embodied, so that bodily processes henceforth take part in its experience, there would now be no experience that would not, among other things, be an impulse undergone. If we replace "embodied soul" with "individual soul," or more briefly with "individual," or finally, in German usage, with "self-being," then we have, it seems, the warrant to examine every experience of any self-being whatever as to what it is as an impulse suffered, and what follows from it for the shaping of experience . Thereupon we turn to the particular kind of con-<sup>5</sup> nection between soul and image in the experience of impulse.

<sup>5</sup> On page 583. — We do not yet have at our disposal here the conceptual equipment that would be needed to limit the general validity of this proposition in such a way as to leave room for an important class of exceptional cases, and therefore add only this one thing: that we have in mind such proper essences whose corporeality at the same time contains the conditions for the experiencing of another's corporeality, or, more briefly, that we have in mind proper essences capable of sensation.

In the state of sheerly psychic beholding, estrangement and connectedness of soul and image stand in equilibrium. Were the soul not to experience the image as something alien to it, it could not experience an image at all; and were it not connected with the image, that would be the end of its experiencing. If, by contrast, we clothe both image and soul with corporeality, [p. 584] then, as regards essence, what remains as it was is the being-estranged, whereas the connectedness appears to us essentially altered. Because, where a body is, no other body is, the embodied image seems to us so severed from the body of the experiencing soul that we now, indeed, grasp the estrangement fully for the first time, but can scarcely any longer comprehend how, then, anything is still connected at all. Solely for the sake of vividness we shall, in what follows, always illustrate by means of seeking drives the guiding proposition, to be formulated thus in the manner of a theorem: both the connectedness and, equally, the incompleteness of the connectedness now show themselves in the fact that from the image there proceeds a pull which acts, in the embodied soul, as an impulse to carry out movements with the goal of touching, or even of incorporating, the embodied image.

To clarify the state of affairs from within, we suitably take our start not from stirrings that first awaken on the occasion of the perception of a possible goal of drive, but from such stirrings as induce the bearer of the impulse to seek out the fulfilling goal. If we ask, then, what it actually is that moves a man or an animal, in the state of thirsting, to seek water, no answer whatever will be forthcoming to us, unless we resolve to declare that there acts within him the *image* of water, in the form of a pull toward water. If the physiologist, say, describes to us with however great a precision the chemical processes that accompany thirsting in the bearer of the impulse, he has not thereby brought us in the least closer to the experience of thirst; and if the theorist of sensation who follows him dissects for us with however great a precision the internal bodily (visceral) sensations of which thirsting is supposed to consist, he has still not betrayed to us by a single syllable how the disjointed sum-total of internal bodily impressions goes about causing movements that fall precisely upon the finding of water! We can therefore in no way get around the assumption of a pull that proceeds from the image of water. The image thus acting in the soul can be phantasied (= dreamed) by the animal, and moreover, in man, further represented (= thought); but such consequences, accruing psychically or even spiritually, presuppose the acting pull, which for its part can occur entirely without them.

Should someone here, out of intellectualist prejudice, raise the question how, then, an image of water can lie within the impulse of thirsting, if one strikes from the soul of the thirsting being not merely the thought of [p. 585] water but even the water-phantasm, we would first pose the counter-question how he proposes to set about giving us the state of affairs of thirsting without taking up into it that toward which thirsting, as its fulfillment, *aims*. Should he reply that, precisely because he assents to this, he sees himself compelled to assume that a phantasm of water necessarily hovers before the thirsting being, then some tens of thousands of examples of stirrings of drive would readily stand at our disposal, with respect to which not even the possibility of such phantasms could be imagined, even for the "higher" animals, not to speak of the "lower" animals such as insects or even infusoria. Is one to make a phantasm of purposiveness responsible for the doings of the polyp, which, in a state of hunger and lack of food, repositions its tentacles every two minutes, though it otherwise lets them hang idly? Does the octopus know the structure of the crab, from which, with its suckers, it conducts the least protected hind side to its mouth? What a treasure of visionary phantasms should we have to attribute to the ants that breed aphids, if we wished to understand from insight why, in spring, they drag the larvae with the utmost care to the roots of the grain, where they find the food most suited to them! What phantasms could it be that prompted the *young* nightingales, starlings, and hoopoes to set out in autumn, without a guide, for Africa, although they have never before been in the south? And would the chick of the moorhen, still within the egg, already have phantasms, because it instantly stops hammering at the shell the moment the hen utters a warning call? If, finally, one takes into account the artfulness — well-nigh passing all conception — of the provisions that countless animals, and above all insects, make, with the most exact adaptation to their conditions of growth, for a brood not yet even in existence, one will for once be cured of confusing the goal-determinateness of the drive-impulse with phantasms of the goal, or even with the thought of the goal.

Calling to mind the 23rd chapter, where kindred examples were already offered, we would have to reply to the exponent of such and similar objections that he had indeed heard it but not taken it in — which is indeed what is most utterly alien to present-day thinking in our manner of conceiving, namely that we hold the images to be something *actual*, more precisely the weaving power of all actuality, just as actual as, on the plane of facts, physical forces, and that we may compare the pull that goes forth from the [p. 586] image to, say, the pull of the magnet on iron filings. He had further heard it and yet not taken it in, that we cannot help calling the images, in and of themselves admittedly non-intuitive, "images" nonetheless, because they are meant to designate, in the actual, that constitution by virtue of which it *appears* in intuitive images. And he would finally not have sufficiently considered why, without the presupposition of an inconceivable actuality of the images, the conceivable things together with their likewise conceivable properties would *not* be able to appear at all. Since, however, as we have learned, the images necessarily live and are thus, in everything that we can distinguish in them by indicative (not conceiving judgements, an expression of liv ing essences, it is in principle a matter of indifference whether one prefers to say that in the thirsty one there is at work the pull of the image of the liquid, or to say that in him there is at work the pull of the essence of water, the essence of liquidity.

Even though the deeply learned philosophy of Romanticism, owing to a devout mind gone astray, was not spared from confusing spirit and soul again and again, and therefore could not work out the doctrine of the actuality of the images, it nevertheless courted, with imperfect formulas, a conception of the drive that stands at least close to our own, and has left us splendid precipitates of a thinking that tried to understand drive and drive-goal from the belonging-together of two poles within the frame of an organism spanning both. By literal reproduction of some passages dealing with this, in which the reader will easily himself sort out what diverges, we hope not only to support his confidence in the manner of consideration still unfamiliar to him, but above all to make our own guiding thought shine forth the more brightly in the today inimitable light that it receives from the means of expression of an already bygone age.

The drive to sense the world, says *Passavant* in his "Untersuchungen über den Lebensmagnetismus und das Hellsehen" (1837), "the drive toward world-consciousness is itself only an utterance of the most general drive, the drive to complete oneself" (50). "The drive and its object relate as two complementary poles. If the North Pole of the earth had a sensation of magnetism, it would have to have an intimation of the South Pole. If a man who had never seen green fixed his gaze on a red wall and thereupon saw a white surface, he would see green through the [p. 587] inner activity of his eye and thus have a representation of this *colour* before he *had* observed it in external nature. . ." Likewise "desire arouses the representation of its complement. This representation is an intimation, until it becomes experience through the finding of the desired object" (55). The *Trevi*ranus whom he cites calls instinct the "productive power of imagination," according to which, upon perceiving or scenting food, the animal is moved in its own way and gains an intimation14 "that the object.. is the means to the quenching of thirst and hunger.." (54). — "The individual thing," says Schubert in his "Geschichte der Seele" (1833), "does not exist for its own sake; it exists for the sake of the other things, lives and dies for the sake of a higher whole" (76). "That physis or nature in which antiquity recognized the formative soul of plant and animal is itself only a harmonious co-becoming of every single essence with the becoming of all. Just as the self-active indwelling life of the individual thing generates for itself its corporeality, the passively receiving (feminine) matter, so the other lives of the universe co-beget *as well*. ." (77). "So too is that instinct, marvelous in its manifestations and movements, which leads the bee over hill and dale to its food in the flowering linden tree.. the movement of a general life working through all that is akin to it.. The taking of food by the animal kingdom resembles, in its relation to the whole, the absorption and excretion of fluids in a living animal body through the vessels appointed for this purpose; each animal species thereby represents, on a large scale, another web of absorbing vessels made expressly for absorption into this part and structure" (106—107). —<sup>6</sup>

<sup>6</sup> On page 587. — *Cuvier*, who, together with Geoffroy St. Hilaire, Burdach, Kielmeyer, Meckel, Carus, von Baer, belongs entirely to the romantic phase of research, or, if one prefers, the Goethean phase, wrote literally in 1836: „One can form no clear conception of instinct except by admitting the assumption that animals have, in their sensorium, innate and fixed *images* (images) or impressions (sensations) that determine them to act; it is a kind of *dream or vision* (de rêve, de vision) that constantly pursues them, and one may regard them, in everything that pertains to their instinct, as *somnambulists*." We know of no researcher who has gained a deeper insight into the essence of instinct than Cuvier does with this sentence, and none who has voiced the insight so gained more aptly. Only the not-quite-fitting word „sensation" betrays a residue of dependence on sensualism. If one compares this with what the subsequent phase of biology, which one may briefly call the Darwinian phase, had to bring forward concerning the phenomenon of so-called instinct, one must concede that what is at issue here is not so much a different mode of thought as rather a regression and relapse into those mechanistic conceptions that Romanticism had refuted in principle. To forestall misunderstanding, let it be added: the humanly most sympathetic *Darwin* was, notwithstanding this, a great researcher, to whom science owes a quite considerable extension of its factual knowledge and, through it, important stimuli; only his research unfortunately stood under the pressure of an eclipse of thought which today we must unreservedly call an *aberration*. That is why his *explanations* are, for the greatest part, simply false.

Let us return to the matter itself, we mean to the peculiar pull with which the image of water or the essence of water acts in the soul of the thirsty one: here the mere acknowledgment of its presence obviously already includes the proof of the existence of a bond between the water-image and the thirsting soul, whereas we hold further clarification to be needed as to why the separateness that results from the fact that drinkable liquid and thirsting essence are two different *bodies* should take the form of a pull from the one toward the other. Could such a pull, one might ask, not arise in a bodiless soul, supposing there were such a thing? It would, the answer runs, be impossible for it to occur in such a soul, because it would also be a placeless soul [p. 588], for which, therefore, between it and the image with which it was momentarily bound up, there would never obtain any distance. Let us assume experimentally that such a soul could, for the fraction of a second, tear itself out of its sinking into the stream of images, and would now long for images that had escaped it — then it would be, in an unthinkably small instant, at the place of its longing, just as we ourselves are at all times, but only "in thought," and sometimes indeed even actually, but only in dream; whereupon, as everyone sees, the pull, scarcely begun to arise, would already have dissolved again! The consideration of this contrary case gives us the key to the origin of the pull.

Thanks to its being bound up with it, the essence of liquidity acts in the soul of the thirsty one, notwithstanding that the matter of the liquid and the thirsty one are at two different places. Were both to be experienced by the soul in the same life-process — the essence of liquidity and the separateness of its body from the matter of the liquid — its being bound up with the image would thereby be found disturbed, and it would seem intelligible that the disturbance be removed and the balance restored through the elimination of the intervening space between the bodies. Because this space is in fact traversed by the thirsting essence, we understand the impulse that moves it thereto from a pull exercised on its soul by the essence of water; of which language, too, gives report, with turns of phrase such as: one feels drawn to something, or attracted *by* something. We underline the seriousness of our attempt at interpretation with the jest that a Schopenhauerian or other world-will, which an unregenerate soul might even now wish to smuggle in, would henceforth, with respect to thirsting, lie in the quasi-wish of the water to be drunk by the thirsty, with respect to hungering, say, of the cows, in the quasi-wish of the grass to be eaten by cows, or of the tiger — to say nothing of the arch-murderer, man! — in the wish of the sheep, calves, zebras to be destroyed by tigers! Should this remark not contribute, precisely, to convincing us of the existence of so peculiar a world-will, then let us at least hope it will all the more cast a light upon the abysmal difference between active impulse of will and pathic drive-impulse, and then also upon the abysmal difference of the millionfold pole-tensions crisscrossing the universe, on which, among other things, the being-driven of organisms rests, from the "vile urge of will" which Schopenhauer, as rightly [p. 589] lamented, as he wrongly fantasized into the world beyond man.

We have just now offered a kind of metaphysical grounding for the pulling force of images. But, one might ask, does the pull in question therefore lie in the experience of impulse itself? If a four-year-old child grasps "impulsively" at the "enticing" apples before it on the table, in order, without reflection, to bring the thickest and reddest to its mouth and bite into it, one may well say that it succumbed to a pull that went from the image of the apples to its soul; only, as readily as we express it in speech, that someone let himself be enticed, seduced, carried away, so do we tacitly think each time of a longing, a desire that comes to meet the enticement out of the person himself, and thereby seem indeed to testify that the experience of impulse contains at least something else besides a pull suffered as though from outside! — Now, even that would not yet be saying enough. The phenomenological investigation ought, strictly speaking, never to have begun at all with the pull in question, because it externalizes in explanation what, considered without a side-glance at itself, would be just as inward a state of affairs as, say, the state of affairs of beholding. However, the metaphysical preliminary discussion not only eases for us the discovery of the pertinent quality of experience, but also offers the advantage of presenting to us at once, in the light of an inner necessity, what is to be found. For we need only think of the disturbedness of the beingbound-up of soul and image, to find it plausible that, for instance, there should inhere in thirsting, as immediately experienced, a specifically peculiar suffering of lack. But just as thirsting cannot be thought without a co-experienced suffering of lack, so in general there is no desiring or longing that would not, during its occurring, be, *among* other things, a suffering of lack, a privation, a need. By the feeling of privation or feeling of lack or feeling of need we designate, in the specific character of the drive-impulse itself, what has been added to the experienced being-bound-up with the fulfilling goal of the drive in the soul of the individual essence, whenever the total experience has the form of an impulse. Let one more passage from *Schubert* show us how Romanticism drew, precisely from the insight just set forth, the courage to work out the thought of polarity in almost hymnic turns of phrase.

"There exists, itself, the life and essence of the soul, no less than [p. 590] the life and thriving of the body through the mere breathing of air, only through communion with a complement that fills out the lack of the single thing, and which has its beginning and its outgoing in the invisible order of things. I see the movement of the one pole of the iron magnet toward the north, that of the opposite pole toward the south; but the complementary other, the movement of the invisible current in which the one pole as much as the other is immersed, I do not perceive. I see, around the weakest and most helpless in visibility, around the forsaken and orphaned, the strongest forces busy; the most wretched and witless worm is preserved by the mightiest and most far-seeing instinct from threatening dangers and led to the help it needs; what my own defective eye sees is only the lack; the help that is to make up for this I do not see. The series of visible forms I recognize, but not the invisible bond on which they hang like pearls on a thread. . . But were it, in the end, even only the lack that my eye.. were to perceive, then even this would already be a worthy object of cognition. Without it, the lack, without the longing for the quickening influence, there would be as little a life present as, without a need of the lungs for breathing, a movement of the blood and the limbs. And this is the ground of all the manifoldness and multiplicity of visible as of invisible creation. Through the fact that, in every single essence, alongside the fullness a lack is found, a something that it has become, and a "much" that it has not become, thereby does the single thing join itself, as a living member, to a whole that is through and through filled with the forces of life. For that which is lack in the single essence is the vessel into which the forces of life flow in; the fullness is that whereby it becomes this particular member, indeed a particular single body in the midst of the greater whole."<sup>7</sup>

<sup>7</sup> On page 590. — If one wants far more astonishing examples of the extra-rational sureness of aim of instincts, one must consider certain provisions made, especially by insects, for their future brood. We give, from *Lloyd* *Morgan*'s book on „Instinct and Habit," the following description of the behaviour of the yucca moth: „The straw-coloured, silvery-shimmering creatures slip out of their pupal cases as soon as the large, yellowish-white, bellshaped blossoms of the yucca — each open for a single night only — unfold. From the anthers of one of these blossoms the female moth now gathers the pollen and kneads this sticky substance into a small ball, which she holds fast beneath her head with her greatly enlarged, bristly palps. Thus laden, she flies off and seeks a second flower. As soon as she has found one, she slits, with the sharp edges of her ovipositor, the tissue at the pistil of the flower and lays her own eggs among the plant's ovules, whereupon she hastens quickly up to the stigma of the style and stuffs the fertilizing little ball of pollen into its funnel-shaped opening. — Now these visits of the moth are indispensable for the plant. It has been demonstrated by experiment that without the mediation of the insects no pollen reaches the stigma, and the plant's ovules accordingly remain unfertilized; and the fertilization of these ovules is in turn indispensable for the larvae that creep out of the insect's eggs in four or five days. It has been established that the larvae feed exclusively on the ovules while these are developing, and would therefore wither if the fertilization of the latter failed to occur. Each single larva now consumes about 20 ovules, and three or four larvae usually come to occupy one flower. The plant's ovary, however, contains about 200 ovules. If we assume, then, that roughly 100 ovules are sacrificed to the moth larvae, there still remain 100 which, solely through the moth's cooperation, attain fertilization and maturity. — This wonderfully adapted instinctive activity of the yucca moth is performed once in its entire life, and this without any instruction, without opportunity to see or imitate it in others, indeed, so far as we can see, without the insect having any inkling of the significance of its actions." (Quoted after: *Carl Haeberlin*, Ärztliche Seelenkunde, pp. 36—37, Barth, Leipzig.)

Before we go further, it seems fitting to commend to the most exact attention two consequences of what has been set forth. No genuine drive-impulse can be experienced in respect of which the co-experienced suffering of lack would not be a suffering of lack in something definite. Thirsting is a need for drink, hungering a need for food, and neither of the two is a need pure and simple. Drive-impulses are never mere intensities or strengths like physical energy, but always directed intensities, even though, as we shall presently convince ourselves, in an essentially different sense than physical [p. 591] vectors. With this we have referred back to the substrates of experience what was above said of the experiences themselves, when we were compelled to establish that to every mood there clings the peculiarity of a particular shape of impulse, to every shape of impulse the peculiarity of a mood. — But just as little as a need is found that would not be a specifically determined need, just as little does there lie in the state of affairs of needing, as such, any indication of what is lacked. Only in accordance with the specific determinateness of what is lacked does a vital feeling of privation occur; but it is a privation not for the sake of the specific peculiarity of what is lacked, but out of a co-experienced separateness from the place of what is lacked!

Accordingly, however, privation, although belonging to the specificity of the impulse, forms the transition to the intensity of the impulse, being in fact intensified along with it. For does it not amount to the same thing to say "strong hungering" as "strong need for food," "weak thirsting" as "weak need for drink"! If we ask whether perhaps the strength of the impulse necessarily coincides with the intensity of the privation, it does not even require an entering into the inwardness of the states of affairs meant, to suggest the mistakenness of such a conjecture. In respect of the circumstance that it is the images from which the pull upon the soul is exercised, receptiveness for it signifies depth of lived experience; in respect of the circumstance that it is only out of the separateness of the bodies that the efficacy of the images becomes a pull, receptiveness for it signifies *disturbability* of lived experience. By virtue of the former the power of the images would announce itself, by virtue of the latter the need, and the intensifications of both would be as little to be confused with one another as the judgement "it entices me powerfully" with the judgement "I feel the lack of it keenly"! Whoever, standing on a rocky cliff, in the face of the surf thundering around it, has ever felt the innermost urge to hurl himself in with outstretched arms, to be dashed to pieces, given up to it, will hardly be inclined to hold a feeling of privation equally responsible for the impulse to do so, as he would for the greedy seizing of the water jug after many hours' wandering over a well-less steppe! Let us keep before our eyes what myths, legends, and fairy tales tirelessly know how to tell of — the enticement of images as siren-song, Lorelei's lament, nixie-magic, as the flute-wonder of a magic rat-catcher, as the sorcery of a fiddle compelling to dance, as the demonically fettering dreamapparition (for instance of the beautiful [p. 592] princess for whom, in every realm of the earth, the fettered prince seeks the archetype), as the mysteriously spellbinding stone that binds whoever beholds it (as, say, in Hebbel's "Rubin") — then we recognize in the image-originatedness of the pull the occasioning ground of creations of popular fantasy as splendid as they are persuasive, and shall feel ourselves fully moved, only then, to distinguish, within its possible strength, what stems from depth of lived experience and what from mere suffering of lack.

Unmistakably, however, it is precisely the magnitude of the suffering of lack that is above all held capable of intensification and is thereby apt to be brought into such proximity to the strength of the impulse, that the further question arises whether it does not perhaps designate a pure intensity, in relation to which alone the enticement of the image would constitute the specific character of the impulse. To this it would have to be answered that both constitutive features, the enticement of the image and one's own need, would leave even the pull into which they merge in the condition of a mere how-constitution of the lived experience, peculiarly mixed of the conflicting colours of the sweet far-feeling of union and the bitter near-feeling of privation, did not the experience of separateness, as co-experienced, enclose within it any obstacles to union whatever. We know of strength of impulse, and can know of it only insofar as the experienced pull of the goal necessarily signifies an experienced counter-pressure against whatever in any way separates from the pulling goal. We need not delve into the riddle of intensifiability in order nevertheless already to see why it is the counter-pressure, and only the counter-pressure, that must appear to us in the light of a magnitude exclusively. For while what, in the impulse, drives *toward* a goal — indifferently whether out of overaccentuated enticement or out of overaccentuated privation — we can also specifically characterize by means of the particularity of the goal, we should, with the impulse simply directed *against* something, hope just as vainly to discover the fulfilling image, in order to read off from it a how-constitution of the process, as to read someone's meaning from the statements of one who would answer *every* question about it with No, thus contesting assertion together with its contradictory counter-assertion!

On the presupposition of the embodiedness of the soul, then, the life-process would present, besides the side of sense-impression, the side of impulse, in which its specificity would stand out against its strength — the former flowing together out of the pull of the image and the suffering of lack of the recipient of the image, the latter intensifiable with the depth of the beholding as with the magnitude of the [p. 593] privation, in the measure of the counter-pressure against obstacles to the realization of the impulse. Now, however, with the capacity for sensing corporeality, the experience of impression is also given, and every impression brings with it modulations of stirring. We will call these reactive drive-impulses, in contrast to the body-originated ones we have hitherto considered. If we bear in mind that impression-images possess a character of presentness, we can distinguish impression and impulse as follows: in the *im*pression the intuitive appearance of the present is at work; in the impulse, the non-intuitive pull of an image not present. But how is it when the impulse is awakened by the intuitively present image, for instance thirsting at the sight of water? Now, the sight of water need not awaken the craving to drink it; but if it does, then those impressions that would correspond to the presentness of the goal — that is to say, those bound up with the drinking of water — are far different from the mere sighting or scenting of the water! There are, then, not two classes of drive-impulses, and in following the non-intuitive pull of images not present, the merely reactive stirring agrees with the body-originated one. In respect of what, then, do we distinguish the two? The most obvious answer — that only reactive impulses occur upon impressions, as the very name "reactive" already lets shine through — leads, however, unawares beyond itself and into a territory of wholly new considerations scarcely yet to be entered here.

Without deciding the question whether spontaneous stirrings of drive can occur entirely without inner-bodily impressions, we hold ourselves exclusively to such as are of the type of hungering or thirsting, whose co-existence with inner-bodily impressions admits of no doubt, and thus arrive, for the time being, at the curious result that in the spontaneous drive-impulse the non-intuitive pull of the not-present image likewise acts by means of impressions — though, to be sure, of inner-bodily impressions that have, if not exactly an intuitive, then at least a character of presentness; in accordance with which we should have to determine the difference between the impulse already, for that reason, called body-originated, and the reactive stirring, to the effect that the latter takes place on the occasion of outer impressions, the former on the occasion of inner ones. Since, however, possibly all, and in any case broad groups of, outer impressions — such as tactile impressions, warmth-impressions, cold-impressions, taste-impressions, strong smells — are likewise accompanied by sensible [p. 594] transformations of the sensing body, the non-intuitive pull of the images would in both cases be found dependent on inner-bodily impressions, even though, to be sure, only those among them that had reactive stirrings as their consequence would have been occasioned by intuitive images. This question, not to be pursued further here for now, may serve us to sharpen our eye a little for the polarity of soul and body, which, for the sake of a survey, may be done point by point. 1. The embodied soul experiences images not immediately, but mediated through impressions. 2. Of the impressions, always in some way inner-bodily, many at the same time serve to communicate outer impressions. 3. With all impressions, impulses go along; according to which, under "embodied soul," must be understood the capacity to receive impressions as well as impulses alike. 4. Whereas we had ascertained the acting counter-pole of the ever-suffering soul in the images, we have now ascertained the acting counter-pole of the suffering of the embodied soul in the living body, which thus, in relation to the images that are no less active on that account, plays the role of the transmitter of their effects. 5. We speak of impressions as such with regard to the overaccentuated intuitiveness of ⦅outer⦆ impressions, and are wont thereby to disregard the impulses likewise bound up with them, to just the degree that these recede behind the former. We speak of impulses as such with regard to the absence of outer impressions, and are wont thereby to disregard the inner-bodily impressions likewise bound up with such impulses, to just the degree that these recede behind the pull of the image.

The foregoing considerations have provided us with a disclosure of great importance. For had we, after all, held it intelligible that the soul should be a capacity for suffering, there would still, in any case, have been the legitimate question of doubt, how mere images should set about exercising effects. Now we have recognized the immediate counter-pole of the soul's suffering in the working of the body belonging to it, though with the addition that it thereby transmits the pull of the images. In this way, to be sure, the soul would be the counter-pole on the one hand to the body of the soul, and on the other to the image, and we should have to give an account [p. 595] of what connection obtains between the working of the body and the pull of the images. But although we must still forgo this here, the mere indication of the fact of the connection in question already suffices to lead us back from the pull of the images to the bodily urge to movement, from which alone, understandably, can develop the sequence of movements that finally brings the bearer of the impulse to the goal that completes its impulse. From this, and only from this, does it now become evident wherein the vital cause of movement differs in principle from the so-called mechanical cause of movement, and that the former can only be determined with reference to an experiencing and thus an ensouled corporeality. For the piece of lime which, as they say, falls from the ceiling to the floor of the room as a consequence of the earth's attraction, the lying on the floor was not, say, the cause of the fall; for the movable compass-needle, which changes its direction as a consequence of a magnetic disturbance, the new position is not the cause of its deflection; whereas for the animal which, because it is thirsty, performs countless movements until it finds drinking water somewhere, the drinking of water is really the vital cause of those movements; for even the most hardened mechanist will have to admit that no consideration of a body as merely a thing movable by pressure or impact or pull would ever enable us to discover such a cause, indeed even so much as to speak of it meaningfully! Only by the interpolation of an experiencing are we in a position to posit the cause of movements in a state of affairs that, at the moment of the beginning of the movement, as well as throughout its entire course up until immediately before its ending, is ⦅not at all⦆ yet present, and only from the goal-determinateness of suffered impulses do we read off causes of this kind. Had physics not, for another purpose, laid claim to the expression "living force," we might be permitted to call drives "living forces," and would have to seek their livingness, in distinction from mechanical forces, in the fact that they are goal-directedly working forces and thus ensouled forces. "Direction" in the sense of physics is never anything other than an — angle; "direction" in the sense of the science of life, however, means the conditionedness of the course of movement by the goal of movement.

However certain it now is that we have thereby made a future event, for instance the drinking of water, into the occasioning ground of a present event, for instance a translatory movement of seeking, and indeed must, among [p. 596] other things, seek therein the sense of the difference of drive-impulse from mechanical impulse, just as certain it is, however, that the reference — already shown in advance — to the unconsciousness of drive-impulses suffices to ward off the thought that the bearer of the impulse is related to the future; for which, indeed, a knowledge of the course of objective time would be required. The direction of every movement, thus also of the movement that owes its origination to a drive-impulse, is direction in space, and the vital time that thereby comes into play signifies not a measurable distance of the now from the later, but the generative ground of what we, objectifyingly, call the future.

Yet it is advisable to draw the boundaries of the concept of drive somewhat more sharply. Just as in physics the word acceleration means three things — increase of speed, decrease of speed, and change of direction — so too can a drive-impulse increase the speed of a movement, that is, convert the state of rest into that of movement, or diminish it, that is, convert the state of movement into that of rest, or finally change the direction of the movement. If I show my dog a piece of meat, he jumps and snaps at it; if I hold my cat out of the window as though I meant to let her fall, she claws fast to my sleeve, thus instinctively seeking to prevent the threatening fall-movement. Furthermore, drive-governed movements need not necessarily turn out translatory. The impulse that causes a bird to utter enticing calls has produced movements, but not translatory ones. Drive-governed colour-change or drive-governed emanations of scent, finally, would indeed require a slight modification of the wording of the conceptual determination, but change nothing in its fundamental content, wherefore we leave them aside here. — Further, one must not overlook that not only movement toward something, but also movement away from something, falls under goal-determined movements, insofar as the tendency to avoidance belongs among their originating causes. Were the lime to fall aslant from the ceiling because there were, plumb beneath it on the floor, a black spot that was disagreeable to it, it would have executed a genuine goal-movement, and we should have to hold it to be living. So when certain amoebae evade the cone of light in the water, or, put in the phrase as learned as it is misleading, are "negatively phototropic," they are possessed of living impulses, and it would not first have to be proved to us that they can be habituated to the light, did the correct apprehension of the state of affairs not still always meet with the extravagances of passionate mechanists [p. 597]. With this it is already stated that the "pull of the images," too, can carry opposite signs. For every individual essence, the actuality of the images that is experienceable by it is stretched between the poles of the appearance of alien essences violently attracting and of alien essences violently repelling, and the obverse of its drives of longing for images of life are formed by its drives of fear before images of death.

Having assured ourselves of the essential difference of physical forces from drives, we may also call to mind the analogies that exist between the two, for the reason that essential elements were unwittingly borrowed from drive-impulse for the purpose of forming basic physical concepts, some of which shall occupy us later. Exactly as, in the working of physical forces, a continual exchange of "potential" against "kinetic" energy and vice versa takes place, so exactly, in the development of drive-impulse, a continual exchange of states of tension against processes of movement. For if a thirsting animal feels itself impelled to seek water, it cannot help but receive, from the impressions of its respective surroundings, impulses that stand in opposition to the body-originated impulse and accordingly call forth a state of tension, which is resolved in the measure of the approach to, say, scented water, so as to make way for an intensified goal-directedness of the movement-processes. As already intimated above, the same state of tension would, in principle, obtain, only unequally weaker, at the awakening of thirst in the presence of attainable water, and it would intensify to the point of unbearableness were the sighting or scenting of water, unattainable either owing to mechanical obstacles (for instance a grating) or owing to body-originated counter-impulses (for instance violent fear of approaching the place of the goal), to accompany body-originated thirsting. Further: just as the drive-force, because goal-conditioned, appears, in respect of objective time, as the generative ground of a future state of affairs, so one ⦅measures⦆ physical force by the speed that it adds to the state of movement of a body — which is to say, with the help of the stretches of space that the body will, in consequence, first come to traverse. But this shall be treated more fully in the 51st Chapter. — Every stilling of a drive brings about a state that, in relation [p. 598] to the state of the suffering of lack, grounds an opposite impulse-constitution; wherefore the concept of the momentary inefficacy of a drive can always be exchanged for the concept of the efficacy of a drive of another kind. A highly oversatiated person, for instance, can be so disgusted by the powerful smell of a roast that he hastily leaves the range of diffusion of a smell that, had he hunger, would make the water run in his mouth. — The exact examination of the development of impulse would acquaint us with a great manifoldness of the properties of drive-life, of which, however, only one more may not be passed over here.

When a person or animal has quenched his thirst, then, within the time of day of his waking, after intervals never indeed mathematically equal, but yet nearly equal to one another — thus now somewhat shorter, now somewhat longer — body-originated thirst appears anew, in consequence of a rhythmic alternation of all the states of life, whereby a pulsing of the universal happening manifests itself in the essence living its own life. Even when unstilled, thirst will, in accordance with such a rhythm, vanish, in order, after only shorter intervals, and then at first ever more violently, to return. And so, indeed, it goes with all body-originated drives without exception, among them also such whose periodic alternation can no longer be determined by days, but only by moons and seasons; one thinks of the pairing of birds in spring, of the rutting seasons of animals in general, of the change of coat at the onset of the colder season, of the twofold change of abode of migratory birds in the year, of the winter sleep of many animals, and so on.

We conclude by drawing together the main points of what we have ascertained, through investigation of drive-impulses, about the constitution of the life of drives: I. In the drive-impulse, the effective pull of essences capable of appearance is experienced, and the thereby necessarily occurring urge to movement receives its direction from images each time polar to the drive. II. In the drive-impulse two sides of the same state of affairs are formed: the body-originated neediness (vis a tergo) and the stilling-promising image (vis a fronte), and the movement toward the latter thus develops of itself out of the former. III. In the ⦅strength⦆ of the drive-impulse, taken absolutely, magnitude of need and depth of beholding are fused with one another into a counter-pressure [p. 599] against everything that in any way hinders union with the complementary image. IV. In accordance with the pulsing of world-happening, the drive is subject to a rhythm of waxing and waning, which the experience of impulse follows with the utmost exactness. V. There are only essences with a plurality of drives, none with only a single drive. The manifoldness of distinguishable drives is in each case equal to the manifoldness of specifically distinguishable states of privation, which are, in their turn, again equal to the specific manifoldness of pull-exercising images.

[p. 600]

#### 46. Kapitel — Trieb und Willensantrieb — Chapter 46 — Drive and Impulse of Will

Against the thesis put forward as a doctrinal premise, that in the moment of passage through the act-bearing boundary-quality, experience stands now under the guidance of impression, now under the guidance of impulse, it could unquestionably and rightly have been objected that the boundary-quality in question, inferred from the character of presentness of the impression, offers not the least handle for supporting the impulse as distinct from the impression. Now, however, we know that the character of presentness attaches also to those inner-bodily impressions that form, so to speak, the reverse side of the drive-impulse, and we find it without difficulty, notwithstanding the presentifying power of the turning-points, to keep impression and impulse apart. The boundaryprocess is called impression to the extent of the preponderance of the intuitive appearance over the pull of the images, and it is called impulse to the extent of the predominance of their pull over the intuitive appearance. The act of apprehension always strikes, immediately, the intuitive appearance, while the only weakly intuitive inner impressions escape it in the measure of the predominance of the non-intuitive pull of the images.

Because it is the impression, mediated by the movement of the soul, to which the I reacts with a splitting deed in the original act of apprehension, we have described the result of the splitting by the transformation of the impression, and inferred therefrom what transformation the movement of the soul thereby undergoes. If, on the other hand, it is an impulse, taking place through participation in the happening (= pull of the images), to which the I reacts with a splitting deed in the act of will, then we must now describe the result of the splitting with the help of the transformation that an ⦅impulse⦆ undergoes from the immediate counter-working of spirit. If we compare the working actuality — whose happening-side may be called, for short, the happening, and whose image-side the specificity of the happening — with the product [p. 601] of the original act of apprehension, the thing, then, in place of the moment of actuality, there has stepped a being, or, that is, in place of actuality itself, being — for which purpose, from the experiential content of being-actual, both the happening and the specificity of the happening had to be detached. Nevertheless, only a little more exact consideration of the thing shows us at once that the being of the how, i.e., the specific property, stands in a different and more intimate relation to it than the being of the happening, i.e., the duration. For while duration belongs merely to the existence of the thing, the properties belong to the thing itself, so much so, indeed, that it may be called the sum of its properties. Through the finding act, then, the happening-side of actuality is simply split off from it, and its appearance is, through it, merely transformed — though, to be sure, transformed down to the root. Whereas, then, the finding of the thing without question presupposes a detachedness of the finder both from the happening and from the specificity of the happening, it is only the detachedness from the happening that has the character of a being-torn-out of it, while the detachedness from the appearance has, by contrast, only that of a being-beside it, and indeed in accordance with the process of presentification that, as was shown, immediately makes the finding act possible. Now the positing of the purpose, too, requires both: detachedness of the willing one both from the happening and from the specificity of the happening. Since it is now, however, the impulse that, so to speak, supplies the material on which the intervention of spirit is directed, the specificity of the happening is simply split off, while its effective pull remains present, transformed — though, to be sure, transformed down to the root. The appearance of actuality was transformed, through the act of apprehension, into a beproperty-ed being. Into what is transformed, and must be transformed, the happening of actuality, through the act of will?

Could mere drive-impulses be split, we should have the answer, in that we should take away from the drive-impulse its specific characteristic, so as to leave over only its strength; for then the drive-impulse would be found detached in the shape of a goal-undetermined urge to movement, which could in each case only be characterized further by ⦅degrees of⦆ difference in experienced resistances. But there is now just as little a wholly directionless urge to movement, as it would be possible for purely animal drive-impulses to be split immediately, and even the so-called naked will will presently appear to us in the light of a willing that is, in one respect, nevertheless already "determined" [p. 602]. Let us recall that only impulses referable to a matter can be split, then the assumption of the possibility of their occurring includes indeed the existence of incentives in place of drives, and thus the existence of the personal I in place of the unity of life. With just this we have also already presupposed that some act of apprehension must be performed, and that through it there must have been impressed upon the life-substance, at least once, that boundary upon its course which we characterized in the 38th Chapter, in order that an act of will may occur. We leave undiscussed for now the relation of the two to one another, likewise pointed to at that time, but preface the derivation of the purpose of will, now to be offered, with a consideration of the recognizability of drive-impulses within the personality, because their separating-off gives us the swiftest disclosure concerning the recognizability of impulses referable to a matter and consequently capable of will.

When goal-giving drive-impulses break through in the personal I, this always happens under a temporary empowering by the will. What would then lie nearer than the thought of certain actions arising out of overstrong surges! Only, with the most violent surge, by no means only a drive can react, but rather, indeed, even an "interest" (cf. Chap. 31), and the "affect-action" can bear witness just as well to the magnitude of an interest as to the strength of a drive. To be sure, in the moment of any surge whatever, the I falls prey to a life-process, and it was precisely with regard to its being-seized that we were able to distinguish, from the experience of undergoing, the experience of being-active, and thus the I from the It; but nothing compels us to exclude impulses referable to a matter from the capacity for "reflection-robbing" surges! Were the I, indeed, nothing but spirit, it could experience no surges, but then it would also arrive at no reflection. If, instead, it is spirit engraved into life, then there ⦅must⦆ be able to become an It for it also a life-stratum that has been saturated through with the effects of acts of spirit. The diminution, or even the complete elimination, of the capacity for self-reflection that goes along with many affects therefore by no means proves the derivation of the surges in question from the drive-stratum of the personality, and only a "not-being-beside-oneself" or "being-out-of-one's-senses" does not yet at all let us recognize whether there is present a mere disempowering of will or a de-selfing.

Let us imagine a sex-hungry vagrant lying in wait for a girl on a deserted field-path, [p. 603] in order to rape her: it is then not, say, his sexual drive immediately, but incentives connected with it, that carries his actions up to the moment when he is on the point of embracing the overpowered and wrestled-down girl, while, for the purpose of sexual satisfaction, the sexual drive now comes immediately into effect. However strong feelings of desire and tensions of expectation may have accompanied the preceding volitions, they were nonetheless genuine volitions and their utterances genuine actions. The process of sexual satisfaction, by contrast, far from being brought about by a willing, comes about only through the fact that, at the moment of the impending enjoyment, all incentives whatever are replaced by drives, and thus, too, all impulses of will by drive-impulses. The sensuous experience of lust that normally accompanies the process of satisfaction to a high degree is, even in cases of only barely perceptible occurrence, a sure sign of the immediate participation of goal-giving drives. Feelings of success, too, can ⦅arouse⦆ the drive-zone; only they themselves have nothing to do with feelings of lust, and their occurrence does not in the least depend on the efficacy of any drives whatever. The pleasure, say, of the man without means who has just won the grand prize, or of the speculator to whom a stock-exchange manoeuvre has brought enormous gains, has not the faintest resemblance to lust; whereas in the pleasure that the violently thirsting man feels in sipping water from a mountain spring, there lies, quite without question, a variety of — though usually only weak-grade — lust.

Anxiety, the pole opposite to lust, has no less certain a sign-value. When we earlier set forth that man alone, by virtue of his capacity for thought, bears constantly within him the consciousness of his impending end, and cited, in confirmation, Hölderlin's word about the child, who is immortal insofar as it knows nothing of dying (Ch. 39), many a reader will in spirit have held the fear of death against us, without whose assumption countless behaviors of thought-incapable animals would remain unintelligible. Here we answer with the disclosure of a far-reaching insight: that so-called fear of death is one and the same as anxiety in general, and that anxiety as such designates a state not referable to any object, which, exactly like lust, rejects not only the thought of death but every thought whatsoever. For an ineradicable feeling for word-meaning compels us to refer the name fear to fear of something definite [p. 604], and the name anxiety to anxiety before something indefinite, exactly analogous to the distinction between *Latin* timor and Latin pavor. Since, in the animals that share both feelings with us, fear too rests on the efficacy of drive-impulses, we must choose the indefinite feeling of anxiety in order to demonstrate its object-unrelated drive-nature in man as well.

Every anxiety is fear of death; but the lived experience of the fear of death coincides so little with the fear of death that accompanies thinking about death, that some have committed suicide — out of fear of death! The intensification of such feelings of anxiety in certain mood-psychoses, incipient schizophrenias, melancholias of age, can, as every physician knows, give the sufferer occasion for self-killing. Anxieties lying ready in readiness can also fuse with apprehensions actually present and produce apparent worries, because the drive to self-preservation is constantly bent on mitigating somewhat the dreadful pressure of indefinite anxieties by tying them to intelligible objects of fear. If at some point an astonishing disproportion shows itself to us between the occasion for apprehension and the expressed vehemence of the fear of the one who fears, we shall, by rough estimate, hit the truth in at least half the cases if we conclude not to excessive timidity but to an anxiety-disposition that finds in occasions of fear, so to speak, welcome opportunities to assert itself before the consciousness of its bearer. In the case of other concomitant properties, however, it may happen that the impression of real danger overwhelms and displaces the dispositional state of anxiety; as a result of which the hypochondriac, previously plagued by imagined apprehensions, suddenly displays calm composure, even bravery. Dispositions to anxiety do not necessarily exclude that their bearer should nonetheless be a warrior fearless of death! — Most closely akin to object-unrelated fear of death is, finally, horror (horror), likewise the pole opposite to bliss.

That in man anxiety — unlike fear — does not rest on an interest of self-preservation, and therefore in principle endangers self-preservation, we show by the example of *panic*. If, on the occasion of the fear of an incipient fire in a theater, or one announced by a cry of "fire," a panic breaks out, then whoever, out of the fear of self-preservation, keeps himself in check indisputably has the greater prospect of escaping with his life than those seized by the panic, who, blindly pressing toward too narrow or even the wrong exit, crush one another in masses [p. 605]. What makes them act so senselessly is no longer the fear of the fire and the thought of rescue at all, but a stirring of quite another kind, welling up from the depths of drive-life, which, be it noted in passing, was set free far less by fear than by the co-fear felt at the sight of so many who are fearing. Whoever has ever experienced even the onset of "panic terror" will afterward know how to distinguish it most sharply from every apprehension, however great, and will admit to himself that no conceivable interest was at play in it, but rather a drive just as elementary as the one that issues into an experience of lust. Between the opposite-pole states of lust and anxiety (as likewise bliss and horror) lies a broad series of distinguishable feelings, or better, feeling-tones, each of which allows us to infer the immediate efficacy of a goal-giving drive. So often, then, as conversely nothing of such mood-tones can be ascertained, we may be certain that our feelings stem from object-relatable impulses.

Let us turn back, accordingly, to these, and take the case that someone occupied with intellectual work suddenly forms the resolve to interrupt it briefly in order to take a walk; let it first be recalled once more that the motive he supposes for this need not always indicate the actual mainspring that was efficacious in the impulse necessarily undergone. It may have been the feeling of fatigue, which our intellectual worker may suppose to have occasioned his resolve; but it may also have been the allurement of the sunshine, and finally both impulses may, as it were, have worked together, even if one of them in the end "tipped the scale." The correct appraisal of the guiding mainsprings on the part of the owner is measured by the degree of personal capacity for self-knowledge and has nothing directly to do with our problem. But however that may stand, one thing is certain: at the moment the resolve was formed, the generic characteristic was split off from an impulse, and because this was now an object-relatable impulse, the spirit thereby actually forged the relation-toobject that had inhered in the impulse as a possibility. If we regard the splitting from the same point of view from which we earlier regarded the splitting of original drive-impulses, we again retain a directionless urge to movement, only with the difference [p. 606] that this now instantaneously receives a direction from the command of spirit. If we regard this from the point of view of the separation, inevitably accompanying it, of the bearer of the impulse from the goal of the impulse, we retain the willing I, which is no longer driven but pursues purposes of its own activity. In relation to the goal proper to the impulse, every purpose is merely a thought or, if one will, a concept. But whereas the product of the act of perception has the sense and the capacity to fix the object within the appearance of the world, and thus to engrave into the personality a direction of relation of its capacity for impressions, the product of the act of will has the sense and the capacity to fix a goal of happening within the happening of the world, and thus to engrave into the personality a direction of effect of its urge to movement. — After this anticipation of the chief finding, we shall now appraise the state of affairs in its individual features.

Should anyone doubt the complete difference in essence between purpose of will and goal of drive, let him only consider that we could not possibly speak of exerting oneself, straining oneself, striving, if we were driven exclusively to every accomplishment. The drive-movements of the animal fall, strictly speaking, under expressive movements, although for reasons to be passed over here we can indeed distinguish, even in animals, expressive movements in the narrower sense from the seeking- or fleeing-movements occasioned by drive-impulses. Perhaps one objects that such movements too could be the utterance of the most violent striving, and points, say, to the climbing feats of a chamois that feels itself pursued, or to the toils and dangers under which animals so often have to fight for their food. Yet one thing is exertion in general — more precisely, the sometimes often-repeated alternation of tension and release that accompanies every satisfaction of a drive — and another thing is striving, more precisely, the lived experience of self-activity. The movements of one seized by panic can manifest the most extraordinary violence; and yet subsequent reflection will teach him that it was not he who exerted himself, not he who strove to escape, but that he was irresistibly swept away. So little did his movements spring from a self-activity that they had rather condemned every self-activity to complete impotence. And it stands the same in principle with all movements in which an original [p. 607] drive-impulse steers toward its goal, however many subspecies may further differentiate themselves within them. In the exertion, tension, striving of willing — comparable to nothing else — it is revealed with irrefutable clarity that, once the vis a fronte, i.e. the pull of the images, falls away, the I has stepped into the place of the vis a tergo, i.e. the directional determinacy of the urge to movement arising from a generically particular privation suffered by the body — the I, whose commands, as we shall show later, can only be realized through a continually recurring conflict of driving with inhibiting movement-impulses.<sup>8</sup>
