<sup>8</sup> On page 607. — We must still call to mind a curious difficulty. If the act of apprehension, no less than the act of will, means the I's answer to an impulse undergone, in such a way that as a consequence a content of impression is split off from the act of apprehension, while a content of impulse is split off from the act of will, then for the act of will we arrive at the seemingly contradictory-looking requirement that the very same impulse that called forth the act must be split off by the act! For the opposite assumption — that an impulse A calls forth the act, which then splits off an impulse B — would be inadmissible if only because it would have to claim, for the occurrence of the act of will, two successive wave-crests of lived experience, between which no agreement could in any case be presupposed with regard to the predominance of the impulse-side, let alone with regard to the content of the impulse-sides. To overcome this apparent difficulty, however, we need only bear in mind that the spiritual act requires no time whatsoever. If the limit-quality that bears it designates an empirical now, and thus needs a — however slight — span of time, nothing at all stands in the way of the act's splitting off precisely that impulse which let it itself „spring forth". In this way, however, we now see the difference between the act of apprehension and the act of will grounded further in the fact that the sustaining impulse helps the spirit, the one time, to the splitting off of a content alien to the soul, the other time, of a content proper to the soul; whereby, in relation to the act of apprehension, the act of will appears in the light of that overemphasized subjectivity which already met us in its merely mediate relatedness to the world of facts, and which has chiefly prevented an adequate characterization of it by the thinkers of an antiquity that looked outward.

If we compare with the bare act of perception: there is something, the bare act of will: I will something, we easily recognize how far it too already possesses a fixed direction of effect. For just as the object of bare perceiving is in any case constituted by something existing, so for the taking place of a bare volition something existing must be presupposed, because otherwise there would be lacking the ground of possibility for the resistance at whose overcoming the volition aims. Because, further, only something now existing can present the obstacle worthy of being overcome, we must call volition, quite simply, an urge to activity directed against the momentary situation of the world and hence also against the momentary situation proper to the one who wills.

This finding makes possible inferences of extraordinary import. First of all, we possess in it, for the first time, the key to the origin of self-reflection, with regard to which it was only set forth in the 12th chapter why it could arise, but not why it in fact arises. Were there a being that indeed possessed (spiritual) apprehensive power but not power of will (which of course would be impossible), it would, notwithstanding the capacity for self-apprehension already lying in its (spiritual) power of apprehension, nonetheless not arrive at the apprehension of itself, because it would lack the motive for doing so. As surely as a man, after discovering his I, can always also judge, instead of "there stands a tree," "I see that there stands a tree," so surely is it not the seeing of the tree or the hearing of its rustling that alone would suffice as occasion for such a turn of view. Rather, the person finds himself, insofar as, on occasion of what is apprehensible, he experiences a volition directed against what is apprehended, and thereby inescapably also experiences himself as a demanding power; and the turning-over of the reflection "there is something" into reflection upon the self-reflecting I is mediated [p. 608] by the *feeling* of self-activity. Whether, with regard to what is to be perceived, I state: there stands a tree, or: trees grow, it seems that, at least immediately, nothing lies in the linguistic expression capable of leading over to the bearer of the statement; whereas reflection upon the content of meaning of an imperative, as soon as it had ascertained that, according to it, something *ought* to happen, could not help but discover the person who commanded it. Even if volition certainly does not coincide with the consciousness of the one willing that it is he who wills there, it is nonetheless indeed volition that gives occasion for self-reflection upon the I, and between the "there is something" and the "I exist" it is the reflection: I will, that mediates for the first time. Instead of "cogito ergo sum," Descartes could have formulated even more aptly: volo ergo sum! It does not contradict this that precisely the typical<sup>9</sup> man of deeds concerns himself least of all with practicing self-reflection; for, although it takes the capacity for will for the I to pass from apprehension of the object to apprehension of the self, self-apprehension nonetheless remains an achievement of reflection and therefore stands in opposition to the *state* of willing, which, in the measure of its predominance, values insight only insofar as it serves the purpose.

<sup>9</sup> On page 608. — This was in fact done by the German philosopher *Bouterwek*, whom the French philosopher *Maine de Biran* later followed in this. Bouterwek was one of the Göttingen teachers of *Schopenhauer*, who thereby received the first impetus toward his metaphysics of the will.

The recognition of the counter-striving nature of the feeling of self-activity further enables us to achieve an essential deepening of our insight into the constitution of the act of judgement. If, by virtue of my self-activity, I am directed against something that is, we understand why the object could appear as something standing-over-against, indeed even as something *thrown* against a movement, and we would have, first of all, to posit in the urge of will the life-ground of *negative* judgements, which would accordingly deserve to be called decisions of will and which, with the garment of statement, would merely conceal the willed act of denial. The proper sense of the sentence "I did not see it" or "brightness is not darkness" would accordingly be: I deny or dispute having seen it (or that brightness is darkness). It is such languages that seem to us to have preserved the primal expression of this state of affairs — languages which, instead of having an independent particle of negation (= not), have negative conjugation-classes (e.g. Bantu), or, as in Finnish, even conjugate the negation in place of the verb, as if we could say: thou not-est to speak, he not-s to speak.<sup>10</sup> — But this is not all: the positive judgement too would, at bottom, have to be a negative judgement, if indeed the act of judgement fell under the acts of will. Although the proof of this has [p. 609] not yet been brought to its conclusion, we need only bring together what we already know of the *achievement* of the act of judgement in order to bring to light the hidden negation of every possible judgement.

<sup>10</sup> On page 608. — We owe this reference to a communication from Dr. E. Ab*egg*, lecturer in general linguistics at the University of Zurich. Compare in this connection notes 19 and 20 of the first volume.

All commandments are prohibitions, and every law signifies an interdiction of transgressions of bounds. But judgement raises its content to the rank of law, and its claim to truth consists in nothing other than the claim to inviolable legal validity. Out of every "so it is" the prohibiting norm springs to meet us: because it is so, it can never again have been otherwise — whereby we are referred back to what was set forth in the 9th chapter on the nature of "assertion." In that the judgement-statement "asserts" something, it denies not merely all conceivable counter-assertions — in view of which precisely it can also be turned negatively — but actuality itself, together with the barrier of being. Just as the judgement-command subjectively forbids forgetting, so it objectively forbids happening by the fixing of having-been, in such a way that it robs actuality of its past and the object of apprehension of that alone through which it had part in the actual: its changeability. If the negative judgement, with the assertion of not-being, indeed disputes an assertion of being, then in the positive assertion of the actuality of a being there lies the negation of an actuality! The positive judgement is the original negation, in relation to which negative judgements bear the character of derived negations. Here we complete, so far as possible, our dissection of the relation between act of apprehension and act of judgement.

If at least one act of apprehension must already have taken place in order that the object-relatable impulse be available whose splitting makes an act of will possible, then it is indisputably the apprehending and not, say, the willing activity of spirit that accompanies the origin of the I, and its primal beginning presents itself as a counter-blow, not against the lived experience, but against the actuality of something lived through. Once again setting aside the vexing riddle of how, out of a lived experience that only just before was still spiritless, the counter-blow of spirit against what is lived can come about, we lay all the more decisive weight on the fact that the bound thereby engraved into the capacity for impressions would fall prey to immediate dissolution, were it not joined by the bound of an urge to movement — and that happens through the splitting of the impulse consequent upon the act of will, which seals the result of the act of apprehension [p. 610]. The apprehensive act, through which I find the object amid the flux of images, would remain ineffectual, did not a judicial act, immediately following upon it, lend the object the form of the inviolable norm. If the former reveals to us the originally reactive bearing of spirit toward life, the latter reveals a self-activity through which spirit first of all binds life; if with the former its dependence on life comes overwhelmingly to the fore, in consequence of which the understanding seems led by the facts and the will in turn by the understanding, then with the latter there is already a dependence of life on spirit, in consequence of which lived experience has to make use of the paths of experience, and experience in turn follows the directions that spirit, by virtue of its capacity to give laws, has pointed out to it. Whereas, accordingly, a judgement-less apprehension would be only incomplete reflection, complete and thus properly speaking reflection rests upon two closely interlinked acts, of which the second is an act of will. That was what those Scholastics divined who sought to stamp willing as the precondition of knowing.

What, according to such insight, do truth and error mean? The statement that someone has apprehended something falsely says, in truth, that he has judged erroneously about something apprehended. Just as lived experience remains on this side of truth and error, because it does not even potentially contain a judgement, so mere apprehension remains on this side of error and truth, because it does not get so far as to actualize the judgement potentially inherent in it. Truths are true judgements, errors erroneous judgements; and outside of judging there is neither truth nor error. This leads us over to the *source* of erring. In apprehending, so far as it is nothing but this, spirit conducts itself reactively, or as wholly compelled by the experience; but in judging it conducts itself self-actively, and thereby runs the danger of not merely fixing what is apprehended but, moreover, of displacing and rearranging it according to the aims of the *will to mastery*, which designates its essence. Here, however, we have to distinguish two principal cases: the case of one-sidedness and the case of falsification.

Every object of apprehension, e.g. "the color red" or "similarity" or "this table here," can become the bearer of countless judgements which, without being wrong, nevertheless make their determinations so predominantly for purposes of thought-facilitation on the part of spirit that they all together contribute to removing it ever further from the actuality-content of the [p. 611] lived experience that originally gave the impulse to find it. We have sought to make this one-sidedness intelligible from a "logocentric" inclination, and have derived from it the shallow reflection which, however considerable the acuity of understanding, is not thereby protected from losing the ground of actuality from under its feet. We fully assure ourselves of its dangerousness when we keep present to mind that every concept which we make the bearer of a judgement was originally the result of a judging act. A judgement indeed created the object of apprehension "color red" or "similarity" or "this table here," and for the displacement that works itself out in judgements about it, it may already itself contain the germ, insofar as a thought-purpose was involved in its production.

Meanwhile let us note that the thought-purpose, in and of itself, signifies indeed one-sidedness but not erroneousness of the finding. Now, however, it is a personal I that bears both the reactive and the self-empowered activity of spirit, and whose peculiar nature can no longer help but intrude, as soon as it passes over from the merely reactive into the self-active bearing. This, taken by itself alone, would indeed be that absolute arbitrary will which is consummated in the concept of an omnipotence, for which even the barrier of the state of affairs would no longer obtain, since together with the boundary it would likewise create the thing-to-be-bounded. If, in the pithy proverb according to which the wish is the father of the thought, we replace the word "wish" with "interest" and the word "thought" with "holding-to-be-true," then with the substitute sentence — that interest is the cause of holding-to-be-true — we would have characterized the most general reason why all conceivable errors may form the object of holding-to-be-true. — Meanwhile, wherein would erring consist?

If the act of apprehension is through and through compelled and dependent on lived experience, one might suppose that the act of judgement must establish truth, provided it confines itself to holding fast the object of apprehension. But in doing so one would have treated the bearer of apprehension as though it were, instead of a personal I, an I-less unit of life. In fact, the dependence of apprehending upon lived experience does *not* guarantee the truth-value of the finding based upon it, because the lived experience could already have been broken at spirit-dependent barriers, and the potential judgement inherent in the apprehension becomes, for the same reason, a source of erring from which the actual judgement directly occasions error — namely, from an interest.

[p. 612] It is other and ever again other contents of lived experience in which we encounter actuality, or which meet us as actual; but their eternal otherness does not exclude the participation of them all in that common element on whose account we suppose we find actuality in each of them. But if it is the actual that the mastering will of spirit exchanges against what is, then the content of every original (i.e. not merely accepted on good faith) error must consist in this: that a being is posited to which nothing actual corresponds, or that a being is denied which, in view of actuality, ought to have been posited. If the true statement translates something actual into the being-language of the understanding, then the erroneous statement asserts the being of an actuality that does not exist, or it denies the being of an actuality that does exist. Examined as to its essential content, every error is falsification of actuality.

Let us place ourselves, as once before, at the beginning of the series of possible acts: the very first act of apprehension, with which the I "enters into existence," can of course not yet contain even the source of an error, whereas already with the very first act of judgement the self-activity of spirit was able to deflect, in the direction of either loosening or falsifying actuality, from the actuality-content of the lived experience that had called forth the act of apprehension. We need not elaborate how, thereby, a mainspring could have a part in the origin of the second act of apprehension which, in relation to the content of lived experience of apprehension itself, would already impart to it a direction either fleeing from actuality or disturbing actuality. If, accordingly, we have to seek the executive power of all erring in the self-activity of spirit, or, more briefly, in the *will*, the ground of the possibility of erring nonetheless lies in the constitution of the basis of lived experience, or, more briefly, of the soul. For be it the act that finds under compulsion of the impulse, or the act that, moreover, self-actively establishes, the act as such can always only sunder, and transpose the sundered from happening into being. Not in it, and not in the occasioning lived experience, but in the manner and degree of its *dependence* on lived experience lies the ground of all peculiarities of thinking and, above all, of all modes of erring. Thinking deepens with the nearness of spirit to actuality; it grows shallow with the remoteness of spirit from actuality; and the most general cause of this its connectedness with life — here rendered sensuous under the image of magnitudes of distance — must [p. 613] be assigned to the *actuality-weight* of the contents of lived experience, and to the capacity of the soul, inferable therefrom, to fetter spirit. With the loosening of the bond between spirit and — not, say, lived experience as such, but — the actuality-content of what is lived through, the precondition is fulfilled for the thought-purpose thenceforth to be dictated by interest alone, and thus to occasion acts of judgement that falsify actuality. If we call the constitution of the soul that would have nearness of spirit to actuality as its consequence the personal sense of actuality, then upon the weakening of the personal sense of actuality rests, on the one hand, the shallowness, on the other, the perversity of thinking, and finally also every abnormality of character and every possible "derangement of spirit."

[p. 614]

#### 47. Kapitel — Vom Willen zur Wahrheit — Chapter 47 — On the Will to Truth

Should one suppose that we have deviated rather long from willing and fallen thoroughly back into the consideration of thinking, it would now be time to emphasize with force that the extraordinarily composite processes that one is accustomed to call willing or thinking, far from coinciding with the act of apprehension and the act of resolve, without exception carry whole chains of acts, among which compelled ones continually alternate with self-active ones! For how indeed should a steered thinking be possible without the participation of acts of will, or a willing without the participation of acts of apprehension! But if steered thinking quite certainly pursues a thought-purpose — indeed, if already with every judgement rendered whatsoever, spirit exercises its will to self-assertion, and if, in this way, in all spiritual activity whatsoever the will-side of the I swells to so threatening a preponderance that it might seem as if, Scotistically, the sense of cognition were shifting for us — then the question presses urgently: what is the fundamental difference between the truth-finding act of judgement and the act of will, which in and for itself is wholly unconcerned with truth!

We have just shown the content of erring to lie in a falsification of actuality, its source in personal interest. Now, among the personal mainsprings there may indisputably also be found the will to truth, with regard to which we accordingly rightly wish to learn whether it belongs to the psychic or to the spiritual constitution of its bearer, and wherein its purpose differs from all other purposes. Were there only the soul — that is, a spiritless soul — it would have no will to truth, because it would indeed live through experience but would not judge about what is lived through. Only a being torn by spirit out of the stream of actuality can thirst after truth, and even through the finding of truth it does not become one with actuality. Yet it is the actuality-weight [p. 615] of what is lived through that draws spirit into the depths and is able to preserve even the colorless schematism of shallow thinking from distortions. We believed we had recognized the driving power of every stirring of drive in the non-intuitable pull of images, and shall therefore hold it at least possible that the actuality comprised within the images too may manifest a drawing force. Under whatever presuppositions this may occur, one thing is certain: that it must be this pull which, through the splitting of the impulse, is found exchanged for the purpose of the spiritual activity that strives after truth. As surely as the sense of actuality means the disposition to receptivity in consequence of which far-reaching acts of apprehension take place, so surely does the sense of actuality become the mainspring of the love of truth, after even a single apprehension has taken place in which the actuality-weight of what was lived through made itself felt. If, then, the will to truth is nothing other than the motor side of the sense of actuality, it belongs to the constitution of the soul — not indeed of the self-being as such, but indeed of the personal self-being. — We pursue the object into all its ramifications, because only a thorough carrying-through gives us hope of bringing the doctrine of the will to a conclusion.

It is customary nowadays gladly to set the superior truth-value of so-called intuitions against the achievements of so-called discursive thinking, thinking in this connection of such sudden ideas as occur on the occasion of strong shocks and have for their recipient the certainty-pathos of "illuminations," "revelations," "inspirations." We have in part already examined earlier, and shall later examine still more closely, for which cases one would hit upon something correct with this; here, on the other hand, two facts are to be pointed out which in principle forbid holding any intuitions to be true intuitions merely because they are accompanied by feelings of certainty that remain more or less inaccessible to grounded refutation. For, in the first place, there are neither findings of insight nor findings of proof that would not, step by step, rest on immediate sudden ideas. Whether it flashes suddenly upon a Goethe, on regarding a flower, that the blossom is the compressed spiral of leaves, or whether a mathematician finds a still "more elegant" proof for a long-since-proven theorem: the eureka of the sudden idea was as little lacking here as there, and only the testing of the judgement decides in both cases whether the personally gladdening idea truly [p. 616] illuminated something or was a will-o'-the-wisp doomed to go out. "Revelations" — and nothing but such — were what helped us, in our pre-conscious youth, to learn our mother tongue, and it is solely to newly streaming-in sudden ideas that we owe it that our thinking does not endlessly repeat itself according to the scheme A is A, but somehow "gets somewhere." — But then again, we have indeed seen that the vehemence of the lived experience by no means yet speaks for the actuality-weight of what is lived through, and can therefore in no way guarantee the truth-value of the judgements bound up with it. — We now take the will to truth as our starting point, in order to uncover a tragic self-contradiction of all volitions whose direction-giving ground must be sought in the life-domain of the personality.

We pass over the fact that the personal mainspring bearing the name love of truth, or, then, will to truth, necessarily enters into opposition with all other mainsprings, because the advantage bound up with the attainment of its goals would at most be an advantage of the soul, but not of the personal self-preservation of its bearer, and we hold fast to the will to truth itself, which we conceive intensified to the temperaturedegree of a passion. Even for the passionate love of truth no fulfillments other than judgements blossom. But if a judgement is rendered, then not only the thirst for truth of the soul but also the will to mastery of spirit has had a part in it, and out of something perhaps only surmised before, a known thing has come to be, which drew forth from the wave-beating flood of actuality not the draught hoped for by the soul, but a lump of ice no longer to be melted! Shallow reflection, of which we are not treating this time, will at once make use of it in order to join it together with other lumps, will thereby build footbridges and bridges and in the end insert an impenetrable layer between actuality and the bearer of reflection. The will to truth, gravitating toward the depths, on the other hand, will feel itself peculiarly betrayed by the result of its seeking, will strive back from the solid to the fluid, from knowing to surmising, and, if it is permitted to continue in the simile, will make use of the one floe in order to steer out into a shoreless sea, suffering agonizingly that it is condemned either to remain separated from the sea or else to have to pay for the annihilation of what separates it with its own destruction. But let us leave the simile and examine the state of affairs.

In that, within the will to truth, sense of actuality [p. 617] and spiritual will to mastery lie in feud with one another, thinking out of will to truth, with its doubting and *tempting* *nature*, attests, for all lived-experience-compelled willing of the grand style, a self-contradiction that, more than anything else, illuminates the life-hostility of the will and hence of spirit. One consequence of this, which we must not pass over, is a kind of criticism very different from the ordinary kind we shall touch on presently. The will to truth will not, with Herbart, work upon concepts, or, if one pleases, measure concepts against experience, whose deceptiveness it saw through, but will approach every concept with the question: of how much feeling for actuality do you bear witness, of how much will to mastery of spirit? If purposive thinking continually climbs upward, contemplative thinking always descends; if the former presses outward, fleeing the center, the latter presses inward, seeking the center; if the former pays homage to restless forward-striding, the latter to unstoppable backward-striding, turning from the content of judgement to the lived experience that called forth the rendering of judgement, from the lived experience to the judgements that preceded it, whose vital consequences had a part in the lived experience. It finds itself on the way to the origins, the archai; it would like to arrive at the root-point of thinking, and — of this there is no doubt — were it to find it, it would tear it out, thereby murdering, *together with* the willing, the ground of the possibility of willing. — Measured against actuality, every truth bears the character of tendentious one-sidedness. The standard employed in this is not, again, a judgement or result of judgement, but the merely beholdable actuality of beholdable images, and is fetched up from the depths of the soul, ordinarily in the form of a feeling of actuality. In the will to truth of such a stamp, then, there contend, unceasingly, with the will to mastery of spirit, elementary feelings and urges which, condensing into claims, insofar as their entry into the course of thought is made compellingly necessary, approach even the true finding with the critical doubt whether life extorted it from spirit or spirit forced it upon life, and drive away from the truths, out of the relational system of the noumena, all that flee actuality. We shall at once set forth still more convincing fruits of the same conflict, but must first characterize its most general outcome of all, which, however, even therein akin to life, bears a Janus-head.

If one calls the form of utterance of judgement an assertion, one [p. 618] has thereby unintentionally already made known that the content of judgement "in itself" belongs to the genus of those achievements of the understanding which, baptized by the Stoa for the broader consciousness of culture, stamped by the modern "natural sciences" as the warrant of all thinking, belong to the genus of laws, and one will agree with us if we, for the sake of clarity of sense, unfold it thus: it is impermissible to behave as though what has been truthfully asserted were not yet asserted at all, and it is impermissible to assert what contradicts it. One thus surveys at a glance the connection between the triumphs of the ever-prohibiting, ever transgression-avenging Jahwism and the jubilant intoxication of "science" over the "lawful order" of the entire course of the world, and one will not be too greatly astonished if here and there some highly significant thinker, as for instance Nietzsche, thanks to his admixture of priestliness (which precisely for that reason he was able, as no other, to unmask), turns back from the concealed-imperative form of communication of science to the personally imperative tone, and tries to transform the researcher into the commander, lawgiver, prophet! The rendering of judgement appears in such a light as what it is named after: as a giving-out of judicial verdicts! — If, on the other hand, one calls the form of utterance of judgement a statement, one finds oneself unexpectedly confronted with the question how the declarative sentence could ever have come about at all, and believes one sees an unbridgeable gulf opening between the act of judgement and the act of will! Appealing to the fact that among the determining occasions of all of them there are to be found either feelings or volitions, we could readily range the assertoric sentence alongside wish-sentences, exclamatory sentences, command-sentences, doubt-sentences, question-sentences, whereas with the declarative sentence the domain of an "objectivity" opens up in which, so to speak, both feeling and will run out of breath!

Now, the conflict we have exposed in the depths comes to the surface, among other things, in that the utterance of judgement is quite as rightly called assertion as statement, and we scarcely make ourselves guilty of too great boldness if we add that the designation "statement" for the linguistic expression of judgement points just as definitely to the first prop of reflection, the act of apprehension, as the designation "assertion" points to the second prop of reflection, the establishing act of will. [p. 619] The recollection of the circumstance that, even in the case of erring, the act of judgement was performed for the sake of the act of apprehension, and to that extent, at least mediately, would have to count as a compelled act, would indeed suffice for an external distinction of the act of judgement from the arbitrary act of will, in relation to which it is the acts of apprehension (together with their associated acts of judgement) that are performed for its sake. But just as the capacity-for-deeds of spirit, when it comes into effect by splitting the impulse, finds "laws" only because it cannot help adapting itself to *apprehended* actualities, so the capacity-for-deeds of spirit, when it comes into effect by splitting the impression, finds existing things only because it cannot help being compelled by sensibly lived actualities. We draw the second-innermost ring around the concept of being with the disclosure: without being ever and again referred to an actuality thereby to be determined, being would rather be non-being! That the actus purus — rooted, to be sure, in life, as it is — must content itself with putting a world that is in the place of the world that happens, instead of dissolving the world altogether into nothing at a single stroke, has as its cause the unconquerable pull of the actuality that has been split off, and from the comparison, already elucidated earlier in connection with the concept of law, of spirit with actuality, we have in the concept of being the original and conditioning formulation. Only because thrown back by actuality does the No of spirit become the being of something extra-spiritual, and the ultimate ground for the surrender of the commanding in favor of a form of communication that resists so-called finality lies in the soul.

Were the opinion right which thinks language to have arisen out of animal expressive sounds, then there would indeed not even be command-sounds, but merely luring sounds, warning sounds, scaring-away sounds; but we should nonetheless like to picture to ourselves that, after the coupling with spirit had taken place, drives became mainsprings and stirrings became volitions, which then, of course, found their linguistic expression, one and all, in imperatives. Even if one disregarded the fact that the command-sentence presupposes the declarative sentence just as surely as the act of will presupposes the act of apprehension, the existence of declarative sentences would in this way remain an unintelligible miracle. The communicating language was preceded by the expressive (but representationally expressive!) language, just as symbolic thinking preceded logical thinking; but if we place ourselves at the point of transition, it is the seeker after truth, or, impersonally conceived, the will to truth that forces spirit down into the depths, to whom we owe the establishing form [p. 620] of speech, and thus a linguistic mode of expression that makes good the claim of the extra-spiritual by pointing to something removed from all arbitrary will. Janus-headed, to be sure, remains the achievement, because the unspoken primal concept of all judging, the concept of being, has, besides its life-dependent side, a spirit-dependent side, and for the unreflective mode of apprehension confuses the two with one another. Precisely what we grasp with the concept of being is the nothing, while the actuality that it indicates, because for the sake of grasping we had to look away from it, is not to be grasped.

With his teaching that the "first substance," i.e. the determinate individual thing, cannot be predicated, Aristotle was grammatically and logically right. But because to the concept of the individual thing belongs that of existing, there already lies within it a predicative determination that denies the happening-character of actuality, and the "first substance" proves — very much against the visible appearance, which is inclined to take it for the bearer of judgement prior to judgement — to be, rather, without exception a product of judgement, which owes its existence to a spiritual deed, through which actuality was severed from the remaining residue of something existing! Yet however much the form of statement contributes to letting the imperative admixed to every "establishing" be overlooked (of which, incidentally, language preserves the memory, in that it permits the strongest command-accent to be laid on the indicative: You are going at once! They are to present themselves at such and such a time!), and thus, as nothing else does, nourished the belief in the actuality of laws, norms, orders, it is nonetheless again the form of statement, and only the form of statement, that keeps alive in the hearer the consciousness that, in the resistance of the fact, an underivable power has a part which compels not only spirits but the will itself. The self-contradiction of the will to truth has set itself a milestone in the concept of being, which, could it speak, would thus address the seeker after truth: I stand, barring entry, at the edge of the world; only as far as me do you penetrate, and never do you get beyond me; but to know this truthfully — that I teach you!

In the language of East Asian wisdom this runs thus: What is to be thought, what is to be considered, in order to know Tao, Knowledge asked in vain of Do-Nothing-Say-Nothing, asked in vain of Wild-Whirl; then she asks the Yellow Emperor. "The Yellow Emperor spoke: \"Nothing is to be thought, [p. 621] nothing is to be considered, in order to know Tao. In nothing is one to stand, nothing is one to grasp, in order to draw near to Tao. Nothing is one to follow, nothing is one to tread, in order to attain Tao.\"" Then Knowledge said to the Yellow Emperor: "You and I know this, but those two do not know it. Who is in the right?" The Yellow Emperor answered: "Do-Nothing-Say-Nothing is truly in the right, and Wild-Whirl is close to being right. You and I are wholly in the wrong. For those who grasp it do not speak it, and those who speak it do not grasp it." Thereupon Knowledge said to the Yellow Emperor: "I asked Do-Nothing-Say-Nothing. He did not answer me. Was it that he would not answer? He could not. I asked Wild-Whirl. He was on the point of speaking, but he did not speak. Was it that he did not wish to? He was on the point of speaking; but he forgot what he desired to say. Now I asked you, and you have answered me. How is it, then, that you should be wholly in the wrong?" The Yellow Emperor said: "Do-Nothing-Say-Nothing was truly in the right, because he did not know. Wild-Whirl was close to being right, because he forgot. You and I are wholly in the wrong, because we know." When Wild-Whirl heard of this, he judged that the Yellow Emperor had spoken like one who knows.<sup>11</sup>

<sup>11</sup> On page 621. From: Reden und Gleichnisse des *Tschuang*-*Tse*, German selection by Martin Buber, pp. 73—74. Insel-Verlag, Leipzig 1920.

Our findings go beyond the wisdom-teachings of Taoism in a direction closed to it (owing to the difference in their origins), inasmuch as they have ascertained the essential content of genuine docta ignorantia in the indicative capacity of judgement, and its brazen limit in judgement's capacity to attain and to conceive, on whose account it is purposive, willing, and deed-laden. What distinguishes the cognitive purpose from all other purposes is that, called into existence through the splitting-off of the pull of actuality, it necessarily takes its *direction* toward the unattainable, toward happening! If we recall that something happens only out of livingness, and that in being-alive the living essence appears, we find an unforced transition to yet another kind of search for actuality — we mean that of the image-maker (artist), and even of the poet (insofar as poets must participate in the image-making), who, at least within the more recent cultural sphere and chiefly since the so-called Renaissance, were likewise compelled to become seekers of truth. — For just as, with the drive-impulse acting on the body of the impulse's bearer, a pull of images operates which comes to its close with the approach to what draws it, or even with union with it, so upon the far-beholding-capable soul of man there operates besides a pull of images that would come to its [p. 622] close with their objectification in an enduring material. And just as actuality fetters the truth-seeker to happening, so it is the images themselves that fetter the artist and make use, as it were, of his spirit in order to come, through him, to appearance in intuitive presentness. Thereby the image-maker finds himself, from inner compulsion, set before the task of shaping — in tone-composing, painting, chiseling, building, dancing, and so forth — with the help of his willing, what would be successful exactly to the extent that it were born, and exactly to the extent unsuccessful as it bore the traces of arbitrary will. If it is no longer granted him to work in a kind of somnambulism — which does in fact hold true for many achievements of primitive peoples, as likewise for certain art-periods of the past — then in him too there would wrest itself free, from the tragic double impulse of having to think what would escape through conceivedness and having to will what would escape through wantedness, a critique which, measuring on and on against image-laden urgencies (comparable to the pangs of pregnancy), compels him step by step to expunge again, with his will, from what has been achieved, whatever in it were made form instead of grown form, disguised gesture of the will instead of expression of life. "Fearful and consuming creation has become. Against arbitrary will it is to realize itself willing. In masterful fire the spirit breaks and hammers unmalleable masses. Wavering between impotence and cruelty it ploughs harvests of potsherds and tears the furrow deeper into a bloodthirsty earth. Therefore the blaze of martyrdom plays about the features of these latecomers of an earlier age, and as though over hollow-eyed gorges they seem to walk on dizzying footbridges."

But no one will deny the fruits of the sufferings and joys of its critique. For it is the works of image-making, whose attainment tears us back out of the sham-actuality of thought-things (= facts) into the actuality of images, while their non-attainment — stamped upon them as the disturbing element, of which since the "Renaissance" no image-work of however great significance remains free — may fittingly remind us that the merely conceived is a false actuality. Now, the precipitates of the deep will to truth are also works, namely in the medium of the word, and to the image-makers both belong, the researcher no less than the artist! What they attain in the service not of some new curiosity but of the voices from the depths of their soul, they attained because they were able, with the will, to lift up again what had been willed; and [p. 623] if accordingly we set the will to deed, as incompatible with it, over against the will to work, we wish thereby to have declared without reservation that the only possible life-affirming achievement of willing takes place through the self-negation of willing. What could not be a miracle wants to become a work; what could not be a work becomes a deed. — If we then return to willing in the narrower sense, or — excluding the will to work, the will to truth included — to the will to deed, then willing would henceforth be spoken of only insofar as the object of thought to be ascertained in judgement became dependent on purposes which the I posited wholly of its own authority. But before we examine more closely the purely arbitrary willing, let us once more touch upon its share in the thought-purposes of shallow reflection, and indeed first of all by characterizing a critique commonly so called, which departs so far from the one just considered that the introduction of different terms for the two would even be advisable. In this connection, however, we may be brief, since everything still to be added has largely been prepared at other places in the book, which the reader will recall without difficulty.

It is one thing to set the object of thought in relation to actuality, another to set it in relation to other objects of thought. Even if, for two judgements by which two objects of thought were found, the pull of actualities was decisive, yet for that judgement which combines both objects of thought with one another, the spirit's will to mastery may be decisive without the result necessarily being false. Now it is, to be sure, again thought-purposes and not the purposes — different in kind from these — of the mere person, that guide the zeal for research even of shallow reflection; but the drive, essentially a drive of appropriation, stands to personal egoisms only as the abstracted stands to the concrete, and therefore fulfills itself — unbeknownst to its bearer — by providing the takings-note, far different from essential truths, of which arbitrary will has need for the realization of its aims. If spiritual connecting is grounded in spiritual separating, and what testifies to the spirit's counter-action against life must therefore be sought in the thinking-activity of distinguishing, then it is a delimiting and, so to speak, planing, turning, tailoring critique on which the usual "progress of cognition" [p. 624] chiefly rests, by which in truth the will creates for itself ever-new footholds in order to extend its domain of power. Newton, for example, a type of shallow reflection paired with great acuity of spirit, undertook to delimit the concept of force against the concept of mass in such a way that both, as well as possible, should be suited to serve as computational units in the analysis of mechanically conceived courses of motion. He "defined" force, and likewise mass, being guided in doing so not by the question of what it actually was that people chose to call "force" and "mass," but by how it — assuming there were such a thing — had to be conceived in order, on the basis of certain simply-given magnitudes (constants), to calculate motions, whether of stars or of terrestrial bodies. Had he instead posed the question of deep reflection concerning the origin of both concepts, he would have received the strange answer that in the judgement that generates them there declares itself so ruthless a will to mastery of the spirit that they properly deserve to be called enemies of actuality. And had the more recent development of the spirit nonetheless continued on this course, we would today indeed have no technology, but also not the belief in a mathematically ordered course of the world, and hence also not the production of that same belief, within the reach of our will, through a devastation of the face of the earth in comparison with which all the misdeeds of the Genghis Khans seem like the foolish pranks of playing boys! Let one recall once more the mountain-moving power of that faith which is demanded in "holy scriptures"!

If the existing thing represents, so to speak, the point of intersection of being with actuality, then every erroneous judgement about things would also have to come into conflict with the thing itself. How, then, one might say, could concepts hostile to actuality assist in the successes of technology! But with this we have already arrived at the question which must occupy us briefly, in second place, with regard to shallow reflection — the question of the manner in which the objects of thinking are co-dependent on the purposes of thinking. Let one grasp hostility to actuality, for this purpose, especially in the sense of extreme one-sidedness, and one has gained the possibility, at the point of intersection of being with actuality, of preserving of the latter exactly as much as is needed in order to be able to — use it! A few deliberately crudely chosen examples shall illustrate this. We take, instead of the [p. 625] images themselves, the intuitive images, and choose as bearer of the capacity to mirror them as faithfully as possible, say, the highly significant landscape painter. And now let one set, comparingly in the mind, beside his apprehension of the boulder in the mountains that of the engineer who wishes to remove it by blasting; beside his apprehension of a grove that of the building speculator who wants to clear it; beside his apprehension of a waterfall that of the electrician who reckons it as a source of power for a rural powerstation — and in the monstrous divergence of their objects of apprehension one has a measure not only for the degree of dependence of the object of apprehension on the direction of the purposes of cognition, but at once also for the degree of the possible estrangement from actuality of the object of thought, with "objectivity" nonetheless preserved!

Whoever holds before his eyes the astonishingly sublime knowledge of facts that had to be incorporated in order to make it possible to grind lenses of more than a meter in diameter for the giant refractor, to carry out weighings accurate to a ten-thousandth of a gram, to sort out the planes of vibration of a ray of light and to penetrate into the structure of crystals far beyond the limit of visibility, to count the chromosomes, of microscopic minuteness, in the fertilized egg, or the wingbeats per second of the housefly, to discover the "hormones," the "vitamins," to measure electrical tensions of a hundredthousandth of a volt, to fix the curves in the photographic image and register the galvanic currents of inconceivable minuteness that accompany every muscular function of our body, indeed every however faint change of our state of soul ,<sup>12</sup> or finally to speak wirelessly from London to Adelaide — such a person might well think that only the most intimate feeling for actuality could enable such achievements. And indeed some feeling for actuality must actually exist for such things to become possible, and in one respect it must go far beyond that feeling for actuality which is allotted to us on the basis of our gift of intuition. Of this we shall speak repeatedly in the coming chapters. But the matter has another side. Let one call to mind a Greek gem of the best period, an old Chinese temple vase, an Egyptian, Persian, or Romanesque column capital, and one first finds oneself compelled to the admission that our capacity to build immeasurably artificial apparatus is paired with an incapacity to set beside those creations anything even remotely of equal worth. [p. 626] But let one immerse oneself in the sight, say, of an old Japanese sword-guard, listening closely to what it tells of the essence of cold-hammered iron, and one finds oneself further compelled to the still more revealing admission of having gained, of the material in question, a knowledge of a kind that one would never gain through the most thorough study of the whole of our metallurgy. Revolutions of the soul are experienced by one who sinks himself into the intuitive images of porphyry, granite, basalt, mica, amber, malachite, rock crystal, ruby, emerald, sapphire, sardonyx, chrysoprase, turquoise, opal, heliotrope, topaz, aquamarine, hyacinth, carbuncle, beryl, tourmaline; but he finds himself utterly abandoned by scientific mineralogy the moment he undertakes to give creative shape to what has thus been stirred up within him. Just as all the noises we enumerated in the twentieth chapter lay outside the domain of physical acoustics, so all the traits of character of stone that the cut chalcedony, the jade vase, the marble column capital can reveal to us lie outside the domain of mineralogy. Every significant landscape painter, be he Ruysdael or Claude Lorrain or Turner or Whistler or Böcklin, discovers with his paintings hitherto unknown essential traits of the atmosphere, and the scholar of art, faced with the frighteningly difficult task of characterizing them in words, would search in vain were he to try to borrow the words for it from physical optics! What would optics and aerodynamics know of the breathing of the air, of a stiff breeze, gusty weather, veiled distance, hovering fragrance, shimmering mist, seething atmosphere, sun-pierced expanse, "hyacinthine night," vast far-off distance, and what would European geometry, Euclidean as well as non-Euclidean, know of the distanceless depth of the merely apparent space that every East Asian painting of the master periods convincingly displays to us! — Thing-reflection and image-reflection unquestionably have but one point of intersection in common, while the directions in which the two range increasingly diverge from one another the longer they go on. If, now, actuality is image, then one will be able to gauge to what extent even the purely objective thought-purpose generates objects that speak less of actuality than of the activity of the spirit, and will know how to appraise, as is due, the degree and significance of the one-sidedness into which merely rational thinking unfailingly falls as a consequence of that dependence on the will which the voluntarist scholastics sensed, without, however, judging it correctly.

<sup>12</sup> On page 625. — The technical term for the galvanometric determinability of the faintest emotions is: psychogalvanic reflex phenomenon. According to the view of the authoritative specialists (Tarchanoff, Veraguth), the fluctuations of the galvanometer depend directly on changes in the secretory activity of the sweat glands; and it is this activity, in turn, that is intensified at one moment and diminished at another by every slightest change of mood. The „string galvanometer" of *Einthoven*, especially suited both for measuring „glandular currents" and for producing so-called cardiophonograms, employs, among other things, a silver-plated quartz thread whose diameter does not exceed 1/100 mm, though in the very finest instruments it amounts to as little as 1/225 mm! With the naked eye the thread can, as goes without saying, no longer be perceived at all! Such achievements of technology *border* not merely on the „miraculous," but are certainly no less marvellous than the „miracles" of an earlier humanity — only, to be sure, in a wholly opposite way.

[p. 627]

### Dritter Abschnitt — Tat und Wirklichkeit — Third Part — Deed and Actuality

#### 48. Kapitel — Zerlegung des Tatwillens — Chapter 48 — Analysis of the Will to Deed

If we now turn to the pure acts of arbitrary will within willing, we must take up again the thread where we began to uncover the purely negating sense of willing. But if what must be split off from the spirit, so that nothing but a commandable urge to movement remains, is the pull of images, then under no circumstances may we regard the strength of this pull as the immediate precondition of the deed that splits it off; rather we must seek that precondition in the strength of that in which the absence of the image announces itself — in the vehemence of privation. For did we not see, in the will to shape of every creative urge, the will to truth of deep reflection included, the will come into conflict with itself through effects, contrary to arbitrary will, of the pull of images! Were we to think it ever more strongly accentuated in the specific character of the impulse, then volition, supposing it had been able to arise at all, would yield either again to the sub-spiritual drive-impulse, or else to the state of ecstasy, which announces a becoming-one with the actuality of happening that is attained only at the far-beholding-capable stage of the soul. It is privation and not plenitude, disturbance and not concord, by which volition prepares itself in lived experience; and, conversely, it is volition that first of all permits the sense of the vital breach — which *also* makes the act of apprehension possible — to be illuminated down to its ground. For even the most violent emotion would not yet, without further ado, be [p. 628] that leap or rupture in which the spirit could, so to speak, nest itself, were the counter-urge against the hindering thing not to gain, within it, the preponderance over what is moving; and only by thinking the image-content of volition as unrestrictedly diminished, and, in proportion to that, the tension arising from the disturbedness of the life-process as retained, do we approach a state of vitality that allows, in a sense, the splitting-off of the pull of images. The question raised in the twenty-seventh chapter, "whether feelings might not be graded according to differences of degree in image-content, and might even perhaps fall apart generically according as, laden with images, they strengthen inwardness, or, violent in movement, they pave the way for their own splitting through the act of reflection," is accordingly to be affirmed without reservation. Whether the capacity for will is, now, more the consequence of desensualization or more of de-souling, it is grounded in any case in a loss of receptivity to images and of image-fecundity, and therefore compels us to grade the feelings themselves according to their image-content. We arrive at the capacity for will of vitality through the pairing of a deficiency in image-content — more briefly, through the pairing of poverty of kind with unbroken strength of impulse — or, to say the same thing in other words, through the overstraining of the, as it were, negating drive-moment of neediness at the cost of the, as it were, affirming desire. From this a few subsidiary traits of volition explain themselves, which up to now have been fundamentally misunderstood.

As surely as the view is peculiarly mistaken that volition forms the conclusion of an "affect" which in turn stems from a feeling, so surely does it not infrequently happen that it is violent surges that are released by energetic resolves, and again surges that at times lend their momentum to the action that develops out of them. For even though volition and surge are indeed wholly different in essence, such that the one excludes the other, still the capacity for will of the life-state is heightened by such surges with which the bearer of life answers disturbances of its impulse-curve. If it was precisely the foreign word "Affekt" that gave occasion to posit the property of "affectability" — in German, excitability, or better still, irritability — then the ever-truthful "genius of language" thereby betrays to us that the vehemence of impulse thought along with it must be understood predominantly not out of depth and fullness but out of the disturbability of lived experience. Certainly, animals too are irritable; but there is not the slightest doubt [p. 629] that, under otherwise comparable circumstances, *irritability* grows with the strengthening of I-hood, thus denoting, in the personal proper essence, precisely that trait so often felt to be objectionable, which the philosophers hoped, mistakenly, to counter with "ataraxia." By failing to recognize — walking in their footsteps — that every feeling of historical man has, besides its life-side, an I-side, and rather substituting the I-side for the life-side, one treated feelings of self-surrender and feelings of self-assertion according to the same scheme, confused the removal of deficiencies with fulfillment, and confused the delight in success that wells up from the successful warding-off of a disturbance with vital bliss or vital rapture. Thus the appearance could arise as though it were the state of feeling that, so to speak, culminates in the state of willing, whereas it is rather the, not infrequently affect-toned, rebound against experienced disturbances of self-assertion upon which, in the spirit-afflicted being, the act of will is able to follow. From this we gather (what had already become visible to us earlier from another quarter): in relation to the life-process, the I is reacting power and nothing but this. But we must go one step further.

If purposing consists in an urge that strives for the being of a non-being and consequently the non-being of a being, then it is only with the help of the act of will that we gain deeper insight into the uniquely isolating effect of the deed of the spirit, which we adumbrated on the occasion of the success of reflection over violently moved surges. Pressing toward the realization of a purpose, the I finds itself set not only out of happening actuality into a being actuality, but even moved out of the existent into a non-existent, which is accompanied by the tendency to detach the "content of consciousness" from the ever-present content of lived experience. We hit the state of affairs more sharply than with the explanation that the fighting soldier does not notice the wound he has received because he is wholly riveted by the sight of the enemy, if we say instead that it is because he has transformed himself wholly into the will to fend off the enemy. A being that were nothing but willing would find itself in a state of desensualization in comparison with which even Buddha under the Bodhi tree would remain an image-bound dreamer; and it is indeed high degrees of precisely this desensualization that underlie so-called black magic as well as every kind of asceticism hostile to undergoing. But prefigurations of this are already offered us by the sensory soul-blindness of every energetic employer, when, for example, he perceives absolutely nothing of the beauty or ugliness of a [p. 630] job applicant, but does perceive the pinpoint stain on his collar, which might give occasion to infer a lack of orderliness — or of the engineer who feels not the slightest thing of the sublimity of the fall of the current, which he nonetheless reckons, quick as lightning, in terms of "horsepower." We need only exchange for the state itself the characteristic feature of the state to recognize clearly that a being actually nothing but willing, being void of all images, would lose consciousness, and, out of the frenzy of its willing, would have ceased — to will; whereby, with respect to the act of will, there is fully disclosed to us, within spiritual activity, a tendency that would find its conclusion in the death of consciousness, or, expressed objectively, in the shutting-down of all happening.

Meanwhile, purpose-relatedness has the character of volition only because the lived experience of the counter-urge remained available, and the counter-urge is the only form of direction-determined impulse capable of existing only because it remains related to the thought of purpose. If in this way even the will-urge is a genuine urge to movement, which, according to the measure of its capability, would pass over into actual movements, and if the (intended) movement strives away from present lived experience and out into the non-existent, then the key to the consciousness of the future, and thus of dynamic time, must lie in the will-urge. Of this we shall give the most exact account.

Every stirring of drive of positive character is directed toward union with an image which, because itself capable of spatial appearance, also has its place in space, and therefore always unfolds itself in movements by which, quite properly, a disturbing Here is overcome. Every will-urge is directed toward a mere thought-thing which, however, has the peculiarity of hovering before us as something that ought to be, and would therefore — were it granted to it to realize itself without bodily mediation — overcome the present moment by leaving it *behind* it. If the drawing drive-goal, measured by thought-objective time, indeed belongs to the future, it is nonetheless, as we have seen, experienced as a spatial not-yetpresence. The absence, by contrast, of a goal that I have "set before" myself is temporal not-yet-presence; and if a consciousness kindling itself on stirrings of drive — supposing there were such a thing — could in no way avoid apprehending an arbitrary manifold of spatial directions, then reflection upon [p. 631] the class of objects of purposes must apprehend the one and only direction of time, and indeed as the direction of a movement out of space! The state of affairs becomes still clearer to us through a comparison of the reflection-on-thefuture thus to be grounded with the reflection-on-the-past already grounded earlier.

Were we to construct, in accordance with the space of the past, a space of the future (however little that might suit the core content of willing), the former would conflict with the impression-image of the present, the latter with the presentness of the impression-image. For there the stress would lie on the sense-spatiality of the phantasm, here entirely on its non-presentness. It is true that the impression-image always has the character of presentness, the moment's lived experience always also the character of impression; but one thing is the disturbance that the present impression suffers from a phantasm, another the disturbance that a wish-image suffers from the presentness of the impression. There the phantasm, out of incompatibility with the impression, finds itself driven back into the appearance-space to which it belongs, or at least could belong; here the Now would be pushed out by the phantasm into a never-before-experienced appearance-space, unless it knew how to assert itself. Where there the line of time became for us the space-analogically conceived distance between two appearance-spaces, here it would become for us the track-line of a movement by which an urge directed against the Now would come to release. — Both conceptions of time have rectilinearity in common with one another, for just as, for two experienced appearance-spaces, no differences of their relation to the bearer of life are conceivable other than differences of distance, so too for two purposes to be attained none other than those of earlier and later. But where-as, thanks to the static conception of time, the human spirit looks, so to speak, at a distance already covered, thanks to the dynamic conception of time it is related to the movement that constantly lengthens this very distance beyond the Now. Only thereby does the concept of time become independent.<sup>13</sup>

<sup>13</sup> On page 631. — But would it not follow from this that all directions of will run parallel to one another, and how would that agree with the fact that they so often „cross" one another? And further, how does the spatial location — which simply cannot be thought away — of *external* goals of will fit with the asserted futurity of *all* goals of will? If I intend to walk from place A to place B, the goal that hovers before me is unquestionably a spatial one! With the answer to the second question we shall at once have answered the first as well. — No realization of external goals of will is conceivable without some change in the outer world, even if it consisted only in the production of a signature; yet the goal does not have the character of purposiveness because it is attained only in the actuality of three-dimensionally extended space. The animal traverses the stretch from A to B with the help of drive-impulses, and even we, when we will it, are capable of carrying it out only because and insofar as the vital urge to movement is at our disposal, by means of which we could traverse that very same stretch even *without* any expenditure of will. The purposiveness of the walk we must seek, under the strictest exclusion of all spatially-related side-thoughts, solely in the fact that it was „undertaken" or „resolved upon," and thus, at the moment of the decision being reached, stands to the state of the one resolving, among other things, as something not-yet-present. Directions of will in fact cross one another just as little as do the lines of time that we think of as assigned to different points in space. The direction of will is that „direction as such" which gave us the impetus toward forming the concept of the straight line. It becomes a *determinate* direction only through projection onto intuitive space. The „crossings" we rightly think of, whenever the volitions of different bearers of will disturb one another, are spatial directions of the impulse-movements that are mobilized in the service of different purposes, or, more briefly: they are mutually „crossing" *actions*. Incidentally we see from this that the concept of the straight line *originally* concerns the course of the time that is an object of thought, and only comes to concern space as well through connection with data of intuition. In order to arrive at the concept of the direction that is an object of thought, we must, to be sure, take as our basis the — invariably spatial — lived experience of direction, which, as goes without saying, the animals have in common with us; but from that alone the former could no more be gained than the concept of the (mathematical) point through even the most far-reaching diminution of intuitive images. Rather, just as the point is the I objectified on the *occasion* of intuitive images, so the direction that is an object of thought is the purposive relatedness of the I *objectified on the occasion* of impulse-directions. The straight line that is an object of thought presupposes the dynamic concept of time, and this, in turn, presupposes the experience of volition! We shall return to this repeatedly.

The equation set up earlier — sense-space = the Now to be experienced — allowed us to recognize in sense-space the immediate precondition for the finding of existence, and of the duration inseparable from it, and at any rate an indispensable one for the finding of the Now, but it could not instruct us as to why the Now, whenever it is thought, is by no means generally identified with the space of intuition; and we did not fail [p. 632] to state in advance that, with the consciousness of the line of time, the consciousness of its dependence on the dimensions of space gets lost. We now know whence it comes that the object of time detached itself from the object of space. If volition aims at something not-yet-present, then its direction of unfolding separates itself from every spatial direction and thus from space itself, and, with the consciousness of purpose, there steps into the place of the space-analogous, the space-opposed dynamic time, as the condition for the realization of an urge to movement dammed up at the Now.

In it we have the foundation of measurable time and consequently of the time-object itself. Measurable time lies "before" us and lies "behind" us as a line which forms, if not the actually surviving, then at least the thought trace of a movement, as it were, of the world-whole — a movement that, in accordance with the purpose-relatedness of the will, goes from the past into the future. The consciousness of time accordingly leads back to the following elements of its possibility of existing. — Were what has hitherto emerged only at the fringe of our investigations, actuality-time, not experienced — however darkly — there would be no succession of occurrences and hence no thought-objective time at all. But if, to the lived experience of actuality-time, that is, of passing as such, we add the standing space of intuition, and the readiness to slip away that attaches, in relation to it, to every content of impression, we obtain the static line of the past, or the sequence of appearance-spaces that are merely still recollectable. Only in the state of willing, however — which is the state of aiming at something that ought to be — does the ever-presentness of the space of intuition become, so to speak, a prison for us, out of which it presses us away, and, as a consequence, the ground that makes possible the intuitability of the manifold of present-qualities detaches itself from that manifold: the Now. And because, in the thought-objective Now, the anticipation of the not-yet-existent breaks against the barrier of what actually exists, the line of the past transforms itself into the line of time "in itself," which — most nearly comparable to a ray — shares with the spatial line only being-directed (here, however, into the future). Seen from the side of dynamic thinking, time is a "rectilinearly" ceaselessly advancing Now-point, and every time-"stretch" is the space-analogically conceived distance between two (thought-objective) Now-points; whereby, then, the deeper ground inquired after in the fifth chapter for the necessity [p. 633] of the spatial straight line for the purpose of measuring thought-objective time as well was at once ascertained. If the spirit fixes and only fixes, that is, sets boundaries, or — with regard to time — apprehends merely *points* of time, then it must first of all borrow from space the being-outside-one-another, in order by means of the points of time to grasp time itself. But the thought-objective straight line — as surely as it cannot be thought without the being-outside-one-another — is direction as such, and "direction as such" is the lived content of the willing being-related to the purpose, seen through the medium of the space of intuition. What is *conceived* of the phenomenon of time, and hence, to be sure, of actuality itself, thus proves to be an objectity of willing, or a precipitate of the change that the eternity of passing suffers within the field of action of the will. — If finally we join the detached time-object once more to the detached space-object, following upon it, we obtain the four-dimensional manifold, or, intuitively conceived, the space that grows unceasingly with the "progress" of time.<sup>14</sup>

<sup>14</sup> On page 633. — On p. 30 of the first volume it was said: „With the concept of the temporal span, the extratemporal object is falsely inserted into real time, or, more correctly, this latter itself is described, though as viewed through the stratum, alien to it, of passing away." We have just now presented the identical state of affairs from the opposite side, but now more precisely, no longer merely as the objecthood of spirit, but of will. Of the space that is an object of thought, or geometrical space, it was said on p. 317 of the first volume that it is at bottom „a present stretched apart". Since we have meanwhile once more, in the experience of volition, pointed out *the* component of the experience of the present which was able to lead to the detachment of this present from intuitive space and thereby to the formation of the (mathematical) concept of the now, the following series of inner dependencies has become certain for us. Time appears to us as a space-analogous straight line with the direction from the past into the future, insofar as we set out from the now that is an object of thought, the „archetype" of the time-point as such; and we feel ourselves driven to do so because, in relation to volition, the *lived* presentness acquires the character of the barrier of an urge which, by its very nature, thrusts beyond any given now, so to speak. If, according to the static conception of time, the time of actuality became a present stretched apart, then, according to the dynamic conception of time, it becomes an unceasingly advancing now-point. But if, accordingly, happening is nullified there just as much as here, it will only in what follows emerge ever more sharply just how far it is precisely the command of will that must be understood solely as the absolute *interruption* of the time of actuality.

We can confirm through self-reflection that, in the vital foundations of our conception of time, now a static, now a dynamic side predominates. Whoever finds himself in a state of lively planning experiences the ever-present moment as a resistance that he would like to drive before him at an ever faster tempo; which finds expression, among other things, in the fact that, if engaged in walking, he involuntarily falls into an ever faster stride, but if sitting, involuntarily feels the urge to rise, in order to pace up and down the room. Whoever, by contrast, finds himself in the state of remembering experiences the moment as the closing point of a line along which his movement, so to speak, gropes its way back into the temporal depth of space; which correspondingly finds expression in the fact that, engaged in walking, he involuntarily strides ever more slowly, or even feels the urge to stop and sit down. It is not by chance that predominantly contemplative antiquity meditated almost exclusively on space and scarcely at all on time, and further made movement the object of penetrating investigations without troubling itself particularly about differences of speed, whereas the voluntarism of Christianity grounds all thinking about happening on the concept of acceleration (Galileo), and is henceforth led, by the ever-increasing need for the measurement of time (and time-utilization , to the invention of ever [p. 634] more artificial chronometers. With still greater sharpness, finally, the opposition of the static and the dynamic conception of time reveals itself in the deliberate reflecting-back upon something past.

If someone finds himself, in the face of a memory-image that at first surfaces involuntarily, prompted to reflect quite precisely on the course of the matter, he will be able, by looking back at every enforced halting-point, to ascertain two states directed against one another: the state of groping one's way back along the line of time, and, incompatible with it, the state of pressing against the momentary Now-point for the sake of realizing the purpose of reflection. Out of the making-present of a moment of the past he is torn again and again back into the moment of the present, off which he rebounds, as it were, with force, in order to bore himself anew into the past. Scarcely anything can shape itself more tormentingly, as the becoming-aware of the powerlessness of the will, than when an effort of recollection remains fruitless in important particulars; whence stems the transitorily almost despairing mood into which one can fall on unsuccessfully trying to recollect a name, a date, a remark — as well as the feeling of paralysis that sometimes takes hold of sensitive natures in an examination, after they have been condemned to remain silent on two or three questions. However wrong an answer may be, it cannot by far be measured, in its depressing effect on self-feeling, against — no answer at all. This may lead us at once to the final clarification of recollecting.

Involuntary recollecting, as we had shown, presupposes the capacity for voluntary recollecting; voluntary recollecting happens with the help of acts of self-reflection; but the act of self-reflection is rooted in the life-conditions not of apprehending but of willing. If, accordingly, that precondition of remembering by virtue of which a phantasm of the past, instead of merely making itself present (dream) or imparting to the impression the coloring of recognizedness or, finally, of mere familiarity, is entered into the now nearer, now more distant past, were to lie in willing, we would arrive at the strange conclusion that the lowest occasioning ground of reflection-on-the-past must be sought in the conditions of reflection-on-the-future. This is in fact the case, and incidentally reveals to us why one so often involuntarily hit upon illustrating the process of will by an effort of recollection — namely, by trying to recollect a [p. 635] name that has slipped one's mind! The conceptual degree of clarity of the formation of past-consciousness corresponds exactly to the conceptual degree of clarity of the formation of future-consciousness, and a deficient formation of the concept of the future regularly goes together with an apprehension of the past that might be termed near-sighted apprehension, and can be attested, both linguistically and cultically, for all primitive peoples. In original man the making-present of the past, e.g., with the assumption of ancestral souls still living on and effective, far outweighs the assumption of their having-been-past, and the "historical sense," which finds its satisfaction in ever more complete registers of data, develops as a law-governed counterpart to the overemphasis on purposing and planning. The verb was originally, generally, a word of process and effect, and is even today, in the Indo-European languages that relate most strongly to time, only incidentally a "time-word."
