But the demand — at first appearing peculiar — to think the static consciousness of the past as mediated by a dynamic consciousness of the future loses much of its strangeness once we take into account that thanks to the former we are related to a no-longer-existent, thanks to the latter to a not-yet-existent, and thus in both cases to a now-non-existent;<sup>15</sup> and it is clarified fully by the review, offered here once more, of the process of finding.

<sup>15</sup> On page 635. — The close interconnection of the consciousness of the past with the consciousness of the future, and likewise conversely, expresses itself most clearly in the fact that, starting from a point represented as past, one is able to grasp the stretch of time up to the now-point also as future, and, starting from a point represented as future, the stretch of time from now up to it also as past; wherein the linguistic forms of the pluperfect and the future perfect have their ground.

We had earlier set forth that in the perception, carried out with consciousness, of something existent there already lies potentially also the knowledge of the succession of its moments of existence, because existence cannot be thought without duration of existence, and because the vital ground that makes possible the apprehension of existence, namely presence, must be understood as a "cross-section" of having-been. We now add the psychological clarification of why, with complete reflection generally, reflection on time necessarily becomes actual. If reflection consists in the pairing of the act of apprehension with the act of judgement — that is to say, with an act of will accomplished on the occasion of apprehension and for the purpose of securing its object — then no finding of existence can be accomplished without the participation of that urge, damming itself up at the Now, which would of itself violently drive the moment before it, were it not held back by the latter's weight of actuality. But if the impulse underlying the act of judgement has, so to speak, *struck against* the Now, then every "ascertainment" must be able, now immediately, now mediately, to be referred to the [p. 636] line of time that ends at the Now-point and aims beyond it. Finding of existence is finding of the Now, because it is, out of the co-participation of a volition, finding of resistance; and the I-am-reflection makes possible the I-was-reflection precisely because it itself was kindled by the lived experience that, raised into consciousness, would yield the I-will-bereflection. But this no more calls into question the independence of reflection on the past than does its connection with reflection on the I. For it suffices for the I that any mere resonance of the lived experience of actuality within the lived experience of the resisting force of being should occur, in order to measure back, remembering, along the line of time, while disregarding entirely its dynamic character.

With the help of the equation: sense-space = the experienceable Now, we explained, among other things, why the static past lies behind us. If, by contrast, the space lying before us sometimes seems to possess less the character of presentness than the character of futurity, this rests of course on the transition from the static to the dynamic conception of time, and on the transfer, attaching itself thereto, of the movement of the Now-point onto the movement, usually directed forward, of our body. But note that it is by no means its remoteness, but only our moving-toward it, that lends the forward vanishing-point the significance of a point of the future. For there is indeed a genuine remoteness of the past, but by no means of the future; more on this later.

Having already earlier stressed the imperative use of the declarative sentence, it will scarcely be necessary to recall that in the same meaning, in numerous languages, the future tense is used all the more emphatically. With a "You will present yourself there at such and such a time" we even reinforce the command that would lie in "You are to present yourself." In Latin the future originally served to denote wishing; in French it not infrequently stands for possibility and probability. If in English it is even built up with the help of the will-and shall-forms, this betrays the dependence of future-consciousness on purpose-consciousness. — Let one finally call to mind the immediate effect of a sharply commanding call, and, in light of what has been set forth, one will feel able to eavesdrop from closest proximity on the detachment of Nowreflection from the intuition of sense-space, and hence on the emergence of abstract time-consciousness. No natural event, were it even the striking bolt of lightning, interrupts the pulsing of happening with so gathered [p. 637] and gathering a suddenness as the properly announced command: Attention — Ready — Stand still — Shoulder arms — March! etc., which may serve us as a kind of symbol of the act itself and of its dagger-thrust-like effect. The fortunate man for whom "no hour strikes" would be torn, by nothing more irresistibly, into the wakefulness of a Now that could be described as nothing better than the most violent disturbance of his happiness by an insurmountable barrier of expiry. Or let one think of the crack of the pistol that signals to the runners standing "ready to start" that they must now — and not a quarter-second later! — begin to run, and one has, as it were, illuminated through and through the connection that obtains between the experienced relatedness to what-ought-to-be and the lived experience of the Now that furnished the spirit with the material for forming the concept of the Now and hence of the concept of time itself. The more we withdraw hoping and willing from the proper essence, the more its present loses the high tone of the Now and approaches once more the actuality-form of the undelimitable wave; and, conversely, it becomes a painfully spurring goad, an ever-and-again-renewing starting shot, and, as it were, the beginning of a race with happening itself, for him who stands under the spell of willing and ought-ing. But what else would duties and the fetters of one's calling be, and what could more effectively chop time into pieces! And here let one admire the unbreakable logic of the inner connections! It was, in contrast to an antiquity that remained still contemplative, the deification of the will by Christianity that called into life the time-measuring, and consequently time-chopping, law-language of the "natural sciences," and it was again Christianity that made of the equally glorified forced labor a time-devouring time-machine, and might fittingly set over every gate of its temples of Mammon, as inscription, the famous article of faith: "Time is money!"

If in such effects the life-destroying nature of arbitrary will confronts us with alarming clarity, the following consideration shows us no less clearly its estrangement from actuality. If we give the proverb, invoked above, of the wish as the father of the thought the turn that it is expectation that is the cause of deception, it reveals to us, in the will-urge, the neverdrying source of untutorable illusions, in comparison with which the dreams of impractical "enthusiasts" pale into graceful shadow-plays. Because the will is satisfied by success alone, and because the making-present of success, which hastens ahead of its realization, [p. 638] has as its object something purely unreal, the will-urge carries with it constant deceptions — partly concerning the nature and controllability of the course of events, partly, and far more so, concerning the degrees of capability of the one willing. Let the understanding recoil from the impossible as it may, the will suggests to it a thousandfold the possibility even of the impossible, and if anything finally breaks mankind's neck, it is the optimism of success of men of will, among whom, again, programmatic world-improvers are the most dangerous of all. — If finally we alter the phrase in question as follows: expectation is the cause of illusion of the senses, we have ascertained the occasioning ground, left open earlier for one half, of if not all, then at least many deceptive perceptions and hallucinations.

Do I not hear the little gate go? / Did not the bolt clink? / No, it was the blowing of the wind, / That whirs through these poplars

Beginning thus, Schiller's extraordinarily beautiful poem "Die Erwartung" carries through, with great consistency, the thought that the expectation of an event is apt to feign the occurrence of that same event. Here, to be sure, it is merely a matter of a feeling of tension that prompts the dream-sense to paint images of fulfillment, which bring with them swiftly self-correcting reinterpretations of the contents of perception. The animal too already undergoes something of this kind, on another plane. Different is the expectation which, bound up with the uncertainty of success of the far-flung goals of willing, colors the life of man — and only of man — with hopes and fears shimmering through almost everywhere, and can in this way entirely blur even the colors of the objects of perception. If the swaying-over of the I from sense-space into dream-space forms the reverse side of the liveliness, strength, and distinctness of phantasms, then, for the imaging-in of phantasms into the space of intuition, we have to seek the cause far less often in the liveliness of the phantasms than in the loss of actuality of images *altogether*, thanks to the enfeeblement of the faculty of cognition through an everready-to-spring intentionality. Fantasy and the magic of memory work together on the fabric of the world of appearance and can, given an overemphasized readiness for making-present, [p. 639] feign semblance-images of the character of impressions; but the chief source of deceptive perceptions and hallucinations lies not in the strength of these, but in the paleness and bloodlessness of the sense-space of a soul whose power of beholding has been extinguished by perpetual aiming-at. The more the actuality of images is displaced by the sham-actuality of purposes (and wishes), the more grows the danger that the object of perception itself be displaced by hoped-for or feared contents of expectation of willing, before whose meager sensory garment there no longer pales the splendor of the world of appearance, but merely its shadowy, dim reflection in an almost blinded mirror. — Oskar Wilde, whose admirable cleverness was denied path-breaking findings only because he lacked the consuming passion of cognition, has strewn his writings abundantly with the gold-dust of tempting paradoxes, of which, all the same, more than one proves to hold up under trial: "Action... is grounded in the want of imagination; it is the last refuge of those who do not know how to dream." And: "When one day, with the help of science, we have come to know all the laws that govern life, we shall become aware that only *one* man has more illusions than the dreamer: namely, the man of action." And: "But we do not wish... to speak any further of the infamous friends of man, whom we may truly leave to the mercy of the wise Chuang Tsu, the almond-eyed philosopher of the Yellow River, who demonstrated that these well-meaning but calamity-working world-improvers have destroyed the simple, innocent virtue that lies in man."

[p. 640]

#### 49. Kapitel — Wollung und Handlung — Chapter 49 — Volition and Action

The investigation of arbitrary will — more precisely, of that side of the volitional process by which alone the efficacy of spirit attests itself — required an extraordinarily far-reaching abstraction from the conditions under which willing is realized; and the appraisal of these conditions, now called for, leads us back to the vital side of volition. We have seen how it is possible that, in the moment of decision, the movement-urge, having become devoid of quality, should remain related to the commanded goal; but we still wish to learn how it is possible that it should also act in the direction of this goal. The assumption that there are two wholly different kinds of acting — one purely inner or mental, by which, for example, we do mental arithmetic, and one purely outer or bodily, by which, for example, we lift weights — will later prove to stand in need of so thoroughgoing a revision that we must call it essentially misleading. Here let only the following remark be sent ahead. Whoever attempts to recall the state he was in during any act of thinking whatsoever will either have to renounce any characterization of it altogether, or will have to admit that he was, throughout, caught up in an abruptly advancing change of bearing, itself grounded in a change of state that could only be described as an inner movement — even though he may have been lying bodily on the couch the while. Only a being capable of inner movements is also capable of outer movements (and likewise conversely), and only a being that produces inner movements spontaneously can also produce outer movements spontaneously (and again conversely). If, accordingly, it seems that in the realization of will everything always comes down to movements, we shall nonetheless choose the movements of the body — movements that are at the same time intuitable — in order to come closer to the process by which will is realized.

[p. 641] In another respect too we wish to simplify the problem. We have established that, and why, the will is as it were constantly bent on instilling in its bearer the belief in the possibility of the impossible. But since an analysis of acting must naturally be grounded in deeds that actually take place and not merely imagined deeds, we shall in principle prefer those volitions whose realization lies within the bounds of the personality's capacity, and in doing so we shall hardly go wrong in expecting that we shall come to know the conditions of failure as well, once we have learned to know those of success. — If it is true — and our discussions of the relation of the impulse of will to the drive-impulse left no doubt of it — that the effect of the act consists not in the generation of a movement-urge but in the fixing of the direction in which a movement-urge runs its course, then every investigation of the grounds that make acting possible must proceed from a truth that has remained unrecognized to this day, and that, put in the form of an equation, runs: willing-to-do = willing-not-tolet-happen. Contrary to a most ancient and universally spread prejudice, the command of spirit belongs no more among the driving forces of the commanded activity than the holding of a course belongs among the causes of the walker's steps. Were we to look about for a simile, we should find none better than the comparison of the bearer of life to a ship, of the movement-impulses to the oarsmen or to the wind that fills the sails, and of the will to the rudder. The simile is defective, because it could naturally arouse the quite erroneous suspicion that the equally goal-determined drive-impulses lack steering; and it is defective further for a reason to be touched on only later. But if we think of one of the enchanted Phaeacian ships that steer themselves, we shall probably have come as close to the state of affairs being compared as can be achieved at all with the help of a simile.

The prejudice that the will drives, when it only directs the rudder, is explained by the tendency of our craving for omnipotence to believe it so, but it knows how to make itself out to be right before reason with the help of at least three states of affairs. First, every willing is a willing-to-do, and in willing-to-do we, in keeping with the activity of the I, are apt to think of the carrying out of movements, as if only these were its expression, and forget in doing so that the willing-tosit-still, the willing-to-be-silent, the willing-to-think-of-nothing [p. 642] are likewise kinds of willing-to-do, whose ends moreover sometimes require a far greater expenditure of will than their respective opposites. When, for example, according to the legend, Tell refused to pay reverence to Gessler's hat, this required a hundredfold stronger power of decision and "energy" than taking a detour would have. The activity of the I that lies in willing-to-do demands expression, and in that expression moments of movement naturally appear even when the end consists entirely in the suppression of movements.<sup>16</sup> But to this something else is added. A willing-to-do could not arise at all were a movement-impulse not already present. Now since this movement-impulse, though it can indeed be sharply distinguished from the command of spirit, cannot be separated from it, and in the lived experience of its exercise works together with it step by step (for which reason the vital movement would really deserve to be called the vehicle of willing), it was bound to appear altogether as though it were the willing I that generated the movement — quite as we say of the builder that he built the house, when in fact he only drew up the plans, leaving the activity of building to the carpenters and masons. — Finally — last not least — between the I and the goal of its willing there lies the distance, as it were, "in itself," or a not-yet-presentness of the ought-to-be, stripped of all data of intuition; as a consequence of which the only movement-intensity still available is transformed, thrustlike, into a straight-line aiming at the objective purpose — or, that is, the no-longer-available pull of distance is exchanged for a state of affairs that one might be tempted to call a mere directional energy. Just as a river we have canalized traverses the stretch from source to sea more quickly, because it is prevented from meandering in bends and spreading out into side channels, so the movement of arbitrary will likewise reaches its goal more quickly than the movement of drive, because it is prevented by the end-positing command of spirit from following the constant vibrations of the impulses of life and "letting itself go" without restraint. But just as the canal walls are not causes of the movement, so too the purpose is no cause of movement. If, notwithstanding this, the purpose belongs among the conditions of the heightened goal-directedness of the impulse-movement just as surely as the canal walls belong among the conditions of the acceleration of the flow of the water masses, then one readily sees why the act of will could be confused with the driving force. To what extent our entire picture of the world was thereby falsified [p. 643] will disclose itself to us overwhelmingly only in the next two chapters, where we shall furnish proof that the basic concepts of mechanics are branches derived from the lived experience of willing-to-do — as tools, that is, of that "exploitation" of the planet earth which would appear destined to end in the destruction of all organisms.

<sup>16</sup> On page 642. — From someone's speaking we conclude quite generally that he wanted to speak, but not equally generally, from his silence, that he did not want to speak, although silence sometimes requires far more effort of will than does speaking, as for instance when someone is restless or has to listen to the most dreadful stupidities. Precisely for this reason, however, wanting-to-be-silent, too, is a wanting-to-do and as such expressive. — A linguistically-historically curious piece of evidence for this, with regard to linguistic expression, is given us by the custom, usual in Sweden, of thinking of complete self-quieting as represented by the sound sipp (pronounced tsib). „When the Swede wants a child to sit prettily silent and upright at table, he admonishes it: You must say sipp!" From: Georg von der Gabelentz, Die Sprachwissenschaft, Leipzig 1891, p. 164.

It remains all the more remarkable that at least the German language expresses the thoroughly goal-directed and fixating character of the will with a consistency that does not even allow the customary exception by which, as the saying goes, the rule is proved. One says of feeling, but not of the will, that it is aroused; one speaks of agitations, surgings, emotions, of shock, violent passion, stormy joy, blazing wrath, raging fury, irresistible craving, of unfetteredness and unbridledness — namely of desire — whereas the more-than-ordinary energy of will, far from being called blazing, unfettered, or shattering, is made known by the following principal words and epithets: strong will, tenacious will, steadfast will, iron will, steely will; firmness, steadfastness, constancy, endurance, perseverance, imperturbability, unwaveringness, unshakeableness of will, power of resistance, singleness of purpose! These are one and all names for a power or force that thwarts being-moved and has not-letting-happen as its consequence; hence with respect to it, deflectability and lack of self-possession count precisely as defects of its capacity! Indeed, by pairing any words that at least co-designate a mobility or displaceability, or even merely the conditions thereof, with their respectively opposite terms, one can determine, for whole series of supposed or actual character-traits, whether they would impair or favor the strength of will. The parts of what is hard, for example, are immovable relative to one another, those of what is soft movable relative to one another; and so hardness in the characterological sense is akin to will, softness on the other hand contrary to will. Cold makes things rigid, warmth softens and spreads; so cold in the characterological sense is akin to will, (warmth of heart) at least ill-suited to support unwaveringness of willing. In an altogether convincing way we find our guiding principle confirmed by the use of the little word "purpose" solely and exclusively for goals of will. Did it not originally mean the center of the target (also called [p. 644] "Zwecke"), which the aiming marksman has any prospect of hitting only if he suppresses every wavering of arm and hand!

Should our example of the steering of the ship for illustrating the performance of the act of will seem after all to be even surpassed by the example of the aiming marksman, it would nonetheless have to be noted that in this case too a steering of movement takes place. Whether we choose the marksman in the state of taking aim, or merely the gazing of the eye in the state of so-called fixating, it is in every case a matter of the setting of a movement into the direction of an object perceived with consciousness. And however great the difference may otherwise be between the movement toward the object and the mere aiming at it, the willed-ness of the process lies without exception in the fettering that a movement undergoes by being compelled to hold to one and the same direction — whether through the arresting of the movement of the arm or eye, or through the prevention of a departure from the direction that the movement of the arm or foot has taken. Steering of movement is and remains the vital achievement of the willing act.

But how could steering of movement through the activity of spirit be *possible*? How can spirit force a movement, occurring out of impulses, into a direction, and how can it even so much as compel it to persist in this direction, when no moving forces whatsoever stand at its disposal, and accordingly no forces whatsoever to arrest something caught up in movement?! The answering of this question makes an intervening consideration of the structure of ends seem desirable, to which we shall first send ahead a recollection of the limits of arbitrary will. — Having presented, in connection with the disclosure of a conflict within every volition with a goal exacted by life, the new finding that it is realized only in proportion to the self-negation of willing, we arrived, for arbitrary volition, at the defining proposition that the acts of apprehension it too requires are performed in the service of the end that the I itself has posited. But if no steering of attention alters what is apprehensible itself, if no steering of the course of thought can annihilate the compulsion that relating, connecting, and distinguishing undergo from the principle of sameness, then we see arbitrary will too pervaded by an oppositely constituted conflict of the same kind, insofar as it may hope to reach its [p. 645] ends only by the accomplishment of objective movements. Just as the executing movements of work-willing break again and again against spirit, so those of will-to-deed break again and again against actuality. I may cherish the wish to fetch the moon down from the sky, because it would seem delightful to me to hold it in my hand; but I cannot normally form the resolve to do so, because that would require belief in the practicability of the thing proposed. In keeping with its estrangement from actuality, the will engenders the most monstrous illusions; in keeping with its enmity to actuality, it seeks to master actuality, and for that it requires that knowledge of actuality with regard to which we repeatedly had to stress that even end-consciousness presupposes mediate relatedness to a world of facts, whose will-independent side finds convincing expression in the declarative sentence.

Passing on from this to the structure of ends, we distinguish the nearest end in each case from the ultimate intention. Let my willing extend to the writing of a letter, to the setting out on a journey, to the closing of a deal, to the building of a machine, to the climbing of a mountain, to an election speech, to the founding of a party, to the improvement of school instruction, to the reshaping of the state, to the making happy of mankind, or to whatever else — of the individual steps of will that even the most distant ultimate end makes necessary, none reaches, immediately, further than the grasp of my hand or the call of my mouth. To be sure, we can make ourselves understood by telephone across hundreds of kilometers; but even for this we must turn the crank, take up the receiver, and speak, entrusting the propagation of the sound to an apparatus that we are not able to master in the same way as our arms or our speaking tongue — as every disruption teaches us, which, very much against our will, brings the conversation to a premature end. (Even "radio" makes no essential exception in this regard!) However terrible the machine of murder may be whose ruin-bringing efficacy a single push or pull of a lever may suffice to "release," *without* that push or pull absolutely nothing at all would happen, and what happens through it we by no means have in hand in the same way as the push or pull itself. A war may be planned and prepared for years; its outbreak requires, among other things, the signature under a declaration of war, for which a pen and a writing hand are needed; and [p. 646] from this moment on, until its ending after years or decades, among the billions of acts of will of all those involved, there is not one whose immediate range is greater than that of the hand that signed that document, or than the sound of a human mouth.

We need only think of this to find it understandable why the opinion could arise that it is precisely the technician, the practical man, and above all the doer in the narrowest sense, who is the true man of actuality, whereas the theorist, on the other hand — the ponderer, the speculator, the "penslinger" and "bookworm," indeed the researcher, scholar, artist, and poet — is a stranger to actuality, a nowhere-dweller. Whoever wishes not merely to plan and build castles in the air, but to carry out his intentions, must remain unceasingly, with the utmost wakefulness and sobriety, "at the matter," because every forward-flying elaboration of pleasant possibilities, every roving deviation from the very nearest end, indeed every purposeless letting of one's thoughts wander, would expose him to the danger of letting an irretrievable opportunity slip by! He finds himself in a permanent state of being dammed up against the counter-pressure of the world of facts, to which he is thereby continually related, and it is for this very reason that he remains protected from that aberration of thought that has so often proved fatal to the merely inwardly willing theorist. If I wish to wage war, I must first of all sign the declaration of war or give the one command; if I wish to improve school instruction, I must at a definite hour, in a definite place, enter into negotiations with definite persons, or, here and now, draft a decree, and so on; whereas the general called war, the general called schooling, indeed even the narrower general of precisely this war, of precisely this schooling, forms no object of my acting (though it does of my willing). The doer, as doer, has to do everywhere and without exception with the locally and temporally determinate individual case, and hence with its unrepeatable particularity, and would fail the moment he let himself be tempted to reify properties and states ideologically. While I make redness, pallor, color, warmth, sound, light, magnetism, or passion, justice, truth, or similarity, manifoldness, sameness, or society, the state, crime, or science, poetry, technology, into the object of the most intense reflection (and, to be sure, also of my willing), it is unavoidably the most determinate individual cases [p. 647] on which something bearing on such concepts can be purposively realized. The doer *as* doer is never a Platonist, but invariably a "materialist"; and however often ideologues have also been doers, it was not by virtue of their ideology that they accomplished deeds — even where they were shattered against it a hundred times over. The object of the deed is what can be seized and grasped; but we have seen that it is precisely actuality that can never be conceived and grasped, and we shall presently see more exactly what other abstractive operation (than the idealist one) must be performed so that of actuality that handle remains which the doer makes use of in order to shatter actuality.

Since a single step of will does not yet mean realization of the intention, it stands, together with all the following steps of will, in the relation of means to end. To say that whoever wills the end must also will the means is to say that the one who wills must first of all bring about certain circumstances that would in turn be capable of effecting the circumstance he has set before himself. The chain of intermediate links may be almost boundlessly long: its reckoning is a matter merely of relating thought, whereas the act of will always consciously calls into existence only the very nearest link of the chain. But that is an achievement of the body of the acting person. We accordingly know, at least in principle, about the practicability of willing, as soon as we have recognized the ground of possibility even of, say, a deliberate stretching-out of the arm; with which we pass over to the main question, which we can now put as follows: how does the willed execution of any movement whatsoever differ, inwardly, from the unwilled execution of that same movement, and how is the former able to reach its goal at all, when neither driving nor inhibiting forces inhere in the thought of the end?

We put natural processes to conceptual use for the purpose of manufacturing an explosive. If now the natural happening that we conceive as a boulder is to be removed, we bring the explosive near it and annihilate the natural force "boulder" by means of the natural force "explosion." Something exactly analogous occurs inwardly in every execution of a movement of arbitrary will. The goal-related movement-urge, namely, which remains after the splitting-off of all the specific marks of a living impulse, proves on closer inspection to be a double urge, divided within itself. If the phrase that an urge, and not merely a consciousness, is related to [p. 648] the end is to have any sense at all, it can only be this: that the urge is now accompanied by a counter-urge, which forces it back again and again into the direction aimed at. But since *this*, of course, likewise stems from the original urge, the deed of spirit that separated the pull of images from the living impulse must itself have split that impulse into two mutually conflicting impulses. This looks like something new, but is, in new lighting, only a state of affairs long since dealt with by us. If one grants that we, in thinking, are related to what is, and bound to our knowledge of what is, one must also grant that this same boundness has the form of a check on the course of our impulses, and hence the form of counter-impulses constantly asserting themselves, insofar as we will something; hence it is a matter of indifference whether we say that volition consists in the fact-boundness of an impulse, or that it consists in the existence of those counter-impulses in which, for all impulses alike, the resistance of facts takes effect. If we earlier called drives vital causes of movement, and mainsprings causes of will, we can now also designate the mainsprings as drives to which the counter-impulse in question is attached, and the will itself as the universal inhibitory mainspring.

Should one suppose that this after all still ascribes a motor efficacy to spirit, one would have confused the splitting of a vital cause of movement with the splitting of a mechanical cause of movement. If I wish to use a portion of the "energies" of the river to drive mills, I must bring some mechanical forces into play, for example erect a weir against which the water is dammed, dig a side channel, and the like. If, by contrast, the vital cause of movement lies in the pull of the impulse's goal, then the knowledge of the resistance of facts *must* likewise be capable of forming the occasioning ground of inhibitory impulses, if the undeniable state of affairs of human being-able-to-will is to remain conceivable at all. With this, to be sure, we have now taken hold of the root of the unresolved, and probably unresolvable, riddle of the coupling of spirit with life. For it is evident that there could no longer be talk of the relatedness of a mere consciousness to objects, and then no longer of consciousness itself, were not all that is apprehensible transformed, through the act of judgement, into inhibitory impulses, and the impression-experience itself thereby first turned into the process of the perception of the time-related [p. 649] thing. Only because, occasioned by the impression, the act of judgement accomplishes on an impulse exactly what the act of will accomplishes spontaneously, does there exist the steered thinking of human consciousness, and logical compulsion is, in the end, the consequence of an inner action, even if an exacted one. For the penetration of spirit into the organic space of life, accordingly, the last attainable condition of life lies in the splittability of the impulse-force of the drives — a splittability that, for its part, indeed first enters together with, and by way of, the splitting-off of their specific character; and to the theoretical achievement of objectification by thinking, the achievement of overpowering objects by willing supplies the corresponding practice.

The arising of vital counter-impulses is, in and of itself, an animal state of affairs; one need think only of the dog, with whose impulse to fetch the meat from the kitchen the acquired counter-impulse of his fear of punishment contends. But whereas in conflicts of impulse of this kind it is always a matter of polar pairs belonging together, in respect of which we can group all original feelings by specific opposites, the inhibitory mainspring named will is found attached to every commandable impulse just as surely as one and the same thing, in the way that it is one and the same being by virtue of which the particular fact represents not merely something particular, but always also, and precisely, something — factual. Accordingly, though the mainsprings need not yield to the drives in manifoldness on their impulse-side, they are nevertheless, on their counter-impulse side, one and the selfsame will — whereby their significance as causes of will has received its final clarification.

Let us consider the state of affairs from the reverse side, and we shall have at once a proof by example. No conceivable drive-impulse is of such a nature as to resist every drive-impulse whatsoever, in which case, namely, it would be capable of abolishing itself. If, by contrast, the will is an absolutely inhibiting force whose origin may not be sought in vitality, even though it is only with the help of vitality that possibilities of realization are allotted to it, then it must be able to enter even into the service of such mainsprings as deny drives their unfolding altogether, and consequently, by means of counter-impulses, render ineffective precisely those drive-impulses on whose satisfaction the continued existence of organic life depends. Now, this is in fact the case. Man, and man alone, is able methodically to deny his drives satisfaction, even at the [p. 650] price of self-annihilation. Religious asceticism, for example, can be intensified to the point of its bearer's dying, and has been so intensified countless times! Political prisoners who die of a hunger strike by which they have raised protest have died by virtue of the strength of their will. — But let us return to the analysis of the achievement of will.

If I will to raise my arm to shoulder height, that which moves it is that vital cause of movement to which, bodily, the arm's capacity for self-movement corresponds, and of which, in the case of the movement's execution, the movement is the expression; and at the same time the willed-ness of this same movement is grounded in an equally vital cause of inhibition, by virtue of which both every deviation of the arm's movement from the commanded direction is prevented, and, in particular, the continuation of the movement beyond the position assumed; wherefore the purposiveness of a movement always, in principle, speaks from an expressively unmistakable narrowing of the range of variation of its natural course. — One might perhaps recall: the merely impulsive movement of the arm is itself already a steered movement, and would thereby have unquestionably rightly made known the thoroughly directed character of all impulses. In view of this, however, the movement of arbitrary will can also be presented thus: what appears in the impulse-movement as an essential connection between urge and goal has, in the movement of arbitrary will, become an energetic magnitude whose whole efficacy consists in preventing, from point to point, the drive-force — now likewise determinable only energetically — from abandoning the direction toward the intended goal-point. But how greatly the life of movement is thereby altered in its very shape from the ground up will become fully clear to us only through richer examples, and through the relation of end and means that comes to the fore with their help. For since, in so simple a movement as the raising of the arm to shoulder height, normally a single impulse is realized, its deliberate execution also requires only a single splitting of impulse, or, that is, a single act of will, and the concatenation of acts of will ordinarily meant by "end and means" falls away.

With regard to the most general meaning of the word, one could indeed maintain that the arm and its mobility were, in this case, the means to the realization of the end — which would come home to us convincingly on the occasion of an injury that abolished the mobility of the arm — [p. 651] and that our knowledge of its manner of use formed a no less indispensable component of the fact-relatedness of our intention to raise it, just as our knowledge of the properties of the steel nib forms an indispensable component of our intention to write with its help. But the applicability of the end-means thought even to every movement of one's own body must not let us overlook that between volition and movement of one's own body there subsists a connection of a different kind, and incomparably closer, than between volition and the movement of a foreign body. Only for one's own body and its capacities for movement, never for a foreign body, do inner-bodily impressions have immediate, and indeed decisive, cognitive value; hence the availability of one's own organs — be it even for the sake of elaborately contrived feats — is rooted in experiences of feeling, and the highest conceivable degree of perfection is always attained only with the return to that manner of exercise which is natural and innate to the animal. We, as beings capable of thought, indeed know that we can grasp a nail with the hand, and make use of such knowledge whenever we do so deliberately; but we could do it even better entirely without the faculty of thought, on the strength merely of possessing organs of grasping proper to our own body; whereas it is spiritual experiences that enable us to drive the grasped nail into the wall. Only the tool in the narrower sense corresponds to the means proper; the organ, by contrast, may be called a means of willing only analogically, just as it is likewise only analogically the tool of the living impulse. But the movement of one's own body does indeed form, for willing, a "vehicle" already in motion, in relation to which only the task of steering falls to it.

If, instead of so simple a movement of arbitrary will as the stretching-out of the arm, we choose an already more complicated one, such as walking from place A to place B, it would nonetheless be mistaken to suppose that as many acts of will as steps of the feet are required for this. Although the first act of will does not, in its immediate effect, extend beyond the initial step of walking, it can nevertheless draw after it, mediately, any number of further steps, which proceed, in proportion to the acquired skill in walking, purely involuntarily or, as one is accustomed to say, automatically. Just as the conversation carried on by telephone is left, for the greatest part, to the workings of a mechanism, so likewise [p. 652] is every action left, for the greatest part, to the self-movement of the organism, or more precisely: the course of movement between any two points of steering is left to it entirely and wholly. Walking, riding, rowing, piano-playing, knitting, speaking, writing, and so forth, are for the one who has mastered them essentially automatic activities, interrupted only now and again by acts of will. We have elucidated with examples the purely factual matter of habit and practiced skill in the 25th chapter, and confine ourselves here to stating the condition under which, once the initial act has taken place, acquired skills are able to take over the further course of the willed sequence of movement for stretches now shorter, now longer.

If the end-relatedness of an impulse comes about thanks to a counter-impulse that binds the act of judgement to the concept of the goal in just the same way as the act of judgement binds the impression-experience to the concept of the thing, then even for the very next step of will its dependence on a more distant end, and finally on the final end, must signify a modification of direction that could not have occurred without it. Just as surely as the final, and by virtue of its finality determining, end of will is a different one when I merely put my foot forward in order to demonstrate, in exemplary fashion, the movement of striding, and again a different one on the occasion of the intention to walk from place A to place B, just as surely can the initial impulse in the first case not be the same as in the second case. There it is found immediately coupled, among other things, with the imperative of a "halt"; here, by contrast, at first only with a spatial consciousness of direction that, moreover, sets no bounds at all to the involuntary course of the walking movement. Given a sufficient degree of skill, vitality takes over the performances of will in principle in proportion to, if not the ultimate, then at least the provisionally envisaged final end; how often, by contrast, conscious steering must actually intervene depends partly on the structure of the intermediate links, partly, and even more, on obstacles that present themselves, but quite especially on that personal property which we characterized above as talent for willing or facility of will — with which the characterologically enormously important, and to this day still nearly unknown, chapter on the relation of individual capacity to willing would be unrolled. To what degree and extent performances of will may thus fall to vitality cannot be stated in general at all, [p. 653] and has as yet never in any individual case been made the object of an investigation; but from various observations on hypnotized persons, and especially from suggestions with so-called posthypnotic effect, it emerges in any case that purposive actions of extremely intricate structure of intermediate links can be accomplished quite involuntarily and unconsciously.

Let us take as an example of a many-membered action the ascent of a difficult peak; we should then have to see the function of the final end first of all in this, that all the partial ends are related to it and set up for its sake. But if the partial ends all stand, with respect to the final end, in the relation of means to end, they will actually fulfill their task only insofar as they call into existence, step by step, the factual conditions of approach to the summit; and since the factual conditions for the occurrence of an event are nothing other than its mechanical causes, and since, accordingly, the prospects of success of willing depend entirely on the state of knowledge of causes, we see end-consciousness bring forth that direction of abstracting, so far removed from the Platonizing one, which sets aside, from the world's state of affairs, everything that has no bearing on the compulsory sequence of processes — the only thing that still matters for will. We need only recall certain equations familiar to the physicist, such as tone = longitudinal vibration (of the air), to find attested a manner of thinking that has forgotten the existence of the How, and that regards as real, of all that exists at all, only those features that can be put into relation with other features in the form of an inviolable and unambiguous succession. Just as the theorist is blind above all to space and time (and therefore brings to the Kantian subjectivizing of both an objectively unwarranted readiness of belief), so the practical man is blind to the world of qualities; hence the "natural-scientific" theory-formation of the modern age, with its energetics estranged from qualities, proves through and through dependent on will-consciousness, and the conception of time prevailing in it proves to be a mere auxiliary construction of a dynamism that concerns itself with nothing less than with temporal actuality. In his "Prinzipien der Mechanik" the physicist Hertz states it unreservedly: "It is the next, and in a certain sense the most important, task of our conscious knowledge of nature that it should enable us to foresee future appearances, so as to [p. 654] be able to arrange our present acting in accordance with this foresight." And: "In fact we do not know, nor have we any means of learning, whether our representations of things agree with those things in anything else than in that one fundamental relation." In the concept of cause, to be considered<sup>17</sup> more closely later, the will has created for itself the tool by which, with the expenditure of a minimum of insight, it nonetheless accomplishes a radical work of destruction upon actuality; just as, conversely, the slightest ignorance in the sequence of cause and effect suffices to turn the claims of the will into illusions and to bring all acting to failure.

<sup>17</sup> On page 654. — Among the noteworthy things in the history of the spirit belongs the following circumstance. The dependence of the supposed cognition of the modern age on the purposes of thinking, and, in turn, of these on the purposes of the will asserting and expanding itself, was seen through, relatively early, by the *philosophers* (e.g. Bacon and, above all, Hobbes). Is it not, after all, the supreme principle of disposition of so-called positivism and monism, which none other than Comte cast into the catchword-like formula of voir pour prévoir! But instead of reflecting, thereupon, that research in the service of human aims of power is an extremely prejudiced research, one that could by no means lead to „pure" cognition, one believed rather to possess, in such a formula, the very ground in right of research as such and the most compelling guarantee for the excellence of its results! If in daily life one likes to quote „One notices the intention, and one is put out of humor" (adapted from Goethe's Tasso), then positivism, quite the reverse, seems to lend credence only to such „truths" as attest their origin by no means from the will to truth, but from other, namely highly „useful," intentions! — The matter loses, however, much of its strangeness as soon as we recall that this merely transfers from the beyond into the here-and-now the alleged „blessedness" that Christianity promises the „believer" as the reward of his faith; whereby alone the point of origin of all „scientificity," of all positivism and monism, would already be exposed, even were it not still to be documented a hundredfold over.

The partial actions can of course again be divided, in the most manifold ways, into subdivisions and again subdivisions, and thus represent, in their totality, a system of end-relations within which the final end signifies the highest abstractum, and, of the partial ends, the nearest one in each case signifies that concretum which admits of immediate realization. Thus, to speak with reference to our example, a wall is to be traversed, a chimney climbed, a crevasse leapt over, a gorge skirted, a glacier scaled — for each of which numerous sub-actions may prove indispensable, many of which would again require intermediate actions, such as the strapping-on of crampons, the securing of the rope, the repair of an ice-axe, and so forth. How, then, are we now to conceive, with respect to each partial end, the efficacy of the inner command, insofar as this command has the final end in view?

In every participant in the ascent, everything is preceded by the resolve to climb the mountain. But what sort of impulse would this be, after whose splitting so remarkable a resolve remained? Let us say in advance: there exists no drive aimed at the attainment of ice-stiffened mountain peaks, any more than there exists a drive to power, a drive to the acquisition of money, or a drive to the making happy of mankind; wherefore such exercises are wholly remote from the animal as well as from primitive man. — Without our being able here already to bring our analysis of the mainspring to a conclusion, it should nonetheless become clear from what has so far been set forth that, in the disposition called "mainspring," a constant condition of impulse-inhibition is united with a condition, in each case particular, of impulse-generation, which would accordingly, like the drive, have to be called a vital cause of movement — a cause of movement, to be sure, that would lack, for the purpose of its realization, the relative [p. 655] independence that we must presuppose for the genuine natural drive, in order for it to move the organism toward the goal that makes itself perceptible with its help.

But how, in the state of affairs "mainspring," the impulse-side, or more precisely a cause of movement that is really none, is to be characterized, belongs among the most delicate questions, whose answering could scarcely succeed without the availability of a fact of consciousness that must at once be called to mind. Nevertheless, provided it is true that already the initial movement of every action receives particularities of its shape from the goal of the action, one will not be able to avoid letting the final end too correspond to an allotted urge, notwithstanding that this urge would take effect only in the modifications of the impulses running, in each case, from one to the next partial end. Now, everyone fortunately knows the fact of consciousness by which his mainsprings can announce themselves before the forming of a resolve, and is able to recall the underlying state, of which perceptive researchers have long since ascertained that it is something quite foreign to the animal: we mean the repeatedly invoked fact of consciousness of wish, and the experience, occasioning it, of *wishing*.<sup>18</sup>

<sup>18</sup> On page 655. — Thus the meaning of wishing and its relation to willing was excellently set forth by Sigwart, whose essay „Der Begriff des Wollens und sein Verhältnis zum Begriff der Ursache," in the second volume of his „Kleine Schriften," is very much to be recommended for reading. We know of no author who has treated of the will more perceptively. Sigwart knows that animals cannot wish. The wish is, according to him, the inner striving, having passed through „thinking reflection," toward a state that I represent to myself as a good, but which I can neither expect with certainty nor bring about myself (loc. cit., p. 149). Further: „The wish rises above the real limitations of the I and its circumstances and creates for itself a world after its own heart; it enlivens us through the imaginary pleasure that a hoped-for or dreamed-of satisfaction of our inclinations affords. Seen from this side, wishing is an idle play and the counterpart of serious . . willing, which is directed only at purposes thought of as constituents of the real world, and it has its meaning solely in the fact that it reveals wherein the individual seeks his happiness and his satisfaction, and is thus a symptom of inclinations and of temperament. On the other side, wishing is again the ever-effective, elastic mainspring that keeps attention strained toward the real world . ., makes us lie in wait for the opportunities that promise the wish the possibility of realization, in order to translate it into purpose-setting willing" (loc. cit., p. 150).

One eases one's insight into the fundamental difference of wishing from willing by reflecting that it was never the common-Germanic "wollen" and "Wille," but rather the West-Germanic "wünschen," that was originally used for magical *actions*, as is still shown by "Verwünschung" [curse] and "Wünschelrute" [divining rod], which have remained to us. If we strip from the state that may have accompanied the exercise of wish-magic the belief in the possibility of magical effects, then for the residual state of wishing become, so to speak, reasonable, we shall have to place the emphasis on the consciousness of the at-least-provisional unattainability of the goal, to which the wisher finds himself related as one nonetheless striving toward it; wherefore his wishing is able to fill the entire compass of his ideas and fantasies, embracing the possible as much as the impossible, the actual as much as the unactual, alike. But however small, in view of this, the fraction may always be of the countless conceivable wishes that is exchanged for resolves, and however much precisely the survivals in the blood of the old wish-magic may contribute to letting the bearer of will sometimes overestimate his capacity, indeed evoke delusions and even delusive ideas [p. 656] of fulfillment, we shall nonetheless have to see in wishing the immediate source of all many-membered volitions, of those doomed to fail no less than of the successful ones. For wishing to be able to awaken a volition, its primevally human magical form must, to be sure, have yielded to the late-age "reasonable" one; or: to the consciousness of the momentary unattainability of the goal there must have joined itself the belief in its attainability by way of mechanical realization — a belief that, for its part, is rooted in knowledge of a necessitated sequence of facts.

The reversal of poles by which original humanity detached itself from animality brought not only the near-experience of sensing into subjection to the far-experience of beholding, but thereby also the near-experience of the drive-impulse into subjection to the far-experience of roaming, faring-forth, and swarming — which appeared only at an already late stage, in the light of magical working. For just as there would be no things at all without the deed of spirit that splits the impression, so too there would be none without the impression bearing the stamp of the intuitive image, of which the animal data of sensation are merely subordinate aspects; and just as there would be no fact-relatable impulses at all without the damming-up of the movement of life at the barrier of being, so too there would be none without the images themselves, besides the pull of images, taking part in the suffering of privation — or, expressed "subjectively," phantasms of fulfillment. Just as surely as nothing capable of being made an end can be thought that would not also, in some respect, be something wished, just as surely is there no fact-relatable impulse without the cooperation of phantasms of the goal. If, then, we were to add to the fact of consciousness of wish a wishing state of life, yet stripped of the faculty for magical wish-fulfillment, we should have characterized, with it, the will-capacity of the impulse just as correctly as when we characterize it as fact-relatability; and the question as to the differing constitution of those impulses, after whose splitting the movement of life would be directed toward the final end of a many-membered volition, would coincide with the question as to the distinguishing constitution of wishing impulses.

Meanwhile it takes no lengthy reflection to see that there could in any case not be a state of wishing in the same sense in which there is one of being-startled, of astonishment, of melancholy, [p. 657] and so forth. The restless feeling of tension, for example, that one might be tempted to adduce as such a state, belongs just as much to expectation, hope, anxiousness, fear, impatience, longing, and so on; and, what weighs more decisively, each of the feeling-states named presents, in man, a side that can be taken as a wish-side, or could at least pass over into a wishing: fear, for example, into the wish to avoid the supposedly or actually terrible thing, even if it is perhaps unavoidable (as with one who, on the eve of an examination that seems to him fateful, sighs: would that it were already the day after tomorrow!); hope into the wish that the expected thing might come about, even though it does not lie in the power of the one hoping to bring it about (as when one wishes for delightful weather for the summer excursion); longing into the wish to be able, in an instant, to bridge the separating interval between oneself and the object of longing, and so forth. Indeed, if we consider it rightly, no human feeling can be conceived that would not have a wish-side; hence we may not, after all, take wishing to be in turn a special feeling, but must rather take it to be a quite peculiar side of all feelings of spiritual beings.

Were one, against this, to repeat what has often been said — that wishing consists in a striving-toward something "represented" — one would only have left in the dark precisely what it would matter most to us to learn: the specific nature of such strivings in relation to the drive-impulses, and would merely have stated, at greater length, that wishing is wishing striving. But we do not wish to carry this dissection, which will probably seem somewhat vivisective, any further, since pointing to dream-sleep should suffice, for the time being, to support the conviction that, if not representing, then at least fantasying is a process that has no need of consciousness, and by whose aid the vital basis of wishing, too, can now be characterized. If, under certain circumstances, animal drives already bear fulfilment-phantasms, then in man there is no concept of fulfilment that could not, at another time, arouse vitality with the power of the phantasm and thereby lend to the being-related-to-the-object-of-thought the character of that inner striving-toward in which the pull of the goal is found exchanged for a — now, however, vital — aiming of the bearer of life toward it, an aiming that, at the moment of resolve, yields to the self-active [p. 658] aiming. If one objects to the introduction of a vital aiming as a dubious duplication, we leave it, for now, only to consideration that an efficacy of phantasms upon the motor side of the bearer of life can hardly be conceived otherwise, and we shall, besides, still have occasion to distinguish the aiming urge of wishing from the aiming urge of will.

But in that we have thereby implanted in all the feelings of spiritual beings, as a mark of their participation, so to speak, in the "eros of distance," a kind of analogue of goal-directedness, we have of course thereby also somewhat modified their impulse-nature, to which we shall henceforth not be able to deny a feature of considerably heightened centrifugality. Already the bodily structure of man furnishes us, in upright gait and the development of the hand, evidence of an overemphasized development of the foundations of expansive readiness for movement; the gesture of pointing — certainly already proper to primitive man, but to no animal — is the involuntary manifestation of a tension aimed at what is, for the moment, unreachable, at least in space, and thereby confirms the connection of every feeling-governed aiming with the experienceability of far-images of intuition; the development of directions of forward motion in the practice of writing, which came to its conclusion in European history, fully corroborates — together with the victory of centre-fleeing over converging movement-impulses, as it finds expression in the generally accomplished transition from retrograde to irreversibly progressive line-direction — the belonging-together of backward-turning with the promethean, that is, contemplatively thinking, and of the inclination to forward-progression with the heraclean, that is, willing and purposively thinking, comportment of life.

Accordingly, in the being capable of thought, we would have to add, to the layer of animal drives that we have understood from the pull of the fulfilling images, tensions in which an unconscious aiming toward phantasms of fulfilment would manifest itself; tensions that, at the moment of release, passed over into centre-fleeing movement-impulses, thereby forming the vital basis of the self-active aiming at the (temporally distant) final purpose, and, precisely for that reason, also of that, so to speak, breathless pressing-onward that distinguishes the exercise of will from the ever-periodic reign of the drive-impulses. — Here one might object: would not everything that was set out concerning the boundness of action [p. 659] to wakefulness for the near and nearest thereby be overturned again? How, further, would the role, demonstrated for all purposing, of a force thoroughly inhibiting impulse be compatible with the centrifugality of the will-impulses? How, finally, could self-mastery be brought into accord with the far-relation newly stipulated here — self-mastery of which not even the outward kind, let alone a willing that in Buddhist fashion aims simply at the rigidifying of life, could dispense with? And would not the "urge into the distance" hinted at here be precisely that luring of the images which, even in the natural impulse, betrays far less a privation-suffering of the organism than the fullness of the streams of the universe flooding through it, and would accordingly form the extreme opposite of the negating *counter-striving* in which, according to the author's far-ranging expositions, the indispensable precondition of the capacity-to-will was to be seen! And does not everyone see, finally, that an urge into the distance would have to lead, for example, to wanderlust and adventurous journeys, and hence to a relatively planless letting-oneself-go, rather than to the weighed planfulness of goal-conscious action!

Had such a questioner also confused will-capable with will-incapable wishing, and rational wishing in general with magical wishing, he would nevertheless have pointed out, to our credit, the inadequacy of our characterization of will-capable wishing — a gap that we shall fill in below. Setting this aside for the moment, it should however be recalled that our sole concern was to explain those bonds that accrue to an action just now unfolding from its being-related to a more distantly lying final purpose. For it is only these that remain, in the realization of will, of the "urge into the distance." But an inhibition does not cease to be what it is merely because the purpose for whose sake it occurs can only be derived from a wish-goal, and the final intention, again, points back to a wishing no less for that, merely because the mastery, fettering, or even the rigidifying of life-processes forms its object. For the goal of the inward-directed exercise of will, by which the Buddhist seeks to disarm every luring of the images and to blunt himself against their stimulus-value, lies, for example, far outside and *beyond* all conceivable drive-impulses! Apart from the very simplest actions, for whose performance a single act of will suffices, the realization of will [p. 660] can accordingly be understood only if we think of wish-states as interposed between the layer of drives and volition, from which the sense of the motive, or "motive-force," now also emerges more clearly. Returning once more to the example of the intellectual worker who temporarily interrupts his studies: the fatigue he perhaps felt could not have awakened the resolve to go for a walk at all without the addition of the wish thereby to gain fresh strength for the continuation of his work — so that only in this wish would the actual motive for the said resolve lie. The assumption of vital wish-states further enables us to draw a sharper distinction between the bases of wishing that are actually effective and those that are merely supposed to be so — that is, between genuine and imagined motives — and opens to us deep glimpses into the exceedingly intricate web of motive-forces. Had our scholar, for instance, actually followed the wish to enjoy the beautiful sunshine, we should stand, characterologically, before the task of ascertaining, besides the motive-force of his action, also the motive-force of his holding-to-be-true, by virtue of which he imagines himself to be organically unfounded tired.

If, with regard to its nature as a vital disposition, we call the motive-force, at the moment it becomes effective, an Itwish, and the conscious wishes, by contrast, I-wishes, then it admits of no doubt that by far the most I-wishes of by far the most people are the results of the often extremely intricate interplay of I-wishes of an entirely different kind — of Itwishes that not infrequently remain hidden from their bearer for a lifetime. If we said above that no conceivable drive is directed at the attainment of an ice-rigid summit, we now add that no aiming wish either, supposing there were such a thing, would ever have brought forth such a resolve. The carrying-out of a life-threatening mountain ascent for the sake of a particularly ample view, or, more generally speaking, out of so-called "feeling for nature," has never yet occurred, notwithstanding that many mountaineers tell themselves as much. What can, however, really have occasioned it is the wish of the bearer of will to furnish other people, or himself, with proof of courage — which is why Nietzsche answered the question why man climbs high mountains with the bon mot: "In order to mock his trembling knees"; further, the wish to surpass other mountaineers by a particularly astonishing feat; or the wish to conquer the mountain [p. 661] as though it were a personal being that, by the sight of its "loftiness," shamed the lowliness of man, and, as it were, to "tread it underfoot" (cf. "the assault on Mount Everest"); or the wish of curiosity, which would like to know what it probably looks like up there; or the wish of the drive to knowledge, whose expression is the strictly factual question. In order to penetrate into human action we should accordingly, in each case, first of all need to know the actual final purpose and, with it, the motive-force whose wish-power supplied the decisive motive for it; for thanks to this manner of regarding things, the whole mountain expedition, for example, would appear not merely in the light of a means to an end, but also as, through and through, wrested from the drives of man.

If we recall the thoroughly grounded proposition that, metaphysically regarded, every action aims at the non-being of a being, and therefore lies vitally grounded in privation-suffering and never in the urge of overflowing fullness, then we shall have to see the cause of the interchangeability of magical wishing with rational wishing in this: that, in the state of wishing, the striving-toward the desired was compelled to subordinate itself to the striving-away from the undesired! The relatedness to a matter that we had to presuppose for all willing striving is underpinned by the wishingoneself-away from a situation appearing in some way unpleasant, and the fulfilment-phantasms attain the capacity to become motives of willing precisely only insofar as they turned over into aversion against phantasms of privation! Just as, in the will-to-work, something does indeed genuinely come to light in a new way from the lurings of the gladdening image — namely in the measure of its own self-negation — so, in the image-negating will-to-deed, only the repulsion of the painful image comes to light: it is only with this plumb-line that we have sounded the ground of the will-capacity of wishing and ascertained the seat of origin of the driving force of "interest." Whoever, on the other hand, looks past the negating essence of the motive-force has confused it with drives or with exuberances, and — in the service of spirit's self-justification — falsifies, idealistically, all human doing and not-doing. It was Nietzsche who, measuring by the state of Dionysian intoxication, tore the mask from the "ideals" and stripped away the "will to power" from every disguise, however deceptive; although he too — captive in this to spirit — did not penetrate to the insight to which his metaphysics of intoxication ought to have obliged him: that the will to power is a will to destruction, and hence a will to the killing of life.

[p. 662] Why positive and negative motive-forces in the narrower sense can nonetheless be kept apart without bursting the frame of our inquiry shall only be indicated here, since it is to be read, in the main, already in our Grundlagen der Charakterkunde. On p. 411 of Volume I we separated "life-scientifically negative stirrings such as fear, terror, hatred, envy, malice, etc., from the positive ones of love, admiration, veneration, etc.," and at once added that this was no ultimate state of affairs, inasmuch as it comes down to the opposed degrees of strength with which the process of beholding takes part in the feeling-process. We now know that, in proportion to the participation in question, will-capacity decreases; accordingly, the feelings called negative are to count as akin to will, those called positive as contrary to will. If we call the one self-assertion feelings, the other self-surrender feelings, then certainly no great acuteness is needed to confirm that the former tend to occasion volitions more easily and more often than the latter, and stand essentially closer to our state-like constitution in energetic resolve and during the course of tenaciously persevering action. If, nonetheless, surrender-feelings too can call forth volitions, they do so only through the medium of assertion-feelings, and hence only in the measure that these are called forth. "Love too commits itself with deeds, but only under bitter self-denial; for at the moment of acting — love does not act!" If, accordingly, motive-forces are without<sup>19</sup> exception negative, because and insofar as they are will-dispositions, they are nonetheless so in extraordinarily different degrees, insofar as they are, besides, dispositional conditions of feelings that fall now more to the side of assertion, now more to the side of surrender. But the more the dispositions to surrender-feelings predominate, the more the motive-forces approach either the (sensory) drives or the (psychic) dispositions to exuberance (= dispositions to ecstasy), and in just that measure their will-capacity is diminished. Or: an exchange of the (wishing) stirring for volition occurs only, and strictly, insofar as the power of the images has yielded to the superior power of the impulse, and, within the impulse, the pulling force of the images has yielded to the counter-urge against something disturbing. — We convince ourselves of this by the mountaineer example.

<sup>19</sup> On page 662. — K*lages*, Die Grundlagen der Charakterkunde, 11th ed., p. 148.

How could one wish to furnish proof of courage, or to surpass others, or to conquer mountains, unless one fell, in the opposite case, into tormenting doubts of one's own worth; and how could one wish to know something [p. 663], unless one felt oneself troubled, disturbed, indeed made anxious, by a lack of knowledge! The wish to accomplish such drive-contrary feats is thus rooted in feelings of insufficiency. But does not something of the kind nonetheless sometimes happen out of that very "feeling for nature"? Was it not this that drove Petrarch, as the first mountain-tourist, to climb Mont Ventoux near Avignon, in order to sink, silently, on the summit, into the sight of the distance? Yet he himself has betrayed to us that he sought nature in order "praeterita oblivisci … et praesentia non videre" [to forget the past … and not to see the present]! However certain it is that springs, mountains, and trees lured him, it is equally certain that there would have been no need at all of anchoretic withdrawal and difficult ascents in order to tower heavenward with mountains, to rush valley-ward with springs, to answer the voices of the storms with trees, had it not become perceptible to him that his soul had been torn from the great accord, and was prevented from regaining it by much that was human around him, and not least by the "all-too-human" in himself!

Nor is this all: what such actions win, in the service of the soul, is not, say, the fulfilment of longing, but, in the good case, the removal of some obstacles to fulfilment, and, in the bad case, *wish*-death from the loss of distance and the decay of that distance itself. Should anyone wish to have us believe that the Icarus-wish to soar up into the upper ether, or the Faustian wish to follow the evening sun in flight, has, since the Renaissance (Leonardo), driven numerous researchers to try their hand at inventing ever-new flying machines, until at last the courted nature of things could no longer withstand fulfilment, we would have to reply that, with the mechanical realization of flight-like locomotion, not merely the "soul-bird" itself died, but also, at least almost, its thought-image, on which Icarian-Faustian urges fed. For one would have to be entirely free of all Icarus-wishes in order to be able to persuade oneself that whoever travels cloud-heights in an airautomobile, whether as passenger or as pilot, is experiencing the flight of the soul! If anyone still has even so much power of recollection as to remember, here and there, the nocturnal dream-flights of his youth, he will have to confess to himself that in the air-motor he is incomparably further from the state of flying than when, with his whole soul, he felt after:

Hurrying clouds, sailors of the air, / who wandered with you, who sailed with you!

[p. 664] The distance cannot be "conquered," but it can indeed be killed by the supposed — conqueror; and it was not the luring of heights and expanses that sharpened and honed human wit until its bearer could "fly," cable, and wire, but rather the aversion to the here of the body and the vexation at the separating power of intervening space, if not indeed envy of eagles and albatrosses!

We interrupt the train of thought for a moment, in order, without any sidelong glance at groundings already sufficiently offered, to let the innermost sense light up together with the end of the road toward which a being unstoppably drives whose soul has become the slave of the will. — There is in man a striving to transform the world into that which he himself feels himself to be. Greatness wants to experience greatness, love a loving being, hatred the hostile, pathos the distance, sobriety the near; and thus greatness poetizes a world of the great, love beings full of loving glow, hatred an enmity of all against all; thus pathos lays a distance-blue, making things elastic, even over the everyday things, and thus sobriety takes even from the firmament the rapt shudder, makes the moist dry and the soft hard. What we behold things as, that is what we do to them. Note the double sense: to do something to someone means, on the one hand, to do him harm, and on the other, to clothe him with something! World-souls want to reveal themselves, and the revealing needs the receiving, which accepts the revelation and radiates back its light. No longer to behold it is already to narrow the life of the images; to behold something worthless into it is to wage a deadly war against it.

The will is the mechanical executor of blindness, and in every blindness lies worthlessness, in every worthlessness blindness. In the will, what is unbelief in blindness becomes soulless destruction-urge, and unbelief, again, is the unfree offspring of the negating power of worthlessness. From negation comes blindness, from blindness the will, which destroys what blindness cannot behold. Because the nothing "entered into life," it became hostility to life; because hostility to life dwells within it, the soul becomes blind; because it is blind, the spirit of man must will. It is therefore the unconscious tactic of the one who wills to shut himself off against the content of what resists: he undermines and degrades the world. The "energy" of his willing is robbed and desecrated water of life; but that it became willing is its [p. 665] adoptive kinship to the blind or blinded soul, which, for its part, in turn does homage to the malice of the nothing. Hence there gapes, through every capacity-to-will, a terrible *rift*: it is the state of consciousness of a soul that, out of an erring urge, storms unceasingly against the edge of the sword and, from moment to moment, perishes cloven in two! Will is ever-renewed lifemurder, and its symbol is suicide.

From energy is heightened the force of willing, but from cleavenness is heightened the will's compliance of energy! The more soul-forsaken the body, the more insubstantial is the resistance to its will; and the more body-forsaken the soul, the more insubstantial is, to its will, the wound it received from resistance.
