If, accordingly, every self-conscious being undoubtedly experiences its corporeality already in its own body — whose limbs are indeed capable of offering resistance to one another, and which is moreover subject to the influence of gravity, to be overcome only by a palpable expenditure of force — it experiences that corporeality, so to speak, in a higher potency in the attempt to overcome the resistance of foreign bodies. Just as certainly as I experience, in the self-active raising of my arm, the impulse that produces it, so certainly do I also experience it heightened in lifting a weight or in arresting a rolling ball. Since original thinking could accordingly not avoid grasping force as the cause of motion, or, more broadly, as the cause of happening, it involuntarily draws a sharp distinction between the mover and the thing-to-be-moved — for which one may compare the dichotomy-table of the Pythagoreans, together with the most extreme working-out of it in Aristotle's proton kinoun akineton [first unmoved mover]! In the latter's polemic against the Platonic doctrine of Ideas, the objection recurs again and again that the Ideas are incapable of moving anything and can for that very reason explain nothing either, but rather that thereby "all consideration of nature is abolished." "And as for physics," it is said elsewhere, "it has for its object a certain kind of being, namely that essence which has in itself the principle of rest and motion..." This remark draws our attention [p. 694] to a circumstance which we do well to impress upon ourselves once more expressly, even though it was tacitly presupposed already in what has just been set forth — namely to the vital difference between rest and motion. For a thinking dependent on life, rest is by no means a motion of velocity zero, but something fundamentally, or in our language polarly, different from motion — which is why, for example, the error the Eleatics committed in identifying rest with position was less grave than it would be in the mouth of the modern physicist. As the passive pole of world-appearance, the body and its substrate, matter, signify something simply at rest and unchanging, to which every motion and ultimately every change first accrues from the active pole, i.e., from the living impulse or the bodily soul.<sup>23</sup>

<sup>23</sup> On page 694. — The more clearly the difference between the two poles was grasped — which happened first on the part of the Pythagoreans — the more one tended to *separate* them from one another and, in this fashion, to distinguish self-moving bodies from bodies incapable of self-movement. The historically earliest determination of the concept of the organically living as that which moves itself of itself (autokineton), by the Pythagorean physician *Alcmaeon*, therefore suffers from a characteristic one-sidedness, since it is only artificially transferable to plant life. Aristotle divides more cautiously: threptikon, kinetikon kata topon, and aisthetikon; a threefold division that, in the form of three developmental stages of life — reproduction, irritability, and sensibility — reaches down into the first half of the 19th century!

Only one who keeps somewhat in view the early history of the concept of cause can gauge the magnitude of the revolution that occurs with the so-called Renaissance, marked by Galileo's *principle of persistence*. In that Galileo, what had formerly been presupposed for the rest of bodies — namely, that an impulse was needed for them to be set in motion — asserted instead precisely for motion, which accordingly, in the absence, say, of inhibiting forces, would continue uniformly without limit, not only was the fundamental distinction between being-at-rest and being-in-motion abolished, but rest itself became a special case of being-in-motion and consequently stood exactly as much in need of explanation as the latter. Coming-to-rest now appears no less questionable than coming-into-motion, and the force capable of bringing about the one as much as the other is no longer sought in the cause of motion, but in the cause of a change of velocity — a shift of conception that at first glance may look trifling, but on closer consideration proves to be the greatest ever demanded of historical humanity.

To be sure, every motion has a velocity, and differences of velocity can become intuitable just as well as the difference between rest and motion. But once, instead of motion, its mark of velocity has become an independent object of thought, the intuitive opposition of rest and motion sinks to the level of a mere incidental matter, and the difficulty that at least gave the Eleatics the impetus to their aporias is found abolished in the [p. 695] thought of mere differences of magnitude, by whose help motion can be characterized even for the strictly mathematical, i.e., temporally unextended point of time — whereby the deed of spirit has definitively become master over the process of lived experience. Modern dynamism means the fulfillment of Eleaticism! If the Eleatic, in place of motion, had found position, and for that reason denied the actuality of motion, the mechanist, by means of the concept of velocity, replaces motion — and ultimately the whole of happening — with mere measure-formulas of happening, which are henceforth treated as though they were actuality itself, and thereby accomplishes, for the first time, what the Eleatic had merely striven for: the displacement of the phenomenal world by a world of noumena. — With these remarks we have anticipated the result of an inquiry for which we must now ask the reader's full attention, even though it will extend only to the school-concepts of mechanics.

Why, one may object to us, should it mean a turning away from actuality and a turning toward formalism if one makes the differences of velocity of motions — which after all simply exist — the object of causal inquiry? That the ancients omitted this, or nearly omitted it, proves how inexactly they — entangled in thought-formations of their own making — had grasped the motions taking place in nature; whereas it was precisely the Renaissance that made war on all mere speculation and drew its insights from nature to a degree not previously attained. How else, indeed, could it be understood that its discoveries have been verified by the successes of technology!

For the reader of this book we need not once again argue at length what we would have to set against this. The technical mastery of nature proves extraordinarily little for the truth-content of the propositions on which it rests. But as for the Renaissance's turn to so-called nature, it must be said that it meant rather a turn to facts — more precisely to things — and consequently a turning away from the world of images! If we compare the speculative schemata of the ancients with those of modernity and ask ourselves on which side the greater urge to abstraction, as well as the greater power to abstract, is to be sought, there is no doubt: on the side of modernity! If ancient man could hold the opinion that a body falls [p. 696] because it "seeks its place," and that heavy bodies fall faster than light ones, we see him wholly under the spell of the world of intuition; whereas when Galileo instead discovers a kind of attractive force of the earth (though admittedly without yet calling it that) and maintains and proves the claim that all bodies fall at equal speed, provided only one thinks away the frictional resistance of the medium fallen through, we have, by virtue of a tremendous feat of abstraction, taken a flight properly into the supersensible. The ancients managed to think the whole world composed of (Euclidean) triangles, or to hold numbers — now, to be sure, conceived symbolically — for what is properly actual. But speculations of that kind are merely exercises of an understanding testing its dialectical skill with self-delight, and moreover extremely harmless, because they leave actuality untouched; it was modern thinking alone that managed, with incomparably more abstract speculations, to close in on actuality's very body. What role actuality itself plays in this we have partly already considered and shall have to consider more thoroughly elsewhere. Here what concerns us is the heightened power of detachment (= abstraction) from it, a power inherently tending to overpower its object.

It was not the more exactly intuitive grasp of motion that gave the impetus to the emphatic singling-out of differences of velocity, but rather the detachment of (phoronomic) motion from the movable thing, whereby motion in itself comes to be regarded as something actual, and its velocity as a property of this actual thing. This emerges drastically in two states of affairs, whose analysis shall now lead us more deeply into Galilean thinking. The first we perceive in the circumstance that the new concept of velocity is essentially punctual and as such related exclusively to the future. "In fact, with this velocity a space is indeed also taken as a basis; but it is not the space which comes into question as traversed, so to speak, behind the operation of the force, but rather the space which the body would traverse quite uniformly and without ceasing if the force no longer acted upon it further" — thus Dühring in his "Kritische Geschichte der allgemeinen Prinzipien der Mechanik" (III, p. 30). If we add that the instantaneous velocity represents the sum of all preceding velocities, we see in it the past effaced at the extensionless boundary [p. 697] and exchanged for a ground of production of the future, to be considered still more sharply in a moment. — To develop the second state of affairs, we take a detour that is instructive to travel in any case.

We reach it by the shortest line through illumination of the second symptom of the predominance of the capacity for detaching the actual from the object of thought — a symptom to be sought in the fact that the mere relational property of velocity figures as a component of force. Let us illustrate by an example what the answer would have to be if we referred the Eleatic problem not to motion but to its velocity, and accordingly asked: what, at the extensionless point of time, is the velocity of motion? Let two arrows of equal weight and equal shape be shot by means of a machine, on the same plane, vertically upward (thus in parallel directions), the second somewhat later than the first, but with a greater initial velocity. If the second arrow flies past the first at the beginning of the third second, in such a way that at the limiting instant when it is just about to overtake it, it has exactly twice the velocity of the first, then an observer sighting normally to the arrows' direction at the same height would, for one element of time, see only one arrow, because the first would completely cover the second — or, in other words, no difference at all would obtain with regard to the intuitable positions of the arrows. We would only need to imagine a wall erected at the point in question, at which, by some contrivance, the arrow-tips were held fast, and we would have demonstrated the Eleatic thought: both arrows would remain at rest, and, in view of their perfectly identical positions, the difference of velocity would seem to have been annihilated, as though it had never existed at all. — The matter appears quite different as soon as we try, experimentally, to put ourselves inside the arrows, which we make easier for ourselves by imagining it to happen at the instant of their impact upon the resisting wall. Then to the doubled velocity of the second arrow there corresponds a fourfold force of its impact, or a fourfold pressure against the obstacle, or, finally, a fourfold striving to penetrate into it. With this, however, we have obtained the answer to our question: just as the motion of a movable thing at a mathematical point of time is a position, so the velocity of the motion at [p. 698] a mathematical point of time is an *urge* (for which one might also say "tension"), and the differences of velocity would be found again in exactly corresponding differences of magnitude of this urge (or this "tension"). The urge is unintuitable, but we can make it intuitable through various consequences. If, for example, we let the obstructing wall be coated with a thick layer of wax, the second arrow would bore into it nearly four times as deep as the first. If previously, and rightly, the attained velocity of the movable thing appeared to us in the light of the "sum" of forces that had operated, it now appears to us, and with equal right, that velocity itself is force; for to the doubled velocity there corresponds, after all, a fourfold pressure or a fourfold weight. If we nonetheless hold fast to seeing in force the circumstance that produces velocities, we are inevitably led to the determination that force is the cause of a change of velocity.

Galileo has not yet expressly formulated this determination; but he made use of it point for point, and that was certainly one of the most extraordinary and, if one likes, most ingenious abstractions to which a human understanding has ever managed to attain. For thereby the possibility of measuring apprehension is opened not merely for any motion whatever, but for happening as such; for differences of velocity also occur with regard to a becoming-larger, a becoming-warmer, a becoming-purer, a becoming-brighter, a becoming-drier, and so forth, and vice versa. Only, the tremendous ascent is paid for with the loss of the maternal ground left behind. Whoever, with Galileo, seeks the source of happening exclusively in the cause of changes of process accessible solely to calculation, has let the operative cause fall, and has thereby, in principle, forfeited the possibility of finding the conditions of the processes themselves, whether in the movable thing or in whatever substrate. He no longer asks: what is the ground why something happens; but rather — presupposing happening together with its conditions — he asks: what is the ground why the velocity of a happening changes? Or, to turn back to mechanics, motion is no longer henceforth the problem, but rather the difference of its velocity from the velocity of another motion. If, for example, a movable thing has such-and-such a velocity, then the ground of this velocity can no longer even be meaningfully asked for the case [p. 699] that it remained in it unceasingly, because, for want of the absence of what is now understood by force, there would for the movable thing be as little occasion to exchange the existing state of velocity for another state of velocity as, for the body resting on a firm base, there is occasion to exchange its rate of fall of zero for a uniformly accelerated fall.

The great initiator of classical mechanics did not concern himself verbally to any great extent with the principle presupposed by his concept of force, with which we began our discussion — though we avoided the designation for it whose coinage, by his successors Huyghens and Newton, betrayed a prescient scent: we mean the "law of inertia," or even the "force of inertia" (vis inertiae). In order that a change of velocity take place in a movable thing, a second movable thing is required, and indeed fundamentally and reciprocally. Were we to traverse, by way of the transmissions of force, the infinity of space and the infinity of the past, we would find no place of origin for force itself, and would see ourselves referred to the transmundane God of medieval belief, if indeed we were minded to come to a halt anywhere at all! Genuine force has been uprooted by mechanics; it no longer has any place in the cosmos, and in fact one seeks it in vain to this day!

It is well known that much has been disputed, and occasionally still is disputed, as to whether the law of inertia is a necessity of thought or a fact of experience, although the sole correct answer has long since been given by thinking physicists as well as by philosophers trained in physics. The suitability of the Galilean concept of force for the computational mastery of actual occurrences was, as is understood, to be secured only by observation and testing, and is so little a necessity of thought that it could even lose its unrestricted validity through an extension of our (physical) store of experience. By contrast, what is brought to consciousness by the so-called law of inertia is merely that presupposition which first makes the concept of force possible at all — namely, the presupposition that the movable thing which forms the object of mechanics indeed receives and passes on impulses, but never generates them, and is thus, in short, lifeless. For the computational application of the concept of force would be over in the very instant that a body in rectilinear uniform motion were able of itself [p. 700] to change its velocity! With this, however, it also becomes palpably evident that the new concept of force owed its origin not to a deepening of insight into the process of motion, but to the detachment of the process of motion from the movable thing, and thus to the making-independent of a property of motion — the making-independent of velocity.

The temporally punctual character of force and its nature as the cause of a change of velocity belong inseparably together. When we think of "force," we refer, in strict turning-away from the past, to the momentary state of a movable thing at any given instant, and indeed as to something that is in turn related to the future and only to the future. To be sure, the force in question signifies an urge, but not an inner one — merely a received, a transmitted urge. Were it an inner urge, we could not analyze it without analyzing the thing that urges, and we could not analyze the thing that urges without taking into account its having-become and its history. The urge, by contrast, that corresponds, for example, to the doubled velocity of the second arrow, is an urge merely lent to the movable thing by another movable thing, an urge with which we are concerned henceforth only as to the difference of its consequences from the consequences of another urge, to which corresponds another — again merely lent — velocity. Force is, from moment to moment, a state of velocity which, instilled from without, is grasped only with a view to the states of velocity to which it in turn gives occasion. We stand in a world without past, without impulse, without necessity, whose headlong rush, nonetheless ever more precipitate, wells up out of ceaselessly accumulating disturbances. In place of creative powers, the disturbance of equilibrium; and in place of growing and grown forms, the summing velocities: that is the change of the age which the name Galileo designates.

Once one has lost the opposition of activity and passivity, one has lost "force" itself, and has in truth and in fact arrived at mere equations of motion, which drag along the semblance of explanations only because they use, for their concepts, names stemming from the biomorphic stratum of human thought. But just as, with the active principle, the passive principle falls away as well, so the actuality of force cannot be surrendered without the surrender of the actuality of matter. That in the end it is precisely the uprooting of matter that [p. 701] is at stake, we shall show not in the foundational — but also merely ground-laying — conceptions of Galileo, but in the concluding ones of Newton. If, philosophically regarded, Galileo is the coiner of the modern concept of velocity and thereby the inventor of force, then Newton is the discoverer of the modern "mass." — The physicist, be it remarked in passing, can take no interest in our considerations; for it is not a matter, for us, of physical criticism of physical concepts, let alone of any proposals for improvement (to which the author, as neither mathematician nor physicist, would in the least consider himself entitled), but rather of demonstrating the subjective point of origin of the concepts in question — in other words, their psychogenesis, more precisely their noogenesis — and of exhibiting their antithetical relation to the concept of actuality belonging to the doctrine of appearance. And this is what shall and will lead us to quite definite results.

Although, as far as we can see, it is not Newton himself who uses the so-called classical formula b = —, which underlies the still-current dimensional formula of force (mlt⁻²), it nonetheless corresponds exactly to his conception of the accelerating magnitude of centripetal force. Before we consider the right-hand side of the equation, which is especially important to us, let us call to mind for a moment the presuppositions of its left-hand side. v (= velocity) signifies change of position per element of time, or, leaving aside the differential signs, in elementary-mathematical notation v = s/t. — Acceleration (b) signifies y<sup>24</sup>

<sup>24</sup> On page 701. — One would of course grossly misunderstand the physicist were one to impute to him the intention of dividing distances by times, which would be just as senseless as, say, a division of dogs by apples! What he means by his equations are not distances, times, velocities, but the *numerical measures* of distances, times, velocities, and each of his numbers in fact signifies the product of the numerator in question and an *arbitrarily* chosen unit. Were a velocity, for example, v = 5, that would mean it is five times as great as a velocity he has chosen as the unit; and were one now to choose as the unit the velocity only half as great, then v = 10 would result, even though the velocity itself would have undergone no change.

V / V / S change of velocity per element of time, or b = —1 = — — -^ We now note in order the presuppositions of the concept of velocity. 1. There exists an objective space and an objective time, whereby, according to earlier discussions, it is entirely immaterial whether one locates the conditions of the apprehension of space and time preferentially in the outer world or in the human spirit, or finally distributes them between the two. 2. Space is measurable. — This assumption includes further presuppositions, which we set alongside the rest. 3. The various spaces of intuition are parts of one and the same total space. [p. 702] 5. The sameness of total space is not affected by the passage of time. (Total space is thus, e.g., today the same as in the times of Homer. As one recalls from earlier chapters, the thought insight in question can also be grasped as a principle of the conservation of space, or, finally, as the renewal of space, congruent with itself, per element of time.) 6. Time is measurable. — This assumption includes further presuppositions, which we set alongside the rest. 7. Time is a space-analogous extension whose sections admit of addition. 8. The passage of time is strictly uniform. 9. The unit of measure of the time-dimension can be borrowed from space. (More precisely: time is measured by a velocity [rotation of the earth, secondspendulum, etc.].)

For our purposes we set aside the circumstance, already mentioned earlier, that time can only be measured by the velocity of a process, while obviously a measure of time is needed in order to measure a velocity — a circle from which, if we are not mistaken, there is no escape for any physical consideration. We further leave aside that measurements take place only with the help of estimations and can therefore only ever be realized approximately. We content ourselves with pointing out that the related assumptions 2, 3, 4, and 5, and likewise assumption 8, are hypotheses that, even should they prove correct, would not admit of verification. Now, however, assumptions 6, 7, and 9 are unquestionably false; for actuality-time is certainly not an extension to which measuring-rods could be applied; and since the three assumptions erroneous from the standpoint of the science of appearance form, together with the five hypothetical assumptions, such a whole that only both together, in their community, satisfy the postulate of measurability, we recognize them one and all as mere noumena and accordingly ascribe to the states of affairs recorded under 1 only the actuality of objects of thought. The one and the same measurable space, and the one and the same measurable time, are in fact thought-things — not, however (as Kant supposed), because the outside-one-another, or the condition of the outside-one-another, resides in the human spirit, but by virtue of the unactuality of the boundaries through whose introduction into the outside-one-another [p. 703] conceivable space and conceivable time first come into being at all. In this way happening, to use an expression we employed earlier, is exchanged for thing-like states of affairs, and, in particular, motion, from the standpoint of the affirmation of being, is indeed no longer denied in the Eleatic manner, but is nonetheless, beyond that, made measurable — and thereby made compliant with the demand for suitability to thought — through the substitution of concepts of being. Against the physicist's presupposed, consciousness-scientific equation, actuality = measurability, we set the appearance-scientific inequality: measurability ≠ actuality. But now let us call to mind what corresponds, on the right-hand side of the equation, to b (= change of velocity).

Were we to imagine the preliminary question indispensable from the standpoint of the science of appearance put to us — what, according to our equation, force is, what mass is — it would at once emerge that the concept of force presupposes the concept of mass, and the concept of mass, in turn, the concept of force. Force is what it is in relation to a mass assumed as known, and mass is what it is in relation to a force assumed as known. Were we already inclined, for this reason, to suspect in both only different modes of presentation of a single state of affairs, this would be made wholly certain for us by the obvious consideration that, in relation to force, mass evidently has the significance of a counter-force. For if acceleration changes proportionally to force and inversely proportionally to mass, then the former is something acceleration-producing, the latter something resisting the production of acceleration, and consequently a counter-force. To be sure, Newton defines mass as the product of volume and density; but later physicists have rightly emphasized the illusoriness of a definition that, with the concept of density (= mass of the unit of volume), already presupposes that of mass. If, then, we take only our formula as a basis, the definition of mass would have to read: mass is resistance to acceleration.

Now, as was shown above, the mechanical concept of force always points back to something outside the system, upon which the change of velocity is to be visited; and insofar as the ground of the effect that a mass suffers must be sought in a second mass, then, according to the law named third by Newton, each of the two masses does something, in proportion to its quantum, *to* the other mass (principle of the equality of action and reaction). [p. 704] Were we now to want to define the concept of mass from this, we would arrive first at that definition which, to our knowledge, the theoretical physicist Mach was the first to prefer: "We call bodies of equal mass those which, acting upon one another, impart to each other equal and opposite accelerations." Further: "If we take the comparison body A as the unit, then we ascribe to that body the mass m which imparts to A m-times the acceleration that it receives in return-action from A." Or, by way of example: a body M has five times the mass of the body m, if it imparts to the latter five times that acceleration which it itself receives from it. Nothing, however, prevents us from placing the emphasis on the resistance to acceleration that mass represents in the "classical equation," and accordingly determining: a body has the mass m which receives from the unit of mass only the m-th part of the acceleration that it imparts to the unit of mass. But if, through this, what goes by the name of mass becomes, with regard to the effects a body exerts, an acceleration-producing power, and, with regard to the effects it receives from another body, a power resisting the production of acceleration, then the essential sameness of force and mass emerges beyond contradiction.

One cannot, of course, tell by looking at mass so defined that masses gravitate toward one another, let alone according to what law the "attractive force" changes with the magnitude of the intervening space. Since, however, according to Galileo's pathbreaking discovery, all bodies at the same place — or, in more modern terms, in a given gravitational field — undergo the same acceleration, weight and inertia must be proportional to one another, and it holds that, with a suitably chosen measure-number, "heavy mass" is equal to "inert mass." — The proportionality of weight and inertia, or, in other words, the measurability of "inert mass" = mass as such by the weight of bodies, has in more recent physics for a time attracted rather more attention than was warranted by the nature of the matter. This is connected, unless we are mistaken, with certain considerations according to which, for the sake of subordinating everything to the concept of energy and at the price of surrendering the constancy of mass, mass is to be conceived as a function of velocity. Yet it is and remains<sup>25</sup> *the same* resistance to acceleration which, in the form of mass, opposes itself to any pressure or impact or pull, and which, in the gravitational field, determines the "attractive force" prevailing between masses.

<sup>25</sup> On page 704. — In modern relativity theory, mass has, as is well known, forfeited its constancy and has become a function of velocity according to the following formula: where E = kinetic energy, c = the speed of light, and v = the velocity of the body. The deviation from the „classical formula" grows the more nearly v approaches the speed of light. Were v actually to equal c, then E, and with it the mass, would become ∞.

[p. 705] As little as Newton yet hit upon the thought of *defining* mass as a force-factor, so little does he leave any doubt at all as to the proper sense of his concept of mass. "Matter," he says, "possesses the power to resist. This force is always proportional to the body (= mass), and differs only in conception from the inertia of matter... wherefore... (it) could be given the very fitting name: force of inertia. The body therefore exercises this force only upon the change of its state, which is to be brought about by another force applied to it, and the former acts, from different points of view, now as resisting, now as attacking force. Resisting, insofar as the body, to maintain its state, counteracts the applied force; attacking, insofar as it, by yielding only with difficulty to the force of the obstacle opposing it, tries to change the state of the latter." Here there is no longer talk of voluminous quanta of mass, but solely of a force which, to be sure, has the peculiarity of becoming effective only then and only insofar as it must, so to speak, defend its own skin — in which our readers cannot fail to divine the self-assertive compulsion of the personal I, transposed into the world of appearance!

The concept of mass rests on the concept of matter, the concept of matter on the concept of body, and the concept of body cannot be formed without the mark of the spatial extendedness of the body; for a body of extension zero would no longer be a body. But if we determine the concept of mass from the applications that a Newton, and the whole of Newtonian physics, makes of it, it gives us not the faintest inkling of the extendedness of mass, and we notice — which, indeed, after the foregoing considerations, will no longer surprise us — that, like physical force, the mass essentially identical with it likewise lacks extendedness. It will come up later that matter *cannot* be derived in thought. All attempts since Boscovich to accomplish this have failed, and all future attempts will fail as well, regardless of whether undertaken with or without belief in the constancy of mass. But however that may be, this much is certain: attempts of that kind lie germinally prefigured in the Newtonian concept of mass, which is in fact an extensionless force. As often, then, as mechanistic thinking made any move, in however serious a manner, to expand itself into a [p. 706] ("world-view"), it issued into a matterless world-picture, now more atomistic, now more energetic, now more dynamistic in character. "By this route," the famous physicist Weber once wrote to Fechner, who likewise professed an atomism without matter, "one arrives at a concept of mass to which the notion of spatial extension does not at all necessarily adhere. Consistently enough, the magnitude of the atoms, on the atomistic view, is in no way measured by spatial extension, but by their mass, i.e., by the ratio, constant for each atom, in which, for the atom, force stands to acceleration." In the comparatively most consistent, but also inwardly most impossible, and most unreservedly revealing of its subjective genetic history form, dynamism offers us, in place of actuality... a system of immaterial, but "materializing," and of course movable, force-centers, whose perhaps most astonishing, and quite properly fantastic, peculiarity inescapably consists in this: that they act, indeed, into the remotenesses of infinity, but not at the place, whatever it may be, of their own existence! But we do not<sup>26</sup> wish to anticipate, and for the present state: just as the left-hand side of the equation that served us as a model of mechanistic thinking annihilates happening by means of the concept of being, so the right-hand side, by means of the spaceless concept of force, annihilates matter, and consequently the corporeal receiving-place of images.

<sup>26</sup> On page 706. — The most consistent execution of so-called dynamism is offered, as far as we can see, by E. von *Hartmann* in his still, even today, worthwhile „Weltanschauung der modernen Physik," 2nd ed. 1909, especially pp. 202—206. In our judgement it is the best book Hartmann wrote — Hartmann, who was a *mechanist*, not a vitalist and metaphysician, as he himself believed. —• Had the equating of materialism with mechanism not become so thoroughly established that the reader not specifically briefed is accustomed to understand by the mechanistic world-view a materialistic world-view, and conversely, the confusion of the two words would be one to avoid. *Genuine* materialism is, like Platonism, a great intellectual achievement of antiquity, forever bound up with the names Democritus, Epicurus, Lucretius. What alone is real for it are indivisible, movable little bodies, called atoms, of a determinate magnitude of extension, fixed shape, and resistant impenetrability. Its point of departure lies in considerations concerning the full and the empty, and its secretly operative pull lies in the particular significance of the experiences of the sense of touch for the formation of the existential judgement. Like all antique types of thought it reaches far into the modern age, and was renewed as late as the 17th century, among others by Gassendi. — Mechanism, by contrast, beginning with Galileo and already culminating in Newton, belonging exclusively to the modern age, aims from the very start at the *denial* of matter, and is consummated, both physically and philosophically, in *formalism*.

The strongest minds among the greatest mechanists became clear, early on, that with such an attitude of spirit one had renounced a knowledge of the world such as, for example, hovered before the thinking Greek and the medieval Scholastic, and that henceforth, in all honesty, one could no longer raise the claim to want to "explain" or "fathom" anything. At approximately the same time as the mechanistic turn, there begins a kind of skepticism unknown to antiquity, namely the formalistic kind, whose creed might be circumscribed somewhat as follows: to know is denied to man; but on the basis of experience he can learn to predict and calculate what will happen under given conditions. Newton himself opens the round. "The designation attraction, impulse, or inclination," he says, "I employ without distinction... inasmuch as I consider these forces not in the physical but in the mathematical sense. The reader should therefore not conclude from remarks of this kind that I wish [p. 707] to explain the manner and way of the operation or the physical cause, or that I ascribe to the centers... actual and physical forces, when I say: the centers attract, or centripetal forces take place." The name of force, thus deprived of force, is henceforth to designate something in and for itself wholly unknown, in connection with which one is no longer to think at all of any operative powers, but only of certain measure-numbers of mathematical equations. Somewhat earlier already, the Englishman Glanvill had invented that subjectivizing of causality which was then further spun out and completed by Hume. Of Kant's "abolition of knowledge" we need not remind the reader again. A little variation is brought into skeptical formalism by *Kirch*hoff, with the concept of description, much favored ever since. "I set it up as the task of mechanics to describe the motions occurring in nature completely and in the simplest way. I mean by this that the only concern should be to state what the appearances are that take place, not, however, to ascertain their causes" (Vorlesungen über mathematische Physik, Lpzg. 1876). But the conceptually strictest attempt at a world-view of causal resignation is furnished, in the "Prinzipien der Mechanik," by Hertz, with what was later called his hylokinetics, which removes from the elementary physical concepts that of force and that of energy, and undertakes to construct a "world-picture" out of the motions of extensionless mass-points, in relation to which "force" falls to the role of a merely thought-of intermediate term between two motions. — To the cynical forms, finally, of modern denial of knowledge that go under the name of "pragmatism," and to the wittily ironic forms of the "relativists," we shall return further below with a few words.

The seeming modesty of such doubt-mongering proves, on closer consideration, to be in truth an arrogant immodesty; for, far from accusing itself of inadequacy in matters of knowing, it elevates the inadequacy in question into a deficiency fundamentally inherent in thinking itself, and plans nothing less than to deny the right to exist to every effort at knowledge that seeks to free itself from such inadequacy! In the gesture of unpretentiousness the formalist disguises, in truth, his bitter enmity against every kind of metaphysics (= inquiry into actuality); [p. 708] hence, in the face of metaphysical claims to knowledge, the doubter at once turns into a furious dogmatist. "Into the fire with everything," the seemingly so matter-of-fact Hume can be heard to say, "that contains neither mathematical investigations nor observations concerning matters of fact and actuality!" Without batting an eye, the skeptic refers the investigations he approves of to an "actuality," and seems not in the least to notice that he first had to eviscerate actuality, and anatomically prepare the eviscerated remains, in order to be able to make *the* observations which his unbelief stands ready to believe!

Newton's "hypotheses non fingo" has been repeated countless times with enthusiasm, without anyone troubling to notice that his natural philosophy consists not merely of nothing but hypotheses, but even of nothing but fictions. A thinking more estranged from actuality has never been devised, not even by those Scholastics who disputed whether and how a camel might pass through the eye of a needle! Let us, however, once more call to mind straightaway on what the semblance of the contrary really rests. When the Algonquin Indian of North America wished to kill a certain animal, he would, reciting spells, shoot an arrow in his wigwam at the grass-image of the animal: the more firmly the arrow lodges in it, the more surely will the prototype be brought down the next day. In their ideograms this people represent the magical fascination of a human being or an animal by a line running from the mouth to the heart. The wolf, for instance, must die whose image, drawn in this way, is addressed by the medicine-man with the spell: "Run, wolf, your body is mine!" The Illinois pierced the image-doll of the being to be bewitched at precisely that place on the body where the harmful influence was to be exerted. Practices of this kind, recurring among all primitive peoples in millionfold variations, rest on the belief in the actuality of images. Whether and to what extent they had success or not, we can no longer verify today, and therefore cannot judge; for, since primitive peoples, *all* primitive peoples all along the line, are in process of dying out, we lack, for a renewed investigation, a wholly indispensable condition — namely the production of the state of *consciousness* that accompanied the accomplishment of the "magic" — whereas we all, one and all, without any effort, share in *the* state of consciousness on the basis of which one observes, weighs, measures, counts, and calculates. Mechanics [p. 709] concerns itself neither with images nor with copied images, but observes, measures, and calculates, sets up experiments on the basis of its calculations, and invents machines. Its arts rest on the belief in the actuality of the measure-number, or, if one prefers, in the applicability of the measure-number to actuality; and we see the successes of this before us in the form of a technology whose interventions into actuality are of such violence and reach that, in comparison with it, the magical procedures of primeval times, even were we willing to grant their efficacy, shrink to a comparatively ineffectual undertaking. Should it not, we feel persuaded, be that what so powerfully and, as it were, irresistibly influences actuality must be highly commensurate with actuality! Yet with this we would have drawn the criterion of the correctness of a judgement from its suitability for satisfying the will's needs for power. With the same right we might discover in the horse a propensity to being whipped, because it runs faster whenever one strikes it, and because thereby *we* arrive more swiftly at our goal! A cruder "anthropomorphism" has never existed; but then, too, no cruder estrangement from actuality. Yet that might still pass, were the estrangement not paired with the inventive eavesdropping that stands in the service of enmity toward actuality. If we consider that technology has already, for the most part, slaughtered the freely living races of animals, and will in due course slaughter them entirely (leaving out of account only the microbes!), that it turns primeval forests into newsprint, and, with poison gases, electricity, and explosives, provides the means to kill even human beings by the millions in the shortest span of time — while it has never once succeeded in generating life — then we shall recognize the seeming commensurateness of its presuppositions with actuality for what it is: for an uncommonly ingenious instrument of destruction. — We turn once more back to formalism.

One deceives oneself with the hope of being able to circumvent explanations by using, in place of the word explanation, the word description. For there is no description that does not enclose within itself countless explanations, and there is, conversely, no explanation that could not be grasped from the standpoint of a description. The possibility of the judgement "Before my window there stands a tree" hangs upon a well-nigh unsurveyable prehistory of thought, according to which we, for example, learned to distinguish trees from [p. 710] plants, plants in general from animals, the window from the wall, the own-I from the alien-I, standing from lying, and, by virtue of a very remarkable generalization, learned to apply the activity of standing to the mere existence of the tree — not to speak of the fact that, in doing so, we referred an indeterminate number of intuitive images to the tree as to something enduring through time, and construed this something in the sense of an *effect*. Were we to pursue further and further the grounds that make this judgement possible, we would infallibly arrive at the result that not a single one of the concepts on which we rely in doing so is necessary, and that this so simple description — or, more correctly, communication — represents a, though admissible, interpretation of a state of affairs that could be interpreted just as correctly in a hundred other ways. Conversely, of course, we can give to every explanation the form of a description. But since the word description, in everyday usage, means a linguistic utterance that appeals particularly to the meaning-experiences, and not to the conceptual thinking, of the hearer — namely for the purpose of the conceptual production of the sensible intuitive content of the described states of affairs — it should, in principle, not be used where objects of thought are concerned, whose adequate apprehension demands precisely the far-reaching exclusion of mere meaning-feelings and the utmost possible detachment from mood-toned intuitive contents. One need only hold the description of a tropical thunderstorm alongside the numerical data that, on the occasion of the same tropical thunderstorm, are supplied by the instruments of the meteorologist, who is intent on explaining the phenomenon, and one will recognize, in the playfulness of such a substitution of names, the failed attempt to take the edge off the renunciation of knowledge by declaring null and void the will to truth as such.

And likewise one succumbs to a self-deception with the view that, by restricting oneself to equations of condition, one has happily steered clear of the reef of having to explain. For granted that actuality were measurable, which it is not, still measuring presupposes something to be measured, and the fundamental equation of the mechanist's religion, actuality = measurability, would merely say that he considers it expedient no longer to concern himself with the What and How; whereby he would have unreservedly surrendered it to the metaphysician. He would then behave like the merchant who knows: this is flour, [p. 711] that is sugar, that is rice, "quality" and "grade" included, and who certainly does not confuse his task of weighing out the flour, the sugar, the rice with an effort at cognition. But just as little as the physicist will ever admit that his renunciation of explanation simply means a renunciation of knowledge, just as little would it help him if he were to rouse himself to so improbable a candor; for his actuality is only measurable because he has previously carried into it a wealth of concepts foreign to its essence, which include just as many highly exclusive *explanations* of happening.

With this, to be sure, it is not to be denied that at least thinkers such as a Newton or a Kirchhoff had cogent grounds to be distrustful of the explanatory value of their formalism. They felt, indisputably, that their mode of research, even if perfected to the utmost, could not offer explanations in the sense in which one had expected them in the pre-mechanistic period of thought and believed one could also offer them with the help of so-called speculations. They therefore gladly indulged in a double bookkeeping, hoping, by the formalistic self-restraint of "science," to save the subjective certainties of "faith." Were not precisely the greatest natural scientists convinced deists! The biological connection is known to our readers. Here we merely remark that anyone who claims for himself the unassailability of mere articles of faith forfeits a hundred times over the right to forbid speculative convictions — however wild they may be — by the legislation of a "science" that has condemned itself to capitulation before the wish-fulfillment phantasms of personal desires! Meanwhile the well-spring of their distrust is exclusively the concept which we may no longer put off illuminating: the concept of cause.

Since Hume, philosophers cannot get out of their heads the notion that the thought of cause stems from the somehow regular succession of two processes, of which the first is called the cause, the second the effect. This is all the more remarkable in that one not only recognized the untenability of Hume's attempt to explain so peculiar a usage of language, but very soon also noticed that he based it on wholly erroneous claims. For however often we might have perceived the succession: sinking of the mercury column in the barometer, or low flight of swallows, and rainy weather, [p. 712] we would nonetheless by no means have held the sinking of the barometer or the low flight of swallows to be the cause of the rain — whereas, given the correct approach to calculation, a single pendulum experiment suffices to let us determine, for a given geographical latitude and height above sea level, the lawfully valid measure of acceleration, and a second experiment at a correspondingly differently chosen location could even suffice to establish the lawful relation between the magnitude of the acceleration and geographical latitude as well as height above sea level. Who, moreover, could fail to notice the circularity in Hume's attempt at explanation! "Now the idea of power," he says (loc. cit. pp. 222–24), "is a new, independent idea, which is not to be met with in the idea of the individual cases. This effect, then, repetition *by itself* cannot have; rather it must first either let us recognize or *produce* something new that can be the source of that idea. . . . Even though the various similar cases from which the idea of power arises exert no effect on one another and can never call forth any new property in the object . . . , yet the observation of this similarity does call forth a new impression in the mind. This now is the true archetype for the idea of power. After we have observed the similarity in a sufficient number of cases, we feel in the mind a compulsion to pass from the one object to its usual companion. . . . This compulsion is the sole effect of the similarity; it must therefore be one and the same with power or efficacy. . ." Hume thus believes he has explained the appearance of the not merely incomprehensible but also unexhibitable working of objects upon one another from — an effect of the objects upon the human mind, thus clearly presupposing, in the same breath, as existing what he pretends to want to refute: the capacity for effect of the objects!<sup>27</sup>

<sup>27</sup> On page 712. — One should not, perhaps, be deceived by the detour through similarity! For this similarity is in fact treated exactly like a property of objects, however much Hume may refuse to hear of it. It *produces* in us the idea of similarity in the very same way that some property of a body produces in us, say, the idea of redness. It stands on *the same* line as the Humean „perception." Does it not, after all, bring forth „a new *impression*" in the mind?

Meanwhile such considerations are superfluous, because Hume evidently confuses two wholly different states of affairs. If the succession of two impressions, which we intuitively distinguish, repeats itself often enough, there arises in us a very strong tendency, upon the first impression, to think of the second; a somewhat weaker one, upon the second, to think of the first; and in any case always the tendency to make present both in that same succession; only that is precisely not what we mean by causing and effecting! Were one to urge against [p. 713] our barometer example that a "savage," or even merely an uneducated and at the same time highly superstitious person, might perhaps actually believe at some point that the sinking of the mercury draws the rain after it, we would have to reply that this happens only because the thought of causality has already become familiar to the one so judging from a wholly different source. This becomes clear to us as soon as we choose an example that excludes such interpretations. If we hear the notes do, re, mi, fa, we perhaps continue in our minds with sol, la, si, do; but it has never yet occurred to anyone that the first four notes are the cause of the following four notes. Conversely, more recent investigators of appearance have rightly pointed out that we are able to perceive causations directly and in fact perceive them continuously, and we add: were it otherwise, the concept of cause could not have arisen at all, neither in the original nor in the mechanistic sense. We see it, and have not merely inferred it or, thanks to a habit of thought, carried it in, that the brook drives the millwheel, the storm bends the trees, the pouring water extinguishes the flame; we hear the "lashing" of the rain, the "raging" of the surf, the "grinding" of the ice floes, and we see just as directly that it is the resistance of the rock on which the surf shatters; indeed, we hear, without looking, the hardness of the ground on which the falling jug breaks. Not some repetition of processes, but perception itself forms the starting point of both the vitalistic and the mechanistic conception of cause, even though the former differs from the latter in an essential respect, in that it grants the working forces the transient character of one that also experiences its working: the rain is an active, the tree lashed by it, in relation thereto, a suffering entity; the surf an attacking, the rock a power asserting itself against it; the falling of the jug a compelled doing, its breaking a befalling, brought about by the counter-effect of the ground. — Yet these already anticipatory remarks are meant only to help fortify our conviction that the concept of cause was won not from the observation of successions but from the perception of effective connections (which Hume of course had to deny, because they would have torn apart the web of concepts of his atomism of perception!), and thus points back compellingly to the far older concept of force.

[p. 714] We now ask: what becomes of force, and what must become of it, after it has — been de-forced? The first answer runs: a compulsorily working force; and the second answer runs: compulsorily working forces are — properties of things! To be sure the thing is certainly something dead, but the force of which we now speak is likewise something dead, and although coupling of dead with dead by no means produces anything living, still an understanding that has chosen, instead of actuality, its corpse as object of investigation can preserve the appearance of explaining something only by restamping the same state of affairs that, in relation to the image of the world, takes the form of how-constitution, into, in relation to the happening of the world, the force that brings it about — all of which, to be sure, again proceeds compulsorily and wholly involuntarily. "With the properties there is thought into the images the timeless substratum of the thus-being of things, with the forces the equally timeless substratum of the constant efficacy of their existence": the content of this sentence from the 21st chapter the following discussion will have to clarify.

If we think away, from the succession of two processes of which the one is to signify the cause, the second the effect, the properties of the states of affairs involved, it shows itself at once that we have thereby likewise thought away the lawfulness or, as it is usually erroneously put, the necessity of the succession in question; whereby our concept of causing or effecting would be abolished. A little heap of gunpowder, brought into contact with a burning match, explodes. It will remain forever a mere dispute over words what one wishes to call the condition of the explosion, what its cause: the approach of the flame to the powder, or the properties of both; for there is not the least doubt that neither the approach could be dispensed with, nor the constitution of powder and flame, for the explosion to occur. If one accordingly calls the totality of causes or conditions, say, the "sufficient reason" for the occurrence of the explosion, it is also clear that we hold the succession of events to be causal exactly and only insofar as we thereby rely on the relation between the heat of the flame and the explosive decomposability of the gunpowder. If the gunpowder does not explode on contact with the flame, we at once seek the cause for this [p. 715] in a change of property either of the flame or of the powder, and find it, say, in the *dampness* of the powder. Dampness is now a property of the powder which we hold, in exactly the same sense and with exactly the same right, to be the hindering ground of the explosion, as we previously saw, in certain other properties of the powder, its enabling ground. Not the succession of any processes whatever, but the presumed compulsoriness forms the object of the (mechanistic) belief in cause, and this compulsoriness rests solely on the time-independent properties of things, which appear in this manner in the light of forces capable of effect. Change in the effect-magnitude of a force can therefore always be described as a measurable change of a property of the object of the force. It is, for example, a matter of indifference whether we let the so-called force of attraction of the earth, or the weight of bodies, be smaller at the equator than at the pole.

When we say: a thing has such and such properties, we do not thereby mean to express either a relation of possession or even a capacity of disposal of the subject over the predicative object, but we mean: both, that is, what we call a thing and what we call its properties, belong together with lawful inviolability; according to which the thing, in relation to its properties, signifies their sum. If we regard "inherence," as the logical term of art is called, from the standpoint of a capacity for activity of the "substance," then the sum of properties, or more briefly the thing, becomes identical with a sum of time-independent conditions of effect and consequently with an association of "natural laws." Far from being a mere sum of how-constitutions, inherence signifies the time-independent and therefore, with respect to time, *constant* ground of all only possible effects of the thing; according to which it is not merely so-and-so, but is compelled to behave so-and-so. With this, however, we have unspokenly postulated compulsoriness for all processes, or for process as such; and if we remarked in the 36th chapter that causes fall into dispositions of the thing and "other conditions of the development of the disposition," we now have to show that, in the spirit of mechanistic thinking, the "causal explanation" reaches its conclusion only insofar as it has traced back whatever happens to properties of things and their relation to one another.

[p. 716] If we again picture the burning match brought near the gunpowder and now ask after the cause of the approach, we ought not to answer that someone has "done" this, whereby we would normally add that he could also have refrained, in accordance namely with his "freedom of will"; rather, the "cause" would only then be ascertained if we could trace the approach back once more to properties, whether of the thing approaching or of third things, that is, to states of affairs that, under given conditions, would have drawn the process in question after them with the same compulsoriness with which, say, the explosion of the powder would draw after it the burning of a nearby scrap of paper. Our altogether everyday example makes vividly evident the character of the mechanical cause as a de-forced force. For we now stand within a world in which all actions are mere reactions, each of which would point back to a preceding reaction, without an original impetus being ascertainable anywhere that would make it comprehensible why anything happens at all! The "sufficient reason," in other words, consists in a combination of forces that requires a preceding combination of forces, and the compulsoriness that alone concerns us, in the properties of things, insofar as they signify just so many (incomprehensible) capacities for effect and were, with regard to this, quite fittingly called by the Scholastics hidden qualities (qualitates occultae). But if (mechanical) causes are the properties of things once again, only now thought as lawfully regulated capacities for activity of things, then in the mere succession of two processes — even were they to occur without exception — nothing whatsoever of causality remains, as soon as we abstract from the properties of the states of affairs involved. The approach of the flame to the gunpowder by a person, for example, although it would never conflict with the merely quantitative law of conservation, cannot be forced into any mechanical equation, because we lack concepts of personal properties that would relate to the process of approaching in the same way as the properties of the powder relate to the process of exploding upon the approach of the flame.

Were there in fact only rules of succession, nothing would remain for us but to attach the name of causality to some arbitrarily fixed degree of frequency of repetitions; but then the compulsoriness of the courses of events would fall away! Were one to decide, say, after tenfold [p. 717] repetition, to hold a succession to be causally conditioned, one would not in the least need to feel embarrassed if it failed to occur the eleventh time; for even after millions of instances there would be not the slightest guarantee for future recurrence. And were the extraordinary thing to happen that someone who had fallen into the glowing molten flow of the blast furnace were to swim about in it merrily and emerge from this hell as from a bath, that would by no means have to count as a miracle or as sorcery, because there would after all be a complete lack of any ground for the occurrence of the opposite consequence. It is astonishing that Hume, generally held to be acute, does not notice the contradiction into which he runs at every step with his attempt to derive eight rules "by which cause and effect are recognized." One of them runs, for example: "The same cause always produces the same effect, and the same effect arises every time from the same cause." This agrees splendidly indeed with the proposition already championed at an earlier point in his book, "that like objects, under like accompanying circumstances, always produce like effects"; but it fits like a fist in the eye with his idea of the frequency of succession as the occasioning ground of the thought of causality. For with phrases like "the same cause" or "like objects" there is rather laid down precisely that which alone can lend a succession, whether it has occurred once or a thousand times, the character of compulsoriness: the thing determined by properties and consequently determined by effect! We have come to know "sensualism" well enough not to be too greatly astonished at such subreptions in a sensualist; but the gentlemen idealists do no better, for which Schopenhauer in particular offers an instructive example.

He clothes what he calls the principle of sufficient reason in the formula: "Nothing is without a reason why it is," and the "law of causality" in the formula: "Every change in the material world can occur only insofar as another has immediately preceded it," or also: "Every change has its cause in another that has immediately preceded it" (W. a. W. u. V. II, pp. 52 and 55), and tirelessly impresses on us that the said law refers only to changes, and that the cause is in no way to be confused with force. Yet scarcely has he stated this than he continues (on p. 58): "This, wholly different from the cause, is nevertheless that which grants to every cause *its* causality [p. 718] (sic!), that is, the possibility of working"! Indeed, matter is nothing other than causality itself, objectively conceived; its whole essence consists in working as such; it is the efficacy of things pure and simple, and "as it were the abstractum of all its various workings" (loc. cit. p. 59). Whoever still believes in the essential difference between sensualism and idealism can here be taught better. Exactly like Hume, Schopenhauer too starts from a succession that he, however, holds to be compulsory from the outset, and exactly like Hume he must introduce forces and, with them, the property-endowed thing, or rather the substratum of thing-hood conceived in addition, matter, in order to lend the succession the character of causality! — The hearth of these peculiar difficulties of thought we find, however, in Newton's manner of consideration, who, as the initiator, by far surpasses the two just-named thinkers in what one might call a well-nigh ingenious acuteness of distrust. We add to the evidence already offered earlier a second, quite especially convincing one.

He distinguishes the absolute, the accelerating, and the moving centripetal force. The moving force is referred to the body as "a striving and inclining of the whole toward the center," the accelerating to the place of the body "as an effective cause which propagates itself from the center to the individual surrounding places," the absolute to the center, "which is endowed with a cause without which the moving forces would not propagate themselves through the surrounding space." "This cause," he continues, "may now be some central body . . . or in some way invisible. Here at least is the mathematical concept of it, for the physical causes and seats of the forces I do not . . . take into consideration" (Mathematische Prinzipien der Naturlehre, ed. Wolfers, 1872, p. 24). Newton has thus recognized that the accelerating effect of the force presupposes the existence of certain properties in the masses gravitating toward one another, because otherwise it would remain incomprehensible why the degree of effect should depend, among other things, on the magnitude of the masses; but when he adds that he speaks entirely only of the mathematical concept of force and wishes to have determined nothing about the actual "seat" of the force, he thereby betrays his knowledge of the simply insurmountable difficulties that every attempt encounters that would try to understand a working of isolated sums of properties upon one another! — Meanwhile it is precisely his [p. 719] considerations that are suited to unveil to us, in yet another way, the mere semblance of the supposed centripetal force. For what, viewed from the attracted mass-point, looks like a force inhering in the attracting mass-point, presents itself, viewed from the attracting mass-point, as an inclination or leaning toward the attracting mass-point inhering in the attracted mass-points (and indeed of such a kind that the various directions of inclination of several attracted mass-points would intersect in a single point). Out of the attraction of the central mass-point there thus becomes, in the twinkling of an eye, an "inclination" of the peripheral mass-points; from which it becomes clear that attraction as well as inclination can only be meant figuratively and in truth designate the in-itself wholly enigmatic something of which only one thing can be stated, namely the relative magnitude, about which the right side of the well-known equation of mass attraction instructs us. — The most recent physics is preparing to let fall the concept of force at a distance; but we do not believe that it has thereby succeeded in removing the difficulty just noted. Let it be remarked here in advance that the question of force at a distance is not a question of physics but of logic. If I have assumed a real unit, for example a very small mass-point, I have thereby delimited this unit against the totality of the world, and in this manner also marked off a sphere of effect, which we may most simply envisage, say, in the resistance that a mass-point offers to the penetration of a second mass-point into the space momentarily occupied by it. Were I now to assert that the mass-point nonetheless acts upon distant mass-points (e.g., attractively), I would have again abolished the sphere of effect just marked off and replaced it with a correspondingly larger sphere of effect; and were I even to let it be understood that it acts without limit, I would have made of it a something that fills the whole of space, and would thereby have annihilated my mass-point. Furthermore, however — and this has always<sup>28</sup> been felt by thinking physicists, and stated a hundred times over by philosophers — it would not help us at all to associate or substitute near-forces for the farforces. It is entirely a matter of indifference whether we let our real units be separated by enormously large or minutely small intervals, because real units enter into connection with one another just as little as one of the five arithmetical ones in the [p. 720] number five could enter into connection with one of the remaining ones. In particular, the sometimes involuntarily co-imagined contact of mass-points is a thing of impossibility. Either they remain isolated at the point of contact (which is of course pictured on the model of intuition), and then something must be between them, whether empty space or ether or whatever else, and the effect of contact differs in nothing essential from an effect across light-millennia of distance; or there would then be nothing more between them, and then they would fuse at the point in question and would thereafter have ceased to be two mass-points. Isolated units purchase their existence at the price of the incapacity to exert or receive effects, and they purchase the capacity to exert or receive effects at the price of their — existence. One sees — Newton had good reasons for denying his "forces" physical significance!

<sup>28</sup> On page 719. — The claim that a something is also there where it acts has been combated with countless arguments, which, on closer inspection, prove one and all to be self-deceptions, because ultimately resting on the reification of a verb. — Here is a mass-point A; it acts on the mass-point B, at any distance of kilometres. Either this *has* a meaning, and then it is this: that the mass-point A reaches with something as far as the mass-point *B*; or one has imagined that the mass-point A sends an „effect" out into space, and then the statement has *no* meaning. Just as surely as the abstraction Running or Standing or Jumping is not capable of existing, but only a thing running, standing, jumping, so surely is abstract Acting not capable of existing, but only something acting. This is not contradicted by the fact that the effect spreads, needs time, grows weaker with increasing distance, and so on, as we assume, say, of light. Rather, the example of the light-ray can, as hardly anything else, make vivid to us the presence of the agent at the place of its action. Whatever we may wish to think in the case of the so-called light-ray, this much is certain: that by virtue of it the luminous thing literally *reaches* all the way to all the points to which it can attain — illuminating them. If we place a light-impermeable wall in the path of the „ray," then, beyond it, the shining is in no way present any longer. But how could the mere function of shining rebound from a resistance?! How could we bolt a door against acting „in itself"?! I may run my head against the door; but it is not my running that can run against the door; I may run across the railway embankment, but it is not my running that runs across the embankment. And it is not the shining that exists, nor the „radiating," but, for all eternity, only the shining thing, the radiating thing, whose peculiarity it is to spread out well-nigh without limit, to meet obstacles which, for their part, then in turn become shining and shiningly self-spreading obstacles, and so on. To be sure, the fantastic assumption of actions at a distance has its reasons. They lie, to put it in a word, in the mystery of *corporeality*, of which we shall still have occasion to speak in the third volume. The luminous *body*, e.g. Jupiter, quite certainly does *not reach* as far as the earth; consequently it — the corporeal planet Jupiter, that is — acts, shining, into vast distances; whence, then, spring the well-known hypotheses: emission theory, undulation theory, ether hypothesis, and so on. Now, the polarity of nearness and farness is an inexplicable further "primal phenomenon." If one *begins* with it, there is a way to make the hereness of farness intelligible as well. If, on the other hand, one begins with the here of the body, one is sooner or later forced onto the path of mechanistic attempts at explanation, and these are forever hopeless.

The puzzling character of impact and counter-impact has often been illuminated with similar considerations; but it has been neglected to draw from this the consequence with which we now come straightaway to the main point of our analysis; otherwise one could not have imagined mastering the embarrassment by replacing the mass-points now with force-centers, now with accumulations of energy, now with other "agents." Since mass, indeed the "matter" of physics, already from the outset, as we have seen, lacks extension, and since it signifies of the "force" of physics merely a factor, it means little when one proceeds to de-materialize and to relativize. For as long as one is still at all minded to measure, to calculate, one cannot avoid positing centers of effect and consequently units of effect, regardless of whether one finds it more fitting to seal what does the effecting with the name mass or force or energy or agent. But once one has marked off spheres of effect, one has also isolated them against one another, and stands with the difficulty of thinking transmissions of effect at exactly the same point!

We hope to have made clear that the modern concept of cause represents only a vague generalization of the modern concept of force, and that the modern concept of force signifies a force de-forced to the very marrow, which — wholly unfit for real working — serves merely for the setting up of mathematical equations, with which one calculates an impending process from a presently occurring process, [p. 721] insofar as one knows it. With this the entire thinking of the modern age since the "Renaissance" moves into the light of a *formal*istic skepticism which, secretly steered by the great physicists and calculators, aims at the subjectivization of the world — namely, through the spiritualization-in of the images, at the subjectivization of the *actuality*-character of the contents of lived experience; through the spiritualization-in of happening, at the subjectivization of the contents of the lived experience of actuality. And we hold in particular the Galilean concept of the powerless force to be the incipient occasioning ground of that volatilization of belief in working causes whose main stages are marked, roughly, by Hume, Kant, and the very latest relativism. However qualitatively different the three may be from one another, they nonetheless mark a sequence of stages toward ever more unrestricted subjectivization.

Hume holds: there are no working powers, but there are indeed constant repetitions of similar successions, and these compel us to hold them necessary. — Kant holds: thanks to a constitution of our faculty of apprehension, happening becomes an object of experience only insofar as it can be thought as taking place according to rules of succession; or: the causal conditionedness of all happening is the consequence of a rule of connection inhering in the human understanding (independent of the personal bearer), without whose application to the world of appearance no consciousness of objectivity whatever would arise. — The relativist holds: so-called actuality is a chess problem, and whoever solves it most successfully has a claim to the Nobel Prize. — According to Hume, it is after all we who are compelled by impressions, even though the occasions of impression do not compel one another; according to Kant it is the (moreover again merely apparent) world of appearance that must submit to compulsions through our "transcendental apperception"; according to the relativist view the whole magic is at bottom a play of our *arbitrary will*. Relativism is, of the three, the most nearly right, though hardly in the sense that would itself be agreeable to it.

Since the Kantian view was held, for more than a century, to be exceedingly enlightened, and still partly is, let it be said in passing that of such a constitution of the human "mind" there can be no talk at all. As soon as one applies the thought of causality to particular cases, it shows itself at once that there is, in principle, not a single one among them that extra-historical [p. 722] as well as prehistoric intelligences have not sometimes conceived against the rule. If, for example, we are convinced that death strictly and lawfully follows the striking off of the head, there were and are, in fairy tales, legends, and even still in the belief of the Middle Ages, miracle-men, devil's servants, and saints enough who, after the said procedure, took their head in their hand and walked off with it. The prehistoric stage of symbolically thinking man knows, broadly speaking, no rules of succession at all, and thus not in the least our concept of causality either, but for that has suffered so little damage to its consciousness of actuality that it, on the contrary, remained wholly untouched by the subjectivistic doubts that have eaten into and riddled the world-picture of modern man. — As for the supposed or actual compulsion to carry a rule of succession into actuality and to interpret causally the happening thus, as it were, falsified, after all that has been set forth it needs no further justification when we assert: that compulsion exists precisely insofar as we regard actuality from the standpoint of the existence of things, and it compels us, in particular, to causal thinking exactly to the degree that our attention is directed not to the how-constitution of things but to the existing of things and to their inseparable-from-it self-comportment. (Existence, be it remarked in passing, is itself already a self-comportment, as we shall soon recognize still more sharply.) But if it has already become evident to us earlier that the thing-point can be nothing other than the I-point hurled out of ourselves into the world, then meanwhile the doctrine of the will has revealed to us a kind of priority of the willing I over the cognizing I, according to which, with respect to its existence, thing-hood would be an analogue of the deed-doing spirit, and the much-discussed causality a volition mirrored back. We now reflect on the extent to which, and only for this reason, the chain of causes is inconcludable.

Had we consciously transferred the I onto actuality, that would be for us an aesthetic play which we certainly would not have brought about in order to explain actuality.
