As it is, however, the transference took place and takes place unconsciously, because the I has no prospect of getting at actuality except by reading I-like entities into it. If, with this, force and finally cause in general become a force effecting by way of will, it nonetheless remains different from actual willing, whose bearer is exclusively [p. 723] the personal I, in that it *lacks* the vehicle of vital impulses. For every world-interpretation grown on the soil of the will to power, the object signifies merely a material for the exercise of will, more briefly a resistance to be overcome. Its goal is calculability (thus measurability), and its interest is directed compulsorily toward the suppression of the living as of that which can never be calculated, and toward the formation of concepts of states of affairs that are simply lifeless. In the will-picture, finally, of happening in general — or at least of extra-human happening — there remains, of actual willing, only the mirroring of willing "in itself," of willing after the subtraction of vitality, and consequently of a willing without the capacity of accomplishment. But if the will alone can bring about nothing whatsoever, neither in the sense of acceleration nor of deceleration nor of change of direction, since it must always base itself on processes already present (in order to split them), then the "force" distilled from it borrows its semblance of working from another force, this again from another, and so on to infinity: that is the ground of the inconcludable chain of causes!

This, to be sure, could not in the long run remain hidden from thinking minds, so that they had to say to themselves: there are no working causes at all. But since they did not recognize the true ground of this, they wished to make us believe that our perception of working powers rests on self-deception (just as, in another respect, they wished to make us believe that the actuality of the world-image is a mere semblance), whereas in truth the will to mastery must not believe in the actuality of working powers (just as it must not believe in the actuality of the images), insofar as it is not prepared to deny all cognitive value to the propositions that were and are asserted of actuality for the sake of enabling its interventions in it. Once we have broken the world up into things, that is, into de-vitalized points, then nothing whatever can happen in it any longer, because the point would already again have ceased to exist as soon as we thought it connected with a second point in any way whatsoever; and so the belief in cause volatilizes, in accordance with its inherent logic, into the belief in mere lawfulness or, more bluntly put, into the calculability of the course of the world. Yet even in this, as was already indicated earlier, there still lies a concession to actuality.

The deed-doing spirit, placed with power of authority into actuality, [p. 724] would of itself, at a single stroke, transform the whole cosmos into nothing, were limits not set to its drive to destruction by the vitality attached to it, without which it would find no place in the universe. Just as it was the intuitive images to be experienced through which the spirit saw itself compelled to multiply the objectified I-point indeterminately often, so it is the happening to be experienced, the ceaseless self-transforming of the images, whereby the spirit sees itself compelled to regard the properties of things as though they were forces or causes or conditions of effect, according to which something could occur among things. In the "lawfulness" that is accordingly supposed to belong to all events, actuality has a share, with the independence of the assumed conditions of effect from the arbitrary will of the spirit; and the spirit, in turn, with the assumption of an unchangeability thanks to which the necessity of happening is exchanged for numerically determined compulsion. The concession extorted from the spirit thus lies in this: that for the purpose of setting up its laws it must simply take something in receipt, while it proves the self-sovereignty of its interventions by forbidding change to what is found and to be found, or, put otherwise, by not ceasing its analyses before it believes itself to have struck upon conditions of effect of the unchangeable character of number, because only such form, for the will to mastery, the through-and-through reliable object. It aims, in the last resort, at a single invariant, in relation to which all world-processes would be its functions (that is the sense of so-called monism); and we have, conversely, to establish that the supposed cognitive endeavors, insofar as they are steered by this very striving, are only executive organs of the will bent on power. Since, further, only in a peculiar intermediate region between the cosmic and the organic world, in the region of the inorganic processes of the earth's surface, does the calculation agree sufficiently to carry through the dominion of spirit as well, while the world of organic life remains outside as a constant miracle, it is by no means an accidental consequence but belongs to the process itself as the immediate manifestation of its origin in the enmity of the will toward actuality, when out of mechanics there grew a technology whose goal reveals itself ever more clearly as the extermination of countless animal species, indeed finally of all living beings of the globe.

[p. 725] The crisis-laden episode of purposive thinking, however, which is just now playing itself out in the form of a relativism that — a kind of gambler — is on the point of surrendering even the last invariant, reveals to us in a flash the hidden driving force of the seeming striving after knowledge and lets it become visible even to duller eyes that the demand for sameness and its counter-image, the fact, designate only the agreement that was extorted from actuality by the ego militans, whereas the ego triumphans takes leave of factuality with an ironic bow, in order henceforth no longer to discover the so-called laws of nature but to dictate them as it pleases. The spirit is as surely counter-logical as it is the deed in itself, or — in relation to actuality — the unbound arbitrary will. — Meanwhile the triumph will prove to be a little premature. One will present to the presumptuous calculating understanding a few of the bills it has drawn: let it hand us means for reversing the direction of time, so that old men may be in a position to begin again as youths, and still more ambitious spirits even to lead their lives back to bygone periods of history that seem to them less corrupt than the present. The calculating understanding will seek evasions, and these wish-fulfillment phantasms of the will to omnipotence will have to abdicate — to make room for other fantasies.<sup>29</sup> For one may henceforth in any case permit oneself, in growing measure, the luxury of denying knowledge, because for the goal-near dominion of arbitrary will, *truth*, with which the spirit previously had to talk itself round, becomes from hour to hour not only more inconvenient but also — more dispensable. And so it is understandable that here and there we already hear a Hosanna flying ahead. — Turning once more to the conception of causality and the history of its volatilization into mathematical equations, the atomized world of physics might now well appear to us like a heap of splintered mirrors, each of which reflects back the willing I, whereby, to be sure, one side of the real world actually became calculable and masterable for it, while the sense of truth, still logically bound, sees itself knotted into inextricable contradictions. The centers of effect, bare of all vitality, cannot possibly work upon one another, and the world-machine into which we find them yoked, similar to the slave-laborer of civilization into the machine of the state, is at bottom a ghostly humbug and, as it were, the shadow, cast upon the vault of heaven, [p. 726] of the soulless and depraved doings of the men of today. Let one only, without prejudice, once fix one's eye on the never meaningless designations! Out of matter, that is, the mother of the world, there has become the "inert mass" and finally the "dead stuff" out of which the spirit kneads the world-devouring golem! The "energy" allegedly read out of nature serves, not by accident, to characterize the will, and the "work" equivalent to it leaves not the faintest doubt any longer as to from which realm of experience the models for the conceptual language of this natural science are taken! Should one wish nonetheless to see in this unimportant externalities, one will no longer be able to, in view of the through-and-through voluntaristic stamp of "force," as the following juxtaposition may attest. 1. For the will, actuality means resistance; for physical force, likewise. 2. The will proves itself in overcoming resistances, force equally so. 3. In contrast to the drives, the will is one and always the same; force likewise, in contrast to the qualities. 4. The will is directed straight at its goal; force no differently. 5. The will is imageless; force no less so. 6. Will-power is, from case to case, greater or smaller; the force of mechanics too. 7. The urge of will is a movement dammed up at the Now, which of itself would drive the moment before it; force is measured by the increase of velocity that is imparted through it to the movable thing that resists. 8. Will as well as force are without a past. 9. The time-relation of both is imaginary, because it goes toward a merely conceivable future.

<sup>29</sup> On page 725. — When a researcher accustomed to Greek thought and to logical rigor comes into proximity with present-day theories of relativity, he always feels tempted to grow "weary of the dry tone." Since, however, relativism is precisely the *trump card*, one will hardly hold it against us that we have allowed ourselves a few jokes at its expense. For this reason let it be shown here, if only in the utmost brevity, why we hold it to be demonstrably false. If relativism meant only a mathematical or kinematic or physical theory, the mathematician, or the physicist, would be ten times right to counter the metaphysician who wished to criticize it with "cobbler, stick to your last!" Mathematics and physics are not poor in logically inadequate conceptions which have nonetheless proved extremely serviceable. To be sure, the writer of these lines has not so far been able to convince himself that the *physical* theory of relativity has actually *achieved* anything in physics, and even less did the evidentiary value of those phenomena which relativism claims to explain seem persuasive to him. The famous deflection of light rays by gravitation, for example, was — according to a "communication" of *Lenard's* in issue 15 of the "Annalen der Physik," [n]th series, volume 65 (1931), p. 69 — not merely asserted but also *correctly calculated* 120 years earlier by the German mathematician *Sold*-*ner*, without relativistic considerations playing the *slightest* part in it. But such doubts may simply be due to the writer's *lack* *of* physical education; and in any case the physical theory of relativity is a matter which the physicists must settle among themselves. What occupies the *metaphysician* is something else. There is no doubt *that* at least since *Mach* the relativists of physics have been setting about presenting us with supposedly new disclosures concerning *actual* space and *actual* time, *actual* motion included. Indeed, entire relativistic "world-pictures" have meanwhile branched off from Einsteinism! But then the situation is reversed; and it is now the metaphysician who feels obliged to hold up to the mathematicians and physicists the "cobbler, stick to your last!" Accordingly, in what follows we are concerned only with the world-view note of relativism, in which, as goes without saying, mathematical considerations play not the slightest part. But so that any possibility of misunderstanding be excluded, our critique rests exclusively on a few literal quotations from *Einstein*, who has taken the commendable trouble to set forth the fundamental concepts of the theory of relativity, with a minimum expenditure of calculation, in terms intelligible to the layman, in the small work "Über die spezielle und die allgemeine Relativitätstheorie," 14th ed., Vieweg und Sohn, Braunschweig, 1922. On page 14 it says there: "At two points A and B, far apart on our railway embankment, lightning has struck the track. I add the assertion that these two strokes occurred *simultaneously*. If I now ask you, dear reader, whether this statement has a meaning, you will *answer* me with a confident 'Yes.' But if I now press you with the request to explain the meaning of the statement more precisely, you notice after some reflection *that* the answer to this question is not as simple as it appears at first sight. — After a while the following answer will perhaps occur to you: 'The meaning of the statement is clear in and of itself and needs no further explanation; some reflection would, however, be required of me if I were given the task of determining by observation whether, in the concrete case, the two events took place simultaneously or not.' But I cannot content myself with this answer, for the following reason. Suppose a skilled meteorologist had discovered, through ingenious reasoning, that lightning must always strike simultaneously at the places A and B; then there arises the task of verifying whether this theoretical result corresponds to actuality or not. The same holds for all physical statements in which the concept 'simultaneous' plays a part. The concept exists for the physicist only once the possibility is given of finding out, in the concrete case, whether the concept applies or not. What is needed, then, is a definition of simultaneity such that this definition furnishes the method by which, in the present case, it can be decided from experiments whether both flashes of lightning occurred simultaneously or not. So long as this requirement is not fulfilled, I am indulging in a delusion, as a physicist (and indeed also as a non-physicist!), if I believe I can attach a meaning to the statement of simultaneity. (Before you have granted me this with conviction, dear reader, read no further.)" The sentence in parentheses at the end deserves our particular attention. With it Einstein makes clear that everything he goes on to present can seem credible only to one who has agreed to this preliminary consideration about simultaneity; and in this he is doubtless right. Before we reproduce the next paragraphs as well, which develop the relativistic concept of simultaneity, let us look a little more closely at the sentences that prepare it. — If we wish to examine whether an actually existing line, for example the edge of a sheet of foolscap, runs *straight*, we can obviously do so only if we know what a straight line is (or rather, what we understand by one). Likewise we must know the circular form in order to decide whether the rim of a plate, an ashtray, a jug runs circular (and not, say, elliptical); and so in every case of a similar kind. But what does Einstein tell us? "The concept *exists* for the physicist only once the possibility is given of *finding out*, in the concrete case, whether the concept applies or not." We can without difficulty recognize in this a special case of the metaphysical equation which we showed in the main text to bring the mechanist's *belief* to its shortest expression, the equation: actuality = measurability. But here it is no longer merely a matter of a metaphysical error, but of the quite ordinary logical blunder of someone making a presupposition which he spirits away in the same breath. Not even with the most ingenious apparatus shall I "find out" whether a concept "applies or not" to objective actuality, so long as I do *not* yet have it. If I judge: simultaneity is an unknown something, then there is no experimental arrangement that could indicate to me the simultaneity of two events. If, conversely, I hold such an experimental arrangement to be possible, then I have already brought with me a quite definite view of simultaneity, and I indulge in a peculiar self-deception if I persuade myself that I still had to ascertain it *from* the experimental arrangement! As we shall presently convince ourselves, Einstein already *has* the concept of simultaneity prior to any experimental arrangement, but he may not admit this to himself, because he would then have to conclude his publication with page 15. First, however, let us *explain* so remarkable a lapse by uncovering its origin in the history of ideas. We have dealt in detail with the progressive subjectivization of actuality through modern thought, and in the course of this repeatedly mentioned the formula by which *cognition* is subjectivistically falsified, Berkeley's formula: esse est percipi. Understood literally, this would indeed be correct, but then, strictly speaking, a tautology: what we conceive are — objects of thought. But since Berkeley means by esse *actuality*, the formula amounts to the following absurdity: actuality *consists* in the thinking of actuality, or: our apprehension of actuality and actuality itself are one and the same, or: the world is a system of thoughts. (Schopenhauer, for variety, said our "representation.") We shall not dwell here on the fact that this destroys the distinction between truth and error. (To restore it, Berkeley, as is well known, called upon the dear Lord.) But we recall once more, with emphasis, that in this way the thinking spirit is in principle freed from the compulsion which it had hitherto experienced from actuality in the form of the demand to *accept* "facts." For if every fact is in the end nothing other than my mode of apprehension, then, for example, the course of natural processes depends on the mode of apprehension and not, say, the reverse. It is not only within my discretion to assume, in the face of a motion, that body A moves relative to the resting body *B, or that B* moves relative to the resting A; the question of what, apart from such assumptions, is "actually" going on has no meaning at all any more. Here, as everyone readily notices, lies the root of Einstein's belief that the experimental arrangement devised by us *produces* the state of affairs (e.g., that of simultaneity), instead of, in truth, merely furnishing us the means of *ascertaining* it with the closest possible approximation. The theory of relativity is Berkeleyism in physical dress. Although our whole work has offered, among other things, a gapless refutation of all Berkeleyism, let a single circumstance be repeated here, for the sake of the completeness of this note, which would suffice to remove the ground from under esse est percipi for good. Dreamless deep sleep is an actual occurrence. If esse = percipi, then sleeping would *consist* in the being-thought of sleeping by the sleeper while he sleeps. Since that is *not* the case, esse is *not* = percipi. Nothing can be bargained away from this. Or should someone perhaps venture the desperate evasion that the sleeping of the sleeper A is an apprehension of the non-sleeper B? We do not know, but for precisely that reason we answer it. If the non-sleeper B is the sleeper *A afterwaking*, then he *distinguishes* his present waking precisely from his past sleeping as from a state that admitted no thinking apprehension whatever, and least of all the apprehension of its taking place. But if the non-sleeper B is a second person, he would know not the least thing about A's sleeping, unless he himself had already slept and thus found himself in that state which excludes the activity of apprehension. To make matters worse, B's judgment would require that the sleeper be present, and would consequently exclude the countless cases of unwitnessed sleep. — We return to Einstein. "After some time of reflection you make the following proposal for establishing simultaneity: the connecting stretch AB is measured off along the track, and in the middle M of the stretch an observer is placed who is provided with a device (say, two mirrors inclined at 90° to each other) which allows him a simultaneous optical fixation of both places A and B. If this observer perceives the two flashes of lightning simultaneously, they are simultaneous. — I am very satisfied with this proposal, yet do not consider the matter entirely settled, because I feel compelled to raise the following objection: 'Your definition would certainly be correct if I already knew that the light which conveys to the observer at M the perception of the flashes of lightning propagates with the same velocity over the stretch A→M as over the stretch B→M. But a test of this presupposition would be possible only if the means of time-measurement were already at one's disposal. One thus seems to be moving here in a logical circle.' — After some further reflection you rightly cast me a somewhat contemptuous glance, however, and declare to me: 'I nonetheless maintain my earlier definition, since it in truth presupposes nothing whatever about light. The definition of simultaneity is subject only to the *one* requirement, that it furnish, in every real case, the means of an empirical decision as to whether the concept to be defined applies or not. That my definition accomplishes this is indisputable. That light needs the same time to traverse the path A→M as to traverse the stretch B→M is, in truth, not a *presupposition or hypothesis* about the physical nature of light, but a *stipulation* which I can make at my own discretion in order to arrive at a definition of simultaneity.' It is clear that this definition can be used to give an exact meaning to the statement of simultaneity not only of *two* events but of any number of events." (p. 15). Here it first becomes drastically apparent that Einstein already *has* the concept of simultaneity, however much he strives to present it as a mere convention. Were we to let ourselves be deceived, tentatively, for a moment, and agree that simultaneity is a matter of convention, what would then have to arouse our utmost astonishment? We put it as a counter-question: why exactly do you place your observer at the *middle* of the stretch AB, why not near A or near B, when you claim to bring with you no prejudice whatever about the meaning of simultaneity? Why, further, do you feel obliged to stipulate that the ray of light from point A needs *the same* time to reach the bisecting point of the stretch AB (= M) as the ray of light from point B? You would, after all, have no occasion whatever to choose equal rather than unequal times for the propagation of light, unless you already associated a quite definite meaning with the word simultaneity. Rather, whoever prefers precisely this and no other experimental arrangement does so, without doubt, because it permits, in his opinion, as precise a *determination* as possible of what he *understands* by simultaneity. In short, we have here a "classical" illustrative example of the cardinal self-deception concealed in esse est percipi. For everything in fact amounts to creating, for an esse laid down as *underlying*, perceptual conditions as favorable as possible! It would weary our readers were we to repeat Einstein's further meditations here. Most of his examples and results have, after all, become almost common knowledge — above all, that simultaneity for the observer at M is not also simultaneity for the observer on a train travelling along the embankment, and that consequently both the temporal and the spatial distance between two events depend on the state of motion of the reference body. For what use are the most ingenious spinnings-out of a train of thought, if this is vitiated by an error in its premises which, moreover, even rests on a fundamental denial of the laws of thought! Let us allow ourselves once more a sidelong glance at the purely logical side of the matter alone. Let a train travel along our embankment from A to B. Since an observer in the train, equipped with the finest apparatus, is travelling toward the flash at B but away from the flash at A, he will, at the moment he passes by (at M), perceive the flash at B a little sooner than the flash at A. The events which take place simultaneously for the resting observer take place successively for the moving observer. With reference to the *empirical* moments presupposed here, one can therefore say: to the moving observer the events *appear* non-simultaneous which appear simultaneous to the resting observer. (The example collapses as soon as one replaces the empirical moments by genuine, that is, temporally unextended, *points* of time, because at the mathematical instant motion = 0. The moving observer perceives the flash at B sooner only insofar as, at the moment of perception, he has *already left* the spatial point M *again*. But the objections that could be raised against relativism with regard to this may be left aside here.) Einstein, on the other hand, secretly believing in esse est percipi, judges: the events are actually both simultaneous *and* non-simultaneous, and the decision depends solely on *our* choice of reference body! What follows from this? Let us assume for a moment that such and similar trains of thought could prove that *actual* (which here means: person-independent) simultaneity of events *actually* taking place could never be decided; even so, this would not touch in the least the actuality of simultaneous occurrence, even though we should now also know that our understanding must renounce the attempt to establish it beyond doubt. But if we make the assumption that actual simultaneity is identical with the product of apprehension of the chosen observer, then we have, at least with respect to simultaneity, abolished actuality — and thereby, as is still to be shown, the actuality-dependence of objects of thought as such. Since the reader of this work has learned in detail, in Volume I, what is to be understood by simultaneity according to the phenomenological conception of actuality, we may state it here purely dogmatically. If the space of intuition is the same as the livable Now, and the space that is an object of thought the same as the punctual Now, then all points of Euclidean space are mathematically simultaneous. Or: the noumenal *space* is that "reference body" in relation to which alone (absolute) simultaneity can be asserted. Whether or not one accounts to oneself for this, it is in every case this concept of simultaneity that guides one's considerations about the simultaneity of two occurrences, even if only in a hidden manner. That is why Einstein, for his observer of simultaneity, chooses the bisecting point of the stretch AB, and stipulates equality of the times for the propagation of light from B and from A to M. For only on the presupposition that the different points of space are themselves simultaneous does it serve a purpose, in establishing the simultaneity of two occurrences at different places, to carefully avoid differences of distance of the observer from them. Were one instead to assume the non-simultaneity of *places*, all these precautions would be utterly senseless! Einstein *conceals* this from himself, because it is the aim of his undertaking to dissolve the concept of simultaneity. There would have been no need at all for the extensive and difficult train of thought that attaches itself to the above considerations, because it secretly already contains what, in the very end, dressed up in fearsome mathematics, leaps out: namely, that each point of space possesses its own time parameter, or, put in terms generally understood, a private time. But with this, noumenal space and noumenal time are annihilated, and, if these two, then the actuality that is the object of thought itself. Hardly a relativist, though perhaps a non-relativist, might wish to object in defense of relativism: such a difference of times refers only to two points (or coordinate systems), of which one is thought of as resting, the other as moving, but not to two systems at rest relative to one another. He would forget that in the theory of relativity there can be no talk whatever of *actually* resting systems, because this would bring back the "absolute space" which the relativist most extremely abhors and, from his own standpoint, must indeed abhor. Incidentally, Einstein leaves us in no doubt whatever as to his opinion. "The fiction of the rigid reference body therefore fails in the general theory of relativity" (loc. cit., p. 66). "One therefore employs non-rigid reference bodies, which are not only moved arbitrarily as a whole, but also undergo *arbitrary changes of shape* during their motion" (p. 67). Indeed, Einstein christens his non-rigid reference bodies with the ever-recurring name "*reference mollusc*": "Every point of the *mollusc* is treated as a point of space" (p. 67). That is convincingly clear, and higher than that it does not go! But, we hear it asked: might he not possibly be right precisely in this? Indeed, might not the author of this book have good reasons to agree with him? Has one not heard that actual space must be distinguished from space as an object of thought, actual time from time as an object of thought, actual happening from happening as an object of thought — and did it not emerge in the course of this that *actual* space, at any rate, could *not* serve as a "rigid reference body"? Could not relativism signify a step *toward* actuality? Is not, in the end, the same breaching of certain bounds of thought hitherto attempted here on the part of physics and mechanics, which the author appears to be attempting from the side of metaphysics? Our answer runs: we have shown that by means of our *concepts* of facts we can *point* to what is actual; but nowhere have we ventured the absurd assertion that what is thus demonstrated could be *conceived*. Our intuition is *possible*; whether it is correct, let others decide. Impossible, by contrast, is an intuition which dissolves the noumena and, notwithstanding this, imagines it can subject what has been dissolved to measurement and calculation! There is a line AB. What enables us to measure it, or also to use it as a unit of measure (of length)? The hypothesis — whether right or wrong, but in any case unavoidable — that the point A is *simultaneous with* the point B. Were both non-simultaneous, A B — then either A would be past relative to B, or B relative to A, and the line would thereby have ceased to exist; rather, it would have become *unthinkable*. And consequently my measuring and calculating would have become unthinkable. Here lies the *self-contradiction* on which the relativistic abolition of simultaneity founders. Either I deny the simultaneity of the points A and B — then I must henceforth renounce all measuring and calculating; or I measure and calculate — then I must think the points A and B as existing simultaneously, and have thereby, unspoken, asserted the simultaneity of all points of Euclidean space. Einstein himself writes down the sentence: "*Even the concept of the straight line thereby loses* its *meaning*," and does not notice that he has thereby deprived himself of the possibility of ever again measuring or calculating anything. — Must we repeat once more that the relativist's customary rejoinder — that he denies only "absolute" lengths, measurements, and motions, but not "relative" ones — has logically no meaning at all? The genuine concept of the relative presupposes that of the absolute, and equally the reverse. But with the abandonment of the simultaneity of all points of Euclidean space, *both* concepts collapse, and the alleged relativization is in truth *annulment*. Only with the help of the assumption of a time-independent space can I measure lengths and velocities, whether relative or absolute! — Only a humanity that has long since inwardly settled itself *beyond* logic could, and can, fall prey to relativistic formalism. — In closing, we do not fail to draw, from the fact of the existence of relativistic world-conceptions, a fresh piece of evidence for our discussion, in Volume I, of "the conceptual kinship of visible appearance." If it is true that Newtonian mechanics — which is not so much overcome by relativism as completed by it — already harbors the germ of the denial of matter, then the physics of the following period, borne by the same tendency, was bound to aim at an ever stronger overemphasis on optics and electrodynamics, which is, as is well known, indeed what happened. Supposed contradictions between the addition theorem of velocities and the propagation of light gave the immediate impulse to the formation of relativistic webs of thought. If we now interpret this stretch of intellectual history, meanwhile completed, by its fruits, the *proximate* ground of the religion of relativity readily discloses itself to us in the neglect of the *tangible* side of the world's content in favor of a boundless overestimation of visible appearance. If I deny the actuality of motion, I have denied the actuality of matter. (Kant's definition of matter as that which is movable is correct!) In order to lend such an undertaking at least an appearance of truth, I will find it expedient to rest on the mere visibility of motion. For *only* on the basis of visible appearance can we in fact never decide whether something is moving or at rest. Because the firmament, with its thousands of stars, is for us nothing but an optical state of affairs, it appears to revolve about the earth in a mighty circuit in twenty-four hours, and no one is in a position to perceive the contrary. (Even from Foucault's marvelous pendulum experiment it is only inferred.) For a world of visible appearance it is a matter of indifference whether we judge: the firmament stands still and the earth revolves, or the earth stands still and the firmament revolves; the embankment is at rest and the train moves, or the train is at rest and the embankment moves; the level of the earth remains steady and the balloon rises, or the balloon remains steady and the level of the earth sinks. But if, through an artificial self-restriction to visible appearance, the *actuality* of motion is annihilated, then visible appearance clearly forms, as it were, the sensory bridge from the phenomenal to the noumenal, and the intellectual overestimation of it forms the beginning of the road that ends in formalism. Exactly the same fate, in the world of mere visible appearance, befalls the body and consequently matter, to both of which henceforth only a reality of *semblance* can belong. For visually there is not the slightest difference between the images in a mirror and the things before the mirror! With the help of visible appearance *alone*, the concept of body cannot be established, and whoever confines his meditations to what is visibly apparent no longer has any need to entertain ingenious considerations about the non-existence of matter, because his aspect of the world excludes matter, and accordingly motion too, from the outset. Since now, as we shall show in Volume III, the *existential judgment* can be rendered only on the occasion of tangible resistances, every world-conception oriented solely on the visual runs out into a denial of existence. With this it was at the same time already foreshadowed that *actual* motion must be something quite different from what falls, by *itself alone*, into visibility: the continuous change of distance of two mass-points. — Since the foregoing note was written in 1927, the noise about relativism has died down, while within physics the dissolution of the fundamental concepts has proceeded rapidly; so that for the outsider there is no doubt that, in relation to the astonishing achievements of ingenious experimenters, theory is beginning to become superfluous. Corpuscles are waves and vice versa; matter is a "wave-packet," or — after the abolition of the search for causes by means of a supposed statistics (as though that in turn did not rest on lawfulness!) — a "probability-packet." According to well-known principles of the science of the soul, this extreme *negativism* has borrowed for itself the name of — positivism. In short, what finally remains is pure mathematics; whereby the tendency toward subjectivization that we have dealt with has reached a climax scarcely to be surpassed. — Only one thing remains to be noted. One is mistaken if one believes one can defend oneself by pointing out that the value of the theory has nothing to fear from the unimaginability of its results. Whoever speaks of waves, that is, of a kind of motion, has presupposed a vibrating *something*. If he dissolves this in turn into waves, he offends against *logic*.

In short, will-power and physical force are the same, only with the one, most tremendous difference, that to the will the vehicle of vital movements stands at disposal, but not to physical force; hence it is a de-forced force, and merely the semblance of one, read into actuality by analogy with willing. For if only something actually working can also suffer effects — since the receiving of an effect is itself a form of working — then the genuine intransitives into which the mechanistic procedure of abstraction has unraveled the [p. 727] world-process are just as incapable of being brought about as they are, by supposition, incapable of producing effects; and so, in truth, even the explanation of the mere propagation of movement from body to body would require that same deus ex machina which the Cartesians found it necessary to install in order to bring thought-movement and body-movement into accord from moment to moment. As long, then, as the physicists were still metaphysicians and not, as today, pure formalists, they had to seek to find and to name this deus ex machina, whereby the following invariably occurred.

If everything moving is something moved, everything driving something driven, everything making something made, then the question of the original impulse, or of the mover, driver, and maker, irresistibly arises. There is scarcely a more convincing proof for the derivation of the belief in cause from the concept of force, and, in turn, of the concept of force from the lived experience of willing, than the circumstance — verifiable without exception throughout the history of thought — that every mechanist who felt a need to let the chain of causes begin somewhere had, willy-nilly, to posit a deed of the Logos or, spoken in Mosaic terms, the simply creative command. With such a performance of will, pushed back to a fictitious beginning, there is revealed, however, only the enabling ground of mechanical causality in general, and there steps forth from its linguistic disguise, as what it is, the actual accomplisher of the supposed working of mechanical forces as such: the "sufficient reason" is de-vitalized will and, causal effecting, objectified "deed in itself." With the imagining of I-analogous existences we have already co-imagined, into actuality, their capacity for acts of self-assertion. If this is nonetheless to remain withheld from things, because only the personal I is capable of doing, and knows itself distinguished from the thing precisely by the separate possession of a capacity for effect, then the belief in the possibility of mechanical effects, indeed even the belief in the actuality of existences, is covertly identical with the belief in unceasing acts of creation of the spirit.

Descartes, the founder of strict rationalism, remarkable for the consistency of his delusions and untiring in thinking-through-to-the-end, had recognized this very well and discusses it classically in the third of his "Meditations". Whoever wishes, he holds, to weaken the assumption of an author of our existence by the consideration that [p. 728] one could indeed always have existed just as one exists now, must be met with the objection that of the innumerable parts into which the time of our life may be divided, none depends upon another. "Hence," he continues, "it does not follow, from the fact that I existed a little while ago, that I must exist now, unless some cause create me anew, as it were, at this very moment... For anyone who attends to the nature of time clearly recognizes that the same power and activity are needed to preserve a thing at each of the individual moments through which it endures as would be needed to create it anew, were it not yet in existence. Hence preservation differs from creation only in our way of thinking, and this proposition is one of those that are manifest by the natural light."

If we said above that the very existing of things is a comporting of things, we now add: the very existence of the I—of which the existence of things is but a reflex, far from being comparable to intuitive continuity—is in truth the substratum, self-identical with respect to time, of ever-renewed acts of self-assertion, or, more precisely described, of the positing of a limit against the surge of a life that persists not for a single instant; and is thus, quite properly, a power that brings itself forth from moment to moment. If we grasp the I as ground of existence, we hold in it the famous and notorious causa sui, which no one has recognized more sharply than Stirner. "I do not presuppose Myself, because I only ever ... create Myself anew each instant. I am creator and creature in one." "I am I only by making Myself..." What Stirner rightly establishes here of the I coincides unmistakably with what a Descartes established of existing as such; whereby, to be sure, no creative power of spirit reaching beyond the I is attested, but rather the instrumental nature of the thought of causality- —indeed, quite generally, of objective thinking in the service of the self-assertion of the will.

The Cartesian unmasking of the principle of causality, as one might call it, shows unfailingly the essential sameness of the mechanistic with the teleological view of the world, since by the "natural light" it should likewise become manifest that the one is as untenable as the other! Teleology understands the cause from the effect, which is as much as to say the willing from the purpose; mechanism understands the effect from the cause, which is as much as to say the purpose from the willing; but both founder on the fact that the causa efficiens, like the causa finalis, would be powerless without the actual [p. 729] happening, in which alone there are no leaps and no I-like separated centers. For even if one were to allow, by way of trial, the assumption that spirit can not only divide but can also create, there would still remain the insuperable counterargument that millions upon millions of supposedly creative acts of spirit would not create so much as a single happening lasting the span of a flash of lightning! Whether one takes the object to be marked off by spirit and thus found, or to be arbitrarily created: it is in every case a being, hence outside of time, and accordingly related to time only by virtue of the happening—which is never conceived, even though it is known, as an inconceivable actuality, by virtue of its being lived.

As long as the logocentric disposition of spirit remains nothing but mechanics and lets itself be guided solely by the need to knit together facts, it leads, to be sure, not to knowledge, but—true to its origin—to the subjection of its object to human purpose. As soon, however, as it enters the field of biology, it only repeats, with each of its explanations, the self-contradiction on which the mechanistic belief in the independence of spirit and the idealistic belief in the independence of life from the object of cognition alike are shattered. Yet this comes to light far more sharply still when the thought of causality, or rather the mere belief in lawfulness, is transferred to the psychology of willing as opposed to that of cognizing. A change which we assume follows another change in accordance with law does not, in any case, have the ground of its occurring within itself. But if it is our lived experience of self-activity, of initiative, of arbitrary will, of "freedom" and self-determination, that alone makes even the lifeless sequences of mechanics credible to us at all—because we secretly interpret them by analogy with the performances of will (of which, in truth, they are the puppet theater)—then higher thinking will invariably come to rest at the I, or spirit, or logos, as the determinant in a world of the determined: the determining that is itself subject to no determination, the cause without cause, which we, beyond question, experience ourselves to be in every act of arbitrary will—a natura naturans non naturata, or the proton kinoun akineton. Around this center of gravity the metaphysics of the West has revolved at least since Plato, to whom, with a little sensitivity to the transformation of the conceptual idiom of thought, one may at the very least ascribe all the preliminaries *of* the invention with which, later, the conflict of [p. 730] "freedom" and natural law—and hence of determinism and indeterminism—was purported to have been settled: the invention of the "intelligible" character and of "transcendental" freedom. The metaphysics of the will stands today, by and large, at exactly the point where it stood two and a half millennia ago. — With the strengthening of I-hood there strengthens not only the consciousness of existence but also the consciousness of arbitrary will and of freedom, and there is sundered ever more sharply, first, one's own existence from alien existence, and then I-hood as such from thing-hood as such. But just as, in consequence of growing objectity, the understanding of its bearer (so long as he is still a mere "observer") becomes ever more dependent upon the demanding object, so, in consequence of growing subjectity, his will becomes ever more dependent upon the resisting object: there as here, spirit builds at the prison of life. And then we understand, too, why the wishing I invents a twofold freedom: out of the robust need for the unboundedness of existence, a postmortal immortality; out of the more sublimated need for the unboundedness of arbitrary will, a pre-existent self-determination.

[p. 731]

#### 52. Kapitel — Galilei und Palágyi — Chapter 52 — Galilei and Palágyi

In order to show that the modern "force" and the modern "cause" are borrowed names, by whose aid the mere belief in law—or, more sharply put, the will-compliant belief in a calculability of the world—disguised itself in a semblance of vitality, we have linked our discussion to the fundamental achievements of the great Galileo. Now if our conception of his significance diverges considerably from the usual one, the reflections by which Melchior Palágyi attempts to give an account of the innermost nerve of Galilean research diverge from it rather further still, only in exactly the opposite direction. If we now take his essay "Galilei und das Übertragungsprinzip" from his "Weltmechanik" as our point of departure, in order, as promised in the first volume, to complete the delineation at least of the main lines of his world-view, this happens at the same time in order to support our wholly different view of the actuality-content of the object of physics, by demonstrating that the attempt—not only probably the most significant but, so far as we know, the only attempt at all—to remodel the basic concepts of physics with a view to enabling their insertion into a polaristic picture of the world, was bound to remain incomplete for the reason that it — abolished itself.

The essay in question runs to only 15 printed pages, and of these a mere 9 are devoted to Galileo. But no one would be capable of fully taking the measure of what stands on these 9 pages who had not studied the 113 pages that precede them and would go on to study the 53 pages that follow them. And even then he might well read past the heart of the matter, were he to read with the eyes of a — physicist, whereas he would have better prospects as a — layman in physics! (Indeed, a physicist declared to the author quite bluntly that he did not understand Palágyi's treatise!) But this, as we shall see, has its good reasons. In beginning, with [p. 732] this treatise, to unfold Palágyi's—unconsciously romantic—thought of polarity, we must nevertheless disclose at least as much of the exposition as is contained in it by the immediately preceding treatise bearing the title "Kopernikus und die Relativitätstheorie".

The most singular thing about it is perhaps that it deals almost not at all with Copernicus and almost exclusively with the theory of relativity, and yet, notwithstanding this, brings out a side of Copernicus's discovery that scarcely exists in the popular knowledge of him. The center of this "seer's" whole manner of thought, it holds, was formed by the "principle of insufficient perception of motion," which therefore rightly deserves to be called the "Copernican principle," and whose most fundamental manifestation is our incapacity to feel or to see the motion of the earth. Unfortunately, however, the principle was soon misconstrued, in that it was falsified into a physical principle. "It was not said that our perception of processes of motion is 'relative'; rather, motion itself was relativized. One no longer spoke of the deficiency of the perception of motion, but of the ambiguity (or multivocity) of motion itself. It was not our human judgment concerning states of motion that was afflicted with an uncertainty, but the processes of motion and the course of nature itself that were said to suffer from an inner (objective) uncertainty. In short, a subjective state of affairs was made into an objective one, which of course entails a fundamental error and the falsification of our entire picture of the world" (loc. cit., p. 105). Even the so-called classical principle of relativity of Newton had already displayed this tendency, but the direct confounding of subjective and objective states of affairs "emerges in the whole of its harshness only in the modernist Einsteinian principle of relativity."

There follows the familiar Copernican simile of the moving ship, to which Palágyi attaches a dialogue between a relativist and a non-relativist. The latter interprets the apparent motions of things and persons within the body of the ship as forms of inertial motion; the former, of course, claims them as proof of his relativism. Palágyi decides that both are in error: the relativist, because he confuses the subjective perception of motion with objective motion; the non-relativist, because he fails to distinguish between motion and the transmission of motion. For [p. 733] such a manner of viewing things, all natural happening dissolves into mere motion, namely into accelerated and inertial motion, "while the actual phenomena of transmission or propagation seem, as it were, to evaporate" (p. 113). It thereby becomes "the typical representative of the mechanistic conception of nature, which traces all natural happening back to processes of motion—something it seeks to achieve by means of the peculiar mysticism of the principle of inertia..." (p. 113). And so we would then arrive at Galileo.

"Copernicus showed us the earth itself in the light of a vehicle or conveyance, which carries with it, in its journey through the celestial spaces, all things situated upon it: Galileo, on the other hand, gently brought this idea of the vehicle back to earth, into our narrow, small human circumstances, and thereby opened the hitherto closed gates of a new kind of cognition. One will perhaps be surprised that we hold the concept of the "vehicle" to be so important that we make it the center-point of all of physics; but we take it in a more general sense than it is usually understood. For us every moving body is a vehicle, for it carries with it, along its path, all particles, molecules, atoms, and so on—that is, it *transmits* its system-motion to all part-systems, which participate in its motion as it were as passengers. In other words: in *experience* there is never a motion without transmission of motion, for one can speak of the motion of a body . . only for the reason that this system transmits its motion to all the part-systems contained within it. However simple and self-evident this proposition may be, it nevertheless forms the foundation and the key to the new doctrine of motion created by Galileo. We shall designate this fundamental proposition as the principle of the *naturally necessary* . . *belonging-together* of the processes of motion and transmission" (p. 114).

Galileo was accordingly, among all natural scientists, the first who, throughout his life, attempted to distinguish two basic types of natural happening: motion and its transmission. At times he regarded the moving body from outside and thus perceived the motion; at other times he put himself inside it and, in consequence, recognized that all the parts of the moving body were, within it (or in relation to it), as "inert matter," in complete rest. The particles of a falling body, for instance, merely go along with the falling motion. They [p. 734] behave like passengers carried along, and are as little involved in the motive impulse as the passengers of a ship are in the forces that move the ship. In this way he discovered the inertial character of matter, according to which "none of its parts possesses a motive impulse of its own, but always only receives impulses from elsewhere by transmission, undergoes them, and converts them into change of place" (p. 116).

Even without following all the subtleties of Palágyi's train of thought, the following will be clear: to the inertial character of matter corresponds uniform happening, to its receptivity for impulses non-uniform happening; the symbol of uniform happening is the straight line, of non-uniform happening the curved line. This, Palágyi holds, hovered before Galileo's mind, though he was not yet able to bring it to clarity and therefore mistakenly designated uniform happening by the same word with which he designated non-uniform happening: the word motion. Thus the conflict was bequeathed, unresolved, to the following centuries, and conjured up "the grandiose struggle between the physics of motion (mechanics) and the physics of transmission (physics of the ether)," which in our own day has broken out in the shape of the ill-starred idea of relativity.

We do not presume to vie with a Palágyi in the interpretation of Galileo. Who, after all, could finally fathom what impulses of thought were at work in the soul of a discoverer like Galileo before he arrived at his epoch-making findings! But we must hold fast to this: that the physics which Palágyi, invoking Galileo's unresolved struggles of thought, now sets about designing for the very first time, was designed neither by Galileo and Newton, nor by Huygens, Fresnel, Faraday, Maxwell, Hertz, and so on. But what sort of "physics" this is, we now wish to ascertain, and in doing so we shall first follow, a stretch further, the thoughts that Palágyi links with his interpretation of Galileo's achievements.

We have, it is true, already heard it, but we bring it out once more with emphasis: he is the first to give the principle of inertia a formulation that unmistakably unmasks its essence as the impulse-lessness of matter. But should one think that this designates, with especial sharpness, that very lifelessness of (physical) matter [p. 735] of which we have treated so extensively, one would at once be taught otherwise by the important addendum that receptivity to impulse is inherent in it. Matter "is the only something in the world," so it reads literally, "that is able to convert an impulse, that is, a mere urge to motion . . into actual motion" (p. 120). If impulse (= unmoved urge to motion) on the one side and receptivity to impulse (= urgeless mobility) on the other are thus sharply set apart, and if we call the bearer of mobility "matter," then a second bearer is evidently needed, namely for the impulse. Now, according to Palágyi, this is the ether. Accordingly, both, matter and ether, are the mutually dependent poles of physical actuality—and indeed in such a way that not only would the ether not exist without matter, but—and it is on this that the emphasis is to be placed—matter, too, would not be capable of subsisting without the ether. For it is evident that nothing in the world would happen if there existed *only* matter wholly without urge, and again nothing, if there existed *only* an ether wholly without motion. The ether is the "static substrate," matter the "dynamic substrate." With this, be it noted, the ether is discovered for the first time (however peculiar the manner may be), in that it has exchanged the embryonic state of a manifoldly self-contradictory hypothesis for the daylight of demonstrable and demonstrated certainty; and with this, furthermore, there is for the first time given a metaphysical interpretation—that is, an insertion into the picture of actuality—of the opposition, admittedly extremely determinate in calculation but essentially wholly unclarified to this day, of "potential" and "kinetic" energy, the law of conservation included.

For the ether is the resting bearer of all tensions and transmissions of tension (= potential energy), matter the ever-moving bearer of all motions (= kinetic energy). Impulses of the ether are continually converted into equivalent motions of matter, and the motion of matter is continually converted into equivalent processes of the resting ether (law of conservation). "If matter is discontinuous, then the ether must be continuous; if ever-moving matter is the bearer of all motor velocities and accelerations, then the never-moving but everexcited ocean of ether is the bearer and propagator of all the tensions and changes of tension of the physical world" (pp. 76–77). Nor does the consistency of a Palágyi shrink back even from the last remaining step. Deeply penetrated by the inner self-contradictoriness of the modern concept of cause, he sets about [p. 736], resolutely, giving it the surprisingly concrete shape of the reciprocal relation of matter and ether. "The struggle, already subsisting for nearly two and a half centuries, between the relativistic and the causal view of nature has in our day sharpened in the most extreme fashion, and Western . . science will now finally have to decide whether it is prepared, in all seriousness, to abandon causal thinking, or whether it will take the trouble to develop a principle of causality as a doctrine of the reciprocal interaction of ether and matter" (p. 124).

Here the question must not be evaded of how "propagations" (spreadings, "diffusions," radiations, energy-transports, and so on) can take place in an ether wholly without motion. The fundamental answer is exceedingly simple. To this end one distinguishes positive and negative impulses (which one may picture to oneself by analogy with pressure and counter-pressure, pull and counter-pull, positive and negative electricity, and so on). If one now imagines "that a positive ethereal impulse calls forth, in its immediate neighborhood, a negative impulse, this in turn a positive one, this a negative one, and so on, then one has a temporal series of momentary impulses, each of which has died away while the next appears, so that they follow one another with a certain velocity, without even one of them ever having budged from the place at which it arose. And yet the series of such impulses possesses a velocity in temporal succession, quite as though the first impulse had "moved onward" and had taken, in turn, the place of the remaining impulses, while in fact none left its place, but each only called the immediately neighboring impulse into being, as it were as deputy for its own extinguished existence" (p. 126). In this way Palágyi arrives at the concept of a "static velocity," whose essential difference from the dynamic velocity exclusively familiar to merely mechanistic thinking leads to consequences of the highest significance. For if the static velocity is by no means a velocity of motion, then it would naturally be a thing of impossibility to wish to add it, according to the principle of composition of two dynamic velocities, into one such velocity. The motion of a source of light, for instance, never adds itself to the static velocity of propagation of light, and the alleged contradiction between the experiments of Fizeau and of Michelson, which the relativists supposed they had to clear up, does not exist at all!

[p. 737] As Palágyi himself emphasizes, his concept of the ether is most nearly akin to that of the physicist Lorentz. Only — and of this Palágyi is sharply aware — the tremendous difference between his ether theory and all ether theories hitherto extant consists in this: that it was not gained through the consideration of optical and electrodynamic processes, but through an entirely novel dissection of mechanical motion—concerning whose extraordinary perspective we now wish to inform ourselves somewhat more precisely, by leaving his meditations on Galileo and turning to his wonderful treatise "Die Relativitätstheorie in der modernen Physik" (1914). — By means of very simple mathematical considerations, which anyone may look up for himself on the spot, Palágyi here carries through the convincing demonstration that rectilinear-uniform motions are impossible in three-dimensional space. This, however, can also be grasped without any mathematics at all, which is why he appends to his proof the—probably by the fewest readers noted—sentence: "All of this, incidentally, is evident from the outset if one considers that bodies moving uniformly relative to one another would stand in absolutely no relation to one another and would consequently be unable to belong to one and the same world" (p. 67). For just as certainly as we must assume mathematical space (that of Euclid) to be homogeneous, just as certainly the space of mechanics, as the field of activity of tensions that change from place to place, is not homogeneous. The smallest displacement imparted to a material point already brings it into a field of forces different from the field of forces in which it had just before been dwelling; not to speak at all of the fact that two bodies approaching one another would have to accelerate their motion in proportion to the approach. — But what holds for the body is fair for world-matter as well: it too can possess no rectilinear-uniform motion in three-dimensional space (whereby the relativistic assumption of the contrary is refuted once and for all).

If we now recall Palágyi's doctrine of "flowing space," or more precisely of the four-dimensional manifold, according to which a fourth axis with an imaginary sign, namely the time-axis, is annexed to the three-axial coordinate system, we readily understand that and why his proposition of the impossibility of rectilinear-uniform motions in three-dimensional space forms only the negative correlate of the positive proposition that a rectilinear-uniform motion of the whole of world-matter does indeed take place, though only in a figurative sense, [p. 738] along the fourth axis (or in "longitudinal space")—a motion that comes to our consciousness as the uniform stream of time. With this the ether becomes at once the bearer of the dimension of time, matter the placeholder of space, and to the polarity of the two substrates, ether and matter, there corresponds the more abstract polarity of time and space.

It would exceed the scope of this discussion were we to go deeper into Palágyi's singular distinctions between singular and collective motions, between microcosmic, mesocosmic, and macrocosmic processes, between original or perpetual and unsteady or transgredient motions, and, finally, into his ingenious attempt to construct a "graduated structure of the cosmos." Although all his statements on this are merely beginnings and give only indications, they nevertheless suffice to let a system of thought of ravishing grandeur shimmer into view. At bottom it is always one and the same polarity that comes to appearance, under different names, in the dualities cited. From mere singular motions of atoms, for example, the collective motion of the body comprising them would never come about, since between atom and atom the binding cement would be lacking—or, in other words, since no atom would be capable of transmitting its own motion to a second atom. This, however, is accomplished by the Palágyian ether. With such examples we feel led back to the point of departure, to Palágyi's interpretation of the principle of inertia, and we now recognize, as the motive of his whole "world-mechanical" movement of thought, the passionate endeavor to make intelligible—by the remodeling of the basic concepts of physics on the ground of mechanics and by means of it—what, in our conviction, can never be understood physically: the transeunt character of all actual happening!

We have set forth and proved that not only the force of mechanics but also the matter of mechanics—indeed any object whatsoever of physics—suffers from the incurable defect of being intransitive by essential necessity, and therefore finds no application at all to actuality itself, which it rather de-souls and splinters, in order to join together, out of the splinters, the admittedly calculable but thereby life-emptied machine. One falls prey to a deceptive semblance if one believes that physics has ever examined how actuality is constituted. Always and everywhere, and with an almost demonic consistency in which [p. 739] the secretly commanding will betrays itself, it has posed the wholly different question, or at least has conducted its research in accordance with it: how can actuality be thought as a machine? We leave it an open question whether a Galileo at times put himself in the place of falling stones; for what alone matters is that what he found, or supposed himself to find, is not at all the impulse-lessness of matter first inferred by Palágyi—which would unfailingly have forced him to devise a second substrate to dispense the impulses—but the impulse-lessness of the (moving) individual body, whose change of velocity therefore appears as a disturbance caused by a second body, for which, as goes without saying, the same "law of persistence" holds! In other words: in Galileo's world, and in the world of the whole of physics, that impulse-emitting power for which Palágyi borrows the name of the ether is simply lacking; and whoever carries such a power into physics has carried an explosive into it, by which its entire structure goes irresistibly to pieces!

To Palágyi's admirable undertaking of replacing the willborn monism of physics with a polarism appropriate to actuality, we could give only the highest assent, and we would know no better physical crowning of our own world-view than through this myth of matter and ether. But we doubt that the physicist will ever come who would translate it into the language of — mathematical theory. For what Palágyi offers is not physics, and is least of all mechanics! Despite more than thirty years of work at shaping it, the great system remained a torso. Was this a malicious accident? We do not believe so; rather, we hold that it was condemned to incompleteness for as long as its creator insisted on bringing it into accord with the concepts of mechanics.

If we take our seat on the ground of mechanistic thinking, question upon question presses in upon us, for which, at least, we ourselves would not even be able to devise the possibility of an answer. The through-and-through immaterial, resting ether is a bearer solely of states of tension, yet is supposed nevertheless to be able to communicate equivalent motions to the three-dimensionally extended matter. How does this happen? Palágyi, who might have answered us, is no more. But we do not even have an inkling of what the answer might be.

To think of contact would be ridiculous; for contact, as we [p. 740] know, is, metaphysically taken, a semblance that conceals the abyss gaping between that which touches and that which is touched, and it is precisely the ether that is supposed to serve to bridge this abyss. Nor, again, would it make the slightest sense to say that the body is "touched" by a—state! The ether, moreover, must permeate matter, since otherwise it would have ceased to be continuous. Finally it "fills"—figuratively speaking—the four-dimensional manifold, and stands to the ever-momentary configuration of world-matter not at all like a spatial without, but rather—as we have already heard- —like the stream of time, according to which matter is forever compelled to occupy new momentary spaces. To be sure, the unimaginability of these processes would be no objection to their actually taking place; but how they would have to be thought—thought in such a way as to become accessible to research—even to vaguely surmise that lies far beyond the combinatory power of the writer of these lines. — And so we would rather content ourselves with declaring in what light the magnificent myth of Palágyi appears to us.

The ether, it was said, is an ocean never moved, but ever excited. "Never moved, ever excited": with this sequence of words we believe we hold in our hands the key to our philosopher's supposedly world-mechanical manner of thought. — Let us assume that I am standing with a friend before a great anthill. We see the creatures busily running about in confusion, and after a while believe we notice, in the colorful swarming, something like a plan. Some strive toward the mound, others away from it. Some carry eggs, others little pieces of wood, gigantic in proportion to their own bodies. They dodge one another with skill, seem to give one another signs by touch, help one another in hauling away a particularly clumsy pine-needle, seem to be in a hurry, as though governed by a common purpose. Now, at one spot, I poke a little with my stick into the surface of the mound. How, indeed, would we describe what now happens, supposing that we surrendered ourselves to the impression without ulterior thought? We do not say: the motions of the ants become faster, more irregular, more complicated; rather we say: the ants have fallen into agitation. We see, compellingly and instantaneously, not so much the more hurried and more complicated motions as, rather, that of which they are the expression: the psychic *agitation* of the ants. "Agitation" is a state of lived experience [p. 741] or it is a nothing! More than that: "states" are inner states, or they are not at all.

To be sure, physics constantly speaks of states and changes of state; but it does so just as certainly in an improper sense as it speaks, in an improper sense, of forces and causes. Were it unable to measure the rise in temperature that accompanies a gas's absorption of heat, or at least to infer it from consequences that are in turn measurable, it would not occur to it to ascribe a change of state to the gas at all. This latter is itself measured only insofar as it is its measurable consequences that are measured. Genuine states, by contrast, cannot be measured, because they do not belong to the world of objects. They appear only in intuitable states of affairs, and their appearance can indeed be analyzed objectively and, in partial features, also measured; but this never leads to a mathematical equation, because what is measured stands, on the one side, opposed to what is on the other side purely and simply a matter of estimate (exactly as, to the measurable motions of a man who has fallen into anger, there corresponds only the estimable strength of his anger) . In short, genuine states, be it of rest or of agitation, have no place in physics. But it is of genuine states—namely, of rest and of agitation—and of these alone, that Palágyi speaks.

His ether stands to his matter as the active principle to the passive principle, as an acting thing to a suffering thing, an effecting thing to a receiving thing, or as the male potency to the female potency, as the fertilizing to the bearing, or, finally, as the soul to the body, as the experiencing inwardness to its externalization in the world of appearance.<sup>30</sup> He solves the physically eternally insoluble problem of transmission, solves the problem of cause and effect, but he solves it by the reintroduction of the genuine polarity of receiving and effecting, and that means: by the vitalization of all the concepts of which he makes use. His ether is as certainly a living and lived-experiencing ether as it is the point of origin of impulses, and his matter is as certainly a living and lived-experiencing matter as it is receptive to genuine *impulses*! (The law of conservation, remarked in passing, need not disturb us—once because the ether must at least have spontaneously expended an initial impulse in order that its intercourse with matter could become manifest, and again because, even were this intercourse thought of as without beginning, the return of the impulses through matter would in no way allow one to foresee in what shape they would come to appear anew in it. In fact [p. 742] the law of conservation has here acquired a wholly new sense, one that will briefly occupy us again in another context.) There are, as one sees, its reasons why Palágyi is not understood, or is rejected, by the physicist. He believed he was building a system of world-mechanics; what he really bequeathed to us are the boundary-stones of the first steps toward a biology of the cosmos.

<sup>30</sup> On page 741. — Since we have thereby, for a moment, set foot on the ground of symbolic thinking, which is at the same time vitalistic thinking, it may be permitted to state here in advance what, seen from its standpoint, the mechanistic — or, as we now more aptly say, the monistic — world-conception presents itself as: it is a special form of the undertaking to abolish, or in a sense to castrate, the *female* pole of actuality. The monon of all mechanistic thinking always *means* the male pole, the one the old-fashioned believer is accustomed to call "God the Father." But because the male pole is just as dependent on the female as the female on the male, it followed that the theoretical abolition of the female pole necessarily entailed the destruction of the male as well. Indeed, this process has meanwhile been consistently completed: the extermination of (female) matter was followed, in relativism, by the elimination of the (male) ether!

[p. 743]

#### 53. Kapitel — Wille und Bewußtseinszustände — Chapter 53 — Will and States of Consciousness

We could conclude the second volume with the preceding chapter; but we hope to have our readers' assent if we append two further chapters, of which the far more extensive first, in summing up the chief yield of our doctrine of the will for the doctrine of the essence and origin of consciousness, at the same time outlines its consequences for the conception of "world-history"; while the much shorter second casts a further sidelong glance at the estrangement of physical thinking from actuality, but for the purpose of rebuffing certain obvious misunderstandings as to the nature of its representatives— whose significance only he could underestimate who would underestimate the power and depth of the life which spirit, with their help, sets about conquering, and, to be sure, also destroying.

Before we recall to mind, at least, the most important features of the state of affairs of the so-called activity of consciousness—in truth, the activity of spirit—according to their dependence upon the will, we repeat what emerged from our disclosures for the all too famous problem of freedom. — The I, of which alone volitions can be predicated, occurs in the world only, and can only occur in it, as a personal I, and its characteristic lies in a change of bearing, comparable to nothing else, of the individual unit of life—not, to be sure, of man as such, but certainly of historical man. That personality is accordingly a willing being, that it disposes over much or little energy and, further, over much or little endowment of will, that its drive-impulses exchange themselves easily or with difficulty for impulses of will, and finally, what purposes it generates under given circumstances—with the subordination of other purposes—all this is unfailingly prescribed to it by its momentary constitution of character at any given time, which in turn draws the "sum" from the original character and [p. 744] its history, and thus in the end goes back to that character as to something as utterly withdrawn from all arbitrary will and free resolve as is the bodily constitution of the newborn infant.

But such "determinedness" does not stand in the way of the insight that in the personal I a power has clamped itself together with organic life, to which the life-processes comport themselves like a material that it presses down, more and more, to the level of a tool. The feeling of freedom grounded in it is in the wrong, insofar as it persuades us that we could ever have willed otherwise, could have acted otherwise, than actually occurred (which is why remorse counts among the deluded states, at least insofar as it is more than mere vexation over stupidities committed); it is in the right, insofar as it lets us know that every decision of will, and thus consciousness itself, testifies to the working-in of extra-vital deed-force into necessity. "Mechanical causality" or "lawfulness," however, is the name of *the* thought that proved to be ultimately effective in dividing up happening into units of computation and forcing it into the obedience of spirit. Neither life nor spirit either is a machine; but the road to the shattering of nature through deed leads by way of the mechanization of nature.

If one wishes to hear it in a manner of speaking that accommodates itself to the one still customary today (which of course stems from mechanics), it may at best be expressed thus: "lawfulness" is causal lawfulness, and causality means computability. Fully, or at least nearly fully, sufficient to it is *only* the machine that we ourselves have made, and "nature" is sufficient to it insofar as we have been able to interpret one *side* of it by analogy with the machine. This shows itself palpably in every living being, which, to be sure, also has a thing-analogous side and therefore, for instance, can be fitted into the equivalence-laws of the exchange of energy, but which, as an unmade and never-to-be-made, but rather born and grown, self-formation, largely escapes computation. We know with certainty of the raspberry-bush that it will bear raspberries and not strawberries; but we are unable to state the number of raspberries to be expected; and we know that it will wither if we withhold light and water from it, but we cannot predetermine the degree of its thriving—since, given equal care, one bush will outstrip another in vigor of growth, out of — the self-sovereignty of life. In the organism of a person there is added, to the incalculability [p. 745] of vitality, the incalculability of spirit.
