We can, with a probability bordering on certainty, strike someone with terror, but we can only, with very much lesser probability, conjecture how he will thereupon act; and everyone knows that the future of a plantspecies or an animal-species, were it withdrawn from human interference, could be reckoned far more securely than the future of the human race, or even of a single people. For the former stands under the sign of necessity, which presents itself in it as the rhythm of the renewal of the similar; in mankind, by contrast, it is the will—itself once again incalculable—that contends with necessity. Whatever we will, and however we will it, we must will it; what we nonetheless, and not merely in fancy, experience as the "freedom" of willing, is the opposition of resolve to drive-impulse, or, more generally put, of the character of the person to the character of the mere vitality of the person. Having thereby already turned onto the road that leads inward, we now turn to the problem of consciousness.

Considerations *based only* on objects of thought or conceivednesses fail, on the one hand, with respect to the livingness of happening, and fail, on the other, with respect to the being-spirited of personal happening. Were we not ourselves seeing beings, no investigation of the eye and the optic nerve would give us even the faintest notion that organisms possessed of eyes were capable of seeing; and were we seeing, but not self-moving, beings, a knowledge of the light-sensitivity of the retina would nevertheless never help us to the surmise that organisms capable of sight could respond to visual impressions with movements. The investigation of living happening, and then, further, of all happening—inasmuch as a happening that is simply and utterly unliving does not take place at all—hangs in the air without the concurrent employment of the concept of experience, which, as we have just once more convinced ourselves, is a demonstrative concept. — But just as the arrangement that we call organism is understood only by a being capable of experience, and by means of experience, and not with the aid of the richest treasures of physical knowledge, so the particular arrangement of the organism of a person is understood only out of being-a-person, and by means of the concept of consciousness. Whatever we might discover about the peculiarity of the human cerebral cortex, it would remain for us a terra incognita without the consciousness already otherwise known to us.

[p. 746] Through a searching dissection of the grounds that make consciousness possible we have found: in order that a consciousness may arise from what is lived and, later, also from the living of it, an extra-spatio-temporal power must have joined itself to the spatio-temporal vitality of the individual bearer of life, a power which, by means of temporally unextended deeds, splits off a group of life-processes; and herein lies the ground of the distinction between life-processes capable of consciousness and life-processes not capable of consciousness. The consequently assumed difference between the bearer of life capable of consciousness and the bearer of life not capable of consciousness we have elsewhere described by the simile of "a displacement of the mid-point of life," according to which the soul, as the mid-point of a life's field of play—now become eccentric—must circle around a new center.<sup>31</sup> The reorientation is inherited as the organic condition of the activity of spirit, whereas the activity of spirit itself cannot be inherited, but sets in ever anew, in every newborn, some moons after birth—and indeed in step with the acquisition of language or of a homologous system of signs—in order only gradually, and at intervals differing in stage, to wrest dominion to itself. (*Once* the organic precondition is given, the assumption of the first intervention presents no metaphysical difficulties, since spirit, as extra-spatio-temporal, is also omnipresent.) The investigation of the inner development of the child—indeed, of youth in general—can be undertaken with success only along the guiding thread of the thought of a power-unfolding of spirit that advances in thrusts. The crises of the transitional years, for example, far from being merely organic thrusts, become enormously complicated in man through the intensifications, bound up with them, of the conflict of spirit and life, and the frequent case of an, as it were, evaded "confrontation" grounds countless varieties of psychic illness. The same holds of the developmental phases of historical mankind, to which we shall presently return.

<sup>31</sup> On page 746. — Compare on this our "Grundlagen der Charakterkunde" (the 9th chapter); further "Vom Wesen des Bewußtseins," 3rd ed., pp. 41–42; further, in "Mensch und Erde," 5th ed., the important essay "Über den Begriff der Persönlichkeit."

Before we proceed, let a train of thought begun in Volume I be brought here to its conclusion. As certainly as elementary similarities must be lived through for that kind of apprehension to occur which makes a thinking-activity possible, so certainly does the apprehension already prepare, and the act of judgement following close on its heels already complete, a given directionally determined *stance* of the will, in relation to which the uninterruptible process of the soul is lived through as motion. Thinking is not a motion, [p. 747] but a leaping transition from stance to stance, which, in proportion to the growing number of intermediate links, takes on the semblance of continuity, and which, with regard to the life-movement that bears it, most nearly resembles a striding.<sup>32</sup> It requires a world of intuitive images as the occasion of its excitation; but what of these declares itself while it is taking place is not the images themselves, but compulsions toward the choice of direction (whose most general axioms are called such); whereas it cannot dispense with a sensuous sign-language for marking the points at which it comes to rest. Hence the, as it seems, never-resting effort of researchers, in "representing," deliberating, planning, calculating, weighing, computing, to find images or more properly phantasms of the intended states of affairs "in" consciousness is misleading. It is not thanks to the phantasms that run strongly through one man's thinking, weakly through a second's, scarcely perceptibly through a third's, that the "motion" of thought gets under way — since it would rather be checked and deflected by them — but thanks to the will's stance, adapted to its goal point by point, which can be felt as a constant change of direction, and which expresses itself in an exactly corresponding mimicry — above all of the eye, which looks now "lost" and "distracted," now "fixed," now searching, now testing, and so forth — and *presents* itself in gesture, or rather in the impulse toward it. Thinking is inward action, and the meaning-bearing signs that serve to support it resemble sightinginstruments, which point directions and do not, say, mirror images. The direction of which we speak, however, is, as was ascertained in this volume, a purposive relatedness conceived by spatial analogy, which we make objective to ourselves with the concept of the straight line.

<sup>32</sup> On page 747. — Of numerous great minds it is reported that they could only work while pacing up and down the room, and many an intellectual worker among the readers of this book will testify the same of himself. Now, such pacing is a genuine expressive movement of combinatorial thinking activity. Its suppression would make thinking more difficult. — Finally, it is no accident that the German language has at its disposal the compound word "Gedankengang" [train of thought].

Meanwhile words like "stance" and "directional determinacy" already betray that *a* phantasm is indeed always at play: the phantasm of sense-space, in relation to which ever-renewed acts of detachment (= abstraction) are therefore always needed, for the purpose of preventing, so to speak, the objects of thought from taking a place within it. For it is, as we have seen, the emblem of all presence and consequently the immediate condition for the occurrence of spiritual acts at all. Through the omission of its detachment, reification ensues — indeed of states of affairs such as justice, science, virtue, logic, contradiction, mathematics, and the like, which have not the faintest similarity to things; for which we found the most incredible and precisely therefore the most compelling example in the undeniable fact that [p. 748] the intellectual history of the modern age let itself be seduced into conceiving thinking consciousness as a spatiality, in which a great deal is supposed to be contained, while other things again remain outside it. — Continuing our retrospect, we recall that the deeds of spirit attach themselves to points of disturbance in the movement of life, which is why the fateful bond between spirit and life must be sought on the side of impulse and not on the side of impression. The essence of spirit reveals itself not in the compelled act of apprehension, but in the spontaneously reactive act of will. In relation to life, spirit is a capacity for deeds, and its awakening is an achievement of resistance which is most briefly voiced by the particle of negation. With the No hurled, on the occasion of a disturbance, against the very current of lived experience (of actuality) itself, there begins the particularity of stance which, taken substantially, is called the I, and, with immediate regard to its capacity of determining, is called the will. The soul lives through experience, and all lived experience pulses; spirit sets a halt, place by place, against the wave-beat of lived experience. Unable to annihilate the soul outright — since it would thereby at once withdraw from itself the site of its working in life, and would destroy, if not itself, then at least its now and its here — it narrows the soul's living room by a net of blocks to its course that grows ever denser; as if one were to force the flood of a sea into a system of canals.

Meanwhile we are already speaking, in saying this, of the history of spirit in the Occident, which, in contrast to the spirit of Asia, has coincided with the history of the will from the very beginning — ultimately, indeed, with the history of spirit in mankind as such, because Asiatic spirituality has succumbed to the spirituality of the West. The struggles that will still be played out in this connection are nationalist powergroup struggles, and no longer those of opposed spiritual groups. — This history, however, now allows us to discern two phases fundamentally sharply distinguished, though in time, folk, and person only hesitantly replacing one another: the phase, wholly prevailing in the early period and still perceptibly so in antiquity, of the life-dependence of the will, and the phase — which, under the leadership of Christianity, supplanted it and has, since the so-called Renaissance, attained victory — of the will-dependence of life. In the former, the direction of apprehension is determined essentially by lived experience, in the latter by the purposes of thinking; in the former the intrinsic worth of knowing predominates, and volition remains bound to truth, in the latter it is the aims of the will to power by [p. 749] which research allows itself to be led; in the former the principal form of the will itself is the will to the work, in the latter it is the will to the deed. Finally, viewed vitally, the former has the distinguishing mark of its character from the depth of beholding, the latter from the vehemence of impulses. The exemplary form of the beholding spirit is called seer-ship, which will occupy us presently and again repeatedly; the exemplary form of the observing spirit is called sobriety, which, wherever it rules, rules in the service of intention. From the former, a sequence of stages of detachment leads first to the logocentric and finally to the formalistic spirituality — a path which the Greek world traversed within a mere three centuries, up to *the* point where the technique of thinking begins to subordinate itself to the technique of willing. With the logic of Aristotle, who was both the ender and the perfecter of the Greek path to downfall, the Greek spirit recalled, before they were torn apart, certain bonds by which, through the sensuous medium of sign-giving — in short, of language — the world of intuition had been able to keep his thinking bound to the actual, even if in the end only by a thin thread. By taking together, on the strength of the mark of opposition to arbitrary will which, however great their other differences, is common to both, the primordial-visionary knowing and the speculative-logical knowing, we distinguish the promethean from the heraclean stage of the will — because no merely conceptual characterization reaches the essential content of these two symbolic figures, on whom we must now explain ourselves somewhat more closely.

Whoever possesses the key to symbolic thinking will henceforth neither seek the genetic history of cultic formations "in consciousness," nor on that account hold them to be senseless, nor even lacking in person-independent meaning merely because he does not consider them "rational" — but will rather, in one and the same stroke, illuminate both their meaning and their genesis by unlocking their — always hidden — essence. He knows that symbolic logic governs even the phantasms with which the myth of peoples, so long as it deserves the name at all, winds about the — always hidden — kernel-layer of essence as with fragrance-laden garlands of blossom, in the process swallowing up actually occurred events — of the strangest selection — and thereby entirely concealing what was already in itself hidden. We indicated, in the 36th Chapter, the direction in which any research must move that seeks to draw nearer to the symbols without sinning against them through mere curiosity for novelty; and we [p. 750] shall, in Volume III, follow a stretch of the path in the direction there indicated. Let it therefore be permitted here to offer, in a more dogmatic form, what the interpretation of two famous cycles of legend presupposes for the disclosure of the meaning-content of the two symbols.

What lends the high-tragic accent to the demonic defiance of the Titan Prometheus, as Aeschylus — rejecting other versions of the legend and in sharp contrast to the Hesiodic conception — set him up for all time, this figure probably the mightiest, but certainly the cultically deepest of the threestarred constellation, is the union of all foreknowing seer's gift with complete inability to forestall the doom. It is not by chance that this same Aeschylus made Cassandra the principal figure of his "Agamemnon" — Cassandra, who, with the clearest consciousness of the double murder, of Agamemnon and of herself, immediately impending, enters the royal palace with the words:

"It has come, the hour; little would flight avail me" — bearing witness to the inescapability of fate. Both, Prometheus and Cassandra, are representatives of the same essential kind, namely of powerless knowledge: embodied there in the form of the immortal daemon, here of mortal man.

It matters little to the point whether the etymology already current among the Greeks and used by Aeschylus himself is correct, according to which "Prometheus" would mean simply the "forethoughtful one," or the one preferred by Kuhn, who traces the name back to the Sanskrit word pramanthas, which denotes the tool with which fire was kindled by the rubbing of pieces of wood; for Prometheus is both: the bringer of fire (pyrphoros) and the bringer of knowledge — the connection between the two events would have to be shown by whoever undertook to interpret the myth itself, a task we hold to be soluble, though it does not fall to us at this point. As bearer of knowledge, however, Prometheus symbolizes the genesis of consciousness. Whoever has read our 39th Chapter attentively (or the 9th of our "Grundlagen der Charakterkunde"), knows the fateful equation according to which consciousness as such coincides with the foreknowledge of having to die, and possesses in it the explanation of why the awakening of consciousness is found to be accompanied by a feeling of helplessness comparable to nothing else. Man, says Prometheus, was "through me made master of spirit, through me made conscious." Further:

[p. 751] "And heard not: like to shapes of dreams they mingled / all things blindly, confusedly, and planlessly together / their whole life long."

But in that the Titan, who foreknows all things and nothing more certainly than what is dreadful, bestows upon men the most fateful of all gifts, consciousness, he limits, out of pity, their foreknowledge of death once more by implanting *hope*; with which trait Aeschylus sets a profound new conception over against the primordial one, which was inclined to see in hope a power that deceptively prolongs the sufferings of man. But enough<sup>33</sup> of this report.

<sup>33</sup> On page 751. — When he has Prometheus say, in verse 248: I stopped mortals from foreseeing death, it follows from this that he *knew* of the connection between the faculty of reflection and the foreknowledge of having to die. But only *one* means did he find — or rather, his Prometheus found — to lessen the horror which only the Titan was strong enough to bear: he planted "blind hopes" (tuphlas elpidas) in the hearts of his wards. This is the new conception of the value of hoping that he represents: hope cannot avert the unavoidable, but it turns it into something *indeterminate*, into a perhaps, which still allows for a "perhaps-not-after-all." — Something quite different, of course, confronts us in Christian hope. Here the name "hope" designates the firm confidence of the bearer of hope in personal immortality. "Death, where is thy sting? etc."

With our key in hand, we recognize in the fettering of Prometheus to the rocks in the desolate land of the Scythians the symbolic expression of the abidingly unresolved earth-boundness of his essence — which appears now in the light of tragic torment for this reason and this reason only, that it is no longer the bearer of life but the bearer of the faculty of *cognition* who remains bound to the powers of the great mother and thus to doom. For is not Prometheus the son of Themis, and is it not the maternal Oceanids whose lament surrounds him with its murmur! — The promethean stage of spirit is the stage of the life-dependence of spirit, of the image-dependence of thinking, of the nearness to actuality of knowing — knowing, that is, out of the will to truth, or knowing as such — and hence of the unintentionality of spiritual doing, and, seen from the standpoint of spirit, of knowing pathic-ness, in whose afterglow the necessity of happening becomes the inexorability of Heimarmene. It marks the final segment of the prehistory of all peoples out of which historical peoples were to arise, everywhere reaches some way into "history," and, for reasons explained in Volume I, permanently retains the preponderance in the history of China, indeed to some degree of Asia altogether. In the Occident, by contrast, the urge to deeds is mixed with seer-ship from the very beginning, and not least in the figure of Prometheus himself — the urge that strives to burst the fetter of tellurism and converts, by degrees, the visionary knowing of the mantis into the reason-bright knowing of the speculative "philosopher." — The essence of the urge to deeds, together with the terrible consequences of its victory over the faculty of cognition, is likewise given to us by the myth, in the figure of Herakles.

[p. 752] From the countless versions of the legend, unconcerned with the never-ending disputes of archaeology over their age, we draw out what alone holds good before the logic of the symbol; for even, say, the "Herakles at the Crossroads" invented late by Prodicus of Ceos is *truthfully* invented. "Already in the cradle he strangles the Agathodaemon, the serpent. Then he decides for the path of toil, of labor, of willing, with a scornful turning-away from the vegetal happiness of the dreamingly idle. Pallas Athena, the motherless daughter of the father, arms him, and now his course of blood-dripping fame begins. Before his arrows and blows of the club there perish not monsters, as the legend, pragmatizing, would have it, but, in an oppressively unbroken series, all the mightiest offspring of Gaia. His triumphal march symbolizes the step-by-step occurring downfall of the telluric world of gods. He helps the Olympians in the battle of the Giants, which is decided in their favor only through him; he slays the Nemean lion, the living sign of primal fire; he destroys, in the serpent of the Lernaean swamp, the chthonic maternal ground out of which cellular life wells up; he overtakes and lames the swiftfooted hind, the animal of Artemis: the venerable symbol of an everywhere-nourishing presence; he catches the boar, the spirit of the thicket in which a creative darkness dwells; he brings about the death of the earthborn centaurs; he drives off the Stymphalian cranes, the brazen voices of the spherical current of air; he tames, in the Cretan bull, the daemon of Dionysian sensibility; he vanquishes the Amazons, the warlike host of the primal night; he strangles, by lifting him from the ground into the naked air, Antaeus — image of the begetting nearness of the clod, invincible through contact with earth; he wounds the maternal Hera; he conquers Troy, the stronghold of matriarchalism; he steals by cunning the innermost symbol of uranian fecundity, the golden apples of the Hesperides; he wrests from death its prey, the wife of Admetus; he overcomes, in Achelous, the original Zeus, the god of impregnating depth, and breaks, symbolically, the power of the underworld, by dragging the three-headed guardian up into the glaring light of the upper day. What was, to the sons of earth, dream and sacred cradle — the Isis-veil of embracing imageglow — becomes to him, the Olympian, a searing shirt of torment: handed to him by a jealous Deianira, and destined, in the purifying penance of immeasurable afflictions, to destroy his body. But out of the pyre there rises — now an immortal — the new Herakles into the higher region of Olympian eternity. [p. 753] We have in him the fully prefigured mold of the Christian world-idea: the spirit which again and again crushes the serpent's head; which, in a life full of martyrdom and temptation, shatters the symbols of the cosmos — of the later hell; which robs death of its sting, and finally passes into an invisible kingdom that leaves behind the world of images as the mere self-deception of lower desires. The history of Herakles gathers onto a single head the struggle, protracted through millennia, and the final victory of this kingdom — called by the Greeks the Olympian — whose truest representative is not Zeus but Apollo, the slayer of Python. As his temple grows only out of the grave of the slain serpent, so must the primeval ordinance of the earthborn be destroyed, wherever the right of spirit and of deeds flourishes."<sup>34</sup>

<sup>34</sup> On page 753. — This passage, composed in the *year* 1903, is taken from the author's *literary remains*.

Who could still doubt what it means, what it must *mean*, that it is precisely Herakles who slays the eagle of Zeus and frees the Titan Prometheus from the rock! Spirit, freed from the bondage of life, steps forth self-sovereignly into appearance as destructive deed, and the activity of thinking is henceforth the instrument of the will to *power*. The heraclean stage of spirit is the stage of the spirit-dependence of life, of the will-dependence of thinking, of knowing out of the purposes of a humanity which subjugates "nature" both within itself and outside itself and today celebrates its triumphs with the "wonders of technology." One sees that it was no accident that the first representatives of the glory of the supposed world-law, the Stoics, chose Herakles for themselves as model and hero!

Let us transport ourselves to the point in time at which spirit first gained entry into life; then between that time and now there lies a path of seemingly gradual transformation of lived experience, which, with regard to the consciousness assigned to each point, we must characterize more precisely as a sequence of states of consciousness, with the stair-landing described by us in the middle and the end to be indicated further below. If we compare, in the usual manner, consciousness as such to brightness, unconsciousness as such to darkness, then, similarly to the solar spectrum, the brightness in question would lie between two darknesses flanking it: psychologically speaking, between the darkness on the near side of consciousness — of lightless yet warm lived experience — and the darkness on the far side of consciousness — of the warmthless "deed in itself"; metaphysically speaking, between the unconscious actuality of happening [p. 754] and the once again unconscious being. Of the living darkness we know from memory of the consciousness-incapable experience of deep sleep, as well as of the consciousness-capable experiences of dreaming and of absorption; the cold darkness of lifeless being, by contrast, we can at first only infer — for example, through the thoughtextension of the degrees of intensification of willing that are experienceable by us, up to the limiting state of a pure willing, a nothing-but-activity which, while certainly not a proton kinoun, would quite certainly, as Aristotle profoundly recognized, be an akineton, and in this way no longer capable of consciousness. If we finally placed the point of fracture, where promethean spirituality is superseded by heraclean, roughly in the middle of the quasi-spectrum, then two coloropposed series of states of consciousness would be distinguished there, one of which would approach ever more nearly the "warm" boundary of consciousness, the other consequently the "cold." If, however, one rejects — as the state of affairs demands — every comparison of consciousness with spatialities and degrees of brightness, then the question forces itself upon us all the more decisively, whether the grounds for the fact that the state of consciousness was driven to progress, stage by stage, from extreme nearness to life to extreme nearness to spirit, are really to be sought only on the side of life, and not also on the side of spirit. For the sequence does indeed seem to be irreversible, or "irreversible," as the physicists say. We give here, in brief, what of this has already become ripe for pronouncement.

If, in relation to the promethean stage, the vitality of the heraclean stage is characterized by heightened vehemence of impulse; if this heightened vehemence can only be understood as heightened reactivity; if, finally, the counter-impulse presupposes the experience of a disturbance — then we shall be inclined to assume, for the entry of spirit into the life-cell as such, a life-disturbability not previously present, stemming from a locus minoris resistentiae, if not indeed from a vulnerable spot, for which, as will have to be recalled later, the mythical thinking of several peoples has left us a riddling symbol. Whereas the promethean stance could appear in the light of an attempt at restoration, and, as it were, of a scarring-over by means of knowledge which, even though it be knowledge of the unavoidable, nonetheless protects the soul by ending what is fear-inducing for it — the *torment of questioning* — the heraclean stance has broken with life, and appears, exactly conversely, in the light of an attempt no longer to protect the [p. 755] spirit-coupled bearer of life against a disturbance of lived experience, but to armor the life-coupled bearer of spirit against lived experience, through its exploitation in the service of the will. It is evident that this requires, equally, a change in the processes of life and also in the activity of spirit, and this holds without exception for every transformation of the state of consciousness from the moment at which, in keeping with the presupposed presence of spirit, a consciousness, in the sense we have laid down for the faculty of reflection, is already present. Without therefore deciding for the present whether the occasion for the change takes place on the side of life or on the side of spirit, we characterize the change itself, but now with emphasis on its character on the side of spirit.

If we consider that the stage-wise heightened vehemence of impulse in the heraclean phase corresponds, among other things, to a growing independence of the basis of impulse in relation to the basis of impression, or, put otherwise, to the progressive emancipation of active life from beholding life, grounded in an increased splittability of the life-processes, then we would have, on the side of spirit, first of all to assert differences of energy among the acts; according to which the splitting effect might reach now shallower, now deeper layers of vitality, and might separate those affected apart from one another with varying degrees of completeness. Spirit resembles, in this way, a wedge driven into the life-cell, whose aim would be to halve it, or, less figuratively put, to de-soul the body, to dis-embody the soul, and in this manner to kill life itself; for, in keeping with the personally, ethnically, and temporally varying inequality in value of the poles of life, now predominantly the one, now predominantly the other actually occurs, without the halving, however, ever having yet been completed. But the more the constitution of life, on the occasion of the energy of the individual act, temporarily approaches complete cleavage, the more it is actually experienced that the vehemence of spiritual activity threatens to shatter consciousness to pieces and drives the state of consciousness to the "upper limit," beyond which consciousness would be extinguished — not as overwhelmed by life, but "as a consequence of the splitting-off of the consciousness-capable outer layer of life from the consciousness-incapable core of life" (Vol. I, p. 266).

With the difference in strength of the acts, measured by the reach and completeness of the splitting-effects upon the living room of life, [p. 756] there now crosses, however, the quite considerable difference in the frequency of their occurrence within equal periods of time (e.g., seconds), and the vital counterpart to this would lie in a series of states reaching from dreamless deep sleep to the utmost wakefulness. Even though, up to now, only here and there has a side-light fallen upon the thorny problem of the polarity of waking and sleeping, the following may nonetheless be taken as established. Whatever the vital difference of waking from sleeping is to be sought in, it signifies for the personal bearer of life, among other things, the rhythmic alternation of two spans, of which the one is unable to subsist without the activity of spirit, the other unable to subsist with it. The memory of the experience of deep sleep bears witness to us of unconsciousness as such, but thereby also of complete incapacity for activity, complete surrender and relaxation. And equally we establish that, with growing tiredness, the state of consciousness first loses spontaneity, in order, the longer this continues, to forfeit even the capacity for reacting; whereas the greatest *freshness* is always required for the purpose of attaining more than ordinary quickness — for example in the deliberate attending to unforeseeably changing occasions of perception. Finally, self-reflection leaves us in no doubt that the quickness of apprehending, combining, deciding, and hence the quickness of spiritual acts, increases with the predominance of active wakefulness, i.e., of willing and acting, over beholding wakefulness, i.e., of contemplating and reflecting, and conversely. It is always, then, the great doers of world history and their lesser kin, the busy ones, of whom it has so often been handed down to us that they were able to carry out several activities, such as reading a book and listening to a speech, "simultaneously" — which in truth, of course, speaks for the more than ordinary quickness of the succession of their spiritual acts. Even though the condition for the acceleration of the succession of acts may be different from the condition for the intensification of their effect, both conditions are without question interwoven with one another in the condition of the predominance of the willing stance over the knowing stance, just as both also drive the state of consciousness toward the "upper limit." For if, upon the completed splitting of the life-cell, spiritual activity ceases because of the standstill of the life-movement that bears it, then, at "infinite" quickness of the acts, spiritual activity would likewise cease, because then arbitrarily many acts would coincide in a single point in time [p. 757] — whereby their connection with the temporality of the life-process would be dissolved. There as here, spirit would henceforth stand alone, and consciousness would be extinguished. But even at finite quickness, the succession cannot be increased beyond a certain limit, if indeed the occurrence of the act produces consciousness only insofar as it takes place at the turning-point of the life-wave, and is thus bound to the latter's pulse, now longer, now shorter.

With this, to be sure, the characterization of the preconditions of the opposed limiting states of consciousness is certainly not yet exhausted. In particular we feel out, as it were, that between deep absorption and ecstatic rapture out of fullness of life, and "transcendental" enrapturement and "unbecoming" out of the might of spirit, still other fundamental differences may well hold sway than those resulting from differences of strength and frequency of the splitting ray, and the question lies close at hand whether the point of impact of the act might not perhaps vary and influence the state-picture of consciousness. To this we shall respond in Volume III with certain considerations which, for the present, admit only of conjectures, but which, precisely for that reason, promise to open new possibilities to esoteric research. Here, by contrast, let it be established, by way of an intervening consideration, that and why the supposed ecstasies of Christian saints, despite the seductive appearance of the opposite, belong to the heraclean stance, and become intelligible only, and entirely, out of enormous overstrainings of the will.

The will to the deed, which, since the beginning of the so-called modern age, has broken out ruthlessly, enslaving the forces of nature, laying waste the face of the planet, draining mankind itself in ever more unceasing "competitive" struggles, was really quite properly "prepared" in the disciplines of medieval monasticism, through a regimentation of the blood lasting more than a thousand years. Whoever wishes to become acquainted with all the intermediate stages the will had to traverse in order to force life completely into the obedience of spirit should study the terrible history of Christian "mysticism," as Görres has presented it to us, on the basis of comprehensive study of the sources, in his five-volume work "Christliche Mystik" — beside which, for grandeur and depth, from the whole of Catholic letters, only the poetry of Dante could at best be set. He will then know that the supposed "freedom," "enlightenment," and idolatry of the understanding of the modern age was merely the releasing of the path outward, after [p. 758] the will had, in the soul of man, in essentials completed its cruel work; and it will no longer strike him as remarkable, though it may well provoke curious reflections, that the Middle Ages closed with two inventions — the invention of the art of printing and the invention of firearms. — If it stands as our book has striven, page by page, to set forth — that spirit, as implanted in life, is, measured against it, will, but that the will is life's inexorable adversary — then, from the standpoint of one still rooted in life but fallen prey to spirit, the turning toward spirit must present itself as a turning away from life, and, with regard to the personhood of the life-bearer overpowered by spirit, as self-overcoming, self-dispossession, and finally self-mortification, and the path thither as a stepwise progressive training in self-tormentings and selfdenials. Now, Christianity, so long as it was still struggling, was, in both practice and doctrine, a systematized struggle with the "temptations of the flesh," and the "triumph" it strove for was the complete subjugation of life — in man, that is to say — to the power-authority of the "Lord," i.e., of the will. Pater vult, filius facit, spiritus perficit! [The father wills, the son does, the spirit perfects.] Its supreme rule of practice was consequently obedience, because of all exercises of the will the strongest is the exercising of oneself in obedience without contradiction.

Let one replace, in the saying of Abbot Daniel — "The more the body flourishes and blooms, the more must the soul wither; the more, on the contrary, the body withers, the more strongly will the soul flourish and increase" — the word soul in both places by the word spirit, and one has, in the one sentence, the meaning and course of development of Christendom up to the elaboration of the completed supreme power of the will, whose bearer must henceforth turn the wiles and cunning of the now soul-poor, once again justified, and purposively worth-tempering body against *extra*human life. — Of Saint Bernard of Clairvaux, scarcely had he entered, at twenty-three, the exceedingly strict Cistercian order, we hear: "Quickly had spirit grown strong in the young man, while what otherwise tends to rule was forced into servitude. The senses found themselves so bound that, seeing, he did not see; hearing, he did not hear; nor, tasting, did he perceive any taste; what he took of nourishment, what he allowed himself of rest in sleep, seemed less taken to preserve life than permitted to hold off death. Amid vigils [p. 759] and fasting, cold and labor, the power of the body was soon broken — indeed, as he himself later sometimes lamented, shattered by all too great zeal; but the spirit had flared up all the more brightly within him" (loc. cit., I, p. 249).

Quite apart from the orgies of self-laceration of the martyrs, from the excesses of self-abasement and the paroxysms of chastisement of the penitents, which leave Indian fakirism behind them in sheer horror,<sup>35</sup> there reveals itself, in the methodical measures for the exercise of the will through the binding of sensibility, the hatred of life belonging to the obedience-demanding power, and the gaping rupture of ascetic inwardness. "So that smell may not have its pleasure in eating, it must put up with everything foul-smelling; and this will be the more welcome, the more nature revolts against it. So that food may not tickle the palate, it is seasoned with wormwood, gall, and everything ill-tasting; the excess of tastelessness and counter-taste, bound almost to a bearer without a body, will soon dull the sense and bind it completely: as is known of many, especially of Saint Bernard, that in the end they lost the power of discrimination, and oil and vinegar counted the same to their tongue. With the other senses it has then been managed in the same way .." (loc. cit., p. 465). The hardest struggle of all, for reasons familiar to us, asceticism wages with the need for sleep! "Hence the many precautions it takes to divert this flooding of the lower life-forces, which brings an ebbing of the higher ones in its train, and to remedy, as far as possible, the daily recurrence of this feverish alternation; hence its endeavor, since a complete abolition of the alternation, like a total renunciation of nature in this life, is not possible, to restrict the need — like that for nourishment .. — to a minimum, which on average is reckoned at two to three hours" (I, pp. 382–383). Thus, however, does the mystic Ruysbroeck express himself on the meaning of these exercises: "In the constant exercise of such self-denial, he who progresses becomes ever more masterful over himself, so that, free and mighty as he has become, the soul is laid into his hand, that he may give it to whomever he will." And indeed we hear of feats of will on the part of great ascetics which one would have to reject as incredible, were they not attested, in the most various places and at the most various times, throughout a millennium and a half, always in similar fashion. "Abbot Elpidius was accustomed, for twenty-five years, to eat only on Saturday and Sunday, and came, in his emaciation, to such a point that one could count all his bones through his skin [p. 760] without effort. Saint John .. had in forty years never once come forth from his cell. Saint Macarius crumbled only bread into a vessel with a narrow neck, and ate each time only as much as he could draw out with a single grasp; 'but that I should eat nothing at all,' he said, 'to that I could not accustom my body, that evil tax-collector.' So prepared, he was able, once, unknown, and admitted only with difficulty by Saint Pachomius into his monastery at Tabenna, to stand throughout the entire forty days' fast in a corner, silent, plaiting palm leaves, eating only, on Sundays, a few raw cabbage leaves, and leaving the spot only for the most extreme necessity .." (I, p. 196).

<sup>35</sup> On page 759. — "Suso tells us at length, in the account that has been preserved to us of his life, in the naive language of his time, how he chastened his all-too-lively nature and what cunning and penance he sought out, that he might make the body subject to the spirit. A hair shirt and an iron chain he wore thus for a long time, until the blood ran from him and he had to lay both aside. Thereupon he had an undergarment made for himself; a hundred and fifty pointed brass nails were fastened to straps, their points turned inward; in this he slept at night. The nights were never so long in winter, nor so hot in summer, that he would have left it off. Then he had made for himself a wooden cross, which was in length as the span of a man's hand, and of a corresponding breadth; into it he had driven thirty nails with projecting points; this he strapped upon his bare back between the shoulders, against the flesh, and wore it thus, day and night, steadily, for eight years; it made him bloody and injured at every bending, or when at night he came to lie upon it, and was so painful that at first his tender nature was terrified by it; he was permitted only to strike it with his fist when he wished to give himself a stronger discipline. So that at night he might not unwittingly help himself, he had leather gloves studded all over with brass pins made for himself; these wounded him whenever he reached anywhere to help himself. This martyring exercise he pursued for a good sixteen years, until his veins had grown cold and his nature was broken; then there appeared to him in a vision a heavenly company, who made known to him that God wished to have it from him no longer. His bed was an old discarded door, on which he had laid a thin mat of reeds; this reached only to his knees. His head rested on a small pillow of pea-straw. As he went by day, so he lay by night, save that he wrapped a thick cloak about himself, which, however, was also very short, so that his feet froze when he wished to stretch them out. To this was added the frequent sharp discipline under the grim blows of his scourges, so that his blood flowed down his body; the great abstinence from all comfort in warmth, in eating and still more in drinking, so that his whole nature struggled to quench an unbearable thirst, and he would often, when he stood thus parched in the choir at Compline and the holy water was, as was customary, carried around, open his parched mouth wide toward the sprinkler, in the hope that perhaps a drop of the water might a little cool his burning tongue. She was almost surpassed by Saint Rosa of Lima in inventions for her own torment. When she had taken the habit, she had made herself a scourge of chains, with which she beat herself without mercy; dealing out the blows she gave herself in such a way that they always struck a different part of her body. When this exercise was forbidden her, she wound the chain threefold and tightly about her loins, closing the ends together with a padlock and then throwing away the key. The skin was soon rubbed through; the chain cut into the flesh, so that it became almost invisible, and finally penetrated as far as the nerve-cords of that region. The consequence was that one night the most violent pain in the hip overcame the virgin, with agonies which, since she could not by any force unlock the chain, threatened to bring about her death. Long had she struggled with it in vain; then she betook herself to prayer, which opens even heaven itself: at once the lock sprang open of itself, the chain gave way; but it had to be torn away by force, so that the skin stayed clinging to it and the blood gushed after. When the wound had healed, she girded herself anew; but her confessor compelled her to surrender the chain to him. She had put on a hair shirt, woven of horsehair and reaching down to her knees, which she wore for many years, here and there reinforced further with points, until it too was taken from her. When she had passed out of her childhood years, she had fashioned herself a crown of tin, furnished on the inside with points, which she wore secretly upon her head for a long time. Then, for the last ten years of her life, she had another made for herself: a strip of silver, set on the inside with ninety-nine spikes arranged side by side in three rows and soldered together into a circle. This she wore hidden beneath her veil. One spike after another wounded her head according to the movements she made. Even speaking became painful to her, still more coughing or sneezing. If any temptation assailed her, she struck it a few times and found help in this. For her bed she had laid seven knotted pieces of wood side by side upon a board, but filled the spaces between them with three hundred sharp pieces of broken pottery, whose points, turned toward her body, caused her such pain that even the mere thought of this dreadful bed, on which she lay for fifteen years, was a horror to her, heroic as she was. Only in the last years of her life, as her infirmities increased, did she spend the nights sitting in a chair, trembling with cold." Thus Görres, in Volume I of his "Christliche Mystik," on pages 405–407. We forgo the reproduction of still far stronger examples, in order to spare the reader needless feelings of disgust. We need hardly add that the so-called ecstasies of these strange saints were throughout accompanied by extreme insensibility (anesthesia); and this was tested and established by experiments, the mere reading of which is apt to make many a susceptible mind of today feel faint.

But it is always such will-mighty "mortifications," understood by the canon of the Church as "purifications," that precede the "raptures" of the saints, as well as the well-nigh incredible feats of unconquerable emissaries. No one, says Görres, may "ascend Tabor of the Transfiguration with the Lord .. unless he shall first have walked with him to Calvary" (II, p. 469). Andreas of Salos, a Byzantine saint of the tenth century who chose the role of the fool, roams homeless through the streets of the city, unprotected from the maltreatment of men and exposed to every inclemency of the weather. Now one day there breaks in a fearful storm, with icy cold and a hailstorm under which the roofs splinter. Niceforus, his biographer, holds the saint for lost, but finds him the next morning in complete cheerfulness of heart, and learns, on asking him where he spent the dreadful interval, the following: "First, he said, he had fled to the refuge of the poor, who, however, had driven him away; then he had gone under the portico to the resting-place of a dog, in case he might find there some protection against the frost. The dog, he said, had risen from its bed and gone away, as though it too did not consider him worthy of its company. Then, praying in despair, he had thrown himself down, and at once an angel in radiant light had appeared to him, who touched him with a lily-stem, saying: Because you have not let go of God, he too will not let go of you; this touch shall win life back for you. He then saw himself transported into a beautiful garden, with trees and flowers without number, unspeakably more beautiful than anything the earth possesses; birds of every color sat upon them, delighting his ear with many songs .. Through the middle of the garden a stream flowed, and on [p. 761] its banks a vine had spread .. Then, as he gazed upon it, a stirring of wind arose and shook the trees, so that the birds began to sing out loudly; all the winds from the west and from midnight and noon then joined this one from the east. But the desire came upon him to view also the region beyond the water, and there a great plain received him. Upon it .. a superterrestrial figure stepped up to him, who led him to the height of the first heaven, on which he saw a great cross surrounded by praying angels. When he now beheld the sea deep below him, a faltering seized him; the angel led him to the second heaven and there stepped, adoring, before a second cross .. until the wanderers at last reached the highest, veiled in a covering. The covering opened, and he saw the Lord in unspeakable radiance .. When he was then led back, he came to himself and found himself again in the same corner of the portico; the storm, however, had meanwhile passed, and clear sunshine greeted him" (I, pp. 241–243). Indeed, the highest grace that can fall to the lot of the rapt is the voluptuously-painful clothing with the fearful wounds of the crucified Savior through stigmatization, concerning which one finds astonishing reports in Görres, which we should advise everyone to read for themselves.

But when the inwardly stored-up store of energy breaks outward, then we see a work-activity of truly herculean irresistibility, endurance, and tenacity come to the fore. John, surnamed "of God," from whom the so-called Hospitallers took their origin, went, in consequence of a vision, to Granada, "was there most deeply seized by the sermons of Avila, and now played, for a time, in order to atone for his sins through humiliation, the fool in that city; was on that account delivered to the madhouse and there so dreadfully mistreated, until he believed it was now enough, and put off the assumed mask of folly. He then served the sick for a time in that house, and here the thought came to him to found a hospital himself, in order to follow, wholly and entirely, the calling of his life within it. He began by gathering brushwood on the nearby mountain and carrying it into the city for sale, from which he fed himself and others. He soon succeeded in renting an empty house; in it he took in as many poor as it could hold; what they needed he soon won for them [p. 762] through his imploring word .. On his own back he himself dragged the sick to the place, so that he often collapsed under the burden; day and night he cared restlessly for his charges. No ingratitude, no maltreatment was able to check his zeal." Then there breaks out a gigantic fire, which spreads to such an extent that no one dares any longer to approach the building, and the central structure is to be razed with cannon. But John, among the first to hasten there, at once forces his way through one of the gates entirely filled with smoke. "Without delay he set to work within. To the sick who could still walk he showed the way; others he led, others were carried, still others sometimes dragged in pairs; those below were let down through the windows: all with such strength and speed that everyone, especially those who knew his body, weakened by fasting and vigils, marveled at it. When the sick were in safety, he rescued of the furnishings what was to be rescued .. He then took an axe and climbed to the loft, to fend off the flames; but while he succeeded with this on the one side, they broke out all the more violently on the other. For half an hour those present had lost sight of him and had already given him up, when he suddenly sprang forth out of the flames, his clothing unharmed, only his eyebrows and eyelashes singed. Seventy witnesses swore to the occurrence under oath" (I, pp. 459–460). With similar titanic feats the founding history of numerous orders begins. The "mission" among the heathen of all four quarters of the heavens, the extermination of the Moors and their culture in Spain, the warlike frenzy of the Crusades: these are "world-historical" evidences that it was an essentially, to be sure, superpersonal will to power that thrust, life-killingly, inward in the penitents and ascetics — not to speak of the deeds of madness that unceasingly accompanied the militant Church, which we know under the name of the persecutions of heretics.

As certainly as, even today, in the age of the will turned ruthlessly outward, there still exist not a few persons who can recall states of absorption, so certainly must it be held doubtful whether even a single human being of the present could bear witness to loss of consciousness arising from will-power turned inward. But this is not needed in order nonetheless to know that the culminating heights of spiritual mysticism, in extreme contrast to the world-surging intoxication of genuine ecstasy, are explicable only through the cleaving-apart of the organism and the consequent [p. 763] standstill of all happening — because it is thus, and thus alone, that what the literary legacy of significant mystics has to report to us of them becomes intelligible. If we take up even so mild a mystic — one secretly inclining, from the Christian denial of life, toward the Buddhist — as Meister Eckhart, we find him occupied, at every step, with painting, by means of admirably well-aimed turns of phrase, states in which there betrays itself the achievement-result of a power that severs from life — a power that actually accomplishes within inwardness what, formerly, the "halters of the world's course," the Eleatics, had, with less success, attempted to attribute to the actuality of cosmic happening. The most highly desired, he says, is complete "detachment" (= absoluteness); the detached spirit is "unmoved" and "unchangeable," and only in the unchangeable does true "being" lie. The object of detachment is formed not by this or that, but by the "supra-rational," the "imageless" (!), and hence the "pure nothing"; on this alone rests the "unity and purity of God," of which we are expressly told that it coincides with the perfect nothing. — We should know, from the history of speculation, no more compelling confirmation for the truth of our disclosures concerning the essence of spirit than the circumstance that, according to the teachings of so-called mysticism, the will turned inward culminates in the production of an unconsciousness which, in relation to elementary being-outside-oneself, appears as the last possible emptiness!

Once, through the "disciplining" of the soul, the supremacy of the will has been finally established, the way outward stands open to it from then on: the man of power replaces the saint, the champion of labor replaces the champion of obedience, and the turning away from the world for the sake of subduing the inner life gives way to the campaign against the world, which it is henceforth the task of research and of sharp-wittedness to wage, supplied with weapons of attack and munitions. Thus there arises, for a brief stretch, the colorful interlude of the essentially "Protestant" (because essentially protesting) personality — for just so long, namely, as the will still needs blood anew in order to gather the thrusting force of spirit against *actuality*, which it was now its destiny to overwhelm and finally to kill: the actuality of ensouled intuitive images. And just as the disempowering of the soul in man was achieved through the regulation and mechanization of the processes of life, so through the regulation and [p. 764] mechanization of the processes of nature the disempowering of the soul in the images of the world is achieved.

"One usually takes the Renaissance as the counterblow of antiquity against the Christianity of the Middle Ages. In truth it is its fulfillment. The aqua fortis of spirit that separates body and soul had, in the Middle Ages, to dissolve the contact between man and the chthonic powers. Allied with the roving instincts of barbarism, it tore the peoples from the nourishing vapor of their house-, forest-, and field-idols and carried the shudder of rapture into the world of its beyond, which therefore seemed to beckon as if from a distance of space. Thus out of the haze and glow of local-boundness there cleared the wandering miracle of "supra-terrestrial" visions. The symbol of chthonism, the ring of walls, transformed itself into the enigmatically unattainable castle of the Grail, whose battlements fade into twilight against a background still cosmically blue. — Now in the age of the Renaissance this rift and cut is fully completed. The paroxysm was incorporated and no longer needs the tutelage of the Church, in whose discipline it grew strong. Its power to draw is gone the moment the goal-setting force has become a component of the human person. Withdrawn from the panta rhei of the world's revolution, man steps into the world alien to him as enemy and newcomer. Every glance of his eye is a petrifying Medusa's glance. The process has a superhuman consistency: first "chastisement of the body" and violent flight from a still-demonic sensory world, whereby this world itself, as though after a violent bloodletting, blooms again, paler, more waning, and at the same time more extravagantly alluring, as a beyond; then execution of the soul by the now rigid and moistureless body, dwelling-place solely of the I-point, which no longer beholds but spies, no longer embraces but dissects — Now, however, it is the peculiar iridescence of the Renaissance that this gaze still remains directed at the sensory world, at a world that, like Botticelli's shivering Aphrodite, has just emerged unclothed from the protecting sea of images. Flashing recollections from life in the All mingle strangely and agonizingly with the curious groping over surfaces already deprived of soul. That is why the smile on the lips of Leonardo's women's heads appears at once sweet and devilish. — And this renewed awareness of nearness to the world, after the convulsive dreams of chastisement of the Middle Ages, which saw every sensory semblance only in the consuming mirror-blaze of the beyond, this renewed awareness [p. 765] led to the belief in a greater kinship with antiquity, from which in truth one was still further removed than in the age of Gothic." — But as<sup>36</sup> this process itself, with the now headlong progress of the mechanization of the outer world, reaches its goal, the presumed self-sovereignty of its bearers finds an end as sudden as it is unexpected.

<sup>36</sup> On page 765. — From the author's literary remains (1907).

Must it not give us pause that, since Kant's doctrine of an "autonomy," which places man in a relation of dependence on the concept of humanity similar to that in which medieval Christianity stood to the concept of God, only fifty-four years elapsed before Stirner's doctrine of an autonomy which dissolves the concept of humanity into a phantasm of the brain? Rid of its life-husk, and mocking the maternal womb, rid at last even of the resistance of the forces of nature (excepting the one: death!), the naked I generates and exultantly attests itself; only the exultation dies before it has gained a voice. For now there is revealed what these pages have labored to reckon out: that the presumed possessor of the will has in truth become the one possessed by the will — fanatic of the mania for records, marionette on the wire of the lust for power, fool of the frenzy for success, racing-machine, fired and driven by the madness of belief in the idol of — the greatest number! — We have shown in part at length, in part at least indicated, why mechanistic thinking, because it is without substance, indeed contrary to substance, flows into formalistic thinking; the calculating of nature into the calculating arts of arbitrary will; destruction out of a pretended sense of utility into destruction out of satanic delight in it. We now reflect on what, presumably, is the end of all this in man.

It can be made clear by reference to mathematical thinking — on which our "Grundlagen der Charakterkunde" gives fuller information — that the very last and thinnest connection of the faculty of reflection with actuality is the connection through the medium of signs, signs, however, taken quite simply, or as it were empty signs, such as are needed to mark the movement of thought; *and* also, that with the growing facility of thinking in mere signs, these, through the growing dispensability of their content of meaning, threaten to become just as independent as happens with concepts in mechanistic thinking. If it is beyond question the goal of formalistic thinking to arrive at results of thought without any expenditure of thinking (emblem: the calculating machine!), [p. 766] answers without the intervening play of searching, then its scarcely foreseen *end* is nonetheless this: dominion of spirit without the means and instrument of a consciousness still always co-dependent on life! "No doubt the wholly consummated formalist would be an unconscious apparatus of precision of uncannily variable capacity for reaction, and might then very well also be assembled — whether in a machine factory, or like the homunculus in the retort." But with that we<sup>37</sup> have, in respect of spirit, reached the end of the road that began with the entry of spirit into the life of man.

<sup>37</sup> On page 766. — From our "Grundlagen der Charakterkunde," 11th ed., Bouvier & Co., Bonn, p. 85.

Original man, as bearer of unconscious beholding and elemental efficacy, is, for all his difference from the animals, just as without history as they are. After the lightning of spirit, on the occasion of some vulnerable spot, had once first succeeded in striking into the living cell, a group of humans began to pass from the historyless into the prehistoric condition, in order gradually to pass over into that of history. Compared with the many-thousand-year prehistory, and still more with the historylessness of more than a *hundred* thousand years, the history of mankind — traceable to some extent back some seven thousand years, which one is accustomed to call "world history" — would signify, even if it should still continue for one or two millennia (which is little probable, since many signs indicate that we are already moving with growing speed toward its end), no more than an exceedingly brief interval of the character of an interruption of the cosmic course. However that may be, historical man is in any case bearer of consciousness (= the faculty of reflection): at first, and in the West at least far into antiquity, on the Promethean stage, characterized by the dependence of willing on cognition and of cognition on the image-forming thinking of prehistory; since the end of antiquity and the incursion of Christianity, on the Heraclean stage, characterized by the dependence of thinking on willing and by the increasingly rapid volatilization of cognition into a more or less emancipated calculating — at first with concepts very poor in meaning, finally with mere signs which, even if still in some way charged with meaning, function as it were of themselves, without reflection on their meaning. The consciousness of will resting on signtechnique, brought to its highest consummation, would be an upper limiting state, beyond which the [p. 767] automatism of a corporeality wholly regulated through and through by spirit would begin. Post-historical humanity, which in our view stands close before the door, will again be an unconscious humanity, distinguished from the unhistorical prehistory, however, by this: that it is now the parasite named spirit that guides the body of its bearer as surely and without any exertion of thinking as formerly the center of life, the soul, did.

How long post-historical humanity will still continue to exist, no one knows; only one thing we know with certainty — that it will end at all — and with probability, that by force of rapid degeneration it will happen relatively quickly, because processes of parasitic character are consuming processes, for which sooner or later the "material" runs out. We perceive the portents of this, as concerns man, in a general imbecility of judgment, indeed in an uncannily spreading *narrow-mindedness*. So-called Americanism, for example — from which we can always read off the next world-minute of humanity — shows us a bondage of individual minds to "public opinion," bordering on the idiotic, which in turn is manufactured by the press. The "soul of the people" boils today or does not boil, according to whether this or that stood yesterday in the most-read daily papers, and the creative man, insofar as such still exist, *has* worth or no worth according as this same press trumpets it abroad or "kills it with silence"; and all this happens day after day, without the broader mass of those thus "reared" and "led" (note the double sense in both words) noticing the least of it — thanks, namely, to their narrow-mindedness. But as for the far shrewder makers and directors, their acuteness reaches only as far as the goals of their lust for power and no further, since otherwise they would have to know, and would know, that with the glozing promises of power Satan himself baits men to the accomplishment of deeds whose final outcome is absolute destruction. If the marionettes are blinded out of narrow-mindedness, the wire-pullers are blinded out of evil *will* — a difference significant for the science of character, but essentially no greater than that — between means and end.<sup>38</sup>

<sup>38</sup> On page 767. — *Schiller's* line "Against stupidity the very gods themselves contend in vain" has a deep meaning, in that it calls attention to the absolute incurability — because complete blindness — of stupidity. "Dumm" [stupid] is related to "stumm" [mute]; but "tump" in Middle High German also had the meaning "deaf," which some philologists, in accordance with the rule that "words for the functions of one sense-perception are readily transferred to those of another" (Kluge), associate with the Greek tuphlos, "blind." In any case, the basic meaning of "dumm" is "insensible, blunt," or, as it were, "deaf and blind." If we bear this in mind, a close kinship of meaning emerges with the still sharper term "narrow-mindedness" [Borniertheit] current today. "Bornieren" means to confine, to narrow. As deafness and blindness narrow the field of sensory experience, so narrow-mindedness signifies the being-narrowed of the soul itself, and indeed by force of inherited limits which, according to our findings, were drawn around vitality by the activity of the will. Narrow-mindedness is the organic *effect* of the "evil will" and is therefore worse than the latter. The evil will can in principle be intimidated or broken, and at least in individual cases sometimes be won over; the *unconscious* evil will, however, which is called narrow-mindedness, can just as little be broken or won over as one could transform the blood of its bearer. — Nevertheless, the essential connection between the two, narrow-mindedness and evil will, is rooted more deeply. For, as has been shown, "instinct" must already have gone blind in some respect in order to deliver up the intensity of the drive as "energy" to the will; hence the following sequence closes into a circulus vitiosus: out of the blindness *or* delusion of beholding grows the will; the will narrows vitality; the blind will of narrow-mindedness is the hardest hammer in the hand of the will that, as it were, sees (just as, according to one version of the myth, the blind Hödur unwittingly serves Loki's intention when he throws the sprig of mistletoe that kills Baldur). Again and again has initiatory arbitrary will triumphed with the help of fanaticized masses!

Presumptuous as the designation "world history" for the interlude in question may be, it is unfortunately not entirely without ground. *The* technology that one has in mind today when one speaks of the "wonders of technology" is not essentially older than four generations, and [p. 768] has nonetheless sufficed to wipe from the face of the planet dozens of tribes of primitives, hundreds of plant genera, twice and three times as many animal species on land, in the air, in the water. The day is not far off when all of them will have been exterminated, save such as it has pleased man to breed for purposes of slaughter or of fashion — excepting only the infusoria and bacteria. The universe is somewhat too spacious for this madness of extermination, but the *Earth*, should no "miracle" occur in time, will die of it; and the power that was able to kill off an entire planet would then in truth have furnished<sup>39</sup> a piece of "world history" — — The hour of counteraction was missed, and all of us, who out of passionate love of life must weep over such horror, are "last Mohicans." But whoever among such as we still dares to cherish wishes should wish only one thing: that a humanity capable of accomplishing such infamy should sink, ape itself into brutehood, and perish as swiftly as possible, so that around its weathering and crumbling arsenals of murder — once more burying, unmixing, and renewing itself — the intoxication of the forests may blaze up. —

<sup>39</sup> On page 768. — Whoever has rightly weighed the preceding note understands better the otherwise astonishing *convergence* of all the partial phenomena of the process of destruction in which we now find ourselves. One need only set side by side: the knowingly evil will to exploitation that stands behind the arts of deception of present-day politics; the incomprehensible narrow-mindedness of broad strata, *even* among the educated, who *believe* in the phrase-mongering of a so-called pacifism, in fraternizations of peoples and leagues of nations, while on the right and on the left, on land, on water, and in the air, men "arm" as never before in five thousand years; finally, technology, which places in the hands of the power-holders and deceivers of peoples machines for the extermination of mankind with which even those of the "World War" cannot bear comparison. — Or one may think of the satanism of the hunt, which has succeeded, within the last ten years, in exterminating almost the entire stock of big game of the continent richest in wildlife of all, namely Africa; of the horrifying narrow-mindedness that does not rise up in revolt when a hard-hearted sense of profit sacrifices, year after year, far more than a *hundred* million of the most magnificent birds to — fashion, for the most part amid unimaginable tortures of execution, or slaughters a further hundred million for the cravings of the palate (the massacre of migratory birds in Italy and Egypt); of the soulblunted thoughtlessness that manifests itself, for example, in the force-fattening of geese to death for the sake of producing a diseased but delicious liver, in the atrocities of American poultry-raising, in pigeon-shooting at "fashionable" seaside resorts, and so on and so forth; of the *hardened* zeal for research of a science that distinguishes itself with vivisections and infectings for the enrichment of medicine, with, at times, simply diabolical extirpations in the service of the so-called animal experiment; *and* once again of technology, which, without the slightest evil ulterior intent, again slays hundreds of thousands of birds with its huge lighthouses, or, with the oil-firing of diesel motors, exterminates in legions not only the water-fowl but the fish of the sea as well. These few examples of, so to speak, systematic works of destruction, with or without deliberate purpose, stand to those actually available as the cartridges in a hunter's pocket stand to the munitions depot of an army. But all of them, the named as well as the unnamed, *converge* with regard to their outcome, namely *destruction*. Now, the same convergence exists in every epoch of humanity's history, or at least of Western humanity, and extends to every individual trait of any culture whatsoever. Whoever has grasped this will, for once, be cured of seeking the forces at work "in the consciousness" of men, in their programs and theories; instead he will seek *and* find them solely and alone in what *happens*.

[p. 769]

#### 54. Kapitel — Antiker und neuzeitlicher Forschertyp — Chapter 54 — Ancient and Modern Type of Researcher

Let us bear in mind that present-day natural science proceeds wholly and entirely from the ascertainment of facts and their relations of dependence; then it becomes evident that the object of mechanics is not merely an abstraction in general but actually a fabricated abstraction: the result of transferring the real being of the thinking person onto the durationless streaming of a never-existing actuality of images; and belief in causality appears in the light of a falsification of what is essentially indivisible into a fundamentally enumerable quantity of computational units, for the purpose of assimilating it to what is essentially dividing. — Now, however, the belief in facts insists upon success. Physical science makes possible, as everyone knows, a precalculation of nature and, on the basis of the calculation, its use in the service of countless human purposes. — To within a fraction of a second the astronomer predicts in advance the onset of a lunar eclipse; far beyond the limits of what is sensibly perceptible the physicist measures the quantity of heat that an electric current of any given strength will produce in passing through a wire of known frictional resistance; and with complete certainty the chemist knows beforehand the nature and quantity of the precipitate when he pours a solution of limewater together with sulfuric acid. More than that: mechanistic science has furnished proof that from its knowledge of the "laws of nature" it was able to infer, in accordance with truth: the existence of stars that no eye had yet seen; the chemical constitution, say, of the sun's envelope, which no one has yet reached; the most important properties of still-undiscovered "elements" of matter. As often as a state of affairs actually experienced and exactly recorded ever diverged from the state of affairs one had to expect according to natural law, it could show that a further natural law was in play, whose connection with what was already known made the [p. 770] divergence necessary. We recall the discovery and calculation of the velocity of propagation of light from the oppositely equal deviation of the occurrence of the eclipses of Jupiter (by its satellites) in opposition and in conjunction from what was correctly calculated for the quadrature, by Römer, or from the "aberration" of near-zenith fixed stars, by Bradley, and quite especially Robert Mayer's ingenious computation of the "mechanical equivalent of heat" from the difference between the specific heat of air at constant pressure and at constant volume. It has, finally, in many cases been able to deduce in advance from its principles, or at least immediately to explain, the possibility of experiences as bewilderingly improbable as, say, "Pascal's paradox" or the mutual self-extinction of meeting rays, and has confirmed its assertions a thousandfold by experiments that far outshine the acuteness of the greatest thinkers. The world of machines made by man seems, above all, to furnish the experimentum crucis for the unrestricted truth of all the formulas that were obtained on the presupposition of belief in the actuality of things and on the ground of the conviction of the I-independent validity of the "laws of nature."

We could, against this, first of all furnish proof that the assumption of an actuality of what the mathematical and phoronomic concepts mean suffers shipwreck on self-contradictions. If, for example, what we count is to be something purely actual, then there would have to exist in actuality countable units, and that is to say: strictly individuated and completely congruent portions of appearance; otherwise we would have counted only noumena, not phainomena. But the very possibility of appearing already excludes the being-for-itself of that which appears, because through its appearing it enters into connection with the impressionability of the beholder. The individuation required for the purpose of realizing the concept of unity would have as its consequence the immediate incapacity of the individuated thing to appear! If accordingly there is no such thing at all as one appearance beside a second appearance (as there certainly is one thing beside a second thing), then let us likewise deduce from this why there would not be two congruent appearances even if we were to consider their spatial multiplicity from the standpoint of a countable quantity. If the supposed individual appearance, together with its momentary beholder, indisputably belongs to the [p. 771] self-transforming nexus of everything that appears, then it can only be understood as the momentarily illumined *place* of the appearing All. If it shifts to another place, then it too has itself become another, because it has thereby infallibly entered into a new nexus of appearances; just as, conversely, every place in space, insofar as it is an appearing place, or, if one prefers, a place of sojourn of appearance, possesses a specific characteristic that distinguishes it from every other place of appearance. The assumption of the congruence of two appearances in space is forbidden by the incongruence of the places of appearance. Made evident to the senses: the same jug becomes a component of a different image with every change of its place, and is therefore no longer "the same." But every temporal locus of the world-picture, too, is just as unrepeatably unique as every spatial locus in it. The thing that remains one and the same in time and space, and is therefore of course countable, whether invisible atom or corporeal sense-thing, is not so much more actual as rather a bearer of appearance merely postulated by spirit, and the first precondition of every physical mode of consideration — the countability of the objects of investigation — cannot come to fulfillment in the actuality of images.

Objections of the same kind arise against the actuality of all phoronomic noumena. They all branch off from the root concept of rectilinear uniform motion.
