At the beginning stands the symbol, and, for the thinking guided by it, the symbolic name; there follows the person, and, for the thinker already believing in man, that which first separates personhood from the impersonal for him: the faculty of judgement, or, for him, spirit; at the end stands a double structure at odds with itself: the concept, screwed up to the self-sovereignty of the so-called Idea, and the object, comporting itself no less self-sovereignly; but in the middle — unbeknownst to the thinkers — stands not, say, the central piece of the famous Chimaera, but the will, preparing itself for real self-sovereignty.

Just as the Greeks, in accordance with the distinguishing bent of the Western spirit to conceive actuality in its entirety out of the actuality of the person, set up hardly-to-be-surpassed model images for the interpenetration of the All with the form of man, so, correspondingly, they were at the outset compelled to understand humanity from the standpoint of its elementary character, and to expand personhood into all-nature by just as much as they narrowed all-nature through personification. In this way they became creators of human types which, in later times, are personified properties, and, in ancient and earliest times, symbols interpreted in person-like fashion. Their psychology therefore, at that time, bore the colours of their cosmology more richly than the latter bore the colour of their psychology.

If, for this reason alone, we may expect of their pathbreakers a manner of thinking as it were akin to nature, there is now added to this the fact that their first and mightiest upswing falls into an epoch of the deepest religious upheaval. The passionate final struggle that the Greek soul, around the seventh to fifth centuries, fights out with its myth already takes place entirely on the plane of consciousness, and gives rise to an uprising of spirits which, kindled as it were by the spraying fire-rain of symbolic knowledge, seeks to hold back the conflagration that threatens, once more before its extinction, to tear rational composure into the frenzy of Dionysian magic. Now miracle-men and "sages," now [p. 852] solitary lordly natures, now founders of sects and prophets, its bearers contend for the realm of spirit with borrowed or plundered weapons of life, just as the motherless father's-daughter Athena wields the terrifying Gorgon's head — thereby preparing, but not yet itself embodying, the type of the "philosopher." If anywhere, it is here that we shall find the essence of life mirrored, provided only that we always keep present to ourselves: first, that every finding must show partisan additions stemming from its discoverer's will to ma⦅ster life⦆; and second, that its true meaning becomes clear less from the meaning-content of the formulas than from the sensuous colouring in which the begetting "intuition" betrays itself. Only he who misconstrues the creations of these men as proper "systems" can be astonished that they, for example, feel no scruple in at once repopulating with hosts of demons the very same nature that they had just explained physically. Systems in the narrower sense arise only where the movement of thought, instead of drawing immediately from language, takes place rather by means of an already fixed stock of philosophical concepts. The condition of those who first won such concepts in struggle with the life of language is wholly different from the attitude of the descendants who let the object of investigation be prescribed to them by ready-made technical concepts. The pre-Socratics seem to us distinguished not by greater acuteness, but by a far greater closeness to life. For the rest, we are not concerned here with the persons, but solely with the findings, namely for the testing of their content of enduring science concerning the nature of life.

A reservation, finally, should not be passed over in silence. If, for the thinkers and discoverers who inaugurate the intellectual history of the West, we do not wish to confine ourselves to a mere reproduction of the scattered fragments that have come down to us from them, but attempt, drawing also on their effects upon later seekers of truth in antiquity, to offer images of their doctrines, then we must remain aware that such images stand, at best, in the same relation to the historical state of affairs as reconstructions or completions of the ruins of the palace of Artaxerxes at Susa stand to that palace. Similar to architectural completions, there are as many philosophical completions as there are completers, and, as there, so here it is understood that the reconstructed images certainly resemble the original works in some particulars, but not in all. Which completion has succeeded better, which worse, can always [p. 853] be decided only approximately, never with certainty. This holds, admittedly, less of the Eleatics, who, as long since discussed, now remain out of play, but to a high degree of the ⦅two⦆ great figures with whom we open the series: of Heraclitus and Protagoras. Heraclitus. — The Eleatics discovered being; Heraclitus discovered actuality, and found for his discovery the valid formula of the Pantarhei [panta rhei, "everything flows"]. The former distrusted the senses because they show movement; he distrusted the senses because they show us things contrary to constancy. The Eleatics, in other words, struck out beholding for the sake of apprehension, and de-actualized temporality; Heraclitus disempowers apprehension in favour of beholding, by withdrawing even being itself into the stream of a happening that never is. All later thrusts of development in the investigation of the "ontological" problem sprang from a renewed reflection, time and again, on the world-historical opposition of Eleaticism and Heraclitism, for which, to this day, no thinker has found a reconciliation! (We know the reason: because there is none!)

Even if the denial of the being of the world did not already presuppose that mere understanding is unfit for genuine formation of knowledge, there would nevertheless not be the slightest doubt that Heraclitus disputed the adequacy of concepts to actuality on the grounds of the indivisibility of that in which alone he sees the truly actual. With full consciousness of its scope, he maintains the assertion of the illusoriness of conceptual contents, and undertakes to demonstrate it from the irrationality of the course of the world beyond man. "Combinations arise: whole and not-whole, concordant and different, accords and dissonances: out of all things one, and out of one all things." "God is day and night, winter and summer, war and peace, satiety and hunger." "Time is a child playing, moving pieces on a board: a child is king."

But his incorruptible clairvoyance sees through, no less, the delusion of freedom of determination in the positing of ends, strikes with tones of tragic scorn the meaninglessness of all purposes and values, and replaces all the poetizing and striving of men with a compelled state of being driven. [p. 854] "They are born in order to live and to fall prey to death... and they leave behind children, that they too may fall prey to death." "All creatures graze under God's whip-stroke." "Man's character is his daemon." "Good and bad are the same." "To God all things are beautiful and good and right; only men suppose that one thing is right, another wrong."

If out of the coupling of such revelations with the poverty of soul of later descendants there emerged the bastard of a "dialectical method" that — a whimsical caricature of scholasticism — undertook with earnest circumstantiality to teach a flux of concepts, it may suffice to recall that our thinker held, quite to the contrary, the conviction of the unalterable *rigidity* of the concept, precisely in order to demonstrate its incapacity to take in the stream of temporality. Nothing could have been further from him than the absurdity already imputed to him by Aristotle, that the concept of day passes over into that of night, the concept of the whole into that of the part; for from the impossibility of this there grew in him, rather, the certainty that actuality does not fall apart into compartments of that kind. The flux of happening refutes for him the dividing and distinguishing line which it is the whole business of the understanding to draw. In contrast to all the guild philosophers, it is precisely the world of objects that bears for him the stamp of deceptive semblance, because it is precisely for the sake of its conceptuality that it fails to show what only mythical thinking had unconsciously been able to mirror: the boundless *mutability*. This constitutes the sensible mark of the pantarhei. "The cold grows warm, the warm cold, the moist dry, the parched moist." "Life and death, waking and sleeping, youth and age are with us one and the same: for this, when it turns about, is that, and that, when it turns about, is this."

Heraclitus, however, does not stop short at propositions of this kind which, despite their profundity, seem to culminate merely in the abrogation of truths of reason, and which would in themselves still leave us in doubt whether their occasioning ground is to be sought more in illumined lived experience or more in the contesting of the understanding's metaphysical transgressions of its bounds. He also completes, affirmatively, his image of the stream of happening, by moving us at a stroke to the outermost limit that an inwardness "hearkening" to the eternal onward-flowing is granted to reach. He discovers [p. 855] rhythm within the pantarhei and opens up what, without itself being law, first makes every law-giving mode of apprehension possible at all: polarity in the alternation of images. The All does not so much flow as pulse, and the semblance of a standing being stems — analogous to the "stationary equilibrium" of mechanics — from a countervailing alternating course, whereby it is unceasingly on the "way up" as much as on the "way down." If one regards this double movement from the standpoint of the opposition of the poles, it appears — comparable to the warring Dioscuri — under the image of eternal discord; if, on the other hand, one regards it from the standpoint of the polarity of all opposites, then — comparable to the allied Dioscuri — under the image of eternal harmony. One can perhaps illuminate the extra-rational place of origin of the thought of polarity no more sharply than by pointing out that, accordingly, the Heraclitean "strife" and the Heraclitean "concord" are one and the same! Just as the circuit of the antique racecourse's two-horse team requires, besides the driving, also the reining charioteer, so the pendulum-course of world-happening requires, if it is to be preserved from real downfall through rigidification in being, the concordance of an unceasingly dissolving process with an unceasingly gathering one, or the ever self-renewing tension of the poles. It is not the vaunted sameness and equality but the gripping strife of opposites that reveals the restlessly pulsing soul: this is a key to Heraclitus's ambiguous riddling word, that invisible harmony is stronger than visible. But because everything not only returns to whence it went out — day into night, wakefulness into sleep, life into death — but will also break forth again to where it sank back — out of night the day, out of sleep waking, out of death life — the menacingly inescapable vortex submerges into the moon-like, soothing semblance of that primordial necessity of fate which, not by chance, is in the wonderful language of the Greeks without exception of feminine gender — Heimarmene, Dike, Ananke — and of which one would scarcely gain deeper knowledge than Heraclitus betrays when he grasps her binding loosing and loosing binding in the singing simile of the palintropos harmonie of the bow as well as the lyre. — It now suffices, however, to keep present to mind the full sense of what we have so far declared of Heraclitean knowledge, in order to grasp, even without his explanations to that effect, that he climbed the uppermost summit [p. 856] of that panzoism which forms the distinguishing mark of the pre-Socratics (more precisely of the pre-Sophists). A ceaselessly self-renewing actuality must be alive through and through, and, so to speak, only the visible expression of a ceaselessly pulsating essence. Everything lives: stone, water, air and ether; the living lives, and the dead lives too; the sense-things that assert themselves in time are nothing but seemingly stable transitional forms of streams of life flooding against one another. And as if that were not enough, he articulates the poles according to the cosmic sense of this life and anticipates a truth that only begins to shine since the Renaissance and celebrates its irresistible breakthrough in Nietzsche's "Birth of Tragedy": the truth that want is fortification, whereas the highest fulfilment of life is release. "Want," says an ancient author, "is according to him the formation of the world, whereas the world-conflagration is superabundance." Death becomes liberation, and the individual being is merely a barrier to life! In this way there separates off, as a phase of want, the animal and always merely self-living actuality from the elemental actuality as the phase of plenitude. If we finally equate the latter with the soul, then we also know what such propositions — commonly misconstrued in a moral sense — mean, according to which the animal lusts endanger the soul and, as it were, drown it. Sleep as a form of life. — "Even the sleeping... work together at what happens in the world." Death as a form of life. — "But now Hades and Dionysos, in whose honour they rave and celebrate festivals, are one and the same." — "Immortals are mortal, mortals immortal: the ones live the others' death and die the others' life." Endangerment of the soul through animal lusts. — "For souls it is joy or death to become moist: we live on in their death, they live on in our death." — "It is hard to fight with lust; for what it wants is bought at the price of the soul." Reciprocity of transformation. — "For the soul it is death to become water; for water it is death to become earth; out of earth water arises again, out of water soul." — "Fire lives on in the death of air, air lives on in the death of fire; water lives on in the death of earth, earth in that of water."

One could not misjudge a Heraclitus more badly than by objecting to him that he too, after all, had to set up conceptual oppositions of this kind, such as death and life, water and soul, in order [p. 857] to clothe his doctrine of polarities in graspable words. In truth his abstracta are no more than signposts toward something that is, in and for itself, merely to be lived through, and hence are not rational concepts at all but genuinely symbolic ones. It attests to the strictest consistency when he expressly rejects rational inquiry and seeks the source of all discovering knowledge not in the understanding but in certain states of the soul, whose fluctuating designation — "faith," "hope," "enthusiasm" — no doubt deliberately evades conceptual determinacy. Among the pre-Socratics Heraclitus was the sole conscious symbolist, and in the service of pre-rational thinking he developed the teaching-form of the allusive aphorism, or the "Delphic style." "The lord whose is the oracle at Delphi neither declares nor conceals, but gives a sign." "He who does not hope will not find the unhoped-for; for it is unsearchable and inaccessible." "Unbelief is the reason why the divine for the most part withdraws from knowledge." "Much learning does not teach understanding." "Pythagoras, son of Mnesarchus, pursued inquiry beyond all other men, and, singling these writings out, made himself a wisdom of his own: much learning, artful knavery."

No scientist, but the symbolist certainly, can make sayings like the following his own: "Human nature has no understanding (gnomai), but the divine has." Or: "Of as many men's discourses as I have heard, none arrives at the recognition that wisdom is set apart from all."

And so there are two primordial symbolic runes with which he undertakes to designate the substance of the world: the circle and the fire. The circle, as Rota and Swastika permeating the world-conception of the whole Pelasgian humanity, carries over into the more general language of symbols the ineradicable cult of that primal fire which reaches from the magism of flame-worship, by way of the sacred Vesta-fire of the Romans, down to the "eternal lamp" of Catholic crypts. "On the circumference of the circle beginning and end coincide": happening is eternal circling, each moment as much a causeless end as a creative new beginning, the boundlessly self-living blaze, out of itself, of the flame that inwardizes itself and unfetters itself. Let us close our attempt at unfolding [p. 858] the most knowing metaphysics there has yet been with two Delphic sayings of Heraclitus whose elementally unpitying metallic ring has scarcely its equal in the history of thought. "The Sibyl, thrusting forth from raving mouth harsh, unadorned, unanointed sounds, penetrates with her voice a thousand years through the inspiration of the god." "This cosmos, one and the same for all beings, was made by neither god nor man, but it was and is and shall be without end an ever-living fire, now kindling, now going out."

Were what has been developed here the whole content of his teaching, we should have in him to venerate the sole wholly unalloyed investigator of elemental life, whom the depth of his beholding participation in it preserved from every "spiritualization" of the cosmos. But, as though the unveiling itself had called down the curse, his clearest disclosure of the "ever-living fire" is also attended by his murkiest aberration. For it is not the Dodonaean Zeus-Acheloos, the mantic voice out of the midst of the eternal circling, but the Olympian Zeus-Helios, the usurper of the throne and titantoppling "orderer" of the world, who signifies for him the sense of this fire, the heart of all wisdom, the soul of the soul! At the torch-race to Eleusis the mystagogue plunged a firebrand into the sea as a sign of the marriage of the ethereal element with the hylic. Heraclitus, the teacher of the flowing of the world, imagines, in an incomprehensible blindness, the flowing-moist to be at enmity with the flaming-dry, rejects the orgies, reviles the entheoi, scourges the poets, and turns toward the parching brightness of the logos; for which it deservedly befell him that the dreariest Protestants of antiquity, the Stoics, plaited precisely out of his sentences the whip with which to drive the pagan soul through the Caudine yoke of an Asiatic "conscience"! He, the symbolist, who knew and declared that wisdom is divine and set apart from all, but reason human and common to all, nonetheless calls thinking the "most excellent property," infects experiencing life with a "self-augmenting" intelligibility, confounds the glowing soul of the world with an "all-governing" spirit of the world, narrows the mystery of Ananke down to a consciousness-accessible "law" (nomos), and paves, without as yet wishing it, the road for those who would afterward disguise the "flamma non urens" of spiritual light in the veil of Maya of images. This was [p. 859] the inner discord that makes Heraclitus's creative "war" shimmer in equivocal colours and that at times shatters his language in the violent thrusts of an underground hatred; hence it was not without reason that the clairvoyance of the ancients wove a dark crown of rays around the austere figure of their greatest thinker — Protagoras. — As Heraclitus *recognized* the counter-pole of the beholding pole within happening, so at least Empedocles and Democritus came closer to ascertaining essential features of beholding itself: the former with the doctrine — to be touched on only later — of the substantial identity of beholding and happening; the latter through the addition that there are corporeal replicas (eidola) of the images, out of whose contact with the organs of the soul intuition as well as knowledge is generated. — Considered according to their position in the history of philosophical problems, both theories are immature preliminary attempts at an interpretation of the process of perception; tested, on the other hand, for their motivating impulses, they radiate, diverging from one another, jointly from the feeling for the fundamental importance of a lived experience through which inwardness enters into real connection with what lies outside it. This, however, had already been disclosed before Democritus, with his genuine and proper doctrine of perception, by the highly significant *Protagoras*, whom only his scepticism could prevent from making a psychological discovery of the greatest consequence. Directed in fact at the sensible experience upon which perception depends (and inevitably, to be sure, confounding this with the act of perceiving), he finds, namely, that it is an undergoing (paschein) of the ceaselessly working happening. Accordingly, not only the aisthesis changes from moment to moment, but, as first generating itself along with it, the aistheton as well. By virtue of the inner actuality of beholding — which is a deed-free state of undergoing or falling-to — the soul enters into intercourse with the *outer* actuality of happening, and the child of the two of them together is, first of all, the appearance of the world.<sup>16</sup>

<sup>16</sup> On page 859. — Although the roughly dozen sentences handed down from Protagoras include the famous saying of man as the measure of all things, "of the things that are, that they are, and of the things that are not, that they are not," our knowledge of his teachings nevertheless rests, even more than in the case of Heraclitus (whose surviving fragments do at least exceed the number 100), on the reports and reconstructions of later thinkers, and above all on Plato's dialogues "Protagoras" and "Theaetetus." How far the figure drawn by Plato (even after removing the features invented to demonstrate the superiority of Socrates) corresponds to the original, opinions may differ. What stands fast, in any case, is that the views existed with whose criticism the two dialogues are concerned, and it is beyond doubt that they at least *tie back* to Protagoras. Among the Sophists, the two most significant stand out as Gorgias and Protagoras. That Gorgias is directly indebted to Eleaticism (whose logic he uses in order to refute Eleatic ontology) emerges from the report of Sextus Empiricus on the principal content of his treatise "On Nature, or On Not-Being." But that Protagoras must have learned, at least mediately, from Heraclitus is no less inescapable in view of the "Theaetetus"; for which the following passage may be recalled. After the, in a sense, sensualist epistemology of Protagoras, according to which perception and knowledge coincide, has already been fairly thoroughly combed through, Socrates continues: "So one must approach this question more closely, as the argument on Protagoras's behalf required, and we must examine this moving being, as though knocking on a vessel, to see whether it is sound or cracked: not a few are those for whom it has become the object of no small contest"; to which Theodorus replies: "Far from being of small significance, it is even gaining tremendously in scope throughout all Ionia! Indeed, the *friends* of Heraclitus open the round-dance for this thesis with great emphasis" (after the rendering of Preisendanz)! Here follows, then, the treatment of the "doctrine of motion," understandably, in order to reduce "the friends of Heraclitus" ad absurdum!

It has occasioned surprise that, if not Protagoras himself then at any rate his pupils, demanded an outer counterpart even for the feelings and passions that may perchance flood through the beholder in the moment of beholding, and thereby included, among other things, in the aistheton what in modern parlance would be called something like the "world's being coloured by the mood of the observer." Yet, were [p. 860] any doubt still able to persist about the sense of the Protagorean opinion, it would be resolved precisely by the supplementary thesis of the estranging power of emotion as well. Human lived experience is, after all, always also feeling lived experience, and whoever therefore seriously asserts a counterpart of lived experience may least of all wish to exempt from it what is nowadays called its feeling-tone! — If Heraclitus had known that in sleep everyone beholds a particular cosmos, then according to Protagoras the very same holds also for the equally undergone world of images of the waking man! Instead, however, of going on to conclude that beholding and the act of judgement on the one side, and the beholdable image and the thinkable thing on the other, are accordingly distinct from one another in origin and content, Protagoras, by throwing both together, soars up to the skeptical view of a lawless particularity attaching rather to the object of thought, and thereby betrays to us that the driving force of even his first step must be set down as the wish to abolish the universal validity of judgement.

We have here to do with one of those curious derailments in the history of thought which, although missing the truth as it were only by a hair's breadth, are nonetheless, in accordance with a directional error of the guiding intention, doomed to end in glaring self-contradictions. Aiming apparently at a de-actualization of objects, but in fact at a sub*jectivization* of *knowledge*, Protagoras avails himself of the ingenious artifice of devaluing the act of judgement by pointing to the incompatibility of the ever-general meaning-content of all thing-concepts with the flowing mutability of the sensed, which they purport to grasp. There is no proposition simply and unconditionally valid; for its original object, the thing to be perceived, does not so much have "existence" as it rather *becomes* continually through the interaction of two processes, of which the one runs its course in the one who experiences, the other outside, and it is therefore what it is only *for* the one who experiences and, strictly taken, only in the generating moment. Thought, however, now with reference to him, the one who experiences, it remains, precisely for this reason, wholly unassailable: (individual) man is the measure of all things! — He did not suspect how swiftly and thoroughly the Platonic Socrates would refute him with the mere counter-objection that this proposition itself could then lay no claim to truth (just as little, incidentally, could one merely mean it; for what would then be asserted is — meaning itself!). "He concedes," [p. 861] Plato makes Socrates say in the Theaetetus, "that the opinion of his opponents, who call his view false, is correct, if he grants that all men mean what is true... And thus he would be conceding the incorrectness of his own opinion..." — But even Plato, with his lifelong search for the essence of the act of judgement, missed the decisive insight which alone deprives every attempt at subjectivizing truth of its ground: that the surrender of the universal validity of what is known can occur only through the abolition of the actuality of thinking consciousness.

We have taken thought of the skeptical turn only so that it should not appear as though we had misjudged Protagoras's aim and, out of benevolent partiality, improved upon the sense of his teaching. His aistheton is once again a thing, although a mutable thing, attestable only by the individual consciousness. Yet one does not thereby step outside the domain of consciousness, still less oppose the value of mere understanding-knowledge, merely by diminishing the number of bearers of consciousness until in the end only a single one remains; and one thus troubles oneself quite in vain over an essential mark of life! Every consciousness is already consciousness as such, and we cannot judge without thereby entering into relation with a person-independent norm! — Notwithstanding this, the Protagorean turn remains a powerful testimony to the compelling force of beholding. Its aistheton is no "deceptive semblance," for it is lived and undergone! But what is capable of being lived, felt, undergone can at the very least attain a force where it crushes the I of the one who experiences and wrests from the depth of beholding pathein the extra-rational certainty that actuality is only — undergone! Plato. — In the composite redemption-philosophy of the already half-Asiatic Plato, with the division of the world into a phenomenal and a noumenal half accomplished for the first time, there now also emerges, fully realized, the threefoldness — inseparable from it — of spiritual, psychic, and corporeal life. Since, on the conception of antiquity, actuality admits of degree, the phainomena too are actual, but the noumena of a higher degree, and the tripartition of the soul out of participation in both appears at first in the form of a threefold *disposition*: its falling prey to the body, its spiritual dominion over it, and a connecting middle state, whose basis is often called thymos. Only later (especially among the Neoplatonists) does the proper psyche [p. 862] emerge from the thymos, the soma from the downward-drawing half, the nous or logos from the ruling half. To the inner triad there corresponds a cosmic one: the world hypo ten selenen to the body and matter, the topos hyperouranios to the spirit, the selene itself or ouranie ge to the soul suspended midway like it. — Regarded as to its aim, Platonic wisdom is, as Nietzsche rightly recognized, "pre-existent Christianity," and indeed of a consistency in carrying through the thought of flight from actuality and enmity to the senses scarcely to be surpassed. No longer beneath the earthly sun does the colour-magic of this most seductive dialectic that ever there was unfold (and which, for two and a half millennia, anticipated all the fundamental questions of European science!), but beneath the "supracelestial" ray of the god of "separateness." What the voice of his Paraclete proclaims under a thousand images and figures and with a thousand beguiling semblances of proof, it finally issues, after all, into the one and only herald's cry of the approaching turn of mankind: "Earth-spirit, your time is up!" "Those," Plato makes his death-ready Socrates say, "who philosophize rightly are occupied with dying." — This, tempting as it would be, we need not pursue here; but we do wish to examine how Plato lays out his three kinds of psychic disposition and what is to be gained from this for insight into the soul's gift of beholding.

There we find at once confirmed, through the most knowing connoisseur of all the courses of thought, that the following belong inseparably together: noumena, Eleatic being, and the spirit's power; phainomena, Heraclitean pantarhei, and the spirit's *powerless*ness! The world of the senses coincides with the world of ceaseless flowing, or genesis, and the soul becomes aware of this insofar as it succumbs to the melting pull or dazing vortex of sweet desires and wild affects. The corporeality that is to be experienced through the senses is also the seat of the epithymiai, to which mankind appears bound, as it were in defiance of precept, through the reflection-clouding efficacy of its epithymetikon. The body prepares countless hindrances for us: "it fills us with love-affairs, with desires and fears and all manner of phantoms." It is not for us to take issue with the priest-philosopher for seeing in the feelings disturbances and aberrations; we have only to hold fast to this, that the world of the ceaselessly changing phainomena is not grasped but lived and undergone, under surrender of the spirit that manifests itself only in grasping. Plato [p. 863] never wearies of painting, with beguiling similes, the "fall" of the soul into the realm of fleeing semblances. Only when the soul's steed has lost its wings of noesis does it plunge, having become unfree, out of the ether of "being" eternity down into the restless revolution of the region of images and deceptive shadows, now entangled with the bodyseduced senses and forthwith forged into the "fearful prison" of belief in "that which never *comports itself* in the same way." It stands fast "that every pleasure and every pain has, as it were, a nail, and nails the soul to the body," bringing it about thereby "that she now supposes to be true whatever the body tells her" (Phaedo). — A doctrine of so unconditionally decided a turning-away from the worldly could, naturally, pay heed to the process of drive-borne, sensuous experience only so far as seemed necessary to illuminate its perniciousness; whence it was a lamentable consequence that mankind has, down to this day, never again got hold of the secret of the senses, and was in the end persuaded to exchange it instead for that experience-cult which comports itself "sensualistically," whose object is merely the caput mortuum of the senseworld after the liquefaction accomplished by the Platonic Socrates! For a Plato the senses were ensouled and capable of lived experience, though he might a hundred times lament the soul for the sake of its being sensualized; the modern-day "empiricist," by contrast, no longer knows any experiencing corporeality, and believes he instructs us more soundly when he recounts the labours of Hercules which the senses perform in the service of calculating understanding. — Equally thoroughgoing and consistent are Plato's disclosures about the thinking part of the soul, the logistikon, and its activity of noesis or phronesis, or, in short, of consciousness. If it was multiplicity and flux that we experienced when body-fettered and with enfeebled reflection, then it is unalterable "being" (ousia, to ontos on) and spaceless "now" (to esti) that we apprehend self-actively. The soul thinks in accordance with reason and grasps what is true when "it is, as far as possible, independent, in and for itself, bidding the body farewell and, without touching it, yearns after that which is" (Phaedo). — But what, then, would properly remain to it itself — to the psyche, that is, in the narrower sense, which is neither the nous nor the soma, and which, mediating between the two and drawn by both, seems constantly on the point of coming apart into opposing halves?

We should hope in vain to fathom its essence even if we gathered together all the passages Plato has set down concerning it. It lies neither [p. 864] in the divided task of the morally disposed thymoeides, nor does the genuinely logocentric sleight-of-hand help us to it, according to which it would consist in the mediation of the moving impulse from the active spirit onto an otherwise dead matter. For this stands to reason in advance: just as certainly as, for the confessor of extraworldly separateness, the world of the senses is the place of becoming and passing away, just as certainly does he contest its aliveness. In order that his most actual actuality should also comprise life, he must, willy-nilly, resolve to think the perceivable nature of life — its coming and going, growing and waning, blossoming and withering — as stemming from being, notwithstanding the cyclopean contradiction that he thereby makes, of all things, the suffering-less and motionless ousia the source of his hell of genesis! It is only the everunavoidable evasion of embarrassment common to absolutely all falsifiers of life, when Plato bestows on the soul the aeikineton, according to which it is her destiny to be the one who first carries the abominable element of motion at all into an actuality in which, without her mediation, "the whole edifice of heaven and all becoming whatsoever would collapse and stand still" (Phaedrus)! — We must seek the sense of the soul elsewhere.

There has never yet been a teacher of the logos — and there never will be one — who did not steal the most sparkling stones of the artificial crown with which he crowned the spirit from the ore-veins and treasure-houses of the earth. So too our thinker gains the sole truly fascinating allure for his highly extolled noesis only by means of the most splendid piece of booty from the temple of life, namely by allotting the gift of beholding to the faculty of discriminating reflection. To be sure, even a Plato remains far too much a Greek to venture so much as to intimate the madness of a persuasion that would let the very medium of all appearing, space and time, be generated by the understanding, and we must search a good two millennia further on to come upon the first traces of this worst blindness of spiritual arrogance. Rather, space, matter, and being-lacking actuality still essentially fall together for him into one. Yet he did also lend a hand toward that, through a raid now conceived, indeed, quite differently.

He knows, with a clarity never afterward surpassed, that his imperishable ov [on] is nothing other than the meaning-content of concepts, and he consistently shows us the way to the "eternal" in the [p. 865] development of a dialectic whose task is to ascertain the "Ideas," with whose help all reflection upon being proceeds. Yet instead of an Aristotelian or Kantian table of the stem-concepts, he thereby bestows on us something fundamentally different! For, pausing at a certain point in its efforts of dissection, the soul *recollects* (anamnesis) the primal images

(katoptetai) suddenly (exaiphnes), the corporeal

barriers, piercing through them, the unchangeably being essence! If ever, then it is for the sake of this chess-move of falsification that one has the right to call Plato a "genius"; for beyond doubt it, and it alone, lent his doctrine of Ideas the magic shimmer with which it ever anew lures away, precisely the enthusiasts and poets, out of the "welling, swelling night" of the cosmic semblances! The dividing and cleaving stride of the image-destroying urge to judgement, notwithstanding that corporeality as well as sense-appearance fall victim to it, culminates suddenly in the epopteia of the self-divested mystic who, seized by the recollection-awakening Eros, beholds primal images of which the sensible object is the imperfect copy (mimesis)! The pious deception is completed by the depiction of a creative achievement of this beholding deed of spirit, through the explanation of the world's coming-into-being from the demiurge's gazing upon the eternal paradigms (Timaeus)!

It does not help that Plato, in preparing the "transcendental synthesis," coins the concept of "synopsis" in order to throw a bridge from the thinking of concepts to the beholding of images: even one who should outdo him a hundredfold in acuity and artfulness of dialectic could never prove to us that the act of conceiving is a lived experience of beholding, the sense of the concept an image, and the activity of abstracting a form of recollecting. Anamnesis, Eros and Opsis are as incompatible with spirit as, say, moisture, colour, and weight are with the figures of geometry! Without reservation, on the other hand, we may grant that Plato knew the heart-point of all lived experience and was in truth the great erotic that he depicts his Socrates as being: he had, indeed, in order to reach his goal of devaluing the body, to transplant into the being spirit what in reality belongs, and belongs alone, to the perishable soul! Thus his consummately logocentric doctrine bears, very much against its own will, the strongest testimony to the constitution of the soul; and we may [p. 866] regard it as vouched for through him: the body has drives and sensations, the soul beholds, the spirit apprehends. The former two are pathic or undergoing, and only the latter is active or spontaneous. Aristotle. — If Heraclitus was the greatest discoverer among the Greeks, Plato their greatest apocalyptist, then Aristotle is their greatest professor. Here it proves the case that even one who masters no longer lived experiences but only concepts — though with the whole energy of a comprehensive understanding — can arrive at new turns of thought. For our purpose, however, at most incidentally come into consideration: his peculiar achievement in logic, his overemphasis on the final cause, and his famous hybrid concept of entelechy; whereas in the first rank stand three individual findings, of which at least two, thought through to the end, would shatter his entire system. First, however, a few words must be said about this system as a whole.

The duality of a stronger actuality of being and a weaker one of happening is taken over from Plato without qualification, partly with Platonic nomenclature. Behind the lower actuality of the hyle, the apeiron and the aoriston, there opens up the higher actuality of the Logos, Eidos, the morphe, and even the paradeigmata. Exactly as with Plato, stripped of its power to form, the maternal Hyle sinks before the supposedly form-bestowing ousia down into the shadow-realm of non-being, or rather of not-yet-being, of being only "potentially." Still, Aristotle has thrown a sharper light on the fact that the "flight of appearances" merely mirrors the incapacity of the understanding to conceive the apeiron of the continuous. The Hyle lacks the plenitude of actual being inasmuch as it wholly withdraws from conceptual determinability: a turn in which one has to see the Greek conclusion of the Eleatic crisis of thought.

Already in his ontology more intent on linking than on separating the powers that differ in essence, and hoping precisely thereby to improve upon Plato, Aristotle now lays the whole weight on the supposed impulse to motion which the hylically boundless is thought to receive from formally-being being, and believes he already has, in the world of sensible kinesis and metabole, a middle term out of "form" and "matter," energeia and apeiron, hen and polla, according to which the two actualities gain the character of merely two distinct sides of an overarching Physis. All the same, he too does not escape the conceptual compulsion of positing that which gives the impulse [p. 867] as existing independently and for itself: as goes without saying, akineton, but, in the character of the end which the whole course of the world is destined to fulfil, a proton kinoun. In this way a remainder is preserved even of Platonic beholding, insofar as happening proceeds not out of causes but rather according to the exemplarity of a telos that simultaneously closes it off. The most important testimony to this is given, with the most daring union of the incompatible, by the almost enthusiastically proclaimed doctrine that the highest bliss of the nous apathes, and hence also of noetic man, consists in the pathos of contemplation, observation, theoria! It stands, however, in the closest connection with the findings shortly to be mentioned, that the perfection of the "theoretical" state requires the gaze of the spirit no longer upon an outside foreign to it, but wholly and solely upon itself. With Aristotle's new coinage of noesis noeseos there thus enters into the history of thought, for the first time, the distinguishing mark of consciousness (I).

In the domain of logic Aristotle is a thorough connoisseur of the principle of identity. Since this grounds the possibility of thinking on the holding-fast to the sameness of sense of a linguistic sound, however often and on whatever occasion it recurs, it must have the power to sharpen the finder's eye for the incomparability of every impression to be experienced with its conceptual meaning-content, and thus for the essential difference of the living from the spiritual as such. Notwithstanding his pantheistic bearing, Aristotle then finds himself driven to two findings which — mutually requiring one another — break through, equally, both the horizon of his predecessors and the frame of his own system.

If, in contrast to the temporally flowing and forever compelled Physis, the Nus is a faculty of self-active accomplishment, then the precondition for its being prompted to any deeds of thinking or willing cannot lie within it. The unmistakable dependence of the spirit's deeds within the organism of man upon impulses of the living body therefore makes necessary the further distinction of the pure nous poietikos from a life-entangled nous pathetikos; whereby the philosopher, in a formulation felicitous also linguistically, ascertains the sense of the personal I, or more precisely the distinguishing psychic constitution of a being whose living scope received, through the spirit's irradiation, the novel orientation toward the midpoint of apprehending consciousness [p. 868] (II). But then the spirit in and for itself (= nous poietikos) can no longer possibly count as the summit and close of that "development" of which, in the Stagirite's opinion, the graded series of individual beings is the bodily appearance. In full contradiction with his idea of an inner-worldly logos, but in equally decided agreement with the correctly inferred freedom-from-undergoing of the logos "in itself," Aristotle therefore lets what is noetic in the strictest sense first join the psychic as such in man's organism from outside (thyrathen)! If this third (III) and greatest finding of the peripatetic school anticipates, on the one hand, the Christian dogma of the extra-worldly God, it prepares, on the other, the counter-thought of the sub-spirituality of the life-process, or, stated with closer reference to our theme and in our own formulation, of the origin of consciousness out of the conflict of two powers, neither of which — whether directly or through subordination to a third principle — could be traced back to the other. Plotinus. — The psychological researches of the Greek late period and of Alexandrianism (in particular the Stoics, Neo-Pythagoreans, and Neoplatonists) stand, in substance, entirely under the sign of the tripartition Nus, Psyche, and Soma, even though, owing to a word-choice that fluctuates considerably and even interchanges the terms, sometimes four, sometimes even five and more essential cores are represented under name. If we strip off all the baroque trimmings and supplement, for each term, the reading of any one school by those compatible readings of the others, we obtain roughly the following determinations of matter: non-being, indeterminacy, steresis, want, formlessness — spatiotemporality, multiplicity, transience, mortality — impurity, badness — femaleness, capacity for conception — sensibility, sensitiveness, drivenness — earthiness and nocturnality; and the following of the Nus: being, determinacy, plenitude, form — eternity, simplicity, changelessness, imperishability, immortality — purity, goodness — maleness, generative power, exemplarity — freedom from undergoing, self-activity — supra-worldliness and kinship with the sun. The soul, on the other hand — mostly, at least, likewise called psyche — is the life-principle sorrowfully set between the two and fought over by both: a moon-like middle world which, in beholding it, passes on the "light" of the spirit to matter, or, having fallen prey to matter, stands in need of "purification" and of [p. 869] "redemption" from the fearful kyklos anagkes. The pull — supposedly upward, but in truth outward — has broken through victoriously along the whole line, and the moral statute, contested seriously by no school, of war against the lusts, is scarcely intensified any further by the flame-thrust advance of Christianity.

However little this age still yields anything creatively new, there nonetheless combine, with the sinking security of the growing Imperium Romanum, the mounting anxieties of soul of dying paganism, so as to set even minds in passionate ferment and to tear the thinkers once more into the nearness of lived experience. The longing for the hopelessly vanishing dominion of the gods brings more sharply to consciousness *what* is going under with it than those could know who, for all their free-thinking, nonetheless stood beneath it, and lets the more illustrious intelligences find, for the first time, words that, as it were, conjure back the consciousness-alien nature of enthusiastic beholding. Plotinus in particular — whom one cannot read without supposing he is writing at this very moment, so full of flickering lights and chasing restlessness are his sentences — never wearies of impressing upon us that the soul attains to beholding only in the moments of being-beside-itself, of that, to be sure, which he too holds to be actuality, the kosmos noetos! Taking up the Platonic doctrine of the world-creating gaze of spirit, he now, however, sharply distinguishes it from the dividing and relating thinking that stands, as it were, midway between unconsciousness and overconsciousness. "If one wishes to attribute a consciousness to nature... one must not ascribe to it such a consciousness... as we do in the case of other things, but it resembles, rather, sleep-consciousness as opposed to waking consciousness. For nature rests, absorbed in the beholding of its own intuition." "Even the animals, indeed, when they beget, are driven by the concepts lying within them, and this is an activity of beholding...: to fill everything with concepts and, if possible, to behold eternally" (Third Ennead, trans. Kiefer). On the other hand, the soul attains to over-being being only when it traverses even the region of reason, "shattering, as it were, the intellect that remains within it" (Sixth Ennead, trans. Müller), in order to become one, in "beholding," with its object. In this way consciousness appears in Plotinus at times quite literally as a phenomenon of disturbance — not, to be sure, as with us, of life, but precisely of spirit and absolute being! Reflection, [p. 870] he holds, only enters into the soul "when it has already fallen into perplexity, when it is filled with care and grows weaker and weaker; for it is a diminution of intelligence to stand in need of the full satisfaction of reflection and deliberation" (Fourth Ennead, after Müller). It is above all to him that there goes back what was later called "intellectual intuition," the pseudo-ecstasy of the spirit-turned Middle Ages, but also, to a great extent, the conceptual language of the Renaissance mystics and the "intuition" still current today.

More important to us at this point is that the world of images, accordingly, cannot in any case be woven out of the content of the faculty of thought alone. Plotinus too must therefore borrow from the soul the creative power with which he wishes to glorify his over-being, over-rational, and supposedly even infinite god. But in wanting to persuade us that what he is not and what he does not have — the world, and consciousness of the world — has broken forth from him raylike, it is precisely the turn that would placate the self-contradiction and explain the impossible that unmasks itself to us: the turn to the image-likeness (eikon) of every deeper stage of realization in relation to the respectively higher one, taken as exemplary, shows that the trick could be brought off only through a complete substitution of a reality of images for the spiritual. Likewise, in the essentially new doctrine of the incorporeality of matter as well — even though it again serves a supra-natural purpose — there simultaneously asserts itself a reversion to the lived experience of beholding, which does indeed truly give us images, and not already, along with them, their corporeality.

Such individually interpretable findings must of course not deceive us into thinking that, taken as a whole, Plotinian wisdom marks the topmost cornice on the Babylonian tower of life-inimical de-worlding, up to which the spiritual aberration of paganism could still climb in its final ascent. As a person, the thinker indeed already belongs entirely to the ascetics, for whom the actuality of the world of appearance is an offense and a stumbling block. When the painter Amelius asks to be allowed to paint his portrait, he refuses — according to the report of Porphyry — with the words: "Is it not enough to bear the shadow-image with which nature has surrounded us? And do you even consider it worth the trouble to leave behind, for future times, a shadow-image of the shadow-image as something worth looking at!" [p. 871] Plutarch. — We conclude our retrospective consideration, tying its end back to its beginning, with an almost complete reproduction of chapters 16 to 18 from the memorable treatise on "The Inscription 'E' at the Temple of Delphi" by the initiate Plutarch, who may recall for us, with the profound splendor of his speech, that the impetus of the whole movement of thought in the Hellenic "age of flowering" was the pre-Socratic problem of the opposition between being and happening, and that the agon of Eleaticism with Heracliteanism, undecided to this day, constitutes the metaphysical content of the entire spiritual history of the West

"If I am now to state my opinion, then this letter denotes neither a number nor a rank nor a connecting word nor any other part of speech, but is rather a self-standing address and greeting to Apollo, which awakens in the soul of the one who utters it, at the same time, a representation of this god's power. Apollo receives each of us who comes to him with the words: Know thyself; a greeting that is certainly no worse than the ordinary 'Chaire,' that is, 'Be greeted' or 'Rejoice.' To this we then answer him with the expression: E i, that is, Thou *art*, and thus offer him the genuine, unfalsified, unique greeting owed to him alone, taken from his existence. For at bottom we can lay no claim to existence at all; rather every mortal nature hovers always between coming-to-be and passing-away, and yields only a phantom, a dark and uncertain opinion of itself. If now one strains one's understanding to grasp it fully and wholly, the same happens to it as to water strongly compressed. For just as the latter, through pressing, trickles away and loses itself entirely, so reflection goes astray when it pursues too clear a conception of some being subject to change, now toward its origin, now toward its passing, without being able to catch hold of anything abiding or truly existing. — Into a river, says Heraclitus, one cannot step twice, and likewise one cannot encounter a mortal being twice in the same state; rather, through the violence of change it is now scattered, now reunited again, now it comes, now it goes away. Therefore nothing that comes into being attains real existence either, but change already begins with the seed, from which first the embryo, then the child, afterward the boy, the youth, the man, the elder, and finally the old man [p. 872] is formed, so that the earlier comings-to-be always perish in those that follow. In truth, it is quite ridiculous that we should still fear death, we who have already died so often and are still dying. Heraclitus says: 'The death of fire is the origin of air, the death of air the origin of water.' But this is perceived far more clearly in man himself. For the man dies when he becomes an old man; the youth dies in the man, the boy in the youth, the child in the boy; yesterday's man has died in today's, and today's dies in tomorrow's. No one remains, no one is a single one, but we become many, since *only* matter drives *round* a single image and slips away again. For how could we, if we always remained the same, now take pleasure in things other than those we did before? How could we love or hate, admire or blame, wholly opposite things? How could we hold other speeches, take on other passions, without at the same time having another shape, form, and disposition? Just as it is impossible to pass into another state without change, so little is he who is changed still the very same. But if he is no longer the same, then he himself *is* no longer either .. What then, now, has real existence? Only the eternal, the uncreated, the imperishable, to which no time can bring about any change. Time is something mobile, which becomes visible only together with moving matter, ever flowing onward and never attaining fixity, as it were a vessel of coming-to-be and passing-away. At least, in the expressions used of it — 'afterward,' 'before,' 'it will be,' 'it has been' — there already lies a confession of the want of existence. For it would indeed be very .. absurd to ascribe existence to that which either has not yet been or has already ceased to be .. Hence one may not say of that which exists that it has been or will be; for these are changes, transitions, and alternations of that which has no enduring existence. But of God one must say: he is; and he is not according to any determinate time, but according to an unmoving, timeless, and unchangeable eternity, in which past, future, and new do not occur at all, which is one alone and *fills* ever-being with a single *now* What is according to such an eternity is really existing, neither past nor future; it has had no beginning and will have no end. Hence we must reverently greet this being either with the expression [p. 873] Thou *art*, or with the one customary among some of the ancients: Thou art *one*. For in the godhead no plurality occurs ..; rather the existent must be only a single one, just as the single one must be existent" (translation after Kaltwasser). Medieval Philosophy. — Under the label of a "Christian philosophy of the Middle Ages" there lies concealed the world-historical process of a gradually accomplished incorporation of the Greek spiritual heritage by oriental dogmas of faith. For a full millennium theoretical reflection no longer produced essentially new disclosures; but, by spinning further, from the motive of grounding a life-hating theology, the errors of the pagans, it unintentionally preserved their truths as well, and in this way carried the tripartite division of inwardness, in changing form, down to the threshold of the modern age. The Pauline trichotomy of the pneumatic, psychic, and somatic man, drawn from the Stoa, forms the most important framework of the inquiry into essence from the oldest Church Fathers down to the latest scholasticism. The scene of thought, to be sure, has been transformed beyond recognition. In place of the ancients' natural guiding concepts such as being, happening, world, matter, body, etc., there are now nothing but delusive constructs of faith such as original sin, penance, damnation, redemption, holiness, the honor of God, the kingdom of the devil, election by grace, prescience, predestination, etc., which the inquiring spirit must torment itself to bring into accord with reason. But what it carries of sense and meaning into such phantasms of faith is Greek wisdom, even if tinged with gloom and, as it were, lit by the flicker of hellfire. The "philosopher" finds himself confronted with the curious task of supplying proofs for propositions whose validity the priest has already decided; and he supplies them, or believes he does, with the help of the concepts of essence available to him from the ancients and by means of the methods of inquiry handed down by them.

If, in view of the logical subtleties in which a thinking almost devoid of actuality alone could excel, one nonetheless wishes to accord scholasticism, in the history of the interpretation of the world, the rank of a distinctive section, then its special character would have to be delimited as follows. Just as it is not questioning reason but a struggling and finally commanding will that determines its course, so the movement of thought runs, now unexpressed, now with clear reflection, [p. 874] toward the attempt to understand the world and the consciousness of the world as an achievement of will, and thus, in opposition to all the schools of paganism, to locate the origin of all knowledge as well in a primordial deed. "If you do not believe, you do not know." From the overnourishment of the inward-directed will, and from it alone, is explained everything that medieval research work bent in the Greek systems, or, if one will, added to them: the reduction of the whole of inwardness, down into receptive beholding itself, to the terms of deed — the consequent doctrine of the origin of the world out of nothing through the bare word of command — the sanctification of personality as the sole possible foundation of commanding and demanding — the now unavoidable anthropocentrism of the spiritual stance (for only human beings are persons) — finally that worst and therefore most enduring delusion of spiritual self-exaltation, according to which even the cosmic course of the world is merely the preparatory school for — "history," that is to say for the register of deeds, not even of mankind, but of the spiritual party of mankind! In the modern delusive notion of boundless "progress" there has only unfolded and become externalized the far more absolute claim of the Christian — reckoning of years! "Faith is perception of the realized will" (Novalis).

But what testifies, as hardly anything else does, to the invincibility of the voice of life is the undeniable circumstance that this thinking, the most estranged from the senses, never dared wholly to disown the power of beholding, and sank back, the longer the more, into a glorification of beholding rapture! Already the fanatic of will Augustine locates "eternal blessedness" in the theorein of divine truth; only a "visio," even if "intellectualis," yet "sine comprehensione," opens the deepest knowledge to Erigena, to the Victorines, to Thomas; a "vis imaginativa," according to Albert, animates sensibility, and only by virtue of "intuition," according to his teaching, does spirit penetrate the actuality no longer demonstrable. Likewise it is experiences of surrender to beholding that ground, for Bonaventure and for St. Bernard, their already mystically tinged belief in a capacity of the soul for deification. — Here, be it noted, we have not been speaking of the Middle Ages but of the philosophy of the Middle Ages, and that means of the philosophy of the monks. The life of the Middle Ages, most strongly and most deeply alive in spirits who wrote not even letters, let alone books, [p. 875] has as yet been uncovered only in the very smallest part (even though it was sensed by the Romantics), and in much of it may well remain forever a riddle to us. Of that, we repeat, we have not treated. The Mysticism of the Renaissance. — The movement of thought of Hellenism ended with the de-actualization of matter, that of the Middle Ages with the de-actualization of its living inwardness Insofar as the falsely so-called Renaissance brought the victory of mechanism (of spirit on the one side, of thing on the other), it was the conclusion of the Middle Ages and by no means, as has been believed, its opposite. Yet just as the entry of the spiritual Orient into the withering paganism of the West was accompanied by convulsions that, in the mirror of retrospection, illuminated the mystery of the senses, so too the entry of the belief in utility — one might call it the material Orient! — into the withering Christianity of the Middle Ages is once again accompanied by convulsions of life, at which, however quickly consuming itself, a high-flaring knowledge of the mystery of the soul is kindled. Not their erring pantheism, to be sure, but rather its inner point of departure really brings some pioneers of the "rebirth" into the neighborhood of the Ionian hylicists, and even enables them to extend the symbolic thinking of the ancients by exploiting a forgotten find of momentous significance. The rediscovery, by Copernicus, of the truth — known in Pythagorean circles — of the earth's motion around the sun was not so much a scientific achievement as the expression of a change of perspective in cosmic lived experience, whose incisive content, because immediately buried over again by Newtonian world-mechanics, has to this day never been appreciated. For with it the karma of the "barbarians," despite roughly a thousand years of bondage under Christianity, broke through the barrier of the karma of antiquity; whereby we have indicated the cause, not indeed of the Baroque, but of that side of it which occupied us in the last chapter, though only as an example of some effects of man's heightened gift of far-beholding. How much else must follow from this, and in fact did follow, shall now be set forth more precisely.<sup>17</sup>

<sup>17</sup> On page 875. — Since three-quarters of this chapter already lay complete in manuscript about twelve years ago, quotations from it were occasionally brought by the author into other writings. The paragraphs now following, from the bottom of page 875 to about the middle of page 878, are reproduced word for word, with a few abridgements, in the first edition of our "Kosmogonischer Eros," which appeared in 192 a, and have also passed unchanged into the reshaped and enlarged 5th edition (Günther 1951) (pp. 119–122).

Greek cosmogony knew Eros as creator of the world; but despite his cosmic nature he remained a Eros of nearness. It does indeed have a deeper sense than present-day astronomy could unriddle [p. 876] when it had the stars nourished by the vapors of the earth; but alongside this it also signifies that relation of nearness which the eye's measure of Hellenic sensibility demands between the heavenly realm and the landscape of the earth Its symbolism, elementary at its core, purchased the charm of architectonic formal definiteness at the price of a narrowing of the soul's circle of vision, which, though it unquestionably first made possible the unique magic of beauty of its human-shaped art, no less *has* hastened the silting-up of the cultic within a now merely logical thinking There is perhaps no more forcefully persuasive testimony to the dependence of the faculty of judgement on the seer's gaze of lived experience than the Copernican rediscovery of the earth's wandering flight! The thought of heliocentrism — which became known to the Greeks early, certainly to Aristarchus, perhaps even already to Philolaus — was for antiquity an improbable "view," which withered away beside the Ptolemaic scheme, because it never underwent the truly vertiginous pathos that alone, as it were, lends the thought a voice and fills a formula seemingly merely astronomical with the significance of the most unprecedented revolution that had until then broken in upon the image of space in the minds of men!

The Greek hylicist stands wide-eyed upon the "well-founded, enduring earth." Grove, cliff, and surf-beaten seacoast ring out together as in an articulated hymenaeus, enclosed and clearly bounded by the radiant bell of the overarching "aether." The flame whirls upward into the more kindred spaces, the falling rain fertilizes the receiving earth, quickening wind, murmuring out of fate-knowing treetops, binds distance to nearness, the above to the below; and the sky with all its stars "grazes its countenance" in the gleam of the waters All things move and wander, announce themselves, unfold and float away, and so it lives, then; drives and desires, longing for satiation or mating, war and fraternization mass the airy, loosen the solid, draw the heavenly fire into the embrace of the marshes, and send the nourishing moisture as mist into the glowing zone of the sun. The belief in universal aliveness, in panmixia, and in unceasing transformation runs through the blood of myth as of the systems of the earliest thinkers. But even though these thinkers raised it beyond the bounds of perception and even taught the cyclical recurrence of polar phases of actuality, one would nonetheless wrongly reconstruct their state of consciousness from that of today [p. 877] if one supposed that they had ever left the geocentric stage.

Opposed to this stood their beholding of space. We are not speaking here of Indian, Chaldean, or even Egyptian space, but solely of Western-antique space. Read it off from myths, symbols, teachings of wisdom, from the Homeric epics, from Aeolic and Pindaric lyric, from the choral songs of the tragedians, from temples and sculptures: it always has the form of the self-enclosing sphere, whose visible half stands, tent-roof-like or dome-like, upon the spread-out plane of the earthly landscape The feeling for life of antiquity is cosmic, but cellular, and takes the macrocosm for an enlarged microcosm. It remains deaf to the discovery of the Aristarchuses, because its space is the macrocosmic cell that holds all happening as the dipping pitcher holds the pour of water, or which places the images of heaven together with the images of earth under the roof of the selfsame house

And now let one try, for a moment, to live one's way into the transformation that must have taken place in the shape of space, in order for Copernican insight to drive apart the Ptolemaic oikos of the universe, and one will understand what it means when we think the capacity for existence of the new coordinate system as grounded, in terms of the science of life, in the secretly already prepared loss of force of the "cultivated" Eros of nearness before the resplendent rising of a "barbarian" Eros of distance. Only the bursting ardor of the soul's pull toward the depth of space shattered the enclosing sphere into pieces and left, of the star-embroidered vault of its visible half, a color-woven backdrop of deceptive perspectives, through which, *reaching* from distances no longer to be grasped by the senses, countless worlds send forth the messenger of light. The brightness even of the bluest day now hangs as a thin veil before the star-heavy chasms of cosmic darkness. The gaze no longer breaks henceforth against the thinly veiled or cloudlessly high "firmament" of the night sky, but plunges into unfathomable shafts, where behind stars ever more distant ones flicker, and even the one glimmering, contourless, in the farthest darkness is never yet the end! Stripped of the protection of its seeming horizons, and resembling a skiff lost upon the ocean, the earth plunges, under the compulsion of an extraterrestrial pull, unstoppably into the bottomless. One must, to be sure, have suffered at least once in one's life the somber wildness and the travailing horror of "Copernican [p. 878] space" — as we the more readily call it, since we too do not hold it to be the final one — in order to hold it beyond doubt certain that it was only then truly discovered, when, once grasped, it at once also possessed the power to seize the minds of thinkers with the violence of a storm and to shake, down to its lowest ground, the foundation upon which the systems of Western wisdom, for all the diversity of their structure, had nonetheless been jointly erected. Then, however, one will not only understand the passionate resistance of the Church, but will also find without difficulty whole series of correlative traits in which this same change of the lived experience of space comes to expression — now in deed, now in creation, now in speech

It is the magic of boundary-dissolving distance that drives the adventurer's urge onto the course of world-circumnavigating Columbian voyages; that sacrifices the antique flatness of the picture to an ever more emphatic perspective; that transforms the inner rooms of baroque palaces, through fantastical wall-painting, as it were into fragrant or draughty landscapes; that, in the panel paintings of the Netherlanders, lets horizon-deep, opened-up expanses of as-though-wandering hills, forests, and clouds swallow up the human groups; that enriches architecture with the romantic problem of those dreamy parks in which one loses oneself with sweet oppression — Many Polynesian peoples give expression to their firm conviction that the sky actually reaches down to the earth at the horizon and thereby holds it enclosed, by calling strangers "Papalangi," that is, "sky-breakers," as ones who had broken in from another world into this one. Now — every "world-view," in the transferred sense, on the basis of Copernican space, differs from every pre-Copernican one no less deeply than the conceptual conception of the horizon does from the sensuous one of those Polynesians! The transformation thus initiated is today so far from concluded that one can still distinguish a pre-Copernican stratum of lived experience from a post-Copernican one. If the world of antiquity was lodged in space as in a vessel, then modern space has penetrated into the world — not, however, as now encompassed by it, but as denying every encompassing. We do not wish at this point to repeat and carry further what we have already set forth concerning the life-conditions of the prevailing intuition of space and the necessity of a further development; instead, however, we shall indicate the three most significant disclosures that biocentric thinking owes to the transformation of [p. 879] the lived experience of space First, however, a remark historical in the narrower sense.

Our account leaves no doubt that, of such a transformation, the discovery of Copernicus signifies for us only the strongest and most tangible sign Just as, notwithstanding it, even today some people go on living in the nearness-emphasizing cosmic space of the Middle Ages (while for others, conversely, Copernican space is already crumbling again), so the decisive change in the intuition of space began long before Copernicus. The, if one may say so, spiritual assimilation of that previously nonexistent "infinity" extends from the beginning of the fifteenth to the end of the seventeenth century and does not coincide without exception with the opinions of those who bore it. Paracelsus, whose coarsely woven autodidacticism still stands with one foot in the Middle Ages, lived from 1493 to 1541, and thus had no knowledge of the work of Copernicus, which, as is well known, appeared only in the year of its creator's death (1543); he nonetheless belongs among those who helped rethink the tectonic universe of Catholicism into an atectonic world-picture. Campanella, on the other hand (1568–1639), a sublime scholar, despite the most exact familiarity with Galileo's researches, takes up, out of Catholicism, a curious intermediate position, in that he indeed acknowledges the circling of the planets around the sun, but at the same time has the sun, together with the planets, circle the earth Yet one would have to cling to wholly external data if one let oneself be deceived, by such retrogressions of thinkers' constructions, about the progress of an inner transformation that had already set in mightily before it had even found a "scientific" expression!

It has long since been established, moreover, that the onset *of* the uprising of spirits, which in Giordano Bruno reaches less a truly consummating than a programmatic high point, is marked, more than a hundred years *before* the appearance of the Copernican work, by the writings of Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), usually called the Cusan This man, the most comprehensive mind of his time, who in an eventful life as a cleric rose to the rank of cardinal, must philosophically be regarded as the one who opened the "Copernican age," and, though more subterraneously than openly, essentially helped determine the subsequent development One cannot recall too often that, on speculative grounds, he did not yet indeed teach heliocentrism, but did teach the axial rotation of the earth, to be thought of as spherical, and [p. 880] the impossibility of a physical center of the world! One could scarcely devise more convincing evidence for the fact that speculation, observation, and calculation depend jointly on changes of vitality, whether gradual or more sudden; since theorein, to be sure, regularly runs ahead of calculating!

The nerve center of the "Renaissance," the notion that has hovered before the mind at that questionable word since Burckhardt, we may unhesitatingly name as a "tendency toward the deification of *proportion*," and its consequences culminate in the mathematical Baroque (or Newtonianism), which, as we heard, overpowers the romantic Baroque by incorporating even "infinity" into the thought of proportion. All the more must we hold fast to the opposition between the vitally conditioned "infinite" and the calculus of infinity, even when in the individual researcher both tendencies cross one another. By tracing the former back to its source, unconcerned with the personalities of its bearers, we bring into view the first of the three aspects for the sake of which the "Renaissance" deserves, at least in some measure, the name of rebirth.

For the Greek — leaving aside the exceptional Greek Heraclitus — the apeiron was the stuff out of which life, whether inherent in it or approaching it from outside, forms the ever-finite shapes; for the mystics of the rebirth, it is precisely form that is the materially limiting thing, which life and soul receive from the boundless! To create means, in antiquity: to form; in the mysticism of the Renaissance: to shatter the barrier of form! In deepest opposition to the whole of antiquity, the weight of the creative powers lies on the scale of boundless infinity The former interprets the happening of the world by analogy with organic happening; the latter interprets organic happening out of the soul-movement of the universe. There, air and fire are elements also of the individual body, because they seem, like it, to strive and aspire; here, the individual body strives and aspires only insofar as it is capable of partaking in the alone truly living streams of the universe. For the Greek even the metals breathe, and the sea arises from the "tears of Kronos"; but for Paracelsus the feverish pulse of the sick man is the symptom of a sidereal storm within, which one masters insofar as one masters the soul of the storm! The Eros of distance has swallowed up the Eros of nearness: no longer is form the source-point of life, but the universal "arcanum"; the essence of the world is no visible stuff but a fluid beyond the senses, which migrates from body to body — [p. 881] the efficacious does not dwell in the here and now, but is an omnia ubique, and its true home the boundless space of the stars. To it, in the most various turns of phrase, a veneration is paid that scarcely falls short of the praise of the godhead According to Campanella, for example, space, without which all physical existence would be uprooted, is an immortal being! — These mystics,<sup>18</sup> far from pursuing mathematical astronomy (and even *when* they do!), are each in his own way astrologers; hence it lay by no means in the nature of the matter that Copernican space later became the playground of mechanics. With this we already touch upon the second disclosure.

<sup>18</sup> On page 881. — We are not aware whether a work already exists on the *epistemological* side of the history of the space and time problem, and especially of the space problem, from the pre-Socratics to the present. It would be an investigation worthy of the greatest historian of the mind! We offer a few sparse data by which at least some main points become visible of the curve that leads from unqualified belief in the actuality of space to the now veiled, now unveiled conviction of the unactuality of space. In the thinking of the Ionian cosmologists, world-substance has in no way yet been separated from space, nor space from world-substance, and the whole is at the same time something divine (to theion).
