This holds of the Apeiron of Anaximander, of the air-stuff of Anaximenes, of the sphere-shaped deity of Xenophanes; it holds all the more of the Pantarhei of Heraclitus. The attack on the actuality of space is consistently opened by Eleaticism: the Parmenidean not-being is, among other things, space as such. What is thereby disputed is not the actuality of space, but rather the actuality of the intervals, or of the void. The later so-called "homoeomeries" of Anaxagoras, and fully the Democritean atomism, mediate: the empty space too is now once again a component of actuality, but in the form of a being — one might almost say a co-being — not-being. This "den" (something), Aristotle therefore says, is for the atomists no better than the "meden" (nothing)! Beyond this stage of the actuality-restriction of space, classical antiquity essentially does not advance. For the Pythagoreans, so far as we may trust the reports, the diastemata — that is, the spatial as well as temporal intervals which, according to a profound turn of phrase, are "breathed in" by the universe out of the pneuma beyond the sphere of the fixed stars — are indispensable to their most actual actuality, namely the geometrically (!) shaped body. Plato, inheriting from them here as in so much else, accords empty space, which, in relation to the being world of the Ideas, again coincides with not-being, the role of a co-cause of the existence of the phainomena. Aristotle, however, the father of the horror vacui, denies the possibility of the void, and knows space at all only as the boundary of moved bodies. In all the considerations of the ancients, space retains the nature of a kind of dwelling-place of the sphere-shelled cosmos (which grows even narrower in the Middle Ages), whereas in the "mysticism of the Renaissance" the irruption of distance becomes apparent, if only from the incomparably greater *intensity* with which the space-problem is now wooed. It is instructive to see, in this connection, how, in accordance with the two tendencies which, with regard to the height of their conflict, we called, in the Baroque, the romantic and the mathematical, the inclination toward the subjectivization of space and time crosses from the outset, and not seldom even interweaves, with an initially no weaker inclination to ascribe unconditional actuality to both. The Cusan (1401–1464), an eminently mathematical mind, comes with his conception of space and time immediately within a single step of *the* conception that makes mere "forms of intuition" out of both. With regard to the concept of time it is said, among other things: "Year, month, hour are instruments of the measurement of time created by man. Thus time itself, since it is the measure of motion, is an instrument of the measuring soul. The reason of the soul does not, therefore, depend on time; rather, the ground of the measurement of motion, called 'time,' depends on reason." One might still doubt whether there is anything to object to in this, were it not known that behind it lies the view that mind *unfolds* the thought of the *now* dwelling *within* it into the so-called time-series; and that this series is time itself. Likewise it is the principle of the point, peculiar to mind, by whose help, through step-by-step progressive constructions, space itself is brought forth. The Cusan's forward-flying speculations remain isolated in the Quattrocento; only in the following century do his problems become a favorite subject of the most significant researchers and thinkers. Telesio (1508–1588) accords space, like time, an actuality wholly independent of the subject and of bodies, and states that the intervals are directly perceived, in particular seen — to which we shall return. Patrizzi (1529—1697), who follows him in this, otherwise goes far beyond him, in that he assigns to space the role of a, albeit incorporeal, primal substance, in relation to which light, warmth, and fluidity signify a sequence of increasing condensations. Here we stand in the midst of those Renaissance philosophers who agree with the Ionian cosmologists in emphasizing the *substantiality* of their worldprinciples, yet differ from them essentially in that they place the strongest accent of actuality on a state of affairs that threatened, for the Ionians, rather to volatilize into a being not-being. Campanella (1568–1639), finally, sees, as noted, in space the manifestation of the deity nearest to its origin. — Between such conceptions of space and the subjectivization of space there would lie an unbridgeable gulf, did they not pursue the secondary purpose of securing for the substanceless propositions of geometry, by underpinning them with the actuality of space, at least a second-class dignity. With this, however, a bridge-arch is nonetheless thrown across the gulf, of which we shall hear more presently. Bruno's (1548–1600) half-atomistic, half-monadological mode of thought remains unfruitful for the space-problem. Gassendi (1592–1655) takes over, along with the Democritean atoms, also the otherwise meaningless intervals. Hobbes (1588–1679), the acute opener of the self-reflection of modern research, is consistently one of the first resolute subjectivists. "By rational cognition," he says, "I understand computation"; and: "Space is the *phantasm* of an existing thing outside us," time "a *phantasm* of motion" or also of "counted motion." Here, as one notices, the coming Kantianism gleams like sheet-lightning. In this respect matters stand, of course, not essentially otherwise with Descartes (1596–1650), for whom space, motion, duration are "innate ideas," by means of which experience and cognition first come about at all. If he nonetheless speaks of "res extensae" and "res cogitantes," this is not in order to lodge a claim to actuality on behalf of *space*, but on behalf of the theorems of mathematics. But the periodic decline of all life has, as we shall still hear, a periodicity of the movements of thought as its consequence too. Among the contemporaries of Descartes personally known to him it is above all the significant (though in the histories of philosophy usually treated rather step-motherly) Henry More (1614–1687) who bends back toward the *mysticism* of the Renaissance, in that he asserts for infinite and immovable space a priority of actuality over bodies and takes it quite directly as an emblem of a divine omnipresence. — We have set forth in the 51st Chapter the extent to which Newton (1643–1727), with his concept of mass, derealizes the extensity of matter. His taking-over of an "absolute space" (together with "absolute time") into theoretical physics would therefore rightly provoke astonishment, had he not stood, in his world-view, under the influence of More's writings: his "absolute space" is secretly a spiritual space and, if not quite a phantasm of the *human* mind, then at least the "sensorium of *God*"! The bridge mentioned above from the mythic spaces of the early Renaissance to the noumenal space of mathematics has proven its load-bearing capacity. Locke's (1632–1704) thoughts on space are wavering, Hume's (1711–1776) wholly indeterminate. Berkeley's (1685–1753) boundless subjectivism, by contrast, leaves no doubt that space must be sought in the human mind and not somehow outside it. If above we heard that, according to Telesio, Patrizzi, and others, space is *seen*, we now hear with the same assurance that it forms no object of perception at all, but is rather the result of an interpretation of sense-data that are in and for themselves non-spatial; entirely "in the same way that the words of any language call to consciousness the ideas which they were formed to represent." Yet this English subjectivism, shallow as all English thinking is, is, thanks precisely to its shallowness, less dangerous than the deeper-reaching doubts that break ground on the Continent at the same time. Here, in their conception of space, the most significant of the French skeptics, Bayle (1647–1706), and the then most significant German philosopher, Leibniz (1646–1716), meet one another; Bayle, in that he declares space *and* bodies to be contents of thought or concepts containing not the slightest indication of a actuality "transcendent" to thought (thereby anticipating the Kantian argument from the antinomies); Leibniz — altogether pre-Kantian — through the doctrine that space and time are mental conditions of ordering or "ideal" rules, on the basis of which the world of appearance becomes an object of experience. The opinion that it is the understanding that gives laws to nature accordingly did not still need to be discovered. — The rationalism of the 17th century culminates philosophically in Leibniz, mathematically in Newton. Both believe in the divine world-machine; but Newton's is still a little more substantial than Leibniz's. A later attempt by Boscovich (1711–1787) to mediate between the two is reported on in the 60th Chapter. It is now the theorems of the 17th century that are further worked out by the 18th century, before the storms and stresses break in. Whoever traces even only in broad outline what is put forward in the process by men like Maupertuis (1698–1759), Crusius (1712–1776), Ploucquet (1716–1780), Lambert (1728–1777), Tetens (1736–1805), and numerous others, would at first likely find it incomprehensible in what way the doctrines of Kant (1724–1804) could impress as being in any way new. According to Maupertuis, for instance, extension and shape are mere appearances no differently than the qualitative sense-data. Crusius sought, in his "Entwurf der notwendigen Vernunftwahrheiten," to prove that the apprehension of existing things presupposes space, time, and force. Tetens, the most outstanding psychologist of his time, who had already partly seen through the hollowness of associationist mechanics, argues at length that certain objects of thought are indeed found on the occasion of "sensations," but only *through* the spontaneous activity of the understanding. The discussions of the so-called a priori and a posteriori, including the supposedly greater excellence of mathematical truths in relation to empirical truths, had not come to rest since Leibniz. Indeed, there are erroneous assumptions of the 17th century that Kant makes his own, notwithstanding that they had already been refuted with all desirable sharpness. We maintain, as will be recalled, the thesis that no ideological philosophy since Plato has been able to state a criterion for distinguishing the perception of a thing from the *thought* of the thing perceived, commonly called representation. The claim advanced many dozens of times (especially by Leibniz, Berkeley, and Wolff) and taken over by Kant, that "objective" objects are distinguished from merely "subjective" representations of the mind by a *rule of succession* necessarily belonging to them, is rejected, ten years before the "Critique of Pure Reason," by Lambert as follows. In the first volume of his "Anlage zur Architektonik oder Theorie des Einfachen und des Ersten in der philosophischen und mathematischen Erkenntnis" (Riga, 1771), it is stated: "The order in which things follow one another in a dream is for the most part interrupted, and neither the beginning nor the end of the dream can be connected with the incidents to which the dream refers.. Whereas in the real world, as we find it waking, such gaps.. do not occur, but rather everything in it follows coherently one upon another, one has sought in this thoroughgoing order the essential feature of metaphysical truth and has defined the latter by the order in things. But it is not thereby yet distinguished from logical truth, because the latter likewise has a complete harmony and coherence. What we see, sense, think of, and represent while waking can, with its whole coherence, be regarded as thinkable even if nothing of it existed" (pp. 295–96). This, as is well known, has not prevented countless epistemological writings of the present from serving up the false criterion of actuality again and again, as though one had never heard anything of the arguments that refute it. We resist the temptation to illuminate the cultural-historical reasons for the tenacity of life of Kantianism all the more readily, since they can, in any case, no longer be hidden from the attentive reader of our work. Only a few more external, and therefore no less effective, moments shall be mentioned. If we set dogmatic skepticism aside, whose prospects of success are always slight, because the untamable thirst for knowledge of man is not in the long run moved to renunciation, then it was precisely for those thinkers who prepared, or even outdid, Kantian subjectivism that their work of clearing away had always been only a means to an end, namely to an *explanation* of actuality that was supposed to be equal to all epistemological doubts, or, to speak in the customary terminology, to a supposedly unassailable "ontology"; whether this amounted in the end to the actuality of atoms, or of representationally capable monads, or of a God who brings forth the individual spirits together with their world-representations. An extreme in this respect is achieved, for example, by Malebranche (1638–1715), who anticipates Kantian subjectivism in all essential particulars, but only in order in the end to give the honor to God as the "place of spirits" as well as of ideas. There was none among these ontologies that was not refuted by one of the others. Kant, however, rejects them wholesale, by fundamentally disputing the legitimacy of ontological thinking, and thereby appears, in contrast to the ontologists, in the light of the bearer of critical circumspection. In truth, however, this is only apparently so. For the ontology that has been, so to speak, publicly driven out is secretly let back in again: partly in the form of a "thing-in-itself" transformed into something sphinx-like, of which nothing further can theoretically be made out than that its being on hand is not exactly unthinkable, partly and above all in the form of *a priori* "postulates" of belief, such as: autonomy, freedom, intelligible character. The justification of belief (belief, that is, in the metaphysical conditionedness of Protestant moral principles) by means of a *critique* that subjectivizes the domain of validity of all knowledge is a chief reason for the successes of Kantianism. But to this is added a terminological invention whose wondrous suggestiveness has sufficed to furnish professors of philosophy with material for exercises in dialectic for a century and a half: the invention of the phrase "empirical realism," said to form the reverse side of a "transcendental idealism"! For if someone were to point to the subjectivism of more or less all idealisms, or even ventured (with Schopenhauer) to say outright that Kant's standpoint at times approaches, disquietingly, the standpoint of, say, a Berkeley, he would be met with the pitying rejoinder that he presumably overlooks the fact that Kant himself exposed the erroneous presuppositions on account of which "good Berkeley" allowed himself to be seduced into degrading "bodies to mere illusion"; and that precisely herein lies one of the great merits of the master, to have grounded the "empirical actuality" of the world of appearance and shown emphatically that only that thinking leads to genuine cognitions which rests upon *experience*. But were the one thus instructed now to conclude from this that our cognition, gladly enough, then concerns *actuality*, the pity in the tone in which he would be answered would grow still further: with such a view he betrays a "naive" realism that has not yet grasped that, according to the disclosures of "transcendental idealism," the object of experience, which alone underlies all legitimate inquiry, has been *prepared* out of an ever merely individual (and moreover wholly chaotic) "matter" of the contents of sensation, by the "forms of intuition of our sensibility" and by the "synthesis of the understanding" (or the "pure concepts of the understanding," or the "categories"), and that "actuality," if one wishes to use that unfortunate word at all, is possessed merely for us, by no means, however, "in itself"! And were our questioner finally, quite intimidated, to inquire what the sciences had in the meantime profited from so significant a discovery — logic, say, or mathematics, or psychology — he would learn, to his horror, that he is given up as hopeless, since he does not even understand that criticism has to do neither with logic (read: "formal" logic, for "transcendental logic," or "logic of synthesis," is what it prefers to call itself) nor with mathematics nor even with psychology, but rather resolves the fundamental problem of what the "relation of cognition to its object" consists in, by the final proof that cognition produces its object by means of a "transcendental apperception." — With this last answer, however, one would have unintentionally given us a third key to explaining the successes of so-called criticism, indeed even its historical course, according to which it has, namely, long since flowed into pure *formalism*. For in formalism we encounter, as we have shown, in the shape of a cast of thought, that same primacy of the will which it was a chief motive of the Kantian undertaking to protect against all challenges to the sense of actuality. — It makes so little difficulty today to display these connections that, on the contrary, it makes some difficulty to ascertain why they are not generally known. Yet in spite of all this, Kant's achievements are obscured by — Kantianism (similarly as, in the 19th century, Darwin's achievements are obscured by Darwinism). We shall not repeat what we adduced in the 17th Chapter concerning those sides of Kantian thought which, in our conviction, must count as merits, and recall here only that Kant, with his "transcendental aesthetic," does indeed retain the *right* of it against all those thinkers who declared space to be a mere concept, or else the correlate of one. His grounds, to be sure, against the conceptuality of space miss their mark, and must miss it, because into his space of intuition there is imperceptibly substituted the space that is an object of thought, which is by no means a "pure intuition." Notwithstanding this, he has, with his argumentation, unintentionally made the *correct* decision between the mutually exclusive judgments of Telesio and Patrizzi on the one hand, of Berkeley on the other. We shall, however, return to this in Note 38.

If individual things are transient states of the infinite, which alone is ensouled, then they can no longer henceforth be parts of the world, whether in the spatial or in the temporal sense. Just as the ensouled gaze of the living eye is not a part of the personality but its expression, so bounded individual being now becomes the expression of life of cosmic eternity. And just as, behind sense-space, there is Copernican space, so behind the processes we perceive there opens a world of universal soul-happening, which alone secures for them sense and meaning Human science seems to stand at a decisive turning point of its development, in that it is preparing, under at least a practical effacement of the thought of (mechanical) cause, to seek its goal in a physiognomics of the universe and thus to issue in the inquiry into essence. This change of direction takes on an almost formulaic shape in the basic thought, illuminating all systems, that the living individual body (though in the first instance that of man!) is once again the boundless universe — namely in the here and now of a necessarily transient expression of soul. The concept of the microcosm, outwardly resembling that of late antiquity, has inwardly undergone a transformation: it is not so much that the cosmos is an all-encompassing animal, but rather that the individual essence is, each in its own peculiar way, the cosmos. In man, according to Campanella, the "world in miniature" becomes manifest. "The second pillar of the art," says Paracelsus in the Buch Paragranum, "is astronomy, for it is the upper part of philosophy, and the knowledge of the upper firmament alone is what teaches us to search out the inner firmament of man, and shows us how the former exerts its uninterrupted effects upon the latter" If one reads Paracelsus,<sup>19</sup> Agrippa, Bruno, van Helmont (together with their forerunner Nicholas of Cusa) from this point of view, then [p. 882] their variously copious fantasies appear in the light of a search which, though led abundantly astray by all the delusive constructs from the age of pacts with the devil, nonetheless sets its sails toward a great goal

<sup>19</sup> On page 881. — We have not succeeded in rediscovering, word for word, this sentence, taken along with several others from Paracelsus, from the book in which we first encountered it some twenty years ago, namely the second edition of *Kiesewetter's* "Geschichte des neueren Okkultismus" (Altmann, 1909), in the "Buch Paragranum" (edited by *Strunz*, Diederichs, 1903). Nor does the selection from the complete "Schriften Theophrasts von Hohenheim genannt Paracelsus," which appeared, edited by Hans *Kayser*, in 1921 from Insel Verlag, contain it. But since the remaining citations are correct, and since, furthermore, the sentences in question agree in sense with numerous others of Paracelsus, we may assume that Kiesewetter had a different edition before him. By way of supplement, the following sentences from the "Buch Paragranum," after the edition of Strunz but rendered in modern High German, may be adduced here. "Now astronomy here is the other foundation and encompasses two parts of man, his air and his fire; just as philosophy likewise encompasses two parts of man, namely earth and water." "Now you must further know that the heavens act within us; how, then, is one to recognize wherein the effect consists, who does not recognize the constitution of the heavens?" "Therefore the outer heaven is for us a signpost to the inner heaven: who wants to be a physician who does not recognize the outer heaven?" "Only outer things make possible a cognition of the inner, and without that no inner thing could be known." Quite especially pregnant in giving the content of the microcosm-thought, in a sense from the standpoint of the medical biologist, is the following passage: "Why does man desire to eat, if not because he is of earth? Why to drink? Because he is of water. Why breath? Because he is of air. Why warmth? Because he is of fire." No one will confuse this with the well-known catchword of materialism, "man is what he eats." For, in the first place, matters here stand the other way around: the life-circumstances nourishing for man in the widest sense are determined by his substantial constitution, not the latter by the former; and further, properties and states of matter such as warmth and fire here figure as essentially of the same kind as the "matters" themselves. This may give occasion for a brief report on sources. For the section on the "Mysticism of the Renaissance" the "Grundriß der Geschichte der Philosophie," in two volumes, by *Johann Eduard Erdmann* (1866 edition) was consulted — a work laborious to read but exceedingly careful in its reporting. For the section "The Role of the Greeks," besides *Zeller's* fundamental work and the well-orienting "Geschichte der Philosophie" of *Windelband* (1892), the best-known translations were used: besides those of *Diels* and Nestle, those of *Schleiermacher*, Kaltwasser, *Kiefer*, *Stöhr*, *Bender*, *Apelt*, *Müller*, *Preisendanz*. Only in cases that seemed doubtful were the originals compared, and here and there a few sentences were also offered in the author's own translation. The section on "Romanticism" rests exclusively on the original works. — A selection as rich as it is well-considered, from the nature-philosophical works of the Romantics, is offered by the book "Romantische Naturphilosophie," selected by *Bernoulli* and *Kern* (Diederichs, 1926). Our retrospective chapter, as was emphasized, makes no claim to offer an outline of the intellectual history of the West. We do not doubt that a *his*-*to*-*rian* could bring forward, from the prehistory of a doctrine of the "actuality of images," still far *more* evidence, and among it perhaps even weightier evidence, than that which met the author, without his having sought it, in the course of the years, and which gained for him a greater or lesser significance. For the rest, a "history of philosophy" on the basis of our world-picture would presumably diverge in essential respects from all previous ones, some of them outstanding!

There now emerge those peculiar concepts, or they at least first move into the center of thought — such as astral matter, sidereal body, ethereal vehicle, Yliaster, Limbus, Stannar, Evestrum, Principium, Archeus, aura, larva, spectrum, matrix, ternary, etc. — which, though at first seeming like a mere doubling of the sensuous world, in reality accompany the attempt at a bending of rational thinking back into symbolic thinking. One means, with full consciousness, no longer merely weighable substances but the souls of the states of aggregation, when one speaks of fire, water, air, and earth as the "elements" There is a soul of the warm and the cold, of the bright and the dark, of the sweet and the bitter, a soul of colors and of tones, of the above and the below, of rest and of the kinds of motion, a soul of suns, planets, and moons, of men, animals, and plants. And because all of these in turn form different formative shapes of the ensouled infinite, somewhat as capacity for envy, capacity for sympathy, memory are different traits of a personality, they are not merely interconnected, but are so in a wholly different and incomparably more intimate way than, for example, effect is connected with cause Only the reflective return to the common soul-center, which in each is undivided and yet particularized, leads to the determination of their degrees of kinship and permits the establishing of "sympathetic" series of similarity, which find no support whatever in the groupings of things. — We scarcely need add that the inadequate attempts at intellectual penetration that entwined themselves about the profound idea of the microcosm at once understood the cosmic center of life after the manner of an I, and therefore, without exception, derailed into pantheism; but a glance at the preferred nomenclature, of which we have just offered a few samples, suffices to put it beyond all doubt that the secret impulse meant a worldessence (in many cases already thought, though not strictly conceived, as "quinta essentia") which shares with things of sense their spatiotemporality but not their being bound to a sensuous place. — This leads us to the third and weightiest point

The Ionian hylicists *exercised*, within the domain of inquiry, a beholding lived experience; the Neoplatonists discovered it; but only the mystics [p. 883] of the rebirth explored it. For only in them, on the ground of the hidden transformation of the lived experience of space, did there occur — though not in abstract formulation, yet in fact — the clear separation of sensuous perceiving from soul-beholding. Just as the space of intuition, thought in Copernican terms, is now merely a pointer to "infinite" space, so the corporeal world as a whole becomes the sign-language of a magical world which — neither concept nor sense-thing — has presence only for the eye of the soul. In sense and in substance, the talk henceforth is not of "intelligible" but of real beholding, whose capacity, fluctuating in kind and degree, appears referable to bodily states that can be precisely described One develops, in modern terms, doctrines of "mediumship," with views partly of an old-fashioned superstitious kind, partly of a novel kind, concerning contemplation, capacity for dream, fascination, telepathy, ecstasy, vampirism, magic, possession — as it were vitalizing, through the secretly guiding belief in images, the materially related considerations of Proclus, Iamblichus, and others. If we strip off the manifold masks of their spiritualization, we find the formative law common to them all in the unquestioned basic conviction that the distinguishing power of the soul is "imagining," and that its counter-pole is an actuality of images, of which sensuous actuality offers signs and "signatures." The following sentence of Paracelsus could serve as a motto for all the significant investigations of that memorable age: "The spirit is the lord, the imagination the instrument, and the body the malleable matter." But the stress lies on the middle term, from which henceforth the two others alone gain their coloring of meaning. According to Agrippa, the imagination can even transport the body of its bearer to the imagined place. He and others hold that, through the power of the imagines, both illnesses and recoveries take place. "I have found," writes van Helmont, "that most diseases .. arise from a conceived image (concepta idea), which afterward clothes itself with a material body." Even for the far "more enlightened" Bruno, it is only with the help of the power of imagination that the human soul breaks through the ever-finite space of intuition and rises to the thought of the infinity of the universe In him, to be sure, that has become a tool of speculative reason which, in the sense of the others, possesses a magical capacity for efficacy For just as what is sensed is not so much a state of the one sensing as rather a body actually to be found outside him, [p. 884] so the imago is not a mere phantasm but an image-actuality "The imagination is a power of the will, which makes sidereal beings out of conceived thoughts; it is not to be confused with fantasy, which is a cornerstone of all folly" — "Just as a wood-carver takes a piece of wood and carves out of it what he has in mind, so the imagination creates with astral matter." — "All imagining .. comes from the heart, and this is the sun of the microcosm, and out of the microcosm the imagination goes forth into the great *world*." — Indeed, the age-old image-magic of the primitive feeling for life now steps forward with the claim to scientific grounding: "Thus it is also possible that through my will I bring the spirit of my adversary into an image, and thereafter bend or lame him in the image according to my pleasure" (Paracelsus).

Such thoughts betray a medieval strand through the inclination to grasp the imagines as something not so much received by the soul as rather wrought by it. But quite apart from the fact that "sidereal beings," even though they may be wrought by the soul, are naturally also, for their part, capable of acting upon souls, and indeed are, in the strictest sense of the word, "received" by souls, it is above all to be noted that the will can indeed guide the imagines, but cannot generate them. Assertions of the contrary, occasionally on record, must not obscure for us the decisive disclosure according to which the coming-to-be of the image must be thought after the manner of a begetting. "Imagining becomes pregnant in man; and out of the imagination springs the deed." From this it is understood without further ado why Paracelsus ascribes the power of imagination predominantly to women ("Women surpass men in imagining"), and why it is (likewise according to van Helmont) inner images of the parents, through whose transference in the act of begetting the resemblance of the newborn, now to the father, now to the mother, is determined.

If we consider that even for the conceptual object, subjectivization in the assertoric sentence unavoidably harbors the danger of reification, we shall not be surprised to see soul and image treated like a second corporeality, notwithstanding that their attributes contradict the essence of the bodily. Yet it is shown not only by the equivalence of meaning between the "sidereal body" and the "light of nature," [p. 885] but especially by the Paracelsian theory of the conjuring of spirits, that the corporeality thus assumed wants to be understood from the point of view of the visibility of what is meant. "The elemental body is tangible, but the sidereal body is not tangible .. Thus the elemental body is seen tangibly, and the sidereal intangibly." — "Just as, in a mirror, the image of the outward man also carries on change, movement, doing and refraining, and yet is a nothing .., so too it is to be understood here that the sidereal body is like the fables and apparitions in a mirror. And as much as one may learn from the mirror about what he does who has looked into the mirror, so much also can one who is a nigromancer learn from the sidereal body."

The key to the interpretation even of the boldest casts of this today remote mysticism is given by the equation: bodily sensing = body = "elemental body"; soul-beholding = imagining = "sidereal body." The thought — though nowhere sharply expressed — that it is granted to the body to sense the spatiotemporal here and to act upon it according to the laws of mechanics, but to the soul, on the other hand, to behold through spatial and temporal distances and to stand in interaction with the placeless everywhere of images that are once again of the soul, sustains together: divination, the interpretation of dreams, and magical practice. Accordingly, the achievements of waking consciousness are distinguished far more sharply than in antiquity from the offspring of beholding, whose constitutional precondition the Romantic school, soon to be discussed, called "night-consciousness." — The "elemental body" must lie enfeebled in sleep, so that the "sidereal body" may awaken to full power, whether to open itself to the inflowing of the most distant imagines, or to send its own images to any distance whatever. "In sleep, where the elemental body rests, the sidereal body is in its operation; for the latter has no rest nor sleep; but when the elemental body dominates and prevails, then the sidereal rests." — "Sleeping is the waking of such arts. For it is the light of nature that works in sleep. More, however, is known to it than the flesh is able to know." — "But to those who are all too clever or all too understanding, the star gives nothing, for self-conceit drives away the operation of the firmament and resists the star. Therefore the firmamental effect works only in those who give the star room." — "In sleep the imagination can send the sidereal man out of the man into the distance, so that he there accomplishes his effect. To the [p. 886] imagination nothing in the world is too far, and one may well imprint over a thousand miles, indeed one may imprint even into heaven." In keeping with the soul-nature of images in general, the medium of beholding is common to all beings and comprises, together with man, the animals in particular as well. "These things, which the birds also proclaim, sleep too presages; for it is the dream-spirit, which is the invisible body of nature."

The foregoing outline sketch of what we mean by "mysticism of the Renaissance" deliberately dispenses with the presentation of any systems, because among them scarcely one is to be found in which what we have singled out does not run together, more or less confusedly, with Platonic and Neoplatonic reminiscences, the Catholic theology of the Middle Ages, Protestant defiance of faith, recipes from the witches' kitchen, and the wildest ghost stories. Not enough with that, the coming age of mechanism also casts its shadows in, so that the systems in question scarcely still deserve their name and could hardly be expounded otherwise than as spiritual documents of a section of cultural history so full of ferment, unrest, conflict, tension, and tinder that, in relation to it, the Thirty Years' War might appear in the light of an unavoidable discharge. For the strict closure of the edifices of thought, whether of the ancients or of late scholasticism, we would search in vain; and what nonetheless sometimes strikes us as a unified style, for example in the writings of Paracelsus, is expression of personality and by no means the expression of a "fittingness together" of thoughts. In the works, admittedly far more rounded, of a Giordano Bruno, however, the Baroque, more and more breaking through, already makes itself felt to some degree from its unwelcome side — partly through a not infrequently disturbing rhetoric, indeed a veritable "euphuism," partly and especially through the fact that beholding seems constantly endangered by the calculus, however enthusiastically delivered, to which, as was shown in the last chapter, the Eros of distance at that time succumbed. The "mysticism of the Renaissance" wants to be peeled out; it does not exist in the manner, say, of the "hylozoism" of the Ionians.

If, however, we hold precisely to the sketch drawn here, we must judge that it offers important contributions to the prehistory of the discovery of images, but by no means that discovery itself For there is entirely lacking in it the very first decisive feature which, were it present, would transform it from the ground up [p. 887] We already know it; but we fittingly test its significance by weighing, with it as a measure of weight, the content of a spiritual transformation.

To be sure, the so-called Renaissance already understood itself as a revival or renewal of something formerly existing, and Bruno gives voice to the conviction of an entire age when, in his dialogue "On the Infinite Universe and Worlds," he puts into Elpino's mouth these beautiful words: "They are felled roots that sprout anew, old things returning, misjudged truths asserting themselves once more; it is a new light that, after a long night, rises again on the horizon of our knowledge and gradually approaches its noonday height." But in this, and in all other turns of phrase of a similar kind that have come down to us in abundance, there is not yet *that* which, in the feeling of life, would guarantee connection with the primal images or even betray any consciousness of it: the shudder of transience. Of this the disposition even of the mysticism of the Renaissance remains untouched. Rather, insofar as the experience of time enters in at all, it is an experience of coming and becoming, anticipating the concept of time of mechanics, and the past — which is thought more than felt — figures in the works of those days as a wish-image, a phantasm of hope, and a design for the future. However far removed one still stood from the idea of development, and altogether from the calamity of the Enlightenment and the madness of progress, there nevertheless announces itself here and there *that* genre of writing for which Thomas More coined the name "Utopias" (with his work, already published in 1516: De optimo rei publicae statu deque nova insula Utopia). It is the image of an impending realm, held now in the anticipated colors of the modern age, now conversely still resembling the coming Kingdom of God of the Middle Ages, for which one borrowed the material of a partly researched, partly dreamed-up early age of history. Behind the far-sightedness even of such mystics their profundity lags, and no breath of the ancestor-cult state of consciousness blows upon us out of their writings.

If we are to name the origin of the not-to-be-overlooked simultaneity of the full bloom of the Baroque with the dominion of mathematics, it could scarcely be done more aptly than with the observation that the eros of distance, which had indeed burst the boundary of the universe and called forth "infinity," was able to shake up the orders of the spirit but not thereby to dissolve them, because from the outset it remained bound to the *spatial image* of the world and could not penetrate through to the primal image of time. [p. 888] Two attempts toward this, likewise prematurely crippled by the counter-spirit, are known — and, as we believe, the last of them, however strange it sounds — only to the nineteenth century: Romanticism. — To want to affix a single label to the movements of spirits in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries would be hopeless from the outset, because numerous strata of very different ages intersect one another confusingly. Only a guiding metaphysical thought can lead to more general formulas, one of which we have offered and developed in the 53. Chapter. But even for the sidereal mystics the word "Renaissance" fits only with reference to the connection of traits singled out there. If, accordingly, the concept of rebirth retains at least a modest claim to right, then for the *other* movement of spirits, to which we now still devote a consideration, the name "Romanticism" is completely and fundamentally wrong. It did not flourish in Romance lands but in Germanic lands, and it attained its highest unfolding where its roots pressed down deepest, and that was in Germany, and in Germany alone. Because, in contrast to the immediately preceding Classicism, which was turned toward Greekness, it cultivated the native past of life and — on its path back to Germanic prehistory, traversing the Middle Ages — was captivated by the Middle Ages, so that the scent of incense mingled with the aromas of its garments, it was taken for Catholic, pointedarched, Roman — no, for "welsch" and "ultramontane"! To be sure, some Romantics were, some became, Catholics; but most were not. To be sure, Spanish romances were translated, Calderón, Camões, Cervantes, Dante, Petrarch were translated, but Shakespeare too was translated, and folk songs, fairy tales, legends, customs, and myths were collected from pretty much every corner of the earth. Historical research — now pursued with the heart — placed the emphasis, as had never happened before, on folklore, philology, and the depiction of manners, and *became* only then, for the first time, what today is customarily called "cultural history." Above all, however — and this cannot be recalled too often — the scholarship of Romanticism extended to absolutely all domains of the spirit and drew, in particular, the whole of thinking about nature into its circle. There was a Romantic astronomy, physics, chemistry, mineralogy, geology, paleontology, botany, zoology, [p. 889] osteology, physiology, biology, medicine, pharmacy — indeed, to some degree, even a Romantic mathematics. What could such an all-encompassing spirituality, pulsing through everything, have to do with "welsch," what with "Roman"! — However, we must pass over this here; for once again our subject is not Romanticism as such, which has only in part been opened up, but what it contributed, through research and intimation, to the discovery of the images. We retain its established name without any qualifying mark, but first send ahead a few sentences on its fathers and ancestors.

If one traces the mostly barely perceptible beginnings, then (literary) Romanticism begins with the "Storm and Stress" of the eighteenth century. Individual Romantic traits — alongside quite different ones, of course, and moreover of an extremely varied kind — are found in Heinse, Herder, Hamann, as well as in almost all vitalistically oriented natural scientists of the same period. To pursue that would not be our purpose here. In Goethe's universalism, by contrast, there lies a component of the Romantic disposition of spirit that would deserve recognition even if it had meant the guiding thought of world-contemplation for no more than one natural scientist of Romanticism, and quite especially for Carus. For did not Goethe coin the concept of the primal phenomenon, and thereby alone already make it known that his inquiring mind pursued not primal causes (a folk-etymological division!) but was on the way to primal images! In contrast to Newtonian mechanics and to the physical mode of thought altogether, it was for him the life-content of the things of perception from which he, as researcher, drew, and hence, given his sensibility turned toward the world, the (visual) intuitive image to which every one of his true words refers back. He had, to be sure, looked about him on every side, he remarks once to Eckermann, yet always only in the direction of such objects "as are perceived through the senses." His nature-studies, it is said elsewhere, rested "on the pure basis of *lived experience*"; and in the "Maxims in Prose" stands the sentence, immeasurable in its consequences, which at a single stroke lays low the ideologism of millennia: "One should only seek nothing behind the phenomena; they themselves are the doctrine!" Yet here too we must not yet come to a stop.

Even had Goethe never been able to think and set down what the youthful Novalis discloses of the substance of faith of the Romantic striving — "The outer is an inner raised to the state of mystery" — the saying could nonetheless be applied without reservation to the genius [p. 890] for whom the primal phenomena are forms of appearance of the divine! Man, he says, "must be capable of raising himself to the highest reason, in order to touch the deity that reveals itself in primal phenomena.." If such divinity is intuited only from the pull and compulsion to which we feel ourselves subjected by its power, then in Goethe it bears the name of the "daemonic"; and to this genius owes its creative capacity, and humanity its ever-living works. — We repeat: this is one line of Goethe's universalism; but one that in any case belongs thoroughly to Romanticism. But even if one were to regard the extraordinary change of illumination that sets in with Romanticism — according to which the multiplicity of colors, the noonday brightness, the atmospheric clarity of Goethe's age suddenly recede, as if fading, before a distant blue and sparkling starlight — as so essential that no kinship of thought, however great, would any longer seem sufficient to make a kinship of soul with Goethe credible, one thing would nevertheless remain that connected both and set both apart jointly from before and after: the predominance of the vital "unconscious" (Goethe's own term) over the wakefulness of the spirit, and hence the predominance of what Goethe called "beholding judgement" over the mere faculty of concepts in all the precipitates of thinking. Both, Goethe as well as Romanticism, are non-uniform; but the wisdom of both is predominantly biocentric, and more so than all Western wisdom before it (excepting perhaps the earliest thinkers of the Greeks). — Nor was Romanticism able to renounce the logocentric error either, but the weather-glow of its soul-born knowledge shines deeper into the night of the cosmic twilight than all preceding mysticism; and it is now above all the Heraclitean thought of polarity that, in spirits of similar vibration, not only clarifies the whole wealth of a many-thousand-year tradition of all myths and symbols, but also seeks to dissolve once more, in the alkahest of the soul, a natural science that had meanwhile grown threateningly strong. If in this the magnetic as well as the electric poles often serve as a model, it must not be forgotten that the discovery of Volta (or properly of Ritter) belongs to Romanticism; just as it is regularly from biocentric ages that the creative insights stem whose noisy exploitation in the service of "humanity," through the hastily following calculating mind, has even brought this latter the reputation of being the refashioner and discoverer! — Accordingly the concept of polarity at once knots itself [p. 891] together with a second thought, which lends the renewed Heraclitism a coloring far different from the original and at the same time completes the siderism of the sages of the age of transition with the emphasis on the interaction of the poles across the distances of space as well as of time. If one takes this for the chief inspiration, one would again arrive at the concept of a beholding, to which the primal image would correspond as counter-pole, and polarity in general would appear in the light of the reciprocal happening between soul and world. This too was recognized at the time, but preferably only with the heart, because on its way to the head, owing to sources of disturbance that were bound to intrude at once, it did not hold to the originally given direction, or at least remained always in danger of losing it.

One teaches a day-pole of inwardness, which wakes and apprehends, and a night-pole, which dreams and beholds.. In the former are lodged body and spirit; the latter is simply the soul, and is accordingly called now the soul, now the unconscious. The "seat" of the day-pole lies in the brain, that of the night-pole predominantly in the ganglionic plexus. The receiving organs of the day-pole are the senses, insofar as they sense; the executing organs are the limbs, insofar as their capacity for movement obeys the helm of the will; the receiving organ of the essentially pathic night-pole is a beholding "all-sense" or "central sense," which, in the opinion of the early Romantics, can be relocated into any limb of the body. "Just as, out of the homogeneous germ of the animal, the individual organs develop through the life-force, so too the outer senses develop out of the capacity and drive to commune with the outer world. But this capacity is not exhausted in the function of the sense-organs, nor is it necessarily bound to them. The central sense as such can also enter into relation with the world *directly*." "The cerebral system is for the spirit the source of experience, the ganglionic system the source of preservation; the former is the tree of knowledge, the latter the tree of life. Since now the whole sleep-life of the soul, and hence its activity in somnambulism, shows polarity with the waking life, the sensations of the solar plexus — seeing, hearing, smelling at the stomach — are to be regarded as a transposition of pole of the function of the sensory nerves into the ganglionic system. Thus the shapes of the world pass into the soul through a gate previously closed" (Passavant).

From such sentences, to which numerous similar ones could be added, we draw two conclusions: first, that people knew of the process of beholding [p. 892] and were inclined to see its enabling ground in the vegetative nervous system; but also, second, that people had not yet been able to shake off the sensualist concept of sensation, and consequently misunderstood beholding as a kind of sensation, and then, quite consistently, invented a second center of sensation alongside the cerebral one. Other pronouncements of later researchers show, however, how one drew ever closer, the longer this went on, to an insight into the proper nature of beholding. "Unconscious perception, not mediated by senses known to us, is not a cognizing such as the day-senses bring to us. Without conscious activity of the spirit, we arrive at immediate *feeling* and beholding. Common feeling and instinctive feeling, odic influence, presentiment, revelation.. are the designations for different degrees of the soul's activity, without any word expressing their essence." "All visions are a product of the beholding, an action of the nocturnal pole of the soul.. Even if the clarity and the scope of beholding vary, the different forms of beholding are nevertheless only degrees of one and the same life-process" (Schindler).

More illuminating, however, than nerve-physiological distinctions or ones akin to them, for what is here in view and properly meant, is the fundamental conviction on which all Romantics agree: that the day-pole particularizes its bearer and sets him over against the world, while the night-pole, deselving him, plunges him back into the fluids of the universe, thereby realizing that connection across distance which, as was shown in the last chapter, first of all makes possible the primal polarity of soul and image. To the day-pole belong will and demonstrative judgement; to the night-pole, healing growth, animal drive, scenting, presentiment, clairvoyance, ecstatic second sight, and magical action at a distance. Everything that occurs there is an activity of consciousness; everything that occurs here takes place unconsciously and makes itself felt, if at all, only through alterations of mood in consciousness. Without regard to repetition or to earlier citations, we bring forward a somewhat larger number of passages (arranged chronologically by author), so that one may recognize, from a weighty example, how much the genuine "philosophy of Romanticism" was a single stream, in relation to which the individual minds resemble, as it were, the arms of the delta into which it divides before the sea receives it. Fr. Hufeland. — The more, from whatever causes, the vegetative system gains the upper hand in a person, the more he merges [p. 893] "through this alteration of his peculiar essence, which brings him nearer to plants and imperfect animals, with universal nature; the partition wall that separated him from the outer world is removed; his intercourse with it is no longer confined to the senses; he enters into immediate interaction with it; his capacity to react to the outer world with spontaneity diminishes, he becomes more dependent on it and hence receptive to certain influences of it that are otherwise foreign to the human organism... Should there be presentiments in dream or prophetic dreams, they could be explained only from this sensitivity of the sleeper to outer influences." Burdach. — "Instinct is the understanding that.. still hangs together intimately with the universal. The individual soul does not intervene here of its own authority, does not deliberate whether to follow the drive now stirring or to adopt a procedure promising something more valuable, nor yet what means it should employ to achieve its ends,.. but surrenders itself to the pull of nature: it acts without.. any representation of the end, without judgement of the means suited to it. It gives itself up to the world-spirit ruling in the life-principle, and therefore the path leading there is made known to it, as if by inspiration, in feeling, so that there is no gap between striving and realization.." Schubert — "The organism resembles a magnetic needle set in the magnetic meridian, through which the current of the universal fluid passes unhindered, out and in. As the pull of magnetic force is directed now toward the distant pole of the earth, now toward that of nearer masses of iron, so the pull of animal instinct goes now toward the distant goal of migration and the still-future need of the unborn brood, now toward the nearer food or sexual counterpart... At every moment, whether we sleep or wake, the pull of planetary gravity acts on our body; so the pull of the befriended forces of surrounding nature acts at every moment on the soul and produces in it that inclination toward the.. counterpart which — as in the sleeping mother the pull toward the suckling — works on continually and without ceasing, even when it betrays itself by no outward movements." Carus. — "In the unconscious the universal existence of the world still floods immediately, and in it, therefore, all the fibers of connection stir, [p. 894] by which the particular is everywhere and forever bound to the whole..." From this it follows, among other things, "that, since our psyche too originally, and even later still to a great extent, remains at the stage of the unconscious,.. it, as a partial idea, must be unconsciously pervaded, now more nearly, now more remotely, first by all the stirrings of the soul of humanity and then of the world as a whole." "If we now know that sleep represents a peculiar imprisonment of consciousness within the unconscious,.. we can also grasp how, in this state, the soul must indeed participate more than in its.. waking state in that cointerweavement in the universal and in that being-pervaded by everything spatial and temporal which belongs to the unconscious as such. From this it then becomes intelligible to us how, to the consciousness imprisoned in the unconscious, various things may become accessible alike in sleep or dream that in waking will never be attainable to it." Further: "The deeper still the organization of the animal, the more intimately does it belong to the whole life of nature.., and the less does it need those particular sense-perceptions which, emerging gradually in individual sense-organs, first reach a considerable height only when the creature *has* raised itself more sharply, as an individual being, out of the circle of nature.." "The so-called second sight, the somnambulistic ecstasies, already some forms of dream — in a word, the states of man as visionary — are reckoned here, and the remarkable, immediate, and, often, even perceptions reaching beyond all bounds of time and space that emerge here recall entirely what has been cited, among the lower animal creatures, as the ordinary manner of sensing." But: "Where the sense clearly cognizes and distinguishes.., there the realm of magic ceases, there the charm of the marvelous vanishes, and the veil of mystery has fallen. Everything, by contrast, that hides itself within us, in the night of unconsciousness,.. is really and properly the field that has, since ancient times, *been* consecrated to Maya..." Schindler. — "Reason is the highest cognition of the subject in its relations to the outer world; the magical pole of the soul is the highest cognition of the subject in its relations to the inner world. While the one pole strives to isolate man from the whole of the rest of nature, the other pole leads him back into the universal life of nature; while [p. 895] the former sets him over against the universe, the latter places him at its center..." "In sleep, where the inner sense is opened, where the individual unlocks its gates to the all-life of nature, where the innumerable rays of cosmic and telluric forces are reflected in it, while on the other hand.. material.. life prevails: there the dream-life too shows those two directions of spiritual activity — on the one hand the confused play of fantasy, aroused by feelings of the lower corporeality.., on the other hand the voice of nature, which, as oracle, explains the past, measures out the present, and proclaims the future, and comes into consciousness as presentiment, inspiration, prophecy." "What appears spatially and temporally bounded in day-polar life loses these bounds in night-polar life; what lives there crowded together in narrow space can here be widely separated, and what there is divided by seas and lands can here touch intimately as close kin."

It is not difficult, on the basis of such views, to bring out the kinship of their proclaimers with the Alexandrian as well as with the Renaissance mystics, and, further, to point out, say, that some Romantics made use of the artistic language of a Böhme. This kinship is not denied — it is rather emphasized by the course of our exposition — and just as little is the pantheistic haze denied, which in thought almost without exception finally takes the form of belief in "God." But if the head pays homage to the idea of God, the heart nonetheless pays homage to the night-pole of actuality, as every one of the sentences cited betrays, and as any sentence whatever, taken from wherever, would confirm. With this, now, in contrast to all other mysticism, and, if we are not mistaken, for the first time in the whole history of the spirit, it is the experience of the time of actuality by which the experience of space is determined, and not the reverse. Never before — excepting Heraclitus, at most — has the world resembled so closely an ever-flooding happening; never before has the faculty of reflection been turned so far backward. "Space is a precipitate out of time, a necessary consequence of time." "All streams and movements are to.. become time." "Nature is nothing but the past" (Novalis). "Only the world is enduring; nothing in it is enduring." "A matter can subsist only through continual *coming-into-being*.." "Space has arisen only out of time.." (Oken). "To live means to come into being and to pass away" (Carus). "Organic [p. 896] bodies are not only subject to constant alteration, but their whole development is a ripening toward death" (von Baer).

The concept of development — thought out in advance by Cuvier, Goethe, Geoffroy St. Hilaire, and others in the sense of a "ground plan" both of the series of organisms and of the differentiation of the individual being — becomes in Romanticism the leitmotif of mesocosmic life-research, in such a way that every process of formation now appears as a renewal of a kindred one that had already occurred countless times before, always similar, never the same. "Ever does the similar return, never the same" (Burdach). Carus therefore grounds and employs, to explain all growth, the thought of the unconscious "memory" of the cell. At least the preliminary form of the cell-doctrine itself (in Oken) owes its origin to the attempt to develop the first coagulation of organisms, in the moist hall of the earth, out of the essential vitality of the liquid and the begetting power of the sea. "The whole sea is alive. It is a surging organism, always rising and always sinking back." "The primal slime out of which everything organic has been created is the slime of the sea." "The primal-organic is a slimy point... The first organic points are vesicles" (elsewhere called "infusoria"). "Organisms are a synthesis of infusoria." "The origin of all animals is water." No individual arises, strictly speaking, out of another, but rather: "The history of generation is a going-back into.. organic chaos.. and a new calling-forth out of it." This is the partly coarse language of a physician who was anything but poetic. But one would go astray to fail to recognize that what even in this language still permits far-sightedness is a spark from the same hearth that the enthusiastic seer Novalis points to in these words: "Water.. cannot deny its voluptuous origin, and shows itself as the element of.. mixture, with heavenly omnipotence, upon earth. Not without truth have ancient sages sought the origin of things in water, and truly they have spoken of a higher water than that of sea and spring. In that water there reveals itself.. the primal-fluid, as it appears in liquid metal, and therefore men may always only revere it as divine. How few have still plumbed the depths of the mysteries of the fluid, and to many this presentiment of the highest.. life has perhaps never dawned in the intoxicated soul. In thirst there reveals itself.. (the) mighty longing for dissolution. The intoxicated feel only too well this unearthly [p. 897] bliss of the fluid, and in the end all agreeable sensations.. are manifold dissolvings, stirrings of those primal waters within us. Even sleep is nothing but the flood of that invisible world-ocean, and waking the setting-in of the ebb."

It is a matter of indifference where all this is tending, and whether, with the individual thinker, the last word is given — now somewhat earlier, now somewhat later, now only timidly and uncertainly, now very decidedly — after all to the "Absolute," to Being, to Spirit: who would wish to deny that, in the lived experience of them all, the distance of the past has opened up, and that on the stream of the ages, once more, those riddles "in the breast of the sphinxes" made themselves audible, "which the old night gave the day to puzzle over" (Görres)! Through this, however, a widening of the horizon is accomplished which, because it is conditioned by the soul, strikes us as essentially different from the predominantly spirit-conditioned widening either of the philosophers of rebirth or of the Classicism then just fading out. Replacing the search for causes — with, at least in part, conscious consistency — by thinking in analogies ("Learn to use the magic wand of analogy!" Novalis), the Romantics open up the meaning of happening in that they encompass, at a single glance: spatially, the maternal egg and the elliptical orbit of the planets; temporally — as we have already heard — the stages of formation of the planet earth and those of its particular beings. And of this again a most important consequence is the tremendous impetus thereby given to *the* thought with which they undertook to characterize the essence of polarity — certainly not for the first time altogether, but for the first time in macrocosmic conception — through the interpretation of the cause of tension as elemental love. The reciprocal duality of wakefulness and sleep, of day and night, of sun and earth, pervading the whole of nature in the most manifold shape, is essentially identical with the duality of man and woman. The bipolar whole in each case — wrongly conceived as an organism — is accordingly "androgynous," and what we behold in it as living is the compensation, ever anew accomplished in the gamos, of an unceasingly renewed erotic tension of the poles. Though one thinker may chiefly emphasize the opposition of the sexes — which are, of course, themselves bipolar — and another that of sun and earth, what remains determinative is the cosmic polarity, which accordingly appears, in each particular essence, as particularized. "The world is the result of an infinite mutual understanding" (Novalis). "Every living creature, at every stage and in every sphere of life, is, as the ancients said, solar and [p. 898] terrestrial, or sidereal and elemental, at once, and the sacrament of life is offered to them all only under these two forms" (Baader). "Only in the All are masculinity and femininity.. without polar difference, as it were merged into a hermaphrodite; in every subordinate part the sexes will emerge as poles.. so too in the solar system. The bearers of femininity in it are the planets.., that of masculinity the sun, insofar as it produces the light.." (Görres).

There is no deeper opposite to the "war of all against all" (of English origin), and doubtless the inclination to resolve hostilities, as dissonances are resolved in the artwork of the symphony, cannot unfortunately be denied. Yet if anywhere the word "esoteric" were in place, it would be here. For even a thinker of the inexorability of Heraclitus, who declared war to be the father of all happening, saw secret harmony in the whirl of becoming and vanishing; from which we may gather that the undeniable dreadfulness of the course of nature is not necessarily incompatible with the knowledge of the visionary enthusiasm for Eros, as the young Goethe had already anticipated in 1782 with his prose hymn on "Nature": "Her crown is love. Only through it does one come near her. She makes rifts between all beings, and everything wants to devour everything else. She has isolated everything in order to draw everything together again. Through a few draughts from the cup of love she compensates for a life full of toil." Yet, lest it be thought that Romanticism supplied merely the commentary to such utterances, we set beside them a few sentences from a hymn of like direction belonging to it, which allow us to conclude, from the tremendous change of illumination, that it was the fusing phase of beholding to which the new seer-ship owed its knowledge, whereas the earlier seer-ship had been grounded in the phase that separates itself, in intuition, from the image: "Whose heart does not stir.. in leaping joy, when.. that mighty feeling, for which language has no other names than love and desire, expands within him like a mighty, alldissolving vapor, and, trembling in sweet anguish, he sinks into the dark, alluring womb of nature, the poor personality consuming itself in the overwhelming waves of desire, and nothing remains but a focal point of the immeasurable power of generation..! What is the flame that appears everywhere? An intimate embrace, whose sweet fruit dews down in voluptuous drops" (Novalis).

[p. 899] A few samples must here suffice to evidence that we are once again dealing with a supra-personal impulse of thought. "The creation of the world is itself nothing but an act of fertilization" (Oken). In the union of the sexes is realized "the universal act of generation, or the marriage of light with gravity" (Hufeland). "The love of the sexes and the fruit-bearing mutual intercourse.. rests on a process of.. rapture of the living soul out of its own body.. into the nature of a foreign one" (Schubert). "To speak and to hear is to fertilize and to conceive." "Property is the female principle, the subject; stimulus is the male principle, the object." With such sentences Novalis brushes, without yet himself knowing it, against the primal polarity: soul and image. — But because the soul had plunged down so deep, the spirit was able to fill the cups of the conceptual faculty far nearer to the source, and the "principles" were able to preserve the color of their Dionysian origin even in the brightest, indeed the most sober, factual research. Solar, to indicate at least the circles this manner of thinking drew: summer, sun, east, day, light (at times also flame), major key, metalloid, animal, brain, man; telluric: earth and moon, winter, west, night, fire (indeed, also embers), minor key, metal, plant, ganglion, woman. Solar is red light, telluric violet light; solar oxygen, telluric hydrogen; solar centrifugality, telluric centripetality; solar the blossoming, telluric the growing; solar the yew and the fig, telluric the walnut, the oak, the willow; solar musk, castoreum, horseradish, telluric thorn-apple, hemp, morphine, belladonna, aconite. — Both poles, in whatever shape they meet, produce a magnetic reciprocal relation with the tendency to equalize the gradient of tension. The magic circle in principle embraces all objects of experience, in such a way that it is a matter of indifference whether one explains the attraction of two cosmic masses from the standpoint of sympathy, or the sympathy of two human minds from that of a cosmic gravitation. The Orphic Eros has become the explanatory principle of metaphysics; the symbol of marriage, pregnancy, and birth takes the place of the solving of the "riddle of the world."<sup>20</sup>

<sup>20</sup> On page 899. — However much our presentation endeavors to show that the source of the most essential views of Romanticism is to be sought in the turning-back from conceptual to symbolic thinking, only he who immerses himself in the writings of the Romantics themselves can gain the right "taste" for it. At least by way of *one* concrete example, however, we wish to illustrate the symbolic *scent* that even the less significant authors of that time did not lack. This addition pursues the secondary purpose of preparing the concluding section of the book. A present-day reader who gets hold of *Oken's* predominantly unrewarding "Lehrbuch der Naturphilosophie" would not be to blame if he soon set it aside, at a loss or out of vexation, because from page 4 to page 42 he would have to listen to *oracular sayings* about the plus sign, the minus sign, and above all about *zero*. Here a few samples! "Zero is nothing in itself. Mathematics is grounded upon nothing and hence springs from nothing." "Mathematics is a system of zeros or nothings." "All number proceeds from zero.." "What zero is in infinite intensity, the numbers are in infinite extensity." "The mathematical monad is eternal." "The eternal is the nothing of nature." "The first form of the extending or appearing of the mathematical monad, or of the O, is the +–." "The eternal thus becomes real through self-bifurcation. When the eternal appears, it is a positive or a negative." "There is no other science than of a nothing." "Zero is accordingly the primal act." "Unity has the striving toward bifurcation, as the O has the striving toward +–." "The primal act appears or acts under three forms, which correspond to the O, +, and –." "A force consisting of two principles is called *polarity*.. Polarity appears at the moment when the creation of the world stirs." "The movement of finite things out of polarity is *life*. Life is movement in a circle." "God has become man, zero has become +–." "Time and space began with the point, with the spatial nothing, with the space-zero. The point.. extends itself in all directions.. Such an extended point is the *sphere*." "Space is.. an infinite sphere." "All things are nothings with different forms. The point is = 0, the surface –+–, the sphere –+0–." These sentences are scattered over more than thirty printed pages and could exchange their places at will: the text as a whole would hardly suffer from it. Although we have moreover picked out those in which "something can be thought" to some extent, a scientist (in the best sense of the word) might well fall into doubt as to whether this is to be taken seriously, or must count as simple-minded stammering, or finally as an affectation of profundity. Well, some affectation is indeed in play (as almost always with Oken); but a kernel of thought is present and could be briefly paraphrased roughly in these words: events rest on polar opposites; at the origin of the world, however, the poles are neutralized. But merely to utter this thought, which runs in a thousand variants through the philosophy of Romanticism, and in Oken goes back predominantly to *Schelling*, would certainly not have needed the peculiar speculation about zero! Certainly, the zero (derived from "nulla figura") is ±0 and thus in a sense a mathematical emblem of the canceled opposites. But that would at most have led to a mention. Oken, by contrast, is evidently fascinated by *zero* as by a mysteriously substantial *nothing*, indeed, as can hardly be doubted, by the sign of zero, whose elliptical shape evokes the neighboring image of the circle and, further, of the sphere, which he claims — with a contradictory addition of the attribute of infinity — as the shape of world-space. In short, in these odd sayings there is, apart from the thought of polarity, something else too: they are an awkward and also not very successful attempt to interpret the *lived experience* of the sign of zero. And thereby they become an example of that symbolism of thought, without knowledge of which one has no prospect of understanding the strangest propositions of the Romantic philosophers. If we now, in passing, contribute something toward explaining the origin of the shape of zero, this admittedly has nothing more directly to do with Oken, and moreover reaches beyond the findings of present-day research. But since it gives an idea of how, with better climbing gear, one can get further along the mountain-paths of Romanticism than one could then, those paths themselves may appear less suspect, and perhaps even — enticing. The author too has, from early on, been occupied by the question why the sign for the absence or negation of numerical value has the shape of a circle, or at least of an ellipse. This is, after all, not self-evident, and was not always and not everywhere so. Let us first hear what science has to say about it. We take the following information from the second part of the rich treatise of E. *Löffler* on "Ziffern und Ziffernsysteme" (Teubner, 1919). In the Brahmi script of the Indians, first demonstrable on inscriptions from the time of King Ashoka in the 3rd century ante, there appear signs for the 9 units, the 9 tens, as well as for 100 and 1000, from which, by the addition of strokes, by combinations and interlacings, far higher numbers (up to 70,000) are represented. The origin of the system is disputed; the signs for 1– 9, by contrast, are with high probability the primal forms of our so-called Arabic numerals. About the 6th century of our era the first traces of writing with place-value and of *zero* can be demonstrated. "Zero," it is stated in Löffler, "was, it seems, originally denoted by a point. This point presumably meant, at first, simply an empty place in the number-series.. Later a circle was used for zero.. The earliest undoubted occurrence of the circular zero is attested in India, according to F. Hill, from the year 876." We add: one can accept the original point-shape of zero without further inquiry; one can also conjecture that it was the circular shape already of the *point* that helped it to this meaning; in any case, however, one will have to investigate why the transition from point to circle took place and why it remained with the circular form. — We continue with Löffler's information. All the Sanskrit names of zero mean: *emptiness*, sky, ether, etc., and it has already been pointed out, too, that it corresponds to the Indian cast of mind to invent a sign of its own for the nothing. The development of meaning of the name of zero is so interesting that we reproduce the relevant passage unabridged.. "The Indians called it sunya, that is, the empty, because it was a sign for the empty place. The Arabs translated this literally by the Old Arabic word *sifr*, which means empty and later took on the meaning zero. This gave rise to the Late Latin word *zefirum*, which, for example, Leonardo of Pisa used; in the 15th century it appears in the contracted form zero. By other algorists the Arabic word was translated, since the 12th century, alongside other designations, by cifra. From this came the French *chiffre* and the German *Ziffer*, a word that today no longer means zero alone, but all 10 signs. Up to the time of Euler (18th century), however, it occurred in both meanings, as it still does today in English, Swedish, Portuguese, and Neo-Arabic. This development shows that zero was unconsciously recognized as the essential feature in the series of Indo-Arabic numerals." As one notices, Oken is not alone with his opinion that zero has an altogether preeminent significance in the number series. — Allow us to weave in a personal anecdote here. In Japan the sect of *Zen* still exists today, in whose views and forms of life Buddhism has fused with Taoism. The late, singular connoisseur of Japan *Julius Grosse* told the author, years ago, the following occurrence. He had been invited to visit an adherent of the Zen sect for the purpose of viewing valuable scroll-paintings from his possession. At the end the host presented the most significant piece of his collection: it depicted a *circle* and nothing further. Grosse at first suspected a feat of skill, similar to that for the sake of which Dürer, in his day in Venice, was awarded by his colleagues the prize of mastery, because he was able to draw freehand a circle whose deviations from "compass-roundness" were scarcely perceptible. The Japanese smiled and explained: it is not the *line* that matters, but the *emptiness* within the line. For the emptiness is — Tao. — In the following rendering from the Tao Te Ching by *Wilhelm*, the word "nothing" is each time to be understood in the sense of "emptiness": Thirty spokes meet in one hub: / on the nothing in it rests the usefulness of the cart. / One shapes clay and makes vessels from it: / on the nothing in it rests the usefulness of the vessel. / One breaks through the wall with doors and windows, / so that a house may come to be: / on the nothing in it rests the usefulness of the house. / Therefore: being yields possession, non-being usefulness. Zhuangzi, Liezi, and other great Taoists are rich in profound utterances on the meaning of emptiness. "Someone said to Master Liezi: 'How can the master esteem emptiness so highly!' Liezi said: 'Emptiness needs no high esteem. It does not depend on the name. Nothing equals stillness, nothing equals emptiness.
