Through stillness, through emptiness one finds one's home; through taking and giving one loses one's *place*.'" Another connoisseur of East Asia, *Otto Fischer*, has in his book "Chinesische Landschaftsmalerei" celebrated this side of Tao, among other things, with the following wonderful words: "Tao is emptiness. But then emptiness becomes streambed and valley, and then Tao increases as brooks and rivers become streams and seas. Just as the hub is the meaning of the wheel, just as emptiness is the meaning of the jug, just as the opening is the meaning of the window, of the door, so Tao is the meaning of the world. In it one experiences perfect oneness. Tao is, so to speak, the zero-point of being. It is the imaginary point at which the rising-and-sinking scale of being remains eternally still and unmoved in equilibrium. Thus Tao is the mother of all things, and all things rest in it. This point the Chinese sought to attain, in order to be one, brotherly, with all things. This zero-point is the secret of Chinese spirituality. From it all opposites are equally accessible, and in it they cancel one another out. But this very zero-point is unfathomable and incomprehensible; it can only be experienced as that which is between the poles" (p. 160). Three times the word "zero-point" occurs there! Fig. 14 gives one of the most usual symbols of Yang and Yin. Here too we see the circle, but as polarized *within itself*; the emptiness which holds the world-poles *enclosed*; the All in the state of not-yet-being-born, or *before* its unfolding into the world of appearances. These juxtapositions leave, it seems to us, no doubt at the outset that the circular shape of zero, as a number that originally meant a kind of nothing, was by no means chance, but grew out of the language of East Asian symbolism. They further allow one to recognize how a world-symbol could pass over into the symbol of an *emptiness* that means at least, at the same time, complete rest and, in the spirit of Taoist-Buddhist speculations, highest perfection. But they do not yet betray to us the primordial motive for the choice of precisely the circle for that line which is destined to encompass, whether it be the world, or whether it be the emptiness. Just as relations can be established between all concepts, so connections can be shown between all symbols, and just as all concepts differ from one another, so too no symbol coincides in identity of sense with another. The content of the circle-symbol is one thing when the circle is thought of as rotating, another when as at rest. In our case it is a matter of the circle at rest. One can, among other things, think here of the vault of heaven, which is indeed suggested, for example, both by the Yang-Yin symbol and by certain Sanskrit names of zero. But that is not the *origin*. We seek, in the concluding section, to make it probable that underlying all those circles — older than they, and, long before their own coming-into-being, alive in the cults of the peoples — is the symbolic egg: the site of life not yet born, in the world of organisms. — And so the zero that Oken courted, in which plus and minus are still undivided, would be a last survival of the egg-symbol, which means, among other things, the form of life in which male and female are likewise still undivided.

It corresponds to the inner logic of such a transformation of the world-view that with it begins that so thoroughly un-Hegelian consideration of the course of humanity hitherto which, among other things, this work seeks to accomplish and — to correct. "This meaning of the old world is.. bearing, while the [p. 900] spirit of the new is begetting; and that meaning is fertilized from without, whereas the spirit of the new age fertilizes itself, and the birth-pangs of that bearing meaning give rise to such appearances as we have just cited from Virgil concerning the Cumaean Sibyl" (J. J. Wagner). "The general character of the old age was telluric life.., that of the new world, by contrast, is solar life and intelligent activity. In the old world there therefore ruled.. the all-sense of night-life instead of the individual senses of day-life, the ganglionic system instead of the cerebral system, instinct instead of free will, fantasy instead of reason.., poetry instead of prose, myth and the hieroglyph instead of historical tradition, the worship of images instead of the enlightenment of ideas, symbolic art instead of philosophy" (Kieser). "History begins only wherever man begins to set himself over against nature.. The first men, not yet torn loose from the creative mother-earth.., feel the most secret stirrings of the outer world vibrate on within them. But from the moment when man feels himself, in opposition to nature, to be something particular.., in order to lead a self-conscious life of his own, the bond becomes ever looser.. So begins with the first *stirring* of consciousness the *error*" (Schindler).

With this last citation, taken from an epigone who, however, handles exclusively the inherited conceptual apparatus of Romanticism, the question comes close to us whether, and how far, Romanticism, despite the logocentric direction of its understanding, was nevertheless able, in feeling, to sense the life-hostile role of the spirit. Here let us first take stock: with the three citations just given, an older section of tellurism is correctly distinguished from a younger one of solarism; but this is not correctly distinguished from the dominion of spirit. Such a confusion did not escape even those Romantics who, like Carus or Schubert, were able to demarcate spirit from soul with sufficient clarity. Only the sharper-sighted Görres separates all life of nature from spirit — but as the strict Catholic that he was, in order, the more and more, to sacrifice it wholly to spirit. There are, by contrast, few Romantics who had not sensed or known that a danger of immeasurable consequence attaches to the coming-into-being of consciousness, and perhaps hardly one to whom the dream-like early states of humanity had not, in some respect, signified a perfection of which spiritual humanity had, through an unblessed event, been deprived [p. 901]. Carus, the Apollonian, cannot impress it upon us often enough that the inner perfection of the formations achieved through the unconscious "infinitely surpasses everything and anything that the conscious spirit could bring forth in a similar way." And when, in the first edition of his "Psyche" (1846), he even states: "Where conscious thinking wavers, and perhaps hits upon the false twice and the true once.., there the unconscious governance of the idea goes its wholly measured way with the greatest decisiveness and.. wisdom, and often presents its essence with a beauty that can never, in its whole scope, be grasped by conscious life, let alone imitated" — this unmistakably preludes *the* disposition which, a good generation later, but now with a sharp turn against consciousness, Nietzsche represents when, in the second "Untimely Meditation" (written 1873), he reckons up for the bearer of consciousness: "He has annihilated and lost his instinct; he can no longer, trusting the "divine animal," let the reins hang loose when his understanding wavers and his path leads through deserts."

We have with this in fact marked out the outermost boundary to which the knowledge of the Romantic thinkers (in connection, moreover, with Goethe) attained, on a consciousness-theoretical basis, concerning the negative nature of spirit; but we shall still have to note other forerunners, insofar as we merely accustom ourselves to no longer understanding by "Romanticism" what the scribes call the Romantic "school." In creative periods there are always to be found<sup>21</sup> powerful lone figures whom only school-understanding attempts to place under one of the usual catchword headings, although, to be sure, not one is to be found even among them who does not share, in some way, in the "spirit of the age." Among such there now stand out, at that time, two men, personally as different from one another as can be, widely different too in importance, and separated in time by the whole span of Romanticism, who in a certain respect are the first to take up the position of combat against spirit, though with a very significant reservation (of which more presently): Arndt, whose birth falls in Napoleon's birth-year (69), and G. Fr. Daumer (b. 1800); the former imperishable for much, and above all for his contributions to folklore, as warm-hearted as they are perfect in form; the latter perhaps only for his well-nigh incomprehensibly beautiful re-creation of songs and sayings of Hafiz. Arndt's true words on spirit are set down in the short tract "Europa und Germanien" (1802) and in the first part of the four-part [p. 902] chief work (of enormous scope) "Geist der Zeit," of which it has rightly been said that it leaves, for instance, a Carlyle behind it in cultural-historical content; Daumer's disclosures stand in "Die Geheimnisse des christlichen Altertums" (1847), one of the most remarkable books of modern literature altogether. Since the anticipations in question are partly little known, partly misinterpreted, we offer richer evidence for them and send ahead a few indispensable explanations.

<sup>21</sup> On page 901. — Perhaps one misses, in our citations from Romantic thinkers, the names of Schelling and *Schopenhauer*. Well, Schelling is, in our judgment, not significant enough to be counted among the essential phenomena. Precocious as he was, he first published, at the age of 24, the "Entwurf eines Systems der Naturphilosophie," a system that at bottom impressed through slogan-like coinages and had above all the success that, still today, in numerous histories of philosophy, most of the men we have mentioned are called his — pupils! Schelling spent his whole life, with great expenditure, recomposing the thoughts of others (Spinoza, Kant, Beck, Fichte, Kielmeyer, Galvani, Steffens, Oken, Goethe, Winckelmann, Schiller, later Baader and Böhme); his own contribution, by contrast, is slight. Schopenhauer, by contrast, a keen-witted thinker of great richness of learning and an outstanding writer, moreover not without a distinctive "mood," belongs to Romanticism only still through manifold incidental features, but in the main marks the transition from it to the mechanistic half of the 19th century. His world-picture is no longer polaristic but monistic; his primal will, nominally unconscious, actually pursues purposes and thereby condemns all events to senselessness; his "Platonic Ideas" are transcendentalized natural laws. Put more deeply: the nimbus is on the point of dissipating; but the swiftly breaking-in dreariness of a mystery-less everyday life is still experienced with strong reluctance and hence "pessimistically."

As regards Daumer, the matter is disposed of with a single remark. It is entirely far from him to mean spirit in our sense; rather he means the spirit of Christianity, and, after his later conversion to Catholicism, the spirit of Protestantism and of the secret societies. He thereby becomes — *not*, to be sure, as a psychologist, which he was not, but indeed as a cultural historian — a forerunner of Nietzsche's "Antichrist." — With Arndt the case lies essentially differently. Thanks to his well-known ardent love of fatherland in the noblest sense of the word, he becomes a critic of the very century in which he grew up, namely the eighteenth, and ascertains, or believes he ascertains, the ground of its deficiencies, faults, and weaknesses in "rationalism," that is, in the cult of the understanding, and sees in this again the manifestations of a spirit that had torn itself loose from soul *and* from body — for which it is also said "from the earth." Proceeding from this, he sketches the entire course of Western human history with great acuity, on the theme that *all* the deficiencies, faults, and weaknesses of the European past rested on the destructive working of a spirit thus severed. It scarcely needs adding that he accordingly hopes for recovery from the reunification of spirit with soul and body, or, more briefly, with the earth.

"I separate out," he says, "from man only three of his chief powers: these are body, soul, and spirit, which almost every human language distinguishes definitely.. I know them only as appearance in a long span of time, which history presents to me.." (Europa und Germanien, p. 8). At the lowest stage of development spirit appears as cleverness and cunning (p. 11), at the highest as "soaring-beyond (transcendence)," and only here does it rage grimly against soul and body (12); the soul, abandoned by spirit, becomes unbridled fanaticism (22); spirit, abandoned by soul, becomes inhumanity (23); its sole dominion turns man into a machine, "usable merely for utility [p. 903], as much for pleasure as for service" (24); in striving for "cosmopolitanism," man has in reality torn himself loose from the native soil, for a love of the universal exists only in the form of the cohesion "of people *of one* land, *of one* city, *of one* village, *of one* family" (112). "When, after this atomization, we shall again be a whole," when we shall have found the earth again.. have, then, and only then, will our culture take its rightful place. Spirit will then rejoice in the renewed form of the world..; it will come to love this earth, which, after a necessary formation of man, it has had to help un-deify... And out of such a seed there will form for man, above the earth too, his more beautiful heaven" (303). "I do not wish to bring down to earth the heaven that I do not clearly understand and probably never shall clearly understand, nor to bind it to earth. I make my people secure and glad upon the earth..: then let them try on which side, and how far, they can climb into heaven.. My people are to be bound by the laws of the earth; but their heaven, where spirit flies, where the soul revels in sweet dreams, that I leave them as free as they need it" (306— 307).<sup>22</sup>

<sup>22</sup> On page 903. — Overeager pupils of the author have thought they could discern, in Arndt's mind-critical pronouncements, a ready-made anticipation of the doctrine of the life-hostility of mind. It would be nice if it were so; but there can be no talk of that, and it is scarcely comprehensible how one could so misunderstand the courageous fighter for freedom whom one might almost call a warrior of God. He, at the very least, would have defended himself most emphatically against such interpretations. For he was, from youth on, a pious Protestant, and remained so into extreme old age — indeed he became more and more so the longer he lived. The "Word of God" runs through everything he wrote. His battle- and patriotic songs are cut from the *same* wood as "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God"; they are texts for Protestant chorales and, as such, passed in no small number into the Protestant hymnals! They would occasionally have gained in poetic quality through a somewhat less frequent recurrence of "God the Father" and of the "Savior" ("Help thou us, that we may win it — thou sweet Savior, Jesus Christ" — "Weep not: my Redeemer wakes," etc.). But even in his splendid books on the "Geist der Zeit" the mind that he combats is, without exception, either the *earth-fleeing* mind, or — and this above all — the "understanding" (grasped in opposition to "reason"), that is, mind in the service of private and state egoisms. In his "Letztes Wort an die Deutschen," the concluding section of Part II of "Geist der Zeit," it is stated: "The understanding has completed its work; it has proved what can be known, learned, and done in earthly things; it has proved what confusion and darkening of the human race must set in as soon as it presumes to want to be judge and interpreter in heavenly and transcendent things also." But: "Reason will in future rule before the understanding — reason, the holiest intuition and the deepest faith of the heart in the highest things: a faith that rests on no proof but that of the innermost breast, and on all that the good and wise of every age and time have felt and hoped... The understanding is, as it were, the small soul of man, reason the great soul; the understanding is man's mediator with the earth and its spirits, reason is the mediatrix of man with heaven and its spirits.." "For without the understanding, reason is as blind on earth as the understanding is in heaven." "What is born of the spirit is spirit, and what is born of the flesh is flesh and will pass away as flesh." "Sense, with its imperishable virtue, spirit, with its immortal life, goes on through all generations and times." — Through long and heavy labors mankind will at last succeed in "joining together again what is separated and uniting again what is distant, in a great league of the spiritualized and sublimated mind!" — Among the peoples, the chief bearers, so to speak, of the lower mind — that is, of the understanding, of ratio, of Enlightenment super-cleverness, of mere analytic skill — are, for him, the French.. "They are, of all Europeans, the most understanding people. As far as the power to order, measure, and weigh given things extends; as far as it is a matter of inventing instruments and measures of things themselves, so far the understanding is a sure guide, and hence, for the lower needs of life, here on the ground of the earth in the first place, it is the surest guide one can have. That is why the French excel in everything where the ordinary and small things of life are at stake. That is why in the Middle Ages they were keen logicians and dialecticians, and are still outstanding in all the sciences where keenness suffices. In the eighteenth century, when the understanding had reached the highest summit of its rule, they were for that reason the first; they still are. But unless all signs deceive, the realm of the understanding will fall, and their splendor will not follow very much longer after. — ... But they were proud as Satan before his fall; they wanted to have no God and no faith any longer; they wanted, on their own authority, to set up for themselves a *clever and moral life of the understanding* (so they called it, well pleased with themselves). And it went with them as with Satan and his companions: they were cast out into hell; the French Revolution broke out." What Arndt sets forth on this is distinguished by native vigor and refinement at once. Especially in "Europa und Germanien" he brings, in this connection, invaluable contributions to the analysis of the origin and significance of the French esprit — the graceful and elegant side, as it were, of the being and unbeing of the understanding — by which the latter has worked bewitchingly on the coarser peoples of East and North and made France the mistress of fashions and manners. He shows the dangerousness of this esprit and casts on the conduct of its inventors and imitators sidelights that are convincing still today. But it is also beyond the slightest doubt that it is precisely here that his critique of mind sets in, and that he, far from rejecting mind itself, wants entirely only to strike at the self-sufficiency of the calculating understanding.

If one wishes to examine what Arndt offers as to its provenance in the history of spirit, it proves without difficulty to be woven of three threads: from the cult of nature nourished on Rousseau of the German "Storm and Stress," the romantic high valuation of the life of feeling, especially its chthonic side, and that enthusiasm for the fatherland active in the Wars of Liberation — which here, to be sure, would more aptly be called "love of the motherland" — and as such, against the dangerous belief in so-called ideals of humanity,

opposes to it the *actuality* of symbiotic associations, with the actuality of body and soil. To know *that* was granted to the peasant's son in Arndt, and that was his best knowledge! However far he then remains from those disclosures that attach to our determination of spirit, yet because it was the blood that granted him his essential insights, he scourged the "rational" self-exaltation of spirit with words of such force that nothing comparable is to be found either before him or among his contemporaries, and that therefore mark the beginning of what a Nietzsche later carried further, from admittedly quite different motives. — We give below his strongest utterances; sentence-parts letter-spaced by us are marked with an asterisk. [p. 904] *Arndt*. — (Germanien und Europa). "The essence of spirit is separating and ordering .. annihilating and de-deifying ..; it is a Proteus that can transform itself painlessly at every moment into a new shape, because it itself has no shape." "Spirit, the high-flier, made the whole of nature into a cadaver, in order to anatomize it." "This spirit, which .. when it stands alone∗ .. cutting like wind and unconquerable like light, drives on and roars down and burns up whatever pleases it, tore brazenly through the sacred veil of Isis that lay chastely over nature and the soul." "The world, which had hitherto passed through the sharply dissecting concept and had lost all warmth, all life and all shape, was now, through the concept, to regain at once, as if by a magic word, the shape and bearing of force upon the firm ground of the earth? In this delusion it shows itself how spirituality itself had lost all presentiment of how a shape, be it man, state, or work of art, comes into being. It cannot be breathed together nor spoken together like a system of words merely crocheted together by arbitrary will: it must form itself in slow germination and growth ..; one must be able to see in it the dark and mystical element of generation. Spirit, however, has no darkness and no mysticism; through it, therefore, nothing can be born into shape, but shape disintegrates before it." "It seems to me that the de-deification of nature, atheism, and the dehumanization of man, irreligion and unbelief, have flowed from no richer source than from derangement through spirituality∗... I say it outright: spirit has turned nature on its head .. This admittedly comes to me only like a presentiment, like a flash of lightning out of the night: but I have nothing better." — (Geist der Zeit.) "The glory of the ancients, too, passed away; how then should that of the moderns not have to, and indeed all the faster, the faster and more destructive their formative principle was? This is spirit. Religion and sense, life and constitution of the medieval and modern world are highly spiritual, further removed from earthly enjoyment and earthly force than those of the ancients. In the fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth centuries this epoch of spiritual formation had its fine force. Mankind still had enough nature and earthly substance to bear it and to let it shine forth in .. sunlit splendor. Later it was volatilized by the ravening fire-force .. into an almost marrowless ghost .. Those who had most to do with promethean matter, scholars and artists, were of course most attacked by it, until at last [p. 905] .. they became almost mummies and skeletons .. Knowledge may be glorious, but life is more glorious, and whoever has lost this can be reborn to no man." Daumer. — "Christianity is the religion of spirit... But what is spirit, spiritus, pneuma in the Christian sense of the word? That which forms the most extreme opposite to nature, to the real being and life of things — which, from this religion on, is determined as something absolutely *not* to be, and under the names flesh, world, sin, devil, is accused, damned, and combated most passionately; the principled abolition and inversion of everything objective, naturally true, and actual into its opposite; absolute subjectivity, hence absolute derangement and unreason; the affirmation and deification of the most isolated human selfhood and particularity; the negation of the whole man and the whole world as a corporeal and living being ..; the most utterly negative, hostile, rending and disruptive, hence the most evil thing there is and that can be conceived. From spirit, in this evil, Christian sense of the word, from this dreadful principle of negation and abstraction, flow all the fanaticisms and horrors that stain the history of Christianity, and these are by no means something foreign to the essence of this religion .., but its true, characteristic, necessary, and unavoidable development and manifestation." The "mystery of holiness" consists, according to Daumer, in "being evil in Christian form, and this evil is the absolute evil, beyond which none other goes and to which none other is equal." To break the "point of evil" is the task of "human nature forming and bettering itself"; with its solution "the kingdom of the cacodaemonically negative on earth, as it has brought itself to unexampled development and appearance in the Christian age, will be at an end forever.."

Only one whom the natural, the elemental, the primordial kindles with love can, as passionately as both men do, declare war on that power which in his opinion threatens it with destruction; and again, the elemental can become an object of *Eros* only to one who did not merely think it, nor even merely feel it, but beheld it. It is no accident, then, that Daumer is at the same time the re-poet of perhaps the only orgiast among the sages before Nietzsche (for besides Hafis even an Omar Khayyám and Jalal ad-Din Rumi are contemplative geniuses), and it is no accident that Arndt, to characterize the fullbloodedly living, [p. 906] chooses with emphasis the name "shape" [Gestalt]. For this now means for him not what it had meant in the mouth of the classicists, but the dark maternal womb of all becoming, insofar as out of it the ever-changing world-formations proceed inexhaustibly. Here, if we do not err, for the first time the last remnant of the Platonic Idea is effaced, and in the lightning-flash of the wrathful element there flickers up, though it be darkened again as quickly, at least a presentiment of the actuality of images. — But what dictated this to Arndt out of wrathful blood, that felt — and perhaps still more deeply — the intoxication of the other, with which, closing the circle of our consideration, we bend back to the beginning.

Not in the thinking but in the poetry of Romanticism there rang out, unmediated, that call of distance-from-thepast which has become for us the "signature" of its "works and days." As beings already vanished from *their* own time, peering through the prison bars of spirit, the poets of that day were seized by a homesickness such as was never endured on earth, and this breathes over what has been with an exuberant gold and a painfully drawing blue. The "spirit of Bacchic melancholy" (Novalis) lies upon their "singing and saying." "Bells go" (in Eichendorff) over "sunken cities," and the "mad songs" of old times shudder, flickering like heat-lightning, through the breast. "Everything is distance, every nearness" (Jean Paul) — and hear this: "Upon the magic circle of the heights stood magic smoke .. Past and future burned bright and near, kindled by the present ... One does not so much recollect the past; rather, it recollects us and pervades us with gnawing longing." When was anything similar ever thought, spoken? Not in world literature — but at times in the songs of the peoples, provided we take the tunes along with the words. Here the actuality of images is — present. — — Dithyrambists of decline. — The span of time still to be touched upon here in passing reaches so far into the author's own life that no conclusive treatment should be expected at this point. We have shown in several writings how far the romantic current — like a subterranean watercourse — continued on beneath the spiritual struggles of the nineteenth century. While in Germany it bore poets such as Droste, Lenau, Mörike, Stifter, it brought forth in Switzerland a late romantic bloom which — apart from the genius to be mentioned presently — is marked by names such as C. F. Meyer, Böcklin, and, in part, Keller. [p. 907] Then, however, once more a breaker-wave rose, which crested around 1880 to 1890, sinking again to end in the year 1905. Why we call the spirits that it pervaded dithyrambists of decline shall still be discussed in a concluding reflection; here we content ourselves with reproducing verbatim what we attempted, in the source-notes to our "Kosmogonischer Eros" — first in 1922, then with a revision that had since become necessary in 1926 — to set up as a monument to three great geniuses, of whom at least two belong essentially to that last period, while one belongs to the interval between. The passage in question follows immediately upon a general appraisal of mythological research since the days of the Brothers Grimm and Creuzer, and its opening words refer directly to that. Should most of what follows seem to repeat what we had already had to maintain for Romanticism, one should nevertheless not overlook: first, that the new disclosures stand to those of Romanticism as knowledge stands to presentiment; and second, that, with regard to the role of spirit, Romanticism was not yet able to draw the conclusions that follow from the conceptions of the opposition of the Dionysian to the Socratic and of matriarchy to patriarchy.

"However high one may rate the discoverer's worth of some of the foregoing works, none of them has brought about a thoroughgoing change in our conception of the "primitive" state of consciousness. It would be saying too much to claim that it has attached itself to the two names now to be opened; but at least this much we may state, that it begins to attach itself to one of them, and we add as our conviction that it is destined to be completed in the second. Nietzsche's "Birth of Tragedy" marks the beginning of a new interpretation of the psychic foundations of antiquity, and hence of the whole of prehistory generally, and *must* henceforth be known and worked through by anyone who would at all venture upon the investigation of symbolic thinking and mythic dreaming. Inessential shortcomings of this highly significant work are to be seen in its adoption of Schopenhauerian terms of art and in its drawing in of problems of music (especially those of Wagnerism); an essential one, however, in that quite indistinctly bounded conception of Apollinism, which prevented the discoverer from noticing that its sufficiently definable meaning-content coincides [p. 908] with the "Socratism" with which he was so thoroughly familiar. — But even before Nietzsche, through his magnificent renewal of the knowledge of the metaphysics of the Dionysian, let the opposition to the daylight world of the Olympians emerge at the primal state of the soul, there had already been completed, in the spirit of another investigator, what the "lower" mythology, and with it the philosophical longing of the whole of Romanticism, sought without finding it: namely the insight that, certainly within the Mediterranean circle of peoples, and in all likelihood within the whole of mankind, a "chthonism" of night-consciousness had preceded the "uranism" of day-consciousness, and had everywhere given way to the latter only after a hard and in part bloody struggle."

"It was J. J. Bachofen (1815–1887) who, with his two principal works, "Das Mutterrecht" and "Gräbersymbolik der Alten" (besides which, scarcely less important, "Das lykische Volk" and "Die Sage von Tanaquil"), undertook to interpret the whole prehistory of the Occident from the standpoint of the struggle between "matriarchalism" and "patriarchalism," laid bare with divinatory certainty, in legends and symbols, the substratum of their oldest formative drives, and was able, with the supporting pillars of unexampled erudition, to sustain the thesis of the existence of a primal religion unconcerned with the boundaries of time and peoples, whose associated forms of society, legal concepts, customs, mores, and conceptions of the gods stand in the starkest contradiction to all — indeed, to all — convictions and commandments of the rational bearer of "world history"! The matter did not go without attracting notice. The ethnologists first concerned themselves with it, and lo: a Morgan, a Kovalevsky, a Lubbock, and others were in a position to demonstrate, among numerous "peoples of nature" as still existing today, precisely those institutions and customs that Bachofen had merely inferred from the cult-notions of antiquity! Ethnology as well as jurisprudence have since incorporated Bachofen's concept of mother-right. Advocates of communism, such as the highly learned Kropotkin, sought with its help to forge, out of the natural history of mankind, weapons against the capitalist dogma of property. Passionate controversies of opinion flared up over the essence, age, and origin of the family, and have retroactively contributed substantially to the broadening and deepening of our knowledge of the earliest tribal associations of mankind. Yet who to this day has even the faintest notion that Bachofen must be recognized as perhaps the greatest discoverer of that primeval state of consciousness, in relation to whose cultic and mythic [p. 909] precipitates, taken all together, without exception all the doctrines of faith of *historical* mankind appear in the light of dilutions or decompositions of the primal source!"

"The writer of these lines confesses that his acquaintance, which fell to him around the turn of the century, with the principal works of Bachofen was the greatest literary experience of his life and decisively co-determined his further life. Of the suggestions he then passed on to a small group of Munich scholars and writers, some — more or less anonymously — have since had further effect. On the whole and in essence, however, the philosophy of religion and the study of myth have still *not arrived* where a Bachofen already stood in the sixties of the last century. For writings such as Dieterich's "Mutter Erde," which, superficially regarded, do indeed appear to travel similar paths (without, moreover, as far as we can see, Bachofen ever even being mentioned!), remain immeasurably behind the works of the pathbreaker in both profundity and breadth of view. — Bachofen furnished, for the romantic idea of polarity, with a wealth of evidence not even remotely exhausted to this day, the proof of its origin in the primal consciousness of mankind. Earth and heaven, night and day, moon and sun, water and fire, left and right, and so forth, belong to one another in pairs of like sense, as body and soul do, and are thought, through the very same reciprocal relation, to renew the world unceasingly, just as the female receiving and the male begetting principle do. The unity thus polarized is grasped in the symbol both of the mother and of the child, whose likewise polar connection sustains the mysterybelief in the eternal cycle. The universal happening itself thereby appears in the image of a maternality perpetually rejuvenating itself through uninterrupted bearing in the child, and accordingly every individual living being enters into a binding relation of dependence, *not*, as Bachofen thought, upon woman, but upon the one and selfsame *mother*, or more correctly upon the egg, the life-cell. From this follows an overvaluation of the soul's readiness for conception and of pregnancy, as against the principle of begetting, which renders, so to speak, merely auxiliary services — consequences that extend immeasurably into the shaping of morals. Bachofen has demonstrated down to particulars that there existed, altogether "beyond good and evil" (we would say "on this side of good and evil"), a "natural law" undisturbed by any arbitrary legislation, which guarded the most intimate connection both of man with the world [p. 910] as also of men with one another. But while, on the one hand, with his heartthoughts, in countless interpretations of symbols, he pursues unswervingly the goal just indicated — we need only recall his disclosure of the primal meaning of all the customs and provisions of the Greek agon, to which nothing in the whole of legend-research is comparable for seer-like clairvoyance — his head-thoughts, on the other hand, stand under the influence of the will-religion of Christianity, and mislead him into taking the process, demonstrable partly historically, partly prehistorically, by which the in-itself utterly image-alien spirit takes possession step by step of the daylight side of life, for a self-overcoming and higher development of the primal state. The very same investigator who, on the one hand, praises, in words that rush like subterranean springs, the self-contained perfection of the maternally embracing chthonism — compared with which everything later means only peaceless unrest — manages, on the other hand, to misunderstand the irruption of the peace-disturbing counter-will as a transition to a "higher stage" of morality! This confusing back-and-forth between heart and head, of which its bearer was not in the least aware, was certainly not the least of what stood in the way of the great discoverer's being understood and recognized."

"Notwithstanding this, Bachofen succeeded in freeing the image of the primal soul from the whitewash of the millennia and in letting us sense its unutterable beauty. To offer the key, drawn from the science of consciousness, to the profundity and truth of this image, is one of our own life's tasks. In this, however, we were helped by the great stroke of fortune of our encounter with that contemporary to whom an earlier note in our book refers. Alfred Schuler's research into the mysteries, in part confirming Bachofen's chthonism, in part thrusting down into still far deeper strata, moves, as already indicated, upon the very ground of symbolic thinking itself, and gives the most living proof of the truth of its findings through the fact, scarcely to be grasped in the present age, of its mere existence!"

B

"The first edition (of the Kosmogonischer Eros) closed with the solemn wish that the bearer of such profound knowledge might, for his unique discoveries, yet in the end find a mode of presentation that would open them, for further reflection, to those who deserve and are permitted to receive them. In the meantime Alfred Schuler died on the 8th of April 1923 after grievous suffering — too early for his work, which had just begun to crystallize [p. 911], far too early for all those to whom it was granted to take part in this extraordinary course of a life. Thus there remains to the writer only the hope that it may be granted to him himself to bring out worthily the legacy — as meager and difficult as it is magnificent — of his companion of many years." Concluding reflection. — Why, the reader will probably ask, should this have been the last of the renewals of the soul; why are its bearers called dithyrambists of decline, and what, generally, stands behind the interplay of primal thoughts now intensifying, now all but vanishing from the memory of mankind? We do not claim to be able to give to such questions an answer that would leave nothing more to be asked. But if we here set forth, so far as we would know how to answer, at least a part of the answer, this happens not only with regard to this comparatively historical chapter, but also in order to prepare, from the insight into the actuality of images, an application that will only come up for discussion later.

Many a one, no doubt, who studies "history" — be it that of political events (1), or of economic formations together with finance (2), or of manners, customs and costumes (3), or of languages (4), or of the fine arts (5), or of music (6), or of so-called belles-lettres (7), or of philosophy (8), or of the sciences (9), or of technology (10), and so on — has perhaps noticed with some astonishment that historians (among whom, as is well known, the most eminent minds are to be found), whenever, after characterizing the sequences of occurrences, they attempt somehow to explain them, ground the sequence of one of the groups just named upon that of another. Thus there is, for instance, a way of looking at things which sees in the history of ideas (7 and 8) the spiritus rector of all the other processes, and is therefore called the "idealist" way; and, opposed to it, a way of looking at things which credits group 2 with such effective power, and is therefore called the "materialist" way. Napoleon, with his famous dictum, "Politics is destiny," claims the leading role for group 1. Close to him, at least, stands Nietzsche, insofar as he thinks the history of mankind to be occasioned by powerful individual spirits. Theology — at least that of the Middle Ages — held it to be the realization of a divine "plan of salvation." The force-and-matter writers of the middle of the last century hoped, from the further progress of physical [p. 912] research, for a future calculability of historical processes as well; and some present-day writers of popular entertainment, who cater to the broad mass of those without means for education, are on the point of bending back to dusty forms of superstition, by holding the position of the planets in the zodiac responsible for the destinies of peoples as of individuals (astrology).

Conceptions such as those of Nietzsche or Napoleon would indeed scarcely be refutable, but they cannot satisfy, because they at once call forth the question whence it comes that here and there an overpowering doer suddenly appears who overturns everything, or an irresistible founder of a religion and "inventor of new values" who likewise overturns everything, though in another way. All the other conceptions, on the other hand, founder on the mere circumstance that, in that case, at least in broad outline the future sequence ought to be foreseeable, whereas, notwithstanding the history of the Occident researched for two and a half thousand years, no one has yet succeeded, with any explanatory principle, in estimating the continuation of a series of occurrences. — Meanwhile there are also investigators who have long recognized that the sequences named (and of course multipliable at will) are, all of them, parallel phenomena; so that a certain kind of occurrences of, say, group 7 plus 8, corresponds each time to certain kinds of occurrences of groups 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9, 10, and, to some extent, even of group 1, and likewise conversely. In a synchronistic treatment one could go on spinning a web of threads without end for the purpose of exhibiting the relations between each group and all the others, and it is fundamentally all one whether someone explains the history of ideas with the help of the history of costume, or the history of costume with the help of the history of ideas. But whichever series one chooses, it can be derived from one of the others just as little as the coming-into-being of a leaf on the tree can be derived from the coming-into-being of one of the other leaves, and the question remains open as to what corresponds to the leaf-bearing trunk.

If historical man is the scene of the struggle of two powers, the actuality that we call life, and the acosmic power named spirit, then every series of occurrences would follow from the reciprocal action of the two, and the momentary situation of all of them at any time from the state of the war just before. If we ask ourselves what, in view of this struggle, can be foreseen and what cannot, the answer runs: [p. 913] always only one thing, namely, that life bleeds itself out more and more the longer it goes on (the consequent phenomena of which were touched on in the 53rd Chapter); and even here there would hold only the admittedly extremely probable, though not certain, presupposition that vitality can bring no other resources into the field than those known to us up to now. But even if that were the case, we would for that reason know little of the actual course of the future, because we cannot foresee how the attacks of spirit will take shape as man's life further weakens. All the same, with our key concepts we can understand the processes hitherto better, and can conjecture more about those to come, than without them.

In that spirit cleaves the life-cell deeper and deeper, both change: the body and the soul. The former emerges directly in the physiognomy of bodies themselves and finds an expression in the intensification of technology; the latter leads directly to a change of feelings and finds an expression in the dwindling of poetry and art. Spirit itself, finally, for which there is no expression, manifests itself indirectly in "ideas." Let us then make the assumption — practically impossible, to be sure, but conceivable — that the germ-cells for the coming-into-being of a Goethe should repeat and combine, right now, in complete equality, and let us ask ourselves why, nonetheless, the second Goethe would turn out different in kind from the first; we would then have to answer: because, in the first place, he would grow up into a world of essentially different intuitive images, and, in the second place, into a state of ideas strongly changed as against that time. Among the intuitive images we might properly distinguish the more technical from the more artistic side, though both in many respects come into effect together. One need only think of a modern great city: many-storied houses, such as did not exist then, tracks with trams, furthermore automobiles, in the air a tangle of wires, huge railway-station structures, nocturnal firework-displays of lighting — by which a contemporary of the age of Goethe would at first be no less bewildered and paralyzed than an Eskimo transplanted all too quickly into a metropolis is even today; add to this the industrialized landscapes. We note at once, too, that we have thereby described only the sensory half of the total transformation, whereas the motor half would deserve our attention to an even higher degree. Could we, by magic, transport a strolling pair of lovers from the Weimar of the Biedermeier period unawares into a traffic center of present-day evening Berlin, they would either, after a few minutes, have sought out a "sheltering [p. 914] roof," or they would, within an hour at most, be dead: so little would they be able to avoid the dangers, wholly new to them, of the traffic there.<sup>23</sup> From such examples it should have become sufficiently clear how differently the sensorium and motility of the second Goethe would have to form themselves from those of the first, with regard to a world of intuition changed partly altogether, and partly, and above all, technically. If we now add further the changed state of ideas, we would have together all the modifications arising from the activity of spirit that had meanwhile taken place, the result of which would accordingly always show, in the main, two sides: a technical one and an ideational one. In antiquity and the Middle Ages the ideational side predominated; since the French Revolution the technical side has predominated by far.

<sup>23</sup> On page 914. — It would be all the more natural to adduce the transformation of the economy and of finance, the uprooting of the feudal nobility, and the rendering-impossible of leisure through the compulsion, becoming ever more all-powerful, to work for the sake of a livelihood, and indeed increasingly in the service of the machine; but all this takes place, at least since 1830, in so close a connection with the "advances of technology" that whoever names the latter has already, in naming it, named the former too. It forms almost a hallmark of the Romantics that those among them who grew up out of the 18th century far into the 19th, even when, like Arndt or Carus, they are natures unshakably believing in hope, saw the machine age coming with secret dread. — In the first part of his "Lebenserinnerungen," which appeared in 1865, Carus, on the occasion of his report on his journey to Rügen in the summer of 1819, remarks, to be sure, contemplatively, as is his way, yet at heart wistfully: "To Berlin, which we now reach in five hours (namely from Dresden), one traveled in those days three whole days! One must really faithfully preserve these antediluvian conditions for posterity, since they will in any case soon be quite forgotten by the generations coming next, and yet so much and such enormous matter in the history of mankind is conditioned precisely by this very turn of events. If I think, for example, of that slow journey, how it carried us over sand and swamp in a small carriage through villages and towns, how time then offered itself for reflections on the fine oak-woods around Herzberg, on individual picturesque pines, on the storks standing in the morning light on the peasants' huts, and a hundred similar small travel-pictures, and if I then compare with that the roaring express train of the railway, which, rushing swiftly past all intermediate states, drives me, together with a hundred other travelers, solely toward the purpose of the journey, then the difference in effect is, in and of itself, altogether incommensurable; but if one considers further how, now, a millionfold, this gap makes itself felt daily and hourly among mankind, and how in general soon nowhere any longer will those simpler, contemplative states occur, then an essential transformation in the thinking and feeling of the masses is truly quite an inescapable consequence. Practical sharpness of understanding, quickness of combination, prose, luxury, and the most immediate craving for enjoyment will be characteristic of the new, just as cordiality, a contemplative cast of mind, poetry, unpretentiousness, and a certain contentment will be characteristic of the old." — More vigorously, in keeping with his temperament, sound kindred utterances of Arndt. Thus it is stated in his book "Meine Wanderungen und Wandlungen mit dem Reichsfreiherrn Heinrich von Stein," which he completed in his 89th year of life: "Amid all the vapors and fumes and railways and their etceteras, what, in the end, will still remain solid of the higher treasures on earth and of the unfading memories and memorials of mankind? Whither will the poetry of the past travel?"

But even apart from what is ideal and what is material in this way, the second Goethe would turn out different from the first, because vitality, even in the absence of spirit, would meanwhile have undergone a change. We speak for a moment of life without regard to spirit, but always of life within the sphere of mankind. It would, to be sure, be erroneous to believe that the oaks or foxes or wild boars growing up in Germany today are still wholly like the oaks or foxes or wild boars of two thousand years ago; but certainly they are far more similar to these than present-day Germans are to the wandering Cimbri. Yet even had the most manifold minglings of races and peoples not occurred, and had spirit not raged for two thousand years, the differences would nonetheless be somewhat greater than those of the trees and animals over the same span, because all vital transformations are more sharply imprinted upon man, who, as the far-beholding organism, is also the most psychic organism, and is therefore engaged in a swifter becoming and passing away. This kind of vital change we wish to call that arising from the grounds of the earth's growing older. To this is added another, which is in principle already known to us

As we know, everything living is subject to an unceasing periodic falling-off. There are periods by the second, the minute, the hour, the day, the month, the year, and periods of various numbers of years besides. Thus extremely wet years alternate with extremely dry ones, abundant and good wineharvests with meager and bad ones, years of mighty grainyields with the scantiest, and so forth. It is not this pendulum-swing that is in question here, but rather that [p. 915] of a spirit-coupled vitality, on which, as can hardly be doubted, the periodic alternation of opposed directions of taste (in the widest sense) rests. "Rational" ages are followed by "mystical" ones; ages to which the starry sky, together with astronomy, seems most important, are followed by ones of passionate microbe-research; periods of literary "realism" and the proscription of verse, by ones of idealistic extravagance and insatiable arts of rhyme-smithing, and so forth. If one notes that, in consequence of the progressive dilution of vitality, the intervals become shorter and shorter, then *the* spans of time, after whose lapse bygone directions of taste return in modified form, can be roughly predetermined in advance — as indeed, for example, enterprising art dealers are said to reckon the revival of interest in past and forgotten painters at about a hundred years, and, in expectation of the ensuing boom, replenish their stock betimes! We call this kind of<sup>24</sup> vital transformation that arising from the grounds of the periodic fall of a spirit-coupled vitality.

<sup>24</sup> On page 915. — An interesting attempt to trace such a periodic decline in the history of *art* is undertaken by W. *Pinder* in his book "Das Problem der Generation in der Kunstgeschichte Europas" (Frankfurter Verlagsanstalt, 1926).

Finally, however, there are vital turning-times that go together with tremendous convulsions of spirits, and whose ultimate cause can be sought only in catastrophes of the life of the earth. No ideological and no materiological historiography will ever explain to us why, about 600 years before our era, there appears almost simultaneously a Lao-tzu and a Confucius in China, a Buddha in India, while on the coasts of Asia Minor cosmological philosophy blossoms with tropical rapidity, and in the south-Italian colonies of Greece the secret league of the Pythagoreans grows up (Confucius died about 479, Lao-tzu was somewhat older, Buddha is said to have died about 477, Heraclitus about 470, Pythagoras about 500, the Law of Manu arose about 500, and so on). The same holds of the sudden clustering of creative spirits in the 16th century, of the new breaker-wave in the second half of the 18th, and of the romantic soul-swell in the first thirty years of the 19th. Who would still believe in so-called chance, when, on the German side, within some five-and-twenty years, there come forward such figures as Arndt (born 1769), Hölderlin (70), Beethoven (70), Novalis (72), Görres (76), Kleist (77), the Brothers Grimm (85 and 86), Eichendorff (88), Carus (89), to name only some of the greatest, while France, with the Corsican Napoleon (69), produces a doer who — rate him as one will — belongs in any case among those demonically driven! — We [p. 916] call this kind of psychic breaker-waves that arising from the grounds of a telluric turn.

What is behind telluric turning-times, whence such turns may again derive, whether they concern the earth alone, or lie grounded in the planetary system, or even in the reaches of the cosmos, since we do, after all, continually pass into other regions of it — of this one may entertain conjectures; a knowledge is denied to us for now, and perhaps forever. On the other hand, a little of the essence of earth-turning-times can be put into words, even if only in the language of symbols. — The "elements," as we have seen, are, for the investigator of actuality, ensouled, and as such accessible neither to physics nor to chemistry. When Nietzsche says, "But the heart of the earth is of gold," this is meant to be understood literally, though it does not refer to the material composition of the earth's core, but to a psychic essence which, in the first place, relates to the vital expressions of the earth similarly to how the heart relates to the vital expressions of the individual being, and which, moreover, wherever it is at work, must be thought of as golden-gleaming. And when he says elsewhere, "The desert grows: woe to him who harbors deserts," or when Novalis already speaks of the "ebbing of the primal waters," this again means to say, literally, that the psychic essence of the earth is diminishing and perhaps could even dwindle away altogether.

Let us now assume that, at wholly incalculable intervals — now of millennia, now of centuries, now of decades — the life-fire of the earth presses outward, and glows through the souls in general that are receptive to it, but quite especially through those, admittedly ever rare, human beings whose blood stands in connection with the elemental processes; then we hold in our hands at least one key to such storm-times of the struggles of spirits, and several otherwise wholly inexplicable occurrences would become somewhat intelligible to us, such as: the independence of such transformations of the inner course of movement from the place of residence of their bearers; their far-reaching independence from the age of these bearers; further, the independence of the change of illumination from the predominantly spiritually conditioned history of styles; and finally the fact that the turning-time itself bears, without exception, the character of inwardness, and consequently, in man, that of a spiritual outbreak, while the effect of this upon the field of deeds occurs only afterward, in a later period. Thus the century of wars followed upon the spiritual struggles of the 16th century; thus, in the 18th, [p. 917] the French Revolution followed upon the society-fleeing "Storm and Stress" of literature (which was telluric-ally conditioned only to the slightest degree); and thus, between 1890 and 1900, the destiny of mankind was decided inwardly, before, then, in the 20th, the executive powers of decline could set in. With these last words we have already anticipated; but we must call a halt to ourselves for one more moment.

The ideological historiography holds that a change of thought, or at least the manifestation of it, brings about physical transformations; the materiological, conversely, traces the former back to upheavals of the economy. But both the ideas and the economic facts, finance and technology included, exist for mankind only insofar as they here and there "come to consciousness." Whoever has, together with the writer of this work, convinced himself that all consciousness is something effected, but never in any way something effecting, must reject both conceptions. The effecting powers are — in man — spirit and life. The latter exhibits a periodic decline of shortening rhythms, and, besides, telluric turns; the former, whose goal is the annihilation of life, must adapt itself to these fluctuations, and answers every telluric turn in particular with a mighty recoil. In the soul-swells and spiritual struggles that we have cited, there manifest themselves — for mankind — transformations of the life of the earth, and upon these there follows each time an outbreak of deeds, for the reason that spirit thereafter finds itself confronted with a psychically altered mankind, and must accordingly master its victim by new means. Both, then — the transformation of spirits and the political or social crisis that follows it — are occasioned by one and the same event within the spirit-coupled scope of life, and stand to one another as action and reaction.

This premised, we offer, for the relative independence of telluric turns from the age of their bearers, a single piece of evidence, which may at the same time serve us to learn to distinguish more spiritual transformations from the unquestionably psychic ones. Among the classicists of the 18th century there are, as mentioned, spiritual forerunners of Romanticism; among the early Romantics, spiritual epigones of Classicism. But now let one make the following test. Let one open at random a page of an author of the "Storm and Stress" period, or indeed of Classicism proper — say Rousseau (born 1712), or Winckelmann (17), or Klopstock (24), or Lessing (29), or Hamann (30), or Wieland (33), or Herder (44), or [p. 918] Heinse (46), or Bürger (47), or Goethe (49), or Voß (51), or Schiller (59): one finds the greatest differences of views as well as of the handling of language, still greater differences of spiritual significance and formative perfection, *and* one finds, between any one of them and the rest, some kinship of ideas, which throughout, though not without exception, is greater for the more neighboring birth-years than for those farther apart. If one then does the same with any author of the birth-period of Romanticism — be it Hölderlin or Novalis or Görres or Kleist or Eichendorff or Schubert or Carus, be it even the earliest of them all, Jean Paul, or such a latecomer as Lenau — then, as regards the very differences and similarities just named, indeed the same holds, both of the Romantics among themselves and of any one of them in relation to Classicism. But this now recedes entirely, at a single stroke, before the circumstance that, in retrospect, all the classicists strike us as comparatively without atmosphere (Schiller too, Goethe too!), while an intensely atmospheric quality seems to envelop every Romantic. There — in a word — the *aura* is (comparatively) lacking; here it is present almost to excess. No aura, it is understood, resembles another: that of a Hölderlin we would call an over-transparent ether, that of a Görres cloud billowing into masses of smoke, that of an Eichendorff distant blue and gold; but it is always "aura," and this depends, qualitatively, not in the least on the age of the one who bears it — it may pale with growing years, or, conversely, even grow stronger, namely when its bearer, according to his birth-year, grows only at a higher age into the telluric turn, as is, for instance, the case with Jean Paul. Still less does it have anything to do with the development of styles, and least of all with spiritual significance. For no Romantic attained the spiritual range and spiritual power of Goethe, and indeed even few attained the spiritual strength of Schiller! It seems to us that a middling degree of fine feeling already suffices to confirm, by checking, what has just been said. — By the aura now, and by it alone (and in accordance with its strength), there announces itself that outward pressing of the earth-essence which is proper only to the times of a telluric turn. — For its manifestations, however, at the most various points of the earth and in spheres of life that are comparable with one another neither in the history of ideas nor otherwise, let a further piece of evidence be offered here too, this time from the subterranean movement of soul [p. 919] of the last decade and a half of the past century. With regard to it too we shall first send ahead a brief survey of the birth-years of its bearers.

In our quotation, besides Bachofen, two men were named: Nietzsche and Schuler. To these the writer himself would have had to add himself, had he not wished to avoid the biographical. For *the* precipitates of experience on which his whole research rests to this day stem from the years 1889–1892, and will, moreover, become accessible to the public only with his literary remains. Likewise still pending is the publication of the spiritual legacy of Schuler, whose most earth-moist fragments fall in the years 1888–1900.<sup>25</sup> The two men are only eight years apart in age; their productions of that time thus belong to the psychic years of youth, and those of the writer were in existence long before he yet knew of the existence of his later companion. If we now cast a glance at Nietzsche, it strikes us that, after the mighty Dionysian thrust of his "Birth of Tragedy," which appeared in 1872, he moves, with his following books (Untimely Meditations, Human, All Too Human I and II, The Wanderer and His Shadow, Daybreak), further and further away from the aura of orgiastic seer-ship, until, about ten years later, that is, at the beginning of manhood, a new shuddering and trembling sets in, which, after the verse-accompanied "Gay Science," comes properly to its outbreak in "Zarathustra" (83–85), only then, in the passionate late works (Beyond Good and Evil 85–86, On the Genealogy of Morals 87, Twilight of the Idols 88, The Antichrist 88), not so much to die away as rather to accompany, as with uncanny gong-strokes, the self-sacrifice of the bearer of such inner conflagrations. Were we accordingly to set the peak of the earth-turning-time at about 1890, then an event might appear to us in a new light which, if we do not err, has scarcely its equal in the exploration — of Africa.

<sup>25</sup> On page 919. — In the meantime, in 1930, the specifically poetic pieces were published from the literary remains by the executors of the estate as a private printing under the title: *Alfred Schuler*, Dichtungen. Aus dem Nachlaß. (Typesetting and printing by the Meisterschule für Deutschlands Buchdrucker in Munich. Distribution through the bookshop Kurt Saucke u. Co., Hamburg I, Bergstr. 23.)

All primitives celebrate, from time to time, festivals of intoxication, by preference on nights of the full moon; many of them know the mantic art of ecstasy; magical methods of healing often proceed amid ecstatic ceremonies, and even the widespread rites of initiation for boys are not seldom accompanied by enthusiastic excesses. The material bearing on this among ethnologists is beyond survey, and yet, in the history of circumnavigators of the world and seekers of new lands, it will not easily be possible to find anything comparable to the [p. 920] tremendous orgy that, in September 1892, seized, with uncanny speed of spread, the whole people of the Warundi, that is, of the inhabitants of the East African land of Urundi. That the reporter, the explorer Baumann, was not in the remotest degree a "poet," but no more and no less than a circumspect leader of an expedition, who traversed the land only in order to press forward to the sources of the Nile, enhances the value of his account, because it guarantees for us its, as it were, photographic fidelity, and relieves us of the trouble of having to cleanse the text of decorative additions. Although a legendary tradition provided the occasion for the events, this is nonetheless only *one* among similarly, multiply attested traditions, and stands in no proportion whatever to the extent of the orgy that followed upon it. For, as gradually became clear, and only with the help of interpreters, the Warundi were said formerly to have been ruled by a dynasty that derived its descent from the moon (mwesi), and whose royal title was accordingly "Mwesi." "The last Mwesi, named Makisavo (the pale face), had long been missing, but, according to tradition, lived on in the moon, and was expected to come from the north. When now suddenly a white man came into the land from the north, they saw in him the longed-for ruler, the Mwesi Makisavo."

Scarcely has the caravan crossed the Kagera river when it is received by endless throngs of black male and female dancers. "They came in single file, swinging foliage and their staffs, sturdy figures with original hair styles and brown-andgrey patterned .. cloaks of bark-cloth .. At the top of the ramp they lined up in two or three rows and performed that curious dance which I was then to see countless times more without its ever losing its charm for me. Under the direction of a lead dancer the masses perform these dances with unbelievable evenness and skill, so that the ground thunders and mighty clouds of dust envelop the dancers. With arms raised high they swing their staffs and foliage gracefully, step forward and backward, execute high leaps at the same time, and never once fall out of the rhythm given by the sole of the foot." — Thus it begins, and this, one will say, is familiar from many similar accounts of the welcome accorded Europeans by primitive tribes. But let one hear further! We confine ourselves to bringing, word for word, a few samples from Baumann's "Durch Massailand zur Nilquelle" (Berlin, [p. 921] Reimer in chronological order, and remark only further that the frenzy continued without interruption for as long as the "Mwesi" was in the land — a full week in all! (Smaller omissions between the passages cited are marked by two dots, larger and very large ones by three or four dots.)

"In the camp regular festival dances developed. In a wide circle the throngs of people crouched and stood around an open space where the dances took place. — Holding the long staff in the right hand, foliage in the left, the warriors of the various regions performed the most difficult "pas" one after another ... After the men, women came forward .. They arranged themselves in a semicircle, the center of which was taken by two beautifully built young girls who, with outstretched arms, performed a charming dance in the Spanish fandango style, accompanied by hand-clapping and pleasantly soft singing.. The melodious, changeful song of the gentle women's voices and the sight of these slender beings, who performed those artful dances with a constant smile, presented a spectacle of peculiar enchantment.. We had no need to worry about provisions here; the wish to buy anything was not even understood; for to the Mwami belongs simply everything that is in the land, he takes what pleases him, and what he cannot take is brought to him in loads from every side. Large-horned cattle, goats and sheep, immense quantities of bananas and legumes, numerous jars of pombe kept arriving continually, without anyone among us asking for or *requesting* anything. . . . The moral strength of my people, especially of the askari, was put to a hard test at that time, for we were fully aware that this mad friendliness of the Warundi, founded exclusively on superstition, could at any moment turn into its opposite through some chance occurrence. It is true that everyone came unarmed and only with long staffs, yet the spearhead was stuck wrapped in foliage under the bark-cloth, and at any moment the peaceful dancers could turn into spear-brandishing, bloodthirsty adversaries.. The awareness of the danger always threatening despite all friendliness, the sight of the thousand-headed mass of people that rolled along beside the caravan like a roaring sea, the din that went on without interruption — all this was capable of affecting even the hardest of temperaments .. When we then camped at Intaganda and the wild stamping and whooping sounded outside, the askari held a council among themselves [p. 922] and sent me a deputation which begged me to turn back .... The fanaticism of the Warundi reached .. its high point. Enormous masses of people, drawn from every side, came and rolled along behind us like a stream. Other throngs went ahead, falling upon everything in the land like a swarm of locusts. They tore provisions and household goods out of the huts, the fields were bare within minutes, whole herds of cattle were driven along and were often literally torn to pieces by my raging escort. The enormous quantities of pombe found in the villages likewise did nothing to calm tempers. — The inhabitants of the settlements did not always let themselves be plundered quietly; bloody skirmishes took place in front of the caravan, in which people were badly wounded and several were even killed. But as soon as I drew near, both sides laid down their weapons, threw themselves literally under the hooves of my riding donkey, and cried their "gansa mwami!" (Hail, chief .) — The con tinual sight of these black bodies pressed against one another, the din that made the air tremble, and the frenzy that spoke from the whole proceeding made the deepest impression on me.. Naturally the fury of (my) people often turned against them, since they wanted to keep the Warundi away from their Mwami. Thus it happened that on 17 September the askari were wounded, first by blows with sticks, then by bites, and finally even by knife stabs. When a young Manyema-Ruga-Ruga actually had his lower lip bitten off, it was no wonder that he opened fire. As is apt to happen in such cases, several shots at once cracked out, and before my whistle, given at once, for "cease fire" could assert itself, some thirty Warundi lay dead and severely wounded on the ground, to my deep regret. — A deathly silence fell, and we now expected to see the long-feared turn of mood occur. But nothing of the kind happened; a piercing trill of joy from a high woman's voice broke the silence, the "gansa mwami" rang out again from a thousand throats, the warriors danced a few steps in front of the corpses of their countrymen, and into the groaning of the dying mingled the jubilant singing of the women. It was a dreadful sight."

This should suffice to give a concept of the fact that something extraordinary was at play here, through which the capacity for ecstasy proper to all primitives (and just as naturally to all the cultured peoples of antiquity and of Asia) was heightened far beyond the limit [p. 923] to which it otherwise attains at their festivals. Should anyone now express astonishment at seeing the description of the frenzies of African "savages" woven into an outline of the intellectual history of the West, he should be told that he has not conceived what we understand by turning-ages of the earth. For if such ages exist (and they do exist!), they must come to light in the most various places on earth, among the most various peoples, and in the most various strata of humanity; and for such ages we have the right, indeed the duty, to set beside the formations mediated by spirit those appearances that break forth unmediated from blood not yet spiritualized.

This wave now was the last, because with it the essence left the globe of the earth . Never perhaps have more glowing<sup>26</sup> shudders been lived through and suffered through by human beings than at that time. The horizons flamed in the evening red of a farewell that in human speech was a farewell forever, and — "all who take leave speak like drunkards and gladly comport themselves festively." Few knew it; fewest know it. Even Nietzsche mistook that woefully mighty glow for the red of a dawning morning. The secret source of such knowledge is known only to one who himself had to drink from it. What we have offered in the way of grounds and facts for the advance of an unstayable calamity is verifiable, but the provenance of the inner certainties is not. Of this no one can wish to convince anyone but the one touched by the same fate; and only for that reason have such words found a place here, so that the reader may know why we called the last bearers of the earth's essence the dithyrambists of downfall. Lemures and vampires surrounded them and have meanwhile all but completed their work . The earth smokes with the blood of the<sup>27</sup> slain as never before, and the ape-like struts about decked in the spoils from the shattered temple of life.

<sup>26</sup> On page 923. — It goes without saying that, seen from coming centuries, the three waves here distinguished — namely the "Sturm und Drang" of the 18th century, Romanticism, and the brief high tide of the 1890s of the 19th century — would foreshorten, in perspective, into three peaks of a single wave, which would then have to be dated, roughly, from 1770 to 1900.

<sup>27</sup> On page 923. — Whoever wishes to learn more precise details on this is referred to our treatise "Der Fall Nietzsche-Wagner in graphologischer Beleuchtung," first published in 1904, reprinted with expanded notes in the collected volume of our essays that appeared under the title "Zur Ausdruckslehre und Charakterkunde" in 1926 from the publishing house of Kampmann.

[p. 924]

### Zweiter Abschnitt — Seele und Leib — Second Section — Soul and Body

#### 58. Kapitel — Das Hier und Jetzt — Chapter 58 — The Here and Now

After the long roads we have covered in getting this far, we feel a little as the sailor does who, at the sight of a stretch of coast, however still distant, cries out "Land at last!" If we have hitherto fared, as it were, upon a heaving ocean of thoughts, looking now aloft, now into the distance, we must now for the first time set foot on land, before we set out on a last, still further-reaching voyage. — The reader will recall that again and again attention was drawn to gaps in the course of the argument, with the remark that they were in part provided for in the plan of the work and in part grounded in the matter itself. Although at bottom we were compelled to leave only a single question open, it nonetheless branches into numerous sub-questions, of which a few may be listed: Why and to what extent can the concept of sameness be applied to the actuality of happening? What makes the existential judgement possible? How does the apprehension of movement come about? How does the consciousness of corporeality? How is intuitability related to corporeality, and corporeality to thing-ness? Whence does the concept of place derive? Is there an actuality of matter, and in what does it consist? — We shall find the answer to all of these together, and to others besides, without difficulty, once we bring our knowledge so far gained of the essence of the now to a conclusion by ascertaining the derivational grounds of the here. But what, seen from outside, concerns the meaning and origin of the hic et nunc [here and now], concerns, with regard to the life-processes involved, the nature of sensation.

[p. 925] In keeping with Goethe's word of wisdom, "To find yourself in the infinite — you must distinguish and then combine," we shall for a while behave as though we had forgotten what has already been established concerning waking and sleeping beholding, concerning original working and the later gift of intuition, and shall furthermore confine ourselves for the time being to the animal life-space, indeed chiefly to that of the single-celled organisms, so that, as far as possible, we may grasp by itself the receptivity to nearness that is polar to the receptivity to distance, and in it come to recognize the essentially decisive impulse toward the genesis of wakefulness — a wakefulness not of beholding, but almost through and through one of judgement-armed willing. A somewhat crude example may give a hint of the goal of this train of thought.

From the dream-image as also from the mirror-image we have satisfied ourselves that appearances which are nothing but appearances lack corporeality. Whatever corporeality may mean in relation to mere appearance, it means at any rate, among other things, that of which an unavoidable consequence is underscored by the world-famous proposition: where one body is, there no other can be. If I cross my room in complete darkness and in doing so bump against the armchair, I experience, as suddenly as uncomfortably, the resistance that hinders the further progress of my stepping, and I suffer an interruption of my state of soul, whatever it may have been. We have repeatedly emphasized "that reflection springs from points of disturbance in lived experience and makes the occasion of disturbance congeal into that lawfully regulated world of facts into which the wakefulness of the thought-reflective bearer of life finds itself inescapably wedged" (p. 280), and we have just now pointed to an occurrence that is involved in absolutely all processes to which, within the animal life-space, the character of disturbance attaches: the occurrence of suffered resistance.
