We believe we can grasp it with our hands: it could not take place if the experiencing being were not, among other things, a body, nor again without this body's capacity for self-movement, nor finally without the corporeality of the resisting something. And this double judgement too seems to us justified on this occasion: the resisting something is here, and at that very same place, at the moment when I come to feel it, am I too. The following equation appears to lie ready to hand: experience of resistance = experience of the hindering of self-movement = experience of the corporeality [p. 926] of the hindering existence = experience of the corporeality of one's own existence = experience of, so to speak, a doubled here. And would not the breaking-point be thereby quite properly indicated, where the separating lightning-deed of spirit might strike? Yet we have, as will become apparent, presupposed a by no means small series of preconditions, and shall not be permitted to shrink from a laborious journey in order to draw them one after another into the light. In doing so we shall not be able to avoid proceeding somewhat more geometrico, in that we first of all state the guiding propositions and doctrines, before in what follows verifying them step by step. This is grounded, however, in the fact that we must afterward again lift the isolation of sensation, which we first drive to its extreme, because it is only through re-connection with the underlying process of beholding that the data ascertained first become capable of life, and in particular fit for deriving what hovers before us as our goal: the corporeality of images.

The psychology hitherto current, which called all sensory experiences simply sensations, has overlooked, and does not know even today, what has for many years been demonstrated by us: that every sensory experience whatsoever falls into two components essentially different from one another — the process of sensing and that of beholding, which, in view of its being bound up with the former, we may also call the process of intuiting. To "reduce" one to the other would be just as fruitless an undertaking, and fruitless in the same sense, as the attempt to reduce right to left, or the North Pole to the South Pole. Since we have reached the point where the consequences of our polaristic world-picture unfold step by step, and where we must accordingly speak again and again of polarities, let it be emphasized once more in advance — though it has already been said more than once — that poles in the sense of the science of life, or, more briefly, vital poles, never exhibit equilibrium or "symmetrical opposition," as we may convince ourselves intuitively from all natural symmetries. "If we lay a vertical plane through the continuous surface-connection of the front view of an animal or human body, the mirror-image halves, for all their exceedingly great similarity, are nevertheless never interchangeably identical with one another. Just as little can the left side of any given leaf be brought by rotation about the medial axis into complete and exact coincidence with the right side.. Just as, in contrast to the constant repetition of a pattern-movement (namely in the machine), [p. 927] natural processes always recur only similarly, so too, on the self-living body, one of the two corresponding halves never forms the exact mirror-imitation of the other." And that is<sup>28</sup> not all: the polarity of vital processes can always be represented as a dependence of the one upon the other. This premised, in order to study the process of sensing by itself we choose, fittingly, a sensory domain where its predominance over the process of beholding comes most strongly into effect: the sensory domain of touch.

<sup>28</sup> On page 927. — From our work "Vom Wesen des Rhythmus" in "Künstlerische Körperbildung," edited by *Pallat* and *Hilker* (Breslau, Hirt 1923, 3rd ed. 1926, pp. 142–191). Later published, revised, as a book

Let us place first the proposition that must occupy us to begin with: *sen*sation is experience of resistance and nothing besides — whereupon we must at once remind ourselves that an experience of touch, especially when thought of as bound up with a movement across the thing touched, always contains still more than merely the experiential content of resistance, namely intuitive features such as smoothness, roughness, stickiness, sharpness, bluntness, coldness, warmth, heat, dryness, wetness, and so forth, all of which are qualitatively different from one another and each of which in turn comprises numerous varieties. If we abstract from all of these completely, a second proposition results, which enriches our first without adding anything new to it: sensation is experience of intensity and nothing besides. If we infer: experience of resistance is experience of intensity, this indeed seems plausible. For we can only ever compare two resistances as to their strength, and if we were to bring in some other distinguishing mark, we would have confused some incidental note with the resistances themselves. Only the comparison implicitly co-thought here actually carries us beyond "pure" sensation and lets us, as it were, already stumble at the threshold: a complete isolation of sensation cannot be carried out, because all lived experience, and hence sensation too, means a change of state, and in this way covertly includes within itself the moment of receptivity to a course of events. Although we for the present close ourselves off against such considerations, our proposition nonetheless says what matters to us. Were we on one occasion touched gently, on another struck violently, neither of the two would indeed become an experience for us without the co-experiencing of the change of state by which being-touched, as much as being-struck, stands out against the moment of life immediately preceding. Compared, however, with the changes of state we experience in passing from the impression of a blue to the impression of a red, it is the peculiarity of the former to be a change of degree of strength and nothing more — provided [p. 928] always that we hold strictly to the experience of resistance. — Our two doctrines, however, suggest yet a further inference, which follows at once if we cast their yield into the equation: experience of resistance = experience of intensity. For this states: not only is every experience of resistance an experience of intensity, but also every experience of intensity is an experience of resistance. The difference between weak and strong brightness, weak and strong noises, smells, temperatures — indeed in principle all contents of impression, insofar as they differ in strength — would be such a difference of degrees of strength of experienced resistances. We confine ourselves here to the dogmatic statement: so it really is. The grounds for this follow later in this chapter.

If I brace myself against a wardrobe in order to push it away, I experience, with regard to the wardrobe, its resistance, and with regard to myself, the strain or exertion directed against the wardrobe; in short: I experience the exercise of a pressure and the occurrence of a counter-pressure. If a heavy ball comes rolling toward me and I want to stop it, I experience the pressure of the ball and the counter-pressure of my hand. Thus our third proposition runs: sensation cannot be separated from the experience of the mutual working of pressure and counter-pressure. The disturbance or interruption of the state of life anticipated at the outset shows itself more sharply as a conflict of experience; hence our fourth doctrine runs: sensation includes within itself the experience of conflict (of two pressures, as it were, measuring themselves against one another). But if someone touches the back of my hand, as it lies on the table, with a forefinger, is the pressure there not felt purely "passively"? We avoid, for the time being, as far as we can, the names activity and passivity, because the feelings of meaning attached to them stand constantly ready to lure the hearer over to the side of spirit and to awaken the wholly misleading secondary thought of processes of will. Here, for the explanation of the matter, let it only be remarked that a being-pressed, in order to be an experience at all, presupposes in any case the capacity for the exercise of pressure and comprises within itself, at least "potentially," the counter-pressure, in the form of a feeling of tension. Without the feeling of tension with which the body-soul meets even the faintest pressure, the pressure would not become content of sensation.

While with our propositions so far we have sought to confine ourselves to the fact of sensing, with the propositions still to follow we shall not be able to avoid touching upon certain conditions of sensing. [p. 929] If one surveys the "theses" already to some extent grounded above, one is easily convinced that the process of sensing, as understood by us, demands the gift of self-movement ("self-movement" [Eigenbewegung] we use as synonymous with "self-motion" [Selbstbewegung], but we prefer "self-movement" for the very same reason for which we have avoided speaking of activity and passivity — namely in order to ward off a secondary thought that the prefix "self" might seem to license, the secondary thought of the sphere of effect of the I) on the part of the sensing being. Only insofar as I am in motion do I bump against the chair; only by mustering impulses do I press and push the wardrobe, do I hold back the ball rolling toward me; and only because I am capable of this do I answer the pressure that befalls a resting organ of my body with that feeling of tension by which alone it first comes to be sensed. Thus our fifth proposition runs: no sensing without self-movement, and conversely.

As certain as it is that a genuine and exceptionlessly valid reciprocity obtains here, according to which a being without self-movement also has no sensations, and a being incapable of sensation has no self-mobility, the examples we have adduced already show — and the behavior of the lowest living beings, to be discussed presently, shows fully — that originally, and, if one likes, genetically, the accent lies on self-mobility, which must therefore count as the ruling pole; wherefore the view that seeks to understand the animality of life out of its receptivities is fundamentally mistaken. In order to throw light more deeply into sensing, we must therefore fix our gaze more sharply upon self-movement. The name self-movement is indisputably deserved only by that movement from which the experience of the impulse to it cannot be separated. Since the drive-impulse was thoroughly discussed (Ch. 46), we content ourselves with merely citing again its most important features, but enrich them with others that have meanwhile become inferable from the nature of sensing. 1.

The drive-impulse is experienced as an impulse that seizes the bearer of the drive. 2. — The drive-impulse is a movement-impulse, more precisely an impulse: now to exchange the state of rest for that of movement, or that of movement for that of rest; now to accelerate the movement or [p. 930] to slow it down; now to change its direction; now to strengthen or loosen the state of clinging (say, to a surface). 3. — The drive-impulse is accordingly a directed impulse. 4. — Experienced drive-impulse and experienced connectedness with the goal of the impulse are two sides of the same thing. 5. — Without prejudice to essentially other features, one well-distinguishable side of every experience of impulse is the experience of suffering want. If, say through a change in the environment, the momentarily habitual or even the optimal circumstances of life alter — for instance as a result of cooling or warming — the self-mobile being lacks its habitual or most favorable life-space and may therefore take flight. A movement out of avoidance of occasions of disturbance does not differ in principle from a movement with which the self-being goes out after prey. — We remark in passing: even the experience of impulse that breaks forth from a state such as hunger can be grasped as the experience of an unsuitability of the surrounding medium: for it lacks, after all, that which would be capable of stilling the hunger! 6. — What we could earlier only hint at has now become essentially demonstrable: the experience of want becomes an experience of impulse only insofar as the bearer of life is capable of suffering a resistance from the life-space of the given moment; for the stimulus toward change proceeds only from that which resists — not indeed of scent or color or a sounding or a shining, but rather — of position, whereby the reciprocity of sensation and impulse emerges most sharply. (Those other processes are, in relation to the genuine impulse, accompanying phenomena of a special origin.) However much, then, the principal accent may originally fall on self-movement, it would nonetheless be unrealizable for a being without sensation. We may therefore, with full assurance, posit capacity for sensation wherever we encounter translatory self-mobility, and, equally, we may not posit it where translatory self-mobility is lacking. (Henceforth we always mean by self-movements movements of locomotion.) Only let the reader never forget that what hovers before us here are not the experiences that have hitherto been called "sensations"! For the occasion of genuine sensation, on the other hand, a name would recommend itself which we have with great decisiveness rejected for the occasion of sensory processes as such: the name stimulus, excitation, irritant. Stimuli understood in this way would accordingly differ from one another by nothing but strength, [p. 931] and the differences of strength would be nothing but differences in the strength of resistances suffered. From this it follows, among other things: those stimuli which, in relation to a song, certainly also occur when the song is heard, and in relation to a picture when the picture is seen — though for the most part only inferable — have no part whatsoever, none at all, in the occasions called song and called painting. 7. — If the resistance suffered is to form the stimulus to a change precisely of position, then the here-experience is lodged within the experience of resistance, and the movement-impulse would accordingly be the generative ground of a process that exchanges a momentary here for another here, whether through displacement of the resistance or, say, through flight.

In view of the full reciprocity of sensation and impulse, there must be, for every datum of impulse, a corresponding one in sensation. We had so far: sensation = experience of resistance = experience of intensity = experience of pressure and counter-pressure = experience of conflict; and we now add: with regard to the movement-process, without which sensation would not take place, the experience of resistance is a here-experience, and with regard to the conflict that lies within the experience of resistance, the here doubles itself into an acting here and a here that receives the effect, and thereby contains an indispensable precondition of the separation of the here from the there. We cast this into two doctrines. The sixth: sensation comprises within itself the here-experience. The seventh: sensation comprises within itself the condition of the separation of the here from the *there*. — Before we now draw from this important conclusions for the finding of the here (as also of the now) and bring to knowledge, from the state of experience that permits the genesis of a capacity for reflection, its most essential side, it seems fitting to us to soften the unusualness of our concept of sensation, and especially the unusualness of the asserted inseparability of sensing from the experience of impulse, by adducing some of the truly astonishing confirmations that fall to us from the behavior of so-called lowest animals.

We confine ourselves to three classes of single-celled organisms: the amoebas, belonging to the unshelled rootfooted animals (Rhizopoda), the bacteria, and the ciliate infusorians (Ciliata), and rely for this chiefly on Jennings's exemplary work on "Das Verhalten der [p. 932] niedersten Organismen" , from which in particular the quotations are<sup>29</sup> taken, except where the name of another author is given. The bacteria, which we bring in, incidentally, only in passing, are reckoned by numerous researchers among the plants and accordingly called Protophyta; but other researchers have agreed to regard the whole world of the Protista as a third kingdom below both animals and plants, which would thus offer, in relation to both animals and plants, their pre-forms. To this view, on the whole probably correct, we shall return in the chapter on the plant, but remark here already that the world of the Protista points more toward the animal branch on the tree of life than toward the vegetative one. It represents, all in all, a mighty — and perhaps premature — thrust toward awakening, and offers, even in microscopic minuteness, throughout the sight of that swarming mobility whose absence is the chief mark of plant-nature. Since we now discern the essence of animality in the never-to-be-separated pair of processes of sensation and self-movement, we must posit at least a preponderance of animal aliveness even where, given unquestionably self-mobile irritability, certain metabolic processes bear more the character of the vegetal, and we accordingly reckon, among other things, all spermatozoa, and likewise most bacteria, either simply among the animals or at least among the pre-forms of animality. — In order to come to the aid of the perhaps not few readers to whom the word protozoon (= single-celled animal) means little more than a name, we sketch in a few sentences what one is to think of thereby.

<sup>29</sup> On page 932. — Besides this outstanding work, in the German translation by Ernst Mangold (Teubner 1910), mention should also be made here of: J. von *Uexküll*, Umwelt und Innenwelt der Tiere (Springer 1921); further, insofar as one is concerned *only* with orientation: G. *Kafka*, Einführung in die Tierpsychologie, vol. 1, Die Sinne der Wirbellosen, Barth 1913. — Jennings, altogether the type of the naturalist in the old and best style, cannot be assigned to any -ism whatsoever and would in any case not count himself among the "Neo-vitalists." Von Uexküll has great merits in the founding of the school of thought just named and is distinguished by a rare originality of presentation, but unfortunately sails somewhat too much in the wake of Kant and Joh. von Müller for him not, after all, to be *more* of a mechanist than he himself knows or would admit. Thus he calls, for example, the sea urchin he examined so closely a "reflex republic"; against which Jennings objects as follows: "When the sea urchin is placed on its back, the ordinary reflexes and their stereotyped connections would not bring the animal back into its natural position, but would only cause it to crawl forward while lying on its back. What appears here, then, is once again the onset of a physiological state that triggers a profound change in the behavior of the spines. They now move in such a way as to turn the sea urchin back onto its ventral side... This adaptation of the spine movements, under extraordinary conditions, to the needs of the organism as a whole seems to abolish all fundamental differences between the behavior of the sea urchin and that of the higher animals."

The (microscopically small) amoeba "is a formless little lump of gelatinous protoplasm that constantly changes its shape as it creeps about the bottom of a pool amid the decaying remains of dead plant parts. From the main mass of the protoplasm, usually in the direction of locomotion, a number of lobe-shaped or pointed processes, the pseudopodia or false feet, are put forth .. and from time to time drawn in again and replaced by others." Although covered with a kind of exceedingly thin double skin (called ecto- and endoplasm, or ecto-and endosarc), which can open and close again at will, and displaying inside a mobile nucleus and a likewise mobile water-bladder (vacuole), the lump, otherwise appearing almost structureless, is nevertheless without interruption engaged in [p. 933] a flowing change of form. The absence of an organic axis forms a chief difference from the bacteria, which — living, as is well known, in masses in the products of putrefaction of organic substances — have definite shapes (egg-shaped, spherical, spiral, rod-shaped, curved, and so on), and further bear, either at both ends or at least at one end, protoplasmic appendages comparable to little whips (so-called flagella), and accordingly move forward in the direction of the long axis. The relatively more highly developed ciliate infusorians, finally, have, besides the fixed axis, also a fixed outer skin (ectoplasm), further a mouth-side (oral side) together with a back (aboral) side, and are moreover set all around with numerous mobile cilia. This should suffice for our purposes. We now line up, point by point, the evidence important for us. 1. The all-dominating self-movement. — The extent to which the amoeba is in unceasing change of form should become impressively clear to us when we hear that researchers who occupied themselves with it most exactly arrived at propositions such as the following: "The animal is an event" (Jennings), or: "Never does a stimulus strike the same animal twice" (von Uexküll). Among the actual movements one distinguishes, as has already been indicated, those of place and those at a place. Taking both together, it holds more or less of the Protozoa in general, but certainly of the ciliate infusorians, that although alternately now remaining still, now seeking a new location, now simply swarming about, they move without pause at their place. It is not probable, says Jennings, "that among infusorians periods of rest comparable to the sleep of higher animals alternate with periods of activity. Hodge and Aikins .. kept a single Vorticella under constant observation for 21 hours, besides the not uninterrupted study extending over several days; they were unable to observe any period of inactivity. During five days the cilia were continually in motion, food was constantly being taken in, and the contractions repeated themselves at short intervals" (p. 279). 2. Self-movement and experience of resistance. — If an amoeba adhering to its substratum is touched somewhere, with sufficient force, by the finely drawn-out tip of a small glass rod, it contracts at that point, [p. 934] gives up its hold on the substratum, alters its internal currents, and moves in a direction leading away from the source of stimulation. If the moving amoeba encounters some resting, resisting something, it will now flow around it and thereby avoid it, now also attach itself firmly to it and, in the case say of a surface suited to it, usually creep along it. — If a moving bacterium collides with an obstacle, a reversal of the direction of movement follows — absolutely so on the part of those bacteria that bear flagella at both ends, whereas on the part of those with only a single flagellum there follows a brief backward movement and thereupon a forward movement again, though in a changed direction. — Among the infusorians, the particularly precisely investigated ciliate Paramecium is engaged predominantly in translatory movement. If it strikes an obstacle with its front side, or is struck there by a blow, it responds by reversing the beat of its cilia, with immediate backward movement, swings itself round in a circle with its front end at some distance from the source of stimulation, thereby, with the help of the ciliary eddy, as it were trying out the surroundings, and then swims forward in the direction found to be least disturbing. This is called the "negative" or "flight reaction"; of the possible "positive" ones, more presently. — The connection of self-movement and experience of resistance (= sensation) should already be unambiguously established by this, but is raised fully beyond any doubt by the circumstance — probably valid for all animal single-celled organisms and certainly demonstrable without exception for Paramecium — that the answering movements occur more easily, more quickly, and more strongly when the moving, rather than the resting, animal suffers the disturbing stimulus. — By this alone it would be shown, even were it not confirmed by all the data, that all movements of animal single-celled organisms are spontaneous movements and by no means, say, reflexes! ("Reflex movements" = stereotyped answers to stimuli, occur only, and indeed exclusively, among the more highly developed multicellular organisms with superordinate and subordinate apparatuses.) 3. First approach to the localization of stimuli. — The resistance could not lead to a change of position were the process through which it is experienced not also, at the same time, an experience of the here. For with the answering functions so far appreciated, a disturbing here is indeed exchanged for a less disturbing here; hence they have fittingly also been christened "avoidance reactions." The discord lying within the experience of resistance thereby becomes [p. 935] the experienced duality of an acting here and a here that receives the effect, of which now the one, now the other indicates the alien existence, and each time the other the own existence. For the single-celled organism in motion, the effect-exercising alien existence is the exceedingly minute cut-out portion of surface with which it comes into contact, and the effect-receiving own existence could coincide with the whole body of the, after all, microscopic being; since this itself would then correspond to the here. Yet already at the very lowest stage a difference of place in irritability appears, whereby, beyond all expectation, the here-nature of a content of experience proves itself, which, scarcely being there at all, already serves the localization of the stimulus.

The amoeba has, it is true, no structural axis, but it does have a functional one in the direction of the self-movement currently taking place. It can transform its functional front end instantaneously into a functional rear end by reversing the internal plasma current and thereby the direction of movement; but the functional front end answers the mechanical disturbance-stimulus in a way well distinguishable from the functional rear end. For whereas disturbance at the front end is followed promptly by contraction, disturbance at the rear end results chiefly in acceleration of the forward movement. — The ciliate infusorian Paramecium, equipped with a fixed axis, behaves in principle exactly the same way; only the difference in irritability between front and back now appears far more distinctly and shows itself especially in a considerably higher receptivity to stimuli at the front end. We may state with certainty: notwithstanding the microscopic smallness of the infusorian, its experience of here-in-front differs from its experience of here-behind! 4. Experience of resistance as experience of intensity. — Intensification of the mechanical disturbance brings about, within certain limits, an intensification of the answering movement of the single-celled organism. Even the ever-mobile Paramecium comes occasionally to rest on a stationary surface of suitable character, but avoids the mechanical impact unconditionally through the flight reaction, and indeed, according to the strength of the impact, with very different degrees of liveliness, ranging from mere cessation of the forward movement, through inconsiderable backward movement, through several intermediate stages, up to complete rotation of the animal's long axis about the axis perpendicular to it — whereby at times an immediate turning away from the cause of the stimulus results. — Another ciliate infusorian, the so-called blue Stentor, shaped like a small funnel, usually attaches itself with its tip, by forming [p. 936] a little tube, to shaded spots, if possible on the bottom, and, by constant beating of its cilia, whirls water together with particles of food into its mouth-side, which opens upward. If the animal now receives a mechanical blow on the mouth-side, or is sprayed with a strong jet of water, it withdraws by immediate contraction into its tube; if, on the other hand, one introduces into the current of the nutrient water only a cloud of fine and, of course, far more weakly stimulating carmine granules, the animal contents itself with merely turning away, thus now assuming a slanted position relative to its location. — We may spare ourselves further examples, since on this side of the matter there does not appear to be any disagreement among researchers. 5. The impulse to searching movement. — On the occasion of the survey, offered once more above, of the principal characteristic features of the drive-impulse, the state of suffering want was adduced as a co-cause of it and discussed conclusively under 5, to the effect that, with regard to it, the movement of impulse could be understood as a process by whose help the bearer of the process escapes an environment that is in some way inadequate. It certainly says no little for the cogency of this train of thought when so exceedingly cautious a researcher as Jennings, to whom our conceptual apparatus is entirely unknown, arrives at the result that, in all likelihood, every movement of impulse is negative. The reflective examination of the whole body of observational material leads him to the following statement: "While the negative reaction is occasioned by new unfavorable conditions, in the endeavor to retain the more advantageous, old state, the positive reaction is released by the old, unfavorable state, in the endeavor to hold fast the new, more favorable one" (p. 464). Further: "The change of behavior rests in every case, in the first instance, on the unfavorable condition, whether of an inner or an outer kind." And: "The positive thus proves to be a secondary result of negative reactions" (p. 488).

This would indeed hold true if the movement of impulse were nothing other than the realization of a need, that is, of a tension arising from suffering want; since, however, this is never solely the case, and at times predominantly *not* the case, it is a fallacy, as can readily be shown *also* from the single-celled organisms. First it is evident: not even the difference of the greater disturbance from the lesser disturbance, let alone that of the less favorable from the more favorable, would be experienced at all unless the attainment of the less-disturbing were accompanied, just as certainly, by an increase of well-being [p. 937] as, on the assumed premise, the intensification of disturbance is by an increase of ill-being. Furthermore, numerous facts leave not the slightest doubt that, already for the self-mobile single-celled organism, certain contacts represent an optimum whose value of satisfaction it does not draw *solely* from the alternation of circumstances, and which is accordingly, as soon as it announces itself, sought, or at any rate can be sought. This holds of the amoeba's encounter with the resistance that signifies the euglena-cyst serving it as food (which it flows around with its pseudopodia and incorporates, and pursues stubbornly should it slip away again); it holds further, at times, of two conjugating paramecia, and shows itself especially in the fact that their sensitivity to stimuli can be lowered even beyond the measure that generally prevails in the interference of occasions of experience. — Meanwhile, this much remains true: that in the experience of resistance alone the condition of the searching movement could never lie! Since the researcher is involuntarily guided by the thought of stimulation and considers self-movement *only* in relation to it, he has, without intending it, furnished us a contribution to the characterization of the process of sensing, insofar as one dissects it out of the greater whole of life, apart from which it nowhere occurs.

We have set this forth elsewhere, and wish here only briefly to repeat, why every experience of intensity, on whatever sensory field, is never anything other than the experience of resistance. If I listen to a song, my experiential content is the song, and in no way my organ of hearing; if I behold a landscape painting, my experiential content is the landscape painting, and in no way my organ of sight. But if a pistol is fired close beside my ear, two experiential contents separate from one another, linked almost only by simultaneity: the bang and a painful sensation in the ear; and if at high-summer noon I look with unprotected eyes into the sun, there likewise separate from one another: the intuitive image of the sun and a stabbing sensation in the eye. If now, as we know, any sensory impression whatever can be intensified to the point of painfulness, then the disturbing resistance lies within every sensory impression as a component, even though it becomes noticeable only when it more or less predominates in relation to the component of beholding; from which it at once becomes clear why, under otherwise similar circumstances, it emerges more decisively in the near senses of touch and [p. 938] taste, thanks to their overemphasized sensitivity to stimuli of contact, warmth, and cold, than in the middle sense of smell, and fully more than in the distance senses of hearing and sight. Were one to point, against this, to the lack of depthmobility in the organs of smell, hearing, and sight, we would have to recall once more that the corporeality common to all organs comprises changing states of tension, and thus the possibility of experiencing occasions of disturbance even *without* actual counter-movement.

It follows self-evidently from our exposition that not only tactile stimuli, warmth stimuli, cold stimuli, heat stimuli, and pain stimuli are qualitatively different from one another, but also that tactile stimuli differing in location are qualitatively different among themselves, and likewise with respect to the remaining kinds of stimuli. In particular the specific multiplicity of possible experiences of pain is extraordinarily great. Not without purpose, and not in vain either, have neurophysiologists therefore taken pains to ascertain special receptor organs for the sensory fields just indicated, and, where possible, to distinguish them again from the receptor organs for experiences of pressure. But this does not affect the fact that experiences of pressure, wherever they occur, and they alone *only*, display differences of degree, that in principle all external organs are capable of reporting experiences of pressure, and that their intensification always issues in the end in experiences of pain. The exceptional cases are, for the science of life, without significance. Thus we are dealing, emphatically, with life-processes by which the bearer of life enters into connection with an outside, and we need not therefore concern ourselves with the circumstance that certain internal organs, through mere intensification of pressure, are scarcely or not at all accessible to the experience of pain. Just as little need it trouble us if, as a result of certain lesions of the nervous system, whose effect can also be artificially induced, sensitivity to pain fails wholly or in part (analgesia); for what occupies us is the nature of life-processes and not their pathology.

Against this, we must bring the enumerated circles of experience into a far more intimate connection with one another, and especially with the experience of pressure, than any one of them with, say, seeing or hearing or even smelling. For it was not by chance that they were all gathered together under the concept of the "skin senses"! They share, namely, with one another the capacity to let us experience, not only the occasion of excitation, but together with it — now sharply and distinctly, now at least vaguely — the region of one's own body [p. 939] at which the exciting agent attacks. They impart to us, without exception, among other things, changes of state of our corporeal being, since, for instance, *even* the experience of cold or the experience of heat can rise to the point of painfulness without its content changing to the degree that it would, under similar circumstances, in the case of a visual experience. On this account let it be permitted to gather together the rich apparatuses which underlie them in the highly developed organism as sensible provisions, and to set them over against the sensory apparatuses to which we owe visual experiences, auditory experiences, olfactory experiences, qualitative experiences of taste, and finally the qualitative element of all sense-experiences. If we now do this, we find our main result mirrored, neurophysiologically, in the fact that the sensible receptor organs are distributed, more or less, over the whole surface of the body, in very different densities to be sure, while the sensory receptor organs are confined to narrow regions of the surface. The former, though never without a specific exponent, report to the bearer of life above all his own body and, so to speak, lift him out of the whole of the world; the latter, though for their part also receptive of degree, report to him predominantly intuitive images, and thus a universe which, in and for itself, does not concern his body at all. For the former the experience of resistance holds good for us as the model; for the latter, the experience of quality as such.

Just as resistance, now, can only be increased or diminished, so the process of sensation harbors only the material for the distinction of degrees, which strike us as something qualitative merely because they fuse, in the sense-experience (and indeed already in that of touch), with intuitive images. Intuitive images are embodiments of formed qualities. If we distinguish in them, so far as language permits, specific kinds such as redness and blueness, noises and sounds, tones of differing pitch, the scent of roses and the smell of petrol, sweetness and bitterness, inviting warmth and prickling cold, and so forth, then none of these would have generated the concept of degree, were it to become an experience for itself; for which, indeed, we would either have to lack wakefulness or be woven out of the illusory material of mirror-images. Since, however, we live as embodied souls in the midst of *corporeal* appearances, every impression whatsoever is accompanied by an alteration of one's own body, now barely noticeable, now extremely violent, whose gradable occasions flow together for us with the intuitive images, on the occasion of which they [p. 940] become effective. Thus we transfer gradability onto features of appearance and have, with the concept of differences of degree of brightness, loudness, sweetness, bitterness, saltiness, warmth, cold, and so on, established the apparatus for measuring — seemingly of "image-properties," but in truth of resistant corporealities that are indicated to us through qualities. Here lies the vital source of comparison as such — One need only, however, bring it to decisive preponderance in order to demonstrate with examples that it is *not* the process of beholding but the process of sensation bound up with it in which alone the idea of intensity and the concept of degree are rooted.

Let us, for example, keep precisely to the two senses whose receptive range, thanks to an overemphasized gift of beholding, extends the farthest — hearing and sight — and let us not stay too close to what is no longer audible or no longer visible; then, from an excessively increasing intensification of degree, the auditory image as well as the visual image is threatened with — destruction. Above the experience of piercing brightness in the eye that I suffer from the unclouded midday sun when I look into it, I lose — as one "dazzled" — more or less the intuitive image of the sun; above the experience of pain in the ear, the intuitive image of the nearby cannon-blast. Each time there still remains an outside, there remains an alienated existence of even fearful irresistibility; but the visualizability of this outside vanishes with the degree of intrusiveness of that existence, until, at the extreme force of the attacking impact, it is at least practically extinguished. If the intuitive image is originally an appearance of essence, then degrees of strength increased to the limit of tolerability leave nothing else of its character but what it has in common with any occasion of violent flight-impulses. Since with this a huge overemphasis of the pole that receives the effect over the pole that exerts it necessarily connects itself, the double experience of alien and own existence passes more and more into the essentially different duality according to which the soul suffers the pain of its body, and in the end not only the intuitive image but the outside itself languishes away; whereby one would, in the science of appearance, even build a bridge from violent pain to "unconsciousness" (cf. p. 267).<sup>30</sup> Whoever properly considers this will henceforth scarcely find it comprehensible how one could fail to recognize the duality of the components in the sensory process and undertake the attempt to compose beholding out of experiences which, given sufficient intensification, destroy every intuitive image.

<sup>30</sup> On page 940. — It is a fact well known in linguistics and often pointed out, that such adverbs as are used for intensification also mean, or originally meant, something *painful*. A typical case: the little word "sehr" ["very"], whose Middle High German form sêre means "painful" (alongside the adjective ser = injured and the noun ser = injury, pain; still preserved in sehren and versehren ["to injure"]). Such a linguistic usage would be highly peculiar, indeed inexplicable, were it not for the connection we have uncovered: intensifiability as such resting on the intensifiability of intensity; original intensity = perceptible pressure; increase of pressure to the highest degree = pain. A few examples! One has been *arg* [badly] or *schrecklich* [terribly] glad, *ungeheuer* [monstrously] amused, has had *furchtbaren* [frightful] fun, laughed *höllisch* [hellishly] (indeed even "died laughing"); someone is *entsetzlich* [dreadfully] boring or *verdammt* [damned] clever, *schauderhaft* [horribly] stupid, *greulich* [gruesomely] talkative, and so on. Because the primal superlative is felt bodily pain, linguistic instinct chooses names for what is adverse in order to designate high degrees, be it even of pleasure!

[p. 941] From everything that has been communicated concerning single-celled organisms, it emerged convincingly that, for the sake of sensing resistances of differing strength and for the sake of answering them with self-movements of differing strength, nothing even remotely comparable to a nervous system is needed. If it is now correct, what we believe we have found through the splitting of our experience — namely that the degree-sensitive component vibrates along in all sensory processes — then beings sensitive to resistance without nerves would have to be able to answer differences of intensity of any source of stimulus whatever with self-movements of differing strength. Now, that is in fact the case. However meager the evidence may be, which out of a great abundance we must content ourselves with singling out, it should suffice for confirmation.

The amoeba shows extraordinary sensitivity to diffusing chemicals and reacts with flight of differing strength to solutions of differing strength of methylene blue, common salt, sodium carbonate, hydrochloric acid, acetic acid, cane sugar, and so on. Spirilla (a kind of bacterium) gather where the slightest quantities of oxygen diffuse in the water, for instance at green diatoms and algae, and answer at the boundary of the most favorable zone with a reversal of movement.<sup>31</sup> Other bacteria avoid oxygen and prefer weak saline solutions, but flee from strong ones. Those that split carbonic acid react positively to moderate brightness, negatively to shading. The infusorian Paramaecium, whose optimal temperature lies between 22 and 28°, answers at the upper limit an increase of temperature with flight, whose liveliness increases with the strength of the warming; at the lower limit likewise a decrease of temperature, only proportionately less lively — If it emerges predominantly from the preceding examples that sensitivity exists for heat-stimuli, light-stimuli, and chemical stimuli generally, the following shows us drastically the operative capacity of degrees of strength. Most infusorians manifest, for stimuli of any kind, a greater sensitivity of the forward end, and this allows us to carry out, with the Stentor already known to us, an astonishing experiment. If the whole vessel is illuminated from one side, with an otherwise uniform distribution of brightness, then in a short time all the Stentors have turned their front side away from the light source and have swum to the side opposite it, exactly as if they could see — in truth, however, because the more sensitive mouth-side only comes into the position to be permanently maintained at the least attainable illumination: truly a wonderful proof of the fineness of the sensed differences of intensity! [p. 942] Finally, all Rhizopoda and Infusoria answer such periodic vibrations of the surrounding medium as signify tones to us, within relatively narrow limits of the number of vibrations, partly with contractions of differing strength of the pseudopodia, partly with acceleration of differing strength of the beating of the cilia.

<sup>31</sup> On page 941. — The process unfolds more precisely as follows: the bacteria swim into the favorable zone without any change of reaction, but then rebound at its boundary and are thus, as it has aptly been put, "caught" within the zone. This mode of reaction characterizes, more or less, the behavior of *all* Protozoa. Here the minuteness of the *smallest* stimuli still responded to exceeds, in numerous cases, our power of comprehension. According to the calculations of *Engelmann*, Bacterium termo still reacts to the hundred-billionth part of a milligram of oxygen, and is therefore occasionally used for the detection of minimal quantities of oxygen that could no longer be demonstrated by chemical means. — According to investigations by *Pfeffer* on bacteria (but also by other researchers on Infusoria), the behavior of these unicellular organisms obeys the Weber approximation law, which concerns the ratio of stimulus increments to sensation increments. Thus, for example, in Bacterium termo the concentration of a solution of meat extract must always be increased fivefold before a reaction occurs!

It is not these facts alone — meager indeed in number and kind — but many others besides, that prompted a Jennings to utterances such as: "All kinds of stimuli that act upon the nervous system and the sense-organs can just as well affect the protoplasm without these organs"; or: even in an animal that possesses a nervous system, "the possibility always remains open that the rest of the protoplasm, by virtue of its own capacities, carries out the action in question." But apart from that, let one consider: there are beings without the power of sight, of hearing, of smell, of taste, even without our power of touch, but animally living beings, and accordingly thoroughly endowed with sensitivity, and this eyeless and earless sensitivity enables them to answer, with locomotions of differing strength, not merely tactile stimuli but also light-stimuli, tone-stimuli, chemical stimuli, temperature-stimuli — in short, in principle all stimuli which we have grown accustomed to assign now to five, now to six, now to seven different sensory domains! Can any doubt still prevail, in view of this, that the sensitivity in question has not the least to do with a so-called specific sensory energy, but betrays the most general receptivity of self-moving living matter, and consequently can be present *without* a developed sensorium, although the latter can in no case exist without it!

It seems to us that only deep-rooted prejudice can block the way to the insight, now lying open to the day, that sensitivity does not inhere in any special sense but belongs rather to the animal protoplasm itself, and then, indeed, after it has, in the richly articulated organism, predominantly taken sensible conducting pathways into its service, serves the excitations of the sensorium merely as support and platform for the purpose of localizing the intuitive images, and thus takes part in every sense-experience, though overemphasized in the domain of touch, underemphasized in the domain of hearing and seeing. The general recognition of the foregoing propositions is merely a question of time, provided only that, once it is "due," one has not already ceased to think about such matters. — [p. 943] We now, however, turn back and reinsert the process of sensation, which we had artificially isolated, into the larger context of life, without which it would not be capable of subsisting. We have spoken of the experience of resistance, of the experience of intensity, of the experience of conflict, of the experience of pressure and counter-pressure, of the experience of alien and own existence, but we have avoided as far as possible drawing in corporeality, and we must now make up for this: that not only no corporeality, but, strictly speaking, not even the outside could be experienced, and thus not the duality either, which is indeed laid out in the experience of resistance, were sensation to exist entirely by itself. Beneath it too lies the effecting-beholding state, already elucidated by the example of the vegetal form of life, and the state of self-moving irritability cannot pair with it without at least some approach, however weak, to the development of the gift of intuition. Since we are just now at the single-celled organisms, let us point at once to a few unappreciated features of the facts adduced, which would not be intelligible from the experience of strength alone, and let us append a few kindred occurrences that have been deliberately passed over. 1. *Receptivity* for specific differences. — Already the fact that for every species of single-celled organism there is a most favorable zone of concentrations, temperatures, light-experiences speaks for the first beginning of the experiencing of qualities. We recognize it more clearly when Paramaecium does *not* come to rest at a glass surface, but does at the fibrous surface of decaying plants, whose bacteria serve it as food, and we become certain of it when we hear that the same result is also achieved with non-nutritive surfaces to which a similar looseness has been given. The experience of similarity — inherent in beholding just as much as the experience of intensity is inherent in sensing — makes possible the transformation of beholding into a vicarious intuiting and forms, for its occurrence, the infallible criterion, when, as here, self-movement is co-determined by similar impressions. One notices, moreover, easily (what we have grounded more deeply earlier) that *without* the experience of similarity qualities would not be distinguished and then, of course, would not have been experienced at all either. We have the essentially identical case when all bacteria that are accustomed to live in weakly saline solutions of decaying vegetable matter are captivated by the likewise similar medium of weak solutions of the salts of [p. 944] rubidium, cesium, lithium, which are foreign to their natural habitat (Pfeffer); or when, by all single-celled organisms, nutrients are quite unmistakably distinguished from others by the kind of reactions. Amoeba terricola answers with immediate opening in the ectoderm the chemical stimulus *only* of such substances as serve it for food. Amoeba proteus flows around and devours the Oscillaria filament nourishing to it, but not indifferent bodies. — If one brings purple bacteria, which require illumination and therefore prefer bright places in the water to dark ones, into the color-band of a spectrum, they gather in the ultra-red and orange-yellow (while avoiding the other colors), notwithstanding that in nature they could never before have tested such distinctions. Each time, here, the feeling of life has reached a decision whose ground of occasion must be sought in its component that is no longer merely degree-estimating but receptive of kind. 2. Voluptuous pleasure and pain. — Here we may be brief, since the essential point was stated above, when we rejected the opinion that on the level of single-celled organisms there is only a mobility of flight and not also a mobility of seeking. The one is as inseparable from the other as the diminution of ill-being cannot be separated from the increase of well-being; and in this, finally, lies grounded that polarity of the behavior of single-celled organisms which gave occasion to the hopeless talk of countless "tropisms." Now, however, let one note: it is not to the apparent opposition, named in psychology as pleasure and unpleasure, but to the genuine polarity of voluptuous pleasure and pain, that the opposition here in mind is the beginning — which, to be sure, taken as a magnitude of difference, may represent, of the magnitude of difference of both ends in *us*, only the billionth fraction, and therefore withdraws from all "imaginability." The apparent opposition of pleasure and unpleasure means the arbitrarily divisible and arbitrarily extendable series of feelings of success from extremely violently disturbed to extremely little disturbed; the genuine polarity of voluptuous pleasure and pain means two polar states of the body corresponding to one another, or more precisely of the body-soul, of which the one binds and isolates one's own essence within its living space, the other releases it and fuses it with its living space; hence a being that did nothing but sense would be capable of neither. 3. The spatiotemporality of experiencing. — However a space of movement may relate to a space of intuition, in any case the following stands firm: if locomotion cannot take place without the impulse to it, then also [p. 945] not without an experience of movement, and if it is accordingly an experienced locomotion, then in it and with it a space of movement must also have been experienced. We hold this to be a logically incontestable conclusion. But whoever, with the aid of the excellent illustrations, immerses himself in the descriptions that a Jennings offers of the manner of movement of single-celled organisms — comparing, for instance, Amoeba proteus to a prey-hunting beast of prey, indeed to some extent equating it — will scarcely trouble his thinking further, because he grasps, as it were, with his hands, that here experiences of movement take place with almost all the peculiarities that we ourselves know from such experiences — for instance the cautious stopping before a body which, violently rushed at, slips away, and the accelerated hastening after it, once it has slipped away! But if experiences of movement take place, then a space of movement is co-experienced in them; for which, again, a being that did nothing but sense would be incapable. If one asks what such a space of movement might look like, then for all single-celled organisms the difference of front from back would have to be established; for infusorians, the beginning of a co-participation of the difference of right and left, while that of above from below only comes into play with lower Metazoa.

The having-been-experienced of a space of movement, however, further includes in itself the having-been-experienced of a time of movement. For in the experience of movement the state just beginning signifies, in relation to the state just passing away, no longer mere change as such, but a phenomenon of succession. We must therefore posit memory, and indeed not merely the so-called memory of all that is vegetative, but genuine memory of impression, according to which the behavior of the moment is guided by preceding impressions. For this, now, apart from the experience of movement, so much evidence can be adduced that here a single instance must suffice us in place of all others. Faced with the carmine cloud that continually molests its mouth-side, the sessile Stentor runs through the following series of forms of behavior: turning aside — turning aside again, until the mouth-side has described a complete circle, and this several times over — ejection of the granules by reversal of the ciliary beat — withdrawal of the whole animal into the root-tube — renewed extension, but now immediate contraction — extension-contraction once more, but in successively longer pauses — finally (after about 15 minutes) detachment from its place and flight. The behavior of each moment is thus co-determined by the change that a previous behavior and its previous behavior, and so on, has effected, and since now each of these behaviors was an answer to something sensed [p. 946], past impressions weave into the behavior of the given present; whereby the temporality of experiencing as such is established once and for all for the level of single-celled organisms. Capacity for habituation to new environmental conditions, capacity for the practicing-in of the "most purposeful" reaction, in short, regular capacity for learning, already belongs to the lowest amoebae. — Concerning the spatiotemporal character of experiencing, no doubt can prevail.

Only, in order to round off the single-cell interlude somewhat, let us indicate in a few sentences what follows, for the overall view of the life-forms of the animal, from the connection of these three features of the beginning of animal life with self-moving irritability. The receptivity for kind discussed under 1 is not sensitivity, because qualities are not sensed; the polarity discussed under 2 merely brings to bear the exponent of that which originally halves them all into: an attracting and a repelling, a gladdening and an adverse, a dissolving of one's own form and a hardening of it — thus marking the beginning of the appearance of two mutually hostile series of beings. (The neutral forms, between the two, a zone of indifference that for the animal is as good as nonexistent.) With the spatiotemporality discussed under 3, the medium is, so to speak, named, without which qualities as well as intensities would remain in eternal concealment: the resisting would not become, for the bearer of life, an experience of the outside, and the state of tension manifesting itself in the impulse, lacking direction, would not become an impulse of movement. But the life-medium, which we must add to self-moving irritability in order for it to become actual, is now of such extraordinary nearness and narrowness that concepts like intuition and appearance find application to it only theoretically and could in no case support the attempt at sensualization. In particular, "intuition" here means *not* that any experience of the initial stage has the slightest similarity to the experiences that are mediated by a developed sensorium. There is no seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, and touching there, but there are changing attitudes, experienced as changing, through which the organism enters into connection with a resisting outside of changing specificity. And here we recall the overemphasized self-mobility and conclude from it: of the two poles of vegetal life, the pole of sleeping working and the pole of sleeping beholding, it is the pole of sleeping working that in the animal kingdom [p. 947] first awakens, or at least manifests greater wakefulness than the beholding pole. But if, in ascending the ladder of development, we can also distinguish an immensely numerous series of stages of becoming-awake and must accordingly posit an ever more widely reaching gift of intuition, still the succession continues, *right up* to the beginning of humanity, in exactly the direction indicated with the protozoon. As surely as, in the soul of the animal, beholding is led by the hand by sensing, so surely is the beholding pole determined by the working pole in the living body of the animal.<sup>32</sup>

<sup>32</sup> On page 947. — Finally, a word on the relation of unicellular to multicellular organisms. Whether the latter arose phylogenetically from the former remains doubtful. Although irritable self-movement may, in principle, extend over every sensory domain for both groups, the species-specific receptivities nonetheless diverge widely in part. Not only does there exist in unicellular organisms a degree of sensitivity to chemical stimuli to which not even our tasting and smelling would offer an analogue; the qualities to which they respond also point at times to a sense of world wholly incomprehensible to us. The phenomenologist is not helped by being told by the natural scientist that ultraviolet and yellow-orange provide the purple bacteria with the most favorable conditions for their metabolic processes; for the circumstance, astonishing to him, of the absence of all color for a being that nonetheless responds precisely to yellow-orange and to a region beyond the spectrum with an immediate change of posture, has thereby lost nothing of its problematic character. Were someone to speculate on what the sensory life of beings must be like in which the sensory life of the Protozoa had become differentiated and heightened, he would scarcely find his way to the sensorium of the mammals! Only one thing certainly connects the two: locomotion responding to specific differences in a resisting outside world.

In now turning back to human experiencing, let us first recall that it was shown, from the behavior of protoplasm, that the here in the content of sensation would not become the sensed here, or would remain, in other words, merely a disposition toward the here, given a complete absence of the spatiotemporal character of what is experienced. — Whereas earlier we developed intuiting out of original beholding, grounded the mirror-nature of sense-space, showed in it the source of presentness, and finally, having already gone far into the process by which intuitive images become independent, had to convince ourselves that they lure us over into the lifediluted state of looking-on, which the spirit, once it had broken the cell open, could and had to use in order to substitute for the omnipresence of hollowed-out forms (eide) the extratemporality of concepts (ideai) — we now arrive at the same point from exactly the opposite side, in attempting to set forth that the disturbance of experiencing by the resisting here forms the reverse side of the state of looking-on, and affords the spirit the fulcrum from which alone that opening of the cell could succeed. Although, in doing so, the emphasis naturally falls on the process of the embodiment of appearance, which indeed predominates over beholding throughout the whole animal world, still every clarification will also help toward the solution of the question how corporeality can appear. So that the reader, however, may know, in everything he hears further on this subject, without any particular effort of memory, in which region of the whole work he currently finds himself, and may be able to establish its "position" as if with the aid of a map, we reproduce verbatim from the first volume a few sentences that point to what is still unfinished, and append each time what tasks are thereby set for us. Beholding — Intuition — Sensation. "As surely as a body without a soul would no longer be a living body, so surely must the psychic sense-process of beholding participate in the bodily sense- [p. 948] process of sensing, if the latter is to deserve the name of life-process at all. The third process, therefore to be inserted, in which the two fuse with one another, now presents itself differently, however, thanks to its participation in sensing, and again differently thanks to its participation in beholding. According to the former we had to investigate the conditions under which corporeality is experienced in images; according to the latter, the conditions under which the unintuitable happening appears, or, then, the conditions of the transformation of beholding as such into an ever more corporeally underbuilt intuiting" (p. 199). It was investigated, we continue, and led nearly to its end, the participation of intuiting in beholding, its emergence from the latter, and its difference from sensing; it is *still* being investigated, insofar as this has not already occurred meanwhile, the participation of intuiting in sensing, and likewise conversely, and with this it is being brought to the final possible clarification, in what respect the appearance of actuality, in contrast, for instance, to mere dream-appearance, is always a "corporeally underbuilt" appearance. Sense-space and *place*. "Without sense-space, no place, and without place, no thing: therein it is expressed that one basis of life for the finding of the thing is the experience of space, the other the experience of place. The latter marks, in the capacity for impression, the bodily side, the former the psychic side, and it is this latter that we shall for the present investigate on its own" (p. 308). The genesis of the space of intuition was investigated; the genesis of place within space is still being investigated, insofar as this has not already occurred meanwhile. Concept and thing. "The timelessness of the general concepts proper to things demands, however, relatedness to the thing, which is for its part related to space and time; hence, in relation to original beholding, the overemphasis of making-present forms only the complementary reverse side to the overemphasis of embodying — no longer, however, as with animals, in the service of the finding of the body, but of the positing of local fixed points for the universals, which are otherwise no longer capable of a home in the totality of appearance!" (p. 387). It was investigated how the conceptualization of the world of intuition was supported by a vital disturbance of equilibrium, which might be called, most briefly, the emancipation of making-present from original beholding; it is still being investigated how the other disturbance of equilibrium, namely in the drive-system, which we came to know [p. 949] on the occasion of the analysis of willing, furthers the (relative) emancipation of sensing from beholding, and thereby brings about *the* state in which the immediate ground of the possibility of the occurrence of spiritual acts must be sought.

Of these three citations, the most important — and the others more or less comprehensive under it — is the one named last, which indeed by no means makes the intuitive image dependent on the contents of sensation, but does make the finding of intuitive images dependent on the finding of their corporealities. If, now, in relation to happening, the space of intuition means the now, and in relation to the space of intuition the content of sensation means a here, then our first step toward verifying the dependency in question will consist in the demonstration of processes through which the now enters into connection with an, in each case, more or less point-like here. — That at least in some indication a sense-space must be experienceable, in order for the here-sensation to be able to take place, need not be said again. But if the space of intuition is available, be it only in the form of a co-experienced space of movement, then a given present here becomes a place upon it, or, more briefly, a place, and from it any other place whatsoever would be separated not so much spatially as rather temporally, because it would become present at another time. That, however, is originally always, and at least predominantly, altogether the case where one is confined to the domain of experience of touch. The behavior of translationally moving single-celled organisms has convinced us that the distance of one here-place from a second here-place wants to be understood from the standpoint of the path-line of an experienced movement, and thus of temporal succession. This, however, is made fully clear to us precisely by a glance at the spiritual acts which, in the developed capacity for reflection, would be occasioned by such data of experience.

If I press the palm of my hand against the tabletop, I require two acts of apprehension in order to note: on the one hand the here at the tip of the index finger, on the other the here at the tip of the little finger, and these two acts are separated from one another by an interval of time, however tiny. What helps us, then, toward the formation of a tactile space is a succession of here-places, and we would doubtless have to marvel at how a side-by-side could ever arise from this, did we not consider that the succession in question is peculiarly different from the succession of such sequences of occurrences of which the [p. 950] one goes when the other comes. I can wander in spirit from the found here at the index finger to the found here at the little finger, and again from the here at the little finger to the here at the index finger, without anything thereby being changed in the position of the one here in relation to the other here; but the before of the first "wandering" would thereby have become the after of the second, and there would thus be distinguished, in the sharpest way, from the irreversible direction of succession of time, one reversible as often as I merely wished, which would thereby become for me the direction of space. It is not, however, this long-known and often appreciated fact that is of importance to us, but the circumstance that, accordingly, the sensible side-by-side of tactile space comes about only through the mediation of the quasi-sensible succession of here-impressions, or more precisely thanks to the inner movement that we experience in passing over from the touched here to the touched there. For the present, however, it is the connection of the here with the now that occupies us, and not yet the experience of movement.

Our sixth theorem ran: sensation comprises within it the experience of the here. We have meanwhile learned: the experience of the here would not become actual and would be no experience of the here at all without the availability of a sense-space. We have further learned: the availability of a sense-space includes within it that of a sense-time. If we transfer this to the experience of the here, it follows: it is always a now-here experience. As surely as we could experience no now at all, did not every available sense-space carry the exponent of presentness, so surely does the now first detach itself from the course of happening and become independent in relation to it, in that it also lifts itself out of the space of intuition through connection with that place of space upon which, in accordance with the here-experience, the high accent of being-present falls. Or: the here-experience is at the same time a now-experience, because the sense-space, with respect to which it is an experience of place, has the character of presentness; *and* but also: the now-experience is at the same time a here-experience, because only on the occasion of the experienced place of space does being-present first of all become, originally, an experience. Since, now, the here can change arbitrarily and does in fact constantly change for the organism that is in motion, and with it also the now, the now thereby *detaches* itself from space, which, as against it, sets about to signify a perennial now, or that well-known "always" of ours, which by degrees leads to real-space and finally [p. 951] to the metric space of Euclid. — We now know why the now connects itself with the here, and we have thereby already, without saying so, expressed that the now-here-place further forms the fulcrum for the sense-space itself, and thus, indeed, in some respect still to be more precisely determined, for the entire world of intuitive images; but we surmise for the present only how the now-here-place gains that relative persistence through which, first of all, the corporeality of the space that bears it would become experienceable, since, indeed, as it appears, its now would be exposed to continual change and would thereby, one might think, sweep its here along into that change.

The life-process, as it was said earlier, is bipolar happening, and lets two sides be recognized: that of the connectedness of the experiencing soul with what is experienced, and that of the alienation of that very thing experienced. That which is to be experienced would not become the experienced, were it not united at some point with the life-process, and it would again not become the experienced, had it not once more become alienated from the life-process: that is the sense of the familiar name "content of experience." We have meanwhile characterized the connectedness more precisely as fusion, namely of beholding with happening, and have shown in it the primal impulse to the experiencing of the unstoppability of every moment, or, more briefly, to the experiencing of real time; and we have found, in the as-it-were pausing turn of beholding, that is, in the process of intuition, the primal impulse to alienation, thanks to which an ever-changing stream of images comes to appearance for the soul in the mirror of sense-space. — For reasons soon to be touched upon, let us attempt to put this result into words in such a way that it would be understood, at least with feeling, even by *one* who had not read our work.

"The sense-impression," we would thus say, "seeks to make the soul like itself," and works, we might go on to say, "in the soul made similar to it, as an impulse to the renewal of its image." We would thereby have set over against one another: sense-impression and soul, or more precisely: the appearing occasion of impression and the process of intuition through which it takes effect in the recipient of the impression; we would thus have posited the possibility of at least momentary fusion of two states of affairs, which can be thought of neither as a unity nor as members belonging together in pairs. We feel, indeed we think we know, that our soul temporarily transforms itself into the *intuitive* image, before which we stand as a still and yet artistically stirred beholder, [p. 952] and it carries conviction when we are told that in this, precisely, is grounded, for instance, the urge to form that may drive us to objectify what has become manifest to us, through inner transformation, out of the appearance of the world. But we had not thought of the — collision with the chair while striding through the room, although this precisely produced an "impression" in the literal sense! One must once consider this in order to become directly aware of the abyss between sensation and intuition, and likewise between the body and its appearance, given, nonetheless, the undoubted rootedness of *both* walls of the chasm in one and the same soil!

If we imagine, in the intuiting just outlined, the being-seized still further intensified, then the soul of the beholder seems to us intermediately permeated by the appearance and thus fused with an image, which then at once again confronts it as something wholly different from itself. If we now set beside this the being-sensed of a resisting existence, then there emerges in it, as essence-determining, *the* feature with which we had begun the investigation of sensing: the impenetrability both of the sensed and of the sensing. In both cases alienation has taken place, but they are alienations of an extremely different kind. If we call — partly relying on all that has already been set forth, partly anticipating still further — the sensed, for the sake of its impenetrability, corporeality, then the difference between the two kinds of alienation presents itself somewhat as follows. Appearance is far more alienated from the one intuiting than its corporeality, insofar as it stands in no connection whatever with the corporeality of himself, and it is far less alienated from him, insofar as it stands constantly in connection with his soul; conversely, the alien corporeality is far less alienated from the one sensing than its appearance, insofar as it stands constantly in connection with the corporeality of himself, and it is far more alienated from him, insofar as it would stand in no connection whatever with his soul, were it not for its never wholly detachable appearance. This description of the more and the less in both cases, however, does not yet suffice us. If we fix our gaze sharply upon sensing alone, then the less of beingalienated coincides with a more, not so much of connectedness as of disturbedness (namely by the alien body), and the disturbedness again, if thought of as, say, growing, [p. 953] with the growth of the having-been-experienced of reciprocal impenetrability. Of this the one consequence, which first concerns us, is the content of experience of corporeality.

We have, in the first volume, elucidated, by the example of the flashing-up of a lightning-bolt over a night-landscape completely darkened, the capacity of the visible appearance to stand in for processes and movements; but the same example also shows the astonishing speed with which visual appearances can change without forfeiting anything of their chief property, their intuitively shaped character. Other examples would be: the ceaseless passing-by of distant and near images of the visible appearance before the gaze of one traveling by railway, or the ceaseless change of shape before the onlooker of a fountain, or a waterfall, or the surf of the sea, or a flickering flame, or a drifting smoke. In comparison with this, the impenetrability of the sensed has, indisputably, the character of persistence. Of an experience of resistance as fleeting as the image of the nocturnal landscape in the moment of the lightning-flash, and nonetheless still preserving the character of intuitability, we can no longer form any concept. But if the empirically shortest intuitability of the impenetrable is unmistakably of longer duration than the empirically shortest intuitability of the merely appearing, then the impenetrable becomes, in relation to the appearing, something that outlasts.<sup>33</sup> These differences of the contents of experience now find support in certain already familiar differences of their essence.

<sup>33</sup> On page 953. — For readers familiar with present-day experimental psychology, a few data may be mentioned here whose proper appreciation requires some reflection. In the case of skin stimulations that produce only pressure-like alterations of the stimulated spot, it naturally speaks only for the originally extraordinary predominance of sensing over beholding, that the so-called time threshold — that is, the minimum duration of stimulation needed to evoke a sensation (through supraliminal stimulus intensities) — is lowest for the "pressure sense," already at least double that for the "pain sense," but three to five times as high for the brightness sense of the eye.
