Such data have been established for the skin senses generally, and for the eye at least predominantly, by means of very brief electrical stimulations. Here too, to be sure, specific differences come into play. Thus, at the very shortest current duration, a sudden sensation arises in the tactile region; at a somewhat longer one, a tingling; at a still longer one, a sensation of warmth. Yet none of this is any more identical with the experiential foundations of alien corporeality than the so-called phosphenes are with visual intuitive images. On the other hand, it may be regarded as a condition of the superior capacity of the visual sense for making-present, that the fraction by which a brightness must be increased for the difference to be just perceptible (the so-called difference threshold) amounts to barely a third of the corresponding value for pressure differences. And the positional sensitivity of the visual sense far exceeds analogous tactile performances altogether. — To the sight of the changing shapes of a fountain, only the palpation of a succession of roundnesses, corners, points, including their smoothness, roughness, dryness, and so on, could be compared. But precisely when we set beside the *sight* of water the comparatively most similar tactile experience — the hand, or the whole body, being washed around by a strongly flowing water — the superiority of the visual sense in intuitive content emerges overwhelmingly, just as, no less certainly, does that of the tactile sense in weight of actuality!

Now that the visible appearance has become for us, to a great extent, a sign of corporeality, it changes nothing in the state of affairs just described that the contents of touch generally recede behind the contents of sight in duration. The experienced resistance in leaning against the wall lasts no longer than I lean against it, whereas the appearance of the walls is constantly present, even if not continuously attended to, for as long as I remain in the room. The same holds of the appearance of the reclining-chair compared with the experiences of pressure during the lying upon it, or of the appearance of the floor compared with the experiences of pressure during standing, or of the appearance of the book-page compared with the delicate experiences of pressure during the turning of pages. Let us further recall what it is at all that calls forth the semblance of that improper continuity which we call duration or persistence, or, in another regard, unchangeableness — [p. 954] it is, as we have learned, for *all* data, thus also for sensed resistances, precisely that renewal of similar images, achievable from moment to moment, exclusively within the domain of beholding. This alone does not prevent, however, that appearance, apart from its corporeality, has *only* presentness and is thus placeless in space; whereas the resisting place, because first experienced by means of it, always lays claim to a now-here. Then, however, the impenetrable can vanish only through change of place, that is, through movement, whereas appearance can vanish absolutely. More sharply put: the impenetrable does not "vanish" at all, it only moves on; appearance, however, vanishes, and of this a subordinate case is transformation.<sup>34</sup> Appearances are capable of transformation, impenetrabilities are merely capable of movement: in this way it emerges most sharply that already the experienced impenetrability harbors the germ of that resistance to non-existence which — unfolded in the awakened capacity for reflection — comes to the aid of an interpretation of the world that scaled its first and at once a lofty peak with the Democritean mechanics of the atoms.

<sup>34</sup> On page 954. — If not all, then at least by far the most so-called conjuring tricks consist in producing the appearance that bodies behave like mere appearances. But they seem to do this always when they suddenly vanish or unexpectedly appear. The model case of this is the transposition of a body to another place without traversing the intervening space. We give as an example a small trick that has been known to Indian jugglers for centuries and is moreover familiar to every reader in Europe as well. A solid little ball of about x cm in diameter is laid before us on the table, and an empty cup is placed inverted over it. At about a meter's distance, a second empty cup of the same shape and size is set down on the table, opening downward. We are permitted to lift the first cup: the little ball is *not* underneath. We lift the second: it *is* underneath. Now while this strikes us as magic, it would appear, at least to the European, not at all wonderful if the mere *image* of the ball were to light up and vanish successively at different places. The "magical" quality thus lies in this: that we are compelled to assume that if a *body* passes from place A to place B, it must have *moved* *there*. By way of supplement, and at the same time anticipating, we further observe: by whatever path the body may arrive, we cannot even think, let alone bring about, that the path-line should exhibit a gap anywhere; more precisely, that there should be found on it a point through which the body had *not* passed. Trivial as such examples may be, they reveal to us all the more drastically the vital ground of the substrate-nature of the *body*; and thereupon also of matter — whence it is one of the strangest aberrations of human thought to wish to "trace back" matter to motion, etc.!

With this, however, we have accomplished what we had first set out to do: the derivation of corporeality. For now we know how to state why the here — always a place of impenetrability — is *not* unrestrictedly swept along into the incessant change of now-moments. For, in the first place, owing to the resisting nature of the here, the now-here is noticeably more persistent than the mere-now of appearance devoid of resistance; and then, moreover, it even takes on, as against it, the character of constancy, because it has laid aside the token of everything that appears — transformability — and has exchanged it instead for mere mobility. It thereby moves into the light of the mobile bearer of changeability, and this, thanks to the self-mobility of sensing beings, is inescapably a threefold extended region of place; whereby the body would then be, quite properly, "fixed and finished." — Corporeality befalls the gift of intuition of self-movingly-sensing beings; it would not befall a merely beholding being, nor equally a merely sensing being. The former, if there were such a being, which would be conceivable, would find itself in the placeless void of placeless transformations; the latter, on the other hand, would be an inconceivable being, because, given the total absence of beholding, its sensing too would be extinguished. The data of intuition of the world form themselves together with the corporealities that bear them, [p. 955] and again these together with the data of intuition that, so to speak, clothe them; but the two do not form themselves in lockstep (which, indeed, does not exist at all in the domain of vitality); rather, in the animal world, *up to* man, in accordance with overemphasized sensation and self-movement, the experience that embodies data of appearance runs ahead of that experience of appearance which *distances* them and turns the distanced into primal images. Finally, let it be pointed out in passing that only experienced corporeality gives the decisive final impulse toward the formation of the idea of the ever-presence of sense-space. For what stands out from its now even more "eloquently" than the fleetingness of appearing and of the transformation of appearance is the change of places experienced and experienceable only in relation to it!

It belongs to every lived experience, among other things, that it estranges the content of experience from the soul. But insofar as the content of sensation is a disturbing content, its intensification can, as we have seen, obscure the polarity of soul and world with the essentially different duality of soul and soul-body. Every sensing harbors within it the onset — however weak, and however imperceptible times without number — of the split that unmistakably prepares itself therein, and it points us back once more to the conflict within sensation that has become known to us on other grounds, and that we must now illuminate somewhat more sharply. This, however, is to take place within the framework of a consideration that will lead us at once from the body to the thing.

[p. 956]

#### 59. Kapitel — Körper und Ding — Chapter 59 — Body and Thing

There is no body that does not have some shape, and just as little is there an appearance that does not have some shape. If, then, we wish to determine the immediate occasioning ground of the act of apprehension precisely in corporeality, we must for the time being disregard entirely the fact that corporeality is shaped. If we do so, corporeality means: impenetrability of the space of intuition; whereupon the question at once announces itself: impenetrable for *what*? Well, certainly *not for* space! If I carry a solid sphere from place A to place B, I have not thereby also displaced the space that fills it, which rather glided through it as though it were nothing; instead, I have made place after place of new spheres of space impenetrable, namely for a second volume of the character of corporeality. Impenetrability thus means a condition of conflict, and with the concept of place at least *two* places are posited — originally real places (= bodies), later merely thought places of sojourn of bodies, thanks to whose independence the concept of objective space and finally of Euclidean space develops. The concept of body rests on the knowledge of the mutual disturbability of that to which corporeality is to belong, or of the possible contest for space; and to the inner split within the process of sensation the actuality of the outer world offers, as it were, a handle in the struggle of bodies for — appearing. Its counter-image in lived experience, if one will, brings with it that heightening of tension at which the rhythm finally breaks.

The double polarity that we claim for every lived experience holds for the process of sensation only insofar as the process of intuition works into it; *without* it, however, *the* reciprocity would be lacking that alone, in the sense of the science of life, is able to ground [p. 957] polarity in the first place — the reciprocity of soul and image — and in its place there would have entered a duality of impenetrabilities. With this we have arrived at the immediate enabling ground of the act of apprehension, the ready-to-intervene presence of spirit, of course, being presupposed. Spirit cannot immediately split a polarized whole, because the splitting ray lacks a point of impact; but it can do so mediately, through the splitting of a duality that has loosened itself within the totality of lived experience and has won relative independence as against the polarity. Not the polarity, but the over-accentuated duality within it alone, harbors the vital analogue of that with which spirit, so long as life lives, must content itself in accomplishing upon life: the separating boundary.

The soul — sensing, in the resistance of the foreign body, the resistance of its own dwelling-place — does not yet experience the boundaries of the two, because the beholding that resonates along with it preserves the connectedness, which in the case of a felicitous touch even grows to a release in voluptuous pleasure; but it is this content of experience which, from the very beginning, makes room for the object of thought named boundary, provided it is struck by the lightning of spirit at the moment of the collision of the soul-body with a repellingly resisting outside. Thereby, at the site of the doubled here, the now bounded and consequently fixed corporeality of one's own existence separates from the likewise bounded and thus equally fixed corporeality of a foreign existence. Before, however, we show that the finding of the corporeality existing here and now coincides with the original existential judgement, and thereupon lay the last and innermost ring around the concept of being, let us call to mind once more the vital sequence of events that has made possible such an over-accentuation of sensing.

The course of development leading to the independence of sensing shows two mutually complementary features, and can accordingly be interpreted more in terms of soul or more in terms of body; the side of the soul presents itself roughly as follows: the formation, unavoidably accompanying growing distance-beholding, of special senses differing in performance, and the thinning of the fluids between soul and world through their surrender to the strengthening sensorium — the growing preponderance of the sense of sight, endowed with the greatest range and the strongest "capacity" — the weakening of elementary sensibility in favor of an incipient spectatorship. But aimed at the same outcome, within the soma, was the scarcely doubtable [p. 958] increase in capacity for pain, by force of which the soul receives ever-increasing impulses toward avoidance of its body. If we survey the history of the — predominantly Promethean — ideologisms from Plato to Schiller, then, alongside a shape-divesting shyness of the body, flight from pain emerges as their chief motive, and in this, despite however great their differences, even the deeper wisdom of Asia at least seconds them. — Turning back with this to the derivation of the thing, we point out in advance that the difficult question of how the judgement of sameness could be passed upon an actuality that is forever changing has meanwhile found its solution. The body (= the sum total of points of impenetrability), once bounded and fixed and thus become a body-thing, has for any arbitrary now of its existence a determinable *place* in relation to the again determinable place of a second thing. We shall call that seemingly fixed thing, outlasting the moment, which it has thereby become for us, the objectively primordially-identical, because all identities that can be found are found in relation to this identity, of which even indicative thinking cannot divest itself, since it too must pass judgements, and judgement presupposes the sameness of that concerning which it takes place, and thus, with regard to the actuality of happening, presupposes its thingness. *Once*, of course, spirit has gained a foothold on the conceivable and conceived foundation of thinking, that is, on the body-thing, it can from here also take aim at happening, at appearances, at primordial images, at souls and essences; it can separate their conceivable from their inconceivable part, and the bearer of spirit can become aware that the thingness of the body is a reinterpretation of the body in the service of making the body thinkable; but it cannot renounce this reinterpretation so long as it does not wish to renounce conceiving itself.

Whoever calls the body-thing the objectively primordially-identical, or the factual primordial object, has thereby already declared that the finding of the thing is the original existential judgement. We have indeed also derived this; but we wish to certify it, and for that purpose must distinguish, somewhat more precisely than heretofore, what reified corporeality means in relation to corporeality. — Not only appearances but bodies too change, on the one hand through inner or outer [p. 959] processes of metabolism, or through both at once, and on the other hand even unceasingly, because from moment to moment they enter ever new spaces of the universe and thereby unavoidably become component parts of ever new contexts. To be sure, unaffected by this remains the place of a sum total of points of impenetrability in relation to a second place of the same character, for at least *two* mathematical instants. But what, we must ask, does the positing of the body's boundaries — through which the body is first reified — mean, in view of a mutability of bodily appearance that is in any case incalculable?

As was shown in detail on pp. 506–508, a boundary, regardless of what it pertains to, must never be confused with shape or form. The boundary as such has no shape. Were, then, the point of impenetrability that indicates to us the corporeality of an appearance not the point of impenetrability of an appearance, the body would have lost its shape and would then, of course, no longer be experienced, let alone found. But just as surely as it is only the intuitive image that makes possible the linking of one point of impenetrability with a second, just as surely it is not impenetrability that confers upon the sum total of all points their determinate shape. And conversely: although every body has a determinate shape at every moment, its shape is precisely not what makes it a body. *One* proof of this we have come to know: everything shape-like about the body can be transferred into the mode of being of visible appearance, and indeed with such success that we sometimes even confuse the untouchable mirror-image with its touchable original, and believe ourselves to perceive, in a perspectival drawing, the three-dimensionally extended scene of three-dimensionally extended corporealities. A second proof we find in the fact that the shape of the body is always only a now-shape, and is therefore, in relation to the happening-defying existence that we have found with its help, a mark that is indeed never absent, but merely additional, and in no case the "constitutive" one.

If on a winter's day, just as the thaw begins, I have laid a piece of ice before my window, the piece of ice changes its shape in incalculable fashion, growing smaller, melting away faster on its sunnier side, acquiring holes besides, and so forth; but that does not prevent me from apprehending in it one and the same piece of ice and consequently an [p. 960] existence, in relation to which *even* the change of shape falls under the root-concept of a change of property; which would without question be impossible if shape belonged among the existence-indices of the thing. But the relative independence of the thing from the shape of the thing goes considerably further still, and allows, for the change of shapes that we must refer to one and the same thing, a range of variation that scarcely falls short, in sensuous conspicuousness, of the change of qualitative properties such as hot and cold, red and green, dry and wet — only that it could of course never in the same way give way to complete shapelessness, as the (actual) color of the thing gives way to colorlessness in complete darkness. If, say, the children in front of my house are busy building a snowman, and have just shaped a kind of pedestal in order to finish the snowman after the lapse of about two hours, I am compelled, within the arbitrarily interpolable series of bodies differing both in bulk and especially in shape, to hold fast to the sameness of the existence that I call this snowman, distinguishing it, for instance, most definitely from a second snowman a hundred meters away, and to it I even still refer the dirty remnant that, after a day and a half of rainy weather, may be left over from it.

From such examples it emerges convincingly that the thingness which we apprehend in spirit on the occasion of experienced corporeality is a mere noumenon — though an unavoidable noumenon, and one that can be produced only with the help of corporeality. If we leave out of play those acts of recognition that the sense of smell makes possible for animals, and especially for insects, and keep to those by means of sight, then not a few animals (birds and mammals in particular) are indeed likewise capable of recognizing a body after a considerable change of shape. Thus many recognize, essentially visually and despite a change of clothes, a particular person by whom they have often been fed and lovingly treated, or repeatedly teased, which one finds ready occasion to test in any zoo. But for one thing, even the utmost achievements of this kind fall immeasurably short of what is humanly possible; and further, to add this at once, there exist limits for all acts of recognition, but not for identifying. If the thin, crumbling flakes of ash of a document just burned still seem to us like the letter, only now in the state of [p. 961] having-been-reduced-to-ash, then, in view of a residue of sensuous conspicuousness, we may still call this an act of recognition; but we shall be in no doubt that such recognition could never take place without the thought of identity, and is therefore simply denied to the animal. It is, of course, a long ladder of abstractions that leads from such quasi-recognitions to the thought of an indestructible world-stuff, and finally to the assumption that the world-stuff consists of nothing but identical atoms, or agglomerations of ether, or similar no-longerdivisible units; but what falls to us at the top of the ladder as the last possible determination, the extensionless *point*, is in truth the thing once again — now, however, stripped of its — corporeality.

Setting out from the consideration that the shape of the thing is only a now-shape, and hence in principle capable of arbitrary change, we have established: what endures through time in the thing, and thus the objectively primordially-identical, is the identity of one place in relation to a second place. We should never have found it, had it not originally been the site of an intuitive image, and had the intuitive image not, in turn, been a district of place within the space of intuition; but what is apprehended in the objective thus constituted, or, more briefly, the factual primordial object, is place as such, thus the point of zero extension — meant, however, as the ideal center, first and foremost, of a minimal district of points of impenetrability, and further of the intuitive images that lean upon these in turn, in relation to a second center of the same import. We can put this into the following equation: factual primordial object = position-determined point of relation for an arbitrarily small, only not vanishingly small, point of impenetrability, which therefore deserves to be called the primordial property of the factual primordial object. From this follows the mobility that does not belong to the merely mathematical point (of Euclidean space), or does so only in a transferred sense; and even the determinacy of position could be absent from the conceptual equation, but was deliberately left standing, so that it might serve as an indication that the finding of the factual primordial object presupposes processes of intuition and their correlate: the space of appearance, embryonic though it be. Once found, the primordial object consequently "attracts" all data of intuition, transforming them too into properties of the thing.

If we survey the course of the argument, it does not escape us that, among all conceivable [p. 962] properties of things, the shape of the thing occupies a unique position, a somewhat more precise consideration of which will, incidentally, furnish us with a contribution not to be underestimated toward answering the question why the ideological undertaking — of positing in shape the primordially-identical, in relation to which the world of things would be something derivative — could repeatedly present an appearance of success. But we are speaking here, be it noted, no longer of the confusion of which one makes oneself guilty in both camps — the confusion of the factual primordial object with actuality — but of the relation of factual identities to one another; and we recall once more, in advance: the materiologist is wrong in assuming that something could be found without the presupposition of experienced intuitiveness; the ideologist is wrong altogether in assuming that shapes could be found without the presupposition of things already found.

Compared with the primordial property of the thing, the arbitrarily small field of impenetrability, all other properties of things — such as visibilities, audibilities, smellabilities, tastabilities, further temperatures, qualitative tangibilities of surfaces, and so on — are, if not outright dispensable properties, then at least such as we may, depending on the vantage-point of the faculty of judgement, call secondary or tertiary properties. But if we ask whether shape belongs among the indispensable or the comparatively dispensable properties, we find it placed, so to speak, between the two, since it seems to us now indispensable, now again dispensable. So original and intellectually powerful a materiologist as Democritus, who laid the ground for all discussions of primary and secondary properties, held it to be indispensable, in that he included among the primordial properties of his atoms, besides hardness, density, and inertia, also size and, above all, shape (σχῆμα), indeed regarding differences of shape as especially important. How does the matter truly stand?

Since the indispensable property that we have called the primordial property, that is, the point-related point of impenetrability, necessarily has some extension, and thus also some bulk, or, if one will, some "magnitude" (though of arbitrary smallness), one is inclined to ascribe to it also some shape, a tiny sphere usually being what is thought of. That is correct, and again incorrect. Incorrect, insofar as [p. 963] the impenetrability of that which is impenetrable has as little shape as the impelling force (impetus) of that which strikes my body; correct, insofar as, in that which is impenetrable, impenetrability is never experienced alone, and in that which strikes, impelling force is never experienced alone. Consistently, we do not speak of an "impact-shape," but we do speak of the shape of the impelling body, because we simply cannot avoid taking up into the content of experience some data of appearance, however vague their shape. But if impenetrability forms the starting point for the conception of the primordial object, then extendedness, and shape thereof altogether, has already flowed to it from elsewhere, and Democritus's bold undertaking proves impracticable. Or, to put it in language already more familiar to us: the absolute hardness that constitutes the Democritean atom does not exclude its being, for every empirical now, the hardness of a differently shaped bulk.<sup>35</sup> Shape is no primordial property of the thing, but it is indeed the one secondary property without whose co-presence the primordial property would sink down into the abyss of mere possibilities. In this, then, one could grant Aristotle right, had he only also recognized the independence of matter, instead of believing that he could exhaust its essence with the determination of a mere possibility of realization for the working of forms — of which at least the highest, and the all-decisive one, must be thought as through and through immaterial.

<sup>35</sup> On page 963. — We can make vivid to ourselves the thought — at first perhaps disconcerting — of a possible change of shape of the atom from moment to moment, and can do so even without recourse to phenomena such as drifting smoke, a flickering flame, a fountain, and so on (against which it might be objected that here there is a constant outflow and inflow of material constituents), simply by recalling that the *appearances* of many *moving* bodies sometimes change without ceasing. One need only think of two dogs chasing each other, of two wrestlers, of the footballer during violent phases of play, of a sprinter, of the gymnast, acrobat, juggler, trick rider, of galloping horses, of a snake uncoiling itself, and so on and so forth, and one has before one's eyes just as many bodies whose intuitive shapes are forever changing, without our thereby running any risk of losing sight of their identity with themselves. Indeed the normal shape which we unconsciously take as our basis in each case is, strictly speaking, a mere noumenon, since the shape of, say, every extended muscle differs, in *actuality*, essentially from the shape of the contracted muscle. (The scientific concept of measurement of constant anatomical length — that is, the length of the muscle in a state of complete relaxation — naturally plays no role whatever for intuition.) Here we have, in the form of a macroscopic state of affairs, what was just now explained by reference to the microscopic state of affairs of the Democritean atom.

What is experienced in that which is impenetrable is, of course, never "absolute" hardness, but always only the relation of hardness between two impenetrabilities; and matter, conceived with regard to the vital occasion of the concept of matter, is thoroughly an intensive, and consequently gradable, state of affairs. If we let a body of clay-like consistency, or, say, the artist's plasticine, be fixed as a whole, then, under the counter-pressure of the fingers, we experience that displaceability of the impenetrable which we are compelled to refer immediately to the stuff of the body, and which we designate as formability, malleability, softness — to which is at once attached the thought of the arbitrarily gradable series from the nearly hard to the liquid. (Let it be recalled in passing: as an adjective to "weichen" [to yield], "weich" [soft] properly means that which yields, gives way, whereas "hart" [hard] — occasionally with the secondary sense of "painfully hard" — is cognate with κρατύς, which means "strong, steadfast.") Now if the inelastic-fluid already lacks almost entirely a shape of its own, [p. 964] this holds all the more fully of the gaseous, notwithstanding that this too can still be experienced, e.g., in the counter-pressure of moving air; and those ultimate and simply unchangeable units, which conceiving thought cannot well dispense with, clearly prove to be mere analogues of the points of relation through which bodies become things, and thus, by their nature, shapeless. At the same time we recognize, in the inclination to assemble the actuality of matter out of primordial units, the — in fact hopeless — attempt to break up into quanta the content of experience of that specific continuity which belongs to every increase of degree, or more precisely to every growth of intensities, and thus to render it pliable to the mental wish-image of countability. On this, however, we shall return in the next chapter.

The concept means the object, and the object, in turn, is an object of thought. The two cannot be torn apart from one another, but the spirit of the person is captivated, now to a higher degree by the concept, now by the object. The content of experience named now-here likewise cannot be torn apart, since no now is experienced without a here, no here without a now; but already within lived experience the accent falls now on the here, now on the now — which we indeed give voice to alternately, when at one time we say that it now lies here, and at another, that here it no longer lies now. Since, however, we have grown accustomed in thought to separating the two members, indeed have separated them so far from one another that some effort of the understanding is needed to recover their belonging-together, it will be understood all the more readily, and followed all the more willingly, when we say that within the now-here it is the here that chiefly bears the primordial object, and the now that chiefly bears the primordial concept that means it. We have shown earlier, in detail, how in consequence every cult of the concept had to be paired with a cult of shape, and we have meanwhile come to know two facts that could help it to apparent successes: the fact that the shape of the primordial object cannot be derived from the primordial object, and the fact that it nonetheless clings to it, though only as a now-shape, and this in contrast to numerous properties that are unrestrictedly dispensable, such as colorations, audibilities, smellabilities, tastabilities, and so forth.

The essential difference between shape and boundary has proved itself most exactly in the factual primordial object: it is not its shape that makes it what it is — an existence unbridgeably bounded and, precisely [p. 965] for that reason, enduring through time — but the impenetrability of each of its shapes for a second primordial object, or, in other words, its own capacity for the assertion of existence. The thing — so we might also define it, though admittedly only for one acquainted with everything expounded thus far — is a self-asserting place; and we would thereby, on the one hand, have grounded the punctual nature of the boundary, through derivation from the character of the primordial object, more deeply than merely logically, and, on the other, have adduced a ground deeper than the merely logical one for the mobility of the primordial object, by interpreting sameness during a change of position as a self-assertion against change, despite a possible change of form! With the foregoing turn, however, we have already branched off, and indeed with a view to a goal that — already surmisable by the reader — is reached more quickly from a wholly different starting point. — With regard to the scope of its immediate working in the world of happening, spirit is the I, which, in relation to the soul of its bearer, can be thought only by analogy with a pivot, and which, together with that soul, makes up the state of affairs called the personal I. If it is true that the primordial act of spirit sets the boundary between body and body, then the bearer of spirit must be a corporeal being (such that a bodiless-soulish being would necessarily be un-spirited), and the person ensouled corporeality, with the I as the center of its receiving and working. Words like center and pivot are similes, inasmuch as here there can be talk neither of a (not even conceivable) midpoint of the shape of the bearer of soul, nor at all of any rotation of that shape about it; but without lengthy discussion it cannot be otherwise stated what is meant by this: the non-extendedness of the I, comparable only to the mathematical point, and the fact that to this immaterial and extensionless point falls the role of sole ruler over all consciousness-capable life-processes of the vitality that it inhabits. With this it is at the same time declared that this said sole rule must be fought for anew from moment to moment against countless life-processes that withdraw themselves from the capacity for consciousness and prepare unceasing alterations — differing in extent and kind — for the processes capable of consciousness. To develop all the in-principle-possible consequences of the primordial discord thereby posited is the task of the metaphysics of personality, whereas here we are concerned only with what was foreshadowed in the 9th Chapter: namely, that, measured against the unceasingly [p. 966] self-changing vitality (the body included, insofar as it is living body), the activity of the I must be grasped as the ever-repeated deed of self-assertion, and the personal I as the abiding disposition to acts of assertion.

Although the proof of this has not yet reached its conclusion, it will already be familiar to the reader from many examples that all vital working, be it begetting or receiving, presupposes polar similarities and consists in assimilations. That similarity, thanks to which alone spirit can succeed in setting the original boundary and, by means of it, in fashioning the factual primordial object, is not a similarity of soul with image, but the mutually like disturbability through which the soul-body, so to speak, "makes contact" with the body of the image: the impenetrability of both; and the assimilation that spirit, though compelled, nonetheless actively accomplishes upon the content of sensation with the act of apprehension consists in the conjuring-fast of the point of impenetrability by a center of self-assertion driven into it. The factual primordial object is generated in that the person, through the primordial act of spirit, shoots into the corporeality of the appearance a copy of the I-point, or rather a case akin to it; and the merely fictitious sameness of the object is nothing but a kind of reflex of the real sameness of the subject.

Here, however, doubts might arise, and the question might be voiced whether this would not continually create new I's, and what spirit, supposing it to be a will to destruction or even merely a will to mastery, would gain by it. New I's are indeed originally created (as, true to fact, still today, as often as the objects are persons) — namely, for exactly as long, and to the extent, as the center of the consciousness-capable life-processes, that is, the I, gives room to the counter-influences of the soul (the anthropomorphic phase of the early history of thinking); and this occurs less and ever less, the more the person, become subservient to spirit, is driven and enabled to bore, instead of a personal I, the I-point itself into actuality — whereupon, finally, this very person could doubt the existence of — persons, and has — how often! — done so. But what would spirit gain thereby?

We know this as soon as we consider that, apart from persons, there is no sameness in actuality, because actuality is unstoppable, [p. 967] unarrestable, ungraspable happening. Just as one originally only "has" what one has made fast — the fish on the hook, the sail on the mast, the slave on the chain, the bird in the cage, and every living thing definitively by killing it — so too spirit "has," or the localized spirit, the I, "has," and can henceforth avail itself, by means of the body of its possession as of a tool, of what it has made fast, in that it — not indeed fishes and birds and slaves, or these only afterward, but rather — tore contents of experience out of the stream of self-changing and pierced them, as with a nail, with the point hurled out from itself, fastening them, forever killed, onto — the spaceless plane of objects of thought. Stat crux dum volvitur orbis! [The cross stands while the world turns] — Could anyone still fail to recognize that "shape" fulfills for the ideologist exactly the same purpose, and merely satisfies a different taste-direction of the wishes for eternalization? Yet "eternalization" is misleading; they are: wishes for de-temporalization. — If one states that something exists, one means to say that it really exists. In colloquial speech, being-actual even predominates, in keeping with the not infrequently resonating secondary thought of something living, and this fits well with the original sense of the Latin ex-sistere, which means to step forth, to step into the light of day, to emerge, and readily takes on the meaning of becoming, of arising. Even though in philosophical language the hidden identity may become more audible, still it always holds: the existent = the really existent; hence we use the word exclusively in this sense. Then, however, the existent would be both a being and an actuality; it would be an actual being or a being actuality, and in it non-being happening would, in whatever way, have become joined with happening-less being, or, to put it as drastically as possible, real time with absolute timelessness!

The course of the investigation has led us, with regard to this riddle-being, to the following principal result: the objectively primordially-identical, that is, the real thing, is, as it were, fused together out of a part that is necessarily merely fictive — the conceivable and countable existence — and the corporeality that is actual independently of spirit, which, however, cannot be conceived, but only demonstrated. But if, accordingly, the paradox just set forth with regard to the factual primordial object thereby dissolves, because only its corporeality, and not its supposed thingness, [p. 968] belongs to actuality, then of the subjectively primordially-identical, that is, the personal I, it holds that the fusion, logically seemingly impossible, has in fact taken place within it, and thereby makes that fictive fusion necessary and possible. Before we give a more exact account of this in the 61st Chapter, we turn our gaze to our scarcely less important secondary result, according to which the original existential judgement means the thingness of the actual, and note that it includes two subassertions: there is no object of thought that would not presuppose the finding of the thing; and: the question of existence, in case of doubt, is always decided by recourse to the existence of the thing.

The first sub-assertion is essentially settled. That properties, states, processes, movements exist only insofar as their substrates do, we need not repeat once again. — Copies and mirrorings, or also dream-phantasms, can indeed be vitally distinguished from that in relation to which they are called copies, mirrorings, phantasms, namely by their bodilessness. But since we ordinarily think of things as often as we involuntarily think of bodies, the statement that something is "mere appearance" has, throughout, the existence of things underlying it as the measure of actuality. — Mathematical and kinematic propositions can be applied to "the actual" only because that actuality, in relation to which the objects of thought of mathematics and kinematics seem to lack being-actual, is the necessarily merely constructed actuality of things, and thus by no means actuality itself. — In the 12th Chapter it was set forth why the finding of the I must take its path by way of the finding of the thing, and in the 46th the role was considered that the will directed against the moment of the world plays in this. On this alone we wish still briefly to dwell, since a few gaps remain to be closed.

As has meanwhile been ascertained, the finding of the thing presupposes the experience of the body, and means, in the first place, the finding of the foreign body. But because the experience of the impenetrability of two bodies lies within the experience of the body, the finding of one's own body necessarily follows upon the finding of the foreign body. Whether the amoeba bumps against the glass thread, or the human against the chair, what is experienced in both cases is the repulsion of two bodies — there dimly, twilight-dark, here sharply and distinctly — so that, if finding joins itself to it, both bodies are at once also reified. If, now, the I has been found by means of [p. 969] the command of the will as the apparently driving power of one's own body, then one's own body henceforth plays a double role: now a thing among things, now the bearer of the I. As bearer of the I, it executes the commands of the I whenever we act; as thing among things, it succumbs to "blind chance" and thus becomes the tormentor of the I whenever we suffer pain; and that is the reason why popular consciousness gladly confuses it with the I, while higher consciousness just as often dismisses it as a disturbing and irksome foreign body. In fact, the stricter conception of the I of one's own begins with its distinction from personal corporeality, and completes itself in the recognition of the essential difference between the two; but a glance at their uniquely close connection allows us to outline still more sharply the dependence of the finding of the I upon the finding of the thing. Were we to think away the bodily dwellingspace of the I, the I would have lost its place in the world, and thus also its scope for activity, and would accordingly no longer be found anywhere; from which we see that the finding of the I requires not so much the finding of a thing in general, as rather the finding of that particular thing which we call one's own body. The I-consciousness of the person is kindled and originally awakens upon the consciousness of the existence of its self-moving corporeality, and primordial existence — that is, the only existence there really is — requires, in order that it may exist within the cosmos, the support of a corporeality in principle capable of appearing. — We now convince ourselves, by means of a few examples, that existence or non-existence is always decided by recourse to the existence of a thing, and in doing so cast a sidelong glance at the problem of the identifying value of similarities, and the distinguishing value of dissimilarities.

In the 34th Chapter (on elementary similarity) the difficulties were considered that we face when we are to specify a mark that would enable us, for any given case of recognition whatsoever, to judge in principle whether it has hit upon what is correct or not. When the dying dog of Odysseus recognizes his master after twenty years, it seems certain to us that the recognition was correct. But what, at bottom, do we have in mind as the identical here? The smell that the dog presumably perceived merely resembled the earlier smell, and was, moreover, not — Odysseus. The dog would probably have likewise given the signs of recognition on sniffing a garment that the hero [p. 970] had worn only a week before, notwithstanding that he might meanwhile have died. His soul was no longer the same as twenty years before, and neither was his body. What, then, is recognized, and how, and by what mark?

The old nurse, as was set forth at that point, recognizes Odysseus in an entirely different way, in that she identifies him, prior to recognition, with the help of a recognized scar. Accordingly, however, the objects of recognition are also different for humans, different for animals. Insofar as, in the ordinary waking state, human recognition at once occasions the apprehension of identities, it concerns the sameness of objects of thought, and only with reference to these is an immediate decision possible concerning truth and error, including that of recognition. If, by contrast, the world of essences and their appearances never preserves sameness, then a recognition not followed by acts of the positing of identities coincides with that cognition of essential similarities which, as we learned, first helps the acts of spirit to their successes, and is subject to deception only insofar as similarities are confused with one another. But what links the thought of sameness with the change of images?

Original sameness means sameness of the thing, and hard on its heels follows the sameness of the person; all other identities are supported by that of things and I's, or, more briefly, by the sameness of ideal points, which as such have no connection with actuality and could, without mediating members, be neither found nor even thought. We recall once more: if the indispensable point of relation of all concepts, namely the consciousness of thinking persons, is itself found only in — figuratively speaking — the reflected gleam of the thing already found beforehand, then no further grounds would be needed (which we nonetheless offer in what follows) to prove that even the arbitrarily abstract object of thought — such as plurality, equality, relation, function, imaginary number, and so on — would be annihilated upon removal of the object of thought named thing. The positing of identities in general goes back to the finding of the thing.

With this premised, let us repeat what we have meanwhile ascertained: between point and world of appearance, the mediating member is the corporeality of the world of appearance, and the original finding of the thing rests upon the at once animal capacity of *re*cognizing [p. 971] of bodies. With the sameness of the thing, be it object or person, we hypostatize the identically persisting body, and to the supposed sameness of the body there corresponds, in actuality, that succession of intuitive images which, for every empirical instant, can be referred to a real place, that is, to a sum total of points of impenetrability.

But in that, in this manner, the in-principle most important means of orientation even for animality, the recognizable body, has become a body-thing and thereby an object of thought, there first takes place a mighty shift in the accent of the marks of recognition: in the place of the tangible, tastable, smellable, and even the audible, there step, and indeed ever more predominantly, those akin to concepts, belonging to the sense of sight; and, further, judgement detaches itself from its starting point, in that between the two arbitrarily long series of members are interposed, each of which is connected with the one preceding it through the thought of functional dependence (as, for instance, when, by force of the system of relations into which the magnetic needle has been inserted, this or that perceived deflection tells of this or that imperceptible process on the — sun). But however many intermediate members may be required, in the individual case, for the reference to the identical to take place, the last member is unavoidably a body; and whatever appearances may allow the inference to its existence, it is its tangible impenetrability alone that can verify it.<sup>36</sup>

<sup>36</sup> On page 971. — Because guided, incomparably more strongly than we are, by the immediate mode of efficacy of vitally important bodies, animals at times display a somnambulistic sureness of recognition. From a great distance the horse finds its way back to its stable, even when, owing to rebuilding, the roof has meanwhile been removed and the front wall torn down; the cat that has grown accustomed to a house over years still wanders searching among the ruins and remnants of walls; the pair of storks, coming back from Africa, chooses the same barn of the Mecklenburg village for its dwelling on which it had nested the year before. Such examples make plain both the positional character of the unreified body and, no less, the corporeality of the still unreified position; and it is understood that recognition is made more difficult by a change of place of the object, and becomes impossible for the animal in the event of any considerable change of appearance besides, as soon as it can no longer rely on scent. Quite otherwise with man, once reification has taken place! Whoever might not otherwise grasp that, and through what, experienceable corporeality differs from mere thinkable thingness, could find it made transparent in view of the differences between animal and human performances of recognition, and especially again in those cases where, in man, the identification precedes the recognizing. Relying solely on my unaided senses, I would not know which of two books, of wholly identical format, identical thickness, identical cover, I held in my hands; but the intuitively exceedingly minor circumstance that one of them is marked on the back with a Roman one, the other with a Roman two, decides the question and makes confusion of the objects impossible. Or consider what minimal differences in the line-patterns of two fingerprints suffice for the criminologist to establish non-identity with certainty, and that the tiny scratch we have made on the two-mark piece suffices to convict the sleight-of-hand artist who exchanged it! The marks of recognition here are of a configurational kind, and are so, for reasons we have considered, for the most part for man's thing-related thinking, but need not be so. Of two gems which even the unpracticed eye, after the most thorough inspection, confuses, the jeweler not infrequently pronounces, with the greatest certainty, the one genuine and the other false — and does so on the basis of a minimal difference of luster which one must learn, over a long time, to perceive.

A thing may, for example, now be characterized predominantly by its shape, as the crystal very often is; now predominantly by its manner of function and effect, as Odysseus is (supposing we wished to assume that his outward appearance had meanwhile changed beyond recognition, and his body had exchanged its matter through and through, there would still remain a manifold of recognizable effects, including, for instance, his bodily scent); now by both together, as, say, the river, whose sameness attests itself through the far-reaching persistence of the position as well as of the forms of its "course," and through sufficient similarities of its functions — yet all this would nonetheless drown in drifting images, would become literally ungraspable, and would withdraw itself from the judgement of sameness, were the sequence of images no longer able to be referred to a district of points of impenetrability, whose existence, through determinacy of place, stood out unmistakably [p. 972] from every other existence, for any arbitrary instant between the perceived intuitive images. Corporeality, and it alone, is the foundation of all judgements of identity, and only what can be attached to it — be it as property or state, be it as expression or effect — is judged as existing.

In waking, Heraclitus said, all have a common world; in sleep, each turns to his own particular one. But what makes this commonality possible for the waking? Certainly not appearance, and least of all the optical appearance, which, of one and the same house, already turns out considerably different for two observers, even if they stand only five meters apart. But indeed the position-determined place of the corporeality of the appearance does. To it the existential judgement of both refers without difference, to it the world-space of both, insofar as it is a judged world-space (= objective space); and so, then, what is common to the waking world of both, despite the difference of their actualities, is the world of things.

The travelers who suddenly saw a palm forest appear in the desert, at a spot where only empty desert is to be found once they have made their way there, call the image a mere appearance, and no longer hope to be able to rest beneath the beckoning treetops. The lack of corporeally graspable existence took from what appeared its existence altogether! — If we dip a straight stick obliquely into water, we see it bent at the point where it emerges. Why do we not "believe" in the bend, when the visual appearance of the bend stands there, after all, irremediably fixed? Because touch assures us of the unbentness of the stick, and because tangible corporeality alone bears the existential judgement.

Everyone knows the countless geometrical-optical illusions that weave into the overall picture of the world of optical perception, and that can, moreover, be demonstrated en masse with simple figures. Why, properly, are they called "illusions"? Why do we not "believe" that the house-walls of the long main street draw together in the distance and finally touch one another, notwithstanding that we see it incontrovertibly? Because at precisely the spot where the touching would have to take place, the tangible walls remain just as far apart as at the original point of observation. Why do we unfailingly hold two parallels, thought of as running on from the observer's body, to be parallel, although to the unbiased (that is, not artificially fixed to the plane of the paper) [p. 973] gaze they seem to diverge upward, as soon as each of them has been crossed with parallel oblique lines that diverge downward (the Zöllner pattern)? Because we can ascertain: the ruler or measuring tape shows the same distance below and above. We "believe" thus the corporeality of the measuring instrument, and are convinced that it is not affected by the shift we must undertake in order to compare the two distances.

But suppose even that we made use of highly abstract methods of measurement, in which the fixed standard did not itself appear directly: they would hang on a chain of prior assumptions whose last and sustaining link would be the — "rigid" body. And suppose further that we subscribed to one of those hypotheses which make the measures of bodies depend on the state of motion of bodies and, for example, take as their basis a contraction of bodies in the direction of motion: without solidity as such, and its constancy at least for an empirical now, the standard itself would have ceased to exist, and we could then no longer even speak of its contraction! Electrodynamics and optics may progress for another ten thousand years, and the computational arts of the mathematicians with them — with no dialectic will one argue away the sustaining link, that is, the solid body, unless one has meanwhile renounced measuring, indeed renounced conceiving as such! If a mode of thought fixes itself upon the mere visible appearance (as, for example, relativism does), it can no longer decide whether something exists or does not exist, and increasingly exchanges its object of research for a system of — rules of the game.

To draw from the significance of the finding of the thing for the existential judgement, from that of the experiencing of corporeality for the finding of the thing, all the conclusions that are possible, a book of its own would be required. Here we confine ourselves to the few that must not be passed over in the service of the main task of the body-and-soul theme: the reconnection of sensing with the wakefulness of beholding, and thus the retaking of the universe of bodies back into the actuality of appearing images.

[p. 974]

#### 60. Kapitel — Materie und Erscheinungswelt — Chapter 60 — Matter and the World of Appearance

*The Underivability of Matter.* — The conceptual determination of matter as the substrate of motion is correct, but insufficient, because the state of affairs it takes as its basis, namely mechanical motion, itself still requires derivation. If the thing means the relational point of its properties posited as actual, then it is undoubtedly something other than the motion of the thing and must be distinguished as sharply from the latter as from the former. But we arrive at matter only by the roundabout way of the body, and the body is by no means itself immediately the substrate of mechanical motion, but rather the appearance-capable site of happening. Before, however, we ground the formula for the essence of matter — repeatedly hinted at elsewhere — we shall recall certain difficulties which no derivation seeking to satisfy the demands of mechanics has yet mastered.

If one proceeds from the thing, as has been done many times since Democritus, one stands sooner or later before two absurdities in which the unreality of the starting point is disclosed. The first has been appraised so extensively that it suffices to name it: since things cannot act upon one another, a matter that is supposed to manifest itself in them would be condemned to complete inefficacy (regardless of whether one additionally invents a force-thing or not) and would consequently be a nothing. The second follows from the first: such a matter could never form the body, since the corpuscles at which the process of division comes to a halt are once again mere absence-of-contact and, figuratively speaking, lack the mortar that would bind them together.

On the long and arduous path that leads from Democritus's still wholly sensuously conceived atoms to the belief in the actuality of extensionless points and finally to mere units of calculation, an instructive way-station is the ingenious attempt of the Jesuit Boscovich to bring Newton's [p. 975] mechanics into accord with the anticipatory formalism of a Leibniz. He undertakes to make the already unavoidable assumption of an actuality of the point metaphysically plausible by conceiving it as a force-point to which a force-*sphere* belongs, according to which the mutual attraction of two force-points, upon a certain diminution of their distance, passes over into a very rapidly increasing repulsion; whereby, among other things, the impenetrability of material places is explained without recourse to the phenomenon of contact, including the enigmatic effect of mechanical impact.

We are not concerned here with the physical side of the theory, but solely with the metaphysical; and there we see at once: it is not the points that matter, but the calculable spheres of action; and these are something just as isolated as any corpuscles whatever, and as it were the ghostly form in which the thing makes a last effort to smuggle itself into the world of happening. What deserves our particular attention in this belated endeavor to force the already self-sufficient mechanistics back into a sublime materialism, however, is the circumstance that with the spheres of action in question the point expands into a *volume*. It speaks for the high consistency of the theory's creator that he accordingly conceives place and position and time-position in the sense of *properties* of the *thing*; and it thereby becomes evident, to be sure, that an actuality of the thing-point, however circumscribed, is purchased only at the price of the unreality of the *continuum*!<sup>37</sup>

<sup>37</sup> On page 975. — Were we to describe the polarity by which alone the relation of the impenetrability of the impenetrable to the shape of the impenetrable can be characterized, on the analogy of the relation of property to substrate, then — in contrast to Boscovich — impenetrability would have to be grasped as a property of shape, or more generally of extendedness, *not*, however, shape or more generally extendedness as a property of the impenetrable. If, to be sure, one proceeds from the finished body, shape will always appear as its property: first, because, for reasons known to us, the body has acquired, in relation to the data of its visibility, audibility, and so on, the meaning of that which endures; and further, because the *rei*-*fied* body, which we can no longer help meaning by "body," is the substrate of all shapes as well.

If mechanistics has in the meantime long since arrived at mere equations of condition, we see in this the proof of the impossibility of reaching matter with physical judgements, and draw from it the confidence that judgements which allow us at least to point toward the inconceivable satisfy, more deeply, any spirit still capable of contemplation. — If sensing and beholding are polar life-processes, then the sensed, insofar as it is only this, and the beheld, insofar as it is beheld, likewise stand to one another in the relation of polarity — in short, the impenetrability and the appearance of the body. We shall show presently, from the most important data of dream-contents, that the making-independent of appearance has a limit, and here we hold fast to its polarity with impenetrability. Impenetrability is wholly dependent on space [p. 976]; space, in order to appear, is dependent on places of impenetrability; matter is entirely dependent on form, form originally likewise on matter. Neither of the two can be reduced to the other, and neither of the two would be capable of appearing without the other. Just as certainly as we can and must distinguish, in the body, spatial form and degree of impenetrability (= strength of resistance), just as certainly would the separation of the two mean the annihilation of the body, and then of matter too; hence the latter can be determined only in *relation* to space.

The formula of the science of life runs: matter is the placed-determinateness of the transformation of appearance, or the bearer of the changeable, or the "receiving-place of images." A subcase of the transformation of appearance is formed by vital motion, and of vital motion, for the detached faculty of conceiving, the lifeless remainder is mechanical motion, that is, the motion of "dead matter." The primordialimaged happening would not come to appearance without receiving-places for it, and what all receiving-places have in common with one another is called matter. Let an intermediate remark be permitted here, one that points ahead to what follows.

The relation of matter and image, or of place and happening, is the relation of a receiving principle to an acting principle, and forms, in accordance with age-old interpretation, the elementary analogy of the relation of the feminine to the masculine. If it is now correct that the offspring of the two, namely the appearance of the happening, takes up the capacity for begetting, thus again acting — but not upon matters, but upon souls capable of beholding-at-a-distance — then it too possesses the character of masculinity, and we would strike, at least by way of intimation, the primal sense of both poles of actuality with the remark that the feminine is the hidden secret, the masculine the secret to be revealed and revealed. The masculine would accordingly depend more on the feminine than the feminine on the masculine, which Heraclitus may have divined when he declared that hidden harmony is mightier than manifest; but the masculine would be, in relation to the feminine, its consummation. The feminine and the masculine would relate to one another, in primordial image, as the arche to the principium, the primordial beginning to the goal of development, to the ancient telete, or as, to actualization itself, the site of actualization. The lyre in the hands of Apollo harbors the sounds that stream from it; but without the god who "plays" it, it would remain forever mute. — [p. 977] In the vitalistic conceptual determination the accent falls on placed-determinateness, and by no means on divisibility, whose sense and consequences we must indicate at least in broad outline. Matter stands out from happening as place stands out from space, and in turn hangs together with happening as place hangs together with space. The appearance of divisibility, however, belongs to the product of its admittedly indispensable fusion with happening, to the body woven out of resistance and spatiality. — Just as place, if abandoned by space, would be derealized, so space could not appear without an actuality of places. Because the one and selfsame actual polarizes itself, among other things, into place and space, these are necessarily, from one and the selfsame connection, two modes of efficacy, through one of which the body stands out from happening, and through the other of which happening comes to appearance together with the body.

The separability — confirmed by the testimony of the senses — of bodies, whether of bodies themselves or of their parts, ineliminable for the individual, does not, in relation to elementary happening, possess with the same certainty the same character, inasmuch as the medium of all connectedness is spatio-temporal continuity. Dividing and separating were first flatly equated only after the thing, that is, the point, had substituted itself for the body, and thereby that between, for space, which then sooner or later appeared in the light of a paradoxically perceivable nothing;<sup>38</sup> Language still judges otherwise today. The executioner does not "divide" the body of the delinquent, but "separates" his head from his trunk. Dividing very often, overwhelmingly, has the sense of allotting, distributing, apportioning: one "shares" something with someone (i.e. gives him a part of it), whence the symbolic "communicate" [mitteilen]; one "divides" something among oneself; one "shares" joy and sorrow with someone; "shared joy is double joy, shared sorrow is half sorrow"; "to partake" and "to take part," finally, let the opposition to separating division be recognized directly. But let us make the metaphysics of the matter clear to ourselves by an example of intuitive division.

<sup>38</sup> On page 977. — Taking up note 18 again, we repeat: Telesio and Patrizzi were right, and Berkeley was wrong: intuitive space is immediately perceived and is, among other things, seen. But more than that: were space not perceived and not, among other things, seen, then nothing at all would be perceived, let alone seen, since, by means of the visual sense, for instance, we can perceive only what is separated from the visual organ by some distance, which is accordingly seen *along with* it. But if space is seen, then the *empty* is also seen; and more than that: were the empty not perceived and, among other things, seen, then *what is spatial* would not be seen at all, since spatial shape can stand out from other spatial shapes only within an empty, and never within a sheer full! — How does it come about that opinions of the kind discussed in note 18 emerged at an exceedingly early date: that the empty, if it exists at all, is in a sense an existing non-being — that nature abhors a vacuum — that empty space cannot be perceived but is merely inferred? The corporeality, in short, of Occidental thought alone does not suffice to explain fully how one could suppose that something unquestionably perceptible was a kind of nothing. A thorough investigation would require a treatise of its own; here we confine ourselves to a few main points. We need scarcely recall that we are moving on the ground of the science of appearances. When one speaks, in the terms of that science, of "empty space," or more briefly of "the empty," what is meant is not some physical vacuum but every intuitive emptiness whatsoever; and when one establishes, in the terms of that science, that empty intervening spaces are infallibly seen along with whatever is seen, this has not in the least to do with the question whether this capacity originally belongs to the visual sense or first accrued to it, say, through tactile experiences. This said in advance, we believe we can indicate at least three occasioning grounds for the above errors. In a very impressive way we become perceptually aware of empty space whenever we look into a large vessel, a barrel, a kettle, a deep pit, a well-shaft, and so on — provided they are empty. Yet they could just as well be full! And in not a few cases that would be more agreeable. Think, say, of an antique amphora: at one time full of wine, at another drunk empty! "It is empty" here means "there is nothing in it." Our exceedingly graphic word "Hohlraum" [hollow space, cavity] lets us fairly experience something of the supposed horror vacui ! ("Hohl" ["hollow"], related to "hehlen" ["to conceal"], originally "not filled within," retains its defensive emotional coloring in numerous compounds: Hohlkopf [hollow-head, blockhead], hollow tones, hollow sounds, hollow howling, to some extent still in "Höhle" [cave]; then faded: hollow lane, hollow way, concave mirror, and so on.) In short, since the emptiness of space was at first and above all referred not so much to intervening spaces as rather to hollow spaces, a negative accent of meaning came to rest upon space as such; and this could favor the prejudice that empty space is not perceived. Instead of dispelling it, the philosophers have nourished this prejudice in a twofold respect: through a confusion born of carelessness, which even today is by no means always avoided, and through — once again a confusion, but of a wholly different nature and origin. The first confusion belongs essentially to the modern age, insofar as the latter, for reasons that have become known to us, was bound to feel inclined to reflect on the space *beyond* the possible limits of the universe. One need only mentally transpose oneself into it, and one has gained the concept of an empty space *without* *places capable of appearing*. But out of the imperceptibility of this thought-thing — which might be called *worldless space* — there arises, in the twinkling of an eye, an imperceptibility of intuitive space, if one neglects to distinguish it properly from the intramundane intervening spaces! There are indeed persons who can scarcely hear the words "empty space" without feeling an impulse to *think away* the world! But there is just as little occasion for this, or even less, than there would be for the purpose of making present to oneself the sense of words like colorlessness or darkness. Intuitive space itself shows us everywhere intervening spaces that are empty in relation to the shaped images, *and* this intuitive emptiness is altogether something other than the negative concept of an absence of all intuitive images! The second confusion, roughly as old as European thinking about man, is that of sense impressions with objects of perception. It was raised to a principle by so-called English sensualism. If we replace the word "sense-process" with the still-prevailing "sense-sensation," and join those false doctrines that compose the process of perception out of sensations, it follows: since space assuredly is not sensed, as pressures, tastes, smells, sounds, colors, and so on are sensed, it is therefore not — perceived either! The theories that have been and are devised to evade this denial of a basic character of sensibility are numerous, ingenious, and full of wit; but not one of them is unassailable. And so the author will not be held it against him if, until further notice, he lives in the conviction that the problem of space is not merely insoluble but is even the source of numerous pseudo-problems, so long as one lacks knowledge of the duality of components in every sense-process: sensation and *beholding*. But in the process which, only together with sensation, leads to intuition — in the process of beholding — there lies, among other things, at the same time the explanation of why, for primal man, the everywhere-perceivable Between, notwithstanding the emptiness likewise seen by him, belongs no less to the *image* of the world than do the resting or moving shapes, and is therefore the bearer of powers that mediate between them. On this, however, the main text provides more precise information.

Let us break an apple in two through the middle: then, instead of one district of places of impenetrability, we have two, and may fittingly call them the halves of the apple. In the separation of the halves thereby involved we shall for the present attend only to the indispensability of its taking place, and consider first of all what we have actually divided and, through the dividing, separated. Not, assuredly, the impenetrability of the apple, [p. 978] but also not the mere volume of the apple. The thought of the divisibility of extents (= volumes) would never have arisen without the intuitive divisibility of bodies; but extents without a corporeal foundation cannot, in view of the gapless continuity of intuitive space, be separated, and are therefore divided only in a transferred sense.

If we compare the parts of the apple, as regards their extents, with the divided whole, we arrive at judgements such as: each is smaller than the whole, and the two together are as large as the whole. If we add still other properties that from some point of view permit comparisons of magnitude, e.g. the weight of the parts, we have entered upon a path that ends in the thought of the quantifiability of matter, but have thereby fallen into the realm of noumena, with which the independence of spirit from life announces itself against life, and shall in the end have exchanged the inconceivable for the self-contradictory, as the history of thinking proves: for every quantification, after all, finally leads out of space! We may, to be sure, make the thousandfold more-and-less with which the world of the senses besets us "manageable" (technicized) by reinterpreting it into quanta: but the vital origin, ultimately, of all quanta is intensity, gradable only by estimation; hence we miss the sense both of happening and of matter as soon as we take the quantum, in their place, to be actual.

We arrive at the following propositions: bodies are divisible insofar as their parts are separable; bodies are separable in relation to one another; they are not separable when considered according to their relation to elementary happening. If we take this as our starting point, then what emerges, out of the divisions that take place or can be performed on bodies, is a change in the distribution of sites of action of happening, or a change of its places of appearance, or an exchange of place of its "partaking." If, now, "matter" is to be understood as the condition, polar to happening, of the actuality of the body, then there is no divisibility of matter that could be thought as absolute separability.

Here, however, the reader will pause and object to us: then it would not, after all, be matter that lets itself be moved! The answer to this leads us back to the distinction between vital and mechanical motion. — If we free the discoverer's core thought of the Eleatics from the erroneous conclusions they believed they had to attach to it, there remains the essential insight that real motion is not [p. 979] what is grasped solely by the phenomenon of motion: the change of distance between two bodies, or points. If we call the former, briefly, motion, and the latter, say, displacement, then the insight in question can be circumscribed with the proposition that displacement, to be sure, is accessible to the understanding, but not the process of which displacement, point by point, represents the result. Bodies, now, are that on which we read off effects of motion in the form of displacements; motion, however, forms, of universal happening, that side, or better, mode of appearance, for whose actualization the actuality of places in space is needed, that is to say, matter. Thus the body would be displaceable, matter, on the other hand, and matter alone, the bearer of a happening that, in contrast to transformation, becomes intuitable as motion, and thereby, within happening generally, helps the spatial pole to preponderance. Motion too, then, would be transformation, in such a way, however, that its otherwise overemphasized temporality would have given way to an overemphasis of spatiality, and the polarity we have posited of matter and primordial image would appear in a new light, in that the one would bear the spatiality, the other the temporality, of happening. If we recall, further, what was discussed at length earlier, that it is the continuity peculiar equally to real space and real time that constitutes, for the understanding, the very cornerstone of offense, then not only the appearance of process withdraws from conceivability, but already the appearance of the outside-one-another, and what remains conceivable in displacement is, in the end, only the distance. It thereby becomes clear, however, that the divisibility which we can scarcely avoid acknowledging for the body resembles divisibility [in the arithmetical sense] only insofar as we mean the reified body. (Compare on this p. 674.)

The determination of matter as the movable is, under all circumstances, to be acknowledged, because it leaves motion the character of a state of something different from motion, instead of treating it, as subsequently happened, as though it were present in itself and a thing-analogous bearer of properties (velocity, direction, acceleration). The question is only what is meant thereby by "motion," and how much of the *actuality* of motion remains available in the meaning-content of the concept of motion. In this connection, however, the following "progress" took place of necessity. — If the (original) body is the appearance-capacity of a place, the bodily appearance the place-capacity of an image, [p. 980] then happening offers two "views," according as we relate corporeality to its appearance with the help of the concept of transformation, or appearance to its corporeality with the help of the concept of motion.
