As soon, now, as the thing has taken the place of the body, the second conception becomes predominant and generates the tendency to consider, first of all, every transformation from the standpoint of motion, and then, next, every motion from the standpoint of displacement; whereby happening succumbs to the essentially always static measurability of mere differences of position, and even the transformation that appears in coming and going succumbs to a division and linkage modeled after the concept of subtracting and adding up.

We are accustomed, for the most part, to pay no attention to the fact that we gain knowledge of the halves of the apple only by the actualization of an interspace which — no more conceivable than real space in general — requires the again inconceivable motion, whether of the one half, or of both at once. — We believe we understand what has occurred better when, in view of the transformation of water into two invisible gases upon the passage of the electric current, we posit two halves which, previously connected, are now separated, and finally, in the case of the thousandfold transformations in the test tube, suppose divisions and linkages of ultimate constituents; only we forget that we always have to accept in the bargain the two just-named inconceivabilities, the interspace and the motion, and that the former, when reduced to a mere distance, derealizes the moved thing through isolation!

A world so behaving would be no world at all, but a heap of separate worlds, between which absolutely nothing would happen, neither linkage nor division. In place of what could really link and divide bodies, in place of motion, it would exhibit nothing more than changes of distance, even if inconsistently alloyed in thought with the attribute of continuity. In short, only the thing is displaceable, and only the reified body divisible in such a way that the parts relate to the whole as the smaller number to the larger. The real body, on the other hand, is besides this an individual, and therefore even mechanically decomposable only into parts different in kind; and real motion is, besides this, a spatially accented appearance of happening, and therefore essentially different from mere displacement.

[p. 981] Down to the unicellular organisms, as we have seen, the actuality of place becomes manifest, in the (at first inconceivably body-near) intuitive space, through the life-process of sensing, and already in the initial state of humanity the body possesses a kind of independence that does not belong to the same degree to the phenomena that *we* call its properties, changes, motions. But for prehistoric or extra-historic and even historical man, so far as he has in no way yet come into contact with "science," the between-bodies is never that absolutely "empty space" that *separates* things, but always at the same time, among other things, an acting space, with whose help bodies converse *among themselves*.

These are symbolic identities, according to which the flourishing and decay of the little tree that was planted at a boy's birth are connected with the flourishing and decay of the youth, even though he dwell far away; or according to which, through magic ceremonies in one village, the sorcererpriests bring about an epidemic in another village. But insofar as the belief in images underlying such identities requires, for magical practices, intuitive images and hence bodies, these convictions would remain unintelligible were not space too taken up into the world of images and thereby become a mediator of effect between body and body. Perhaps it emerges still more drastically with the manifoldly attested fact that primitives conceive even the cardinal directions altogether as substances; of which mention was already made in the first volume. — We today marvel at such "superstitions"; but we do not want to forget that the impulses which come to realization in them — however wide of the mark — attest, as immediately lived, a polarity without which even we ourselves could not get along: the polarity between the actuality of happening and the actuality of places of appearance. Its example, hitherto longest investigated, is called, in the language of science: gravitation.<sup>39</sup>

<sup>39</sup> On page 981. — Our purely phenomenological investigation has nothing to do with physics. Since, however, the theories of physics have at least a *point of intersection* with actuality in common, they may not, *to that* *extent*, stand in contradiction with the results of the science of appearances. Weighing this requires, from case to case, an extensive investigation (of the kind carried out in Chapter 51), which is not planned here as regards matter. Only one point, concerning, so to speak, its distribution, including the "ether," is not to be passed over entirely: namely the question whether matter may be thought of as continuously spread through the whole of space (and of course of varying density). 1.) Just as two bodies (say, two wax spheres) can be melted together, so too can they be separated from one another to any distance. They are really separated insofar as we relate the one body to the other, and they remain connected with one another even at distances of light-millennia, insofar as we relate both together to what happens, or, that is, to the space in which it happens. Put differently: the parts into which we can divide matter are true and proper parts in relation to the body thereby divided; they are not parts in relation to the world. If we confuse that relative quantifiability with quantifiability as such, then even the relative quantifiability is uprooted, because its ground of possibility, namely the motion of the parts, becomes not merely incomprehensible but downright unthinkable. Or finally: every body may be conceived as a part of matter, and thus also of world-matter, but exchanges, in relation to the universe, its role of being-a-part for the role of a site of appearance of the whole. 2. From the fact that matter is the actuality of *places*, it follows with certainty that it could in no case be "everywhere." For then space would coincide with its places, place with space, whereby both would be annihilated, since place has standing only in relation to space, while space, without places, would no longer appear and thus also no longer be apprehended. 3. It is undecidable, from the standpoint of the science of appearances, whether the space in which things happen must be thought of, physically, after the manner of an immaterial substrate, that is, the ether; but it is entirely certain that every attempt (whether meant metaphysically or physically) to "trace back" one of the two poles of actuality to the other is doomed to failure and sooner or later perishes in mere feats of calculation.

If we look back upon the admittedly still short stretch that we believe to have traversed on the way to the reconnection of matter with the actuality of images, it should have become clear to us that from matter to primordial image the intuitive space, as it were, strikes the bridge, because without it neither of the two would appear: matter not for lack of the now, the primordial image not for lack of the here. With the demonstration [p. 982] of the first proposition the second is already demonstrated as well; but we wish to vouch for the second without reference to the first, by illuminating the placelessness of "pure" appearance. The Placelessness of "Pure" Appearance. — In the reader's interest it is advisable, before taking cognizance of the discussion that follows here, to go once more through the chapter on the "conceptual kinship of the visible appearance." Presupposing thorough acquaintance with its content, we refer to a single passage. After the result of far-ranging expositions had been summarized in propositions such as the following: "The process of seeing and the seen shape are placeless. The bodily shape is really located where it is felt by touch; the image-shape, without the body, is located nowhere or everywhere," the possibility of an objection was borne in mind with the words: "To be sure, we too locate mere visual images at determinate places of space, but only because for us the space of fact coincides with the space of touch, the — for reasons not yet ripe for discussion here — immediate bearer of the space of fact." We have since learned why the space of touch is the bearer of the space of fact; we no longer doubt (let this be assumed) that images, in order to appear, need place, and that the actuality of place is one and the same thing with the actuality of matter. But we also believe we know that, were matter wholly removed, no appearing would take place at all, and we wish to see the placelessness or freedom-from-place, which has so often been claimed for appearance as such, demonstrated in the evident sense of a mark of its distinction from the body, because otherwise doubts might arise. It is, one might want to consider, indeed correct, and curious enough, that of the waterfall the image can be in many places at once, and thus, in relation to the waterfall-body, leads a kind of "placeless, hovering existence," but it is nonetheless no less certainly associated, each time, with a definite place, just as certainly as its never-dispensable corporeal foundation, be it newspaper, film-strip, projection-screen, be it layer of air, wall of mist, curtain of rain. The detachability of appearance, or at least of the visual, from its corporeality plainly exists; but may we for that reason call it placeless, when indeed it would vanish without any material-local support whatsoever?

The theory would undoubtedly have to submit to at least certain modifications [p. 983] of its naming, had we no means at all of demonstrating what we mean by placelessness of appearance. Such means, however, do exist, though their application calls for a preliminary remark. — At bottom all so-called laws of nature — which one is accustomed to stress only for those where it becomes obtrusive — are "ideal limiting cases," which states of affairs can approach in the extreme without, however, ever reaching them. The gas equation, for example, which expresses the relation of the change of volume to changes of pressure and temperature quite "classically" simply, holds far from exactly, since, first, the behavior of any given gas deviates from it, and second, the behavior of each again deviates more or less from that of every other, and to some extent even in each case in its own particular way. Nevertheless it is a serviceable measure for the behavior of gases. Now we are not concerned here with "laws of nature," but with results of the science of essences; but the recollection of the "ideal limiting case" is admirably suited to elucidate the method we must employ for the purpose of demonstrating the placelessness of appearance.

If "pure" appearances do not and cannot exist, because they would then not merely not be anywhere, but would not be at all any longer, how shall we nonetheless demonstrate the placelessness of appearance? By attempting to show that the more one takes from appearance its bodily support, the more it takes on the character of placelessness. But before, on the path of increasing disembodiment, it would reach the limiting case of "pure" appearance, it would have ceased to be present. If, however, we can furnish evidence for the parallelism just indicated, then, drawing on everything that has already been established, in the course of our inquiry, concerning the essence of images, it is permitted, indeed required, to count placelessness among the criteria of appearance as such.

Copy-image and mirror-image, both placeless in the space of fact, but both connected in different ways with the existence of things, nonetheless each have, mediately, from case to case, a place: the former a real one, coinciding with the body that bears it; the latter an apparent one, whose apparent position is determined by the real position of the original before the mirror. This lies, however, already in the concepts of both, inasmuch as they could not be formed at all without reference to things in the always fully articulated space of fact and to their ever-determinate position and change of position. [p. 984] For the purpose of exhibiting the placelessness of appearance we therefore had to be able to exchange the scene of bodies for a scene of bodiless appearances. Is there a state of life that makes this possible? We have long known it: it is the state of nocturnal as well as waking dreaming.

Someone remembers the garden in which he played as a boy, he calls before himself the beds of periwinkle, the caper bushes rich in bloom and sternly fragrant, the dusky arbor of wild vine, the noise of carriages rolling past, the drowsy sultriness of the blue summer day; the mood of those longsunken days resounds within him, and as it captures and enmeshes him more and more, suddenly his soul is carried off into dream-space, where before the inner eye there forthwith takes place what a moment ago was only "represented." He is once again the boy of that time; the appearing images have gained a life of their own, they unfold, similarly to the images of a world of perception, out of themselves, he follows them instead of calling them forth, and what occurs, as though it were really present, is now neither remembered nor need it unfold as it would correspond to a faithful recollection. Reflecting momentarily, he knows: that was at another time than the one in which I now find myself, that was another space than the one that presently encompasses me; but during the reign of his phantasms he has left the now and here of factually present existence and exchanged it for the scene of bodilessly present images. Would these, then, be placeless images? Certainly not, certainly not yet. For, in the first place, our dreamer is by supposition awake, and therefore engaged in a continual swinging to and fro between dream-space and the here-now of waking space, and to that extent half and half a spectator of his waking-dream visions; and, in the second place — and this holds even for the accomplished dream — he is a dreamer who has often and long been present in waking space and who therefore carries the treasure of experience of his waking into his dreaming as well. In any case, even the play of phantasms of his waking offers, by way of intimation, some features that distinguish it from the proceedings of his world of perception: sudden leap of the chain of images and the emergence of another that could not be reconciled, in factual time, with the previous one; sudden change of scene, such as would not occur just as abruptly in the space of fact. These features, however, become dominant features with the completion of the dream-state in sleep.

[p. 985] Of the genuine sleep-dream, no longer disturbed by any world of perception, no one has hitherto been able to say what it actually is; nor will anyone ever be able to say without a knowledge of the two components of all sense-processes: sensation and beholding. We may, "to a first approximation," as the physicists say, determine it as sensationless beholding. Here, however, an insertion cannot be avoided. For scarcely have we said this than one will recall the countless theories that seek to derive the contents of dreams from external or internal "stimuli," in relation to which the consciousness of the sleeper resembles, say, a distorted mirror: as, the dream of the Alpine glow from the sunbeam playing in, which has struck the sleeper's never wholly closed lids; the dream of wading through snowfields from the cooling of the feet, which were bared of the blanket; the dream of the waiter who lets the plates fall with a clatter, from the beginning rattle of the alarm clock; the dream of soaring up and rushing down on the swing, from palpitation of the heart; the dream of the sumptuous drinking-bout from the inner bodily sensations of thirst, and so on.<sup>40</sup>

<sup>40</sup> On page 985. — The stimulus-origination theory of the dream is found, more or less, in all researchers who have worked on the dream. Some emphasize the outer, others the inner stimuli more strongly. As the chief representatives of that variety we name: D'*Hervey*, *Hildebrandt*, *Strümpell*, *Maury*, *Wundt*, *Weygandt*, Gieß*ler*, Monroe, Beaunis, and above all Vold; of the other: *Schopenhauer*, *Börner*, Krauß, *Scherner*, Volkelt, Radestock, *Simon*, Spitta, Tissié. Incidentally, the "stimulus-origination theorist" of the dream need not strike his colors in the face of the intervention of far-acting "fluids." Were dream-visions perhaps co-determined by a change of weather, snowfall, foehn pressure, the full moon, or even by the lengthwise position of the body relative to the magnetic meridian; did they themselves credibly hang together with distant events or with the soul-stirrings of another person, whether waking or dreaming — still, the stimulus-origination theorist could maintain, the facts in question would in every case have had to produce some modification in the bodiliness of the sleeper, and it would be this modification alone that, in a manner admittedly still to be more precisely described, occasions the dream-contents. In short, he would leave the Romantic conception of the sleep-dream an open question, confining himself instead to demonstrating the derivation of dreaming from bodily processes of the sleeper, and attempting to build up the dream-visions out of the sensation-contents bound up with these. — Such thoughts, to be sure, tend to lie quite remote from this group of researchers.

Against speculations of this kind little is to be objected, so long as they do not suppose themselves to have thereby explained dreaming to us. Who could seriously deny that the bodily processes of the sleeper contribute to the fabric of his dreams, and who would not at bottom know it? Aristotle knew it. "One supposes," he says in the first chapter of his treatise "On Prophesying by Dreams" (in Rolfers's translation), "that it lightens and thunders, when a faint sound strikes the ear; believes one is tasting honey and sweet flavors, when one swallows a little phlegm, and that one is passing through fire . . . when particular limbs grow a little warm." The Romantics especially have made use of such connections with predilection, in order to captivate us with magnificent dream-visions, for which one may compare, say, the artfully attuned and splendid poem "Ein Sommertagstraum" [A Summer-Day's Dream] by Annette von Droste-Hülshoff, or the charming dream-episode in the third chapter of Eichendorff's "Taugenichts." Here, however, an account is to be given of what happens with the "stimuli" whenever they occasion dream-visions instead of, as in waking, processes of perception.

If a luminous flame shines through a strong solution of alum, its luminous element passes through almost undiminished, while its warming element is for the most part absorbed, so that on the other side almost only light-effects [p. 986] take place: in some such way, of everything that acts within the body of the sleeper, indifferently whether it arises within or outside it, only that reaches the soul which is convertible into visibilities, whereas the sensible remains "on this side." We have used the simile for the sake of abbreviating the course of thought, and let it drop now that it has done its service. For here it is not the case that on one side of the sleeping body stands the bodily appearance, and on the other the dreaming soul, so that from the former the intuitive images would have to detach themselves, as the luminous element of the flame detaches itself from the warming; but rather, to retain at least the spatial element of the metaphor: to the left of the sleeper's state, vegetative bodily processes take place, or, psychologically speaking, sleeping beholding and sleeping acting; to the right, of this the soul becomes aware, in whatever can present itself in the form of appearing. It would take a book to show how from this all, literally all, the characters of dreaming become intelligible. Such a book, entitled "Vom Traumbewußtsein" [On Dream-Consciousness], was begun by the author several years before the war; the first part, headed "Charaktere der Traumstimmung und des Traumes" [Characters of the Dream-Mood and of the Dream], appeared in 1914; of the second, "Das Wachbewußtsein im Traume" [Waking Consciousness in the Dream], the first half — wrested only with difficulty from the psychic disturbances that the calamity of mankind brought with it — appeared in 1919 (94 printed pages together); but the second half, though almost completely written down, was never published, because the elaboration of the third and last part, "Das Traumbewußtsein im Wachen" [Dream-Consciousness in Waking], had to be abandoned. Since the work is very difficult of access , let it<sup>41</sup> be permitted to reproduce here a few passages from it pertaining to the matter. Since these, however, particularly bring out the significance of dreaming and of dreams for man's entire view of the world, the result shall be anticipated, as it were, in bare words and shown by a few examples, chosen precisely from the most nearly meaningless dream-visions.

<sup>41</sup> On page 986. — The work "Vom Traumbewußtsein" is to be found in the "Zeitschrift für Pathopsychologie," which ceased publication many years ago, namely in the volumes for 1914 (pp. 1–38) and 1919 (pp. 373–429).

Suppose that dreaming were sensationless beholding, and mere appearance were placeless: then dream-visions would have no fixed position in space, and consequently also none in time, and hence, despite every semblance of being real, not the character of existences; from which there follow, among other things, the following dream-characters, which everyone will confirm who still dreams here and there vividly enough to be able afterward to recollect what happened in the dream: [p. 987] 1.) The dreamer has unawares changed place without the participation of any process of motion. — 2.) He suddenly finds himself in another time, in relation, of course, to the time-situation of his dream. He is, for example, once again a child who has not finished his schoolwork, and yet at the same time knows that he has long since been practicing a bread-winning profession. — 3.) The same transitionless interchange of spatial and temporal positions takes place, in principle, in regard to any content of the dream whatsoever. — 4.) The sameness of the seeming objects of the dream ceases. Each is what it is, and *can* at the same time be something entirely different, without the dreamer having to be astonished at it. — 5.) The same fate naturally befalls the linguistic designations of the units of meaning.

*A few examples may make this vivid.* — The dreamer is driving in a carriage on the highway and is already, at the same time, riding in a boat on a canal — "the kiss of Judith," so the "Green Henry" of Gottfried Keller relates in the "Heimatsträume" [Dreams of Home], "was actually a piece of apple cake, which I ate eagerly" — the dreamer perceives two rows of naked boys moving against one another, and unexpectedly takes a set of dentures out of his mouth, since it was, after all, the rows of teeth that had been moving against one another — the dreamer sits in an arbor and sees, through a narrow gap in the garden fence, a cow; this suddenly springs, as though it were quite natural, through the gap; the dreamer flees — the dreamer sees how someone has set his own head, which, however, is made of wax, before the window in the sun, and perceives with the utmost discomfort how the head begins to melt and run — the dreamer talks without surprise with a friend who, as he knows, has long been dead, and sees at the same time (again without surprise) himself standing on the balcony of a nearby house — the dreamer leafs through a book of his own notes, where each next page offers ever more momentous disclosures and depths of insight; he feels himself approaching the page on which the "solution of the riddle of the world" will stand; he opens it, reads, seized by shudders, the solution of the riddle of the world, awakens, and can just still recollect what he had read, which ran: "It is a settled matter that everyone paints a goat on the wall" — These few examples are taken, some exactly, some in somewhat abridged form for the sake of emphasizing what is here important to us, from the real dreams of different [p. 988] persons, insofar as the criteria which the science of essences provides could guarantee the unfalsified character of the dream-reports.<sup>42</sup>

<sup>42</sup> On page 988. — A rarely beautiful collection of genuine sleepdreams, outstandingly well rendered, is given by the little book: *Friedrich* *Huch*, Träume (Berlin, Fischer 1904); as well as volume IV of the "Gesammelte Werke" (Stuttgart, Deutsche Verlagsanstalt).

If it is the boundness-to-place of appearance that makes it possible for the animal to recognize and re-recognize the world of bodies, and makes it possible for man to hold fast appearances by linking them to identifiable things, then the thousandfold attestable loss of sameness of dreamed units of meaning proves that their appearances largely lack spatially and temporally determinate places. Were one to object that even in the dream, from case to case, definite situations are after all given, hence a side-by-side and a one-after-another, it would have to be recalled: first, that "pure" appearance is a mere concept, since with complete placelessness it would itself come to nothing; and second, as already indicated above, that in the form of acquired dispositions the sleeper carries the whole past of his waking into the state of sleep, since without this presupposition he could not dream at all any longer.<sup>43</sup> The dream-appearance possesses, rather, in fact, lability of place in any degree whatsoever, and therein we find the confirmation that appearance as such would lose place, were it experienceable *without* any reference to the corporeality familiar to us. We call visions that presuppose the appearance-space of place-bound wakefulness phasms of the waking state, and may therefore define, "to a second approximation": dreaming is sensationless beholding, but in regard to phasms of the waking state.

<sup>43</sup> On page 988. — A being that would *not* carry the past of its wakefulness over into its dreams could not dream, for this reason: that it would lack the phasm *of corporeality*, since anything *really* corporeal is, after all, experienced only in waking. But were it to lack the phasm of corporeality, the appearances would literally become placeless, and the intuitive character of space would consequently vanish away; or: the very stage-setting of the dream-visions would be annihilated. Should it therefore be the case, for example — as we shall later make probable — that the plant does *not* wake, and consequently does not experience corporeality (or does so only in rudiments too weak to be of use), then the plant could not dream either, in the manner of animals and men. With the "phasms of the waking state," as one notices, two things are set in relation to the dream state: on the one hand the corporeality of the world, on the other the wakefulness of the sleeper, which, however, in sleep belongs to his past. This explains why the one group of researchers has always been inclined, and still is, to hunt for occasioning "stimuli," while the other group, by contrast, is inclined to interpret the dream-visions as after-effects of past experiences of the waking state. Both are right, insofar as they wish to search through the materials of which the dream state must avail itself in order to weave dreams out of them; and both talk entirely past the matter, insofar as they suppose that in this way they can illuminate dreaming itself!

This determination, too, does not coincide exactly with the state of affairs, because dreaming, owing to the varying depth of sleep, is variously disturbed by contents of sensation (= waking-stimuli) that no longer belong to the dream-state itself, but accompany its passing over into awakening. To this belongs, for example, a suddenly flashing-up consciousness of the dreamer *that* he is dreaming; to this belongs every equally sudden recollection of data of the past of wakefulness; to this belongs the welling-up of real voluptuousness and real pain, which, both of them, when taken over from the dream-state, arouse feelings of bliss or of anxiety, but on the other hand wake the sleeper as soon as their degree of intensity no longer permits the transposition.<sup>44</sup> If we hold all this together, it need not be discussed at length why the nightly dream-visions, of every degree, can turn out poor in primordial images and accordingly silly, [p. 989] confused, lacking a view of the world, but equally, of every degree, rich in primordial images and accordingly meaningful and world-revealing. In general their essentiality will grow, among other things, sometimes with the depth of sleep, always with the fullness of the sleeping soul, further with the, in terms of the science of life, ambiguous circumstance of the relative independence of the soul from the body. How, by this means, at the same time a great manifoldness of differently constituted occurrences becomes accessible to interpretation, such as somnambulism, fascination, hypnosis, "slumber-images," seemingly unmediated sympathetic action, so-called clairvoyance, and much else of the kind, cannot be set forth here. The dependence of the mythic state of consciousness on the dream-state, however, strongly emphasized in the reproductions now following from our work on dream-consciousness, needs all the less to be elucidated further, since it in any case comes up again in the concluding section of our work.

<sup>44</sup> On page 988. — To forestall a misunderstanding: dreamed feelings of anxiety on the one hand, feelings of bliss on the other, can have still *other* causes than those just touched upon.

"Not deep enough had we dug, when to the transience of the world in the dream-mood we found the correspondence in the dream-phantasm itself, in its transformability, when we said that even it, in turn, is a transposition of only the ultimate character of appearance: in the flux of time to remain, without ground, not the same, indeed already at one and the same time to be both one thing and another. We see the principle of identity vanish, and with it the concept of the fact, and dispose of the assumption of the essential sameness of representing now by pointing out that with every representation the spirit means, after all, facts, from which it proceeds, of its own impulse and often with effort, to other facts. Viewed more closely only one form of thinking, representing fails just as this does in the face of the dream-appearance, in such a way that one may say it is precisely for this reason that the dream dissolves, because one attempts to represent it . . . !" The process of fantasying, dreamlike yet different in essence from it, "governs the poetry of myth and of Romanticism, whereas from fairy tale, folk song, and legend the unbroken dreaming itself speaks, completing every transformation without onset and sequence, yet leaving the transformed thing its familiar features. In the fairy tale of the "Machandelboom" [Juniper Tree] (after Grimm) the magic is worked upon the bones of the slain and eaten boy, after the little sister has carried them under the tree, as follows: "Mit des so güng dar so'n Newel von dem Boom un recht in dem Newel dar brennd dat as Führ, un uut dem [p. 990] Führ dar flöög so'n schönen Vagel heruut, de süng so herrlich un flöög hoog in de Luft, um as he wech wöör, do wöör de Machandelboom as he vürhen west wöör, un de Dook mit de Knakens wöör wech." Now the uncanny soul-bird begins to sing its gruesome verses:

My mother, she who slaughtered me, / My father, who ate me, etc.; but whoever hears it, the goldsmith, the shoemaker, the twenty miller's lads, each one is edified by it and gives the bird what it desires: the golden chain, the shoes, and, as a ruff for its neck, the hundredweight millstone. No astonishment arises that a bird could tell such a prior history and bear a threefold burden; rather, for the dream-consciousness there is sensibly present in it the demon of avenging fate. Thus its song fills the father with bliss, the little sister with joyful expectation; thus it brings gift to both, chain and shoes, but to the murderess, seized with horror, the crushing millstone. And scarcely has this happened than fiery smoke again billows up, and living and unharmed the murdered, dismembered, and eaten boy steps forth, and, as though they had forgotten everything, the three, father, son, and daughter, go "into the house to table and eat." In the world of things the gruesome drama becomes a fleeting phantom and shadowplay, however gripping-real it was in the world of appearance."

"As though bathed in the vapor of primordial poetry, German Romanticism created a literature of dream-consciousness that finds no equal among any other people, and in the best pieces of a Tieck, an Eichendorff, a Hoffmann it lets us not even wake up in between. Through the latter especially we gain insight into the essence of genuine magic and enchantment, for the interpretation of which modern suggestion-literature courted in vain. Different from the autonomously dreaming consciousness, for which there are only appearances, the fascinated consciousness remains bound to things in that it experiences, now in a truly spectral manner, the mythical change of shape and loss of identity precisely in them. Commonly compelled by the magician with the help of fear, but also surrendering from itself and forthwith subjected to the imaginative affect of a voluptuous dread, the transformed one believes he perceives what can only be beheld: on the bronze door-knocker in the hand of the student Anselmus, "the metallic face .. " twists "into a grinning smile"; it is the [p. 991] demonic apple-woman — the grasped bell-cord sinks down and becomes a transparent serpent — among the bushes and trees in the house of the archivist Lindhorst (who is in fact the prince of spirits) there seem, on closer inspection, to stretch "long corridors into the far distance" — a fire-lily bush suddenly begins to stride, and it is the archivist himself, whose "dressing-gown gleaming in yellow and red" had "merely deceived" Anselmus — from the eyes of the green serpent the beloved gazes at him in unspeakable longing — a stream of fire surrounds him; but, looked at more closely, these are "after all only great books with gilded edges" — embracing the serpent as his beloved, he hears from her the tale of the wonder-land of Atlantis, only to find it afterward, apparently written in his own hand, in the unfamiliar characters of the mysterious script he was to copy — a droll little man appears for the punch-evening, delivering the archivist's compliments, but as he strides out the door, all now see that he "was in fact a gray parrot" — the old coffee-pot with the half-broken lid is in truth a witch, who in turn is at bottom a mangel-wurzel, and so on. But no passage in the "Golden Pot," from which we quote, lets us see more deeply into the transformation-delusion of the bewitched one than the following. As punishment for the fateful ink-blot, Anselmus, amid the wildest magical uproar, ends up in a wellcorked crystal flask on a shelf in the library-room of the secret prince of spirits. He floats motionless "as in a frozen ether," his breath comes heavily, his pulse-veins swell, and through the crystal glow that holds him captive all the objects around seem to waver in trembling rainbow colors. Lamenting, he calls out to his beloved — "then someone right beside him said: 'I really do not know what you want, Herr Studiosus, why do you lament so beyond all measure?' The student Anselmus became aware that beside him, on the same shelf, five more flasks stood, in which he beheld three choirboys and two clerks. 'Ah, my gentlemen and companions in misfortune,' he cried out, 'how is it possible for you to be so composed, indeed so merry, as I observe from your cheerful faces? You after all sit just as well locked up in glass flasks as I do, and cannot stir . . , indeed cannot even think anything sensible .. without its buzzing and roaring in your heads.' 'You are surely raving, Herr Studiosus,' replied a choirboy, 'never have we [p. 992] fared better than now, for the species-thalers which we receive from the mad archivist for all sorts of confused copying do us good; .. we go now every day to Josephus's .., let the double beer taste good to us, also look a pretty girl in the eyes now and then, sing like real students .. and walk diligently up to the vineyard, instead of sitting between four walls at tiresome copying-work.' 'But my best, most worthy sirs!' said the student Anselmus, 'do you then not feel that you are all, each and every one, sitting in glass flasks and cannot stir or move, let alone walk about?' Then the choirboys and the clerks burst into a bright laugh and cried: 'The Studiosus is mad, he imagines himself sitting in a glass flask and is standing on the Elbe bridge and looking straight down into the water. Let us just go on!'" — One believes, with the breaking-off of the voice, that one feels the instantaneous extinguishing of the memory of the whole occurrence, and being caught once more in the tormenting spell of the appearance which overwhelms the flashing perception-image."

" . . . We would remain incomplete, however, if we did not also carry the thought over to the medium of all dreaming as of all waking, and furnish the proof that de-reification seizes space and time as well... Were we to separate extension and uninterruptedness from space and time as alone we can "represent" them, there would no longer be an earlier and a later, and the straight line would no longer be the shortest line between two points. We can think it traversed at speeds a million times greater than that of lightning, and still it would be traversed by means of motion (either of the moving point or of itself) and in time, and nowhere would room remain for a gap. But dreaming, we experience how utterly unthinkable it is for the encompassing space to be bereft of the power of extension and for time to be interrupted from point to point, so that both are surmountable in an instant, every There a Here and every Once a Now! Not only do things de-objectify themselves insofar as they appear in the dream, but space and time too sink down to the state-of-affairs level of mere mirror-images, and thus the element of all separation — extension — loses its efficacy. The apart ceases to have the sense it has in waking; what was, is there again, and what is only going to happen is already taking place. Motion itself, as the [p. 993] perceptible form of the union of time with space, goes under in the dimensionless sphere of appearance and leaves behind, in the most proper sense, a phantom of motion, whose spectral play — sometimes gladdening, more often tormenting — we still have to consider. We no longer find ourselves in the flux of time, where for every Now the Once unstoppably flees back, but in an everlasting present with an unboundedly mobile *now-point*, and we find ourselves just as little in outer space, which takes time to traverse, but rather in an unboundedly mobile *Here*. . "

" . . . We understand the meaning of the lack of memory in the dream. It is not that it lacks recollection, which, as is well known, can indeed reach far beyond that of waking; rather, it lacks the spiritual form of recollecting, because, owing to the instantaneous shift of the point of the present, the recollected at once enters into the present as well. Scarcely does green Henry wish, in the dream, to recall the apples which he ate years before with Judith, when these apples are already present in the shape of the apple-cake into which her kiss is transformed. And likewise every distance of space is found effaced the moment it merely enters the beholder's point of view, just as, on the other hand, it can be reached by no exertion or willed movement, so often as it is represented in the dream after the manner of waking. Before we look more closely at the latter point in particular, we must still especially recall the shifts — so utterly incomprehensible to waking consciousness — to which all relations of magnitude succumb, because the dimensions are enfeebled and permit the instantaneous interchange of the distant with the near, the great with the small, the wide with the narrow, the containing with the contained, in this way filling, with a meaning intelligible of course only to the dreamer, "the true element of nonsense." The singing of the mango-child Mouli (in the Indian fairy-tale) sounds twelve days' journey through the forest and lures Koila, without needing on that account to be especially loud — the princess Anar Rani is wont to sleep with her two maidens in pomegranates, of which each nonetheless encloses a complete bed — Allerleirauh (in the German fairy-tale) packs her sun-, moon-, and star-dress, as though nothing were more natural, into a nutshell — the tent of the fairy Pari Banu, which spans four armies (in the Arabian fairy-tale), nonetheless has room in a closed hand, and the astonishment at this is no greater than would in any case seem fitting in view of so roomy a [p. 994] covering — in Hoffmann's "Nutcracker" little Marie climbs with the Mouse King up through her father's fur sleeve to a wonder-world. The conscious impossibilities in the so-called lying-tales of the Greeks and Tatars prove, on closer examination, at least in part not to be ordinary jests but caricatures drawn from the actuality of dream-consciousness: a man slips through a needle's eye or through a finger-ring — in the middle of a white flea lies a gleaming city, in which a king dwells — someone relates that at fifteen he rocked his father in the cradle, or that at that time his mother was still his daughter. Mixed of genuine dream-spectrality and willed distortion is the witch's magic spell in Faust:

Und Neun ist Eins / Und Zehn ist Keins / Das ist das Hexen-Einmal-Eins." — And nine is one / And ten is none / That is the witches' one-times-one." / Our interpolations have, we hope, also scattered the last dark remainder that might still have clung to the thought of the "placelessness of pure appearance." It was shown, on no small body of material, that with the growth of the dream-state the bodiless visions fall prey to a growing lability of their spatiotemporal place, from which it is to be concluded that "pure" appearance would lack place, were it not already beforehand robbed of appearing; further, that with vanishing capacity for place the unity-ofmeaning of the appearing essence vanishes as well; from which it is to be concluded that only a place-bound corporeality admits the existential judgement. For the characterization of the space of intuition, then, the perennial Now does not suffice; there is added the Here fixable at or in it. If, then, the intuitability of space is grounded in the possibility of experiencing the Now as present here and the Here as present now, then the Now too must change if the here-ness of the Now begins to waver, and the transformation that accompanies the de-corporealization of appearance reaches into the very scene of appearances. The essence of the space of intuition, and equally of the time of intuition, lies in the polarity of nearness and distance. But if we make serious with an "unboundedly mobile Now" and an "unboundedly mobile Here," then we have de-actualized both distance and nearness, and phantomized the movement that in bodily space connects the two. The dream-space, the phantasm of the [p. 995] space of intuition, lacks, through the lability of its Now and Here, the opposition of distance and nearness, and thus offers only the *phantasm* of presentness.

It was mentioned in the first volume that in East Asian antiquity the process of making-present possessed a considerable preponderance over the process of embodiment, and what in part wondrous, in part also strange occurrences resulted from this. Here we recall once more the "distanceless depth of the *merely* visible space" in the incomparable Chinese landscape paintings, but now also indicate the reverse side of the magical dream-beauty of those forms, not in order to exercise criticism, but for the sake of pointing the way to a beauty and greatness of an opposite kind. Sprung from dream-space, Chinese landscape art knows the far-depth intoxication of Occidental pictorial arts not at all or hardly, but just as little, or even less, our coarse-handed nearness. While the horizons of Chinese landscapes are mostly barred, usually by fantastically sky-high mountains, even their foregrounds already offer the character of distance and *are* not at all "foregrounds" in our sense. Everything is distant, one might say, and again, nothing is "properly" distant; rather it hovers before us as a melancholy-blissful semblance: realms of the dream-world as though mirrored by walls of mist. Certainly this perfection of the arts of mere visible appearance is granted to no Occidental heroism steeped in actuality. But if we set aside for once the height of perfection of the form and gather our gaze upon its essential content, then before many a color-poem of Böcklin's, "Triton and Nereid" say, perhaps the shudder of *the* distance touches us, a distance that is purchasable only at the price of the actuality of nearness! And this, finally, be said here in closing: only in bodily space do distance and nearness become demonic actualities, which, with the tragic inescapability of the must-separate, conjure up from the darkest grounds the wildest blazing of life. — The site of primal disturbance. — Before ideological actuality degenerates into a world of mere concepts, it is a world of bodiless forms. In Plato and in Schiller we have shown how, among the motives for according belief to such worlds of semblance, flight from pain goes hand in hand with the overemphasis of visible appearance. In [p. 996] fact, nature has now shown a fearsome inventive skill, in that it endowed every sensation with the capacity for heightening into the painful, and each, moreover, with its own variants of painfulness, such as: nausea, ringing in the ears, limpness, dazedness, palpitation, seasickness, chill, headache, migraine, fainting spells, suffocation, belly-ache, stitch in the side, toothache, muscle cramp, joint pain, lumbago, rheumatism, labor pains, sciatica, neuralgias, and so on. But if it is thus indeed the sentient corporeality that "prepares for us countless hindrances" (Plato), it is nonetheless no less the sentient corporeality to which the soul owes just as many degrees and kinds of inconceivable feelings of well-being, beginning with the flattering breath of the fragrances of spring up to the sinking into the fire-chalice of voluptuousness. "Does not even the mere transition from greater to lesser pain infallibly bring with it that likewise bodily feeling of well-being which one summarily calls 'relief,' although it means, each time, quite different delights, according as, for example, a wound ceases to burn, a throbbing heart grows calm, after paralyzing sultriness a storm fans coolness, a tormenting thirst is quenched, after hard muscular labor complete rest refreshes the strained body.. Think further of the delights of skin- and touch-sensation in high-summer bathing in flowing waters, in barefoot wandering on soft turfcarpet, in the sinking of the body into a swelling pillow, in letting the hand glide over the smooth surfaces of polished stones, in stroking heavy furs, a dense plumage, and not least the forms of the human body. Look at the certainly quite unspiritual well-being that the smallest children show in scrabbling in sand or in stirring and shaping wet earth, and one will no longer dare to doubt the felt-ness of what is thus experienced." And what soul-sweetnesses can pair them-<sup>45</sup> selves, in the sense-awakened human being, with experiences of taste! With what wealth of invention, which leaves all human fantasy far behind it, does nature, as we partake of food, delight us, who offers us the spring-drink and grapeblood, who bestows on us honey and grain-fruits, peaches, apples, oranges, raspberries, pineapples, or at least allows such to be won from her!<sup>46</sup> Even the wonder-world of scents, though more strongly interwoven with beholding, requires thoroughly the sentient substratum, and would remain on this side of the threshold of the shadow-realm of forms which, according to ideological delusion, is supposed to compensate for the loss of the body. [p. 997] Who, finally, would wish to deny that a healthy, strong, and well-trained corporeality can lift one to heights of the joy of life, where delight resolves itself into dances, overflows in jubilant songs! Beginning with the orchestics of the Greeks down to the recently reawakening cult of the body, everything that has become known to us, gladdeningly, from word and image and living presence, of the rhythmic play of the limbs, would sink into ruins, were actuality robbed of its corporeality.

<sup>45</sup> On page 996. — *Klages*, Vom Traumbewußtsein, loc. cit. 1919, pp. 408 and 409.

<sup>46</sup> On page 996. — To substantiate the quite extraordinary significance of precisely the experiences of taste for the entire soul-life of man, a great number of proofs could be adduced, of which only two shall be cited here. The Latin sapiens, "wise," comes from the verb sapere, "to taste." In German the verb schmecken ["to taste"] developed early from the noun Schmack, and, though originally related to the sense of taste, and alongside it to the sense of smell, was very soon also applied to lofty and the loftiest experiences: to "taste" heavenly gifts, to "taste" rest and peace, to "taste" death — in Jean Paul even: "sie schmeckten sich einander gut" ["they tasted good to one another"]. The word "Geschmack" ["taste"], which arose later, has then, in imitation of the French goût, since the beginning of the eighteenth century, been used, as is well known, just as often for someone's *artistic* "taste" as for the taste-direction of his tongue!

Not in the capacity for pain as such, therefore, may we seek the site of primal disturbance; rather we must seek it, and have already found it, in the experience of resistance, which points back to the impulse of movement and the hindrance that befalls its working. Since, however, in the animal domain of life, from the amoeba up to man, *all* disturbances originally attach themselves to this — which is why, for example, primitive man traces every illness back to a foreign body that has magically penetrated the body of the sick person — it follows, as has again and again been emphasized, that, regardless of polar reciprocity, animal sensibility depends more on animal motility than the reverse; and correspondingly, it is, within the special domain of humanity, the predominance of the willing attitude over the cognizing attitude through which the worst misfortune broke in upon the soul, until at last the spirit could emancipate itself and attempt to slay the one forever fettered. It is the body as barrier that has put it into his head to make war upon the here and now and to seek to enfeeble distance, and it is the body as tool that has enabled him to bring about at least the vanishing of all earthly intervening spaces.

With the uncovering of the primal-original occasioning ground for the entry of the act, we have solved the question left open earlier, "whether the susceptibility to disturbance of the drives and interests might not perhaps be intelligible from a trait of essence common to all of them, one that would explain to us even better than has just been done even the almost indifferent acts of involuntary attention to a matter" (p. 265). As will be recalled, nothing sensed would become an object of perception without the assistance of a wave of feeling bound up with it. Were all feelings to fall to the zero point, no more "awakening of attention" would take place and we would sink into unconsciousness. Since now, during waking, we constantly notice numerous things without, on reflection, finding [p. 998] feelings that would have attested their presence to us, it might seem as though the indifferent were exempted from the rule just named. But this is not so, because even to the object perceived without participation there clings *that* by which it occasions fine changes of attitude: its existence within the domain of a bodily world, with regard to which every wave of feeling, indeed every faintest impulse, is first of all to be realized.

It constitutes the essential mark already of the animal form of life, and altogether of the human faculty of apprehension, that everything that falls within the domain of perception stands in connection with what is bodily actual, now immediately, now mediated by intervening links. To be sure, the characters of actuality appear and determine the formation of all original unities of meaning; but only the linking of the data of intuition with corporealities makes possible for the animal an instinctive recognition, for man the perception of existing things. — We established earlier, and documented with examples (especially from language), why in an actuality of *mere* images substratum and property, or subject and predicate, would be interchangeable, and one will now easily supplement that in it there would also be lacking the impulse its goal and, still more, the intention its purpose. The origin of the grammatical subject, too, is of course the I; but its original representative is the foreign body, insofar as we attend in it not to what makes it the receiving-place of images, but to what makes it the ground of hindrance to self-movement.

Here we interpolate that with this an occurrence has now also found its explanation, of which we made mention on p. 444 in connection with the attempt to demonstrate intuitively the accomplishment of the act of boundary-setting division, by placing side by side the still-unapprehended content of impression and the object of perception that it signifies once the act of perceiving has taken place. "He who is woken from deep sleep by a knocking at the door not seldom *knows*, at the moment of perceiving, that it had already knocked twice before, without his being-there having gained the character of selfhood and the awakening sound the character of thing-ness." With such and similar occurrences there attest themselves, as it were, hovering processes of intuition that have not yet, or only imperfectly, accomplished their union with a place-determined process of sensation, whether, as here, out of half-sleep, or owing to a still-predominant dream-state, or finally thanks to distracted attention. [p. 999] For so long, namely, as through this the recipient of the impression finds the place of his own being-there fettered to the actual or notional place of an alien being-there, the new intuition-image, though as an intuition-image it has already come to have effect, does not have the power to bring the *place* itself to validity, in relation to which alone it would first gain existence. Here it comes surprisingly to light in what sense awakening and disturbance are one and the same state of affairs, and that it is not images that can awaken and disturb, but strictly only objects of perception, i.e., embodied images, or in other words intuition-images, which take their place in space as the abode of bodies. This, however, can also be expressed thus: intuition-images become perception-capable in virtue of the sensed intensity of the beheld, and in this, in turn, the actuality of self-movement confronts us as estranged.

The last turn of phrase reminds us that it is a matter of indifference whether we think the site of primal disturbance characterized by the experience of resistance or by that of a degree of strength. Both, essentially one and differing only in degree of generality, form, as it were, the bony framework of the perceptual world and prompt every being to whose nature an impulsive capacity belongs to answer the actual with changes of attitude — namely the always simultaneously intuitable corporeality with the *how* of the change, the strength of the resistance with the how-much. In this way, however, the site of primal disturbance, insofar as it becomes the breaking-point that admits the intervention of spirit, harbors a precondition not only of the act of apprehension but even of the act of judgement as well. If, in the primal state-of-affairs called "bodily resistance," we place the accent on the corporeality of the resistance, we hold in our hands the vital condition of the grammatical subject nearest to its origin; but if on the strength of the resistance, then the vital condition of the predicate nearest to its origin. In that the primal act, striking at the site of primal disturbance, reifies the bodily resistance, it has separated not only the bearer of life as an existing "subject" from the content of experience as an existing object, but also, within the content of experience as the objective primal object, the what from the how-much; since, then, out of the compulsion of the experienced connections, the how-much is related, as predicative determination, to the what as grammatical subject; or: to the primal object of the original act of apprehension, the primal act of judgement attaches a strength of resistance peculiar and distinct to it.

[p. 1000] The existential judgement is therefore at the same time an intensity-judgement, and must be so, because "existence" after all means self-assertion of the existing thing and thus its now greater, now lesser sphere of power. Herein lies the ground for the fact that every apprehension still close to its source, whether that of children or of primitives, links with every object of perception, and ultimately with every state of affairs whatever, an immediate feeling of its capacity for effect and presumed power, and is related not so much to existences of abstract meaning as rather to their experienced spheres of power. If consciousness is already unavoidably comparing consciousness, then, in turn, the most original of all comparisons is the comparison of degrees of strength. Since, now, the primal predicate of the primal object, intensity, thanks to its participation in all the intuition-data of the actuality of self-moving beings, furnishes the mediating link for *all* predicative connections, the essential content of the faculty of judgement could scarcely be more sharply outlined than by the remark that it enables the bearer of thought-consciousness to grade and to compare; from which, at the summit of the self-sovereignty of the understanding, there remains the quantifying and finally the mere counting!<sup>47</sup>

<sup>47</sup> On page 1000. — As will be recalled from note 53 of the first volume, the most recent ethnology tends to deny the primitive state of consciousness any belief in the soul whatsoever. A magical fluid — called mana, imunu, wakanda, orenda, voduu (tamaniu, atai, mauri, hau, etc.) — is supposed, for the primitive, to fill things and processes somewhat as electricity does, now more, now less. Occasional turns of phrase such as that such-and-such a stone or fetish is, for, say, the Maori, especially "mana-charged," reveal to us unmistakably the origin of this conception, namely in the physical concept of energy. What in truth is the case with the soul-belief of primitive peoples will occupy us later in more detail. Here, however, a remark on mana may be permitted. The energetic interpretations stem predominantly from scholarly commentators, and less from the *traveling* researchers who made their observations on the spot and rendered the name of the supposed fluid now as soul or soul-stuff, now as life-force, now as potency. If one goes through a large series of examples among the most various peoples, one can readily discern three components of the meaning of the name, each of which fits smoothly into the extra-historical soul-state. — First, for any state of affairs of significance however arisen, the accent of mana falls on that character-trait of appearances which belongs, not only in primitive but also in prehistoric experience, to the world as such: the character-trait of the *mysterious*. Every greater or lesser weight of significance originally means a greater or lesser content of mystery. Then, to be sure, the content of soul is not to be separated from the content of mystery either, insofar as by soul one understands the (somber or serene) *sense* of images. But to this a third thing is added. However much the *corporeality* of the world may be but one *side* of the *appearance* of the world (as in primal man), however much it may come to speech with equal significance, or even have the leading voice (as for not a few primitives): it is always corporeality that, as bearer of underivable intensities, adds still further *spans of power* to the essential mystery of images; and these will then, if not intensify, at least more or less *emancipate* themselves, and, in the measure of their growing independence, let mystery and essence dwindle away, the more the experience becomes a mere support-point for the existential judgment, and the body thereby becomes a thing. This self-independence has of course long since come about within the realm of civilization (even though mystery and soul may otherwise continue a sham existence, partly in the customs of the Church, partly turned into art and literature); but the idea of power, among various circles and strata, stands on very different levels of *abstractness*. — Of the, for the time being, most abstract level, the symbol of its practice is money, to which, theoretically, corresponds the recasting of the world-picture into mathematics; of the, for the time being, most concrete level, the most typical expression is the belief in the master-value of the *record*. In advance of certain linguistic-historical testimonies, to be discussed more precisely later, to the fact that the power-comparing state of consciousness has nowhere developed more strongly than within the Indo-Germanic family of peoples, let it be recalled here that only the languages belonging to it know the three-stage form of comparison (positive, comparative, superlative) of all adjectives. Now, since in North America the Anglo-Saxon group mixed with the offscourings of all cultures, and not least with semi-primitive Indian tribes, there developed there, alongside the most brutal Mammonism, that barbaric record-madness which, to the peoples of the Old World, insofar as they have not themselves already wholly succumbed to it, appears in the light of a kind of uncouth childishness, or more correctly of clownery.

[p. 1001]

#### 61. Kapitel — Das Sein — Chapter 61 — Being

*The concept of unity.* — Taking as basis the objective primal object, we now show which quite different directions the activity of detachment can take from it, and how it thereby arrives at objects of thought not only of different degrees of abstractness but also of different genera, all of which are nevertheless neighbors of one another, in that they form, so to speak, the retinue and innermost ring around the concept of being, with whose final clarification we shall conclude the series. — If the (relatively at-rest) sense-thing is the point of relation, identical with itself in relation to the course of time, of an aggregate of properties, of which we recognized a threefold-extended impenetrability as the most original, then no sense-thing is apprehended without some of its properties. Were we to confine ourselves to the narrowest district of the tactile domain, the sense-thing would nonetheless, besides its relative impenetrability, also have its shape in every empirical time-interval, and would thus already, at the lowest stage of abstraction, admit the distinction of two properties, but at a higher stage of three, by the separation of general impenetrability (= materiality) from its respective degree. Were we to include the beholding-capacity of touch, the series would grow considerably, in that numerous specific properties of tactile contents, among them especially warmth and cold, would come into play. With the aid of the sense of sight, finally, there would be added: colors together with their distribution and their relation to the conditions of lighting, glosscapable smoothness and gloss-incapable dullness, as well as surface-data of the most manifold kind for characters of matter, whose number is legion and most of which still await scientific investigation into appearance. Here it suffices us to establish that, in relation to the thing, its properties stand under all circumstances in the plural, or that, in relation to them, the thing is the unity that holds together the multiplicity of its properties. [p. 1002] No further "aesthetics" whatever is needed to establish the famous "unity in multiplicity": it stands before our eyes with any thing whatever. As surely as the thing is an "aggregate" of properties, so surely does it harbor the original impetus to the formation of the concept of unity.

Once we have it, we can of course in principle apply it to any state of affairs whatever. It is, however, precisely erroneous, and a typical case of false reification, to start from the world of appearance and to try to demonstrate on *it* the "unity in multiplicity"; for the more the appearances, in place of the things, captivate and take hold of us, the condition of the thought of unity, so to speak, dissolves away. To growing influence of the appearances there corresponds, in the soul, a growing preponderance of intuiting over sensing, and to growing fullness of the content of the appearances a growing participation of original beholding in intuiting. As the way to appearance leads away from the thing, so it can at least lead to the original images and finally to the primal image. Seen from it, however, neither unity nor multiplicity takes place in the intuition-image, but an undivided and indivisible cohesion, understood as the transformation-capable appearing of happening, or, put more boldly, as a self-revealing of elemental souls. But even if we leave aside the very source of the thought of appearance and hold, without depth-vision, to the intuition-images, it is beyond doubt that *they* are not what could support the thought-objective opposition of substratum and property. This the late art of European Baroque may help us once more to confirm.

As everyone knows, one main character-trait of it developed into so-called Impressionism, which pointedly wished to represent not objects but appearances, in that it thereby proceeded in painting after the words of Faust: "In the colored reflection we have life," it dissolved on its canvases the things and, with them, also the unities familiar to our thought; one need only recall the boundary-blurring shimmer on Renoir's "Pariser Boulevard" and the still, after all, vibrating, though already decay-threatened liveliness that expresses itself precisely therein. — We need scarcely add that the concept of unity is a late thought, which could only become conscious once one was, for other reasons, [p. 1003] in possession of number and of counting. This leads us at once to the origin of the One. The One. — Not by chance does the so-called indefinite article bear the name of the One! According to the testimony of linguistics, it is throughout the Indo-European languages the One that let the indefinite "a" for "any whatever" emerge from itself, since even the Indo-European oinos underlies most of the names of the One within this linguistic domain. The ground, in the science of consciousness, is scarcely to be missed if we resolve upon the assumption that the One originally meant a thing in relation, as goes without saying, to yet another thing. But how could it do so, and how, if it was so, could it detach itself from the thing? — We ask that it be noted that the following derivation of the One concerns the inner conditions of the origin of the One, and not the prehistoric processes by which it came about that the concept of the One "entered consciousness" here and there.<sup>48</sup>

<sup>48</sup> On page 1003. — In the *phylogeny* of the One, as in principle of all concepts that are not gained by combination out of other concepts, two phases must be distinguished: the arising of the experiential content out of which the concept was drawn, and the process of concept-formation *on the* *basis* of that experiential content. As regards both, it is not settled in advance, for any concept, whether the course of development was the same among all peoples capable of forming the concept — even though this may in fact have occurred in at least the majority of cases.

As with any thing whatever certain properties of the thing are unfailingly present, so with any thing whatever other things are unfailingly present as well; but that requires a between. If we recall that the primal act of thing-finding is an act of boundary-setting separation, by which body is sundered from body, then it becomes altogether certain to us that a between-the-things belongs to the thing. — We arrive at the same result in the following way. If the thing of perception is the objective primal existence, then it is, for one, a being-there that asserts itself in the course of time, and for another, a bearer of sensuous data in the space of intuition. If it is to be able to withstand the stream of happening, then the nature of the for-itself belongs to it, and if it is nonetheless to be able to bear data of intuition, then it must be separated from every other for-itself always by a spatial between, and, with regard to the change of places of abode, also by a temporal between. The former we express with the judgement that the same thing cannot be in several places at once; the latter with the judgement that at the same place several things cannot be at once.

Now, however, we wish to look away from all the properties of the thing, and we ease for ourselves an undertaking that seems so difficult by pointing out that the personal I, too, is a bearer of properties, but not of data of intuition. If, then, we accomplish the required detachment, what we have left over is what individual things and [p. 1004] individual I's have in common: the for-itself pure and simple, or the naked separate-being. If finally we detach from it also the spatial and temporal place, there remains: one and yet another and yet another. Separate-existences, stripped of all properties and thought without regard to their place in the spatiotemporal whole of the world of intuition, are ones. It is at once evident: insofar as the for-itself belongs to every individual being-there, be it thing, be it I, indeed finally even to the object of thought itself, the One, in the form of the so-called indefinite article, can be assigned to every object of thought, and thereby takes on the function of naming it with regard to what it has in common with all the objects of thought of the group designated by the noun.<sup>49</sup>

<sup>49</sup> On page 1004. — This is possible because here the One hovers before the mind as a genus, of which more will be said in what follows. In certain cases, however, the individual instance may also be meant; as when we say: only one gentleman had come. If, by contrast, the well-known fairy-tale opening "Once upon a time there was a man" emphasizes, with the "a," merely the class of sex, thus leaving undetermined *which* man it was, then this at the same time characterizes, far more, the *generality* of the case than its abstractness — and this holds predominantly for the use of the indefinite article. — Since, thanks to such indefiniteness, we feel little called upon to *think*, the *appearance* of the state of affairs gains the upper hand, which, in this kind of narrative art, strengthens the poetic, indeed dreamlike, stamp. (Or, as it is usually put, "wide scope is left to the imagination.")

Should one object that individual things are at any rate also something actual, while the ones, on the other hand, are nothing but objects of thought, one would have overlooked that among the divisions we have carried out in order to get from the thing to the One, there is one, namely the last, by which even existence itself was stripped from what previously remained. Something exists independently insofar as it must be thought as immediately related to the spatiotemporal continuum, dependently as a property, state, motion of something independently existing, and it no longer exists at all after the removal of relatedness to space-time altogether. — In view of the careful prior discussion, we may, without fear of misunderstanding, once display the process schematically by its catchwords, indicating the decisive division by a vertical line that halves the word separate-existence:

Individual Thing

• Separate-existence = Separate I Existence / . / One I Being The right-hand half of the division, being, will presently be derived by another route.

That older logicians brought counting, and thus the element of number, the One, into connection now with space, now with time, or even with both, was certainly a mistake; but the newer and newest logisticians, who suppose that spirit generates all this out of itself, go astray all the more. The ground of thinkability of the One, the ideal between, points back to the intuitable between of individual things, and marks the One as the empty for-itself. Should one object that every object of thought requires an ideal between in order to be distinguishable from other [p. 1005] objects of thought, it would first have to be noted that precisely this attests the thing as the objective primal object, in relation to which, to be sure, every object of thought is either something derived from it or an analogue to it; and then it would have to be recalled that the sense of no object of thought, save that of the One, is exhausted by the for-itself alone (from which, indeed, its relation to the indefinite article followed). — Proceeding from the result that the One is the naked for-itself, we offer, of the countless consequences, only the few that are suited to place the result itself in another light and thereby to confirm it.

If, in relation to the One, space, time, the whole world of intuition are mere co-relatednesses, and moreover of a higher degree than, say, in relation to the faculty of reflection, then the One's for-itself belongs to it *only* in relation to another One, and belongs to it, in relation to this other, *only* as for-itself. This lends it, among objects of thought, a unique position with regard to the relations laid out within it. Every object of thought can be brought into logical connection with any other whatever, by a chain of intermediate links now short, now long; but every one also includes, as belonging to it, demands for relation that determine its relation to other objects of thought and finally its "place" in the system of objects of thought: the concept of the full its relation to that of the empty and conversely, the concept of the great its relation to that of the small and conversely, the concept of the lover its relation to the object of inclination, and not conversely. The first two demands for relation are reciprocal, the third is one-sided. In the One there lies immediately only the demand to be related to yet one more One; but this has a peculiarity of its own. The relation *can*, to be sure, take place reciprocally, and would always do so for intelligences that could only count up to two; and it can just as well be one-sided, in that the second One is related to a third, the third to a fourth, and so on; whereby the series of ones opens up, similar to a series of things, but far more abstract, more similar to a series of points, but still more abstract, because the points would be either points of space or points of time, whereas the ones are neither of the two, but, so to speak, the series "in itself."

But how do we come to posit the One ever anew without limit? First of all, its origin betrays itself herein once more, because, quite analogously, [p. 1006] individual things after individual things enter into the field of vision, each of which can be thought as one. But whereas the number of possible things is, by thought-necessity, a determinate one, there is no ground by which we could be induced to command a halt anywhere in the positing of ones; hence the progression continues beyond every conceivable One and is in this respect unclosable. If, namely, we apprehend only the for-itself, in relation to a thought second for-itself, the relation contains nothing by which it could be distinguished from the relation of the second for-itself to the third for-itself, and so forth. This can of course also be turned subjectively, by pointing to the arbitrary repeatability of the counting-steps, or then to the arbitrary extendability of the activity of counting. Many significant scholars have taken part in the solution of the — as one notices — difficult problem of deriving the position and order of the ones, of ascertaining the ground that makes the how-much possible, and finally of determining the essence of number and counting in such a way that from it all the numberforms and arithmetical operations that were developed and mathematically tested in the course of two and a half millennia, but quite especially of the last century and a half, would become intelligible; yet their successes have remained, to this hour, contested.<sup>50</sup> At this point *only* the One is under discussion.

<sup>50</sup> On page 1006. — Among the significant mathematicians (as well as physicists) who, in the course of the last century and this one, have earned merit in the logical foundation of mathematics (and theoretical physics), it is customary to single out, among others: Riemann, Hamilton, Weierstraß, Cantor, F. Klein, Frege, Dedekind, Poincaré, Duhem, Peano, Zermelo, Veronese, Picard, Hilbert, and others; among mathematically trained logicians and epistemologists, among others: Drobisch, B. Erdmann, Petzoldt, Russell, Couturat, Enriques, Husserl, and many others. As a non-mathematician, the author has no judgment on the mathematical and logical merits of these men, and must leave it to the specialists to decide what progress, whether of mathematics or of the clarification of its fundamental concepts, has been achieved through the labors of so many researchers. On the other hand, a misgiving shall not be passed over in silence which forced itself upon us, from the standpoint of the *science* of *consciousness*, in every attempt to work through one or another of those writings belonging to the epistemological group. We can make ourselves understood most quickly with the help of an admittedly considerable exaggeration.
