The philosophers of the Middle Ages had to prove what the priest had laid down; of the philosophers of the modern age one sometimes has, and to a small degree always has, the impression that it is their concern to secure, epistemologically, what the mathematicians and physicists have determined. But just as little as the philosopher holds any propositions to be truths merely because a belief demands them, just so little should the researcher of consciousness hold any propositions to be truths merely because mathematics and mathematical physics *need* them. If the science of consciousness is to preserve its independence, then a weighing of the mathematical concept of truth by means of the metaphysical concept of truth would have had to precede the *logical* endeavors; but this we miss. Now, to be sure, a "personal union" of tendencies has taken place and still takes place throughout: just as the thinkers of high scholasticism *wished* to hold true the propositions which, in their opinion, they had proved, so for most epistemologists of mathematics the mathematical concept of truth is a welcome support for the concept of truth at which they aim, out of an unconscious or conscious interest in the assumption of world-creative gifts of the human mind (or even the *actuality* of the objects of mathematical truths). We hold it to be almost certain that the logic of mathematics has thereby registered significant achievements; but we have not so far been able to convince ourselves that the science of consciousness has been enriched thereby. — We take the opportunity to append an addendum which — by no means indispensable — may perhaps be welcome to one reader or another as a brief review, so to speak, of the *logical* method of our work. — Everything we have put forward concerning the origin of the concept of the One, of matter, of the thing, and so on, extreme logicists will dismiss with the remark that it shows only our relapse into long-outmoded "abstraction theories." For it has indeed gone out of fashion, the taste for the logic of abstracting and subsuming, and come into fashion instead the taste for a logic of orderings, series, rules, principles of connection, functions, and so on — in short, the belief in mere *lawfulnesses*, as that in which, above all, the self-sovereignty of the mind is held to manifest itself. Yet we wish to judge more fairly: this is less a fashion than the fitting expression of that *formalism* which, under the pressure of the enormous upsurge of mathematics in the nineteenth century and of theoretical physics in the present one, has begun more or less to permeate all thinking (analogous to the development of pre-Nietzschean thought under the pressure of the mechanics of Galileo and Newton). Now we have, to be sure, and certainly not with a hesitant voice, declared that we do not assent to *the* abstraction-theories according to which the concept of, say, the tree would come about by one's having left out the particularity of the beech, the oak, the linden, and so on! Yet, since conceptual thinking *without* the activity of abstracting in any case does *not* take place, we wish to take a somewhat closer look, from this side, at the formalist turn that logic has taken. For it seems to us that formalism does not always look for its difference from, for example, Aristotelian logic in the right place. We tell the attentive reader nothing new with the sentence that may guide our consideration: the capacity of the mind to comport itself, according to a rule, with objects of thought of any degree of abstractness whatever, is in principle no different from its capacity *to form concepts at all*. If it is true that the act of apprehension (together with the act of judgment coordinated with it) lifts what is apprehended out of the time of actuality, then, with respect to the time of actuality, the object of thought is the substrate of a rule: the thing, for instance, of the rule of a self-asserting; the property of the thing, of the rule of a comporting-itself; and each, like the other, the substrate of rules of acting upon other objects of thought. If we make, in just such a way, an object of thought (= conceptual content) out of, say, the motion of the thing, or a change of property, then we possess, in this object of thought, the rule of a *sequence* of comportments or the rule of a *recurrence* of the mode of effect. Since present-day epistemologists generally think first and at length of mathematics, and at most, quite last, in passing, of actuality, it may not be superfluous to recall that *variable* relations of dependence, too, were grasped en masse before man thought of grasping them numerically. If the sun sinks, it grows darker; if the warmth of the air increases, the snow melts; if one runs faster and faster, one grows hotter and hotter — such are these rules. If, however, one succeeds in expressing the relation of two properties, say long and short, in numerical measures, then sooner or later one will also succeed in expressing *changes* of property in numerical measures, and thus in translating the dependence of one process upon another process into the language of mathematical "functions." How immense this second step was, we have attempted to show by reference to Galileo's concept of force. But the immensity did not lie in the process of concept-formation having changed, but exclusively in the fact that such a height of *abstractness* first becomes attainable to a faculty of thought that has largely detached itself from the exigencies of life. When a contemporary author, who conceives it differently, aptly judges: "Out of a sum of properties, the 'thing' now becomes a mathematical epitome of values that are fixed with respect to some scale of comparison" (Cassirer, in his admirably orienting book "Substanzbegriff und Funktionsbegriff," p. 197), we believe we see before our eyes how, thanks to the supposed progress, a comparatively actuality-laden epitome was exchanged for one nearly devoid of actuality. Something of this sort is, so to speak, self-evident, once one has assured oneself of the sameness of the thing with an epitome of laws of effect, and of the indispensability of the concept of the thing for the formation of the concept of number as well. (The "scale of comparison," as is understood, is as surely always there as any property whatever can in principle be *compared* — though, to be sure, not thereby also multiplied.) Once the property of the thing has been exchanged for the property of number, what was previously exercised on the basis of concepts of things — distinguishing and relating — now takes place on the basis of mere relational concepts. The procedure has remained the same. But because the substrate has forfeited its immediate connection with the spatiotemporal continuum, certain barriers to the movement of thought have fallen away, and the play of combinations is left largely to the discretion of the mind. — But how would that be possible, one might object, if, according to our account in Chapter 38, the splitting act of mind leads to distinguishing only because what is divided is related back to one another out of the exigency of *experienced* connections? Would not everything, on the plane of pure thought-things, have to disintegrate, so to speak, into atoms of thought, and every combining thereby come to a standstill? Our resolution of the seeming antinomy is known. In a twofold respect, mental activity remains, even now, bound up with vitality: first through threads that nonetheless still exist between image and thought-thing, and further by virtue of the unavoidably sensuous signs (figures, numerals, letters), without which not a single thread could any longer be spun, even in the region of mere brain-phantoms. With regard to these, the formalist stage of thinking can be determined as follows. Granted that thinking as such were, in a certain respect, a function of language (which will be more precisely characterized and grounded in a later chapter), then formalist thinking would, in that very respect, be a function of signs whose *symbolic* content had volatilized down to a bare minimum scarcely capable of further reduction. — Having now informed ourselves somewhat more precisely about the procedure of formalism, let the relation of our mode of consideration to the (Aristotelian) abstraction-theories now be touched upon. It is not the emphasis placed on abstracting in all thinking activity that is subject to criticism, but rather the neglect of its participation in the perceptual process. So long as the co-activity of the human spirit in human perceiving is not recognized, every theory of abstraction hangs in the air (just as does the distinction of factual from apodictic truths, or of aposteriori from apriori judgments). Were the object of perception not, among other things, an *object* — that is, an object of thought — but rather a pure content of experience, it would remain inexplicable how comprehending thought could subsequently take possession of it. Given the transience of everything actual, it would then lack precisely that *identical element* with regard to which alone comprehension can take place! We repeat (what has certainly been said a dozen times before): whether one judges that the water in the kettle is already boiling, *or* whether one judges that water under such-and-such air pressure boils at such-and-such a temperature — in *both* cases one has made (metaphysically) *abstract* statements about (metaphysically) *abstract* objects, and only the degrees of abstractness differ. Expressed vitalistically: in the second case the relation to actuality is mediated by a greater number of members than in the first. — We deny the "constructive" activities of the spirit so little that, on the contrary, we regard the mathematical natural sciences, for example, as a "logocentric construction" (cf. p. 67); but we have shown and established that all, even the highest, products of construction have one and only one basis, namely the *thing of perception*. We hold the judgment by which it is "ascertained" to be the immediate consequence of an act of division (and distinction), and we have shown that it is this act which precedes *every* judgment, regardless of what object it concerns. Whoever does not find the inviolable validity, and accordingly the (hypostatized) "law," in the individual perceptual judgment — by distinguishing from it, say with *Kant*, the "judgment of experience," through which alone "connections according to rules" first take place, "rules which determine the connection of representations within the concept of an object, and the extent to which they can or cannot stand together in one experience" — such a person has, to begin with, made a chaos out of the indispensable *occasion* of the perceptual judgment, that is, out of the world of intuitive images, a chaos in relation to which the spirit (however named) becomes necessary in order that a cosmos may arise out of the chaos; and, following the thought through consistently, he ends infallibly with the *striking-out* of the occasion itself, as the history of Kantianism has proved. But by this, mere *constructions* of the *understanding* are declared real — indeed, the only actuality there is. *Hume*, whose atomism of perception (as we called it) has been sufficiently appraised, furnished, with a thoroughness never seen before, the proof — quite unwelcome to himself — that sense-impressions can convey to us not the slightest knowledge of objects that *exist* independently of our perceptions and hence uninterruptedly. Whoever reads through the second section of the fourth part of his treatise "Of the Understanding" is easily convinced of the impracticability of the feats of skill which the author must credit to the "imagination" in order to explain the origin of the "fiction" of existing things, and will credit it to him — since he visibly feels little satisfaction with his own arguments here — that he does not let himself be tempted to make "repetition" and "habit" responsible for the existential judgment, much as this would have suggested itself according to his interpretation of the causal idea. Those formalists might well take a lesson from this, who, in their endeavor to raise mere rules and laws to the rank of a world-creating deity, outdo their master Kant. For once the bearer of spirit has, by virtue of the *act* in the perceptual process, ascertained a *thing* on the occasion of the (corporeal) intuitive images, then in principle all the rules or laws that the process of dissection subsequently *unfolds* are already given along with it; whereas, conversely, no system of rules, however rich and free of contradiction, would be capable of guaranteeing existence! In closing our "review," we recall that only in this way does it become apparent what abstracting actually is. It does not consist in the understanding comparing and dropping away, but in its splitting the object of thought, splitting the halves of the split again, and so on. Regarded from the standpoint of the science of consciousness, abstracting is merely a concomitant phenomenon or result of *dissection*. That comparisons accordingly do take place already lies in the concept of relating, and becomes entirely certain to us when we attend to the position of the object of thought relative to consciousness, for which it is well known to coincide with a "direction" of the spiritual "gaze" — a direction which of course only subsists in relation to at least one further direction (cf. the following chapter). With that-which-is-to-be-compared, we might say, the comparison is here also given, but the object of comparison does not arise through prior comparison. Just as the object of thought is an embodiment of relational dispositions, so its split halves are in turn embodiments of relational dispositions; hence our abstracting, however high it may climb, could never break through the web of relations. Only — if a comparison may be allowed for gauging the content of thoughts — the web of relations, a carpet in the regions of thinking close to intuition, becomes a spider's web in the highly abstract regions. And this comes about as follows. With the growing abstractness of the object, the number of mediating members grows between the content of the judgment and the bearing surface of all thinking: the world of intuition, which is immediately present only in the (consciousness-capable) perceptual process. But if this world means the spirit-side head of the bridge whose world-side head is the *actuality* of the *images*, then removal from it means loss of *actuality-content*. And indeed we were able to show: already with the first splitting, that is, with the act of apprehension in the perceptual process, a splitting-off occurs; with every splitting of the halves it occurs again, and so on ever further, down to the ultimate attainable products of splitting, which are therefore, however rich in relational dispositions, exceedingly poor in weight of meaning. If one calls the meaning of the object of thought its *character*, then for any given procedure of dissection one can readily identify which character thereby disappears. Galilean phoronomy and mechanics, for example, rest, among other things, on the following *splittings*: first, of the moving body into body and motion; second, of motion into motion and velocity; third, of velocity into velocity and change of velocity. With the first splitting, the character of corporeality is split off (it follows that the moving body can be represented by the moving point); with the second, the character of activity and passivity (it follows that rest becomes a special case of being-in-motion); with the third, the character of motion itself (it follows that the abstract change of velocity becomes autonomous and is applied to any change of state whatsoever). It suffices to bring this fully to consciousness, and in place of actuality one has a system of equations. This would not, as is sometimes said, abolish the "ontological" mode of consideration — for, on the contrary, no On (= nothing) exists that is *still* more unmixed than number (which grants actuality no more than a concession of multiplicity); but rather the On that remains has become almost substanceless. — But at last, enough of the review!

Every object of thought is subject to the principle of sameness; but the sameness of the One with itself is now at the same time sameness with any One whatever! For if all spatial, temporal, specific marks and all distinguishing relational dispositions, apart from the naked for-itself-being, have fallen away, then nothing more can be found by which the individual One would be distinct from the other One, or would, in relation to it, be anything else at all, notwithstanding that it in turn needs the other in order to be thinkable itself, and accordingly it holds, for the One as pure object of thought, that individual and species coincide. If we have nonetheless distinguished, and had to distinguish, the one One from the other One, and thus doubtless also the individual-one from the One as species, this was possible only because we had unnoticed taken up into the empty concept of for-itself the content of meaning that flows to it from the for-itself of the thing. We think the sequence-capable ones thanks to the separated presentness of individual things, and without that we could indeed no longer think even the One detached from the "earthly remainder" of that co-relatedness, since, robbed of its capacity for back-relation to the [p. 1007] individual-one, it would have dissolved away: a, as it were, monumental example of the fact that even the most abstract products of the activity of spirit are attached, by a thread sometimes almost invisible and yet always capable of being made visible, to actuality!

Is now, perhaps, the equation 1 = 1 an identity-equation? No. For were *it* so, then all equations would be so, and one would need to trouble the art of reckoning no further. (As often as, for the sake of convenience, identity is once expressed in the form of an equation, the writing always has only symbolic meaning.) We hold that, for the purpose of ascertaining the consciousness-scientific sense of the equation, one must not start from such equations as 1+1 = 2, or indeed from still richer ones, which are after all all already derived equations, but from the equation 1 = 1, which might be called the primal equation. The One on its left side is a different one from that on its right, by virtue of the co-related content of meaning of the One, and each of the two coincides identically with the other by virtue of the sameness of the pure concept of it with the concept of the One in general. From this results the sense of the equals-sign, and with it the unique position of mathematical science within the totality of the sciences: the equals-sign means interchangeability without *loss of sameness*. As surely as the left side of any equation whatever is different from its right side, so surely is that of the two sides, on whose account they are set equal to one another, however one may determine and name it, the same on both sides. This manifests itself, after the pattern of the primal equation 1 = 1, in the phenomenon of the equation, among other things, by the fact that the equation remains the same if one makes the right side the left, the left the right. It is a matter of indifference whether one writes: a = b, or: b = a.

Once more, in this connection, the kinship of the numberworld with the thing-world lights up for us, but also, however, the difference between the two, when we note that two things, though certainly not interchangeable like two sides of an equation, are nonetheless, on the basis of far-reaching similarity of their properties, mistakable for one another, and on that account likewise called "equal." To the mistakability of things there corresponds, after the removal of all determining pieces that would permit localization in the spatiotemporal world, the genuine interchangeability of the sides of an equation, and, toward the desired goal of all calculating consideration of nature — to resolve thing-relations [p. 1008] into equations — the preparatory measure forms the reinterpretation of thing-properties into magnitude-values.

We arrived at the One from the thing by isolating its being-for-itself in relation to the being-for-itself of other things. But what remains, if we isolate self-assertion — without which the mutual being-for-itself would likewise collapse — in relation to boundless happening? Being remains. Being. — What is being? Empty sameness, not indeed related to objective time, yet with co-relatedness to it; for without that the thought of sameness would no longer be executable. — We would not need to discuss this again, insofar as it has already been shown in earlier chapters and in part in the present chapter; but let it now once more be elucidated with regard to certain consequences suited to consolidate it.<sup>51</sup>

<sup>51</sup> On page 1008. — The noun Being [Sein] is the substantivized infinitive of the process-word sein [to be], in whose inflected forms three different stems participate: es- or s-, in "sind" [are] and "sein" [to be], in Greek esti, Latin est, meaning existing most immediately; bheu-, in "bin" [am] and "bist" [art], in Greek phyō, Latin fui and fio, indicating in part more a growing and becoming; ves-, in "war" [was], "gewesen" [been], also "Wesen" [essence/being], meaning in Old Indic something like "to dwell" or "to abide." In higher thinking all three converge upon the abstract concept of Being, which, once more richly furnished, gives way to the concept of — always more or less determinate — existing, and which then allows one to emphasize, now more the actuality of an existent, now more the existence of something real, that is, the sameness of it throughout the change of moments; in and for itself, however, it means nothing but the empty sameness. In order not to repeat at length what has already been set forth earlier, and above all in order to preserve the main line of the exposition in the body text, we refrained there from meeting an objection that would concern the concept of "empty sameness"; we make up for this now, on this occasion, at least by way of a note, though in the greatest brevity, and avail ourselves for this purpose of the famous phrase of the in-itself. If we replace "empty sameness" with "sameness in itself," and Being accordingly with "Being in itself," then sameness in itself and Being in itself would be one and the same. Here the following objection might perhaps be raised: sameness belongs, among other things, to every *concept* — for example to the concept "identity" or "imaginary number" or "chimera"; but how could one ascribe *Being* to mere concepts, mere "units of validity," laws, and so forth? We answer: if by Being one understands Being in itself, then Being belongs to concepts, "units of validity," and so on, just as certainly as sameness belongs to them. The principle of identity does not, correctly understood, read: A=A or A is A, but rather it reads: *A is*. We refer to the third chapter, where it was set forth that *this* Being never means anything other than the timelessness of all objects of comprehending thought (= of the object of thought), and we add: concepts too are objects of thought, as soon as we occupy ourselves thinkingly with *them* instead of with the objects which we mentally sight with their help. The concept of the chimera *is*, insofar as we think it, and what it means *is* likewise, insofar as we think it. Were we now to add, with regard to this, say: it *is* as a (by-us-intended) phantasm, but not, for example, as a possible thing of perception, we would have brought into play a special relation of the posited Being to actuality; and this, as is well known, happens throughout wherever we form concepts for the purpose of sighting determinate objects of thought. In doing so we involuntarily behave as though we had each time to answer the question: sameness in relation to what, or also: Being as what? If we now rise to the high-level abstractum: sameness in itself (= *Being* in itself), then a secret in-relation-to-what does indeed still hover before us here too, namely the *character of actuality* of all merely possible contents of experience. For three reasons, however, we avoid defining Being in itself as sameness in relation to actuality. First: since actuality-time also belongs to actuality, Being would thereby become ever-being [Immersein], hence a concept that is a whole degree more concrete and can, for example, be predicated of physical space (as, for the time being, also of physical mass and energy); second: it would thus be explicable only by roundabout ways why the concept of Being in itself (= sameness in itself), whenever it emerges in pure form, *displaces* that of actuality; third, and above all: Being in itself is conceived precisely by *making autonomous* the sameness that holds of every object of thought, concepts included. Anticipating, we add: just as the *experience* of actuality — or, more sharply, the weight of actuality of all contents of experience — comes into its own in the (indispensable) co-relatedness of actuality-time, so, in the tendency and capacity for making Being in itself autonomous, indeed for reifying it, the *experienced* power of the spirit comes into its own.

For the concept of being at the highest level of abstractness, which alone occupies us here, two important consequences follow. First, that we exhaust its content when we predicate it of itself. If someone utters: God *is*, he may think a great deal at the word God, e.g. that God is omnipotent, omniscient, omnipresent, and need by no means suppose that with this utterance he has exhausted the essence of God or even characterized it in any meaningful way. But if we say: being *is*, we have then predicated of being everything that can be immediately predicated of it at all, and have thus indeed exhausted the whole content of being. We may well make this very state of affairs the point of relation for countless other states of affairs, but we thereby add no new characteristics to being itself. As in the case of the concept of the One the individual coincides with the kind, so in the case of being the "substance" is identical with its "accidents," or, as it was occasionally expressed, the esse with the essentia.

But since, further, sameness "obtains" or "holds" with regard to every object of thought, the verb to be could "fade" (as it is usually put) into that so-called auxiliary verb which now has only the meaning of a copula — namely, preferentially, that copula which links whatever attributes to the subject of the statement. The difference of function of "is" in the sentence "God is" and in the sentence "God is good" could of course be expressed in manifold ways [p. 1009], and it is so expressed; but that, for instance, the Indo-European languages among others hit upon exactly this form of expression goes back to the identity of the concept of being with the concept of sameness.

Although the content of being is already exhausted by the statement that it *is*, one judgement, among the other judgements that can be rendered about being by including further states of affairs, nevertheless enjoys a privileged position, whose great age is attested to us by the previously cited passage from Plutarch: the judgement that being is one; by which, more precisely, is meant: being is *only* one. This confirms for us, among other things, that the concept of being requires, as its counterpart, that of individual existences, and could only be found in relation to them; and thereby the sense of that split by whose aid we arrived above at the One stands out still more sharply, since we thought of the meaning-content of the disembodied individual existence as halved, whereby it fell apart into the unrestrictedly repeatable One and the unrepeatable being. Just as, with the antithesis of Eleaticism to Heracliteanism, the two paths fork, of which the one leads to the science of facts, the other to the science of happening, so too, on the side of belief in objects, the Greeks carried out the very split just indicated, whereby the Eleatics' certainty of being was met by the Pythagoreans' certainty of number — inwardly similar and yet, comparatively, opposed.

The ground of the kinship of essence between being and the One thus expressed is known to us. For there is one and only one metaphysical place where the changelessly existing intersects with the changing actuality: the personal I. We need only think of the I to know at once why it forms the primal source: of the unextended point, of the existing thing, of the One and of unity, of separate existence, of existence as such = the "thing in itself" = being = empty sameness = positive nothing. Now, since, in view of the circumstance that within the life-sphere of personality the I forms the point of origin and the center of those acts which make possible the activity of willing and of thinking, one can hardly avoid calling the generative ground of the I spirit, there results, first, the equation to be understood metaphysically: spirit = being = positive nothing; then, that the spirit, whenever it succeeded in apprehending itself, was conceived as one and only one, as likewise as a unity [p. 1010] in relation to its possible modes of operation and finally to everything that entered into any relation to it; and finally, why one liked to characterize it as the "absolute" I or the "pure" I, and why it presented no particularly great difficulties to determine it — mistakenly, though — even as a person.<sup>52</sup>

<sup>52</sup> On page 1010. — Here, from the history of thought, some of the most famous testimonies to this: The supreme world-principle of the Pythagoreans is the oppositionless Monad, out of which the successivelycapable One first arises as a second One. — Parmenides, the discoverer of Being, at once discovers also its non-manifoldness, more precisely its beingonly-one, and, by essentially equating it with the thinking of Being, opens the round-dance of what were later called the philosophies of identity. — The Nous of Anaxagoras, notwithstanding its capacity to dwell materially in ensouled beings, is "alone and by and for itself." — For Plato the Good is an indivisible hen [ἕν]. — Aristotle's highest final cause is separate from everything (chōriston) and hence the absolute for-itself. — The equating of the following basic concepts, with only slight differences, runs through all the sects and schools of the Alexandrian age: the One, or the unit, or the superone = unity, which comprises all multiplicity within itself = Being or superbeing = spirit, for which a long series of names stands ready for the sake of emphasizing, heightening, and over-heightening its transcendence. — According to Origen, God is timeless, and the eternal Being brought forth by him is identical with spirit. — The God of Augustine is of course spirit and as such above all an unum, but is, in keeping with the Christian turn, conceived as personality and accordingly, for example, also endowed with the verum and the bonum. Even this age, incidentally, knows the formula that God is the nihil; and a nihil does not multiply well! — In Eckhart, the Godhead, which for him signifies the transcendent ground of both Being and knowing, is called without circumlocution the Nothing. — For Nicholas of Cusa it is the unity which, similarly to Neoplatonism, embraces all manifoldness, and above all every opposition, except that now the main emphasis falls on the "infinity" of this unity. He too, incidentally, stresses that God stands closer to the nihil than to the aliquid. — The God of Descartes and his followers is "infinite Being," which presents itself to the human intellect in the res extensa and the res cogitans; a conception taken over, with alterations of no substantive significance, by Spinoza. — According to Leibniz, substance is unity in multiplicity, and God the "central monad." — The Fichtean Ego and the so-called systems of identity close — for the time being — the series.

At two points we may not pass by, before we leave being, since otherwise they might appear as "dark points." The first is the phrase "positive nothing." The word nothing, originally conceived as the genitive of not, refers, in a purely logical respect, only to the non-presence of something — e.g., when we say, here lies nothing — but was early substantivized and has behind it a memorable history of meaning in philosophy. Plato set over against being not exactly nothing, but rather non-being, yet by this means by no means the contradictory but a contrary opposite to the world of the ideas that are, and this, for him, coincides with space. Likewise, for Aristotle, being in matter is present only "potentially" and is actualized only through the shaping power of "form" that supervenes.

While here non-being carries the meaning of a positive something in opposition to being, there prepares itself, in the Alexandrian age, among the Neopythagoreans, Gnostics, early apologists of Christianity, and above all among the Neoplatonists, the so-called negative theology of the Middle Ages, and with it the equating of being with non-being, indeed downright with nothing — and this on the ground of a motif of thought which Spinoza's famous formula, in its sharpest form, offers us: omnis determinatio est negatio [every determination is a negation]. For the more decisively being as such — that is, the opposite of all actuality — was and is conceived as the true, proper, highest actuality, and thus as the one and only deity, the more forcibly the thought had to press itself upon one that every property one might ascribe to the ens realissimum would entail a restriction and limitation of its nature as "sheer" being, and consequently a diminution of the boundlessness one felt compelled to ascribe to the deity in every and all respects. — Here we can proceed at once to explain our phrase of the positive nothing. Being is doubtless the same as nothing, insofar as any determining feature whatever that we might borrow from appearing and appearance-capable actuality cannot and may not [p. 1011] be predicated of it. But it is not, on that account, the mere non-presence of actuality, because it produces, through the mediation of the human I, changes verifiable in terms of data within and in the actuality of happening — changes that could in no way be derived from actuality itself and without that otherwise indescribable nothing; whence the addition "positive" is justified.

One sees from this, incidentally, that the phrase "positive nothing" positively forces itself upon us. In pre-conceptual thinking there is no meaning-content that would correspond to the concept which philosophical and religious doctrines link to substantives such as non-being or nothing or analogous names; for whenever and wherever such designations occur, either something real is meant by them, or the highest, proper and sole "actuality" itself; and in relation to it, every pre-conceptual actuality sinks to the level, now of a merely preparatory existence, now of a hell, now — and above all — of a merely apparent world, whose origin the thinkers could of course never succeed in explaining. Thus, for instance, "Nirvana" means roughly "extinction" and actually intends to signify the state of one for whom any content of intuition whatever, the alluring as much as the repugnant and terrible, has entirely lost its excitatory value and is, in this way, according to the Buddhist conception, annihilated. Yet, although absolutely nothing remains that could be predicated of Nirvana, it counts as a positive state — indeed as the only positive one, in whose afterglow the universe, demons and gods included, dissolves like a haze or foam into *the* nothing, which even the unphilosophical mind would understand without explanation. In short, the substantivized nothing is, without exception, understood as a positive nothing; and the positive nothing is spirit.

Secondly, we need once more to look back at the concept of duration. — Every physicist knows, and it stands to be read in every recent physics textbook, that the rendering, say, of a process of motion by means of an equation or a curve comes about only through interpolation of the data that observation has supplied. However closely we may bring together the points in time to which correspond the successive stretches covered by a falling stone, there always lie between them intervals of time to which perception can no longer extend, and for which we accordingly supply, in thought, the corresponding rates of acceleration. The same considerations hold [p. 1012] for the trajectory of a motion, hold in principle for all distinguishable features of all distinguishable processes whatsoever; but they hold, beyond that, even for the ascertainment of any fact whatever. If I rise from my desk and, turning my back to it, face the bookshelf, then during the half-minute that taking hold of a book required, the desk could, for instance, have vanished for a second, and my conviction that it stood uninterruptedly where it stands rests on involuntary interpolation. And that is not all: even while I am working at it, it could repeatedly have vanished, say for thousandths of a second, without my having noticed the least thing of it, because the intervals within which, however great their freshness, the acts of my spirit follow upon one another are without doubt far longer than microseconds. Even if, by ingenious apparatus, we were to increase our perceptual power for spatial and temporal differences a millionfold beyond what is today already attainable telescopically and microscopically, we would nonetheless remain unable to compose the spatiotemporal continuity of the actual out of perceptual elements that no longer enclosed any unperceived intervals within themselves. It is not necessary to point to the limits of such an enhancement of perception in order to bring the limits of observability before our eyes, because the limitedness is in principle established for anyone who has recognized that the apparently uninterrupted activity of the spirit in truth consists of a series of temporally unextended acts, and that therefore no consciousness can "catch up with" the continuity of happening.

But just as the assumption of the continuity of subsistence, for the factual primal object, is merely an indispensable aid to thought, so too it is, in the first instance, only an aid to thought with regard to the subjectively primally identical, the personal I. — For if one were to raise the question whether our I exists in the sense of continuous presence while we lie asleep, the answer would have to be: No. No reasonable sense could be attached to the contrary view. Even appeal to possible dreams would not help us, because into the state of dreaming we carry along only the phasms of the waking state, and thus also only the phasm of our person. But even during the interval between two acts in waking life, one can hardly speak of the real presence of the I, since this is attested by nothing whatever. Although now [p. 1013], however, no difference at all obtains in the relation between the duration of things and the duration of the I, we must nonetheless ascribe real existence to the I, and this in view of the circumstance that it is identically present at every moment of its operation. All existences of the universe change unceasingly and really, which, for reasons repeatedly weighed in the meantime, does not exclude our isolating in thought certain embodied sums of properties and, within temporal limits, treating even them themselves to some degree — but especially the more abstract world of their properties and relations — as invariants. The I, by contrast, really has the character of an invariant, not indeed as continuously filling the intervals between the acts, but rather as repeating itself identically with each act.

Since, further, our thinking, which always posits substrates, cannot avoid positing, in the organism of every being that has become the scene of operation for the I, an I-disposition or I-basis, through which it comes about that those repetitions of the identical take place, it takes on the appearance as if there were nonetheless something identically filling time, or, so to speak, the non-thing of a real synthesis of rigid sameness and self-changing continuity. To resolve the metaphysical riddle thereby confronting us would mean being able to answer how it came about at all that spirit found entry into the living cell — which we forgo; but the logical difficulty can be mitigated and, apart from that metaphysical remainder, removed. The I-basis, repeatedly elucidated by the simile of the unextended center around which a life-nexus is compelled to revolve, can only be conceived as a functional constitution which, so long as the functional nexus called organism persists, makes possible again and again the presence of the one and same act-accomplishing I — notwithstanding the changes to which it too, in the stream of happening, is not exempt. Bases (dispositions,<sup>53</sup> faculties, existences, etc.), personal as much as factual, are necessarily co-thought real grounds of determinable behaviors, and none of them accompanies, in *actuality*, the continuity of happening; but the I-basis, or, more briefly, the I, is, of all conceivable bases, the one and only one according to which that trait of behavior which it is destined to bear is unrestrictedly the same, whenever it becomes "actual." Therefore we must attribute reality of existing to the I, and to the I alone, and may unhesitatingly elucidate this with the [p. 1014] addition: the I, as basis, endures throughout the lifetime of the being possessed of an I.

<sup>53</sup> On page 1013. — We are — at least for the present — unable to state more precisely wherein consists the change in the functions of the organism which permits the recurrence of existence of one and the same something within it; but with regard to the disposition in question we can point to a variety of *transformations* which both empirically confirm its vital character and allow us to recognize that it must be anchored in the core of the organism and more or less alters the whole system. If we cast a glance, for instance, at the (personal) feeling of self, without whose mediation no knowledge of one's own existing would take place, it is shown that it — like every feeling — is subject to varying amplitude of swing, or, spoken with a physiological ring, to fluctuations of tonus, according to which, for example, the age of puberty regularly brings with it a passing heightening of the selfemphasis of all experiences (together with manifold and often not harmless consequences), middle age frequently leads to a form of self that might be called a hardening of selfhood, and old age either continues this to the point of "ossification" or brings forth weakness of self. The center, however, with regard to which the person is precisely I or self, remains throughout one and always the same, and remains so even in cases of the gravest disturbance of self-consciousness. The patient who, say, puts forward: I do not exist at all, I am nothing, I am not at all, or who denies the existence of his own body, has, with the "I" in the little sentence "I am not" or with the "my" in the statement "my body no longer exists," already attested to the existence and presence of that which alone enables him to judge anything at all — even though he may use his capacity for judgment precisely in order to deny his I, his body, his existence.

And so, in conclusion, let it once more be recalled: the word continuity, today used metaphorically a thousandfold, signifies, by derivation and original sense, *the* character trait of the world of appearance without which this world would have ceased to appear. Continuous is the appearance of the single-colored wall surface before my eyes, continuous the appearance of the interval between it and me, continuous every intuitive process such as, say, the appearance of a tone, a sound, a noise, continuous above all every intuitive movement such as the appearance of the beating of waves, of the falling stone, the appearance of the movement of my arm between its starting position and its end position (and this continuity — namely that of movement, as will be shown later — perhaps forms the pattern for all the rest). It is not, as has been claimed here and there and still is, that we arrive at the intuition of continuity by interpolation; on the contrary: continuity is that primal experience of the gift of intuition for the sake of which the faculty of thought, capable only of discrete acts, must interpolate, when it wishes to transpose the world of appearances into the world of things alone comprehensible to it. Near-character of objects of thought. — Let us take into account that animal aliveness presents two poles, a comparatively receptive and a comparatively active pole, and let us ask, from the standpoint of the science of the soul, what, accordingly, within the life-sphere — now, in the first place, of man — the body is, what the soul is, and what spirit is; the answer runs: the body is the bearer of sensing and of self-movement, the soul the bearer of beholding and working (= "weaving"), the spirit the bearer of acts of apprehension and acts of will. To the living body there corresponds, accordingly, the corporeality of the world or, more abstractly conceived, its materiality; to the embodied soul, the appearance of the world's characters, growing in psychic content with growing predominance of soul; to the localized spirit, a world of objects identical with themselves. These determinations put us in a position to name with certainty the share of the body, of the soul, of the spirit, whether in any of our — consciousness-capable or non-consciousness-capable — life-processes (such as nourishment, growth, mating, breathing, excretion, sleeping, dreaming, waking, sensing, beholding, perceiving, recollecting, apprehending, judging, [p. 1015] thinking, wishing, planning, willing, doubting, hoping, fearing, reflex movement, expressive movement, drive-action, arbitrary movement, etc.), or in whatever technical, formative, poetic, thinking, religious, social, or even wholly sleepwalking precipitates of human "doing and letting-be." Since, in the weightiest of them all, namely language, *also* the conceptual faculty has a share, the question arises through what, in it, the body attests itself, through what the soul, through what the spirit.

Scarcely any other question lets us recognize as immediately as this one what research can achieve thanks to a correct metaphysics and what it must fail to achieve thanks to a false one. Since, from the Renaissance onward, the soul fell into oblivion, only the corporeal now being distinguished from the spiritual (apart from the repeatedly considered exceptions), the science of language knew, and for the most part still knows today, only what is linguistically-bodily alongside what is linguistically-spiritual, and thereby became entangled in manifold difficulties which cannot in principle be resolved and which mock every subsequent patching-up. The body of a name is of course the sound, the spirit is the concept; but to want to grasp the origin, development, and essence of language from these two alone would not be particularly different from thinking to grasp a piece of music from the musical instrument and the score, while forgetting the composer over it! What, then, is the soul of the name? The meaning of the word. We shall send a few examples ahead, for the difference between word-meaning and concept.

Who would not know the differences in meaning between bowl, cup, dish, basin, sauce-boat, tureen, pot, jug, tankard, pitcher, urn, beaker, goblet, amphora, vase, crucible, pail, tub — and who, with the help of such knowledge, would not be able to assign specimens actually before him to one of these kinds; but who would undertake to fix them conceptually, even with recourse to their purpose of use, so precisely that the delimitation would exclude confusion? It is the same with board, plank, beam, batten, joist, or with axe, hatchet, hammer, hoe, pick, or with forest, grove, wood, copse, or with twig, bough, shoot, or with puddle, pool, pond, and so forth. The names Lenz [poetic "spring"] and Frühling [spring] designate the same concept but have different meanings. If we read in a calendar the word "vernal equinox" [Frühlingsgleiche], this strikes us as fitting; but if we were instead to read "Lenz's equinox" [Lenzesgleiche], it would strike us as a joke, notwithstanding that the meanings of both words stand extremely [p. 1016] close to one another. In other cases they diverge, despite the sameness of the concepts, so widely that it would be impossible to put the one in the other's place. If someone were to write in an obituary, instead of "Yesterday evening our good aunt gently fell asleep," something like "Yesterday evening our aunt gently perished," legitimate doubts about his state of mind would be voiced. If one merely holds together the following series of German words, with each of which the concept of dying recurs, though here and there somewhat specialized — partly with regard to the respect or disrespect paid to the deceased, partly with reference to the cause of death: to pass away, to depart, to fall (in war), to go over, to perish, to go round the corner, to croak, to die like a beast, to bite the dust, to bless the temporal — then one will surely never again be in danger of confusing concept and unity of meaning! As an — incidentally instructive — parlor jest, the following recommends itself: He did away with himself, sank to the ground bereft of soul, and gave up his spirit. — This has, of course, not escaped the science of language. Much, and much that is ingenious, has been written about it,54) but, entangled in the —<sup>54</sup> moreover misleading — opposition of body and spirit, the differences of meaning among conceptually identical names have been interpreted subjectivistically, in that one hoped to find the ground for them in processes of feeling supposed to accompany the hearing as well as the uttering of the names, whereas in truth it is rather the meanings to which feelings attach themselves, of a strength and kind that is, moreover, quite variable from person to person! It is not our business here to show how many wholly erroneous views necessarily arose from this; instead, let the occasion be taken to survey in flight the principal oppositions between concept and meaning. 1. The meaning inheres in the name as the soul in the body; the concept is exhausted through the setting of the meaning's boundaries. 2. The meaning can never be absent; the concept is an artifact, whose absence changes not the least thing about the intelligibility of language. 3. Meanings are as old as language itself; concepts are no older than historical mankind and are indeed even now still younger. 4. Meanings change just as names do, only faster than they, just as the soul too changes faster than the ensouled body; concepts are, at some time, first discovered and must, at some time, yield their place to new concepts, but they themselves do not change. [p. 1017] 6. Meanings are lived through and are consequently never definable; concepts, always definable, are thought. 6. The meaning of a name is inexhaustible, as the soul is; the concept as such is entirely devoid of content. 7. The meaning of a name changes, if at times imperceptibly, with its appearance, and is therefore never exactly the same in any sentence — indeed not even exactly the same in the sentence heard as in the sentence read; the concept, wherever it occurs, occurs only as the same. 8. Word-meanings cannot be exactly transposed into any foreign language; concepts can be transposed absolutely exactly into any foreign language of equal or nearly equal historical age. 9. Meanings, and they alone, serve indicative thinking; concepts serve conceptual thinking, i.e., the faculty of judgement (in the word's non-specialized meaning).

<sup>54</sup> On page 1016. — Particularly rich material in this connection is offered by K. O. *Erdmann*, Die Bedeutung des Wortes (2nd ed., Leipzig 1910).

Although the psychic content of the word will be discussed in detail in the 66th chapter, let at least one remark forestall a possible misunderstanding already here. Because, without regard to the change of meaning, the change of sound is subject to its own laws, the meaning, even under the most considerable change of the sound, may be so little changed that any attempt at a definition of the difference would have to fail. All the more, for reasons sometimes of a historical and, to that extent, purely accidental nature, is the meaning of a name not infrequently exchanged for a wholly different one — that is, without the least change of sound. But how, one might then ask, would the name be an appearance of meaning?

To the answer must be prefixed the reminder that neither the difference nor the sameness of concepts furnishes any measure for the degree of difference of the meanings that can only be lived through. The answer itself, however, is already partly contained in points 6–8, which bring home to us in a threefold way the inexhaustibility of meanings; and it completes itself with reference to the circumstance — to be considered presently — that in not a few words the psychic content recedes far behind the spiritual content, in relation to which the sound indeed signifies no more than a — token. But finally (and with this we come to the main point): as surely as, for the soul of language, the soul of the speaker forms the medium, just as surely may the former not, say, be equated with the latter. The meaning stands to the sound as the [p. 1018] soul of the organism stands to the appearance of its body; but the soul of sound is a supra-organic soul, whose manner of appearing — to be discussed later — surpasses the appearance of living individuals in inconstancy at least as much as the world of — noises and sounds surpasses the material body.

We have touched, only in a few cases, upon the parallelism of this opposition with the opposition of soul and spirit, because the reader will readily supply it in the remaining ones. Mastery of language, as it will scarcely still need to be said after this, rests upon the availability of word-meanings, or upon the effectively operative presence of the soul of language in the owner of the language; it is therefore subject, from moment to moment, to now finer, now coarser fluctuations, and is as much withdrawn from the speaker's arbitrary will as, say, the mood that happens to govern him. We can, ordinarily, utter whatever we wish — the what understood in the sense of the content of judgement — but the how of the giving of form, and with it the content of meaning, is present and gift, and is therefore, like every gift, indeed practicable, yet never capable of being raised beyond a personal optimum, and, even up to it, only in the best of cases. Whoever wishes to be more precisely informed that, and how greatly, the depth of the capacity for reflection therefore depends on the degree of mastery of language, we refer to the 7th chapter of our book Ausdrucksbewegung und Gestaltungskraft [Expressive Movement and the Power of Form]; here, however, we bend back to our main subject, by making an application of what has just been said, one that should justify, even without further explanatory addition, the comparative breadth of the preliminary consideration.

As surely as it is only the sentence-structure that decides the respective strength, depth, compass, color and luminosity of a word-meaning, just as surely, in every language that has a long history of thinking behind it, there separate out "concept-weak meaning-words" and "meaning-poor concept-words." Only now can we win the full sense of these phrases, used by us earlier, and at the same time explain it. — Since by the "object of thought as such" we mean, and must mean, the conceived of a state of affairs, objects of thought are conceptual contents and, as such, extra-spatiotemporal. Were there names whose function was exhausted in the designating of concepts, they would differ in nothing from the essentially conventional signs of mathematics, and the favorite wish, especially of the Baroque age, to invent a logical algorithm would no longer be utopian: [p. 1019] the names in question would, unhindered by the spatiotemporal rhythm of movement of language, designate extra-spatiotemporal objects of thought exactly and coincidingly. Now, no such names exist, and none will exist, so long as human beings communicate by means of language; but the meaning-content of every name fluctuates quite extraordinarily, according to whether the manner of presentation seeks to bring itself into its own validity (whether that succeeds well or badly) or, on the contrary, is bent on communicating only the concept to which it has been stuck. Such an endeavor, however, which gives scientific treatment of language its characteristically sober stamp, is found supported, now more, now less, by the names themselves. If the reader flies in spirit over the most important termini of the last two chapters for principal and guiding concepts, thinking merely of the series just dealt with, such as: matter, the thing, resistance, the point of disturbance, unity, the One, being, he will not hesitate to admit that they themselves already breathe, to some degree, the sobriety so desired by science, compared with words such as: the dawn, winter, the primeval world, the sea, the climate, the flame, the firmament, the storm, the curse, sin, misery, destruction. We have, then, in the former, quite convincing examples of "meaning-poor concept-words." (Compare, on this, chapter 11, page 93.)

But whoever is even a little practiced in catching meanings and in listening in on the attitudes by whose aid the soul assures itself of them, that person cannot fail, in the end, to notice that meaning-poor concept-words more or less lack distance (whereas the others never do), and bring what remaining residue of meaning there still is into a nearness that is, so to speak, tangible. Since, however, objects of thought, being extra-spatiotemporal, have no relation either to distance or to nearness, and can least of all be touched, the cause of this must lie in the vital process which has made it possible to exhaust the concept out of the meaning of the name. And so the almost painful near-character, proper without exception to the meaning-content of every name that either long use in the service of conceptual thinking or the communicative technique of eloquent sharpness of understanding has striven to dry out into a mere conceptual label, gives us the not-to-be-underestimated confirmation that we have to seek, in the here and now of the resistance felt as disturbing, the place of origin of all concepts, indeed of conceiving itself. Whether one calculates the angle of refraction of light or scales the Platonic obelisks [p. 1020] of dialectic, whether one skewers infusoria or captures nebulae of the universe on light-sensitive plates, whether one dissects the concept of the triangle or the concept of God: his thinking is distance-blind and resembles a razor-sharp knife, fit for precise cutting into ever narrower slices; and with the successes of thinking of this kind, its shallowness grows. The materiologist seeks his pride in this; the ideologist conceals it from himself; but his conjuring tricks are in vain. Let one read whatever idealist system one will, be it the most significant we know, the edifice of thought of Plato, let one test the meaning-content by its psychic aftertaste, and one will know that it is exactly as atmosphereless and bare of all depth as any atomistic one, or as a scientific computational feat of Newtonian descent. But insofar as such an aftertaste judges otherwise, one will infallibly find that, for the materiologist as for the ideologist, the objects of thought had momentarily slipped away, because the never-to-be-conceived soul of language asserted its claim, flooding even the thinker's understanding with mystical fullness of meaning.

But yet another piece of evidence falls to us unbidden. As the finding of the existing thing forms, in principle, the first step of spirited finding, so the finding of the willing I forms, in principle, the second. It was the one and same primal point of disturbance, namely the Here doubled in the experience of resistance, from which we had to set out for the ascertainment of the vital enabling grounds of both. And accordingly it appears that that essenceless something to which we owe the Danaan gift of consciousness of existence — that our I, always poised to spring, obtrudes upon and draws near to the soul, as often as our spirit is indeed wakefully present but not otherwise occupied. To the distancelessness of the object of thought there corresponds, in us, the distancelessness of the personal I; to the victory of distancing images over concepts and things there corresponds, in us, an exuberance of enthusiasm or the fervor of the body — but always self-forgetfulness. — Our discussion of the near-character of objects of thought pursues yet a secondary aim.

What was earlier circumscribed time and again, and has now been conclusively illuminated, shallow reflection — this very thing is what we ourselves have, up to now in this section, been exercising, with all the power of thought at our command. For, just as it would be impossible, with its aid, to bring into view what vanishes before its near gaze (as, say, the stars in the dull [p. 1021] gray of afternoon) — the essence of the world — so it is only with its aid possible to find what, whether vitally or spiritually, let it itself arise in man; since, to be sure, the impulse thereto again does not stem from it, which is loath to see its own essence unmasked, but from the opposing side! With this it is already stated that the same procedure cannot now serve to carry through, step by step, to its end, what here and there has indeed been spun out and prepared, but not yet sufficiently carried through: the reconnection of the near-world of sensing with the far-world of beholding. Whoever gives himself over to Eichendorff's stanza that begins with the verse "Es redet trunken die Ferne" ["Distance speaks, drunken"], does not think distance, but he has experienced it; and whoever now wanted to reflect on what was experienced by taking pains to think distance, would find, in an instant, something so-and-so-far-removed slipped in its place, and he would be thinking the so-and-so-great distance. But this shares with the small and the smallest distance the near-character of all objects of thought, and holds, for one thus related to it, no more distance than, say, the dial of his pocket watch.

It is not everyone's affair to exchange the world of conceptual contents, all too familiar to us, for the world of meaning-contents, or discursive sighting for discursive immersion. — When the poet — we mean the real poet — momentarily beguiles even the shallow-reflective spirit, the verbal magic that enables him to do so is aided by the circumstance that the listener and reader console themselves with the wholly perverse conviction, natural though it is to shallow-mindedness, that the content of a poem is, after all, not actuality. The advocate of deep reflection has it far harder, because, in musing and in speaking, he can only point toward what can never be conceived, and yet demands that it be acknowledged that this very thing is actuality! In accompanying him on such paths, he may therefore invite only him to whom the truth would not seem too dearly bought at the price of the collapse of all the ramparts of opinion behind which the strongest driving force of historical man, self-assertion, has barricaded and entrenched itself against the power of the will-killing gaze of distance. — But we have hurried ahead, since for the present we must still linger in the near-world of conceiving.

[p. 1022]

### Dritter Abschnitt — Nähe und Ferne — Third Section — Nearness and Distance

#### 62. Kapitel — Vom Bewegungserlebnis — Chapter 62 — On the Experience of Movement

*Sensibility and motility.* — Less the matter itself than its relation to the present-day situation of the science of the soul brings it about that we frame an inquiry devoted to the experience of movement with some considerations on the perceptibility of movement. As a consequence of the errors of approach of sensualism, known to us, researchers have for some three hundred years been at pains to explain the behavior of organisms (= motility) with the aid of concepts that were, admittedly, created to explain the capacity for impression (roughly = sensibility). In view of the auxiliary assumptions that one consequently had to invent in order to make movement-perception intelligible, one feels a little reminded of the Ptolemaists in the days of Copernicus: just as epicycle upon epicycle was then piled up, so in the meantime one has furnished the "five senses" not only with the famous local signs, but also with sensations of position, sensations of force, sensations of tension, sensations of impulse, sensations of innervation, muscle-sensations, joint-sensations — indeed, one may marvel — sensations of movement. However much that is acute, ingenious and significant has been put forward on the problem of movement-perception, there is no doubt that one could not, in principle, free oneself from the error that the effector processes of the soul must be resolvable into receptor ones. One has wanted to establish (especially by experiment) what the sense of sight, the static organ, the sense of touch, the joint-sense, [p. 1023] the sense of temperature, etc., contribute to movement-perception; but one has not won through to the insight that no interweaving of impression-data, however rich, could produce the least experience of movement, because the experience of movement is of equal originality with the experience of impression. However great the value of such researches, by which knowledge of the sense organs was multiplied, they do not concern the experience of movement and are therefore, indeed, also not sufficient to make movement-perception plausible.

If today one speaks of movement-perception, one is generally inclined thereby to think of visual movement-perception, that is, of the visible evidence of movement. Now one may hold the most varied opinions about what is usually called real movement as opposed to apparent movement; in any case one will have to distinguish: appearances of movement that are referred to objects actually in motion, and appearances of movement that are referred to objects actually at rest. Here a colorful survey of the second kind! — If I watch a game of football, I perceive real movements; if I watch the same game of football on the screen in the movie theater, I perceive simulated movements, occasioned by a rapidly passing succession of positions. If a stone falls into the middle of a pond, it looks not as though the wave propagated itself in concentric rings, but as though the water itself rolled from the middle toward the shore. Whoever, in a railway train that has just come to a halt, glances leisurely at another train halted on the neighboring track, not infrequently believes his own train to have begun moving, when the neighboring one departs in the opposite direction. If we look up at a steep rock face against which clouds are driving in the blue of the sky, it happens to us that the appearance of the clouds stands still and the appearance of the rock face leans threateningly toward us. Stars, sighted for a longer time, begin to waver. If one fixes, in complete darkness, a stationary point of light, it will presently describe circles, sometimes of considerable diameter. The — now, to be sure, interpolated — loops and knots which the planets traverse, now slowly, now swiftly, would appear from the sun as nearly uniformly traversed circles. — But we need not continue, since the facts are known to everyone, and we remark only further that there exist comprehensive experimental investigations on this, which give a truly imposing notion of the manifold possibilities of the mere apparentness of [p. 1024] visible movement.

Here, of the illusions of movement in visible appearance, it is not their manifold conditions that concern us, but only a few consequences relevant to the science of consciousness. If visual movement-perception occurs both thanks to real movement of the object apparently moved and despite its real rest, then, in the first place, mere visible appearance cannot, with regard to movements, bear the judgement of existence; and further, visual appearances, entirely without the aid of other life-processes, can occasion no movement-perception whatsoever. A being that consisted only of the faculty of sight would arrive at no perception of movement, because it would lack the bodies with reference to which movement is first of all to be realized. Should this conclusion — simple, though even today still unfamiliar — surprise the reader, we may refer him to later expositions, in part already of this chapter, but especially of the next. Palägyi's "virtual movement." — Not such considerations alone, yet they above all, gave a highly significant thinker the decisive impetus to settle, once and for all, with the situation in the history of the spirit just indicated. It is Palägyi and, as far as we can see, only Palägyi, who uprooted sensualism with his doctrine of the equallyweighted originality of motility. We called it, in the 40th chapter, epoch-making, but immediately added, with reference to "later expositions," that it could not be regarded as concluded in the same sense as the doctrine of the intermittence of the acts of reflection; and we now attempt, now that its reproduction has become ripe for judgement, to set forth, at least in its main features, what in it appears to us finished and imperishable, what unconcluded, what, finally, in need of modification.

Of Palägyi's three classes of process, sensation, feeling and phantasm, we have here to do only with the third, for which he alternately uses the following names: process of imagination, movement-phantasm, vital movement, movement-imagining, imagined movement, virtual movement, tactile fantasy, and, in his very latest writings — following the terminology of the present reporter — tactile beholding. All mean thoroughly the same thing, which we prefer to call virtual movement, and which we shall elucidate with the following passages from Palägyi's writings. "Only a being that is capable of moving itself, i.e. that possesses the capacity to [p. 1025] move its body or one of its limbs, can also possess the capacity to perceive movements"; but this requires a class of experiences of its own, which enable it to refer its feelings and sensations to the mechanical process of movement. "We are in a position to live our way into a movement, without therefore having to carry out the movement in actuality. I call that kind of life-process, by which we live our way into a movement without actually carrying it out, imagined movements or also movement-phantasms... The production and perception of movements is bound to living one's way into the movement, and without this... there would be nowhere any capacity for arbitrary movement, and likewise nowhere any perception of any movements whatever, hence also no perception of a mechanical world... Lifeless things can indeed be caught up in real... movement, but they have no... vital movement, by which is meant that they cannot, in imagination, transpose themselves into other positions. The wonder of higher animal life is this vital transposing of the body from one place to another, without the transposition... having to be carried out mechanically." "Every human fantasy is, at its ultimate root, nothing more than movement-fantasy..."

Conceptions of this kind, however many citations one might adduce for closer characterization, retain something indeterminate so long as one does not recognize with full clarity what they serve, what they accomplish. Only a few considerations of another kind are needed, however, to have the most important application immediately before one's eyes. We cannot envisage an intuitive space in which places or positions would not also have to be kept apart, no intuitive place without a co-intuited space. If we think here of any tactile impressions, they are incomparably different from any visual impressions; nonetheless we inevitably locate tactile contents and visual contents in one and the same space and, for all objects of which we gain knowledge both through processes of touching and through processes of seeing, normally refer both experiential contents to the same places in space. We are, as one notices, at the famous problem of localization, and thereby stand at the same time before the far more comprehensive question of how the perception of space as a medium is possible — a medium which all data of intuition have in common. "Because space in itself," says Palägyi, "is incapable of awakening any sensations in us, it is also not sensation [p. 1026] taken by itself through which its existence is disclosed to us. But although space is nothing capable of being sensed, it is nevertheless something perceptible: an apparent paradox in which the enigmatic nature of space attains its most concise expression." Here now, proceeding from his concept of virtual movement, begins the most important application, which we wish to hear from him himself.

"If a foreign body touches the point P of our skin surface for a moment, we know, even with our eyes bandaged, with fair accuracy at what place the touch occurred. As proof we can ourselves at once carry out a movement with the hand and touch approximately the same skin-point P. But even if we do not actually carry out the movement, we nevertheless find the point P by means of an imagined movement aiming toward it, by means of a movement-phantasm. To be sure, in us who can see, the optical phantasm of the touched place on the skin obtrudes upon our consciousness so strongly that we scarcely become aware of our movement-phantasm; but since the born-blind person, too, is able to find the touched place on the skin by means of an actual or imagined movement, one sees that in the so-called localization of a touch-sensation the movement-phantasm.. plays a decisive role." "The whole localsign hypothesis is only an intuitive presentation of the impossibility of coping with the problem of localization on a sensualist basis.. What is puzzled into the tactile sensations is, after all, in the end again only sensation: there simply is no such thing as a place-sensation. Places are namely nothing of the sort that would have the power to awaken sensations in us. Sensations are aroused in us only by physico-chemical processes. But since places are no such processes, no reasonable person will ascribe to them the capacity to act upon our sensible nerves." "If I cover the circular opening of a beaker with the palm of my hand, I do not perceive the circular form of the opening by means of the sensations that the rim of the glass awakens; rather, these sensations must first arouse my imagination and prompt it to an imagined movement around the rim of the glass, so that I am able to apprehend its circular form."

Virtual movements — let the reader always keep this in mind — are real life-processes, hence also bodily processes, which appears, among other things, from the fact that each of them induces a sensation, [p. 1027] mostly an imperceptibly weak one, but at times a noticeable one of fairly considerable strength. If, for example, someone observes a point of our body sharply, we feel a sensation there, because our imagination "begins to occupy itself with that fixated point, and the imagined movement.. awakens a sensation there too." All perceptions therefore rest on vital circular processes.<sup>55</sup> For the localization of every content of intuition depends on the virtual movement, which in this way weaves all contents into one and the same domain of movement! It is set forth in extraordinary detail how, in particular, the seeing of places in space comes about only through the fact that we cannot touch and view one and the same point at the same instant. "If we draw the finger along a red line, the point that has just come forward for visual perception is the one that the touching finger has just left. Since, then, through the touching finger a point is covered up for visual perception at every instant, the latter.. can follow the moving finger, bring itself into concordance with it. Visual perception is, so to speak, "educated" by tactile perception.., and one is able to locate a visual sensation at a determinate place only because the trailblazing sense of touch has already arrived at a perception of place."

<sup>55</sup> On page 1027. — Several physicians who are friends of the author consider it regrettable that Palágyi, in the second edition of his "Naturphilosophische Vorlesungen," omitted the fifteenth lecture of the first edition. As we hear, the grounds put forward there by Palágyi *for* the fibril doctrine and against the neuron hypothesis are said still today to be highly alive. Following the Hungarian neurophysiologist Apáthy, he champions, with life-scientific grounds, the principle of the closedness of the entire nervous system (analogous to the closedness of the vascular system).

Since all the achievements of the virtual power of movement are already practiced by the infant, above all through ceaseless self-touching, they detach themselves early from the activity of spirit, become for the most part entirely unconscious, and fulfil their tasks "automatically," in perception as in one's own movement. If someone walks along sunk in thought, giving no heed at all to his steps, one says "the legs did their duty 'automatically'." But what does one mean by this enigmatic word? Does one perhaps believe that the automatically moving legs have been robbed of their guide, the imagined movement? If the automatic movements had lost their helmsman, the virtual movement, they would have to sink back to that primitive stage of development which betrays itself in the infant through the aimlessly flailing little hands. An automatized movement remains a purposive movement only because it has not lost its helmsman, namely the virtual movement; though, to be sure, this virtual movement has forfeited contact with consciousness.. By an automatized movement we therefore understand such a movement whose [p. 1028] virtual rudder has been switched out.. of connection with consciousness."

In finally distinguishing, from the "direct" movement-imagination, which is stimulated by sensations and first of all makes possible the perception of an outer world, the "inverse" movement-imagination, which is stimulated by vegetative processes (~ feelings) and withdraws from the outer world, Palägyi arrives at essentially new conceptions of fantasying, dreaming, emotions, expressive phenomena, and hypnotic suggestion.
