The unfamiliarity of his views may justify our adducing yet one more passage, which leads, as it were, up to the summit and allows the most important disclosures to be grasped in a single glance. "It is a wonder without equal that life, without departing from the place where it finds itself, can nevertheless behave as though it had escaped to another place in space or to another place in time.. This self-liberation of the life-process from the bonds that hold it captive in actuality is called, in popular speech, "the flight of fantasy." If, then, there is any process through which life stands out from the mechanical with perfect distinctness, it is the process of imagination... As.. life nowhere confronts the mechanical so distinctly as in the process of imagination, this is to be regarded as the highest unfolding of the vital .. Thus it now also becomes intelligible why even what is present cannot be perceived without the help of imagination. For what, for example, is taking place two meters away from our body can evidently be perceived at this determinate distance only through imagination. A perceptual activity is impossible without imagination."

Rich as our selection of testimonies may be, it accounts predominantly only for results, while for the whole wealth of grounding states of affairs and their interpretations reference must be made to Palägyi's writings. Meanwhile we expect nothing other than that the reader still unacquainted with them, even with the greatest readiness to understand, will not shake off a feeling of doubt, asking himself again and again what this "virtual movement," to which he can recall himself little or not at all, actually is. The deeper ground of such justified wavering will occupy us presently; here, however, we conclude our report by reproducing a few sentences with which we have elsewhere tried to bring virtual movement into the domain of intuitability [p. 1029]. "Should anyone, with the most willing effort, fail to succeed in envisaging the state that is meant by the virtual movement-experience, let him think of the following. If one merely reads a letter or a novel or even a poem with the eyes, one finds oneself unceasingly in the state of virtual speaking. It is at every moment immediately present to self-reflection and stands out with the greatest sharpness both against any images one may have of word-sound-forms (be it of one's own voice or of a strange one) and against the urge to read aloud. If one is fully occupied with vivid reflection, the intensity of virtual speaking increases so much that movement-impulses now even connect themselves with it, which discharge themselves in fine but soundless movements of the lips and tongue. Reflection upon virtual speaking seems to us the most excellent means of becoming aware of virtual movement as an original class of experience."<sup>56</sup>

<sup>56</sup> On page 1029. — From our "Introductory Foreword" to the "Wahrnehmungslehre," which was published from Palágyi's literary remains.

Three things we hold to be fundamental, established, and indisputable in the foregoing findings: the originality of inner movement, polar to the experience of impression — the solution of the problem of the apprehension of place with the help of "virtual movement" — the indispensable participation of the latter in the apprehension of differences of distance. Before we now express in what respects we diverge from Palägyi's propositions, we draw attention to a few curious gaps in his teaching. The obvious question, whether virtual movement generates the image of space or merely shapes an image of space that befalls us in any case, remains undecided; and, what calls forth our utmost astonishment, virtual movement is not called upon for the derivation of — the perception of movement! However often its discoverer assures us that without virtual movement neither one's own movement nor the perception of movement takes place, it is nevertheless nothing but static data such as place, shape, and distance whose apprehensibility he explains, really or supposedly, by means of it, and nowhere is even an attempt made to explain the perception of movement. The deeper ground is this: that the perception of movement cannot be explained at all by means of "virtual movement." We shall establish this step by step, beginning with the problem of the apprehension of shape.

If virtual movements are needed for the finding of place, one easily sees in what respect virtual movements can take part in [p. 1030] the apprehension of shape. If I cover the opening of a circular beaker with my hand, virtual movements bring it about that the rim of the beaker, and with it the whole beaker, signifies for me a place in space and has, for example, distances differing by direction from my shoulders and my feet; further, that the part of the rim turned toward me lies a little closer to me than the part turned away from me. If, then, it is meant that we find, by means of virtual movement, for the empirically distinguishable places of every shape, their position relative to one another as well as to us, this would be correct; but if it is meant (and this is how Palägyi means it) that the same virtual movement itself brings forth the experience of shape, then we must first remark that it is not evident how it could do so. Granted that the succession of pressure-contents in covering the beaker with the hand is not the circular form, we ask ourselves in vain how we should thereby bring about the circular form by connecting any two points of resistance with one another through virtual movement. Just as the circular appearance underlies things whenever we inscribe any polygon in a circle, so too it underlies a vital movement which has the task and the capacity to support, upon itself, the finding of the mutual position of two places; or: the polygon which at best arises in this way is precisely the circular form *not*

Because Palägyi has most probably sensed this, he calls virtual movement, with respect to the apprehension of shape, metaphorically an "imaging" movement, and in doing so evidently makes no distinction between it and *the* movement that, say, the tip of the index finger would trace if it circled the rim of the beaker. Now everyone of course sees that with the word "to image" precisely that is already presupposed at bottom which was supposed to arise only through the movement, namely the movement-shape; but further (though we attach no importance to this either) that circularity does not belong to the shape of a path — lying, as it were, at its back — because it can be apprehended from place to place from the standpoint of a direction of movement. The appearance of the contrary stems from phoronomy, and Palägyi's doctrine of the genesis of shape rests on a confusion of the science of appearance with mechanics.

If we think of the rigid circle as traversed by an actual movement, or by the inner movement exactly corresponding to it, the circular line appears, as it were, as the trace left behind by it, and we may, with regard [p. 1031] to this, attribute its shape to the movement itself. This shape, however, can in no way be understood from the aiming impulses with which Palägyi invests virtual movement, and it alone, with the capacity of finding places. Only a kinematic manner of conception suggests such a misinterpretation. For since kinematics is not concerned with movements at all but with movement-results to be arrived at by calculation, it first resolves the so-called movement-shape into tiny partial segments and in the end replaces it by the "infinite" series of tangents that can be laid, point for point, against the curvature, thereby substituting for the movement-shape a sequence of directions. Guided secretly by considerations of this kind, Palägyi overlooks the essential difference between directional impulses and the shape-properties of a path of movement, and therefore lets the appearance of shape be produced by the former. There is indeed no moving-oneself of which one side would not be the experience of direction, now extremely vague, now extremely determinate, and with regard to this the doctrine remains uncontradicted; but from ever so many feelings of direction there does not flow together the experience of a shape.

We have so far scarcely distinguished between the visible shape of a rigid line and the invisible shape of a movementpath of the same kind, because it mattered to us first of all to point out the contrast that prevails between the continuity of both of these together and the discontinuity of *the* movement-impulses that help us to the finding of places, distances, positions. In now appraising that distinction somewhat more closely, we wish to illuminate a second motive of thought of the discoverer of virtual movement, and with it the ground of his silence in the face of the question of the genesis of the intuition of space.<sup>57</sup> — One speaks of the direction of a blow and not of the shape of the blow; one strikes out, in wandering, in this or that direction and does not, say, describe a shape of locomotion; one even lets the roads "run" in this or that direction, and would, by contrast, refer the shapes of the roads — setting aside their serviceability for the realization of purposes of movement — chiefly to the images of intuition as they stand ready before one's eyes as a whole, say on a map. In short, as was set forth in the first volume, shape is, in the most pronounced conceivable way, now-shape, and is therefore fit as nothing else is to exhibit the content of intuitive space in a perennial now. In view of this, movement [p. 1032] as such and shape as such would be appearance-opposites of a tension only a little less wide than — time and space; and supposing it should turn out that no experience of shape could act upon the soul without stirring experiences of movement (and it will turn out so), it would still not be precisely the being-shaped, and so it would have to be something else that is thereby made manifest to us from the appearance of the world. But it is not only the appearance of shape, but to some degree even the experience of place, that demands intuitive space.

<sup>57</sup> On page 1031. — Only in one, very latest essay of Palágyi's, entitled "Raum und Zeit," is there a remark (Wahrnehmungslehre, p. 113) that might perhaps be read as meaning that the intuition of space *arises* out of virtual movements. The passage runs: "We express this fact in the fundamental proposition of *the belonging-together* of *virtual* and *real movements*. In its sense our intuition of space (which is actually contained in the virtual movement of tactile beholding) could not develop if the virtual movement did not manifest itself in directed real movements. Hence there would be no intuition of space without directed real movements . . ."

Just as no space would grow together out of mere places, so space could not become intuitable to a being that merely felt resistances and answered them with directional impulses; but were intuitive space to be entirely lacking, even the experience of place would dissolve already in the state of its coming-to-be, because all sensations would fall apart in time. That is why, indeed, happening really does not lead to the appearance of happening so long as the pulsatorily recurring turning-points of mirroring beholding have not yet been introduced into slumbering beholding (as is at least nearly the case in the life of the plant); and, conversely, precisely for this reason, if the experience of place and virtual movement are to be possible, mirroring beholding *must* have set in and have established at least the embryonic form of that to which, in the incomparably more awakened beholding, the intuitive space alone conceivable to us corresponds. For indeed even something resistant could not be felt at all without some, however slight, extendedness of the resisting thing! If, accordingly, the process of intuition is independent of an unfolded sensorium — as the level of the unicellular organism bore witness, though with motility overwhelmingly emphasized — then the question of what, after the unfolding of a sensorium, the one sense and the other sense and finally virtual movement contribute to the intuition of space becomes in principle moot, since each of them merely supplies distinct footholds for an ever-increasing orientation, and in particular neither touch can be endowed with intuition of space by sight nor sight by touch. But then we may not wish to deny entirely to either of the two senses just named the gift of conveying that in which the appearance of space is, so to speak, crystallized — the conveying of the appearance of shape — and still less may we wish to burden the sense of touch alone with it on account of the mobility of its organs, whereby it would rather occupy, to some degree, the position of an antagonist toward the shapeside of the world's appearance!

[p. 1033] It is not least Palägyi's innermost resistance to the modern relativization of actuality that enables him to reconquer for research the fundamental significance of the sense of touch for all processes of perception, and, in the closest connection with this, to set the originality of one's own movement against the will — as hopeless as it is for the present unteachable — to volatilize the universe into mere sensations and "perceptions." But as not infrequently happens with great discoveries, so it went a little here too: the principle first correctly recognized was overstrained, and, in the counterblow against penetrated prejudices, just as much too much was taken from the sense of sight as ideological partiality had previously added too much to it at the expense of the sense of touch. Striving, by pointing to the full sensuousness of passive-active touching in relation to the overemphasized activity of looking, to secure for the experience of movement the leading role in the process of perception, Palägyi forgets that he would rob the contents of sight of intuitability if they were, of themselves, as he assumes, shapeless. Were we to agree with his assumption that precisely what is shaped cannot be seen immediately, we should have to resolve to deny colorfulness, too, to the contents of sight, and to leave to the sense of sight only receptivity for degrees of brightness. For it is an absurdity to posit the superficially spread-out manifold of colors and yet to deny it the visibility of the forms that inescapably co-appear with it!

Were it as Palägyi thinks, the concordance of virtual movement with the contents of sight could moreover not be established even if this movement actually bore experiences of shape, because it would be inconceivable how a visible appearance quite unarticulated in space should offer any footholds at all for the reception of the movement-shape. What Palägyi sets forth, for example, concerning the visible disappearing and reappearing of the places successively to be touched in guiding the finger along a line, presupposes, among other things, a visual image of the gliding finger, and hence also of its shape, whereas the finger would not be seen at all if its shape were invisible! The whole arrangement would remain without effect: contents of sight and contents of touch would, despite the granted movement-shape, never make contact with one another. We once more summarize what, from our train of thought, bears upon Palägyi's achievement.

[p. 1034] Palägyi called himself a Pythagorean, and this may hold true with regard to the role he assigned to spirit in life; as a biologist, however, he was a Heraclitean to a degree scarcely to be surpassed. He could not have formed such conceptual opposites as those of beholding and mirroring beholding (= beholding and intuiting == beholding and making-present), because his thinking was incomparably more strongly fettered by the stream of time than by intuitive space, which therefore, together with shape, threatened to dissolve for him into a succession. However much this bent of his spirit had to qualify him for the deepest understanding of precisely the appearance of movement, and did indeed prove fruitful in two discoveries, namely the four-dimensional manifold and virtual movement, just as much did his likewise innately conditioned belief in mechanics bring it about that his life-scientific thinking was constantly crossed by physical research-intentions and turned aside, on the way to the primal phenomena, before reaching its goal. If we earlier had to set forth that he determined sensation and feeling essentially only according to their relations to the apprehension of a mechanical world, and did not essentially distinguish them, exactly the same has meanwhile emerged for his determination of vital movement, which was largely devised by him on the model of mechanical movement and therefore consistently conveys only static data. The more we now leave, step by step, the field of mere intuitabilities, the more it will show itself that his "virtual movement," which without doubt really exists, offers of the experience of movement only, as it were, its geometrical view. 1. Main varieties of movement-feelings. — If we ask ourselves what the meditation on movement thus far has extracted from its object, we must answer: the direction of movement. Now, however, the rigid straight line, too, has direction; the surface of the roof has direction relative to the surface of the house-wall, and there is direction from moment to moment; vital movement is intuitively no different from mechanical movement, except that the latter finds itself fixed intuitively at the same time by an angle, the former unintuitively by a goal. It is the direction, for example, of looking of which<sup>58</sup> Palägyi recognized, penetratingly, that movements toward the goal must run ahead of it before it, "educated" by them, is able to seek *its* goal in untouchable distances. This is confirmed not only by the behavior of the infant, repeatedly adduced by him, [p. 1035] who in the first weeks of life is notoriously unable even to grasp, let alone fixate anything, but subsequently learns fixation literally "in looking toward" touching and grasping; it also stands in accord with the behavior of the unicellular organisms we have discussed, which have impulse-experiences and consequently experiences of place, of position, of direction on the basis of an unarticulated sensing, and in particular without the least power of sight. But even if we were to disregard the fact that ever so many directions do not form a shape, there would still not lie in the experience of direction even the continuity that would belong to the transition from place to place by means of movement, but solely and only the goal of movement. In the concept of the direction of movement one has detached and isolated something from the experience of movement, whereby the experience of movement forms the counterpart of isolating sensation and of the data isolated by it; and just as one must take the place back into space in order for it to be what it is — a position in space — and for that requires the intuition of space, so one must tie direction back again to a happening, in order for it to be what it is — direction of movement — and for that requires the lived experience of original time.

<sup>58</sup> On page 1034. — We do not wish to pass by the disclosures that the word "richten" [to direct/straighten] harbors in this connection. According to *Paul*, richten means first of all "to make something crooked straight" (hence Richteisen [straightening iron], Richtstock [straightening rod], etc.); in particular "to bring something into an upright position"; further, the fastening of bodies in determinate directions to one another: a house is "gerichtet" [set upright/framed] when the timberwork is joined (hence Richtefest [topping-out feast], Richteschmaus [framing feast], etc.). If in all these cases the predominantly angle-determining function of richten, related in this way to the *statics* of the result, comes to the fore, then from its dynamics comes *rectilinearity* and accordingly the aiming nature in the directing [Richten] of a missile (at something), of glances, of eyes, of the heart, of thoughts; which is why Paul defines without restriction: "to bring an object into such a position that it moves (in a straight line) toward a goal." Likewise "to direct [oneself] *after* something" and "to be guided by something" actually means "to determine the position of one object by means of another." The transitions of meaning toward richten in the sense of "putting something in order" we may leave aside here.

If the object of perception, whatever its other features, is in any case an empirical now, then, under strict restriction to the intuitive content underlying it, the perception of visible movement would be impossible, in that we should see, instead of it, either the moving object only at successive places in space, or the traversed distance in the form of a rigid figure — as indeed actually happens at a certain degree of speed, as when, instead of a circling spark, a luminous circle appears. Present intuitability alone can never support intuitability of movement, and a being that could do nothing but — look on would find itself in that timeless world of shapes from which Plato consistently excluded movement, indeed every change. What, then — so runs the question — is the experience of movement in relation to the present intuitability of position? Before we attempt to give an answer to this, let us call to mind the main varieties of movement-feelings by way of a survey of the main varieties of animal movements.

To avoid roundabout circumlocutions, we shall henceforth make use of the terms activity and passivity, but ask that, even when [p. 1036] movements of arbitrary will are mentioned, one not think of resolving, purposing, willed striving, but of what is experienced on the occasion of such activities of spirit. So that this may always stand before our eyes, we shall in what follows speak preferentially of movement-feelings. If, then, we distinguish active and passive movement-feelings, one could further halve the active ones, which will occupy us exclusively for the present, into spontaneous and reactive, could split both the spontaneous and the reactive once more into several subdivisions, and would finally bring to light a great manifold of kinds of impulse, with regard to each of which some particularity would also have to be distinguished in the corresponding movement-feelings. But refinements of this sort need not concern us in an investigation that pays attention to drive-impulses only incidentally and only so far as is required for the elucidation of movement-feelings. With regard to the latter, however, we must now circumscribe still more sharply the moment of activity in the drive-impulse. Just as the sensation of resistance makes possible for spirit the act of objectification, so the drive-impulse, polar-opposite to it, makes possible the act of positing a purpose. The willed effort, particularly familiar to man, now shares with the drive-impulses, spontaneous as well as reactive, what may be called, with respect to the pertaining movement-feelings, the dynamic. Since this, however, for reasons considered in detail, congealed into the forceless concept of force of physics, we must first recollect ourselves upon its vital content.

Whether we call it a feeling of tension with regard to the posture that precedes the impulse, or a feeling of impulse with regard to the connection of this posture with the goal of the impulse, or a feeling of exertion with regard to the resistances that the impulse, developing itself in movements, seeks to overcome, or a feeling of force with regard to the realization of the overcoming, or, say, a feeling of achievement with regard to the reaching of the goal, including the successpromising approach to it — all this would dissolve into thin air without the capacity to experience the opposition of alien and one's own corporeality. Only a being that, in experiencing, co-experiences corporealities, and exactly only to the extent that this is the case, can experience tensions, impulses, forces, exertions, can experience spontaneous and reactive stirrings, can, summarily stated, experience impulses of movement and, in this way, dynamics both within itself and outside itself. Because kinematics, borrowing, to be sure, the never-to-be-comprehended [p. 1037] continuity which intuitive space has in common with time, sets bodies aside for purposes of calculation and replaces movement by the movementschema, the deceptive appearance could arise that the spatial presentability of movement is the process itself, and that movement could be understood from the visible appearance of movement. But to the (at times astonished) question why laws of movement, which are reckoned logically and mathematically! by means of points, lines, curves, should be verified by the actual behavior of moving "masses," the correct answer is that it is not laws of movement at all that are confirmed by the actuality of movement, but laws of the figural movementschema that are confirmed by the visible appearance of movement. From mere data of intuition alone we do not extract even the actuality of dynamics, let alone of movement, and what makes those into appearances of movement is an *inwardness* paired with the image of space, of which even vital dynamics, as will presently be shown, forms only one side.

With this, incidentally, the explanation is found of why, in the doctrine of will, we made in principle no distinction between the self-active generation of so-called inner and so-called outer movements, and among other things essentially equated *the* movement customarily called "movement of thought" with a movement of one's own limbs (and specifically with walking). Just as little as the dynamic that one would not deny to the latter consists in data of intuition, just as little would the former have to belong to it in a lesser degree, or even be lacking, because the play of tensions and releases does not come to appearance directly here; and just as surely as the appearing dynamic, for the images from which we read it off, lays claim to corporeality, just as surely would a disembodied soul be capable not only of no intuitable movement, but also of no "movement of thought." But that the genuine dynamic, from which the seeming dynamic of physics was won through anatomizing, concerns only one side of the experience of movement, will become recognizable to us more deeply than from the above considerations on Palägyi's virtual movement, through a retrospective glance at the nature of the drives.

In examining the drive-impulse in Chapter 45 we distinguished in it, from the pull of the images, the magnitude of privation-suffering, and thereupon pointed out, in its strength peculiar from case to case, two "motives" (understood literally!): the depth and the disturbedness of experiencing. [p. 1038] Neither of the two can be dispensed with for the origination of an impulse of movement; more intimate, however, as we had to emphasize, is the connection between need and the intensity or strength of the impulse than between need and the quality or kind of the impulse. The investigation, since then almost concluded, of the relation of impulse to sensing has fully disclosed to us that, in the experience of impulse, the image-character of the goal recedes, more or less, behind the goal-character of the image. Into the impulse there enters from the image only so much as is required for the generation of the selection of direction, while the strength of the impulse and the speed of movement are determined quite predominantly by the magnitude of privation-suffering; hence we should grasp the inwardness of the experience of movement most incompletely, were we to restrict ourselves to the dynamics of impulse, whether original or reactive. To the source-point of movement-feelings leads the consideration of the temporality of movement, and to this again the way leads by way of the passivity of movement, and this means by way of feelings not of moving oneself, but of being moved and of falling into movement. Meanwhile we continue our survey of the varieties of vital movement.

We may pass over all movement-automatisms. Even granting that the acquired ones among them, such as automatic walking, chewing, throwing out the arms (in falling), etc., rest, according to Palägyi's doctrine, on the efficacy of virtual movements, this only designates one condition of their taking place, while the taking place itself is indicated to us merely through sensations. This holds fully only of the inherited ones, which are called "reflex movements," beginning with the closing of the eyelid when the cornea is touched, the pupillary reflex, the "knee-jerk," the Achilles-tendon reflex, by way of the so-called chain-reflexes such as swallowing or vomiting, down to, say, the flying of decapitated pigeons: they can become perceptible through weak as well as through strong sensations, and have considerable significance for the steering, measuring, and coordinating of impulse-movements, but they themselves are not experienced as movement-feelings, because their immediate sphere of effect depends on apparatuses that are to some extent autonomous. "Mechanisms," to be sure, as one is fond of calling them, their mechanisms of drive are by no means. For even with reflexes the living body always answers only similarly to the similar, not, as the machine does, identically to the identical, and only this much is true: that the conditions of the reflexes stand, in the [p. 1039] overall structure of the body, in a relation of auxiliary arrangements to the wakefulness of its liveliness, and possess, so to speak, an instrumental nature — a circumstance that mechanistic thinking has exploited quite immoderately for the purpose of transferring the concept of the machine to living beings. For even today the biology of animal life-processes is still governed, to a wide extent, by the concept of the "reflex arc"!

Against this, the so-called expressive movement now strikes the connecting arch to the pivot of all movement-feelings, and with it we shall linger a moment. It scarcely needs to be said that all bodily processes of the animal being are in some way expressive, and indeed in principle not only the perceptible ones but also those playing themselves out imperceptibly within the body, such as heartbeat, breathing, digestion, glandular processes, chemisms of a thousand kinds. But their expressive content sinks, for one thing, as automatism rises; and for another, it comes to appearance directly only in such processes as give outward notice of themselves, and are therefore, e.g., on the sub-human level, at the same time the sole means of communication. Of these too there is an extraordinarily rich manifold, such as changes of scent, skin-color, secretions, voices, sheens, etc.; but the nearer one comes to man, the more decisively the expressive modification of movement comes forward, that is, that sensible characteristic of the impulse-movement with which, without regard to occasion and goal, the constitution of the impulse — by strength, kind, tempo, etc. — comes directly to expression, and with it, to some degree, the whole that has been seized by the stirring in question. An example will make this clearer to us. Just as little as we can tell from the locomotion of a higher animal whether it serves, say, the search for a mate or for its young, just as surely do we not infrequently really see from it whether it owes its origin to seeking, or fleeing, or attacking impulses; from which it follows that features cling to the appearances of movement in which the soul-state of the bearer of the movement becomes intuitable, at least in accordance with its participation in the life of the drive-impulses. Here we wish to bring to bear two sides of the state of affairs that are mostly not sufficiently appreciated by research on expression, namely that every expressive movement is suffered by its bearer, and that it — expresses — something only for that reason. The suffering-tone of expressive movement. — If we gather together all the [p. 1040] feelings enumerated above, the feelings of tension, of impulse, of force, etc., under the concept of dynamic feelings, we notice that they are described chiefly by degrees of strength, but scarcely or not at all by *that* which we are accustomed to think of first and foremost at the word feeling, namely the qualitative constitution of state, for which the German language offers us the admirably suited word "Stimmung" [mood]. We have set forth elsewhere that, with the growth of the dynamic in relation to mood, feeling more and more assumes the form of the so-called affect; but we have also always, and repeatedly in the course of this work, emphasized that no dynamic lacks the mood peculiar to it, and no mood lacks a dynamic that at least plays along in some hint. If the excitable soul answers with dynamics to the goal-character of images, then the beholding-capable soul answers with mood to the image-character of goals, and hence the former appears in the light of spontaneous or reciprocating activity, the latter in the light of pathic being. If, now, excitable drive-nature is only the incipient wakefulness of slumbering beholding and acting, and, as it were, its upper layer, then, in the domain of life, the so-called activity stands to passivity somewhat as a dependent to an independent magnitude, or as the outer side to an inner that bears it, or as the vigorous play of the limbs to the beating heart, without which it would be all over with their moving; and we must reckon pathic being into account for all life-processes, while dynamics is added to it, namely in the special domain of animality. The life-process, in other words — and indeed even the one quite predominantly dynamic — is suffered, never done, and the infallible sign of this in it itself is the mood that clings to each and every one.<sup>59</sup>

<sup>59</sup> On page 1040. — In order to meet certain doubts that might, after all, be entertained about the meaning here assumed for mood-tones in particular, a brief casuistry may be advisable. We first convince ourselves that "mood-tones" are in fact always present. Whether it be a matter of feelings in which we are obliged to emphasize the character of mood, or of those in which we are obliged to emphasize the character of surge, and if we pick out, from the former, pronounced lasting moods such as cheerfulness, contentment, resignation-in-devotion, faintheartedness, grief, resignation, sorrow, and from the latter pronounced momentary states such as overflowing joy, sudden rapture, boundless being-surprised, bewildered consternation, extreme embarrassment, fit-like fear, unfettered rage — it would seem to us that dynamics is rather lacking in the former than any coloring of mood is lacking in the latter; whereby the presence of the latter *also* in momentary affect would be sufficiently attested. But now it might perhaps be objected: if it is indeed true that even the most violent surge never lacks the color of soul, still it is more the *being-* *moved* than this color by which the dependence of the bearer of life on the life-process manifests itself. Here, however, either "dependence on the life-process" is confused with a *different* dependence, or it is overlooked that a being-moved comes to notice only thanks to a highly characteristic mood. For the violent surge, however it may be laid down in the organism, normally occurs on the occasion of sense-impressions, is therefore involuntarily related by the bearer to these, and is grasped more or less as having sprung from them; one need only think of being startled as a result of a bang. But this kind of dependence is *not* what we mean. It is one thing to be startled as a result of a bang; it is another thing to act in such-and-such a way as a result of the same bang. Only in the latter case, not the former, has the life-process that accompanied the perception of the bang become master over the recipient of the event. In losing one's composure, being overwhelmed, being carried away, and whatever else it may be called depending on the case, the *suffered character* of the process attests itself even where the dynamics of the bodily reaction are strong; and this suffered character forms the core of that *mood* which belongs more or less in common to surges and is their mark of recognition. If in this way one is inclined to locate the character of being-suffered of emotional movements in the wrong place, and consequently easily overlooks the symptomatic value of the mood-tone, then conversely, in the case of lasting states — at least of contentment, of comfort, of being happy — one not infrequently tends to underestimate their being-suffered, and doubtless because the vegetative processes underlying them remain hidden from us, while at the same time no external occasion is found with which we might try to connect them and "explain" them. From this it follows, first, that the absence of recognizable occasions for a state detracts no more from the pathic character of a mood than the pressing occasion of a surge could add anything to it; and second, that however strong the dynamics may be, this stands in no contradiction to that *suffered character* of the movement of which the mood of being-seized is the sign. — Incidentally, all this becomes clear to us at a stroke when we consider that, in principle, the expression of every affect can indeed be mastered, but never directly the mood *itself*!

If we were to bring that dynamic which announces itself in drive-impulses, and which, in keeping with the vehemence of feeling-emphasis, visibly stamps even its own ductus with the mark of vehemence, to a last and supreme formula together with the pathic being that manifests itself even within it, we should have to say that it is not distinguished from the vegetative processes by being less compelled, less suffered, but rather by being compelled as movement overcoming resistance and appearing at bodies in space. With this, however, we have not only brought to our knowledge the relation of the life-process as such to movement as such, but at once also its essence. For were it true that every vital movement is the, if not sole, then at any rate original [p. 1041] form of appearance of happening, then it will also be the stirring of an inner happening by virtue of which movements appear, in "standing" space, to the being capable of intuition, or, to put it still more pointedly: just as the experience of one's own movement would present itself as, in a sense, the more massive form of being moved, so it would in the end be a feeling of being driven, by virtue of which space could afford, for the bearer of intuition, the scene not only of images but also of their movements within it. But we must not rush too far ahead!

If we turn back to expressive movement and call to mind being seized, being overpowered, being overwhelmed — in relation to which one speaks of stormy joy, blazing anger, unfettered rage, enfeebling fear, paralyzing terror — we know indeed that this takes place not only directly in the bearer of such emotions, but also indirectly in the onlooker of their outward expressions, namely through the medium of being co-moved. It is co-movedness, as is scarcely disputed any longer, that first of all enables us to perceive grief in the features of the grieved, agitation in the gestures of the agitated, anger in the voice of the angry, however often it may also rebound off our own state of life and then have, for our consciousness, merely the significance of a sign.<sup>60</sup> And we know further that co-movedness gains ground the more powerfully — finally filling the onlooker with vehement excitement of his own — the more, from the manifestations of surging emotion he witnesses, there speaks resistanceless being-seized. Here we have, for the first half of<sup>61</sup> what has just been explained — namely, that a life-process expresses itself and becomes manifest in accordance with its degree of having-been-suffered — an almost excessive example, and we note in passing that we have hereby come upon an instance of that trait of symbolic thinking according to which elementary similarity forms the ground of all efficacy. We co-experience, thanks to some degree of being-seized, the experience of another (and recognize it in immediate connection therewith), insofar as it too, without prejudice to its other features, is likewise a form of being-seized! The actus purus, for example (== the pure == absolute deed), we cannot, accordingly, co-experience, and therefore can never recognize immediately either; or, to put it more graspably: spiritual activity, indeed all doing whatsoever, has no expression at all, and is gathered only indirectly from the admittedly unique inhibition of all utterances and precipitates of one's own life, which we may fittingly call their regulation.

<sup>60</sup> On page 1041. — All counter-arguments of those who still cling to the long-refuted view that psychic processes could be inferred prove to be merely apparent arguments. It has been urged, for instance: the malicious rejoicer *takes pleasure* in the displeasure of him upon whom the harm has fallen, the cruel man in the torments of the tortured; how would that be possible if he were co-excited by the other's displeasure, the other's torments?! And now suppose another person *is indignant* at the malicious joy and at the cruelty — would he then have experienced co-malicious-joy and co-cruelty? The answer is: without doubt! If the cruel man could not in the least share in the torments of his victim, his cruelty would come away empty; and if the person indignant about it could not in the least feel along with the state of the cruel man, this indignation would not come about at all. Among other reasons, this is why a sadist who frequently indulges his sadism must intensify the torturings if the sight of them is still to bring him satisfaction; this is further why the person indignant about it will gradually become less violently indignant if he had to witness the cruelties very often; for the same reason, too, we react differently where we perceive cruelty than where we recognize the cause of permitting torments to lie, say, in indifference. We would not soon come to an end were we to adduce all the facts that confirm that, for the perception of another's psychic states, *some* degree of co-excitation is entirely indispensable. But the most important is this: as the capacity for co-excitation dwindles more and more — whether from indifference and habituation, or from increasing dullness with advancing age, or from counteracting will (example: the coldness and sobriety of the scientific vivisector) and self-mastery — affective perception passes in lockstep into unaffective perception (not forgetting that even the most unaffective matter-of-factness in turn has its feeling-tone, whose analysis — successfully begun by Nietzsche — can hardly be regarded as complete). If, then, for example, the cruel man were to watch the torments of the tortured with affectless matter-of-factness, or, put differently, with the utmost minimum of participation in them, then at most his curiosity, his thirst for knowledge, and whatever else might find satisfaction — only not, precisely, his cruelty. — We have used the word "participation" here, as is understood, in its literal sense and not in the sense that came to predominate in colloquial speech, where it means, like "sympathy," a helpfully disposed compassion. The participation we have in mind is finally heightened to a state for which the German language has the apt phrase, that one is "drawn into fellow-suffering" [in Mitleidenschaft gezogen]; and for this degree of participating — which would more correctly be called almost a being-made-toparticipate — childhood offers the most striking evidence. The often-repeated example of this: a child cries because it cannot find its toy, and presently its two playmates likewise begin to cry "for no reason." Such a kind of co-excitability has rightly been brought under the concept of suggestibility, but has thereby been placed in a light that seems to furnish a new argument to the advocates of the belief in the inferability of psychic processes (as, incidentally, also to the advocates of the belief in an "inner perception"). For must not, so it is thought, highly participation-capable adults (now understood in the sense of colloquial speech) at the same time be very suggestible? Such a concurrence of capacity for participation and suggestibility, however, by no means holds. There are exceedingly suggestible persons whose capacity for love is slight and whose participating warmth of heart remains far below average; and conversely there are warm-heartedly participating persons of far-below-average suggestibility! We enter here all the less into a detailed discussion of the relevant range of questions, since it has already been offered by us in several places (compare especially the 7th chapter of our "Grundlagen der Charakterkunde"); only the main point shall be briefly recalled. As certainly as the co-excitation of the child, leading at once to corresponding expressive phenomena, which may indeed count as a form of suggestibility, immediately reveals to us the being-drawn-into-fellow-suffering and with it the primal source of every feeling-with, every participation in the widest sense of the word, so certainly does genuine, authentic sympathy come about only then, when and insofar as the being-moved-with *sets itself* *off* from the being-moved-of-one's-own. Whereas up to a certain age the child is characterized by the fact that every one of its co-excitations immediately becomes an excitation of its own, in the adult the own state *asserts* *itself against* the co-excitation and notwithstanding it; from which it is an immediate consequence that the origin of the co-excitation is referred to the alien soul. As one notices, it is only through this that the state of co-excitation becomes a state of (consciousness-capable) participation in the alien excitation. *To this extent*, then, sensing predominates in the child as compared with the adult, and beholding predominates in the adult as compared with the child. — Even if we were to leave aside the inhibition of the expression of feeling that naturally sets in with the adult, that *interiorization* of co-excitations which resonates in the concept of feeling generally is further accomplished as a consequence of this. Suggestibility is therefore in any case ambiguous: it *can*, among other things, have its source in an overly easy co-excitability (with which, incidentally, nothing would yet be settled about the depth of the feelings); but it *can* also be a consequence of poverty of images and lack of definition of the soul, and in this way speak for the *weakness* of "psychogenic" feelings. (In fact the latter occurs far more often.) With this it should be sufficiently clarified what we had in mind when we said that the co-excitation indispensable for the perception of another's feelings has in many cases only the significance of a sign, in that it rebounds off one's own state of life. Thus the being-moved-with through another's torments rebounds, in the cruel man, off *those* feelings which, on that occasion, accompany the satisfaction of his will to power; thus the feeling-with of another's cruelty, in the person indignant about it, rebounds off his own — pity for the victim of the cruelty, with whom he temporarily identifies himself; thus, finally, the "sympathy" of one who is captivated by the mere state of affairs of a process — say, as a researcher — rebounds off intellectual feelings of his own.

<sup>61</sup> On page 1041. — The circumstance that *even* in the adult, undoubtedly genuine sympathies, co-affects, and the like, not at all rarely pass over again into *such* affects in which the difference between the alien and the own stirring appears once more abolished in experience, is a further strong argument for the source of all perception of feeling. Here it is characteristically not the depth but the violence of the stirring that tends to build the bridge from the one state to the other. We give an illustrative example of this, whose demonstrative value rests in the primitiveness of the occasions of feeling that come into play in it. Since the oldest days, and in part still today, animal fights, or fights between animals and men, have been popular. What excitements accompany these among the festive crowd of spectators in Spain is well known. But even one who has never attended such a spectacle has often been present when, on the street, two dogs tore into each other, in the henyard two roosters clashed, in the garden two tomcats, on the meadow two bulls, in the zoo two bears, and so on, and has surely noticed more than *once* that the onlookers, himself included, not merely fell into co-excitation but soon enough even took sides for one of the two animals and, so far as possible, intervened — not so much in order to separate the animals as out of shared anger *against* one of the two. With this the pathic trait in any surge whatsoever becomes, so to speak, tangible. For if the co-excitation of those vividly involved, or in our case the shared anger, can finally pass over into genuine anger of one's own, then we recognize, even in the most dynamic drive-impulse, the underlying layer of suffering, and see "doing and driving" break forth out of being-done-to, the impulsive moving-of-oneself out of being-moved.

[p. 1042] To make plausible also the second half of our preliminary consideration, which concerns the life-scientific standing of movement in particular, let us recall in advance that, under otherwise comparable circumstances, the resting image of intuition is surpassed in expressive content by the intuited process, and, again, the uniform process by the non-uniform: the redness of a face falls short, in this respect, of the blushing; paleness, of the growing pale; sweatiness, of a sudden outbreak of sweat; the gleam of the eyes, of the "lighting up" of the gaze; the roughness, loudness, softness of a voice, of its becoming rougher, becoming louder, becoming softer; and, most of all, every uniform movement falls short of every change of tempo, fullness, briskness, force, and of every change in the rhythm of its course. Now, however, many usages of language, repeatedly mentioned, bear witness that movement is beheld not only in a process, but even in a rigid line. When the resting tendril "winds itself," the resting branches "spread out," the resting banks of the river "rise," the resting rock-face "plunges" or "falls" sheer downward, the resting path "meanders," "curves"; when the moon "waxes" and "wanes"; when darkness, brightness, warmth, cold can "grow" — it can scarcely meet with doubt any longer that more or less the whole world of appearance, and above all every appearance of process, is involuntarily interpreted as an appearance of movement, and is opened to understanding only through this. If, for convenience's sake, we call the beholding of movements that are not perceived co-perception, we may say: one understands movement as perceived, in perceiving a hopping, jumping, dancing, raging, clenching of fists, wringing of hands, shaking of the head, frowning, starting, trembling, twitching, chattering of teeth; and one understands movement as co-perceived, in perceiving a blushing, growing pale, lighting up of the eyes, sighing, groaning, panting, weeping, sobbing, wailing, screaming, laughing, exulting, etc. Co-excitability is essentially co-movability. One expresses this, incidentally, literally in German when one says: he took it in "moved" [bewegt], or, say: he remained, through all of it, "unmoved" [unbewegt].

It is precisely such examples that now bring home to us, with full force, that movement as the all-governing means of expression — vital movement, for short — is itself already something expressed, at times, moreover, perceptible as movement and then intuitively [p. 1043] indistinguishable from mechanical movement, far more often not perceptible as movement and yet not experienced essentially otherwise than if the movement did perceptibly take place. Because, in the sense of the science of life, something exercises effects by expressing itself, the investigation of expression coincides with that of vital efficacy, and ultimately with that of efficacy as such, provided one has become convinced that efficacy and living efficacy are the same thing, mechanical efficacy however only a noumenon in the service of the calculability of one side of what "in actuality" takes place. We have, if not already established, then at least made probable, and subordinated to the principle of elementary similarity: 1. Vital movement in the individual essence acts by awakening co-movements in other individual essences. 2. The passivity that, in relation to the acting movement, belongs to the co-movement thereby brought about, already belongs, in some other way, to the acting movement itself. 3. Vital movement in general is accordingly pathic movement, or a form of being-moved, and in particular self-movement is a having-to-move-oneself. If one transfers such propositions to movement as such, then, despite all that has been set out at length, on the one hand concerning the mechanical concept of cause, and on the other concerning the opposition of lawfulness and necessity, a faint feeling of disquiet may perhaps still rise up, prompted by the collateral thought whether that very constrainedness — borrowed from the running of the machine as its model, and denoting the essence of the mechanized universe — has not thereby crept into living efficacy. This, however, would only set us the task of giving a still more precise account of what the pathic character of life-movement amounts to — quite generally, and not merely with regard to such cases of expressive movement and co-movement as were just now adduced. We link up here with a few open questions from the doctrine of drive-impulse, and ease our train of thought by setting side by side, for a stretch, as though they were two distinct states of affairs, the soul receptive to distance, or beholding-andacting soul, and the stimulus-sensitive, self-moving bodily soul. The latter would then be the bearer of drive-impulse and self-movement, the former of an inwardness of movement through which spatial and temporal distance is enabled to come into effect [p. 1044] in the here and now of the animal body. The one would coincide with the condition of the dynamic life-processes, the other with the condition of their operative pathic character. On the origin of movement in the individual essence. — In the 45th chapter we called to mind the inner-bodily impressions that accompany every drive-impulse, and surmised in them a connecting link between the pull of non-present images and the soul, insofar as the images signify goals to it; from which two questions seem to arise, which one might be tempted to frame as follows: how are inner-bodily impressions connected with non-present images; and by what are they distinguished from the inner-bodily coimpressions of outer impressions, which mediate the presence of intuitive images? The first of the two questions alone would be quite unanswerable did one not know of the full originality of motility, and credit inner-bodily impressions with the capacity to bring about impulses — notwithstanding that these have not the least similarity to the goals of the impulse, and are rather weakly intuitive indications that other processes are taking place, out of which the impulse develops. Sensations, for example, that can be a mark of the state of thirsting, of the state of hungering, are not therefore also a mark of the tensions that likewise belong to thirsting, to hungering, and that directly occasion the impulses of the same name; sensations in the joints are no constituent part of the impulse from which a movement of extension or flexion proceeds. Such sensations, however, and all others of kindred sort, are indeed the symptoms of processes that either underlie the impulse to seek food, to seek liquid, to let the limbs play, or that accompany its realization, and as symptoms are at times indispensable to the involuntary steering of the course of movement. We should accordingly have to ask as follows: what kind of inner processes are they through which their bearer is connected with non-present images?

But the second of the above questions, too, would conceal a misunderstanding, should the thought — still widespread today — hover before us that inner-bodily impressions could build up intuitive images, or at least contribute to their building. Bodily sensations in the eyes, for instance, that can occur in producing the convergent position of their axes, and that may at most be accompanied by feelings of slight exertion [p. 1045], do not themselves produce the wholly incommensurable visible evidence of the image's nearness, even though they are in turn a symptom of its nearness and may have some value as points of support for the process of intuition.<sup>62</sup> In short, what is sensed and to-be-sensed upon the body as well as within the body is always a here and now, and therefore, with respect to every there or then or hereafter, a signal of an efficacy unfolding elsewhere; hence we decide, more generally than the question was put, that inner-bodily sensations provide aids toward the vital oversight of the success both of impulses and of processes of intuition. The diversity of their contents thereafter offers scarcely any further interest.

<sup>62</sup> On page 1044. — From the "sensualist" false doctrine, that data of inner-bodily sensation enter as elements into our intuitive images, the more significant among the psychologists of Germany have in fact long since departed; by no means, however, have the psychologists of the Western peoples, in particular of France, England, America. Thus we read, for example, in *Poincaré*'s "Science and Hypothesis" (translated by Lindemann, 3rd ed., Leipzig 1914), p. 55, verbatim: "Sight, however, allows us to estimate distances and consequently to perceive a third dimension. But everyone knows that this perception of the third dimension reduces to the sensation of an effort in the accommodation the eye must make, and to the sensation of the convergent direction which both eyes must assume in order clearly to perceive a determinate object." — As it continues in this vein, the *intuitability* of a space of four dimensions is incidentally demonstrated to us in advance. "Nothing prevents us from supposing that a being which has an understanding as fully developed as ours, and which has the same sense organs as we do, is placed in a world where light reaches it only after having passed through refracting media of a complicated kind. The two indications which serve us for estimating distances would then cease to be connected by a constant relation. A being which, in such a world, accomplishes the education of its senses would doubtless attribute four dimensions to complete visual space" (p. 67). On page 59 the derivation of the so-called representation of movement ends with the following words: "When I say that we represent these movements to ourselves, I mean by this only that we represent to ourselves the muscular sensations which accompany them and which have no geometrical character whatsoever, which consequently in no case imply the pre-existence of the concept of space." — Total unfamiliarity with the originariness of motility could hardly be voiced more drastically. Conversely, however, it should become clear, precisely in the countershine of such backwardnesses, that the whole sensualist doctrine of sensation shatters against the knowledge of the polar reciprocity of drive-impulse and sensation!

If we return to the main question, what kind of processes they are through which their bearer is connected with non-present images, the answer runs, in the language of the science of the body: vegetative processes; in the language of the science of the soul: processes of sleeping efficacy and sleeping beholding. What presents itself, seen from the standpoint of the one who lives it, as the pull of non-present images, is, seen from the standpoint of the investigator, life-processes through which distance becomes present in the here, and the impetus that thereby falls to the stimulus-sensitive bodily soul signifies, in relation to what gives the impetus, its awakening: originally, and in the animal generally predominantly, the awakening of its efficacy, gradually more and more, and in man predominantly, the awakening of its beholding. In the living body, then, insofar as it serves, so to speak, as the dwelling-place of a soul receptive to distance, the non-present images are, after all, present — but not as intuitive images — and their efficacy, too, is present — but not as drive-impulse; and thus the genesis of the process of intuition appears in the light of a transposition of the form of actuality of the image into the form of actuality of the intuitive image, through the pairing of beholding with sensing; the genesis of the drive-impulse, in the light of a fine transposition of the form of actuality of efficacy into the form of actuality of dynamics, through the pairing of efficacy with bodily mobility. Of these, only the second case concerns us here.

We can avoid the perhaps somewhat too abstract-sounding word "transposition" by placing ourselves within the opposition of sleeping to waking. As "primal phenomenon" each of the two states can be described only in relation to the other, since being-awake inescapably becomes being-for-itself, and being-for-itself in any case signifies corporeality, [p. 1046] because it is only through it that a real now-and-here sees itself set apart from a real then-and-there. Accordingly, insofar as efficacy awakens, a separation takes place between a sleepingly present, which we shall call the co-present, and a wakingly non-present; and in place of the sleeping efficacy there steps the drive-impulse, which, with regard to the co-presence of the efficacy of the images, is a pull thereby determined and directed, but, with regard to the bodily non-presence of that which thus pulls, is urge to movement. If we replace "efficacy," since it means the efficacy of images, by "happening," we can say more briefly: in the mobile individual essence, as a body appearing as an actuality, the happening of the original actuality necessarily becomes space-traversing movement, and the impulse to movement becomes urge against resistances.

In passing we recall that the thought of the microcosm has thereby now been circumscribed more sharply than in the 56th chapter. The opposition of individual essence and world remains untouched, because the former, as body, is unquestionably a part of the latter, and therefore depends on it in some other and greater way than the universe depends on the organisms within it; but mere part-being grounds no connection between the two. Rather, the individual essence has any relation to the world at all only because, thanks to a soul receptive to distance within it, its here and now signifies at the same time a there and then, or in other words a place of passage of elementary efficacy, and is thus an inner scene of the very same powers that weave the appearing cosmos. In fact there is no process between outside and inside, or conversely, that would not also be a process within; and what, for example, "a human being, whether willed or involuntary, accomplishes outwardly, is never anything other than a process of inner life that has become objective in rebound from the world."<sup>63</sup>

<sup>63</sup> On page 1046. — *Klages*, Vom kosmogonischen Eros, 5th ed., p. 171.

The foregoing reflections confirm for us what we sketched above in passing and by way of anticipation, with the following warranted conclusions: 1. Considered in relation to the efficacy of the soul receptive to distance (which is for its part cosmos "on the spot"), the drive-impulse of the stimulus-sensitive bodily soul is compelled. 2. The compulsion in question assumes the form of dynamics, because in the actuality of the body only movement brings together what is separated, and parts what has come together. 3. If, accordingly, self-movement is, so to speak, the outer side of being-moved, [p. 1047] it holds nonetheless no less that such compulsion, however often it may answer the onrush of impressions, is inner compulsion, and thus not to be compared with the mechanics of the being-pushed of non-living things. 4. Since the pathic character of self-movement becomes intuitively evident and attestable to us only at the distance-beholding-capable stage of co-movement, we must take co-movement as our basis for the purpose of clarifying every kind of coming-into-movement. 5. This leads finally to the question of the manner of the transition from original happening into movedness.

That we cannot witness such transpositions by any dissection of bodily processes however far pursued, goes without saying. We shall not, however, for that reason hold certain fundamental experiences to be of quite slight account, even though they are ordinarily regarded only physically, and not, as is here our task, according to their expressive content. The lowest protists, as we have seen, respond not only to mechanical but also to thermal, chemical, optical, and other stimuli with movement, in that, for example, within the *interior* of the amoeba the plasma-streaming takes other directions. Fluctuations of temperature or fluctuations of brightness — to stay with these two, which are not themselves movements — can "convert," as it is customarily put, into mechanical movements; but, as often as they act as stimuli, the movement that now ensues from them breaks forth from within the individual essence, and indeed in connection with chemical and probably electrical processes whose possibility of arising is grounded in living matter. In the human nervous system, indeed, it is demonstrably electrical waves into which the outer influence is transformed, and by which the answering movement is called forth. Brought to the briefest formula: outer happening induces inner happening, and this induces self-movement. In the language of the science of essence, the following interpretation would at least be admissible: real happening in the cosmos occasions real happening in the individual essence in accordance with the elementary similarity of the two; but wherein, now, would lie the elementary similarity between this and the phenomenon of self-movement? — Supposing we have come to agree that self-movement is movedness, we find the key to its connection with happening perhaps at the highest stage of distance-beholding-capable wakefulness. [p. 1048] Demonstration of the pathic character of movement. — Whether an animal flees or seeks or attacks, we see that it moves itself; but in countless other cases we see that something is moved, and we see it not because we had hastily interpreted the process mechanically, however natural that may seem to most people nowadays, but thanks to a deeply original state of being seized, behind which, even in the case of utmost compulsion, all animal being-driven remains far too dynamic and outward, falling short of innermost and genuine pathic character. In this kind of being-seized are rooted those feelings, conjured up by poets, that can fill us when we are wholly given over to the sight of a sail gliding across the lake's surface, of leaves fluttering on the tree, of clouds drifting through the vault of the sky. Even one for whom the like is already threatening to drown in the mist of memory should be able to bring enough of it back into clear view, as soon as he ranges side by side, comparatively: other appearances of the same movement-soul, others of a predominantly dynamic soul, still others that more or less compel a mechanical interpretation. Thus akin in soul to the examples cited is the appearance of the wave-beating pond, of the wind-billowed cornfield, and, to some extent, of the gliding river; a little more dynamic is the appearance of streaming rain or the roaring waterfall; a little more dynamic still is that of a nocturnal flight of storks migrating southward; already predominantly dynamic is that of a herd of fleeing deer; wholly dynamic is that of a sprinter; and finally the appearance of the thrown stone, of the water flowing from the kitchen tap, as well as the movement-appearance of all machines, call for a mechanical interpretation — though even these still in varying degree. Compared with a mechanics of movement that intuitively forces itself upon us, all the remaining images are, for unreflective feeling, without doubt alive — but those that are markedly, pathically alive are animate in a quite peculiar sense, because caught up in a self-movement wholly without impulse. With this, however, we should have come upon a through-and-through living being-moved within ourselves, which, with the deepest conceivable passivity, would at the same time be entirely without the reactive pull that stood out so obtrusively in surge-like being-driven, and, in view of the immediacy with which we can behold this movedness in images, we should have to posit a virtuality of movement that would differ enormously from virtual dynamics, in that it would above all not exhibit the latter's erratic guidance [p. 1049], and would thus seem alone truly called to lead into the essence of movement. But then we should have to be able to point to its seat of origin, no less than to that of the virtual impulses, in earliest infancy.

Now, its origin falls, as it seems to us, into a still earlier dawn-time of individual life than the origin of virtual dynamics. If not all, then certainly most peoples know how to still a crying infant by rocking, and to lull the quieted infant to sleep by cradling. If we further think of being-carried, which sets in from the moment the umbilical cord is cut and, if not at once, then a little later, can bring about similar effects, we do not doubt that the experiential content of being-moved signifies a primordial datum of the unfolding human soul, and we see the doctrine of the preponderance, distinguishing it, of the wakefulness of beholding over that of efficacy — or, put with the concepts meanwhile acquired, of the preponderance of its image-receptive pathic character over its stimulus-sensitive dynamics — surprisingly confirmed by the circumstance that the, in the animal world unparalleled, long immaturity of the human child essentially coincides with the period of incapacity for self-active locomotion, during which, in its place — the stimulus-sensitive dynamics as it were groping about on the spot — being-moved-along becomes, quite predominantly, the experience. Here in particular lies the ontogenesis of that supra-animal capacity for co-movement of man through intuitive images to which our examples referred, and without whose presence the pathic character of movement would have become known to no one, and this reflection would never have been undertaken.

But just as the self-movement of the limbs corresponds to virtual dynamics, so the letting-oneself-be-carried of adults of all times and peoples, too, corresponds to virtual pathic movement — and the longer, the greater in extent. If we disregard the merely useful arrangements of "traffic life" and the fever of will belonging to sport, it admits of no doubt that the pathic character of movement is involved in every, even the slightest, preference for locomotion by means of a vehicle (such as carriage, railway, motorcar, ship, aeroplane, etc.), and, for reasons we shall touch on presently, still more in such activities where self-movement fuses with an alien mover, as in riding, tobogganing, swimming, rowing, skiing, cycling, gliding over a smooth surface by means of steel skate or roller skate. Should we wish to doubt that man owes the invention of many artificial and the taming of many living vehicles not to the will to [p. 1050] power alone — though certainly to it above all — but also, alongside it, at least to the passionate urge toward being-moved-along, we should be incontrovertibly instructed to the contrary by the merest glance at the modes of amusement of children and adults. What is it, indeed, with which, at any popular fair whatever, apart from spectacles, old and young amuse themselves so predominantly that all other kinds of amusement, such as target-shooting, strength-tests, sack-races, and the like, sink into the shade beside it? The surrendering of oneself to contrivances by which one is (with or without musical accompaniment) jolted, shaken, jostled, thrown, swung, hurled, spun, rolled, or carried off at furious speed! Examples: ordinary swings, "Russian" swings, ordinary carousels, those with seats revolving about themselves, those with boats flying centrifugally through the air, rotating drums through which one tries to pass, straight and spiral sliding surfaces, "topple-slides," rollercoasters, and so on and so forth. But who would fail to recognize that from pleasures of this kind the path leads, by way of children's delight in the swaying beam and the "swing," in a straight line down to the pre-conscious delight of the infant in the rocking cradle!<sup>64</sup>

<sup>64</sup> On page 1050. — In the author's youth the cradle was (at least in Germany) generally widespread; at present it has more and more ceased to exist; indeed, the rocking of infants and small children is now frowned upon as inexpedient. Every reader who has made himself inwardly familiar with the expositions of our main text will know how to appreciate this "progress" as a weighty symptom on the way to the complete subjugation of life by the spirit with the help of unconsciously logocentric measures of education. — That, moreover, the extraordinary increase of locomotion-machines likewise speaks for a dwindling pathic capacity is self-evident. For ever more powerful equipment is needed if a dying-out drive is still to be granted satisfactions!

Compared with the state of being-moved-along, beingturned, being-rocked, the feelings of tension, of impulse, of exertion, and so forth, discussed above, present themselves fully as feelings of force, which are at the same time feelings of movement only because the self-movement that develops out of them bears, in relation to the impulse, the character of what has been brought about — on account of which, notwithstanding all activity, a kind of being-moved is invariably co-experienced even in self-movement, and can also without difficulty be noticed. With this we have at the same time found the key to the origin of a widely held opinion, which appears already in prehistoric thought and has been noted again and again by thinkers for two and a half millennia — the opinion that the primal cause of all movements is the soul, the body that which is set in motion by it; the former essentially self-active and engaged in unceasing self-movement (aeikineton), the latter of itself at rest, except insofar as it receives impulses to movement from the soul. Neither from the prehistoric perception of the immobility of the corpse, nor from the later reflection on the activity of spirit — which was, after all, [p. 1051] confused early enough by thinkers with the soul — nor finally from the attempts to determine the concept of matter (are not, for example, the Democritean atoms of themselves in motion!) does this opinion draw, for countless human beings, its still unweakened power of conviction, but from the two-facedness of the feelings that accompany the transition of an impulse into the movement of the limbs. For that which clearly separates out whenever, by self-movement, one sets a foreign body in motion — especially a non-living one, such as a ball — namely the acting impulse and the movement of the foreign body brought about by it, that same thing is found distinguishably coupled already in self-movement itself, insofar as, once again, though less sharply, because constantly crossed by new impulses, the movement stands out from the acting impulse as something relatively brought-about; wherein, therefore, the most original impetus for that opinion is presumably to be sought.

In fact a being that were able to experience only the release of the tension that precedes the course of movement as urge to movement, and nothing whatever of the coming-intomovement and being-moved of the limbs, would not experience movement at all — just as, conversely, of course, neither would a being to which the interplay of tension and release were denied. But the interpretation guided, beyond question, by the incomparably more intuitive process of the thrust against the movable foreign body, confuses, as it were, the beholding-and-acting soul with the stimulus-sensitive bodily soul, vegetative with merely animal aliveness, and genuine efficacy as such with mere dynamics, in that it fails to recognize the psychic content that distinguishes, ahead of the moving, precisely the being-moved, insofar as this is understood as occurring from within outward. But let us separate more sharply wherein that opinion is right and wherein it goes astray! If we take the body, as has constantly been done here, as embodied soul, then psychic occasioning grounds are unquestionably needed for any experience of movement whatever to take place, be it of being-moved, be it even of self-movement, and to that extent the belief in the moving power of the soul would be in the right. But because one — inspired by the will to self-assertion — did not see through the fact that the dynamics of movement speaks predominantly precisely of the nature of the body, and only its pathic character of the nature of the soul, one overburdened the soul with what belongs exclusively to the body, namely movement, and was consequently bound to miss entirely, in psychic happening, its character of cosmically conditioned [p. 1052] compulsion. Or, as briefly as possible: without psychic happening no movement of the body would take place; but it is only by virtue of corporeality that this happening assumes the form of movement.

With our now already less questionable formulation — that non-intuitable happening, which one calls the soul, passes over, by the means of urge and tension of living corporeality, into that intuitable happening which one calls movement — even the word "transposition" used above should have justified itself, because now, through the interposition of the impulse-capable body, one form of happening would continue into another form of happening, and movement itself would resemble a process of propagation, though not in the sense of physical nomenclature, and for the present only a process of propagation from the domain of the non-intuitable interior into the domain of the world of intuition.
