The body would thereby be the indispensable point of support of the original happening, and the occasion for the transformation of an acting pathic character into a brought-about pathic character, and the incentive to compare this "wonder" with the relation of compelled co-movement to compelled movement would find itself brought somewhat nearer to satisfaction. But, one might ask, though passive movement, and co-movement in particular, may well lack the tonus of doing, and indeed be accompanied by feelings of complete surrender, may one for that reason move it into such proximity to non-intuitable happening that it would become, quite properly, an appearance of it? Movedness as the appearance-form of happening. — To this question, too, we find the answer only by following the methodical rule of first of all isolating the object of investigation, notwithstanding that it might have the logical character of a property — that is, in our case, of considering movedness in movement strictly and exclusively by itself, or, what amounts to the same thing, of disregarding entirely its dynamics and thus, of course, its bodily bearer. If we do this, we find in it a continuity of change of state, of once more continuous augmentability, and perhaps of a still more particular kind; but not the moment that cannot be separated from any self-movement or any perceptible movement of another: the moment of change of place. The addition "of a particular kind" is probably superfluous, because it can be doubted whether, in differently constituted intensifications of state such as growing warmer, growing colder, growing damper, growing drier, growing thirstier, [p. 1053] growing hungrier, growing wearier, growing livelier, growing sadder, growing more cheerful, growing more anxious, growing bolder, growing more impatient, growing more dazed, growing lazier, and so on, an original continuity is ever co-experienced at all; since the tendency, which we have repeatedly exemplified, of grasping all of them, for the sake of easing understanding, as though they were movements, seems rather to speak for the fact that continuity is thereby first carried into any process whatsoever. Should there nonetheless lie, in movedness, besides the exemplary continuity of change of state, still a further specific peculiarity, this, as goes without saying, would admit of description no more than, say, the colour blue. But as regards change of place, nothing of it whatever can be contained in mere movedness, because movedness has absolutely nothing to do with the state of affairs "place"; but if not in movedness, then also not in the experience of movement, insofar as this, in order to take place, is fed from the pathic character of movement. We hope to convince even those of our readers to whom this might seem quite implausible, by pointing to three facts which, though repeatedly mentioned, have not yet been sharply placed in this light.

In the first place, it is from this, and from this alone, that the possibility of virtuality is explained, whether we think of Palägyi's virtual dynamics or of the virtuality, underlying it, of being-moved. How, for example, should there be, in reading, virtual movements of speech without the least movements of the lips; how the co-experience of dynamic movements at the sight of fighting animals, of pathic movements at the sight of drifting clouds or fluttering leaves; how, in general, the mere inwardness of being-moved, from whatever occasion, could exist at all, if that in which we have shown the nourishing source of all feelings of movement — movedness — were bound to the experience of the change of places!<sup>65</sup>

<sup>65</sup> On page 1053. — Here we see anew that, entirely without at least an embryonic phantasm of intuitive space, *virtual* movement would not become *actual* movement, and would then, even in Palágyi's sense, be unable to occasion any perception of movement! Only through the coupling of movement-virtuality with space-phantasms do experiences of place, experiences of position, experiences of direction, experiences of distance arise, and furthermore, above all, dynamic experiences of locomotion, and finally experiences of form (in such a way that in experiences of place and direction the space-phantasms depend on the movement-impulse, while in the experience of form the movement-impulses depend on the space-phantasm). Because, so to speak, the heart-point of all movement-feelings is formed by the state of a simply continuous being-moved, which is indifferent to the change of places, we understand why the experience of movement can break forth at all out of every depth of inwardness and, in turn, dive back down into it. Just as there really is a storm of thoughts or a storm of the soul, so too the movement-content of intuitive images of the sea's surf or of the autumn gale awakens only through *en-souling* [Einverseelung].

If we further look back once more at the state of dreaming, it is the lability of place in dream-space that forbids its traversal by means of self-movement and allows only movement-phasms to arise — which, incidentally, explains the grisly dream-spectre of fleeing and running away while nonetheless seeming to stick to the spot; and it is, by contrast, the pathic character of dreaming that permits the pathic pull of the feelings of movement to work itself out with a strength and purity that far exceeds the waking state, and thus makes possible a dream-experience that has no like in waking: the dream-experience [p. 1054] of flying. Whoever has dreamed vivid flying-dreams not all too rarely, even if only in youth, will confirm the following data. There is a dream-flying that, wholly or nearly free of relation to place and without the faintest tinge of activity, exertion, and self-movement, is thoroughly a gliding, swimming, and floating in the bearing element of the air, or an appearance-form of a moved weightlessness, by means of which the faintest wish and gesture of the dreamer is converted into the desired direction, curve, speed, rise, descent. But even where dream-flying — akin in essence still more closely to swimming — consists in the dreamer, for instance, plunging headlong down from the ridge of a roof as with a header, sweeping rushingly close above the ground, gliding up again beside a tower or a cliff, only to hover suddenly, say, in empty airspace, the basic feeling of effortless flying remains, to which the phasm of the change of places and images attaches itself only as though to attest it. Just as the experience of movement of the starting racer, who strives to reach a goal-point in the shortest span, is distinguished from the experience of movement of one who, lying on his back, lets himself be raised and lowered by a light swell of the sea, in that the latter exhibits almost nothing more of change of place, so the through-and-through pathic dream-flying movement is aimless, indeed wholly alien to any goal, and is not directed, even then, from one place to another place of dream-space, when the change of state moreover occasions a gliding-past of images.

Thirdly and finally, we need only call to mind dance — understood in the widest sense of rhythmic bodily movements that take place to the beat either of a melody or of mere noises — to recognize the essence of the deep pleasure in it, which among primitives grows into psychic intoxication, in the fact that the at times exceedingly variegated wealth of dynamic self-movements, thanks to a mighty being-seized, is more and more borne, and, in the case of perfection, wholly engulfed, by the once again goal-alien pathic character of being-moved, or, as it were, by a surge rolling through the soul. The more the dancer is graced to be absorbed in the dance, the more it is not a self-moving, not a change of places and traversal of distances, but the will-less, indeed almost impulse-less resonating-along within the element of a wave-beating movedness, that is now experienced and, in being experienced, at the same time "wrought and woven." In the rhythmically perfect dance there is consummated into an original experience of one's own [p. 1055] what, at the sight of fluttering leaves, drifting clouds, or the surf of the sea, is at first only co-experienced: the being-borne by the stream of happening — and this now to such a degree that it even *takes* the self-movement directed from one place to another up into itself, thereby revealing to us intuitively, on our own body, the dependence of dynamics too upon the "working and weaving" of the elements.<sup>66</sup>

<sup>66</sup> On page 1055. — An outstandingly fine attempt to illuminate, by way of the concept of happening, the "essence of the primal dance" is offered by the essay of the same title by *Rudolf Bode* in "Rhythmus und Körpererziehung" (Diederichs, Jena, 3rd ed.). The fact that Bode does not shy from the paradoxical turn of phrase that the center of gravity of original, and especially of Asian, dance lies not in the "*generation* of movements" but precisely in the most perfect possible "*suspension* of movement," is especially well suited to jolt awake *the* reader whose taste has been spoiled and whose understanding of the essence of original dance has been lost through our most recent European schools of art-dancing with their acrobatic leaping feats. What Bode *means* is exactly what we have set forth in the main text: the taking-back of movement into happening as such.

Since the watchword of the "stream of happening" has now, after all, already slipped from us, let the end be anticipated at once: in the experience of movement, whose essence is movedness, the experience of happening pairs with the experience of impulse, weaving itself into it; but in the experience of happening there are neutralized: image-receptive and stimulus-sensitive soul, experience and content of experience, movedness and self-movement, suffering and acting, passivity and activity. Stream-like we call an efficacious agency without activity, without dynamics, without beginning and ending, and the stream-like of this stamp is, between the actuality of happening and the actuality of movement, the connecting third term, with regard to which the actuality of movement resembles the actuality of happening in just the way that co-movement resembles movement. And so the stream we mean would be the time of actuality, with a view to the possibility of its appearing; and the ground of all real efficacy — now, passing through the body, first generating the image of movement, now, with the aid of intuitability, passing it on — would be *the excitation of similar rhythms*. — Let us now bring both sides of the state of affairs before our minds! Without the inflow of what is excited in the phase of happening, the place of the impulse and the place of the goal would remain unconnected, space would be threatened with disintegration by over-emphasis of the positions within it, and the world of appearance itself through loss of that continuity which is not affected by the change of the moments of impulse. The sense-impression would have ceased to be sense-excitation, and the utterance of excitation would resemble a calling into the void, because it could awaken co-excitation nowhere. The character of infinitude belonging to continuity would emerge overwhelmingly, and with it the insurmountability of every between for everything that is not happening; in consequence of which mere dynamics would find itself separated from something distant by only a thousandth of a millimetre by the literally immeasurable and never-to-be-traversed (as has indeed become frighteningly evident in the life-threatening spectre of forces in physics!).

[p. 1056] But the last sentence has already, imperceptibly indeed, yet none the less compellingly, shifted us over to the opposite side, in that, along with the indispensability of becoming-one for the realization of movement, it indicates the indispensability of estrangement as well. For if happening overcomes the immeasurability of the between, it is not because it "traverses" it, but because, in its actuality, the places and positions, with regard to which the continuous becomes for us a between, are one and all connected with one another — or rather are not there at all in the way they are from the standpoint of wakefulness, but are there unarticulated, unfathomable to discursive thinking and comparable only in a likeness to an uninterrupted exchange of rhythms between primally polar essences, which never began and never ends. Time as the soul of space, every distance a distance-of-thepast, nearness and distance themselves the two mutually complementing primal qualities: we should not know how to make it more convincing that movement does not take place in an actuality a few main features of whose physiognomy can only be attempted, and that but haltingly, to retrace with formulas as runic as these. For this it lacks the actuality of position, or, as the physicist would prefer to say, a frame of reference; but the actuality of position is no mere frame of reference, but a body.

Although there can indeed be happening without movement, but not movement without happening, primal image without appearance, but not appearance without primal images, yet happening does not suffice for there to be movement, nor primal image for there to be appearance; rather, for that, there must step apart: the duality, neutralized in happening, of activity and passivity; the duality, neutralized in the primal image, of place and space. The enabling ground of their separation is called: living body, and this is, within the domain of animalism, at the same time an epitome of conditions of impulse. From the determinateness of place of the mobile body there follows, for the bearer of life, the possibility of the appearing of images; from the mobile corporeality of its place, the possibility of the efficacy of resistances; from the interplay of both, the transformation of happening into appearing movement, or, explained in terms of inwardness, into that excitable wakefulness in relation to which original happening now for the first time comes to resemble dreamless deep sleep. Dependence of the world-images upon self-movedness. — Having shown [p. 1057] the connecting links by force of which an elementary similarity prevails between original happening and the appearance of movement, and having in particular determined, in the living body, the bearer of the assimilations of the two, we now characterize somewhat more precisely the significance that, on that account, belongs to the experience of movement within the total experience of animals as of man. Even if we were to disregard the fact that self-movement, as well as the impression of movement, fulfils, at the lowest stages, its there almost sole task of steering behaviour without the aid of a sensorium, their lead in originality over other appearances of change, such as change of brightness, change of warmth, change of scent, and so on, would nonetheless follow incontrovertibly from the fact that only movement brings the near bodily into connection with the nearer, the there with the here, and finally the distant with the near, and accordingly adds, to the separating power with which the space of intuition confronts the wakingly mobile individual essence, the means of overcoming it. As the extreme case of the spatialization of happening, and the exemplary form of its intuitability, movement forms the basis of every appearance of change, just as the mobility of the bearer of intuition forms the basis of every intuition of movement.

But that is not all: if animal excitability is in any case virtual mobility, then the experience of movement resounds through all forms of experience at the level of wakefulness; and it is no accident that it seems to us wholly fitting when we express the time-stressed noises and sounds with process-words, each of which occasions the co-flashing-up of an appearance of movement; when we speak of the "plunge" or "fall" of the temperature, or even of thoughts that have "driven" or "gone" through our heads; when we let the hours "trickle away," the days "hasten off," the years "flee," and paint time with similes of something restlessly moved — notwithstanding that no space could be found, nor thought, through which time might move itself as a body moves through the space known to us. For in this is expressed the fact that, without co-excited feelings of movement, no change would become intuitable — and then not even the rest that sets itself off from it in form!

Although we are not here concerned with the problem of the perceptibility of movement, which will come up again for discussion only in the next chapter, we mention, nonetheless, because it contributes to supporting the weight of significance of the feelings of movement, that, at least by all higher animals, as everyone knows, something in motion [p. 1058] is noticed a thousandfold, and answered, say, with flight, which, had it been at rest, would not have been noticed. It is not the scarecrow most similar to human appearance that has the most lasting effect, but the most mobile one, and, among the mobile ones, in turn the one whose movements occur with the least machine-like regularity. The same holds of man. A noise as such, under otherwise comparable circumstances, falls short in effect of one that seems to be approaching, or of one that is to us the expression of an actual movement, like the whistling of the wind, or of one in which we perceive, without reflection, a result of movement, as in the thud of an (unseen) apple falling beside us, or even in the delicate sound that, in autumn, the falling leaves produce on touching the ground.

Among the results of experimental research let it be noted here that the "threshold" of "movement-sensitivity" lies lower than the "space-threshold." For every area of skin of the human body there is, as is well known, a specific minimum distance that must not be undershot if it is still to be recognizable that not one spot is being touched, but two separated by a slight interval. If, instead, one moves a point within the same area of skin, then a distance of about a quarter of that length already suffices to produce the impression of a movement having taken place, and thus also of the distance it has traversed. Likewise, in indirect vision, the decrease in the graspability of small movements proceeds considerably more slowly than that of rigid lengths.<sup>67</sup>

<sup>67</sup> On page 1058. — Of the investigations relating to this, the earliest is at the same time one of the most important; for although some of its findings are still disputed today, there is hardly any doubt as to the correctness of the main point. It was *Exner* who, already in 1875, carried out the relevant experiments, which, incidentally, formed the basis for decades of all this researcher's further experiments. In his expositions ("Pflügers Archiv für die gesamte Physiologie," vol. XI) two points above all deserve our attention: first, that his chief motive was the endeavor to demonstrate by experiment that it is *not* an inference by which one arrives at the apprehension of movements; second, that he was thereby led, and misled, into the opinion that the perception of movement rests, in just the same way, on a special "sensation," such as, say, the perception of the color blue. From the former one sees (and today probably everyone with astonishment) how far the thinking of the nineteenth century, for all its cult of dynamics, was removed from any insight into the essence of movement, being led on a leash by a moreover misunderstood Eleaticism; from the latter, that a researcher to whom it was in the extreme repugnant to classify the impression of movement among the "sensations" could nonetheless hardly avoid doing so, because the knowledge of the *originariness of motility* lay entirely beyond the horizon of his age. No one today will any longer believe that one perceives movement as a result of the perceived change of places; and only a few stragglers will still believe that movement is "sensed." But who has known about the originariness of motility, that is, not merely verbally, but truly?! One must once call this to mind in order rightly to appreciate the pathbreaking significance of Palágyi's conception.

Whoever, with us, holds the life-form of animality to be characterized by the translatory self-mobility of the animal body will see manifested, in the demonstrated preponderance of receptivity for appearances of movement, the same inner necessity by virtue of which, at the initial stage of unicellular organisms, any stimulus whatsoever signifies an incitement to a change of posture by means of movement, and will find confirmed in it the expressive, indeed the unconsciously communicative, character by which we let ourselves be guided in order to press forward to the seat of the feelings of movement. Now that it has already been shown how far even the case, exemplarily given at that stage, of the transition of outer happening, through the medium of inner happening, into self-movement, may be regarded on the analogy of a capacity for co-movement, a supplementary addendum seems called for concerning the connection — mentioned, indeed, but not yet fully clarified — of the co-movedness [p. 1059] that lurks in every "fellow-feeling," with the dependence, peculiar to man alone, of the capacity for sensation upon the capacity for beholding.

The sense-impression is sense-excitation, and excitation can give occasion for self-movements precisely because it is at the same time movedness, indeed a surge, however often of an imperceptibly slight degree. Intuition as such, then, requires the virtual mobility of an impulse-capable body, and since it is intuition that first of all makes perceiving possible, the same holds of the process of perception. What becomes tangible to us here is co-movedness in the perceiving of appearances of movement; but here the road forks, both within man from case to case and, in particular, in principle, according as animal or man perceives. For out of every co-movedness of the animal there develops instantaneously a self-excitation in the service of the care of life, whereas in man now this, now the opposite of this, occurs. Whereas, for example, in the grazing deer, occasions of perception that do not glide by unnoticed excite either impulses to flee or impulses to seek, man is able to remain with the intuitive image of the object of perception and can fill himself with its content of meaning; and this takes place and makes possible an immersion into ever deeper strata of essence, in proportion to the degree of participation of original beholding in the process of intuition. Goethe called a thinking that is thus fertilized by appearance "intuitive judgement," and has left us, in the "Maxims in Prose," a sentence that every investigator of appearance would do well to choose as a motto: "All that we call inventing, discovering in the higher sense, is... a revelation kindled within, at the outer."

Just as even with so simple an example the "excitation of similar rhythms" stands out in the efficacy of images, so it forces upon us, even more with this example, the inner oppositeness of the gift of intuition and the capacity for sensation, of co-movedness and that dynamics which, notwithstanding the indispensability of its achievements, can appear, in relation to co-movedness, as a ground of weakening and a cause of disturbance, and which therefore, at the human stage, mostly moves into questionable proximity to a willing that is simply contrary to rhythm. We need no longer spell out, since everyone notices it readily for himself, why in so-called affective agitation self-movement does injury to co-movedness, dynamics to pathic character, and why, conversely, pathic character dissolves the reactive impulse to movement by means of that surrender — indeed that absorption — which, [p. 1060] under certain subsidiary conditions, empowers Goethean "revelations." For it, too, admittedly has a dynamic counterpart: on the psychic plane, the orgiasm of ecstasy, for which an example was given us in the wholly moved self-movement of one wholly pulsed through by the rhythmic surge of the dance; on the spiritual plane, creativity.

Yet even without weighing the degree of participation of the two poles of inwardness, we are informed and apprised, by the messengers of all life-processes, by the feelings, how far dynamics, how far pathic character is in play, in that, in lockstep with the growth of the former, the dimension of feeling of vehemence grows, with the growth of the latter, the dimension of feeling of depth; whereby, however, it should not be overlooked that "depth" could not be intensified at all, were it not the embodied soul, coupled with the drive-system, by which it had to be experienced. In the orgiasm of perfect ecstasis there are no longer any feelings, hence also no depth of them, finally not even any longer being-seized and movedness — with which, after all, dualities would still be interspersed within the unio mystica; hence, to the reflective among great ecstatics, the event thereafter not infrequently appeared in the light of rapture, namely also in relation to the body. In view of this the true word becomes intelligible: "Feelings are the wealth of men and the poverty of the gods." On the movement-content of forms. — We approach the close of our discussions of the experience of movement by once more assuring ourselves of the movement-content that, on this account, inheres in all intuitive images. If all being-seized passes through the medium of movedness, then in principle every datum of intuition can stimulate experiences of movement — and thus, then, so can form! Not only the strongly, over-emphatically temporal appearances of movements, processes, sounds, noises, but also the strongly, over-emphatically spatial forms of mountains, houses, implements, of images and ornaments, and finally the outlines of all solid bodies whatsoever, can be pathically beheld and, in proportion to the movedness of the bearer of soul, understood as symbols of happening; with which, then, the significance of the feelings of movement, and especially of the feelings of movedness, for the intuition and apprehension of the universe would be completely circumscribed.

But this does not mean that the pathic, or even the dynamic, generates shapes. [p. 1061] So far is it from doing so that, left to itself, it would rather dissolve everything shape-like. — The pattern of the experience of intensity, as was shown, is enhanceable strength of resistance; the pattern of the experience of continuity (thus, for instance, also of steadily increasing degrees of strength, or even of the continuity of intuitive space) is probably the continuity of being-inmotion. But even were we to hold this to be as certain as the former, it would by no means follow that continuity is already attended by shape, simply because we had first carried continuity, as a form of space, over out of motion-character.(1) Even if shape-like continuity — which doubtless expresses the continuity of virtual motion — should after all first arise through virtual motion-character, the ground of the genesis of the shape of movement would nonetheless lie not in motion-character but inescapably in intuitive space. Just as surely as intuitive space is the empirical now and the counter-pole to the temporality of happening, just as surely does its temporally opposed essence emerge most decisively with shape, and to the very highest degree with the visible shape that becomes intuitively given to us fundamentally in the moment of experience. There is, moreover, no need of any metaphysics of space and time; for who could seriously believe that the shape spatially present to the eye's momentary glance (!) is first made known to it through the memory-image left behind by the temporally unfolding — and, strictly speaking, never present — movement!

In short, shape — and above all the visible shape, in which we may confidently posit the pattern of all shape-character — stands furthest from process and motion-character, and precisely for that reason offers itself as an emblem to the faith in being and to the Ideas. And here we now point to the wholly undoubtable circumstance that, while the intuition of shape does indeed harbor pathic experiences of movement, it does so to an extraordinarily different degree from person to person. While one man, contemplating with absorbed attention the column, the tree, the ridge of a roof, the line of the horizon, or even ornament, perceives such strong co-motion that he even feels faint impulses toward — apparently imitative, but in truth shape-character-expressing — movements of his own, other observers can trace only with difficulty the co-motion that is likewise not wholly absent in them, because it is too weak. One would go wrong to see in this a sign that the one group stood nearer to the actuality of happening and the other to the semblance-actuality of being, in the way that, say, the contest between the experience of touch and the experience of sight actually underlies the worldview-opposition of materialism [p. 1062] and idealism; for the grounds of such difference, merely in the experiencing of shape, may lie on the surface, and by no means always coincide with the grounds of the opposition in the valuation of shape-character. But this the experience of shape does let us recognize: that in essential features it accommodates the tendency that would hollow shape out and, detached from it, turn it into a mere object. This very thing the geometric apprehension of figures now accomplishes, and has developed to the highest artfulness. Lines and figures form the object of geometry; lines and figures form the object of every Moorish ornament; but the distance between the content of geometry and the content of ornament is only a little less than the distance between the imageless world of being that belongs to spirit and the actuality-in-happening that belongs to images. And so it was no accident that the pathbreaker of ideologism forbade entry into his school to anyone who had not studied geometry, and, leaning on the admittedly deeper wisdom of the Pythagoreans, reinterpreted the world of bodies more and more, the longer the better, into a structure of — triangles. —

[p. 1063]

#### 63. Kapitel — Zum Problem der Bewegungswahrnehmbarkeit — Chapter 63 — On the Problem of the Perceivability of Movement

If we now renew the question with which we began, namely how *perc*eption of movement is possible, and confine ourselves here to visible movement, we shall ease our task if we send ahead, point by point and in flight, what — thanks to the elucidation of the feelings of movement — already lies before us in the way of valid propositions bearing on this problem as well. 1. — If intuitive images can appear as conceived in motion only because they have aroused virtual co-motions, then every appearance of movement is expression, and the question of its perceivability is a problem of expression, which we may formulate somewhat as follows: under what conditions does movement appear in an intuitive change of position? — Here we interpose: even though we cannot entirely avoid touching on physiological conditions such as the position of the eyes, the movement of the eyes, the movement of the retinal image, these are nonetheless not our object, but rather the psychological conditions and, so far as necessary, the metaphysical ones. 2. — If we confine ourselves for the present, without a side-glance at causes, within that range of speed of intuitive changes of position which is neither too fast nor too slow to be seen as movement of images, let it be stressed in the first place that, during perceiving, a perceived movement is never "relative" in speed, path-shape, and especially direction. The direction may suddenly reverse of its own accord, or be interchangeable through acts of will; in the moment of perception it is infallibly determined unambiguously. We see either that the moon hastens toward the cloud or that the cloud hastens toward the moon; but we never see merely a steady lessening of the distance between the two, leaving it uncertain whether it is the cloud that is moving or the moon. But the reversibility of merely visible movement meets the relativization desired for purposes of calculation [p. 1064], as it were, halfway! 3. — We have just adduced two appearances of movement, one of which falls under the movement-illusions mentioned earlier; for it matters to us to strip our assertion — that a being that were nothing but seeing would not perceive movement at all — of its dialectical husk, precisely by reference to the unambiguously visible direction of movement. For movement is seen only because the process of seeing — which by itself would not be capable of it — is always at the same time the experience of a touching and touchable body. Since the word "frame of reference" would, for obvious reasons, be out of place here, we call it the indicator, and understand by it the (however caused) supposed resting or being-in-motion of one's own body, against which all visible appearance is involuntarily measured and, accordingly, now seen at rest, now in motion. To this indicator belongs unconditionality, because it cannot be exchanged for any other in the world; and the visibility of a movement always consists in this, that either a visible intuitive image is posited as moving in relation to the experienced resting of the body, or as resting in relation to the experienced being-in-motion of the body (whether in fact one of the two is moving, or both, or neither, as for instance in the case of the apparent movement of a point of light fixated for a long time in the dark). A being that were nothing but seeing would thus not even perceive apparent movements, because it would have to do without the indicator. 4. — Before we ask how correction of illusion is possible by means of it, we draw attention to the fact that, merely through its existence, one's own living body forms, for the bearer of intuition, the center of a system of positions. — One has occasionally wondered at the following state of affairs, which calls for a brief preliminary consideration. If a bird flies past someone's resting eyes, the retinal image glides considerably faster than when he follows the bird's appearance with his gaze by turning his eye (in which case, however, jerky displacements likewise occur, because the movement of the eye always lags somewhat behind that of the visual image); by which one thought to explain why a perceptible movement seems to proceed more rapidly when the gaze is at rest than when it follows along. Now, eye-movements are experiences of movement that are now pathic, now dynamic, and are moreover accompanied by faint sensations, and are therefore certainly of significance for the apprehension of movement.<sup>68</sup> But since, in keeping with a sensualist manner of thinking [p. 1065], one held above all to the gliding retinal images, one asked oneself — and indeed had to ask oneself — why, when someone scans a bookshelf standing before him with his gaze by turning his eye, normally not the slightest impression of movement arises, when here too a displacement of the retinal images occurs, in that, say, a spot just fixated is seen only indirectly immediately afterward. We add at once, by way of reinforcement, that it makes not the slightest difference whether the turning of the gaze in question proceeds quickly or slowly, or whether it takes place through a turning of the eye or even of the head with the eye at rest. — The difficulty is at once resolved by pointing out that the position of the bookshelf in relation to the body of the one seeing is ascertained with a single glance and thereafter "stands fast." 5. — But if we now see the moon hastening toward the cloud, and in the next moment, voluntarily or involuntarily, the cloud hastening toward the moon, was it not, then, the first time the appearance of the cloud that was the indicator, and the second time the appearance of the moon? By no means. The indicator was, both times, our body; but the first time we had brought the appearance of the cloud into fixed connection with it, and thereby taken it up into the one and the same system of positions, and the second time the appearance of the moon — as a consequence of which the virtual co-motion of the soul took place there with the appearance of the moon, here with the appearance of the cloud. In accordance with the intuition of space, or, if one prefers, with the conditions of the intuition of space, our sensing and sensible corporeality has assigned to it not only the unconditioned and thus in every case conditioning Here, as opposed to the There, but also, for every empirical interval of time, the determining position with respect to a system of positions intuitively bound up with it; which is why the perception of movement, at the level of lived experience, is always grounded in a division between a position of the body felt at any given time with respect to intuitive space, and the virtual co-motions of the soul. — Thus far, roughly, extend the results of our investigation of the feelings of movement, and we therefore break off the preliminary consideration.

<sup>68</sup> On page 1064. — Of the numerous facts from which the significance of eye-movement for the apprehension of movement emerges, at least one may be named. If the muscle that effects the turning of one eye, say the right one, is paralyzed (M. rectus lateralis), then, with the left eye closed, the visual field turns to the right for the patient. If he reaches quickly for an object which he fixates only with the right eye, he reaches past it to the right. From such and similar data the co-dependence of visual perception of movement on the habitual magnitude of the impulse to the turning of the eyeball becomes clear.

*Before we proceed, a supplement to Point 1 is needed here.* — Although our whole work teaches, among other things, that all intuitive images are expression or, more correctly, appearance — namely of efficacious essences, meeting the capacity for near-beholding in a friendly or hostile manner, and moreover revealing, to the gift of far-beholding, their own nature — the now deeply rooted habit of thought might, in view of the special expressive significance of movement stressed here [p. 1066], nonetheless perhaps feel prompted to ask whether, then, movement forms an object of perceiving at all. Now, even the being-angry of the angry man is perceived, the being-cheerful of the cheerful man, the being-sad of the sad man, even though what is thus perceived cannot be pointed out in the same way as the lines, forms, and color-tones of the angry, cheerful, sad countenance; and neither this nor even so much as a movement or any other change would be perceived at all, were the intuitive image to consist of those timeless data out of which "sensualism" thought to compose it, in the way one puts together a mosaic picture out of colored little stones.

If, on the other hand, vital presence is intelligible only as the shape-character of a having-been and as a passingthrough-point of a happening, then there is no present intuitive image in which the fore-moments of beholding lived experience, and with them the life-past of the bearer of intuition (including that of his forebears), would not have a share; and each of them, be it an image of rest or an image of movement, is not some mere system of features but is at once and wholly a unity of meaning. Pointed-out data of intuition are indeed just as indispensable as intuitive space, which makes such presence possible; but they are present only as appearance-indices of happening, and form, for the bearer of experience, footholds for the perceiving of appearing essences; hence an anatomizing with the aid of the understanding is needed in order to bring them themselves to consciousness. In perceiving them, we cognize objects, just as the animal, in beholding them, cognizes bodies; we cognize, for instance, a faint ill-humor in the features of the man who is faintly illhumored; but we do not, originally, also perceive the timeless data in which, from case to case, the ill-humor becomes present.

Let someone who is not precisely an architect describe from memory the facade of the railway-station building he has seen a hundred times, and one will experience one's rude awakening at all he does not know, or reports quite wrongly; and let one ask him, if he is not precisely a student of expression, to state the features of a faint ill-humor, and it will become apparent that he knows of them not much more than — nothing. It was only the artificial hollowing-out of the world of appearance — through ideological aesthetics on the one hand, through mechanistic physics and technology on the other — that allowed the monstrous [p. 1067] opinion to arise and take hold that the intuitive image, and even more the object of perception, is an agglomeration of timeless data, and that thereby turned the state of affairs called meaning into that more-than-sphinx-like riddle which ideology and mechanics have for centuries labored in vain to resolve.

The appearance of rest and the appearance of movement would, in this respect, thus not differ in essence at all, and the latter would fundamentally be perceived no differently from the former. But this, now, was what we sought to show in the preceding chapter: that from the — in short — presentable appearance to that which appears by means of it, it is the appearance of movement, and only the appearance of movement, that throws the bridge, because it is the most immediate shape-character of happening; according to which, with respect to any intuitive image whatever and any object of perception whatever, experiences of meaning as well as thoughts of meaning would take place through the medium of virtual movements. — Were we to call all theories of perception that, with idealist or mechanistic intent, proceed from presentable data as the "given" (instead of from the unity of meaning) geometrical, then, by contrast, our own would deserve the name of a physiognomics of the universe, according to which every involuntary interpretation, also of all forms and shapes — beginning with the intuitive images of the most distant stars and extending to those of the human skull, or of the lines of the hand, or of the lobster's claws, or of the rib-lines of the oak leaf — would be grounded in inner movements. If, accordingly, the perception of being-in-motion were superior to the perception of resting in weight of meaning and, as it were, in content of primal image, then the perception of movement — whose conditions we are just now about to state — would fall to the role of the paradigm case of the perception of meaning as such. Or, to say it once more in other words: the apprehension, bound up with every perception, now of the outer, now of a merely inner movement-character of the object to be perceived, is the immediate condition for the perceiving of all those states of affairs that we call, in the narrower sense, psychic — and thus the immediate condition of the perception of meaning as such. From this it would follow, remarked in passing, that an attempt at a physiognomics in the narrower sense would have to begin with the interpretation of processes, and not, say, of shapes.

We too, as goes without saying, have had to abstract. For originally, never simply movements as such are perceived, but always at least *eit*her [p. 1068] pathic or dynamic movements, and, again, from case to case, always still more concrete forms of the one or the other. That, however, the mere fact of the perceivability of movement — and indeed of it alone (assuming, that is, that the supposition holds that the appearance of movement is the prototype of all appearances of process) — suffices to cut the ground from under the geometrical apprehension, is given its most monumental proof by Eleaticism (together with Platonism), in that, for the sake of carrying through the belief in the actuality of being and of an ever-present shape-character, it had to abolish movement and thus all happening. Of the geometrical apprehension, finally, the modern variant is the mechanistic, which, as was argued at length, likewise purchases its interpretation of movement at the price of de-actualizing movement. So much, then, on this.

Point 2 also still requires a supplement. Whenever we believe we perceive that our body is being moved, whether this is actually the case or not, there comes into play, more sharply than in the examples above, should any correction of illusion be needed, that body which we take, not only thanks to thousandfold experience but even on metaphysical grounds — which, however, may be passed over here — for something resting absolutely, and which we may therefore call the auxiliary indicator, namely the earth. If the standing train in which we are sitting seems to us to be pulling out, because the train on the neighboring track is pulling out in the opposite direction, then the steady change of position of our body relative to the intuitive image of the neighboring train has given the soul occasion to attach its virtual co-motion to the vehicle that belongs to the same system as the body. If the last passing carriage now frees our view of a pillar of the station, which, for easily apparent reasons, represents the earth for us, then instantly a kind of switching-over of the system of positions occurs, and the virtual co-motion necessarily attaches itself to the neighboring train. Control by touch for the sake of correcting illusion is spared us here, and in countless similar cases, by the unambiguous appearance of the auxiliary indicator (as, for instance, also when we sight the moon, apparently moving against the cloud, with the aid of a lightning-rod); but even the apparent movement could not have taken place without the system of positions whose center of relation is one's own body!

With this, the most important cause of the perception of rest despite virtual co-motion with lines and shapes would at the same time have been shown more sharply than above [p. 1069]. Remarked in passing: with respect to them too, in the moment of perception, the co-motion is never relative, and in by far the most cases can even be reversed only with some effort. A spiral may now seem to us to unfold from within outward, now to shrink together from without inward; but the opposition of the vertical to the horizontal, which governs the space of vision by itself alone, is found to be predominantly determined unambiguously, in that, for instance, the rock seen from above unfailingly plunges into the depth, the poplar unfailingly strains upward from below to its slender crown, and the piers that lose themselves in the pointed vault of a Gothic arch tear the beholder upward. Yet, regardless of the soul feeling itself driven by these forms to such powerful co-motions, they all belong, together with the body of the bearer of perception, to one and the same system of positions, according to which, from any given standpoint, the same lower-lying datum of intuition continually corresponds to every higher-lying one, the same datum lying further to the left to every one lying further to the right, the same nearer one to every more distant one — in short, not the least changes of position become visible, not to speak of the firm connectedness, at least of the examples of appearance chosen here, with the appearance of the earth. The utter rigidity of places and directions lends to the virtual co-motion that is awakened by shapes its character, at once emphatically incorporeal and emphatically inward. Here, however, a somewhat more precise characterization may be called for.

We spoke above of a division within experience present in every perception of movement. It occurs once again, in a different way, in every self-movement of the body, whether it proceeds actively or passively (as, say, when the arms of one person are moved by a second person). In both cases an opposition prevails between the self-movement and the intuitive system of positions of the surroundings, which is in principle always felt by touch and, in most cases, moreover also seen. And indeed, the virtual co-motion attaches itself, in the form of a co-resting, to the intuitive image, insofar as the self-movement stands out from it.

Let us take, say, the case of someone hurrying to the railway station: into his experience of moving-himself there unavoidably enter two components — the experience of bodily dynamics, and the experience of the unmovedness of that section of the surrounding world in relation to which his moving-himself takes place. In between, he may perceive numerous other movements (of people, carriages, birds, and so on) or else [p. 1070] pay them no further heed: he at least *liv*es through, and ordinarily also perceives, the unmovedness of the street, of the houses, and finally of all objects that stand in fixed connection with the earth; for which, for the sake of brevity, we may say: the unmovedness of the earth. But this is not the same as the perception of shapes; for whatever he may, even in hurrying past, still apprehend of, say, architectural forms, the high accent of his experience lies nonetheless on the unmovedness of the earth, in consequence of the virtual co-unmovedness of his far-beholding-capable soul in relation to the active self-movement of the body. In the dreamspecter of not-getting-anywhere (owing to the body's having become a mere phantasm of corporeality), the virtually present experience of the standing-still of the surrounding world reveals itself, so to speak, palpably, in that it penetrates into the phantasm of moving-oneself as a hindrance to movement.

In an essentially different respect, the same opposition reveals itself in passive co-being-in-motion on the occasion of the perception of resting forms. And indeed, in this case it consists not between the actual resting of one's own body and the virtual co-motion of the soul with an intuitive process, but between the unmovedness of the intuitive image and the virtual being-co-moved with the movement-content of the *forms* of this same intuitive image. Whereas the perception of merely outer movement normally shows only slight differences from person to person, great differences of receptivity naturally appear with respect to those movements which, in being expressed by resting forms, no longer bring merely a happening as such to appearance, but at once also its life-content. Now, in as much as the far-beholding-capable soul of the bearer of perception is, in this way, claimed for itself, so to speak, the inclination and the growing capacity for apprehending the life of forms can bring with it both an interiorization and also, however, a de-materialization, whereby the genuine language of forms would then volatilize into those merely subjective abstracta that have been worked over by "aesthetics" for a century and a half.<sup>69</sup>

<sup>69</sup> On page 1070. — In this connection the line of development leads roughly from *Herder* by way of *Lotze* to *Lipps*. At the beginning (Herder), with admittedly extremely uncertain formulation, constantly wavering between belief in actuality and subjectivism, stands the endeavor to find the world of forms, shapes, movements full of living content; at the end (Lipps) what remains of this is a *mechanics of feelings*, by which the world of shapes — now conceived as material — is credited with an illusory content. In this the science of art has gained little or nothing, but the science of the perceptual process has gained a good deal (especially in the field of geometrical-optical illusions). On this occasion let it once more be recalled that the specifically psychic content which the only-co-perceivable movedness of resting forms *demands* that we experience and find, the directly perceivable movement likewise *makes possible* our finding — provided, in both cases, sufficient participation of the process of beholding. Indeed, the very apprehension of the difference between pathic and dynamic movements was already a chief example of this!

There remains for us still the last, and for the problem of perception admittedly the most significant, question: namely what the conditions are for the co-motion to be related immediately, precisely, to *changes of position*. We see changes of position of the sun, of the moon, of the hour-hand, of the glacier's tongue, [p. 1071] of the tip of the growing blade of grass, but no movements of them; we see neither change of position nor movement of a point of light rotating fast enough, but instead a fiery circle; and finally we do not see at all the cannonball that cuts across our field of vision. How does it come about that changes of position appear as movement only within a relatively narrow range of speed, and what follows from this for the impression of movement? A thoroughgoing exposition would lead to numerous sub-questions and individual questions, whose treatment is neither planned nor required, where in the end it is only the contribution that the perceivability of movement, too, promises to furnish toward clarifying the essence of movement that attracts us. Only in this sense, then, does our extremely simplifying answer wish to be understood.

For some seventy years it has been known, at least in principle, that there exists a "spatial threshold" as well as a "threshold for intervals of time," different for different sense-zones, but for each of them a minimum spatial extent and a minimum span of time that can still be apprehended with the aid of a sense, say with the aid of the sense of sight; and for just as long, significant researchers have made considerations as to how the appearance of the world would change with an enlargement and with a diminution of what, if one may say so, the appearance-atoms of space and the appearance-atoms of time, or also of both together; considerations which, through far too great a simplification, frequently did violence to the states of affairs, but which nonetheless theoretically anticipated by half a century the extensions and condensations of time that the achievements of instructional films nowadays lay before us intuitively.

In truth, of course, there can be no talk of appearance-atoms of space and time, but there can certainly be talk of limits to the distinguishability of their parts; which is why a change of position is not yet seen as movement when the distance traversed per second of time falls short of a minimum length, or, to put it the other way about, when the time consumed per second of arc exceeds a maximum length; and is no longer seen as movement when the distance traversed per second of time exceeds a maximum length, or when the time consumed per second of arc falls short of a minimum length. The limits of distinguishability are now vitally conditioned, as follows from the single fact alone that they can be extended little or not at all through the activity of spirit (though, of course, indirectly through apparatus such as [p. 1072] magnifying glasses, "slow-motion" devices, and time-condensers). Both magnitudes, length of path and length of time, stand to each other in a relation of reciprocity, the scope of which becomes intuitively clear to us as follows.

Seen magnitudes are, as we know, always apparent magnitudes, because they become smaller with increasing distance — rapidly at first, more slowly later. Accordingly, we can eventually bring any visible movement of a body to vanish by enlarging the intervening space between us and it. The same railway train that hurtles past us at great speed when seen from a hundred meters away seems to us, as is well known, when seen from ten kilometers away — say, viewed from a mountain — to creep slowly along. This can be accounted for either in this way: the visible appearance of the distance covered per second has now shrunk enormously; or in this way: the time that is now needed to traverse the previously per-second-covered distance of visible appearance has grown enormously. There would then be two reciprocal changes in the intuitive capacity of the bearer of soul, by which the visible appearance of the earlier speed would be restored: with the power of distinguishing time-intervals remaining constant, an enlargement of the power of distinguishing distances; or, with the power of distinguishing distances remaining constant, a diminution of the power of distinguishing time-intervals. In the first case, our "spatial threshold" would have been lowered. We would no longer distinguish only minutes of arc (which, for the sense of sight, represents approximately the minimum length), but, say, seconds of arc. In the second case, our "threshold for time-intervals" would have been raised in the same proportion, and the spans of time that we could still just distinguish would be sixty times longer than before.

From this we can read off without further ado through which two changes in the bearer of intuition, at a fixed distance from the moving object, its visible speed would be increased, and through which two it would be diminished. It would be increased: a) through the diminishing of the path-lengths still just apprehensible, b) through the growing of the time-spans still just apprehensible; it would be diminished: a') through the growing of the path-lengths still just apprehensible, b') through the diminishing of the time-spans still just apprehensible. It was similar considerations — and indeed especially with respect to the "sense of time" (thus b and b') — that originally gave occasion to bring to bear a dependence of the appearance of movement (and thus, admittedly, of the entire world of appearance) upon the constitution [p. 1073] of the capacity of intuition. Partly because the works in question tend to be known only to specialists, and partly, and above all, because alongside truths belonging to the science of consciousness they harbor the beginnings of metaphysical errors, let it be permitted to reproduce their principal results here.

It was the significant biologist K. E. von Baer who, in his address delivered at St. Petersburg to the Congress of Entomologists in 1860, "Welche Auffassung der lebenden Natur ist die richtige?" [Which conception of living nature is the correct one?] (printed in: Reden, Part 1, 1864), advanced the hypothesis that for every being there exists a vital measure of time, which probably corresponds to the arterial pulse. Since he posits this, for man, at an average of 60 beats per second, he even believes he has ascertained a vital motive for the choice of the second [as a unit]. In any case, the power of distinguishing time-intervals is supposed to increase and decrease, according to some ratio or other, with the speed of the pulse-beats. We had to make mention of this, as goes without saying, untenable assumption only because otherwise the quotations would remain unintelligible, and we remark in advance that von Baer's decisive considerations are not affected by it at all. For what he in truth wants to derive are certain changes that the world-picture of the bearer of soul would undergo through the acceleration or retardation of its moments of perception.

"Let us imagine, then," he says, "that our pulse-beat went a thousand times as slowly as it actually goes, and that we needed a thousand times as much time for a sensory perception as we now need; correspondingly, our life would then run its course not, "at most, for 80 years," but for 80,000 years." "The course of a year would then make upon us an impression like that which 8¾ hours now make. In our latitudes, then, we would see, in the course of little more than 4 hours of our inner time, the snow dissolve into water, the ground thaw, grass and flowers shoot up, the trees put forth leaves, bear fruit, and lose their leaves again. We would really *se*e the growing, in that our eye would directly apprehend the enlargement; but some developments, such as, say, that of a mushroom, could scarcely be followed by us at all, and we would see the plant only once it stood there complete, just as we now see a shooting fountain-jet only once it has shot up." In the four hours of summer time, day and night would alternate uninterruptedly "like a bright minute with a dark half-minute," and [p. 1074] "the sun would, to our feeling, complete its whole arc across the sky in one minute and be invisible for half a minute." "Man could, in the course of one earthly year, make only 189 perceptions; for almost twice 24 hours would be needed for each sensation."

We have here, as one notices, the case b. The opposite case, too, that is b', is treated by our researcher, though not quite so exhaustively. — It is the merit of Sigwart to have detached the essential matter from its connection with the arterial pulse, and to have supplemented it by giving due weight also to changes of the "spatial sense"; his treatise "Über die Natur unsrer Vorstellungen von räumlichen und zeitlichen Größen" [On the Nature of our Representations of Spatial and Temporal Magnitudes], in the second volume of his Kleine Schriften (1884), is still worth reading today.

"Let us imagine," it says, among other things, "that our measure of time remained the same, while our capacity to perceive small spatial differences increased a hundredfold or a thousandfold... then at once much that now seems to us at rest and shows no trace of change would fall into distinct motion; we would see the grass grow, the leaves of a tree develop, the hands of a clock run their course in rapid progression; the changes that we now only infer would be present to our immediate perception." Here we have the case a. If, further, with spatial power of discrimination remaining the same, the speed of our "moments of consciousness" were so diminished that we could just still distinguish minutes (case b), then "the dance around us would rise to an ever more rapid tempo." "Sun and moon would rise and sink again in the sky like fireballs, the bright stars like rockets; and with magical speed the earth would clothe itself in spring with a green that would change color just as quickly." "But a great many of the movements now visible would vanish completely from our perception; we could no longer make out the movement of an animal's legs, any more than we can now follow the vibrating of a string; a long symphony would be a momentary roar, and we could understand a speech only if the syllables followed one another at intervals of minutes." If, on the other hand, with spatial power of discrimination remaining the same, our capacity to notice small spans of time were to grow, say, tenfold (case b'), then "the impression of the speed of movements would be diminished by just as much; living creatures would move with unbearable [p. 1075] slowness; much that we now see in motion would seem to stand still, like the hour-hand of a clock, because in a long series of moments of time we could observe no perceptible progress. In solemn procession, raindrops and hailstones would float down from the sky; the floods of a waterfall would sink deliberately downward, and would leave us time to count the drops it flings off. We would then be able to follow the vibrations of a string just as we now follow the to-and-fro swing of a clock's pendulum, and the whirring of an insect's wings would seem to occur more slowly than the rare beats with which a circling falcon holds itself hovering aloft. The recollection of what fills the span of an hour would comprise a much greater series of distinguishable moments, and to the same degree this span of time would have to seem longer to us."

Sigwart concludes his discussion with the sentence: "Thus our estimation of magnitudes of time, and with it every representation of the speed of movements and changes in the world, depends on the speed with which our consciousness passes from one moment to another." This holds true doubtlessly enough in itself, and yet leads astray, insofar as the dependence of appearance upon the capacity of intuition is meant to be one-sidedly emphasized — something at least not avoided by either researcher, and which happens nowadays quite completely on the part of those biologists who mistakenly hope to escape mechanistics through a subjectivi*zat*ion of actuality. Since the idea of the plurality of worlds, and everything connected with it, will be discussed at length in later chapters, we confine ourselves here to freeing what is correct in the above statements from what is incorrect in the tendency standing behind them.

First of all, it is immediately clear: all the transformations of the world of appearance painted here would take place, with the power of intuition unchanged, just as well, thanks to a corresponding transformation of — the actual world! For among them there is not one that we could not imagine, and among them, moreover, are very characteristic ones of which we today even occasionally become witnesses: one need only think of those motion pictures that show us the growth of a plant's root in the form of a highly agitated stretching, bending, swerving, and so on, or that, conversely, let us see the rider slowly floating over the crossing-barrier, his mount meanwhile displaying positions [p. 1076] we had never before perceived. (Only when one fantastically increases the figures and, for example, forces a million "moments of consciousness" together into the second does the world of appearance imaginable to us decompose, in that all tones and sounds would now have vanished and the colors would be altered in an unthinkable way.) The dependence, in other words, on which the main accent here rests — namely, the dependence of appearances on the constitution of the bearer of intuition — is rather a reversible function; and what we are in truth instructed about, with the aid of exaggerations, is that relation of polarity between appearance and soul, according to which every change on the one side is accompanied by some correspondingly answering change on the other.

Let this, however, be mentioned only in passing. Somewhat more important to us is the circumstance that neither researcher actually thinks in the manner of the science of appearance, but rather in the manner of the science of things; at the very least, they speak of objectively actual organisms, and thereby unavoidably, at the same time, of an objectively actual world. With this in view, however, one would have to recall that the power of intuition of microcosms is incomparably more determined by the image of the macrocosm than the image of the macrocosm is by the power of intuition of microcosms! Were it otherwise, we would most certainly have to expect to meet many animals endowed with fully developed powers of sight that did not see movements which we see, and just as many that saw movements which we do not see. Now, biology has indeed been able to demonstrate extraordinary differences in the capacity of the color sense, in the capacity for the intuition of shape, in the fineness of the power of distinguishing sense-data generally; but it has to this day, for instance, discovered no animal that reacted to a seen movement in a case where, for us, with the naked eye, complete rest would prevail. Why one may nonetheless say, indeed must say, that every animal species lives in its own world, will occupy us later. — Just as, in those days, for reasons of the spirit of the age, a strictly appearance-scientific investigation could hardly have been possible, so, within the framework of a thing-scientific investigation, still less possible was any attention to the consequences of the knowledge, meanwhile gained in addition, of the independence of motility. Let one picture to oneself the muscular system and the movement-life of a human being for whose power of intuition the trees in springtime would literally "burst into leaf," and one grasps it as if with one's hands that [p. 1077] there is no room, in the world of bodies, for such phantasies out of the world of visible appearances!

Far more important to us, however, than these remarks — to which one might object that both researchers resorted to fictions only in order to bring the indisputably existing significance of "moments of consciousness" for the apprehension of movement into sharp relief, by exaggerating their consequences — is the pointing-out of the, even if unconscious, guiding belief of both in a dependence of actuality-time upon metric time. To the more superficial view, admittedly, the opposite rather seems to take place, in that, for the purpose of explaining transformations in the picture of world-processes, precisely the so-called inner time, or more exactly the subjective distinguishing of time, is called upon. Yet the very idea of a distinguishing of time-intervals stands entirely on the ground of measuring thought. It is not out of transformations of the experience of time that the temporal appearance of the world changes here, but out of a change in the apprehension of temporal contents of experience. What underlies it is the second, thought of, as it were, as a container of the process; what is derived are changes of the appearance of movement, which arise from the fact that the function of the second is taken over by some arbitrary fraction, or some arbitrary multiple, of it. It is thus, in fact, a matter of an alteration of the subjective metric of time, and the consequences that would have to follow, if the process of perception were able to regulate itself accordingly, are developed with great acuity. But it is no accident that it is not also added that this is excluded; rather, there betrays itself in this a subjectivism, not to say individualism, which is inclined, indeed, not to separate the individual from the world, but certainly to separate it, together with its world, from all other individuals.

The somewhat lengthy setting-right was necessary so that a finding of high importance for the theory of consciousness might be preserved from metaphysical aberrations. All the more freely may we, on the short stretch of way that still lies before us, now make use of it as a lamp whose beam reaches at once into the vicinity of our goal. — If we imagine a fixed value assigned to those elements of space that, under certain conditions, are just still visible, whose magnitude, for the individual human being as likewise for every animal species, goes back to structural properties of the organ of sight, then it admits of no doubt that the magnitude of the time-elements just still [p. 1078] distinguishable depends on the length of the "waves" whose "turning-points" carry the moment of making-present. If we make the assumption, still uncertain today but not wholly improbable, that in the state of fully conscious wakefulness there occur (by means of the sense of sight) at most 16 moments of making-present per second (in man, accompanied by acts of spirit), then whatever, of an appearance of process — be it discontinuous succession, be it movement — had occurred in substantially shorter spans, and thus within the just-named interval of time, would be lost to intuition (as to apprehension). If, for example, two intuitive positions, separated by a distance of 3–5 cm, follow one another in about 1/8 of a second, then the visible appearance of succession corresponds to the actual succession; if they follow one another already in about 1/16 of a second, then the one position appears to move through the intervening space; but if in about 1/32 of a second, then there arises the visible appearance of a present figure formed by both positions.<sup>70</sup>

<sup>70</sup> On page 1078. — Among the exceedingly numerous experimental investigations that have appeared since the days of Exner on the problem of the perceptibility of movement, the "Experimental Studies on the Seeing of Movement" that Max *Wertheimer* published in 1912 in the 61st volume of the "Zeitschrift für Psychologie," pp. 161–265, stand out in importance. He works chiefly with brief expositions of two lines — some parallel, some inclined to each other at an acute angle — which are led past the observer at intervals of 1, 3, and 5 cm, and finds the optimal impression of movement at a time interval between the expositions of about 60σ (= 0.060 second), simultaneity (that is, instead of two lines, a single *figure*) at about 30σ, distinct succession at about 200σ. Among the rich individual findings of his work, particular interest is deserved by the finding that under certain non-optimal conditions the impression of movement indeed arises, but without the impression of a moving object. With this fact — however it may be interpreted in relation to its objective presuppositions — it is experimentally confirmed that, *from the standpoint of the science of appearance*, movement belongs among the "primal phenomena" and thus certainly cannot be composed out of "elements." At least the following further experimenters may be named: Aubert, O. Fischer, Zoth, Basler, Marbe, Schumann, Witasek, Hanselmann, Linke, Benussi (the latter especially as an investigator of tactile movement-phenomena), Korte, Hofmann, Wittmann, Hildebrand, L. Hartmann, Metzger, Higgison, Rubin. It is the task of the specialist to take note of the manifold results of these and other researchers and to appreciate the increase in our knowledge of the physiology of the sense organs and of the nervous system that we owe to them. To a final clarification of the basic question, however, they could not and cannot lead. For, first, by far the majority of investigations are guided not by biological but by neurophysiological points of view; second, none of the investigators takes as a basis that autonomy of motility which, through Palágyi's theory of virtual movement, must be regarded as established since 1916. Out of receptor life-processes *alone* — we repeat it — the intuition of movement cannot be understood.

It is, however, not on figures of this kind, still rather uncertain, but on this that it matters to us: that the perception of movements, and especially by means of the sense of sight, is determined just as much by the tempo of the moments of making-present, or, as has been said metaphorically, by the "pulse-frequency of lived experience," as it is by the changes of position of the appearance. In order that the continuity of inner happening — unintuitable between two turning-points — may take part, in the form of co-motion, in the essentially spatial displacement that meanwhile takes place, the speed of the displacement may neither lag considerably behind the speed of succession of the turning-points, nor outstrip it by a multiple.

In view of this, the conviction irresistibly forces itself upon us that movement is always expressed by an actual change of position, and indeed can be expressed only insofar as that change was able to fulfill the conditions for arousing virtual movements in the bearer of intuition. However much such ingenious elaborations — how, with an acceleration of the tempo of the moments of making-present, the drops of a waterfall would float down deliberately and countably, while, with an equally great deceleration, the sun would glide across the vault of heaven with visible haste — might seduce one into wholly erroneous opinions about the vital self-sufficiency of the bearer of intuition, they have at least this much to offer us: namely, to make clear to us, with the aid of exaggerations, [p. 1079] that, in movement occasioned by changes of position, there comes to spatially-intuitive expression a happening that is itself unintuitable, which indeed has in common with it the continuity of fleeting-away, but which must borrow its differences of speed from the world of matter and of body.

Finally, however — and this might perhaps be reckoned an even greater gain in knowledge — the pulsatory character of the happening in the life-bearer is thereby removed from the domain of contested opinion and brought to unshakeable certainty. Without it there would indeed be no capacity for intuition and no appearance at all; but without it there would above all be no appearance of movement, because within an unarticulated continuity of lived experience "moments" could no longer be told apart, and consequently there would be no before and after at all, and thus also not that by which every appearance of process, and the pattern of all of them, the appearance of movement, differs fundamentally from happening "in itself": the coming and going. This very fact is, so to speak, underscored by the circumstance that the appearance of movement (be it visual, auditory, or tactile) proves bound to a relatively narrow range in the speed of succession of that coming and going; in keeping with which research should sooner or later succeed in determining, at least approximately and exactly for the sensory domain of seeing, the duration of the moments of making-present and then also the duration of the intervening "waves" (with which the "counting of spiritual acts" — cf. Chapter 40 — would be most closely bound up). We spoke earlier of the shudder of transience and recognized in it the state of life that stands nearest neighbor to a fusion with happening; but even it occurs only insofar as the stillreverberating irresistibility of happening has begun to stand out from the equally inescapable here-and-now of the life-bearer, owing to the intermediately slowed movement of life. In the fused-togetherness of lived experience with happening, by contrast, neither an intuitive image nor even the irresistibility of all intuitive images would be "experience."

No less compelling, however, is now the final conclusion, which runs as follows: world-happening itself is pulsing world-happening, or: there is a rhythm of actuality, or finally: actuality-time pulses. Were happening itself not to pulse, it would not merely remain inconceivable but would be downright unthinkable how the [p. 1080] proper being, with which and through which actuality-time comes to appearance, could ever have arisen, indeed could exist at all! And so it is more than mere simile when poets and thinkers have at times compared the "course" of the great and small worlds to the surge of waves, where the smallest waves are borne by larger ones, the larger by still larger ones, and all of them by the greatest waves of a sea — for whose symbol language, with deep intuition, found the name of the "world-ocean." —<sup>71</sup>

<sup>71</sup> On page 1080. — In order to satisfy even the acuteness of hairsplitting, let the following objection be raised. We measure time by naming some *duration of a process*, which we assume to be always the same however often the process repeats itself, "unit of time." With the help of this unit we can then compare processes as to their speed and ascertain increasing and decreasing changes of speed. But what sense would it make to think of the course of time itself as occurring now faster, now slower? In this way time would evidently be treated like a process in time, and thereby a second time would be unreflectingly presupposed, of which the passage of that first time would have used up now more, now less. Only this second time would then be the true and "real" time, and with respect to it, in turn, unarticulated continuity would obtain.
