The answer is: if one translates the pulsing of actuality-time discussed in the main text into the language of pure conceptual capacity, what remains is a *rhythmic* change of qualities in non-intuitable world-happening. This must at least be assumed, if the rhythm in the life of all organisms is not to be artificially removed from the cosmos that makes it possible again and again, and the whole world of organisms falsely turned into a foreign body of the universe. Considered as a science of things, we may pause here; considered as a science of appearance, we need not be satisfied with so general a characterization. As was shown, there is a datum of experience that enables us to equate actuality-time with sheer fleeing, and there are further, richly varying data of experience according to which time now seems to us to linger, now to hasten (subjective feelings of time). Grasped by analogy with such data of the appearance of time, the rhythmic change of qualities of world-happening becomes a pulsing or rhythmic fleeing — and this, then, would be actuality-time, insofar as we thought of it as taking place in the form of appearance. By this, and by this alone, the metaphysical ground of the fact would moreover be made recognizable that only from complete surrender to a *rhythm* of happening does that experience of becoming-one with the happening flower, of which the most striking example for us was the orgiasm of the dance. Every wholly undisturbed course of organic life-processes would accordingly appear at the same time in the light of a harmonious interfering with the "world-pulse." Because, however, the organism is not *only* a microcosm but, in view of its corporeality, is also part of the universe, lasting undisturbedness of course remains a wishful image. Even the plant can be sensitively disturbed by its outer world and even brought to ruin, even if we leave aside the interventions of man (devastating storms and hailstorms, overlong droughts, drowning periods of rain, the sudden irruption of hostile hosts of creatures such as locusts or the nun moth, the overpowering growth of a parasite, etc.). Incomparably more manifold, however, are the disturbances within the affective and motor animal world, whose species must fight one another en masse (animal and prey-animal). Yet what follows from this in the way of *inner* disturbances is in principle compelled, is a reacting that does temporary violence to the organism's own rhythm, and is *not* a breaking of that own rhythm itself. Man, by contrast — equally exposed to all disturbances through outer fate — is subject in addition to the lasting disturbance caused by the presence of spirit within him, and that means: to the ceaseless being-disturbed from *within*; wherefore for him the rhythmic course forms the fortunate exception, which falls to his lot, when consciousness is paused, that is, in the state of sleep, indeed more often, but in the waking state only rarely. (Even in the state of sleep it very often does *not* fall to his lot. Man owes it to his spirituality that he is the only one of all beings who can suffer severely and at length from "sleeplessness," and who, even while asleep, again and again experiences disquiets of a scope far exceeding the animal's.) It does, however, fall to him with certainty in the state, repeatedly appreciated, of surrender, where the I is shattered or dissolves. That in the orgiasm of the dance (and in numerous cases of a similar kind) this comes about by means of beat is one of the deepest and most alluring problems of the science of the soul, concerning which something is to be found in our treatise on the essence of rhythm, cited in note 28. —

[p. 1081]

#### 64. Kapitel — Von der Pflanzenseele — Chapter 64 — On the Plant-Soul

Although man belongs, in natural-scientific terms, to animality, the transformation through which the soul of the original human being arose out of the animal soul reaches deep enough to justify distinguishing three principal life-forms among the beings of this planet: plant, animal, human. The origin of the original human soul and its essential difference from the animal soul has been set forth. Of the plant-soul it was said that it is essentially sleeping beholding and working, or, to a large extent, the presence of the distance of time and space within the locally fixed here of the living body. The plant thus seemed, in relation to the animal, to be even more soul-like than the latter, and to stand closer to the original human being, who, through the preponderance of the wakefulness of beholding over self-moving irritability, would again be woven into the cosmos more intimately than the animal — though not in the manner of the plant, but through dependence on distant appearance. This might suffice to characterize the three kinds of soul, were it not that it seems to be contradicted by some of the astonishing disclosures with which natural-scientific biology has, roughly since the days of Romanticism, enriched our knowledge of plant life-processes. Indeed, we hear even seasoned specialists speak of a sensitivity even surpassing that of animals, which reveals itself both in the response movements and in the spontaneous movements of the plant! If we therefore attempt to resolve these inconsistencies in broad strokes, we hope at the same time to draw profit from this in another respect, by now energetically taking the content of matter back into happening, and thereby reaching the point from which to gain a view into the essence of the elemental souls.

Natural scientists as well as philosophers have again and again emphasized that a sharp separation of plant and animal is impossible, because there is no distinguishing mark that does not suffer exceptions; [p. 1082] if one nonetheless wishes to draw boundaries, one must either content oneself with "weighing the marks" from case to case (Miehe), or form an opinion, from the courses of phylogenetic development, as to what the splitting of the world of organisms into plants and animals is really "aiming at" — in short, adapt the conceptual determination to the respectively most highly developed forms. If by "higher" forms one understands more richly articulated (= more differentiated) forms, which are of course usually also phylogenetically later, and if one keeps at bay every secondary thought of so-called natural purposes, then scarcely any objection could be raised against such a selection of species for the purpose of delimiting the great realms of nature; and in any case, on the ground of natural science, the problem of definition could not be solved otherwise than so. What accordingly generally counts as specifically plant-like, what as specifically animal-like, is in all likelihood known to most readers. The survey nonetheless offered below is meant only to make it easier to fall back upon one point or another. It should be expressly noted that of the — real or supposed — exceptions, never all but always only some, either especially important or especially conspicuous, are cited in catchword fashion.

1. The plant: The cells throughout surrounded by a firm membrane. — Exception: slime molds; swarm spores and spermatozoids of algae and fungi; spermatozoids of mosses and ferns. — The animal: The cells are for the most part naked.

2. The plant: The parts of the plant preserve, relative to the whole, a comparatively great independence. Consequences of this are the considerable capacity for regeneration and the ability, persisting even alongside sexual reproduction, for vegetative multiplication (budding, spore formation, cuttings; model case: mosses). — The animal: The individual cell has become less independent in relation to the cellular whole; "division of labor" and "centralization" have advanced; body cells and reproductive cells have throughout become separated; the capacity for regeneration is, relative to the plant, slight. — Exception: Stentor and other infusoria, polyps, worms.

3. The plant: [p. 1083] Growth in principle unlimited. Always young parts alongside old ones. — The animal: Growth with a finished final state. Aging affects the organism as a whole. Exception: the coral colony.

4. The plant: The growth surfaces predominantly developed outward: in the air the leaves, in the soil the roots. Surface area very large compared to the whole body. — The animal: The respiratory surfaces and the osmotically active surfaces such as the intestinal canal are throughout relocated into the interior of the body. Surface area predominantly small compared to the whole body.

5. The plant: Incorporates in general only liquid nutrients. Exception: slime molds and, insofar as they digest animals, the insectivorous plants. — The animal: Incorporates solid nutrients as well. In higher animals a special provision for their liquefaction, namely the stomach, which is thus a specifically animal organ.

6. The plant: Draws its nutrients from minerals. An important subcase of this: the decomposition of exothermic carbonic acid and the building-up of endothermic carbohydrates. Exception: fungi, which for that reason thrive in the dark; further, many bacteria; finally certain parasitically living phanerogams such as the wholly chlorophyll-free Lathraea and the almost chlorophyll-free Cuscuta ("devil's twine"), Orobanche ("strangler"), and some others. — The animal: Forms no chlorophyll and requires organic food, and is thus reliant on endothermic compounds.

7. The plant: Does not respond to stimuli with visible movements. Exception: among the insectivorous plants, especially the Venus flytrap (Dionaea), the admittedly only slow sundew (Drosera), also Aldrovanda; further the sensitive plant (Mimosa), which reacts vividly to jolt, shock, and wounding [p. 1084]; and similarly, though more weakly, some leguminous plants and oxalis species. — Naturally, of paratonic growth movements, all those only inferred do not belong here. — The animal: In principle responds to stimuli with movements, and predominantly by far with locomotion.

8. The plant: No translatory self-movement, but predominantly a fixed location — exceptions in the text. On the other hand, autonomous growth movements take place continually on the spot, of which however only a few are directly perceptible, e.g. in Desmodium gyrans ("telegraph plant") and Oxalis hedysaroides. — The animal: No fixed location, but translatory self-movement. — Exception: coral, moss animals, sea lilies. — With the progressive differentiation of the stimulus-sensitive movement dispositions (7 and 8), the formation of muscles and nerves takes place, which plants lack.

9. The plant: Main direction of effect lying between above and below. — The animal: Main direction of effect lying between front and back. — Exception: some radially built animals (such as starfish, brittle stars, etc.).

On point 8 a few additions are needed on the plant side. To begin with, translatory self-movement does indeed take place in many bacteria, in all flagellates, including the Volvocaceae, as well as in swarm spores and spermatozoids. Further, there is a lack of fixed locations together with passive mobility in all freely swimming aquatic species, of which may be cited: some conjugates, the peridineans, and numerous diatoms, which together with unequally ciliated green algae take part in the formation of plankton; also the brown algae, e.g. of the Sargasso Sea; finally, protoplasmic movement in various blue-green algae, slime molds, and diatoms brings with it amoeboid crawling of the whole structure. — To what extent genuine exceptions are hardly to be met with in all this will presently be considered.

If we survey the oppositions in order, there is indeed not one among them for which no exceptions occur; for even no. 4, which in any case is of rather slight importance scientifically, admits exceptions, in that, for example, the surface area of not a few cacti, Aizoaceae, and Euphorbiaceae [p. 1085] is exceedingly small in relation to the whole body. — Continuing from our guiding idea of the relative lack of self-moving sensitivity in plants (7 and 8), we now wish, however, to gather together, in colorful succession, several further individual occurrences, each of which seems rather to indicate the opposite of that idea.

Not, to be sure, with visible movements, but indeed with growth processes whose course can be made visible, the green plant responds, for example, to illumination, and not only aligns its tips and stems in the direction of the rays but also distinguishes the intensities of irradiation with extraordinary fineness. Thus "the stems of the Indian nasturtium... curve in spring, under weak illumination, out toward the window, but under the strong light intensity of summer, from the window into the room" (Molisch). If a plant is struck simultaneously by two sources of light, "it usually aligns itself exactly in the direction of the resultant of the two light intensities" (Molisch). Further, the so-called law of quantity of stimulus holds, according to which the magnitude of the effect is decided by the product of the strength of the stimulus and the duration of its presence. Finally, the circumstance that in certain cases either an exceedingly brief presence of the stimulus source or an astonishingly slight strength suffices to initiate growth processes seems to speak for the preponderant significance of intensities. Thus, for example, phototropism is already stimulated by the pale gleam of luminous bacteria, or an oat seedling is induced to turn afterward toward a flash of light that lasted no longer than 1/2000 of a second. The same holds for sensitivity to differences of moisture. The fruiting bodies of certain slime molds, which require dryness, turn toward an iron rod fastened beside them, because, owing to the accumulation of moisture on its surface, the air nearer to it is somewhat drier than the air farther away. Shoots of twining plants, as is well known, execute self-displacements that combine into cyclical movements, and answer the touch-stimulus of a pole suitable for support with growth processes directed the same way, which result in the enclosing of the supporting body. The sensitivity especially of tendrils is adapted to the purposeful unevenness of the resistance: it fails to occur when the tendril is struck by heavy rain, by a jet of water, or pressed by the smooth surfaces of heavy mercury; it occurs upon contact with an ever more or less rough cotton thread, even though [p. 1086] the contact pressure amounts to only the four-thousandth part of a milligram (Pfeffer)! Some researchers even believe they have identified specific sensory pits as organs of such high "sensitivity."

But even these already rather forceful examples could still be surpassed in manifold ways — if, for instance, we were to translate the growth processes, by "time-lapse," into visible movements (as everyone knows from film screenings), or let them express themselves, through magnifying devices on the growth-recorder, in curves of any desired amplitude, or were to draw upon the perceptibly locomotive plants such as Dionaea, Drosera, Mimosa, Desmodium, Biophytum, which were partly cited under 7 and 8, or were even to proceed from the already-mentioned bacteria, flagellates, swarm spores, spermatozoids, regarding which there can no longer be any doubt that they are endowed with an intensity-sensitive capacity for self-movement. But it is precisely here that the pointer seems to us to be set up from which we can read that our path was a wrong path. Are we actually speaking of the plant-like? All that is animal-like rests upon something plant-like within the animal itself, and is moreover directly or indirectly reliant on the plant-like as nourishment; but the plant-like, too, could partake of the animal-like within the plant itself, so that for some species it could no longer be decided whether they are more animals or more plants. This, however, would not affect the principles that have compelled us since ancient times, and still compel us, to distinguish the "flora" of a land from its "fauna"! Let us consider our examples more closely.

To be sure, there are mineral bacteria (e.g. the nitrogen bacteria in the soil), but by far the most decompose living or dead organic matter and moreover form no chlorophyll. The plant-like forms among the flagellates, in turn, resemble the saprophytic and animalic infusoria so closely in structure and mode of function that a strict division of the whole group is no longer possible at all. As for the swarm spores and spermatozoids, they too are indeed "flagellate animalcules," and are so no less because they are formed not only by unicellular algae and fungi but in part even by organisms possessing the character of rather highly developed plants (ferns, horsetails, even vestiges in the cycads). If the world of protists is, as already remarked earlier, a world of pre-forms in which the bifurcation into the plant-like and the animal-like is indeed intimated but not carried through, then [p. 1087] we cannot draw our distinguishing marks from it, though we may test marks already established elsewhere on its species as well, and thus have it in our power, for example, to place bacteria and swarm spores, thanks to their self-moving irritability, on the side of animality — from which it would follow, among other things, that widespread groups of beings such as algae, ferns, horsetails, etc. exhibit an alternation of phases of plant-like and animal-like life-forms (with a preponderance, all the same, of the vegetative). — Before we proceed further, however, we wish to reinforce the grounds for our guiding idea, and recall first that it is a primal idea of humanity, one that stems from immediate intuition.

If one asks anyone who has never occupied himself with zoology, botany, or even philosophy, to draw what he imagines under the word "plant," we get to see a line vertical in relation to the line of writing, meaning the trunk or stem, at its upper end obtuse-angled lines starting out and diverging, meaning branches or leaves, at the lower end similar but more wavily downward-spreading lines, meaning roots. But if we wish to obtain just such a schema of the animal, some persons may indeed think at once of domestic animals and attempt to suggest something four-legged; the more reflective, by contrast, hesitate, then ask, say, whether aquatic animals, land animals, or birds are meant, and declare themselves unable to comply with the request if one simply insists on the schema of the animal as such. For a pike looks almost incomparably different from a sheep, and the buzzard again quite different still, and into what further different forms again would one fall if one took, say, starfish or polyps or spiders as the model! The result of this little experiment is confirmed by the vegetal ornamentation of all times and peoples. Notwithstanding the unthinkable wealth of forms in the plant world, the unit of meaning "plant" is represented by a single schema, whereas for the unit of meaning "animal" the unlearned consciousness has at least three schemata at its disposal, and the zoologist an indeterminately large number.

What humanity has at all times imagined under a plant does not, to be sure, yet decide the actual state of affairs that science, say, connects with the name; but the two main marks of the notion in question, sessility and tree-like structure, are confirmed by at least three facts. First, fixed [p. 1088] treeforms, even where roots are still lacking, reach far back into the Paleozoic age (fossil horsetails, ferns, sigillarians, club mosses in the form of mighty trees, further conifers); second, the number of species of freely swimming plants is far exceeded by the species with a fixed location; third and above all, development in the succession of the earth's ages proceeds from water to land, thus from the rootless to the rooted, and clearly completes itself in the exceedingly species-rich group of the angiosperms (covered-seed plants). — And with this, an opposition of another kind crosses it in the same sense.

As already intimated earlier, the plant-covers of the continents, and among them especially the forests, represent, in the form of the beings composing them, the element of the liquid, and therefore stand in polar connection on the one hand with the earth-element, on the other with the air-element; whereby moisture is constantly drawn from the soil by the roots and constantly given to the atmosphere by the leaves. It has indeed been estimated that a single birch evaporates about 400 liters of water on hot days, a hectare of beech forest about 20,000 liters daily! Now if some dryness of the air is already required for "transpiration" to take place, this is fully the case as well during flowering for the purpose of fertilization, in that it falls to the wind and the insects to bring the wholly passive pollen grain to the stigma of the style, so that it may grow from there into the ovary and to the egg cell. In exact contrast to this, precisely the liquid element is required for the purpose of multiplication by all plants that produce self-moving spores: from the algae, the water of rivers or seas; from mosses and ferns, rain (of which the last survivals meet us in the cycads and in Ginkgo biloba, the Japanese temple tree, for whose only feebly motile spermatozoids the requisite droplet of liquid is formed within the pollen tube itself). Such a language of facts is hardly to be misunderstood! On the one side: forms articulated into root, stem, and leaf (cormophytes), an unexchangeable location, germ cells without self-movement, kinship with wind; on the other: unarticulated forms without roots and in part without distinct leaves (thallophytes), a location now immobile, now mobile, animal-like self-movement of either all, or at least of the male germ cells, kinship with water. The developmental line that ends in the earth-rooted tree meets with the developmental line that aims at the loss of every participation [p. 1089] in translatory mobility. We may not only, we must, see in the "site-bound" tree the appearance of the plant nearest to its primal image, and can then never hope to gain an understanding of the essence of the plant from its participation in translatory mobility. That would not be much different from someone letting upright gait drop as the distinguishing mark of the human being, because the small child, like the land-dwelling mammals, is accustomed to crawl on all fours! But how does it now stand with movements on the spot? Here a preliminary remark cannot be avoided.

It is, from the standpoint of the science of appearance, an unparalleled falsification of the state of affairs when, in a time-condensing motion picture, the tobacco plant shoots hastily upward, roots glide apart snake-like, unsupported circling shoots of climbing plants set about wrestling with one another, and the like, or when one equates growth processes with visible movements because, by means of magnifying leverage, one is able to transfer even the most delicate course of events into curves of any desired size; and let it not be overlooked that it is again the confusion of the actual with the visible appearance of actuality that first of all permits such illusions! Underlying both the compression and the stretching of time is, as we know, the detachment of metric time from actuality-time. Since units of measure possess no content of their own, it is open to us to think compressed into a second what actually plays out over hours, or to take up in thought into it only a fraction of what actually happens in the second, and precisely this can be made visible within certain limits. One will, however, only then learn a good many useful things from it if one resists the temptation to exchange the processes emancipated, in the image, from their basis, for corporeal processes!

What projects, so to speak, into all the counting and measuring sciences from actuality are the "constants," which are never relative but always absolute. Even to mere magnification, therefore, the scientist of appearance will attend with some caution. Were we to imagine, for example — freely after Gulliver's Travels — the fly swollen, with its geometric similarity preserved, to the size of the elephant, it would be all over with the glory of the fly, because, according to the laws of mechanics already familiar to Galileo, this creature would at once break into pieces. But the enlargement and diminution of visible intuitive images is [p. 1090] something everyday to us, thanks to the changing distance of bodies, and in any case changes nothing in the proportions; acceleration and deceleration of the visible appearance of processes alone, however, as well as magnification of the visible appearance only of their amplitude of deflection, without a corresponding change of their bodily appearance, means a distortion of actuality and requires a rethinking of a quite peculiar kind if it is to instruct us and not deceive us. The movements of the previously invisible infusoria, visible under the microscope, correspond exactly to the real movements of the animals, because the bearers of movement were magnified, and remain true in that respect; the deflections of the lever (or the deflections of a mirrored beam), on the other hand, which a millionfoldmagnifying growth-recorder presents to us, report with fearsome precision every fluctuation in the course of vegetative life-processes, but have, incidentally, no more similarity to these than, say, the bell tones by which such fluctuations could in principle likewise be indicated by electrical means. Strictly speaking, the scientist of appearance may directly admit only those movements that are themselves seen under the most favorable conditions and, if necessary, with the armed eye, not equally those only inferred from displacements or traces of movement or other movements. If he nonetheless takes the often unavoidable detour, he will redouble his vigilance so as not to stray onto one of the side paths that lead, here and there, right and left, into the realm of — mechanics and units of calculation! We speak first of movements that are not, properly speaking, growth movements.

One distinguishes self-originated (autonomous) movements and stimulus movements (paratonic), and among the latter again those dependent on the direction of the stimulus, which are called tropisms, and those without relation to the direction of the stimulus, which are called nasties. Unfortunately things have gone with words like<sup>72</sup> tropisms and nasties much as they did in the science of the soul with the name association: one has, after prolonged use, confused designations that may possess a certain value for classification with explanations. But when one later took pains to find explanations, one found oneself pressed, by the concept of the stimulus — originally tailored to the animal form of life — in a direction whose goal, at first unknown, subsequently deliberately pursued, is the interpretation of more or less all growth phenomena by analogy with effects of contact. Now a mistaken prejudice need by no means hinder the [p. 1091] researcher from making discoveries; and so, too, the attempt to understand growth processes from reactions to stimuli has contributed to the increase of knowledge. But in principle it means a dead end, as may be shown by a single example.

<sup>72</sup> On page 1090. — It would be strange were we to cite here specialist literature which the specialist in any case knows a hundred times better and more comprehensively! To non-specialists in botany, on the other hand (to whom the author too belongs), two excellent little volumes of the series "Aus Natur und Geisteswelt" may be recommended for orientation on questions of plant physiology and related matters: H. *Molisch*, Pflanzenphysiologie, and H. *Miehe*, Allgemeine Biologie. Whoever wishes to be more precisely instructed, however, we refer to the wholly outstanding "Lehrbuch der Botanik für Hochschulen," founded by *Straßburger*, *Noll*, *Schenck*, and *Schimper* (Jena, Fischer), whose 14th edition, with contributions by *Vitting*, *Jost*, *Schenck*, *and Karsten*, was the author's most important aid.

The embryo of every seed grain is polarized toward root and shoot. The root grows downward, the shoot upward. One now speaks of a gravitational stimulus that acts positively on the growth direction of the root, negatively on that of the stem; and Darwin already believed he had observed that the positive stimulus attacks only at the extreme tip of the root and is conducted from there to its more highly situated growth zone. Under the impetus proceeding from the concept of the stimulus, later researchers (Haberlandt and Němec) then identified, in the cell tissue of the root cap, comparatively easily mobile starch grains and assigned to them the significance of animal statoliths. If, then, the root is brought, say, into a horizontal position, the starch grains "fall" to the side and thereby exert a pressure on plasma sites unaccustomed to anything of the kind. From this pressure, felt — one is tempted to say — uncomfortably (and it *is* said), the self-regulation is supposed to result, which ends with a renewed curving of the tip downward and continued growth in the natural direction. We leave aside what was advanced *for* this view and what against it; for only through observations and experiments can the possibly important role of "statolith starch" be decided! It is, by contrast, fundamentally wrong to wish to ground the earthward tendency of root growth on any irritabilities whatsoever.

Even if we regard it as of little account that roots behave quite differently according to the task allotted them in the service of the plant's life, and, for example, penetrate the soil now straight, now obliquely, occasionally even grow on horizontally beneath it, yet at once change their direction in the sense of earthward tendency if they should happen upon an open slope; that they further sometimes exchange their earthward tendency for a light-ward one (the respiratory roots of certain mangrove plants); that they, again, strive downward even in the absence of starch (the "roots" of certain fungi) — great confusion would in any case result, if earthward tendency depended on localized pressure stimuli. If we sow a sackful of grain, then, according to the calculus of probability, as many of them lie with the root pole upward as downward. [p. 1092] Whether we now assume that the radicle already breaking out of the seed coat contains those starch grains, or assume on the contrary that it does not yet contain any, it would not be foreseeable how, with the root end pointing upward, it should nevertheless grow downward, because in the second case the pressure stimulus would be lacking, in the first the inverse pressure stimulus would lack the character of a disturbance (which it would after all only have thanks to its deviation from normal pressure!). But even if we make the scarcely very probable assumption that the "geotropic" capacity for orientation of the root is somehow bound to the existence of "statolith starch," it would be no less wrong on that account to interpret the connection according to the schema stimulus → reaction. For in the first place the pressure in question is certainly not "felt," and in the second place it is in no way to be comprehended how it could occasion earthward tendency in a wholly non-intuiting being, were this not already prescribed in some other way! Of that presently.

For the plant's tendency toward light too, Haberlandt and his followers believed they had found eye-like provisions in the epidermal cells of the leaves, each of which was supposed to collect sunlight at a focal point. From such conceptions it is of course only a few steps to crediting the plant with a capacity for intuition, a faculty of perception, world-consciousness, and finally a power of judgment that assesses what is purposeful and gives occasion for well-considered actions. All spiritualizations, however, notoriously form only the reverse side of the mechanistic; it is no accident that it was precisely a Fechner, who presented us with fanciful dreams about the soul-life of the plant, who incidentally also invented — "psychophysics"! Meanwhile, what occupies us here is not this or that exaggeration but that widespread mode of thought of science in which we recognize an effect of English sensualism reaching even into the doctrine of plants. A more recent author, who caused a stir through outstanding experiments, claims already to have discovered the heart, the blood vessels, the nerves of the plant;<sup>73</sup> but even those researchers who do not yet believe in a "reflex arc" of the plant let themselves be governed by the corresponding scheme of conception: the "stimulus," acting after the manner of contact, is "felt" by the plant, if not indeed perceived, and answered with a curving movement, however usually only a slow one. Curiously, the same researchers have found that the light stimulus — as also, in touch-sensitive plants, the touch stimulus — produces inhibition of growth on the illuminated side, [p. 1093] increase of growth on the shaded side, and consequently, quite naturally, the light-ward curving; a course of events that has exceedingly little resemblance to the reflex arc! We turn once more to the "gravitational stimulus."

<sup>73</sup> On page 1092. — We mean the J. C. *Bose* who has recently become almost popular, who has set down his findings in generally intelligible form in a work with the sensational title "Die Pflanzenschrift und ihre Offenbarungen." By "writing" are meant the curves which Bose's ingeniously improved auxanographs (= growth-recorders) trace from the most delicate inner processes of plants. By means of these curves several important findings have been achieved, of which the following may be mentioned: irritations of all plant organs produce an electrical potential-gradient; excitability sinks through frequent repetition of stimulus (analogous to animal fatigue), through shading, cooling, and narcotics; the likewise general (though for the naked eye usually invisible) proper movement of the leaves is diminished by dryness, anesthetics, alkaloids, poisonous acids, whereby phenomena analogous to cardiac poisons appear; *the* *growth* processes *run rhythmically* (Bose's biologically most significant finding!) and can again be raised or lowered by irritations, now the one, now the other (the former, for instance, by weak, the latter by strong radio waves); the internal pressure, too, is subject to pulsatory change; the uptake of carbonic acid is slowed by electrical stimuli, accelerated by microdoses of chemicals. The experimental results are certainly valuable, even if not all so new and of such import as the daily press seeks to present them; but the interpretations given by the experimenter leave something to be desired. Bose's manner of thinking is thoroughly unbiological. He pays homage to that variety of mechanism which can be turned into spiritualism at will. — Popular examples of spiritual mechanism are plentiful in plant physiology. We name, for instance: A. *Wagner*, Die Vernunft der Pflanze (Reißner, Dresden). Here the consciousness of present-day man is wholesale burdened upon the plant. Maeterlinck too, as we hear, is said to have expressed himself similarly. Decidedly superior to this literature of epigones remains *Fechner* with his book "Nanna oder über das Seelenleben der Pflanzen."

There is, in the whole animal world, no sensation of position, of equilibrium, and of disturbance of equilibrium, and again no sensations of weight, sensations of movement, or sensations, for example, of vertigo. Until the year 1824 no one knew that injury to the semicircular canals disturbs the experiences of position and can severely impair orientation regarding bodily posture, and it took another half century before the significance of the whole vestibular apparatus, including the otoliths, for the feelings of movement and position could be clarified to some extent. The research directed at this is far from concluded even today.<sup>74</sup> But, however much we have in the meantime learned and come to know through it, we still cannot succeed, even now, in discovering sensations of the semicircular canals (e.g. in rotational vertigo) or even sensations of otolith displacement (say, when rapidly ascending in an elevator); and even the objection of some specialists can and will not help us further here. For here, with the name of the fundamentally localized and consciousness-capable sensation, life-processes are being designated which, only in conjunction with consciousness-capable life-processes, furnish data that are by no means sensible but are indeed intuitable, and which are important and in part indispensable for our conception of bodily posture.

<sup>74</sup> On page 1093. — Deaf-mutes in whom, at the same time, pathological changes of the vestibular apparatus are present never become dizzy through rotation about their own axis, however rapid; the orientation of *their* experiences of position and movement in space has thus developed, without the auxiliary data of the otoliths, etc., solely by means of tactile and visual impressions. In return, however, they lose the apprehension of position when diving in water, where the requisite visual impressions are lacking. — A shark deprived of its otoliths loses orientation completely and may even stand on its head. A crayfish has at its head a pouch open to the outside, in which nerve-endings are found above and grains of sand, serving as otoliths, below. If it comes to lie on its back, the grains of sand fall onto the nerve-endings, from which the signal to right itself then proceeds. Much discussed is an illuminating experiment by *Kreidl*: instead of sand he put iron filings into the otolith-receptacle and brought a magnet close to the animal's head, with the result that the crayfish turned away from it every time. — From such observations it emerges that the spatial intuition of fishes, amphibians, and other swimming water-animals depends to a far higher degree on those inner data than does, say, that of man, and thus falls considerably short of the latter in intuitive content.

Since the translatorily self-moving animal constantly changes its position and continually compensates disturbances of equilibrium through counter-movements, it is still somewhat understandable that one could confuse the inner-bodily life-processes by which it is thereby supported with sensations of position. With the transfer of the same manner of consideration, however, to beings that are stimulated by possibly somehow analogous inner processes *at all* not to locomotion but to growth processes, the consequence of which consists partly in displacements, partly in changes of form, one betakes oneself onto the ground of that hybrid thinking in whose hopeless mongrel concepts life-scientific and mechanistic motives have become indissolubly knotted together. It is indeed henceforth a matter of taste whether one uses the animalization of everything vegetative thereby set in motion in order to burden the plant with the life-wakefulness of the animal stage, and thus to make it into a [p. 1094] lifelong, mercilessly chained animal, or whether, conversely, one traces plant-like as well as animal-like life-processes back in the end to the play of thrust and counter-thrust! — As we now bend<sup>75</sup> over into the consideration proper to the science of appearance, we henceforth have in view only intuitable data, and not the — physically, but also only physically, highly interesting — apparatus by which they come about in the spirit of physical thinking.

<sup>75</sup> On page 1094. — Thus it is, for instance, something quite ordinary that, in order to be able to compare irritations and reflexes with mechanical processes, one makes use of some such account as this: the irritation effects a "release" of the energy embodied in the plasm, *similarly* as energies in gunpowder or dynamite might be "released" by an electric spark. Now when it is by no means so rare an occurrence that scholars who pay homage to this either meaningless or fundamentally erroneous mode of viewing things speak, alongside it, of the "ego-tone of the cell" or something similar, this again shows, to one's astonishment, how splendidly mechanistic and spiritual conceptions get along with one another!

With words like gravitation, light, magnetism, electricity we designate, in the language of physics, what in the language of metaphysics would have to be named with "forms of distant presence in the here and now." A being above all opened to these bearers of effect and shaping itself by means of them would accordingly be a being condensed out of sleeping beholding and working, in whose compelled "actions" as well as "reactions" an immediate intercourse with the cosmos would become intuitable. If we remain for the moment with gravitation, we see the rooted tree, which shall henceforth count for us as the model of the plant, incorporated into the "field of gravity" — something entirely different from the capacity, possessed more or less by all animals, to bring their changing positions into the vitally necessary accord with gravitation. For the growth axis of the tree coincides, if not exactly, then nearly, with the local radius of the earth, whereas the axis of the animal cannot objectively be determined at all, because it runs from front to back. Conversely, there is for the tree no back and front, no left and right. One would have to have gone blind, over the measuring of thousandths of a millimeter, to the world of intuition, to wish to overlook such essential differences or count them as nothing.

To be sure, in the realm of sponges, polyps, medusae, corals, and in part still the echinoderms, we meet forms now fungus-shaped or tree-like branching, now radially radiating outward; but just as one does not choose precisely algae or myxomycetes for the purpose of elucidating the essence of the plant, so too one does not choose plant-like coelenterates for the purpose of elucidating the essence of animality; rather one will take as a basis at least the articulate animals, but above all the vertebrates. Meanwhile the infusoria already attest not only to the originality of the front-back axis of the animal but at once also to its independence in relation to the space of gravity. The infusorian can move in all directions of space and thereby lend, alternately, to above and below the role of front, [p. 1095] and likewise fish, likewise birds, likewise insects. It is true that a preferred position, and in particular that of rest, can usually be indicated. Thus the front of the sea urchin is always the below, its back always the above, and thus the preferred position of the longitudinal axis falls, for by far most vertebrates, roughly into a plane parallel to the water's surface; but they can turn themselves out of it, and every direction within it stands open to each of them. With this we have brought to consciousness a side of the state of affairs of translatory mobility that is, to be sure, little regarded: the comparative freedom of the body axis of self-moving beings from the direction-giving powers of the earth, and we may at the same time have been taught that for the beings of at least this planet, sessility for the most part goes together with a vertical body axis.

As little as the by now almost worn-out words "objective" and "subjective" ever hit the core of the matter, we wish nonetheless to make them our own for a moment, in order to state, with the utmost brevity, the most important features of the opposition just developed. The axis of the plant is an "objective" axis, that of the animal a "subjective" axis; the former designates, from place to place, the cosmic direction from nadir to zenith, the latter has no generally statable relation to cosmic directions; all other directions, positions, situations of the plant and its members must be construed according to their relation to the "objective" axis, that is, to the vertically upright direction of the trunk's growth, all positions and situations of the animal according to their relation to the "subjective" longitudinal axis; from the coincidence of the plant axis with the direction of the effect of gravity follows a highly heightened receptivity to position of the living plant cell, but from the existence of a vegetative substratum in the animal too, a capacity for discrimination, progressing by degrees, of changes of axial position (regardless of what particular reporting provisions were formed for this, and are drawn upon).

Continuing from the last-named difference, we can present the state of affairs conversely as follows: the protoplasm is, among other things, receptive to gravity, and this receptivity to gravity determines the growth axis of the, for that reason, highly position-dependent plant, but forms in the animal, by contrast, the standing ground for the construction of intuitive space through the two mutually complementary senses of touch and sight. Accordingly, receptivity to gravity would be a side of sleeping beholding, which takes part in the awakening of the soul only in connection with sensory processes, [p. 1096] but never and nowhere itself a sensation or anything even remotely akin to sensation. This results, incidentally, more simply as follows.

The essential thing, both of sensing and of beholding, in the sensory process, is the alienation of the content to be sensed and beheld, whereby first an again-corporeal environment stands out from one's own body, and then, on one's own body itself, its outer and inner places delimit themselves against one another. But now gravity permeates every individual body wholly and entirely; and were we to break it down (with physics) into atoms, gravity would permeate even the atoms. A bearer of effect whose "laws" depend exclusively on distance, as though it coincided with space itself, can, however, obviously never give occasion for the local separation of two impenetrabilities. (The differences of density in matter, too, measured by "specific weights," require, as is understood, the process of sensation as their counterpart.) Seen thus, we at once understand a datum of appearance that alone would suffice to uproot the fantasies of the stimulus. Naturally, the receiving organs of animals for genuine stimuli lie on the outer surface of the body; but it is then equally natural that specific reporting provisions for changes of position lie *never* on the surface of the body but in the interior of the body. On the surface they would indeed have nothing to seek, because "gravity stimuli" or "position stimuli" or "displacement stimuli" simply do not exist. The "statolith starch," too, if a role in reporting position really did belong to it, makes no exception to this.

In order for the classical equation of mass attraction to hold rightly, physics was compelled — and not, as is sometimes believed, only recently, but for about a century and a half — to set "inert mass" and "heavy mass" equal to one another. Although such concepts as inert and heavy mass, as late products of abstraction of objective and formalistic thinking, have no place in the doctrine of life, we shall scarcely search in vain for the features of actuality from which calculating thought had to strain them off for the purpose of forming them. As we found, in the experience of contact, a resisting something, and thus, without question, the state of affairs corresponding to the concept of inertia, so it would now be a receptivity of sleeping beholding by virtue of which the inert appears at the same time as gravitating. What the differentiating sensation [p. 1097] could comparatively isolate is thus, for the sleeping stage of life, something connected with, and connecting to, the world as a whole, indeed quite simply the most general form of the presence of the cosmos in the here and now. We can also put it this way: thanks to its resisting nature, matter realizes place in space, but thanks to its gravitating nature, the place, and thus in turn matter too, belongs to the cosmic happening which — itself placeless — only works through place. Only by means of both signatures, weight and resistance, is the characterization of matter completed, in such a way, indeed, that resistance suffices to indicate its existence, while weight lets it appear, as it were, in the light of condensations of the happening of the All. Since translatory self-movement would be unthinkable without feelings of position, the sensing of resisting corporealities, too, is founded upon a sleeping participation in the condensing power, drawing "downward" in the intuitive image, in which we have just now identified the connecting link between matter and "ether." But while the animal, owing to its wakefulness, is increasingly determined, the longer the more, immediately by drive-complementary alien bodies, we find the plant, owing to its predominantly sleeping form of life, immediately bound up with the soul of matter, and sunk that much more deeply into the life of the earth, the less capable it is of resonating to the life of the alien body. One will already understand it now to some extent if we give to the opposition of sleeping and waking, with reference to the opposition of the plant to the animal, the formulation — which, without what has just been explained, might indeed seem strange — that in the animal matter depends on the body, in the plant the body depends on matter.

As we approach the last section of the work, which is to guide us a few steps into the world of symbols, we shall from now on weave in, more often than before, pointers to results, each of which will gain its full power of conviction only from data of the primal history of spirit, and this somewhat in the sense of a schooling in "thinking in images." Thanks to the earth-boundness of axis and life-space, the plant is a symbol of the earth itself, and shares, in both respects, the nature of the clinging and predominantly telluric soul of woman. One must descend into such depths to understand fully why, at all times and among all peoples, the preference of women for flowers is more widespread and more intense than that of men, why it was and is women who wind wreaths and bind bouquets, adorn themselves with flowers [p. 1098] or fill their garments with the scent of blossoms, why among folk names for flowers the feminine predominate alongside the neuter, why the herb-lore of ancient times was administered by women, why the poets never tire of fetching, for the real or supposed excellences of woman, similes from the plant kingdom (as, conversely, from the animal kingdom for men)!

We have been at pains to equate the sleeping forms of beholding and working — from which alone the chief character-traits of the plant are to be explained — with the essence of growth as such, and thus also of the animal, and to distinguish them, so far as possible, from the sensory-motor processes which, in relation to those, constitute an upper and outer layer. This we find confirmed both linguistically and symbolically. With the Greek zoon, from zen = to live, lifehaving is expressly ascribed to the animal; with the Latin animal, of the same stem as anima, which means both life-principle and soul, ensoulment is expressly ascribed to it (in keeping with an old attempt at distinction, which runs: plantae vivunt, animalia vivunt et sentiunt [plants live, animals live and sense]); but according to the Greek phyton, from phyein = to cause to grow, as likewise according to the German "Gewächs" [growth, plant], the plant embodies the principle of growth. In keeping with this, even to present-day man nothing may still serve better as an emblem of swelling fullness of life than luxuriant plant growth in and around swamps, or in the hothouse, or in the tropical primeval forest; and this is one side of all vegetative symbolism. But the opposite side, too, becomes at once intelligible to us.

Growing is, among other things, self-nourishing, and the plant's self-nourishing takes place, among other means, by way of the roots, that is, of the part of it that it has sunk into the earth. Earth and underworld are the same, and to the underworld belong the dead. As, accordingly, the well-spring of life bubbles up out of the realm of the dead, so must that which is swollen by it into growth in the airy space wither, and, once it has borne fruit, sink down to death, into the space beneath the earth; even as its ruler, in the myth of the Greeks, was, as Pluto, the joy-bestowing giver of gifts, and, as Aidoneus, the inexorable king of the departed and of all death-bringing powers. We need no more than this to see why the wreath befits the mystic, the ruler, the bride, but no less the dead, and why flowers keep company with graves.

Let one more step be allowed, a little bolder than those just taken. We do not yet speak of the fact that the tree dies when it is [p. 1099] felled, that from the felled tree is fashioned or hollowed out not only the cradle but also the coffin; but we recall that whoever thinks of the foliage of the tree, at least in temperate latitudes, will scarcely fail to think of the fall of the leaves. And this, according to the testimony of the myths of all ages, is an age-old symbol of the return into the realm of those below, and the poets' favored simile for eternal transience. And here now the symbolism of falling would open before us. The prostration of those at prayer, face to the ground, reinterpreted as a gesture of humility, has in certain initiation rites preserved its original meaning still, namely that of symbolic dying; whoever is killed in war has "fallen," and the word "cadaver," which arose from the Latin (from cadere = to fall), makes the body's long, long contact with the earth the mark of its lifelessness. Whoever is still unfamiliar with symbolic modes of thought will find it strange when we set beside this the fact that, of the manners of self-killing, woman particularly favors the plunge from the window and the leap into water.<sup>76</sup> We return to the study of appearance with a brief weighing of the plant's masculine "heliotropism."

<sup>76</sup> On page 1099. — Here belongs also the widespread inclination of sporting airwomen toward parachute jumps.

As, by means of the growth of the stem, powers of the earth take body in the plant, so, by means of the growth of the leaves, do powers of the sun. It has long been recognized that seed-leaves, scale-leaves, bracts, sepals, petals, stamens, and carpels are transformed foliage-leaves; but the typical foliage-leaf is the plant in miniature. And so the life of the plant is found to be bound to the existence of the leaf every bit as much as to that of the root — indeed, in view of the leaf-like parts of unrooted thallophytes, even more to the former. In the leaf takes place — and by this the plant is most clearly set apart from the animal — the transformation of light into the plant's living building-material, and the most original light is sunlight; hence it has rightly been said that what warms us in the coal-fire is embodied sunlight of primeval time. In the plant's in-principle limitless receptivity to light its connection with the sun attests itself, or rather a participation in light that leaves mere consequences of irritability far behind. Indeed it has been shown that the carbon-dioxide uptake of certain plants is measurably diminished by so much as a shadow passing over them! Whoever cannot free himself from confusing the growth processes we call phototropism with the animal's answering movements to stimuli of brightness need only consider [p. 1100] that the plant, in so far as it receives the effect of light, also consumes it. "Among other things," then, it nourishes itself partly by means of the roots, through the absorption of water containing nutrient salts, and partly, as we must now add, by means of the leafgreen, namely on — light. The "illumination" and "imparting of light" sought since ancient times by the neophytes of the mysteries — the plant receives it in sleep; for it feeds on light as the animal feeds on the matter it is to incorporate. By means of light, distance materializes itself in the plant!

Here too a prospect onto the symbols lies near at hand. Man shares with the animal the horizontal axis, but with the tree the vertical, plumb-line carriage of the body. What most sharply distinguishes the bearer of the wakefulness of beholding from the animal — the upright stance, to which corresponds the equally unique posture of sleep: front-above — back-below — is precisely what joins him to the unawakened state of the plant. If we translate the unconscious wisdom of symbolic thinking into doctrines to be stated, then, as will be shown later, the most important of these would be that man is descended from the tree, is transformed into trees or plants (and conversely), holds converse with prophesying trees, and so forth. The axis of the predominantly sleeping tree and the carriage of the waking man both form with the earth's surface the angle that, of all angles, was first grasped and named, and that furnished the measure, as the true or "right" angle, for all the rest. The "right angle" (almost more even than the right hand) is the primal pattern of right conduct — though, at that, more the man's than the woman's — and right-angledness originally means the perpendicular, the plumb, the vertical. Hence the turn of phrase "the upright man," or, in the — ever archaic — language of students, "the only vertical" comportment; hence the closely related praise of "straight sense," "straight character," "straight understanding"; hence the misgiving attaching to the "inclined plane" and the "crooked posture," to what is "askew and crooked"; hence "to take amiss [krummnehmen, literally to take crookedly]" for "to take ill"; hence, in the sign-languages of the American Indians, the movement of the forefinger from the mouth in a straight direction, that is, at right angles to the body, as the sign for "truth," and in a direction slanting downward as the sign for "lie." — To these symbolic similarities come yet others, which we can unlock with our own insights. — To the root-end of the tree [p. 1101] the crown-end stands as the masculine day-side stands to the feminine night-side. Both are in the sleeping state of beholding and working; but, though the direction of the earth's axis belongs to both in so far as it determines both poles, still tellurism rules at the lower pole and has to share the rule with siderism at the upper pole. The former expresses itself in the root's turning toward the earth, the latter in the stem's turning away from the earth, and above all in the foliage's turning toward the sun. One understands why the receiving organs of animal sensibility lie on the outer surface of the body; one understands too why the forward ends of animal bodies must be more richly endowed with sense-organs, since the forward prolongation of the axis-line chiefly indicates the animal's direction of locomotion; but only when we know that in man alone the sensing of bodies becomes subject to the beholding of images do we understand the necessity of his in turn plant-like carriage. For by this, in the waking state, his front has become his above, and has thus become, out of a steering-point of locomotion, at once and even more decisively a place of overview (and indeed, be it well noted, not only while standing, as is likewise the case with most birds, but also while moving about). The positional superiority *of* the sense-organ, whose reach is in principle limitless, asserts itself sharply as spatial aboveness, and the eye's function as watcher recedes, in the gaze of pelasgian man — compare the images of the gods of antiquity — behind the eye's kinship with the stars. Man's essence forms the utmost antithesis to the plant's essence, in so far as, of all self-beings, and far beyond the animals too, man is the greatest mover on this planet; and yet again: man has found his way back to the vegetal, in so far as that same beholding and working which, in sleeping growth, there weaves the bodies, became in him the beholding and working of the soul, under a considerable narrowing of his sensing-instinctual animality. The presence of what is distant has been transformed into the appearance of what is distant, by virtue, namely, of the ensouling of the near-world of animal sensation, and it is the form of appearance of this when, in the tree as in man, the light-receptive bodily pole lies above, turned literally toward the ether — there thanks to the vertical axis, here thanks to the upright carriage.

The "tree of life" is a genuine symbol, the "tree of knowledge" a sham-symbol. But sham-symbols too, above all ones so [p. 1102] persuasive as this, have their grounds of possibility. If one replaces the "light of nature," which alone actually exists, with the "light of spirit" invented by man, then kinship with the stars becomes kinship with spirit, the seeking of light becomes the seeking of ideas, sun-intoxication becomes "enlightenment"-zeal, and indeed true cognizing, which is granted only to deep reflection, becomes that supposed cognizing which forges for the will to power its tools for the sacrilegious destruction of life. If one has in this way confused the wakefulness of beholding with the wakefulness of conceiving, it is no longer far to the confusion even of sleeping beholding with conceiving; whereupon the symbolic tree could first of all be doubled into one of life and one of knowledge. This happened, as is well known, several thousand years ago. But the science of today has gone considerably further still. Over the "tree of knowledge" it has lost sight of the "tree of life," in that it seeks to understand the leaves' receptivity to light not from sleeping beholding but rather from a kind of sensing of brightnesses or even of beholding of colors, and the growth-processes of phototropism not from sleeping working but rather after the manner of the movements with which the animal, among other things, flees from or seeks out stimuli of brightness. Perhaps the following quatrain of Goethe's is fit to give one or another researcher pause:

All our most honest endeavor / succeeds only in the unconscious moment. / How, then, could the rose bloom, / if it knew the splendor of the sun. / We could go on enumerating other distance-receptivities of the plant or, physically speaking, its receptivity for other kinds of rays. There would be no lack of material for this. The efficacy of ultraviolet waves, of infrared, of electrical waves, and of radio waves is beyond doubt. But the most astonishing thing in this connection is surely the discovery of the "mitogenetic rays" by Gurwitsch, to which must be added the substantially extending findings of Reiter and Gabor. According to these, from growing tissue — for instance from the tips of young onion roots — there issue invisible rays, subject to the laws of refraction, diffraction, reflection, and so on, through which, in another [p. 1103] onion root, an increase in nuclear division occurs on the side turned toward it, and a decrease on the side turned away. Although the results<sup>77</sup> of these careful experiments, continued over years, are still contested, still the path they indicate must, even should gaps in the evidence come to light, be regarded as in principle promising and as leading, sooner or later, to its goal. For here, in one particular case, the reciprocity of working and beholding would be demonstrated — not only in general, but for an exchange between one distance and another.

<sup>77</sup> On page 1103. — T. *Reiter* and D. *Gabor*, Sonderheft der wissenschaftlichen Veröffentlichungen aus dem Siemens-Konzern, published by the Zentralstation für wiss.-techn. Forschungsarbeiten des Siemens-Konzerns (Springer, Berlin 1928). — Review by *Belar* and *Houtermans* in "Die Naturwissenschaften," 17th year, issue 21. — Of quite special interest in these extraordinary experiments is the circumstance that only growing tissue excites the mysterious rays (whose wavelength is assumed to lie between 330 and 350 μ). Thus, for instance, a mash of heads of very young tadpoles is effective, but not that of full-grown tree-frogs; malignant tumors, further, are effective, but not benign ones!

In so far as it is something bodily distant that, by the means of sleeping beholding, weaves the living cell, then at the bodily-distant cell too the here of sleeping working must be able to co-weave. The ancients knew the genius loci, the nimbus, the aura, and we too still speak of the "atmosphere" of a person, a house, a region. Now this "atmosphere," overheard by so-called sensitive natures, felt by the fine-feeling, unknown to more robust temperaments, is a working actuality — giving and enriching or draining and weakening, enfolding and warming or hollowing out and chilling, accelerating and exciting or checking and damping, widening or narrowing, uplifting or paralyzing — and its working is essentially different from the mutual touching of bodies. The physical concept of induction touches not on a physically soluble problem but on a mystery of life. Every living being produces innumerable "induction-effects" in other beings, just as it in turn forms the center of the innumerable "induction-effects" of its fellow-beings. Evidence for this, first physically established on the living being, would be offered by the "mitogenetic rays." — Yet even without all this, the two facts of geotropism and phototropism would suffice to secure for the plant an inwardness — though, to be sure, an inescapability too — of connection with the cosmos, compared with which the animal has been granted a far greater independence, but also a proportionate detachment.

But how, now, does matters stand with the plant's receptivity for what is bodily near, for differences of intensity, for genuine stimuli of touch? It would weary the reader were we to run at length through the evidence for this. Not only the contraries of the presence and absence of pressure, of wetness and dryness, cold and warmth, are mirrored in the behavior of the plant's organs, but even differences of degree of the most extraordinary minuteness. On temperature fluctuations — to single out only one matter in this connection [p. 1104] — depends, not least, that alternation of plant life-processes which corresponds to the cosmic alternation of day and night. The opening of the European water-lily by day, its closing by night, rests on a different "sensibility" of the two sides of its petals to warmth: the "more sensitive" inner side grows, with rising temperature, more rapidly, and with falling temperature more slowly, than the less sensitive outer side, from which follows, in the first case, a curvature of the leaf outward, and in the second, inward. The vegetative feeling for differences of moisture we have already explained above in connection with the fruiting bodies of the mold fungus. It sounds still more astonishing when we hear that roots "search" for the moisture of the soil; in accordance with which the plant that, rooted in moist earth, sends down roots no longer than a finger, drives its roots, in desert sand, a meter deep, and multiplies their water-absorbing hairs! As for receptivity to effects of touch, finally, we need not even appeal to movements, since, for the purpose of demonstrating it, the mere circumstance would suffice that, for example, in a root-tip encased in plaster, the growth-pressure directed against the obstacle can rise as high as twelve atmospheres!

It may be expedient for the natural-scientific doctrine of life to interpret these and similar phenomena as reflexanswers to stimuli; the doctrine of life founded on the science of soul must not follow it in this, but must hold fast, down to particulars, to the essential difference between cellular growth-processes and the sensory-motor processes that rest upon them. "Were the distance-processes," it was said in the 56th Chapter, "to preponderate considerably, the tension between nearness and distance would diminish"; if the plant, we now continue, is predominantly a sleeping-beholding being, then for it the opposition of nearness and distance vanishes, if not wholly, then nearly so, from which it follows that its experience of the distant and its experience of the near bear essentially the same character. Likewise it follows from the circumstance that there is a soul of matter too — which will disclose itself to us fully only in what follows (whereby the withdrawal of soul into happening comes to its close) — that matter is that form of happening which admits of the separating-out of local actualities, and thereby, indeed, first of all makes possible their appearing. It is not, then, as though nearness were closed off to beholding; rather: by virtue of beholding, beings hold converse with what is bodily distant just as with what is [p. 1105] bodily near, whereas by virtue of sensing they hold converse *only* with what is bodily near; by virtue of beholding, the world-elements are present in the self-being "working and weaving," while by virtue of sensing it becomes a body among bodies situated outside one another; by virtue of beholding, in a word, it is microcosm, by virtue of sensing, *part* of the universe.

We have long known this, even if it has not hitherto been so expressed. For we have, indeed, had occasion more than once to assert, with reference partly to primal man and partly to the state of ecstasis, that in step with the increase of the power of beholding over the power of sensing, what is near and nearest too becomes image, and that, at the perfection of beholding, even the bodily self-movement of the bearer of soul melts into the world-pulse of happening. Therefore, so far as vegetative receptivity really is a state of beholding, there may, for the plant, no more obtain a distinction between distant, near, and nearest bearers of working than for the ecstatic, and the deep contrariety of its sleeping beholding to the wakefulness of beholding (in primal man) lies solely in this, that its connection with the surrounding world is not so much that of a soul of the body with the appearance of happening as rather that of a soul of matter with happening itself; in consequence of which every change in the surrounding world that becomes feelable to the plant embodies itself in the plant. The expression of this it is when, among the palpably manifest consequences of the "working" of the plant, by far the most appear as consequences of changes of growth.

The plant does not see, does not hear, does not smell, does not taste, does not touch; it does not sense and it does not intuit — and an abyss gapes, moreover, between its intercourse with the surrounding world and that of a being which perceives its surrounding world. If it has been said that it does not sleep (as men and animals sleep), one should not fail to add: because it does not — wake (as animals and men wake). The experiences incapable of consciousness within the interior of the human body, which one rightly calls "vegetative processes," become known to us indirectly through the moodcoloring of our feelings, and come fully "to speech" with the phantasmal images of nocturnal dreams. We have also been able to show that, in the state of dream-sleep and of deep sleep, the separating wall between the local actuality of the ensouled [p. 1106] body and general happening becomes thinner, indeed in part vanishes; and we need, of the exchange thereby opened up, stress only *the* side that belongs to it from the body's participation in the essence of matter, in order to find the reflection of the surrounding world in the soul of the plant somewhat comparable to the reports that may flow to us ourselves from the world through moods and dreams. From the plant's surrounding world, to be sure, the plant's mood brings to the plant-body far more faithful tidings than mere moods bring to consciousness from our own surrounding world; but in return we are possessed of the power of intuition and of perception, which remains wholly denied to it.

Once one has understood the *sense* of the chief marks by which the plant sets itself off from the animal — the sense of its sessility, and of the earth-turning and light-turning character of its structure — one readily sees that none of its other basic properties stands in contradiction to these. It would indeed be a wonder without parallel if differences of intensity did not also weave into the plant's growth; but the assumption that these are experienced as intensities is admissible only for organisms that answer to them with translatory self-movements. The investigation of life would have surrendered its object were it to assent to the molecular-theoretical equating of the consequences of growth with movements. Only for a being that becomes aware of a foreign body do intensities exist; but even this being, in doing so, rests upon the sleeping-beholding layer, thanks to which the data of strength attach themselves to data of kind. If, then, we strike out sensing, or at least think of it as so far diminished that it practically no longer counts, there remain *only* qualities, and the distinguishing of these from intensities — a distinction familiar only to the more wakeful stage — becomes void of object.

We have grown accustomed to seeing, in the differences of light from dark, of loud from soft, of more from less strongly scented with wallflower, of more from less bitter, moist, hard, warm, and so on, differences of strength, whereas in and for themselves these are nothing but differences of kind, which we are able to arrange in scales of strength only because we, as beings that are always also sensing, are, or at least can be, bodily altered by data of intuition through that in them which we for this reason take to be high degrees of intensification. But were the degrees of strength that we thus detach not likewise kinds, then intuition would cease altogether, and [p. 1107] in the end even the sensing of resistances would be extinguished, because already the spatial extendedness, without which they cannot be thought, carries an exponent of kind. One needs, for instance, only call to mind intuitive contents such as the pointed, the blunt, the rough, the smooth, the hairy, the woolly, the floury, and so on, or the scarcely less numerous sense-data of the liquid, to be assured of the qualitative nature of all contents of touch. If, accordingly, there simply occur no differences of strength that are not accompanied by changes of quality, then it speaks not in the least against the far predominantly beholding nature of the plant if its growth-processes are also participated in by such changes of the surrounding world as it is more convenient for us to characterize as contents of sensation.

The transfer of the stimulus-response schema onto plantlore has occasioned important discoveries, but it has also given rise to delusions, one of the worst of which is surely the one that culminates in the judgment that the plant is ⦅only⦆ receptive to differences of intensity — by which, of course, our interpretation of its receptivity would be overturned. It is scarcely comprehensible how such a thing could be said, after it had been established, for example, that for phototropism blue and violet light are decisive, but not red, while for the uptake of carbon dioxide it is precisely red, and not violet! Meanwhile we have repeatedly documented plant receptivities to quality, behind which the receptivity to quality of animal, and even of human, intuitive gift, remains immeasurably behind. One need only recall the tendril, which answers with changes of growth to the touch of a cotton thread swaying in the wind, while remaining "mute" under the crushing pressure of mercury! How utterly explanation by way of differences of strength fails here! It is not the difference of pressure but the difference between smoothness and roughness that determines the behavior. This one example can give us the right concept of the beholding-power ⦅also⦆ of touch. Another would be the earlier-mentioned parasitic plant Cuscuta europaea (dodder). For it makes use of its capacity for twining and for tendril-climbing only when living supports (such as a willow twig) are at its disposal that serve it as nourishment, but not, for example, in the case of brass rods. We need scarcely add that the surrounding world of the plasterencased root spoken of above deviates qualitatively to an extraordinary degree from the natural surrounding world of the root, [p. 1108] even were we to leave aside the differences of kind that can never be separated even from a mere increase of pressure. The "law of stimulus-quantity," finally, brings us only a fresh confirmation, in that the significance which, according to it, attaches to duration of time could scarcely be understood from mere sensing. But that the life-form of the plant stands quite properly "under the sign" of receptivity to kind becomes fully certain to us when we hold the following before our eyes.

Of the countless passively mobile pollen grains that the wind scatters abroad, only relatively very few ever reach the place of their destination. Some fall into water, some into grass, some onto stone or sand, some stick to foliage-leaves, some land on the stigma of flowers of an utterly foreign kind: in all these cases nothing happens. But if the pollen grain comes to rest on the stigma of a flower of the same kind, or at least of a similar kind, then and only then does there begin within it that highly intricate, multi-staged growth-process which ends with the union of male and female reproductive cells in the ovules of the ovary. Here, then, we should have the fundamental example of a receptivity to kind on the part of the plant cell, which goes beyond the receptivities to kind of our own intuitive gift to the point of incomprehensibility; for surely no one today would still venture the nonsense that the pollen grain, deprived of all self-movement, perceives the stigma of its own kind.

The reader has long since noticed that, with the foregoing exposition, the contribution we offered in the 58th Chapter toward a metaphysics of the life of the cell is at once completed and closed. Already there it was stressed, and supported with numerous examples, that the stimulus-sensitive self-movement of many single-celled organisms is founded on a receptivity to kind which appears as a basic property of living matter and manifests itself organically in the diversity of the protoplasms of all kinds. In the plant, which has remained predominantly in the sleeping state of life, the cell's receptivity to kind has developed into the organism's supreme receptivity to kind; in the animal, only a modest part of this has passed over into the gift of intuition, while, for the sake of ever-increasing wakefulness, sensibility had to develop, on which rests the seeking-out and avoiding of bodies.
