For anyone can see this: we could now, in principle, compare the souls of the images of brightness and darkness, of warmth and cold, of storm and stillness, of rock and tree, river and sea, forest and desert, of sunlight and moonshine, starry night and daytime sky, ravine and summit; we could do so far beyond what was attempted above with the appearance-contrast of the liquid to the solid. And supposing a little had become known to us of the elemental souls, we could pursue them right into living beings and in the end into man, thereby ascertaining the essences on which, within mankind, the differences of the characters of individual persons, of the characters of peoples, races, ages, would depend. The postulate in Heraclitus's ethos anthropo daimon [a man's character is his daimon] would be fulfilled in the spirit of its proclaimer, and sciences would arise wholly incomparable with those known up to now! Only, in part, this would no longer be the task of a work that has set itself the exploration of the border zone where souls stand in the most terrible of all struggles, the struggle with spirit; in part, the closing section will at least indicate, and substantiate with a few examples from the prehistory of conceiving thought, what means of such a mode of research would stand at our disposal. But even if we did not have to content ourselves with less, those sciences would nonetheless remain unborn. It has become too late for them. The powers are departing from the devastated face of this star, and the power of primal reflection, even of the most deep-rooted among the living, would have to grow faint before it caught sight once more of what is fleeing in its escape. With this we come to the end of this consideration.

Let us transpose ourselves into the highest wakefulness of beholding, and we find the whole world of appearance pervaded by a polarity that surpasses in significance those already adduced: the polarity of distance and nearness. Since, for the sake of the reciprocity of the impenetrable, we have just called sensation a special kind of beholding, let us also reflect on the mark by which we might characterize this special kind: it lies in the "nearness as such" of everything experienceable as resistant. Sensation would thus be the beholding of nearness as such, the sensed a nearness- [p. 1139] appearance, or, grasped by analogy with the beheld, it would be the *cha*-*racter* of nearness. We grant this seemingly perverse conception a moment's space because it thereby emerges with particular sharpness that *genuine* images, which are unimaginably present in *sleeping* beholding, gain the character of distance only as a consequence of the co-appearance of the near-character. Only to a being that, through sensations, has intercourse with the appearance of nearness as nearness do *images* come to appearance or, put otherwise, does distance *appear*. The elemental souls are unreleased souls of images, even when they are souls of matter, and are thus souls of distance differing in kind. Just as they require the appearance of nearness in order to appear, so they require the appearance of distance in order to reveal themselves.

Appearing distance is always distance in space; but the soul of spatial distance is distance in time, and distance in time is distance in the past. To the degree of the participation of beholding in the process of intuition corresponds the degree of the participation of the past in the present, and with the growing depth of beholding grows the distance of the ages conjured up in images. (This is why, in the cult customs of ancient as well as of unhistorical peoples, the elemental souls are at once souls of the dead and ancestral souls.) We need not have investigated it; we can feel that the primal image of man is younger than the primal image of the animal, the primal image of the animal younger than that of the plant, but that older than both, and truly age-old, are the primal images of the high mountains, of the sea, of the starry sky. Were we to call beholding primal recollection (without, however, forgetting that its images of recollection appear), we might say that the gaze of primal recollection presses on from distance of the past to distance of the past, passing from the animal soul to the soul of the plant, and plunges into far deeper gulfs of time yet in its thrust onward to the soul of the primal granite.

Within the framework of the mechanistic mode of thought of the previous century there was a genuinely *materialist* island. We cannot today read the language in which people came to an understanding with one another there without finding it repellently superficial. This is justified insofar as, for those materiologists, "matter" itself, against their own will, kept splintering ever again into atoms; it is unjustified insofar as the computational arts of today are still immeasurably more superficial. "The secret of mechanics lay heavy upon these anchorites in the deserts of the understanding" (Novalis), and so their matter [p. 1140] remained an unrefreshing hybrid thing of earthly desire and figment of the brain. Yet the elemental souls had not entirely fallen into oblivion (how else could a Böcklin have come into being!), and more still lingers on in present-day minds than people are willing to concede, out of deference to the spirit-glorification theater that belongs to good form. Perhaps we shall make ourselves more intelligible to one or another reader if, for once, we express ourselves a little improperly, leaning strongly on a materialism of yesterday.

Supposing man were the latest microcosm in a sequence of stages of microcosms that was to fulfill itself in the bearer of the beholding of the primal images, then there would have to dwell within him the souls of the animal, of the plant, of the primal mountain-range, of the sea, of the starry sky. His outermost layer would be the human, beneath it would lie the animal, beneath that the vegetal, beneath that the elemental. Now his corporeality really does contain the conditions of spiritual, animal, vegetative processes, and the condition of all of them is a chemistry that likewise governs the happening of unliving matter. The soul's gaze, were it to press through into the soul of its own matter, would be at the same time a look back into the souls of the oldest ages of the earth. — To be sure, it was not quite thought in this way at the time. Chemical elements were allowed to come together into protoplasms, protoplasms were allowed to "develop" over millions of years into man, the embryo in the mother's womb was allowed to pass, at an accelerated tempo, through the series of animal forms that man — so it was thought — had earlier been. But since some held fast to a kind of ensoulment of matter as well, there nonetheless remained a presentiment that the beholding of actuality could only be compared to recollecting.

Let us return to the world of images! The elemental layer too is present, but as distance. Distance slumbers in the vegetal layer; it narrows, in that it begins to awaken, in the animal layer; it appears to primordial man; it is whitewashed over, papered over, and tamped down by the unnatural layer of the faculty of concepts. The power of the elements in man must double itself if it is, bursting the dungeon, nonetheless to be able to pair with the powers that want to appear to it. But that is not yet enough. As spirit, breaking outward as will, accomplishes through its henchman, herculean man, the same work upon the earth: it clogs her pores, robs her of her breathing air, cuts off her exchange with the [p. 1141] cosmos — clearing of the forests, extermination of freely living races of animals, drainage of terrain, regulation and poisoning of the rivers, exploitation and destruction of all the treasures of the soil are some of the widely visible signs of this. But if the cradle of images is shattered, then the elemental souls flee and abandon the violated planet, and after them dies out the gift of primal recollection in the desolating souls of men. It has become too late for the wardens of the meaning of the earth. — One of the deepest of Novalis's words of wisdom runs: "The seat of the soul is there, where inner world and outer world touch one another," and one of the worst of the aberrations of belief in the actuality of things has led to the delusion that one arrives at the "seat" of the soul by the paths of anatomy. The opposition of symbolic depth and symbolic flatness holds good; but the "way inward" (in Heraclitus, tellingly, "the way upward") is the way from the appearances ("surfaces") to that which appears in them ("depth"), and not, say, the way from the natural outside of the body to the matters filling it, which in turn become outside as soon as the body is cut open! Where else, indeed, could the soul be sought but at the natural outer surfaces, if it is the soul that appears in the ensouled! Just as we rightly hope to find the characters of men in their physiognomies, so the souls of animals speak from the physiognomies of animals, not likewise from their entrails (whose metaphysics, as practiced in the haruspicy of antiquity, rests on a different ground), the souls of plants from the physiognomies of plants, the elemental souls from the physiognomies of the earth.

But the saying of Novalis discloses to us this too, that the ground of the appearing of souls is the same as the ground of the intercourse between soul and soul, and especially of the intercourse between soul and world. The happening that we call the soul occurs ever anew through the interplay of the poles of actuality, and just as the elements are released through their gamos [marriage] with the soul of the beholder, so their being-present is grounded in the flux of happening and, with regard to the earth, in the uninterrupted exchange between earth and cosmos. Therefore, whoever destroys the face of the earth murders the heart of the earth and robs of their "seat" the powers now vanishing into the "ether."

The devastation of the face of the earth, which is bringing forth such fearful consequences, has perceptibly begun only since Goethe's death, and has maintained the frenzied, ever- [p. 1142] increasing tempo with which we see it wading forward today for no longer than about fifty years. Since about 1830, therefore, there began, unceasingly, to break apart in mankind what one is accustomed to call "culture" and what is nowadays generally distinguished from so-called civilization (— embourgeoisement); hence that "world history," which we can trace with some reliability for about five thousand years, notwithstanding the growing victories of the herculean will over the last roughly two thousand years, remains predominantly within the spell of the earth up until the year 1830, but no longer from then on. This is the reason why we designate the elemental souls as "having been" and had to take the detour by way of image-forming spirits of the past, in order to make it easier for ourselves to furnish proof of the actuality of their working. One will now know better what the difficulty is with sighting elemental souls today, even in the work of the almost still-contemporary Böcklin. But after everything we have attempted to elucidate concerning this, one will also, at least with the organs of presentiment, be able to grope toward that whose essence a forgotten poet enclosed in these verses:

The trees roar, yet they speak only / to him whose soul once fared within the storm.

[p. 1143]

### Vierter Abschnitt — Vom Wirkungsvermögen der Bilder (Zusammenhang und Beziehung) — Fourth Section — On the Efficacy of Images (Connection and Relation)

#### 66. Kapitel — Vom Wirklichkeitsgehalt der Sprache — Chapter 66 — On the Actuality-Content of Language

*Preliminary remarks.* — To the door of my room, which I attentively regard, I am related without being connected with it; but if my wrist and the door-handle have been tied together by means of a corporeal band, then I am connected with it, whether or not I attend to this, or am inwardly occupied with something else. Door-handle and chair could likewise be connected, although neither of them establishes a relation. In order that I be able to perceive the moon, I must indeed have suffered the influence of its light, and this points to a kind of connecting that always takes place in the case of perceiving, even if this mostly goes unnoticed; but the astronomical moon experiences no influence from the glances of men directed toward it, and this holds in principle again for every object of perception in relation to the process of perceiving. If, on the other hand, we take corporeal connecting as the model of connecting, then in the state of affairs of connecting there are always reciprocally occurring influences. If I tug at the band whose resistance I suffer while fettered, then the thing which the band links me with also experiences the influence of my pulling and tugging. It is one thing to see the island which the sailboat approaches, another to set foot upon it: there mere being-related, of which only the bearer of perception can become aware, but not the island; here a connection, of which, for instance, the footprints of the soles remain to the object in the sand of the shore.

[p. 1144] Crude and palpable as our examples are, they may nonetheless help to make it easier for us to unfold, in the life-scientific sense, the differences of meaning between connection and relation in the following propositions: 1. Connection is not relation. 2. Connections are not to be thought without reciprocal influences; relation as such has no influence as its consequence. 3. Every connection is something real; every relation something conceptual. 4. Connections are immediately experienced, but not conceived; relations are conceived, but not immediately experienced. 5. Connections rest on the actuality of the spatio-temporal continuum; relations on the being of the extra-spatio-temporal spirit. 6. Connections can take place without relations being added; relations never take place without the presupposition of connections. 7. In order that a relation may arise, connections must be abolished.

Of the foregoing propositions, it is above all the seventh that shall occupy us. For reasons we have spelled out, conceiving thought proceeds from the assumption of the conceivability of corporeal connections, by which we have just now illustrated connecting; but this very assumption was recognized as erroneous. Corporeal is the connecting of the strictly near with the strictly near; and this, as we know, would not take place without the connecting of the distant with the distant. If now the connecting of the distant with the distant is inconceivable, then so too is the connecting of the near with the near, and consequently connecting as such (4th proposition). Against this, the history of logocentric thinking signifies the unworkable attempt, for the sake of "making the world thinkable," to resolve connections into relations.

In our comprehensive account of the relation of the concept to the individual case (Chapter 38), it was announced on p. 429 that "in a much later chapter" the "fundamental confusion" would be uncovered that caused every attempt to make intelligible how the concept occurs in the "cases" to which it is applied, to fail. The solution has become ripe: it is a matter of the confusion of relation and connection. That only relations obtain between concepts may be granted; but on the basis of a belief that reinterprets spirit either as the source or as the flower of the world of appearances, one has not forced one's way through to the insight [p. 1145] that this must hold equally of objects. Between the general concept "tree as such" and the individual concept "tree here in this particular place" there certainly obtains no connection, but indeed a relation; so too there obtains a relation, and not a connection, between the contents of the opinions themselves. The relation of concepts is elucidated by the relation of objects, but neither of the two is to be explained from the other. The most penetrating acuity founders when it seeks to derive the relation of concepts from a relation of objects, or, conversely, the relation of objects from such a relation of concepts. The vehemence — unmatched by any successor — with which a Plato undertook the second attempt has, down to this hour, made it difficult for Western science to master the means of thought that would open access to connections.

We have shown that it is now proper beings, now elemental souls, which, by the medium of their appearing, allow those units of meaning to arise, without whose secret efficacy relating thought would remain in the — beyond of space. The general concept holds for the individual case because the meaning of the name, out of which it was demarcated, is as it were the reflection of an essence for which the boundaries in question do not exist. Insofar as the conceptless meaning concerns characters of appearance, the scope of the cases is already given within it. Only with the separation of the essence from the appearance of the tree does tree-appearance separate from tree-appearance, and the individual tree from the generic concept of the tree; and in the place of real connections there step the merely conceivable relations of objects of thought. The ground of their relatability does not lie in them, and from them one cannot recover what had to be stripped away in order to think them: actuality.

Modern ethnology, as is well known, passionately circles around the state of soul of primitives. Yet without a knowledge of symbolic identity, that is, the identity of the essence in its numerically and specifically diverse forms of appearance, it will at best mark out problems and forgo their solution, or at worst offer sham solutions. In symbolic thinking, individual and species are not essentially distinguished. With the sacred sacrificial bird all birds of its species are sacrificed, and the body of the god that is eaten in the form of the wafer is one and always the same, regardless that each believer partakes of a different [p. 1146] wafer. Understanding-bound thinking runs into self-contradictions here only because it has won its identities by surrendering the connections without whose efficacy — no longer manifest, yet still secretly persisting — it would itself in the end collapse. — But the arts of formalism, which raise the claim to need no actuality, would dissolve away without the efficacy of the intuitive — signs, in whose abusive handling they consist. With this we come to the role of names, one often adduced by us but never thought through to the end. The evocative power of language. — No one can really wish to conceive of really operative powers; but one can name them, and by means of naming (or other forms of sign-giving, which however remain outside our consideration here) refer to them those persons who have at some time suffered their working strongly enough to be able to "call it to mind." What is operative here is, as the phrase betrays, the meaning of the name or the linguistic content. Then, however, language must, among other things, be an expression of experienced images in the medium of human sounds, or a phonic representation of image-characters, and in any case only insofar as it either still is this, or at least offers equivalents for it, does it possess the gift of evocation, for which we shall first bring forward a handful of instances familiar to everyone, even if not consciously so to everyone.

Magic was always essentially image-magic, and one kind of image-magic was the world-wide magic of the name, from which scarcely any human being even today wholly escapes. "Curses" have indeed gone out of fashion; but with the "cursed fellow" and the "ill-reputed house" the custom of cursing reaches into today's everyday speech. When one accompanies the report of the excellent state of health of a beloved person with the thrice-repeated "touch wood," what strikes us as still more noteworthy than the aftereffect of a once wide-awake fear of the envy of listening demons is the presentiment — easily attested by self-observation — of the power that inheres in the uttered naming. There have always been, and still are, many concealments arising from the anxiety that one runs the risk of forfeiting certain goods, such as fortune, talent, favorable circumstances, if one speaks them aloud (or "cries them up"). The proverbial "lupus in fabula," in turn, is rooted in the at least [p. 1147] felt conviction that something somehow baleful is summoned by naming.

We scarcely need remind ourselves that, with regard to "nomen est omen," prehistoric man agrees entirely with extra-historical man. Among the ancients it was a common thing for mighty gods to bear, besides their usual name, a second one that had to remain secret, because otherwise they would fall into the power of whoever came to know it. Ra, a supreme god of the Egyptians, who, before the world yet existed, created himself by the utterance of his own name (!), loses his power after Isis has by cunning succeeded in inducing him to surrender the stubbornly withheld word. As Bramanaspati, that is, "lord of prayer," or at least as his human embodiment, the Indian priest was a kind of over-god, who could not only perform deeds like the gods but could even bend these themselves to his will. No lesser a capacity is attributed by the Mohammedans to those prophets who are in possession of the "great name" of the deity. The name of the tutelary deity of Rome was kept secret, so that no hostile people who learned it might make the god subservient to itself and seize the city. — And this very same thing meets us now in a thousandfold form among primitives and semi-primitives. The name of the newborn child is, in the overwhelming majority of cases, not chosen but found, on the basis of the priest's inquiry into the ancestor reborn in it. In many cases, however, it may not be spoken, because the child would thereby be endangered, and is therefore called only by a nickname; and even at the grave, not infrequently, the name of the totem appears instead of the proper name (Tylor). The naming of a dead person could moreover cause him to return as a vampiric ghost, for which reason his name and all similarly sounding names sometimes fall under a taboo, whose significance for the development and rapid transformation of many primitive languages has been thoroughly appreciated by researchers.

In so-called verbal suggestion (= instillation by means of speech) we practice and experience daily a similar effect of words, only detached from the survival of former word-magic. — People have looked a great deal for invisible forces in these instillations, chiefly no doubt because verbally identical requests succeed in the mouth of one person and fail in the mouth of another, and certainly much depends on various attendant circumstances [p. 1148] such as manner of utterance, appearance and bearing of the speaker, the "atmosphere" of the surroundings. Also (though not necessarily) those fluids which Romanticism called "vital magnetism" may play a part; yet there is no doubt whatever that of a hundred instillations by the most skillful instiller, ninety-nine would fail if the receiving person were not master of the language which the instiller employs.

Of the effect of the uttered word in diplomatic conversations, or in parliamentary negotiations, or indeed in the popular speeches of an agitator, by far the greater part is known to fall to immediate instillation. In more primitive times this power attached, for reasons yet to be touched on below, predominantly to the songs of the "singers." "The Finnish word laulaja means both singer and conjurer, magician"<sup>84</sup>; and indeed one could fill volumes with evidence for the "sorcery" of singers. Has not even in historical times one condemned to death not too rarely sung himself free, and thereafter on occasion even attained high honors! But even today the name, and only the name, occasionally attains, with a force reminiscent of similar phenomena among primitives, an efficacy in certain children's games. A fanciful boy, for example, who in the game "The wolf is coming" represents precisely the wolf, feels himself to some extent pervaded by powers that are lacking to him in his average state, and his playmates do not deny an admixture of fear that refers to the wolf and by no means to the person of the one representing it.

<sup>84</sup> On page 1148. — Otto Böckel, Psychologie der Volksdichtung, p. 191.

Indeed, if we reflect rightly, we recognize that the evocative and transforming power of the word in some form still pervades our whole life. Whoever, on his daily walk, has repeatedly passed by a person who is, say, working in a field, feels his innermost bearing toward this person changed down to its very ground from the moment when he has "exchanged a few words" with them (however indifferent the content!). Finally, the power of instillation of the printed word — above all of poetry, then of exciting entertainment literature, further of all pictureless advertising in the service either of commercial or of political ends, including catchwords and fashionable words — furnishes the incontrovertible proof that,<sup>85</sup> in relation to the soul of the one perceiving it, language itself — thus apart from the manner of utterance — is an operative power of the highest rank. The schemata of the forms of relation. — [p. 1149] Of the confusion of operative connections with merely conceivable relations, that form of representation on which at the same time all the other forms and cases depend, is the un-realization of the name — never to be completed before the downfall of thinking, yet willed and, in waves, furthered by logocentric thinking for two and a half thousand years — in favor of a supposed actuality either of the concept or of the fact. In order to be able to indulge its belief in the actuality of things, "naturalism" rests, now unconsciously, now consciously, on the assumption that name as well as concept are determined by the thing, as the following schema indicates: In order to be able to indulge its belief in the actuality of concepts, ideologism rests, now unconsciously, now consciously, on the assumption that both the name and the thing are determined by the concept, as the following schema indicates. One readily surveys the following facts: 1. As mere noumena, concept and object of thought are indeed related to one another, but are not connected with one another. The concept can never, the thing only to the extent, be made intuitively present, that for the appearances which have made possible the act of objectification, representing images are available (which is the case with river or to jump or blue etc., but not with duty, unjust, to answer for, deceit, because, disfavor, absent, patience, appropriate etc.). 2. It is a (spiritual) act of apprehension through which thing and thing-concept arise together with one another, but an act of will through which, with the splitting-off of the name's meaning, the name becomes a sign for the concept. Though we may in this be co-determined [p. 1150] by feelings of meaning, we nonetheless have, to a great extent, freedom of choice, of which the history of the sciences offers examples enough. — Could we even wholly free ourselves from feelings of meaning, which is of course impossible, then the name would be attached to the concept in a manner similar to that in which, say, a mark of ownership, a trademark, a publisher's imprint, an ex-libris, a badge of rank etc. is attached to other states of affairs; or, in other words, it would have to the concept the relation of a — proper name. These are exaggerations, but they show what matters. 3. This premised, let us reflect that both schemata indeed indicate relations, but are silent about their ground of production. The ideological schema at least allows us to recognize that the object is a content of apprehension, but not how the apprehension comes about, and least of all what the name really has to do with it. Rather, it appears in both figures in the light of a mere appendage, as which we have just sought to characterize it — which stands out especially when we compare the two with one another, since then the relation between concept and thing recurs in both, while that between concept and name is missing in Fig. 9. If we now consider that it is precisely the name to which, under all circumstances, immediate intuitiveness belongs, then the devaluation visibly intended for it in both cases leaves no doubt that here, in the place of the power through which alone something is connected for its bearer, in the place of the soul, there has stepped the power that alone establishes relations, namely spirit. Basic forms of connections. — The schema of connections looks different. In the animal it has the following form: Thanks to the predominance of sensation, something corporeal in particular is experienced in the intuitive image, whose own significance recedes quite extraordinarily behind its significance for the weal and woe of the bearer of life, and to this there attach immediate reactions which, [p. 1151] with regard to their capacity to make manifest the state of life that occasioned them, are called expression. Since the triangle of Fig. 11 schematizes the connection in the experiential domain of the awakening soul of the living body, we call it the schema of animal cognition, or more briefly the "animal schema." It is closed; for the process runs from K not only by way of L to A, but also by way of A to L, though never with equal strength. If A follows immediately upon K, it is called "reflex," and, in relation to it, the corporeal appearance "stimulus." But even the reflex participates in principle in the generation of meaning: partly by the establishment of optimal conditions for the arising of intuitive images, partly by directives for the imageappropriate utilization of sense-data. One need only recall the role that accrues, for visual beholding, to accommodation, pupil-width, and the position of convergence.

<sup>85</sup> On page 1148. — That name and verbal formulation are in countless cases more decisive than the thing meant by them is known to every professional writer of advertising copy. But this also holds for the history of the sciences. Without the splendid catchwords "adaptation" and "struggle for existence," for example, so-called Darwinism would hardly have conquered the world in the last century as swiftly as it did; and that even the intellectually curious cult which the second half of that century carried on with "the conservation of energy" was favored by the choice of the word "energy" admits, for the student of appearance, of no doubt. The name rises to quite decisive importance above all in the language of literary men, by which present-day colloquial speech is very strongly co-determined. This has often and aptly been discussed by opponents of unlovely fashions in foreign words. One need only imagine the word "international" rendered by "interstate" and ask oneself whether it would then still have been possible to make of it so mighty a lever of nation-uprooting theorems as it in fact served, decade after decade! Or let one reflect on the notorious "pogrom" in place of "persecution of the Jews." Whoever occupies himself here and there a little with literary fashionable words and phrases will, incidentally, likely arrive at the conviction that the suggestibility of present-day educated man has reached a degree never before attained. Scarcely had the self-important word "mentality" turned up somewhere during the war, than there was soon scarcely a leading article, indeed scarcely a "feuilleton," in which it did not occur at least once, notwithstanding that it says nowhere *more* than "disposition" and can besides, depending on the case, be rendered by "turn of mind," "state of mind," "condition of mind," "manner of thinking," "way of thinking." A few more examples may be permitted. The false compound "beachtlich" (from commercial language) in place of the correct "beachtenswert" is just now forcing its way in even into highly learned treatises. Minds of significance, or of rank, or of weight, etc., have for the time being had to yield all along the line to minds of "format." In the author's youth one knew, indeed, of various "services" (such as punishmentservice, night-service, military service, etc.), but not of a service *to* something. Today, by contrast, even the most reckless business practice is a — service to the customer. The certainly unobjectionable, indeed beautiful word "Aufbau" [structure, building-up] is at present spreading with the speed of an epidemic: it may pass when there is talk of the structure of the world of perception, of personality, of man, etc.; tolerably still, when of the structure of mathematics, or — already more questionable — of perception, of intuition, etc.; but it is, after all, asking rather much when we are even supposed to think of a structure of, say, the cognitive *function*! The turn of phrase "it is a matter of" [es geht um etwas], formerly reserved for grand or dangerous or at least delicate matters (e.g., a matter of life, of being or not being, etc.), is, through excessive frequency, being so trivialized that it will presumably shortly have taken the place of "it concerns something." We scarcely need add that every fashionable word, every fashionable turn of phrase, represents a piece of cultural history and can be interpreted, in terms of the science of the soul, with just as much certainty as articles of faith, styles of building, party divisions, etc.

By naming the apex of the triangle "corporeal appearance," the participation of the beholding soul even in the sensing of the soul of the living body is meant to be noted. We pass over, as sufficiently set forth, the persistence of the animal schema in man, further the perfecting of beholding in the moments of having-become-fused, and offer at once the schema of connections for the experiential domain of, say, the Promethean stage, presupposing, that is, the presence of a language, which provided the ground for that of concepts. It has the following form:

Name

Meaning / Character of appearance / Fig. 12. Biocentric schema. / We have shown in Chapter 36 why original language is always, among other things, symbolic language, further, that this consists in the transferring of the "thought of sameness to characters of appearance of essential similarity"; finally, how, without unconscious impulses from the symbolism of names, even conceptual thinking, which has consciously turned away from it, would run dry. Yet it is not only for this reason that we must now place the name at the apex of the triangle, but even more because without it the creation of units of meaning, with whose help the images can be evoked anew, would be impossible. Only insofar as the soul feels the urge, and is able, to meet the experience of the image with the [p. 1152] symbolic sign, or, what chiefly concerns us here, with the symbolic call, do there arise for it, for the first time, such image-characters, whose meaning the sound thenceforth preserves and "propagates."

The schema holds, as has been said, not for beholding souls as such, but for souls already inspirited, yet still at the stage of unshaken dependence on life; hence it is called the schema of life-guided thinking, or symbolic schema, or — more comprehensively — biocentric schema. By juxtaposing it with the animal schema we readily rediscover the familiar features by which animal and human cognition are distinguished. To the extent that the working of the soul gains ascendancy over the working of the body, it is no longer states of one's own but world-characters that decisively determine the mode of utterance of the bearer of life. If one takes the term "expression" in so extended a sense that it also embraces linguistic utterance, then language would be the phonic expression essentially of features of appearance, and not, say, equally of the life-processes which an occurrence of appearance would have occasioned in the body of the recipient.

Even animal expressive sounds of man become constituent parts of language only by losing, through assimilation to pre-existing forms of language, their own expressive value, in order thenceforth to signify now the state of which they were an expression, now an utterance of it. Thus we may perhaps find, in the interjectional "ach," certain states of feeling expressed at least somewhat similarly to kindred states of feeling, for example in weeping; but the word "ächzen" [to groan] derived from it (in Greek similarly pheuzein, aiazein, achesthai) has, like every word, a content of meaning which the kinship of sound with possible sounds of lament — a kinship we still feel into it — would by no means suffice to make audible out of the word. More on this presently.

In view of this, and in order to bar the way to the still occasionally haunting "bow-wow theory" of the origin of language, it is better not to call language expression at all, but rather phonic representation of units of meaning, or, with reference to a very original state that would not yet bear the traces of millennia-long collaboration by spirit, more boldly, say, a phonic mirror of characters of appearance.<sup>86</sup> In any case, however, names are not expressions of the state of the speaker, but expressions of meaning, which of course can also serve to communicate the [p. 1153] state of the speaker incomparably more thoroughly than would happen with mere expressive sounds. — As, in the precedence of the name over expression, the preponderance of the working of the soul over the working of the body appears, so, in the correlative precedence of image-characters over corporeal appearances, the preponderance of beholding over sensing shows itself. From the ensuing independence of the gift of intuition follows that inclination and capacity — peculiar to man alone — for the consolidation of world-characters into images, whose significance was appreciated in Chapter 35.

<sup>86</sup> On page 1152. — The fundamental distinction between movements that involuntarily express and movements that involuntarily represent was carried out by us in our work "Ausdrucksbewegung und Gestaltungskraft," which first appeared in 1917. For the theory in general, compare chapter 5, headed "Das persönliche Leitbild" (in the *3rd* and 4th editions of 1923, pp. 92–106), and for its application to language, especially chapter 7, headed "Die Gestaltungskraft," pp. 146–192.

If we now set the ideological schema beside it, we read off without further ado the following "events": 1. The connection between name and meaning was sundered. The finding of the concept presupposes, then, the splitting-off of the name's meaning, or the abolition of that connection by virtue of which the original speech-sound formed, with its meaning, a two-poled whole. 2. With this the name has become a relatively arbitrary sign, merely attached to the concept and consequently subordinate to it. 3. Units of meaning are experienced, and with them the characters of appearance that are "mirrored" in them; states of affairs, insofar as they are "conceived," are not experienced: consequently there was likewise sundered the connection of meaning and character of appearance; and it is in principle immaterial whether one illustrates the thesis, that the founding of a relation requires the prior abolition of connections, by the devaluation of the weaving-power of the intuitive image, or by the devaluation of the weaving-power of the name. We shall concern ourselves first chiefly with the weaving-power and devaluation of names, then chiefly with the world of appearance, without, however, sharply separating the two. Language and elemental actuality. — As has been mentioned several times, there appear periodically, in the intellectual history of the West, thinkers who hope to gain new insights, or to secure ones already gained, by taking literally the names which they need for the utterance of essential thoughts. However many erroneous derivations of words may play a part in this, one need only recall the pre-Socratics, the Romantics, Nietzsche, to see confirmed the proposition — surmisable on general grounds — that it is the most strongly biocentric thinkers who are quite properly "fettered" by language. But [p. 1154] what perhaps deserves our attention to an even higher degree is the circumstance that language itself manifests a similar belief in its own hidden knowledge; for which at least one example may be offered (on the basis of the German dictionary of Paul and the etymological one of Kluge).

"Name" is a word proper to all Germanic and Indo-European (IE) languages, "of the highest antiquity and the widest distribution." To it correspond Old Saxon namo, Dutch naam, Anglo-Saxon noma, nama, English name, Old Norse nafn, Gothic namo, Old Slavic ime, Old Prussian emmens, Old Irish ainm, Sanskrit nama, Greek onoma, Latin nomen. The probable source, perhaps of all, in any case of most, formations is the IE root gnō (Greek gno-, cf. English to know), "so that 'recognition' would be the basic meaning of the word." So far Kluge. As the Greek logos means now word and speech, now book and writing, now deliberation, reason, and therefore in New Testament Greek even serves to designate the embodiment of God in the Son, so the derivation of the word "name" would point to an original identity of meaning with cognition. That in fact "being named" and "naming" were among other things understood in the sense of a making-present of essence is confirmed by the following linguistic usages, each of which leads us back to the stage of word-magic: in Middle High German (according to Paul) wibes name designates the female sex, likewise Mannesname the male; whoever speaks "in the name" of the king, of the law, of God, holds not only the right but even the power to accomplish everything that the king, the law, indeed God, would accomplish; "in the name" of supposedly higher powers, conjurations and magical performances therefore took place; sanctification of the name is sanctification of the named; a "great name" means fame, and consequently a power reaching far beyond the life of its bearer. — With such turns of phrase, which could be further multiplied, the name attests the life-content of — the name.

In order to give some notion of the leading role of language in the formation of all units of meaning, we must above all recall the leading role which language occupies, even now, despite the effort of spirit to withdraw from its embrace, for the development of thinking. In his "Völkerpsychologie," Wundt remarks at one point that the question "whether reason or language was the earlier" has "as little sense as the famous disputed question, whether the egg or the hen was earlier." He has scarcely considered here that the question of the priority of egg or hen, before it became a jesting question, was a mystes' question [p. 1155] to which the initiate was able to give a very definite answer (of which we shall hear more in the concluding section). The reader doubtless correctly surmises what answer the author would have to give to this question, and he already knows our answer to the first: languages were long present before man began to think, the condition for which we today call now reason, now understanding.

These two names are especially instructive. Vernehmen [to perceive/apprehend] (whence Vernunft, reason) originally means "to become aware of" in general (one "vernahm" the wind, "vernahm" the darkness) and was then restricted to becoming aware by hearing; and Verstehen [to understand] (whence Verstand, understanding) referred chiefly to the grasping of sentences, as indeed we still say that someone "understands" a foreign language. The two names, then, which in everyday usage, at least of German, at present best render the core sense of the already more learned word "faculty of judgment," proceed from the audibility of contents of meaning, as though thinking were a consequence of speaking and not, say, the reverse!

It would lead us here away from our subject were we to attempt to depict how pre-rational primal languages of mankind may have looked. It is more than probable that we would call them sung speech, could we hear them; but certain, that it was images which, in the medium of the beholding soul, created for themselves the sound-body that was itself again a happening; in relation to which the expression of whatever feelings could only ever play a partly furthering, partly hindering subordinate role. Metaphysically this would remain simply incomprehensible unless one resolved upon the assumption that it is noises and sounds in which the elemental souls themselves most immediately express themselves; hence, for example, the merely colored, or even over-emphatically figural, appearance lags somewhat behind the sounding one in immediate primal-image content, it being understood, given equal "potency" of both. A pre-rational primal language would accordingly be more comparable to what later detached itself from it as song than is our present-day language; and assuredly poetizing is the primordial creativity out of which the impulses to formation have only later become differentiated, and from which each of them is secretly nourished so long as it has not yet become wholly artified and stunted into an "aesthetic" matter of the brain. Music, too, has branched off from song (in the meantime to suffocate more and more in the airless space of abstraction).

If accordingly the whistling were not at all peculiar to the wind, the soughing to the treetops, [p. 1156] the roaring to the sea, but rather were the "language" of the air, of the tree, of the sea, this would not mean that this "language" wishes or is able to be imitated by the language of man. The most authoritative representatives of present-day linguistics would scarcely withhold their assent if we maintained the proposition: so-called sound-imitating words have, for the formation and development of languages, by far not the significance that one was formerly inclined to ascribe to them, and are above all, essentially, not what the designation "sound-imitation" seems to suggest.

There are ventriloquists and variety-artists who can imitate the crowing of the cock, the scarcely describable noise of the plane, the "song" of the nightingale so deceptively that every listener at once recognizes the noise meant; but no genuine speech-sound accomplishes the same. We understand readily enough why, in Japanese children's speech (according to Wundt), kokko means hen, yet find the German children's word "gackgack" no less fitting; and had we been told konkon instead of kokko, it would likewise have seemed credible to us, and we should by no means have heard in it that the Japanese children mean by it — coughing. "Bim-bam" or "bim-bam-bum" seems to us strangely fitting for the ringing of bells; but the Manchu finds that bells say kilang-kalang.<sup>87</sup> This series could be continued endlessly.

<sup>87</sup> On page 1156. — *Georg* von *der Gabelentz*, Die Sprachwissenschaft (Leipzig 1891), p. 164.

As has long been known, and was already partly documented in the first book, speech-sounds moreover symbolize by no means only noises, but also phenomena of movement. If one compares, in German, only the following verbs, certainly of sound-symbolic origin: stolpern [to stumble], flattern [to flutter], (flink [nimble]), schlottern [to shake/totter], humpeln [to hobble], baumeln [to dangle], bummeln [to saunter], knutschen [to smooch/crush], kribbeln [to tingle/crawl], krabbeln [to crawl], rempeln [to jostle], torkeln [to stagger], lodern [to blaze], klimpern [to jingle/tinkle] — or the following, in which sound-symbolism is at least interwoven: schnüffeln [to sniff], kratzen [to scratch], scharren [to scrape], zerren [to tug], sausen [to whizz], zausen [to tousle] — one at once convinces oneself that the inner belonging-together of each with the process meant forces itself upon us no less compellingly than that of the sound-imitating words with the sounds meant. Conversely, we do not hear, in the very pictorial "zupfen" [to pluck], that it was derived from "Zopf" [braid/plait], a sound whose meaning would scarcely allow the assumption of a like manner of origin.

Much is said of the euphony of poems, and poems do indeed possess euphony, if one sets beside it the prose of an official ordinance in the same language. Yet this euphony, though it does not [p. 1157] wholly vanish, vanishes to an estimated nine-tenths for one who does not "know" this language. If it is true, as surely no linguist doubts, that we correctly hear only the language we can also speak, then it is fully true that the euphony of one and the same sentence bears wholly different and immeasurably richer features for one who understands the language than for one who does not understand it. Finally, a glance at the so-called homonyms suffices to acquaint even one who has never before attended to it with the experience that, with the exchange of meaning, the character of what we mean to hear or read also changes. A few examples: Der Bauer pflügt das Feld / der Vogel singt im Bauer [The farmer ploughs the field / the bird sings in its cage] — Auf dem Grase funkelt der Tau / das Tau wird am Mastbaum festgemacht / das Tau ist ein griechischer Buchstabe [Dew sparkles on the grass / the rope is made fast to the mast / tau is a Greek letter] — Wer wüßte voraus das Geschick der Völker / sein Junge hat mehr Geschick als der meinige [Who could know beforehand the fate of the peoples / his boy has more skill than mine] — Ein schlimmerer Tor ist mir niemals begegnet / ich "durchwandelte sacht das Tor mit dem gotischen Bögen" [A worse fool I have never met / I "wandered softly through the gate with its Gothic arches"] — Die Blätter wehen im Winde / die Blätter der Linksparteien verurteilen diese Zollpolitik [The leaves blow in the wind / the newspapers of the left-wing parties condemn this tariff policy] — Es sind acht Pferde / geben Sie acht / er wurde in die Acht erklärt [There are eight horses / pay attention / he was placed under the ban] — Der dritte Band ist erschienen / ich brauche ein Band zum Verschnüren [The third volume has appeared / I need a ribbon for tying] — Er steht am Steuer / die Steuer wurde erhöht [He stands at the helm / the tax was raised] — Die Schale ist aus Ton / im Gesänge reiht sich Ton an Ton [The bowl is made of clay / in the song tone follows upon tone] — Ein Linsengericht / das Reichsgericht [A dish of lentils / the Imperial Court of Justice]. Who could fail to notice that each time we are literally compelled to hear differently! If, then, by word-sound is to be understood what phonetics understands by it, we may not hope to find the sense of the words in the sound of the words; and this now holds also of the so-called sound-imitating ones.<sup>88</sup>

<sup>88</sup> On page 1157. — *Wundt* speaks of "sound-imitations," of "soundimages," of "sound-gestures," of "pointing sound-gestures," and finally of "natural sound-metaphors." He holds that what is at issue is less sound-imitation than imitations *by means of* sound. Such, he says, are "movements which, in expressing the subjective feelings aroused by the impression, involuntarily also reproduce the very process that arouses the feeling." If such groping formulations are meant, so to speak, to leave several doors open, in truth they favor the confounding of functions that directly express with functions that involuntarily represent. Whoever conceives of feeling as something merely "subjective" can in no way make it intelligible to us how its expression should be capable of *reproducing* the "arousing process." Nor, moreover, does the capacity of speech-sounds to represent depend at all on the movements of speech, but on the intuitive image of the sounds thereby produced. Finally, without a knowledge of the fundamental manifoldness of the modes of appearance of beheld *characters*, it can of course never be explained how sounds could "reproduce" processes of quite a different kind, for example the process of tingling.

If already those visual images in which the preponderance of the gift of intuition manifests itself are, far from being comparable to photograms, rather representations of characters of appearance under a strong claim, to be sure, upon evident similarities, then this holds in an even far higher degree of formations whose material is furnished by the essentially temporal sounds and noises. If one wishes here too to seek similarities, for instance between the noise of the striking of drops in heavy rain and the word Pladdern [to patter], or between the experienced course-form of skin-sensations and the word Kribbeln [to tingle], one must first have reflected that one is here touching the very same mystery by virtue of which noises and sounds are the "language" of the — elements. Here we have a primal phenomenon that can be experienced a hundredfold and with overwhelming [p. 1158] certainty, but cannot be derived from anything still more original.<sup>89</sup> This does not, however, exclude that other kind of inquiry which pursues the relations of kinship among the various sides even of primal phenomena. Thus it can be shown, and was shown by us elsewhere, that the application of the units of meaning above and below, or height and depth, to tones is grounded in the opposition of the characters of brightness and darkness, that this in turn comes to appearance in the pointed and the broad (or blunt) as well as in the light and the heavy. Were we to add, say, that, other things being comparable, blue has more depth than green, or even yellow, then compounds like Klangfarbe [timbre] and Farbenklang [color-tone] would for us have finally ceased to be metaphors, and we would understand why one sound is related to another sound somewhat as green is to blue. If one considers finally that, apart from the epithets here adduced, the following too are predicated of sounds and tones in an immediately intelligible way: full and empty, soft and hard, thick and thin, smooth and rough, blaring and melting, one senses the immensity of the field that would still lie open, in the science of language, to the study of appearance. Only, this would presuppose the primal phenomenon not only of the kinds and degrees of kinship, but also of the capacity of noises and sounds to be, in principle, the nearest and mightiest form of revelation of the elements of the world.

<sup>89</sup> On page 1158. — This too should not be forgotten: even copies are appearances and thus always also image-appearances, even where they are already meant as thing-appearances. Only a being that was originally "appointed to behold" could degenerate into that spectator of the world and finally that gaper at the world who invented, among other things, — photography!

The discernible connecting link is called: similarity of rhythms. Elemental happening transforms itself, through psychic happening, into linguistic processes whose product brings the image-characters to phonic representation by means of melos, tempo, measure, stress, smooth or hard joining, fluency and isolation, etc. Even nature-sounds audible out of speech-sounds resemble the latter through kinship of character, and this in turn is produced less by identical partial tones than by, now manifest, now hidden, similarity of rhythms.<sup>90</sup> When the famous Ovidian verse:

<sup>90</sup> On page 1158. — Compare our work "Vom Wesen des Rhythmus." (See note 28.)

"Tamquam sint sub aqua, sub aqua maledicere tentant" — calls up before the soul the croaking of frogs, then the modest share of credit that is due, after all, to the word aqua recedes considerably behind the mighty effect of the twice-repeated sub aqua in the midst of a verse that compels every qua to be stressed and lengthened, and thereby also brings into play the echo of the preparatory tamquam. Thus a degree of vividness is attained that a merely prosaic use of the undoubtedly onomatopoetic ooaxare could scarcely have achieved.

[p. 1159] The magic of language, of which every great master of language, but in the highest degree the poet, disposes, consists in the renewal of primal sounds by means of a linguistic material that is separated by many millennia from the pre-rational sources of language. The How, unteachable and unlearnable, has nothing to do with bold new coinages, nothing with the seeking-out of antiquated words and turns of phrase, but rests on the readiness of elemental rhythms to follow. The ever predominantly spirit-conditioned logic of the sciences, the still more thoroughly spirit-conditioned teleologic of commerce, of trade, of law, of statutes, of officialdom, of the professions, of the estates etc., has engraved scar upon scar into linguistic material, has made it "rational" in the service of life-hostile interests, has sought to screw it down into a mere tool of an ever more swiftly working technique of communication. If nonetheless the genuine poet still, in even the latest languages, makes primal sounds resound, which snatch our soul out of the anxiety-dream of evil facticity into the actuality of images, then the ground of this possibility can lie only in the mystery of rhythm. The impossibility of signless thinking. — After this intervening consideration, further words are superfluous in support of the proposition that the beholding of images itself only first perfects itself in the elemental speech-sound. As to the ordinary impression there belongs an animal expression, so to psychic beholding there belongs either orgiastic rapture or the working of the soul that utters itself in rhythmic sung-speech; whereby at the same time the misconception is disposed of that speaking and languages were hatched out of wishes to communicate. If, accordingly, at the pre-rational stage, character of appearance and its representation through song-like sounds are bound to one another, then already at the stage of symbolic thinking the generative power of names predominates over that of the contents of experience, in accordance with which, in Fig. 12, the process runs from the apex more often to the left than to the right; and it predominates overwhelmingly in rational thinking, to be sure, insofar as this remains fettered by the will to truth.

Arrogance of spirit has brought up the tasteless phrase of the "poverty of language," and still keeps alive the fantastic view that there is a wordless thinking, indeed that language is comparable to a wardrobe in which the finished thought picks out the garment that suits it, sometimes after shorter or longer hesitation as to which material it had best choose, and not so rarely, [p. 1160] without having found the linguistic material that could serve it, to deck itself out festively. Since one occasionally finds similar nonsense maintained, if in other words, even in learned books on language, we may not well go around it. — Let it be remarked in advance that "wordless" and "speechless" would have to be replaced by "signless," insofar as one were to bring in the, admittedly soundless, sign-language of the deaf-mute or of primitives.

Mere apprehensions without thoughts about what is apprehended are possible, and can to a great extent co-determine the behavior of their bearer, even where the urge toward sayable reflection is not even vividly felt. Were one to wish to call this already a thinking, then one would have posited a kind of thinking to whose nature it would belong not to be put into language, and could in any case thereby ground no deficiency of language; for, at the moment of incipient judgment-formation, something could also be predicated of what was apprehended. But judgments without an inner linguistic form of the judgment neither exist nor will exist. — Toward explaining the tenacity with which a contrary belief has here and there managed to maintain itself, the following three remarks may contribute something.

Before, in the researcher, inventor, thinker, the thought that matters has been worked out, the spirit of the one thus inwardly active finds itself, with regard to it, in a preliminary state that lets now stimulating, now paralyzing moments relieve one another: trying, missing the mark, doing otherwise, wrestling down obstacles, circumventing the "insurmountable," and so forth. In other words, there constantly take place, in searching thought, impulses whose direction is co-determined by the not-yet-sightable goal of the thinking; but such characteristic experiential forms of an inspirited vitality are not for that reason any the less mere experiential forms, precisely because it is the strongest activity of the understanding that unavoidably needs them. (This holds, of course, all the more for strong efforts of spirit on the part of one endowed with a weak understanding!) One does not, after all, confuse motive and deed either! But every judgment that springs forth on the way to the goal, whether it be more a question or more a partial answer, is also inwardly spoken, and a eureka without sayability has never yet occurred!

Matters stand essentially otherwise with the supposedly speechless thinking that one might be tempted to insert between the thought and its most successful formulation. One succumbs to a self-deception in supposing that linguistic expression can be altered without altering [p. 1161] what it expresses. That holds true even for a thinking guided solely by the intention of comprehension — how much more so for biocentric thinking! If, for example, a name is unwittingly used that ought to be assigned to a different concept — even if the difference seems at first quite slight, as when for the concept of gravitation one says "the earth's force of attraction," or for that of the propagation of light "the motion" of light — a later exchange of names will unfailingly mean also an exchange of the old concept for a new one. — Indeed, the considerably shallower zone of merely reporting or demanding or entreating speech does not entirely escape the same principle. It is one and the same content of judgment that the following two sentences communicate: "Lying is forbidden" and "It is not permitted to speak untruth"; yet they are considerably different thoughts that present themselves in such different forms: there the imperative of a police regulation, here an educative admonition.

One may, incidentally, call "subtleties" of thought what first comes to light through "subtleties" of formulation; such "subtleties" grow into essentials in step with the growing participation, in the process of thinking, of a questioning that presses into depth, and they are quite simply decisive for the truths in which such questioning finds fulfillment. If, by contrast, under certain circumstances the linguistically most meager hint suffices to betray the campaign plan for the next day, or a technical invention, or the solution of a riddle-joke; if to the buyer of a commodity the bare statement of price, or to the accused a "two years' imprisonment" whispered before the pronouncement of the verdict, says as much as a sentence of the utmost formal perfection could no longer say — that speaks only for the extraordinary poverty of content of — purposive thinking, and for the once again admirable capacity of the word to satisfy its demands as well. For the rest, let us not forget that "striking" and "well-aimed" brevity which precisely and fully comprehends what wordiness would let slip.

Finally, it admits of no doubt that even the most linguistically powerful speaker lacks words for countless states. Yet here the matter always stands thus: if one can only think of such states, and by no means yet think about them, then they are simply unsayable; but what and how much one thinks about them, that and exactly that much one is unfailingly capable of expressing. We need by no means fall back here on the "awakenings," [p. 1162] "elevations," "illuminations" that so-called mysticism admittedly holds to be supra-conceptual, because the very same thing already holds, to some degree, of ordinary moods and especially ill-humors, and holds completely of countless contents of sensory experience. In most cases one will strive in vain to capture in a few words the particular smell of a house, or the fragrance of a flower whose name one does not know, the taste of some rarer dish, the timbre of a musical instrument, the newfangled color-tone of a silk fabric, the texture of a wood, the bark-quality of a tree, or to describe with anything like satisfying clarity a hitherto unfamiliar pressure in the stomach. And it was here that one of the strongest sources of language-forming creativity formerly lay, since the successful putting-into-words of a matter under consideration always goes somewhat ahead —

Every glance at the languages of primitives and semi-primitives confirms this. There, distinct names stand ready, and often in great number, not only for many varieties of birds, fishes, trees, but also for different parts and places of the arm, foot, leg, for different manners of walking, lying, sitting, standing, carrying, for different shadings or occasioning grounds of joy, terror, grief, for different kinds of cloudimages, rain-showers, sunshine, for countless particularities of rock formations, coastlines, river bends; for which reason research has again and again found occasion to marvel at the abundance of words in general, and especially at those words that we could only render with the help of whole descriptions.

Since, with the later increase of abstract names, the capacity for the actual "composition" of objects of intuition grew (objects that only thereby became "concreta" in the first place), the inclination toward the immediate vocalization of sensory data of experience receded more and more; hence, as one notices, the language-forming impulses of highly civilized peoples deviate considerably from those of primitive peoples. If we, then, faced with relatively unfamiliar sense impressions, are not seldom at a loss to express them adequately in language, this is in any case only owing to the preponderance of the conceptual content of our words and the compulsion, going along with it, to use them more or less thinkingly; from which it follows that, conversely, with the onset of comprehending orientation the words for it likewise immediately present themselves. There can thus be no talk whatever of a sub-linguistic or supra-linguistic thinking. — So much for that. [p. 1163] Manner of speaking and manner of thinking. — We come now to the propositions that carry forward this train of thought. Since every "activity of consciousness" occurs only through the coincidence of temporally unextended acts of spirit with life-processes, the question arises in every case of what such life-processes are constituted. If we understand by "thought-activity" an inner progression from judgment to judgment, now more in the form of doubt and question, now more in the form of answer, then the life-process immediately involved is evidently a virtual speech-process, or, taking also into account the soundless language of the deaf-mute, a process of virtual sign-giving; hence we must first of all establish that thought-activity requires speech-processes and would cease with the loss of every capacity for sign-giving.

We cannot expound this here and must content ourselves with a few indications of the extent to which numerous varieties — of leading and of accompanying thought-activity, including characteristic disturbances of it — might be derived from this and organized accordingly. Just as animal expression has, unintended, the incidental effect of communication, so a will to communicate accompanies linguistic representation almost at once, growing stronger and stronger toward it in the course of time; and just as communication in neither case belongs to the essence of the matter, so we must see in the communicative values of language its surface and outer layer, in relation to which the representable contents of meaning form an inner layer of many-graded depth, whose lowest and innermost contents of sense it may be given only to rare thinkers, as well as to seers and genuine poets, to bring to validity. Now the more the communicative values predominate in inner speech, the more thought-activity flattens out, and the strongest manifestation of this is the "hollow flood of words" or unending garrulity; but the more the representable values of meaning predominate, the more thinking deepens, and its form of utterance is not too seldom a weighty terseness, more often richness and a thought-bearing stream of speech. — Both kinds of thinking can now again be more or less steered, and the helm is held now chiefly by spirit, now chiefly by soul. If the former grows slack, there follows, among other things (!), the so-called idea-fleeing urge to speak, whose choice and sequence of words depends especially on shifting momentary impressions, among them virtually or actually heard sounds of the words; if the latter grows slack, there follows that profound stammering and murmuring in which madness and poethood can at times touch [p. 1164] one another. There is no centrally conditioned speech disorder that would not also, in some respect, be a disorder of thinking.

If we remain, however, with steered thinking that has no immediate communicative purpose, it has all the more the character of deep reflection the more it is guided by the symbolism of language, and all the more the character of an at best sharp but shallow reflection the more it is boundaries drawn by spirit that mark out the paths for its "course." If that former thinking leads, as it were, along mountain trails through dense forests, and not so seldom through untrodden thicket, this latter keeps to roads as straight as a die and lays them out with whatever equipment is required, wherever they are still lacking. In clearing and breaking ground, "empiricism" and "naturalism" distinguish themselves; in straightening and shortening roads over territory long since mapped, every kind of scholasticism and formalism does. But let us set the similes aside! Since mere boundaries, without that which is bounded by them, would be a nothing, no thinking, however conceptual, is capable of tearing itself free from language without itself becoming nothing. One comprehends in German, in French, in Latin, but one never comprehends in no language at all, and the deaf-mute, who lacks sounds, comprehends in virtual gestures.

The boundaries created by comprehension are, in turn, likewise "assimilated" by language, and have in this way at least helped to shape many habits of inflection, of the use of relational words, of sentence structure in general — habits whose mighty steering power over the thinking of the linguistic descendants is well known and has repeatedly been appreciated by us.<sup>91</sup> But however inseparably comprehending thinking may remain fastened to language, it "lives and has its being" only in its outermost layers, and draws its values of representation precisely from the communicative values, which in principle can be replaced by any sign whatever. In this way it must remove itself ever further from the images that originally, through the transmission of similar rhythms, had gained a sound-body not only in the name but even in the earliest forms of unfolding. Comprehending thinking and speaking for the sake of "communication" (!) are two sides of the same thing. Consciousness, says Nietzsche in his posthumous notes toward "The Will to Power," "is only a means of communicability: it is developed in intercourse and with a view to the interests of intercourse."

<sup>91</sup> On page 1164. — Were it otherwise, that science could hardly already, two and a half thousand years ago, have gathered its first fruits of knowledge which undertakes to abstract communicable rules from language and to translate its mighty growth into a logically articulated system — the science of grammar!

The technically, to be sure, immeasurable superiority of the language of having-comprehended over a language that "brings primal sounds to resound" is thus [p. 1165] in any case bought at the price of a loss in imagistic content of speech which, were there a common measure here for advantage and disadvantage, would appear far greater than the gain. If we consider, however, that language indeed bears from this a richly meshed network of traces, but has by no means died of it, nor even yielded to an artificial system of signs — which would, after all, still be an inheritance from it — but rather lives and continues to grow, albeit at a slackened tempo and in many ways fenced in, then we understand why among all the bequests of humanity's life there is none that could come even approximately close to it in the capacity to make present those remotenesses of the past which appear in "primal images." There is no receptive mind that would not feel the shudder of high antiquity before the Via Appia, the Pyramids, the menhirs of Carnac. But the antiquity that, in heightened moments, can waft upon the poet out of the now-living language is uncounted millennia older than tombs and dolmens and menhirs: for it reaches back, in unbroken growth, into a primeval time in which it was, among other things, truly the language of the elements, whose "voices" the one graced by its genius still hears out of it and utters by means of it! Thinking a kind of speaking. — But it is not only this that we wish to maintain, that no thought-activity of whatever kind occurs without virtual speaking, but beyond that, that thought-activity is through and through nothing but a manner and mode of speaking! Note well: a kind of speaking; whereby it is forbidden to invert the sentence. There are enough uttered as well as purely inward modes of speaking that have little or nothing to do with thought-activity. In poetry, thought can rise to its highest and most distant flights; but it can also fade to a phantom behind the round-dance of images, and in song it often vanishes entirely. Depictions and descriptions on the one hand, exhortations and commands on the other, are indeed always also something of thought; yet thought-activity in the narrower sense plays only a subordinate role in them. There is, further, an automatic reading-aloud, reciting, and especially an enumerating, during which the speaker's thoughts dwell on something quite different, not to mention the manifold cases of oral as well as written utterances of madness that consist of senseless strings of words, or even of mere fragments of names and echoes, of which it can often not be decided whether they have a meaning merely hidden from us [p. 1166] or stem from utterly meaningless impulses to speak. Only thus, then, is our proposition to be understood: among the manifold kinds of speaking there is to be found one for which the name "thinking" has, since ancient times, become customary.

That was certainly an advantage not to be underestimated, both in general and quite especially for the language of higher reflection, which could now without difficulty demarcate an inner speaking from outer speaking, and in turn single out, from within inner speaking, that speaking in which acts of spirit take part, now ruling, now serving. But it was also a disadvantage, because it first of all came to the aid of the opinion that thinking is not speaking but merely makes use of speaking, and then at least lent support to the false doctrine that thinking has no need of speaking either, and becomes all the "purer" a thinking the more it leaves language behind it. Here we have a truly monumental example of the fact that one and the same language, which endows with unerring truths the one who knows how to listen to its voices, is busily engaged in enmeshing, in hopeless errors, the arrogance of spirit that scorns it!

The further back we go in the history of humanity, and the more we draw in this connection on the at least partially kindred primitives, the closer we approach a state of soul for which everything we today call "inner life" stepped directly outward: now in shaping work upon stone and wood, reed and flax, metal and clay, together with the making of all tools and their use in the service of hunting, herding, and tillage; now in cultic ceremonies and the dance-orgies of festivals; now in the language of exchanged speech and of songs. One spoke, one sang, one kept silent; but only late and gradually did there grow up alongside this the silent "thinking." For it was only when the reign of spirit had succeeded in more and more dissolving the symbiotic bonds, and thereby inwardly isolating the individual tribal companion, that the imagined friend hesitantly presented himself, until he finally became a constant companion, an alter ego, the ever-present partner of the mute conversation!

Perfect poetic making, because entirely free of communicative purposes, is perfect monologue, or a duet with actuality, or else — and here it touches upon its limits — a dialogue of the singer with his own soul ("lyric"). Thinking, however, is the soundless dialogue of the I with the other I within the same person, and mostly indeed of a predominantly [p. 1167] speaking I with a predominantly listening I, and beyond that it is — nothing! No other people has thought so immoderately, so close to its prehistory, as the Greeks; yet scarcely any other was so addicted to conversation as this one. It is in truth no accident that a system of thought as vast in scope as the Platonic is presented in the form of conversations that unfold between sharply drawn speakers, often with almost dramatic accents! With the help of this ingenious device, Plato erected a monument from which we may read off that precisely the most sovereign of our thoughts are those speeches that remained victorious in disputation with the inner Peripatetic! Evidence for this development is found in<sup>92</sup> abundance. The typical man is more of a "thinker" than the typical woman; thus women more often think of something than about something, men usually the other way round; thus thinking about something, in the spirit of the woman, frequently proceeds from conversations that have really taken place, or shapes what is communicable with a particular person in view; and thus, under otherwise comparable circumstances, women even today are mostly superior to men in the writing of diaries and letters, mostly inferior in the writing of treatises.

<sup>92</sup> On page 1167. — Plato, incidentally, did not reach for the dialogue form merely involuntarily, but consciously and deliberately. Thinking, Socrates holds in the Theaetetus, is "a conversation which the soul carries on with itself about that which it examines," and it seems to do nothing else in thinking "than to converse with itself in question and answer, whereby it affirms and denies." "Hence," it continues, "I understand by opining a speaking, and by opinion a *speech* which, however, is spoken not to another ... no, in all stillness, to oneself."

We pass over, as shown elsewhere by us, that the interiorization of speaking received a mighty impetus from the invention of writing.
