But now that, for many centuries already, book and card-index and writing implement have belonged to the scholar as leather and lasts and awl belong to the shoemaker, that threesome has to some extent taken the place of the mute fellow-interlocutor: the proper scholar "discusses" it with the paper, and has forgotten that thinking is a dialogue without a second party. With this the knowledge has vanished entirely that, of the little the individual thinker adds to the store of thought of humanity, he owes by far the best of it to a language that thought through him. "To philosophize is to attempt an interpretation of word-magic." Language as the workshop of thought — Schiller's distich, in which he expresses that language composes and thinks on behalf of the versifier, holds in a deeper sense for the human being as such, and in a yet more particular sense for the greatest poets and thinkers. But these know it; the other usually does not. — If someone says the matter seems to him to be in order, he uses the same process-word that he uses to remark that today the sun is shining. Of the two essentially different meanings [p. 1168], the second is by far the more original. Let one consider now what a long road covert thinking had to traverse in order to get from the name for the shining of the sun, by way of the mere appearing of what is only apparent as against what is unrestrictedly real, to the use of this same name for the possibility or probability (modeled on the Latin verisimilis) of an existing or taking-place; and let one ask oneself whether a human understanding could ever have arrived at the sublime thought "it seems to me that" without the help of the name! But as here, so it goes in a thousand times a thousand cases: the meaning of the name itself, as its sound-body exchanges place after place, lets new meanings flash forth and endows the one virtually speaking with new — thoughts.

The linguists class "denken" [to think] as a factitive of "dünken" [to seem], and explain that its original meaning was in turn "to shine, to appear," so that the initial sense of "denken" was "to make something appear" (Kluge). The associations are, as far as we know, uncontested; but even should the threads run otherwise still, what recurs for us in any word whatever would remain unaffected by that, so long as we are able to accompany it far enough along the road to its origins: namely, the derivation of every noumenon from a phainomenon. The history of languages teaches us that no name that means something merely conceptual, no relational word however abstract, no prefix and suffix, no inflectional, intensifying, or generalizing ending, in short no distinguishable element of language, is to be found that would not at some earlier time have named the appearing state of affairs or, as we know it better, its character. Just as thinking is in fact and inescapably a kind of inner speaking, so that derivation of the German name for it locates its original sense in the generation of that very same appearing, out of which, through the reciprocal intercourse of the soul with it, every unit of meaning arose in primal beginning!

To bring further evidence for the descent of language from the world of appearance is superfluous; for on the one hand, in principle any word whatever can serve as an example; and on the other, it is no longer the fact itself that stands in need of proof, but its consequences. No one, for example, is any longer unaware today that "wissen" [to know] goes back to an Indo-European root wid, which means roughly "to see and find" (Skr. vid — to find, Gr. idein, Lat. videre = to see, Goth. vitan = to observe); but not everyone considers that, accordingly, original knowing would rest on finding out of an undergoing of images [p. 1169], and would thus be most nearly neighbored to Goethe's "intuitive power of judgment." But let a few classes of occurrence be recalled in passing, each of which at once makes it possible to demonstrate that development, as it runs on toward the more general, unintentionally eases for the deeds of spirit the construction of concepts that disavow their origin.

All attributions effected by genitives or adjectives, by which we today declare the properties of a bearer of properties, originally meant the property of an owner, of which an unmistakable residue lies in the linguistic usage of letting a state of affairs "have" its properties. (Instead of "the color of the leather is brown" we say with equal correctness "the leather has a brown color.") The generalization rests on the co-experiencedness of the character of a belonging-together of owner and owned (which among primitives is not seldom grasped as downright organic, for example in the joint destruction of all possessions along with the corpse of their owner), and the transference to the relation of part to whole, of property to substance, of effect to cause, and so on, was a discovery prefigured by language, whose bearing on the formation of symbolic units of meaning of a higher order can scarcely be overestimated. But as soon as deeds of spirit now follow, through which concepts arise, the tendency toward isolating the objects of thought in question is also there. No one would hit upon letting the owner consist of his possessions; but to sensualism the object of perception is a "bundle" of properties, to ideologism and formalism the world as such is — mysteriously enough — a system, become intuitable, of merely thinkable predicaments!

To a European who has never yet occupied himself with linguistics, the four to six (or, finally, even eight) cases of the Indo-European languages seem the natural thing, indeed almost the self-evident thing, and in particular the nominative and accusative seem the two pillars that bear the edifice of all possible "cases." Linguistics judges a little differently! That Chinese, for example, has no cases at all is, after all, already striking enough, though in the end it might not seem too significant, given a language that handles only uninflectable words, each consisting of a single syllable, and must therefore, among other things, place into the kinds of wordorder what we accomplish by means of inflections. But if a highly developed language such as Finnish disposes of at least 15 cases, among which of our cases only the genitive [p. 1170] occurs, or if Hungarian, presumably still more highly developed, among its roughly 21 cases in any case has neither nominative nor accusative, then the four to eight cases familiar to us first of all lose entirely the character of "self-evidence," and furthermore the weight that we involuntarily attach to the nominative and accusative becomes a problem — and indeed a very weighty one!

If we cast a preliminary glance at the abundance of cases which has its counterpart in numerous primitive languages, it becomes apparent that this abundance serves not at all to express those syntactic relations that we must be inclined above all to think of in this connection, but rather mirrors spatiotemporal connections: led thereby from the immediate intuitability of the overemphasized spatial, thanks to the co-experienced character of the images, to the merely mediate intuitability of the overemphasized temporal. It is the where, whither, whence, before-what, behind-what, beside-what, out-of-what, into-what, upon-what, under-what, throughwhat, with-what, together-with-what, away-from-what, and so on, then the simultaneous, the successive, the while, the earlier, the later, further the when, the until-when, the sincewhen, the how-long, the how-short, and so on, that is originally marked by such cases; and it is, in turn, discoveries occasioned as a linguistic consequence, by force of which some of these cases come to be applied, for example, to the relation of an achieved result to that by which it was attained, or still more generally to the relation of the supposedly effected to the supposedly effecting state of affairs — applications each of which is accompanied by the fresh acquisition of a unit of meaning.

Even into the four most usual of our purely grammatical cases there play, as has long been established, residues of the memory of the co-presence of spatiotemporal relations, of which our prepositions tell us without any recourse to the history of language. One could write a deep-probing chapter merely to mark the main stages of the creative events thanks to which the following three prepositions gained, in addition to their initially merely intuitive values of meaning, which still persist today, values of a high degree of abstractness: durch [through], von [from, of], and in [in]; but we must forgo that here.<sup>93</sup>

<sup>93</sup> On page 1170. — If we here give at least a hint of the course of meaning of "in," this is because precisely this preposition furnishes a contribution that is not only uncommonly forceful but also exceedingly transparent, both for the building activity of language and for the dismantling activity of spirit. We confine ourselves, however, to marking a few main stages, and refer otherwise to the admirably arranged compilations in *Paul*'s dictionary. If one sets alongside local uses such as: in the water, in the air, in the ether, in the earth, into space, into the tunnel, into the forest, or further: in the lecture, in the treatise, in the book; and temporal ones such as: in a year, in the night, in the future, in old age, already in the Middle Ages quite abstract ones such as: in good circumstances, in need, in doubt, in jest, in deed, or even: in general, all in all; and then passes on to expressive ones such as: to fix in view, to keep in view, to catch the eye, and further to the distinctly psychical ones such as: to carry someone in one's heart, to put something into someone's head, in spirit, in mind, in the mind's disposition, in fancy, in memory, etc. — then it should not really be hard to read off, from the still-living meanings of the one little word "in," an entire network of paths and cross-paths that the human spirit has traversed since time immemorial. Here we call to mind once more the fateful consequences of the detaching of the object of thought from the pictorial content of the unit of meaning, out of which the comprehending consciousness lifted it by means of delimitation; restricting ourselves, however, to the "in" that governs the dative. The primordial "in" means the being-within of something corporeal in something corporeal: the fish is in the net, the water in the hose, the hut in the kraal. The transfer to space at first makes no exception to this, inasmuch as space that is simply "empty" is a late thought, which the creation of "in," or of equivalent forms, preceded by millennia. Nor, at the prehistoric stage, is any reinterpretation of time as an extension needed in order to apply spatial data to temporal relations, because space and time are by no means yet objects of thought, but rather, in the appearances of happening, the spatial is filled with *history* along with the temporal. The *character* of the encompassing may, finally, even be attributed to the "heart," the "head," and further to the mind, the sense, the memory, in relation to the experiences undergone and especially to the intuitive images of this heart, head, mind. But once, through the splitting and delimiting deeds of spirit, the body has been conceptually *severed* from space, space from time, and each of the three from the soul, etc., then, apart from the first-named use of "in," all the remaining ones become improper uses, and there is now need of reflection upon the *meaning-content* of the *name*, so as not to fall into ghastly false doctrines! We do not repeat what, precisely with reference to "in," has already been said at several places in the work, and call to mind only once more that most reckless folly which lurks at the end of the path of logocentric misconstruals of the content of "in": consciousness, although it is supposed to be spaceless, is the space-like encompassing in which the universe sits; or: the universe together with its "history" is a — content of consciousness; or: in place of the being-within of bodies within a larger body, there has stepped the being-within of all bodies and spaces in something absolutely non-spatial, man himself included, whose body, too, is after all merely an inmate of consciousness. With the help of the preposition "in," spirit has managed to have the cosmos swallowed up by nothingness!

The seat of origin of the opposition between nominative and accusative lies far elsewhere, namely at just that point where — presumably a little earlier — the opposition between noun and verb arose. One is scarcely guilty of exaggeration in generalizing: to the sharpness and distinctness with which, in a given group of languages, the one opposition [p. 1171] attains expression, there corresponds an equal or nearly equal sharpness and distinctness in the expression of the other. Instead of starting out from two important findings of linguistics, we shall place them at the end of a short path of thought that rises up to them, as it were vertically, from deeper strata.

"Essentially meaningful is the interconnection of the distinguishable members of a manifold, and the most original manifold is a twofold. The going-back to this twofold, far from following any mere arbitrariness of dividing and counting, is demanded by the polarity of appearing actuality to the soul that experiences it — a polarity without which there would be no concept of a living being, and then also none of a thinking being." From these sentences, with which our far-ranging consideration, on page 251, of the difference between the living and the mechanical process approached its end, it becomes at once intelligible why the pre-rational speaker must already have come into the position of discovering appearance in relation to beholding, or the world of intuition in relation to the bearer of life, and of finding the polar primal twoness. This, then, also occurred early, and carried the thought of reciprocal intercourse — not only of the strange person with one's own person, but quite generally of efficacious and fructifying daemons with the souls opened to and receiving their working — a duality that is found, more or less, in all the cults of prehistory, and not least in the mysteries of antiquity. But a strange fate has willed it that it was not the same glance of the soul that opened the gates of language to the Janus-headed twin-form!

We call it Janus-headed because the two states of affairs that meet together in it are polarly connected with one another only in that they are, at the same time, estranged from one another (cf. Chapter 26). The peoples bearing the far more numerous group of languages, for whose formation interconnection predominated, were, it seems, for all the depth certainly to be credited to them on that account, afflicted with a certain dullness that did not let them penetrate through to the full experience of polar reciprocity, but let them remain instead in the basic feeling of a more oppressive dependency on the world. Thus arose those formations and usages, met with a hundredfold by the linguist, by which the conception of being-determined asserted itself not merely for the expression of feeling, sensing, and beholding, but for the whole doing and forbearing of human beings.

[p. 1172] The few examples here — multipliable into the immeasurable, and offering, incidentally, very different secondary features, from a consideration of which we abstain — are meant to do nothing more than illustrate for the reader, at least to some degree, the sense of that formative motive. — As was mentioned in Chapter 26, Greenlandic avoids describing processes with names for activities; but it goes further and even depicts activities with names for processes. Not content with that, the depictions of process actually consist of a noun with a possessive suffix; thus instead of "I weep," more exactly "my tear." Literal translations remain, of course, always only attempts at approximation, but they show what matters. We take the following in part from Finck's "Main Types of Linguistic Structure." Instead of "I kill him" it reads, approximately, "he dies to me"; instead of "I throw it away," approximately "it flies away from me"; instead of "I hear," as exactly as possible "to-my resounding"; instead of "I hear him," equally exactly "resounding-of-him mine"; instead of "I procure for myself something suited to a fishing-line," something like "fish-implement-suited-attainment-mine." Likewise frequently in the Melanesian linguistic region, among the Athapascans, in the Quechua language. Here, for example, "carried I" (literally) can be translated both as "I am carried" and as "I have carried," when nearer determinations of the carrier and the carried are lacking (Wundt after Müller). Turkish does indeed have active forms, but even its verbs are partly nominal, partly participial in character: instead of "I love," "you love," and so on, roughly "loving I," "loving you," and so on. Similarly in Finnish: "my loving" in the sense of "I love." Astonishing evidence can be adduced from Basque: to go = in the going, I go = I am in the going, you carry me = I am in the being-carried by you.

Since here, and in countless kindred cases, the conception of process — admittedly unmistakable — is dominated by the feeling of being-determined by something, it not only overgrows, now to some degree, now completely, the conception of activity, but even lets the event-character of the process step back, more or less, behind the state of that to which the event happens. But a mirror of actuality that throws back all events according to the measure of the states of the bearer of life, and that even brings out of the impulse-experiences almost only their undergoing-nature, testifies to disproportionately emphasized feelings of dependency on the world, and can therefore hardly reflect with sufficient clarity the reciprocal intercourse between soul and world.

[p. 1173] What had not succeeded here succeeded elsewhere and in an essentially different way. There occurred a linguistic event tragic, in a certain sense, for "world history": it was not the soul that, in being estranged, affirms interconnection, but the soul that is certain of its estrangement within interconnection and is goaded from undergoing to promethean venture, that found that twin-form; but it found it by exchanging the essence of the poles, making of the suffering pole a pole that attacks in retaliation, and of the acting pole one to be attacked! The primal sense of the nominative, or the naming case, is the bearer of the will to deed; the primal sense of the accusative, or the target-case, is the counter-world of that bearer's volitions. Nowhere was the work made easier for spirit; for only a single further step is needed, and the nominative has become the real "subject," the accusative the real "object" — which confirms for us anew, to our astonishment, how little it was chance that grammar names the arbitrary sentencebearing word precisely subject, and the arbitrary target of the activity to be predicated of it precisely object! The separation of the two cases thus goes hand in hand with a clear separation of noun from verb, and this in turn presupposes the use of a verb that has at least begun to mean, not so much processes or states, as activities. However manifold, then, the data of spatial intuition that once again play in at the start, they have henceforth to subordinate themselves to the determinations of an incipient willing.

Leaving the Chinese aside, whose monosyllabic language stands, in several respects, on a leaf by itself, it is really only two groups of peoples that brought the opposition of noun and verb to its sharpest expression: the bright group of the Indo-Europeans and the dark group of the Semites; and precisely in the languages of these two, the naming-case and the target-case are likewise distinguished with the utmost sharpness, and actually form the pillars of declining thought.<sup>94</sup> With this we have reached the one of the two linguistic findings to which we wished to ascend from below. But the other, too, is already there unspoken. We need only think of Latin to obtain, as answer to the question why the form of the neuter so often coincides with that of the accusative, a rule that holds for most Indo-European languages. The answer runs: because the neuter was originally (among other things) the real object or target of personal working, and hence, like the target-case, is the passivus, in relation to which the nominative, as real subject, represents the activus (or ergative). — [p. 1174] Finally, one more example from the realm of suffixes. The independent word corresponding to the ending "-heit" meant, in Middle High German, "state" and also "constitution"; in Old High German, "rank, standing," also "person," and it goes back, together with "heiter" [bright, serene], to a root-word for "gleam, shine," also "to see"! The course of the development of meaning, exceedingly similar to that of shining, thinking, and knowing, from the concretely intuitable, by way of its character, to a kind of characteristic quality in general, lies within the field of operation of symbolism. But the much higher generality that follows upon the transformation of the word into a mere word-ending was also originally experienced, and was at first not so much the abstraction that hovers before us today with beauty, truth, wickedness, and so on (similarly with the words in "-keit" or "-schaft"), as the somewhat divine power from which this proceeds and which bestows, for good or for ill, what appears in the individual instance of beauty, truth, wickedness, and so on. Even out of collective names in "-heit" such as "Menschheit" [mankind] a residue of something distinctively proper to the human being is still more audible than out of mere generic names like animal or human or plant.

<sup>94</sup> On page 1173. — Naming-case and goal-case can of course be expressed somehow in most, if not all, languages (for example through word order, which has indeed remained essential even within the Indo-European family); but it does not follow from this that corresponding case-forms must already be present. Further, there are indistinct formations which occupy a middle position between the wholly unformed and the sharply formed. Thus in not a few languages nominative and accusative are marked off by special particles, or even by suffixes, when names for living or active or otherwise significant beings are concerned, but coincide with the word-stem in the case of all names for lifeless or insignificant beings. Here too, of course, there can as yet be no talk of the *sharpest* formation of both case-forms.

The most important reasons for this have become known to us in the course of the work, but let them here still be supported by a few strong pieces of evidence. If the first step of spirit, in order to take possession of precisely such classes of meaning, consisted in personifying them, then their nature and origin is nonetheless attested by the exceedingly remarkable circumstance that spirit was compelled to assign to these quasi-persons, overwhelmingly, one and the same of the two sexes. Why precisely the feminine is one of those questions of linguistics, to be passed over here, that find their solution only on the ground of metaphysics. To be sure, we form neuter abstracts en masse, now out of process-words, by prefixing the infinitive with "das," now out of adjectives, again by means of "das." But if we succeed in making a "proper" noun out of such a neuter, it is of feminine and never of masculine gender!

A few examples. Das Gute [the good, neut.] or die Güte [goodness, fem.], das Harte or die Härte [hardness], das Rote or die Röte [redness], das Warme or die Wärme [warmth], das Kalte or die Kälte [coldness] each denote general objects of nearly the same scope. Ordinary usage tends to alternate between such formations and those in "-heit": die Wärme, not die Warmheit; die Wahrheit [truth], not die Wahre; yet their fundamental equivalence also emerges alongside this in double forms: thus instead of "Schönheit" [beauty], in poetic language, at times —

[p. 1175]

#### 67. Kapitel — Vom Wesen der Wirklichkeit — Chapter 67 — On the Essence of Actuality

*Actuality as a singulare tantum.* — We devise a curious objection, one that may, however, seem to not a few readers not so curious at all. If actuality itself is to attain to phonic representation through the transmission of similar rhythms in the sounds of speech, how could thousands of different languages then arise? How can the same speech-sound have quite different meanings in one language? And finally, how would transferences still be possible, when the new sounds would no longer represent the same images?

We could make it easy for ourselves by recalling that this capacity for representation was, after all, claimed only for a pre-rational stage of language-creating processes. To be sure, such processes did not entirely cease even later, but fell into the minority as against formative motives from already spiritualized strata of the feeling for language. We could further recall that actuality also includes the ever-individual soul of the language-former, whose speech-sound, even at the greatest adequacy of appearance in its contact with the world, would nonetheless have to diverge from that of another soul, because in both the image-characters themselves turned out differently. Such considerations carry weight, but would for the moment scarcely be of use to us. For at once the question would arise by what standard, under such circumstances, the actuality-content of speech-sounds is to be judged. We must reach further back and dig deeper.

Not only the objection, but also what has just now been tentatively advanced to refute it, stands on the ground of the belief in a actuality of objects, and knows nothing of a actuality of images. If we hold the two turns of phrase "actuality of objects" and "actuality of images" side by side, measuring the sense of the one against the sense of the other, then the thought that would of course at once present itself — the [p. 1176] ... at times "die Schöne" [the beautiful woman], just as in the artistic German of the newest philosophy, alongside "die Ganzheit" [wholeness] from the particle "ganz" [whole], there is also "die Gänze" [entireness]. And this has now occurred, presumably similarly, in all the Indo-European languages, but in exactly the same way in Greek and Latin (together with their daughter languages). The following names, out of the unsurveyable series of cases belonging here, denote, according to choice, either objects of thought of a high degree of generality (in which case they were written with a small letter) or goddesses: Sophrosyne, Nike, Demokratia, Dike, Aretae, Eleutheria, Hybris, Themis, Nemesis, Galene, Eirene, Eunomia — Natio, Veritas, Justitia, Fortuna, Virtus, Aequitas, Libertas, Clementia, Prudentia, Pietas, Fides, Juventas, Pudicitia. We shall return to this in the final section.

The further progressions of spirit have become known to us. They lead from Plato's reified concepts bearing the name "Ideas," by way of the "universals" of the so-called realists of the Middle Ages, through the complete splitting-off of the aura of meaning, to objects that are now merely thinkable, whose actuality-content evaporates as they disintegrate either, sensualistically, into the compulsory misinterpretations of sense-data that are themselves again inexplicable, or, spiritualistically, into products of spirit. In both cases, as one observes, the origin, both of these objects themselves and especially of the values attaching to them, is relocated into the subject; of which the worst variety runs as follows: beautiful or ugly is what someone, or more often a group of persons, "finds" beautiful or ugly; true or false, what a group of persons is pleased to hold for such; right or wrong, what strikes them so. One seeks today to avoid such subjective turns of phrase; but relativism and formalism have raised this very same subjectivism to the principle of the explanation of the world. — With this our exposition of the actuality-content of language is by no means concluded; but the still-missing final piece requires such far-reaching preparations concerning the nature of actuality that we shall traverse it more quickly if we now proceed from the opposite side: from the actuality-content of the world of appearance and its devaluation through the activity of spirit. [p. 1177] ...the difference between things and intuitive images would by no means suffice to open up the sense of the second turn of phrase, before we had also thought through the difference of that which, in both cases, recurs under the same name, under the name "actuality." To be sure, hardly anything else remains for us than to attribute "actuality" at least to the things of perception as well, because those concepts of being by which we refer to their being-real are directly co-occasioned by the appearances, and stand out thereby sharply from the nothing-but-objects-of-thought, whose relation to what is real is mediated by an often long series of intermediate links; but to equate the things of perception with actuality on that account would mean: to confuse the product with one of the two conditions of its production, namely the vital condition, and to suppress entirely the at least equally important second condition, namely the spiritual one.

Because the appearance of the forest that one approaches from afar continually and softly changes, and becomes wholly and essentially different upon entering it, it is easy to set forth, and easy to grasp, why the forest as thing and the appearance of the forest are two different matters. But the threshold of understanding a doctrine of the "actuality of images" has been crossed, in the first instance, only by one for whom the appearing forest and the forest as thing fall apart — or, more exactly: for whom the actualities that come to appearance in the images of what is called "this forest here" fall apart from the one and selfsame thing that is likewise so called. For only now is it a different actuality that appears as referable to "this forest here" from afar, and a different one that appears as referable to it from nearby. "The forest here," as one and the same from afar and from nearby, is at best perceived; "the forest here," as a change of innumerable actualities between distance and nearness, is at best experienced, undergone, beheld on the occasion of perceiving; to the former the bearer of perception is related, while with the latter, or better with its changing actualities, the bearer of beholding is bound up.<sup>95</sup>

<sup>95</sup> On page 1177. — We began this work by setting apart appearing actuality and existence, and had to convince ourselves, right at the threshold, that it is not existing things that appear, even though it is existing things that in principle always co-depend on appearances, and, as it has meanwhile emerged, even on the corporeality of appearances. None of the manifold sides of the intuitable world seemed so well suited to this as the visible evidence of the eyes. But so long as one chooses spaces whose distances can be canceled out by motion, by drawing, for instance, on the difference between the "views" of a tree or a tower or a mountain (cf. chapter 2), the thought all too easily remains stuck in the concept of the difference between thing and appearance, and falls back, before one is aware of it, into the error that it is, after all, in the end the things that are perceived by means of intuitive images and especially by means of the visible evidence of the eyes — whence, indeed, they also bear the name "things of perception." Only when one brings cosmic ranges of the eye into play does actuality and existence, or, that is to say, *the* actuality that appears, part inexorably from the so-called actuality of things. For this, an example remarkable also for other reasons shall here be offered. Appearances of, as it were, vertiginous distances can be released from the soul by means of the sense of sight at every glance into the sparkling splendor of stars of a winter sky — mighty already in their effect when we take what we see for lights that greet us out of the depths of space, mightier still when we take them for "worlds." Our account of the psychical consequences of "Copernican space" has left no doubt that even astronomical thoughts of this kind can be "assimilated" by such an experience, and then deepen that "deceptively remote distance" still further. But because the actuality of the stars has, now, the peculiarity of appearing to us only insofar as we see them, it allows the direct demonstration of the *spatio-temporal separability* of what appears to us in the visual image from the things by which we suppose ourselves led to think these very visual images. Here, however, the discussion is not of the bodilessness of visible appearances, nor even of the phantasms of dream-seeing, but of the spatio-temporal disparateness of the — as it has been put — "seen-thing" and the so-called real thing; and this becomes, so to speak, palpable to us when we reflect that no mortal has yet seen what the calculating astronomer understands by Saturn, by Orion, by the Omega Nebula! We do not know whether the conception, which for a time became popular and which must be touched on here, is still expounded to schoolchildren today. Among the older generation, however, there will scarcely be anyone who does not still recall the astonishment with which he listened to the following explanation by his teacher: from such and such a star, the "ray of light" takes ten years to reach the earth; thus, in perceiving the star, we see not its present existence but its existence as it was ten years ago; there are also stars from which the light has been on its way for two thousand years (nowadays even ones estimated to be some three million light-years distant); these could meanwhile long since have crumbled to dust, and yet we should still see them; and so it would be given to us to *perceive* distant pasts, perceiving them no differently than we perceive the wall of our room! Here we can take hold, right at the root, of the confusion of two actualities, one appearing and one necessarily thought in addition. We have shown: whatever is at all capable of appearing to us, and quite especially the visible evidence of the eyes, is framed by the empirical now. For the space of intuition, from moment to moment, is indeed the appearance of the — moment, and, to be sure, only for that reason actually bears this determination of time, because and insofar as it forms the "cross-section" of that co-experienced happening, participation in which alone makes possible the *intuitability* of processes and movements. Just as certainly, then, as only ever the present becomes intuitable to us, just as certainly is an objectively past thing never perceived. If we proceed, then, from the assumption that the astronomical stars are the "actually real" stars, it is unshakably certain that we, in any case, never "get to see" them! Rather, what we "behold" in *relation* to them, whether with the naked eye or with instruments, would be — spoken in the language of physics — their "projection" onto the space of intuition, or still more clearly their "projection onto the space of the now," and thus, under all circumstances, something now-present, which sees itself separated by unimaginable spaces and times from the stars that are objects of thought. If we already give thought-room to light-years, then it is literally out of "deceptively remote" distances (Platen) that the stars sparkle; for these distances neither form a possible object of our perceiving, nor have they the least to do with the distances in which, occasioned by the perception of constellations, even distances of the past can — appear — to us! — Were we, however, to arrive at the stars of astronomy, then what would *then* appear to us, thanks to the (possible) co-participation of experiences of hearing, of smelling, of temperature, of touch, of movement, etc., would differ almost beyond comparison from the *merely* visually apparent appearances of before, such that only on the strength of a belief with which spirit burdens us — the belief in the actuality of objects — would what then appears to us be taken for the same actuality as what had appeared to us before, but never on the strength of the contents of experience!

Even perception, to be sure, presupposes for fractions of a second a connectedness; but this, before it has even become a recollectable experience, falls prey to the cleaving deed of the spirit and finds itself, scarcely arisen, already detached from the discriminating state-of-being-related; and such cleavage and separation is one and the same with that which tears the inner speech-sound, and hence thinking, away from the magical sphere of efficacy of the soul, thereby transforming the bearer of beholding into the bearer of a consciousness [p. 1178] which, driven as it now is to want to "comprehend" the world of perception, seeks to master it by violent intervention. It is therefore not a matter of the multiplicity of appearances, but of the multiplicity of the actualities that appear in them: it is this that is meant by the "actuality of images."

Linguistics has coined the term "collectives" for names whose singular denotes a multiplicity, such as servantry, library, grove, crowd, army, brushwood, people; the term pluralia tantum for names which, despite a singular meaning, occur only in the plural, such as castra = the camp, litterae in the sense of a record, letter, message, or "Pfingsten" [Whitsun], which in point of linguistic form is a dative plural; but it has not likewise formed a "singulare tantum," which, strictly speaking, would be a name of only singular form with a plural meaning. Grammatically singular names there are enough of: on the one hand proper names, on the other such as: the will, the world-all, the universe; yet these have at most a collective, not however a plural, sense. For objective thinking, names such as: the sun, the moon, the earth ought to be equivalent to proper names. Yet they characteristically do not resist the grammatical plural, which occurs ever more often, especially since Nietzsche: suns, moons, earths. The likewise pluralizable "actuality," finally, seldom occurs in the plural, since instead one commonly speaks of the various "worlds," say, of two personalities, or likewise of animals and men; a usage that would be just as fitting as it would be sufficient, were only the difference of the characters of actuality thereby co-intended, without which different "worlds" cannot be thought at all. So that this may stand inescapably before our eyes, we call the word actuality a singulare tantum, and mean thereby to express without qualification that its singular signifies an uncountable multitude—

With this, however, the origin of the multiplicity of languages would have ceased to be a problem, even if we brought the manifoldness of individuals into play not at all, and even passed over the differences that must have arisen from the collaboration of the spirit; and against the life-tenacious fiction of a single primal language that is supposed to have released all particular languages out of itself, let it be expressly stressed that it is rather this that would stand in need of explanation—why a language should be found at all that extends to more than, say, a dozen persons. Strictly speaking, this is not even the case at all. If we listen keenly enough, the languages change from village to [p. 1179] village; even the "scribes" in the cities never wholly escape the "dialects"; at bottom every single human being speaks his own language, which resounds even into and out of his own writings. Only the codification of a more or less artificial "written language," the habituation to the uniform jargon of the daily press, and, in the purposive use of speech, the enormous preponderance of the will to communicate over the will to represent, have prepared and enabled us to hear a single language wherever there are thousands upon thousands of languages.

Just as the representational urge of poets and seers created the abundance of languages and of speaking, so the general will to communicate aims at a single "world-language," and hence at just the sufficing minimum of stock of sounds as well as of derivational forms and rules of combination: the languages of mankind that are today felt to be different are the result of the counteraction of both powers, of which the one unmistakably stands on the side of life and the soul, the other, by far preponderantly, on the side of the spirit. In particular, many languages had to perish at the hands of the will to communicate, others had to fuse together, before there arose such languages as are, each of them, common to numerous millions of human beings, at least to the extent that, in relation to their highly heightened capacity to serve mutual understanding, individual differences are scarcely noticed any longer.

In actuality, to be sure, translation always takes place between speaker and hearer, because the former cannot communicate without adding to the communicative values of the general language some representational values of his own idiolect, and the latter cannot apprehend what is communicated without stripping off the foreign values and exchanging them for representational values of his own; only that such a requirement of translation is first noticed when the "dialects" differ considerably. — The conditions of the capacity— reached by one person incredibly quickly, by another incredibly slowly or not at all—to translate merely the communicative values of any given foreign language have never yet been precisely investigated, but must in any case be distinguished from the ability also to render the foreign language's representational values. Since this latter is always genuine new creation (not, of course, as goes without saying, of what is identical in content, but indeed of what is similar in content), it requires, in order to be accomplished, gifts of linguistic formation of a strength scarcely to be overestimated. With so-called literal translation, say, of poetic works into another language, precisely that is not translated [p. 1180] which makes the foreign text the text of a poem; wherefore, in the contrary case, one rightly speaks of a "re-creation in verse."

It may sound a little strange to find one—though an exceedingly modest—variety of re-creative achievement already in the ordinary conversations of speakers of the same tongue. Had we instead said that everyone thinks in some measure in a personal way, that would seem self-evident, and one would only forget thereby that it is at the same time asserted that he also speaks in some measure in a personal way. Naturally the degrees of individuality vary extraordinarily from person to person. The stencil-man, who thinks thoughts thought out beforehand, also speaks a language spoken beforehand; the creative and formative human being, who among other things thinks new thoughts and above all thinks in a new way, speaks in a strongly divergent way even when, by no means as with the writer, thinker, poet, language forms the medium of his shaping, but rather, say, color or wood or stone or steel or living beings. Whether someone unfolds creative gifts as craftsman or technician or farmer or great entrepreneur or statesman, and so forth, his written as well as his spoken word bears traces of this as surely as it is an immediate form of appearance of his thinking! Only, linguistic artistry must not be confused with linguistic individuality. The former belongs to the shaper of language, the latter goes hand in hand with every kind of formative power and may, in the process, not too rarely play over into linguistic artistry.

It happens partly, indeed, even today, but it was quite especially the custom in the eighteenth century that every man of any significance, in his more advanced years, composed his "memoirs." Now, let one read the biographies of the punctiliously pietistic oculist Jung-Stilling, or of such rather unruly adventurers as Trenck, *Laukhard*, Casanova, and one will be astonished at their linguistic qualities. As for the old sea-dog Nettelbeck, who of his eighty-six years of life spent more than half upon the water, he writes his "wondrous lifestory" in a prose of which no Goethe would need be ashamed!<sup>96</sup>

<sup>96</sup> On page 1180. — As evidence of this, at least one passage shall be offered. Nettelbeck's ship lies at anchor in Lisbon. He himself and several other captains are invited to table by a Portuguese merchant. One is surprised at this, since one does not know the gentleman more closely. Here our text-passage begins. "This did not, however, prevent our being called together once the exchange-hour was over. There were nine of us ship's captains, in the motliest mixture, like the men in the Pentecost epistle — Danes, Hamburgers, Lübeckers, Swedes, Swedish Pomeranians, and men of Danzig. We also found, on arriving at our host's house, that several merchants were already assembled there and a savory meal prepared, at which, too, valiant drinking was carried on; for our host understood thoroughly the art of pressing drink upon one, and so, once the table was cleared, it soon degenerated into a bacchanal. With me, however, who knew exactly the measure I must not exceed if I was to remain in my senses and my honor, every word of the host, good or ill, was soon lost. 'Basta, and not another drop!' was and remained my last trump, which in the end had to be respected too. Less well did the other ship's captains fare, who so overreached themselves that at last, every one of them, they sank beneath the table. I, for my part, had meanwhile been conversing with the merchants present, until, weary of the bestial sight, I took my leave and betook myself aboard my ship. — All the same, I rubbed my eyes somewhat bewildered the next morning, when I saw our host of the day before enter, in the company of those merchants. They shook my hand heartily and disclosed to me, laughing, that yesterday's drinkingfeast had been deliberately arranged by them in order to pick out, from among the nine of us, the right man, to whom, as the most solid and level-headed, they might entrust a cargo of value. Their choice, they said, had fallen on me unanimously, and so they asked me whether it would suit me to take on a full cargo of tea for Amsterdam. It is easy to imagine that I did not say 'No!'" *This* narrative grace runs through the whole of Nettelbeck's lifestory!

Meanwhile, a further difference must not be passed over, between great shapers of language and those speakers whose speech, though without effort, mirrors the strength of their psychic and spiritual individuality, yet is not at the same time an expression of their own relation to language. In their linguistic individuality there comes to appearance chiefly the individuality of their [p. 1181] essence; but in the linguistic individuality of mighty shapers of language there comes to appearance chiefly the actuality which, to experience and to behold down into more than ordinary depths, their mastery of the word has, not least of all, enabled them to do. Through the poet above all, as often as he brings "primal sounds to resound," elemental actualities have gained a voice—actualities in relation to which the essence of the poet almost resembles the harp or lyre upon which world-weaving "powers" play. In thus turning back once more to the primal source of languages and of speaking, we do not fail to bring forward a confirmation of our conception from the lore of myth.

In his beautiful treatise on the "Origin of Language," Jakob Grimm reports an Estonian folk-legend that undertakes nothing less than to explain the origin of the multiplicity of languages. The old god has the tribes step up to a water-kettle over the fire, so that each may take away from it a voice of the singing water; thus the various languages arose. Here, as it seems to us, there is expressed with unsurpassable vividness not only the actuality-content of languages, but also this, that actuality is a—singulare tantum. As many voices as sing confusedly together in the seething of the water, so many worlds of appearance; and as many worlds of appearance, so many actualities appearing in them. On the Character and the Characters of Actuality — But now two misgivings demand a hearing: a logical one, concerning the concept of actuality, and a metaphysical one, concerning the world of images and its reverberation in the sounds of language. We turn first to the logical one. — Should there be no such thing as actuality at all, but strictly speaking only actualities, how then would it still be possible to decide whether one means what is actual or what is not actual? Could we not think the star or stone or river in unity, how would we ever set about thinking stars or stones or rivers in plurality? Certainly several stars, several stones, several rivers differ from one another, and not merely numerically; but the stars would no longer be stars, the stones no longer stones, the rivers no longer rivers, did there not at least allow itself to be named some single mark that belonged distinctively to all stars, all stones, all rivers alike—in short, to every unity of meaning of which we meaningfully form a plural. But if a plurality of actualities is posited, then [p. 1182] none of them could have anything in common with any other, and the plurality in question would be a mere word. Either, then, this plural has no sense at all, or there is indeed something common to all actualities, whereby the one and only actuality would have returned again—an actuality to which, in virtue of other grounds of distinction, we may indeed well ascribe the greatest manifoldness.

The objection looks unsurmountable, and would be so, if one held the process to be comprehensible by which it comes about that a content of experience raises the claim to actuality. Since, however, such a process is an "ur-phenomenon"— indeed the ur-phenomenon of all ur-phenomena—the circumstance that, to be sure, all actualities have one character-trait in common does not conflict with the fundamental multiplicity of actuality. We know this trait and have often made use of it: it is the state of being estranged of that which the soul experiences as actual. This, and this alone, defines, in the life-process, that whereby it becomes the process of an experiencing; but it defines it only by pointing to a state of affairs whose somewhat closer consideration will fully unveil to us its nature of multiplicity.

The proposition is not convertible, because there is also apparent actuality. By this, however, we do not mean optical illusions, afterimages, semblance-images (of the "eidetiker"), not dream-phantasms, contents of suggestion, sequels of empathy, delusive-perception formations, hallucinations, pseudohallucinations, and the like; for here, generally speaking, only the question is at stake whether existential judgments attach themselves to them or not. These, insofar as they occur, are always to be refuted by logical and factual incompatibilities, and can for that very reason be rejected by the bearer of the experience himself. But we need only think of certain "inner perceptions," "awakenings," "illuminations," "suprasensible revelations," "secret signs," alienations, raptures, and so forth, whose contents are assuredly not what they give the appearance of being, in order to see that the convictions of actuality borne by them could for the most part not be invalidated by an appeal to facts. In order to distinguish justified claims to actuality from unjustified ones, we must therefore assume some distinguishing peculiarity of all the appearances to which those claims can be assigned, and this now changes from case to case, without thereby forfeiting its power to hold good.

If we try to give it a name, then what offers itself is not, say, [p. 1183] "strength," but rather "depth"—and again not depth in general, but depth as the immediate occasioning ground of that penetrating urgency which always harbors the guarantee of an extra-personal origin, and is never to be confused with what one might call obtrusiveness, which owes its weight merely to violent alterations. Now it is the peculiarity of depth in every form, and hence also of our particular variety of depth, that its at least analogical capacity for intensification cannot be separated from a transformation of qualities. One can make this vivid to oneself by simple sense-data. If, for example, we pass through a sequence of imperceptible intermediate stages from yellow to green-yellow, from green-yellow to green, from green to blue-green, from blue-green to blue, from blue to blue-violet, then, together with the change of qualities, we at the same time experience a progression from shallower to deeper colors, or, in short, an intensification of depth. What here hovers before us is, as one notices, just as little to be grasped objectively, and hence just as little comprehensible, as the color-tones themselves, and yet is just as determinate an experience as these. Let us recall, in order to come closer to the sense of this capacity for intensification of depth, the correspondence that holds between shallowness and nearness as nearness, between depth and distance as distance; then we may essentially equate the character of deepening with the character of the growing of distance, and accordingly the content of depth with a content of distance, whose more or less can, as an expedient, be made spatially present.

The state of being estranged, which guarantees the extra-personal origin of the image, or, spoken less relationally, the metaphysical ground of its foreignness, is thus attended by an exponent which, even as it changes from image to image, moreover runs through rising or falling degrees. Since it naturally fuses with the image, co-operating in its own peculiar "coloring," it follows: in general, the multiplicity of actualities, but in particular the comparatively gradable content, of the actuality present in each given instant, of—actuality! The antique formula: actual, more actual, most actual—already grasped ontologically by the Greeks, and in that way misunderstood—holds good as surely for the actuality of images as it becomes senseless through transference to Being. — Two applications of this thought to readily accessible states of affairs should bring it as near to understanding as is at all possible with a truth that can only be demonstrated.

With growing content of actuality the image becomes more and more a [p. 1184] *world*. Let one recall the examples by which, in the 65th chapter, the appearing of elemental souls was elucidated, and one will confirm that the images there adduced, of overwhelming landscapes or astonishing wonders of art, bring with them, again and again, their own universe. This, however, can be made still more palpable with more modest examples. — Having earlier set forth that the most significant works of so-called Romanticism surpass works of equal significance from Classicism through strength of aura, we could now say instead that they are of greater weight of actuality, and therefore empowered to a higher degree to take us, from case to case, into unrepeatable worlds.

Goethe, too, comes closest to achieving this as well, though only with numerous scenes of the first "Faust." But let one then read, in Mörike's "Stuttgarter Hutzelmännlein," the "History of the Fair Lau"; let one surrender to the narrative without any ulterior thought, and ask oneself only whether one is at all able to refuse the actuality of what is narrated— and one will have to answer the question in the negative. Now the tale deals for the most part with wholly legendary occurrences, in which, at least today, no one any longer is wont to "believe"—with water-nymphs and mighty water-spirits, with the tooth of the kraken that renders one invisible, with the magic humming-top whose wondrous melodies would soothe every quarrel—and these legends weave themselves in turn with the life and doings of a village monastic community of the Middle Ages, more or less as it may actually have taken place. But then the versified actuality can only compel our acknowledgment of its actuality because the poetry has succeeded in tearing us away from the objective world and leading us into one of the uncountable worlds out of the actuality of images.

This succeeds with our Classicists mostly only in part (one of the unmistakable signs of which is that here and there the personality of the poet intrudes, be it with outbursts of feeling, be it with maxims); it succeeds, on the other hand, with very many fairy tales of all times and peoples; it succeeds with Homer; it succeeds with Shakespeare in "Julius Caesar"; and evidently there are just as many worlds into which we are in this way transformed, incompatible among themselves and wholly incompatible with the world of existing things, whose presence masters us hourly, and whose past is laid before us by the records of the historians, the conclusions of the researchers into prehistory and the geologists, the calculations of the physicists and astronomers. We would not know how to say what we mean more clearly [p. 1185] than in these words: that the way is opened to the doctrine of the actuality of images by the thought that the worlds just named, and all worlds essentially akin to them, out of the actuality of the poets, are exemplary images of what must be understood under the unrestrictedly actual. With this, however, the last remnant of obscurity that might still have clung to the "singulare tantum" should be cleared up.

Only in passing do we call to mind the head-turning distortion by which the actuality of images, and then in particular the content of poetry, is beset by the involuntarily prejudged belief in the one and only "actuality" of things. It leads, as everyone knows, to the form of consideration most falsely called "realistic" or "naturalistic," which judges the essence of images by the chronicle of things and, for example, accords the greatest fullness of actuality to that verbal work which has transcribed some or other factual relations and occurrences as exactly as possible. One is wont to call this its "truth," and thereby strangely forgets, as a rule, that of this sort of truth every properly kept transcript of a court proceeding contains more than the most "realistic" narrative, however realistic. But one by no means escapes such a habit of valuation by hunting instead for sublime general thoughts and so-called Ideas, of which the artist is supposed to furnish illustrative examples, or even by degrading creative works into silly trifling with "aesthetic" frippery. On the contrary, we would far rather take pleasure in factual truths and sharply outlined reportage— which need by no means lack all artistic charm—than let ourselves be duped into taking for essence a mere—masquerade of Ideas! Let no one deceive himself about this: either the mightiest poetry and art of all times is blue—no, gray—haze, or it is the magical means of unlocking for us actual worlds to which we, out of our own dungeon of belief in facts, could by our own strength no longer find our way. — Let a brief retrospect be sent ahead of the second application that we wish to offer. — The event would not come to appearance without the actuality of place, and the actuality of place means the actuality of the corporeal body, or, generalized, the actuality of matter. Since it is the corporeal body, and the corporeal body alone, that permits the reification of the event and allows the existential proof to be carried out, there is, for the actuality of images and the so-called actuality of things, a line of intersection, in accordance with which [p. 1186] we distinguish thingsof-thought from actual things and ascribe to the latter a participation in actuality. Now the life-process that announces actuality to us with respect to things, namely the process of sensation, is wont to be made to underlie the finding of actuality generally, and indeed proves itself especially serviceable for the rejection of false claims to actuality—for example, of an abstracted visible appearance, and altogether of "pure" concepts. We have, to be sure, sufficiently shown that a sensible resistance is able to indicate the corporeal body only insofar as it is the resistance of an already estranged image; that, hence, the origin of actuality must be sought in the state of being estranged and not in an obstacle to motion; we have furthermore, since then, linked event with matter, distance with nearness, ever more closely, and have learned to appraise our intercourse with both from the standpoint of two kinds of connectedness.

If, for the sake of its gradability, we replace depth by distance, shallowness by nearness, and conceive of nearness for once as diminished and, at most, smallest-possible distance, then we have given to the opposition of depth and shallowness that form which allows us to surmise a polarity dawning even behind it, thoroughly different from the ordinarily coresonating opposition of deep and shallow thinking. The nearness with which the thing besets us by way of touch is, as such, a distanceless nearness, and to the reflection that is kindled by it there belongs accordingly a depthless shallowness, from which, above the calculating with existences, the actuality of images vanishes ("shoals" [Untiefen] are still today the name for shallow places in the sea, where—sandbanks lurk . But even this nearness would lose its power of conviction (and has in part already lost it in formalistic world-webs of thought) without the co-participation of the nearness of the corporeal body; and this latter need not be distanceless, but can be, toward distance, either the opposite pole, or, on the contrary, afford that presence which we found consummated in the life-domain of the plant. This, however, occurs insofar as, thanks to the preponderance of its qualitative content, the sensed corporeality of the soul becomes the occasion for it to melt together, in the instant, with the event within it—the sign of whose consummation is a voluptuousness pervading the living body of the soul. As surely as there is a deep voluptuousness, just as surely can depths of actuality, on occasion of the very process of touch, stream in even into the utmost nearness.

The image is born when the soul has lost itself temporarily in the event. The event is essentially distance (more precisely: distance of the past); but even in what is simply present the distances are weaving [p. 1187] and can, by means of it, become perceptible to the soul, so far as its beholding is kindled precisely at the "stimulus." Compared with the ecstatic beholding of the appearance of distance, this kind of beholding approaches somewhat the occurrences of sleeping beholding, but differs from them by a suddenness similar to a breaking wave, which can be experienced only within the domain of wakefulness. Yet one may, after all, call it a diving-down of the soul into the night of the chaotic, whereby it is impregnated with distance and becomes partaker of the image in the medium of the living body. (This is not, but here would branch off, among other things, the metaphysics of the pairing-drive and of "propagation.") This we must now apply to the vanishing of distance in the appearance that approaches us or that we approach. The actuality itself, it was said, of the one and only objective forest is another when it appears from afar, another when it appears from near, an essentially different one again when it envelops him who enters it and thereby also him who becomes aware of it through his touchings. We now understand why the utmost nearness, which finally extinguishes the appearance of distance, need not necessarily mean a loss of distance, but also how deeply actuality must transform itself if, despite the vanishing of the appearance of distance, what appears on paths newly to be broken for the soul is to remain actuality.

Finally, however—and this is more important to us—we now know that actuality can transform itself without any transformation of the intuitive image, whether spatially distant or spatially near, namely thanks to a sudden breaking-out of the soul from the cage of the object, or thanks to a gradual yielding of its numbnesses. And if, therefore, the brook, the hut, the misting land—but a moment ago indifferent things of perception or sullen phantoms—now stand at a stroke in a luminous or gloomy aura, gazing with nameless mysteries; if the trembling soul, between the one and the other actuality, finds the wall of things riven asunder, and suddenly awakens as from a long and heavy dream of dread; if out of the distances of an unfathomable once-upon-a-time still more terror-laden gleams flash forth, until, just as suddenly, everything has sunk away again, and brook and hut and mist-land, together with the lost wanderer, once more eke out their "existence" in the frosty day of consciousness—then we shall henceforth no longer wish to refute, by the actuality of corporeal bodies and of matter, worlds in relation to which corporeality, as it is commonly understood, would be but a possible indication of them, while the world of things would be a dungeon walled up out of the mortared [p. 1188] splinters left over from actuality in general after its shattering by deeds of the spirit. (Fundamentally the same holds, as goes without saying, for the actuality-revealing content of that deep voluptuousness which sinks one into the "chaos.")

Were one to describe all this in the following way—that the objectively identical intuitive image, which yesterday struck us as devoid of essence, may today appear to us filled with deep meaning, and thereby disclose to us, as it were, its hitherto hidden soul—one would have described it more comprehensibly, yet unfortunately all too comprehensibly, and would scarcely have brought to bear what is decisively at issue: that this so-called soul, if it is anything at all, is an actuality to whose nature appearing belongs, so that it must necessarily have been a different actuality that had appeared to us in the soulless intuitive image. We are never, in the waking state, wholly without intercourse with an appearing actuality, since even between the least living and most habitual things and the soul some connectedness must continually be accomplished, so that the perceiving relatedness of the bearer of soul to them can take place at all. But the actuality through whose influence every present moment of our wakefulness signifies a co-presence of scarcely heeded things is far different from that by force of which the co-presence of these selfsame things becomes a rune of illuminated and illuminating sense, or a fatefully alluring riddle. Just as with the telescope we perceive objects that without it we do not perceive, and with the sharper telescope again new ones, so it is other and ever deeper actualities that can appear to us without any change of the things, when, out of the soul within us, more and ever deeper things awaken, and it, ever more unrestrainedly, loses itself out of its depths into powers at work.

We pass over, as having already been discussed elsewhere more or less, what can be gained from this for the recognition and cognition of the states that are most, and those that are least, favorable to the reception of deep actualities, and recall only once more that the content of actuality of the word, too, in order that it may appear, requires an appropriate receptive capacity of the soul that apprehends the word. The most perfect and deepest poem opens wider and more wondrous worlds to the bearer of a deep soul than to that of a shallow one, to the bearer of a soul capable of being addressed(!) than to that of one incapable of it, finally to the bearer of soul in a state of unforceable readiness for life than to this same bearer in a state of ill-humor or care or exhaustion, and so forth. [p. 1189] What differences nonetheless obtain between every mediated dialogue with the elements and the immediate one will presently have to be considered. — After such far-reaching, yet scarcely dispensable, considerations in connection with the logical objection, we shall be brief regarding the metaphysical objection. — If it may already be difficult to understand what shines forth, and should shine forth, from those considerations with a force scarcely achieved to a like degree before—namely that the actualities to which we there pointed are ever-transforming, that they are actualities that happen, and are nonetheless images—then it seems altogether inconceivable how anything of this could be captured in the sounds of language, without thereby forfeiting precisely the non-abiding soul and being—de-actualized. For, even if one were to adduce also the change of sound and the change of meaning in language, and further, what gives secret impulses thereto, the vibrations of sense and sound at the exchange of a word's position in living speech, adding to this the faint displacements, now cancelling one another, now accumulating, through the continually occurring transmissions of what is spoken by those who hear it—and if, with all this, one brought oneself to the awareness that language too is a piece of happening—still a single glance at the literature of the ages and peoples, which was possible only through at least a relative persistence of languages, suffices to see that no language of mankind could possibly offer a counterpart to the restless going and coming of appearances of actualities of ever-different strata.

Certainly, we today no longer read and hear Pindar, Ovid, and even Dante, in the way Pindar may have read Pindar, Ovid Ovid, Dante Dante, and some contemporary of each of the three may have apprehended what was read. We recognize that even such masterworks of language do not, across the centuries, reach across to us their content of meaning so exactly as their merely communicable and comprehensible content; and we are willing to believe that even the word set down in writing does not withdraw itself from the change of the times; but it holds that change back! For we do not doubt that much of the soul of the poetry renews itself similarly even in another age. For otherwise poetry as poetry could no longer be experienced once the time that created it were past!

But according to the doctrine of the "actuality of images," the sun of Homer no longer shines for us, and has long ceased to! The heavens with all their stars, the earth with its rivers, mountains, and storms—though still ever findable [p. 1190] points of reference for comprehending thought—exchanged actuality for actuality; the "change of the times," of which we speak so lightly, has taken on a terrible meaning: space and time are no longer the same as they were then; every moment is somehow a deep otherness; and even if we may indeed doubt that, as is rumored, the elemental souls have in the meantime vanished forever, still they too went and came; the primal waters ebbed and rose and ebbed; and finally: what does the one still know of the actuality of the other?! But how then shall the word, how shall speech, how shall any human work at all be able to conjure world-weaving powers! The Visionary Act. — Suppose it were the case that, while every particular being is indeed a microcosm, only with man, after the intermediate realm of animality, had there begun to awaken: the distances, the event, the cosmos—then the images of ecstatic beholding would be, at once, the goal and consummation of world-happening and, again and again, its creative primal beginning; and it would be the sense of the precipitates of every moment of image-intoxication to be the objectively become means of their renewal. But with this, one would have named the macrocosmic sense of human creating and working altogether, once it had been wrested away from the magical rotations of a primal age in which soul and world had fused with one another in rhythmically uninterrupted, eversucceeding embraces. — It is essentially all one whether one demonstrates this by buildings, statues, paintings, by ornamentation and objects of use, by writing and "signs," by musical works, songs, and poems, by dances and mystery-plays, or whether one chooses language for it instead, because what guarantees the content of actuality in any one of these fundamentally guarantees it in any arbitrary creation of mankind whatever. But language offers, as an object for demonstration, manifold advantages.

For one thing, it is in the possession of all, and so it becomes manifest in it, as nowhere else, that everyone is "called" to co-operate in the creative advance of mankind, even if only few are "chosen." Then again, it is language that has, with unsurpassable sharpness and distinctness, in a certain sense immortalized all the stages and resting-places of the soul's wrestling with the spirit. Finally, so we have heard, it is only thanks to it that the wonder has come to pass that, after millennia of the decomposition of human formative powers by the spirit (of which it is precisely language that bears the history within itself), voices of the elements still live on, together with it, in the working [p. 1191] of the human beings of today. To be sure, with pyramids and menhirs, remote ages tower into the present; but it is not we who erect menhirs, who build pyramids. Yet we still speak, and speak, even though we do not think thereby of languages full of age-old mysteries. The arts might long since have died, poetry might be dead: as long as language had not wholly decayed, so long would "spirits of the primal age" not have wholly vanished from our deeds.

"The rain is streaming," says Peter, glad in his understanding, / Content, because he dwells beneath a roof; / Unwitting that, veiled living in the word, / Out of the rain's dull mouth its soul roars forth. / Meanwhile, what concerns us here is no longer the elemental pulse-beat in the life of sounds, and still less the development toward the partly sharply precise system of conceptual signs and means of fixing judgments which the historical languages have taken on under the compulsion of the purposive and of the scientific spirit; rather we have to do with the language-creativity of thinking, or more precisely with the thought-creativity of that mode of speaking capable of it. We do not dive down as far as the pre-rational stratum of language, but still beneath the promethean stratum, and down into what is in any case a prehistoric time, where the world of symbols was born forth rather than created, and out of which stems the mighty legacy of works to be understood only symbolically—symbolic through and through, from the mighty rune-stone to the tiniest ornamental piece of a potsherd. Whatever wonder-works the historical age brought forth at all, it is the more laden with actuality the more, in all its immediacy, it at the same time hands on the heritage of symbolism.

Only a relatively late age distinguished the visionary from the poetic, and it was reserved to an even later one to think of both as distributed between two persons. Certainly, too, this had already begun to articulate itself apart even in antiquity; but just as certainly, down to the most recent times, one will find no truly great poet who does not here and there display visionary passages, nor, in turn, any genuine visionary whose visionary states did not in many respects resemble the state of the poet in those moments which, tellingly, have been called precisely with regard to him "inspired." Only, we must here set aside the "sign-interpreters"—the palmists, astrologers, cartomancers, augurs, haruspices, [p. 1192] rhabdomancers, geomancers, and so forth—who prop themselves upon handed-down systems of supposed omens, even though their arts of interpretation are not seldom fertilized by unconsciously coresonating visionary gifts. In any case, let the word visionary [Seher] here be understood in the antique sense of the vates.

The visionary in this sense originally formed, together with the poetic, a whole, whose bearer, in the moments of ecstasis, gave utterance now more visionarily, now more poetically. We pass over the in-themselves significant, and, as it seems to us, also graspable differences between the two kinds of utterance, and hold ourselves solely to the visionary, because it certainly would not take place without the participation of deeds of the spirit. We may not only, we must, speak, with regard to it, of deeds of visionary thinking, and we hold visionary thinking to be essentially the same as the symbolic thinking of which repeated mention has been made. Were the source of the language-creativity within a mankind, accordingly, to be found in symbolic thinking, or more precisely in that mode of inner speaking which avails itself of a symbolic language—a mankind that, though its soul unconditionally rules, is nevertheless no longer compelled merely to experience primal images, but, with regard to them, also to accomplish acts of apprehension—then it can at all times only have been favored single individuals to whom we owe the creation of symbols, and thus of language itself: of language, insofar as it presents itself as the sound-body of symbolic units of meaning. Language, then, which in favorable cases still brings "primal sounds to resound" even today, is, on our conception, the work of visionary poets or poetic visionaries- —or rather, what is their work in it is what permits undertakings so improbable.

The metaphysical objection took as its ground a relative persistence of language (and thereby of the work as such). In our approval of it, given straightaway, the symbolic word (and thereby the work containing symbols as such) was called the objective means of the renewal of actualities that have happened. "Renewal," chosen in contrast to "repetition," means, or ought to mean: the bringing-back of the similar. One recalls that similarity is at bottom elementary similarity, and thus a similarity that is experienced and can be pointed out, but whose scope never admits of delimitation. With this it is said: if, by means, say, of the poetic word, the actuality objectified in the sound-body is renewed a hundred times, then it is renewed a hundred times differently—not [p. 1193] simply differently, but in a hundred ways of similarity; or: the worlds that, by virtue of the relative persistence of the poetic word, are called forth a hundred times, are a hundred different actualities, but each similar to the other, and all similar to the original one, which, in the moment of the birth of the image—that is, in the moment of the streaming-in of powers at work into the soul of the poet given over to them—gained, through this soul, a sound-body. We wish to make the extraordinary thing that is with this, for the present, only posited, vivid to ourselves at least by one example.
