It will always be a key to baneful depths in the essence of Nietzsche that, in the third part of his "Zarathustra," after the proclamation of the tragic truth "To every soul belongs another world," he lets Resignation answer the comfort-seeking, feeling-forward question, "Are not names and sounds given as a gift to things?"—disguising her bitter answer in the grace of speech: "How lovely is all speaking and all the lying of sounds! With sounds our soul dances upon many-colored rainbows." We do not inquire into what Zarathustra thereby tells us of his creator; but we wish to say that it is not the sounds and names that lie, but at most only he who misuses them, and again only he who misunderstands them. We wish to say that one whom, in a favorable hour, Sappho's Poikilothron' athanat' Aphrodita carries away is granted entrance, if not yet into the world of Sapphic actuality, then indeed into a similar actuality, and in this way learns more of the Aeolian Greekdom of those distant days than through years of archaeological study without the good fortune of interspersed "illuminations."

Though not quite in this same way, yet not essentially otherwise, "similarities and sibling-features" of vanished actualities become manifest to him who understands how to listen into the symbolic depths of language. But then "symbolic identities" would have to be linguistic precipitates of the apprehension, not of intuitive images, but of primal images, since otherwise it would scarcely be comprehensible how the "transference of the thought of sameness onto appearancecharacters of essential similarity" could have taken place. But how would that be possible?! We know: if the act occurs at the turning-point, then either, by splitting off an event from the intuitive image, the thing is fixed, or, by splitting off the intuitive image from the (impulse-)event, the purpose is fixed. In both cases, accordingly, there is separated: the receiving soul from the powers that fructify it; the thing from space and time; space from time; the localized [p. 1194] I from the world; but above all, from every living body, the soul appearing through it, which henceforth eked out a hypothetical existence, an existence resting on doubtful conclusions never to be made unassailable. Neither of the two members in each pair, by contrast, may have been separated from the other by that deed of the spirit whose success would be a knowledge of "symbolic identities."

We do not consider it idle to say the same thing once more in other words. We had repeatedly to establish that the conviction of identity "has, in the moment of its being found by the act of apprehension, torn its object out of the stream of time" (p. 433). If, now, there is to be a content of actuality belonging to names, then, despite the act of apprehension having taken place, the appearance must have kept its nimbus, or the image its ever-momentary world. Instead of becoming an identically referable, and hence simply past and irretrievable, point (upon the line of time as an object of thought), the moment would have had to "immortalize" itself in the symbolic cry of language in such a way that it would be renewed by, let us say, a magical use of names. We do not investigate by which mode of the use of language the wonder succeeds of dissolving the moment of time and realizing the moment of eternity incomparable with it. One comes closest to it if one calls it (as was done above) the consummately poetic mode, which would then no longer even need accompanying acts. We ask, on the other hand, how language could harbor a knowledge of moments of eternity, and recall that, without this knowledge, comprehending thought too could not have arisen.

With such questions one stands entirely on the ground of esoteric inquiry, and will therefore not disdain solutions to which at least a value of probability must be conceded. Before we ground our conjecture concerning the essence of the visionary act, however, let us try, in a few words, to characterize the experience that surrounds it like a storm-cloud, and in doing so let us rely on two utterances or precipitates of it. We think first of the Sphinx. At that time (still before the Promethean stage), when the intruder Spirit ventured its first mighty thrusts, visionary acts of the utmost reach occurred, thanks to tremendous recoils of life, before which fate and mystery of the world changed into doom and riddle of the world.

In the "ray" of such cognition the darknesses deepen, the problems multiply the more of them one has solved; the meaning [p. 1195] of the world, formerly kept silent in images, becomes manifest as a tormenting or threatening question. Wherever, instead of the secret twilight, the flickering of uncertainty lies upon the landscape of the soul (as often in Nietzsche), there is Spirit — but in cosmic space more convulsive, flaring up against infinity, glowing in the phosphorescence of the soul. Before its flashing-up the image of Isis veils itself more densely, and in the sidereal primal murk those terror-inspiring idols mass together, of which Babylon, India, Egypt have left us such mighty examples. An entire world of prehistoric symbols of horror wants to be understood from this point of view.

The second expression of experience — abundantly attested among an overwhelming number of thinkers, mystics, so-called prophets, and poets too, wellspring-spirits of every kind — is the comparison, indeed the equation, of the visionary act of cognition with the flaring-up of lightning. Instead of many passages we give one: "What is grasped always stands there — it does not flow and change; but in mere perceiving, veil-less and naked, a thing among things, isolated and ultimately definable; in visionary far-sight, by contrast, illumined for an instant as if by flashes of weather, emerging from a stream of dreams, or from a twilight of presentiments, or from a surf of feelings, and always from a vortex of happening. Perception meets what is factual; that 'gaze,' on the other hand, is met now by the core of something streaming and surging, now by the nearness of a flight of distances. Thus something elemental inheres in what is grasped: as the possibility of streaming forth again, as something pointing beyond itself, as the threat of dissolution. What is thus be-held exists only in the unrepeatable eye-blink, yet lives on in the secrecy of the symbol." — Since, after all, it is inner experiences of this kind that give one the courage still to risk explanations where mere understanding no longer remotely suffices, let us recall once more the peculiarity of the visionary state, which can be described only, and inescapably, by the self-contradictory phrase of a rapt repose in wild motion.

In our preparations our reasons already lie unspoken. If it is to become intelligible that the symbol-finding act does not separate all this but rather comprehends in one what, on the level of objective thinking, would fall apart into the experienced and the experiencing, object and subject, world and I, there and here, once and now — then only the assumption remains that it flashes up, or strikes in, however one wishes to take it, not at the beginning or end of the pendulum's swing, but in the moments of its most violent momentum, thus producing the structure in which the separated halves strike back together, [p. 1196] differing from the primal image through their distinguishability, yet akin to it in essence through their inseparability.

We may unhesitatingly ascribe the choice of the Greek symbolon — whose profane meaning is "contract" — to designate what was thus brought about, to hidden influences of the visionary spirit, which will have heard out and fetched out symballein = to throw together. In any case, by reference to the verbal noun we hit upon the essence of the matter more deeply than even with Ramler's excellent rendering by "Sinnbild" [image of meaning], which can tempt one to think of the intuitive representation of the non-intuitive concept, and *has* tempted all interpreters of the Sinnbild to do so. — For the purpose of a schematic representation of the process we replace the wave-motion with paths of the pendulum-motion strung one after another, whose rounded connecting lines are meant to correspond to the turning-points, where the acts normally arise. The arrows, by contrast, denote the points of impact of the acts in the state of visionary ecstasy.

Fig. 15.

Whoever today, unacquainted with ethnology and the history of antiquity, hears of "seers," will think first of fortunetelling and the interpreting of signs, and would understand from our characterization of the visionary state as "rapt repose in wild motion" presumably the repose, but by no means the wild motion, on which, according to Fig. 13, the main stress actually falls. Wholly uncomfortable to him would be the demand to link the seer so closely with the poet as our account requires. Since, of all symbolism, linguistic symbolism is always the first to become transparent, we do not want, in closing, to fail to question language itself as to what it has to report to us of the visionary and the poetic.

With the German loanword "dichten" [to compose poetry] (from Latin dictare = to dictate/copy down, later to draft) naturally nothing can be done. It only draws our attention to the regrettable circumstance that, out of the ear-poetry of the true singer, there increasingly arose the eye-poetry of such "singers" as wrote their songs down. For the Greeks, however, it remains highly characteristic that, thanks to an excessive sense of art, they saw in the poet not so much the one inspired by the god as a shaper, and therefore called him [p. 1197] poietes, that is, the maker, the fabricator — namely of exceedingly artful structures of words; just as the sublime daring of Greek metrics at times oversteps the bounds of artifice. In compensation, however, they gave validity to the Dionysian origin proper to seer-hood with the word mantis = seer, which names one caught up in demonic frenzy, since it branches off, together with the Bacchic "Mainas," from mainesthai = to rage. Here one should recall also the barely translatable thymos, from thyein = to storm, rage, rave, roar, foam, insofar as it forms the point of departure for the designation of precisely those Bacchai or Mainades as "Thyiades," and of the god's wild festal throngs as "Thiasoi." (From our "heart" or "temper" one can no longer clearly enough hear what Thymos originally meant: an ever-surging blood-soul; the old meaning of "Geist" [spirit], on the other hand, would correspond to it — a word which, like spiritus (from spirare) or anima and animus (akin to aeiv = to blow and anemos = wind), is traced by philologists back to a root meaning to rush, to blow, to ferment, a root still present in an Old Norse geisa = to break out roaring.) Meanwhile other testimonies of the greatest weight stand at our disposal.

The developmental history of no Germanic god is as instructive as that of Wodan (Norse Odin). It is set forth concisely and comprehensively in Mogk's Germanische Mythologie. Here we merely note that Wodan appears, common to all Germanic peoples, as a demon of the storm and leader of the "raging host" of the souls of the dead, but that his rise to become the chief god of the Germanic peoples took place not in the North but in Lower Germany among the Saxons and Lombards, and only from there spread to Scandinavia, England, and Iceland (with a magnificent late flowering in the Viking age). We cannot here substantiate what we hold to be strictly demonstrable — that his numerous and in part apparently widely divergent meanings have, one and all, sprouted from a single root, even if brought out only successively and in part cultivated with a partisan selectiveness by the warrior class especially devoted to him. It can be shown that and how the wind- and storm-demon belong together with, and are aspects of, a single being: the god of weather and fertility, the god of battle and of heroes, the inventor of the runes, the "father of magic," the god of the magical healing art, the possessor and steward of all wisdom, the god of seers and poets. Here what concerns us is only the linguistic side.

"Wodan," to whom in the Vedas corresponds the demon Vata = wind, of [p. 1198] whose chariot it is said that it presses forward thundering and shattering everything, spreading a red glow across the sky and whirling up the dust of the earth,<sup>97</sup> "Wodan" is primally akin to "wüten" [to rage], to Latin vates, meaning "god-inspired singer" and "seer," to Old Irish faith = poet. If we further note that Old Norse óðr (akin to Óðinn) means both raging and furious as well as poetry, song, we will certainly no longer believe that the skalds at the courts of the jarls had first to remake Odin into the god of the wise, of seers and poets.<sup>98</sup> With this, however, language has furnished us with several mutually complementary testimonies of the strongest kind — first for the common descent of seer and poet, and then, above all, for the fact that vitally underlying both the visionary's and the poet's self-utterance is that condition which the mystery cults of antiquity knew as hieromanic. With the famous Rune Song of Odin, finally, which opens with the verses: "I know that I hung — On the windy tree — Nine nights long," we find it confirmed by the myth that out of the inspired state language itself grew up, or at least that in it by which it is able to hand on and to keep working magical knowledge:

<sup>97</sup> On page 1198. — *Oldenberg*, Die Religion des Veda, p. 225. —

<sup>98</sup> On page 1198. — The author owes the reference to the Old Norse óðr and its relation to the meaning of Odin to Dr. *Martin Ninck*. Compare note 117.

Word led me from word to word, / work led me from work to work.

"Rune," incidentally, as may be recalled in passing, means "secret word, secret song, secret sign" (hence the runes are always also magic runes).

[p. 1199]

#### 68. Kapitel — Von der Coincidentia oppositorum — Chapter 68 — On the Coincidentia oppositorum

Circle and Center — The famous formula of the Cusan holds still more, and something other, than what he himself wished and was able to put into it: namely an unwitting knowledge of the essence of connectedness and of its opposition to being-in-relation. Hardly more sharply than with its help can we measure the incomprehensibility of any connectedness whatsoever against the comprehensibility of the relations that step into its place thanks to the abolition of the connection. And indeed the opposita that "coincide" in the form of connectedness are, in relation to the whole thereby posited, either sides or poles. Always the experience of elementary similarities underlies this — there the similarities of characters of appearance, here those particular similarities whose primal source is the coincidence of the receiving soul with the acting happening in the process of beholding. Before we show why the postulate of polarity holds at least for the similarity of features of appearance as well, let us call to mind the nature of connectedness and the counter-nature of being-in-relation, in both cases.

If we become aware of the character of spatial appearance, which somehow belongs to every appearance, we can call to mind that it is not by virtue of its spatiality that one appearance stands out from another appearance. A volume that we assume really exists, e.g. the volume of the Heidelberg Tun, is connected with every volume of which we assume the same, e.g. the volume of the Pyramid of Cestius; or: the space of intuition is a form of appearance of real space, and thus, indeed, of cosmic space. Only through the spiritual act which, on occasion of the always local corporealities, abolishes the connection, do the spatial extents become opposita, and does the appearing of cosmic space within the space of intuition become a mystical coincidence. — Likewise every span of time thought of as real, e.g. the lifetime [p. 1200] of Napoleon, is connected with every other, say the lifetime of Hannibal, and again the same holds for distinguishing. Since this, in both cases, has the form of dividing, its objects stand to the thereby-divided whole as the summands to the sum. We need only recall that neither spaces nor times — but only things — can be summed or subtracted, in order to assure ourselves of the inapplicability of all measuring to actuality. But the incomprehensibility of connections emerges more sharply in the following way.

Only the space of intuition can be thought of as a part of cosmic space, which has already been detached from real time, which together with real space forms that double-poled whole that appears to us. If we compare the relatability of thought-objective space to thought-objective time with the proposition: real presentness is the space of intuition, we recognize that the deed of Spirit has not merely divided the poled actuality but has even dismembered it, by making its poles independent. — Within spatiotemporal actuality, again thanks to elementary similarity, every (thinkable) segment of an intuitive process or an intuitive movement is connected with every other segment of this same process; or: movement appears in the empirical instant. Measured, however, against the counterpart of the spiritual act — the temporally unextended point — all movement ceases and yields its place to the ingeniously contrived sum of an "infinite" series of "infinitely small" summands. This repeats itself for every concrete case.

The river is a real whole, whose character becomes intuitable to us at the sight of any arbitrary point of the river; likewise, say, the living tree. Now the mouth depends on the source differently than the source depends on the mouth, the blossom depends on the root differently than the root depends on the blossom; but in each case neither of the two dependencies would be what it is without the other. The coming and going of moments, which we plot, as objects of thought, along the line of time, cannot be interchanged in such a way that coming would become going, and going, coming; but if between the two there obtains a connection like that between the rising and falling of a wave, then the way in which the present depends on the past cannot be separated from a way in which the past depends on the present. We shall return to this later.

The actuality of reciprocal dependencies can be pointed to, but not conceived; every conceived relation, by contrast, is as such [p. 1201] one-sided (or reciprocal only in the sense of pairwise-belonging one-sidednesses), and therefore "directed" in a wholly different sense than actuality would be from the irreversibility of coming and going. Just as certainly as, in the mechanical world-picture, the present second of happening depends on the preceding second of happening, never the reverse, and consequently no interactions whatever take place (in this Schopenhauer was right), just as certainly does actuality know only interactions, however different in kind and strength they may always be. (The improper reversibilities of physics concern merely the undoing of objective effects.)

In order that I may catch sight of the cloud, something of the essence of the cloud must, to be sure, have appeared to me within the fraction of a second. But as soon as, thanks to the immediately occurring act of apprehension, the connection has dissolved — the appearance having separated itself from the soul, the cloud-thing from the bearer of perception — I stand, in seeing, only related to the cloud, and to this direction of perception issuing from the I there is nothing corresponding on the side of the object perceived. When Eckhart taught that it is one and the same thing to see and know God and to be seen and known by him, and when afterward, quite analogously, the Cusan saw the goal of world-history in the attainment of a state in which our loving of God coincides with our being loved by him, such boldnesses of thought confirm for us that, with the beginnings of the knowledge of the nature of beholding, its essential difference from the nature of perceiving and thinking at once began to emerge. For although the glances of two persons may "meet" and "cross," they are opposita that never coincide. Whoever doubts it should try to picture how the direction of person A's gaze from A to B could be thought as a process that could not be separated from the process of person B's gazing from B to A (and equally the reverse).

Through the "crossing" glances of two persons, vital processes can indeed be stirred up in them — whether in both, or predominantly in one; but this happens not through the act of apprehension, which always remains self-contained, but insofar as, on the occasion of the process of perceiving, either each of the two persons, or at least one of them, was able to let something of the essence of the other person appear and assert itself against what is merely objective. (In more familiar language: it happens [p. 1202] through the working-in of the expression of the alien soul into the soul of the bearer of perception.) If, in the extreme case, the primal image of the one person appears to the other, then a bond is woven between it and the recipient of the primal image, even though the bearer of the primal image has not the slightest inkling of it, and the influence of this on the soul of the recipient of the image will ultimately even come to light objectively, in that the life-conduct of the "induced" one changes in some way. But how far the process also concerns the "inducer" — let a brief consideration teach us of that state of affairs by which the intercourse of man with man is determined in its depth.

If we set side by side the bearer of the primal image and the recipient of the primal image, the former is an unconsciously acting self-being, the latter a suffering self-being, to whom, out of what is received, something throughout becomes conscious. If we said earlier that every living being forms the center of the innumerable "induction-effects" of its fellow beings, the example just given reminds us that, without prejudice to the truth of that, we must divide self-beings in general, and human beings in particular, into those from whom "inductions" predominantly issue, and those who predominantly receive "inductions" — or, more briefly, into predominantly acting and predominantly receiving bearers of soul, whereby we can hardly avoid recalling the primal polarity of the male to the female. If we compare the former, with reference to our sun, to suns, and the latter to planets and satellites, we see at once that not only does every planet need its sun and will therefore seek it out if it lacks it, but also that every sun needs its satellites. One can, though one need not, illustrate this by the forms and instances of what is commonly understood by love. "Circles" and "centers" have formed themselves as long as there has been a humanity, and will only fully disintegrate in post-historical humanity; and they originally formed themselves not out of a will to power on the part of the centers, out of urges to submission on the part of the group "circling" around them, but as a consequence of the vital polarity of an acting bearer of the primal image toward the recipient souls, which fulfill themselves in that, aroused by the numen of the center, they mirror it.

That the recipient souls are changed by this needs no further word. But from the greatest to the smallest one can also demonstrate, for acting souls, the reciprocity of receiving and acting. The "born ruler," cast into a humanity that has passed beyond "the age of [p. 1203] kings," and thus condemned to exchange the sublime solitude of the king for the abandonment of a king without a people, suffers under this and transforms himself into a ruler over inwardnesses, one different from the ruler over men. Whoever kindles love often experiences in himself some consequence of it, differing according to his otherwise nature, whether he consciously attaches much or little weight to it. He grows to a different outcome than would have happened without the vis attractiva, and certainly suffers a decline of life when it wanes. Whoever is met throughout with indifference becomes, without exception, inwardly poorer for it; and whoever tends to arouse reluctance or even hatred either breaks on account of it or grows into a greater doer of deeds than he would have become without it, through a strengthening of sheer evil within him.<sup>99</sup>

<sup>99</sup> On page 1203. — Compare, on this, our treatise "Über den Quell der unmittelbaren Neigungsgefühle," already published in 1899 and reprinted in the collected volume of our essays "Zur Ausdruckslehre und Charakterkunde" (Kampmann, 1926), pp. 19–24.

Let us turn once more to the vital center of a vital circle: both the center and the circle are as little opposita as they are in the geometric circle, but poles, and what coincides in the streams from within outward with the streams from without inward falls under the ancient concept of Eros, which cannot be covered by the concepts of love current today. Were the word "organism" not so badly misused today, one might at most compare such circles to organisms — but not at all to states (compounds too, like "bee-state," "ant-state," "termitestate," are fundamentally mistaken!) — though one would at once have to recall that symbiotic associations of the widest significance are supra-individual organisms, and thereby occasionally come into the neighborhood of cosmic associations (like satellites and a central star). We find both — the connectedness of vital "circle" and vital "center," and the originally cosmic nature of the "circle" — in the highest perfection among the ancient Peruvians, whose Inca was, as is well known, the adored representative of the sun-god (as his wife and sister was representative of the moon-goddess) and was connected with his people as the heart, or indeed the head, is with the living body. Pizarro, at the head of 168 Spanish bandits, "conquered" and subjugated the entire Peruvian people by capturing their king Atahualpa through Christian methods of treachery and infamy: the people, in order to ransom him, brought the demanded mountains of gold (estimated at a value of 72 million marks, an unheard-of sum in those days!), stripping the temples of their treasures, indeed of their roofs, and fell, as if beheaded, into the hands of the white villain, after [p. 1204] the latter, following spiritual exhortation, had strangled the Inca and burned his corpse upon the pyre. — What here held sway in its highest perfection is found in a thousandfold form in all associations retaining even a trace of participation in life. The "patriarchal" relation of the great farmer of former times to his servants, of Nordic or Greek Anaktes to their retinue (Odysseus and Eumaeus!), the loyalty of retainers among the Germanic peoples and in the Germanic Middle Ages, at best even the bond between Caesar and the people, between "Little Father" Tsar and the Russian muzhik: these and countless reciprocities of a similar kind cannot be understood without assuming at least the resonance of an Eros between acting centers and receiving members of the groups closed into a circle around them (not to speak of the primitives, for whom we shall later have to assert even an excess of reciprocal bonds).

The shattering of the symbiotic circles is a long, sad, and terrible episode in the life of humanity, an episode as young or as old as — world history, accompanying with the utmost exactness, through many intermediate stages and attempts at compromise, the wave-by-wave decline of symbolic thinking before conceptual thinking, and completing itself with the victory of the Heraclean will. It would be doing too much of a good thing to still want to furnish proof today for the deadly opposition between the communist programs of the present, which annihilate human beings into rods, pins, and belts of the state-machine, and the fellowship-Eros of the old village community, which stands under the sign of the cults of motherhood. Only "ill will" fails to see the deadly enmity here. But it is not superfluous to say that out of shattered poles there always arise opposita, namely in the sense of two "opponents."

One recognizes this easily where the brutal violence of a despot enslaves a people; what one too often overlooks, on the other hand, is that the so-called democratic constitutions — the more democratic, all the more so — never were, and are, anything other than the straightest paths to the unbounded rule of the money-bag! America is Dollarica, and Soviet Russia will be a super-America! The opposita of the rationalized state are called: the omnipotence of the holders of the greatest "capital," the impotence of the utterly "destitute." From this opposition of the two follows the uninterrupted "struggle for competition," follow party struggles, class struggles, crimes, revolutions, wars among peoples. The calculable end is either: the destruction of all, or: the automatization of all.<sup>100</sup> [p. 1205] Macrocosm and Microcosms. — If we think of a distant place, of what happened yesterday or will happen tomorrow, of the room next to our own, we have always also thought of a between. Objective space, objective time, objective matter — together they ground the never-to-be-penetrated between, without which the object would not exist at all, and with respect to which coincidences do not take place. In actuality, insofar as it is to be conceived, nothing coincides, since of any two of its states of affairs, which we let coincide by way of experiment, either both, or one of them, would by that very fact have ceased to exist. Hegel was certainly a clever and thought-rich mind; but his doctrine of the "turning-over" of concepts into one another is a childish thing, and amounts in the end to the attempt to master, by means of the faculty of judgment, the boundaries in whose drawing that very faculty consists, by legitimizing a confusion of principle. — If, by contrast, we think of the incomprehensible world of images, which are appearances not of objects but of essences, then out of that same between, which with respect to objects is what separates them, there arises, with respect to images, a bond that links them. The spatial and temporal being-outside-one-another also has a share in this, insofar as it partakes of continuity; but we did not need merely to point to indecomposable features of the facts, because we were and are able to call the connecting element itself by name: it is called happening. This, however, as we have meanwhile learned, is in principle a reciprocal happening between polarly opposed similarities. The word "connection" [Zusammenhang] expresses precisely this in a spatially intuitive manner, and "coincidence" means, in the last analysis, the inseparability of polar processes (for which, in the history of thought, Heraclitus offered us the first example, with the "way up" and the "way down").

<sup>100</sup> On page 1204. — This is not the place to describe the path to that point; only one intermediate stage shall be mentioned, because it eases the understanding of a phenomenon of the present that disgusts educated taste almost more even than the mutual slaughtering for Mammon's sake. The bearer of the earliest advances of the will to power that *detaches itself* from life is the medicine-man, the priest. Since Nietzsche we know, or can know, that the progress from a straightforward intelligence, such as was proper to the hunter and warrior, the herdsman and tiller of the soil, and, among peoples, to the master peoples, toward the *cunning* intelligence that invented, among other things, dialectic, was at first caused far more by the priest than by the merchant. In possession of magical recipes, but no longer of magical gifts, he knows how to spread about himself the nimbus of power through magically flickering *jugglery*. He invents, knows, and masters all the arts of suggestion, and puts in the place of images not concepts (as the philosopher later did) but a theater of images. A master in the deceit of masks, and a dazzler with false semblances, he takes possession of men's minds by poisoning, through the instilling of preposterous fears, the instincts of men, and by setting himself up as their savior, physician, and redeemer. Although the secret methods have been profaned since Mesmer, the type has splendidly maintained itself down to the present day. And so bourgeois society teems far and wide with sects, "secret" leagues, lodges, orders, conventicles, groups partly fanatical, partly saccharine, gathered each around a medicine-man who, as "Master," "Adept," "Seer," "Saint," "Priest-King," celebrates blasphemous consecrations, promoting feeble-mindedness in the adoring congregation of his disciples, little lambs, and fools, while attending, for *himself*, to the business of his fame — a "business" that, as everyone knows, today never comes up short. This mischief, a repulsive caricature of vital community-formations, decomposes the arts, the sciences, literature, with a contemptible cult of personality, and works rapidly toward the extermination of the meager remnants of *independence of judgment* that have here and there still remained amid the raging of the struggles of interest. —

The chief task of the inquiry into essence that results from this — a task in whose service stand all parts of our work that are not charged with rebutting the false claims of "pure understanding" — is the discovery of a polarity in every elementary similarity, and the demonstration of the bipolar character of all connections. Going hand in hand with this is the formation of homologous series of polarities by virtue of a primal polarity running through them all. If, for example, in the following series: space and time — night and day — matter and ether — left and right — female and male, all the first terms are to correspond to one another, and likewise all the second terms, this can only be the case insofar as, in each pair, the primal polarity of suffering and acting, or of receiving and fructifying, has become particularized [p. 1206]. This, in turn, leads us back to the intercourse of the suffering soul with acting powers, which we must now investigate more closely in a twofold respect.

While it is generally grasped at once that, as a result of the crossing of the glances of two persons, connections can be forged between two souls — regardless of whether, say, one of the two were a predominantly impressing soul and the other a predominantly impressed one — the breath of his spirit tends to fail the merely objectively thinking man when one asserts the same for the relation of the soul of the beholder to the essence of, say, the cloud. For in thinking of two persons he thinks along with them two souls, to which he credits some sort of reciprocal effects upon the bodies and their comportments, whereas in thinking of a person and a cloud he thinks along with it only one soul; he thereby evidently confuses the appearance of the cloud with the cloud-thing, which without doubt remains untouched by whether one looks at it or not. Yet even if one avoids such confusions, one encounters a difficulty.

We have set far apart the soul of the self-being and what we have called the elemental souls. But if we consider that, in the process of beholding, the outer world — for which the cloud here serves as our symbol — is something purely acting, and the soul something purely suffering, then the primal polarity would be most perfectly realized precisely when the outer pole possessed only the capacity to act, as in the case of the cloud, and not, besides that, also a capacity to suffer, as in the case of the alien person; and so the reciprocal happening, in which we have recognized the meaning of connectedness, would have to attain its highest perfection precisely in this case. If, however, objective consequences of this seem to us possible only on the one side, namely on the bearer of soul, but not on the other, namely the cloud, then — and here lies the emphasis — the polarity of the connected members would remain exposed to certain doubts for just as long as reasons were not shown, together with it, for the impossibility of factually graspable consequential appearances on the acting pole.

That weather, climate, soil, or, more briefly, the landscape (in the most comprehensive sense) not only shapes plants and animals directly and powerfully, and shapes man considerably, but shapes him further, mediately, through the senses, is well known today. An extensive body of material has been produced to prove the transient influences of environment upon comportments, and the lasting influences upon [p. 1207] the permanent constitution — including the "constitutions" — of all living beings.<sup>101</sup> Indeed, the merest feeling for intuitive images suffices to discover the incompatibility of the appearance of the Eskimo with the equatorial landscape, of the appearance of the Negro with the landscape of the Arctic; and what thus becomes readily perceptible in the large and the gross also occurs — only less noticeably — down to the smallest and finest details. According to the measurements of the anthropologist Boas, for example, there can hardly still be any doubt that in the United States the skull-forms already of the immediate descendants of immigrant Europeans (even when still born in Europe) undergo a slight alteration in the direction of assimilation to the average measurements of the American! From the standpoint of what we may call a science of happening, there is, finally, no change of air pressure, humidity, or electrical potential-gradient without changes in the vegetative system of the self-being, no process of beholding in man without a transformation of the beholding soul. But where would we find the signs of this reciprocal intercourse, or, to place the stress on what is missing here, where would we find the signs of a dependence of the macrocosm, too, upon the souls of the microcosms?

<sup>101</sup> On page 1207. — Compare *Hellpach*, Geopsychische Erscheinungen.

We could call to mind many passages of this work; but one need only think back to what was set forth on page 664-65 in order to come at least very close to an answer to the question. "As what we behold them, so we do unto things ... No longer to behold them is already to narrow the life of images; to behold something worthless into them is to wage a deadly war upon it." In order to draw out the full content of such sentences, we must consider both sides, the positive and the negative, one after the other. — If this is the meaning of cosmic happening, that it should appear, then it completes itself only for the first time in that it works its way into beholding souls. Only through pairing with the suffering of the soul-pole are primal images released out of the happening of the acting pole, whereas the happening by itself would remain the primally-mighty but unparticipating blaze which the ancients labeled with the easily misunderstood name "chaotic." In relation to intuitive images, and with reference to them, primal images are intuitive images within the "nimbus" or the "aura," or also appearances of distance. Without the beholding of the beholder the cloud would not be present as an appearance of distance, notwithstanding that, among other things, the condition of what we mean, in the language of understanding, by the thing-like cloud, would be present. But with this we have not yet exhausted the cosmic consequences of [p. 1208] the working-in of elemental powers into beholding souls.

In relation to the beholder, the image is indeed, as has been shown at length, the counter-pole of such processes of his inner being as translate themselves into compelled movements of his body; and these in turn emerge immediately in the whirlings of the dance as in rhythmic chant-speech, and mediately in all activities aimed at incarnating primal images. Just as, without the soul of the beholder, the cosmos would not come to appearance, so, without the body of this soul, the actuality-laden work would not arise — the lasting condition of the constant renewal of primal images. But since the earth itself is thereby altered, we have in this an irrefutable testimony to objective consequences of cosmic happening, which would be lacking without its pairings with microcosms capable of far-beholding.

The transformations of the earth, insofar as it let continents rise, wander, and sink again, welled up lavas, layered mountains and made them weather away, created lakes and deserts, dammed, released, and diverted rivers, are of an essentially different origin from those of its transformations that occurred through the spreading life of single-celled organisms, plants, and animals, of whose significant share in the structure of the planet such legacies as coal seams, diatomite (of the diatoms), chalk cliffs, coral reefs, and shell masses tell us. But an incomparably deeper difference in essence separates the wampum belt — woven from the polished shells and pierced pearls of the Venus clam and the horn shell — from these, and separates the totem figure carved from the wood of the sycamore, and the pyramid towered up from the limestone of the Nummulites, from their raw materials in the same way. If, resting on our account in the 65th chapter, we take such works of man to be just as unadulterated res natae as the shell, the sycamore wood, the foraminiferal limestone, then they are palpable precipitates of the gamos of distance with the soul of the beholder, and confirm the real presence of transformations of the face of the earth arising from the presence not so much of living beings as, rather, of beholding souls.

The earth, as it were a dwelling-place of elemental souls, would accordingly crown itself with the works of naturedependent shapers, and their cosmically compelled working would in turn be a fate-necessity awakened in beholding and consummated in the birth of images. And this consummation would stand in accord with the consummation brought forth by the unawakened, [p. 1209] shaping powers; for it belongs to the mystery of the "blind" governance of earthly as of sidereal forces that, though unconcerned for the torments and joys of the self-beings sprung from them, with frost and drought and flood and storm and fire and ashfall and quakings of the ground they snap life after life before it ripens, sparing not even their strongest and most beautiful "children," yet with inexhaustible generative power tirelessly give birth anew to the perfect. In nature outside of man one will not find the flower whose bold colors do not fuse into a chord, the tree whose leaf-forms would not fit inimitably to the linear character of its branches, the meadow or prairie whose stones and plants and animals would not sound together symphonically. Insofar, then, as souls and world are not opposita but poles, whose vibrations interfere harmonically in the process of beholding, just so far does all the acting as well as the omitting of man not break the rhythm of the landscape but crown it with memorial marks of eternity.<sup>102</sup>

<sup>102</sup> On page 1209. — This is the theme of our book "Mensch und Erde."

To this belong the productions of human artistry, from houses to garments, but no less the so-called sacred groves, sacred springs, rivers, lakes, rocks, mountain peaks, trees, bays, animals — in short, all the sites consecrated by Pelasgian piety of mind and thereby withdrawn from the encroachment of arbitrary will — inasmuch as those works are able to crown the landscape only by leaving untouched in it what must remain unviolated, if its rhythm is to keep rolling on undisturbed through what has been created by man.

If we now let, in thought, the gift of beholding grow weaker and weaker, the process of perceiving grow ever more naked, until finally, in place of world-receiving souls, there remain almost only will-tautened "subjects," and in place of fructifying powers only "objects," hard and cold resistances to the blows that shatter them, then, within humanity, elemental acting has yielded to self-willed counter-acting, the will to work in general to the will to deed, and demiurgic building to an amok-run of destruction; with which we would then have arrived at the negative sense of our guiding thought: "to behold something worthless into things is to wage a deadly war upon the life of images." But precisely because it is only through the tearing-apart of the reciprocal intercourse between soul and cosmos that the murderous violences come into play, which break the rhythm of the landscape and, on their path of annihilation, now race faster and faster [p. 1210] toward their goal — namely, the killing of the earth itself — we become fully certain of the original polarity, and find irrevocably confirmed the dependence of the macrocosm, too, upon the events in the heart of the microcosms!

Since our work in general, and not least this work, is strewn with examples of the appalling devastations which the will to power — that is, the will, that is, Spirit — daily, no, hourly, wreaks upon the inhabitants of the earth, man himself included, it seems superfluous to swell those already offered with further ones. Should one wish to take in the counterregions at a single glance, one may set beside the torturous extermination of eagles, condors, herons, birds of paradise, albatrosses, and so forth, for fashion's purposes, the circumstance that formerly there were not only sacred ibises, geese, and cranes, but even sacred crocodiles and snakes; or set beside the shattering of any landscape of the earth whatever, however overwhelming its splendor, whenever it is a matter of erecting derricks for the extraction of petroleum, laying out a racetrack for automobiles, building factories for the swiftest possible transformation of the last whales into whalebone, oil, and — fertilizer, the fact that, not one human generation ago, in the interior of China a railway line could not infrequently be laid, and, in spite of the most tempting offers of capital-rich companies, had to be abandoned, because it could not be done without displacing several ancestral graves by a few hundred meters. — In order to secure for themselves, before closing time, at least a semblance of a power of disposal even over the slain, people today hasten to petrify it in manifold ways: for instance by capturing everything that crawls and flies "from the cradle to the bier" with the camera and putting it on show in lucrative picture-books (or, still more profitably, by means of films), or by gathering it, stuffed or otherwise "prepared," into museums, where too, abducted from the places of their destination, torn away from the remotest temples and the deepest graves, the legacies of a still-glowing human past are surrendered to curiosity. America has carried this furthest in such curiosity-shops, some of which house even exterminated peoples in the form of — wax figures. That fits none too badly with the American, of whose gruesome pre-history the bloodiest chapter has been told us by a brave author of the present, Friedrich von Gagern, in his Grenzerbuch. The history of humanity is a chain of atrocities; [p. 1211] but all of them are surely surpassed in hideousness by the roughly century-and-a-half of devilries by whose aid the emergent American succeeded in the complete annihilation of the landscape of a mighty continent and the slaughtering-down of nearly all the Indian tribes, to which, for heroism and wilderness-beauty, little has compared since the earliest days. We would not know how to document the desecration of the earth through human outrage more powerfully than is done in a few sentences from the very book just named:

It speaks of the sending out of the bold spy Christopher Gist by the "Ohio Company," founded "for the disenfranchising and despoiling of the Indians and the filling of a few large money-bags," into the region of the upper Ohio around 1750. "Where today the turbines and motors of unstoppably growing cities — Columbus, Dayton, Springfield, Cincinnati, Toledo — roar, rage, devastate, annihilate, driving the feverish metabolism of a mechanized humanity gone mad, there the dark bison, the herd of the great Spirit, once grazed peacefully in the blue-grass and white clover of lovely little prairies; graceful groves of hard sugar maple and wild sour cherry, of black walnut and tall-trunked ash, of huge hickories and mighty poplars accompanied and lined, in most pleasant alternation, the many small waters, thickly peopled with red deer and strong flocks of wild turkey, bears and tree-felling beavers.... Think of the old Norse hero's hall with its smokeblackened timbers and its baring trophies, set somber, silent chieftains upon delicately tanned buffalo hides daintily adorned with colored picture-chronicles around the shadowcasting fire — and one is in the romantic America of a longsunken heroic age, in Picqua on the great Miami, a hundred miles behind primeval forest and prairie, far from the last white settlement.... Ohio, the beautiful river, la belle Rivière, stream of paradise. — In mightily princely repose the broad mirror of the flood glides on through the solemn primeval forests. Hundreds of deer stream across, this way and that, through the sacred waters, in silver-plowing wake; hundreds of peaceable bears cool themselves on the bank under the roof of the wide-spreading sycamores. Tens of thousands of ducks drift with the gentle current, ten thousand rise up roaring, it rushes from their wings like a thunderstorm's rain. Blessed garden-islands dream, transfigured by evening, in the shimmering current; above them hover the bright choirs of herons. — That was the Ohio. White man has made it into the sewage of his great slaughterhouses [p. 1212] and ash-heaps, into the cloaca of black iron cities, into the gutter. White civilized so-called man, the beast. Not the child of the great Spirit — the Indian. —" And: "Today almost the whole of America is a single ghastly waste of rock and slag; the fire-breath of the iron machine-dragons, the poison-breath of the American soul, has devoured its sacred forests."

One more step remains for us to take, and it is taken at once, in order to clarify the connection between soul and the actuality of images. Whether the power of beholding grows faint because the aura pales, or whether the aura pales because the power of beholding grows faint, may differ from case to case and matters little once we know that, thanks to the polarity of the processes, changes in the one cannot occur without changes in the other. Only for this reason can the life-hostile will ever gain a foothold: because in the process of perception the beholding, to which the actuality of images would disclose itself, has grown faint — and even if this were to happen from disturbances of vitality in the bearer of perception, still, through the blocking of the path of its efficacy, on which alone it would first come to completion in images, the event itself would thereby lose in potential besoulment. In relation to this we spoke in the 65th Chapter of the escaping of the powers, and we might equally well speak of the vanishing of the essences. They are really present, because they can break forth as aura, and they are never objectively present, because actuality assumes the spiritual form of objecthood, and in particular of thinghood, precisely and only insofar as it has become essence-less in the life-medium of the bearer of perception. If we place the sense of the essences into the symbolic unity of meaning of the primal fire, then we may say that through the pairing of primal fire in the blood of the beholder with effective powers, the primal fire of the event is set free — and we would thereby even have opened a gate to the today, admittedly, wholly esoteric doctrine of the essences of actuality

We recall in passing once more Heraclitus's πῦρ ἀείζωον, the cults of the flame-worshippers, Nietzsche's saying that the heart of the earth is of gold. We point to the fact, unexplained to this hour, that the Homeric Greeks lent the gods, instead of ordinary blood, ichor, that is, a luminous blood; we mention that Schuler coined for the primal-fire-content of the blood the beautiful name "blood-glow," and that even in incomparably richer times than our [p. 1213] own he believed he had to grant blood-glow only to a few people, though under otherwise comparable circumstances to blooming youth in the highest degree. A first, and unless we are mistaken, also the only attempt at an archaeological mastery of the relevant facts was undertaken as early as 1859 by Ludolf Stephani with his study "Nimbus und Strahlenkrone," in which many proofs are to be found that, according to the testimony of the ancients, ecstatically excited persons often appeared to those present in radiant glory.<sup>103</sup> Mystical "illuminations" and ritual "distributions of light" have their origin here. Finally, let it be recalled that every eros kindled from within by blood-glow — regardless of which image it embraces — sets out to flow into the state that we know from ancient consecration customs as "cosmogonic" eros.

<sup>103</sup> On page 1213. — Characteristically, the "halo" remaining from this tends to confine itself to the head, and then, growing ever narrower and more delicate, to hover *above* it, before it is lost altogether!

Realms grown strange to us today would be entered by whoever made the investigation of auras his concern. He would find the polar opposition of bearers of the ember to bearers of the flame: the former are clinging, the latter roving; the former tellurian, the latter sidereal; the former essentially feminine, the latter essentially masculine; the former preservers and keepers, the latter disseminators of the primal fire; the former founders of the house, the wall, the city, the latter heroes, adventurers, conquerors, and so forth. He would press deeper than scholarship has been granted to do into the essence of the sacred lamps, into the essence of the Vestaflame, of the Yule-log, of the need-fire, of the tree of lights, of the Midsummer fires, and of all festivals that stand under the sign of the torch or the burning wheel; and he would gain a knowledge of the symbolism of colors that would leave far behind what even a Goethe was able to teach about it. — This we now leave unspoken, and instead sum up the result of our inquiry, with reference to the example of the cloud, as follows. The soul of the beholder changes at the primal image of the cloud, and while certainly the cloud-thing does not change, the essence of actuality that appears to us as cloud does indeed change, through pairing with the beholding soul: it renews itself and grows stronger with the birth of its image, it dwindles by escaping wherever the "way inward" is barred to it

One cannot prove esoteric truths in the customary manner, but neither can one refute them in the customary manner. Meanwhile let us not forget that we need not invoke the symbol of the primal fire in order to raise the two-sidedness of the dependencies in the exchange between the macrocosm and the souls of the microcosms above all doubt. For suppose that the bodily graspable consequences of the working of the soul-bodies [p. 1214] are essentially different when the soul predominates than when the will predominates in the bearer of life, then the body of the earth is altered differently in the one case than in the other, and with it unavoidably the tellurian event 1 The process of destruction, for example, that goes hand in hand with the unleashing of arbitrary will, has already today transformed climates and weather to such an extent that the fine instruments of the meteorologist are no longer needed in order to become aware of the changes. Karstification of wholly deforested regions brings dreary droughts in its train (there are islands that have died off from it); broad clear-cuttings heighten the suddenness of violent changes of weather; the canalization of great rivers leads, as a result of considerably accelerated flow, with almost periodic regularity to flood catastrophes of dimensions formerly unknown; the draining of swamps, lakes, and marshes alters the groundwater level, which again has incalculable consequences; the enrichment of the atmosphere with coal dust in the vicinity of extended industrial centers brings about a considerable rise in the average yearly warmth. The effects of the masses of iron raised above the ground, of the countless electrical "currents" that race around the globe along wires, of the radio waves that ceaselessly shake the planetary space up to the stratosphere, will certainly one day prove to be monstrous; not to speak of the wholly incalculable after-effects of the extermination of all plants and animals outside of human agriculture. In short, even he to whom the doctrine of the actuality of images remains closed cannot deny the mightiest upheaval in the life of the earth as a consequence of an upheaval in the soul-constitution of man; but we need no more than this

By this, the profound difference between the mutual intercourse of two souls and that of a soul with cosmic powers is neither denied nor diminished: here, on the one side, only suffering and receiving, on the other only acting and fertilizing; there, suffering and acting, receiving and fertilizing, alternating more or less, and even where the acting of the bearers of the primal image predominates and the suffering of the recipients of the primal image predominates — not, on the one side, unbeholding event and, on the other, beholding rapture, but rather, on the one side, magical communication of images, comparable to that through symbols and eternity-works, and on the other side its magical mirroring. For just as the essences of actuality are renewed through the release of images, so the blood-glow of the creative soul renews itself, among other things, in the reflection of its primal image in the mirror of the selflessly loving soul. — [p. 1215] The Polarity of Present and Past. — We complete our result through a brief consideration of the other side of the matter. The line of metric time runs from the past, through the present, into the future, by continually extending itself in this direction. Because, accordingly, the moment of the event now taking place, which also in the end underlies it, means the real ground or the cause or condition — or whatever one wishes to call it — of the moment next following, and nothing besides, every past moment too is nothing but past and thus irrevocably over. Now, to be sure, without doubt nothing that has ever happened happens again. The important document that was accidentally burned does not come back; the friend who has died, likewise not; the exterminated plants, animals, and races of men do not come back; nor does the landscape of the Indians that the Americans have laid waste and entombed, and: "What has once been struck from the minute — No eternity gives it back." But that is not at all what is meant

The invention of metric time has, rather, led to the coinvention of reversible processes and has raised that phantom of endlessly self-repeating sequences which draws nearer and nearer to realization with the triumphal march of the machines. It is not insight into the eternal otherness of every moment of actuality but the belief in the equality and calculability of moments that has produced the concept of a time which, in truth, is de-temporalized time, a measuring-tape of the never-to-be-measured, and an imaginary coordinate. But if, for the confessor of the time-specter and the passionate calculator of the future, precisely the past is what becomes derealized, then we have no doubt where, in himself, the natural ground of his believing this lies: he has lost his past and "lives" only in the projects of a future he himself is to fabricate, in relation to which his present, grown empty, is nothing more than a foothold and a means to an end. Let us not hesitate to reverse the proposition decisively: only the present escapes the danger of running idle, which is kindled by primal images of the past, and only that moment fills life to the brim for which souls of former times renew themselves

We need not repeat that the appearance of distance is the appearance of the past. Whoever holds the one to be possible has likewise held the other to be possible, and has thereby envisaged the coincidence and interaction, in which we recognized the sense of connectedness, even for [p. 1216] the poles of present and past — poles which, to the factual logic of millennia, appeared so entirely in the light of the most irreconcilable opposites that it could only try to soften the irretrievability of what has been by the fiction of "supraheavenly spaces" and of a "better beyond" as the place of reunion. Just as not only the souls of the beholders depend on the cosmos, but also, though differently, the cosmos depends on the souls of the beholders, so now not only must present actuality depend on past actualities, but also, though differently, past actualities must depend on the ever-present.

One gauges at a single glance the unbridgeable abyss between the logic of symbolic and of conceptual thinking when one considers that nothing is more offensive and more absurd to the intellect than the thought of a kind of dependence of what has been upon the present (despite relativism!), and nothing more absurd to the soul — and more incredible — than the assumption of the opposite! Let one try, for a moment, to live one's way into the cult of the dead of an earlier age, for which something of the essence of the ancestors was present in the lar-figure, the anointed stone monument, the statue — growing stronger, to the blessing of the descendants, through the libations and votive offerings of adoring piety, growing cold through indifference, threatening ill to whoever desecrated its site — and one has one of the most eloquent testimonies to the belief in the reciprocity of intercourse between the departed and the living! Whoever now sees in this only "superstition," or even a somewhat exalted form of our so-called piety, might perhaps be given pause by the following.

After all, not so many are yet so utterly dead to the connection with the past that, in their feelings at the sight of the Colosseum, the Doric temple of Segesta, the Sassanid palace at Ctesiphon, or a Neolithic clay jar, a Bronze-Age blade, a scarab, a coin from the Rome of the Caesars, a Gothic chest, nothing of the shudder of high antiquity would resonate along; and if, accordingly, through the destruction of such objects a piece of antiquity is destroyed, how can one deny that the past too depends on the present, and not only the reverse! Would anyone be so dull as not to feel that, with the brutal destruction of the most wondrously powerful churches still remaining, the Russian ones, a people is robbed of its past and its soul thereby surely extinguished, after the most horrifying [p. 1217] slaughters had not fully succeeded in doing so; indeed, do not such atrocities betray an instinctive knowledge on the part of the perpetrators? And can the thought not yet have occurred to any reader that the stone axes, palstaves, idols, fibulae, face-urns dug out of the ground, that the kantharoi, lekythoi, and lamps, the statuettes and statues of antiquity in the mortuary chambers we call museums, are no longer what they were in the places of their working; and would he not thereby have conceded that they are more and other than mere things? And is not, likewise, a thousand-year-old oak a piece of antiquity? Is it not, all the more, a so-called untouched landscape, and are antiquities not once again murdered when such landscapes are murdered?

The false belief in actuality that supports and spurs on the merely objective mode of thinking is, of course, ready with its objection: even if, on the occasion of landscapes, stone axes, churches, and so on, one may recall various pasts, these themselves are not pasts but present facts, through whose destruction, at most, monuments of the past are abolished, but not facts that have been are altered. Meanwhile let one ask oneself: is Rembrandt's painting "Saskia" a piece of canvas with so-and-so many oil colors upon it, or is it something other and more? Would one who scraped off the oil colors have merely cleaned the canvas, as one might clean a palette? Should one answer the second half of the first question in the affirmative and deny the second question, one would thereby have unavoidably attributed actuality to the "more and other." Well then: by however much Rembrandt's painting is more and other than canvas together with oil colors, by at least so much is what is old more and other than what is new. Whoever wishes to make this palpable should call to mind the patina that has already become symbolic, or the actually present layer of weathering on all structures of great age, and should then no longer evade the unavoidable decision that, among other things (!), there are present in it distances of the past, waiting, as it were, for the beholding soul whose gaze would renew them, withering and dying under the piercing glances of curiosity, the dull glances of indifference, the caustically sharp glances of unloving criticism; wherein, after all, there would surely lie a kind of dependence even of what has already passed upon what is just now present.

Considerations of this kind make understanding easier, but they do not strike the core of the matter. We reach that core only after having made the transition from the seeming actuality of things to the real actuality [p. 1218] of images, within whose frame the actuality-laden structures of nature as much as of mankind take on the form of symbols of the event — and this means of an event that can only be thought of as interaction. Were one to assign it a direction by analogy, it would come out of the future and tear every present into the past, carrying it off into ever more remote distances. This becoming-ever-more-distant in time would then be a process exactly as real, with exactly as real consequent appearances, as the becoming-ever-more-distant in space of, for instance, the appearance of a mountain range as the observer's distance from it grows. Were we to translate this into the language of metrics, then what is a thousand years past would have more content of distance than what is a hundred years past, and would thus have become more completely "image," and in particular would be more thoroughly stripped of all those features which, in relation to the actuality of the event, would have to count as merely disturbing features. Feeling assents, as often as we still today sometimes let the dead be "transfigured," and fully so when, in the death-cult consciousness of earlier peoples, the ancestors became the mightier the further their having-been receded into the depths of the past, finally becoming gods thanks to their entry into that distance of the past which no longer admits of differences of distance

Let us call to mind in swift review in which conclusions two modes of consideration so fundamentally different as the objective and the symbolic more or less agree with regard to temporality, and in which they diverge widely; it is advisable first to point out once again that the objective conception of the event — as always, so here too — does not dispense with the presupposition of an occurring actuality, in that it too posits a kind of dependence of present upon just-preceding processes, and has thereby formed that self-contradictory concept of a merely one-sided connectedness which — burdened at first still with the thought of cause and effect — is ultimately determined only to underpin the calculability of the sequences. But let a certain essential difference of consequence be thought along with this at once. In accordance with the "near-character of the objects of thought," what has been loses, for the dependence-conception of objective thinking, in quasi-efficacy to the extent of the length of its having-beenpast; whereas for the symbolic conception it gains, precisely thereby, in genuine capacity for effect. The single similarity of conception now to be named will prove to be merely apparent. If the event "flows" into the past, then [p. 1219] there can no longer be any talk of reversibilities, and consequently still less of a once-more of something that has been. Whether we stand on the ground of objective or of symbolic thinking, there is no shaking the pastness of the past.

But it is precisely here that the roads fork, never to meet again! One thing is the actuality of what has passed, another the chronicle of facts! The concept of what has been coincides with that of a fact no longer being. If, now, one has subordinated being to actuality, then what has been a fact becomes something utterly unreal; and behind the ever-present moment — including, at most, the immediately preceding moments involved in it — actuality plunges into the abyss of nothingness. The growing line of time is a growing nothingness, ceaselessly pushing before it the, as it were, foot-wide sheer wall of the present. To think of something past, or to recollect something past, here means as much as to think of something derealized or to recollect something utterly unreal — an evidently fruitless undertaking, from which the mind reluctantly turns away in order to throw itself entirely into bringing about futures which, in and for themselves, are equally devoid of actuality. Were the reflection directed toward goals of the will not, in its depths, unreflective, Heraclean mankind would long since have voluntarily sought, out of horror at its present hovering groundlessly, the death that it will involuntarily suffer at the end of the road.

The actuality of the event looks different when it oscillates between the poles of spatiotemporal nearness and spatiotemporal distance! Just as surely as, in the space of intuition, graspable nearness is connected with ungraspable distances, so surely, in the actuality of the event, is the wave just now cresting connected with the waves on the horizon-rim of the sea of the past; and just as it is past images that renew themselves again and again vegetatively in like fashion, so it is pasts that appear anew and ever anew, in a mighty circuit, to the beholding soul. The turn of phrase "flowing into the past" leaves, indeed, no doubt that without connection to images of former times the moment of the soul would be wholly empty! But if, accordingly, the past belongs to the very same event that becomes present in the moment — and, to be sure, only in the moment — then it follows, first, that precisely by virtue of passing away the image changes from moment to moment, and thus — in the language of metrics — is, after a thousand years, really other than it is after a hundred years; and, second and above all, in order to [p. 1220] adapt this to present-day thinking, that the primal-imagistic nature of the past is essentially co-determined by the image-receiving capacity of whatever bearers of soul are present at any given time. It had, and has, the deepest sense that among the Chinese, the Indians, and many primitive peoples, offspring had to be begotten and, where they were lacking, were replaced — and in part still are — by adoption, because otherwise the soul of one departing from the life of the day would necessarily lack the tending which alone is able to preserve it from de-realization.

How much could be gathered from this for a science of character drawing on the well-spring of essential thoughts cannot be set forth further here. Only two remarks shall be woven in that contribute a little more toward clarifying the metaphysics of the matter. If beholding awakens on the occasion of distances of space made present, then the soul feels, before it is carried away, above all the mighty pull of distance and a losing of itself in the expanse; if, on the other hand, beholding awakens on the occasion of distances of time made present, then, in the same phase of development, the soul feels, though drawn no less, above all a pulling power of its own self and an inner summoning of the distance of the past. Both states, as sides of one and the same underlying state, differ only in the distribution of accent and pass easily into one another. From the predominance of the distance of space, which accords with the roving type of soul, come, among other consummation-phenomena, the mystical excursions; from the predominance of the distance of time, which accords with the clinging type of soul, come, among others, conjurations and, as a late degenerate form, so-called necromancies. From both preliminary states of beholding, but quite especially from the approach of the image of the distance of the past, the mighty feeling of longing is fed. The relation to the future is added to longing merely as an elective affinity of thought; longing itself aims at the recovery of something that has flowed away, and therefore dies off with the vanishing of the values of the past. For distinguishing vital and, at most, magical wishing from wishing that is rational and capable of will, there is no more infallible test than examining feelings of wishing for their content of longing. With this, enough of this.

We now know: the past lives by virtue of the present, or it dies through the present; the one as much as the other, however, determines the content of the present. Everything set forth above concerning the vanishing of the essences and auras of appearance, and concerning the consequences of this in the realm of facts, can be described with equal correctness as the vanishing [p. 1221] of the essences of the past. But having just touched upon certain differences in the way of experience of the beholder, according as the image accrues to him more from the distance of space or more from the distance of time, we now briefly recall the particular form in which disaster works itself out for the present as a consequence of the killing of the past, and in doing so tie in with our remark that, for the mere intellect, every past thing is a nothing, or, spoken in an arithmetical simile, is, as it were, the one factor of a product whose other factor would be zero.

It does not conflict with this remark that everyone, even today, constantly bears the consequences of actions and events that have flowed away, and can become conscious of such relations; for reflection upon processes that have taken place by no means includes the thought of a possible vitality of the past. On the other hand, something of the past does indeed tremble on in every violent regret over something done, left undone, or otherwise come to pass, far more still, and even of a morbid kind, in every violent remorse; and it is, entirely, the past that rises threateningly against the perpetrator in the shape of — penal law. Yet the sharper-sighted observer will not overlook two things that considerably weaken this strongest remnant of the actuality of the past. The penal law of more or less all civilized peoples guards, with in part still cruel severity, property — not, however, property as such, but what is understood by it in a capitalist society that, as is well known, hangs the small thieves and — legitimizes the great ones; apart from this, it moves, here faster, there slower, toward — dissolution. (One must, of course, leave aside criminal prosecutions of political acts, for these are always genuine "persecutions," lightly masked with paragraphs.) Furthermore, all still-existing penal law derives itself, increasingly, from the thought of rendering harmless, if not indeed of "reforming," the criminal for the purpose of protecting the non-criminal — which has, to be sure, long corresponded to the actual state of affairs, but by no means to the sense of law, which by origin and intent is just retribution. One need not be a prophet to predict: as surely as mankind, which was the bearer of soul and of the past, dies off, so surely does penal law too, sooner or later, die off, and with it the concept of law altogether, to make room for a struggle for power no longer regulated by paragraphs. The maxim "he who has power has the right" [p. 1222] will soon be a generally sanctioned custom, and is, indeed, today already nearly so in business, in finance, and wholly so in politics!

We shall treat the origin of the concept of law only in the concluding section. Here, however, let it be stated what else, besides the emptying of its present, threatens a mankind that has not only turned away from what has been, not only destroyed its monuments, but has also long since paid scribes whose task it is to falsify, to lie away, to poison what has been: it is threatened by the avenging recoil of that, an ur-phenomenon that in the mythic language of the ancients was called the vengeance of the Erinyes. One need not necessarily think here of snake-haired hags or, say, of apocalyptic riders; it suffices to see with unclouded eyes what has already begun mightily, and of which these sentences from the above-cited work of F. von Gagern remind us: "World history is nothing but the history of an eternal blood-feud; and who knows how near to us is the time when the accursed white master-peoples of the Occident, in mutual self-laceration, perish through their own civilization, through their own delusion and essence, as an atoning sacrifice for the true, the innocent children of God, whose bones lie silent beneath the iron-sown battlefields of their murderers, whose spirits hover lamenting over the sites of their devastated home-gardens, their ravaged paradises." It seems to us that this self-laceration has set in with blows so mighty that it might be hard to decide which comes sooner: man as an unconscious machine, or the globe without man. The former would be the consummation of the running-idle that follows from an annihilated past; the latter, the downfall through the vengeance of the desecrated past.

[p. 1223]

#### 69. Kapitel — Urbilder und Phantome — Chapter 69 — Primal Images and Phantoms

Insofar as the world of intuition is a world of appearances, and the world of appearances is the only possible form of the revelation of the event, we must judge every content of intuition whatsoever as an appearance of the event, and may then not even exempt the ordinary world of perception from this. Making use once more of the often-employed metaphor of stratification, one could say: whether extremely deep or extremely shallow strata of the event appear in the content of intuition on which the act of perception rests, some event must underlie it, since otherwise nothing at all would be beheld and thus nothing further perceived either.
