What appears here, under the name of the sea, before the inner eye, has the actuality of an image and of an image only; it has nothing of the actuality of that object bearing exactly the same name, in whose [p. 1256] water one can fish, whose depth one can sound, whose plants one can press for a herbarium. And it admits just as little of comparison with the "representation" of that object. We find the objective sea as ever the same, in one and the same universe, in the ever-same place, and we can think it or represent it in virtue of this selfsameness. The poet's sea we find never and nowhere, except at a favorable hour in his poem, and there never a second time as it was but a moment before! In vain does our spirit wish to seize it: for, in order to become aware of it, we would rather have to renounce all activity, to such a degree that, un-spirited and given over, we would be nothing but ones seized by it. The perceptible sea is grasped and thought; Lenau's sea was experienced and beheld by the poet. With the corporeal body of the former, the thing designated by the sound masks itself, as it were; in the naming sound-body of the latter, there appears the unseizable but gripping image. In the language of the mysticism explained earlier: the sea of the poem has a "sidereal body," which "is seen ungraspably" and comes to appearance for the hearer according to the measure of his capacity and readiness to be taken up by the magic of the word.

We have just now again suggested it: the thing could not have "appeared" at all, and consequently could not have been grasped and comprehended, without the actuality of that image which only the poet, and at times the seer, succeeds in loosening again from the captivity of thing-hood — and even they only in the rare moments of a love rapt beyond reflection. If it is beyond question images that live in the wordbody of poetry, and if through them there becomes alive for us whatever at all may seize us in the actually existing world, then the counterpart of the soul that seizes spirit must be an actuality of images, and of images alone! — Should one object that toothache too is an experience, we ask that it be remembered that this too, among other things, was emphatically argued and illuminated from many sides in earlier chapters. Notwithstanding this, it holds without restriction, even for the most violent bodily anguish, that its soul comes to effect and "expresses itself" again only in images (whereas, without the possibility of such an effect, the experience of anguish itself would be annihilated and sunk in the dark of unconsciousness). The cry of pain striking our ear would remain an essenceless noise so long as it did not touch the soul. But if it does so, then spirit is now seized by the very images, set into commotion, that light up beholdably in the [p. 1257] word of the poet when he "sings" the pain of the tortured one. This holds rightly, too, for all conceivable bodily feelings whatsoever: if it is truly the anguish, and even the "mute anguish," of the martyred that a poet is able to "say" (and we should not understand him, were it otherwise!), then the content of undergoing of the tormented soul of the body must be one and the same with just such images — which alone, after all, can be given voice in the word, both, of course, dis-thingified and freed from the dominion of the body. Poetic Genius and Prehistory. — The objective sea is always found in the selfsame place of a selfsame universe. The sea of Lenau's "Sturmesmythe" generates itself anew each time in the soul of the one experiencing the myth, and with it, at the same time, a whole earthly and heavenly universe that belongs to it. It is ensouled, otherwise it would not "speak" to the soul; and its soul must be a "demonic" one, provided we are right to choose this name for a soul of the universe. Suppose the poet had beheld the image not only inwardly but on the occasion of a perceived landscape, and suppose he still had a spirit just as believing as, at the moment of the releasing conception, he unquestionably had a believing soul — then he, sobered once again, would take those waters to be inhabited by demonic beings, and would perhaps erect altars there on which sacrifice might be offered. So it happened generally in the age of "Pelasgianism," and so it happened, at least essentially similarly, down into the most recent past among all "nature peoples," insofar as, amid the scorching desert wind of a humanity's godless fury of destruction, they were able to preserve age-old customs. We have repeatedly offered examples of the belief in images of prehistory and its reflective form of thinking — not conceptual, but symbolic. But we now wish, out of wonderlegends and divine service, out of fetish-veneration and sorcery, out of divination and superstition, out of hallowed customs and observances, omissions and commandments — in short, out of the entire legacy of the prehistoric round of humanity — to assemble in a definite sequence a larger series of testimonies to show that spirit fettered to life, notwithstanding the boundless diversity of its formations, and no less in the degenerate and disintegrating than in the healthy and perfect ones, rests upon the dominion of the belief in images over the belief in the actuality of things, and lets the efficacy (though certainly [p. 1258] not a discursive consciousness) of the following basic thoughts be recognized in without exception all its precipitates: the oneness in essence of images generally with the efficacious powers of the world; of images among themselves according to the measure of elemental similarities; of the particular image with its symbolic sign, and again with the human soul that receives the image as with the one that gives the sign.

Greek legend knows, among other things, two races of "autochthons," of which, in the course of time, the one is superseded by the other. The original (that is, earlier) one is the race of the Pelasgians, and this perishes in the mighty flood, with the exception of a single human pair, Deucalion and Pyrrha, from whom (in a magical manner, as will be discussed in detail later) the race of the Hellenes derives itself. We now choose the name "Pelasgianism," which even a Bachofen did not disdain after Romanticism had seized upon it and, with prescient instinct, made it into an essence, in order, for the present, to designate by it, in at least three, otherwise widely separated, groups of human beings, that in virtue of which they are, in the sense of the formulas just offered, bearers of a still pathic consciousness that thinks in symbols. The first consists of the genuine poets of all peoples and ages, insofar as they were not so much personalities as receiving organs for language-capable waves of the soul; the second, of the unhistorical "nature peoples" — if not of the present, where they scarcely exist any longer, then at least of the very recent past, to which may be partly added all remnants of unbroken strata of folk-life within the boundaries of culture; the third, of the prehistoric ancestors, especially of the European peoples of culture, whose essence is disclosed from divine images, cults, symbols, mysteries, and myths, but which besides lives on in not a few historically attested facts of (Promethean) antiquity, of which, accordingly, many features, taken in their psychic sense, belong to prehistory. But the emphasis here lies on the third group. It is this that furnishes us the standard for evaluating the other two. — With particular regard now to the poetic genius here included, certain differences must be indicated, alongside the similarities of the phenomena we have in view, since otherwise grave misunderstandings could scarcely be prevented.

We are far from equating the three groups named as wholes with one another. The "cultured" poet, even during poetic conception, no longer experiences the same thing, nor in the same way, that a Patagonian offering sacrifice experiences, and each of the two experiences [p. 1259] something other, and otherwise, than the Indra-priest of the oldest Vedas or an Inca of the Peruvians. The Pelasgianism of the two last named, although likewise not subsisting without spirit, lets the characters of pathic consciousness be recognized in their purest form; that of the cultured poet, as already spiritualized, is most often subject to the danger of disintegration (of which presently); that of the primitive, finally, exhibits, along the whole line, though in varying degree, distortions that are easy to characterize but hard to explain. Since we could only offer conjectures as to the causes, we restrict ourselves to a brief statement of the most important features in which degeneration-phenomena are to be discerned, arising from the misleading compulsion of spirit, and must, to be sure, avail ourselves each time, for this purpose, of the word "excess," inasmuch as these phenomena, quite simply, all and severally meet us again among the confirming marks of Pelasgianism! What distorts its countenance in the domain of the primitives is an excess of the boundness of each individual to the group, and of the group — and by means of it, again, of each individual — to the powers experienced as efficacious.

Today much is said of "collective" consciousness, "collective" states of life, and the like, as though of an initial condition of mankind out of which individual attitudes toward life had only gradually formed themselves, and we shall see in the course of our further exposition what is really the case here. But the excessive dependence of the life of primitives upon the images that signify fate to them cannot be understood from the strength of any communal feelings whatever; it must be understood from the fear that, thanks to the isolating intervention of spirit, had taken possession of the souls in those groups of peoples. We pass over here — since it will be investigated in detail — how, in consequence, a superstitious reification of idols and fetishes could gain ground, and mention only the second trait of degeneration, which forms the reverse side of the excess of boundness: the excess of magism arising from the warding-off of fear. Both traits fuse in the boundless tabooings by force of which the primitives were, indeed, above all preserved from "progress," but by which their Pelasgianism, too, could never come to completion. To choose at least one single example in advance: according to the belief of not a few primitives, the monthly course of woman can disturb the course of the universe, indeed threaten it with annihilation; and conversely the observance of the uniformly cruel prescriptions that are therefore to be heeded in this regard can [p. 1260] prevent such disturbances, indeed even wrest favorable turns for the fate of the world. — With this premised, we now seek to strip out what is common to all three groups. But before we thus arrive at the elemental symbols of Pelasgian thinking, we wish, with the help of graphic evidence, to try to approach that character of actuality of the world from which alone the "truths" of a consciousness can be derived that throve wholly and entirely on the ground of belief in a world of images.

[p. 1261]

#### 72. Kapitel — Bilderdienst und Wirklichkeitssinn — Chapter 72 — Image-Worship and the Sense of Actuality

*Image-Worship and Art.* — We have just now thought of the genuine poet as a belated preserver of vanished forms of life, but must now unfortunately add that it is precisely artists, and even poets, who, though they are the tardy heirs of an image-mighty prehistory, have, with and without fault of their own, contributed not a little to obscuring the true state of affairs in the mind of thinkers. For since we, living as we do in the actuality of things, can no longer very well concede an actuality to the world of the artistic work, and yet would gladly see justified by reasons what it is that makes it valuable to us, there has, in enthusiastic minds, and favored by philosophizing poets, allied itself decoratively with the creed of mechanism the saccharine doctrine of "aesthetic" semblance — as which, without the substratum of an actuality, indeed precisely out of a supernatural freedom from it, privileged intelligences so formed offer the exquisite joy of "pure forms." The pernicious repercussion on the consideration of the primal phenomena has, however, consisted in this: that one either, disputing the deepest disclosures of Romanticism, simply denies outright that in which genuine art stands connected with them — namely its content of symbolism; or else allows the symbolism, at most conceded, to count only as a "crude" preliminary form of "higher" stages of development, on which it would first have to be cleansed of the still all-tooearthly admixture of belief in the actuality of what it signifies. In the face of this it seems necessary to establish the following.

Besides that drive — if one wishes to call it a drive — which since the most ancient times has occasioned a creative doing on the part of man, there exists an animal impulse of imitation which, in mankind, under the influence at first of its dominant beholding, later of the development of its concepts, passes over into the urge to represent. This urge now fuses, indeed, in differing degree from case to case, with the creative capacity (for which [p. 1262] we may then also say formative power), but it is not the same as this. For while the urge to represent can be spiritually accented to any degree whatever, in that it strives, say, now toward the more imitative and so-called realistic, now toward the more independent and so-called idealistic image-formation of something thought (perceived, represented, conceptual), the formative drive aims solely and exclusively at the conjuring-fast of the image; and if, therefore, the former belongs to the expressive side of a person, the latter belongs to the expressive side of elemental beholding.

For a wholly and entirely elemental being that would still be free of consciousness, the formative drive would coincide with the formative capacity, and formative activity would occur not in the form of an achievement, but of that immediate transformation which we still see carried out, in the realm of sleeping life, by the living body — which, though ceaselessly passing away, ceaselessly weaves anew, bearing and growing, the specific images of organisms. The Pelasgian, by contrast, already spiritual but still soul-fettered, accomplishes the conjuring-fast of images either by "magically" summoning them forth, or by the in-formation of his impregnated inwardness into a receptive material, whereby, among other things, arises that genus, well known to us, of actuality-laden "signs," which, in souls ready for conception, renew the births of images in a manner similar to how the communicating word renews the act of comprehension in the perceiving mind. Now even if drive and capacity no longer coincide henceforth, because with the pull of life the commands of spirit lie in feud, and hence a sign-forming thinking is in principle just as exposed to derailment as the comprehending kind, still the formative power had, at least since the younger Stone Age, "incorporated" into itself the urge to represent, and only after long struggles for independence did it come to be wholly at variance with it — ever since, under the pressure of the victorious Logos, it has sought satisfaction on its own authority in a haughtily separated practice of "art."

By contrast, the art-productions of prehistoric man, from bodily ornament through the adornments of weapons and household implements to buildings, sculptured works, tonal patterns, songs, had their whole and sole dignity in the significance of a symbol-language of prehistoric belief. Reaching far beyond the limits that our culture of concepts has drawn around the creative urge, it was the formative power of language and writing, and of quite simply everything that we today use as sign in the service of purposes of communication. Even the tool [p. 1263] as such — that is, apart from decorative addition — originally stood on one line with the idol. One need only call to mind the legend-laden symbolism of, say, hammer, bow, arrow, spear, wagon, sword, wheel, spindle, belt, staff, ring, mixing-jar, cup, ship, to convince oneself that in those days there was no invention without a divine sense. — As for our "art," now dying, by comparison with this, it must be said that the value distinctively peculiar to it today, of a "speaking" or "form-filled" physiognomy, it then had to share with every formation of the human hand, and that of the unsurveyable wealth of original form-characters it has preserved a remnant only insofar as the soul of the creator harbors enough of the soul of prehistory to be able — temporarily de-selved — to receive that alone from which birth occurs in accord with the rhythm of the universe: the inflow of images. Art, if it is to be more than a sophistical parading with peeled-off surfaces, is believing, and accordingly symbolic, art. Image-Worship and Polytheism. — One ought quite simply to know today that Pelasgian "gods" are, in the first instance, nothing but unfolded symbols, which only quite gradually, and never without resistance, accommodated themselves to bearing human shape. The "soul-bird" had stood for millennia in the clear mirror of beholding reflection before, compelled to the embrace of spirit, it gave birth, for a humanity of beginning I-liberation, to the bastard of a jackal-headed Anubis or ibis-headed Thoth or the claw-footed siren; and again it was a still far longer road of the soul that led from such bird-daimons of planetary humanity to the eagle of Zeus or the owl of Pallas Athena. The "thunderbolt" had long been a demonic being before such a one became Jupiter, the hammer long before Thor, and the "furious host" raged through the forests before ever Wodan stood at its head.

Every thing, every process, every property, no less than the feeling-excitement of the beholder which is for us only "subjective," has the dimension of the demonic. This, however, is one in essence with the space-temporal singularity of an image which, without itself being comprehensible, points the way, for the symbolic thinking of the ensouled understanding, in place of things, for the comparison of things and properties that have been judged. — For us there is, say, space and parts of space, time and parts of time; for the [p. 1264] life-fettered spirit there are, in the first instance, as many spaces and times as there are space-temporally experienceable images: thus not only a night-space alongside a day-space, a house-space alongside a heaven-space, a forest-space alongside a temple-space, an east-space, south-space, west-space, north-space, but under certain circumstances as many spaces of the house as there are houses, and finally as many spaces even of the same house as there are moments of the efficacious inner-becoming of the house-shaped space-appearance. The preliminary form and root of the knowledge of the actuality of images is polydemonism, and the manifoldness that declares itself with it multiplies every content of signification, measured against the oneness of the concept for it. The genuine daimon is the daimon of a place, a region, an element, changing with the appearances of the same, receives the sacrifices of its devotees in temporal rhythms whose daily, monthly, or yearly measure is grounded in the forms of its becoming manifest, and holds sway in such events or performances as spirit was driven to accept as powerfully efficacious, through their pathically beheld images.

In the first volume it was mentioned how many living remnants of this have survived in the believing life of Catholic portions of the populace; here, where equivalent occurrences of paganism will meet us at every step, it scarcely seems necessary any longer to send examples ahead. The Egyptian Ra, for instance, was called differently in the morning, differently at noon, differently in the evening — was thus three times an other, without, however, ceasing to be Ra. Likewise there was not one Baal of the Semites, but a thousand upon thousand Baalim (among them, besides male ones, female and malefemale ones as well), each of whom was named after the place of his epiphany and usually further surnamed after his zone of efficacy, again to be understood in graphic, concrete terms. Thus one was, say, "Baal of the Sun-Pillar," another "Baal of the Palms," a third "Baal of the Flies," a fourth "Baal of Heaven," a fifth "Baal of the Dance"; and yet each of them the whole and real Baal.

Hegel, who with exuberant equanimity of soul carries the dialectic of "monotheism" through to its self-sublation, could calmly pronounce the sentence that might fittingly be called the "truth of paganism": "Nothing is essential that does not appear"! The admirable truthfulness of the Hellenic sense for fine distinctions derived theion from theaton, the visible and, in the fullness of appearances, the venerable, and thereby gave the most exact account — if not of the derivation of the word, then [p. 1265] certainly of the psychic place of origin of its sense. Since, now, concepts cannot appear — each of them being a unity beyond time, while appearance is of a temporally streaming manifold — the genuine divinity that grounds the name, and of which there are images, and that merely supposed divinity, which is grasped through and through only conceptually, exclude one another. No bridge leads to the conceptual god from the uncountable multiplicity of images of real, that is, experienced, daimons, whose domains of power and properties — inexhaustible as the sea of images — surpass the entire conceptual stock of mankind by just as much as does the wealth of human speech-sounds flowing from the same source. Unigodhood is only another turn of phrase for the conceptuality of that which one would like to clothe with divine dignity, and unigod-worship a mere transitional form toward the victory of ungodly spirituality over the "object" of every stirring of the soul: the god-filled world of appearance. "He who seeks God will never find gods."

In view of this, one can hardly go more badly astray than with the assumption that the mere centralization of customs, say in consequence of the political welding-together of groups of peoples, is as such already on the way to some sort of "monotheism." One speech-sound and yet another speech-sound can be placed alongside each other, or fuse into a new sound, or the one can displace the other; but through their coming together they cannot simply vanish altogether, so as to leave behind only their meanings, or even the bare concepts! Likewise, when two pagan tribes come into contact, whether warlike or by treaty, their divine images associate, pair off, displace one another, accumulate, and gradually fuse according to the degree of similarity; in accordance with which an equalization of their modes of beholding is accomplished among the peoples — but by no means its replacement by the concept of God. Neither the baroque accumulation of divine attributes of power, such as Hellenistic sculptured works show us, nor the dying-out of entire divine lineages in consequence of the loss of freedom of their worshippers, resembles in the least the dwindling-away of image-worship before the corrosive ray of godless will-reason, which triumphs under the sign of that supposed God whose vaunted oneness forms only the reverse side of his — invisibility. If, in particular, many daimons of the large-state confederations of peoples of later paganism had to submit to the monarchy of a supreme god, they themselves nevertheless neither ceased thereby to exist and to hold sway, nor did their [p. 1266] ruler forfeit, in the consciousness of the people, the character of a primus inter pares, in exchange for the image-repugnant incomparability of an other-worldly Nous.<sup>108</sup> Meanwhile history teaches us that the displacement of gods occurs far more rarely than the accumulation of gods, and that in times of spreading intermixture of gods the number of daimons tends not to decrease but to grow; so that in imperial Rome there are said to have been some 30,000 of them. The concept of a pantheon, meant to embrace, together with one's own, all foreign gods as well, was known to the Greeks even before the Romans, and the custom of inviting the gods of subjugated peoples into the capital of the victor, by creating for their statues, dragged there en masse, their own places of veneration, or by setting them up in the temple of all the gods, was practiced, like those peoples, among others also by the Peruvians.

<sup>108</sup> On page 1266. — What is said here naturally holds not only for the merging of divine figures, but generally. We choose an example of quite a different kind. The Greek underworld had not merely one entrance in general, but one at the Acherusian lake in Thesprotia, another in Hermione, a third at the promontory of Taenarum, a fourth near Cumae, a fifth near Heraclea on the Pontus. Now even if one among the oracles of the dead situated at these places had become famous above the others, and had caused the others' claim to be entrances to Hades to be forgotten, the entrance-gate assigned to that one would nonetheless remain no less bound to the particular landscape of that quite particular locality, and would by no means have acquired the significance of an entrance to the underworld "as such"!

For the hostile opposition between the ostensibly singlegod, in actuality ungodly, direction of thinking and the ineluctable multiplicity of gods of beholding, the history of religious belief offers an example that in immediate evidentiary force perhaps even surpasses the instructive course of development of Jewish "monotheism." We mean the attempt of the Egyptian king Amenhotep IV, who called himself Chuen'eten, i.e. splendor of the sun disk, suddenly and by decree to replace the numerous demon-cults of his people with the service of the one god "truly living." Notwithstanding that by this he still understood even an image, namely that of the sun disk (though already with an abstract emphasis on the "infinity of life" within it), the result was: on his side an embittered, fanatical struggle against all the holy sites, which not even the sarcophagi could halt; on the side of the people, whom he had thought to bless with "higher" wisdom, the passionately outraged resistance that after a few years shattered his work, razed his magnificent buildings to the ground, consigned his teaching to the death of complete oblivion, and secured an unlimited polytheism in Egypt forever.

But as concerns that proper "monotheism" which, thanks to a world-historical error, claims the Theion of the soul for the Monon of spirit — the victorious "monotheism" of the Israelite prophets, who brought off the astonishing feat of raising unbounded hatred for the very godliness of this world into the personal "Lord" of the entire world — everyone today knows, or could at least know, that the vampiric will to power that inspired it [p. 1267] meant that Jahwe was never permitted to tire for a single hour of pouring out his curses on "idolworship," not only of the whole of extra-Judaic heathendom but chiefly also of the folk-part of the Jews themselves! Let us note in passing that the name "Götze" [idol], to which Luther with deep linguistic understanding essentially gave its present-day meaning, originally meant a "holy image-work," but in the sense-feeling of the present-day hearer designates, on the one hand, any god whatsoever, so long as he is only one among several, and on the other hand, any representation — were it even of the One God himself — so far as it wishes to signify him in place of the concept of him! "Idols" are Baal, Hecate, Indra; but an "idol" would also be the Christ nailed to the cross, insofar as the veneration were paid to the sensibly present likeness. With words such as these, for example, Jahwe turns, through the mouths of the prophets, in the first instance to the people whom he has "chosen," but in truth to all who do not acknowledge "Jahwe's law" (following the outstandingly beautiful rendering by Duhm):

For three transgressions of Judah, / or for four, I will not turn it back: / because they have despised Jahwe's law . . . / led astray by idol-lies, / which their fathers already followed. / (Amos) / And now they transgress further still / and make themselves a molten work / of silver in the form of images. / The work of artisans is all of it . . . / Man shall kiss calves. / (Hosea) / As often as I call them, / they run from me: / they bring sacrifices to the Baals, / incense-offerings to the image. / (Hosea) / I hate, I despise your dances / and cannot smell your feasts, / I want not your gifts, I do not / look upon your fattened-calf offerings. / Take away from me the noise of your songs! / I will not hear the playing of your harps! / (Amos)

[p. 1268] And I will kill their last ones by the sword; / not one of them shall flee, / not one of them escape. / And should they break through to Sheol, / from there my hand shall fetch them. / And should they climb up to heaven, / I will hurl them down from there . . . / I set my eye upon them / for evil and not for good. / (Amos) / Who could fail to hear the death-hatred in the voice of the speaker, and who could fail to recognize that the opposition of one-god-worship to manygod-worship only clothes, in the sublime form of a cultic speech, the truly intended opposition of naked destructionwill and image-laden soul! And indeed the substrate of the former image-worship shines through, even among the Jews, in numerous customs and even in the most pious of the sanctioned legends. We recall the blood-sacrifice; the "Asherah," the holy tree of the village altars; the divining palm of the prophetess Deborah; holy spring-waters by which one swore; the mountains Sinai or Horeb as "mountains of God"; the "burning bush," which was beyond doubt the hallowed seat of a demon; the occasional storm- and thunder-accompaniment of Jahwistic wrath. — Inseparable from every demon remains the earthly face of its place of appearance. "When Jacob," says R. Smith, one of the most cautious judges of primitive faithimpulses, "saw in a dream an appearance of the deity at Bethel, he concludes from it not merely that Jahwe was present there for a while, but that the site itself is 'the house of God and the gate of heaven.'" After their defeat in the highlands of Samaria, the Aramaeans of Damascus consequently hold the god of the Jews to be a god of the heights, with whom one may dare to fight only on the plain. "The Babylonians whom the king of Assyria settled in the Northern Kingdom brought their native gods with them. But when they were attacked by lions, they believed they must invoke the help of the god of the land, who . . . in his own domain of rule had power over wild beasts just as over men." — Now just as, notwithstanding countless differences, all appearances of the air are more like one another than the appearances of the waters [p. 1269], and these again more like one another than the images of meadows, forests, steppes, deserts, and fields, so too, among the most various peoples, without ever coinciding, the customs of veneration toward their gods of the air resemble one another, and again those toward the gods of the waters, and finally those toward the gods of the underworld, and likewise the magical customs belonging to them. The offerings for the upper gods are burned, for the gods of the waters thrown into springs, wells, lakes, rivers, ponds, seas, for the gods of the underworld dug into the ground. What knits the cult together with the demonic soul to which it applies is always the totality of an image which, more fluid than any concept of things and properties, remains akin, through a thousand traits of similarity, to all possible images. With wondrous sharpness the belonging-together of both always comes to light in such observances as touch even a sense-fleeing side of the divine appearance. The Saracens, of whose faith-customs the holy Nilus (d. 430) reports to us, could perform their wild morning-star sacrifice (the tearing apart of a camel and the devouring of its stillbloody flesh) only within the short span during which the light of the star had not yet vanished before the rays of the sun, and had to have it completed by sunrise! One may gather from this how even the cosmic flight of the soul is held fast by the maternal ring of the image, preserving the swarming soul from the wrong path that leads out of the blazing circle of ageless happening to the "supra-heavenly" place of rigid and formless being! Idolity and Symbolism. — It escaped no researcher that this "primitive" thinking, which we still notice here and there similarly in children, is always inclined to take the likeness, or even a sign of the thing, for the thing itself. But, caught in a way of looking that proceeds from things as the domain of supposedly "correct" contents of thought, and hopes unhesitatingly to understand every actuality-mirroring that deviates from this out of merely subjective compulsions of mental association, it sees in it only a substitution, and fails to ask itself whether it might not be better advised by the less schoolmasterly assumption that the original understanding was able to hit what it meant no less exactly than ours can, and is therefore not to be judged from the standpoint of a millennia-long derangement of minds. Shall we have correctly understood the opinion of primeval times if we make it constantly confuse image and thing [p. 1270], or does not the deception perhaps lie rather with us, who in thinking no longer know how to take our bearings by images, and therefore impute errors of fact to those whose units of meaning were from the outset not related to objects at all, but rather, even then, to images, when the states of affairs they concern appear to us in the light of ordinary things of perception? Error as much as truth of logical thinking presupposes an experiencing for which essentially real are durable things; error as much as truth of elementary thinking presupposes an experiencing for which essentially real are present images. It has the thing in the likeness and the sign, not because it would have confused the two with each other, but because for it the real element of the thing is its image, and the entire All is only the sum-total of restlessly fleeing and therefore essentially ever-momentary images.

Should one doubt whether the rapt earnestness with which the playing child devotes itself to its play entitles us to conclude that the toy, while it is playing with it, is unrestrictedly also what it seems to it to be, a glance at kindred customs of primitives would at once lead to an affirmative answer. — Among many North American tribes, the mother who had lost a child would fill its cradle with black feathers, carry it about with her for years, and tend the clump of feathers with words and deeds as though it were still the living child. Among the Wanyamwezi the same office was performed by a bottle-gourd wrapped in skins. The Ostyaks used to make, of such of their deceased tribesmen as had enjoyed particular favor, a wooden likeness that was not, like our "monuments," merely regarded with indifference, but was the object of a care — on the part of the wife especially — of continued tokens of love, such as befit meaningfully only a living human being. Let us leave out of consideration, for the moment, what in these examples already touches on the cult of the dead, and hold fast only to this: that such customs, drawn from the closest neighborhood of our children's actuality-play, become intelligible only on the one presupposition that for the "savage" the appearance-form that clings equally to the thing and to the likeness is more real still than the thing itself.

Child and bottle-gourd, man and wood modeled into human form, are in each case two different things, of which the one can replace the other the less, the more it "reminds" one of what is to be replaced. For if an A reminds me of a B, then in the moment of remembering I also know that B is precisely not present, but absent and withdrawn from my perception for now or forever [p. 1271]. The Indian mother and the Ostyak widow, however, deal with the bundle of feathers and the wooden idol in no way as though these were signs of remembrance, but rather as though they were the very objects of which they offer likenesses. For them, then, what is pictured is present in these, and their consciousness of actuality is accordingly grounded not in the things — of which there are, in both cases, one and yet another — but in the image, which in both cases, by virtue of a similarity not indeed conceived but deeply and vividly felt, is nonetheless one and the same, or, stated as exactly as possible, is, however considerable the factual differences of appearance, the appearance-form of one and the same essence. Their perceiving follows the lead of experienced appearances, whereas we at best notice the appearance of the thing established once and for all and changelessly persistent. They seem to "fantasize," even while they wake, and what they perceive with open senses, as sharply as we do and sharper, is nonetheless woven out of a stuff that at least resembles that of dream-visions.

When a researcher occupies himself long and searchingly with such problems, it sometimes has the appearance as though, for moments, the proper light of the object wished to part the dense mist of false doctrines that bar the imagestripped consciousness of the present day from a view into the wellspring of thought, and suddenly to reveal itself without the will of the one who holds it captive. Tylor, from whom we take the above examples, pays homage throughout to the false doctrine of exchange. Yet in the midst of a well-documented discussion of magic and divinatory arts, there escapes him unawares the astonishing remark that all we still observe of magical belief, and even what we might draw from tradition, is perhaps only the degenerate remainder "of a system of errors" (!), which "more perfect and more harmonious" might have been in a state of humanity "where its life was more like a long dream than even the life that the Puris deep in the forests of South America lead today (!)." At once, however, the flashing gleam is again extinguished that, even if caught only in the miner's lamp of research, might have lit the way into the primeval forest of — the soul. — But, it might be objected, even granting that the manner of behaving of the Indian mother and of the Ostyak widow must be understood from their relation to the appearance of the thing to which it applies, still the bundle of feathers and the wooden model are not merely images but also, besides, things; and inasmuch as these now receive a treatment as though they were themselves that from which they had only borrowed their shape, there is nonetheless a confusion of dead things and living beings [p. 1272]. To raise such an objection with awareness of its bearing, one would first have had to ask and decide whether, at least in the cases mentioned and all similar ones, "things" are apprehended by the primitive at all, and would further have had to ask and decide how their likewise only experienceable corporeality relates to the experienced appearance. The first question would have to be answered in principle in the negative, insofar as thing-hood does not belong to the essence of idols and therefore, wherever it intrudes, falsifies the apprehension of idols (of which we shall hear more presently). To the second question the answer would have to be, as we know, that man, insofar as he not only beholds but also senses — or, more briefly, man in the waking state — does indeed need, for the sake of intercourse with the merely beholdable soul, the mediation of a body, which might accordingly deserve to be called its house or "receiving-place." All the veneration-customs of primeval times apply to living, present souls; but the living soul — understood, of course, in the spirit of primeval times — is a manifoldly mutable and essentially fleeting image, in relation to which the corporeality, say, of a bodily living child plays just as much the role of its not indispensable abode as does the appearance-similar bundle of feathers that offers the disembodied child a substitute for its missing sensory husk. — But it is objected that the view that the primitive sees in the idolic likeness only a dwelling-place for the objects of his love or fear or longing remains at least questionable and is scarcely to be reconciled with numerous customs, partly of peoples outside history, partly of prehistoric peoples. Let us then examine whether the idols in the narrower sense are able to give us some information on this.

Ethnologists, as is well known, have never come to a fully settled conclusion whether idols and fetishes are seats of souls or are themselves already (demonic) souls, and even the most comprehensive collection of the relevant facts does not at all allow one to come to clarity about it. When at the feast of the Durga Puja the Brahmin touches the breast and eyes of each idol and says the while, "Let the soul of Durga remain long and blissfully in this image," there is no doubt that the bodily figures count only as seats of a demonic being. But when other peoples, in the case of two rival gods, ascribe victory to the one whose idol [p. 1273] has remained unharmed in the violent collision with the idol of the other; or when Tibetan lamas let pieces of paper fly from a mountain peak so that the magic horses depicted on them might come to the aid of exhausted pilgrims, then the idolic body does indeed here seem to coincide with its demonic soul. On the other hand, we perhaps still resist placing, however great the outward similarity, on quite the same level the behavior of a Germanic warrior who not only sacrifices in a god's temple the charmed weapon with which he won his victory, but even renders to it itself divine honors — or, to draw on what is historically attested, when the Thessalian tyrant Alexander of Pherai (369–359) adorns with woolen bands the lance that had helped him kill his uncle, and honors it with abundant offerings as a demon named "The Striker" (Usener).

Still greater obscurity prevails over the meaning of the symbol. If one leaves aside the Romantics and their perfecters, and assembles definitions of the symbol from numerous writers, philosophers, myth-researchers, ethnologists, "folklorists," one will find the authors, however great their differences of opinion, agreed at least on this point: that the symbol is a sign for something invisible, "supersensible," and thus flatly spiritual — whether what hovers before the mind is now a result of spiritual activity, now this activity itself. Since the relation of the concept to the meaning-filled sound is thereby falsely smuggled into genuine symbolism, it is naturally not difficult to invent a ladder of ascent that leads from the cultic symbols of earliest prehistory or of the most remote primitives up to the language of the most abstract sciences, indeed up into the sign-systems of higher and highest mathematics. Following our detailed exposition of conceptual and symbolic thinking in the first volume, we forgo a renewed refutation and confine ourselves to recalling only the little that is required to mark the differences, but also the agreements, between symbolism and idolity.

Were we to render "symbol" in German as "expressive sign" (which, incidentally, would correspond almost exactly to our "Sinnbild" [emblem], if only one refrained from thinking, at "Sinn," of conceptual sense, and thought instead exclusively of "essence," "essentia," "soul"), we would indeed have blocked that worst wrong turning, but would not yet have sufficiently made clear how the expression-world of symbols relates to the one familiar to us [p. 1274] of organic life-processes. Were we to do so with the remark: just as the laughing or weeping countenance is a gesture of the glad or afflicted disposition, so the symbol is a gesture of the primal-image soul, then it would surely be sufficiently made plain: first, that every symbol, what it means, at the same time also is; and second, that the essences or souls with which it is connected as one of their revelation-forms are such of the appearance-world in general, or, so to speak, cosmic characters, and thus reach by far beyond the range of expression of individual beings.

It is accordingly a matter of seizing the images in what is, as it were, the fruitful moment of their most expressive presentness, and there arises, as we know, the symbol in accordance with elementary similarities that are found through the seer's deed of a reflection which, in spirits capable of it, follows upon the falling-due of a past-laden event. We recognize it, to be sure, only afterward, which feature of the images determined the choice of epithets in a poem or lent magic power to the savage's fetish, but we do not know it beforehand and could never contrive it. For the similarities of which we speak do not grow out of a drive-conditioned or even sober comparison of things, but out of the soul-kinship of images present only to beholding. We understand why the symbol of the ship means, among other things, the mother's womb in the language of concepts, and we readily grasp how the phrase "screaming red" arose; but we know no law, and shall find none, why it is precisely the ship that stands for the mother's womb, the noise of a scream for the degree of intensification of the essence of redness. We may have understood a symbol as deeply as is conceivable, yet we could, should it still be alive, no more calculate its future in advance than we are ever able to predetermine the development of meaning of any given word. — We return to the idols.

Could we place ourselves deeply enough into idols (fetishes, talismans)<sup>109</sup>, we would probably find that each of them means a likeness of the demonic that is to cling to it — in whatever manner — although we would often see only blocks, staves, metal plates, rings, stones, at most ornamented with circles, spirals, horseshoe-lines, triangles, pentagrams, dots. The detailed descriptions that we owe to well-known ethnologists, for example, of the totemic stones of the Australian Aruntas (called churinga or tjurunga)<sup>110</sup>, have encouraged present-day ethnology to a number of ventures of thought that one would not have expected even thirty years ago, and today even make it easier for an interpreter of Pelasgianism to draw at least somewhat nearer [p. 1275] to the layer of experience where idols grow, without having to exchange the language of scholarship for the language of absorption.

<sup>109</sup> On page 1274. — One can distinguish, from a certain point of view, between idols on the one hand and fetishes and talismans on the other, and this has been done; but these classifications, legitimate in themselves, lie outside our train of thought.

<sup>110</sup> On page 1274. — The most important research findings in this regard are owed, on the one hand, to *Spencer* and Gillen (1899), and, on the other, to *Strehlow* (1908).

The idolic likeness is, among other things, body and house of the soul of the image, or, more briefly, of the image, remote in something the way the "aspects" may conceal and, so to speak, clothe the thing for us; and it transforms itself, among other things, for the one cultically stirred, into the image-soul itself, remote in something the way, for the artist, the visible appearances take the place of the thing. In both cases something soul-like, essential, demonic (or whatever we wish to call it) becomes present with the help of the idol, and in this, as one notices, the idol agrees entirely with the symbol; but the mode of turning-toward that avails itself of the idol diverges not inconsiderably from that which avails itself of the symbol, and accordingly meets with a good many other features of the demonic image. If we take symbol and idol for once as two sides of a single primal phenomenon, then the one relates to the other somewhat as the soul to the body, or, in a bolder turn of phrase, as the flame to the blood. Every symbol, one might say, has an idolic body, every idol a symbolic sense, and it corresponds to this that the idolic shudder is above all a shudder of the begetting body, the symbolic shudder above all a shudder of the winging soul.

With the mystery of images a visionary spirit comes to an understanding through their symbolic runes, an image-receptive body through the bodily present fetish. In the state that makes the former possible, the stream of excitation runs from the soul-pole to the body-pole; in the state that makes the latter possible, from the body-pole to the soul-pole. The "man of spirit" succeeds only exceptionally in an after-feeling of the symbol-receptive experience, and he succeeds almost not at all any longer in an after-feeling of the idol-receptive experience; with "the people" (especially the Catholic) it is the reverse. But even if the fervor of a primal Eros kindled at the idolic body can at best still be surmised by the bearer of will-understanding, he can nonetheless, supported by what has just been offered, trace the chief character-traits of the idolic likeness in thought, and most easily with regard to the efficacy that the Pelasgian is inclined to ascribe to his idols: in magical custom the meaning of the idol becomes tangible to us.

[p. 1276] Insofar as the image clings not to the thing but to the body of the thing, the practice of any magic with the idol requires in principle not so much a thing of such-and-such a kind as rather a determinate thing in a determinate place at a determinate time. Further, because the body possesses magical power only by virtue of its participation in the image, it is, for one thing, its generic properties that permit it to be used with magical effect — whereby, for instance, inspiration comes to the seer only at the scent of laurel, or when the mirror from which he reads it is made of polished copper; for another, properties of its form: staff-form, cross-form, ring-form, eggform, hand-form, finger-form, eye-form, and so on; and it is also both together, as when for a healing to succeed it is required that the touch be made with a body of fig wood and of the shape of the phallus, or when a "divining rod" requires not merely a forked branch but one specifically of hazel. With the first sort of determinateness the emphatically idolic character of the idol declares itself; with the others, and especially with the required properties of form, its symbolic character. According as, in the manner of using this primal precipitate of the human soul, idolatry or symbolism has the lead, magical practice or "gnosis" steps into the foreground.

Now when the soul begins to dwindle, there becomes independent, in the symbol its sign-nature, in the idol its nature as a body. From that beginning of cleavage, before it is followed by a complete resolution into concepts and things, one aberrant path runs to an empty pantomime, which can mostly continue by leaning on pragmatic reinterpretations after its meaning has evaporated for centuries or even millennia; another aberrant path to a codified sign-divination and, with predilection, to a mystical arithmetic — as both are just now again in bloom here and there, partly in the service of a mantic pursued for gain. From this same beginning of cleavage — namely of the genuine idol into departing soul and — wonder-thing — runs the aberrant path to the likewise thoroughly artificial practice of dull sorceries. The symbol, in other words, is degenerate insofar as it is confused with mere signs and gestures; the idol is degenerate insofar as it is confused with things allegedly endowed with wonder-working power. But because even the sham-symbolic sign took its origin at some time in symbolic thinking, the sham-idolic thing in idolic thinking, it must in principle be of no consequence whether one draws the evidence for the dependence [p. 1277] of original thinking on the merely beholdable unity of the image from the purest cults or from the corner-lurking arts of a malicious, fearful superstition. However, before we pursue this a while further, let us cast a side-glance at the mystical "double." The "Double." — Scarcely anything else attests, with such doubt-excluding certainty, the dependence of all original cults on the belief in the actuality of images as does the otherwise inexplicable fact that almost every Pelasgian people, in the period of transition from it to the actuality-affirmation of things, appears, with fully awakened consciousness, related to the juxtaposition of two worlds, of which the one is the "double" of the other. For the more the idea of the thing begins to triumph — but before the original image yet abandons every claim to actuality and fades into a mere illuminating coloration of solid "states of affairs" — the images take on the form of objecthood, thereby once more attaching themselves to the things of perception and to objective doings, though in a mystically altering light. This transitional period can also be historically attested among such Pelasgian peoples as were able only hesitantly to tear themselves from the ring of the still life-fettered spirit, and who carried the eggshell-fragments of the protecting shell that they too broke to their own undoing over into late and glorious periods of their history with all the more painstaking care, the more they had forgotten its origin. Of these, the Persians made fast the thought of the double into a teachable world-view system, but the Romans, who not without reason linked their descent to Asia of the Orient, put it most strongly into practice.

To illuminate the doctrine of the actuality of images by the thought of the double, we must repeat in a few words what is generally known. — The adherent of the Zarathustrian religion sees the whole world of all things doubly: once in its corporeality, and alongside this in incorporeal primal-imagehood. Whereas most transcendental systems grasp supraworldly being as a unity, the Persian assumes an unbounded multiplicity of "eternal" pre-forms of all created beings. Every individual being — stars, trees, animals, or men — already existed in primal-image purity (or as "word" of Ahura Mazda) before it stepped bodily into appearance [p. 1278], and will exist again, once more disembodied, after the downfall of its impermanent bearer. We leave aside the relation to the divine word or name, in which already lies the seed of the Platonic identification of the primal image with the concept, and hold fast only to the application to everyday life. There the doctrine has led to the sharply outlined conviction that every being — be it well understood, besides man also animals, plants, stars — unceasingly has a double, who, over against the threats of Angra Mainyu, at the same time plays the role of a guardian spirit, thus a "demonic" double: the Frawashi or Fravashi. The number of the Frawashi, in rank and range, is as great as the number of the differently constituted beings themselves that, after the pattern of those, step into existence in endless succession. In the moment a being bodily arises, the Frawashi must leave the place of eternal light in order to betake itself to the place of the transient body, which, as it receives life from it, henceforth becomes its abiding likeness. During the span of bodily life the Frawashi remains united with its bearer, but swings back, as soon as this expires, like a bird into heaven. When the Parsee prays, he does it not only for himself but also for his Frawashi: this is, literally, an "other I."

The Frawashi of the Romans is called, for images conceived as male, the "Genius," for those conceived as female the "Juno" (without distinction of sex, sometimes also "numen"). If we look up in any dictionary, for example that of Georges, we find under the word "genius" the following: "Genius, from gignere = to beget, designates the god presiding over human nature, who was active at the begetting and birth of man, who as his guardian spirit accompanied him through life and determined his fate, who also shared joy and sorrow with him, and who, even after the man's decease, lived on in the Lar and could continue to work protectively. Just as man, so too did every place (region, forest, town, house, gate), every state, every herd, and individual conditions, properties, and doings have their genius, which was intimately bound up with the existence of the place, etc. One entreated and adjured someone and swore by one's own genius and by the genius of respected and valued persons (slaves, for example, by the genius of their master, subjects by that of the monarch). On feast-days one propitiated the genius with flowers and wine, especially on the birthday with a cake. To one who joyfully enjoys life the genius is [p. 1279] gracious (albus); to the mopers and to those who, out of avarice, stint their own existence, ungracious (ater, sinister); hence a glad enjoyment of life was as much desired for the genius as for the man himself: whence "genio indulgere" = "to indulge one's genius" = "to cheer life through gladness" and, mindful of its transience, to prolong it through wise enjoyment."

Essentially the same conceptions, only not so fully elaborated, are elsewhere too nothing unusual in instituted religions and schooled wisdom-teachings. "Likeness" [Ebenbild] of God is, at least, man not only according to the "Holy Scripture" of the Hebrews, but also in younger teachings of the Indians (= murti). As a guardian-spirit-like second self the Frawashi attained world-fame through the Socratic "Daimonion," whose shimmering-over into the "voice of conscience" no one will fail to recognize. But quite especially does the Kabbalah indulge in the elaboration of the concept of the double, from which above all it flowed, manifoldly ramified, into the mysticism of the Renaissance. — As evidence, the following passage from the Zohar may suffice: "In the moment of earthly union, the Holy One, blessed be his name, sends down from heaven a form in the likeness of man, bearing the imprint of the divine seal. This form assists in the act of which we speak, and if the eye could see what happens there, one would behold above its head an image perfectly resembling the human countenance, which is the model according to which we are made. If it is not sent down by the Lord, no begetting takes place, for it is written: 'And God created man in his image.' This image received us at our arrival in the world; it develops as we grow, and leaves the earth with us. Its origin is in heaven. At the moment when souls leave their heavenly abode, each soul appears before the highest King, clothed in a sublime form, in which are engraved the features that it is to bear here below. The image of which we speak consists in this sublime form; it comes as a third behind the soul, it goes before us on earth and awaits our arrival from the moment of conception."<sup>111</sup>

<sup>111</sup> On page 1279. — Quoted after *Kiesewetter*, Der Okkultismus des Altertums, pp. 420–421.

More important still for us is the circumstance that such teachings translate into the language of a higher gnosis nothing but a constituent piece taken over from the ancestor-cult belief of late-primeval folk-life. Something thoroughly of the same kind is given, among others, by the ka of the Egyptians, the shen and kwei of the Chinese, the daimones and tychai of the Greeks, the Nordic fylgjur, the German [p. 1280] followingspirits and shadow-spirits, the Lithuanian gelbys devas, the medieval spiritus familiares, tutelares, fatidici; and still today, within Christendom, the "guardian angel" and the "genius," transposed into the higher-spiritual, of significant personalities. — Indeed, according to the far-ranging findings of ethnology, it admits of no doubt that at least the pre-forms of double-like ancestor-souls were already known to numerous primitives and were spread over wide regions of the earth. To this class would belong, say, the arlus of the Eskimos, and especially the guardian-spirit-like atka of their children, the ininkugua of the Central Australians, the kra of the Ewe, the okra and okrabi of the Ga-Negroes — more than merely resembling the genius albus and ater — the ntovo of the Ashanti, the musedi of the Ba-ila, the la and the kelah of the Karen, the "medicine" of the North American Indian, and so forth.

Usener, whom his researches into the history of language had led to the original plurality of every demon-cult, sets the thought of the double likewise in the earliest period of religious meaning-feelings, and believes he ought to understand it out of that momentariness, known to us, of "demonic" seizure, in which, already according to the Greek conception, the presence of the (seizing) god alone comes to immediate expression. This interpretation, however, mistakes the essential difference between image and object. Just as certainly as the consciousness of the ensouled understanding — precisely in the measure of its originality — does not set the corporeality of things and persons beside their always momentary images, but rather *subordinates* it to these in just the way that we, conversely, subordinate the changing images, as — now merely "subjective" — appearance-forms (aspects, "views"), to the conceptually meant states of affairs, so certainly, too, can it not separate the "demon" from its bearer in such a way that it would become a copy resembling it point for point. Because it rather first takes hold of the thing at all within the frame and, so to speak, under the law of images, it transfers to all objects whatsoever, in clear testimony of all original cults, what it really experienced in images and similarities: the possibility of unbounded transformation, in which we see the heart-point alike of magic and of myth.

As, however, with the beginning of the predominance of thing-apprehension the image sets about taking part in the essence of the thing and, so to speak, begins to congeal, it becomes necessarily a secondary-thing repeating the thing, or more correctly its appearance-forms, which now steps up, as a third, alongside the "soul" only now taking flight into the "supersensible" [p. 1281] — only not so definitely as in the Zohar passage above. None of the doubles named: Frawashi, Ka, Genius, Numen, Daimonion, following-spirit, guardian-spirit — partly reckoning in also those of the primitives — is any longer fully identical with the soul, yet each, in relation to the life-bearer assigned to it, is on the one hand a being not merely human but demonic, on the other the ward's "likeness." Only the disintegration of the original unity — arising from the beginning of the desiccation of the body or the evaporation of the soul, which comes to the same thing — shows us, as so often, with unmistakable clarity which of the parts held them all together: "the dimension of the demonic," as we called it above, forced to become singular, takes on neither the form of a body nor of an extra-sensory soul, but rather that of — an image, which, however, to be sure, frozen fast to the place of a thing grasped as its "likeness," now plays only the role of a ghostly follower and in the end must congeal into a powerless and forgotten phantom. Shadow and "Visions." — Inwardly akin to the double, and sometimes merging with it, but always one of the strongest testimonies to a actuality-certainty determined by intuition (and ultimately by beholding), is the nearly earth-spanning symbolism of the shadow, from whose unconscious after-resonance in the souls of readers the fame of "Peter Schlemihl" derives. In that the Pelasgian, in many cases, ties the weal and woe of man to the presence and unimpairedness of his shadow, while the primitive throughout downright reifies the shadow, so as then, among other things, to count its very — irreproachability among the preconditions of personal dignity (the Fijians!), both attest the dependence of the original apprehension of actuality on at least three character-traits of appearance: bodilessness, shape, and mutability.

When in China mortal danger threatened the mourner whose shadow had by chance fallen into the open coffin, not too few Europeans might, in a vivid realization of the situation, still find it a little uncanny, and therefore bring to such a belief a certain feeling-based understanding. But were we to think through wherein the uncanniness actually lay, and how it could obtrude itself so strongly that the "shadow in the coffin" threatened to become an advance sign of the "shadowcaster in the coffin," then the first thing we should establish, along with other researchers [p. 1282], would surely be that the shadow was by no means known to the Chinese as a mere "negation of light"; the second, that the "negation of light," as a physical interpretation, belongs not in the least to the image of the shadow; the third and decisive thing, however, that precisely the mutability and incorporeality — by virtue of which the extensions, changes of form, and movements of the shadow cannot be arrested or fettered by what bodily offers resistance — while yet the shape has at every moment its own momentary determinateness, could ground for the Pelasgian's spirit a deeper connection with the soul than for the bodily shape of the man whom it accompanies. Darkness and ground-boundness are added, serving chiefly to let the bodiless soul of the sometime enfeebled, sometime powerful dead appear in the shadow.

Insofar as by firmness, steadfastness, unshakability we mean dispositions of will whose opposite would be, say, want of hold and fickleness, we cannot help but associate with these the feeling of the value of strength that is lacking in the latter; and even, for instance, the "impenetrability" of personality enjoys a certain high esteem on essentially the same ground. Yet even one never touched by "classical education" would likely be inclined to think of hosts of shadows when he hears of the realm of the dead and of the underworld, and might then perhaps, by the roundabout way of the memory of ghost-stories, be given pause and venture the surmise that it is precisely to penetrability that a power sometimes belongs which is lacking to the impenetrable. With that he would have taken a path leading out of the world of things and into that of appearances, even though it would remain uncertain whether, at the forking-point of the night-blue road, he followed the one into the sea of images or the pale one into the intermediate realm of phantoms. Between the two stretches the symbolism of the shadow.

According to Tongan legend, the crew of a boat that had come to Bolotu, the island of the gods and heroes, report that there one strides through houses, trees, and chieftains, and an Algonquin hunter, carried off in a state of ecstasy into the realm of the dead, has the same to tell of it. As air-forms and shadows, ungraspable to the living, the souls of the dead swarm about the blood-filled sacrificial pit of Odysseus at the edge of Hades. Because themselves shadows, "spirits" are shadowless. The shadow-nature of the dead-folk of the Cimmerians is intimated by the fact that fog and starless night continually envelop them. Not only the Greek skia and [p. 1283] the Latin umbra can mean spirits of the departed, but elsewhere too the name for shadow is exceedingly often at the same time a name for soul, or at least for one of the souls, as can be gathered from the customs and myths of a tribe, for which Tylor especially offers many examples. This holds, say, for the Tasmanians, Algonquin, Quiche, Basuto, and numerous others. The Patagonians had one word for soul, image, and shadow; likewise the Arawak. Itongo, the long shadow, is for the Zulu the ancestor-spirit, the short shadow a soul-like appurtenance of the dead. The shadow, or "dark spirit," of the Fijians descends at a man's death into the underworld; the "light spirit," as a kind of mirror-image, remains near the grave. The Abiponian word loakal means shadow, soul, echo, image. Of the at least five distinguishable kinds of soul of the Sioux, the four of the Egyptians, the three of the Yakuts, one is in each case identical with the shadow.

But just as we too still know the shadow as something enveloping and embracing, so likewise — in contrast to its bodilessness, shading over into the spectral and the deathannouncing double — it is its earth-kinship and nocturnality by force of which telluric powers of a motherly, sheltering, and past-guarding disposition reveal themselves through it. If we enter properly into linguistic formations like "leaf-roof" and "forest-cathedral," our astonishment will lessen when we learn that there were Estonian tribes who brought sacrifices to the shadow of sacred trees, or that the sacred groves of the Estonians extended as far as the shadow-boundary, within which therefore no twig might be broken, no leaf plucked, and where the dead were often buried. The strongest oath of the women of Priene was "by the darkness of the oak"; to which Bachofen remarks: "Higher than the tree of the god stands the primal shadow, which as a dark maternal womb gave rise to it, to which the dead return, and which the women therefore ... raise to their most sacred oath." The shadow as guardian of the grave belongs to the "elementary thoughts" of mankind.<sup>112</sup>

<sup>112</sup> On page 1283. — Numerous instances are offered by *Negelein*, Bild, Spiegel und Schatten im Volksglauben, ARWS, 1902.

If, in short, the wakefulness of a thinking beholding is more akin to our dreaming than to our waking — not because of some twilight unresponsiveness of its bearer to the corporeal outer world, but thanks to the depth of its connectedness with the characters of its phenomena — then dream-images and visions, though sharply distinguished from the occasions of perception, must partake of one and the same actuality as these, and must therefore in principle be able to intervene in the conduct of life [p. 1284] just as much as the events of the day. This much has become most widely known and has remained even to the consciousness of today somewhat familiar. Indeed the so-called veridical dream, whose influence upon historically attested deeds would fill a stately volume, reaches even into the narratives of the present; hence it strikes us as almost still familiar when we hear that, for example, the North American Indians used to set out on the bear hunt only after the bears had announced themselves to numerous tribesmen in nocturnal dreams.

Yet the man of today does not for that reason also approve the wisdom of the Aeschylean verses, according to which "the senses of the sleeper behold more keenly," because "the semblance of day conceals the lot of men" — though most thinkers of antiquity and the Middle Ages assent to this, as do the mystics of the Renaissance down to the writings of a Jakob Böhme, and afterward, as we have seen, some of the greatest Romantics. But this very thing was the unspoken conviction of the whole of Pelasgianism, and no less of all primitives. And it is indeed the bodilessness of dream-visions that associates them with mirror-images and doubles, their mutability that associates them above all with shadows, and that makes the dream-state the preferred vehicle of intercourse partly with absent friends, but partly and above all with gods and the dead — in that the dream-soul either "sets out" on a far journey, or is visited by beings unreachable to it in waking.

In "incubation sleep" the cave-spirit Amphiaraos or Trophonios appeared to the Greek, to give him means of recovery from bodily ailments or indications for the future; but not essentially otherwise is the Zulu warned of dangers in dream by the Itongo, the shadow-shaped ancestral spirit, or even temporarily taken along into the realm of the ancestors. Whatever arcs of the boldest span we strike across ages and peoples, we everywhere come upon the same "elementary thought." Only in dream could the Finn hold converse with his dead, but the Finnish shaman could do so even in waking, namely by virtue of his gift of heightened beholding. His soul has loosened its connection with the body and can go on a journey for days, to bring back the most exact tidings of persons and regions as far as distant Iceland, while the body lies in cataleptic rigidity. But from antiquity we hear stories of the same type: one need only think of Hermotimos (or Hermodoros, as Plutarch calls him), whose body, during too long an excursion of the soul, is burned as lifeless by his [p. 1285] wife at the instigation of ill-wishers; or of Thespesios (in Plutarch's "On the Delay of Divine Vengeance"), who as the result of a fall lies enveloped in unconsciousness for almost three days, while his soul passes over into a kind of beyond, where it attends both supernal joys and the infernal torments of the departed. As a result of the warnings and instructions thereby imparted to it, its bearer, the now "recovered" Thespesios, changes his manner of life entirely and turns from a dissolute into a pious man.

Let us recall here further the quite extraordinary cultic significance attributed without exception to the intoxicating drink — for which it suffices to recall the Soma of the Indians, which the eagle of Indra brings, the nectar of the Greeks, which the eagle of Zeus brings, the mead of the Germanic peoples, which Odin in eagle-shape steals from — heaven: in this thought the dream-conception of Pelasgianism is fully rounded out for us: the highest wisdom, initiating knowledge, momentous inspirations are granted to the soul not in the state of ordinary wakefulness, but now in deep sleep, now in a rapture akin to dream; and only from the stupefactions of the spirit do the images blossom forth by which, fructified, it becomes "seeing." Whether Mohammed, Cardanus, Campanella receive "revelations" from "visions," or the West African Negro Doalu receives from the dream-image of a white man the instructions for a syllabary of his tribal language; whether the visions light up in natural sleep-dream or in those narcotic excitations by force of which the Pythias and Sibyls discern the threads in the fabric of fate of individual men as of peoples (without — in the view of St. Justin — carrying any knowledge of it over into the state of sobriety); whether finally the mystic knowledge is attained in such a way, or perhaps in the whirl of orgiastic dances (which, for example, among the Hupa in California were continued for months on end for the purpose of attaining shamanic powers): it always comes down to breaking apart the merely-perceivable world of day, or plunging it into night, in order, through the liberated power of beholding, to bring oneself into accord with the actuality of images. Semblances, mirrorings, visions, dream-visions, and shadows are not in and for themselves bearers of soul (or the souls themselves, however one wishes to take it), but rather, as it were, messengers and scarcely surveyable weather-signs of a happening that becomes demonically present in images and only in images, and precipitates itself into "symbols" [p. 1286]. Image-magic. — Just as between idol and symbol an almost continuous transition takes place, so too between the magical act and mystical knowledge. Where in custom the gnosis recedes, image-magic predominates; in the other case, sign-magic. The former is so well known that even a cursory treatment of it might be dispensed with, did it not present a side that seems to correspond to a wholly different mode of thought, and that without the doctrine of the actuality of images would remain either unintelligible or misunderstood: we mean magic with cuttings of the body, which loses nothing of its power to instruct precisely because, wherever it appeared most decisively, it degenerated earliest into superstition. For if, according to the actuality-sense of Pelasgianism, intuitive images are one and all appearances and thus, among other things, centers of psychic efficacy, then conversely all that we call materials, substances, matters likewise become essential traits of the world-appearance, and thus share the signature-meaning with the magically efficacious images. An example will make our meaning clearer.

The Pelasgian becomes entheos, that is, filled by the daemon and a partaker of its powers, in that he beholds the daemon, that is, a primal image, for which a transient de-spiriting and "hieromanic" intoxication is required. If he now attains this now in narcotic sleep, now in dance, now in wineintoxication, but now also by devouring certain bodies, then it cannot be their (in our sense) material constitution, but must rather be their connection with essence-appearances, that fits them for this. For the world-wide "eating of god" this follows from the fact alone that the tearing apart of daemonic animals, the drinking of their blood, the swallowing down of the raw flesh, could in the most various places on earth fuse with cultic dances. One would not soon come to an end were one to assemble even the strongest analogues among primitives to such observances of the Thracian-Hellenic Dionysos festival. At the snake-dance of the Moki, for example, dancing snake-priests carried rattlesnakes in their mouths, which were prevented from biting by the feather-wand of a fellow dancer, thereby at least suggesting the orgiastic devouring of snakes. The Aztecs, on the other hand, at the festival of their rain-god Tlaloc (which took place every eight years) did not content themselves with suggestion, but seized live snakes in their mouths while dancing, and bit and swallowed them while dancing. Let us add at once that at the rain-magic dances of the Cora the magically most significant act was the [p. 1287] eating of an enormous locust — which, however, consisted of maize: then there can be no doubt as to the dependence of substances to be cultically incorporated upon essential appearances.

It is no different, however, with every magically conditioned choice of food. If according to Egyptian prejudice the flesh of doves kept one pure, the flesh of serpents made one cleverer, the flesh of vultures, wolves, lions strengthened the lust for murder or for lust itself, this was unmistakably so because the animals in question were conceived as distinguished by purity, cleverness, lust for murder — which was suggested, in a manner here even easily intelligible, by the total picture of their vital activities. In accordance with exactly the same mode of viewing, even today the young men of the Dayaks abstain from the flesh of the roe-deer so as not to become timid, while the North American warriors give preference to the flesh of stags and boars because it is thought to confer courage and swiftness.
