As surely as no one will think of seeking the ground of such differences of valuation among foods in any assumptions about the material constitution of the preferred kinds of flesh, so surely does the belief in the edibility of the essence of the slain animals go back to the appearances of their behavior, and shows us the process of eating in the light not so much of an incorporation as rather of the in-imaging of efficacious essences. — The same principle now holds for all the features of magical belief, even where at a cursory glance they seem to rest on mere material magic.

One recalls what importance — strange to us — attaches, partly in the protective, partly and especially in the injurious magic of all times and peoples, to cuttings and products of the human body. What has, at the stage of culture, volatilized into either a pious or a lascivious prizing of "living keepsakes" — from which medical science derived its none too fortunate concept of "fetishism" — was earlier everywhere, and is still today among the remnants of dying-out primitives, a matter of fateful weight. The time is not too distant when, among the lower folk of Italy, a man entrusted a lock of his hair to strange hands only with the utmost reluctance, because he feared being bewitched or entangled against his will in love affairs. On the New Hebridean island of Tanna there is, or at least was, a whole colony of disease-makers who lived by their art, in that they collected every conceivable kind of refuse of the natives — not merely hair-clippings and fingernails, but with special preference also spittle, excrement, urine, and food-remains [p. 1288] — and slowly burned them, each time, of whomever was to fall ill from it. If someone there was then seized by an illness, one blew on conch-trumpets and thereby implored the sorcerers to desist from their undertaking, and to expect the gifts with which one intended to reward their goodwill (Tylor). — We choose deliberately an example from the proper superstition of a comparatively low-standing group of men, in order to hold fast, even against the visible appearance, that the ground even of such customs — which confuse the image with its bodily seat — must be sought in the preponderance of actuality of the appearance over the thing. Leaving aside the grounds already considered earlier, why the space of efficacy of every magic can be thought only as image-space, even a merely material conception of the body-cuttings would conflict with the individual nature of their capacity to act. We have medicines against palpitation, insomnia, fever (or against the supposed causes of such disturbances), but not one that would help only A against fever, a second against the fever of B, a third against that of C; and we have general poisons like arsenic, belladonna, strychnine, but not one that would harm only A, a second to the sole detriment of B, and so on — whereas A, and only he, falls ill through magic worked with cuttings of his body, etc. It is not human kidney-fat in general that matters to the primitive Australian, but that of the man just slain, and he prizes it the more highly, the braver an opponent he was whom he has slain.

We need not continue, since the difference lies plainly before us. Now the individual essence is something unrepeatably unique, from moment to moment resembling itself in appearance, a change of images held together by the streambed of the body; and the limb of the body or an excretion of the body stands to it as the pebbles of the bed or a piece of the bank stand, in place of the whole bed, to the stream bordered by it. It is one thing, to stay with the simile, to relate the pebble to its find-site, another to relate it to its lime-content; the former has an intuitive basis, the latter does not; and intuitability is rooted in a context of appearance, as when, in the case of magic with body-cuttings, the object's power to act derives from its provenance. But that is not all: the pars-pro-toto principle, which pervades all procedures of symbolic thought, yields for body-cuttings that they represent not so much the body from which they stem [p. 1289] as rather impressive appearance-forms, partly of that body itself, partly of essential functions of it, and is therefore suited to disclose to us the symbolic ground of the "material language" that reigns in the domain of Pelasgian thought.

The capacity of body-cuttings to serve as substitute coincides, as goes without saying, with their significance; their degree of significance is one with their specific value, and the orders of value that thereupon open up can never and nowhere be understood from any actual importance of the body-fragment in question for the functions of the body, and stand in part in unbridgeable opposition to every "rational" conception of their essence. According to such a conception, the significance of the eye, or of the hair, or of the hands might indeed be intelligible to us — less so already that of the earlobes, still less that of the fingernails, which play the greatest role in numerous legends and customs, and probably not at all any longer that of excrement and urine, venerated by all of Pelasgianism. We undertake the ticklish venture of a lifedoctrine of the body on the basis of the body's appearance here all the less, as it would undoubtedly require a whole book for that; but we point the way there in a few sentences by characterizing only a single state of affairs: namely, that magical symbolism, born as it is out of "beholding thought," is by far predominantly, if not exclusively, determined by indices of the outer side of the body.

One has adduced, for (just excreted) dung and urine, their steaming warmth, and sought thereby to interpret the scarcely doubtable fact that, for example, the Aztec sun-gods were originally fire-daemons — the fire-daemons, however (like other creative powers as well), brought forth fire partly through the warming breath of the mouth, together with the warm-moist spittle, partly through their excrements. But Preuss<sup>113</sup> to whom we owe valuable special investigations into Aztec cults, at once also considered the special significance that attaches, in connection with this, to all the openings of the body, insofar as through them — so we add — there come into appearance the gates of the organism, through which in waking an unceasing interchange takes place between outer and inner, macrocosm and microcosm, between begetting happening and image-bearing soul; an interchange that continues even into sleep by means of breathing.

<sup>113</sup> On page 1289. — K. Th. *Preuß*, Der Ursprung der Menschenopfer in Mexiko. Globus, vol. LXXXVI, 1904; further, in the same place and in vol. LXXXVII, 1906: Der Ursprung der Religion und Kunst.

The eyes are such openings, as are the ears, the nose, the mouth, the [p. 1290] navel, the anus, and the organ of sex; to each of which, in keeping with this, there can and in the course of time here and there did attach intuitive articulations of essential receptivities as well as capacities. Thus tattooings accumulate in the named zones; thus nose-rings and nose-sticks appear, piercings further of tongue and lips (sometimes with those lip-plugs that to our taste disfigure the countenance beyond measure), filing or removal of the front teeth, not to speak of the countless and in part horribly painful operations upon the organ of sex, and indeed preferentially that of the man.<sup>114</sup> From these same regions of the body's surface, then, consistently, there feeds a widely spanning symbolism of cultic idols (one need think of the manifoldness of representations of the phallus, of eyes, of the mouth, etc.), of magical customs, and of the earliest systems of signs, where they sometimes congeal directly into ideograms: as when, say, a schema of the lip-lines signifies the activity of eating or of speaking, or in the Aztec picture-writing the little cloud before the mouths of human figures signifies "speech."

<sup>114</sup> On page 1290. — Even though the idea of beauty at bottom goes back to Hellas, a feeling for beauty nonetheless already exists among the primitives, but it must be regarded as an altogether independent driving force, which *crosses* with the demands of symbolism, case by case, to varying degrees.

To be sure, to the appearance of breath, of spittle, of excrement there also belong moisture, warmth, steaming vapor, and so they can belong to the essence appearing therein; but what distinguishes them from — here deliberately passed over — blood, what further distinguishes them from the vapor of hot springs or of boiling water, from the smoke of the fire kindled under the drill, and from countless process-images essentially akin to them, is their intuitive connection with the gates of the body, whose phenomenological consideration would present us with numerous special disclosures. Let it suffice us here to have derived the weight of significance and the substitutive capacity of all of them from the appearance of the body. If in particular the pars-pro-toto role falls also, and here and there even preponderantly, to excrements — held for that very reason to be creative — we may consider this sufficiently grounded already by the intuitive connection of the excretory organs in question with the organ of procreation (with which, to be sure, a phenomenological doctrine of the body would find itself faced with a formidable problem).

We pass over the symbolism of hair, since something of it has survived and is besides known from a few data of historical fashions ("long-haired" Achaeans as well as Germanic peoples in contrast to shorn unfree men and slaves; the full-bottomed wig as an expression of power in the age of the Baroque; the priest's tonsure in connection with celibacy [p. 1291], etc.), and remark, on the symbolism of the hands, that it is not, or hardly, their animal chief property of instinctive grasping, but partly the predominantly human one of giving and offering, and partly and especially the image-linking one, peculiar to man alone, of pointing, by which they are governed — or, if indeed of seizing and taking, then that magically appropriating touch from which healing and restoring, indeed begetting and bearing effects can proceed (Daktyloi, Tom Thumbs, and other hand-births). Linguistic echoes tell us of this: the finger-pointing of fate; the finger of God; to lay one's hand on something, or to lay one's hand upon someone, whereby one, magically taking possession, protects, blesses, soothes, heals, and — "puts under guardianship" (belonging to the extinct Old Germanic mund = hand); to withdraw one's hand from someone, by which originally, likewise magically and not merely in a transferred sense, the opposite of this is brought about; to hold one's thumb for someone, etc. From the jesting phrase that one cannot suck it out of one's fingers, we hear the nourishing magic of the hand (the ring-finger of the left hand of Isis was milk-dispensing!); from the remark that the little finger tells one so, the magic of the indicating hand; and even still the witty characterization of someone as one who has more talent in his little finger than another in his whole body, follows unconscious impulses from that barbaric chirology according to which the cutting-off of finger-joints, for instance of Australian girls or Mandan youths, was a most essence-laden and hence indeed most lucrative sacrifice. There were indeed tribes who thought the life-principle of a mythical being contained likewise in the little finger, as the strength of Samson lay in his hair! — Finally, even a glance at the artistry and the technical achievements of hand and fingers, as they come directly to representation in postures and movements, then in the countless activities of spinning, weaving, carving, kneading, building, etc., would suffice to make understood the accent of value that, among other things, singles out these members from the image of man; and whatever else besides may contribute to the symbolism of the nails, the pars-pro-toto series — nail = finger = hand → pointing, protecting, weaving, "efficacious," begetting life-principle — suffices to endow the easily detached fingernails with magically efficacious essences.

Decisive, however, for the image-theoretical grounding of all magic with body-cuttings is the fundamental assumption, generally peculiar to Pelasgianism, [p. 1292] of an essence-changing power of moulting. We shall illustrate in the next chapter, by means of a definite cultic custom, the symbolic identity of skin and garment, and confine ourselves here to the anticipatory remark that, were it so, man would become the being of the tree whose mantle of foliage, the being of the animal whose pelt, the being of the daemon whose skin enclosed him. The Mexican spring-god Xipe was called "the Flayed One," because his idol was periodically clothed with the skin that had been drawn from the sacrificial man who represented him. But if daemons could in this way once literally "jump out of their skin," we shall not overlook what the following turns of phrase contribute to confirming the symbolic identity of skin with life (a), essence (b), and sphere of power (c): a) to defend one's skin, to carry one's skin to market, to stake one's skin on something, to sell one's skin (in military service), to escape with a whole skin — b) an honest skin, to be ill at ease in one's skin, someone is not comfortable in his skin — c) to pull the skin (or also the hide) over someone's ears (that is, to strip him of his power). Perhaps the most striking example of the magic of skin-changing is offered by the versipelles = skinturners, by which, as is well known, one understood those animal-men who had turned the wolf's pelt inward and therefore, by the mere turning of their skin, became daemonic werewolves. It becomes apparent thereby that not even the skin as such, but at bottom only its visible outer side, determined the character of its bearer — or, generalized: that with every change of appearance a change of essence went hand in hand!

Accordingly it was the intimation of transformation into some daemonic animal, indeed the beginning of it, when the Indian warrior hoped, by wearing the claws of the grizzly bear, to increase his boldness; when jaguar-claws worn as a necklace augmented strength, deer-hooves swiftness; when the shaman, by fastening eagle-feathers to his staff, shared in the supposed omniscience of that far-sighted bird of prey; when from Australia to America it was precisely feathers that were able to transfer the essential content of birds to the "feathered" man.<sup>115</sup> From the soul-possession of parts of the body's outer surface there speaks unmistakably the physiognomic ground of origin of their magical value: in all the customs we have adduced, bodies and substances owe their power to act at a distance or to transform, to their fitness to stand in for a likeness, and thus for the transmission or renewal of the efficacy [p. 1293] ascribed to the being depicted. The image-character of these connections comes wholly to light when the efficacious or effect-receptive fetish is neither part nor product of the body to be bewitched, but an accessory of its appearance. In a witch-trial of the 17th century the sorceress confessed to having struck a lord with fatal illness by letting rot in the earth — not some cutting of his body, but a glove of his!

<sup>115</sup> On page 1292. — However much fashions have long since become a matter of mercantile speculation, it nonetheless seems to us that, in the astonishing readiness of countless women to have their hats adorned with bird feathers and stuffed birds, although the devastating consequences for the earth's stock of birds must today be generally known, an after-drive from mankind's prehistory is involved — without, of course, the least consciousness of it!

The image-magic in the narrower sense of the word, to which we have thus arrived, reaches so far up into the latest times (we recall the punitive form of hanging "in effigy") that mere mention might suffice to call the matter to mind. Yet a few examples may help toward understanding. — The transition from seemingly material magic to pure image-magic is offered by the custom of the Hindus of kneading hair-shreds and other bodily refuse into little figures, pronouncing mantras over them, and consecrating them by sacrifice; whereupon countless evils befall the bewitched person through the Grahas, or planet-spirits. From here it is but a single step to the baptized wax doll, which, as everyone knows, was the preferred fetish of all harm-magic in the Christian Middle Ages. In the 11th century the Jews made a waxen image of Bishop Eberhard, had it baptized by a priest, and burned it; whereupon the bishop fell ill and died (Grimm); but even today wax figures of the enemy are still made in Borneo: as they slowly melt at the fire, so the enemy sickens and perishes. Since, in the spirit of symbolic thought, the foot, for example, represents the whole man, and in turn the shape of the foot represents the foot, one can in principle bewitch the pedestrian by magical operations upon his footprints. Hence when the Karen in Burma wished to strike a person dumb, they lifted out that person's footprints, formed from them a likeness of the owner, and stuck it all over with cotton seeds (Tylor). Note the threefold image-relation: the footprints as image of the foot and consequently of the whole person, the earth-model as second representation of the person, the covering with cotton seeds as image of the closing of the mouth. The same thought, however, sustains that well-known custom of Germanic antiquity known as the so-called earth-cutting: "One cuts out, namely, the earth or the turf on which the man who is to be destroyed has stood, and hangs it in the chimney, that he may perish [p. 1294] as his footprints dry up and shrink" (Tylor). — A single example of this kind seems to us sufficient to fix the conviction that there has been a stage of consciousness of mankind as a whole whose manner of reflection was informed by belief in the actuality not of things but of images; and who could fail to recognize how nearly related to it still is the Democritean eidolon empsychon, and the whole early Greek image-theory of perception, down into Plato's theory of Ideas!

However much the image-customs tended predominantly to serve harm-magic, there is scarcely one among them that would not also appear, alongside this, in the service of healing-magic, love-magic, protective magic, birth-magic, fertility-magic, rain-magic, hunting-magic, etc. Among the South Slavs, for example, the footprints of the beloved were dug out by the girl, put into a pot, and planted with "unwitherable" flowers (Frazer). "In the South Sea Islands one hangs up charms to keep thieves away from plantations; a few coconut leaves, plaited in the shape of a shark, cause the thief who disregards them to be devoured by a real shark" (Tylor). In Sumatra childless women tried (and perhaps occasionally still try) to bring about pregnancy by holding a self-made image of a child between their thighs. The custom, prevailing among Bulgarians, Turks, and several other peoples down into the latest times, of drawing a boy who was to be adopted through the clothes of the chosen mother, or from behind between her legs, reaches back into antiquity, from which the same procedure is told us, for instance, of Hera adopting Heracles (Frazer). From an essentially like motive, the sorcerer in Borneo eases childbirth by imitating the movements of the woman in labor with a wrapped stone bound in front of himself. With bison-dances, snake-dances, bear-dances the Indians, with emu-dances and kangaroo-dances the West Australians lured the game; with fish-mask dances the natives of the Torres Strait, and likewise, say, the aboriginal inhabitants of Central Brazil, lured the fish. By the whirring of the whirled bullroarer boards the thunder is called forth; by the smoking of cigarettes — cloud-formation is favored! The rain-causing libation of water, of which we shall presently hear more, is found in the antiquity of all the Indo-Germanic as well as Semitic peoples; but no differently among the Samoan "rainmakers" of the most recent past! Likewise [p. 1295] the ancient Israelite "scapegoat" has countless relatives among primitives. In West Africa the devil was banished into dolls. "In Siam the doctor makes an image out of clay, sends his patient's illness into it, then carries it into the forest and buries it" (Tylor). The waxen reproductions of afflicted limbs, with which even today pious feeling purchases healing by consecration before the image of the Redeemer, or renders thanks for a cure happily achieved, need no further mention. Sign-magic. — Just as idolatry occurs not without symbolism, symbolism not without idolatry, so no image-magic without a resonating sign-magic, no sign-magic without components of image-magic. The cross would be an intermediate thing between image and sign, insofar as it signifies, say, the tree; already predominantly sign, if two crossing paths; only sign, if the process of pairing, which even today zoology and botany often call "crossing"; and this sign-nature would seem to be still heightened by replacing the figure of the cross with the gesture of "crossing oneself." If our eye is thereby sharpened for the image-content of acts, activities, movements, processes, events, we should nonetheless remember that metaphysically the matter stands the other way round: insofar as all intuitive images are for the Pelasgian above all appearances, even the merely figural likenesses already carry the meaning of signs of living powers and of their now steady, now sudden working, and the gesture, whether representing or sign-giving, only accentuates the experience of movement, which can never be separated from any receptivity to idols.

Among our examples of image-magic there were already not a few from the border-zone of so-called analogy-magic, which is characterized by image-like correspondences. They emerge palpably in the following healing-magic. Among North American Indians the likeness of a daemon was painted on the ground with colored powders; those in need of healing let themselves down onto certain places of the magical image, and the medicine-man rubbed the aching parts of the body, after first pressing his spittle-moistened hand onto the corresponding parts of the image. In similar fashion the Chinese physician used crown, middle piece, and roots of the plant as medicine for the head, trunk, and legs of the patient. Among the Germanic peoples the crown of the tree generally corresponded to the head of man, the bark to the skin, the [p. 1296] bast to the entrails. The plant ginseng, in German "likeness of man," was held in China as among the Iroquois to be curative on the ground of a beheld similarity of its root to the shape of man. "Bloodstone" proves effective in staunching blood; the "serpent-stone" helped in Hellas against snakebite, and in Albania it is said still to occur that young mothers carry the "milk-stone" to increase their milk.

The astrology of the Middle Ages walks entirely in the same paths. A child born under the sign of the Lion becomes courageous; one born under the sign of the Crab does not get properly ahead; one born under the sign of the Water-Bearer must beware of drowning. "From this it follows of necessity," says Albertus Magnus in his work on the kinds of stones, "that if one duly observes a celestial figure and impresses its image upon some work of nature or of art, a part of the powers of the former then flows into the latter." Accordingly, images fashioned, say, under the so-called fiery triplicity ought to mitigate fevers and make one witty and eloquent, while those produced under the watery one strengthen mendacity and luxurious living.

Name-magic, already touched on earlier, as the purest and highest form of sign-magic, mingles curiously with the most massive forms of image-magic, when the Chinese physician makes the sick man swallow the ash of the prescription, or Mohammedans drink themselves healing with the help of water into which verses of the Koran have been dipped! Deeper into the domain of sign-magic, by contrast, leads us the following healing custom. In Vorarlberg, not too long ago, one drove the lichen from a sick animal by breaking off, at sunset, three shoots from an elder bush, binding the affliction into them under certain ceremonies, and then hanging them in the chimney: as the shoots dried up, the lichen vanished. Of the three main motifs — the elder bush, the binding-in of the affliction, and the drying-out of the loop in the chimney — we pass over the drying-out, familiar to us in principle, and, setting the elder bush aside for the time being, direct our attention to the binding-in of illnesses. It is found in countless variants. Thus, for example, headache is driven away by binding a thread three times round the head, then hanging it in the form of a loop on a tree, and waiting to see whether a bird flies through it: if this happens, it carries the affliction away with it. If in such cases the gesture [p. 1297] of knot-tying or of forming a loop obviously has real binding as its consequence, then even our own logic would demand that the magically understood gesture of loosening a knot must bring about real unbinding. This is regularly the case at the stage of beholding consciousness. When, for example, the Lappish sorcerer sold sailors bundles of knots, so that they might find as many knots to loosen as they needed of favoring winds, then the knot, by being loosed, gives what the knot, by being tied, took. From antiquity we recall the bags of Aeolus. We see this same elementary thought applied to the symbol of the ring, of the gate, of the lock, of the chain, indeed of any bindingdevice whatsoever, when among numerous peoples the delivery of the pregnant woman was made harder by the presence of knots, rings, locked locks, corked bottles, folded hands (!), and eased by their opening, loosening, or removal.

Though the severing of the umbilical cord may have helped promote the use of the word "unbinding" for the process of birth, the usage nonetheless betrays — whereby one can be "unbound" of an oath, an obligation, an office — the originally symbolic nature also of all bodily binding and loosing; hence one would haughtily underestimate the judgment of Pelasgian man by supposing that he meant to enclose the storm in his loops, knots, and bags, or to release it by loosing them, the storm that we hold to be real with the concept of storm. The connection for him subsists not between the objective movement of air and the objective knot, but between the image of the former and the gesture of knot-tying. What he binds with his pantomime of binding, looses with his loosing, is the beheld image of the wind, or, in the language of school-understanding, the "spirit" of the wind. He believes, even in the state of reflective sobriety, what even the educated poet, in the state at least of enthusiastic excitement — insofar as he is a poet — cannot but believe: in the actuality of that of which, in contrast to the merely thought, not to say the re-thought, world, the lived and only livable world is the appearing and manifesting; in the actuality of soul perceptible to sense! And he links — though, to be sure, out of immediate necessity and without consciousness of the possibility of a fundamentally different order — the properties of things along the thread of pictorial similarities, and thereby of their kinship of life [p. 1298]. On the magical contrary-sense of symbols. — Why must the healing shoots be broken precisely from the elder? Because it was the elder that sent the affliction! What had already suggested itself several times, and came fully to light with the knot, holds for every symbol: with regard to every meaning that can be predicated of it, it has at the same time the contrary counter-meaning. Just as it is originally the achievement of one of those seer-like acts that snatch themselves directly from the gamos of receiving soul and efficacious happening, so it repeats, in the medium of signs, the bipolar character of actuality, and offers, case by case, a coincidentia oppositorum. With this key in hand no one will henceforth be able to confuse it either with the concept or with the metaphor! All that we shall further adduce in this section serves, among other things, to trace the symbolic polarities back to their root and to let the primal polarity, from which all particular polarities branch off, come to light. Here, however, we close with a few instances of the magical contrary-sense of symbols, for the understanding of which, however, a preliminary remark is required.

It is grounded in the corporeality of all magic that, with the predominance of magical uses, the symbol too becomes more corporeal and idol-like; and from the increasing corporeality there follows so intimate an interlocking of the poles that it is at times hard to discern the polar powers whose alternating emergence entails the opposite effects. It is evident how the one and the same knot can bind and free, according as it is tied or loosed; but only after the symbolic equation of the removal of a ring with its breaking do we understand how the removal can ease childbirth. We should be inclined to hold the elder bush to be only curative, had we not learned that it also sends certain illnesses; and again, insofar as it appears in the light of a possible seat of the illness, it is able to take the illness into itself and thereby, as it were, to entice it away from another seat.

The path to reification, upon which we have entered with so external a conception of the states of affairs, has, as has already been intimated several times, also been trodden by magical thinking; only that, since the cosmic symbolism (in the following chapters) leads us back to its beginning, we shall find, at the bottom of all symbolic thought, that "reversal of opposites" discovered by Heraclitus and falsified by Hegel, [p. 1299] according to which the polarity of substances or shapes proceeds from a polarity of "efficacious and weaving" happening, and day would not be there without night, the kindling not without the extinguishing of the light. Even the thought, repeatedly involved in our examples, that one avoids the harm which one takes upon oneself symbolically (or even actually!), conjures away the danger which one undergoes in effigy or with which one marks oneself, feeds in the end on the — if not known, then at least beheld — polarity of happening. — Although our instances favor the magical contrary-sense, they should nonetheless already let it be glimpsed that symbolic polarity pervades the realm of primal gnosis as well. — Dog's hair heals dog-bite, according to the Hávamál. — The rope of the hanged brings luck in popular belief; the blood of beheaded criminals heals epilepsy. — Because it was the lance with which Achilles dealt Telephus his wound, Achilles heals the wounded man with scraped shavings of the same lance; likewise the seer Melampus heals a cut wound by giving to drink of the rust of the knife. — According to late Egyptian pharmacology, stone preparations help against bladder-stone; leaves of St. John's wort, because they are perforated and look like wounds, against wounds; yellowish plant-extracts (of caraway, crocus, wormwood) against ailments of the yellow bile, blackish ones against those of the "black bile." — The sacrificial blood of the bull consecrated to the gods was for the Greek poison and remedy at once. — The healing god Apollo is also the sender of pestilence. — Oven-heat, in popular belief, drives out fever-heat; the coldness of the frog, feverchill. We need not recall the doctrines of homeopathy. — The ring of Gyges makes visible and invisible. — A dreamed wedding-dance signifies among the Zulus an imminent funeral. — In many places the opinion prevails that whoever rescues a drowning man is himself threatened with drowning. — The Mexican maize-goddess made the seed thrive, but also sent famines; the fire-god was at the same time lord of the sign of water, the fire-goddess of the sign of rain. — The water of the springs at Thyana was, for those who swore truly, sweet and pleasant, while the perjurer was struck blind by it. — According to the belief of by far the most primitives, magical power is heightened by abstinences and mortifications of the most various kinds, such as sexual abstinence, enforced silence, sleep-deprivation, bloodletting, amputations, etc. — Piercing of the tongue can strengthen mouth-magic, that of the testicles procreation-magic. — Piercing of the ear meant [p. 1300] among the Arapaho being struck by lightning, and counted as protection against arrows in battle. — A "thunderbolt," brought into the house, guards against being struck, likewise a hearth-brand, kindled at the primordially generated "need-fire," against the flame of lightning. — Hölderlin points to age-old knowledge when he sings of the "holy-sober" water: the Greeks knew springs that made one mad, and springs that instantly made one sober. — Loki, the irreconcilable enemy of the gods, is nonetheless blood-brothered with Odin and helps Thor win back his hammer. — Poseidon, the earth-shaker and rock-breaker, builds the walls of the cities of Troy and Byzantium. Similarly the magical sound of the tuba: it "awakens" the walls sleeping in the ground and draws them up into the light, and it topples them. — He who falls into the deep well of Mother Holle finds himself high up among the clouds.<sup>116</sup>

<sup>116</sup> On page 1300. — Here would belong the thesis, advocated by *Abel* in his tract "Über den Gegensinn der Urworte" (Leipzig, 1884) and supported by many disputed, but also some scarcely deniable, examples, that originally all names in all languages once meant, besides the state of affairs they signified, simultaneously the opposite state of affairs as well; according to which, for instance, the name for "strong" would also have been the name for "weak." The *thought* is correct, but unfortunately unprovable: first, because the *separation* of the poles occurs earlier in languages than in cultic symbols (and their mythical paraphrases); and second, because the will to communicate, making more and more use of languages, brings into play motives of separation of a *spiritual* origin, which no longer let that primal motive "come to word."

[p. 1301]

#### 73. Kapitel — Elementarsymbole — Chapter 73 — Elemental Symbols

*Symbolic thinking in examples.* — Having discussed the most important forms, as well as the degenerate forms, of symbolic thinking and magical custom, and having assessed the relation of both to the sense of actuality, we now turn more decisively to Pelasgianism, the word understood in the sense set out at the beginning. Here we are no longer concerned with the actual condition of extra-historical social groupings, and at most only incidentally with their actual prehistory, but with the efficacious image of Pelasgianism, so far as it can be inferred from cults, myths, and symbols — and has for the most part already been inferred, thanks to the researches of Bachofen. With this in view, the phenomena of the human organism now recede in formative power behind the phenomena of the cosmos. Just as in the previous chapter, for the sake of the "primitive peoples," we had to emphasize the animal traits in the physiognomy of the idols, so now we must lay the stress on the cosmic ones, because the Pelasgian conception of the world overwhelmingly mirrors the reign of the elements: "It is an all-governing basic view of the ancient world that things earthly and things heavenly obey the same laws, and that a great harmony must pervade the transient and the imperishable alike. Earthly development struggles on until it realizes in full truth the cosmic prototype of the heavenly bodies" (Bachofen). Mountains and caves, stones and swamps, storms and downpours, stars, the clod-earth and the drift of clouds: all of them weave together in the ever-passing, everarising soul-appearance of the Pelasgian sensory world, and the field of consideration would widen into the boundless if we did not choose reference points or formative centers from the outset. From the manifold of elemental symbols, as we shall call them, we single out three: the moon, water, the tree, and shall attempt to descend to the "Mothers" by taking as our guide the elementary [p. 1302] similarities that link the moon with water, both with the tree, and each of them with every possible image. We begin with a cursory survey, meant to make us more familiar with the symbolic mode of contemplation and at least to sound the principal motifs of the later exposition.

To the factually perceiving eye, the moon presents itself as a shimmering circular disk that can be compared, analyzed, and fixed according to color, shape, luminosity, movement, corporeality, and other properties. Not one among these but its appearance also falls within the experience of the beholding soul; yet none of them either could determine the mode of apprehension of a being whose inner eye is opened to the life-content of images and their kindred similarities. For a "beholding consciousness," rather, the lunar appearance belongs, on the one hand, to the totality of the nocturnal earthly space, of which we shall treat only later, and on the other, to a sequence of events through which it is renewed every night — still in a forcefully self-attesting manner, as, according to the genuinely Pelasgian dictum of Heraclitus, the sun is too, day by day: namely as, moreover, life-altered, image-different from its previous appearance, restlessly transformed in its wandering return. And to transformation as such is joined directly the double sense of the rhythmic change of phases. Thus the beheld moon becomes the pulse-gauge of time, the visible rhythm of the event that oscillates restlessly between dying and becoming, the celestial chronoscope. We need only follow this thread to find it comprehensible even today why trees must be felled and plants gathered when the moon is waning, whereas one sets grafting-scions and begins every deed-undertaking when the moon is waxing.

With this we enter at the same time the domain of divination, which appears as the magical exploitation of primordial gnosis and therefore plays wholly within the bounds of symbolic thinking. Among earthly images, all those with a constantly changing sensory body have, in like manner, oracular significance. If the moon's power to "measure" time already lies in its very name — granting that the derivation of the stem men from the Indo-European root me or mä (= to measure) still holds its ground against more recent challenges — then, conversely, phrases like "the stream of time," "the flowing-away of time" likewise attest that the beholding primal reflection mirrors the everlasting coming and going from the image of water as well, and that water too is thereby joined to the time-pole. Living time, however, as we know, is not that [p. 1303] ever-selfsame straight line which the accumulating succession of factual time signifies to us, but the expression of eternal otherness, or the appearing form of all-encompassing fate. Thus the Pelasgians found in the liquid element the convincing symbol of never-calculable, yet itself all-knowing powers of fate. Beginning with the spirits of springs, wells, and ponds, by way of the royal rulers of the sacred rivers — Ganga, Euphrates, Nile, Jordan, Aphaka, Achelous, Alpheius, Maeander, Tiber, Danube — down to the thousand-shaped monsters and gods of the sea, the water-dwellers are for peoples as for individuals incalculably capricious increasers and disturbers, yet in the smallest matters as in the greatest, always knowing of the future.

From the animality within us we came to know that water quenches thirst; with the understanding within us we learned to shatter it, and believe ourselves the better instructed since we can artificially make it out of two gases. How differently the world opens to us on the ground of the reflection of beholding! For here we learn what neither a thinking animal nor ever a merely rational mind could learn: that to one who knows of the soul of water, the willing element grants, out of its "spirit," a foreseeing clairvoyance. How much German "popular superstition" alone tells of this! If one washes one's face beneath three bridges while the bells ring for Christmas midnight mass, one foresees all the events of the coming year. Vessels of water, set out in the open during a lunar eclipse, show the girl who gazes into them her future bridegroom. — Germanic women prophesied from the eddies of rivers and the murmur of brooks. In antiquity, the power of prophecy was bestowed by, or bound up with, chthonic oracle-sites — among others, the spring of Amphiaraus at Lerna and at Oropus, further the one at the foot of the oak of Zeus at Dodona, the one on Cithaeron, at Patrae, at Delphi, near Antioch, at the temple of Jupiter Ammon. By marshy lakes stood the most famous oracles of the dead. In an echoing seagrotto the Cumaean Sibyl prophesied. Compelled or entreated by the practices of age-old hydromancy, which continued through the whole of the Middle Ages, the images of coming events emerge from the water or are mirrored on its surface. Speaking or counseling reeds and rushes are nothing rare in myth. Of the inspiring power of the draught from sacred wells we have already heard; and it is enthousiasmos that makes one "seeing." Of the oracle at Colophon, Iamblichus says: "It is known throughout the whole world that the oracle at Colophon gives its answers through water. In an underground grotto [p. 1304] there is a spring, from which the prophet drinks, and after he has drunk, and after several nights in which all the prescribed rites are fulfilled, he prophesies." Knowing rivers made known, in the Middle Ages, the guilt or innocence of supposed witches — and likewise in India, Arabia, Palestine, Syria, Carthage! Stygian streams that unveil and avenge perjury existed alike in the East and in the West. According to Wellhausen's researches, age-old Hebrew tradition derives the Torah from the judicial pronouncements of Moses at the sanctuary of Kadesh, which lay by the demonic spring "En Mishpat" — in German, the "spring of justice." — It takes no great acuteness to recognize the connection between clairvoyance-bestowing waters of popular "superstition" and the sweepingly grand legendary motif according to which the highest of the gods, the Nordic Odin, borrowed his wisdom from Mimir, the — spirit of the well!

The framework of a time-relation common to both symbols nonetheless leaves room for essential differences, of which the following two may also be grasped intuitively: the formal determinacy of every lunar appearance, the formal indeterminacy of every water-image; an articulated succession of images there, a flowing succession here. If, accordingly, the moon determines the pulse-beat of time, works out periods of fate, and is joined, either portending or with intensifying presence, to the turning-points of life, then water makes the unstoppability of what happens appear, and reveals in the language of signs why the soul of images can never become anyone's own possession: its restless transformation. In view of this, the water-beings of the most various peoples are marked by a startling suddenness of surfacing and vanishing, by a cunning now teasingly playful, now shrilly mocking, and by that sorcery of protean costume-changing behind which the demonic element slips "ungraspable" and derisive from the grasp of human curiosity. Yet whoever, by decree of the gods, knows how to bind his "spirits" — Nereus, Proteus, Glaucus, Achelous, Thetis, and the like — to him they proclaim, with never-failing certainty, a future often consoling, more often dark and dreadful.

But what transforms itself in an instant must also be able to transform whatever comes into soulful contact with it; and so a bewildering abundance of customs repeats the primal thought of a power that renews down to the deepest depths — and hence, of course, often also bewitches — a power that belongs to sprinkling, to washing with water, to immersion in it, to drinking it, indeed even to the barely felt moistening of it. Upon the plunging of oneself into water there usually follows [p. 1305] in myth a complete transformation, as of Asteria into a quail, of Alcyone into a kingfisher, of Derceto-Atargatis into a fish. With sprinkling, in the oriental fairy tale, the evil sorceress works upon the person to be cursed the calamitous exchange of shape (for example, of human form with the form of a dog), while the good sorceress works the reverse transformation upon the bewitched one. Every waterconsecration, baptism, ritual purification is rooted in that belief in a change of essence through the self-changing element, and in "rebirth" out of a change of essence, into which the most direct insight is given us by the — despite all the diversity of its forms, always identical in meaning — "fountain of rejuvenation." German folk custom knows: "Whoever washes himself in the village puddle on Walpurgis Night becomes young and beautiful." — It speaks for the sleepwalking certainty of symbol-forming thought that, with its distinction between the loosening and transforming "waters of forgetting" and the binding and banning "waters of remembrance," it shows itself knowledgeable of the influences that polar states of life exert upon consciousness.<sup>117</sup>

<sup>117</sup> On page 1305. — Besides *Pfannenschmidt*'s "Weihwasser," rich material, together with deeply penetrating observations on it, is offered by M. *Ninck*, Die Bedeutung des Wassers im Kult und Leben der Alten. Eine symbolgeschichtliche Untersuchung (Leipzig 1921).

More closely akin to the moon than to water, though standing partly in a relation of Gamos to the latter, the plant-world finally symbolizes once again — but more closely and intimately — the rise and fall of the courses of fate with their rhythm of growing and withering. Everywhere there holds the symbolic double-equation between human happiness and the blossoming of the plant, human misfortune and its withering. It is one and the same primal thought whose bright side inspired the opening of the Psalm: "He is like a tree planted by streams of water, that bringeth forth his fruit in his season, whose leaf also shall not wither," and whose dark side speaks more movingly from these verses of the Hávamál: "The tree that stands alone in the village dies, and neither leaf nor bark keep it warm; so is the man whom no one loves — why should he live any longer?"

Divinatory customs like the following, from British Guiana, occur, along with many akin in meaning, in the antiquity of every civilized people of the present day. When two young children are betrothed, the parties plant trees to confirm the agreement: if one of the trees dies, the child symbolically identified with it dies as well. In the Aargau, down to the latest times, it was customary to plant a little tree at the hour of a child's birth — apple trees for boys, pear trees for girls: the thriving or failure to thrive of the sapling then foretold the growth or stunting of the child. "Still within the last generation," reports Mannhardt, [p. 1306] "it happened that an Aargau father, in wrath over a wayward son who was just then abroad and hence beyond paternal chastisement, went out into the field and cut down again the birth-tree planted there." The seeming sameness of the corporeal being with its likeness corresponds to a seeming sameness of the corporeal being with its symbol: yet in both alike — because for a consciousness for which essential actuality lies only in appearance — there is found, in each of the three, merely housed in a different way, one and the same truly identical primal image.

Our presentation has perhaps already made it evident that the time-symbolic trait comes to expression most strongly in the water-image, next in the image of the moon, and only in third place in the plant-image. In the latter, however, alongside that trait there stands out, more and more sharply, until finally it emerges predominant, the space-symbolism — the more we turn from leaves and blossoms and ground-plants to the tree. And here it is, as already discussed earlier, the polarity of below to above, the capacity of the tree to reach down, clinging with its roots into the night-realm of the depths, and to reach up, bearing into the light-realm of the height, from which new series of similarities develop in customs, idols, and magic formulas, often expanding into the grandest configuration of the world-tree that branches through heaven and earth — of which, as no other legendary figure does, the Nordic Yggdrasil sets before our eyes. "In Lydia," says Bachofen, "the belief held that the trees were older than the earth. That is the idea of a tree of life."

That the tree of life is, in turn, also "tree of fate," and hence, notwithstanding its full form that mightily articulates the heights, depths, and breadths of the world, a resounding symbol of what happens, is shown to us (after Mannhardt) by a dramatic magic-song with which Russian women ward off a threatening plague, drawing at the same time, with the plow, the evil-hindering furrow around the village. In the twelve maidens of the song a sea-born doom is embodied — here especially the doom of deadly bodily ills; the trees are to be won over to drive the fire of annihilation across the earth; they seem ready, and the death-cauldrons begin to seethe; but out of the inwardness of their cosmic fullness of life there rises in the trees the watcher's voice, and their rustling swells into a droning song of life, before which the spirits of plague lose themselves farther and ever farther away. [p. 1307] Twelve maidens came; they took their way, no short one it was, to the steep heights, up to the mountains, to the three old elder trees. "Make ready the white oaken tables, sharpen the knives of steel, make hot the seething cauldrons, cleave, pierce unto death every life beneath the heavens." In these seething cauldrons brews, with unquenchable fire, every life beneath the heavens. Round about the seething cauldrons stand the old elders. The old elders sing, they sing of life, they sing of death, they sing of the whole race of man. The old elders grant to the whole world long life; but to the other, to evil death, the old elders appoint a wide and long journey. The old elders promise abiding life to the whole race of men. Symbolism and personification. — We interrupt the course of an inquiry devoted to the conditions under which three elemental symbols arose, because there is reason to fear that, despite our defense taken beforehand, it will be misconstrued by virtue of an erroneous, yet all-dominating, habit of thought of the present. We have, to be sure, emphatically rejected the view that the efficacious powers to which a beholding consciousness felt itself bound were originally man-like powers; [p. 1308] yet the belletristic subjectivism that falsifies all the primal thoughts of mankind will, without perhaps even noticing it itself, nonetheless be inclined to smuggle, under the assumption of the mere presence of unquestionably soul-like powers, an assumption of secretly personal powers — this notwithstanding that even the poet who speaks in similitudes, even at the highest level of cultivation, can in no way escape the pull of that thinking already prefigured by language itself, which explains, not the cosmos by man, but, quite to the contrary, man by the cosmos.

Scarcely any other symbolism has grown so deeply into language, and has interlocked so far-reachingly with poetry, as the symbol of the plant. Is the plant, then, humanized, or is man, conversely, made into a plant? In ancient Chinese lyric poetry the royal bride is called a "tree in a robe of silk foliage," each of her hands "a five-parted branch," her colored nails are likened to blossoms, her teeth to "moist melon-seeds." In the Vedas it is said of the singer that he "drives forth the blossoms of songs" like a tree; in the Mahabharata, of the heroine, that she breathes upon her husband's breast like "the flower, when morning refreshes it." Homer, in his world-famous verses, which will occupy us further below in particular, sees the coming and passing of the generations of men in the sprouting and falling of leaves; and, as though the millennia had changed nothing of it, Schiller in turn calls Wallenstein, forsaken by his followers, a "leafless tree." — And, quite without poetic intention, whoever speaks of "sappy" or "swelling" youth, of "withered" or "dry" old age, of "blooming" health, "budding" maidenhood, "fully blossomed" beauty — what has he really "compared": the plant to man, or rather man to the plant? Without any doubt, the latter! And accordingly, among genuine poetic words there will scarcely be found even one of another kind than that in which the immediately intelligible is precisely the plant-like, while the human is a merely mediated thing that first, through relation to the former, comes into a participation-demanding light. If man has thus indeed become a kind of plant, we must not understand it as a humanizing of the plant when the plant, in turn, has "eyes," "feet," "head," or "hair," when it can "speak" or "sing," "sigh" and "groan," and when the tree, struck by the axe-blow, "bleeds" and "cries out." For such turns of phrase [p. 1309] presuppose a plant-soul whose utterances can in the end be depicted only in the same terms as those of the human mind — not to mention that (as was shown earlier) the meaning-content of the words in such turns of phrase undergoes a perceptible change.

As the sun goes down, / there is a last tree, / that stands as though in morning flames / at the farthest rim of the sky. / It is a tree and nothing more, / yet if one thinks, at night, / of that last wondrous light, / one thinks of it as well. / In the same way I think of you, / now that youth has left me; / you hold its last gleam for me / fast for all time. / The gripping power of these verses of Hebbel wells up from the identification of a whole human fate with the image of the tree, beheld as though in cultic rapture — and certainly not the reverse! Not an inclination toward the personification of all-nature, but rather toward the re-naturalization of the human person, marks the poet's experience; and with just this it takes part in the symbolism of prehistory!

If, in Westphalia, the farmer once announced to the beehives, the grain-sacks, and not least to the trees, the death of the master of the house — "The master is dead" — or if the Moravian peasant-woman stroked the fruit tree, saying, "Little tree, bring forth much fruit!" — or if people even greeted the trees with reverence, "Good morning, Gylde" — the cultivated modern man may, if he likes, misunderstand this to mean that his forebear took beehives, grain-sacks, and above all trees for persons. But when the Curetes spring from the ground after a mighty rain, or the Phrygian Corybantes are driven up tree-like (dendrophyeis) from the Great Mother; or when the Eranian creation-myth lets the first human pair grow out of the earth in the shape of a Reivas-plant and only gradually change into human beings; or when we hear of the Sioux [p. 1310] that their tribal ancestors clung with their feet in the ground for centuries, until a great serpent gnawed at their roots, whereupon they, now for the first time truly humanized, went their way — then anyone must recognize, who is not yet wholly blinded by the nonsense of empathy-projection, that here it is not so much the tree that is personified as, rather, the human person that is taken back into the more original realm of the vegetative.

But should even such evidence still seem ambiguous to anyone, let him open his eyes to the popular customs — as Mannhardt gathered them for us, from past and present, out of almost the whole of Aryandom, for tree-veneration — in an unparalleled wealth and with a wholehearted engagement that lets us scarcely notice, over the astonishingly happy success of his conjuring of the speech-exchanging voices of the forest, even his inadequate attempts at explanation: and he might, despite the theoretically wavering stance of the mediator himself, perhaps find his own belief in the explicability of primordial essence-concepts shaken loose from that self-mirroring habit which has, to be sure, become a kind of second nature to us. — What myth only poeticizes, the demonic transformation of man into a tree- or plant-being, is accomplished, namely — and precisely on the occasion of the enactment of a cult-idea to be touched on later — by festive customs, not merely in a theatrically eye-catching but in a tangible actuality. We mean, however, the idea of sacrifice, and we anticipate here, for the time being without proof, what will later be more precisely grounded: that to bring a demon a sacrifice always means to sacrifice the demon himself. This granted, then, on the basis of the belief in the actuality of images, the living gift — be it plant, animal, or human — must, in order to be fit for sacrifice, exchange its own form for that of the demon, by virtue now of a soul-symbolic, now of a bodilyidolic magic. The bodily exchange of form is now brought about — as was intimated in the last chapter — for an imagebelieving consciousness by what has already become, for a fact-believing one, a mere externality: the magic change of clothing; which is why, indeed, among absolutely all "primitive peoples," a ritual meaning still inheres today in forms of dress, quite especially the festive mask, which, as is well known, passed over into Greek tragedy and would alone suffice to guarantee its sacral origin. If this is so, then we need only determine what clothing the participant in the festival deems necessary for the object of sacrifice, in order to know with certainty what image [p. 1311] stands at the focal point of his veneration and of what kind, accordingly, the demonic being is to whom his celebration is dedicated.

All the tree-veneration customs that express a change of essence on the part of those who perform them — hence, in particular, all those descended from former sacrificial rites — now show us, as magically potent, the plant-mask, examples of which, following Mannhardt, we here assemble in a few exemplary instances. — In the Bavarian Franconian Forest, on Walpurgis Day, "a man wrapped from crown to toe in straw, with ears of grain bound together over his head in the form of a crown — the Walber" danced round the planted Walbertree. In Russian Lithuania the spirit of the May-tree was symbolized by the loveliest girl of the village, entirely wound about with birch branches and resounded about by the ever-recurring cry of Bacchic jubilation: O Maja, O Maja! In modern Greek villages, in times of persistent drought, an orphan child was stripped naked and then wrapped, from head to foot, in herbs and field-flowers: having thus become the demonic "Pyrpiruna," it had gained the power to conjure the longed-for rain, provided each father of a household poured a small cask of water over its head. Likewise, in Romania, the leaf-clad "Paparuda" was solemnly led about and drenched with water; in Bulgaria a "Perperuga"; in Serbia a "Dodola" — each accompanied by magic-songs, of whose incantatory cadence the following fragments of strophes give an impression:

"Papaluga, climb up into heaven, / open its door" — "Off flew the Perperuga; / Give, God, rain..." — "We go through the village, / the clouds go across the sky; / We go faster, / and faster go the clouds... / Out of the clouds fell a ring, / which the chorus-leader caught."

Lest one suppose, however, that such things may be taken for any arbitrary "mummery," [p. 1312] we shall henceforth choose only such examples as leave it, moreover, beyond doubt that the drenching was, once again, a "real-symbol" of the *drowning* that was for that very reason meant in full earnest.

In Slovenian Carinthia, on the feast day of St. George (April 24), an orgiastic procession wound its way, with wild music, to the May-tree festival ground, and in its midst the "Green George," a lad wrapped from top to bottom in birch, whom, at the moment the celebration reached its climax, they threw into the water! Whether this was done directly, or only symbolically upon a substitute effigy, it was in every case a genuine sacrifice — one that, by its very principle, no more requires a "real" killing in the factual sense than it knows, or may know, mercy for a life that has been transformed into the demon who is to be killed — yet who, through that killing, nonetheless does not die! In Lower Bavaria the leaf-man called the "Pfingstl" wore a tall, tapering cap of marshmarigolds ending in a wreath of peonies; only two openings were left for the eyes, with wreaths of vetch above them; the sleeves of his garment, too, were made of water-plants and hazel-leaves. On either side, guides walked holding the outstretched arms of the Pfingstl, and all the boys carried bared swords. As they passed through the village, the demonic mask-wearer was now pelted by the farmers, from their hiding places, with copious showers of water, then led into the brook up to his waist, and pantomimically beheaded there with the sword by one of the guides. In Swabia the herdsmen disguised one of their fellows, the "Pfingstbutz," with flowering broom, covered his face besides with tree-bark, set a pointed leaf-cap upon him, hung him with cowbells, led him solemnly through the village, and finally buried him under straw and dung. In Bohemia they drew forth, from a leaf-hut, the Pentecost-king, disguised idol-like in tree-bark, hunted him, caught him, whipped him with rods, and, with ceremonies of archaic, grim formality, condemned him to death, whereupon he was beheaded by the so-called headsman with a swung sword — by the striking off of his crown — and carried away upon a bier. Among the Mexicans, finally, "in summer a feast was celebrated in honor of the goddess of maize... Centeotl, in the course of which she bore, after the soft ear of maize, Xilotl, the name Xilone. On the last day of the feast a woman, who represented the goddess, danced, and was afterward sacrificed." "In May, that is, at the onset of the rainy season..., the yearly feast of Huitzilopochtli himself was celebrated there... [p. 1313] Then an image of the god was made of edible plant-matter and honey... The maidens were called, on this day, sisters of Huitzilopochtli; they wore on their heads wreaths of dry maize-leaves, in their hands split reeds... Among the priests there was a captive, destined for sacrifice a year in advance, called 'wise lord of heaven,' who represented the god himself and had the freedom to determine the hour of his own sacrifice..."

We have brought forward here the idea of sacrifice, not yet ripe for full discussion, only because it guarantees, with a certainty beyond all surpassing, that the demonic mask really does refer to what the veneration of primitive peoples is directed toward. This image, however, leaves no doubt that, in order to become what the beholding gaze found in plants and trees, it was not the plant that exchanged its elemental essence for the personal essence of man, but man who exchanged his personality for the personless character of the plant — no differently than what myth, for an already higher reflection, attests, when it represents, in an unmistakable turn, the primal-thought truth that the soul, before it became the soul of man, had traversed the extra-human life-circle of an all-capable tree-nature. — We ask: what aesthete, imagining he has animated the landscape when, world-estranged and unbelieving as he is, he had to invent his own feelings of selfhood for it — would ever have hit upon any one of these myths, let alone upon those customs, before which, rather, we are condemned to stand ever more helplessly the more we have fallen victim to sentimental "anthropomorphism"! Myth, as we now see, unfolds, by the medium of a fantasy now more popular, now more personal — and, incidentally, under conditions whose investigation is in its very earliest beginnings — what lives more directly in customs and usages, and is known, out of a primordial mode of reflection, only in symbolically intelligible "signs."

Were we to try to express in sober words what, of the treeexperience of the Pelasgian — and finally of everyone who still harbors remnants of primordial feeling — can be translated into the form of a judgment, it would not run: the tree too has fates like a man, so it too must probably be something man-like; but rather: I too, man that I am, am a growing and again-withering thing; me too, just as though by roots, the earth holds and tirelessly nourishes from the lower depths, while heaven waters me from above with rays and rains; I too — however far I may have strayed and [p. 1314] become a stranger to this actuality of clouds, streams, downpours, lightnings, storms, trees, and forests, whose voices I no longer understand, even though they still touch me with an age-old familiarity — am not yet wholly an outcast fellow-dweller of a world-homeland in which all individual beings are bound up with one another. Losing myself, and it giving me back to myself, I dive, un-selved, back into the life of the tree that branches through it! "Coming to myself again" out of an admittedly incomparably deeper "sinking-under" than that which is meagerly expressed in the venture of such sentences, the life-conjoined reflection mirrors the character of the plant-demon, not narrowed within the bounds of personality.

Convinced that genuine poetry wells from the same source as genuine myth, we call once more, in closing, and all the more gladly, upon the genius of the poet for help, since above we disputed the claim to mythic truth of that supposedly poetic thing which knew how to secure for its usurped rank, unfortunately, unrestricted applause — it is no comfort to add, of a mankind grown misshapen, since that applause is the judgment-determining one of today! — we think here of the incomparable forest-songs of Lenau, at whose center the poet, with sure instinct, placed the figure of a magician, the sorcerer Merlin. With that power of language that belongs only to image-drunkenness, the following short fragment brings to expression not only the tree- and weather-shudder themselves, but, in the closing verses, their meaning and essence as well.

Full of storm-desire, / Merlin flings off, / in the tempest, his garment, / that the winds may cool, / that lightnings may bathe / his naked breast. / Root-threads the oak / stretches into the ground, / below, hidden, its mouth / sucks a thousandfold / life from secret springs, / that swell the trunk toward heaven.

[p. 1315] To and fro in the storm-night, / and the fiery-tawny lightnings spray, / to anoint his head; / nature, the manifest one, / intimately entwining sisterlike with him, / waters his heart, when crackling lightnings / kiss his black hair. — Dual polarity of the elemental symbols. — After this digression, which we could not spare ourselves, returning once more to the contemplation of the symbols — moon, tree, and water — we must now make plain, more sharply than has thus far been done by way of intimation, that "basic principle," as one might call it, of all symbol-forming thought, on the presupposition of which alone insight into the procedure of the ensouled understanding can be deepened. Already the little that was brought forward, from the point of view of their significance for fate, concerning the essence of the moon, water, and the tree, has shown each of the three to us in the light of a symbol at once of life and of death, of arising as of passing, of coming as of vanishing; and it should be self-evident, without further explanation, to anyone who has followed us through the third part of our work with even some attention, if we were to bring the same opposition to expression further through the following pairs: brightness and darkness, white and black, above and below, driving and reining-in, utterance and inwarding. The members thus paired with one another stand, in each case, in a relation of interchange that can equally well be regarded in the sense of conflict as of complement, and that could, in any case, not be severed without the co-abolition of the members themselves; they stand, in a word, to one another in that relation of polarity of which we know that it marks the structural character of actuality itself. The attempt to trace the form of polarity back to its point of origin requires a brief preliminary remark.

Were one to carry over the opposition, familiar to us from natural science, of a "positive" pole to a "negative" pole into the intuitive realm of symbols, one would at once run the risk of grasping it evaluatively, and thereby de-realizing, from the very ground up, the world of appearance with reference to which alone symbols can be spoken of at all. As against this, it must be emphatically [p. 1316] stressed that every real vanishing and passing is, of course, no less "positive" than every real coming and arising, the "death-side" in no way less full of content than the "life-side," every severing power no less indispensably engaged in the weaving of the "veil of Maya" than every connecting one, and neither of the two the end or the means of the other!

This premised, it follows, to be sure, without further ado, that the required like-sensedness of all polarities, however it may be designated, links each symbol doubly with every other, and thereby opens up the series of similarities of symbolic thinking, whose labyrinthine interweaving of analogies mocks dissection by a schoolroom-trained faculty of judgment just as the arabesque filigree of Moorish temple ornament mocks the measuring arts of the geometer. To illustrate its "method" with the completeness sufficient for our purposes, we shall content ourselves with establishing, in detail, for the following twice-twelve pairwise-belonging properties of appearance, their symbolic kinship of meaning: the capacity for conception, below, rest, darkness, earth, space, night, dying, reining-in, inwarding, "heart," left, on the one side; the power to beget, above, movement, light, sun, time, day, arising, impulse, utterance, "head," right, on the other. One can without difficulty multiply this brief series of analogies; one can extend it to colors, sounds, degrees of warmth; to the "elements" of the ancients, to constellations and atmospheric phenomena; to animals and plants, to the outer and inner parts of the human body; finally — what, in the wake of Orphic sectarian wisdom, the Pythagoreans first attempted, what the Kabbalists later unwittingly parodied, and what the Romantics afterward thought to renew — among other things to numbers and geometric figures; but even without that it suffices to let us discern, not only in symbols and customs but even in all only somewhat primordial legends, with the deepest astonishment, a consistency of unconscious connection compared with which the handed-down achievements of conscious inference, throughout the history of the understanding, resemble a groping about in the densest fog, in which the successful grasp only ever manages to succeed after a thousandfold missing of the mark, and more by favor of chance than out of itself.

After this we hardly still need to reject the belief that one has ascertained the wellspring-point of all symbol-formation once one christens the two sides after the difference of the sexes. Understood from an original feeling, [p. 1317] this currently most favored classification is, to be sure, exactly as justified as any of the others, but — without being in any way deeper — is far more helplessly exposed than other forms of opposition to the worst distortions, as soon as it is construed "materially" from the outset. Not, then, in order to lend support to a habit of thought of more than questionable worth, but rather in order to accommodate the receptive powers of today's readers, and besides for the purpose of preparing the next chapter, where we take up Bachofen's research findings, we offer a cursory outline sketch, to serve the picture to be elaborated as a ground-plan, with the linking lines of connection set upon the division of the sexes, which, from the point of view of the idea of polarity, presents itself roughly as follows. Regardless of whether we choose as our guiding image the distinguishing peculiarities of behavior in the mating process, or other differences of bearing between the two sexes, there is always, on the male side, a preponderance of self-movement, of going-out-from-oneself, of expenditure of powers; on the female side, of abiding, receiving, and conserving of powers. Accordingly there correspond, to the male: revealing brightness, mobility, hurling-power, upright posture, the Heraclitean "way upward," the shaping of what is coming; to the female: veiling darkness, rest, drawing-power, recumbent posture, the Heraclitean "way downward," an inclination toward what has been. Further correspondences will be easy for anyone to find. But if each of the two sides is grasped as a pole, and not, say, as a severable half, then we must conceive the symbolically intended manhood as pervaded by the feminine, womanhood as pervaded by the masculine. The split of the sexes accomplished today, on the other hand, into two parties now warring against and using one another, now passionately seeking one another, is only the practical consequence of that same rending of life which comes to conceptual expression in the separation of space from time, of both from the properties of kind, in the splitting of these into individual contents, and in the thereby unavoidably bound-up disembodiment of the soul and desouling of the body — in short, in the de-imaging and atomization of the world by the calculating will.

If we now fix our eye, first of all, upon water, the change of calm and storm, already intuitively evident in itself in the image of the sea, also separates out materially in the opposition between the comparative stillness of wells, ponds, swamps, and marshes and the restless movement of rivers and rain. By the former, water would fall on the female [p. 1318] and receiving side; by the latter, on the male and begetting side. As, in sense-space, either situated below or in any case striving toward the depths, it again shares in the essence of the woman; but as always also above, namely at home in the clouds and, evaporating, rising into the heights, it likewise shares in the essence of the man. If we further presuppose, for the time being without proof, that the space-pole of the world corresponds directly to the woman, the time-pole directly to the man, then water belongs, by virtue of its capacity to fill any space, to the female half, and, by virtue of the unavoidable time-relation of its everlasting change of form, to the male half. — Equally Janus-faced traits are shown us by the face of the moon. White and shining, in relation to the blackness of the earth, it stands under the sign of the male pole; light-receiving, in contrast to the brightness of the sun, under the sign of the female pole. Again, in the change of the seasons, full-moonlight alternates in it with sheltering newmoon darkness, and that signifies: male revelation of power and overflowing utterance, alongside female withholding of power and securely renewing inwarding. Because, finally, the stars vanish before the moon's radiance, it becomes, in the female night-space, a likeness of the male day; but because it itself, stripped of its radiance, pales in the manlike sunlight, it becomes a likeness of the female night within the space of day. — Equally the appearance of the tree is divided between the sides. An almost house-shaped spatiality, of which even compound-words like "leaf-roof" bear witness, the immovability of its place, the earthiness of its root-base, the inwardness of its living moisture, give it the character of the woman; but the mighty urge of the trunk upward, the wind-akin restlessness of its branches and leaves, the radiance-steeped nearness to heaven of its crown, its never-silent rustling, give it, in equal measure, the character of the man.

Just as certainly as primordial gods are never persons, just so certainly can the character-traits of person-like god-figures be understood only from the characters of the symbols that underlie them in essence and have preceded them in time. In view of the double sense of the symbols, it follows for all man-like demons in general, and hence also for those of water, of the moon, and of the tree, that among every people they must be divided by sex, appear preferentially in pairs, and can finally appear in hermaphroditic form. A cursory glance will confirm this.

Beside the German Nixe stands a male Nix; beside the Nordic Nichessa, [p. 1319] the Nøkk or Nekken; beside the mermaid, the merman; beside the sea-wife, the sea-husband; beside the sea-giant Hymir, his wife Frilla; beside the oceanic demon Ägir, as his consort, Rán; beside the male water-horse of the storming surf, the equally mighty ray-mother. — To the Nereids and Oceanids are joined Tritons; to Amphitrite, Poseidon and Pontus; to Phorcys, Ceto. Of the six hundred springs and streams that, according to Hesiod's Theogony, exist on the earth, the three hundred rivers are sons, while the three hundred springs and brooks, by contrast, are daughters of Oceanus. Greek river-names end, by a wide preponderance, in the masculine — one need only compare Achelous, Asopus, Alpheus, Ister, Pactolus, Scamander, Eridanus, Inachus, Caicus, Hermus, Cayster, Maeander — and among their animal symbols, besides the ambiguous serpent, the fertilizing ones likewise predominate: boar, bull, and horse; whereas springs, brooks, and wells stand under the protection of Artemis and are peopled with virgin nymphs, among whom Calypso, Amaltheia, Arethusa stand out. And even these, in turn, have their male counterpart in the original Sileni, the spring- and well-spirits of the Phrygian cult of Cybele. Not only Proteus, Nereus, Achelous practice the deceptive art of transformation, but, in accordance with a legendary motif proper to the elf-belief of the whole of Indo-Germandom, the divine Thetis too knows how to do so, when she seeks to escape Peleus, who is pursuing her, by a lightning-swift exchange of shape with that of the dog, the serpent, the camel, and fire! If turns of phrase like "bosom of the sea" still decide, in today's usage, for the femininity of water, then it becomes, on the other hand, the chief symbol of all earthly begetting-power in the Pelasgian god-figure of Poseidon, the greatest seducer of women in Greek myth, whose animals — horse and bull and ram — point to phallic urgency, and who bears the byname phytalmios, that is, the one who fertilizes the earth.
