A thousandfold the sacred goose represents the feminine aspect of the element; yet to the goose-shaped Nemesis-Leda there draws near a swan-shaped Zeus, and closer investigation shows that among the water-signifying animals of the swamps no fewer are male than female: we may name, for instance, the crab, the stork, the dragon. To the women of Argos, and likewise to those of Elis, the god with the ox-foot rises up out of the sea; from the sea emerges the demonic bull that impregnates Pasiphaë, clad in the wooden cow-phantom; across the sea the bull of Zeus carries off Europa. The Athenian women decide, against the wave of Poseidon, in favor of the olive [p. 1320] tree; as streaming rain, the male power impregnates Danaë and Cybele. Conversely, however, the Persian tree of life inseminates the receiving rain-lake Vouru-kasha; and from Sophocles the words are handed down to us that moisture is feminine, because it begets and nourishes much.

As regards the moon, zealous "folklorists" have calculated that, taking all primitive peoples into account, contrary to a widespread view, no fewer male than female deities are to be found among the moon-gods; though, as is then still added, scarcely of equal weight. Still, alongside its background and dominating femininity, a foreground and, as it were, flatter masculinity is nowhere to be mistaken. Thus the Asia Minor Men increasingly contested the primacy of the Greek moon-goddesses. Thus, together with the Dea Luna, Helena, Achilles as Deus Lunus circles the moon-island Leuke. But above all, the land of the deepest and most knowing moon-worship, Egypt, tells us that in the sexually differentiated moondemons, only the poles of the in actuality "androgynous" symbol parted asunder into a deceptive semblance of their own: Isis, opposite the day-star, nocturnal, needful of light and receiving it, while the Egyptian moon, opposite the earth, becomes the fructifying Apis, whose ray, as a seed-ray touching a calving cow, magically transforms her bodily fruit into the sacred Apis-bull. — Among trees we saw above the pear tree already conceived as female, the apple tree as male, and would now, on closer examination, again find the tree- and forest-beings of the most various peoples divisible by sex. In the custom and legend of the Germanic sphere, wood- and moss-maidens, Fanggen, blessed maidens, wild maidens, weather-witches, Lohjungfern, shaking-women, elder- and ash-women stand opposite male wild-folk, wild men, Schrate, Nörgen, wind-wolves; forest Fanken and Celtic wild-folk appear paired; the Swedish Skogsman or Hulte even somewhat outweighs the Skogsfru; the Russian Ljeschi entirely outweighs the Lisunka. In the Greco-Roman sphere, the hosts of Oreads, Dryads, Hamadryads, Meliads (nymphs, Naiads, Danaids) are matched by no less numerous hosts of satyrs, fauns, sileni, Pans, centaurs, cyclopes (Curetes, Corybantes). — Plant as well as tree are in legend often transformed women (Daphne), but often also transformed men (Narcissus, Hyacinthus). Sometimes, in the folk tree-customs, the May-, Whitsun-, or summer-trees are adorned with women's garments and [p. 1321] silver belts, and are brought into closest relation to womanhood especially through hung egg-shells; sometimes they are decorated with the "bread-man" or bear the name of the lad who, wooing, sets them before the door of the desired girl. Predominant tellurism of water, moon, and tree. — If, up to this point, each of the three symbols has appeared to us fitted together out of two mutually complementing powers, a somewhat deeper-penetrating consideration now leads us to insight into the preponderance nonetheless of one pole — and indeed, if we measure for the time being once more by the opposition of the sexes, in each case of the female pole. The way there runs by way of the cosmic ordering-place of the below and the above, which we have indeed intimated but not thought through. Should something already said seem to repeat itself here, it happens nonetheless from a new perspective, and for the purpose of carrying over the symbolcharacters that have become known to us out of a world of still relative nearness into the world of the Pelasgian universe. For since the oppositions of above and below, right and left, front and back are oppositions of spatial appearance, they determine for the image-forming consciousness the coordinates of the structure of the whole world of appearance, and thereby gain a cosmic rank of actuality, for the understanding of which merely objective thinking lacks the categories.

Seen from the standpoint of the earthly observer, the Pelasgian All is built up, so to speak, in three storeys: the below of the earth, the between of the moon, the above of the fixed stars and the sun. Equivalent to the earthly below, thanks to its own repose, is the solid; to the lunar between, thanks to changing motion, the liquid; to the sidereal above, thanks to its own motion, the fiery. This fiery element thus resembles the Heraclitean primal fire, in relation to which the humoral "elements" appear as its forms of transformation; it thus, on the one hand, in the guise for instance of volcanism, even partakes of the stony, and on the other leaves behind it the world of matters that is essentially bound to place, in that it girds it firmamentally round. We need only recall the correspondence of self-repose and femininity, of self-motion and masculinity, to rediscover the symbolic polarity of the sexes in this articulation as well. Accordingly, though every symbolically generalized image would have to be thought of as differently mixed from masculine fire-substance and feminine matter-substance, the opposite regions nonetheless stand apart polarly, [p. 1322] in such a way that the lower zone is found bound chiefly to the cosmically female pole, the upper to the cosmically male pole, the middle layer to a cosmic "hermaphroditism." All demonism of primal time divides into the chthonic, the poseidonian, and the uranic; into that of the underworld, of the moon-world, and of the zodiacal world; into that of stone, of the waters, and of the ether; and after all that has already been set forth there can be no doubt that in the same order the line runs from the symbolically conceived essence of the woman, by way of that of the hermaphrodite, to that of the man.

The reason for the assignment of three primal substances — the solid, the liquid, and the fiery — to three regions of cosmic space is revealed still more clearly when we consider the opposition of below and above from the point of view of an opposition of modes of efficacy, since to the lower pole falls everything succumbing to its influence, while to the upper pole *rises* everything receptive to it. Now evidently only the flame-appearance has the urge and the capacity to blaze away, never to return, from the place of its earthly origin; whereas the solid weighs down and, if undermined, plunges into the depths; the liquid, as vapor, indeed (nourishing or hostile) scales cosmic heights and as a cloud-dragon even threatens planets, but must always, as rain or sinking mist, return into earthly space. To be sure — in appearance and mythologically — a heavenly world-ocean joins the earthly world-ocean; but even though this may extend up beyond the moon (for the appearance of the moon does not necessarily hover above clouds and storms, but sometimes right in the midst of them, sometimes even still beneath them), it sinks, as the tear of Kronos, again and again back onto the earth that thirsts for it; and only that luminous, airy, flaming thing which we see burning in the highest heaven as abiding lights, and congealed into the glowing ball of the never-aging sun, remains forever withdrawn from the demonic pull of the earth. The solid and the liquid symbolize, though in differing degree, the movement-form of centripetality, the flame, on the other hand, that of pure centrifugality. But that finally, despite its position between the zones and modes of efficacy, the moon nonetheless belongs preponderantly to tellurism — as a sterile earth and Isis-ship, crossing the ocean of the earthly heaven safely indeed, yet not reaching out into the weightless ether of the sidereal All — follows from the impermanence of its luminous form, which early awakened the surmise that it shines with borrowed light. It is neither its [p. 1323] change of place, which it shares with the stars and the sun, nor the time-determining transformation, but rather — as bound up with this for it — its constantly repeated waning of light, that draws it into the current of sinking and, so to speak, of "frailty," and holds it fast in the outermost ring of the earth's field of efficacy, of the below, and thus of the woman.

If we now, drawing also on what has already been established above, gather together the main characteristic traits of the three symbols, they take up, in the Pelasgian image of the cosmos, roughly the following places. Notwithstanding that the tree, with trunk and crown, articulates the airy space, is mighty in voices of rustling, and turns its leafy crown to the light, chthonism predominates in it owing to the underworldliness of its roots, the steadfastness and immovability of its place, and not least the fluid-solid character of its substance, through which above all it belongs to inwardness, to night, to the life hidden in matter, and thus to womanhood. But where it clings, sheltering and overarching, the moon traverses that same realm of night: wedding time to space, a light to darkness that does not shine of itself — a sign of Gamos, and therefore preeminently the symbol of the soul in the narrower sense, insofar as it constantly blossoms and breathes forth from the body through the constant Gamos of within with without, of the suffering substance with the working substance, of the capacity for conception with the capacity for begetting. Water, finally, breaking from the darkness of the earth's depths, rising into the high world of the stars and plunging again into Acherontian chasms, brings to appearance, within the bounds of planetary space, the mystery revealed in the unstoppable cycle of becoming. Wrested from womanhood, yet without being able permanently to escape its pull, it carries, with the force of moving masculinity, the temporal revolution into the very heart of the rocks, thus dissolving, in the pantarhei, the apparently most rigid of spaces, and stands, in relation to the ever-renewed pregnancy and the eternal need for rejuvenation of matter, in the nature of the impelling seed.

Essentially the same relation holds among the three animal-shaped soul-symbols of original Pelasgianism; all three extremely mobile: the serpent, however, in the lower, the fish in the middle, the bird in the upper element; the serpent the most bound, hence a genius loci and appearance now of the receiving soul, now — according to the principle of polarity — of its phallic partner; the fish already partaking of the freedom of the flowing, [p. 1324] hence a moon-kindred appearance of the fructified soul; the bird, akin in essence to the heavenly waters, a sign of the soul released from the body, bacchically swarming. And it is in the bird that chthonism now turns over into uranism. As griffin, phoenix, golden swan, the soul-bird leaves the earthly space, scales the heaven, and attains — literally, after a Veda-passage — "union with the sun."

Having above established, for all tree-, moon-, and water-beings, their divisibility by sex, let us here first confirm, for the moon, its nonetheless preponderant tellurism, with the following two items of legend and custom. — While there is, to be sure, a great multiplicity of male moon-gods, it nonetheless holds true in no mythic world for the male gods in general what may be said at least of the majority of the female gods of any people whatever: that each of them, on occasion, also becomes a goddess of the moon. All female demons without exception shimmer more or less into the lunar, and there is scarcely a goddess or demigoddess who has not at times been confused by legend-lore with the "proper" moon-goddess. From Hellas and its neighboring spheres, apart from Selene, Mene, Pandia, Artemis-Diana, at least the following legendary figures of the female sex bear a now weaker, now more strongly accented lunar significance: Hecate, Antaia, Empusa, Medea, Gorgo, Circe; Demeter, Despoina, Persephone, Kore; Rhea, Hestia, Hera, Io, Urania, Aphrodite, Athene; Themis, Dike; Pasiphae, Telephassa, Ariadne, Phaedra, Iphigenia, Helena, Europa; Atalanta, Phaethusa, Arethusa, Eileithyia, Britomartis-Dictynna, Brimo, Bendis, Chryse, Eiresione, Pheraia, Laodike, Hyperoche — Ma, Anaitis, Mylitta, Astarte, Cybele, Isis. And it is no different among Indians, Phoenicians, Carthaginians, Egyptians, Romans, Celts, Germans. — But in such visions the myth only mirrors the fact, true in the history of custom, that at the cosmic division of the sexes the men, without exception, enter into the following of the sun, but the women into that of the moon. The cosmic division of the sexes was brought, as is well known, into a fixed system by the Peruvians, whose Inca was in each case son and representative of the sun, his wife and sister, on the other hand, of the moon. Just as one fashioned the sun-demon as a golden disc with a male countenance, the moon-demon as a silver one with a female countenance, so too the mummies of the deceased Inca kings sat on golden thrones along the inner walls of the sun-temple [p. 1325] at Cuzco, those of their wife-sisters likewise in the temple of the moon. — And to this there is now added the second circumstance, that (real as well as legendary) Pelasgian peoples, at that (more original) stage of their manner of association for which, following authors of antiquity, Bachofen uses the easily misunderstood name "gynaecocracy" — like the pre-Incan Peruvians, the Caribs, Etruscans, Libyan nomads, Scythians, the earliest Egyptians, Lycians, the Germans of Tacitus (at least in part), Troglodytes, and "Cimmerians" — if they do not reckon time by nights and moons instead of by days of the solar year, nonetheless grant a fundamental position of preference to the moon before the sun, to the night before the day, a matter to be treated more exactly further below.

For tree and plant, whose lunar kinship perhaps finds its most intimate expression in the moon-relation, developed by the Indians, of the sacred Soma-drink, let us here for the present recall only the following circumstance. Though it is indeed the case that the tree at times appears as a fructifying force, it is nonetheless, in such cases, not so much the tree itself as rather the seed grown upon it that is the fructifying agent. Whereas it is the plant-being itself that is, as it were, impregnated by a male demon: thus in Greek myth Philyra, that is, the linden, fructified by Kronos, bears Cheiron; Melia, that is, the ash, bears to Poseidon Amykos, to Silenus the Centaur Pholos; to Inachos, Phoroneus and Aigaleus. But with this we already touch upon that deeper mystery which alone is properly fit to reveal the true meaning of symbolic polarity: the essence of the unity that embraces both poles. In order not to have to repeat ourselves, we shall confine ourselves to preparing its more exact characterization with a single consideration drawn from the circle of thought of primeval tree-worship. Homer's, if we may put it so, tree-cultic simile runs:

Even as leaves in the forest, so are the generations of men; / leaves the wind now scatters to the earth, but others in turn / the budding forest brings forth again, when spring comes freshly to life: / so it is with the race of men — this one grows, and that one vanishes.

On the tree of life (= forest) grow the generations of men, thus men as well as women; there grow upon it, as it were, the "fair maidens," but also the phallic life-wands, the "breadmen" and doll-children, [p. 1326] and there have, at bottom, grown upon it the fertility-symbolic apples, nuts, cakes, eggstrings, grapes, jugs, coins, the festive ribbons, taeniae, banners, wreaths, gold-paper chains, lights, with which folk custom still today adorns its fetish-trees and May-birches, and Christmas custom the wintry fir and spruce: the tree itself, neither man nor woman, bears and carries the masculine and the feminine, the light and the dark, coming-to-be and passing-away. Remaining behind the poles and forking into them, it has, in relation to them, the meaning of the principle that brings both forth, the metaphysical arche, or, conceived in accordance with organic bringings-forth, the meaning not indeed of the woman, but well of the mother.

Breaking off here with this indication — to which, taking it up again, we shall at once point out the decisive turn from which the Janus-face of primeval thinking is explained — it may suffice, for the tellurism of water, to advance for the present only the one fact that, notwithstanding its so frequently begetting role vis-à-vis the earthly solid, it always appears in the meaning of the receiving pole vis-à-vis the airyfiery. In every marriage, according to the view of antiquity, the male fire-power mates with the female water-power. This means, rightly understood, that the water-nature too has its begetting force from the fire indwelling within it: in the most exact agreement with which the demons of male tellurism, such as Hephaestus, Achelous, Dionysus, Bacchus, Varuna, Osiris, Prometheus, Bellerophon, Achilles, are always marked by a double relation, namely on the one hand to water, on the other to fire, while the sidereal light, the pure "pneuma," mythically embodied in figures such as Apollo, Mithras, Ra, Helios, Ahura Mazda, Serapis, being thought of as through and through active, is never thought of as femininely receiving, and already in the earliest myths and initiations (at least of the Indians, Egyptians, Greeks) stands on the point of turning over into that matter-estranged "light of the spirit" which, through negation of the suffering (and experiencing) pole, enters into opposition to polarity as such, and thus to the living cell itself. Mother-meaning of the symbols. — Having come this far, we have only a few more steps to take in order to answer the question wherein, then, actually lies the meaning of that third thing which in each case holds the poles together. — If "drive" and "inclination" are to form a totality of efficacy, [p. 1327] then the former may neither scatter into infinity nor may the latter shrink together into the mathematical point. If, therefore, in order to do justice to both necessities, we were, following the symbol-language of the ancients, to choose for the spatial schema of the courses of events movement on the line of the circle, we would have determined actuality-time essentially by a pull inward, and raised a resting center to dominion over all that is in motion. — Customs and turns of phrase still today attest the primacy of the appearing midpoint. The target at which one shoots presents a grouping of concentric circles, and the spot to be hit by the marksman, hence the most significant spot, is their midpoint. As the heart lies in the midst of the body, so lay the heart of the Roman city, the forum, in its midst; likewise, among both Romans and Greeks, the hearth with the fire hallowed to Hestia lay in the midst of the house; and still today graveyard and church lie in the midst of the village. One calls the one who sets the tone of a social community its center; the political or spiritual leader gathers about himself a "circle" of followers, believers, disciples. In the language of some primitive peoples it is one and the same word that means both midpoint and one's own body. But if, accordingly, in the spatial schema the place that connects the poles coincides with the center, then we arrive at the today somewhat surprising conclusion that in the actuality of cosmic space the lower pole could at the same time be the symbol for the unity of the poles! For evidently below and earth relate to above and heaven, in appearance, as the midpoint relates to the circumference; but then likewise rest to motion, darkness to brightness, night to day. Whoever hits the middle of the target has in every case also hit the "bull's-eye," although a white mark on a black target would actually be still easier to see! Understood in the sense of the middle, night gains the primacy over day, rest over motion, and, in opposition to the earlier-established and to us by far more habitual valuation, the below over the above. It is the life-fettered, psychic, "earthly" estimation that speaks out of the overvaluation of darkness, of inwardness, of the root, whereas spirit seeks its likeness in the outer, the above, the pointed, in the "ethereal" and "heavenly" — for its own devaluation of life itself!

Since, among the correspondences of the midpoint just adduced, from the two sexes the woman also belongs, the question arises what is to be understood by the woman when she is conceived not as one of the [p. 1328] two ends, but as the middle of the symbolic threeness. — Just as the stream of happening as such unfolds into the unceasing alternation of passing-away and coming-to-be, so does the temporality of the living individual being unfold into the alternation of dying and being-born. If, now, both processes are to be polarly belonging sides of a single process, then death can no longer be mere ending, and must at the same time and preeminently signify a new beginning (though, as may be remarked here in advance, under no circumstances a beginning of the mortal individual being!). Exactly like coming-to-be and passing-away, being-born and dying are now moments of passage on the line of the circle, where every end marks the onset of one just beginning, every beginning the conclusion and full completion of a movement already traversed. As, further, the circular movement appears determined and governed by its center, because it can only subsist through the uninterrupted pulling-force of this center, so the course of the individual being, swinging between dying and being-born, is determined by a resting life-abode which bears within itself both, beginning and end of life, but unexpanded. Not the being-born and not the dying, not the being-alive and not the being-dead, but rather their underlying relation of exchange, calls for the assumption of a common third as the — so to speak lawful — necessity by virtue of which the living present must forever return into the past, and a formerly existing thing must forever constantly renew itself.

What the cyclical course of all the stars, the change of the moon's phases, of the seasons, of night with day, sets cosmically before our eyes, is now repeated, for the life-cycle of every self-living being, sensibly in the image-change of the plant, which, sprouting up out of the seed-corn, after passing through all the stages of coming-to-be and growth, finally ends again in the seed-corn, and, thus withering, reaches precisely the point from which it once again *begins* to come to be. And just as, in relation to the circling celestial sphere, the earth is the resting and determining middle, so, in relation to the never-abiding image-change of the individual life, the seed-corn has the meaning of the all-embracing life-place, because it is only with reference to it that the falling life-movement ends at the point of the newly beginning ascent, the rising leads toward the point of the return-movement to the end. As the middle is the unexpanded circle, so the seed-corn is an unexpanded life-destiny, and is therefore neither beginning nor end, and yet, in turn, both at once. What in the symbol-language [p. 1329] of the great cosmos is called "earth" is, in that of the small cosmos, called "seed-corn," or, in accordance with animal renewal of life, "egg," or indeed, after its dwelling, "womb," and finally simply "mother." And because finally macrocosm and microcosm are two forms of appearance of the same totality of life, the primal-symbolic equation holds good from left to right as from right to left: earth = seed-corn = egg = womb = mother. Womanhood no longer signifies a pole of the symbolic threeness, but the pole-linking middle, insofar as it signifies motherliness, and motherliness signifies the preserving and sheltering place equally of the coming as of the past life. It is to say one and the same state of affairs only in different words, whether one speaks of the threefoldness of the symbol, its double meaning, and finally of the mother-character of the symbolic unity. But one cannot keep it present to oneself insistently enough that womanhood, in this sense, does not form the counterpart to manhood, but rather a still unexpanded this-side both of the sexes and of all possible oppositions whatever; and just as little does maternal darkness, maternal night, maternal space, maternal rest, maternal below represent the opposite of brightness, day, time, motion, above, but rather the undivided this-side of dark and bright, night and day, space and time, rest and motion, below and above. The unity that takes on sides in every symbol stands under the sign of the woman as the mother (= of the "egg," the "seed-corn," the "earth"). She alone is *the* coincidentia oppositorum, from which the radii run to all elemental symbols, and which imparts, concerning the essence of polarity as such, the ultimate attainable disclosure.

[p. 1330]

#### 74. Kapitel — Die Magna Mater (Randbemerkungen zu den Entdeckungen Bachofens) — Chapter 74 — The Magna Mater (Marginal notes on Bachofen's discoveries)

*All-motherhood of the earth and earth-meaning of the mother.* — There is no Pelasgian people whose entire symbol-language is not governed by the conception that comes to expression in the equation just developed. We wish to furnish the proof of this, and indeed with somewhat richer evidence for the earth-meaning of the mother, which we shall trace — down to the end of the subsection headed "Primeval Piety" — into its most important symbolic, cultic, mythic ramifications, but with only the indispensable evidence, by contrast, for the essential identity of the Mater with the egg, and for the position of the woman, resulting from this, within Pelasgian tribal associations. A renewed return to our elemental symbols will conclude the consideration, which trails off into the thought of sacrifice.

In the most extreme contrast, say, to the Jewish creation-myth, which lets the world come into being through the command of a male god, it arises, according to heathen belief, in the manner of a birth, whether the maternally conceived earth brings it forth just as it does trees and plants, or through the splitting of a primordial egg. — The conception, to be touched on here in advance in view of this, of the all-motherhood of the earth, is too well known and even today still too current for us to need to dwell on it any longer. A terra mater, and as such a panton meter, is the Pachamama of the Peruvians, Centeotl of the Aztecs, (Yin of the Chinese), Prthivi of the Indians, Isis and Neith of the Egyptians, Gaia and Demeter of the Greeks, Tellus and Ceres of the Romans, Nerthus of the Germans, Belisana of the Celts. The same belief was shared by the Finns, Estonians and Lapps, the Polynesians, Karens, and finally also the North American Indians, who used to say that one sits down on one's mother's lap when one sits down on the earth. The earth has, motherlike, given birth to everything, and the earth in turn takes all that has come to be back into her darkness. The [p. 1331] womb that she signifies is also the grave of all that has gone forth from it (and thus, symbolically, of the whole world); and the grave that she signifies is at the same time womb and cradle of a life ever newly sprouting from it. Hades is often called in antiquity the "all-bedding bridal chamber" and thalamos Persephoneias. In the crouching posture which the early Mycenaeans used to give their dead, the position of the embryo in the womb is repeated.<sup>118</sup> The dead man, in that he has completed his life, thereby stands once more at life's very beginning; he has returned into the life-preparing lap, or has, as it is literally put, become a "Demetrian." In every Pelasgian people, at least the nobles regarded themselves as autochthonous, that is, earth-born. Out of the caves of the earth, a legend of the Peruvians relates, all men came forth, and according to another, of the Indians, the "Great Spirit" stuck arrows (!) into Mother Earth, from which first the women (!), then the men arose. According to Numa's law, whoever murders a fellow citizen is "parricida," hence a parent-murderer; for in every human being one touches, one touches the motherhood of the bearing power of nature. The parricida is not buried, but is excluded, by being sewn into a sack, from all contact with the common mother.

<sup>118</sup> On page 1331. — For the crouched position of the dead, at least half a dozen, if not more, quite different explanations are offered, among which, among scholars, the following in particular enjoys widespread assent. The crouched position — which, incidentally, is a lying one — is found (and indeed already during the Aurignacian) in southern and western Europe, further in Thuringia and on the Danube, but *not* in the megalithic graves of northern Germany and Scandinavia. This is said to stem from the fact that only in the warm countries did people sleep on the bare ground, curling themselves up to preserve warmth. The position given to the dead is thus supposed to have imitated, in each case, the sleeping position customary in the place. Compare on this *Carl Schuchhardt*, Alteuropa (Trübner 1919). — Such and other explanations, provided only that they do not exclude one another, may have something valid to say for themselves, but do *not* for that reason conflict with a symbolic conception of the matter besides, because in early times no matter of any significance whatever existed without symbolic content!

However easy it may still seem to us to follow such trains of thought, and in particular, with an eye to the seed-corn, to understand along with it the circle-like constitution of earth-life, we nonetheless attain from it at most a presentiment of the essence of the mother-symbol only once we also appreciate its far more alien reverse side, according to which the mother in general must be regarded — and therefore only the woman can be regarded — from the point of view precisely of this all-bearing and all-devouring earth. Just as the earth, when it appears as mother, is both the bearing-forth womb and also the receiving-back burial-place, so, because it is capable of becoming mother, the woman alone, of the two sexes, symbolizes the circle-moving midpoint, and the primally-conceived maternal womb counts as the eternal place equally of the kindling as of the quenching of life.

Even high historical antiquity, in its own way, held fast to a memory of the prehistoric concept of the sanctity of the motherly woman, when it beheld in her a representative of the bearing principle of the earth. According to Bachofen's pathbreaking researches, to which we shall from now on again and again return, there belong together from the very outset: [p. 1332] the chthonic character of the female deities, the mother-meaning of the woman, and the structure not merely of the convictions of belief, but even of all legal and communal forms of life, in accordance with that territorial subordination under an all-governing motherhood which, for some Pelasgian peoples, reached at least temporarily the degree of a so-called gynaecocracy. (Most unmistakably attested for the Cantabrians by Strabo: "Among the Cantabrians the men bring a dowry to the women. Among them also the daughters alone are entitled to inherit. The brothers are given by the sisters in marriage to wives. In all these customs lies the rule of women.") A living legacy of this, still in the latest times, was the widespread cult of the "Great Mothers," whose orgiastic rites show, without exception, the fusion of passionate jubilation over the source of inexhaustible coming-to-be with an equally passionate lament over the necessity of inescapable passing-away. We pick out, from the well-nigh unsurveyable abundance of evidence that Bachofen has brought forward for the earth-nature of the woman as mother and its double meaning, a few examples.

Black is the color of the earth's depth as of the — womb. Thus is explained the blackness of the Arcadian Demeter Hippia of the Phigaleans and her byname Melaina; thus the blackening of the face which, according to Strabo, the women of the mother-right Troglodytes practiced with great care. But this blackness points now equally to the moist arable earth and the luxuriant generative power of the marshes as to the darkness of the subterranean grave, and thus lets not only the earth, but likewise the woman as mother, appear in the light of the middle, by virtue of which both poles come into appearance. — Of the marsh-relation of the mother-deities the symbolism of the Pelasgian world gives most manifold testimony. "In the midst of the marsh-reeds sits Isis on a monument… just as the Nile-reed sari is called Isis's hair." In the land of the Nile, Io, driven about by Hera's gadfly, gives birth to the black Epaphos. From the union of Osiris with Nephthys, goddess of unbounded lust for begetting, springs the lotus of the marshes. Artemis is surnamed limnaia, limnatis, and is worshipped as the Great Goddess of the Ephesians at the marshy mouth of the Cayster; Aphrodite is worshipped with preference in moist grounds (en kalamois, en helois); Helena is called outright helos (= marsh). Perigyne, daughter of the earth-demon Sinis, hides herself from the wooing sun-hero Theseus between reeds and wild asparagus, wherefore, according to Plutarch's report, in memory of this deed of their [p. 1333] ancestress the Carian Ioxids kept up the custom of "burning neither reed nor wild asparagus, but honoring both as sacred." To the Lycian Leda-Latona the frogs of the marshes sing their hymns; the tortoise is the animal-sign of the Elean Aphrodite, and the bird of the wet lowlands, the stork, which to this day has been able to preserve its relation to female pregnancy, symbolizes the supreme deity in the marsh-land of the Peneus.

If, in this way, the mother-deities seem to signify, as it were, an abiding pregnancy, and are mere human-shaped likenesses of the all-nourishing earth-realm, then, on the other side, their connection with the darkness of death's night and the depth of the grave stands out no less sharply. Aphrodite, the goddess of the finding-of-each-other of all lovers, is also the eldest of the Moirai, and sees fulfilled in herself the inexorable fate that *parts* at the very moment of most blissful fulfillment. Clothed in the black garments of mourning, a lamenting mater dolorosa, she seeks Adonis, torn from her by death, as Cybele seeks Attis, Demeter Kore, Isis Osiris. Like the Assyrian Ishtar she descends to the underworld and appears veiled on graves as epitymbidia (= grave-loving deathgoddess). Likewise Venus laeta transforms into Venus lugens, and performs, as Libitina, the business of washing the dead. The death-relation of the Amazons, in whom Bachofen finds expressed the revolt of the mother-age against male violence, emerges partly from the frequency of their occurrence on sarcophagi, partly from various legend-lore traits, as when the warlike Antiope becomes the mourning mother of Hippolytus, carried off in youthful bloom. — And according to the model of sorrow of the Great Mother, the fate and bearing of the mortal woman is ordered. "On the height of the Sipylan rock-face Niobe mourns, in eternally trickling springs, over the destruction of all her offspring: an image of the primal mother Earth, to whom, of her many children, not one is at last left." It is the affair of the philothrenoi gynaikes to perform the lament for the dead; indeed among the Lycians, whose mother-right overall constitution Bachofen's researches place beyond doubt, the law held that the citizens, when they mourned, had to put on women's clothing. "As the dead become and are called Demetrians, so too can the earth's pain only be represented by the mother and in the mother's form." — Because the wheel of life would stand still if the destroying power were not joined to the bringing-forth, nourishing, and guarding power, Isis must herself again release Typhon, [p. 1334] whom she has bound — "Typhon's destroying power, the Egyptians teach, does not always keep the upper hand; often it is overcome and bound by the generative power; and just as often it tears itself loose again and fights with Horus. This, however, is the world surrounding the earth, in which destruction and bringing-forth alternate with one another" (Plutarch in his treatise on "Isis and Osiris"). — On Aegina the double being of the mother-deity divides into the two figures of Auxesia and Damia, of whom the latter again takes back into her womb what the former has sent up into life. The Germanic Holda, as goddess of death, receives in the cloud the souls of the dead, and releases in turn, from her mysterious cloud-well, the souls of the newborn. Artemis, as paidotrophos the goddess of nurses and their charges, also wields the killing arrow, and sends blight, dearth, and death upon the herds; wherefore human sacrifice and bloody scourgings mark the oldest form of her cult. Symbols as well as rites of Ishtar, Astarte, Alilat, Anaitis, Ma, Mylitta, Isis, Kotytto, Dione, Dindymene, Rhea, Cybele, Maia, Urania, Berecynthia, Ino-Leukothea, Juno, Bellona, Dido, Anna Perenna, Mater Matuta, and under whatever other names the Great Mother may still appear, proclaim alike the exuberance of life and the unavertable force of dark death. Fully in Demeter, Persephone, Proserpina, Despoina, Erinys, Hecate, as in the Germanic Hel, the underworld-nature of womanhood has found its most eloquent expression. Immense, further, is the host of the lower terror-figures of the female sex with which the imagination of all peoples has painted the dread of death; for which it may suffice to recall Greek legendary figures such as Poine, Antaia, Gorgo, Gello, Echidna, Empusa, the Lamiae, Striges, Harpies, Graeae, Sirens, Stymphalides, Keres. But that even such demonic she-fiends are nonetheless only the reverse side of the bearing power of all life flashes out surprisingly now from this, now from that trait of myth: the bleeding trunk of Medusa, after she has been beheaded by Perseus, releases Pegasus, the thunder-bearing moisture, and Chrysaor, the fructifying lightning and "lord of the golden harvests"! A most primevally gripping embodiment of the doom-shudder that lures precisely to the boldest venture is offered by the figure of the Egyptian Sphinx. Birth as fulfillment and end. — But it is not the unfolding-apart of the oppositions, but rather their complete interpenetration into that coincidentia oppositorum, which [p. 1335] we can render conceptually only by self-contradictions, that the sense bound in the mother-mystery is concerned with. — Being of beginningless eternity, the earth is also ageless, and is therefore — in the language of concepts — both the oldest and also the very youngest of all beings. Eternally new, she stands eternally in the first moment! Therefore the mother-deity presents herself now as a wrinkled crone, now in the beguiling charm of budding youth; is at once child-rich mother and virgin, and transforms out of the former into the beloved of the man. Adonis, at one time son of Aphrodite and blossoming youth, is at another her begetter, and is worshipped as Papas, as father of himself! The Aphroditic Beroe, according to the earlier legend of one essence with the earth and of one origin with Aion, "never-aging time," stands nonetheless, according to the later one, in the nimbus of a beauty so youthfully fresh that two of the mightiest gods, Dionysus and Poseidon, inflamed with love, fall into strife with one another for her sake. Anna Perenna, like the Moira Eileithyia "older than Kronos," nonetheless appears every year in the garb of spring and dallies with Mars in the shape of the loveliest maiden. The Roman Feronia, in whose temple, for reasons soon to be touched on, the slave received his freedom, is called both Mater and Juno Virgo. — No expenditure of acumen, however great, could disentangle in scholarly fashion what the conception of the virginal mother or motherly virgin, which perhaps gained its most significant expression among the Celts, gathers together into a single symbol. Of the various sides accessible to a logical understanding, we devote to the one most important for us, the Pelasgian experience of space-time, a special consideration, but for the present sum up what this lets us know of the meaning of original motherhood.

It is not the woman in the image of the motherly virgin at whom the reverent worship of peoples is directed, but rather the undivided source of life and the place of origin of happening itself. As the receiving and conceiving pole, the woman needs the man as the giving and begetting pole; whereas to the mother, because she is the unity in respect of which polarities can first of all obtain at all, there belongs not the man, but the child. Mother and child are of one essence. The frame that spans both bears the completion of life, the balance standing in equilibrium, the telete of the ancient mystery-initiations. If motherliness signifies the possibility and readiness of life, underlying every change of becoming [p. 1336] and passing-away, and therefore at every time equally original and hence eternally virginal, to become manifest in the cycle of happening, then childhood signifies the once-more oppositionless and supra-sexual fulfillment in which, after the accomplished Gamos of the begetting with the receiving power, the life-movement finds its end. Out of the virgin becomes the mother; but the mother is now once again the virgin anew: what lies between virgin and mother — love, marriage, and pregnancy — is the path of the circle running back into itself! Out of the child becomes the old man; but he, dying, returns into that same maternal darkness out of which he stepped forth as a child: what lies between being-born and dying is again the path of the circle running back into itself! In order not merely to illuminate logically the deep incompatibility of objective and symbolic thinking, let us cast a side-glance at a few practical consequences of the mother-symbolic feeling for the world.

While the consciousness of historical man sees in the child the uncertain beginning of an awaited future, the Pelasgian consciousness beholds in it the fulfilling conclusion, in each case, of the whole past of life. The child, and not the adult — or the adult then only in the measure of his participation in the essence of the child — is, for this way of conceiving things, the expression of perfection and the revealed meaning of life; of which, among other things, the cult of the "divine child," still echoing into our own days, bears witness, but out of primeval time a wealth of symbolic traits as well. If, with the "divine child" — in the starkest contrast to the Mosaic belief in God — the mother is conceived as "Mother of God," and the essence of the deity itself is seen under the sign of the child, then it is an easily understood turn of the same thought when the primally-imaged earth-sons of a fabulous prehistory are wont to burst forth at once, out of the bearing stones, trees, or clods of field, in full stature and even terribly armed: thus the giants armed with gleaming lances, thus above all the Theban Spartoi out of the dragon-seed of Cadmus, or the bronze men out of that of Jason. But if the thing-born thus stands on a level with the ripened and falling fruit, and thus at the end of that sequence of process which was merely inaugurated by the sowing, then the bearing takes its place beside the harvesting, and the man's achievement of scattering the seed vanishes behind it as without essence. Bachofen has, with regard to the legitimacy of children, furnished from the jurists of Roman antiquity the proof that the significance which the law of the state attaches to the [p. 1337] moment of conception was wholly unknown to the "jus naturale." "According to the natural system the prima origo coincides, in one and the same point of time, with the completed formation of birth. Becoming and being-completed are here synonymous. In the system of paternity, by contrast, the two are distinguished, and it begins with the sowing, not with the fruit… With fatherhood is bound up, just as definitely, the idea of the beginning, as with motherhood that of the completion. There the sowing, here the fruit and the harvesting are kept in view. There the becoming is the beginning, here the end of the development. There there is a future, here only a past; there a beginning, here only an ending… According to mother-right the ripeness of the wheat is its prima origo, and its harvesting at once its coming-to-be and passing-away. Therefore the earth-born spring forth complete from the earth; but only in order to be mown down in the very same moment; just as Jason is to accomplish the whole work before the setting sun… According to father-right, by contrast, the origin lies in the sowing, not in the harvesting; according to it, hope is heeded, according to the former, only fulfillment.'" Cosmically the equating of bearing and completing comes to expression through the relation to the last phase of the moon, according to which, by the common belief of the ancients and of many primitive peoples, the moon-goddesses are almost all likewise goddesses of childbirth, and women give birth most easily on nights of the full moon.

To name only one more of the further consequences, whose factuality is as familiar to every scholar of saga as the sole correct interpretation which a Bachofen alone was able to give of it is usually not, it follows with necessity from the mother-right world-view that the privileged position belongs to the youngest-birth. It can have escaped no one who has read even Grimm's folktales with some attentiveness that it is regularly only the youngest of three brothers, the youngest of three sisters, who succeeds in solving a seemingly impossible task, in overcoming dangerous monsters, in disenchanting the bewitched prince or the bewitched princess. Just as little do the legends and sagas of antiquity leave any doubt about the auspiciousness of the youngest-birth: Joseph is the youngest of his brothers; Kronos, who himself comes to rule by emasculating Uranus (according to Hesiod), is the youngest of the Titans; and again Zeus, who alone escapes the fate of being devoured and overthrows Kronos, is the youngest of his sons. "Of Neleus's twelve [p. 1338] sons, eleven are slain by Herakles; only Nestor, the youngest, remains alive. Of the serpents that the oak of Melampus harbors, the old ones are slain, the young alone reared: it is they who impart to the seer the understanding of the future." Even into proverbial sayings such as "the first shall be last" (and conversely), into winged poetic words like "last not least", indeed into figures of speech such as the climax ad majus, impulses continue to work from a primal thought whose basic sense is self-evident from what has gone before, even though its various aspects are to be characterized differently. Because those born earlier are already no longer children by the time the last one comes to light, "youngest-birth" is only another expression for the child as such, and becomes, for beholding reflection, the symbolic sign of that fortune-favored submission to fate which only the unconscious concord of childlike piety with the powers of the world is able to bestow. Light is thrown on another side of the matter by the consideration that it is always only in a last and youngest event that the eternal pastness of all life has the character of momentary presentness — But, one might object, does not the strongest aura always rather surround the first impression, the first friendship, the first love; does not precisely the earliest and most bygone stand there in the nimbus of irretrievable beauty?! Now, the strange reversibility of all symbolic truths can perhaps be brought into no sharper light than if we reply at once: this first and earliest and that youngest and latest event are one and the same, but are apprehended intuitively only in the present! Just as the mother is once again the untouched and conception-willing virgin, the dead once again a mundus in nuce, ready anew to burst the shell of maternal darkness, so in the ageless cycle of telluric life every youngest and latest moment has the gripping power of the earliest and most bygone; the last-born is the first-born a second time and shines forth in so dewy a radiance as though only with it did the visible cosmos itself come into appearance! Wholly opposed to logical consciousness, which, groping along the straight line of time, holds everything past to be annihilated and sees in the present only repetitions of it, Pelasgianism, bound to the circle of time, lives and knows and teaches the eternal restoration of the origin. Turning back thereby once more from the divine child to the divine mother, we can now bring to full clarity in what sense woman, when conceived as representative of the Mater, appears removed from the opposition [p. 1339] not only of the sexes but especially also of becoming and passing away.

The earth, when it bestows the ripe fruits, is one and the same with the earth which takes the seeds back into its womb for new begetting; and again the earth of the present year is one and the same with the earth of all years gone by; and finally, if this is called "mother", then there is only one mother, around whom the natura naturata circles in eternal repetition — not indeed of things, but of the becoming and passing away of things — and every woman, in respect of her capacity for motherhood, is the same as every other woman: something like this is how the wisdom of primeval times would sound in the language of today. The earth, as often as it has completed its begetting in the round of the year, is new, untouched, no further from the origin of its appearance than on the "first day", virginal, divine; every mother is the virgin that once was, every virgin a rejuvenated mother; the actuality of life means the agelessly ever-original cycle from having-been-completed through pregnancy to completion, while the succession of generations is merely the human parable for a presentness of all the past that appears in the fullness of the completing moment: thus it might have sounded in the language of former times, had that language stood in need of rendering symbolic knowledge in didactic speech. Availing himself of the first manner of expression, Bachofen, by means of the legend of Deucalion and Pyrrha, penetrates so deeply into the essence of the mother-mystery and its opposition to the male and logical mode of apprehension that we should like to reproduce his most important sentences here in full, notwithstanding that some of what was said above thereby finds mention once again: "Upon the maternal earth-stuff all the generations of men pass in succession, fructifying it. The son becomes husband and father, the same primal woman begotten today by the ancestor, tomorrow by the grandson." For "men and women are the bones of Pyrrha's body; in their substance all stem from her as the formless stone stems from the earth. The stone-people and the mother-people are identical. The stone-lineage has no father, but only a mother. They are the apo Pyrras. They remain this also in the succession of generations; for every woman of this stone-people is Pyrrha herself, a feminine stone, thrown by the primal mother, now representing her and continuing the first work in her stead. From this the feature preserved in all versions of the legend, according to which Themis commanded that the bones of the progenitress be thrown backward, also receives [p. 1340] its explanation. Mother-right has only ancestors, father-right has descendants. The father, as the proton kinoun, appears as the first impulse of a motion that extends outward before him, as the stream flows away from the spring. The mother, conversely, is never the principium, but always the end. In the long series of successive mothers, each is representative of the primal mother earth. This latter therefore always comes to representation in the living form. With the generations the primal mother too moves forward, hence meter isodrome, the primal mother earth who keeps equal step with the successions of the generations; embodied in the youngest, she forms the end, not the beginning, of the long line, which is why in this system too it is the youngest, the hoplotere, the one furthest advanced, and not the oldest, who receives the preference. With every new birth the primal mother moves forward; the birth, that is to say, thus has the significance of a throw of the stone toward the rear. So shapes itself the view that considers only the maternal substance. Different is that view which regards the man as former and demiurge. The motion proceeding from him propagates itself from generation to generation without the proton kinoun ever leaving its place and following the generations as isodromos. The man sees the generations come to unfold before him, just as the material woman — not moving but moved — has them behind her. The father is only beginning, the first father the first beginning, the woman always end, the last the first, the first the last.<sup>119</sup> That is why, in the Pyrrha myth, man and woman throw their stones backward, whereas the opposite direction alone would have corresponded to father-right." (The letter-spacings are our own.) But whoever might wish to take this for a mere caprice of myth-forming fantasy should be persuaded otherwise by the following fact. In the flood-legend of the predominantly mother-right Central American Indian tribe of the Caribs, a human pair likewise saves itself upon the high mountain Tamanacu; there they throw fruits of the Mauritia palm behind them: from the kernels arise women and men. — The Spatial Significance of Woman. — We have repeatedly placed space on the side of woman, time on that of man, and found ourselves thereby led to equate, symbolically, the connecting middle in which the two interpenetrate with a cosmic *place*. Now we know indeed that primal-image space is only unfolded time, primal-image time only the transformation of space; and the development of the mother-symbol with regard to the central body of the appearing universe may have confirmed, at least [p. 1341] by way of parable, the maternal character of space . Yet the course of our consideration has imperceptibly led us back to the point from which we began the way, when, anticipating, we attempted to ascertain the basic meaning first of the moon, then of water, and finally of the tree, from the standpoint precisely of their time-shape, and thereby arrived at the result that each of them, in its own particular way, is to be determined as a symbol of the fate of the world. For if we survey everything that has been said about the relation of the Mater to the certainly temporal state of affairs of becoming and passing away, she appears primarily and fundamentally to be the mother of all fates, and thus to be connected far more closely with happening and consequently with time than with image-like extended space. A single glance at primeval times suffices to show us legend as well as custom wholly permeated by the fate-relation of woman (which was already indicated for another purpose on pp. 545– 46, but shall here be briefly repeated once more). From the Wala Odin learns the fate of the gods; from his mother Themis, Prometheus learns of it. The reigning necessity of fate, to which even the highest gods must at times bow, bears without exception the features of femininity. Ananke, Heimarmene, Nemesis-Adrastea, Tyche, Fortuna, Regina, Fatua, the Parcae, the Norns, fairies, Valkyries, swan-maidens: these are all only different names for the same thing, for the feminine-conceived power of fate. If we think finally of the Pythias, the Sibyls, the Cassandras, the Druidesses, the Alraunas, of Veleda, Aurinia, Ganna, to whom many a historically attested individual figure of prophesying women might be added, it takes on the appearance that the position of power of the Pelasgian woman rested chiefly on the conviction that she was woven into fate far more immediately than the man, and was therefore initiated into its dispensations. Before we now briefly set forth what is the case with the time-relation of the Mater, let us first document, from the symbol-language of primeval times, the affinity of woman with space.

<sup>119</sup> On page 1340. — We have letter-spaced these words because, as nothing else does, they let it be recognized that, in relation to the straight line of objective time, a supra-temporality belongs to the Mother, one which will reveal itself to us, in the sub-section after next, as the form of actuality-time. — This, however, is not contradicted by the proposition, repeatedly set forth by us, that man stands to woman as the revealed stands to the unrevealed mystery. For if, according to the Pelasgian conception, woman first attains the perfection possible to her in motherhood, then the revelation lies in the appearance of the *child*; and this, as we shall see later, is indeed not necessarily, but nonetheless typically, the boy.

If in German the grammatical gender of "space" [der Raum] is masculine and that of "time" [die Zeit] feminine, this only shows that the present-day gender-conception of nouns may depend on quite different grounds than those operative in primal symbolism. Yet some attention may still be due to the precisely opposite gender-characters of the Greek names chora and hedra on the one side, and aion and chronos on the other. More important already appears the history of the Greek kamara, which originally denoted a [p. 1342] receptacle with a vaulted roof, then a bedroom, a room, and as such passes over into the Romance "camara" (French chambre), from which the German "Kammer" is borrowed. Add to this "Kammer" in the sense of "chamber of justice", then "parliament", further "chamberlain" [Kämmerer], "chamber-estate" [Kammergut], and one has a certainly not accidental example of the equation of the essence of woman with that fundamental property of appearing space which is organically emphasized above all in the maternal womb: namely, to encompass like a receptacle and thereby to enclose what is encompassed. Analogously, our "Kamerad" [comrade] arose from the feminine camarade (French), as denoting a company that *has* a house in common. Likewise feminine is the name "bursa", which underlies today's "Bursche" [fellow, lad], but originally means "purse", "pouch", and then a fellowship — again by virtue of the community of its house. In "Frauenzimmer" [woman's chamber, an old word for "woman"], finally, the woman's room is used for the name of woman herself. — Of the numerous passages in ancient thinkers that emphasize the spatial character of woman, let only the following two be recalled. Plato calls woman: hedra geneseos, chora kai dexamene en hē gignetai — in short, then: place and receptacle of coming-to-be. Connecting with him, Plutarch teaches in his treatise on Isis and Osiris that the Egyptians gave Isis three different names, namely Muth, Athyri, and Methyer; of these the first means "mother", the last "fullness and cause", but the middle one "house of Horus". Intuitively, Goethe utters the same truth when he puts into the mouth of his Mephistopheles the words about the "proud light that now disputes with Mother Night her ancient rank, her space".

In order for the space-image to close together like a receptacle, it is above all necessary that the appearing boundaries of space be fixed immovably against one another; for only thereby does space become the "resting pole in the flight of appearances", the schema of all adhering and of all sensuous duration; and time confronts it as the condition of change, of unboundedness, of roaming. If woman belongs on the side of space, she must also belong on that of rest and persistence; and if man belongs on the side of time, he must correspondingly belong on the side of locomotion. The Pythagoreans give expression to this when they connect the symbolic number of the female sex, namely the even, among other things also with rest, and that of the male sex, namely the odd, with motion. In agreement with this, woman is on inscriptions actually called [p. 1343] Domiseda (= she who sits at home), and as gravemother is shown almost regularly seated. Here an important contrast in the formative drives of human forms of community attaches itself. The roaming nature of man aims at a nomadic wandering life, at the vicissitudes of war, of the hunt and of seafaring, and finds itself satisfied at most still in the mobile occupation of the shepherd or the fisherman; the clinging nature of woman aims at settledness, clings fast to the soil once trodden, and becomes the creator of the concept of homeland. Accordingly the old tribal confederations knew no "fatherland" — which rather comes to predominance only with the preponderance of the concept of the state — but instead a "motherland", beside which there further stand "mother-city", "daughter-city", "mother-tongue", "motherchurch". The binding center, in turn, of all settledness is the firmly-joined house, or else the clustered group of houses: therefore in the deity of the domestic hearth a feminine Hestia is recognized, and in the mother of the gods the foundress of cities. Most visibly of all, finally, the power of unswerving persistence, together with the capacity of holding-within-itself, attaches to the enclosing and protecting wall: thus the mural crown is an inseparable attribute of the Great Mother! Indeed, the scope of this symbol reaches considerably further still. Not only does the wall enclose the courtyard, the village, the city, but it also conceals them from the gaze of those outside, exactly as the maternal womb conceals the as-yet-unborn child. In this way, like the veiling veil of Isis, the unloosed girdle, the flickering flame, the proliferating thicket of thorns — a symbol no longer merely of feminine adherence but even of the pre-sexual Mater herself — it holds what is enclosed captive in the eternal dream-sleep of the unrevealed mystery, past which the stream of time rushes powerlessly (as past Vesta and her priestesses), but precisely thereby also guards it against the change of fates and the doom of withering. Only when the phallic thrust breaks the encircling wall does the eternal virgin become mortal woman, surrendered without resistance to an unstoppable and everuncertain development. We stand in reverent astonishment before the consistency of elemental thinking, which passes all comprehension, when we set side by side, in comparison: Brünhild amid the ring of fire, Sleeping Beauty amid the hedge, and, behind the walls of Troy, the ever-bridal Helen! Every time it is the possessive will of man that conquers the ageless soul; every time she falls to him after the bursting of the magic girdle that protectively surrounds her [p. 1344] abode; every time it is the phallic thrust that breaks the spell of the maternal ring; for even the downfall of Troy is brought about not by a warlike deed of the Achaeans, but by the breaching of the wall through the demonic horse, which, as can also be demonstrated elsewhere, signifies the death-phallus! Whoever has grown accustomed to understanding so-called world history too out of the wisdom of symbols will regard the sinking of the walls around city and citadel as the most fateful turning-point in the destiny of all settled peoples, because with it began the dominion of motion over the resting middle, the uprooting of woman and the derailment of moving man into the tangential wayward path of that restless and unreturning, and therefore unavoidably destructive, "progress"! — We mention in passing that, in exact correspondence with what has just been set forth, the primal mode of apprehension did not view the wall as the performed achievement of a male demiurge and "mason", but as something come into being either through growth or through elemental magic: the Romans, where the wall of the city was to arise, dug into the receiving earth the child-bearing furrow with the phallic plough, which therefore had each time to be lifted wherever space was to remain for a gate; and again, to the sound of Amphion's lyre, the stones of the mighty walls of Thebes joined themselves together by magic. — From the realm of art one might further adduce the entablature-bearing female caryatids. — To the space-shapedness and place-boundness of the feminine pole, the time-shapedness and motion-energy of the masculine finally gives the complementary counterpart: winged are Eros, Phallos, Pegasus, Hermes, Mercury; winged steeds draw the chariot of Poseidon and the quadriga of the sun-god, and, most of all, Wodan's storming spectral steed reaches back into Indo-Germanic prehistory, but precisely thereby, to be sure, connects to still more fatefully deep strata of Pelasgian destiny. Herakles, surrounded by lion and ox-hide and bearing the epithet chronos or chronos pater, is represented on Cilician coins as Dromeus, abducting the maternal egg at a swift run.

Meanwhile, everything said here about the place-relation of woman is perhaps still surpassed in evidential force by another testimony, whose disclosure was again achieved by Bachofen's clear-sightedness. What was indeed already known to the scholar of antiquity before him — namely that Greeks as well as Romans each possessed two different concepts of holiness — first found through him its immediately convincing explanation. Both peoples [p. 1345] distinguished, in a thoroughly similar manner, that which was sanctified through consecration, which the Greeks called a hieron and the Romans a sacrum, from that which was already holy by nature, the hosion or sanctum. The sanctum stands always under the protection of the subterranean gods and ultimately of the Great Mother, the sacrum under that of the celestial gods and ultimately of Zeus or Jupiter. If one now seeks an essential feature of sanctitas, it turns out that it is grounded in that inviolability, unswervingness, untouchability which has led to the often-discussed formula of akineton me kinein, or quieta non movere. Whatever is holy to the Great Mother, such as the wall, the boundary-stone, the grave-monument, the treasure resting in the earth, is to be eternally untouchable, may never be moved from its place and never be altered: a "monument" unchangeably enduring through all curricula vitae. Because it is torn from the holy maternal darkness, a curse lies, in the otherwise most various legends of the world, upon the raising of the golden hoard. Indeed, in the extraordinary horror that, down to the latest times, hovers about nocturnal treasure-digging, in the sense of sacrilege that among rustic strata of the people still today tends to follow the secret shifting of boundary-stones, and finally in the holiness of the burial place, not even yet wholly forgotten by educated consciousness, we have to see the last rings of waves from the center of disturbance of an outlook grounded in the metaphysics of place, and thus predominantly of the body, and in this manner of space. The Time-Circle of the Mother-World — Although serving a precisely opposite purpose, the foregoing explanations now already put into our hands the means for understanding the relations between the Mater and the time-world of fate. The goddesses of fate too are not infrequently winged, stand on racing griffin-chariots or on the winged wheel, and the meter, as we already heard, is even called isodrome, as though, restlessly moved, she led the restless happening at an equal pace. Yet they also carry the bestowing horn of Amaltheia, the rudder, the measure, and the scroll of fate, and thereby seem to show themselves as powers that apportion, weigh out, balance, and nevertheless regulate the incalculable change of chance occurrences according to a mysterious plan. Are they to accompany the storm-flight of fate, yet not as a driving but as a restraining force, and to be the directing rudder in the wave-tossed ship of life? So indeed it is! "Athena possesses the secret [p. 1346] of bridling the wild Pegasus." We must at this point in our considerations on the Mater approach more closely a side of the primal thought that, like no other, estranges the mind of today. If the Mater is the symbol of the balancing of the poles and the ruling middle of the eternal circling, then she must also be the bearer of cosmic order and the inexorable avenger of every offense against it. Just as surely as in primeval times, no differently than today, will and deed were the affair of man, just as surely was wisdom and judgeship the affair of woman! The great weaver who weaves the garment of the world and of all fates bears the name "Harmonia". Justitia and aequitas count as inborn properties of the feminine principle of nature. The laws were kept at Athens in the temple of Demeter Thesmophoros, the so-called Metroon, at Rome in that of Ceres Legifera; testaments and legal documents also in the temple of Vesta. As priests of Ceres, the aediles were also partly charged with the administration of justice, and expressions like "Justitiae sacerdos", "Dikaiosynēs hiereus" let this very administration appear in the light of a priestly exercise of the service of the Mater. The Syrian Aphrodite, who "weighs in her scale both life and law", is called justi inventrix. Dike, Eunomia, Eirene are the holy authoresses of every lawful order. The left hand of Isis, whose cast is carried on display in the festival procession, is called "Justitiae manus" or "Aequitatis manus". Of Venus, Ovid says: juraque dat coelo, terrae, natalibus undis; of Nemesis, Ammianus Marcellinus says she is causarum et arbitra regum. In solemn procession, women and virgins carry the sacred books of law to Eleusis on the day of initiation.

Whoever today were to weigh the characters of the sexes against one another, even were he the greatest friend of women, would find himself, on the basis of a thousandfold experience, without doubt occasioned to grant to man the preference of greater justice, but to regard woman as afflicted with a propensity to personal partiality — and might well ask, in view of this, whether it is in any way probable that the sexes have since then so deeply altered their natures, when at least the woman, as a comparative glance at primitives betrays, has been able to preserve so many traits from the age of originality, and not always to her advantage? The answer runs: it is not woman who, notwithstanding all the transformations to which she too succumbed, has so altered herself; but that "right" which, in the name of justice, the man indeed administers far better than she, is something wholly other than that of [p. 1347] primeval times. We must first of all learn to divest ourselves, from the ground up, of all moral habits of thought, in order to find again the concept of right that could flourish on the soil of a thoroughly nature-bound thinking. In the apprehension and exercise of moral right, woman still lags behind man as before, and will never attain him so long as she is not yet wholly virilized; but for that, the spirit of man has become so hopelessly blind to the apprehension of a "natural right" that he no longer comprehends at all how such a thing could even exist, and unwittingly confuses the "beyond good and evil" with the admission of a kind of criminality! Before we now, relying on Bachofen's disclosures, which in our opinion are here simply definitive, sketch in a few lines the outline drawing of the right of nature, we place first the thought through which it proves to be anchored in the time-relation of motherhood, and is able, shining back, to clarify this relation itself.

In place of the concepts of space and time, to which two never-to-be-united objects correspond, beholding apprehension has symbols of actuality itself, in which space and time interpenetrate inseparably. Logically speaking, as we know, actuality-space would be the time unfolded in the momentary image, actuality-time the flowing of the image; and, with regard to its spatiality, the world-image would find itself in unceasing vanishing or going, with regard to its temporality in unceasing becoming or coming, but with regard to both together in the same pulsatory alternation of arising and passing that governs the world of the senses in the greatest as in the smallest — But in having to call upon words like pulse or rhythm in order to catch the sense of the symbol at least in a likeness, we also notice that we have likewise subordinated the fate of the world to a "law", whose complete difference from the laws of the understanding has indeed been discussed from every side, yet may once more be called to mind, namely with regard to the relation of actuality-time to actuality-space.

Even though the space of the coming moment may be, for the gaze of the soul, other than the space of the going moment, still the coming space resembles the going space, the coming image the going image; for otherwise not even the shape of an image, let alone of the thing, could have arisen, and consequently the existence of the very faculty of [p. 1348] judgment would become impossible. Here too, then, recurrence takes place; but this is now not repetition, but that which is never to be grasped by the intellect: namely renewal! Penetrating to the place where the pulse of the Pelasgian cosmos arises, we come upon the same principle in which we found the formative power of Pelasgian thinking, elementary similarity, and recognize more sharply than before its sense-bestowing source: unlike factual similarity, which can be divided up into identical and non-identical data, elementary similarity links a thing just now becoming to a thing just now vanishing, through the renewal of the latter, and reveals in the present even what was formerly past, as though it, only now arising, were beginning its course anew: another and yet the same, the same and yet another! The effective space of things is constituted by the law of the ever-repeating repetition of the same; the effective space of images by the rhythm of the ever-resembling return of the similar. The law, essentially bare of temporality, binds the moment, thrusting it into life, and lets it, a prisoner, age irreversibly, grow grey, fade; rhythm, the eternal form of appearance of actuality-time, releases it, in that it unceasingly rejuvenates what unceasingly sets about aging.

Transferred to human doing and leaving-undone, the one relates to the other as the dance to the drill-step, play to work, the natural movement of the living body to the machine. Only in the heart of the cosmos itself do we find the key to why every "nature-people" performs the labors of sowing the seed, of mowing and raking, of grinding the grain, of flax-breaking, weaving and plaiting, to the beat of communal songs — that is, dancing; why the whole of antiquity ascribed a magical influence on body and soul to instruments of sound, and thought the mightiest gods symbolically denoted by such (Apollo by the kithara, the Bacchic throng by the flute, the Muses by the lyre); why finally, throughout the whole Pelasgian earth, cult and orchestics flow together indistinguishably, and even a Plato still holds gymnastic and musical education of youths as of maidens indispensable for the realization of his concept of the state. In all this a primal feeling expresses itself, which places human rule under the scepter of demonic rhythm and dissolves the glassy brittleness of law in the vibrating ether of the cosmic pulse.

We have repeatedly touched on similar disclosures, but must now go one step further. If space, insofar as it takes up time, falls in the same instant into pastness, how then could the moment just now [p. 1349] opening even resemble the one just now elapsed, when indeed the momentary, in elapsing, is already de-momentized and consequently de-actualized — or in other words: with what dimensions would a world be endowed whose pastness proved to belong to actuality through constant return in rejuvenated shape? If we attempt to bind, in explanatory speech, what once was livingly present in the depths of the "unconscious", this could happen only with the help of a judgment of, as it were, boundless absurdity: the time-pulse itself signifies rhythmic time-renewal, and cosmic time, if it is permitted to say so, has the shape of the circle and flows, again and again, into its own beginning!

We have already made use of this thought above, but so imperceptibly and in passing that the reader will scarcely have felt what it actually demands of us and with what violence it tears apart the bounds of our capacity of comprehension. The primal contradiction comes fully to light when we hold up beside it another thought which, through the extravagant flight it takes, at first as it were robs the mind of breath, but then proves at least achievable in representation, and finally even as resting on a merely fantastic heightening of a constantly practiced procedure: we mean that of "eternal recurrence". Hatched already in the school of the Pythagoreans and, as is known, advocated in recent times by Nietzsche (forced upon him too, certainly, by a primal experience which is, to be sure, misconstrued by the one who bore it), it teaches by no means a circularly-shaped time, but the circular shape of the processes of things in time — this, however, not with regard to the general features of the individual process, whereby only the basic law of all experience would be fulfilled and no one could be surprised, but with regard to the totality (thought of as finite) of the processes. It wants to overcome the concept of mechanism, but in truth leads to its most extreme exaggeration, and may to that extent count as the fully realized opposite of the Pelasgian restoration of the origin.

"Eternal recurrence" means the constant once-again of all states of affairs that have ever been; "circular time", by contrast, means the constant renewal of unstoppably flowing images. According to the former, the world, after every full revolution, would have aged by the measure of the aeons of years elapsed meanwhile; according to the latter, what is to be experienced anew in the sense of recurrence is precisely the historyless novelty of the moment, its character of [p. 1350] creative inception, its never-diminished *youngestness*. In the former, a selfsame thing repeats itself into the unbounded; in the latter, the "infinite" renews itself; the former, striving after immortality, clothes the thing beyond time with a deceptive mask of eternity, by multiplying its duration-measured existence a thousandfold along the straight line of time; the latter beholds eternity, rather, in the restlessly passing, and transforms what is coming into an eye-opening glance of primeval time.
