There, nothing is renewed, but it merely repeats itself; here, conversely, even that which has been present a thousand times, the habitual and the aged, has its actuality only from participation in the mystery of the rebirth of the soul.

What we must now pay particular attention to, however, is the circumstance that, with this, on the one hand arising indeed becomes a "function" of passing, but on the other hand time becomes a function of space. — The world-schema of the Pythagoreans, which for apocalyptic purposes largely recurs in the last chapter of Plato's "Republic", gives an instructive account of this: beyond the circle of fire, namely, which as the outermost surrounds the inner nine of cosmic space (more precisely, of Olympus, of Kosmos, and of Uranos), is found the Pneuma, out of which the world breathes in time. Time appears accordingly as a spherical outside of space conceived as hollow-sphere-shaped. It is Pneuma, that is to say: the cause of all change and of all manifoldness, more precisely of the motion of divine stars in the sidereal circles (Olympus and Kosmos), of becoming and passing in the sublunary world (Uranos). But time itself, because it became world-capable, now finds itself enclosed within the field of effect of a space which, in its totality, circles about the resting middle of a Hestia, a Harmonia, or — according to another version — about the world-spindle that rests in the lap of Ananke. With this we are at the deepest attainable ground of the time-relation of the Mater.

If womanhood is the soul of space as such, then the Mater is the soul of the restoration of space in the medium of *time*. The moment always sinks backward, but not along the straight line of objective time, but along the ring of this metaphysical space, where passing flows, wave upon wave, into arising. As the Parca holds the thread of life, so maternal space holds the stream of time captive, by bending it into the path of the circle; and though each thing races on in unstoppable flight, still nothing escapes the resting Mater, who — if a bolder simile befits what can never be grasped — holds the eternity of the [p. 1351] presence-less actuality-time on the rein of the ever-and-again present eternity of a spherical space; or, then: Pelasgian time is the rotation of Pelasgian space — in view of the infinity of both, a thought logically doubly unperformable! And in this, now, consists the sameness and the comparability of every opening moment with every closing moment: that each of them, insofar as it "steps into appearance", begins the course of world-happening; but in this consists the eternal otherness of the moment just now coming: that, precisely for the sake of the primal beginning it signifies, it repeats none that was before it. To the irretrievability of everything ever present is joined, as was already set forth earlier (ch. 14) for another purpose, for everything ever becoming present, the ever-same originality. But any transformation striving beyond this would be an offense against the "law" of Ananke.

There is no order of things, no duration, no preservation, no property, no possessable world; for there is neither thing nor number, but only present corporeality and its downfall, not to be held up for a single second. But this most truthful "moment" is drawn about with limits of no less inviolability than those which the law of cause draws for things: namely by the primal image of the beginning, which by its means embodies itself anew each time. Because in the life-circle of the Mater the stage of childhood means completion, the stage of childhood is therefore already the turning point, in comparison with which adulthood represents merely a form of having-been. Whoever were now to forget this, or were to contend against it with the demand of a "higher" goal, would have broken through the magic circle, and would either have to be able to master fate, or would succumb to its inexorably crushing wheel. Terrible atonement threatens every arrogated freedom of arbitrary will, and especially the will-believing innovator who plays the duty-commandment of futurefatherhood off against the primal commandment of eternal past-childhood. Arbitrary will and lawfulness so little exclude one another that the latter consists, rather, only in the generalization of the former; for every law stems from the arbitrary will of a legislative act; but arbitrary will and lawfulness contend equally with necessity, in that both erect the barrier of the fixed and deny the unalterability of happening. Cosmic rhythm means: an immovability circling about itself; and it becomes audible to Pelasgian consciousness as the primal commandment of eternal turning-back and eternally purposeless [p. 1352] new beginning. — From this we gather, trait by trait, both what the jus naturale permits and what it demands and forbids. Natural Right and Its Idea of Freedom. — The supreme principle of all natural right is expressed by Pindar in the words: "One is the race of men, another that of the gods, yet both live and breathe from one mother." If we add that animals, plants, stars, clouds and winds counted as divine, then accordingly all formations of the visible universe would be leaves from one stem and members of the one and same symbiotic association.

From this follows, first, with regard to all possible beings, the admission of the boundlessness of Eros; but with regard to human tribal confederations, even the requirement of the rejection of erotic private possession, and therefore, from the very primal beginning, even of sexual tabooings. As already indicated above several times, there originally exists no resistance to the pairing, whether of sister and brother, or of mother and son, or of daughter and father; for in the mirror of the mother-symbol, sister, mother, and daughter embody, in three different ways, the *one* primal image of womanhood. Indeed, such unions, as soon as they have once become at all conspicuous within a richly articulated community, soon appear endowed too with the dignity of higher originality, of more fateful intimacy, and the first step toward their limitation is taken not by moral defense, but quite on the contrary by the wish for special consecration, in that it reserves the right to them for magicians, the powerful, and kings. So it is above all the divine legends of the whole world that not merely occasionally but regularly and preferentially pair the father-god with the daughter-goddess, the divine mother with the mortal or immortal son, and, in a thousandfold reading, demonic siblings with one another. In Rhea's womb the twins Isis and Osiris perform the sacred gamos; Hera is sister and consort of Zeus, Camisa of Janus, Libera of Liber; the ruler and "Son of the Sun" of the Peruvians may "wed" only his own sister — if, that is, we are not to disdain, for pairings of this kind, a name that owes its present-day sense to an opposing manner of thinking. Running parallel with private property, monogamy arises only in that very same post-Pelasgian circle of humanity which, moreover, also represents the jus civile; and the "sacrament" of marriage, above all, is an invention of Christendom.

[p. 1353] Even that religious conception of marriage which Bachofen assigns to the Demetrian stage he posits does not do without symbolic cultic acts of feminine self-surrender, of which presently; and there has never existed a monogamous legal order of society without a prostitution, either highly praised or deeply despised (in some form or other) — not to speak of the other phenomenon which, on the ground of inner polarity, accompanies the exchange of soul and blood between the sexes through times and peoples: homosexual love, with its blossoms, richly varied in kind, especially among men. The path from the animal stage of pairing to the primordially human stage is not also the path to monogamy, but leads from the native uniformity of the sex-drive to the unsurveyable multiformity of an Eros which, just as it is rooted in beholding and kindles itself at the image, likewise reaches by far beyond the limits drawn for the sex-drive, effecting under a thousand shapes the gamos of the soul with the world-mystery — whereas monogamy, when conceived as the canon of life's conduct and the structural law of society, satisfies a requirement no longer of life, but of spirit.

With this it is already said, in passing, that Eros and Sexus by no means necessarily coincide. Rather, the two will diverge from one another all the more, the more sexuality is subjected, under the compulsion of emergencies — one is accustomed to call them economic problems — to obligatory determinations which, in keeping with the manifold of occasions as well as of tribal characters among different groups, can as is to be understood take on quite different forms, and in the course of the ages actually have done so (exogamy, class-marriage, polyandry, polygyny, marriage by rank, marriage in service, and so on). The attempts, undertaken again and again now from the side of the man, now from the side of the woman, now by the old, now by the young, to bring the two, Sexus and Eros, into accord by means of a principle of order, have never succeeded and will never succeed, because attempts at order can only appear once the process of disintegration has already begun in the living cell — a process called to end with the cleaving-apart of soul and body. Eros and law resist one another as soul and spirit do, and every intervention of will, instead of closing the rift, widens it.

Rightly, therefore, the greatest and most perceptive researchers have long since given up wanting to read off the early conditions of humanity — whether among primitives, or from the reports and remains of antiquity — precisely [p. 1354] from the regulations governing the drive toward sexual pairing, and have instead turned their attention preferentially to those customs, partly extralegal or merely tolerated, partly prevailing as something taken for granted, which, being charged with feeling, always point back to older forms of society. From the abundance of examples we single out two. — However much Tacitus stresses the strictness of the marital life of the Germanic peoples, and in doing so, for readily intelligible reasons, underlines the rarity of extramarital relations, he nonetheless does not fail to recall the peculiarly high significance attached to the relation between siblings and to the mother's brother. "The sons of sisters stand as near to their uncle as to their own father. Some even regard this blood-kinship as still more sacred and intimate, and when hostages are demanded they insist especially on such children, as though these constituted a firmer bond for the conscience, a more comprehensive one for the family." Now, since Bachofen's researches, which furnish the richest evidence for this from the myths and customs of antiquity, it has been generally known, and ethnologists have confirmed it, that the predominance of the blood-bond between brother and sister's child over the blood-bond between children and father stems from the early period of the mother-cult (the so-called avunculate) and accordingly is grounded in a conception of community essentially different from that of a sanctified monogamy; a point to which we shall return.

More important for us here is a matter of another kind already touched on above. A thought still falling within the turn of prehistory, and speaking irresistibly for the lateness of the marital law and its opposition to the order of the Mater, shines forth from important strands of legend and, above all, from numerous customs: namely, that the husband's claim of ownership was tantamount to a theft committed against the woman's original aphroditic destiny — a theft that could only be offset by surrendering, at first before marriage or in the interval, her own person, and later also her symbolically vicarious hair, to the privileged goddess of love. "Herodotus's description of the Babylonian custom shows entirely this character, and stresses in particular the obligation to follow anyone, without will or choice. This view reaches as far as Italy, as Justin's account of the vow of the women of Locris, and the reconciliation of Aphrodite thereby intended, proves. We find it again in Etruria and on the Balearic Islands. It also underlies the Cyprian institutions, stands in connection with the early history of Carthage, emerges at the innermost [p. 1355] bosom of the Adriatic in the myth of Cinyras, and at Corinth and in other seats of the cult of Aphrodite takes the form of the dedication of hetaeric hierodules" (Bachofen).

Kinship, not right of ownership, binds these children of the world — the smaller kinship from the commonality of the tribal mother, the greater from the commonality of the mother of the All — and this kinship declares itself in the elective determinacy of race-feeling and is sealed through the real or symbolic mixing of blood. Already contained in this is the fact that no one is entitled to set himself up as lord, whether over animals, plants and soil, or over his fellow man. Here there is no personal supreme power, only personal belongings — foremost among them the belonging to the house, itself again mother-symbolic, further the belonging to the native soil, to the district association, to the craft guild — and in all this what possesses is always the — past, out of which the human being emerges, either in fact or through the incorporating consecration of adoption, whereas he himself is the possessed: not having, but had; not ruling, but given over. Natural law rejects and punishes, wherever it should show itself, every "will to power." At this point let a further backward glance at certain disclosures of language be permitted once more.

Having earlier appraised, chiefly from the standpoint of exaggerated feelings of dependence on the world, the quite extraordinary richness of possessive formations that characterizes the languages of many primitive peoples but also of some peoples of culture, it seems fitting also to point out the reverse side, according to which such linguistic usages express, among other things, the predominance of an inward direction and the, as it were, clustering and centering tendency of representation — a tendency to which, in the Pelasgian world-picture, the Mater corresponds as the midpoint of the universe and ultimately of all happening. — And here, then, let the promised hint be given as to where the path to understanding must be sought for the highly peculiar fact that, in the most various languages that have developed grammatical gender, highly abstract nouns far more often bear feminine than masculine endings, or are marked by the feminine article (in German, for instance, all nouns in -heit and -keit and - schaft and -ung and -sucht: Schönheit [beauty], Wissenschaft [science], Regierung [government], Sehnsucht [longing], further Mathematik, and finally Güte [goodness], Treue [fidelity], Stärke [strength], and so on).

As has been shown, certain concepts are residues of the splitting of very general unities of meaning, so that their names rest on the exploitation [p. 1356] (reshaping, extension of use, and so on) of incomparably older general names, by which originally, without exception, divine centers of happening were meant, and consequently connections that come into appearance through their working. "Universalia" properly precede the abstracta, and the universal, traced back into the formative and nourishing stratum of still unconceptual contents of meaning, is the symbol of belongings-together, communities, kinship groups. Being essentially splitting, dividing, separating, spirit, as has often been stressed, would not even arrive at distinguishing, because it would not arrive at relating, were the linguistic symbols of connections not at its disposal — symbols which it was the soul's lot to find thanks to its beholding of images. But if it is the great bearer-of-life, in view of whom the original blood-bond and accordingly every community of Pelasgian humanity closed together, then it must be, insofar as they also name gender-characters, precisely the symbolic names of the greatest spheres — or, more soberly put, the widest general names — that bear the gender of the Magna Mater. Since it was naturally on these that the will to analysis of bold pioneers of thought first tested itself, those cosmological concepts arose which, above all in Greece, open the history of conceiving, and the inclination of speculative thought to mark more or less all abstracta linguistically by the feminine gender remained thereafter. — And so, incidentally, the capacity for so-called synthesis, of which the hubris of the understanding boasts, would be, as it were, unmasked by language itself, and the ground of possibility of relating would be traced, with the help especially of high-order general concepts, to the — heart. Not even the "figment of the brain," let alone what is called a "rational thought," would take place without a, however anemic it may have become, "figment of the blood." — We return to the development of the main thought.

To be a vein or a little vein in the network of blood-vessels, a thread or little thread in the veil of Maya, a leaf or little leaf on the tree of life — that is the meaning, and indeed the sole meaning, of Pelasgian "equality." As autochthons, standing over against one another, the members of the tribe stand under the "law" of their ancestry; all beings whatsoever rest inseparably in the "womb of Ananke"; but among themselves they all enjoy the same inviolable freedom. Indeed, even clothing, the warrior's weapon, the manifold household goods, and whatever else makes even the dead man's dwelling, the grave, [p. 1357] homely, are not so much his possession as rather signs of his participation in the nourishing and weaving being of the world, from whose inexhaustible source he regards as given, just like the rain of heaven and the fruits of the field, even that which first took shape through the mediation of his own making. Because his acting, working spirit remains bound to the elemental rhythm, what he accomplishes, too, has the character of the born and the grown, is ensouled like this, and breathes, from generation to generation, always the same originality — a state of affairs that still today gives to all the products of "nature peoples," their houses, implements, costumes, ornaments, songs, the so often admired and never artificially achievable uniformity of stamp. The "freedom" we are dealing with here is only another expression for the boundless omnipotence of life; it therefore disenfranchises the I and rejects, as fetter and constraint, every self-glorifying claim of spirit! In a hymn to Isis it is said: "Before our highest royal power they tremble; but the constraint of fetters not pleasing to me, I loose." A Roman jurist explains to us in sober words the significance of this for the relation of human beings to one another: Jure naturali omnes homines liberi sunt, servitus venit ex jure gentium [By natural law all men are free; slavery arises from the law of nations]. All female and male deities who represent the maternal center also bear the epithet "Loosener" or "Liberator." The slave who was permitted to sit down in the temple of Feronia upon the stone seat, a symbol of the earth, rose up again as a free man. This is the *jus* talionis. — But this "freedom" is to be had only at the price of unresisting submission to the unalterability of a happening that made transience the condition of coming-to-be, dying the condition of being born, night the mother of day. Infinite past, flashing up in the fullness of the moment, the living tolerates no constraint from outside, bursts every barrier of spiritual laws, but succumbs, without any possibility of escape, to the inner compulsion of unstoppable reflux into — having-been. If the Platonist and the Christian long for "redemption" from the kyklos anankes and strive after "immortality" in the "beyond"; if present-day man, with all his science, at bottom wants to master only the one thing — how to free existence from the measuredness of being alive and win boundless duration — then for the Pelasgian this would be precisely the most extreme [p. 1358] wish for sacrilege and a criminal encroachment on the right of nature, which, for the sake of the eternity of life, demands unconditional renunciation of persistence. As regards this "law," which tolerates no exception, there joins itself, without contradiction, to the words of the mother goddess just cited, the inscription of the Isis-column: "I am Isis, the queen of the whole land, and what I have legally laid down, no one can loose." What we have thus far appraised from the standpoint of a, so to speak, blind force of nature now appears in the light of a right whose application to human forms of sociability conflicts with all concepts of right grounded in the statutes of "morality."

The "freedom" of life coincides with the commandment to die. It is, with double reference to the fugitive character of the soul's existence and to its dependence on the living-place of the maternal egg, called: "outlawry"! The eternity of life demands that it wander from one hand to another; whoever receives it has received it only as a fief and must pass it on, just as it was given to him. "The lot of death appointed to creatures is an act of never-ending justice" — with this iron sentence Bachofen carries back into the mode of thought of primeval time a truth that Goethe had ventured to put only into the mouth of the "spirit that ever denies": "For all that comes to be — Deserves to perish wretchedly." The moment that steps into life kindles itself at a dying moment: so it too must die, that the one to come may live. The Fates spin the thread of life, the Fates cut it off: only through the pulse-beat of coming-to-be and passing-away is the world's renewal, in the medium of time, secured. Nemesis, the "justly-apportioning one," is, just like Ate, Hybris, Erinys, at the same time the doom of death that overtakes everyone, because and insofar as he ever dared to live at all! But this thought reaches further.

The individual living being has its life only as a fief not merely because it could not live had not another individual living being sunk back into the night of death, from whom it inherited its life, but also because, spatially, it stands within an ever-pulsing nexus in which each lives only at the expense of the other, being compelled to feed its own flame of life with the fire it robbed from another. Primal man finds not the thing in images but the images in the thing, and beholds in things, as in the properties of things, the appearing features of living souls: in clouds, winds, and waters no less than [p. 1359] in animals and plants, in these no less than in man, in man no more than in the implements made by man. Hence, even if he could nourish himself on dust, or, like the cicadas of a Greek tale, on dew, his being alive would still become a consequence of unceasing encroachments upon the life of the outer world, and even the breath he cannot forgo for a single minute is a constant plunder of the universally diffused breath of life. If, then, out of the primal feeling of having been graced, the feeling of doing begins fully to awaken — the feeling of wanting-to-live — then every moment of life increases the magnitude of a "debt" that can be discharged only by the sacrifice of life. With this we already touch the essence and innermost ground of the jus talionis: an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, blood for blood; or, in a less sensuous formulation: suffer what you have done!

Few teachers of wisdom have thought more deeply about original revenge than Nietzsche. Again and again the question occupied him: how could the thought of the possibility of retribution arise at all; how did the wholly peculiar belief arise that the pain someone suffered is offset by producing yet another pain, namely in the one who caused it; how in particular can the deed of killing make a second killing desirable, when the first nonetheless remains no less irrevocable on that account? "Whence this age-old,.. perhaps.. ineradicable idea.. of an equivalence between injury and pain?" he asks in the "Genealogy of Morals." "The feeling of guilt," runs his answer, "..has its origin in the oldest and most original relation there is between persons, in the relation between buyer and seller, creditor and debtor." And indeed the settlement "is given by the fact that, in place of an advantage accruing directly against the damage (that is, in place of a settlement in money, land, possessions of any kind), the creditor is granted a kind of feeling of well-being as repayment.., the feeling of well-being of being allowed to vent his power without misgiving upon one who is powerless.., the enjoyment in violation.. By means of the punishment inflicted on the debtor, the creditor participates in a master's right.. The settlement consists in a warrant and title to cruelty." — It would lead too far, and could profit us little, were we to try to untangle the thick knot of fundamental errors that such propositions offer in place of a solution; only the error of presupposition ought not to remain uncontested, the exposure of which alone suffices to invalidate all the conclusions drawn from it: original retribution never rests on a "relation between persons," [p. 1360] but is always a matter of the clan, the household community, the district association, the tribe, and so forth. Private revenge develops only after the pattern of clan revenge, and this is grounded neither in the angry irritability already proper to the animal, nor in the feeling of that thirst for vengeance which we today are inclined to think of preferentially at this word. According to testimony valid for numerous peoples, the obligation of revenge of the kin-group can extend over many generations (to the third, indeed to the thirteenth degree!) and can in this way concern persons who are no longer in any contact whatsoever with the wrong to be avenged. In the case of a killing that has occurred, it is accustomed to leave entirely out of consideration whether it happened intentionally or not, and, as compensation for the life of the slain, it does not necessarily demand that of the murderer, but that of some member of his clan, or else that of a — sacrificial animal. Oedipus, for instance, stained his land with kin-murder, even though he neither intended to slay Laius nor could in the least have known that the man he struck was his father. — Nietzsche's statements nonetheless have a twofold merit: first, to have awakened, to a degree not achieved before, astonishment at the sequential linkage of having-to-suffer and having-done; and second, to have compared the commandment of revenge with the creditor's demand upon the debtor. The opinion that this relation made the beginning is, to be sure, so far from correct that it could not itself have arisen without the foundation of another thought, which will at once disclose to us the meaning of retribution; for exchange requires the concept of value, which in turn is rooted in feelings of value and was consequently mediated by an original experience. It does, however, hold true that the act of retribution corresponds to the exacting of a debt, and gains the sense of a restoration only insofar as it appears to take back what had previously either been lent or wrested away. But the "creditor" here is precisely not a person, not a power-hungry I seeking to be paid for a suffered disadvantage by satisfying drives of cruelty, but a blood-bond, a corporate member of life itself, and its demand aims not at feelings of pleasure of whatever kind (of the individual human being or of a group of human beings), but at the renewal of the original image of life through the restitution, to be brought about, of what was taken from it.

[p. 1361] It could not escape perceptive researchers that, within the framework of the duty of blood revenge, the atonement for a homicide under certain circumstances recedes entirely behind the atonement for blood shed. There are Arab tribes among whom a killing that took place without the shedding of blood demands no blood revenge, whereas a mere blow that happened to bring a wound to bleeding makes it necessary. If, then, here it is not the killing at all but the shed blood that "cries out for revenge," it follows compellingly that the primal impulse to retribution must be sought not in the personal feelings of disturbance of the one who executes the retribution, but rather in the disturbance of life itself that was produced through the encroachment upon the appearance of life. The clan takes revenge for its slain member, or the soul of the slain avenges itself, or the Erinyes avenge him: these are only three forms of a single process, and this process is not so much what present-day man understands by taking revenge, as rather the process of undoing something that happened before, insofar as it had, according to the life-belief of primeval time, the sense of a robbery. Personal desires for revenge would never assume the form of a statute, would never be shared by a second person merely because that person had a common descent with the first, could not gain a foothold on occasions such as those we have just heard of, and could not in the least awaken the thought that marks the essence of primal retribution: the thought of re-accomplishing, upon the doer, the deed that is to be atoned for.

If we take our stand on the ground of the I-dependent conception of things, it remains forever incomprehensible how a homicide should be offset by yet another homicide (for it is a matter of offsetting, as Nietzsche rightly recognized!), shed blood by a further shedding of blood, the tooth one lost by one that is knocked out, the eye one forfeited by the one that is torn out — in short, suffered pain by the infliction of injury. For it is not the avenger who gains by the act of revenge, and it is not the personal loss of the one doing penance that is in question (however much motives of this kind may have contributed to the reshaping of the matter in a less "barbaric" age, when one already did — business with advantage!). If, on the other hand, we take our stand on the ground of beholding thought, for which the real is not the thing but the appearance of the soul, and the person only its dwelling-place, then killing becomes, quite literally, the taking of life — just as even today it is said of the murderer [p. 1362] that he "takes" someone's life, or his own — the shedding of blood becomes the taking of blood, since it was indeed sometimes actually drunk, and, similarly, every disturbance of the soul-body becomes an appropriation of that which is essentially unpossessable and which, according to the rhythm of life, can indeed be exchanged but can by no means be surrendered to the will to power, and is therefore reclaimed from it. Because, by virtue of elementary similarity, the letting of blood is above all a giving of the same actuality that was taken by the shedding of blood, atonement by talion, far from being a new injury, stands there in the light of a healing — a healing "mystical," to be sure, for our consciousness — performed upon the wound of the image through the taking-back of what was purloined from the image. Let one consider the following deeply "barbaric" example of the jus talionis, and one will find confirmed, in crude palpability, both that primal retribution aims at the healing of life's wounds through the restitution of what was robbed, and, at a single stroke, recognize it as impossible to derive it from reactive impulses of an injured claim to power of a personal I. In the Wendhagen peasant law there is found (according to Grimm) the provision: "If anyone bark-strips a willow, he shall be made to cover the damage with his own entrails; if he can get over that, the tree can get over it too." We may spare ourselves the more precise dissection of this statute, in view of the preceding development of its fundamental content. — Finally, a glance at a few facts of the history of the language is worthwhile. The word "Schuld" [guilt/debt], related in Old High German "sculan" to "sollen" [to owe/shall], originally means the legal obligation to a performance, then, in the narrower sense, the obligation to atonement; this, in turn, still has in Middle High German the sense of "remedy against something," in accordance with which the derived verb "büßen," etymologically related to "bessern" [to improve], is still used in some places (for instance, in Switzerland) for "to repair," "to mend." Compare: "Lückenbüßer" [stopgap] = "one who fills a gap," further "seine Lust büßen" = "to still one's desire." Likewise "sühnen" [to atone] originally means "to reconcile," and occurs even in more recent literature still in precisely this sense (in Keller, after Paul: "until a bad farmer brings about the reconciliation"). "Vergelten" [to requite], finally, originally means simply "to pay back."

Here it is now time to reject with all emphasis the view, which has become a veritable fixed idea among present-day apostles of morality, that the mere circumstance of the universal bindingness of a standard already [p. 1363] suffices to require that it be thought grounded in the lawfulness of spirit, and to dismiss the possibility of its origin from "nature." According to them, without exception every valuation would be, in essence, moral valuation; an outside of ethics would be simply renunciation of valuation, and the "beyond good and evil" would at best be the formula of complete indifference. — We take up again the thread of thought exactly where we earlier let it drop, when we assert, in opposition to this: just as mythical thinking, because it is a "thinking of the blood," turns out in many respects far less "subjective" than "scientificity," so too the normings of the mythical stage are rooted in sub-personal strata of being, and thus natural law bears, not only in scope and depth but even in the kind of limits it sets up, whether hallowing or forbidding, to a far higher degree the character of generality than any right of spirit ever does. — In the same work in which Nietzsche wants to derive the thought of retribution from barter, he also strives to refute the proposition, held especially by Dühring, that the concept of justice grew out of "reactive affects," against which he objects, among other things, that experience shows nothing is so hard and so late to be conquered by the spirit of justice as the ground of "reactive feeling." Wherever justice prevails, one sees rather a stronger power, in relation to a weaker one subordinate to it, seeking means to put an end to the senseless raging of "ressentiment"; and it achieves this above all through "the establishment of the law, the imperative declaration of what in general, in its eyes, is to count as permitted, what as forbidden, as wrong." By this alone, in the long run, the opposite is achieved of what all revenge wants, insofar as revenge lets only the standpoint of the injured party count — namely, the ever more impersonal assessment of the deed, in the end even on the part of the injured party himself. "Accordingly," he continues, "'right' and 'wrong' exist only from the establishment of the law onward, and not, as Dühring would have it, from the act of injury onward." — Everything that is here brought forward against the doctrine of the origin of justice from personal revenge is doubtless correct; yet it must strike us as highly strange when a thinker like Nietzsche unmistakably takes the side of a "justice" whose existence rests on that universal lawfulness of the will which Kant called a categorical ought. If we hold together with this what Nietzsche correctly uncovers, that every law is grounded in the decision of will of a [p. 1364] personal lawgiver, then the "beyond good and evil" would unquestionably have become a declaration of renunciation of essentially impersonal valuing altogether, and Nietzsche would have had no occasion left at all to rage against the "moral world-order," whose essentially identical origin was indeed familiar to no one better than to him. Had he too not been led astray by his belief in the vital significance of the "will to power," he would at once have noticed that the norm of the will indeed depersonalizes willing, but by no means also de-selves it, and can therefore indeed free it from "subjectivity" out of "interest," but not from the far worse partiality into which we fall by setting up spirit, of which we alone are the bearers, as judge over life; and the question would have had to arise before him whether ichless life did not itself contain the very stuff that enables it not merely to act, but also to balance out actions against one another — indeed, whether it is not in a cosmic rhythm that the very ground of possibility both of experiencing and of norming first lies! But then he would hardly have overlooked that the possible model cases of human behavior can be halved by yet a wholly different dividing line than the one that separates a self-personal doing from a lawful one. From mere states of feeling, such as angry irritability, or, further, so-called ressentiment (= hatred against life arising from poisoned life — envy of life), the idea of equality and "conscience" (= receptivity to "categorical imperatives") are distinguished, as attitudes of the reason of the will: but all of them have this in common, that they take as their basis the person of the injured party. It is this person for whose affront the "reactive feeling" demands retribution, and again this person in respect of whom alone spiritual right can be violated. In contrast, the jus talionis is determined exclusively by the damage inflicted. This can concern a person, an animal, a plant, a place (for instance, a gravesite), a region, a human implement: it is always the disturbance in the image of the world that here stands in need of healing, and this is meant even when, by chance, the bearer of the image was not merely a living thing but, in addition, a personal one. Only thus is it explained — but then also without any residue of questionability — why the intent of the doer of the damage plays no role at all, why the atonement does not necessarily concern his person, and can, depending on circumstances, also be accomplished symbolically. Instead of the merely depersonalized justice of spirit, there reigns here, by force of fate, the [p. 1365] inhuman justice of life, which cannot be carried out by persons without danger of ruin for the executor himself!

Meanwhile, German in particular allows one to keep the two kinds of right apart according to the kinds of offense by which right can in each case be violated. At least within "civilization," that is, under the influence of the Christian corruption of the blood, the conception of the immoral has undergone that most extreme sharpening which took shape in the concept of "sin." But just as certainly as there is sin only for a moral consciousness, so certainly is there sacrilege only for a life-consciousness. Every sin is a sin against spirit, every sacrilege a sacrilege against life! "Sin against game" or "sin against a tree" would be ridiculous; "sacrilege against game" and "sacrilege against a tree," by contrast, are indeed still understood to some extent even today. "Sin" corresponds roughly to the Greek hamartema, "sacrilege" exactly to the Greek hybris. All hybris consists, in the end, in the criminal rebellion of the I-shaped spirit against the landscape-bound belonging of man too to the realm of the Great Mother. Hence, just as "virtue" stands opposed to sin, exalting its bearer here or beyond, so sacrifice stands opposed to sacrilege, shattering its bearer — not "to the glory of God," but rather so that the aura of the — gods may shine forth the more radiantly!

Now that the connection with the mother-symbol that grounds it has, it is hoped, been clarified, it is neither our task nor our intention to pursue natural law into its particular forms. With regard to the connection, already briefly touched on, between the jus talionis and the thought of sacrifice, that perhaps most bewildering of all propositions from the Janusbelief of primeval time — whose consequences for magical custom we have already made recognizable earlier — may at least be brought nearer to sympathetic understanding: what takes life, that same thing is also able to lend life. "In a similar way," says Ivo in his "de rebus ecclesiasticis," "like is set against like. According to this similarity our physician healed the death of our flesh, which derives from the serpent, through the death of his own flesh."<sup>120</sup> If, accordingly, sacrifice too can take the place of retribution — whether of a human being or an animal, or even of a lifeless thing — and if this evidently requires a repetition of the deed to be atoned for, it follows incontrovertibly that the thought of retribution alone and exclusively serves the restoration of a disturbance of supra-personal life, and undertakes to accomplish this by healing, according to the "law" of the similarity [p. 1366] of images, the wound of life with an accomplishment similar to the one by which the wound was dealt it. Against the present-day belief in the "conservation of matter," or of force, primeval time sets its belief in the constant renewal of images, and, instead of our violently ever-advancing method of converting mechanical processes, it puts into effect the palintropos harmonie of an everlasting exchange. We have found such exchange anchored, at bottom, in the life-necessary alternation of perishing with coming-to-be, and have in this way tied its origin to the most comprehensive of all conceivable circles: to the very possibility of the appearing of actuality. So far-reaching a depersonalization of human motives, however, not only does not exclude but in fact positively fosters that retribution, like sacrifice, should fill the person of the executor with the deepest and most powerful pathos. A concluding glance at this may at least help us toward an intimation of the extent to which the empowerment of personality is nonetheless compatible with a clear separation of "pious" from "impious" courses of life. Primeval piety — In view of the unconditional inviolability of natural world-appearance, it might seem to us as though the mere enjoyment of life on the part of the person were already a crime worthy of death. Yet, however certain it is that a person's right to life is indeed truly bought with the obligation to die, it is equally certain that, on the basis of a formerly unknown conceptuality of our thinking, we would have wholly misapprehended the sense of the justice that "atones" every being-alive with death, were we to want to equate mere participation in life with the defiant sacrilege against life, and the self-fulfilling "atonement" of the former with the vengeance of the pursuing Erinys. To be sure, it is the life of the All to which the sacrificial faith of the Pelasgian is directed wholly and solely, but this becomes present to his beholding thought only by the medium of sensuous Eros. He does not yet know, and neither may nor can know, man, animal, plant as such; rather he knows only that with which he hangs together in living fashion: his dead, his hearth-place and native soil; the men, animals, and plants that surround him; the spring that quenches his thirst, the crop of the field that stills his hunger; the sun of here and today, the star above his roof. Because he himself is an eye of the world, what he beholds and loves is the world — not, however, that for which we, with the [p. 1367] name for it, designate a mere concept. Our thought-of All is a mechanical jumble of things; the living All, by contrast, to which we can only linguistically point, not conceive it, is beheld in the momentariness of its appearance flashing up here and now. In this lies grounded, now, a twofold division of values of the life-dependent disposition of spirit.

<sup>120</sup> On page 1365. — Quoted after *Cassel*, Die Symbolik des Blutes (Berlin 1882), p. 8.

Because, out of gratitude for having been given, she is willing to give herself up for everything to which her Eros belongs, she stands armed for war and ready for revenge against every encroachment from without. Brotherliness within, readiness for war without, belongs, by the unanimous judgment of ancient reporters, among the ever-recurring traits of mother-right tribes. The Scythians and the Getae, for example, with their community of goods and women, are called eunomoi by Aeschylus in regard to their love of justice. It is the willingness to stand up protectively for grave, home, and district association to which every Pelasgian people knows itself bound; death-despising bravery in battle against the disturber of the peace, which bestows fame on its bearer above others; the lack of inwardness of attachment to the statute of the ancestors, hearth, and district, which demeans him; timidity in defense, which degrades him; and betrayal and faithlessness already count among the sacrileges that call for an extinguishing revenge. It is one thing to kill a foreign warrior in battle, and another thing again to kill one's own tribal fellow, since it is only with the latter, not with the former, that the double bond of blood and Eros is tied, and it is only through this deed, not through that one, that the body of life is sacrilegiously violated. But because here kinship prevails on the basis of commonality of the mother, and because the mother, thanks to her essential oneness of being with the Magna Mater, that is, with the eternal place of the world's renewal, ultimately spans the whole natura naturata, the circle of significance can widen into the circle of significance of the kinship of all human beings with one another, and, further, of man with animals, plants, and things; as indeed we heard above, that out of a natural-law impulse of Roman penal provisions, the killing of even a mere citizen already sufficed to brand the doer a parricide.

It is paternity, opened to spirit, that divides: first into groups, then into families, finally into single human beings; maternity, on the other hand, fundamentally denies all bounds of objecthood. "As in the paternal principle lies limitation, so in the maternal lies that of universality; [p. 1368] as the former brings with it restriction to narrower circles, so the latter knows no bounds, no more than natural life does. From child-bearing motherhood stems the universal brotherliness of all human beings, whose consciousness and recognition goes under with the development of paternity. The family grounded on father-right closes itself off into an individual organism, whereas the mother-right family bears that typically-universal character with which all development begins.." (Bachofen). Were one, however, to want to read off from the tolerances and prohibitions of the mythical stage something like a moral recognition of the personality's right to exist, one would have to fall silent in the face of the fact that even murder, in the Pelasgian judgment, is still capable of an intensification up to that most extreme sacrilegious deed, no longer atonable by anything, which, within the framework of natural law, corresponds to what, within the framework of moral right, would be the mortal sin against the "Holy Spirit": we mean matricide! "Just as in the religion of.. spirit," says Bachofen, "the sin against.. spirit has no forgiveness to hope for, so in that religion of material force, the sin against its principle, the motherhood of the earth." One must read it in his interpretation of the Aeschylean Oresteia, which alone would already suffice to bear out his fame as the greatest rediscoverer of primeval time so far, how the matricide, according to the primal conception, has fallen prey to a kind of eternal damnation, and escapes the startled avenging spirits of the Mater struck to her innermost core only because her right of revenge is broken forever by the motherless father's-daughter Athena, and must thenceforth yield to the moral right of the spirit-god Apollo; and one will perhaps, even more than in reading Aeschylus himself, sense a breath of the demonic crushings by which the catastrophes in the life of a humanity of ineluctable fate were accompanied.

The concluding stroke in this painting, full of somber grandeur, of this side of the right of nature is added by the thought of the today almost inconceivable power which, thanks to the far-reaching validity of the duty of retribution, the past exercises over every present of the pre-world. On the inexorability of the primal commandments the Pelasgian sense of actuality is formed and strengthened, the astonishing truthfulness and long-enduring steadfastness of Pelasgian remembrance. It is not facts and deeds in the sense of "history" that primal memory records; but with a brazen stylus it engraves into itself original custom and tribal commandment, and, with the imprescriptible [p. 1369] necessity of a force of nature, it carries out the call for revenge for every sacrilege against the form of life: the most ancient ancestor lives on, bestowing and judging, among the latest descendants! Everywhere it is the subterranean gods, the semnai theai of the Greeks, by whom the most dreadful oaths are sworn, and who bind even the rulers of heaven to the given word with a Stygian fetter. — To this division of values arising from the contrast of the distant with the near there is now joined, however, another one, which shows us the countenance of the pre-world in a far friendlier light and lets it appear, notwithstanding a sublimity certainly not to be called idyllic, nonetheless incomparably more peaceful than the bloody grimace of life today. — Just as certainly as every moment of being-alive is a gift of the universally diffused life, so certainly does it lie within the power of the beholding soul to render tribute of thanks for it, by taking living things round about it into its care and keeping, and by restoring to the primal source of life, out of the best that it enjoys, the best; and just as certainly as not even the most insignificant purpose is realized without changes to the image of the world, so certainly is it able to hallow the purpose, that it bring to expression, in the spirit of man, the formative drives of "eternal life," and thus become a means for those drives to crown themselves, in the first place, with completion. It is not encroachment upon life as such that is already necessarily a violation of life, but the high-handed encroachment that breaks the rhythm instead of carrying it forward. Whoever builds himself a roof must fell trees; whoever erects a gravestone must break stone: this would be a sacrilege against the image of the world on the part of one who did it in consciousness of the mastery of his spirit and had the plan for it only from himself; it is, on the other hand, permitted and indeed demanded collaboration at the loom of fate on the part of one who, given over to the voices of the soul, fulfills, with a sleepwalker's compulsion, in his own doing, only the growth-wishes of the earth — from which the thoughtful reader may gather why it could become necessary to inquire from divine signs where a house, a temple, might be allowed to arise, and to purchase participation in the shaping of the place by the "genius loci" through sacrifices at once conciliatory and seeking protection. And again: whoever tends a flower, waters it, kills its pests, unquestionably intervenes in the weaving of Maya, but not in order to destroy caterpillars and lice, but in order to bring flowers to their highest unfolding. His doing is determined by Eros toward the image, and what, arising out of this, became [p. 1370] a surpassing value is precisely that in which life itself has "set itself the goal" of culminating; for only in the elective impulse of love does the creative urge of the telluric powers awaken! The origin of the world from the egg. — After a relatively so detailed discussion of the mother-thought itself, we may be brief concerning the two other pieces of evidence which we still intended to adduce for the germinal point of Pelasgian symbolism. As regards the one — namely the origin, whether simply of the world and of the world-creating gods, or at least of the stuff of the world and of the law of its transformations, from a primordial egg, in which the double nature of hidden fate is symbolized through the opposition of two colors — we have only to single out a few, essentially well-known, facts from the almost unsurveyable abundance of those which Bachofen brings together in his "Gräbersymbolik."

Taking as his starting point the "mystery-egg," as it repeatedly appears depicted on initiation vases, on bronze figures, on reliefs, sarcophagus images, tomb paintings, or is found, modeled in fired clay, in the necropoleis, he gives, with reference to hundreds of supporting passages from the literature of antiquity, the following abbreviating overview: "The Orphic primal egg is half white, half black or red, just as Typhon too, the destructive force, is depicted red. Indeed these colors pass into one another as constantly as life and death, day and night, becoming and passing away." As the center of the Dionysian religion it shows us "the highest law that governs the transitory world, as a fatum inborn in the feminine substance... From the two halves of the egg heaven and earth have come forth. According to the Indian cosmogony Brahma dwells long concealed within the primal egg, then divides it into two halves and makes of the one the heaven, of the other the earth. According to Egyptian doctrine Kneph begets the primal egg from his mouth...: Ptah, who in Suidas is called Dionysos, opens it; from the one half arises the heaven, from the other the earth... Among the Chaldeans Bel, the demiurge, cuts asunder Omorka (the material primal mother conceived as primal waters and moon); the upper half is the heaven, the lower the earth... The half corresponding to the earth is black, that of the heaven bright." According to the Persian doctrine Horomazes encloses 24 gods within the egg, and Arimanius as many. The one sprang from the purest light, the other from darkness, and is in all things opposed to the former, [p. 1371] locked with him in eternal war. The 24 gods engendered by Arimanius break through the egg, and from this stems the mixture of good with evil, out of whose struggle the life of the universe consists... Thus not only is every telluric organism contained spermatikos in the egg, but heaven and earth too still lie within it undivided, side by side. In both respects the egg — the elementum of the material world, or Moth, the maternal primal slime — is destined, at a further stage of development, to let its content, still hidden, step forth into the light. In this unfolding the black half becomes the earth, the white the heaven... But as once they rested within one another, so in their separation they long for constant reunion... In this longing is rooted the origin of all things and the stream of becoming that begins with it, to which the equally strong stream of passing away eternally flows in opposition. The power that brings together again what was cut asunder is that god born from the egg whom the Orphic doctrines call Metis, Phanes, Erikapaios, Protogonos, Herakles-Chronos, Eros; the Lesbians call Enorches, the Egyptians Osiris..." Thus the egg encloses "all parts of the material world, heaven and earth, light and darkness, the male and the female potency of nature, the germ of all telluric organisms, of the higher and the lower creation, and the whole world of gods, which has one and the same mother in common with men, animals, plants. According to the Indian doctrine the tree grows forth — from which the lotus and the Trimurti, with the remaining gods, grow upward — out of the egg of the primal waters, which bears that very primal mother, in threefold form, upon its lap. Likewise Syria is born from the egg, likewise Leda-Nemesis, likewise Helena, no less Demeter... All moon-goddesses are connected with the egg. From it come forth the Molionidai and the Dioskuroi, from it Osiris, from it Chusoros, from it finally Enorches, Dionysos, Eros." This survey could be extended, through further mythic material, through symbols and customs, almost without limit. Ptah-Eshmun is depicted forming the world-egg upon the potter's wheel. From the moon-egg that fell into the Euphrates, which fish roll to the shore and doves hatch, the Babylonian Atargatis is descended. The apotropaic Gallic serpent's-egg makes the cult of the primal egg probable as the original religion of the Celts. According to the belief of the Peruvians three eggs fell from heaven, one golden, one silver, one of copper; from the first arose the princes, from the second the nobles, from the third the people. Leda-Nemesis, impregnated by Zeus in the shape of a swan, bears, according to the most common turn of the legend, an egg [p. 1372] from which come forth Helena, Castor and Pollux. That is why the caps of the Dioskuroi are formed from the two halves of the egg, and this egg-cap, called Pileus, becomes the distinguishing headgear of the free man. "When the close-shorn head is covered by the egg-cap, the slave returns to that freedom which belongs to all births of the primal mother." On the so-called Harpy Monument of Xanthos the Lycian egg-mother is depicted: winged, with bird's feet, an egg-shaped body, maternal breast-formation, and a virginal countenance. From a golden egg the Persian king drinks water mixed with wine, the bright fluid with the dark, thereby declaring, in this manner, the maternal origin of his power and its doublemeaninged nature. — According to the most varied testimonies of the most varied peoples, then, the pre-polar totality of life, and its destiny to unfold itself into opposites, is brought to intuition partly directly through double coloring, partly through the oppositional nature of its content, in the image of the egg. The ever-recurring relation to the mother-deity confirms the equation: Mother = Egg. (Compare on this note 20.)

If accordingly the doctrine of man as a genuine microcosm — which already emerged in Pythagoreanism and was never afterward wholly forgotten — unmistakably has its origin in the egg-symbol, then it proves itself thereby to be one of those remnants of the image-forming thinking of the beholding understanding, of which it constitutes perhaps the best, if not the only, merit of so-called philosophy to have preserved not a few, in conceptual paraphrase, and rescued into later times. All the less, then, do we wish to forget that no veiling is able to blur its thoroughly image-like stamp, or to deceive us as to its incompatibility with a mechanistic view of the world. — As already emerges from the examples above, and could moreover still be attested a thousandfold, the egg-cell, expanded on the ground of experienced similarities into a world-cell, gains a hold, convincing even to the senses, in certain intuitable similarities: from the small world of life, above all the egg-shape of the human head and the ellipsoidally conceived trunk — we recall the canopic jars touched upon above —, from the great world, in the first place the nearly hemispherical shape of the unbounded visual space, then the circular disk especially of the speckled moon, finally even the elliptical orbit of all the wandering stars. We need not argue in detail what is self-evident to every competent judgment: that from the standpoint of science the appeal to similarities of this kind would not merely fail to prove the belief [p. 1373] — according to which the universe has the shape of an egg and hence the egg has the shape of the universe — but would even suffice to reject it as a fiction. For even if, for the at least remotely egg-shaped formations of the moon, the head, and the trunk, an objective basis were granted, the chief item of comparison, namely visual space, would have entered the series only through a confusion of the thing with the mere appearance of the thing. But the thought would be removed altogether from any possibility of scientific consideration by the fact that it asserts not so much a similarity of the world to the egg as rather the identity of the two, in that it makes the universe into an egg-cell writ large, the egg-cell into the universe writ small! One must hold this immovably before one's eyes, so as to be armored in advance, in the face of the intellectual exertions of later philosophies that have forgotten the origin of the concept of the microcosm, against every temptation to bring it, by generalizing formulations, into accord with objective science. The objective egg-cell would remain, even then, only a part of the objective universe, and would in no way be the cosmos reduced once more in size, even if it consisted — which, as is well known, is by no means the case — of a mixture of all the chemical "elements." Philosophical efforts have accordingly never seriously moved in the hopeless direction of this proof, but were always guided by the, however unclear, conviction of an essential identity of the two. But essential identity indicates a similarity of images, as became apparent, betrayingly, on our problem every time one felt driven to grasp the relation of macrocosm to microcosm after the manner of that of primal image to copy, or of object to mirror-image; and images are nothing but appearances in need of explanation within a world-system in which real and efficacious power belongs only to things that push and press against one another (and today, as we know, not even to these any longer, but merely to numbers and equations). "As the world is the image of God," says Agrippa in his "Philosophia occulta," "so is man the image of the world. Hence some interpret it thus, that man was created not simply as the likeness of God, but, as it were, as the image of the image; wherefore he is called microcosm, that is, small world."

Only he can undertake to make the science-contradicting thought of the microcosm the foundation of a — science, who cuts through the knot of enemies by resolving, without evasion, [p. 1374] to seek the primal contradiction in the very inadequacy-to-actuality of conceiving thought itself, and to hold the world of things, causes and forces to be, not the real world, but rather the product of a labor of some five thousand years' duration which the de-imaging logos has performed upon the spirit-alien actuality of images. With the word "microcosm" is designated not a factual concept but a symbolic unit of meaning, and indeed precisely that one in which the whole "world-view" of a life-fettered spirituality gathers itself together out of inner necessity, and which therefore forms, to be sure, an inexhaustible source of possible insights for the pointing thought of the investigator of appearances (who, in our language, is the — investigator of actuality). Whoever, knowing this, now holds fast to the thought of the microcosm, should be clear that he has thereby decided the age-old dispute, whether the hen presupposes the egg or the egg the hen, in the sense of the mystery-wisdom, by declaring the world to be the sign-language of an eternal vivum, and the ageless, ever-present ovum to be the indivisible place of origin of ceaseless occurrence. — Still more briefly we dispose of the third point, the prehistoric so-called gynaecocracy, since it is in any case still further illuminated by the application of the mother-thought to the symbols of water, tree, and moon. Insofar as the symbols of the night-polar side of the world are at the same time also those of the pole-connecting middle, night must, as was noted earlier, receive precedence over day, darkness over brightness, the below over the above, rest over motion, space over time, the left over the right, and so forth, and within the human-shaped symbols the woman as mother must receive precedence over the poles man and woman. The correctness of this assumption Bachofen has demonstrated in comprehensive fashion for the whole of Pelasgianism, but has — at least in part — gone too far in the conclusions drawn from it, in that he, as was hardly otherwise possible in his time, did not always sufficiently keep apart religious states of affairs from social ones. Before we now offer some examples for this too, we devote a brief separate consideration to the polarity of left and right, partly because its grounding is still owing, partly and above all as a prelude to the weighing of "gynaecocracy." The polarity of left to right. — That for the Pelasgian not only [p. 1375] above and below, front and back, but also right and left, have substantial significance, needs no further word; just as little the correspondence that holds between the front, as the goal-direction of all seeking, fleeing, attacking drives, and the above, as the active pole of all bearings; further, between the back or rearward, as the direction of gaze of comparatively driveless beholding, and the below, as the passive pole of bearings. More precisely: through the above and the front are determined, in the same sense, elementary directions of efficacy, next directions of drive, finally, on the plane of incipient spirituality, the principal directions of doing; through the below and the back are determined, in the same sense, directions of elementary beholding (for the beholding gaze, into whatever distance, is essentially a gaze into the distance of the past!), next of comparatively driveless suffering, finally, on the plane of incipient spirituality, the principal directions of inclination, of self-surrender and of letting-oneself-go; in accordance with which, to the man, by virtue of his masculinity, belong standing posture and locomotion, to the woman, by virtue of her femininity, lying posture and persistence.<sup>121</sup> Why, however, should precisely the right correspond to the front and the above, precisely the left to the back and the below?

<sup>121</sup> On page 1375. — With this, incidentally, the old disputed question is settled, as to which of the two sexes is the "more beautiful." To show this here as well, we of course set aside the difficult determination of the concept of beauty and entrust ourselves to the sufficiently determinate feelings of meaning that unfailingly accompany the words "beautiful" and "ugly." Whoever compares the form of the typical man as such with the form of the typical woman as such has no common measure and will always only bring his personal direction of taste to bear. From the application of the principle of polarity, by contrast, it follows at once why both sexes can be beautiful to the same *degree*, if one compares the upright standing form of the youth or the mature man with the reclining form of the young girl or the mature woman. If, then, one were to choose, say, a very beautiful youth and a very beautiful young girl, the girl would fall short of the youth in beauty when the upright forms of both are compared, and, conversely, the youth would fall short of the girl when the reclining forms of both are compared.

The question is already answered as soon as we make that presupposition which may suffice for our purposes: namely, that among the achievements of the right hand the spiritually as well as vitally active ones predominate, among those of the left hand the spiritually as well as vitally passive ones. It would, on the other hand, be the task of a new direction of research — namely that of the phenomenological science of the body — to investigate and establish why so peculiar a division of labor between the hands could gain ground, whether it exists generally and always existed or not, and whether it is owing to a merely peripheral or perhaps even a metaphysical significance.<sup>122</sup> Because that no longer belongs to our subject, we confine ourselves to a few purely dogmatic remarks, for which we hope to adduce further grounds elsewhere than those already contained, at any rate, in the exposition that follows. The by far greater number of all human beings has from of old been, not indeed ambidextrous, but left-right; the active achievements fell always and everywhere in principle to the right hand, the passive achievements to the left hand; and the specific difference of the use of the hands rests, finally, upon a thoroughgoing asymmetry of the human body in relation to the vertical median plane; with which, as we scarcely need add, the demand for a metaphysical grounding [p. 1376] of the state of affairs would be pronounced, and the exceptional conditions both of the comparatively rare cases of ambidexterity and of the more frequent ones of left-active, right-passive would have to be sought, both corporeally and psychically, in the innermost strata of essence.

<sup>122</sup> On page 1375. — Reference may here be made to the treatise: *Friedr.* S. *Roth*schild, Über Links und Rechts. Eine erscheinungswissenschaftliche Untersuchung, Zeitschrift für die gesamte Neurologie und Psychiatrie, vol. 124, issue 4, pp. 451–511 (Berlin 1930). — Its significance is to be sought not so much in the contributions the work furnishes to the psychology of the difference between the left and right halves of the body, as in the fact that it carries the method of the science of appearance into the physiology of the nerves, and thereby brings the idea of the microcosm felicitously to bear.

This premised, we need, for the purpose of a distinguishing characterization of drive-conditioned achievements and their successes, think for the right hand only of grasping, taking, appropriating, acquiring, thrusting, striking, hindering, warding off, and, in part, of holding fast; for the left hand, of allowing, being taken, receiving, and again of a holding fast, but for the purpose of giving, distributing, bestowing — so as to find the one hand bound in kind to the male pole, the other to the female pole. But since the phenomenal characters of womanhood recur, each time more deeply in meaning, as phenomenal characters of the Mater, the left, together with the below and the backward, belongs without doubt to the maternal middle, and thereby gains, in addition to the gifts already made good, that of healing, nourishing, indeed of birth-giving bringing-forth. Although Bachofen devoted the 14th chapter of his inexhaustible work on "The Three Mystery Eggs," which forms the main part of the "Gräbersymbolik," principally to the polarity of left and right, the theme is nevertheless not sharply carried through even here, and one must take in addition what is found on the same question of inquiry in the "Mutterrecht" (scattered over more than thirty places throughout the whole work), if one wants a survey of the material available from antiquity. Taking everything together, what is offered remains, to be sure, still fragmentary, but suffices in any case to ground the quite specific significance that matriarchal Pelasgianism attached both to the opposition of left and right and especially to the left side. We single out a few of the most vivid pieces of evidence.

Peruvian Cuzco was divided into an upper and a lower city: the upper was dedicated to the king and was to count as much as the right arm of man, the lower, dedicated to the queen, as much as the left arm. On the occasion of the attempt to distinguish gods from daemons, Plutarch remarks in his treatise on "Isis and Osiris": "That is also why Plato assigns to the Olympian gods the right side and the odd number, but the opposite to the daemons." In memory of the ivory shoulder of Pelops, beloved by Poseidon and led by him to victory, all the Pelopidai, according to one turn of the legend, bear [p. 1377] the white mark of their patron on the right shoulder, but on the left upper arm the Gorgon's head. On a vasepainting one sees the Dionysos-child in the egg, in the act of breaking through the shell, with a band around the left arm. Helle holds the scepter in the left hand; Dike, the daughter of Astraios, is enthroned in the starry sky with a full ear of grain in the left hand. — If here, in the first instance, only the connection of the left side with the woman, the underworld, and the egg emerges, the following examples show us its kinship with the maternal, nourishing and renewing power. According to the "Metamorphoses" of Apuleius, in the Isis procession the fourth priest carries a cast of the opened left hand of Isis (symbol, as has been said, of Aequitas) and at the same time a golden bowl full of milk in the shape of a woman's breast. According to Macrobius the finger of the left hand next to the little finger possesses magical healing powers (digitus medicinalis), is therefore adorned with the ring, and is anointed with fragrant salves by the priests at the godimages of the Egyptian temples. Bachofen doubtless hits upon the truth with his assumption that it is precisely this finger which Isis (according to Plutarch), in her role as nurse, puts into the mouth of the child of the king of Byblos, Malkander, and his consort Astarte, in place of the breast.

Other legendary traits and (real or legendary) customs finally speak for the special power and dignity of the left side, for the major honos laevarum partium and thus of the woman, insofar as she is grasped as representative of lifeteeming Chthon. In the oldest auguries it was (according to Bachofen) not the right but the left side that was auspicious. Jason, half son of the sun, half son of the earth, and as such, among other things, the favorite of maternal Hera, goes unshod on the left foot, which an instructive legend explains by symbolic gamos with the chthonic depth: his left sandal, it is said, got stuck in the mire when he waded through the muddy river Anauros! In accordance with the fundamental principle of symbolic thinking, it is, as goes without saying, the same valuing accentuation of the left side that can be expressed by distinguishing unclothing as well as by clothing. When, according to Herodotus (IV.191), many agriculturally occupied Libyans shaved the left side of the head, then through this hair-offering their dependence on the mother-goddess finds expression in a manner similar to the reverence paid to her through the custom of another Libyan tribe, the Adyrmachidai (further the Hernici and the Aetolians), of clothing only the left leg. [p. 1378] On prehistoric gynaecocracy. — With our remarks on left and right there is now evidently confirmed only what shines forth from all the other symbols that we have let pass by: namely, that the mother-symbol created the order of values of the Pelasgian world-picture, consequently determined the cults or, if one prefers, the religious bearing of prehistory, and accordingly assigned to the woman, psychically, indeed a value-height for whose understanding historical man lacks the experiences requisite thereto. Nor can it be denied that, in keeping with this, women temporarily and occasionally fell into a position of power of an extent that did not recur in later times in equal measure; only it would mean substituting merely conceptual facts for symbolic actualities, and consequently confusing the middle of the poles with one of the poles — we mean the woman as the sexual partner of the man — were one to derive from this, for the social associations of prehistory, a fundamental rule of the woman over the man! This would also decidedly contradict natural law, which — at least ideally — knows no ruling such as we understand it, but rather a distribution of centers of power and spheres of efficacy according to the measure of the principles of all self-alive growth. Even had a regiment of women existed, the Pelasgian primal thought would not have been realized by it. But indeed, it did not exist at all.

According to the ethnological researches to which Bachofen's discoveries gave the impetus, and with which he himself, the longer the more, made even the beginning, it admits of no doubt that gynaecocratic associations in the literal meaning of the word, or even so-called states of women and Amazon realms, formed the rarest exceptions, in that, rather, even under pronounced matriarchy — more correctly, by virtue of matriarchy — the exercise, and one might almost say the physics, of power was ever the affair of the man, whereas the selection of the bearers of power and the articulation of competencies followed the requirements of the cult of the Great Mother. We ought not to be surprised that even the initiator himself did not entirely succeed in always clearly keeping the two apart; for that would have required the consciousness-scientific insight into the fundamental difference between symbolic and conceptual thinking! All the less, however, need we fear that findings of ethnology should be capable of invalidating even a single one of the disclosures bearing on the essence of the Magna Mater. — [p. 1379] Hardly anything else could be so well suited to illustrate the distinction in question as the previously touched-upon position of the mother's brother. Were we, in order to gain, by leaving aside all intermediate forms, something like a model case of the social form that would correspond to the most nearly perfect matriarchy possible (and indeed, without regard to the rules of pairing, purely with respect to the distribution of rights of power), to compile from the far-flung material of ethnology at least the chief determinations in which the mother-right character of society's, for the rest, quite various orders finds expression, then the picture would at first look roughly thus: the child's belonging to the clan of the mother (who thus gives the name) — consequently (at least originally) no kinship with the father — predominant right of possession of the women (understood, of course, insofar as, alongside clanproperty, there can be talk of special property at all) — descent from the mother to the children, and especially to the daughters — the daughters' duty of support toward the parents — the husband's dowry to the wife — the women as administrators of the treasure of the tribal community — priestly and judicial competencies of the woman — heavier penalties for insults, offenses against honor, robberies, killings of a woman than of a man. But in this we would have forgotten one of the chief traits, namely the preponderant significance of the mother's brother. Only with it, first of all, may the picture count as sufficiently developed.

Let us note at once the peculiar double meaning of such a position of preeminence! It speaks for the powerlessness of the woman, if in the foregoing enumeration she does not appear as chieftain, king, commander, and so on (which, as has been said, is not typical, but counts among the exceptions); it speaks for the limitation of her power, if it is the brother, sometimes furnished with wide powers, from whose rank and dignity the rank and dignity of, say, the sister's son derive; and it speaks for the power of the woman, if not only the possession of the man, but even — as, for example, in the Pharaonic kingship — the highest dignity passes, not to his own son, but to that of his sister.
