Herewith the quite decided superiority of the female principle makes itself known with regard to the distribution and transmission of competencies and rights, whereas with the sole entitlement of the man to the assumption and actual exercise of such, the superiority of the male principle comes to light no less unambiguously. — Exactly the same relation repeats itself when, in many tales [p. 1380] of the most various peoples (and down into the best-known fairy-tales of the Grimm collection), some jumped-up adventurer becomes king of a foreign land because he has succeeded (however it may be) in winning the heart and hand of a princess: it is she, then, on whose possession it depends whether one may be king or not; but it is her husband who exercises the rule.

Yet the basic thought that regulates, in Pelasgianism, the distribution of powers among the sexes is rooted more deeply. We have indicated, anticipatorily, on p. 976, how far the principle of the woman is a hidden or veiled secret, that of the man the disclosure and revelation of the secret, and in this way constitutes the full-completion. We had to make the same relation good once more for the purpose of characterizing the polarity of mother and child. Both are the same secret, but there in unrevealed, here in revealed form. Not without intention have we just spoken, with respect to the rights of the man, and only with respect to them, of a "coming-to-light"; for these rights are grounded, in the last resort, in the relation of the son to the mother, and have from it both their greatness and breadth and also their limits.

The "divine child" need not by any means always be a boy (Demeter and Kore); but it is a boy in the vastly preponderant majority of cases; and in this it declares itself that, measured against the darkness of the pregnant chaos, the cosmos, because it "steps into appearance," is of masculine and begetting essence. The wall, in Latin murus, come to being through growth, born forth, and child of the earth (as we saw above), is often found clothed with the image of the evil-averting phallus, and is thereby clearly designated as a male child. Not the murus still "sleeping" in the ground (a phrase familiar to the ancients), but only the one "awakened" to the light of day, is able to protect the space consecrated to the Mater, and is, by virtue of this capacity, no less phallic in nature than the blows that it wards off and to which it can succumb. It alone embodies perfection and being-completed, in that it brings a previously secret working into appearance; and that is why the power of accomplishment lies on the side of the man, and mother-cults and phallus-cults belong together. But if, accordingly, in the polarity "mother and son" the male pole seems even to have precedence over the female pole, then it is nevertheless, by virtue of the same polarity, in the filial dependence of all natura naturata upon the Mater, that the mother-boundedness of the male principle of nature is above all and especially emphasized.

[p. 1381] "The woman stands first as mother, the man first as son. Out of the mother-furrow the day is plowed forth" (Bachofen). As mother, then, the woman towers not so much over the woman — who, by virtue of her very womanhood, likewise has a share in motherhood — as rather over the man, who, with respect to his manhood, is indeed only ever born, but does not bear. — Far more convincingly still than in the mother-sonship of God, this comes to representation when antiquity, in works of art, gladly gives to the Great Mother a male assessor (paredos, assessor) in doll-size, who, according to the testimony of legend, is by no means always the son, but perhaps also a foster-child, a ward, or a dwarfish daemon destined for the service of the goddess. Now standing on the ground or on a column, now sitting on the shoulders or knees of the mother-goddess, now borne in her arms, there appear thus: the winged boy Eros beside Aphrodite, Amor beside Venus, Iakchos beside Demeter, Euamerion or Telesphoros beside Hygieia, Sosipolis as well as Plutos as boys with cornucopia beside Tyche or Athena Ergane, the Genius Jovialis beside the Praenestine Fortuna, Anxurus beside Feronia, Melikertes-Palaimon in the arm of Matuta-Leukothea. — If, further, it is the preponderant and usual case, after the victory of spirit-addicted light-gods, that of the male rulers of heaven one descends to the mortal daughters of men in order to beget with them heroes or demigods, then in the older legend the mystical marriage is closed just as preponderantly between the mortal man and the immortal goddess who blesses him with her favor: we recall Eshmun and Astronoe, Tammuz and Ishtar, Attis and Cybele, Adonis and Aphrodite, Endymion and Selene, Jasion and Demeter, Peleus and Thetis. — In the transitional legends the light-heroes often owe their victories to the help of a maiden who appears endowed with magical powers, thus Jason to Medea, Theseus to Ariadne; or they must, temporarily, bow even to the power of the wanton woman, as Herakles to Omphale, Samson to Delilah. Finally, as noted above, the woman steps forth in the legend-mirror of prehistory, if not, as for instance the Egyptian Nitocris herself, as ruling, then at least as that power which has, in the first place, the royal authority to bestow upon the man. The legendary Scottish queen, of whom, according to Saxo Grammaticus, another queen knows to boast: "Whomever she deemed worthy of her bed was at the same time a king, and she bestowed her realm together with her person; thus scepter and person belonged together with her" — thereby lends expression only to that [p. 1382] conception of the descent of the royal dignity which belongs to the type of mother-right society, and traces of which can be shown among almost all the peoples of the earth. Thus Omphale grounds the Lydian Heraklid rule, Semiramis the Assyrian kingship, Hersione raises Priamos to the throne, Tydo raises Gyges, Tanaquil Tarquin and Servius. The memory of many a historical and semi-historical female figure of the early period, and even from the high culture of antiquity, such as Tomyris, Zarina, Artemisia, Kandake, Cleopatra, Julia Domna, Mammaea, the Bohemian women Libussa and Wlasta, the Russian women Olga and Polenitsa Nastasia, may strengthen us in the conviction that those legends faithfully mirror a stage of mankind whose actual community forms stood under the sign, not indeed of a physical rule of women, but assuredly of the cultic preponderance of the Mater. — In accord with this, many symbolic trinities, in sharp contrast to the Christian one, confirm that the psychic preeminence of the woman is only a valuing expression for the real middle position of the Mater between the poles. She is the One who first transforms the two halves of the Two, which without her would fall apart, into poles of the necessarily threefold totality of life, and therefore stands between the left One and the right One as the connecting One in the midst: we recall, for instance, Helena between the two Dioskuroi; the world-creating triad of Pherecydes, which shows us the female Chthon between Zeus and Kronos; the three-shaped Chimaira, whose feminine name derives from the circumstance that it is the maternal she-goat whom we see enclosed by the dragon, the symbol of the fluid element, and the lion, the symbol of fire. Motherhood of the tree. — Having now made intelligible the lowest ground of the double meaning of all symbolic concepts, from their participation in the mother-mystery, there remains for us only still to add, for the symbols of water, moon, and tree — with restriction, however, to the most essential — further evidence to that which we have already offered for a, though variously strong, predominance of the mother-character, and indeed especially from the domain of derived secondary symbols. We begin with the tree, whose motherliness, the most preponderant of all three, emerges especially convincingly in the profound legend-cycle of the oriental Adonis-Attis-Osiris.

We shall here concern ourselves neither with the manifold variations and in part [p. 1383] exceedingly instructive individual traits of the sacred legend that accompanies the service of the Great Mother in Mesopotamia, Phrygia, Libya, Caria, Syria, Phoenicia, Egypt, Hellas and Rome, nor with its kinship relations, placed beyond question by Mannhardt, to the tree-cult observances of the Germans, Slavs and Celts, but direct our attention only to the one circumstance, that each time the tree appears as the symbolic place out of which the bearerperson of all life-revelation springs, and into which it again enters for eternal rebirth. — In the Adonis legend, Myrrha, the king's daughter made pregnant by her father Cinyras, is transformed into a balsam-tree: in the tenth month the bark bursts, and Adonis steps into the light. His return to the place of being of the beginning is found at least indicated by the transformation of his flowing-out blood into anemones and roses. — Attis, indeed, is borne by the daughter of the rivergod Sangarios, yet not by a man, but from the fruit-kernel of a mystical almond-tree, whose prehistory we must presently still touch upon. As he thus stems, at least mediately, from the tree, so his blood goes into the violets, but his soul into the pine-tree, under which he perished after his self-emasculation. But not only the violet-entwined pine accordingly appears in the service of the Great Mother, but the self-emasculation, too, of consecrated "Metragyrtai," "Kybebai," "Galli" becomes a sacred custom in the crushing orgies with which, in Phrygia and Lydia, the wild death-feast of her favorite sweeps by. If we still close our eyes, for the present, to the horrifying violence of these deeds of a "sacred madness," in order for the time being merely to ascertain their meaning, the myth alone would already offer the key. For that fructifying almond-tree has arisen precisely from the severed medea of a bisexual primal being that Agdistis, the goddess of the mountain Agdos, had brought forth, and which the gods thereupon unmanned out of fear of its immeasurable power of generation. Even were it not expressly attested that Agdistis is none other than the primal mother Kybele, the legend itself would betray it, in letting Agdistis appear as mother-goddess and lay claim to Attis for herself at the very moment when the youth, celebrated for his beauty, is on the point of being wedded to the king's daughter of Pessinus. The tree, to which he owes his origin, is thus the primal mother, and the attribute of bisexuality expresses, with reference to her, the capacity for self-active bearing through inner begetting [p. 1384] of the still-unseparated poles. Measured against this, the mutually dependent begetting-urge of the two sexes, each referred to the other, now appears as the half-ness that separates from the fullness of the divine, and the self-emasculation presents itself as an actattempt at bending-back into the state of a super-sexual inwardness of life. In the spirit of the legend Attis returns, through denial of sexual one-sidedness, into filial belonging to the mother, and purchases, at the price of his manhood, the expectancy of rebirth. As the tree was the cradle of his life, so now the tree becomes his grave, whereby the equation proves itself most perfectly: tree = mother's womb = place of the hidden = cradle of what is to be revealed = grave of the revealed life. — In exactly the same double meaning the tree appears in the Osiris myth. The coffin-chest, in which Set and his conspirators have enclosed the murdered Osiris, is driven by the Nile as far as Byblos in Phoenicia; there a heather-tree grows around it, which the country's king sets up as a pillar beneath his house. From it the mother-goddess Isis frees the dead Osiris, and only now can Horus, that is, the Osiris reborn from Isis, take vengeance, while the first Osiris henceforth reigns in the realm of the dead. The devouring and again-giving-birth mother-darkness appears here in the threefold image of the tree, the pillar, the coffin, each of which accordingly at the same time stands in for the place of the other.

Several rites of the Osiris cult transmitted to us confirm that the myth (as it fundamentally always does) merely clothes the meaning of the far older symbol and the customs that sprang from it, in the tendrils of phantasms, and thereby, at the same time, reveals it. Thus, according to the account of Firmicus Maternus, the image of the god, to be sacrificed by burning every year, was made from the wood that had been hollowed out a year before from a felled pine-tree, and which, during this interval, had lain in the hollowed-out trunk as in a coffin — a report whose reliability is illuminated by the circumstance that "in the hall of Osiris at Dendera the coffin with the torch-headed mummy of the god is clearly represented as enclosed within a tree, apparently a conifer, whose trunk and branches become visible above and below the coffin" (Frazer).

Once one has convinced oneself, from such by no means misunderstandable examples, of the mother-meaning of the tree, ever new and further evidence at once streams in, and while, in one respect, astonishing agreements of the legendmotifs among the [p. 1385] most widely separated peoples now first strike the eye, in another, customs and myths of externally the greatest conceivable diversity prove explicable from one and the same point. — Tales after the pattern of the following occur, manifoldly varied, but under strict observance of the motif of motherliness, among the most various peoples. A tree-nymph, living in conjugal community with a human man, returns nightly to her willow by the brook; the man learns of it and fells the willow, whereupon his wife instantly perishes. But out of the willow there now becomes the sheltering and lulling cradle, in which the child left behind, motherly guarded, grows up. — Under a wild strawberry-tree, according to Boeotian local legend, the child Hermes grew up, and Dionysos was known among the Greeks as "Dionysos in the tree" and is depicted, among other things, as pressing forth from a dense bush. — Odin, before he became the most knowing of the gods, hangs nine nights in the tree, exactly the number of months of pregnancy, whereby one should not take it for chance that the month is represented by the night; and again it is the tree, in whose crown those who are sacrificed to Odin, the "hanging god," find their end by hanging. The tree is tree of life and receptacle of the germ, insofar as it releases life out of itself; tree of death, insofar as it takes it back into itself; finally tree of fate (and thus felix as well as infelix arbor of the Romans), because it comprises both what has been and what is not yet come to be, and out of the grave-darkness of its welling inwardness ever anew gives birth again to the original life.

If one wished to detect Christian influence in that Edda passage in the Havamal, one would in any case have had, with incomparably better right, to see in the crucified Christ a pagan tree-sacrifice, to which only a logocentric reinterpretation lent a spiritual-ethical sense; since indeed the legend occasionally transforms the cross back into the tree of life, and well-known works of art bring the Christian redeemer to representation as hanging on a fruit-bearing tree. Even were one to leave it undecided why, in the sacrificial cult and in the profane execution of punishment, which borrowed its instruments of torture from the symbols, the image of a cross came to be made precisely out of the tree-image (three-branched, four-branched, many-branched, straight and slanting), and why in particular the killing occurred quite preferentially at the upper end of the stake or cross (instead of, say, by entombment), no one will nonetheless be able to close himself off from the unity of the basic thought [p. 1386] if he compares side by side: the pagan custom of burying the dead in hollowed-out trees, the Christian egkolpia, that is, cross-shaped reliquary-shrines, and the crosses, so exceedingly frequent by the wayside in Catholic lands, which show, in a hollow in the middle, the image of the divine mother with the divine son, and beneath it the inscription "in gremio matris." — The Christian poetry of the Middle Ages calls the son of God the rod from the root of Jesse, the "fruit on the rod" (Mary), the "wheat in the sheaf" of Mary, the bread of heaven, the satisfying grain. As such he is mown, bound, beaten (martyred), ground (crucified), put into the oven (buried), taken out after three days, and serves as food for the satisfying of thousands. A French custom designated the last sheaf as the "sheaf of the Passion" and carried it home in solemn procession, adorned with laurel branches and a consecrated wooden cross. According to a belief widespread in Silesia, Austria, Swabia, the Mother of God with the Child is supposed to be perceivable in every grain of spelt. "The tree of life," says an office of the Greek church for the eve of Christmas, "blossomed forth in the cave of the Virgin." "And elsewhere Mary is depicted as the blossoming and imperishable garden, in which the tree of life is planted, which imparts to all, without hindrance, the fruit of immortality" (Mannhardt). — If in the execution-customs of impaling, hanging on the gallows, and crucifying, the death-pole of the symbolic tree seems to have hardened into terrible self-sufficiency, we nonetheless sense how even the driest instrument of torture can sink back into the againbearing womb, when we hear that, according to an oriental legend, someone to whom it was granted, after the Fall had taken place, to look once more into Paradise, found the tree there withered, but in its branches a — little child lying. — Yet we can trace the symbolic thinking here even into individual details. If we lay the emphasis, namely, on the relation that the mother-place gains, through its middle position, to the poles, then it appears in the symbol of the trunk that forks into that middle position; whereby there opens at once to understanding, in the first place, the substitutability of the tree by the cross, and especially by one of tau-shape (Taugestalt, that is, T-shape); further, the necessity of the fork-form for the life-rod, the divining-rod, the original Hermes-staff, and the preference enjoyed, in tree-veneration, by forked, twin-branching trunks that grew together again above; [p. 1387] finally the widespread custom of drawing crippled children through such a fork for the purpose of healing. — But because both poles come to appearance most grandly in the intuitable contrast of heaven and earth, the tree's cosmic mother-place lies high above in the crown, and is, as such, both an air-akin place of sacrifice and dying (impaling, hanging and crucifying) and also the place of the resurrection of so many sacrificial gods to an "eternal" life. To withdraw the Zeus-child from the pursuing Kronos, the nurse Amaltheia hangs it in the crown of a tree, so that, as the legend knows to explain, it might be found neither in heaven nor on earth: the mother-place that guarantees rebirth is the undivided middle of actuality, the cosmic egg before its splitting, the stillunfolded inwardness, and is therefore not discovered in the visible world, which fell apart, polarically, into heaven and earth, above and below, brightness and darkness, man and woman, coming-to-be and passing-away. — With this we have, incidentally — and let it be mentioned only incidentally — discovered, if not the sole, then certainly the decisive ground of the world-spread belief in the all-surpassing holiness and the well-nigh unbounded magical efficacy of certain plant species that thrive not in the ground but (parasitically) in the crown of trees; to which, besides a special species each of the rowan and mountain-ash, above all, as is well known, the legend-shrouded mistletoe belongs. The Druids, according to the report of Pliny, cut it, under solemn ceremonies, from the sacred oaks with golden sickles, and it had, if it fell down, to be caught, so that it might not by any chance touch the ground. — It is worth our while to turn aside for a moment from the tree-cult, and, in connection with the foregoing examples, to illuminate the connections that the beholding thinking, in strict boundedness, pursues.

Insofar as the creative life-place lies between the poles, we may expect from the outset that the bearing and renewing efficacy will quite generally attach itself to the passing through the middle of all those appearances that can in any way be thought of as bearers of living rule. Accordingly, for example, covenant-making parties among the ancient Hebrews passed between the two halves of the divided sacrificial animal; in East India the mothers passed with their newborns between two fires. To the same order belong all the original baptismal acts, in which the one being baptized was drawn through, whether by water or by a flame (up to a fourfold [p. 1388] repetition); to the same order belong the customs, spread over all the peoples of the New World as of the Old, of youths and maidens leaping through sacred fires, of driving herds through them for the purpose of averting feared evils or freeing from present ones. — Insofar, on the other hand, the creative life-place lies as the unformed unity in the darkness of the interior, rebirth presupposes passage through the most various kinds of caves (of rocks, earth-mounds, trees, animal bodies), the choice of object again resulting, as is to be understood, from elementary similarities. Age-old rites of rebirth have given the impulse to fairy tales of this kind: such as that of Jonah in the belly of the fish; of Herakles, who according to one version of the Hesione saga slays the sea-monster by diving down into its gullet, in order to emerge again on the third day unharmed, if hairless; of little Monedo of the Ojibwe Indian tribe, who is likewise swallowed by a fish and cut out again by his sister; of Tom Thumb in the cow, of Little Red Riding Hood or the seven kids in the wolf, and so forth; and this can often be demonstrated quite directly in other legends as well. According to a Zulu legend, forests, rivers, lands, dogs, and men are swallowed by the "Great Elephant"; a warrior slays him, and at once all step out again one after another, each in its own way uttering the words: I see the world! In the Scandinavian Eirek saga the hero must, on his wandering toward paradise, cross a stone bridge before which a dragon lies as guardian: he crawls into its belly and at once finds himself in the world of the blessed. Maui, the cosmic hero of the New Zealanders, is to overcome Hine-nui-te-po, his mighty ancestress. While she sleeps he creeps into her for that purpose; she wakes, however, and crushes him between her thighs. Thus death came into the world; but had Maui penetrated her body and emerged again unharmed from her mouth, mankind would be immortal. — In certain mysteries of Isis the novice was, after the model of Osiris, enclosed in a coffin; in those of Mithras he received the blood-baptism in the interior of a pit covered with planks; in an Indian rite of purification he crept through the interior of an artificial cow. According to a fertility charm of the New Caledonians, the girl, on entering the age of maturity, is buried in the earth, and this is struck with the (phallic) rod. — Insofar, finally, as the creative life-place is the connecting Third of below and above, earth and heaven, woman and man, [p. 1389] its symbol is every threefold form, and in its most abstracted version becomes the Three, the uppermost of all sacred numbers. As in the countenance of the All, so it rules in the symbols, customs, and legends of practically the whole of Pelasgian mankind. We have again and again come to know evidence of this, and here recall once more the parting of the ways or the three-way crossing, the place of "three-formed" Hecate and of all nocturnal magic.

Nebenher have we now also at once learned of the maternal significance of the sacred basket or chest, which, out of incomparably older folk-conceptions, penetrated — one may well say — into every secret cult, and always plays in that double light according to which it is, as cradle, also again coffin, and, as coffin, also again cradle. It has now the form of a basket (kystos) or of a fruit-bowl, now of the box or the chest (cista), now of the ash-urn or coffin (larnax, arca), of the sieve (cribrum), of the barrel (dolium), of the bushel (modius), and finally of the winnowing-shovel or grain-fan (likmos, liknon). Among the formulas by which, according to the testimony of the Orphic gold tablets, the soul of the dead proved itself before the goddess of the underworld to belong to the band of the initiated, there is found, besides others, the so-called Eleusinian formula: "I have fasted, I have drunk the mixed drink, I have taken out of the chest, and after I had done this, I laid it in the basket and then again back into the chest." According to a Roman relief, the mystes stands veiled before the deity while a woman holds a grain-fan over him. The identity of essence with the cradle emerges, among other things, from the folk custom of giving cradles the shape of the Demetrian grain-fan. On the other hand Demeter, as also the Erycinian Venus, is gladly depicted with a great modius upon her head. The sieve of Vesta, the cask of the Danaids, the barrel of Diogenes all belong to the same basic conception. The oneness of meaning of all of these with that of the tree is grounded not so much in the fact that each of them is made from its wood, as rather in the intuitive property of an enclosing hollow space, which, just like the shading crown, the concealing thicket of leaves, or also the enveloping bark, has a mysterious interior to hide. Legend often brings this to expression far more definitely still than happened in the Osiris myth through the assignment of the very same role to coffin-chest, heather-tree, and pillar, in that it either, for example, adds to the tree-birth of a demigod a second birth out of the cista [p. 1390], or has the sacred chest made out of a tree that is, for its part, itself already sacred. Thus, according to one turn of the Adonis legend, the tree-born child is enclosed by Aphrodite in a small chest and handed over to Persephone. Of the cult-place of the Praenestine Fortuna, where formerly her oak-wood lots had broken forth out of the shattered flint stone, Cicero reports in his treatise on divination: "This spot is to this day conscientiously fenced in, close beside the temple of the boy-Jupiter, who, sitting as an infant with Juno in the lap of Fortuna, reaches for the breast and is venerated by mothers with the greatest devotion. And at that same time, where the temple of Fortuna now stands, honey is said to have flowed from an olive tree, and the sacrificial seers are said to have declared that those lots would attain great renown, and at their bidding a small chest was made from that olive tree and the lots kept within it, which are now drawn at the beckoning of Fortuna." This means, in the form of communication proper to legend: Mother-goddess = olive tree == chest (as dwelling-place of the lots of fate). — Like the tree and the egg, the mystica vannus too harbors what is coming and what has been, white and black, the male phallos and the female ear of grain, and, like the maternal womb of Rhea, it withdraws from the gaze of the uninitiated the unceasing gamos of the opposites still joined within it, of which the eternal cycle of appearing happening is the revelation that abides only in change. But just as we found, in the preference for the image of the divine Mother with the divine Son, the opposition of secret and revealed actuality expressed at once through the polarity of the bearing power turned into the begetting one, so too what the chest releases from itself is preferentially the male phallos, just as the Eleusinian mystes lays this too out of the basket into the chest — although still in the itself again ambiguous form of the serpent, which does not thereby forfeit its participation in both poles, in that it does indeed become, over against the receiving soul of the epopt, a symbol of the fertilizer. So it is, for instance, the male earth-daemon Erichthonios whom Athena locks into the mother-chest; so Dionysos, after his birth, is laid in a basket woven of willow and venerated at Patras as Dionysos arcanus, in that the symbol of the hidden god, the larnax, is carried about in nocturnal procession. — But this chest now has yet another kindred companion-image, which leads us over to the maternal character of water: we mean the ship, which shows its significance [p. 1391] as the maternal womb enclosing all seeds of life most unmistakably perhaps in Noah's Ark. Motherhood of water. — As surely as water is the wet that fertilizes, when we think above all of swiftly hurrying streams or indeed of falling rain, so surely does it become the nourishing wet where it breaks from the earth as a spring, and the maternal moisture pure and simple in the swamps, marshes, and inland lakes that cover themselves inexhaustibly of their own accord with the most luxuriant plant growth; and this meaning forms, in keeping with the gravitation of beholding thought toward the maternal center, the essence-determining background of the water-world as such. In the spirit of this same mode of apprehension stands the ship, whose thousandfold relations to the cults of the Great Mothers we must forgo discussing in detail, which stands to water not in opposition but belongs most intimately together with it. As it bears life, so is it itself borne by the wave; as it embraces and shelters life, so does it itself take shelter in the embracing flood. "The Egyptians," says Plutarch, "do not have the sun and moon perpetually driven about on chariots, but in ships, to indicate that these derive their origin and their nourishment from moisture." The Greek legend too knows the ark that saves life from the all-destroying floods: in a chest Deukalion and Pyrrha land on Mount Othrys. But if the water has already swallowed up an entire mankind, it is likewise the water that presents the land with the life-sheltering chest, and it would therefore lie close at hand to think the meaning of the creative place transferred onto it. Accordingly, for example, according to the local legend of Prasiae, the Dionysos-child is washed ashore from the sea in a chest and then raised by Ino. Who would not at once think of the like legends of Moses, Siegfried, Perseus, and who would fail to notice that we have thereby already come into the neighborhood of the notion of the seed-pregnant nature of water itself, according to which newborns come, say, from the children's well of Frau Holle or from the pool of Bethesda! Equivalent to the ark is the fish, which bears the god or demigod as the dolphin bears Arion and Dionysos, or which harbors him alive and unharmed in its belly; further, seaweed, sea-grass, reeds, rushes, out of which he must be peeled like the child from the mother's womb. In a Polynesian legend the hero's ship is wound about by the tentacles of a giant octopus; in [p. 1392] another it is the Polynesian sun-god Maui himself, whom his mother hid in the sea-grass and wickerwork of the sea and wrapped about with slime-fish, until his ancestor, the sky, freed him from it. With this the essence-creating role widens into a world-creating one, and the terra mater steps to the side as a second manifestation of cosmic motherhood alongside the maternal sea, he thalassa tes geneseos symbolon, in which meaning the oldest of the Ionian natural philosophers carried it over into scientific consideration, in that he declared water to be the primal matter out of which everything whatsoever had arisen. The model for this thought too may be counted as the common property of symbol-forming thinking. The Buddhist Mongols have the foam come first from the sea, but all living essence derive from it; according to a legend of the Peruvians, everything created proceeded from Mama Cocha, the sea. From Lake Copais the Boeotians, from Lake Titicaca the South American Collas, derived their origin. Elsewhere the same opinion is expressed by having, not the world itself, but that being which for its part brings forth the world, or at least its most flourishing life, arise from the sea: from the foam of the sea emerges the Indian Lakshmi, the Greek Aphrodite, the Peruvian Viracocha. Those arriving on ships were held there to be immediate "children of the sea" = "Viracochas," namely the Spaniards, and for a long time afterward every European. The "water of life," with its regenerating and rejuvenating efficacy, which nonetheless discloses its double nature in the twofoldness of the springs, that of forgetting and that of remembrance; the legend of the Savior's mother Mary as the "Stella maris" or the "sempiterni fons perennis" — these are all only different forms in which the same basic thought is shaped, according to which, alongside the earth, a symbol of the cosmic mother of all destinies is the nourishing as well as devouring water; wherefore, in the cults of the Great Mothers of the whole of Pelasgianism — from the Germanic Nerthus to the Phrygian Cybele — the bathing of her image (together with ship or chariot) belonged among the most sacred observances, which were woven about with the darkest of shudders.

Meanwhile, one thing should not be forgotten amid all trains of thought of this kind. Everything that we can adduce, by pointing to the inner logic of beholding thought and by the aid of intuitive similarities, in order to bring existing symbols nearer to understanding, tells us nothing about how a symbol arises, but only [p. 1393] with which others it belongs together by essential kinship, and to what kind of world-view it would lead if one undertook to make the symbolic unity of meaning the starting point of judging reflection. Whoever thinks in symbols does not at the same time think about symbols, and remains as far removed from all such considerations as he already possesses in them the result of a differently constituted questioning, by which he is guided in place of the question of fact. The demands of symbolic reflection are at work in him, but — in contrast to logical reflection — he would at the very same moment be unable to go on fulfilling them, were he, like us, to become conscious of them. If we could not avoid carrying out an operation of understanding-bound dissection upon certain symbols, this happened and happens solely for the sake of the proposition to whose establishment our efforts are exclusively directed, namely that the object of ensouled thinking is not things but images — a proposition that is to gain its decisively probative confirmation only from the connections that its most various findings show us in the light of a "system" of connections just as unbroken as, for us, is the system of causally connectible facts. However certain it is that the connections in question exist, just as little are they there because they would have been thought. The "logic" of which we speak is a logic not of the spirit — for the spirit would rather contradict it point by point — but solely and entirely of an experiencing that wrests its decisions from the spirit, from case to case, in an immediate way. No symbol was ever hunted down by an effort of reason; each is rather "given from within," and only through such inward giving could one become aware of a state whose knowledge is a knowledge in symbols; only through the poetic content of clairvoyant speech, finally, would it be communicated. How the symbols of the tree, of water, of the moon may once have formed themselves — that only one could know who had at least relived the crushing shudders that ran down upon the Pelasgian from the crowns of sacred oaks, that murmured mysteriously out of the babbling of springs, that in silvery moonlit nights spanned the soul with a magic net; since he would then, to be sure, not lack indirect testimonies for the actuality-value of his beholdings. One need only compare what a Tacitus tells us of the sacred grove of the Semnones, which one entered only in bonds, and through which whoever had stumbled in it had to roll himself along the ground, and one will

 [p. 1394] sense something of the demonic fullness of revelations that could fall to the soul's eye at the sight of a forest, and recognize it as hopeless to wish to bridge the gulf that separates our condition of standingalongside reflectiveness from the condition of a mankind situated within world-happening itself. To penetrate into it, even if only from without, say by the hand of genuine poetry, does not belong among the tasks of this book; and even the exposition of the "laws" of ensouled understanding is meant only to help deepen insight into the life-foundations of the unensouled, into the opposition of the ruled to the ruling Logos, and finds its conclusion with the ascertainment of those life-processes under whose presupposition the intervention of spirit, and with it a conceptual apprehension of the world, can alone be thought possible. Motherhood of the moon. — The complete grounding of the maternity of the moon would first require a complete grounding of the meaning of night, for whose motherhood we already argued above that mother-right peoples reckon not by days but by nights, and not by solar years but by lunar years, for which the rest may be referred to Bachofen. According to the original conception of the whole of Pelasgianism, it is "the darkness that bears the light for itself," the day thus a hemera nykterine, a fatherless offspring of Mother Matuta, and comparable to a mortal being enclosed between two darknesses, the one out of which it breaks forth with the dawn, and the other into which it sinks with the evening glow. The cosmogony of Hesiod has Aether and Hemera arise out of Erebos and Nyx, and the name of the mother of the light-god Apollo, Leto, was already derived by the ancients from lethein, lanthanein. But to convey insight into the nature of the inner necessity that compels the equating of the maternal center with the nocturnal pole of actuality, more than one sensory point of connection would be offered already by the familiar togetherness of that pole with space, with inwardness, and with the below. It is not space that shines, but within it the fire of the stars, which it for its part surrounds with eternal darkness, just as the darkness of the mother's womb surrounded the child that, like the stars, broke forth out of it; and the rays of these heavenly flames flicker from above downward. In keeping, moreover, with a similarity intelligible to us even without further ado, death is brothered to [p. 1395] sleep, falling asleep therefore to dying, and awakening to coming-into-being. If we can accordingly call the place of unrevealed life also that of sleeping life, then it becomes wholly evident that it can be understood only as the soul of the image of darkness.

With this said in advance, there result for the maternity of the moon at least four equally essential grounds, most of which have already been adduced earlier: its property as the ruling star of the night — the changeability of its luminous form, which places it within the cycle of becoming and passing away — its ever-recurring egg-shape — and its neighborhood to and likeness with the earth, believed in by all Pelasgians, which for its part again rests on a manifold of appearances. To begin with the last point, it would be an easy matter to demonstrate, from testimonies of every period, that mere feeling-bound contemplation was and is always inclined to hold the moon for a kind of heavenly earth, situated much nearer to the earthly earth than the sun and stars. Beside designations of the ancients for the moon such as ourania ge and aitheria ge, or familiarissimum nostrae terrae sidus (Pliny, Cicero), one need only set the following two verses of Hölderlin, sprung from immediate inspiration, in order to convince oneself, across ages and peoples, of the likeness of the underlying feelings:

See, and the image of our earth, the moon / comes now too in secret; the rapturous one, the night, comes! / But even more than the feelings that speak from such turns of phrase and

poet's words, it must rather have been bodily feelings, indeed genuine sensations, to which the belief in the moon's earthly nearness chiefly owes its origin. Let us call to mind only the generally assumed influence of the moon upon growth, upon the hatching of eggs and upon births, the quite unusually high significance that magic everywhere attaches to the moon, the periodically recurring assumption of a "moonsickness" that manifoldly determines the life of certain people — and we shall scarcely doubt influences of the moon, or rather of its light, which — hidden from "science" — were perhaps experienced by the world-open soul of prehistoric man as strongly and regularly as ebb and flow were experienced from the sea, and are thereby led to seek in them the chief cause for the earth-belonging of this wandering star [p. 1396]. And with this there fused the likewise intuitive connection between moonlight and the vapors and mists that weave over meadows and moist grounds on star-clear nights, as the favored expression of the udae ignes of the heavenly queen alone already shows. According to the opinion of the Egyptian astronomers, Plutarch relates, the moon has "a fertilizing and moistening light, which favors both the thriving of animals and the growth of plants"; and: "So too the Stoics say that the moon receives from spring- and marsh-waters sweet, gentle exhalations." Finally, the mild and cool shining of the moon, and especially, in southern lands, its contrast to the boiling, blinding, and parching violence of the sun's rays, may have strengthened the assumption of the earthly essence of the moon.

As has already been set forth above in another connection, what places the moon on the side not only of the earth but preeminently of unceasing passing-away, and hence of receiving and suffering, of passivity, is its ever-recurring, alternating waning of light, in which, since the earliest days, custom and legend have been accustomed to see the stellar prototype of the inconstancy of all earthly life, entirely in the manner of the old Frankish song that begins with the verses:

It surely cannot always stay this way / here beneath the changing moon.

— The intuitive similarity to the egg, which is still today apt to be independently rediscovered by every child, completes the relation to motherhood. It is the cosmic moon-egg that the world-mothers Artemis, Persephone, Hecate carry in their hands, and whose primal-image identity with their own essence the legend grounds now in its arising from the mother-goddess, now in the mother-goddess's arising from it. All moon-women, the ancients judged, are egg-bearing.

But more sharply now than in the tree and in the water — insofar as the latter is equated with maternal moisture — there emerges, in the motherhood of the moon, by virtue of its luminosity, the revealing and bearing power, and — since this comes to efficacy only through the constant union of the already separated poles — the motherliness that, needing to be fertilized, takes the male into itself and, through new birth, transforms it back into a child. The "man in the moon," beheld together out of the [p. 1397] spot-appearances of the full moon, is equally the man who, begetting, has entered into femaleness, and the — embryo in the mother's womb; and when even today the helplessness of more soulful natures in the life of the day is occasionally characterized by the turn of phrase that someone behaves as if he had "fallen from the moon," there lies in this an unconscious allusion to the symbolically real moon-descent of Pelasgian mother-man, whom Hesiod, in the race of the silver age, describes thus:

For a hundred years now was the child, beside its worthy mother, / tenderly reared, and grew up a minor in its own house.

Thus it is explained that the moon can also be grasped as male. The lion is without doubt a symbol of fire and of manhood; but the Nemean lion, which the bloodthirstiest of all heroes of light and spirit, the child-murderer Herakles, slays not by chance before its cave, belongs, together with the serpents of Hera, the Hydra of the Lernaean swamp, the hind of Artemis, the Centaurs, the Erymanthian boar, the Stymphalian birds, the Poseidonian bull, the mares of Diomedes, the Amazons, Antaeus, the giant Geryon, the guardian dragon of the apples of the Hesperides, the underworld hound Cerberus, Acheloos — to the demonic retinue of the Great Mother; for it had fallen down from the moon onto the land of Apia! Offspring and champions of the moonmother are the egg-shell-covered Dioscuri and Molionidae, and it is the torch of night with reference to which Dionysos, like Osiris, is called nyktophaes and lampter. Instead of many individual examples we adduce, in support of the foregoing, a few passages from Plutarch's essentially accurate and deeply learned account of the Egyptian moon-cult (in "Isis and Osiris").

The moon, he says, "they call the mother of the world and ascribe to it a hermaphroditic nature, in that it is impregnated and fertilized by the sun, but then itself also spreads and scatters seed-particles into the air." "Isis is supposed to be none other than the moon, and this they prove from her statues, which are furnished with horns to represent the change of the moon. Her black garments, however, they interpret as referring to the moon's concealments and shadowings, in which she longingly follows after the sun." The god who enters into the moon-goddess, and thus in turn also proceeds forth from her, is Osiris. For Typhon, according to the interpreters' opinion, signifies [p. 1398] the sun's power, Osiris on the other hand the moon-world. "Osiris had lived twenty-eight years... and it is likewise as many days in which the moon appears and travels through its course." His death occurs at full moon, and his corpse is divided by the conspirators into fourteen pieces, corresponding to the number of nights of the waning moon from full moon to new moon. "At the new moon of the month Phamenoth, which is the beginning of spring, they celebrate a festival that is called Osiris's entrance into the moon... They also say that there he cohabits with Isis, who is the coming-into-being." The double sense of this moon-world, whose side of death was called Gorgo by the Greek, Nephthys by the Egyptian, he elucidates, with the whole subtlety of late-antique interpretive art, by means of the sacred sistra. "The sistrum is round all around at the top, and in its rim are fixed the four movable rods. This is meant to signify that whatever arises in the world and again passes away is encompassed by the moon's disk, and that everything in it is moved and changed by the four elements: fire, air, water, and earth. Quite at the top, on the rim of the sistrum, is placed the image of a cat with a human face; below the movable rods, however, on the one side the face of Isis, on the other the face of Nephthys. With these two faces one points to the coming-into-being and the passing-away of things, which are the changes and movements of the elements; but with the cat, to the moon, because this animal is many-colored, active by night, and fruitful." In sentences as simple as they are exalted, even if evaluative after the manner of the Platonists, he finally unrolls the image of an eternally-becoming, never-being actuality. "According to Heraclitus, it stands with the world just as with a lyre or a bow, whose strings are now drawn taut, now let slack; and Euripides says:

From the good the evil cannot be parted; / in right measure the two are ever mingled.

Hence, then, also stems that age-old opinion, which was carried down from the theologians and lawgivers to the poets and sages, and which, even though its first originator cannot be named, is for that reason no less certain and reliable, since it does not rest on mere legends and rumors, but is taught, in connection with mysteries and sacrifices, everywhere among Greeks as among barbarians alike: namely, that this universe is neither left ungoverned to chance, nor [p. 1399] is it ruled by a single rational being as though by a rudder or a rein... but that there must be two distinct primal beings and mutually opposed forces, of which the one leads to the right hand and straight ahead, while the other turns aside and drives back again. Hence, then, human life, and, if not the whole world, at least this sublunary earth, is so unequal, so manifold, and subject to changes... To this opinion, now, the most and the greatest of the wise are inclined." We have come to know this same primal thought in a thousandfold refractions, and know that it governs the entire symbol-world.

A Roman tomb inscription reads: Priapus mortis et vitai locus. — Shiva is depicted with a necklace of skulls and the lingam in his hand. He dispenses life and death; so too Varuna, so too Odin, so too Sesostris, so too Isis. — "The former of light," says Isaiah, "is also the author of darkness; the creator of peace is also the founder of calamity." — Creusa possesses two drops of the blood of the dying Gorgon: the one drop brings death, the other healing. — Mercury's staff lulls to sleep and awakens from death. — On sacred Delos no one may die, but neither may anyone be born. — The wreath adorns the bride, but also the coffin. — The color of death is black, like the veiling dark and Wodan's helm of concealment, and yet again also white: the souls of the dead prefer to appear as white doves. Many peoples mourn in black, some in white. — The Chinese used to, and in part still, put on their burial garment on their birthday. — The Getae wailed at the birth of a child and, conversely, celebrated the death of their tribesmen as a festival. All ancient festivals are festivals of the dead. — Now that, in step with the moralizing of mankind, the profound law of compensation that determines the way beholding reflection apprehends events has had to yield to the mere demand- and wish-thought of "guilt and atonement," we do not want to fail to recall the essentially different decision that early thinking, under the aftereffect of the symbols, knew how to win from it for the course-form of fate. The whole (especially Greek) legend, and in particular the poetry of the great tragedians, is pervaded by the basic assumption — as uncanny as it is touching to every feeling sense with the power of a hidden truth — that man brings about the doom precisely by those very measures of his forethought [p. 1400] by which he seeks to avoid it. One need only think of the house of Tantalus, and above all of Oedipus! With this disposition, equally foreign to the Christian as to the scientific man, historical antiquity, notwithstanding its boundless drive toward spiritualization, confesses itself to a pathic morality, for which ruin comes not from sin but from transgression, and which holds hybris — that is, self-willed volition, and ultimately the deed as such — to be the primal source of all transgression —

[p. 1401]

#### 75. Kapitel — Nachtrag über den Ursinn des Opfers — Chapter 75 — Supplement on the Primal Meaning of Sacrifice

But there is now a deed that is so little to be separated from the cults, of Pelasgianism too, that it forms rather their probably most important act: the deed of sacrificing. Insofar as by this were understood only the expression of the duty of repayment arising from the feeling of being a debtor of life, and, as it were, that perpetual tribute of thanks of which we have treated at length, no further words would indeed be needed. But the deed-character of sacrifice, as it confronts us fearinspiringly wherever violent incursions are made, on the part of those who sacrifice, into the life-sphere of those who must furnish the sacrifice with goods or with blood, does call for explanation.

We recall first of all that, in principle, everything attainable by the will can be sacrificed, insofar as it signifies a good in any respect: the virginity of the woman (ritual duty of surrender), the expectancy of the woman, or also of the man, of satisfying the sexual drive (ritual commandment of chastity), sleep (ritual vigil), food (the tabooing of certain foods as well as temporary complete fasting, under some circumstances unto death), personal freedoms of every kind and every degree (up to the utmost enslavement of the sacrificial person), in particular free movement (up to lifelong imprisonment); further, any and all property (in things, implements, field-crops, animals, and so on); finally, living bodies or cultically essential parts of such (of plants, animals, humans, in particular hair, teeth, skin, and — not to be forgotten — blood), which, though not always, yet very predominantly, involves the killing of the sacrificial being, in part under frightful tortures. In view of the foregoing possibilities we now have to establish in advance: one will not find the god or demon to whom sacrifices are not offered, nor the desirable possession of which one has not divested oneself in sacrificial service, nor the natural manifestation of life [p. 1402] whose temporarily violent omission or mastering does not occur somewhere among the indispensable sacrifices; and one need not think of the sacrificial frenzies of the Aztecs, which led to the depopulation of the surrounding Indian tribes, of the Carthaginians' gruesome service of the child-devouring Moloch, of the headhunters of the South Seas and the like, in order to find human sacrifice; for it was without question spread over all peoples. "The god whom one eats," as familiar to the Christian as to the heathen, was at some time perhaps everywhere a "man whom one ate," in that one drank his blood and consumed his flesh. So-called cannibalism reaches up into Pelasgianism itself; just as it, conversely, of course roots without exception in prehistoric mysticism.

Were one to go through these same myths and legends and rites, from which we have sought to win back the contours of the Pelasgian world-picture, for all the data that reveal, with more or less great certainty, customs of human sacrifice — one would find them everywhere, one would find them with regard to every class of human being, from the male infant to the old man, from the female infant to the old woman, and one would find an uncanny manifold of ways of practicing it. Frazer, indeed, in his well-known work "The Golden Bough," could undertake a traversal of the entire domain of the cults of primitives and of Pelasgianism by way of the theme of the "sacred regicide," as though along the middle road from which one arrives, by cross-paths and connecting paths, at the darkest ceremonies of the most remote groups! Since everything pertaining to this subject can be read up in him, we may content ourselves with quite a few indications.

Not only in the orgiastic cult of Dionysos were sacrificial victims, according to the testimony of legend, torn apart (Lycurgus, Pentheus, likewise also Romulus) or even devoured (Hippasos), but also the magical ceremonies of more or less all the Indo-Germanic peoples at sowing and harvest, at the beginning of spring and of winter, at the solstices and equinoxes (the pretended throwing of a man or a girl into the fire, the burning of effigies or figures), at the conjuring up of rain or of drought (one need recall the customs from the sphere of tree-worship) — leave no doubt that on such occasions, at an earlier time, among other things, human beings were crushed, cut to pieces, quartered, roasted, burned to ashes, drowned, beheaded, strangled, buried alive, and in some circumstances also eaten. Stories such as that of Tantalus, who feasts the gods [p. 1403] with the cooked corpse of his son, or of the intended slaughter of Isaac by Abraham, or of Kronos, who devours his children, speak of the wide diffusion of the sacrifice of the firstborn. The ever-recurring fairy-tale motif of the beautiful king's daughter who must be delivered up to a dragon that would otherwise lay waste the land, the legends of the type of the sacrifice of Iphigenia to obtain a favorable sailing wind, the story of King Moab, who hopes to save the besieged city by offering his son as a burnt offering on the wall, the periodically recurring human tribute of the Athenians to the legendary Minos of Crete, the swallowingup of celebrated heroes by an opening earth-chasm, or their perilous descent into the underworld — all this and countless more testifies incontrovertibly that there has hardly been an adversity of fate, a want or an emergency, that one did not attempt to meet, hindering it or warding it off or forestalling it, with human sacrifices.

But historical evidence, too, is not lacking. Thus in the cult of Attis the high priest of Pessinus was slain every year; among the Egyptians, at the grave of Osiris, a red-haired man was burned every year; among the Babylonian Sacaea a criminal was regularly sacrificed (in place, however, of the king, of which more presently); according to the unimpeachable testimony of ancient authors, numerous sacrificial victims were burned alive by the Druids every five years; captives of war were at times offered up to the gods by the Germans — not to speak of the fearful self-mutilations that meet us in manifold form in Oriental and Asiatic cults. Were one further to bring in the "superstitious" sacrificial rites in the narrower sense, which extend well into historical times, such as the wallingup of a human being (usually a child, but often also of adults) for the purpose of securing the durability of a newly erected house, a bridge, a rampart, and so on, one would not soon come to an end. Among all these customs, moreover, there is not a single one to which similar customs of primitives, described by eyewitnesses, would not correspond!

The wrong path that the excess of bloody sacrifice in heathendom generally, and especially among primitives, without doubt marks out, man could not have taken without spirit. In that spirit at least strove to isolate souls still wholly woven into the life of the community, it produced in them, first, the (essentially indeterminate) anxiety, [p. 1404] and, as a consequence of it, presently the *fear* of the mystical causes of the anxiety, and, finally, the will to ward these off by magical measures against — the frightened soul itself! Whatever in the magism of prehistory presents itself to us as excess is, in its sense and origin, defensive magic arising from a beginning loosening of the connections of one's own essence with the cosmos, and from the darkening of the operative powers inseparable from this. We have already spoken of this at the beginning of the section (as also elsewhere) and content ourselves now with pointing out that the demons round about him, with whom the primitive stands in more intimate connection than with the facts round about him, sorted themselves in a manner similar to that in which, for the animal in him, beings in general sort themselves, namely into friendly or so-called good ones and hostile or so-called evil ones — except that now all of them become dangerous powers, since, by virtue of their demonism, their friendliness too can turn into hostility at any moment. Perhaps the most convincing example of this is offered by the circumstance that without exception every taboo owes its sphere of power not so much to the abundance that it might be destined to guard, as to the scope of the ruin that the non-fulfillment of its demands would bring with it, and therefore everywhere manifests the tendency to transform itself from something holy into something poisoning. Stronger than the Eumenid in him is the Erinys; in keeping with which the cults of the renewal of the past (through deeply erotic ancestor-worship) become ominously entangled with the somber rites of warding-off, the bloody ones for the appeasement of vampiric ghosts. — Only if we now leave this line in the life of prehistory entirely aside — a line that has been traced exclusively by folklore studies up to now, and, to a considerable extent nonetheless, by the science of myth as well — can we hope perhaps to see the shadowy outline of the primal meaning of the idea of sacrifice begin to dawn.

But even so we should not succeed, were we not granted three states of affairs, of which, however, two are already established, while the third is fortunately confirmed by the disclosures of precisely the most outstanding students of myth and of peoples. — In the first place we presuppose that, wherever primal content still inheres in human sacrifice, the state of consciousness both of the doer and of the one who suffers it deviates entirely from that in which we find ourselves whenever we mentally place ourselves in the one or the other. The more the sacrificial act, with regard to the sacrificial being, and especially to the human victim, seems to know nothing at all of the compassion natural to us, with all the greater [p. 1405] certainty must we assume that there occurs, in some form, what becomes unmistakable to us too in the model cases of its manifestation: the state of that encompassing rapture which temporarily tears apart or dissolves the barriers of personhood. (One gauges the span of the possibilities when one calls to mind, one after another, some cultic orgy and the raptures, rare today but formerly widespread, on the occasion of — the Eucharist!) With the help of at least a theoretical knowledge of "hieromania," but not otherwise either, do we understand, or at least surmise, how the deed of sacrificing can cease to be a deed, in that, at the moment of fulfillment, the one sacrificing is granted to merge mysteriously with the sacrifice.

In the second place we presuppose: that which is to be offered, however it may properly be named, is in essence images or, to give at once with the word the kernel of its meaning, primal images. In saying this we are transferring, as will be noticed, to the process of sacrifice only the leitmotif of our entire train of thought, and would have nothing more to add, were it not advisable to protect the sacrificial rule that follows from it — according to which a symbol of the object to be sacrificed is, without restriction, equivalent to it — against that still-prevailing misunderstanding which, among other things, was able to split Protestant Christendom into two groups: the misunderstanding that genuine symbols could mean something without at the same time also being it. Against this, nothing is more certain than that symbol and symbolized are two forms of appearance of one and the same essence, so that it makes no fundamental difference whether, in cultic practice, a human being is burned, or an image shaped like a human being, or finally a genuinely symbolic "sign"; nor whether the beheading or drowning or dismemberment of the sacrificial victim is carried out actually or in genuine symbolic form.

It can (need not) be a "softening of manners" that leads to offering an animal in place of the human being, or the human being's hair, or, in place of the organically living altogether, clay figures; but such a motive does not also explain the choice of the substitute objects, which were rather present long before that motive existed, and which at that time were not yet distinguished from what they were later to "represent." Certainly no one will credit the Aztecs with so much as a spark of "humanity"; the altars of their gods dripped almost continuously with human blood! But that did not prevent them, precisely at the two festivals that were held — [p. 1406] in May and December — in honor of their chief god Huitzilopochtli, with the most solemn pomp, from offering, among other things, a huge image of the god made of dough, and consuming the pieces of the broken image as a sacrament; "the dough cakes being taken for the flesh and bones of the idol," adds the Spanish historian Acosta, to whom we owe the detailed account of all the ceremonies that took place there. And just as here a people of the cruelest sacrificial customs offers now real human beings, now mere images, thereby attesting the essential sameness of the two, so too we find in numerous cases both side by side or even mingled with one another. At their great spring festival the Chinese sacrificed both a real buffalo and the image of a buffalo which — made of clay or colored pasteboard — held several kinds of grain inside it. The most usual mode of sacrifice among the Druids was to enclose the sacrificial human beings (together with sacrificial animals) in a huge wicker *figure* and set it on fire. Now if at European summer festivals (especially in France and Belgium), well into the nineteenth century, giant wicker figures were carried about in procession, not infrequently to be burned at the end, then it can hardly be shown more plainly that the supposed substitute objects with which late and latest times satisfy a sacrificial custom no longer understood were originally themselves among the images to be offered; and from this alone we may read off that the sacrificial cult was only one side of the worship of images.

In the third place we presuppose — something that indeed follows from the foregoing, but must be stated on its own because it is the most important point — that at the outset the sacrifice was always at the same time the demon to whom it was offered. For if one sacrificed primal images, one sacrificed gods, and if one sacrificed gods, one brought, every time, a god as a sacrifice to himself. That myth-research and ethnology are coming more and more to the same conclusion in this matter carries all the more weight in that this happens far from any doctrine of the actuality of images, under the pressure of the facts themselves (with, unless we are mistaken, some contribution from the secret pull that the Christian religion exerts on the minds of thinkers, at the center of which, after all, stands the sacrificial death of a god). With this it is already stated that the evidence reaches exactly as far as our knowledge of sacrificial acts, regardless of which people, which age, and which cultural stage one [p. 1407] singles out; however variously colored the articles of belief may be with which those who sacrifice justify their sacrificing to themselves. Consciousness of the matter could grow dim early on, and did so already in Pelasgianism, because, thanks to the unbounded transformability of the primal images, several forms of appearance were available for every demon, of which — owing to a tendency toward humanization asserting itself everywhere — the older, inhuman forms tended to be retained for the image of the victim, the later half-human or wholly human forms for the image of the god. The goat or bull sacrificed to Dionysus is an image of the original Dionysus; the sacrificial animal of Demeter, the pig, an image of the original Demeter; that of Ammon, the ram, an image of the original Ammon — which here, indeed, is also indicated in the later god by his ram-headedness. Besides the plant or animal companions of the gods, it is above all mixed forms of this kind that silence every doubt as to the sameness in question, and that illuminate at a single stroke why sacrificial plants, sacrificial animals, and sacrificial human beings are, without exception, holy plants, animals, and human beings. Certain sacrificial ceremonies themselves, moreover, speak a language that is if anything still plainer. Did we not see, in discussing the sacrificial customs of tree-cults, that the human being who was symbolically to be offered first had to be transformed, through a magical exchange of garments, into the image of the vegetation to which he fell as a sacrifice!

It is a convenient way of speaking, and for one who knows the score also an unobjectionable one, to say that the Pessinuntine priest who was sacrificed to Attis every year was a "representative" of the god; but one must beware of thereby taking as a basis the concept of representation, which, as is understood, would prompt one to think of one being and then a second being. The priest was the appearance (epiphany) of Attis himself, at that very festival and in that very moment in which he — a sacrifice — fell: Attis to Attis. This discloses to us in a new way what "in place of" means at all in the sacrificial cult, and what consequences it can have that strike us as strange. Because the appearance clings to its material bearer no more than, say, a garment does, the sacrificial act, on the one hand, does not necessarily require an actual killing, and on the other hand the actual killing can be transferred from one person to another person, from the person to a lock of her hair, from a human being to an animal, and so on. The criminal who, among the Babylonian Sacaea, died the sacrificial death [p. 1408] in place of the king was beforehand clothed in all the insignia of royal power and honored as king for five days. He was thus the appearance of the essence of the king, but in this way at the same time the appearance of that being of which the king, for his part, was the appearance: the Babylonian demon Marduk. If we add that, at the moment the sacrifice is performed, those who sacrifice merge psychically with the sacrifice, just as the sacrifice merges with the god, we recognize in the sacrificial act a process of the deification of the human being through his participation in — the demise of the god; with which we have already gone considerably beyond our preliminary consideration and have drawn to within a few steps of the original sense of sacrifice, insofar as it can still be surmised at all.

If we place the emphasis on deification — which for the Pelasgian would admittedly be better called "demonization" — we are led sooner or later to a disposition within the striving for deification that ultimately turns hostile to life, and that unfolds in precisely the measure in which the spirit takes over the place of the soul. Demonization, referred to the soul, means the utmost unleashing of the life of the soul and thus of life itself; deification, referred to the spirit, means the deification of the person — but that would be the utmost outlawing of life. The deification of the person was raised by Christianity to a principle, in that it demanded that God be thought of as a person and declared every extra-personal image of life to be ungodly (which is why the technique of this mode of deification in Christian mysticism, despite its outward opposition to the Church, actually only perfected what the canon of faith had already prefigured). But already in Pelasgianism we come upon enough occurrences in which — unthought and unknown — the demonization of the soul becomes confused with the deification of the person. We cannot go through them here and note only that among them belongs, above all, the excess of tabooing by means of which the priest-king is here and there not so much moved into the center of life as rather isolated in idol-like fashion and set outside the cycles of life. It is no longer pagan belief alone, it is already pagan superstition, when, say, at his enthronement the god-king must swear that henceforth he will let the sun shine and the field be covered with fruits (Mexico).

If, on the other hand, we place the emphasis on the going-under, as that through which alone the fulfillment of life first becomes attainable, then we have arrived at the original sense of sacrifice and see gathered in it, as in a focal point, all the [p. 1409] primal impulses of the Pelasgian attitude toward life. Here, however, we must distinguish what concerns everyone from what concerns only those graced with the highest fullness. The necessity of sacrificing as such concerns everyone, because everyone, as we have seen, receives the share of life and of all the goods of life that is within his grasp — the original suum cuique — only by constantly giving and giving back. But what is meant here is not exchange in the sense of ordinary exchange of goods (which of course likewise received its consecration, in earliest times, from the thought of sacrifice), but the exchange of fluids or essences through the surrender of one's own soul to the sustaining and nourishing life of the world. This could happen continually, and would in fact happen, as it were eventlessly, within a wholly demonic humanity; it happens unavoidably in thrusts, and as it were in moments of breaking surf, as soon as the adversary, the spirit, has a say — even if for the time being still bound and serving. And thus there would arise the painfully joyous festival of sacrifice, in that one voluntarily — that is, out of an irresistible inner compulsion — periodically divests oneself of all that is best and most beautiful, or rather of that to which one is bound by the strongest ties of love: be it implement or plant or fruit or animal or human being, be it the claim to fulfillment of image-laden drives, be it even the "sweet habit" of living on. The one who sacrifices lives in the gift he sacrifices as he lives in his own body, or at the least: he becomes one with it in the moment of sacrificing, thanks to the heightening of Eros through the necessity of parting. And the gift becomes a holy gift, indeed an image of the divine itself and of its eternal going-under through its falling prey to the unmixing elemental powers.

But fullness was apportioned differently, and to the richest fullness corresponds the greatest and heaviest sacrifice. Its bearers — call them heroes, poets, kings, sons of the sun, priests, magi, vestals — stand in immediate connection with the cosmic powers; the others only in mediate connection, namely by virtue of the cults and works and bodies of wisdom that gained shape through those figures. Not because these live for others, but because it is their life, and can be their dying, through which the fullness pours itself out over the others too, their life is a constant self-sacrificing, and their dying can be the sacrificial death that weds whole peoples anew to the "ever-living fire" and weds the primal age to the blood of those now living. Here we have, in god-manhood, the bright and light-streaming side, and we wish to hold it before our eyes as well, by adding to the Mexican [p. 1410] example a counter-example. It can be the therefore effectual "sign" of the perfect concord of the bearer of the primal essence, become personless, with the governance of fate, when, say, the regularly repeated circuit of Pharaoh around the temple guarantees the regular course of the sun. (Certainly, the physical sun would rise and set even without him; but the connection of the souls of the people, of which he is the primal image, with the sidereal images would run the risk of being interrupted, if the change of the stars did not work its way through him and mirror itself in his own change.) — But let us turn our gaze from such forms of sacrificial service, grown strange to us, to the intoxicated excess of self-surrender, thinking, say, of the blood-sacrifice of the warrior in battle, the preferred form of sacrifice of heroic peoples, as Schiller expresses it imperishably in the Cavalry Song: "And if you do not stake your life — never will life be won for you" — then it may become fully clear to us why all the greatness and depth and breadth of life would vanish along with the tragedy of life, and why only in going-under lies fulfillment, only in the dying of the divine images the guarantee of their eternity. — It has been said, and documented with many cultic customs, that every sacrifice ultimately amounts to the rebirth of the victim and, since the victim is after all the demon himself, to the rejuvenation of the life in him, which would otherwise be exposed to aging and withering and growing powerless. There is no doubt that something similar was mirrored here and there in the consciousness of the Pelasgians; but one must have made oneself familiar with the "time-circle of the mother-world" in order to understand to some degree what could be experienced in this, and how, in keeping with such an experience, the originally pagan "eternity" was constituted, in contrast to the false "immortality" which, with the delusive notion of the person's endless continuance, already intruded disastrously into the initiation rites of antiquity before it attained complete victory in Christianity.

In many regions of Central Europe (Franconia, Thuringia, Meissen, the Vogtland, Silesia, Lusatia, Bohemia) there existed, well into the nineteenth century, the custom of the so-called "carrying-out of Death" (usually on Laetare Sunday), in which, characteristically, the essential ceremonies were without exception the affair of girls and women. They carried Death — in the shape, say, of a straw puppet clothed in a shift — out of the village amid solemn songs, destroyed it now symbolically by stripping off its clothes, now literally by [p. 1411] tearing it apart or drowning it, and brought it back in again, now however as Life, by, for instance, clothing the loveliest girl in the garment of the sacrificed Death, or else distributing the pieces of the torn straw image among the young men, who scattered them on the fields for the sake of increasing — fertility! One killed and sacrificed, then, but one killed Death; one won life, but one won it from the hand of death and at the price of killing. The roots of this homely and childlikeseeming folk custom reach down into the very heart of the metaphysics of paganism.

We need not necessarily think, at the word "immortal," of everlasting existence, and will presumably even want to avoid doing so in some way, as soon as we consider that we would thereby be thinking of an everlasting unchangeability. But because we usually do not consider that, the word already tempts us into forming a self-contradictory hybrid concept. For this much we may take as settled: strictly unchanging is only the empty sameness, or, as it is more temptingly called with regard to the temporality of the world of appearance, absolute being. Absolute being is the spirit, and the place by virtue of which the spirit exists in the world is the personal I, or, in short, the person. Were the person deprived of its essentially transient place, the spirit too would vanish, and it would be over with its being, but also with its existing. Every literally understood belief in immortality therefore rests on the conflation of two concepts: the concept of timelessness with that of a presence whose necessarily temporal duration is imagined as unmeasured and immeasurable.

This immortality was now in fact always and everywhere related only to persons, and the famous "beyond" into which, for its sake, the person had to flee outward is a beyond not merely of space but also, and indeed in the first place, of time. Wholly different is Pelasgian immortality, insofar as, true to its primal source, it means the immortality of images.
