The Greek athanatos and the Latin immortalis have indeed undergone the same development of meaning and can unreservedly be rendered by "immortal," but they literally say "deathless," and thereby seem to indicate to us that it is not dying that is avoidable, but rather death that can be annihilated. "I have passed through the gates of death," it rings from the mouth of the mystes who attained "rebirth" in the mysteries of Isis. He has become deathless in that he has already once [p. 1412] — but without loss of existence — undergone the transformation that he will another time undergo with loss of existence, at the going-under of his body (or at least would have undergone, had the consecration remained with him until then).

The reaped ear of grain was the symbol of consummation of the Eleusinian mysteries. What, then, might it have been that could become manifest to the illumined mind of the initiate at the sight of it, in the moment when the consecration had been accomplished (regardless of whether his understanding afterward interpreted it truly or falsely)? Certainly not the immortality of "his" body, of "his" soul, or of whatever other thing or being he might have called "his own"; since, on the contrary, if he had still harbored doubts beforehand, it would among other things have become certain to him that all such things, one and all, would irrevocably pass away. For this ear of grain surely withers and dies; indeed, no sooner grown and reaped than it has already fallen prey to going-under: a painful symbol of that having-been into which everything present is destined inescapably to sink back. But out of its very transience, and confirmed precisely by it, the primal image of the ear of grain rises up, shining and deathless: symbol of the eternity of the bodily renewal of every life-form in the womb of the Mater. Christian eternity is timelessness and the delusive notion of the endless continuance of the person; pagan eternity is the eternity of the being-less transformation of that which passes away into that which arises, and of the unaging formative power of the image. The one flees dying and therefore outlaws being born; the other kindles, at dying — which is for that reason to be affirmed — the ever-identically-original new beginning of life, with which, from moment to moment, it attains consummation. Seen in Christian terms, there lies upon the world the curse of having to pass away, which weighs on every one of its appearances, and from which to be "redeemed" and to flee outward into the timeless Nothing is called "immortality"; seen in pagan terms, the transience of every appearance of life harbors the guarantee of eternity, in that life *circles back* into itself in unceasing transformation.

*Once more we pause.* — Every motion is a form of change, every change also a transformation, every transformation can present itself in the light of going and coming, of waning and waxing, of passing-away and arising. Mere change, to be sure, would have remained nameless, since it would not even be experienced, let alone found. Just as surely as, for us, there can be "eternity as time" only because every arriving moment is other and different from all that went before, so surely, for that very reason, [p. 1413] is there "time as eternity," because it resembles those that were. For the sake of the similarity that appears together with the otherness, we experience, in the fleeing of the images, a going and coming, and out of the fullness of beholding we are able, in the alternation of the two, to experience the eternity of the world's self-renewal. Yet this passing-away and arising is a cosmic state of affairs that may become vivid to us in the change of the seasons, in the imagephases of the moon, in the starry firmament generally, in the alternation of night and day, of ebb and flood, in the periodic appearances of vegetation and, at most, of the individual plant as well, and finally in certain periods of one's own body and in the transformation of its psychic moods. But such sinking and rising, waning and waxing, darkening and clearing, comparable to the image of the rhythmic beating of waves, resembles somehow still, though only very distantly, and with other features decidedly conflicts with the alternation of dying and being born, and conflicts with it all the more, insofar as the being subject to this alternation *bears* the center of its being-alive within itself. — For to the degree that this is the case, dying and being born are catastrophes, already far different from the withering and sprouting of the plant, almost incomparably different from the waning and waxing of the moon. And that is not yet enough: dying is now no longer such an ending as would be followed by a new beginning, but an ending of that world absolutely, which without the life-center of the one who is dying can never, and never again, be experienced. Age-old songs lament it: spring returns, and with it, in virginal firstness, the blossoming that vanished in autumn — but the human being, once he has died, never.

Only when we keep this present to our minds do we perhaps understand what demon-hood would mean, and do we surmise what the Pelasgian — far closer to it than we are — regained from it by bringing gods as sacrifices to gods. Demonic would be the being that was wholly microcosm, that is, in the here-and-now the cosmos, and in the form of its own essence the soul of the elements. Because its own center would coincide with the center of the All, its being born and dying would truly resemble the waxing and waning and re-waxing of the moon, the coming and going and returning of the seasons, the rising and falling and rising again of the tide; and even though the elements themselves are shaken by catastrophes as the world-ocean is by hurricanes, still, whatever of that would surge through elemental souls — the bright and the somber intoxications — would be [p. 1414] an event in the life of the gods, and not an event of its own beginning and ending. — If it is true, as we have heard from Bachofen, that in Pelasgianism earthly development did not rest until it had succeeded, so far as possible, in "realizing the cosmic archetype in full truth," then its deepest striving must have been directed toward magically transforming back the catastrophes of dying and being born into the cosmic rhythm of passing-away and arising. Only when and insofar as dying resembled elemental passing-away, and being born resembled elemental arising, did dying stand in the light of a process from which a new becoming could be kindled through the return of what had been, in rejuvenated form. In what ways so great a thing might be attainable, and whether it was ever fully realized by human beings at all, may remain an open question; suffice it that one way was the surrender of the divine element of the soul through the sacrifice of the bodily images of the god. In the shudder of going-under, experienced by the sacrifice and co-experienced by the participants, death melted away, and out of the depths of a dying that had become wholly a passing-away there rose up the image of the newly arising demon.

There was quiet and loud sacrificing, slow and sudden sacrificing; there was a dissolving as in falling asleep, a burstingapart as under the stroke of the axe. And between the essence of the elements and the essence of the human being, already hardened and falling prey to incipient self-hood, there were mediating beings, among which, recognized across the whole Pelasgian earth as worthy of deepest worship, was the double-poled and mother-symbolic tree. Around the forest, from the inconspicuous herb to the roaring treetop, myth weaves lavishly its most golden net; in the god-consecrated darkness of sacred oaks the sacrificial cult unfolds and harbors its deepest mysteries. How much the seers may have known of this — who is to decide! But they knew more than we "let ourselves dream," and they still ask us, too, who is to interpret it:

I know that I hung / On the windy tree / Nine full nights, / Wounded with the spear, / Given to Odin,

[p. 1415] On that tree / Unknown to all / From what root it springs.

In the language of Christendom: the god sacrificed himself on the tree, and he rose again by loosing himself from the tree. But he did not die and rise "for mankind"; rather, in loosing himself he found the runes of knowledge ..

[p. 1416]

### Rückblick — Retrospect

The "synoptic table of the main results" originally planned has become superfluous, partly because of the repeated references to main results in the section on Pelasgianism, partly because we have meanwhile committed ourselves to offering something similar elsewhere. The "Retrospect" to be given instead pursues different purposes. It wishes, first, to ease the understanding of the basic thought of the spirit as the adversary of the soul, by dispelling some misunderstandings that keep cropping up here and there; it wishes, further, to point out a strongest source of the emotional resistance to the author's writings and to show to what extent it too is to be reckoned a — misunderstanding; it will finally dismiss the reader with a question meant to prompt him to his own retrospective survey of the whole work, the answering of which would give him the opportunity to check how much of its essential content he has managed to make his own; all this, of course, in the utmost brevity. — First, then, let the adversaries of the "Adversary" have the floor, especially those who have precisely never read the "Adversary": Since the author calls the disposition toward all possible disvalues "spirit" and that toward all possible values "soul," he has an easy game of making the one the adversary of the other. In truth he confuses the spirit itself with certain degenerate forms of its activity, and especially with the boundless rationalism, intellectualism, and so forth, which dominated the second half of the past century. A thoroughly time-conditioned reaction against it is served up to us as an allegedly spirit-hostile philosophy. The spirit itself can by no means be grasped merely as "analytic potency," but must be grasped in the first place as "synthetic potency." (1) — Here there is apt to follow the opinion that it is precisely through the spirit [p. 1417], and only through it, that the harm which a false application of it has brought about is to be remedied. Not infrequently there follow glimpses of the transcendental or religious position of the spirit, now Kantian, now Catholic in coloring, but always with the ultimate goal: spirit = God. Finally the reproach is also apt to be voiced that the author is an incurable or arch-romantic laudator temporis acti. (1a) Are we then supposed to abolish thinking understanding, the will, reason? This demand condemns itself to senselessness. For, in the first place, no one is free to decide in accordance with it; and further, even if we could, the result would be a ghastly barbarism! (2) The author is caught in a personal self-contradiction. Is he himself not afflicted with the very spirit he rejects, and would he not, without it, have been unable to produce his entire work! (3) — Although the following objection is an altogether different one, it nevertheless runs together with the one just heard almost as a matter of course, which is why we likewise link it with that one. It runs roughly thus: here the intellect is being combated by — the intellect! A thousand subtleties are mustered to stage a refutation by means of that very disposition of the human being which alone and exclusively is capable of such subtleties: the dialectically trained understanding. Consequently the author is caught in a logical self-contradiction. (3a)

We begin by shedding light on 3 and 3a, and for that purpose must of course pull the two apart. — On 3, only a few words are needed. So extreme a subjectivism as finds expression in it may today be regarded, at least theoretically, as settled, and already seems almost a little — old-fashioned. Must someone who possesses property a, and knows it, therefore hold a to be valuable? To affirm this would mean denying the possibility of even the most modest self-criticism, and would moreover set itself in contradiction with the fact that there are not a few persons who suffer from the properties a, β, γ, etc. of their own being. The relation of a thinker's (poet's, artist's, etc.) driving forces to the values that he represents with his work is a psychological problem of high importance, and incidentally one of the core questions of the psychological part of our own books; but, however much may still remain to be done there, this much at least we should know since Nietzsche: that in [p. 1418] this relation both far-reaching agreement and far-reaching opposition can prevail; from which it follows, among other things, that even correctly ascertained properties of an author never furnish the least contribution to the criticism of his work. Only after one has, through objective examination — and indeed exclusively of the work — discovered, say, errors, can the ascertaining of the author's personal properties become important and instructive, for the purpose of illuminating the individual grounds that occasioned the error. Conflicts of properties are one thing entirely; self-contradictions are quite another!<sup>123</sup>

<sup>123</sup> On page 1418. — The questions concerning the relation of a work to the properties of its author are found discussed at the most various places in our writings, but especially in our book "Die psychologischen Errungenschaften Nietzsches" (2nd ed., Leipzig, Barth, 1929); further, in most concentrated form, in the essays "Der Fall Nietzsche-Wagner in graphologischer Beleuchtung" (1904) and "Nietzsche und seine Handschrift" (1927); both in the collected volume "Zur Ausdruckslehre und Charakterkunde."

Against this, it would be not merely an objection but even a fatal objection, if the logical self-contradiction that 3a wishes to allege actually held good. — Now, here an opportunity offers itself for us to dig out the root of a prejudice almost universally current today! Let us first of all unfold what is actually meant; it looks roughly like this: whoever refutes something judges, in any case — one can judge only with the help of the spirit — and likewise every evaluating, and consequently, say, every condemning, is a kind of judging — whoever denies the value of the spirit denies, among other things, the value of the faculty of judgment — consequently: the faculty of judgment, in judging, denies its own value — but that is absurd! — No, that is *not* absurd; and whoever holds it to be so thereby proves only that behind *all* his judgments there stands a — not necessary — *belief*, namely the secret belief in the *sanctity of the spirit*. Let him just try to prove the alleged absurdity: he will never succeed!

We have shown that there is a spirit-dependent, but also a life-dependent, thinking, or in other words a spirit-dependent and a life-dependent faculty of judgment. The faculty of judgment is in both cases the same; but the vital impulses that occasion the decisive acts of judging are, in both cases, different. We have further shown that the only *form* of the life-dependence of spirit still possible at the highest level of judging reflection is called logic or objectivity (for logic and objectivity are two "views" of one and the same state of affairs!), and that *truths* are ascertained only with their help, never without them, however much their content and substance may lie a hundred times beyond — more correctly, this side of — all comprehensibility. (Compare here the chapters on "Comprehending and Pointing Thinking," on "Shallow and Deep Reflection," and above all on the "Will to Truth.") But we have finally also shown [p. 1419] this: as surely as truth is never actuality, just as surely are we able to recognize, to know, and consequently to judge, that the state of being interwoven into actuality is incomparably more perfect than that of seeking truth and finding truths; or, put differently, the finding of truths relates to the experiencing of actuality not, to be sure, as life-denial relates to life-affirmation, but still always as lack relates to fullness. Only truth instead of actuality — that is the least, and for that no less painful, price we must pay for having been enabled, thanks to the irruption of spirit into life, to adopt the stance of objectively judging reflection (which, as such, excludes the experiencing stance!).<sup>124</sup>

<sup>124</sup> On page 1419. — Said as briefly as possible: the faculty of judgment does not deny its capacity to judge, but rather the value of the judging state in relation to the value of the judgment-free, experiencing state. — The resolution of an apparent self-contradiction, outwardly similar but inwardly of a different kind, is furnished by the consideration that, on the presupposition of a purely negating nature of spirit, spirit must *also* be capable of negating the results of its own life-negating activity. But however important this finding may become for certain consequences and successes of the efficacy of spirit, it does not concern the case that occupies us here: namely, that it is not the value of the finding of truth, but the value of thinking and cognizing in relation to the value of life and experiencing, that is called into question; wherefore we do not enter into a discussion of the range of problems belonging to that topic.

But we must dwell a moment longer on the prejudice in question. One hears a great deal nowadays of so-called irrationalism, a word that is also found here and there in our own writings, but only rarely. For from the name itself one cannot tell whether it denotes a concept that plays off life against spirit, or, quite the reverse, a concept that plays off spirit against life. If by rationalism one understands the cult of the understanding or the cult of reason, then our work rejects rationalism and would therefore, if one likes, represent an irrationalism; but if one understands by it the fundamental disempowering of objectivity (= of logic) in favor of, say, a subjectivist or relativist thinking (and that is at present predominantly the case), then our work would stand on the side of rationalism, in sharpest rejection of this so-called irrationalism, which is obviously a last and worst trump card of — the spirit! For, as has been shown, it is not the spirit of itself that is the creator of the logical (= objective) stance, but the spirit under the compulsion of necessities that stem from the experiencing of actuality. Let one consider for a moment that it is through and through two different things, whether one holds, with us, the state of thinking, in relation to the state of experiencing, to be a state of lack that could only gain a foothold through a disturbance of life, or whether, with so-called irrationalism, one disdains — in thinking — truth, which alone is found within the framework of the objective stance. — If, then, the prejudice that it is absurd to see in thinking consciousness a disturbance-phenomenon of life — life being held the more valuable — must obviously proceed "irrationally" (here = detached from objectivity = alogically) in order to put itself in the right before itself, we shall not be surprised that the secretly ruling belief in the [p. 1420] sanctity of the spirit sacrifices, with great readiness, indeed with unacknowledged satisfaction, precisely — the intellect. With this we come to objection 1.

The belief in the sanctity of the spirit has its good reasons for sacrificing the intellect; for the intellect, in the sense of the strictly objectively judging faculty of reflection, forms, to speak in a simile, an intermediate realm, where the spirit asserts itself only thanks to considerable concessions made to life (Promethean phase). If we measure through — always speaking in the simile — this intermediate realm toward the side of the spirit, we come into the region of the will, that is, of a power that indeed also makes use of logic, but not out of logic and not for the sake of knowing. We would insult the champions of objection 1 were we to assume that they had taken cognizance of the second volume of the "Adversary," bearing the title "The Doctrine of the Will," or even only of our "Foundations of the Science of Character"; and only on the assumption that this has not happened may we repeat: our work finds the key to the essence of the spirit not in the intellect, but in the will. It seeks to prove that, as the self-sovereignty of the spirit (= the positive nothing) grows, objectivity must yield the field, in that thinking enters more and more into the service of the will (= Heraclean phase); it proves further that the will, the more it frees itself, the more it comes to coincide with absolute arbitrariness, and that accordingly, finally, spirit as such must be determined as deed "in itself," and spirit in the organism of the human being as the constitutional center of deeds; with which everything collapses that was brought forward under 1 against the conception of spirit as the adversary of the soul, from the point of view that this was a matter of confusing a struggle against ephemeral cults of the understanding with metaphysical insight.

We shall not repeat our demonstration that the deed "in itself" can only destroy (= dissolve = analyze), more precisely can only cleave apart; nor the further demonstration that therefore, in the faculty of judgment, only the capacity for distinguishing attests the spirit; but we devote a few more words to the attack on the name of the spirit. It is known that we are not of the opinion that a name is "sound and smoke," and we hold, in particular, that in present-day usage, and for some hundred and fifty years now, the undertaking to say soul for spirit and spirit for soul would be scarcely less hopeless than if someone insisted on calling the sun moon and the moon [p. 1421] sun. Whoever doubts it should above all read R. Hildebrand, Geist (separate edition of the article of the same name in Grimm's Dictionary, Halle 1926), and should moreover ask himself whether Hegel could also have entitled the work to which he gave the heading "Phenomenology of Spirit" "Phenomenology of the Soul." But since what is disputed here is the matter, not words, we recommend — as elsewhere already — to all who have fallen in love with the word spirit, that they denote the center of deeds that we mean by the letter X, and the soul that we mean by the letter Y. (The difference between soul and life may be neglected in this consideration.) After one has, in this way, everywhere inserted X where we speak of spirit in the metaphysical sense, and Y where we speak of soul, let one put to oneself, in order, the following questions.

Has the author succeeded in showing that both X and Y actually exist? Has he succeeded, in particular, in showing that the two are unmistakably distinguished from one another? Further, that X cannot be traced back to Y, nor Y to X, and equally that X and Y together cannot be traced back to some other Z? Finally, that the existence of X has life-threatening consequences for the existence of Y? For some thirty years the author has been waiting, in vain, for the proof that he has not succeeded in these tasks, although he has missed no opportunity to challenge the most significant of his contemporaries, whom he encountered in the course of his life, to dispute them. This does not exclude the possibility that some future thinker will cogently demonstrate that X can after all be traced back to Y, or Y after all to X, or that X and Y can both be traced back to Z. In any case, however, one of these proofs would have to be furnished by anyone who wished to undertake to dispute what is already indicated in the title of our work — the life-threatening character of the spirit for the soul; whereas nothing at all is achieved by enthusiastic invocations made "in the name" of the spirit. — As for the transcendental conception, however, which culminates in the formula spirit = God, it has indeed been heard that we approve of it in the most decided way, only, to be sure, just as decidedly disputing the role that is almost universally accorded to the spirit-god with respect to the universe. — And so it would still remain for us to answer the laudator temporis acti under 1a, and objection 2. But we wish to arrive at that by another route, all the more since objection 2 would first have to be dressed up before it could be possible to take it — seriously.

A chief source of the emotional resistance to the author's writings is to be sought in the circumstance that the present-day reader [p. 1422] expects almost from every book, but certainly from every metaphysics, a *pro*gram, and is consequently disappointed when it is lacking, and falls altogether into an uncritical aversion where, among other things, the nullity of all programs seems to follow from the insights set forth. We bring well-founded results of research, nothing more; and we thus have a right to be refuted, should we have erred. But the opinion that a philosophy is erroneous because, among other things, the imminent downfall of mankind follows from it, stands on the same level as the opinion that the physician has judged wrongly because he has declared that, "according to human estimation," the patient will not survive the coming night. If he perhaps sometimes adds that with God, to be sure, "nothing is impossible," well, we too have added, at various places (and not only in the present work), that the "miracle" remains reserved which would prevent the merely logically foreseeable annihilation of the life of the earth by the spirit, and would bring about rebirths that no human understanding could foresee. But although, in the context of a system that holds the ways of fate to be strictly beyond reason and thus incalculable, such a reservation carries more weight than the rhetorical gesture toward an almighty God in the mouth of the physician, it nevertheless remains untouched by this that a cross-section through the present state of "world history" shows no fact that would justify hopes, but countless ones that demand the worst prognosis. And that suffices to repel everyone who is looking for promises or, more bluntly put, for prescriptions (in the first place, as is understood, for his own person, and incidentally, if possible, for "mankind" as well). Nothing can be argued away from such feelings; only no one should mistake them for refutations!

One could naturally dig deeper here, and in doing so gain many a valuable insight into the state of mind of the greater part of our contemporaries. Thus an insatiable craving for programs speaks of a boundless overvaluation of that thought-thing, the future; and out of this, in turn, speaks a flight from the present scarcely capable of further intensification, and, in this fashion, complete joylessness. If this already betrays the deepest inner disturbance of equilibrium, then the dreadful overemphasis on willing and will comes to light all the more plainly once we consider that only he can hope from phantoms of the future for what ever-present actuality withholds from him who fancies himself able to fabricate the future. The happy man [p. 1423] — and even the merely contented and self-satisfied man — has no occasion to concern himself unceasingly with what neither was nor is; but even the man who mourns, the disappointed man, indeed the man who despises joy on principle, need not live on hopes at all, but can find recompense, for instance, through a turning-away from actuality (Buddhism, Taoism, Christian eremitism of the first centuries). No doubt the feverish belief in a coming omnipotence of man of some kind is the consuming wish-image of man's extreme impotence, and is indeed one of the strongest symptoms of the approaching end. — Still stranger disclosures would come our way. Today's average man is, in some form or other, always a "monist." He may have traversed the whole history of the mind, may have made himself at home in each of the thousand-and-one philosophical systems — one thing remains denied him to reflect upon: that, comparable to the misfortunes of human life, there could be such a thing as a metaphysical misfortune, one which, under certain circumstances, might have a fatal outcome for an entire planet. — For the present, however, we shall not pursue such considerations further, since something else lies close to our heart.

However probable, in view of our knowledge of the mind's hostility to life, the self-attrition of mankind may be, the stillopen possibility of renewal could nonetheless prompt the question: what would we have to do, what to leave undone, in order to hasten it, or at least not hinder it? Not too far removed would then be the thought: if mind is hostile to life, one ought really to wish that it did not exist at all. And at once a whole series of questions would follow: are there means and ways to eliminate mind from life, or, failing that, to render it ineffective, or, failing that, to compel it anew into the service of life — and would mankind then sink back into the prehistoric or even the original condition? We repeat: it is not our task to seek the answer to questions of this kind; and if we nonetheless behave for a moment as though we did, it is only in order to dispel the misunderstandings underlying the two objections still outstanding. It should be needless to say, yet let it be said for the sake of clarification: one cannot, by any measures whatever, eliminate mind from life, or render it ineffective, or force it back into subjection to life, let alone return to any past. How, indeed, could a thinker ever do homage to such articles of faith who has not [p. 1424] grown weary, and does not grow weary, of impressing upon us that nothing which has ever happened is ever repeated!

This does not deny, however, that the conduct of life of anyone who has become deeply imbued with the knowledge of mind's struggle against the tragic divinity of life would proceed differently in essential respects than without such knowledge — and consequently so too for mankind as a whole, provided such knowledge became, if not common property, then at least the possession of its leading strata. For this, however, as little need of any programs would be required as a program is needed for a man to flee or do away with what he abhors, to cherish and protect what he reveres and loves. In view of the mass's lack of judgment, educators and leaders might then perhaps set up signposts; but it remains certain that the "knowing man" would find such signposts for every one of his decisions, the greatest as well as the smallest, within his own inner being.

It would be an easy matter for us to set down countless "guidelines"; but we hold that only he would be free to follow them for whom they would at the same time mean — wishes of his heart! Just as there is certainly no return, so there could be — a turning-about. But what work could exhaust what the desirability of this turning-about would bring with it in incalculable consequences for every course of life? Since the bearer of the wish for this turning-about would precisely not let himself be determined by thoughts of the future (apart from the next one, to which everyday life obliges him each time), he could by no means plow the field of deeds, and would take the unavoidable spells of sheer having-to-will merely "into the bargain." He would never do work for the sake of work, but, insofar as it could not be avoided, for the sake of making possible an existence able to renounce most "claims" save one: periodic hours of leisure.

What he would have instead is an ambition, if that is the right word for it: to perform everything he does as perfectly as possible. For, however indifferent or worthless the deed might be to him, he would know that it is by the work, and by it alone, that man was given the possibility of arriving, by the paths of doing, at some kind of consummation, however modest. The moments of great experience come or do not come, and once come, pass away again: no willing, no activity, could force them to appear. But every perfectly accomplished piece of work bestows a minute of happiness which, far from being the highest and deepest happiness, is nonetheless a pure happiness, and indeed the only one which man was granted the power to bring about [p. 1425]. We do not speak of the excesses of heroism, of star-drunkenness, or of the creative frenzy of inventive geniuses, but of the possible wealth of any activity whatever. For an accomplishment can be more or less perfect, whether it be called house-building or boot-soling or kettlemending or book-carting or dust-wiping; and the successful one always repays the worker and doer, like a grateful essence (it is an essence!), with a glance of joy that is warmer than the joys of the onlooker, and before which the hollow pleasure of success turns pale. But in the reflected shining of even the humblest fabric made by one's own hand, kindred forms from every past bloom and glow, softly wooing love. — But why paint out what either paints itself out, or else remains forever mute to the soul?

We shall not linger even to suggest how utterly different things would go, compared with today, in a mankind possessed of such or similar dispositions, and content ourselves with merely touching on the question of what this or any other unquestionably mind-averted stance might mean for the future of mind. — Just as certainly as no measure is conceivable that could effectively counter mind's intervention in life, so certainly can — indeed unfailingly will — every man sworn to life wish that mind might once more become subservient to life, or, better still, that it might forsake forever the cosmic actuality which is no home to it: an Ahasuerus finally come to rest. Could such wishes have consequences lying in the direction of their fulfillment, or not?

Here two cases must in principle be kept apart: the one, that the content of the wish lies within the realm of the fulfillable, and the other, that it does not. We give an example of the latter. — There have always and everywhere, to be sure, been individual men who held life to be an evil not merely in theory; but the overwhelmingly preponderant majority, at least of historical mankind, held life to be a good and death to be the greatest of evils, and therefore had to wish to abolish it, even though firmly convinced that this could not be done (apart from a handful of fools, of whom some are said to exist here and there, especially today). We shall no longer speak of the part this wish played in the state of consciousness of Pelasgianism, nor of its effects on the images of the world; but we do recall that, despite a clear insight into the [p. 1426] impossibility of abolishing death, it has nonetheless produced *actual* consequences lying in the direction of its fulfillment, in that hygiene and the medical art, spurred on among other things by it, have managed to disarm numerous causes of death: today a far greater proportion of those born remain alive than in earlier centuries (prevented and diminished infant mortality); far fewer women die in childbed (antisepsis); countless people are no longer struck down by epidemics to which they formerly succumbed (disinfection) — so that, all in all, average lifespan has risen considerably. — Whether this is metaphysically gratifying or ungratifying cannot be discussed here; only the fact itself concerns us, and that as an example of the important possibility that the unfulfillability of a wish does not necessarily exclude successes bearing a relation to the fulfillment of the wish similar to that which some slight alleviation of a poor man's poverty bears to the riches he vainly strives for. The analogy lies at hand: a "turning-about" of mankind, compelled from within, could lead to a weakening of the efficacy of mind in life, whether because life grew stronger in the face of it, or because it found itself, here and there, less open to it, whereby ground would, as it were, be withdrawn from mind here and there.

Meanwhile, the content of the wish directed against the existence (= Dasein) of mind by no means belongs among the impossibilities. Just as certainly as the life of plants and animals surely runs its course without mind — and that of primal man too, with high probability — so certainly could the life of a future mankind once again be rid of mind, without thereby ever again becoming what it was before the eruption of mind; and thus the wish for the exclusion of mind from life would even have better prospects of fulfillment than the wish for the removal of death! Yet a tremendous difference obtains here: discoveries can indeed be made, and on the strength of these discoveries measures taken — certainly not against death, but well against supposed or real causes of death; whereas no discoveries can be made, and no measures taken, against real or supposed causes of life's vulnerability to mind; or, were such to exist, they would be magical measures, and moreover measures of a magic yet to be invented. Never could a disposition toward turning-about lead directly to partial fulfillments; the only thing it might venture to hope for, without self-deception, is that gradual changes of vitality would accompany the "doing and refraining" corresponding to it — changes favorable to the consolidation of life, unfavorable to the further advance of mind [p. 1427]. And this would then already find expression in the doing and refraining itself.

For just as it is not merely willing and doing in general that correspond to a mind-turned disposition, but action in the narrower sense — the undertaking, the deed, the "conquering" expansion — so, thanks to the renunciation of seizure, violation, and "future," it is refraining that corresponds, with respect to all "actions," to the mind-averted disposition (whose ambition for accomplishment would, after all, be the perfection of the work). And refrainings would occur partly unwilled, but partly also willed, in such a way that, of all resolutions, by far the fewest would stand in the service of attack, the most in the service of defense. Refraining would come about unwilled insofar as the drivingsprings required for volition were lacking. One may picture to oneself how many actions would fail to occur simply because as many millions of individual men as those to whom the opposite appears alluring today would hold it not worth striving for, but even an evil: to possess more than one's neighbor, to attain a "public name," to "impress" others, to make persons dependent upon one's own person, to acquire a "fortune" for the sake of increasing the power of those to whom one hopes to bequeath it (be this family, clan, district association, or a people, a state, or a race, or finally an international group, usually called "mankind"; one thinks of charitable foundations, of scholarships, of Nobel prizes, and so on). Or, to leap from individual persons to peoples and empires, one may picture to oneself what it would mean if not a single people were minded to play police chief over all the rest (this is called striving for "world domination"), but instead felt precisely this to be the most painful of burdens! — But there would also be no lack of volitions arising from defense, of which, in bringing our excursion to a close, we offer a single example.

During the war a brisk trade was carried on in Neutralia, among other things, in — walnut trees, because their wood was needed for rifle butts. Prices rose, and to the tempting offers even centuries-old trunks fell victim in droves — needless to say, without any hardship on the part of those country folk who thereby enriched themselves for a time. We pass over why this was not even "economically" thought through; suffice it to say that in a mankind predominantly disposed toward the [p. 1428] turning-about, nothing of the kind would happen , since, with existence unthreatened, volitions springing from "business interest" would have to yield to the counter-will which — to speak in connection with our example — love for such "natural monuments" would be able to muster almost effortlessly. As one observes, not even a belief in "sacred trees" and the like would be necessary to bring about those refrainings on which the life and doings of today's mankind founder. — Let the reader not forget that with such considerations the author has left the ground on which alone he is willing and able to move. Educative minds with economic knowledge could carry this out far more comprehensively and persuasively without difficulty. But the meager sketch was not meant to satisfy any need for a program; rather, it seeks to support the refutation of a mistaken view by calling upon the power of intuition. Everything set forth here, unquestionably lying within the realm of the conceivable, would aim at a weakening of the will to deeds, a strengthening of the will to work, and slow modifications of vitality could not fail to follow in consequence. It is needless and superfluous to try to work out how the history of mankind's formation would further shape itself along such paths of turning-about; rather, it belongs to the disposition of turning-about itself to abstain, so far as possible, from all forward-flying speculations about the future. Should, however, some reader perhaps still object that these are manifest utopias, in that men so constituted as we have assumed would be found perhaps once among millions, and would therefore never have any prospect of prevailing against the selfish urge to power of the rest, we would have to remind him that this is exactly our own view, and one of the strongest supports of our conviction of the inevitability of the downfall. It was not a future shape of mankind that we wished to sketch, but only this was meant to be illustrated: that, should anyone wish to derive a canon of conduct from the results of our researches, the table of his values and aims would indeed conflict with the values, aims, and properties of today's mankind, yet would nonetheless remain thoroughly within the bounds of the humanly possible, and would least of all impute to us the nonsense of an abolition or suspension of the understanding. — Finally, it is perhaps not superfluous expressly to emphasize that here we have spoken solely and exclusively of behaviors subject to the arbitrary will, and by no means of the drives and effects by which life [p. 1429] itself would come to the aid of its own resurgence. For whether, and how far, that which serves life out of life itself comes to fulfillment — Eros, ancestor-cult, and festival — lies so entirely outside the reach of disposition and effort of will that it would infallibly suffer harm through any intervention of the will. And with that, enough of this. — That, thanks to the existence of this work, anything should come to pass in the direction of the goals we have just characterized, the author does not believe. But were it even, against all expectation, to be the case, it would nonetheless lie, as a merely mediated appearance, wholly outside the zone of efficacy for which the work could form the center. — In this the findings of deep reflection agree with those of shallow reflection: that they can and will occasion further research; likewise in this, that they will kindle only him for whom a kind of fulfillment of his "poetizing and striving" means knowledge independent of person. But whereas in mechanistic thinking, matter-of-factness and logic serve at best the task of establishing objective relations between objects of thought, metaphysical thinking reserves the name "truth" exclusively for insights into traits of character of actuality, and establishes its relations with a view to these. Since knowledge so understood consists ultimately of demonstrations, "proofs," indeed makings-present of "primal phenomena," it necessarily has, at the same time, the form of a doctrine of world-view, and resembles, in respect of its content, a world-picture or even a structure of cognition. These are, to be sure, similes; but they express, in an unobjectionable way, why immersion in such a "system," or, more generally, participation in a thought-image of the meaning of the world, can mean, for one who is willing and able, a specific happiness, and a sheet-lightning gleam capable in principle of illuminating every path of life, in that it lets depths of meaning flash up even in the supposed nullities of the dreariest everyday — wherein, of the work's possible effects, the strongest and highest would then be contained. And so, at the end, let it be granted to him who had to create it to express wherein, for him, the best assurance lies that he has not searched wholly in vain, but has, among other things, also found — not, however, without first repeating once more in what respect finding remained denied to him.

Although a great, if not the greatest, part of our researches [p. 1430] was directed toward ascertaining, in the soul, the points of "least resistance" to the inroads of mind, and, as we would like to believe, not without success, we have nonetheless failed to explain or to make comprehensible in what manner, once upon a time — that is, millennia ago, in some group of men — the first eruption of mind could have taken place. We do not doubt that one or another of our critics, out of personal disinclination, will joyfully seize upon this and seek to give us to understand that the whole system founders on this inadequacy. Yet surely no great acuity is required to expose the spuriousness of such an objection. If someone conclusively proves that something exists or obtains, the proof would suffer no detriment even from the certainty of the proven state of affairs being in principle inexplicable, let alone merely provisionally inexplicable. Evidence for this could be adduced in abundance from the camp of the "sciences," but this seems to us dispensable. On the other hand, the inadequacy in question would indeed constitute a formidable problem for — future metaphysicians, should there still be any to reckon with. — After this repetition of a lack often pointed out, we may offer, in closing, a reference to something we consider achieved.

Let us leave aside the theologians (in the widest sense), and further the leaders of sects, creeds, occultisms, because, while they claim — sometimes more, sometimes less — to be in possession of "knowledge," they either disdain to furnish proof of it or are not in a position to do so; and let us hold instead to those, no longer sparse today, students of religion, researchers into myth, ethnologists, and so on, who are inclined to grant essential features both of the prehistoric and of the extra-historical — or, in our language, the Pelasgian — state of consciousness a basic legitimacy, indeed, under certain circumstances, for all their difference, an equal value with our own. Then, unless we are mistaken, there is not one among them for whom it would not present the greatest difficulties, if it were not downright impossible, to give a conclusive answer to the following question, which may be introduced in a few words.

Just as present-day man in his thinking and behavior is, in any case, related to facts, so, in the thinking and behavior of the Pelasgians, there is, in any case, a further relation to demons (for which, if one prefers, one can also say "souls," or "primal images," or "mystic fluids," and so on). We do not underestimate the essential and ingenious [p. 1431] contributions that have been brought, in accordance with such insight, to the illumination of the differences between rational (= merely logical) thinking and thinking that is, in addition, image-forming (= symbolic); nor the psychological disclosures concerning the manner of sensibility and state of mind of Pelasgianism; but nowhere do we find it decided whether magism — which forms, now advancing, now receding, the reverse side of symbolism — likewise possesses basic legitimacy, apart, that is, from the not merely possible but also actually occurring degenerations of it into genuine superstition. Here, however, the escape route of today's fashionable subjectivism is entirely barred, the subjectivism which fancies itself entitled to posit a merely inward correctness, by bringing into play, say, the maid-of-all-work "the unconscious," or suggestions and suggestibility, or else, with the help of the arts of the usual "theory of knowledge," having the outer world fabricated out of certain proceedings of the inner. For here the question, to make it graspable with an example, runs thus: was the weather, say, ever actually changed by magic at some time, and more, can such a thing happen or not? If yes, then the hic Rhodus, hic salta applies in this case. We have looked about in earnest; but we have not found the researcher by whom the question was even raised with the necessary definiteness, let alone one by whom it was answered without ifs or buts. — The cause of this, however, is to be sought in a more general prior question, which one shrinks from answering for obvious reasons — the prior question: if this was at some time possible, would not the laws of physics thereby be overthrown, laws which — wholly apart from their metaphysical worth or unworth — have in any case proved themselves, objectively, in the achievements of technology, and leave no room for an objectively effective magism?!

Now, the "laws of physics" need not necessarily hold for every distance in space — whereby we are free to bring millions of "parsecs" into play — nor, still less, need they hold for every past — whereby we are free to bring trillions of years into play. Suppose, however, that the same "laws of physics" as hold today had held for at least hundreds of thousands of years, and suppose further that a change, say, of the weather by means of magic is at present impossible, then we believe we have, for the first time, disclosed why, notwithstanding this, a magical participation in the events of the terrestrial universe might once have been possible — because it was not so much the actuality of the inner [p. 1432] as rather actuality itself that was other than it is today. We believe, speaking more generally, to have demonstrated that and why the most consequential transformations of telluric actuality cannot be discovered by the research methods of physics, and therefore exert no influence either on the shaping of "physical laws." Whoever among our readers is able to substantiate this has appropriated to himself the best and deepest of the content of our work. —
